Ripasudil, also known by its research designation Y-39983 and commercially available as Selleckchem S8443, is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor developed originally as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil containing protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. Members of the ROCK inhibitor class have seen prior use in settings that require modulation of actin cytoskeleton dynamics, such as the treatment of glaucoma via enhanced aqueous humor outflow, and have also been explored in contexts involving wound healing and anti-fibrotic effects in various ocular tissues (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, ripasudil has been approved in Japan for the treatment of glaucoma and ocular hypertension, where it is delivered topically in the form of eye drops, demonstrating a well-established safety profile and a low incidence of systemic adverse effects. In preclinical models, it has demonstrated efficacy by increasing ocular blood flow, modifying trabecular meshwork cell contractility, and reducing intraocular pressure, thereby serving as a stepping stone and proof-of-concept for the utility of ROCK inhibitors in ocular disorders. Beyond its approved use in glaucoma, investigations of ROCK inhibitors—including ripasudil—have extended into experimental applications in corneal endothelial regeneration and have been evaluated in combination with anti-VEGF therapies for diabetic macular edema. Although direct clinical evidence specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is not available, multiple lines of preclinical research have shown that the ROCK inhibitor class modulates pathways which are believed to underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Notably, the mechanistic studies have identified the role of ROCK signaling in cytoskeletal reorganization, matrix contractility, and fibrosis, all of which are processes particularly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier dysfunction seen in dry AMD (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ripasudil exerts its therapeutic activity by competitively inhibiting the ATP-binding site of ROCK isoforms, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of downstream effectors such as myosin light-chain (MLC), myosin-binding subunit of MLC phosphatase (MYPT1), and LIM kinase. These phosphorylation events normally lead to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, focal adhesion assembly, and ultimately contribute to a contractile, stiffened cell phenotype. In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, this contractility is thought to be exacerbated under conditions of oxidative stress, contributing to disassembly or mislocalization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity. By inhibiting ROCK, ripasudil reduces actomyosin-driven contraction and stress-fiber formation, thereby promoting cortical F-actin remodeling and facilitating the proper membrane relocalization of tight-junction proteins. The specificity of ripasudil has been demonstrated by its greater than 100-fold selectivity against other kinases such as protein kinase C (PKC) and myotonic dystrophy kinase-related Cdc42-binding kinase (MRCK), highlighting the mechanistic precision by which it modulates ROCK-dependent signaling cascades (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Additionally, while several studies indicate that the ROCK inhibitor class generally targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2 isoforms, quantitative biochemical data have shown that ripasudil exhibits potent enzyme inhibitory activity with IC₅₀s in the low nanomolar range (with values reported around 51 nM for ROCK1 and 19 nM for ROCK2 in some studies, though the candidate hypothesis posits values of approximately 29 nM for ROCK1 and 68 nM for ROCK2). This inhibitory profile is particularly relevant because emerging research indicates that ROCK2, in particular, is upregulated in the pathological conditions of dry AMD and plays a key role in mediating cytoskeletal changes that disrupt RPE tight junction integrity (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). The inhibition of ROCK thereby is expected to have a dual benefit of cytoprotection and restoration of cell junction architecture, ultimately leading to improved barrier function (Ghenciu et al., 2025; Singh & Singh, 2023).

The central hypothesis for repurposing ripasudil for dry AMD is that by blocking ROCK activity in oxidatively stressed retinal pigment epithelium cells, the compound will lead to a reduction in actomyosin contractility, thereby alleviating the formation of pathological stress fibers that otherwise disrupt the organization of tight junction complexes. This specificity is critical when repurposing drugs for chronic conditions such as dry AMD, where long-term ocular safety is paramount (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Despite these strengths, there are notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before ripasudil can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. A primary limitation is the paucity of direct experimental evidence in RPE models of dry AMD. While the hypothesis is supported by data from related in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative stress), robust in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of dry AMD pathophysiology are still needed. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Alagebrium chloride (ALT-711) is a synthetic small molecule designed as an advanced glycation end product (AGE) crosslink breaker. Chemically identified as 3‐phenacyl‐4,5‐dimethylthiazolium chloride, it belongs to the thiazolium salt family—a class noted for its reactivity toward α-dicarbonyl substrates found in AGE crosslinks. Originally developed as an analog of N-phenacylthiazolium bromide (PTB), ALT-711 was synthesized specifically to overcome the instability and in vivo degradation that hampered PTB’s clinical potential, and thus represented a more stable, easily synthesized candidate with retained crosslink-cleaving activity (Alam, Ahsan, & Alam, 2013; Borg & Forbes, 2016). The design rationale capitalized on the unique nucleophilic properties of the thiazolium core—similar in some respects to the vitamin thiamine structure, though it lacks the pyrimidine moiety—to facilitate cleavage of carbon–carbon bonds between protein-bound glycation products, notably interfering with the formation of deleterious cross-links such as those involving pentosidine (Furber, 2010; Coughlan et al., 2007). Over the past two decades, this class of AGE breakers, including ALT-711, has been primarily explored for applications in cardiovascular and diabetic complications, with the underlying therapeutic hypothesis being that reversal of AGE-mediated crosslinking could restore tissue compliance and function (Kim & Spiegel, 2013; Toprak & Yigitaslan, 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
The historical development of alagebrium is rooted in efforts to counteract the progressive accumulation of AGEs—a hallmark of chronic hyperglycemia and aging—that contribute to decreased protein turnover, tissue stiffening, and dysfunction. ALT-711 was developed and advanced by pharmaceutical entities like Alteon Pharmaceuticals (later Synvista Therapeutics) for its ability to reverse AGE-mediated crosslinking in the extracellular matrix, particularly in collagen and elastin-rich tissues (Alam, Ahsan, & Alam, 2013; Velichkova, 2020). Preclinical studies in diabetic rat models demonstrated that ALT-711 not only increased cardiac output and improved left ventricular diastolic function but also reduced arterial stiffening by breaking protein crosslinks, an effect that was correlated with improved vascular compliance (Coughlan et al., 2007; Kim & Spiegel, 2013). In clinical development, ALT-711 progressed through human trials—being evaluated for conditions such as heart failure, systolic hypertension, and vascular stiffening—although its program ultimately faced setbacks due to financial constraints and discontinuation of further clinical studies (Toprak & Yigitaslan, 2019; Vasan et al., 2003). Despite robust preclinical evidence in cardiovascular models, there is no established record of alagebrium being previously used to treat ocular diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); however, the underlying mechanism of AGE crosslink reversal suggests potential utility in tissues that undergo similar AGE-mediated structural changes, like the Bruch’s membrane (BM) of the eye (Krautwald et al., 2011; Nagai et al., 2012).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of action of ALT-711 centers on its ability to cleave AGE-derived protein crosslinks via a nucleophilic reaction targeting α-dicarbonyl moieties within these adducts. In biochemical models, the thiazolium ring of ALT-711 acts by facilitating the hydrolytic cleavage of carbon–carbon bonds that form between juxtaposed carbonyl groups in AGE crosslinks. This cleavage is thought to reduce the irreversible linkages that normally render long-lived extracellular matrix proteins (such as collagen and elastin) resistant to proteolytic degradation, thereby restoring their turnover and normal biomechanical properties (Borg & Forbes, 2016; Coughlan et al., 2007). Additionally, several studies have indicated that ALT-711 may exert secondary effects such as chelation of transition metals, thereby mitigating metal-catalyzed oxidative modifications that fuel further AGE formation (Kim & Spiegel, 2013; Velichkova, 2020). While there remains some controversy regarding the specificity and efficiency of its crosslink-breaking capacity in complex tissue environments, experimental evidence from enzymatic and cellular assays supports its role in reducing crosslink density in collagen matrices (Velichkova, 2020; Yamagishi, 2013). Molecular modeling studies have further delineated that the compound retains structural homologies with thiamine derivatives, and its phenacyl substituent is critical for reactivity, promoting interactions with dicarbonyl groups and facilitating reversible bond cleavage without extensive disruption of peptide backbones (Krautwald et al., 2011; Chen & Tang, 2007). These combined actions—disruption of AGE crosslinks and antioxidant/chelation activity—constitute the basis for its therapeutic potential in tissues rendered pathologically stiff by AGE accumulation.

In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration, the central hypothesis posits that ALT-711 can act on the collagen/elastin-rich Bruch’s membrane (BM), a structure whose biomechanical integrity is compromised by AGE accumulation. AICAR’s journey from a metabolic intermediate to a pharmacologically active compound has been well documented across a range of biomedical research areas. In preclinical studies, AICAR has been extensively utilized to activate AMPK in various cellular models, thereby providing critical insights into the regulation of energy balance, mitochondrial biogenesis, and lipid metabolism (Green, 2013; Pokrywka et al., 2014). Its early applications in skeletal muscle and cancer cells underscored its ability to stimulate glucose uptake and shift cellular energy dynamics in favor of catabolic pathways (Dolinar et al., 2018; Longnus et al., 2003).

In cardiovascular research, AICAR was instrumental in elucidating the mechanisms underlying glycogenolysis and vasorelaxation, where its conversion to ZMP led to the activation of AMPK in vascular smooth muscle cells, resulting in beneficial metabolic adaptations (Pyla et al., 2022). Although these studies did not directly target ocular tissues, they established a robust framework for understanding how AMPK activation can mediate protective responses under conditions of metabolic stress.

The transition of AICAR into the realm of ophthalmological research was driven by the observation that AMPK is a pivotal regulator of RPE function and tight junction assembly. Publications have demonstrated that oxidative stress—a significant contributor to AMD pathology—can impair RPE barrier integrity by disrupting the organization of tight junction proteins, while AMPK activation appears to counteract these deleterious changes (Qin, 2012; Villarroel et al., 2011). In one study, treatment with AICAR in RPE cells under H₂O₂‐induced stress not only increased TEER but also elevated levels of phosphorylated AMPK, thereby indicating enhanced barrier stability (Miyagishima et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the dual role of AMPK in regulating autophagy and lipid metabolism has been a focal point in dry AMD research, as dysfunctional autophagy and lipid accumulation are hallmarks of RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011). The protective effects of AMPK activators in other models of cellular stress, such as in cardiomyocytes and hepatocarcinoma cells, lend additional support to the hypothesis that similar mechanisms may be beneficial in preserving RPE function (Kawashima et al., 2020; Sid et al., 2014).

Despite these promising findings, it is important to note that the therapeutic history of AICAR in the context of ocular diseases remains in the preclinical phase, with limited direct clinical evaluation for dry AMD. Some studies have even suggested that AMPK activation in the RPE could have dual outcomes, potentially inhibiting phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments under oxidative conditions (Qin & De Vries, 2008). This observation highlights the intricacies of AMPK signaling in retinal cells and underscores the need for rigorous dose–response and context–specific studies. Nonetheless, the accumulated preclinical data from both ocular and non‐ocular systems provide a strong rationale for further exploring AICAR as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Expected Impact on RPE Function and Dry AMD Pathology:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of AICAR in dry AMD is that its ability to activate AMPK will lead to a concerted improvement in RPE barrier function and energy homeostasis—two crucial aspects compromised in AMD. In vitro models of RPE, particularly those derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC‐RPE), have shown that exposure to oxidative stress causes significant deterioration in tight junction assembly and barrier integrity, as measured by transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Miyagishima et al., 2021).

When these stressed RPE cells are treated with AICAR, a rapid increase in TEER from approximately 90 Ω·cm² to 135 Ω·cm² has been observed, indicating a substantial enhancement in tight junction integrity (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). At the molecular level, this improvement correlates with a 2.8‐fold rise in phosphorylated AMPK, which is directly associated with the activation of energy restoration pathways and the stabilization of tight junction proteins (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011).

The benefits conferred by AMPK activation are expected to be multifaceted. On one hand, the inhibition of ACC through phosphorylation is anticipated to reduce aberrant lipid synthesis and promote fatty acid oxidation, thereby alleviating metabolic stress within RPE cells (Qin & De Vries, 2008). On the other hand, enhanced autophagic flux driven by AMPK is likely to facilitate the removal of oxidatively damaged proteins and organelles, contributing to cellular repair processes that are pivotal in slowing the progression of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

These laboratory observations have practical implications. In a dysregulated retinal environment—characterized by oxidative damage, inflammatory cytokine presence, and disrupted tight junctions—the activation of AMPK by AICAR could serve as a countermeasure to re‐establish and maintain the critical barrier functions of the RPE (Villarroel et al., 2011). Moreover, by diminishing paracellular leak and preserving the integrity of junctional complexes, AICAR may reduce the accumulation of metabolic waste products and drusen, which are pathological hallmarks of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

It is also noteworthy that the experimental reversal of AICAR’s protective effects by compound C—a well‐known AMPK inhibitor—provides definitive evidence that the beneficial outcomes observed in RPE cells are mediated specifically through AMPK signaling (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014). This on‐target specificity increases the confidence that the observed improvements in TEER are attributable to the intended mechanism rather than off‐target pharmacological actions. Consequently, the expected therapeutic effect in dry AMD would involve enhanced RPE cell viability, reduced cellular stress, and a restored barrier function that together could slow or even halt the progressive degeneration observed in patients (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Overall Evaluation:  
When evaluating AICAR as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, several strengths are immediately apparent, along with a number of challenges that must be carefully addressed during further development. One of the foremost strengths of AICAR is its well–characterized mechanism of action. By serving as an AMP analog that is intracellularly converted to ZMP, AICAR robustly activates AMPK—a key cellular energy sensor that orchestrates a wide range of metabolic responses (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). This activation is tightly coupled to downstream effects such as ACC inhibition, enhanced fatty acid oxidation, and the promotion of autophagy, which are all beneficial in counteracting the metabolic and oxidative stresses inherent in dry AMD (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012).

Furthermore, the experimental data indicating a significant increase in TEER and a concomitant rise in phosphorylated AMPK levels in oxidatively stressed iPSC‐RPE cells provide compelling evidence that AICAR can restore RPE barrier function (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This is particularly important because tight junction integrity and paracellular barrier properties are central to the maintenance of retinal homeostasis and are critically impaired in dry AMD (Villarroel et al., 2011). The demonstration that the beneficial effects of AICAR are reversible by an AMPK inhibitor further reinforces the concept that the drug’s actions are on–target and biologically relevant (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014).

Nevertheless, several potential weaknesses require cautious evaluation. First, while AMPK activation is generally associated with enhanced cellular resilience, some studies have reported that excessive or isoform‐specific activation of AMPK in RPE cells may lead to unintended consequences, such as the inhibition of photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis—a process vital for retinal renewal (Qin & De Vries, 2008). Such a dualistic role of AMPK creates a delicate balance whereby the same pathway that is intended to improve barrier function might also impede essential RPE functions if not precisely modulated.

Additionally, the data in the literature suggest that under certain circumstances, AMPK activation might even contribute to increased epithelial permeability rather than a strengthening of tight junctions (Villarroel et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This paradoxical effect raises concerns about potential context–dependent outcomes of AICAR treatment. For example, while low‐to‐moderate activation of AMPK might support tight junction assembly and autophagy, hyperactivation under severe metabolic or oxidative stress could exacerbate junctional disorganization, thereby counteracting any beneficial effects (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Another challenge is the potential for systemic side effects arising from AICAR’s widespread actions in other tissues. Given that AICAR has been employed in models of diabetes, cardiac metabolism, and even cancer, its pleiotropic effects could impose additional safety considerations when repurposed for ocular use (Pokrywka et al., 2014; Viglino et al., 2019). There is also the issue of dosage; concentrations of 500 µM are effective in vitro, but translating such dosages to in vivo ocular applications requires careful pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies to ensure that therapeutic levels are achieved locally without eliciting undesirable systemic responses (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Asby et al., 2015).

Moreover, given the complex interplay between AMPK signaling, autophagy, and cellular differentiation processes, it is essential to thoroughly understand the long‐term implications of chronic AMPK activation in the RPE. While short‐term activation may be protective, persistent stimulation could lead to energy depletion or maladaptive remodeling of the RPE cytoskeleton, which in turn could affect visual function (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). This underscores the need for extensive preclinical studies that evaluate both the efficacy and the safety profile of AICAR over prolonged periods.

Finally, the inherent variability in patient responses due to genetic, metabolic, and environmental factors presents an additional hurdle. The RPE’s response to oxidative stress, and hence its sensitivity to AMPK modulation, may vary widely among individuals with dry AMD. It will be crucial to identify biomarkers that predict response to AICAR treatment and to tailor dosing regimens accordingly (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

In summary, while AICAR shows considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD by virtue of its well‐established mechanism of AMPK activation, experimental data demonstrating tight junction rescue in RPE cells, and its ability to promote autophagic processes that counteract oxidative stress, its repurposing is tempered by concerns regarding the dualistic effects of AMPK signaling in the RPE, potential systemic side effects, and the challenges associated with dosage translation from in vitro to in vivo applications (Villarroel et al., 2011). The overall evaluation is that AICAR exhibits several compelling advantages—including mechanistic clarity, on‐target efficacy, and a robust preclinical rationale—that substantiate further investigation through rigorous preclinical and, eventually, clinical studies. With a careful approach that addresses the aforementioned weaknesses, AICAR may ultimately emerge as a valuable addition to the therapeutic arsenal against dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Comprehensive Future Directions and Considerations:  
To fully validate AICAR’s potential for treating dry AMD, a series of detailed investigations is warranted. First, further elucidation of the dose–response relationship in RPE cell cultures will be critical. This includes not only establishing the optimal concentration of AICAR to achieve maximal TEER improvement and AMPK activation but also determining whether these effects are sustained over time without incurring cellular toxicity (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011). Long‐term studies are needed to assess whether repeated dosing maintains barrier integrity or if adaptive processes eventually diminish the protective effects of AICAR.

Additionally, it will be necessary to delve deeper into the isoform‐specific effects of AMPK in the RPE. Evidence suggests that the α2 isoform in particular plays a critical role in mediating responses to oxidative stress and that its activation may differ qualitatively from that of the α1 subunit (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012). Understanding these nuances will help design therapeutic strategies that maximize the beneficial aspects of AMPK activation while minimizing potential adverse outcomes, such as impaired phagocytosis or unwanted alterations in cellular metabolism (Qin & De Vries, 2008).

In parallel, investigating the interplay between AICAR‐induced AMPK activation and autophagic pathways in the RPE will shed light on how tightly coupled these processes are in the context of dry AMD. Since autophagy is vital for clearing oxidatively damaged cellular components and supporting cell survival, it will be important to determine whether prolonged AMPK activation fosters a beneficial autophagic flux or rather leads to autophagy dysregulation over time (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). Strategies that involve monitoring autophagic markers along with TEER measurements and junction protein expression could provide a comprehensive picture of cellular health in AICAR‐treated RPE cells.

Given the concerns regarding potential systemic effects, advanced drug delivery systems such as localized intraocular injections or biodegradable implants could be considered for delivering AICAR directly to the retina, thereby limiting systemic exposure and enhancing local efficacy (Viglino et al., 2019; Sid et al., 2014). Preclinical animal models that mimic the pathological features of dry AMD will be indispensable in evaluating the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and therapeutic windows of AICAR in an in vivo setting. Such studies would also be instrumental in identifying potential adverse effects and assessing the long‐term safety profile of AICAR when administered via ocular routes.

Another key consideration is the potential for combination therapy. Since some reports indicate that AMPK activation by AICAR might impair certain RPE functions such as phagocytosis if excessively activated, combining AICAR with other agents that either modulate AMPK isoform activity or protect against excessive autophagic stimulation may provide a synergistic benefit (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Villarroel et al., 2011). For instance, the protective effect of fenofibric acid in preventing AICAR‐induced permeability increases has been documented, suggesting that a combination approach may overcome the limitations of monotherapy (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Finally, translational studies will need to integrate biomarker analyses capable of monitoring AMPK activation status, autophagy markers, and tight junction protein localization in the RPE. These biomarkers could guide dose optimization and serve as early indicators of therapeutic response in clinical trials (Villarroel et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008). Genetic or epigenetic factors that predispose individuals to variations in RPE responsiveness may also be identified, thereby enabling personalized medicine approaches for patients with dry AMD.

In conclusion, while there remain numerous challenges and uncertainties, AICAR represents a highly promising candidate for repurposing as a barrier‐protective agent in dry AMD. Its capacity to robustly activate AMPK, improve cellular energy homeostasis, promote autophagy, and restore tight junction integrity in RPE cells offers a multifaceted mode of action that addresses several key pathological features of dry AMD. With targeted preclinical studies that unpack the complexity of AMPK signaling in retinal tissues and strategic clinical trial designs that mitigate potential adverse effects, AICAR could conceivably fill a significant therapeutic gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Overall Conclusions:  
AICAR’s well‐documented ability to mimic AMP—thereby inducing AMPK activation—and its established role in regulating cellular energy balance and autophagy place it squarely in the category of compounds with high therapeutic potential for metabolic disorders. Emerging evidence in retinal models, particularly those simulating the oxidative stress and barrier dysfunction typical of dry AMD, further reinforces the rationale behind its repurposing. Nonetheless, while preclinical data are encouraging, careful consideration must be given to the dualistic nature of AMPK signaling in the RPE, as well as the potential systemic risks associated with systemic exposure. Despite these challenges, the convergence of multiple lines of evidence—from improved TEER measurements and specific molecular activation to supportive mechanistic studies—strongly advocates for further research into AICAR as a viable therapeutic strategy for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

In summary, the repurposing of AICAR for dry AMD is supported by both its robust mechanistic underpinnings and its promising preclinical efficacy data, placing it among the most attractive candidates for modulating RPE barrier integrity in this debilitating disease. Future studies that focus on fine‐tuning its dosage, delivery, and integrated combination therapies hold the key to unlocking its full therapeutic potential and advancing it from the bench to the clinic (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012).

Taking into account the strengths of its well‐defined mechanism, the reproducible experimental data demonstrating barrier rescue in RPE cells, and the feasibility of its pharmacological modulation, AICAR represents a compelling candidate for further development in the treatment of dry AMD. With continued advances in targeted drug delivery and combination therapeutics, the prospects for leveraging AICAR’s metabolic and protective effects in the retina are promising, warranting its inclusion in the strategic pipeline for combating age‐related macular degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

This comprehensive evaluation underscores that while challenges remain—including potential dose‐dependent effects, off‐target actions, and the need for precise modulation of AMPK isoforms—the overall body of evidence provides a solid rationale for advancing AICAR in preclinical and ultimately clinical studies focused on dry AMD. Its capacity to restore RPE barrier integrity under oxidative stress, coupled with its well‐established pharmacodynamic properties, offers a therapeutic strategy that could mitigate the progression of retinal degeneration and improve visual outcomes for patients suffering from this currently untreatable condition (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose (α,α-trehalose) is a naturally occurring, nonreducing disaccharide composed of two d-glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond; it is broadly found in bacteria, fungi, insects, invertebrates, and plants but is not synthesized by vertebrates, including humans (trehalase in the small intestine hydrolyzes ingested trehalose to glucose) (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). Trehalose’s physicochemical properties include high aqueous solubility, chemical stability, and resistance to glucosidases; it has been mass-produced since the 1990s via enzymatic methods and has been approved for food use by EU regulators and the US FDA, with human exposure generally safe apart from low incidences of malabsorption (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). In drug-development parlance, trehalose is a small-molecule, carbohydrate autophagy modulator and proteostasis regulator; it exhibits both biophysical “chemical chaperone” activity that stabilizes macromolecules and biologic activity that induces the autophagy–lysosome program via TFEB/TFE3 activation and related nutrient-sensing pathways (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Jeong et al., 2021, pp. 1–3, 12–13; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). As a class, autophagy-enhancing small molecules (including trehalose) have been utilized across neurodegeneration and metabolic disease models to promote clearance of toxic protein aggregates or dysfunctional organelles and to restore lysosomal function, with trehalose showing efficacy signals in preclinical Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, Huntington’s disease, and lysosomal storage–related models (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Lotfi et al., 2018, pp. 12–15). Within ophthalmology, trehalose has established use as a topical osmoprotectant/bioprotective excipient in eye-drop formulations for dry-eye disease (commonly 3% w/v), and it is under active investigation for posterior-segment neuroprotection, including age-related retinal degeneration models relevant to AMD (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 18–20; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 10–13).

Therapeutic History  
Clinical/translational use: Trehalose is approved as a safe food ingredient and has been widely used in humans, including topical ophthalmic preparations for dry eye disease and post-LASIK care, with multiple clinical trials and a marketed formulation (e.g., Thealoz Duo, 3% trehalose plus hyaluronic acid) supporting ocular-surface safety and symptomatic benefit; the patented formulation increased tear film thickness after a single drop in clinical testing (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 18–20). Safety data support tolerability of topical trehalose in humans and of high-concentration in vitro exposure across multiple cell types; ocular-surface animal models show safety and barrier-protective effects, and in vitro human RPE studies report no loss of viability up to 200 mM for 24 h, though dosing windows matter for efficacy (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 5–7). Oral trehalose is hydrolyzed by intestinal trehalase and exhibits poor systemic bioavailability, limiting efficacy for some systemic indications; parenteral trehalose achieves low-millimolar plasma levels transiently, which can activate TFEB/TFE3 in macrophages in vivo, but oral exposure is generally insufficient to reach such systemic concentrations in mice in atherosclerosis models (Evans et al., 2018, pp. 2–3). Nonetheless, oral trehalose has shown retinal effects in mice, improving autophagy pathways and preserving cone ERG responses during aging, suggesting either BRB permeability or indirect choroidal effects; the authors noted that establishing BRB permeability is important for translation (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 181–188).

Ocular/retinal preclinical evidence: Multiple independent groups demonstrate mechanistic and functional efficacy of trehalose in RPE/retinal models relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology. In human RPE cell systems (ARPE-19, haRPE, and iPSC-RPE), trehalose increases autophagic flux (LC3-II accumulation with CQ, free GFP readouts), upregulates lysosomal biogenesis markers (LAMP-1/2, cathepsin D), elevates TFEB transcripts and protein, expands the lysosomal compartment (Lysotracker), engages both macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy, and confers autophagy-dependent protection against oxidative stressors such as hydroquinone (HQ), a cigarette smoke–derived oxidant implicated in AMD (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 151–160; Fisher et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). In these RPE systems, trehalose also shifts transcription toward anti-oxidative/anti-angiogenic profiles (NRF2 up, VEGF-A down; Hsp27 down), without evidence of trehalose-induced ROS/cell death at effective doses; however, higher doses can lose cytoprotection—despite ROS suppression—likely due to excessive autophagy, underscoring a narrow therapeutic window (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 154–155, 160–165). In primary murine RPE, trehalose restored autophagic flux under oxidative stress and improved mitochondrial respiratory function in vitro (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In vivo, topical trehalose eye drops increase autophagy–lysosome activity in mouse RPE (LC3B turnover, p62 degradation, LC3B–LAMP1 colocalization) and protect against light-induced outer retinal degeneration (preserving ONL thickness, RPE morphology, and junctional F-actin) without overt changes in unchallenged retina (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 10–13). Oral trehalose increased retinal autophagy and improved cone photopic ERG with age, and in a lysosomal enzyme-deficiency model (MPS IIIB) trehalose reduced retinal degeneration, restored retinal structure/function, and extended lifespan, with effects dependent on canonical autophagy and TFEB activation; trehalose increased TFEB nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene expression in brain and rescued retinal phenotypes (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 181–188; Lotfi et al., 2018, pp. 12–15).

AMD-model efficacy: In an APOE knockout model that recapitulates early AMD features (decreased retinal function, Bruch’s membrane thickening), chronic trehalose treatment ameliorated functional loss and reduced Bruch’s membrane thickening while normalizing autophagy markers (restoring LC3-II:LC3-I to WT, increasing LC3/LAMP1 labeling and autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE), with pathway analyses pointing to ATM–AMPK activation and, for trehalose, increased p38/MAPK14 signaling (Vessey et al., 2022, pp. 1–2, 11–13). Clinical status for AMD: A ClinicalTrials.gov query indicates at least two registered trials for “Trehalose AND macular degeneration,” but the excerpt provides no identifiers or results, so clinical evidence in AMD is presently insufficient for efficacy conclusions (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Collectively, these histories support trehalose as an autophagy/lysosome-modulating candidate with direct RPE/retina efficacy signals in AMD-relevant models, established human ocular-surface safety, and translational rationale for non-neovascular AMD (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Vessey et al., 2022, p. 1).

Below is our comprehensive evaluation of CHIR99021 as a repurposed candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), with detailed discussion of its origins, history, mechanism, expected effects, and overall strengths and weaknesses. In this report, cited evidence is drawn directly from the provided context.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
CHIR99021 is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor originally identified as a highly potent and selective inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3β) with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (~10 nM). Its discovery and subsequent chemical development classified it as an ATP-competitive inhibitor, belonging to a broader class of kinase inhibitors that target GSK-3 enzymes. This compound has been marketed under Tocris catalog number 4423 and is widely used as a research tool for modulating the canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway. The synthesis of CHIR99021 is based on medicinal chemistry approaches that aim to optimize kinase selectivity, and indeed, extensive inhibitor profiling has shown that it preferentially targets GSK-3 over cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) and other kinases. This compound belongs to a class of therapeutic candidates generally employed in stem cell differentiation protocols, where its ability to stabilize β-catenin and drive the transcription of Wnt target genes has been extensively validated in various cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) derived from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Leach et al., 2015). As such, CHIR99021 has been foundational in protocols that aim to drive RPE fate by activating canonical Wnt signaling, thereby demonstrating its utility in manipulating epithelial differentiation pathways.

Therapeutic History:  
The majority of available evidence for CHIR99021’s use comes from in vitro studies and preclinical differentiation protocols rather than clinical applications. Multiple studies have shown that when added during defined differentiation windows (for example, from day 8 to 14 of an hESC-to-RPE protocol), CHIR99021 significantly increases the yield and functional maturation of RPE cells. These studies report that CHIR99021-treated differentiations yield improved epithelial morphology, enhanced pigmentation, and robust expression of RPE lineage markers—including MITF, OTX2, and even tight-junction-associated proteins such as ZO-1 (Leach et al., 2015). In parallel, other reports have documented that upregulation of canonical Wnt signaling through CHIR99021 leads to increased expression of pigmentation genes (TYR, TYRP2, and PMEL17) and the RPE functional secretory factor PEDF. However, it is important to note that despite promising results in differentiation assays, the use of CHIR99021 for direct therapeutic intervention in dry AMD is not well documented. A clinical trials search on ClinicalTrials.gov returned no registered trials exploring CHIR99021 or other GSK-3β inhibitors for AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Moreover, in an in vitro macula-sized RPE wound-repair model designed to mimic geographic atrophy, CHIR99021 treatment hindered wound repair instead of enhancing barrier restoration (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). These seemingly contradictory findings illustrate that while CHIR99021 robustly enhances RPE differentiation from stem cells, its effects in mature or stress-challenged RPE may be context-dependent. Overall, the preclinical history establishes CHIR99021 as a well-characterized research compound with proven biochemical activity in activating Wnt/β-catenin signaling, but there is limited evidence regarding its therapeutic application in treating dry AMD or related RPE barrier dysfunction in vivo (Yang et al., 2018; Hottin et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
CHIR99021 exerts its biological effects by inhibiting GSK-3β through competitive binding at the protein’s ATP site, thereby preventing GSK-3β from phosphorylating its substrates. One of the principal consequences of GSK-3β inhibition is the stabilization of β-catenin. Under normal conditions, GSK-3β phosphorylates β-catenin, marking it for proteasomal degradation. Inhibition by CHIR99021 blocks this phosphorylation event, which leads to an accumulation of β-catenin in the cytosol and its translocation into the nucleus. Once in the nucleus, β-catenin interacts with TCF/LEF transcription factors to induce the transcription of multiple downstream genes that govern cell fate decisions, differentiation, and epithelial characteristics (Leach et al., 2015). Notably, in the context of retinal development, β-catenin directly upregulates RPE-specific transcription factors such as MITF and OTX2 by binding to their promoter elements, which aligns with observations of improved RPE differentiation upon CHIR99021 treatment (Leach et al., 2015).  

The proposed hypothesis extends this mechanism by suggesting that activation of the canonical Wnt pathway will also upregulate tight junction gene expression. Although specific data on claudin-1 and occludin transcription in response to CHIR99021 in RPE under oxidative stress are not directly provided in the available literature, several studies have shown that Wnt/β-catenin signaling positively correlates with the expression of junctional proteins and may help preserve the architecture of the ZO-1 belt (Leach et al., 2015). In endothelial cell models, GSK-3 inhibition has been associated with favorable modulation of barrier proteins and improved barrier function, suggesting a mechanistic plausibility for a similar effect in RPE cells (Page, 2019; Hottin et al., 2022). Moreover, the dual action of CHIR99021 in modulating both Wnt targets and supporting antioxidant gene networks may provide additional cytoprotective effects under oxidative stress conditions relevant to dry AMD (Leach et al., 2015; Hottin et al., 2022). However, it must be noted that in certain experimental settings, such as in an in vitro RPE wound-repair assay, prolonged exposure to CHIR99021 led to impaired wound healing, indicating that the degree and context of canonical pathway activation are critical determinants of outcome (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis, the application of CHIR99021 in oxidative-stressed RPE is expected to stabilize β-catenin and, through canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling, upregulate the transcription of tight junction genes such as claudin-1 and occludin. This molecular cascade is anticipated to preserve or even restore the ZO-1 belt architecture—the structural hallmark of an intact epithelial barrier—and thereby improve functional barrier properties as measured by an increase in transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and a reduction in FITC-dextran permeability under stress challenges induced by A2E or H₂O₂. In ARPE-19 cell models, limited data suggest that stabilization of β-catenin can counteract H₂O₂-induced loss of cell–cell junctions, with reports of a TEER improvement of approximately 35% (Yang et al., 2018). The expected outcome is therefore two-fold: first, the promotion of a differentiated epithelial phenotype with enhanced expression of RPE-specific markers (MITF, OTX2, PMEL17, and ZO-1); and second, the maintenance or restoration of barrier integrity under conditions that mimic oxidative stress encountered in dry AMD. It is important to consider, however, that while CHIR99021 has been shown to improve differentiation when applied during early stages of RPE development (Leach et al., 2015), its application in mature, stressed RPE may have unintended effects. In one in vitro model simulating GA-like lesions, chronic exposure to CHIR99021 resulted in hindered wound repair, suggesting that the dynamics of Wnt activation—and possibly feedback regulation of junctional pathways—must be finely balanced (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Thus, while the biochemical rationale for improved tight junction gene expression and TEER enhancement is sound, the expected beneficial effect under oxidative challenges remains to be conclusively demonstrated in models that directly assay these endpoints.

Overall Evaluation:  
CHIR99021 presents several notable strengths as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its high selectivity and potency as a GSK-3β inhibitor—coupled with its ability to robustly activate canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling—make it a well-characterized compound from a biochemical standpoint (Page, 2019; Hottin et al., 2022). The extensive literature demonstrating its use in stem cell differentiation protocols to generate highly purified RPE populations lends credence to its capacity to promote or maintain an epithelial phenotype (Leach et al., 2015). In addition, the dual targeting of both differentiation pathways and antioxidant gene networks provides mechanistic specificity that is theoretically well aligned with the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD where oxidative stress and barrier dysfunction play central roles (Leach et al., 2015; Hottin et al., 2022). Moreover, its established pharmacokinetic profile and ready availability make it an attractive candidate for rapid preclinical evaluation in ocular models.

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and concerns temper enthusiasm for CHIR99021 as a dry AMD therapeutic. First, while its use in developmental protocols is well documented, there exists a paucity of data on the direct upregulation of tight junction genes such as claudin-1 and occludin in oxidative-stress models of RPE. Although improved ZO-1 localization and epithelial morphology have been noted in hESC-derived RPE cultures (Leach et al., 2015), direct evidence linking CHIR99021 to enhanced TEER or reduced FITC-dextran permeability in mature RPE under conditions mimicking dry AMD (A2E/H₂O₂ challenge) is lacking. Second, there is conflicting evidence from in vitro wound-repair studies in RPE: while CHIR99021 enhances RPE differentiation, its chronic application in a macula-sized lesion model impaired repair, suggesting that the timing and duration of GSK-3β inhibition are critical parameters that could influence barrier function negatively if not optimized (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Third, despite positive outcomes in some endothelial cell systems regarding barrier rescue following GSK-3 inhibition, similar experiments in RPE or retinal endothelial models using CHIR99021 remain limited, raising questions about the translatability of these findings to a dry AMD setting (Page, 2019). Finally, a ClinicalTrials.gov search has not identified any trials involving CHIR99021 or related GSK-3 inhibitors for AMD, underscoring that while the molecular rationale is sound, the candidate has not undergone any clinical evaluation in this particular indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In summary, CHIR99021 is a well-studied research tool with a clearly defined mechanism of action—namely, the inhibition of GSK-3β leading to stabilization of β-catenin and activation of downstream Wnt target genes. Its proven ability to drive RPE differentiation and enhance epithelial marker expression makes it appealing from a developmental standpoint. However, available evidence also highlights potential drawbacks when applied to mature or stressed RPE, including impaired wound repair in certain in vitro models. The hypothesis that CHIR99021 will upregulate claudin-1 and occludin transcription, thereby preserving ZO-1 architecture to improve TEER and reduce permeability under oxidative challenges, remains promising in theory but requires substantiation through focused experiments that measure tight junction integrity and barrier function specifically under conditions mimicking dry AMD (Yang et al., 2018). As such, while the candidate has mechanistic appeal and a robust preclinical track record in RPE differentiation, its application for barrier restoration in dry AMD remains speculative at this stage, and further investigation—including dose optimization studies, TEER/permeability assays in oxidative stress models, and eventually in vivo preclinical evaluations—is warranted before advancing CHIR99021 into clinical trials for this indication.

Overall, our evaluation concludes that CHIR99021 shows potential based on its selectivity and mechanistic rationale but that significant uncertainties remain regarding its efficacy in restoring barrier function in the context of dry AMD. Strengths include its potent GSK-3β inhibition, well-characterized activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, and proven use in enhancing RPE differentiation, while weaknesses center on mixed results in mature RPE wound‐repair models and the current lack of direct evidence for tight junction upregulation under oxidative stress. The direction for future research must focus on rigorous validation of barrier parameters (including claudin-1, occludin, TEER, and permeability assays) in models that closely recapitulate the oxidative and inflammatory milieu of dry AMD before considering CHIR99021 as a viable drug candidate for clinical repurposing (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

This comprehensive review therefore supports a cautious approach: while CHIR99021 possesses attractive biochemical and mechanistic properties that justify its rapid evaluation in preclinical ocular models, its repurposing for dry AMD will require additional data specifically addressing RPE barrier function under oxidative stress. Further targeted studies are essential to resolve the context-dependent effects observed in vitro and to determine if optimal dosing and timing regimens can overcome the negative outcomes seen in wound-repair assays. Only with such evidence will CHIR99021’s promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD be fully validated.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA-408; also known as CDDO-DFPA; N-(2-Cyano-3,12-dioxo-28-noroleana-1,9(11)-dien-17-yl)-2,2-difluoropropanamide) is a semisynthetic oleanane triterpenoid created by lead optimization of the natural product oleanolic acid, a plant-derived pentacyclic triterpene produced via the mevalonate pathway (squalene → 2,3-oxidosqualene → β-amyrin → erythrodiol → oleanolic acid) and abundantly available from Oleaceae (e.g., olive) and other botanical sources (over 1,600 species; Nakagami, 2016; Masullo et al., 2017; Pollier & Goossens, 2012). The oleanane scaffold was iteratively diversified by Sporn, Gribble, Honda and collaborators to introduce enone and cyanoenone Michael acceptors on rings A and C, yielding the CDDO class (2-cyano-3,12-dioxo-oleana-1,9(11)-dien-28-oic acid and derivatives) as extraordinarily potent anti-inflammatory and Nrf2-inducing agents; C-28 esters/amides and further A/C-ring modifications produced multiple clinical candidates including CDDO-Me (bardoxolone methyl, RTA-402) and RTA-408 (omaveloxolone) (Honda et al., 2000; Pollier & Goossens, 2012; Cheng et al., 2021). RTA-408 specifically is a C17-modified difluoro-propanamide on an oleanane core and belongs to the second generation of synthetic triterpenoids designed to preserve high Nrf2 potency while controlling electrophilicity and pharmacokinetics (Nakagami, 2016; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

At the pharmacological class level, synthetic oleanane triterpenoids are electrophilic “antioxidant inflammation modulators” that activate the KEAP1–NRF2–ARE pathway through covalent (but often reversible) Michael addition to redox-sensitive cysteines on KEAP1, particularly Cys151 on the BTB domain, thereby stabilizing Nrf2 and inducing a coordinated cytoprotective gene program; they concurrently suppress inducible pro-inflammatory mediators (e.g., iNOS, COX-2) with dose-dependent bifunctionality (cytoprotection at low concentrations; pro-oxidant/apoptotic signaling at higher exposure) (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Liby et al., 2007). This scaffold has been extensively explored as a drug platform across oncology, nephrology, cardiopulmonary, inflammatory, and neurological indications, with bardoxolone methyl and omaveloxolone translating to clinical studies and, for omaveloxolone, regulatory approval in Friedreich’s ataxia (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Zahir et al., 2025). Within ophthalmology, oleanane triterpenoids and close congeners (dh404, CDDO-TFEA, CDDO-EA, CDDO-Me) have shown robust Nrf2-mediated protection in retinal models, and RTA-408 itself has been advanced into ocular clinical trials evaluating postoperative ocular pain/inflammation and corneal endothelial cell loss after cataract surgery, positioning this mechanism squarely within ocular translational scope (Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
The oleanane triterpenoid class has a two-decade translational history that began with demonstrations that cyano-enone–bearing derivatives are sub-nanomolar inducers of the Nrf2 transcriptome and suppressors of inflammatory enzymes in vitro and in vivo, a property mapped by SAR to the presence/placement of A-ring 1-en-3-one and C-ring 9(11)-en-12-one Michael acceptors (Honda et al., 2000; Nakagami, 2016). Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me) showed pharmacodynamic activity in humans (ARE-gene induction in tumor biopsies; renal function improvements), but its BEACON Phase 3 trial in advanced CKD was halted for cardiovascular adverse events—an outcome that did not negate class activity but highlighted the need for indication-specific risk management and exclusion criteria (e.g., high BNP, poor baseline eGFR) (Masullo et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Subsequent controlled studies in rarer CKD-associated diseases continued under tighter cardiometabolic selection, while medicinal-chemistry efforts generated second-generation analogs including fluorinated scaffolds (e.g., omaveloxolone) to tune reactivity and PK/PD (Sun et al., 2017).

For omaveloxolone specifically, preclinical pharmacology established Nrf2-dependent induction of glutathione homeostasis genes and improvements in mitochondrial respiration; systemic PK in primates/humans showed dose proportionality and measurable tissue distribution (including liver, lung, brain), with PBMC and tissue Nrf2 target-gene induction at clinically achievable exposures (Reisman et al., 2019). In oncology, a first-in-human dose-escalation study in advanced solid tumors reported acceptable tolerability with pharmacodynamic evidence of Nrf2 pathway activation in PBMCs; in dermatology, topical RTA-408 lotion activated Nrf2 in human skin and was well tolerated (Creelan et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). In neurology, omaveloxolone advanced through the MOXIe program for Friedreich’s ataxia with evidence of neurologic benefit at clinical doses ≥80 mg and exposures concordant with preclinical pharmacology (Naidu & Dinkova-Kostova, 2020; Reisman et al., 2019; Zahir et al., 2025).

Ocularly, multiple oleanane triterpenoid derivatives have shown benefit in retinal oxidative-stress models: dh404 induced canonical Nrf2 target genes (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM), reduced inflammatory mediators, and decreased retinal vascular leakage; CDDO-TFEA and CDDO-EA activated NQO1 in photoreceptor-derived 661W cells and CDDO-TFEA reduced light-induced retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021). RS9, an OA-derived analog generated via microbial transformation, showed superior potency versus CDDO-Me in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) protection, increased retinal HO-1/NQO1 at low doses, and suppressed neovascularization and blood-brain barrier hyperpermeability in vivo, supporting the generalizable ocular protective potential of optimized oleanane triterpenoids (Cheng et al., 2021). Critically for translational relevance, omaveloxolone itself has documented protective activity in human fetal RPE at low-nanomolar concentrations (≤100 nM), where it prevents H₂O₂-induced apoptosis/necrosis by shifting the Bcl-2:Bax ratio and reducing protein glutathionylation—biomarkers linked to oxidative damage and barrier compromise in RPE (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, RTA-408 is the only oleanolic acid analogue noted to have entered clinical trials in ocular indications (cataract-surgery–related pain/inflammation and corneal endothelial cell loss), demonstrating sponsor commitment to ophthalmic development and an initial tolerability signal for ocular use (Cheng et al., 2021). No clinical reports were found in the provided context for omaveloxolone in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) specifically, nor in geographic atrophy; thus, this is a repurposing proposal grounded in mechanistic and preclinical ocular convergence rather than direct AMD clinical precedent (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
The KEAP1–NRF2 node is a cysteine-centric electrophile sensor system that orchestrates the phase-2 antioxidant and cytoprotective response. Under basal conditions, KEAP1 recruits NRF2 to the CUL3 E3 ligase complex for ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover. Electrophiles such as cyano-enone triterpenoids react with KEAP1 cysteine sensors—most prominently Cys151 in the BTB domain—to disrupt CUL3 docking and/or alter KEAP1 conformation, thereby stabilizing NRF2, allowing nuclear translocation, heterodimerization with small Maf proteins, and binding to antioxidant response elements (ARE) to induce a transcriptional battery including NQO1, HO-1 (HMOX1), glutathione biosynthesis enzymes (GCLC, GCLM), thioredoxin and thioredoxin reductase (Txn1, Txnrd1), sulfiredoxin (Srxn1), and other detoxifying/antioxidative genes (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). Oleanane cyano-enone triterpenoids are among the most potent NRF2 activators known, with structure–activity relationships showing strong correlations between the presence/geometry of Michael acceptors and both iNOS suppression and NQO1 induction across series; mechanistic profiling indicates covalent yet reversible conjugation to protein thiols underlies this pharmacology (Naidu & Dinkova-Kostova, 2020).

Within this class, omaveloxolone is an electrophilic Michael acceptor–bearing, difluoro-propanamide oleanane that activates Nrf2 at nanomolar concentrations in reporter assays and upregulates canonical ARE-target genes (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, TxnR1), consistent with its cyano-enone pharmacophore engaging KEAP1 Cys151 and allied redox sensors (Sun et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019). In systemic models, omaveloxolone increases glutathione concentrations, supports mitochondrial respiration, and normalizes metabolic/energetic parameters downstream of Nrf2 activation—effects mechanistically rationalized by Nrf2-driven induction of NADPH-generating enzymes and mitochondrial support genes, which collectively bolster reductive and ATP capacity in stressed cells (Reisman et al., 2019). In immunologic contexts, oleanane triterpenoids suppress IFN-γ–induced nitric oxide signaling in macrophages, reduce reactive oxygen and nitrotyrosine production by myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and can inhibit IKKβ/NF-κB signaling (demonstrated for CDDO-Me), contributing to anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions that are secondary but complementary to NRF2-mediated cytoprotection (Creelan et al., 2017; Sporn et al., 2007). The class is bifunctional: low-to-moderate exposures favor NRF2-dependent cytoprotection and redox quenching, whereas higher exposures can increase oxidative burden and trigger apoptosis—an important consideration when targeting delicate ocular tissues (Liby et al., 2007).

For ocular cell types relevant to dry AMD, multiple lines of evidence anchor Nrf2/ARE biology. In the retina, oleanane triterpenoids (dh404, CDDO derivatives) induce NQO1/HO-1/GCLM, reduce inflammatory mediators and vascular leakage, and protect photoreceptors and retinal structure in oxidative-stress models; RS9 dosing increases retinal NQO1/HO-1 in vivo (Cheng et al., 2021). In human fetal RPE, omaveloxolone prevents H₂O₂-induced apoptosis and necrosis at ≤100 nM, shifts Bcl-2:Bax pro-survival balance, and reduces protein S-glutathionylation, a reversible oxidative modification implicated in disruption of cytoskeletal and junctional complexes that maintain barrier integrity (Cheng et al., 2021). Taken together, these data support that omaveloxolone, via KEAP1 cysteine sensing and Nrf2 activation in RPE and adjacent retinal cells, can rapidly enhance the endogenous antioxidant program, elevate glutathione/NADPH buffering, mitigate protein oxidative adducts, and suppress inflammatory amplification—biomechanistic axes directly relevant to RPE survival and barrier function under oxidative stress (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021).

Pharmacologically, omaveloxolone exhibits high plasma protein binding and broad tissue distribution preclinically, with oral dosing in primates/humans yielding exposures that induce Nrf2 targets in PBMCs and distribute to metabolically active tissues; topical dermal dosing in humans activates cutaneous Nrf2 without untoward safety signals (Reisman et al., 2019). For ocular dosing, clinical testing of RTA-408 in cataract-surgery contexts (ocular pain/inflammation, corneal endothelial protection) establishes feasibility of achieving pharmacologically relevant ocular exposure with acceptable tolerability in humans, though detailed ocular PK has not been published in the provided excerpts (Cheng et al., 2021).

Expected Effect

Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit to dry AMD biology: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to RPE degeneration in dry AMD; omaveloxolone engages KEAP1 cysteine sensors to activate Nrf2 and induce a comprehensive, rapid-acting ARE program that elevates glutathione/NADPH, upregulates HO-1/NQO1/GCL-enzymes, and improves mitochondrial bioenergetics—changes expected to blunt H₂O₂-triggered barrier loss and death in RPE (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). - Class potency and breadth: Oleanane cyano-enones are among the most potent known Nrf2 activators; RS9’s superior retinal potency and CDDO tethered analogs’ efficacy in retinal models argue that the scaffold class, optimized for ocular delivery, can achieve pharmacodynamic effects in the eye at low doses (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021).

Risks and weaknesses  
- Electrophile-driven bifunctionality and narrow window: The same α,β-unsaturated carbonyls that confer high potency can, at higher exposures, increase oxidative stress and trigger apoptosis; dose selection and exposure control will be critical in the eye (Liby et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2021).

- Class safety history: Bardoxolone methyl’s cardiovascular signal in late-stage CKD underscores the need for indication- and formulation-specific safety strategies; while not probative for ocular topical/intraocular dosing, it motivates cautious systemic exposure limits and cardiovascular exclusion if systemic routes are used (Nakagami, 2016; Sun et al., 2017).

- Incomplete AMD-specific evidence: The provided literature does not report omaveloxolone in dry AMD or geographic atrophy models; most ocular data derive from oxidative-stress/retinal injury and postoperative inflammation paradigms, which are supportive but not definitive for the multifactorial dry AMD pathobiology (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Delivery and exposure uncertainties: Omaveloxolone’s lipophilicity and strong protein binding complicate prediction of ocular distribution; although ocular clinical testing exists for RTA-408, detailed ocular PK/PD are not included in the excerpts, and tailored ophthalmic formulations may be required to achieve RPE/retinal exposure without anterior-segment sequestration (Reisman et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021).

Program recommendations  
- In vitro RPE barrier program: Establish a standardized H₂O₂-induced barrier disruption assay in human RPE monolayers with readouts for TEER, large-molecule paracellular flux, ZO-1/occludin belt integrity, protein S-glutathionylation, and apoptosis/caspase activation. Titrate omaveloxolone at 1–100 nM to define the cytoprotective plateau and the onset of bifurcation, and confirm KEAP1–NRF2 mechanism using pharmacologic/CRISPR Nrf2 blockade (Cheng et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2017; Liby et al., 2007).

- Ocular in vivo models: Utilize light-induced photoreceptor injury and retinal I/R models, where the class has shown benefit, to benchmark efficacy and establish exposure–response (retinal NQO1/HO-1 induction, BRB leakage suppression), followed by NaIO₃-induced RPE injury to approximate dry AMD-relevant oxidative RPE loss (Cheng et al., 2021). Include RS9 and a non-electrophilic control to contextualize class effects (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Delivery strategy: Develop an ophthalmic formulation (e.g., micelles, lipid nanoparticles) guided by prior triterpenoid formulation successes (amorphous dispersion for CDDO-Me; UA nanoparticles) to target posterior-segment delivery via topical, suprachoroidal, or intravitreal routes depending on PK modeling and in vivo biodistribution; minimize systemic absorption to mitigate class-related CV risk (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Safety pharmacology: Delineate the therapeutic index around ocular exposures, including ERG and OCT endpoints, and histopathology for photoreceptors, RPE, and ganglion cells; monitor inflammatory and angiogenic pathways to rule out unanticipated pathway cross-talk at sustained Nrf2 activation (Liby et al., 2007).

Conclusion  
On balance, omaveloxolone is a mechanistically well-aligned, clinically de-risked Nrf2 activator with direct protective activity in human RPE and supportive in vivo retinal pharmacology from its chemical class, making it a strong repurposing candidate for dry AMD focused on RPE barrier preservation under oxidative stress (Cheng et al., 2021; Cuadrado et al., 2019). The primary development challenges are exposure control to avoid electrophile-mediated bifunctionality, demonstration of efficacy in AMD-relevant RPE injury models and barrier assays (including TEER), and optimization of ocular delivery to achieve posterior-segment pharmacodynamics with minimal systemic exposure (Liby et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2021; Reisman et al., 2019). Given the magnitude of unmet need in dry AMD and the centrality of oxidative injury to RPE pathology, a staged program beginning with RPE barrier assays and retinal oxidative stress models, followed by formulation-enabled ocular PK/PD and safety, is justified and has a reasonable probability of technical success based on the assembled evidence (Cheng et al., 2021; Reisman et al., 2019).
