Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ripasudil, also known by its research designation Y-39983 and commercially available as Selleckchem S8443, is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor developed originally as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil containing protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. It belongs to a class of therapeutics that act in an ATP‐competitive manner to inhibit the activity of ROCK isoforms, enzymes that are critical regulators of actomyosin contractility and cell adhesion. Ripasudil was synthesized following the structural optimization of earlier compounds such as fasudil and Y-27632, with the aim of increasing both potency and ocular tolerability. Its chemical origins are linked to the rational design strategies that sought to improve enzyme inhibitory selectivity and to enhance the pharmacokinetic profile for local ocular application. Members of the ROCK inhibitor class have seen prior use in settings that require modulation of actin cytoskeleton dynamics, such as the treatment of glaucoma via enhanced aqueous humor outflow, and have also been explored in contexts involving wound healing and anti-fibrotic effects in various ocular tissues (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, ripasudil has been approved in Japan for the treatment of glaucoma and ocular hypertension, where it is delivered topically in the form of eye drops, demonstrating a well-established safety profile and a low incidence of systemic adverse effects. In preclinical models, it has demonstrated efficacy by increasing ocular blood flow, modifying trabecular meshwork cell contractility, and reducing intraocular pressure, thereby serving as a stepping stone and proof-of-concept for the utility of ROCK inhibitors in ocular disorders. Beyond its approved use in glaucoma, investigations of ROCK inhibitors—including ripasudil—have extended into experimental applications in corneal endothelial regeneration and have been evaluated in combination with anti-VEGF therapies for diabetic macular edema. Although direct clinical evidence specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is not available, multiple lines of preclinical research have shown that the ROCK inhibitor class modulates pathways which are believed to underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Notably, the mechanistic studies have identified the role of ROCK signaling in cytoskeletal reorganization, matrix contractility, and fibrosis, all of which are processes particularly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier dysfunction seen in dry AMD (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Moreover, the ocular pharmacokinetic profile of ripasudil—demonstrated by rabbit intravitreal studies showing a half-life of approximately 14 hours and negligible systemic exposure—is supportive of repurposing this candidate for posterior segment indications, including dry AMD (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ripasudil exerts its therapeutic activity by competitively inhibiting the ATP-binding site of ROCK isoforms, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of downstream effectors such as myosin light-chain (MLC), myosin-binding subunit of MLC phosphatase (MYPT1), and LIM kinase. These phosphorylation events normally lead to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, focal adhesion assembly, and ultimately contribute to a contractile, stiffened cell phenotype. In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, this contractility is thought to be exacerbated under conditions of oxidative stress, contributing to disassembly or mislocalization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity. By inhibiting ROCK, ripasudil reduces actomyosin-driven contraction and stress-fiber formation, thereby promoting cortical F-actin remodeling and facilitating the proper membrane relocalization of tight-junction proteins. The specificity of ripasudil has been demonstrated by its greater than 100-fold selectivity against other kinases such as protein kinase C (PKC) and myotonic dystrophy kinase-related Cdc42-binding kinase (MRCK), highlighting the mechanistic precision by which it modulates ROCK-dependent signaling cascades (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Additionally, while several studies indicate that the ROCK inhibitor class generally targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2 isoforms, quantitative biochemical data have shown that ripasudil exhibits potent enzyme inhibitory activity with IC₅₀s in the low nanomolar range (with values reported around 51 nM for ROCK1 and 19 nM for ROCK2 in some studies, though the candidate hypothesis posits values of approximately 29 nM for ROCK1 and 68 nM for ROCK2). This inhibitory profile is particularly relevant because emerging research indicates that ROCK2, in particular, is upregulated in the pathological conditions of dry AMD and plays a key role in mediating cytoskeletal changes that disrupt RPE tight junction integrity (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). The inhibition of ROCK thereby is expected to have a dual benefit of cytoprotection and restoration of cell junction architecture, ultimately leading to improved barrier function (Ghenciu et al., 2025; Singh & Singh, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing ripasudil for dry AMD is that by blocking ROCK activity in oxidatively stressed retinal pigment epithelium cells, the compound will lead to a reduction in actomyosin contractility, thereby alleviating the formation of pathological stress fibers that otherwise disrupt the organization of tight junction complexes. Under normal physiological conditions, tight junction proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin are localized at the plasma membrane in a continuous, belt-like manner that is essential to maintain TEER and restrict paracellular permeability. However, in dry AMD, oxidative damage, inflammation, and mechanical stress lead to cytoskeletal reorganization and a discontinuous distribution of these critical proteins, resulting in impaired barrier function and contributing to the pathogenesis of the disease. Preclinical studies, particularly those employing ARPE-19 cell models subjected to toxic insults such as paraquat or sodium iodate (NaIO₃), have demonstrated that ROCK inhibitors can dose-dependently restore TEER (with reported improvements up to 70%) and re-establish the membrane continuity of ZO-1, suggesting that these agents can “rescue” the RPE barrier phenotype under injurious conditions (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). It is expected that ripasudil, with its potent ROCK-inhibitory activity and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics (including intravitreal retention times supportive of sustained action), will similarly promote the cortical redistribution of F-actin, leading to the re-localization of junctional molecules back to the cell membrane. This mechanistic restoration should result in improved transepithelial electrical resistance and a concomitant reduction in paracellular permeability, effectively reinforcing the RPE barrier—a central therapeutic target in dry AMD. Moreover, the activation of protective cellular pathways through ROCK inhibition may also confer additional anti-apoptotic and anti-inflammatory effects, further contributing to the survival and functional integrity of the RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating ripasudil as a candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths become apparent. First, its established clinical use for glaucoma means that its safety, tolerability, and ocular pharmacokinetic properties are well characterized—attributes that significantly lower the translational barrier for its application in other ocular diseases. The intravitreal pharmacokinetic data, with a half-life of approximately 14 hours in rabbit models and negligible systemic exposure, suggest that therapeutic concentrations capable of modulating ROCK activity in the retina can be achieved with acceptable dosing regimens (Yamaguchi et al., 2016). Second, the mechanistic rationale is compelling: ROCK signaling is intimately involved in mediating actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, and subsequent disruption of tight junction architecture in epithelial cells. Given that ROCK2 in particular is implicated in the pathological processes observed in the RPE in dry AMD, the ability of ripasudil to inhibit this pathway could translate into measurable improvements in barrier function, as indicated by preclinical assays demonstrating TEER restoration and the re-localization of ZO-1 in ARPE-19 cells (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Third, the compound exhibits a favorable selectivity profile, with negligible off-target activity against other kinases such as PKC and MRCK, which minimizes the risk of unintended effects in non-target tissues. This specificity is critical when repurposing drugs for chronic conditions such as dry AMD, where long-term ocular safety is paramount (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Despite these strengths, there are notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before ripasudil can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. A primary limitation is the paucity of direct experimental evidence in RPE models of dry AMD. While the hypothesis is supported by data from related in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative stress), robust in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of dry AMD pathophysiology are still needed. In particular, data demonstrating that ripasudil can restore tight junction integrity and improve TEER in the context of chronic, progressive RPE dysfunction remain limited (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Furthermore, although the compound’s ROCK inhibitory activity is well documented, the available literature does not consistently detail the isoform-specific effects in RPE cells; given that ROCK1 and ROCK2 may play distinct roles in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, clarifying the relative contributions of each isoform is essential. The candidate hypothesis posits specific IC₅₀ values for ROCK1 and ROCK2, yet discrepancies exist across reported studies regarding the precise inhibitory concentrations, which indicates that further biochemical characterization is warranted (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). Another consideration is the potential for adverse effects when repurposing a drug originally optimized for anterior-segment diseases for posterior-segment applications. Although the ocular safety profile of ripasudil in glaucoma is well established, the long-term impact of ROCK inhibition on RPE cell biology in an aged population—especially in the context of dry AMD—remains uncertain. Off-target cytoskeletal effects in other retinal cell types, possible modulation of inflammatory responses, and the risk of inadvertently triggering compensatory signaling pathways are all factors that must be carefully evaluated in preclinical studies (Iancu et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2025). Lastly, while the pharmacokinetic data support retinal exposure after intravitreal or possibly topical administration, optimizing the delivery method to ensure sustained and localized drug levels in the RPE without causing ocular surface toxicity (such as conjunctival hyperemia or corneal epithelial disturbances) will be critical. Innovative delivery systems, such as sustained-release intravitreal implants or depot formulations, may offer solutions but require further development (Yamaguchi et al., 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023).

In conclusion, the repurposing of ripasudil for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and a favorable safety profile derived from its established use in glaucoma. The compound’s capacity to inhibit ROCK-mediated actomyosin contraction and promote cortical F-actin remodeling positions it as a promising agent for restoring RPE barrier function—one of the key pathological features of dry AMD. However, the current literature reveals significant gaps in direct evidence regarding its effects on RPE tight junction proteins, TEER restoration, and the isoform-specific roles of ROCK in the RPE under oxidative stress. To advance ripasudil as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, additional preclinical investigations—ideally incorporating robust animal models of dry AMD and detailed biochemical analyses of ROCK isoform activity in RPE cells—are required. Additionally, optimizations in drug delivery methodology to achieve sustained posterior-segment exposure while minimizing adverse ocular events will be imperative. Overall, ripasudil presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, with its strengths in mechanistic specificity, favorable ocular pharmacokinetics, and established clinical safety underscoring its potential. Nonetheless, the outlined weaknesses and knowledge gaps necessitate a rigorous program of targeted research to validate its efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity and to ensure its long-term safety in the intended patient population (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023; Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Adams & Papillon, 2020; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
JQ1 (Selleck S7110) is a synthetic small-molecule thienotriazolodiazepine developed as a first-in-class, highly selective competitive inhibitor of the bromodomain and extra-terminal (BET) acetyl-lysine reader family (BRD2/3/4, BRDT) that binds the acetyl-lysine pocket of BET bromodomains (BD1 and BD2) to displace BET proteins from chromatin and suppress transcription at dependent enhancers and promoters (pan-BET, BD1/BD2 non-selective) (Zhao et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2023). BET bromodomains recognize acetylated histone tails at active enhancers/super-enhancers and recruit coactivator assemblies that couple to RNA polymerase II to drive high-amplitude transcription of inflammatory, immune, and stress-response genes; small-molecule BET inhibition collapses these assemblies and blunts stimulus-induced transcriptional programs in immune and neural cells (Zhao et al., 2017). Within ophthalmology, JQ1 has been deployed intravitreally or systemically in multiple preclinical models, including inherited photoreceptor degeneration (rd10 retinitis pigmentosa), oxidative-stress retinal injury (sodium iodate), light-damage photoreceptor injury, experimental autoimmune uveitis (with other BET inhibitors), corneal fibrosis, and proliferative vitreoretinopathy, where it has shown neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory, and anti-fibrotic activity (Zhao et al., 2017; Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023; Eichenbaum, 2020; Liao et al., 2024). The BET modality also includes domain-selective ligands (e.g., BD2-preferring apabetalone/RVX-208) and targeted protein degraders (e.g., dBET6, a cereblon-recruiting JQ1-based PROTAC) that achieve complementary pharmacology by either sparing BD1 or depleting BRD2/3/4 protein, respectively (Zhu et al., 2023; Shahid et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
- Inherited photoreceptor degeneration (rd10, Pde6b mutant): A single intravitreal injection of JQ1 (2 µl of 0.1 mM at PN14) preserved photoreceptor number through PN24 (>90% of baseline), improved ERG a- and b-wave amplitudes, reduced TUNEL-positive photoreceptor apoptosis and caspase-3/7 activity, and markedly suppressed retinal microglial activation/infiltration (IBA1, TSPO, CD68) with cytokine mRNAs (TNFα, MCP-1, IL-1β, IL-6, RANTES) reduced to WT levels in whole retinas and in sorted retinal microglia (MCP-1 also lowered by ELISA) (Zhao et al., 2017). Complementary in vitro work showed JQ1 pre-treatment abolished LPS-induced upregulation of TNFα, MCP-1, IL-1β, IL-6 and RANTES and reduced microglial proliferation and migration by ~70%, with mechanistic dissection implicating BET2 (BRD2) and the BD2 (Brom2) domain in microglial activation; a BD2-preferring ligand (RVX208) suppressed cytokine induction more effectively than a BD1-preferring ligand (Olinone) (Zhao et al., 2017). In vivo, BET2 protein is increased at PN24 in rd10 retinas, correlating with peak microglial activation and photoreceptor degeneration (Zhao et al., 2017).  
- Oxidative-stress retinal/RPE injury (sodium iodate, SI): JQ1 suppressed BRD4-induced STING transcription by decreasing chromatin accessibility (reduced H3 acetylation, RNA Pol II recruitment) at the STING locus, curtailed cGAS–STING activation, reduced microglia/macrophage accumulation (IBA1+) in retina/subretinal spaces, prevented RPE/retinal degeneration, and preserved retinal integrity without detectable adverse retinal morphology when used alone (in vitro ARPE cells and in vivo SI models across ages) (Zou et al., 2022). Mechanistically, BRD4 upregulation under oxidative stress promotes STING and inflammatory outputs; JQ1 or BRD4 depletion enhances autophagic flux (LC3II), accelerates autophagic enclosure/clearance of cytosolic DNA, reduces dsDNA accumulation, and thereby attenuates STING-mediated inflammation; autophagy inhibitors (BafA1, chloroquine) block these effects, indicating an autophagy-dependent mechanism (Zou et al., 2022).  
- Light-damage photoreceptor injury: The JQ1-based PROTAC dBET6 delivered systemically degraded BRD2/3/4 in mouse retina, improved retinal responsiveness and visual acuity after light damage, suppressed macrophage/microglia activation and Müller gliosis, reduced photoreceptor death, and inhibited LD-induced cGAS–STING activation in retinal microglia; importantly, the PROTAC strategy is motivated by compensatory BRD4 accumulation observed with JQ1 (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- RPE cell inflammation (ARPE-19): Multiple BET inhibitors (including JQ1) reduced etoposide-induced IL-6 and IL-8 secretion, decreased NF-κB p65 activity, and reduced acetylation of p53 at K382 in human RPE without major cytotoxicity; the anti-inflammatory effects appeared SIRT1-independent (SIRT1 inhibition or knockdown did not reverse IL-8 lowering), although SIRT1 pharmacology altered the p53 acetylation response (Hytti et al., 2016). BET inhibitors slightly decreased baseline MTT conversion but reduced etoposide cytotoxicity (lower LDH release, higher viability), consistent with modest cytoprotection under this stressor (Hytti et al., 2016).  
- Endothelial barrier inflammation: In HUVEC transwell monolayers, TNF-α decreased TEER, whereas pretreatment with JQ1 or BD2-selective apabetalone prevented the TEER drop, maintaining monolayer integrity; BRD4 inhibition reduced inflammatory marker expression and midkine, and the authors concluded BRD4 inhibition preserved barrier function under inflammatory challenge; while promising for barrier biology, these data were generated in vascular endothelial cells, not RPE (Shahid et al., 2022).  
- Other ophthalmic signals: BET blockade has downregulated Th17-associated genes in experimental autoimmune uveitis, ameliorated acute RGC loss after NMDA by suppressing retinal cytokines (~50% reduction in TNFα, IL-1β, MCP-1, RANTES) and preserving RGC number/gene expression (~2×), and reduced/reversed corneal scarring via BRD4 inhibition and Nrf2-dependent antioxidant induction without impairing epithelial regeneration (Eichenbaum, 2020). A separate RPE-centric multi-omics PVR study used intraocular eNano-JQ1 to show potent anti-fibrotic efficacy (reduced αSMA, thinner membranes) with favorable ocular safety (ERG, histology, TUNEL) over seven days, supporting feasibility of sustained intraocular JQ1 delivery (Liao et al., 2024).  
- Application to AMD: JQ1 has not been tested clinically for dry AMD; however, in vivo SI oxidative-injury studies model RPE/retinal degeneration relevant to geographic atrophy and identify cGAS–STING repression and autophagy-mediated cytosolic DNA clearance as protective mechanisms; moreover, cGAS/STING promoter accessibility is increased in macular retinas from GA patients, strengthening translational plausibility for dry AMD (Zou et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
BET chromatin reader displacement and inflammatory super-enhancer suppression  
- BET proteins, particularly BRD4, bind acetylated histone tails via BD1 and BD2 to stabilize enhancer/super-enhancer coactivator complexes and recruit Mediator and RNA Pol II, enabling rapid, high-output transcription of stimulus-responsive genes (e.g., NF-κB target programs and innate immune effectors) (Zhao et al., 2017). JQ1 competitively occupies the acetyl-lysine pocket in BD1/BD2, displacing BET proteins and causing collapse of the transcriptional assembly with consequent repression of inflammatory/immune gene expression; this has been demonstrated across macrophages, microglia, brain, and retina (Zhao et al., 2017). NF-κB drives dynamic super-enhancer formation during inflammation, providing a mechanistic intersection whereby BRD4 coactivation of NF-κB can be neutralized by BET inhibition to broadly downregulate cytokine programs and adhesion molecules (Zhao et al., 2017).  
- In retinal microglia and degenerating retina, BET2 (BRD2) and the BD2 (Brom2) domain appear to dominate cytokine induction and activation phenotypes; pharmacologic BD2 targeting (RVX208) and siRNA to BET2 blunt expression of TNFα, IL-1β, MCP-1, IL-6, and RANTES and curb microglial proliferation/migration, whereas BD1 targeting (Olinone) exerts narrower effects (notably migration and RANTES) (Zhao et al., 2017). In vivo, intravitreal JQ1 suppresses microglial infiltration into ONL/subretinal spaces and lowers retinal cytokine mRNAs and MCP-1 protein, consistent with an immunomodulatory mechanism downstream of BET displacement (Zhao et al., 2017).  
- In ARPE-19 cells, BET inhibition reduces etoposide-induced IL-6/IL-8 secretion and NF-κB activity without major cytotoxicity; the anti-inflammatory effect persists when SIRT1 is inhibited or knocked down, indicating SIRT1 independence for cytokine suppression in these conditions, even though BET inhibition reduces acetyl-p53 (Lys382) via a SIRT1-interacting axis (Hytti et al., 2016). These data collectively establish BET blockade as a chromatin-level anti-inflammatory mechanism across retinal microglia and RPE contexts (Hytti et al., 2016).

BRD4–cGAS–STING repression and autophagy-dependent cytosolic DNA clearance in oxidative stress  
- Under oxidative stress in RPE and retina, BRD4 is induced and directly promotes STING transcription; JQ1 counteracts this by reducing histone acetylation (e.g., H3 acetyl marks) and phosphorylated Pol II occupancy at the STING locus, thereby reducing chromatin accessibility and transcriptional output (Zou et al., 2022). This leads to reduced cGAS–STING activation, dampened downstream NF-κB/IRF-mediated inflammatory gene induction, decreased retinal microglia/macrophage recruitment, and protection against RPE/retina degeneration in vivo (Zou et al., 2022).  
- Beyond transcriptional repression, BRD4 inhibition potentiates autophagy: JQ1 or BRD4 knockdown increases LC3II, accelerates enclosure of cytosolic dsDNA by autophagosomes (visualized with GFP-LC3 and Cy3-DNA), reduces accumulation of oxidized cytosolic DNA (a potent innate immune agonist), and these effects require intact autophagic flux (blocked by chloroquine/BafA1), directly linking BET inhibition to enhanced clearance of DNA debris that drives cGAS activation (Zou et al., 2022). This dual mechanism—STING transcriptional silencing and autophagic DNA clearance—aligns with decreased innate immune activation in SI-injured retinas and provides a mechanistic bridge to geographic atrophy in which cGAS/STING promoters exhibit increased accessibility (Zou et al., 2022).

Barrier biology and tight junctions: what is and is not known  
- In vascular endothelium, BRD4 inhibition with JQ1 or BD2-selective apabetalone preserved TEER and monolayer integrity during TNF-α stimulation, reduced NF-κB activation, decreased pro-inflammatory markers, and lowered midkine expression, indicating a direct barrier-protective effect in inflamed endothelium (Shahid et al., 2022). While the cell type differs, these results are proof-of-concept that BET inhibition can functionally maintain barrier resistance under cytokine challenge.  
- Critically, across the RPE literature excerpts provided, no direct measurements of RPE barrier function (TEER), tight-junction proteins (ZO-1/TJP1, claudin-19/CLDN19), or junctional continuity were reported for JQ1 or any BET inhibitor in ARPE-19 or primary RPE under inflammatory/oxidative stress; multiple excerpts explicitly note the absence of tight-junction/barrier metrics and recommend further study in advanced models (Hytti et al., 2016; Eichenbaum, 2020; Zhu et al., 2023). Therefore, a mechanistic claim that JQ1 increases H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19 enhancers and directly raises ZO-1/claudin-19 transcription in RPE is not supported by existing evidence in the provided corpus.

Pharmacology, delivery, and safety considerations  
- JQ1 exhibits a short systemic half-life (~1 h reported elsewhere and noted in the retinal context), and in rd10, photoreceptor protection after a single intravitreal dose waned as drug dissociated from targets and diffused, with higher intravitreal concentrations not improving efficacy, motivating sustained ocular delivery strategies (e.g., nanoparticles, osmotic pumps) or alternative modalities (e.g., BET PROTACs) (Zhao et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2023). Local formulation advances such as eNano-JQ1 achieved seven-day intraocular release with favorable safety and efficacy in a PVR model (Liao et al., 2024).  
- BET competitive inhibitors can trigger cell-cycle arrest and modestly reduce metabolic activity in vitro; ARPE-19 studies showed slight decreases in MTT conversion at baseline but no major viability loss, and in some assays BET inhibitors reduced etoposide cytotoxicity (Hytti et al., 2016). In SI models, JQ1 alone exhibited no overt adverse retinal morphology/viability, and systemic dBET6 achieved retinal BET degradation “without detectable toxicity” at the reported regimen (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). Notably, compensatory BRD4 upregulation was observed with JQ1 in certain contexts, potentially blunting efficacy—a liability that targeted degradation (dBET6) may overcome (Zhu et al., 2023).

Therapeutic implications for dry AMD  
Collectively, the ocular data support an anti-inflammatory/innate-immunity–modulating, neuroprotective role for BET inhibition in retina/RPE that is directly relevant to dry AMD pathobiology: oxidative stress-driven cytosolic DNA leakage, cGAS–STING activation, NF-κB–dependent cytokine induction, microglia/macrophage recruitment, and downstream neurodegeneration are all attenuated by JQ1 or dBET6 in preclinical models (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). However, there is no direct evidence that JQ1 improves RPE tight-junction expression or TEER; any barrier benefit inferred for RPE is, at present, extrapolated from endothelial TEER preservation and from general anti-inflammatory rescue in RPE/retina (Shahid et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016).

Expected Effect  
The proposed hypothesis states that JQ1 will relieve repression of tight-junction enhancers in RPE under inflammatory/oxidative stress, increasing H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19 loci, boosting ZO-1/claudin-19 transcription, and enhancing TEER; mechanistically, it posits that BRD4 occupancy at inflammatory loci displaces transcriptional machinery from tight-junction enhancers, and BET displacement by JQ1 restores enhancer-promoter function. Based on the available literature, this precise enhancer-activation model is not supported; instead, JQ1 typically represses transcription at BET-dependent loci and reduces histone acetylation and Pol II recruitment at targeted promoters (e.g., STING), thereby closing chromatin accessibility rather than increasing it (Zou et al., 2022). No data in the provided corpus demonstrate increased H3K27ac or enhanced transcription at TJP1/CLDN19 in RPE after JQ1, nor any RPE TEER restoration with JQ1 in IL-1β or oxidative-stress paradigms; multiple sources explicitly note the absence of RPE barrier metrics and tight-junction readouts in prior BET/RPE work (Hytti et al., 2016).

A more evidence-grounded expected effect in IL-1β- or TNF-α-treated RPE is indirect barrier preservation via upstream anti-inflammatory mechanisms:  
- JQ1 should reduce NF-κB–driven cytokine induction (e.g., IL-6, IL-8) in ARPE-19 based on prior findings with etoposide models, and suppress cGAS–STING signaling under oxidative stress by repressing STING transcription and promoting autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA (Hytti et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2022). These actions plausibly decrease paracrine/autocrine junction-disrupting cues, which could secondarily stabilize tight-junction structure and TEER, as supported by endothelial TEER preservation in HUVECs during TNF-α challenge (Shahid et al., 2022).  
- In microglia-RPE co-culture or in retinal tissue, JQ1 would be expected to reduce the load of microglia-derived cytokines/chemokines that exacerbate epithelial barrier dysfunction and photoreceptor stress, via demonstrated suppression of retinal microglial activation and cytokine production (Zhao et al., 2017).  

Given the lack of published RPE barrier data, the appropriate experimental expectations and measurements for the proposed IL-1β RPE assay are:  
- Primary outcome: TEER rescue and paracellular permeability under IL-1β with and without JQ1 (0.1–1 µM), benchmarking against endothelial TEER precedent and aligning with ARPE-19 cytokine suppression (Shahid et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016). Secondary outcomes: immunofluorescence continuity and membrane localization of ZO-1 and CLDN19, and western/RT-qPCR quantification of TJP1/CLDN19 transcripts/proteins to test whether barrier maintenance arises from preserved junctional organization versus increased transcription.  
- Mechanistic chromatin assays to test the stated enhancer hypothesis: ChIP-seq/ChIP-qPCR for H3K27ac and BRD4 at TJP1/CLDN19 promoters/enhancers in IL-1β±JQ1, plus Pol II occupancy; based on STING-locus data, we predict decreased rather than increased H3 acetylation and Pol II occupancy at direct BRD4-dependent loci after JQ1 (Zou et al., 2022). A finding of increased H3K27ac at tight-junction loci with JQ1 would represent a novel and unanticipated RPE-specific BET effect that would require rigorous validation and mechanistic clarification.  
- Parallel readouts to anchor known mechanisms: NF-κB p65 nuclear activity (TransAM), STING expression, cGAS–STING pathway markers, LC3 flux with/without chloroquine, and cytokine ELISAs (IL-6, IL-8), all of which are supported in prior RPE/retina work and will clarify whether barrier effects track with established anti-inflammatory and autophagic actions of BET inhibition (Hytti et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2022).

Mechanistic expression support in the assayed cell type  
- BET target genes relevant to inflammation (e.g., IL-6, IL-8, STING) are expressed and modulated in ARPE-19 and in mouse retina; BRD4 is induced by oxidative stress in RPE and retina, and cGAS–STING components are present in retinal microglia (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2023). The corpus does not provide explicit documentation of TJP1/CLDN19 expression modulation by JQ1 in RPE, underscoring the need for primary measurement within the proposed assay (Hytti et al., 2016).

Therapeutic plausibility in dry AMD models  
- RPE oxidative stress, cytosolic DNA leakage, cGAS–STING activation, microglia/macrophage recruitment, and chronic NF-κB activity are central to dry AMD pathogenesis; JQ1 has demonstrably suppressed cGAS–STING signaling and protected RPE/retina in SI-injury models, and PROMOTER accessibility of cGAS/STING is increased in GA patients, providing a mechanistic and translational bridge (Zou et al., 2022). In light-damage injury, BET degradation with dBET6 improved functional outcomes and repressed microglial STING expression, suggesting that BET-targeted therapies are effective across different sterile-injury paradigms relevant to atrophic disease (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Therefore, for dry AMD, the most defensible expectation is that JQ1 will reduce innate-immune and NF-κB–driven inflammatory signaling in RPE/retina and microglia, attenuate microglia recruitment/activation, and protect photoreceptors/RPE via transcriptional repression of STING and enhanced autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA, rather than directly upregulating tight-junction genes; any barrier rescue measured by TEER would likely be an indirect consequence of reduced inflammatory burden (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective efficacy across ocular models that capture key elements of dry AMD biology:  
  • In vivo oxidative-stress (SI) models demonstrate that JQ1 represses BRD4-driven STING transcription, reduces cGAS–STING signaling, limits immune cell accumulation, and prevents RPE/retinal degeneration with favorable safety in the absence of stressors (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Inflammatory microglia suppression is consistent and robust: intravitreal JQ1 reduces microglia infiltration and cytokines in rd10 retina and abolishes LPS-induced cytokine induction and activation phenotypes in vitro; BET2/BD2 targeting emerges as a key effector axis, aligning with innate-immune pathophysiology in atrophic AMD (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • dBET6 (systemic) degrades retinal BRD2/3/4, improves retinal function/acuity after light damage, and suppresses microglial STING and inflammatory responses, offering a mechanistically stronger alternative to JQ1 where compensatory BRD4 upregulation occurs (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Mechanistic depth linking BET inhibition to innate immunity and autophagy:  
  • JQ1 reduces histone acetylation and Pol II engagement at the STING locus, silencing a central innate immune amplifier in RPE/retina (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • BRD4 inhibition increases LC3-dependent enclosure/clearance of cytosolic DNA; this autophagy-dependent mechanism is integral to lowering cGAS activation (Zou et al., 2022).  
- Feasibility of ocular delivery and safety:  
  • Intravitreal JQ1 achieved durable rescue for at least 10 days in rd10 despite short systemic half-life; higher doses did not improve efficacy, highlighting the need for sustained delivery rather than dose escalation (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • eNano-JQ1 provides a practical intraocular slow-release platform with favorable ERG/histology safety and anti-fibrotic efficacy in PVR, supporting translatability of sustained local BET blockade (Liao et al., 2024).  
  • dBET6 showed retinal target engagement and no detectable retinal toxicity under the tested regimen (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Ancillary barrier-preserving precedent:  
  • In HUVECs, BRD4 inhibition (JQ1/apabetalone) preserved TEER and monolayer integrity during TNF-α challenge, lending plausibility that BET blockade can maintain barrier function under inflammatory stress, though cell-type differences warrant caution (Shahid et al., 2022).

Weaknesses, risks, and key unknowns relative to the current hypothesis  
- No direct evidence that JQ1 increases H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19 or upregulates ZO-1/claudin-19 transcription in RPE; the available mechanistic data actually show decreased histone acetylation and Pol II recruitment at target inflammatory loci with JQ1, arguing against a generalizable H3K27ac-increasing effect at tight-junction enhancers (Zou et al., 2022). Multiple sources explicitly note the absence of RPE barrier (TEER) or tight-junction data in BET-RPE studies to date (Hytti et al., 2016).  
- BET inhibitors can cause cell-cycle arrest and slightly depress metabolic activity in vitro; while ARPE-19 viability was largely preserved and etoposide toxicity was reduced by BET pretreatment, these on-target cytostatic effects will require dose/formulation tuning for chronic intraocular use (Hytti et al., 2016).  
- Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics: single-dose intravitreal JQ1 protection wanes over time, and systemic administration risks off-target tissue exposure; local sustained delivery or newer modalities (e.g., dBET6) are likely needed for translational development (Zhao et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2024).  
- Feedback and compensation: JQ1 can increase BRD4 protein levels in some contexts, potentially compromising effect; PROTAC degradation (dBET6) may mitigate this but brings its own safety and distribution questions (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Cell-type selectivity: The strongest in vivo efficacy signals (rd10, light damage) include microglial suppression and photoreceptor rescue; dry AMD pathogenesis is centered on RPE/Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with secondary photoreceptor involvement; while SI and oxidative-stress data in RPE support relevance, dedicated chronic AMD-like models (aging, complement dysregulation, diet-induced) and RPE barrier endpoints remain to be tested (Zou et al., 2022).

Go/no-go assessment and recommendations  
- Go decision for mechanism-driven validation in dry AMD-relevant preclinical systems, but with a revised primary hypothesis and fit-for-purpose endpoints. The most compelling AMD-relevant mechanism for JQ1 is epigenetic suppression of cGAS–STING and NF-κB inflammatory programs in RPE and resident microglia, plus autophagy-mediated clearance of cytosolic DNA, not direct activation of tight-junction gene enhancers (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017).  
- Replace the current primary mechanistic claim (increased H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19) with a testable, literature-anchored hypothesis: JQ1 prevents inflammation- and oxidative-stress–induced RPE barrier breakdown by (i) repressing STING transcription and dampening cGAS–STING signaling; (ii) promoting autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA; and (iii) suppressing NF-κB–driven cytokines in RPE and microglia that secondarily disturb junctional integrity. TEER and junctional continuity should be primary outcomes, but mechanistic attribution should center on cGAS–STING/NF-κB and autophagy rather than TJ enhancer activation (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Shahid et al., 2022).  
- Rapid experimental plan:  
  • ARPE-19 and/or primary human RPE on transwells: TEER, paracellular flux, ZO-1/CLDN19 localization under IL-1β or TNF-α ± JQ1 (0.1–1 µM), with NF-κB activity, cytokine ELISAs, STING expression, LC3 flux, and dsDNA imaging to anchor mechanism (Hytti et al., 2016; Shahid et al., 2022; Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Oxidative stress model (H2O2 or SI-conditioned medium) ± JQ1: replicate cGAS–STING repression and autophagy findings in RPE; use autophagy inhibitors to confirm flux-dependence (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • ChIP-qPCR/ATAC at STING and at TJP1/CLDN19 enhancers/promoters to directly test the tight-junction enhancer hypothesis; set expectation that STING chromatin accessibility/acetylation will decline with JQ1, while TJ loci changes are unknown and likely neutral or reduced (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Microglia–RPE co-culture: test whether microglial cytokine suppression by JQ1 protects RPE TEER/barrier vs IL-1β, isolating paracrine contributions (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • In vivo oxidative-injury model (SI) with intraocular slow-release JQ1 (eNano-JQ1) to assess RPE barrier integrity (flat-mount ZO-1 continuity), microglial recruitment (IBA1), and function, leveraging prior safety/feasibility data (Liao et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2022).  
- Modality strategy: Given compensatory BRD4 upregulation with JQ1 and BD2 dominance in microglial activation, parallel exploration of BD2-selective ligands (e.g., apabetalone analogs) or BET degraders (dBET6-like) for retina-directed delivery is warranted to optimize therapeutic index while maintaining target engagement (Zhu et al., 2023; Shahid et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2017).

Conclusion  
JQ1 is a mechanistically well-grounded epigenetic modulator that suppresses inflammatory transcriptional programs and innate immune activation in retina/RPE and microglia, protects photoreceptors and RPE from oxidative and inflammatory injury in vivo, and has feasible ocular delivery paths with encouraging preclinical safety signals (Zou et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2017; Liao et al., 2024). These features position BET inhibition as a credible therapeutic strategy for dry AMD, targeting core disease drivers (oxidative stress, cytosolic DNA sensing via cGAS–STING, chronic NF-κB activation, microglial recruitment) rather than exclusively downstream consequences (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). However, the specific hypothesis that JQ1 restores RPE barrier function by increasing H3K27ac at tight-junction loci (TJP1/CLDN19) is not supported by available evidence; on the contrary, BET inhibition generally reduces histone acetylation/accessibility at target loci like STING, and RPE barrier metrics after JQ1 remain unreported (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016). We therefore recommend proceeding with JQ1 (or improved BET-modality variants) in dry AMD-relevant models with primary endpoints focused on cGAS–STING/NF-κB suppression, autophagy-dependent cytosolic DNA clearance, microglial modulation, and functional RPE barrier preservation (TEER, ZO-1/CLDN19 continuity), while explicitly testing and likely revising the proposed tight-junction enhancer mechanism based on direct chromatin measurements (Zou et al., 2022; Shahid et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SS-31, also known as Elamipretide, is a synthetic, cell‐permeable tetrapeptide that was originally discovered serendipitously during efforts to optimize opioid receptor peptide analogs and has since been rationally designed to target mitochondria by binding the lipid cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3). Its chemical structure, typically denoted as D-Arg-Dmt-Lys-Phe-NH₂—with “Dmt” representing 2,6-dimethyltyrosine—confers a unique alternating pattern of cationic and aromatic residues that endows the compound with high membrane permeability and preferential accumulation in the mitochondrial inner membrane (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 2–5). The molecular weight of SS-31 is approximately 639.8 g/mol, and its synthesis is generally performed via solid-phase peptide synthesis, which allows for efficient production and structural modification; this synthetic origin situates SS-31 within the class of mitochondria-targeting peptides or “stealth peptides” that have been extensively studied for their bioenergetic and cytoprotective properties (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In addition to its capacity to target cardiolipin, the compound’s design leverages both electrostatic attraction—owing to its positively charged arginine and lysine residues—and hydrophobic interactions from its aromatic side chains to facilitate a stable binding to the anionic membranes of mitochondria (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). As a member of a broader therapeutic class initially developed to improve mitochondrial function, SS-31 has been applied across various models of mitochondrial dysfunction, making it a promising repurposed candidate for diseases where mitochondrial impairment is a key pathological driver, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SS-31 is extensive and spans several preclinical and early-phase clinical investigations across a range of indications characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction. Preclinical studies across more than 150 peer-reviewed publications have demonstrated that SS-31 exerts robust mitochondrial protection in models of cardiac and skeletal muscle myopathies, where it improves mitochondrial structure, enhances ATP production, reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and ultimately ameliorates organ dysfunction (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3, 10–11). In the cardiovascular arena, animal models of heart failure and ischemia-reperfusion injury have documented that SS-31 treatment leads to improved left ventricular function and reduced tissue biomarkers of injury, effects that are attributed to its ability to stabilize cardiolipin and maintain the integrity of the electron transport system (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 10–12). Further, in neuromuscular and metabolic disease models, the compound has been shown to enhance mitochondrial ATP production and reduce oxidative stress, with early clinical studies in rare mitochondrial disorders such as Barth syndrome (a condition involving cardiolipin abnormalities) and primary mitochondrial myopathy providing supportive translational evidence (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 10–11, 16–22). More recently, SS-31 has been explored in the context of ocular diseases, including nonneovascular age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) and diabetic macular edema, where preclinical studies in murine models report that subcutaneous administration of SS-31 can reverse electroretinographic deficits, facilitate the clearance of sub-retinal pigment epithelium (sub‐RPE) deposits, and ultimately reverse vision loss (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Clinical trials—such as the Phase I ReCLAIM study in intermediate AMD and the ongoing Phase II ReCLAIM-2 trial—have begun to assess SS-31’s safety profile, pharmacokinetics, and preliminary efficacy in preserving visual function, thereby positioning it as a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Although its use in dry AMD is relatively novel compared to its established preclinical record in other mitochondrial disorders, the existing scientific and regulatory trajectory supports its potential repurposing for diseases in which mitochondrial dysfunction is a central pathogenic mechanism (Nashine, 2021, pp. 9–11, 16).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism by which SS-31 exerts its cytoprotective effects is centered on its highly specific interaction with cardiolipin, an anionic phospholipid unique to the mitochondrial inner membrane that plays a pivotal role in maintaining the structural integrity of cristae and the proper assembly and function of electron transport chain complexes (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). Detailed biophysical studies, including nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations, have demonstrated that SS-31 binds to cardiolipin via both electrostatic interactions (through its basic residues) and hydrophobic interactions (via its aromatic side chains), resulting in the “neutralization” of the negative surface charge on mitochondrial membranes and a favorable modulation of membrane fluidity and curvature (Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4; Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 16–22). This binding not only stabilizes cardiolipin against oxidative peroxidation but also promotes the optimal assembly of electron transport chain complexes into respiratory supercomplexes, thereby enhancing electron flow, reducing electron leakage, and ultimately decreasing the generation of ROS (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 4–6, 15–16). In addition, SS-31 has been shown to mitigate proton leakage and restore pH stress resistance in aged mitochondria by enhancing the function of critical proteins such as the adenine nucleotide translocator (ANT), which is central to ADP/ATP exchange and overall mitochondrial bioenergetics (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 10–12). Although SS-31 was initially characterized as an antioxidant, its primary mode of action is now understood to be the preservation of mitochondrial structure and function through cardiolipin stabilization rather than direct radical scavenging alone (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4). In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress—a key pathological hallmark of dry AMD—the hypothesis posits that by stabilizing mitochondria via cardiolipin binding, SS-31 will maintain normal electron transport chain efficiency, preserve ATP production, and limit ROS production, thereby protecting the integrity of RPE cells (Tong et al., 2022, pp. 14–16). Although direct experimental evidence linking SS-31 to the preservation of tight junction proteins such as ZO-1/occludin or to the restoration of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE cells is limited in the current literature, the well-documented mitochondrial protection afforded by SS-31 in other cellular models suggests that secondary benefits on cellular barrier function are plausible given the tight coupling between mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and loss of epithelial integrity (Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Based on its molecular mechanism, the expected effect of SS-31 in an oxidative-challenge assay using RPE cells is multifaceted. Overall, SS-31 (Elamipretide) presents as a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, with several key strengths that support its potential utility and a few noteworthy challenges that will need to be addressed in further research. One of the primary strengths of SS-31 is its well-characterized mechanism of action; its ability to bind cardiolipin and thereby stabilize mitochondrial inner membrane structure, enhance electron transport chain efficiency, and reduce ROS generation is supported by robust preclinical data across multiple models of mitochondrial dysfunction, including cardiac, skeletal muscle, and retinal systems (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4). This mitochondria-targeted mechanism is particularly attractive in the context of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are recognized as major drivers of RPE degeneration and subsequent photoreceptor loss (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Furthermore, early-phase clinical studies in ocular disease have demonstrated that SS-31 is safe and well tolerated and have hinted at functional improvements in visual acuity and reduced progression of retinal degeneration, which supports its translational viability (Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5). The repurposing of SS-31 from conditions such as heart failure and primary mitochondrial myopathy to an ocular application leverages its established bioenergetic benefits and broad mitochondrial stabilization properties, thereby enhancing its appeal as a novel intervention for dry AMD (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 10–11, 16–22).

However, there are several challenges and weaknesses that merit consideration. First, while the molecular mechanism of SS-31—centered on cardiolipin binding and mitochondrial stabilization—is well supported, direct evidence linking its activity to the preservation of tight junction proteins (such as ZO-1/occludin) and the restoration of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE models remains limited in the current literature (Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40). This represents a key knowledge gap given that the hypothesis posits that protection of RPE barrier integrity is a critical outcome in preventing disease progression in dry AMD. Additional preclinical studies that specifically measure the effects of SS-31 on RPE tight junction organization, using immunostaining for ZO-1 and occludin as well as quantitative TEER assays, would be essential to fully validate its proposed mechanism in the context of epithelial barrier protection (Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Second, although early-phase clinical trials have shown promise in improving functional visual metrics, some clinical studies in related indications (e.g., Phase 2 trials in cardiac conditions) have produced mixed results with primary endpoints not consistently met, suggesting that optimal dosing regimens, treatment durations, and patient selection criteria may need further refinement (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 9–10). In the case of dry AMD, where the pathological changes evolve over extended periods, longer-term studies and careful endpoint selection will be critical to demonstrate sustained therapeutic benefit (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Third, while the pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of SS-31 appear favorable for reaching mitochondrial targets, ensuring sufficient ocular penetration and accumulation in the RPE—whether via systemic subcutaneous administration or topical formulations—remains a logistical and pharmacological challenge that must be addressed in future clinical development (Tong et al., 2022, pp. 14–16; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

In conclusion, SS-31 (Elamipretide) exhibits a strong mechanistic underpinning based on its targeted interaction with cardiolipin to restore mitochondrial function and mitigate oxidative stress—a mode of action that is directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD owing to the central role of mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE degeneration (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). The compound’s extensive preclinical validation in models of mitochondrial diseases, coupled with encouraging early clinical data, makes it a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Nonetheless, key gaps in directly demonstrating its effects on RPE barrier integrity and tight junction preservation (as measured by ZO-1/occludin levels and TEER) necessitate further targeted preclinical studies. Additionally, addressing challenges related to optimal dosing, treatment duration, and efficient ocular delivery will be paramount for the success of subsequent clinical trials. Overall, given its robust mitochondrial protective effects and plausible secondary benefits on epithelial barrier function, SS-31 warrants further investigation as a novel therapeutic strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 10–12).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ (mitoquinone) is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant generated by covalently linking a ubiquinone headgroup to a decyl triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation, yielding a delocalized lipophilic cation that partitions across biological membranes and accumulates several-hundredfold inside the mitochondrial matrix driven by the large negative inner mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Chico et al., 2016; Smith & Murphy, 2010; Fields et al., 2023). Within mitochondria, MitoQ adsorbs predominantly to the matrix-facing leaflet of the inner mitochondrial membrane where the ubiquinone moiety is reduced by the respiratory chain to the corresponding hydroquinone (mitoquinol), which then acts as a chain-breaking antioxidant that intercepts lipid peroxyl radicals and limits cardiolipin and phospholipid peroxidation in situ (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Vlachantoni et al., 2011). The TPP⁺-driven mitochondrial targeting strategy (also used by related agents such as SkQ1, decylTPP conjugates, and TPP-Niacin) was devised to overcome the poor organelle-level bioavailability and off-target scavenging that limited earlier, non-targeted antioxidants in clinical translation (Fields et al., 2023).

The compound and its class were developed and extensively characterized by Murphy and colleagues, including in vitro uptake/antioxidant activity, radiolabeled biodistribution, and oral tablet formulations suitable for animal toxicology and human dosing (Smith & Murphy, 2010). After oral dosing, MitoQ exhibits low but measurable bioavailability (~10%), undergoes first-pass metabolism (intestinal wall and liver), and is excreted as unchanged drug and conjugated metabolites of the reduced quinol form (glucuronides/sulfates), with phase I human pharmacokinetics showing a Cmax ≈33 ng/mL at ~1 hour after an 80 mg dose (Zinovkin & Zamyatnin, 2019; Smith & Murphy, 2010). Long-term oral administration in rodents was tolerated at 500 μM in drinking water without overt toxicity; quantitative LC/MS/MS confirms tissue distribution to heart, liver, brain, and other organs over weeks to months (Smith & Murphy, 2010). In a retinal context, oral MitoQ accumulates in mouse retina to steady-state levels on the order of ~1.3 nmol/g wet tissue (with no retinal toxicity in wild-type mice at 500 μM dosing), establishing biological access to ocular tissues via systemic exposure (Vlachantoni et al., 2011).

MitoQ belongs to the broader class of mitochondria-targeted quinones (short-chain quinones conjugated to lipophilic cations), which includes plastoquinone analogs such as SkQ1 that share the same TPP⁺ carrier but differ in the redox headgroup and, potentially, in reactivity and recycling kinetics within mitochondria (Chico et al., 2016; Baksheeva et al., 2018). This class has been deployed across neurological, cardiovascular, inflammatory, and hepatic models, with mixed clinical translation; importantly for ophthalmology, SkQ1 has advanced to ocular topical formulations (Visomitin) with evidence of retinal protection in animal models of light-induced damage and age-related retinopathy, illustrating that TPP⁺-conjugated antioxidants can reach and act within retinal tissues when appropriately delivered (Baksheeva et al., 2018; Grigoryan et al., 2012; Lukashev et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical and clinical experience with MitoQ spans multiple organ systems and disease models. In animal studies, orally administered MitoQ has shown protective effects in models of ischemia-reperfusion, endotoxin/sepsis, and neurodegeneration, consistent with its mitochondrial antioxidant mechanism and tissue distribution profile (Lukashev et al., 2014; Fields et al., 2023). For example, MitoQ decreased inflammatory cytokines and liver enzyme elevations in sepsis models, reduced neurological deficits in an Alzheimer’s transgenic mouse model, and modestly prolonged survival with improved pathology in the SOD1-G93A ALS mouse model when given chronically in drinking water (Lukashev et al., 2014). Additional preclinical reports include beneficial effects in diabetic kidney disease via Nrf2/PINK1-associated mitophagy and in sensorineural hearing loss driven by mitochondrial ROS, supporting broad bioactivity against mitochondrial oxidative injury across tissues (Shyam et al., 2021).

Human experience includes long-term oral dosing in Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients (40–80 mg/day for 12 months) without slowing disease progression but providing important safety data for year-long administration, as well as shorter trials demonstrating improved vascular function and reduced oxidative stress biomarkers or decreased hepatic transaminases in chronic hepatitis C without antiviral benefit (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Zinovkin & Zamyatnin, 2019; Mason et al., 2022). Across randomized studies of mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, MitoQ was generally well tolerated (with occasional non-serious gastrointestinal adverse events), but the evidence base remains short-term and of low-to-very-low certainty for many endpoints (Mason et al., 2022). Crucially for AMD, no registered human clinical trials testing MitoQ in age-related macular degeneration were identified on ClinicalTrials.gov, indicating an absence of clinical translational activity in this indication to date (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Ocular and retinal history is mixed. On the positive side, MitoQ is orally bioavailable to the retina in mice at nanomole-per-gram levels without overt retinal toxicity in wild-type animals (outer nuclear layer thickness unchanged; no TUNEL-positive photoreceptor cells), supporting general ocular tolerability and access (Vlachantoni et al., 2011). In vitro, MitoQ (as a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant) has been reported to protect RPE cells from blue light–induced oxidative stress, providing cell-level plausibility in a phototoxic paradigm relevant to RPE oxidative injury (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012). However, in an independent oxidative RPE insult model (NaIO₃ in hTERT RPE-1), MitoQ failed to rescue cells from mitochondrial depolarization and apoptosis, whereas a CD36 ligand (MPE-001) that enhanced autophagy did prevent cell death, directly documenting a negative result for MitoQ in this RPE oxidative-stress paradigm (Dorion et al., 2021).

In vivo retinal degeneration models have been largely negative for MitoQ efficacy. Multiple inherited photoreceptor degeneration (IPD) mouse models—Pde6brd1/rd1, Pde6batrd1/atrd1, Rho⁻/⁻, and Prph2rds/rds—showed no mitigation of photoreceptor loss or apoptosis with oral MitoQ; outer nuclear layer degeneration progressed on schedule, and TUNEL-positive cell counts were unaffected by treatment (Vlachantoni et al., 2011). Mechanistic biomarker analyses in these models also failed to show improvements in Complex I activity or reduced glutathione (GSH), consistent with a lack of impact on core mitochondrial oxidative endpoints in this setting (Vlachantoni et al., 2011). These negative outcomes likely reflect the mismatch between MitoQ’s primary antioxidant chemistry and the dominant ROS species present in these models (see Mechanism of Action), as well as disease-specific drivers beyond ROS that dominate in fast-progressing genetic photoreceptor loss (Vlachantoni et al., 2011).

By contrast, SkQ1—another TPP⁺-linked mitochondrial antioxidant with a plastoquinone headgroup—has repeatedly shown retinal protection in animal models, including light-induced retinal damage in rabbits (preservation of photoreceptors, suppression of H₂O₂ accumulation, inhibition of arrestin disulfide dimerization, improvement of antioxidant capacity; topical administration achieved nanomolar retinal levels) and prevention of RPE atrophy and retinopathy in senescence-accelerated OXYS rats (systemic dosing) (Baksheeva et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2022). SkQ1 also protected RPE and choroid structure in long-term organotypic rat posterior eyecup cultures at nanomolar concentrations, reducing apoptosis and preventing RPE detachment from Bruch’s membrane (Grigoryan et al., 2012). Beyond preclinical studies, SkQ1 has been formulated as an ophthalmic solution (Visomitin) and advanced into human trials for dry eye and ocular indications, demonstrating the feasibility of TPP⁺-linked antioxidants in topical ocular delivery; although not directly probative for AMD, this trajectory indicates class-level translational potential with appropriate formulation (Lukashev et al., 2014).

This body of work positions MitoQ as mechanistically plausible for mitigating mitochondrial oxidative damage in RPE and retina, with retinal access established in mice, but with mixed-to-negative efficacy in photoreceptor degeneration models and at least one negative RPE oxidative injury study; critically, there is no published evidence of MitoQ improving RPE barrier function endpoints (TEER, ZO-1/occludin) or preventing RPE atrophy in AMD-like models in vivo (Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Dorion et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
MitoQ exploits the Δψm-dependent electrophoretic uptake of the TPP⁺ carrier to concentrate within mitochondria, where the ubiquinone moiety is reduced by the electron transport chain (predominantly at Complex II) to the hydroquinone mitoquinol, which is the active antioxidant species (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Gueven et al., 2017). The quinol intercalates into the inner membrane lipid bilayer, where it donates hydrogen atoms to lipid peroxyl radicals, terminating chain propagation in lipid peroxidation and thereby preserving mitochondrial membrane integrity and function; it also reduces reactive nitrogen species such as peroxynitrite-derived intermediates in membrane environments (Smith & Murphy, 2010). After oxidation back to ubiquinone, MitoQ is recycled by the respiratory chain to maintain antioxidant capacity, making it a “rechargeable” mitochondrial antioxidant under conditions where electron flow remains sufficient (Zinovkin & Zamyatnin, 2019).

Two mechanistic constraints are salient for RPE/retinal applications:

- ROS selectivity: MitoQ shows negligible direct reactivity toward hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) and has limited ability to decrease mitochondrial superoxide generation; its predominant efficacy is in lipid radical interception within membranes, not in neutralizing aqueous ROS such as H₂O₂ (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Vlachantoni et al., 2011). Under some conditions, MitoQ or the TPP⁺ moiety can exhibit pro-oxidant behavior, increasing ROS in endothelial cells and isolated mitochondria, underscoring context-dependent redox outcomes (Gueven et al., 2017).

- Dependence on Δψm and ETC activity: Uptake and recycling of MitoQ rely on sustained mitochondrial membrane potential and electron transport activity; in severely depolarized RPE mitochondria (for example, after NaIO₃ injury or intense oxidant exposure), mitochondrial accumulation and bioactivation to the quinol may be compromised (Gueven et al., 2017).

In retinal phototoxicity and AMD-relevant oxidative stress, mitochondrial ROS from photoreceptors and RPE are central drivers, with H₂O₂ acting as a major mediator of phototoxicity; oxidative protein modifications such as arrestin disulfide dimerization and lipid peroxidation products (e.g., malondialdehyde) are robust biomarkers in illuminated retina (Baksheeva et al., 2018). In rabbit light-induced retinal damage, a mitochondria-targeted TPP⁺ antioxidant (SkQ1) suppressed H₂O₂ accumulation, prevented protein oxidation, reduced lipid peroxidation, and improved antioxidant enzyme dynamics (AOA, GPx), consistent with neutralizing mitochondrial sources of ROS and stabilizing redox homeostasis in retinal cells (Baksheeva et al., 2018). The success of SkQ1 in H₂O₂-centric retinal injury contexts may reflect differences in redox kinetics or membrane interactions of the plastoquinone headgroup compared to ubiquinone in MitoQ, or differences in delivery (topical eye drops achieving local retinal exposure) (Baksheeva et al., 2018).

For RPE barrier integrity specifically, tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin) and TEER are degraded by oxidative stressors including H₂O₂, blue light in A2E-loaded RPE, and NaIO₃; mitochondrial dysfunction (Δψm loss, increased mitochondrial ROS, impaired ATP generation) is causally linked to RPE injury in these paradigms (Tong et al., 2022). Mitochondria-targeted antioxidants can restore mitochondrial membrane potential and limit mitochondrial ROS in RPE cells, as shown with TPP-Niacin in H₂O₂-challenged ARPE-19, which preserved Δψm, reduced ROS, and upregulated antioxidant and mitochondrial biogenesis programs, albeit without reported barrier readouts (Kim et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022). Related TPP-conjugates (e.g., TPP-D-NAC) demonstrated selective quenching of mitochondrial ROS in RPE and established an experimental pipeline for assessing RPE bioenergetics, mitochondrial ROS, and structural endpoints that would be directly applicable to evaluating MitoQ (Datta et al., 2023).

Taken together, MitoQ’s molecular pharmacology—robust lipid peroxidation interception when mitochondria are polarized, limited H₂O₂ reactivity, dependence on ETC for recycling—supports a priori efficacy in oxidative paradigms dominated by lipid radical propagation and intact Δψm, while suggesting reduced performance in H₂O₂-dominant or severely depolarizing insults (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Gueven et al., 2017).

Expected Effect  
The proposed hypothesis is that MitoQ will accumulate in RPE mitochondria to scavenge mitochondrial superoxide–derived lipid peroxyl radicals, preventing oxidative degradation of tight junction proteins (ZO-1/occludin) and restoring TEER in A2E- or H₂O₂-challenged monolayers. Mechanistically, if Δψm is maintained sufficiently to support TPP⁺-driven uptake and ETC recycling, mitoquinol should suppress membrane lipid peroxidation and secondary oxidative cascades, indirectly preserving junctional complexes that are susceptible to ROS-driven damage (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Gueven et al., 2017). This expectation is supported in part by prior in vitro RPE photostress data where MitoQ afforded protection against blue light–induced oxidative stress, a model in which A2E photosensitization generates lipid peroxidation and singlet oxygen that could be intercepted effectively by a membrane-localized quinol antioxidant (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Tong et al., 2022). In such A2E/blue-light paradigms, measuring reductions in lipid peroxidation endpoints (e.g., MDA/4-HNE) and preservation of ZO-1/occludin belts would be consistent with MitoQ’s established lipid radical scavenging capacity (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Tong et al., 2022).

By contrast, in H₂O₂-dominant paradigms (e.g., acute H₂O₂ challenge), the compound’s negligible direct reactivity toward H₂O₂ and reliance on Δψm for accumulation predict weaker effects, especially if H₂O₂ exposure collapses Δψm and impairs recycling of MitoQ to mitoquinol (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Gueven et al., 2017). Indeed, in an NaIO₃ oxidative injury model in hTERT RPE-1 cells—a paradigm with mitochondrial depolarization and apoptosis—MitoQ did not rescue cell viability, underscoring this mechanistic limitation in certain RPE oxidative injuries (Dorion et al., 2021). Therefore, for the H₂O₂ arm of the proposed assay, any TEER restoration or preservation of ZO-1/occludin is less certain a priori and should be interpreted alongside direct mitochondrial readouts (Δψm by TMRM, mitochondrial ROS by MitoSOX, ATP, spare respiratory capacity) and lipid peroxidation metrics to delineate the operative ROS pathways (Datta et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2022).

Assay design considerations that align with the compound’s mechanistic strengths include:

- Using A2E-loaded ARPE-19 or primary human RPE under blue-light exposure to generate a membrane-lipid–centric oxidative insult and monitoring junctional integrity (ZO-1/occludin immunostaining), TEER, MDA/4-HNE, and mitochondrial function (Δψm, OCR by Seahorse), with MitoQ pretreatment titrated across a sub-cytotoxic range (proposed in vitro non-toxicity up to 10 μM in some systems) (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Gueven et al., 2017; Datta et al., 2023).

- Including positive mitochondrial antioxidant controls from the TPP⁺ class with stronger retinal/RPE evidence (e.g., SkQ1) to benchmark effects on oxidative markers and junctional integrity, recognizing that SkQ1 has demonstrated in vivo retinal protection and topical ocular bioavailability (Baksheeva et al., 2018).

- Incorporating NaIO₃ as a severe oxidative RPE stressor to test the boundaries of MitoQ efficacy relative to autophagy-restoring agents (e.g., CD36 ligand MPE-001), given the prior negative result in NaIO₃-challenged hTERT RPE-1 cells (Dorion et al., 2021).

- Emphasizing lipid peroxidation readouts in addition to TEER/ZO-1 because MitoQ’s most robust and direct antioxidant activity is at the level of lipid radical chain termination (Smith & Murphy, 2010).

In vivo, the most directly relevant AMD-like model for RPE mitochondrial oxidative stress is the conditional RPE Sod2 knockout mouse, which recapitulates progressive RPE dysfunction with photoreceptor loss and choroidal changes; this model provides a suitable platform to test whether chronic MitoQ can stabilize mitochondrial redox status, preserve RPE structure, and protect photoreceptors, while carefully monitoring retinal function and structure (Mao et al., 2014). Given the earlier negative outcomes in fast photoreceptor-degeneration mutants (rd1, etc.), any in vivo testing should prioritize RPE-centric oxidative stress models rather than photoreceptor-centric genetic degeneration (Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2014).

Parallel formulation and delivery research should address MitoQ’s low aqueous solubility and micelle formation to enable ocular delivery if systemic exposure proves insufficient, learning from SkQ1 topical development but recognizing the physicochemical differences between ubiquinone and plastoquinone analogs (Zinovkin & Zamyatnin, 2019; Lukashev et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths

- Strong mechanistic rationale for mitochondrial targeting in RPE/retina: Mitochondria are a major ROS source in RPE and photoreceptors, and mitochondrial oxidative stress is causally linked to RPE degeneration, photoreceptor loss, and AMD pathobiology; targeting antioxidants to mitochondria is a coherent strategy to limit oxidative injury at its source (Tong et al., 2022; Mao et al., 2014). The TPP⁺ carrier ensures several-hundredfold mitochondrial accumulation of MitoQ under polarized conditions, concentrating antioxidant capacity in the organelle most relevant to RPE oxidative damage (Chico et al., 2016; Fields et al., 2023).

- Documented retinal exposure and systemic tolerability: Oral MitoQ accumulates in mouse retina without retinal toxicity at doses producing steady-state nanomole-per-gram retinal levels; chronic oral administration in rodents and year-long oral dosing in humans are generally well tolerated, supporting translational feasibility from a safety perspective (Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Smith & Murphy, 2010; Mason et al., 2022).

- Class precedent for ocular efficacy: SkQ1, a closely related TPP⁺-linked plastoquinone, demonstrates robust retinal protection in light-induced injury and age-related retinopathy models and achieves retinal bioavailability via topical eye drops, underscoring that the TPP⁺-mitochondrial antioxidant modality can succeed in ocular tissues when appropriately matched to the injury context and delivery route (Baksheeva et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2022; Lukashev et al., 2014).

- RPE in vitro plausibility under photostress: Literature indicates that MitoQ protects RPE from blue light–induced oxidative stress, consistent with efficacy in A2E/blue-light paradigms where lipid peroxidation is a key damage pathway that mitoquinol can intercept in membranes (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Tong et al., 2022; Smith & Murphy, 2010).

Weaknesses and Risks

- Mixed/negative retinal efficacy data in vivo: MitoQ failed to protect photoreceptors in multiple inherited degeneration models, with no improvement in apoptosis, ONL thickness, Complex I activity, or retinal GSH, indicating that in at least some retinal pathologies MitoQ does not deliver functional benefit (Vlachantoni et al., 2011).

- Direct negative RPE oxidative result: In hTERT RPE-1 NaIO₃ injury, MitoQ did not rescue mitochondrial depolarization or cell death, whereas autophagy restoration via a CD36 ligand was effective, highlighting a boundary condition where MitoQ’s dependence on Δψm and limited H₂O₂ reactivity may undermine efficacy (Dorion et al., 2021).

- ROS selectivity constraints: MitoQ is a potent chain-breaking antioxidant for membrane lipid peroxidation but reacts negligibly with H₂O₂ and does not suppress superoxide generation; H₂O₂ is a major mediator of light-induced phototoxicity in retina, and RPE oxidative injury often features elevated H₂O₂, suggesting that MitoQ may be less effective in H₂O₂-centric insults unless upstream mitochondrial ROS generation and lipid peroxidation dominate (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Baksheeva et al., 2018).

- Delivery/formulation uncertainties for ocular use: Although oral dosing achieves retinal levels in mice, the absolute concentrations, human ocular PK, and durability required for AMD are undefined; MitoQ’s low aqueous solubility and propensity to form micelles complicate formulation, and no ocular/topical PK data are available for MitoQ (as opposed to SkQ1) (Zinovkin & Zamyatnin, 2019; Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Smith & Murphy, 2010). There are no registered clinical trials of MitoQ for AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

- Potential context-dependent pro-oxidant effects: Reports of increased ROS in endothelial cells and isolated mitochondria under certain conditions suggest a non-zero risk of paradoxical redox effects, mandating careful dose-ranging and redox biomarker monitoring in RPE systems (Gueven et al., 2017).

Evidence Gaps for the Proposed Hypothesis (TEER/ZO-1 Rescue)

- No published data were identified that directly demonstrate MitoQ preserves ZO-1/occludin localization or restores TEER in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE under A2E/blue-light, H₂O₂, or NaIO₃ challenge; extant RPE data are limited to blue light–induced oxidative protection without barrier metrics and a negative NaIO₃ rescue (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Dorion et al., 2021). In vitro work with related TPP-conjugates (TPP-Niacin) shows rescue of mitochondrial function and ROS but did not report barrier outcomes, reinforcing that barrier-protective efficacy remains unproven for this class in RPE (Kim et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).

Go/No-Go Assessment and Development Path
