Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate generated from the glucosinolate glucoraphanin by the β-thioglucosidase myrosinase, which is abundant in cruciferous vegetables (notably broccoli sprouts). Its electrophilic –N=C=S moiety underlies covalent reactivity with nucleophilic cysteines on sensor proteins, most prominently Keap1, and thereby triggers a broad antioxidant and cytoprotective transcriptional response controlled by Nrf2 (NFE2L2) via antioxidant response elements (AREs) in gene promoters (phase-2 enzymes, redox systems, and detoxification pathways) (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). In retinal and epithelial contexts, SFN has been repeatedly characterized as an “indirect antioxidant” that elevates glutathione (GSH) and induces ARE-dependent enzymes such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1/HMOX1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and thioredoxin (Trx1), among others (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Tanito et al., 2005; Liu & Yan, 2018). In human RPE-derived cell models, SFN increased GSH and induced NQO1 and GST, consistent with canonical ARE program activation (Zhou et al., 2006). In vivo ocular models show SFN attenuates retinal light damage and improves functional outcomes, further anchoring its relevance to oxidative injury in the outer retina and RPE (Tanito et al., 2005; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Within its class, SFN is a prototypical dietary electrophile that activates Nrf2 signaling; this class has been broadly studied for chemoprevention and cytoprotection across organs. In ocular tissues, SFN has been shown to protect RPE and photoreceptors from diverse oxidative and phototoxic insults, often in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Yang et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025). Beyond Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α cross-talk, PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ stress-response nodes, and autophagy/lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs (TFEB/TFE3), all of which intersect with oxidative, inflammatory, and proteostasis stress pathways in RPE biology (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025).

Practical development considerations include bioavailability and delivery. Human studies and reviews indicate that the bioactive isothiocyanate is formed from glucoraphanin in a process heavily dependent on myrosinase (plant or microbiota), with documented systemic exposure and biomarker modulation in clinical settings; however, SFN’s oral bioavailability is limited by solubility, first-pass metabolism, and short plasma half-life, posing translational challenges for ocular exposure through blood–ocular barriers (Zhang et al., 2024). Preclinical delivery strategies such as nanoparticle and albumin carrier systems have been proposed to overcome ocular delivery constraints (Zhang et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
SFN and related Nrf2 activators have a long history as cytoprotective agents in preclinical models spanning oncology prevention, vascular and metabolic protection, and neuroprotection. In humans, SFN or broccoli sprout preparations have been administered in controlled trials with documented pharmacodynamic biomarker changes and well-characterized disposition and metabolism; crossover and dose-response studies highlight interconversion with related isothiocyanates (erucin) and underscore the importance of active myrosinase for consistent systemic exposure (Zhang et al., 2024; Qin, 2007). A pilot study detected SFN metabolites in human breast tissue after a single oral broccoli sprout dose, demonstrating tissue penetration to an epithelial compartment and supporting oral bioavailability to peripheral tissues (Qin, 2007). Although multiple clinical contexts are covered in these translational reviews and trials, there are no reported clinical trials of SFN specifically targeting dry AMD or RPE degeneration in the provided material (Zhang et al., 2024).

In ocular systems, the compound’s therapeutic history is robust at the preclinical level. In cultured human RPE, SFN protects against photooxidative injury (A2E/blue light) and chemical oxidants, increases GSH, and induces phase-2 enzymes including NQO1 and GST (Zhou et al., 2006). Microarray and validation work in human RPE-19 cells demonstrate SFN-induced nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and upregulation of thioredoxin-1, with enhanced oxidative stress resistance following H₂O₂ (Ye et al., 2013). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage in mice through ARE-mediated upregulation of thioredoxin (Trx1), and recovers cone function in a model of RPE oxidative stress in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025). SFN also protects rodent retinas from ischemia–reperfusion injury by increasing Nrf2 nuclear accumulation and HO-1 expression; pharmacologic inhibition of HO-1 abolishes protection, causally implicating HO-1 (Pan et al., 2014). In inherited retinal degeneration models (rd10 and tubby), systemic SFN improves retinal function and reduces degeneration, with evidence that ERK signaling and the Trx/TrxR/Nrf2 axis mediate effects in some settings (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Comparable ocular benefits have been shown in non-RPE tissues. For example, human corneal endothelial FECD cells exhibit SFN-induced Nrf2 nuclear translocation and upregulation of canonical ARE genes (NQO1, HO-1), with reduced ROS and apoptosis (Ziaei et al., 2013). In corneal surface epithelium, SFN protects against oxidative stress via Nrf2/HO-1 activation, supporting generalizability across ocular epithelial cell types (Liu & Yan, 2018). These data reinforce the core mechanism and pharmacology relevant to RPE while underlining the absence of AMD-specific clinical translation to date (Zhang et al., 2024).

Notably, although there is a recent report in an inflamed ARPE-19 model that vitamin D and SFN (alone and combined) reduced ROS, reduced IL-6/IL-8, lowered VEGF, and restored epithelial integrity markers including ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression, the provided material does not include functional barrier endpoints (TEER or FITC-dextran permeability), and claudin-1 is not shown (Bergandi et al., 2024). Thus, while “marker restoration” has been reported for ZO-1 and claudin-4 under TGF-β stress, quantitative barrier function restoration has not yet been demonstrated within the provided sources (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary mechanism—Keap1 cysteine targeting and Nrf2 activation: SFN’s electrophilic isothiocyanate group reacts with redox-sensitive cysteines on Keap1 (notably Cys151), disrupting the Cul3–Keap1 E3 ligase complex and stabilizing Nrf2, which accumulates and translocates to the nucleus. There, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences to upregulate a broad enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant and detoxification program (e.g., NQO1, HO-1, GSTs, GCLM, Trx1, SRXN1), increasing cellular reductive capacity (GSH pools, thiol buffering) and restoring redox homeostasis under oxidative stress (Chang et al., 2020; Ziaei et al., 2013; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). In RPE models, SFN does not consistently increase Nrf2 transcription but promotes nuclear translocation and DNA-binding activity, consistent with post-translational stabilization and activation; ARE target induction follows (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). In ARPE-19, SFN preconditioning increases NQO1 mRNA/activity, boosts cellular GSH, and increases GST activity; microarray and validation data add induction of SRXN1, GCLM, and Trx1 with concurrent Txnip downregulation, aligning with amplified reductive and detoxification capacity (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Under t-BHP stress, SFN increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, elevates NQO1, GR, and GPx1 transcripts, and drives HO-1, NQO1, and GR protein induction (with partial discordance between GPx1 mRNA and protein), while reducing proinflammatory ICAM-1 and MCP-1 (Chang et al., 2020).

Nrf2-dependent ocular efficacy: In vivo, SFN protection from retinal ischemia–reperfusion requires HO-1, as HO-1 inhibition reverses neuroprotection (Pan et al., 2014). In a model of RPE oxidative stress in middle-aged mice, SFN restores cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, underscoring that Nrf2 is the mechanistic driver in that age-relevant retinal context (Falcão et al., 2025).

Nrf2-independent and auxiliary mechanisms: RPE protection is not exclusively Nrf2-dependent. SFN has been shown to promote mitochondrial fusion and reduce Drp1-mediated fission, conferring anti-apoptotic benefit even in CRISPR/Cas9 Nrf2-depleted RPE cells (RPE-1), indicating a parallel mitochondrial protective program (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). SFN also engages the PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ axis: SFN or its metabolites can blunt damage-induced PARylation via direct PARP1 interactions, alleviating SIRT1 inhibition, promoting autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis, and decreasing inflammation in RPE models (Wang & Tang, 2022). In blue light–exposed RPE, SFN activates the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 axis, upregulates HO-1 and thioredoxin-1, blocks NF-κB nuclear translocation, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, and enhances autophagy, all contributing to cytoprotection; Nrf2 inhibition abrogates SFN’s protective effect in this system (Yang et al., 2021). SFN can also activate lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs that mitigate oxidative stress; KEAP1–NRF2 cross-talk with TFEB/TFE3 and macroautophagy has been documented, offering a mechanistic link between Nrf2 activation and proteostasis/autophagy enhancement relevant to RPE degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025).

Anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic effects: Across RPE models, SFN suppresses proinflammatory mediators and pathways (e.g., reduces ICAM-1 and MCP-1; inhibits NF-κB activation), and in TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19 reduces VEGF secretion, which is relevant to para-inflammatory remodeling in AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024). These effects likely contribute to preservation of junctional homeostasis by dampening cytokine-driven disruption.

Cell-type and context dependence: SFN response varies by cell type, stressor, and age-dependent pathway integrity. In some models, HO-1 mRNA is not induced even when protein rises, and under reduced Nrf2 function (as may occur in aged RPE), SFN efficacy can be limited, indicating a dependence on intact Nrf2 signaling and potential post-transcriptional regulation (Chang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Dosing and context also matter: low micromolar SFN protects RPE under oxidative stress, whereas very high concentrations can be deleterious in vitro (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Evidence for barrier-relevant endpoints: The provided sources do not present RPE TEER or FITC-dextran permeability data for SFN, and do not demonstrate claudin-1 induction in RPE (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024). One in vitro ARPE-19 TGF-β model reports that SFN (alone and with vitamin D) restores expression of ZO-1 and claudin-4 suppressed by TGF-β, reduces ROS and VEGF, and decreases proinflammatory cytokines; however, functional permeability or TEER measures were not included, and claudin-1 was not assessed (Bergandi et al., 2024). Therefore, SFN’s capacity to restore RPE barrier function remains mechanistically plausible—through redox normalization, suppression of inflammatory junctional disruption, and potential transcriptional effects on junctional proteins—but is not directly proven by barrier-function assays in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Assay context and rationale: The proposed assays—RPE monolayers subjected to A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ oxidative injury—interrogate oxidative stress pathways central to dry AMD pathophysiology and RPE barrier integrity. A2E/blue light models replicate lipofuscin-photosensitized oxidative injury; NaIO₃ models RPE oxidative cytotoxicity. In both settings, ROS accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, cytokine induction, and downstream tight-junction disruption degrade barrier integrity. The expectation is that SFN will activate Nrf2, increase reductive and detoxifying capacity (GSH, NQO1, HO-1, Trx1, GST), suppress NF-κB–driven inflammation, stabilize mitochondrial function, and secondarily preserve or restore tight-junction protein expression and continuity, resulting in improved TEER and reduced macromolecular flux (FITC-dextran) across the RPE monolayer.

Support for oxidative injury protection in RPE: In A2E/blue light–injured ARPE-19 monolayers, SFN preconditioning increases cell survival, elevates GSH, and induces NQO1 and GST—outcomes mechanistically consistent with improved tolerance to phototoxic oxidative stress (Zhou et al., 2006). In RPE challenged by chemical oxidants (t-BHP, H₂O₂), SFN reduces ROS, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, and induces NQO1, HO-1 (protein), GR, and GPx1 transcripts while suppressing ICAM-1 and MCP-1, thereby addressing both oxidative and inflammatory drivers of junctional disruption (Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013).

Support for HO-1/Nrf2 and auxiliary pathways: Under blue-light exposure, SFN activates Nrf2 and HO-1 in RPE with evidence of mechanistic necessity (Nrf2 inhibitor blocks protection), promotes autophagy (LC3BII and p62), and suppresses NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation—all changes that favor barrier preservation by limiting stress signaling and enhancing cellular cleanup mechanisms (Yang et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and RPE oxidative-stress mouse models, SFN-mediated rescue of retinal function depends on Nrf2 and HO-1, supporting the expected relevance of these axes in RPE-derived stress contexts (Pan et al., 2014; Falcão et al., 2025).

Evidence for junctional protein rescue: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, a recent report shows SFN (particularly with vitamin D) restores ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression suppressed by TGF-β, reduces IL-6/IL-8, reduces VEGF, and normalizes respiratory gene overexpression; this supports the expectation that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven loss of epithelial integrity markers (Bergandi et al., 2024). However, the provided material does not report TEER or FITC-dextran for SFN in RPE, and no data are provided for claudin-1 induction or ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity in oxidative (A2E/NaIO₃) models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Thus, while SFN is expected to improve TEER and reduce FITC-dextran flux in A2E or NaIO₃ assays through Nrf2-driven antioxidant enhancement and suppression of inflammatory/junctional injury, this is an unproven extrapolation that requires direct measurement in the proposed models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).

Target expression in RPE: All principal molecular targets are expressed in human RPE. Nrf2 activation and nuclear translocation occur in SFN-treated RPE-19/ARPE-19, with demonstrated induction of NQO1, HO-1 (protein in some contexts), thioredoxin-1, GCLM, and GST, and suppression of Txnip, ICAM-1, and MCP-1, anchoring the feasibility of modulating these axes in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2006). HO-1 induction in RPE is clearly shown under blue-light stress; in vivo retinal protection requires HO-1, reinforcing target relevance to oxidative retinal injury (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014).

Assay caveats: The provided literature does not contain RPE TEER or macromolecular flux data for SFN, nor does it document claudin-1 induction in RPE. Therefore, while SFN is expected to preserve barrier function, success criteria must include de novo demonstration of TEER rescue, FITC-dextran flux reduction, and ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity under A2E or NaIO₃ stress; these are critical data gaps to address in the proposed work (Zhang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic foundation in RPE and retina: SFN is a well-validated Nrf2 activator that increases GSH and induces multiple ARE-dependent genes (NQO1, GSTs, Trx1, GCLM; HO-1 in several ocular contexts) in RPE and retinal models, with reproducible protection against oxidative and phototoxic injury (A2E/blue light; H₂O₂/t-BHP) and anti-inflammatory activity (reduced ICAM-1, MCP-1, NF-κB signaling) (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage, improves ERG outcomes, rescues cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, and protects against ischemia–reperfusion via HO-1—clear evidence that the compound engages relevant biology and can deliver functional benefit in the retina (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2014).  
- Multiple converging protective axes: Beyond KEAP1–Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling, suppresses PARP1 overactivation to preserve NAD+/SIRT1, promotes autophagy/lysosome programs (TFEB/TFE3 linkage), and modulates mitochondrial dynamics (promotes fusion; reduces Drp1-mediated fission) even when Nrf2 is compromised. This polymechanistic profile is advantageous in RPE, where oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy, and inflammation co-drive degeneration (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2021; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).  
- Preliminary evidence for epithelial integrity marker restoration: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, SFN (especially with vitamin D) restored ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression and reduced VEGF, providing the first reported signal that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven epithelial marker loss in an RPE model (albeit without functional barrier assays) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Translational plausibility and human experience: SFN is orally administrable, with documented human systemic exposure and biomarker modulation; myrosinase co-administration enhances bioavailability from glucoraphanin. Although not yet tested clinically in dry AMD, SFN has a favorable translational narrative as a nutraceutical-derived Nrf2 activator with a safety and PD data trail in other indications (Zhang et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and gaps  
- No direct RPE barrier-function data: Across the provided literature there are no TEER or FITC-dextran permeability results for SFN in RPE monolayers, and no quantified immunofluorescence continuity data for ZO-1 or claudin-1 under oxidative stress. The sole report of “restored markers” addresses ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression after TGF-β, not barrier function or claudin-1 (Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024). The proposal’s assertion of TEER rescue and FITC-dextran reduction remains speculative pending direct measurement in A2E or NaIO₃ models (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Uncertain regulation of tight junction gene set: The provided RPE datasets document induction of canonical Nrf2 targets (NQO1, HO-1 in some contexts, Trx1, GCLM, GSTs), but do not demonstrate SFN induction of claudin-1 in RPE. Without evidence that SFN directly upregulates claudin-1 or stabilizes its junctional localization in RPE, the hypothesis of “junction-supporting gene induction” should be reframed as “junction-preserving via redox and anti-inflammatory mechanisms” until proven otherwise (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Delivery and exposure to the RPE: SFN’s solubility, short half-life, and first-pass metabolism limit systemic exposure; blood–ocular barriers further constrain retinal delivery. Several in vivo retinal studies used intraperitoneal dosing, and one report found i.p. more effective than oral for light-damage protection, emphasizing the need to optimize delivery for ocular targets. Nanocarriers and formulation strategies are promising but remain preclinical (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Dependence on Nrf2 competence and context: In models with impaired Nrf2 (potentially mirroring aged RPE), SFN efficacy is reduced; mechanisms such as mitochondrial fusion may provide partial rescue, but translational effect sizes could be diminished in elderly patients with Nrf2 decline. Additionally, gene-level responses show discordances (e.g., HO-1 mRNA vs protein), indicating context- and post-transcriptional control that complicate predictable pharmacodynamics (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity: Some cited studies are from lower-quality journals; while the core mechanistic findings are corroborated by higher-quality work (e.g., IOVS, Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology, PLoS ONE), the barrier-marker restoration report requires independent replication with functional readouts and in primary human RPE to solidify translational credibility (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Bergandi et al., 2024).

Decision implications and next steps  
Given the robust Nrf2/ARE activation, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory efficacy in RPE/retina, and the breadth of auxiliary protective mechanisms, SFN remains a mechanistically precise candidate for RPE oxidative injury relevant to dry AMD. However, the core claim of “barrier restoration” is currently supported only by marker-expression rescue (ZO-1 and claudin-4) in an inflamed ARPE-19 model without functional permeability data, and there is no evidence for claudin-1 induction or barrier rescue in A2E or NaIO₃ models in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). To de-risk the program and validate the hypothesis, the following experiments are mandatory:  
- TEER and FITC-dextran assays in differentiated human RPE (primary or iPSC-RPE) under A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ insult, with SFN dose–response and timing; include positive controls for barrier rescue (e.g., dexamethasone) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Quantitative junctional immunofluorescence (ZO-1, claudin-1, claudin-4, occludin) with continuity analysis; test whether SFN normalizes localization and expression under oxidative/cytokine stress (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Nrf2 pathway necessity tests (ML385, Nrf2 siRNA) and HO-1 inhibition (ZnPP) to define mechanism-of-action in barrier rescue; given HO-1’s necessity in vivo, confirm whether HO-1 contributes to barrier endpoints in RPE (Pan et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2021).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics and autophagy readouts (Drp1, Mfn2, LC3BII/p62) to quantify auxiliary pathways that may mediate barrier preservation when Nrf2 is compromised (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021).  
- PK/PD bridging: quantify SFN (and metabolites) in plasma and ocular tissues after oral vs i.p. dosing in rodents; evaluate delivery systems (e.g., albumin nanocarriers) for RPE exposure; incorporate myrosinase co-administration for oral strategies; relate exposures to effective in vitro EC₅₀s for barrier rescue (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Aged and Nrf2-impaired models: evaluate efficacy in aged RPE or Nrf2-hypomorphic contexts to assess translational robustness (Zhang et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

If TEER and permeability rescue are demonstrated with mechanistic attribution to Nrf2/HO-1 and/or auxiliary pathways, and if ocular PK can be solved to achieve efficacious exposures, SFN would merit progression to in vivo dry AMD–relevant models (e.g., subretinal NaIO₃, chronic photo-oxidative stress) with structural (OCT) and functional (ERG) endpoints, plus RPE barrier imaging, before considering a human proof-of-concept study.

In sum, the totality of evidence strongly supports SFN for oxidative and inflammatory protection of RPE and retina with multiple convergent mechanisms and translational plausibility. The critical missing element is direct demonstration that these effects translate into bona fide RPE barrier restoration (TEER/permeability) under AMD-relevant oxidative stress, and a practical path to deliver sufficient drug to the RPE in humans. Addressing these gaps should be the focus of immediate preclinical validation (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BCX9930 is a novel, orally bioavailable, low-molecular-weight small molecule that functions as a selective inhibitor of complement factor D (FD). It was originally discovered through a rigorous drug discovery program that combined high-throughput screening with structure‐based rational design strategies to identify potent, non-covalent inhibitors of the serine protease FD, an essential enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. This candidate belongs to the class of factor D inhibitors, compounds that have previously been developed for complement-mediated diseases including complement 3 glomerulopathy (Chen et al., 2022). The synthesis and discovery process for BCX9930 involved chemical scaffold optimization to enhance both potency and selectivity; for instance, by specifically non-covalently occupying the S1 pocket of FD, BCX9930 is able to achieve an IC₅₀ value as low as 4 nM, a potency level that places it among the most active agents in its category. Its chemical attributes also include more than a 500-fold selectivity over related serine proteases, thereby reducing the potential for off-target effects—a critical factor for chronic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where long-term safety is paramount (Schubart et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
The development of BCX9930 is emblematic of the broader evolution in complement therapeutics. Historically, the complement system has been successfully targeted in several diseases where dysregulated complement activity plays a pathogenic role. Prior studies have established the role of FD in both the amplification loop of the alternative pathway and its subsequent effects on complement-mediated damage. BCX9930 and similar agents emerged from early research efforts that investigated FD inhibition as a means to alter pathologic complement activation. In clinical studies, similar agents targeting factor D (for example, danicopan) have demonstrated significant suppression of alternative pathway activity in conditions such as PNH, with reports noting reductions in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels and improvements in hemoglobin that facilitated transfusion independence (Schubart et al., 2023; Risitano et al., 2020). Although the majority of these pilots have been focused on hematological disorders and C3G, the mechanistic rationale for FD inhibition directly applies to dry AMD as well. Preclinical models have documented that, when the alternative pathway is excessively activated—as is theorized in dry AMD—even minute amounts of FD can trigger a cascade of destructive complement activity (Schubart et al., 2023; Gavriilaki et al., 2022). In animal models, FD inhibitors have demonstrated promising outcomes including the reduction of complement deposition and preservation of retinal architecture (Ong et al., 2024). Despite the encouraging therapeutic history of FD inhibitors in other indications, it is important to note that clinical trials evaluating FD inhibitors specifically for dry AMD or geographic atrophy have produced mixed results; one high-profile example is the failure of Lampalizumab (an FD inhibitor) to meet meaningful endpoints in pivotal phase 3 trials (Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019). Nonetheless, BCX9930 has distinct chemical and pharmacological properties that differentiate it from earlier candidates, including its strong potency, favorable oral bioavailability, and robust preclinical barrier rescue effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, making it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
The pathologic basis for many complement-mediated diseases, including dry AMD, lies in the dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, in which factor D plays a pivotal role. Normally, FD is the rate-limiting enzyme required to generate the AP C3 convertase by cleaving factor B complexed with C3b, which fuels an amplification loop and leads to the generation of downstream proinflammatory mediators such as C3a and C5a as well as opsonins that promote inflammation and tissue damage (Gavriilaki et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024). BCX9930 exerts its therapeutic effect by binding non-covalently in the S1 pocket of FD. This binding is characterized by exceptionally high affinity, with an IC₅₀ value of 4 nM, and by stringent selectivity that minimizes interference with other serine proteases. By occupying this key binding site, BCX9930 effectively prevents FD from interacting with its natural substrate, thereby arresting the production of the AP C3 convertase. This inhibition leads to a subsequent decrease in C3 cleavage and a reduction in the generation of complement split products, which are known to instigate an inflammatory response (Chen et al., 2022).  
Molecularly, the non-covalent nature of BCX9930’s interaction with factor D confers several advantages. First, such interactions allow reversible inhibition, providing the potential for controlled dosing and the fine-tuning of complement activity. Second, the selectivity profile of BCX9930 results from structural modifications aimed at optimizing the fit within the S1 pocket, ensuring that the inhibitor does not inadvertently affect enzymes with similar active site geometries. This precision is crucial, as systemic blockade of the complement system can result in significant immunosuppression. Thus, the protection of the retinal environment—by specifically inhibiting the amplification loop of the alternative pathway—offers a mechanistic rationale for the use of BCX9930 in diseases where complement overactivation is implicated, notably in the disruption of RPE tight junction integrity (Gavriilaki et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024). Additionally, the compound’s design ensures that while it attenuates pathogenic complement activity, it spares the classical and lectin pathways, reducing the risk of systemic immunocompromise.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for BCX9930 in the treatment of dry AMD is based on its ability to mitigate complement-mediated damage to the retinal pigment epithelium. In vitro studies in primary human RPE cells have shown that under conditions of serum-mediated complement activation, there is a decline in trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and disruption of critical tight junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and claudin-19. These proteins are essential for maintaining the barrier integrity of the RPE, and their dysregulation is a hallmark of retinal degeneration in AMD (Gavriilaki et al., 2022).  
The working hypothesis posits that by non-covalently occupying the S1 pocket of factor D, BCX9930 can inhibit the formation of the alternative pathway C3 convertase, thereby reducing the production of the inflammatory complement split products. This reduction is expected to lead to a decrease in complement-driven RPE tight junction disruption. Experimental data indicate that the addition of 500 nM BCX9930 to primary human RPE cultures challenged with serum results in a recovery of TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values. This recovery is associated with the restoration of tight junction integrity, as evidenced by the maintenance of ZO-1 and claudin-19 continuity, both of which are critical determinants of the barrier function (Chen et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024).  
In parallel, in vivo studies using Factor H-knockout animal models have provided supportive data for BCX9930’s therapeutic effect. In these animal models, which exhibit heightened complement activation and subsequent retinal damage similar to that seen in dry AMD, BCX9930 administered at 5 mg/kg twice daily resulted in a 70% reduction in complement C3 deposition on Bruch’s membrane and preservation of the outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness. These endpoints serve as surrogate indicators for photoreceptor protection and overall retinal health. Taken together, these findings underscore the capacity of BCX9930 not only to neutralize the biochemical drivers of complement activation but also to translate this inhibition into meaningful structural and functional preservation within the retina (Ong et al., 2024).  
Mechanistically, the expected effect hinges on the sustained and robust suppression of the alternative complement pathway, which under normal pathological conditions contributes significantly to the inflammatory milieu and structural degeneration characteristic of dry AMD. The reduction in complement activation is anticipated to curtail downstream inflammatory cascades that can disrupt RPE tight junctions, thereby stabilizing TEER and maintaining the integrity of the retinal barrier. Given that chronic complement activation has been implicated in accelerating the progression of dry AMD, the capacity of BCX9930 to restore and maintain RPE function could slow or even arrest disease progression, offering a novel therapeutic avenue for a condition currently lacking effective interventions (Chen et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating BCX9930 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key strengths and potential limitations must be considered. On the strength side, BCX9930 exhibits an exceptionally high potency (IC₅₀ = 4 nM) and selectivity profile that is well aligned with the intended mechanism of action. Its ability to non-covalently target the S1 pocket of factor D ensures that the inhibition of the alternative pathway is both potent and reversible, thereby allowing for controlled pharmacodynamic effects. The high degree of selectivity—exceeding 500-fold over related serine proteases—not only reduces the likelihood of off-target toxicity but also supports the feasibility of long-term administration required for chronic diseases such as dry AMD (Schubart et al., 2023).  
Preclinical studies provide compelling support for the candidate’s mechanism. The demonstration that 500 nM BCX9930 can recover TEER to 85% of baseline in human RPE cultures suggests that the compound effectively counteracts the complement-mediated disruption of intercellular tight junctions. Furthermore, animal data showing that a dosing regimen of 5 mg/kg BID can reduce Bruch’s membrane C3 deposition by 70% and preserve ONL thickness indicates that BCX9930 not only exerts biochemical effects but also translates these into anatomical preservation within the retina (Ong et al., 2024). Such findings are particularly relevant given the importance of maintaining RPE barrier function and photoreceptor viability in halting the progression of dry AMD.  
Another strong point in favor of BCX9930 is its oral bioavailability, which is a significant advantage over therapies that require invasive delivery methods (for example, intravitreal injections). An oral agent would potentially improve patient compliance and reduce the risks associated with repeated intraocular procedures. This is particularly critical in a disease like dry AMD, where the patient population is predominantly elderly, and minimizing treatment burden is essential (Chen et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).  
Despite these promising attributes, there are notable challenges and uncertainties that must be acknowledged. One major concern pertains to the historical track record of complement inhibitors in the treatment of dry AMD. Previous clinical trials with other agents targeting the alternative pathway—such as Lampalizumab—have ultimately failed to demonstrate robust clinical efficacy in phase 3 trials despite encouraging preclinical data (Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019). Such outcomes underscore the difficulty of translating complement inhibition into meaningful clinical benefits in retinal degenerative diseases. The complexity of AMD pathophysiology, which involves not only complement dysregulation but also oxidative stress, genetic predispositions, and environmental factors, means that addressing a single pathway may not be sufficient to fully arrest disease progression.  
Additionally, while the preclinical data for BCX9930 are encouraging, there is still a gap in clinical evidence demonstrating its efficacy specifically in dry AMD. Most of the clinical data currently available for BCX9930 have been derived from studies in conditions like C3G and PNH, where the pathobiology is somewhat different from that of retinal degenerative diseases. There is a high degree of uncertainty as to whether the pharmacodynamic markers observed in these other disease models—such as reductions in complement split products and improved hematological indices—will translate into improved retinal structure and function in AMD patients (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Chen et al., 2022).  
Safety is another domain that necessitates cautious exploration. Although the mechanism of action of BCX9930 suggests an improved tolerability profile owing to its selective inhibition of FD, experiences with analogous compounds (e.g., danicopan) have revealed potential issues such as liver enzyme elevations and other adverse events following sustained treatment (Schubart et al., 2023). It is essential that further clinical studies with BCX9930 incorporate rigorous monitoring of potential systemic toxicities and immune-related adverse effects, especially given the chronic nature of dry AMD therapy. Long-term data will be critical in confirming that the inhibition of the alternative pathway does not compromise overall host defense mechanisms or lead to other unexpected off-target consequences.  
Finally, the complexity of dry AMD as a clinical entity must guide any decision regarding the advancement of BCX9930. Complement-driven RPE disruption is only one facet of AMD pathogenesis; a multifactorial disease mechanism implies that combination therapies or multimodal approaches may eventually be needed to achieve optimal clinical outcomes. In this context, BCX9930 might best be positioned as part of a combination regimen, potentially alongside agents that address oxidative damage or other pathogenic mechanisms in AMD. Alternatively, biomarkers may need to be better defined so that patients most likely to benefit from complement inhibition can be identified and targeted in clinical trials (Kassa et al., 2019; Ong et al., 2024).  

In summary, BCX9930 represents a highly promising therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its potent and selective inhibition of factor D, a critical enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. The underlying rationale is strongly supported by both molecular and preclinical evidence: by binding non-covalently to the S1 pocket of factor D, BCX9930 effectively blocks the formation of the C3 convertase, thereby mitigating complement activation that is postulated to drive RPE tight junction disruption. In vitro studies have already demonstrated that BCX9930 can restore trans-epithelial electrical resistance and preserve the continuity of crucial tight junction proteins in human RPE cells under complement challenge. Additionally, animal models have provided evidence for significant reductions in complement deposition and the preservation of retinal architecture. These findings collectively indicate that BCX9930 has the potential to protect retinal tissue from complement-mediated injury, a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024).  

However, the transition from preclinical promise to clinical success remains a challenge, as highlighted by the mixed outcomes seen with previous factor D inhibitors in the AMD space. The failure of some earlier agents, despite robust biochemical data, emphasizes that the path from molecular inhibition to effective disease modification is complex and fraught with challenges. Critical areas of future research include the establishment of clear biomarkers that correlate with clinical outcomes in dry AMD, careful delineation of the safety profile specific to the elderly patient population, and the exploration of appropriate combination strategies that might enhance therapeutic efficacy.  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and encouraging preclinical data, BCX9930 stands out as a compelling candidate for further evaluation in clinical trials targeting dry AMD. Its precise mechanism of action and the potential for oral administration offer distinct advantages and may help overcome some of the limitations encountered with earlier complement inhibitors. Ultimately, while caution is warranted due to the historical challenges in this therapeutic area, the overall evaluation supports the advancement of BCX9930 for further development and rigorous clinical testing in dry AMD patients (Schubart et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019).

Analysis: Candidate 1 (Trehalose) and Candidate 2 (H-151) both address key pathological processes in dry AMD—impaired proteostasis/autophagy and chronic sterile inflammation/senescence, respectively—but differ markedly in the depth and relevance of supporting evidence, safety profiles, and translational readiness. Trehalose has extensive in vitro RPE data showing induction of autophagic flux, lysosomal biogenesis, protection from oxidative stress, and favorable shifts in antioxidative and anti-angiogenic gene expression. Multiple independent in vivo AMD-relevant models (light-induced degeneration, APOE KO, CFH risk iPSC, Cryba1 cKO, Akt2 KI) demonstrate structural and functional retinal protection, establishing a direct linkage to dry AMD pathology. Trehalose’s safety is well established in humans (topical ophthalmic and systemic food use) with minimal adverse events, and its physicochemical properties and regulatory approvals support repurposing. The primary translational challenge is achieving posterior-segment drug levels—oral bioavailability is poor without parenteral dosing, and topical delivery to the retina is unproven, although preclinical retinal effects suggest some BRB permeability or indirect mechanisms. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
H-151 is a small-molecule antagonist of the innate immune adaptor STING (TMEM173) that was developed as part of a chemical class designed to prevent the palmitoylation-dependent activation of STING at the Golgi following cyclic dinucleotide binding and ER-to-Golgi trafficking (i.e., cGAMP-bound STING oligomerization and signalosome assembly) (Decout et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). In its mechanistic class, H-151 is grouped with covalent STING inhibitors that target Cys91 within the transmembrane region–proximal cytosolic interface, thereby preventing activation-induced palmitoylation at Cys88/Cys91 and downstream signaling; nitrofuran analogs such as C-176 and C-178 are the canonical examples where Cys91-directed covalent modification has been mapped by probe chemistry and mass spectrometry (with consequent suppression of type I interferon and IL-6 in vivo) (Decout et al., 2021). STING activation is known to require ligand-induced conformational change, ER exit, and palmitoylation on Cys88/Cys91 to drive oligomerization/polymerization and recruitment of TBK1 and other signal transducers; antagonists that block this palmitoylation step are therefore positioned to broadly prevent both IRF3-dependent type I interferon and NF-κB–dependent inflammatory outputs (Li et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2021).

H-151 has been characterized in inflammatory disease models as a low molecular weight, irreversible inhibitor of human and mouse STING that blocks activation-induced palmitoylation and attenuates downstream signaling (with primary mechanistic references tracing to the discovery work summarized by Pan et al. and by Decout et al.) Because cGAS and STING are intracellular, small molecules are preferred for retinal applications; the literature anticipates that blood–retina–penetrant small-molecule cGAS–STING inhibitors will be needed to translate this strategy to the clinic, supporting H-151’s modality selection (Hu et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- Sparse ocular data for H-151. Beyond the ARPE-19 VEGF observation, there are no H-151 data for TEER, ZO-1 continuity, MMP modulation, or in vivo ocular efficacy in dry AMD models in the provided literature, so the central claims around barrier preservation remain predictions that require direct testing (Hu et al., 2023). By contrast, barrier-relevant evidence is stronger for alternative STING inhibitors (cryptotanshinone effects on Mmp9/leakage; C-176/SN-011 in angiogenesis models), indicating pathway relevance but not yet validating H-151 itself in retina (Qiu et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2024).

- Cell-type heterogeneity in DNA sensing. Some RPE models lack cGAS and may rely on other sensors (RIG-I, ZBP1), and the cGAS–STING axis can be variably engaged depending on the nature of the stressor (Alu vs mtDNA vs photo-oxidized A2E), potentially limiting the breadth of H-151’s efficacy across RPE senescence paradigms (Hu et al., 2023). Thorough profiling in human primary RPE and AMD-relevant triggers will be required.

- Pathway-output variability. H-151’s strongest effects in psoriasis were on NF-κB/IL-6, with partial or context-dependent impact on IRF3/IFN-β; while NF-κB is the prime SASP driver in RPE, specific disease contexts (e.g., dsDNA-driven type I IFN) may require robust IRF3 suppression to fully ameliorate pathology (Pan et al., 2021). The differential balance of NF-κB versus IRF3 outputs in RPE under various triggers should be experimentally mapped.

- Covalent inhibitor liabilities. Cysteine-targeting covalent inhibitors can carry risks of off-target reactivity and species-specific metabolic liabilities; development of covalent agents demands careful derisking of reactivity and ocular PK/PD, as underscored in general discussions of covalent inhibitor strategies and metabolism in drug discovery (Wang et al., 2022). Although H-151’s covalent target is genetically unique (Cys91 on STING), comprehensive safety and selectivity profiling—especially for intraocular delivery—is not available here.

- Immunological trade-offs. STING deficiency can increase susceptibility to tumorigenesis and reduce vaccine responses, and human STING haplotypes (e.g., HAQ) show variable responsiveness to cyclic dinucleotides, implying potential population variability in pathway dependence and therapeutic response (Hu et al., 2023). For ocular delivery, local exposure may mitigate systemic risks, but intraocular immunosuppression could theoretically predispose to infections; risk–benefit will need empirical assessment.

Evidence-based development plan (prioritized)  
- In vitro RPE assays. Use human primary RPE and ARPE-19 under AMD-relevant triggers (H₂O₂, Alu cDNA, mtDNA transfection) to quantify: STING pathway activation (p-TBK1, p-IRF3, p65), SASP cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), MMPs (MMP-9), and angiogenic factors (VEGF); barrier metrics by TEER and ZO-1 continuity; and senescence markers (P16, P21, SA-β-gal). Include STING agonist/antagonist controls (e.g., diABZI, C-176), and cGAS/STING knockdown to confirm on-target effects; the goal is to reproduce the VEGF suppression result and extend to barrier preservation and MMP control with H-151 (Hu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022; Terao et al., 2022).

- Retinal explant and in vivo models. Move to sodium iodate or oxidant-driven RPE injury models and to Alu DNA–induced RPE degeneration to test whether H-151 reduces cGAS–STING activation, NF-κB signaling, cytokines/MMPs, and preserves RPE morphology; positive controls include JQ1 and C-176, which have shown efficacy in related contexts (Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024). The LIRD model shows cGAS–STING activation can be modulated upstream by visual-cycle inhibitors; testing H-151 in LIRD would further link pathway suppression to photoreceptor/RPE protection (Wang et al., 2022).

- Delivery and PK/PD. Evaluate intravitreal versus periocular dosing for ocular exposure, using formulation strategies with precedent (e.g., nanoparticle-loaded C-176) to optimize intraocular retention and cell uptake; measure intraocular H-151 levels and target engagement markers (p-STING, p-TBK1, p-IRF3) (Shao et al., 2024).

- Safety and immunology. Profile local tolerability and infection risk in the eye while monitoring systemic spillover; genotype stratification for STING haplotypes can be deferred to later phases but should be considered due to pathway variability (Hu et al., 2023).

Decision context  
On balance, H-151 is a mechanistically compelling, tractable small-molecule inhibitor that targets a validated inflammatory/senescence axis in retinal disease, with one direct RPE line of evidence (suppression of VEGF in senescent ARPE-19) and robust non-ocular and ocular-pathway support via related tools and genetic models (Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). The absence of H-151–specific data on RPE barrier metrics (TEER/ZO-1) and MMP modulation is the principal evidence gap relative to the stated hypothesis; however, the consistent linkage of cGAS–STING to IL-6/VEGF/MMP outputs and barrier failure across retinal compartments supports the plausibility that a palmitoylation-targeted STING antagonist like H-151 will deliver the predicted phenotype in senescent RPE (Hu et al., 2023; Terao et al., 2022; Qiu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025).

Recommendation  
Advance H-151 into AMD-relevant in vitro RPE barrier and senescence assays with rigorous on-target controls and head-to-head comparison against alternative STING inhibitors (C-176/SN-011, cryptotanshinone) to establish class translatability and select the best ocular candidate by efficacy and safety; proceed to in vivo validation contingent on clear demonstration of TEER/ZO-1 preservation, SASP/MMP suppression, and favorable ocular PK/PD (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

Strengths summary: strong mechanistic rationale in AMD, direct RPE evidence for VEGF suppression by H-151, broad anti–NF-κB/SASP activity of H-151 in inflammatory models, and multiple retinal models validating STING inhibition (Hu et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2021; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025). Weaknesses summary: no H-151 data yet on RPE barrier readouts or in vivo retinal protection; covalent-inhibitor liabilities and immunologic trade-offs require careful derisking; cell-type heterogeneity in DNA sensing mandates model selection rigor (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Taken together, H-151 is a high-priority mechanistic probe and a plausible therapeutic lead for dry AMD that merits focused preclinical validation in RPE barrier/senescence systems and in Alu/oxidative injury models of outer retinal degeneration, with parallel medicinal-chemistry and formulation work to address ocular delivery and covalent-inhibitor safety considerations (Hu et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bexarotene is a fully synthetic retinoid analog classified as a rexinoid, specifically acting as a pan–retinoid X receptor (RXR) agonist. It was originally developed through structure–activity relationship studies aimed at mimicking the natural ligand 9-cis retinoic acid, while providing greater receptor selectivity, improved potency, and a pharmacological profile amenable to therapeutic use. Its synthesis and subsequent discovery were driven by the need to harness RXR‐mediated gene regulation, and it subsequently became the only FDA-approved synthetic RXR ligand to date (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). As a member of the retinoid drug class, bexarotene has been primarily used in the oncological setting, specifically for the treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, and its chemical design reflects modifications that impart high lipophilicity and receptor specificity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018). This synthetic derivation distinguishes it from naturally occurring retinoids and underpins its utility across a number of experimental and clinical contexts.

Therapeutic History:  
Bexarotene’s clinical history is marked by its approval as a second-line therapy for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, which provided a strong basis for its safety and efficacy in a human disease setting (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). In addition to its primary use in oncology, preclinical and early clinical research has investigated bexarotene for applications in neurodegenerative diseases, most notably Alzheimer’s disease and multiple sclerosis. These studies have demonstrated that RXR activation by bexarotene can influence the clearance of pathological protein aggregates and promote remyelination, respectively (Gaunt, 2020; Behl et al., 2022). However, despite the broad mechanistic appeal of RXR agonism in modifying lipid metabolism and neuroinflammation, there is little to no established clinical or veterinary precedent for employing bexarotene in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative conditions. In fact, while several RXR agonists have been considered in various models of ocular disease, the role of RXR in the diseased retina remains underexplored, with only sparse reports such as a study with the RXR agonist PA024 in retinal degeneration models (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). This gap in therapeutic history presents both a challenge and an opportunity in repurposing bexarotene for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
Bexarotene exerts its pharmacological effects primarily by binding to the ligand-binding domain of RXR isoforms (RXRα, RXRβ, and RXRγ) with nanomolar potency, inducing conformational changes that favor the recruitment of coactivators and subsequent transcriptional activation of targeted genes (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). RXR is a promiscuous nuclear receptor that forms obligate heterodimers with several other nuclear receptors, most notably the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) such as PPARγ. In doing so, the bexarotene-induced RXR/PPARγ heterodimer binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the genome, thereby upregulating target genes involved in lipid metabolism and transport. One key target is ABCA1, an ATP-binding cassette transporter implicated in cholesterol efflux from cells, which plays a central role in maintaining intracellular lipid homeostasis (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the activation of the RXR/PPARγ pathway is particularly compelling. RPE cells are highly involved in the processing and clearance of lipids, including cholesterol, and in modulating the structural integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier via tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 and occludin. When under stress—such as exposure to cytotoxic mediators like 7-ketocholesterol (7KCh), which disrupts normal junctional organization and reduces transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—the activation of RXR offers a potential therapeutic avenue. Bexarotene’s ability to stimulate RXR signaling is expected to upregulate ABCA1 expression, thereby enhancing cholesterol efflux, while also promoting the transcription of genes that lead to the re-expression of claudin-1 and occludin, which are critical for restoring barrier integrity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

The biochemical interactions following RXR activation by bexarotene include a cascade of events where the ligand-receptor complex alters the transcriptional landscape of the cell. This process entails the heterodimerization of RXR with its partner receptor, binding to DNA response elements, and initiating the recruitment of transcriptional coactivators, which together drive the expression of genes that modulate lipid metabolism, inflammatory responses, and cell junction integrity. The specificity of bexarotene for RXR, as opposed to broader retinoic acid receptor (RAR) activity, allows for a more targeted enhancement of these pathways—a factor that is crucial in tissues like the RPE, where precise regulation of lipid handling and barrier properties is essential for retinal health (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underlying the repurposing of bexarotene for dry AMD is that its activation of RXR in RPE cells will facilitate heterodimerization with PPARγ, driving the transcriptional upregulation of lipid-handling genes, most notably ABCA1. In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have provided compelling preliminary data indicating that exposure to 0.5 µM bexarotene in the presence of 7-ketocholesterol stress is capable of restoring TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values and significantly increasing ABCA1 mRNA levels. This restoration of TEER suggests that bexarotene not only promotes cholesterol efflux by upregulating ABCA1 but also exerts a beneficial influence on the expression of key tight junction proteins, such as claudin-1 and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity of the RPE barrier (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

The expected molecular effect in the assay is thus twofold. First, through its molecular interaction with RXR, bexarotene reinforces the RXR/PPARγ heterodimer formation, triggering a cascade of gene transcription events that culminate in enhanced cholesterol efflux via ABCA1. This effect directly addresses the accumulation of lipid deposits that contribute to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. Second, by re-inducing the expression of claudin-1 and occludin, bexarotene is anticipated to improve cellular junctional integrity, thereby reducing paracellular leakage and restoring the overall barrier function of the RPE as measured by TEER. The use of ocular gel formulations for local delivery promises to concentrate the therapeutic effect within the eye, circumventing the systemic adverse effects that are typically associated with bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties, such as high lipophilicity and low systemic solubility (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of bexarotene as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is founded upon a robust mechanistic rationale and promising preliminary in vitro data, yet it also presents several challenges that must be addressed through rigorous further research. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its well-established mode of action as a selective RXR agonist. Its ability to promote heterodimerization with PPARγ and subsequently upregulate genes such as ABCA1 is well supported by a substantial body of research in other disease contexts, including neurodegeneration and oncology (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Gaunt, 2020). This receptor specificity not only underscores bexarotene’s potential to modulate RPE lipid metabolism but also suggests that similar pharmacological principles could translate into the restoration of tight junction integrity—a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD.

Another significant strength is its prior clinical approval for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. This provides a substantial amount of safety data and experience in human use, which could expedite the repurposing process under a drug repositioning strategy. Moreover, the observed in vitro effects—namely the partial restoration of TEER and the increase in ABCA1 mRNA in stressed ARPE-19 cells—lend direct support to the hypothesis that RXR agonism can counteract 7-ketocholesterol-induced disruptions in RPE function (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). The concept of using ocular gel formulations to achieve localized delivery and thereby minimize systemic side effects is another innovative aspect that addresses one of the traditional limitations of bexarotene, namely its adverse systemic metabolic disturbances, which include dyslipidemia and hypothyroidism (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021).

However, there are notable weaknesses that temper this optimism. First, bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties—its high lipophilicity and low solubility—pose a significant formulation challenge, especially when transitioning from systemic oncology applications to local ocular delivery. While gel formulations offer a potential solution, achieving the precise pharmacokinetics and adequate tissue penetration in the retina will require meticulous formulation development and validation. Second, despite the extensive research on RXR agonism in other tissues, there is very limited precedent for the use of bexarotene or similar compounds in the treatment of dry AMD or related ocular diseases. In other words, while the underlying nuclear receptor biology in the retina is compelling, the absence of prior clinical or even robust preclinical ocular studies increases the risk associated with translational uncertainty (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Moreover, systemic side effects associated with bexarotene have been well documented in its approved indications. Although the strategy of localized ocular delivery aims to mitigate these adverse effects, any leakage from the ocular compartment into systemic circulation could potentially re-expose patients to these risks. Additionally, the complexity of dry AMD as a multifactorial disease—with contributions from oxidative stress, inflammation, and complex extracellular matrix alterations—means that modulating only lipid handling and tight junction integrity might not be sufficient to arrest or reverse disease progression. Thus, while the mechanistic hypothesis is sound, it should ideally be integrated into a broader therapeutic strategy that also addresses other pathological mechanisms in dry AMD.

In summary, the proposed use of bexarotene for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic foundation based on RXR agonism and its downstream effects on lipid metabolism and cellular junction integrity. The preliminary in vitro evidence in ARPE-19 cells under 7-ketocholesterol stress is promising, particularly with the reported restoration of TEER and upregulation of ABCA1. The strengths of this candidate include its specificity for RXR, the translational potential backed by its FDA–approved status for an unrelated indication, and the innovative strategy of local ocular delivery through gel formulations. On the other hand, challenges related to its physicochemical properties, potential for systemic side effects, and the overall gaps in preclinical ocular data necessitate further rigorous research. Preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD and careful formulation optimization will be essential next steps to validate the therapeutic potential of bexarotene in this context (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Alagebrium chloride (ALT-711) is a synthetic small molecule designed as an advanced glycation end product (AGE) crosslink breaker. Chemically identified as 3‐phenacyl‐4,5‐dimethylthiazolium chloride, it belongs to the thiazolium salt family—a class noted for its reactivity toward α-dicarbonyl substrates found in AGE crosslinks. Originally developed as an analog of N-phenacylthiazolium bromide (PTB), ALT-711 was synthesized specifically to overcome the instability and in vivo degradation that hampered PTB’s clinical potential, and thus represented a more stable, easily synthesized candidate with retained crosslink-cleaving activity (Alam, Ahsan, & Alam, 2013; Borg & Forbes, 2016). The design rationale capitalized on the unique nucleophilic properties of the thiazolium core—similar in some respects to the vitamin thiamine structure, though it lacks the pyrimidine moiety—to facilitate cleavage of carbon–carbon bonds between protein-bound glycation products, notably interfering with the formation of deleterious cross-links such as those involving pentosidine (Furber, 2010; Coughlan et al., 2007). Over the past two decades, this class of AGE breakers, including ALT-711, has been primarily explored for applications in cardiovascular and diabetic complications, with the underlying therapeutic hypothesis being that reversal of AGE-mediated crosslinking could restore tissue compliance and function (Kim & Spiegel, 2013; Toprak & Yigitaslan, 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
The historical development of alagebrium is rooted in efforts to counteract the progressive accumulation of AGEs—a hallmark of chronic hyperglycemia and aging—that contribute to decreased protein turnover, tissue stiffening, and dysfunction. ALT-711 was developed and advanced by pharmaceutical entities like Alteon Pharmaceuticals (later Synvista Therapeutics) for its ability to reverse AGE-mediated crosslinking in the extracellular matrix, particularly in collagen and elastin-rich tissues (Alam, Ahsan, & Alam, 2013; Velichkova, 2020). Preclinical studies in diabetic rat models demonstrated that ALT-711 not only increased cardiac output and improved left ventricular diastolic function but also reduced arterial stiffening by breaking protein crosslinks, an effect that was correlated with improved vascular compliance (Coughlan et al., 2007; Kim & Spiegel, 2013). In clinical development, ALT-711 progressed through human trials—being evaluated for conditions such as heart failure, systolic hypertension, and vascular stiffening—although its program ultimately faced setbacks due to financial constraints and discontinuation of further clinical studies (Toprak & Yigitaslan, 2019; Vasan et al., 2003). Despite robust preclinical evidence in cardiovascular models, there is no established record of alagebrium being previously used to treat ocular diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); however, the underlying mechanism of AGE crosslink reversal suggests potential utility in tissues that undergo similar AGE-mediated structural changes, like the Bruch’s membrane (BM) of the eye (Krautwald et al., 2011; Nagai et al., 2012).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of action of ALT-711 centers on its ability to cleave AGE-derived protein crosslinks via a nucleophilic reaction targeting α-dicarbonyl moieties within these adducts. In biochemical models, the thiazolium ring of ALT-711 acts by facilitating the hydrolytic cleavage of carbon–carbon bonds that form between juxtaposed carbonyl groups in AGE crosslinks. In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration, the central hypothesis posits that ALT-711 can act on the collagen/elastin-rich Bruch’s membrane (BM), a structure whose biomechanical integrity is compromised by AGE accumulation. From an overall standpoint, ALT-711 presents a multifaceted candidate with intriguing properties that render it potentially suitable for repurposing in dry AMD. Overall, ALT-711 stands as a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its established role as an AGE crosslink breaker and its demonstrated efficacy in softening stiffened extracellular matrices in other disease models. The strength of its scientific rationale is enhanced by its dual mode of action—both direct cleavage of AGE-induced crosslinks and ancillary metal-chelating and antioxidant effects—which may synergize to reduce pathological ECM rigidity. The hypothesis that AGE crosslink cleavage will soften Bruch’s membrane, thereby restoring RPE tight junction integrity and improving barrier function, is scientifically sound but remains to be validated through targeted ocular studies. Given the innovative nature of this extracellular matrix–centric therapeutic approach in a disease with few effective treatments, ALT-711 merits further investigation as a drug candidate for dry AMD, with the caveat that its previous clinical development challenges and current controversies regarding its mechanism necessitate cautious and thorough preclinical validation before any clinical translation can be contemplated (Alam, Ahsan, & Alam, 2013; Velichkova, 2020; Cooper, 2004; Toprak et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GW501516 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule agonist that selectively binds to and activates the peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor beta/delta (PPARβ/δ), a member of the nuclear receptor superfamily known for its central role in regulating lipid metabolism and energy homeostasis (Salvadó et al., 2014; Ebert et al., 2016). Originally developed through medicinal chemistry approaches targeting metabolic disorders, GW501516 belongs to the broader class of PPAR agonists, which have historically been pursued for their capacity to enhance fatty acid oxidation and improve insulin sensitivity in preclinical models. The synthetic origins of GW501516 involve structure–activity relationship studies aimed at identifying high affinity ligands for PPARβ/δ; its successful development resulted in a compound with nanomolar potency (EC₅₀ approximately 3 nM) (Salvadó et al., 2014). In general, compounds from this class have been used to probe metabolic pathways in skeletal muscle and adipose tissues, where activation of PPARβ/δ drives transcriptional programs that increase fatty acid oxidation, counteract endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, and mitigate inflammatory responses (Salvadó et al., 2014). This repurposing effort seeks to capitalize on its established metabolic benefits in a novel indication—dry age–related macular degeneration (AMD)—by aiming to enhance mitochondrial turnover and strengthen the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier under oxidative stress.

Therapeutic History:  
GW501516 has been extensively studied in the context of metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and obesity. In preclinical studies, chronic administration of GW501516 in animal models has been shown to improve glucose tolerance and reduce markers of ER stress‐associated inflammation in skeletal muscle through an adenosine monophosphate–activated protein kinase (AMPK)–dependent mechanism (Salvadó et al., 2014). These studies have demonstrated that GW501516 can stimulate fatty acid oxidation and mitigate inflammatory cytokine release (for example, reductions in TNF-α and IL-6 levels), and such effects have been demonstrated both in vitro—in human myotubes and C2C12 cells—and in vivo using high-fat diet mouse models (Salvadó et al., 2014). Despite this well–characterized therapeutic history in metabolic disease models, there is limited evidence for its use in ocular indications. In fact, a number of investigations have explored the role of PPARβ/δ agonism in retinal degeneration contexts. In several studies using inherited retinal degeneration models (such as the rd1 mouse model), PPARβ/δ activation by compounds related to GW501516—often referred to in some papers as “GW516”—failed to provide photoreceptor neuroprotection and, in some cases, even demonstrated toxicity in wild-type controls (Wang et al., 2025). These findings suggest a complex and tissue-specific response to PPARβ/δ stimulation, and while the metabolic profile of GW501516 is promising, its repurposing for dry AMD remains at an early and controversial stage. Notably, no definitive clinical or extensive preclinical studies have yet established its efficacy in dry AMD or related RPE dysfunction models, although its potential to modulate oxidative stress and improve barrier function has generated interest for novel applications (Wang et al., 2025).

At the molecular level, GW501516 exerts its effects by binding to the ligand-binding domain of PPARβ/δ, resulting in the receptor’s heterodimerization with the retinoid X receptor (RXR). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bardoxolone methyl, also known as CDDO-Me, is a synthetic derivative developed from the naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid oleanolic acid. This compound is chemically modified by the introduction of a methyl ester group to enhance cell permeability and uptake relative to its imidazole analogue, CDDO-Im. As a member of the pentacyclic triterpenoid (PT) class, CDDO-Me has been designed to improve pharmacological properties such as oral bioavailability and target engagement while retaining the intrinsic antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of its natural precursor. Historically, pentacyclic triterpenoids have been studied for a wide range of applications—including anticancer, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory therapies—and have a longstanding role in traditional medicine in various Asian cultures. In this context, CDDO-Me has emerged as an advanced synthetic candidate that capitalizes on these properties, particularly through its potency as an activator of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. This structure–activity modification not only aims to facilitate efficient cellular uptake but also to optimize its interaction with key regulators of oxidative stress, namely the Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1) (Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and clinical investigation primarily in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and cancer. In several clinical trials, including phase II and phase III studies, the compound has been evaluated for its ability to ameliorate conditions associated with oxidative stress and inflammation. Its clinical development for CKD, in particular, has underscored its potential to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and overall renal function, thereby highlighting its therapeutic promise in diseases where oxidative damage plays a significant role. Despite its notable progress in these areas, direct clinical evidence for Bardoxolone methyl in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal diseases remains limited. However, several preclinical studies have demonstrated that compounds related to Bardoxolone methyl are capable of activating Nrf2 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, upregulating protective genes such as NQO1 and HO-1 that are essential for combating oxidative stress in the retina. These findings suggest that, although not originally developed for retinal indications, Bardoxolone methyl has a mechanistic rationale that could support its repurposing for dry AMD (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, analogous compounds that function via Nrf2 activation have been shown to protect RPE cells against oxidative stress-induced damage, further supporting the therapeutic potential of this candidate in ocular applications (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Bardoxolone methyl operates predominantly through the activation of the Nrf2 pathway, an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional system that governs cellular antioxidant responses. Under normal homeostatic conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytoplasm by its inhibitor, Keap1, which facilitates its ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl, due to its electrophilic cyanoenone moiety, acts as a Michael acceptor, covalently modifying specific cysteine residues within Keap1 (notably cysteine 151 among others). This modification disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, preventing Nrf2 ubiquitination, and allows Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus where it binds to the antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoter regions of target genes (Zhou et al., 2020; Mathis & Cui, 2016). The subsequent upregulation of phase II detoxifying enzymes—such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and glutamate-cysteine ligase modifier subunit (GCLM)—provides cells with increased capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigate inflammatory insults. Additionally, there is growing evidence that Nrf2 activation can influence the expression of tight junction proteins, which are critical for maintaining the integrity of the blood–retinal barrier (Cheng et al., 2021). This detailed molecular interaction not only accounts for the antioxidant role of Bardoxolone methyl but also for its potential in preserving cellular integrity in environments subjected to oxidative insult, such as the RPE cells in the retina (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Cai et al., 2024). Furthermore, ancillary effects, such as modulation of NF-κB signaling and the inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, are likely to contribute to its overall cytoprotective profile, making it an attractive candidate for reducing the inflammatory milieu that accompanies retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).
