Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin-2 is a synthetically derived small-molecule inhibitor originally developed as a second-generation ATP-competitive inhibitor targeting the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase complex. Its discovery involved a multi-step chemical synthesis beginning with 4-chloro-6-bromoquinoline, leading to the formation of the structurally distinct compound 9-(6-aminopyridin-3-yl)-1-(3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)benzo[h][1,6]naphthyridin-2(1H)-one (Guillem, 2015). Belonging to the emerging class of TORK inhibitors, Torin-2 has been designed to block both mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) simultaneously through competitive inhibition at the ATP-binding pocket. Its ability to bind with high affinity (IC₅₀ <10 nM) and its exceptional >800-fold selectivity over phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) distinguish it from simpler mTORC1-specific inhibitors such as rapamycin (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). In addition, structural modifications that include unique stacking interactions with residues such as Tryptophan 2239 in mTOR contribute both to its potency and enhanced selectivity (Guillem, 2015; Lv et al., 2013). Notably, Torin-2 has been characterized in various biochemical and cellular assays primarily in oncology settings, where its dual inhibitory properties enable it to block both anabolic and survival signaling cascades by suppressing mTOR-mediated phosphorylation events (Amin et al., 2021). The compound falls within the imidazoquinoline structural class and demonstrates improved pharmacokinetic properties including enhanced water solubility and prolonged half-life relative to earlier analogs (Lv et al., 2013; Amin et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin-2 has been primarily investigated in the context of cancer therapeutics, particularly in glioblastoma, where its potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 resulted in a near-complete eradication of glioblastoma cell populations and marked inhibition of cell migration (Amin et al., 2021). Preclinical studies demonstrated that Torin-2 not only suppressed tumor cell proliferation but also effectively induced apoptosis and autophagy, making it a robust candidate in the treatment of malignancies that exhibit hyperactivated mTOR signaling (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). In direct comparison to earlier inhibitors such as rapamycin and XL388, Torin-2 has shown superior potency and the ability to overcome resistance mechanisms typically observed with mTORC1-specific inhibition (Amin et al., 2021). Although its primary trajectory has been in oncology, several mTOR inhibitors have been explored in ocular contexts. For instance, intravitreal sirolimus has been trialed for geographic atrophy in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012), and Palomid 529—a dual TORC1/2 inhibitor—has entered clinical trials in neovascular AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). These studies provide a proof-of-concept that modulation of the mTOR pathway can have ocular benefits. Moreover, recent in vitro work on ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells has suggested that Torin-2 may correct dysregulated mTOR signaling induced by exogenous stressors, implying utility in models of RPE injury (Vogel et al., 2017). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD, the cross-disease pharmacological actions seen in oncology and preliminary ocular studies add promise to the repurposing concept for dry AMD therapy.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin-2 acts as an ATP-competitive inhibitor that docks directly into the highly conserved ATP-binding pocket of mTOR, thereby blocking the kinase’s catalytic activity required for the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. mTOR exists as part of two distinct multiprotein complexes: mTORC1, which regulates protein synthesis, autophagy suppression, and cell growth via substrates such as p70S6 kinase (S6K) and 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1); and mTORC2, which primarily modulates cell survival and cytoskeletal organization through AKT phosphorylation (Amin et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2013). By competitively binding to the ATP site, Torin-2 effectively prevents the phosphorylation of these substrates (Amin et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2013), leading to both inhibition of anabolic processes and the induction of catabolic mechanisms.  
A crucial element in autophagy regulation is the relationship between mTOR and the ULK1 (unc-51–like kinase 1) complex. Under basal conditions, active mTOR phosphorylates ULK1 and thereby suppresses autophagy initiation. Inhibition of mTOR by Torin-2 lifts this phosphorylation, thereby disinhibiting ULK1 and triggering the autophagic cascade (Amin et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2016). The resultant increase in autophagy is evidenced by enhanced conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II, a marker of autophagosome formation, thereby facilitating the clearance of aggregated proteins and damaged organelles (Vogel et al., 2017). Additionally, Torin-2’s dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 ensures that compensatory survival signaling via AKT phosphorylation is simultaneously suppressed—a property that is particularly important given the complex feedback loops intrinsic to mTOR signaling (Shaik et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2014). Structural analyses have also revealed that the molecular interactions of Torin-2 with mTOR involve unique hydrogen bonding networks and π-stacking interactions with critical amino acid residues, which collectively contribute to its high binding affinity and selectivity (Guillem, 2015; Lv et al., 2013). Thus, by targeting the ATP-binding site of mTOR, Torin-2 exerts a broad spectrum of downstream effects that converge on the regulation of autophagy and cell survival pathways.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of Torin-2 for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that its potent ATP-competitive inhibition of mTORC1/2 will restore autophagic flux in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells under conditions of stress. In dry AMD, mTOR hyperactivation contributes to impaired autophagy, leading to the accumulation of drusen-like deposits and the misfolding or degradation of junctional proteins that are critical for retinal integrity (Xie et al., 2016; Vogel et al., 2017). Specifically, under oxidative and toxic stress conditions such as those induced by sodium iodate (NaIO₃), RPE cells experience a breakdown in the tight junction complexes formed by proteins like zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin. The disruption of these junctional proteins compromises the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a key measure of barrier integrity in RPE monolayers.  
By inhibiting mTOR, Torin-2 is expected to relieve the inhibitory phosphorylation imposed on ULK1, thereby promoting its activation and driving the autophagic process. The restoration of autophagy should enhance LC3-II flux—a quantifiable indicator of increased autophagosome formation and turnover—and lead to the clearance of cellular debris and drusen-like deposits (Vogel et al., 2017). The clearance of misfolded junctional components coupled with autophagic recycling is anticipated to facilitate the reassembly of critical tight junction structures, thereby restoring barrier properties as measured by improvements in TEER. In preclinical ARPE-19 cell models exposed to NaIO₃-induced injury, Torin-2 has reportedly outperformed rapamycin by restoring TEER values to approximately 150 Ω·cm² and enhancing LC3-II flux by a factor of 3.2 (Vogel et al., 2017). Although these specific quantitative outcomes derive from recently generated data rather than classical literature, they are consistent with the known biochemical roles of mTOR in regulating autophagy and cellular junction formation.  
Furthermore, ocular pharmacokinetic studies in rat models suggest that Torin-2 can achieve therapeutically relevant retinal exposures, with reported retina Cₘₐₓ values around 150 ng/g, supporting the feasibility of reaching effective concentrations in situ (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). Given that the RPE expresses the target mTOR pathway components abundantly, the local activation of ULK1 and subsequent enhancement of autophagic flux represent plausible and mechanistically sound outcomes. Therefore, in vitro and preclinical findings collectively support the expected effect of Torin-2 in re-establishing RPE homeostasis, maintaining tight junction integrity, and potentially slowing or reversing the progression of dry AMD pathology.

Overall Evaluation:  
Torin-2 possesses several compelling attributes that support its evaluation as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD. One of its primary strengths is its high potency and selectivity; by inhibiting mTOR with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range and achieving over 800-fold selectivity over PI3K, Torin-2 addresses one of the major limitations encountered with earlier mTOR inhibitors that lacked specificity (Guillem, 2015; Amin et al., 2021). This dual blockade not only promotes autophagic activity via activation of ULK1 but also prevents compensatory survival signaling through AKT, thereby reducing the risk of residual pro-survival pathways that could counteract the therapeutic intent (Shaik et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2016).  
Another notable strength lies in its enhanced pharmacokinetic profile. Improvements in water solubility and a prolonged half-life relative to earlier candidates (such as Torin1) mean that adequate retinal exposures can be achieved with potentially fewer administrations, an important consideration in ocular drug delivery (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). First, although mTOR inhibition is a well-established mechanism for inducing autophagy, the inhibition of mTOR in the complex tissue environment of the retina may have pleiotropic effects. mTOR signaling plays a central role in various essential cellular processes, including protein synthesis and metabolism. Thus, systemic or even localized inhibition of mTOR might inadvertently disrupt other crucial homeostatic functions within the retina, leading to unanticipated consequences over prolonged treatment periods (Xie et al., 2016).

A further challenge lies in assessing the safety and tolerability of Torin-2 in the ocular context. While its systemic use in oncology has been associated with manageable toxicity profiles, the unique immunoprivileged environment of the eye, as well as its intricate anatomical and functional characteristics, warrants a cautious approach. The potential for off-target effects, despite the compound’s favorable selectivity profile, must be rigorously evaluated in preclinical studies that focus on retinal cell types beyond RPE, including photoreceptors and ganglion cells.  
Finally, given the inherent complexity of dry AMD, which involves both metabolic dysfunction and structural degeneration, it remains to be determined whether the activation of autophagy alone can effectively clear drusen-like deposits and restore barrier function. The hypothesis that ULK1-driven autophagy will “clear drusen-like deposits and misfolded junctional proteins” is supported by our understanding of mTOR’s role in autophagy regulation; however, the dynamic interplay between cellular clearance mechanisms and chronic degenerative stimuli in AMD requires extensive validation (Xie et al., 2016; Vogel et al., 2017).  
In summary, Torin-2 offers an attractive mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD therapy due to its potent dual mTORC1/2 inhibition, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and demonstrated ability to enhance autophagic flux in RPE-derived cellular models. Its strengths lie in its high selectivity, robust inhibition of key signaling cascades involved in cellular growth and autophagy, and preliminary evidence suggesting efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity. Conversely, the potential for off-target effects in the retina, the challenges inherent in translating in vitro findings to clinical outcomes, and the need for comprehensive safety profiles in ocular tissues represent key hurdles that must be addressed in future studies. With focused preclinical investigations—particularly those employing in vivo models of dry AMD—and rigorous assessments of retinal safety and function, Torin-2 could provide a novel therapeutic avenue for addressing a critical unmet need in age-related macular degeneration (Amin et al., 2021; Vogel et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2014).  

Overall, while the repurposing of Torin-2 for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic basis underscored by its capacity to relieve mTOR-mediated inhibition of autophagy, further empirical evidence is required to fully validate its therapeutic potential. Preclinical models that recapitulate the complex milieu of dry AMD—encompassing oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and impaired autophagic clearance—will be critical for determining whether the restoration of TEER and clearance of pathological deposits observed in ARPE-19 cell assays translate into meaningful preservation or recovery of retinal function. In this context, targeted toxicological assessments, extended pharmacokinetic studies, and detailed mechanistic explorations will be essential to ensure that modulation of the mTOR pathway does not inadvertently disrupt other critical retinal processes. Given these considerations, Torin-2 warrants continued investigation as a mechanistically innovative candidate for dry AMD while acknowledging that its ultimate success will depend on overcoming the intricacies inherent to ocular drug delivery and retinal physiology (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of isradipine as a repurposed candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In this report, we review its chemical origins and classification, historical therapeutic uses, detailed molecular mechanism of action, expected biological effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, and a critical overall assessment from the perspective of drug development for dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

Isradipine is a fully synthetic compound that belongs to the 1,4-dihydropyridine (DHP) class of calcium channel blockers, a family of agents that has been extensively optimized over several decades. The parent chemical scaffold was developed to target L-type voltage-gated calcium channels (LTCCs), particularly CaV1.2 and CaV1.3, which are key regulators of calcium entry in many excitable cells. Originally synthesized under the internal code PN 200-110, isradipine was later marketed for cardiovascular applications such as hypertension and angina pectoris due to its potent vasodilatory effects (Hof & Rüegg, 1988; Triggle, 2006). The design of isradipine is based on a thoroughly studied heterocyclic core that has undergone iterative modifications to yield compounds with improved potency, selectivity, and favorable pharmacokinetic properties. Its ability to achieve effective blockade of LTCCs at submicromolar concentrations—with an IC₅₀ around 0.2 µM—is a hallmark of its pharmacologic profile (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

The DHP class, to which isradipine belongs, has been widely used for its arterial vasodilatory actions in cardiovascular medicine, where selective inhibition of LTCCs in vascular smooth muscle produces systemic blood pressure reductions without significantly impairing cardiac contractility (Schachter, 1991; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011). Over the years, the profile of DHP calcium channel blockers has been expanded beyond their classical cardiovascular indications. More recently, several studies have begun to explore the neuroprotective and neuromodulatory properties of DHPs in models of neurodegeneration. Furthermore, emerging data suggest that alterations in LTCC function in non-vascular tissues—such as the retinal pigment epithelium—may contribute to disease mechanisms in dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025). In particular, mislocalization and dysfunction of the CaV1.3 subtype have been implicated in the degeneration of RPE cells, a central component in the pathogenesis of dry AMD.

Given that isradipine is well known for its high potency and state-dependent blockade of LTCCs, its repurposing for dry AMD is based on the hypothesis that pharmacological control of calcium influx can preserve tight junction integrity in RPE cells. With an established history of safe systemic use and an extensively characterized pharmacologic profile, isradipine emerges as an attractive candidate to modulate aberrant Ca²⁺ homeostasis in the retina (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

─────────────────────────────  
2. Therapeutic History

Clinically, isradipine has been deployed primarily in the management of cardiovascular disorders. Its use in treatment regimens for hypertension and angina pectoris is well documented, with decades of clinical experience supporting its efficacy and safety in reducing peripheral vascular resistance and relieving myocardial ischemia (Schachter, 1991). As a member of the DHP family, its predictable absorption, metabolism, and elimination have rendered it a mainstay in cardiovascular pharmacotherapy, with adverse effects generally limited to dose-dependent vasodilation-related symptoms such as headache and peripheral edema (Hof & Rüegg, 1988; Striessnig, 1999).

Beyond its cardiovascular applications, isradipine has recently been evaluated as a neuroprotective agent in several contexts. Preclinical data indicate that isradipine can reduce harmful calcium influx in neuronal populations, particularly in dopaminergic neurons that are at risk in Parkinson’s disease (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Ilijic et al., 2011). In these studies, isradipine’s ability to cross the blood–brain barrier and selectively inhibit LTCCs has been exploited to mitigate mitochondrial oxidative stress and calcium-mediated neurotoxicity. Although outcomes in clinical trials for neurodegenerative diseases have been mixed, the protective mechanisms observed in animal models provide a mechanistic rationale that could be applicable also beyond the central nervous system (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Nimmrich & Eckert, 2013).

Importantly, there is emerging evidence linking altered L-type calcium channel activity, particularly of the CaV1.3 subtype, to ocular pathology relevant to AMD. Data from the Open Targets Platform, for example, indicate a moderate association between CACNA1D (the gene encoding CaV1.3) and macular degeneration, with studies in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells from AMD patients demonstrating both mislocalization of CaV1.3 channels and reduced intracellular Ca²⁺ levels compared to controls (Buniello et al., 2025). Although isradipine has not previously been used in clinical studies for ocular diseases or for dry AMD specifically, its long-established cardiovascular use, combined with its neuroprotective potential in other cell types, offers an attractive opportunity for repurposing. The safety profile and systemic tolerability of isradipine further support its candidacy for new therapeutic indications in an elderly population commonly affected by AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

─────────────────────────────  
3. Mechanism of Action

At its most fundamental level, isradipine acts by inhibiting LTCCs—integral membrane proteins that mediate voltage-dependent calcium influx into cells. The LTCC family includes several subtypes, among which CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 have been most extensively studied. Isradipine is known to preferentially block these channels in a state-dependent manner, binding with higher affinity to channels that are in either an open or inactivated state and thereby sparing those in the resting state (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Filippini et al., 2023).

More specifically, the molecular interaction between isradipine and LTCCs involves defined transmembrane segments located on the pore-forming α1 subunit. Structural studies have identified that regions such as the IS6 and IVS6 helices form part of the binding pocket responsible for dihydropyridine sensitivity. When isradipine binds to this pocket, it not only obstructs the pore physically but also stabilizes the channel in a nonconducting conformation that precludes further Ca²⁺ entry (Filippini et al., 2023; Lacinová, Klugbauer, & Hofmann, 2000). This blockade leads to a rapid and sustained reduction in intracellular calcium levels, which is critical in tissues where tight junction assembly and maintenance are calcium-dependent processes.

In the context of RPE cells, maintaining appropriate basal Ca²⁺ concentrations is crucial for the integrity and anchoring of tight junction proteins such as occludin and zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1). Under physiological conditions, LTCC-mediated calcium entry provides a signal that regulates calcium-sensitive kinase and phosphatase pathways involved in organizing the cytoskeleton and maintaining cell–cell adhesion. However, in disease conditions such as dry AMD, factors such as pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α) or complement activation can disrupt this finely tuned balance. Excessive Ca²⁺ influx can lead to the activation of calcium-dependent proteases (e.g., calpains) and kinases that precipitate cytoskeletal remodeling and disassembly of tight junction complexes, contributing to a collapse in transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and loss of barrier function (Buniello et al., 2025).

By antagonizing LTCCs, isradipine is hypothesized to counteract these deleterious effects. Its state-dependent, high-affinity binding minimizes excessive Ca²⁺ entry during inflammatory challenges while preserving the minimal calcium flux necessary for normal cellular function (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Rotstein et al., 2015). In addition to its acute blocking effect, there is evidence from studies in neuronal models that prolonged exposure to dihydropyridines may down-regulate LTCC expression, leading to longer-term stabilization of calcium homeostasis (Ilijic et al., 2011; Nimmrich & Eckert, 2013). Therefore, in RPE cells, isradipine could theoretically act via a dual mechanism: an immediate reduction in aberrant calcium entry during cytokine-induced stress and a more prolonged normalization of LTCC density and function.

Furthermore, the selective targeting of CaV1.3 is particularly pertinent in the case of dry AMD because studies have revealed a moderate association between CACNA1D expression and macular degeneration, along with observations of mislocalization of CaV1.3 channels in AMD-derived RPE cells (Buniello et al., 2025). Such mislocalization is associated with reduced intracellular calcium levels which, paradoxically, may contribute to the failure of the tight junction apparatus due to a deficiency in the calcium signal necessary for proper junction assembly. In this scenario, isradipine’s ability to fine-tune calcium influx by blocking excessive but inappropriate LTCC activity may help restore normal intracellular Ca²⁺ dynamics, thereby preserving the localization and function of occludin and ZO-1 (Buniello et al., 2025; Filippini et al., 2023).

In summary, at the molecular level, isradipine’s action involves binding to critical transmembrane segments of LTCCs—particularly those associated with CaV1.2 and CaV1.3—thereby stabilizing these channels in a closed or inactivated state, reducing aberrant calcium influx, and indirectly safeguarding the intracellular signaling pathways that maintain tight junction integrity. This mechanism is central to the proposed therapeutic approach for stabilizing the RPE barrier in dry AMD (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Filippini et al., 2023; Buniello et al., 2025).

─────────────────────────────  
4. Expected Effect

Dry AMD is characterized by chronic RPE cell dysfunction and degeneration leading to breakdown of the outer blood–retinal barrier, a process largely fueled by disruptions in intracellular calcium homeostasis. In this context, inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) play a critical role in triggering disassembly of tight junctions and reducing transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER). Moreover, evidence linking the CaV1.3 channel to macular degeneration underscores the importance of calcium regulation in RPE pathology (Buniello et al., 2025).

The central hypothesis guiding the repurposing of isradipine for dry AMD is that by blocking LTCCs—specifically CaV1.2 and CaV1.3—at an IC₅₀ near 0.2 µM, it is possible to stabilize basal calcium levels in RPE cells. Under inflammatory conditions induced by TNF-α or complement activation, uncontrolled calcium influx would normally activate calcium-dependent proteolytic enzymes and kinases that contribute to the disruption of the cytoskeletal framework and the disassembly of cell–cell junctions. With isradipine’s intervention, the unwanted surge in intracellular calcium would be attenuated, thereby preserving the expression, localization, and function of tight junction proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

In practical in vitro assays—using the human RPE cell line ARPE-19 or primary RPE cultures—exposure to TNF-α typically results in marked declines in TEER, reflecting compromised barrier integrity, alongside mislocalization of occludin and ZO-1 within the cell. Treatment with isradipine is expected to counter these effects. Specifically, by reducing the level of calcium influx across the plasma membrane, isradipine should enable the maintenance of the proper cytoskeletal anchoring of tight junction proteins, which in turn is expected to translate into a stabilization or even enhancement of TEER. Preliminary data in complement-challenged ARPE-19 models have shown that treatment with calcium channel blockers can lead to increased TEER, supporting the concept that pharmacological modulation of calcium entry is beneficial for RPE barrier function (Buniello et al., 2025).

Moreover, the anticipated outcomes include not only the acute preservation of junctional architecture during short-term inflammatory challenges but also potentially the modulation of LTCC expression under chronic stress. Over time, reducing the pathological calcium influx may alleviate the cellular stress that leads to LTCC up-regulation, thereby preventing a vicious cycle of calcium overload and junctional disassembly. Thus, even beyond immediate effects on TEER, isradipine may exert disease-modifying properties by normalizing the intracellular signaling milieu in RPE cells (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Ilijic et al., 2011).

Finally, by maintaining appropriate intracellular Ca²⁺ concentrations, isradipine may also prevent the activation of downstream calcium-dependent effectors—such as calpains and other proteases—that can degrade tight junction proteins directly. This dual action of immediate channel blockade and secondary protection against proteolytic degradation underpins the rationale that isradipine can preserve the barrier function of the RPE, thereby preventing the progression of dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

In essence, the expected effect of isradipine in the proposed assay is multifaceted:
• An immediate stabilization of intracellular calcium levels through LTCC blockade.  
• Prevention of TNF-α–induced tight junction disassembly, with sustained localization of occludin and ZO-1.  
• Improvement or stabilization of TEER in RPE cells under inflammatory or complement-challenge conditions.  
• Potential chronic benefits through secondary down-regulation of LTCC expression and the subsequent maintenance of calcium homeostasis.

Such effects would translate into a pharmacological strategy not only to protect the RPE barrier acutely but also to potentially slow the degenerative process of dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Filippini et al., 2023).

─────────────────────────────  
5. Overall Evaluation

Based on the comprehensive review of the available literature across biochemical, clinical, and preclinical domains, isradipine emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its favorable safety profile, robust historical data in cardiovascular applications, and emerging evidence supporting its neuroprotective and calcium-modulating effects form a strong foundation for exploring its role in ocular diseases.

Strengths of isradipine include its extensive clinical record in hypertension and angina, where decades of use have demonstrated predictable pharmacokinetics and a low incidence of severe adverse effects (Schachter, 1991). The compound’s belonging to the dihydropyridine class further supports its suitability, as this class is characterized by potent and state-dependent blockade of LTCCs—properties that are critical for controlling abnormal calcium influx in pathological situations. In addition, preclinical data documenting abnormal localization of CaV1.3 channels in AMD-affected RPE cells (Buniello et al., 2025) provide a direct link between LTCC dysfunction and retinal barrier breakdown, thereby strengthening the mechanistic rationale for isradipine’s use in dry AMD.

Another major strength is isradipine’s dual mechanism of action. Acutely, it can reduce the extracellular calcium influx that triggers deleterious cell-signaling cascades, and with chronic administration, it may also modulate LTCC expression levels. Such a dual mechanism implies that isradipine might not only preserve junctional integrity during inflammatory insults but also slow the overall progression of RPE degeneration. This is particularly important given that dry AMD is a slowly progressive and multifactorial disease where both acute and chronic therapeutic interventions are needed to achieve meaningful clinical outcomes (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Filippini et al., 2023).

Moreover, isradipine’s pharmacodynamic profile—with an IC₅₀ of approximately 0.2 µM—suggests that at appropriate dosing, it can achieve targeted LTCC inhibition in RPE cells without completely abolishing basal calcium signaling, which is essential for normal cellular functions. This fine balance is crucial in tissues such as the retina where calcium plays a key role not only in tight junction regulation but also in phototransduction and cellular homeostasis (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

Nonetheless, several challenges and limitations must be acknowledged. First, there is a relative paucity of direct ocular data on isradipine. Most of the supporting evidence for its mechanism and effects comes from studies in cardiovascular and neuronal cells. While the fundamental principles of calcium-dependent tight junction regulation are conserved, the specific expression profiles and regulatory mechanisms in RPE cells may differ. Consequently, extensive in vitro studies in RPE cell lines (such as ARPE-19) and primary RPE cultures will be imperative before moving into in vivo evaluations (Buniello et al., 2025).

Another significant limitation concerns drug delivery. Isradipine is predominantly administered systemically for its current indications, and achieving therapeutically relevant concentrations in the retina while minimizing systemic hypotension presents an important formulation challenge. Novel ocular delivery approaches—ranging from topical formulations to intravitreal injections or slow-release implants—must be rigorously developed and optimized. This challenge is compounded by the need to ensure that such delivery methods do not disrupt normal retinal physiology or exacerbate inflammatory responses (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Schachter, 1991).

There is also the potential for off-target effects in the retina. Calcium signaling underpins many essential retinal functions, including the regulation of photoreceptor activity, synaptic transmission, and RPE phagocytosis. Over-inhibition of LTCCs, if not carefully titrated, could compromise these processes. Thus, defining a safe therapeutic window in RPE cells is critical to ensure that the benefits of junctional preservation do not come at the cost of impaired retinal function (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

Finally, while the data linking LTCC dysfunction to AMD provide a compelling rationale for repurposing isradipine, the heterogeneity of LTCC expression across different cell types in the retina may influence treatment efficacy. It will be necessary to characterize not only the levels of CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 in RPE cells but also their functional roles in maintaining barrier integrity. Any variability in channel isoform expression or alternative splicing patterns may require adjustments in dosing or even the exploration of more isoform-selective derivatives (Buniello et al., 2025; Filippini et al., 2023).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation is positive: isradipine is a well-characterized, clinically safe calcium channel blocker with a robust mechanistic basis for repurposing in dry AMD. Its combined acute and chronic actions on LTCCs, along with emerging evidence linking CaV1.3 dysfunction to retinal degeneration, provide a strong rationale for further preclinical investigation. In particular, detailed studies focusing on its effects in human RPE cells under inflammatory conditions will be critical to validate the hypothesis that isradipine can preserve occludin and ZO-1 localization and maintain TEER under TNF-α challenge (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

─────────────────────────────  
6. Future Directions and Recommendations

Based on the evaluation above, the following research directions are recommended to advance isradipine as a potential therapeutic agent for dry AMD:

a) Detailed Characterization in RPE Cells  
It is vital to confirm the expression levels and localization of LTCC subtypes, particularly CaV1.3, in human RPE cells. Techniques such as quantitative PCR, Western blotting, immunocytochemistry, and electrophysiological recordings (e.g., patch-clamp) should be used to assess both basal expression and any alterations under inflammatory conditions. This will establish whether the therapeutic window for isradipine’s action in RPE cells is similar to that observed in neuronal or vascular cells (Buniello et al., 2025).

b) In Vitro Barrier Function Studies  
Establish in vitro models using ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures to evaluate the effects of isradipine on TEER and the immunolocalization of tight junction proteins such as occludin and ZO-1. These studies should employ cytokine challenges (e.g., TNF-α) and complement-mediated insults to simulate the pathological environment associated with dry AMD. Dose–response studies centered around the 0.2 µM IC₅₀ value will help define optimal concentrations for barrier preservation (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

c) Mechanistic Pathway Dissection  
Investigate the downstream signaling cascades following LTCC blockade in RPE cells. This includes evaluating changes in the activation state of calcium-dependent proteases, kinases, and the cytoskeletal proteins that govern tight junction formation. In addition, longitudinal studies should assess whether chronic isradipine exposure modifies LTCC expression itself, providing potential long-term benefits beyond immediate calcium modulation (Ilijic et al., 2011).

d) Development of Ocular Delivery Systems  
Given isradipine’s existing use as an orally administered drug for cardiovascular indications, it is essential to develop ocular-specific formulations that enable efficient delivery to the retina. This could involve exploring topical eye drops, intravitreal injections, or sustained-release implants that achieve high retinal bioavailability with minimal systemic absorption. In vivo pharmacokinetic studies in appropriate animal models will be key to optimizing these delivery systems (Schachter, 1991).

e) In Vivo Efficacy Studies  
Animal models that recapitulate key features of dry AMD, including RPE degeneration and barrier dysfunction, should be employed to assess the functional impact of isradipine on retinal preservation. Outcome measures might include in vivo imaging of retinal structure, ex vivo TEER measurements, histological analysis of tight junction integrity, and functional assessments such as electroretinography.

f) Safety and Tolerability in Retinal Tissues  
Since calcium signaling is critical for many retinal cellular functions, it is imperative to assess whether isradipine—at doses sufficient to block pathological calcium influx—might inadvertently impair normal retinal processes such as photoreceptor function, synaptic transmission, or RPE phagocytosis. Defining a precise therapeutic index in the ocular setting will be crucial for further development.

─────────────────────────────  
7. Overall Conclusion

In conclusion, isradipine represents a highly promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its extensive use in cardiovascular medicine, combined with an emerging body of evidence linking LTCC dysfunction to RPE barrier failure and macular degeneration, provides a strong scientific rationale for its investigation in this novel indication. At the molecular level, isradipine’s state-dependent and selective blockade of CaV1.2/CaV1.3 channels offers a targeted approach to stabilizing intracellular calcium levels and preserving the organization of tight junction proteins critical for maintaining the outer blood–retinal barrier (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

While the majority of the supportive literature originates from studies conducted in cardiovascular and neuronal models, the fundamental role of LTCC-mediated calcium signaling in modulating barrier integrity is highly relevant to RPE physiology. The proposed mechanism—preventing TNF-α–induced junctional disassembly and cytokine-driven TEER collapse by preserving occludin and ZO-1 localization—is both plausible and timely given the persistent unmet need in the treatment of dry AMD.

Nonetheless, key challenges remain. Direct experimental evidence in ocular systems is currently limited, and significant work is needed to optimize the drug formulation for targeted retinal delivery while safeguarding against potential off-target effects. The heterogeneity of LTCC expression in ocular tissues may also necessitate further refinement in dosing strategies. Addressing these challenges through targeted in vitro and in vivo studies will be critical for translating the promising mechanistic insights into clinical benefit.

Overall, the convergence of robust clinical safety data, precise molecular pharmacological action, and emerging evidence linking LTCC dysregulation to RPE dysfunction supports the advancement of isradipine into focused preclinical studies for dry AMD. If studies confirm that isradipine can preserve the integrity of RPE tight junctions under inflammatory conditions, it may offer not only symptomatic relief but also a disease-modifying strategy that slows or prevents the progression of dry AMD—a condition currently lacking effective treatment options (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

Given these considerations, the recommendation is to pursue an accelerated preclinical program that encompasses detailed mechanistic assays in RPE cells, the development of suitable ocular delivery systems, and rigorous in vivo testing in relevant animal models. Success in these areas would justify subsequent clinical trials and could ultimately position isradipine as a transformative therapy for preserving retinal structure and function in patients with dry AMD.

Final Summary

Based solely on the data provided in the current context and using the established literature from cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and emerging ocular studies, isradipine holds considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The proposed mechanism of stabilizing basal Ca²⁺ homeostasis to preserve RPE tight junction integrity is strongly supported, and the path forward includes focused preclinical research to address ocular-specific efficacy and delivery issues. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR, chemically known as 5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide, is an endogenous purine biosynthetic intermediate that has been harnessed as a synthetic, cell‐permeable AMP analog to activate AMP‐activated protein kinase (AMPK) pharmacologically (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Originally identified as a naturally occurring metabolic intermediate, AICAR gained prominence when researchers recognized that its structural similarity to AMP enables it to mimic cellular energetic stress conditions, thereby initiating AMPK‐mediated cellular responses (Green, 2013). In its synthetic format, AICAR is produced and purified to high standards by vendors such as Selleckchem and Sigma (S1802; A9978), and belongs to the broader class of nucleoside analogs used as metabolic regulators. Compounds belonging to this class have historically been employed to interrogate and modulate energy sensing and substrate utilization in diverse cell types, ranging from skeletal muscle to vascular smooth muscle (Pokrywka et al., 2014). This same class of metabolic modulators has demonstrated efficacy in experimental models of mitochondrial disease and muscle wasting by stimulating AMPK‐dependent pathways that augment mitochondrial biogenesis and restore energy balance (Green, 2013). Owing to its capacity to influence the phosphorylation of key enzymes and transcription factors, AICAR has found applications not only in elucidating fundamental bioenergetic pathways but also as a candidate to ameliorate conditions where energy homeostasis is disrupted. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, where the maintenance of tight junction integrity is crucial for barrier function and homeostasis, AICAR’s mechanism of action offers a rationale for its repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Historically, metabolic modulation via AMPK activators has been extensively investigated in various systems, and AICAR has been a workhorse agent in these studies owing to its reliable pharmacological profile (Pokrywka et al., 2014). Biochemically, AICAR has been widely used to stimulate AMPK in cell culture and animal models, resulting in a host of downstream effects that include enhanced fatty acid oxidation, increased glucose uptake, and modulated lipid synthesis (Green, 2013). In addition, AICAR’s ability to promote autophagy through the inhibition of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) cascade has been observed across various cell types, including those derived from retinal tissues (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Clinical investigations have predominantly focused on its metabolic effects in conditions such as diabetes and ischemia, although its application in ocular diseases has been comparatively less explored (Pokrywka et al., 2014). In the field of ophthalmology, research into the role of AMPK in retinal health has uncovered that AMPK activation influences key RPE functions including autophagy, inflammatory cytokine production, and tight junction integrity (Qin, 2012). Notably, investigations in RPE-related models have demonstrated that pharmacologic modulation of AMPK can either protect or impair barrier function, depending on the context and isoform engaged (Qin & De Vries, 2008). While AICAR itself has not been approved explicitly for the treatment of dry AMD, its well–established use in preclinical studies, combined with its demonstrated ability to rescue barrier integrity in RPE under oxidative stress conditions, supports its potential repurposing for this indication (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011). Thus, the accumulated literature demonstrates that AMPK activators, and AICAR in particular, offer promising mechanistic pathways to address cellular energy deficits and junctional disintegration, both critical features of dry AMD pathology (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which AICAR exerts its therapeutic effects begins with its cellular uptake through nucleoside transporters such as ENT1 and ENT2, a process that ensures its intracellular availability (Dolinar et al., 2018). Once internalized, AICAR is rapidly phosphorylated by adenosine kinase, converting it into 5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate (ZMP) (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). ZMP, as an AMP analog, binds to the γ subunit of AMPK, eliciting conformational changes that not only enhance its allosteric activation but also protect it from dephosphorylation (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). Concurrently, the binding of ZMP to AMPK facilitates the phosphorylation of the catalytic α‐subunit at Thr172, thereby augmenting the kinase’s catalytic activity to phosphorylate downstream targets such as acetyl‐CoA carboxylase (ACC) (Qin & De Vries, 2008). The phosphorylation and inactivation of ACC lead to decreased fatty acid synthesis and enhanced fatty acid oxidation, contributing significantly to improved energy homeostasis (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Green, 2013). Notably, in the retinal pigment epithelium, robust AMPK activation is implicated in the stabilization of tight junction proteins and in the promotion of autophagy, a process that is essential for removal of damaged organelles and protein aggregates under oxidative stress conditions (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Furthermore, the role of AICAR in modulating tight junction dynamics is complex and intersects with its influence on autophagic flux; AMPK activation can downregulate mTOR signaling, which not only contributes to increased autophagic clearance but also appears to correlate with improved organization of junctional proteins, ultimately enhancing transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). In experimental settings using RPE cells, the administration of AICAR under oxidative or high‐glucose stress conditions leads to a cascade of phosphorylation events that foster an environment conducive to tight junction assembly while simultaneously stabilizing cellular energy stores (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This biochemical cascade is further verified by the reversal of the observed effects upon the use of compound C, an AMPK inhibitor, which underscores the specificity of AICAR’s action being mediated through AMPK activation (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Villarroel et al., 2011).

It is also critical to note that the effects of AICAR on AMPK activity are influenced not only by its rapid intracellular conversion but also by the intrinsic cellular context—including the balance of energy substrates, the presence of other nucleosides, and the isoform‐specific roles of AMPK (Qin & De Vries, 2008). The resultant activation of AMPK leads to multifaceted downstream responses, such as cellular adaptation to metabolic stress, regulation of inflammatory mediators, and modulation of cytoskeletal elements that cooperate in the maintenance of cell–cell adhesion within the RPE monolayer (Villarroel et al., 2011). This detailed mechanistic insight provides the foundation for hypothesizing that AICAR may effectively drive energy homeostasis and promote tight junction assembly in RPE cells, addressing one of the core pathological features of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
In the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration, the primary pathological hallmark is the degeneration of the RPE accompanied by impaired tight junction integrity and compromised barrier function, resulting in increased paracellular permeability and accumulation of metabolic waste. Based on the observed effects of AICAR in in vitro RPE models, it is expected that AICAR will allosterically activate AMPK within RPE cells, leading to enhanced energy homeostasis and improved assembly of tight junctions (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Experimental data have demonstrated that when induced with oxidative stress, as is common in AMD, treatment with 500 µM AICAR increased TEER from 90 to 135 Ω·cm²—a clear indicator of enhanced barrier integrity (Miyagishima et al., 2021). This increase in TEER is paralleled by a 2.8‐fold elevation in phosphorylated AMPK levels, which confirms that AICAR is effectively engaging its intended target in these cells (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011).

The underlying mechanism for this improved barrier function is thought to be twofold. First, through ACC inhibition—mediated by AMPK activation—there is a shift in the cellular lipid economy, reducing the deleterious lipid accumulation that can disrupt tight junction architecture (Qin & De Vries, 2008). Second, the activation of autophagic pathways facilitates the clearance of oxidatively damaged proteins and organelles, thereby enhancing the overall health of the RPE and reinforcing its capacity to maintain tight junction complexes (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). This dual action not only addresses the immediate energetic deficit induced by oxidative stress but also contributes to the structural resilience of the RPE monolayer.

Moreover, the observed reversal of AICAR’s protective effects by compound C serves as strong evidence that the benefit is specifically mediated through the AMPK pathway rather than off‐target effects (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014). This mechanistic specificity is critical when evaluating a compound for clinical translation, as it suggests that downstream effects such as TEER enhancement, tight junction stabilization, and modulation of paracellular flux are directly attributable to AMPK activation. Additionally, AICAR‐mediated autophagy has been implicated in maintaining cellular integrity under chronic oxidative stress—a condition that is intrinsically linked to the progression of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Given the central role of AMPK in RPE physiology, particularly in the regulation of junction protein stability and energy metabolism, the expected therapeutic effect of AICAR in dry AMD is to restore and preserve RPE barrier function. This restoration is anticipated to limit paracellular fluid leakage, reduce the deposition of extracellular debris, and ultimately slow the degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011). The projected outcome is an improvement in cellular homeostasis and reduced progression of retinal degeneration, which translates into a potential clinical benefit for patients with dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History and Prior Applications:  
AICAR’s journey from a metabolic intermediate to a pharmacologically active compound has been well documented across a range of biomedical research areas. In preclinical studies, AICAR has been extensively utilized to activate AMPK in various cellular models, thereby providing critical insights into the regulation of energy balance, mitochondrial biogenesis, and lipid metabolism (Green, 2013; Pokrywka et al., 2014). Its early applications in skeletal muscle and cancer cells underscored its ability to stimulate glucose uptake and shift cellular energy dynamics in favor of catabolic pathways (Dolinar et al., 2018; Longnus et al., 2003).

In cardiovascular research, AICAR was instrumental in elucidating the mechanisms underlying glycogenolysis and vasorelaxation, where its conversion to ZMP led to the activation of AMPK in vascular smooth muscle cells, resulting in beneficial metabolic adaptations (Pyla et al., 2022). Although these studies did not directly target ocular tissues, they established a robust framework for understanding how AMPK activation can mediate protective responses under conditions of metabolic stress.

The transition of AICAR into the realm of ophthalmological research was driven by the observation that AMPK is a pivotal regulator of RPE function and tight junction assembly. Publications have demonstrated that oxidative stress—a significant contributor to AMD pathology—can impair RPE barrier integrity by disrupting the organization of tight junction proteins, while AMPK activation appears to counteract these deleterious changes (Qin, 2012; Villarroel et al., 2011). In one study, treatment with AICAR in RPE cells under H₂O₂‐induced stress not only increased TEER but also elevated levels of phosphorylated AMPK, thereby indicating enhanced barrier stability (Miyagishima et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the dual role of AMPK in regulating autophagy and lipid metabolism has been a focal point in dry AMD research, as dysfunctional autophagy and lipid accumulation are hallmarks of RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011). The protective effects of AMPK activators in other models of cellular stress, such as in cardiomyocytes and hepatocarcinoma cells, lend additional support to the hypothesis that similar mechanisms may be beneficial in preserving RPE function (Kawashima et al., 2020; Sid et al., 2014).

Despite these promising findings, it is important to note that the therapeutic history of AICAR in the context of ocular diseases remains in the preclinical phase, with limited direct clinical evaluation for dry AMD. Some studies have even suggested that AMPK activation in the RPE could have dual outcomes, potentially inhibiting phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments under oxidative conditions (Qin & De Vries, 2008). This observation highlights the intricacies of AMPK signaling in retinal cells and underscores the need for rigorous dose–response and context–specific studies. Nonetheless, the accumulated preclinical data from both ocular and non‐ocular systems provide a strong rationale for further exploring AICAR as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Expected Impact on RPE Function and Dry AMD Pathology:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of AICAR in dry AMD is that its ability to activate AMPK will lead to a concerted improvement in RPE barrier function and energy homeostasis—two crucial aspects compromised in AMD. In vitro models of RPE, particularly those derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC‐RPE), have shown that exposure to oxidative stress causes significant deterioration in tight junction assembly and barrier integrity, as measured by transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Miyagishima et al., 2021).

When these stressed RPE cells are treated with AICAR, a rapid increase in TEER from approximately 90 Ω·cm² to 135 Ω·cm² has been observed, indicating a substantial enhancement in tight junction integrity (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). At the molecular level, this improvement correlates with a 2.8‐fold rise in phosphorylated AMPK, which is directly associated with the activation of energy restoration pathways and the stabilization of tight junction proteins (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011).

The benefits conferred by AMPK activation are expected to be multifaceted. On one hand, the inhibition of ACC through phosphorylation is anticipated to reduce aberrant lipid synthesis and promote fatty acid oxidation, thereby alleviating metabolic stress within RPE cells (Qin & De Vries, 2008). On the other hand, enhanced autophagic flux driven by AMPK is likely to facilitate the removal of oxidatively damaged proteins and organelles, contributing to cellular repair processes that are pivotal in slowing the progression of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

These laboratory observations have practical implications. In a dysregulated retinal environment—characterized by oxidative damage, inflammatory cytokine presence, and disrupted tight junctions—the activation of AMPK by AICAR could serve as a countermeasure to re‐establish and maintain the critical barrier functions of the RPE (Villarroel et al., 2011). Moreover, by diminishing paracellular leak and preserving the integrity of junctional complexes, AICAR may reduce the accumulation of metabolic waste products and drusen, which are pathological hallmarks of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

It is also noteworthy that the experimental reversal of AICAR’s protective effects by compound C—a well‐known AMPK inhibitor—provides definitive evidence that the beneficial outcomes observed in RPE cells are mediated specifically through AMPK signaling (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014). This on‐target specificity increases the confidence that the observed improvements in TEER are attributable to the intended mechanism rather than off‐target pharmacological actions. Consequently, the expected therapeutic effect in dry AMD would involve enhanced RPE cell viability, reduced cellular stress, and a restored barrier function that together could slow or even halt the progressive degeneration observed in patients (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Overall Evaluation:  
When evaluating AICAR as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, several strengths are immediately apparent, along with a number of challenges that must be carefully addressed during further development. One of the foremost strengths of AICAR is its well–characterized mechanism of action. By serving as an AMP analog that is intracellularly converted to ZMP, AICAR robustly activates AMPK—a key cellular energy sensor that orchestrates a wide range of metabolic responses (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). This activation is tightly coupled to downstream effects such as ACC inhibition, enhanced fatty acid oxidation, and the promotion of autophagy, which are all beneficial in counteracting the metabolic and oxidative stresses inherent in dry AMD (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012).

Furthermore, the experimental data indicating a significant increase in TEER and a concomitant rise in phosphorylated AMPK levels in oxidatively stressed iPSC‐RPE cells provide compelling evidence that AICAR can restore RPE barrier function (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This is particularly important because tight junction integrity and paracellular barrier properties are central to the maintenance of retinal homeostasis and are critically impaired in dry AMD (Villarroel et al., 2011). The demonstration that the beneficial effects of AICAR are reversible by an AMPK inhibitor further reinforces the concept that the drug’s actions are on–target and biologically relevant (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014).

Nevertheless, several potential weaknesses require cautious evaluation. First, while AMPK activation is generally associated with enhanced cellular resilience, some studies have reported that excessive or isoform‐specific activation of AMPK in RPE cells may lead to unintended consequences, such as the inhibition of photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis—a process vital for retinal renewal (Qin & De Vries, 2008). Such a dualistic role of AMPK creates a delicate balance whereby the same pathway that is intended to improve barrier function might also impede essential RPE functions if not precisely modulated.

Additionally, the data in the literature suggest that under certain circumstances, AMPK activation might even contribute to increased epithelial permeability rather than a strengthening of tight junctions (Villarroel et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This paradoxical effect raises concerns about potential context–dependent outcomes of AICAR treatment. For example, while low‐to‐moderate activation of AMPK might support tight junction assembly and autophagy, hyperactivation under severe metabolic or oxidative stress could exacerbate junctional disorganization, thereby counteracting any beneficial effects (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Another challenge is the potential for systemic side effects arising from AICAR’s widespread actions in other tissues. Given that AICAR has been employed in models of diabetes, cardiac metabolism, and even cancer, its pleiotropic effects could impose additional safety considerations when repurposed for ocular use (Pokrywka et al., 2014; Viglino et al., 2019). There is also the issue of dosage; concentrations of 500 µM are effective in vitro, but translating such dosages to in vivo ocular applications requires careful pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies to ensure that therapeutic levels are achieved locally without eliciting undesirable systemic responses (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Asby et al., 2015).

Moreover, given the complex interplay between AMPK signaling, autophagy, and cellular differentiation processes, it is essential to thoroughly understand the long‐term implications of chronic AMPK activation in the RPE. While short‐term activation may be protective, persistent stimulation could lead to energy depletion or maladaptive remodeling of the RPE cytoskeleton, which in turn could affect visual function (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). This underscores the need for extensive preclinical studies that evaluate both the efficacy and the safety profile of AICAR over prolonged periods.

Finally, the inherent variability in patient responses due to genetic, metabolic, and environmental factors presents an additional hurdle. The RPE’s response to oxidative stress, and hence its sensitivity to AMPK modulation, may vary widely among individuals with dry AMD. It will be crucial to identify biomarkers that predict response to AICAR treatment and to tailor dosing regimens accordingly (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

In summary, while AICAR shows considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD by virtue of its well‐established mechanism of AMPK activation, experimental data demonstrating tight junction rescue in RPE cells, and its ability to promote autophagic processes that counteract oxidative stress, its repurposing is tempered by concerns regarding the dualistic effects of AMPK signaling in the RPE, potential systemic side effects, and the challenges associated with dosage translation from in vitro to in vivo applications (Villarroel et al., 2011). The overall evaluation is that AICAR exhibits several compelling advantages—including mechanistic clarity, on‐target efficacy, and a robust preclinical rationale—that substantiate further investigation through rigorous preclinical and, eventually, clinical studies. With a careful approach that addresses the aforementioned weaknesses, AICAR may ultimately emerge as a valuable addition to the therapeutic arsenal against dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Comprehensive Future Directions and Considerations:  
To fully validate AICAR’s potential for treating dry AMD, a series of detailed investigations is warranted. First, further elucidation of the dose–response relationship in RPE cell cultures will be critical. This includes not only establishing the optimal concentration of AICAR to achieve maximal TEER improvement and AMPK activation but also determining whether these effects are sustained over time without incurring cellular toxicity (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011). Long‐term studies are needed to assess whether repeated dosing maintains barrier integrity or if adaptive processes eventually diminish the protective effects of AICAR.

Additionally, it will be necessary to delve deeper into the isoform‐specific effects of AMPK in the RPE. Evidence suggests that the α2 isoform in particular plays a critical role in mediating responses to oxidative stress and that its activation may differ qualitatively from that of the α1 subunit (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012). Understanding these nuances will help design therapeutic strategies that maximize the beneficial aspects of AMPK activation while minimizing potential adverse outcomes, such as impaired phagocytosis or unwanted alterations in cellular metabolism (Qin & De Vries, 2008).

In parallel, investigating the interplay between AICAR‐induced AMPK activation and autophagic pathways in the RPE will shed light on how tightly coupled these processes are in the context of dry AMD. Since autophagy is vital for clearing oxidatively damaged cellular components and supporting cell survival, it will be important to determine whether prolonged AMPK activation fosters a beneficial autophagic flux or rather leads to autophagy dysregulation over time (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). Strategies that involve monitoring autophagic markers along with TEER measurements and junction protein expression could provide a comprehensive picture of cellular health in AICAR‐treated RPE cells.

Given the concerns regarding potential systemic effects, advanced drug delivery systems such as localized intraocular injections or biodegradable implants could be considered for delivering AICAR directly to the retina, thereby limiting systemic exposure and enhancing local efficacy (Viglino et al., 2019; Sid et al., 2014). Preclinical animal models that mimic the pathological features of dry AMD will be indispensable in evaluating the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and therapeutic windows of AICAR in an in vivo setting. Such studies would also be instrumental in identifying potential adverse effects and assessing the long‐term safety profile of AICAR when administered via ocular routes.

Another key consideration is the potential for combination therapy. Since some reports indicate that AMPK activation by AICAR might impair certain RPE functions such as phagocytosis if excessively activated, combining AICAR with other agents that either modulate AMPK isoform activity or protect against excessive autophagic stimulation may provide a synergistic benefit (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Villarroel et al., 2011). For instance, the protective effect of fenofibric acid in preventing AICAR‐induced permeability increases has been documented, suggesting that a combination approach may overcome the limitations of monotherapy (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Finally, translational studies will need to integrate biomarker analyses capable of monitoring AMPK activation status, autophagy markers, and tight junction protein localization in the RPE. These biomarkers could guide dose optimization and serve as early indicators of therapeutic response in clinical trials (Villarroel et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008). Genetic or epigenetic factors that predispose individuals to variations in RPE responsiveness may also be identified, thereby enabling personalized medicine approaches for patients with dry AMD.

In conclusion, while there remain numerous challenges and uncertainties, AICAR represents a highly promising candidate for repurposing as a barrier‐protective agent in dry AMD. Its capacity to robustly activate AMPK, improve cellular energy homeostasis, promote autophagy, and restore tight junction integrity in RPE cells offers a multifaceted mode of action that addresses several key pathological features of dry AMD. With targeted preclinical studies that unpack the complexity of AMPK signaling in retinal tissues and strategic clinical trial designs that mitigate potential adverse effects, AICAR could conceivably fill a significant therapeutic gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Overall Conclusions:  
AICAR’s well‐documented ability to mimic AMP—thereby inducing AMPK activation—and its established role in regulating cellular energy balance and autophagy place it squarely in the category of compounds with high therapeutic potential for metabolic disorders. Emerging evidence in retinal models, particularly those simulating the oxidative stress and barrier dysfunction typical of dry AMD, further reinforces the rationale behind its repurposing. Nonetheless, while preclinical data are encouraging, careful consideration must be given to the dualistic nature of AMPK signaling in the RPE, as well as the potential systemic risks associated with systemic exposure. Despite these challenges, the convergence of multiple lines of evidence—from improved TEER measurements and specific molecular activation to supportive mechanistic studies—strongly advocates for further research into AICAR as a viable therapeutic strategy for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

In summary, the repurposing of AICAR for dry AMD is supported by both its robust mechanistic underpinnings and its promising preclinical efficacy data, placing it among the most attractive candidates for modulating RPE barrier integrity in this debilitating disease. Future studies that focus on fine‐tuning its dosage, delivery, and integrated combination therapies hold the key to unlocking its full therapeutic potential and advancing it from the bench to the clinic (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012).

Taking into account the strengths of its well‐defined mechanism, the reproducible experimental data demonstrating barrier rescue in RPE cells, and the feasibility of its pharmacological modulation, AICAR represents a compelling candidate for further development in the treatment of dry AMD. With continued advances in targeted drug delivery and combination therapeutics, the prospects for leveraging AICAR’s metabolic and protective effects in the retina are promising, warranting its inclusion in the strategic pipeline for combating age‐related macular degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

This comprehensive evaluation underscores that while challenges remain—including potential dose‐dependent effects, off‐target actions, and the need for precise modulation of AMPK isoforms—the overall body of evidence provides a solid rationale for advancing AICAR in preclinical and ultimately clinical studies focused on dry AMD. Its capacity to restore RPE barrier integrity under oxidative stress, coupled with its well‐established pharmacodynamic properties, offers a therapeutic strategy that could mitigate the progression of retinal degeneration and improve visual outcomes for patients suffering from this currently untreatable condition (Villarroel et al., 2011).
