────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

Torin-1 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule compound that belongs to the second generation of mTOR inhibitors. Its discovery originated from high-throughput biochemical screening efforts led by Nathanael Gray’s research group, and later advances were carried out in both academic and industrial settings (Ali et al., 2022). Unlike the first-generation mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin and its analogs—agents that inhibit mTOR activity by forming a complex with FKBP12 and acting allosterically—Torin-1 belongs to a class of ATP-competitive inhibitors that target the catalytic site of mTOR directly (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). Chemically, Torin-1 is built on a quinoline or pyrazolopyrimidine core scaffold; such a design was informed by molecular docking studies and X-ray crystallographic analyses that revealed the ability of these scaffolds to form critical hydrogen bonds with residues in the mTOR ATP-binding pocket, notably with Asp2195 and Lys2187 (Ali et al., 2022; He et al., 2017). The compound’s outstanding potency is reflected in its low nanomolar inhibitory concentrations – with reported IC₅₀ values near 2 nM for mTORC1—and its ability to simultaneously inhibit mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) distinguishes it from macrolide-based compounds (Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Schenone et al., 2011). As part of the so-called “TORKinibs,” Torin-1 is representative of a modern strategy in kinase inhibition, leveraging structure-guided design to achieve comprehensive blockade of the mTOR signaling cascade.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

Since its initial discovery, Torin-1 has primarily been employed as a biochemical and cellular tool in preclinical research rather than as a drug that has advanced to the clinical arena. Its potent inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 has allowed researchers to dissect the functional roles of mTOR in diverse cellular processes such as protein synthesis, metabolism, autophagy regulation, and cell cycle progression (Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013). In oncology studies, Torin-1 has been used to demonstrate that complete inhibition of mTOR signaling—especially the blockade of mTORC2, which is seldom affected by allosteric inhibitors—can lead to robust antiproliferative effects and induction of apoptosis in cancer cells (Xie et al., 2016; Amin et al., 2021).

In the retinal space, there is emerging evidence supporting the use of ATP-competitive inhibitors in models of photoreceptor and RPE dysfunction. For example, studies in the rd1 mouse model of retinal degeneration have shown that treatment with Torin-1 results in marked suppression of mTOR phosphorylation; such inhibition correlates with an increase in autophagy markers (elevated LC3B-II/LC3B-I ratio) and consequent neuroprotective effects, including a reduction in photoreceptor apoptosis (Yang et al., 2021). Furthermore, investigations employing human retinal pigment epithelial cells, such as ARPE-19 or transformed RPE lines like hTERT-RPE1, have demonstrated that Torin-1 treatment can effectively promote autophagic flux and exert protective effects under conditions of cellular stress (Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017). Despite promising preclinical data in RPE and retinal degeneration models, Torin-1 has not yet been formally evaluated in clinical trials for dry AMD; rather, previous clinical efforts for AMD have focused on allosteric mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2006; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008). Thus, while Torin-1 itself remains a potent research probe, its clinical utility in ocular diseases awaits further validation.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

At its core, Torin-1 functions by robustly and directly inhibiting mTOR kinase activity through an ATP-competitive mechanism. Unlike rapamycin, which requires the formation of an FKBP12 complex and employs an allosteric mode of inhibition that selectively attenuates mTORC1 activity, Torin-1 enters the catalytic domain of mTOR and competes with ATP for occupancy of the active site (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). Structural studies have detailed that Torin-1 establishes multiple hydrogen bonds within the mTOR pocket—specifically, two hydrogen bonds between its urea NH groups and Asp2195, and one bond involving a carbonyl moiety and Lys2187 (Ali et al., 2022; He et al., 2017). This binding configuration not only accounts for its superior potency (IC₅₀ values as low as 2 nM) but also ensures a high degree of selectivity compared to kinases within the PI3K family (Schenone et al., 2011).

The inhibition of mTOR by Torin-1 leads to immediate downstream consequences. In mTORC1, the blockade results in the complete ablation of S6K phosphorylation, thereby reducing protein synthesis and halting anabolic growth processes. Concurrently, inhibition of mTORC2 is evidenced by decreased phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473, implicating effects on survival signaling (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). One particularly important downstream effect is the release of ULK1 (unc-51-like kinase 1) from mTOR-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation. Under nutrient-rich conditions, active mTOR phosphorylates ULK1 on serine residues (such as Ser758) to prevent its activation, keeping autophagy in check. When mTOR is inhibited by Torin-1, ULK1 is derepressed, allowing it to drive the conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and initiate autophagosome formation (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017). This induction of autophagy plays a central role in the compound’s proposed mechanism in RPE cells, linking enzyme inhibition to the clearance of potentially toxic cellular debris, including complement components that compromise intercellular junctions.

It is also important to note that, given mTOR’s central role in regulating metabolic homeostasis and proteostasis, the dual inhibition of both mTOR complexes by Torin-1 shifts the cellular balance from an anabolic, protein-synthesizing state to a catabolic, degradation-oriented state (Guillem, 2015). In this context, the activation of autophagy via ULK1 is not only a marker of cellular stress response but also a potential mechanism to clear aggregated proteins and damaged organelles that may contribute to disease pathology.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

Dry AMD is characterized by the progressive dysfunction of RPE cells, which is associated with chronic, low-grade complement activation and the deposition of sublytic membrane attack complexes (MAC). In dry AMD, the persistent presence of complement fragments and sublytic MAC can lead to a collapse of the zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) belt that normally maintains tight junction integrity between RPE cells. This disruption is usually accompanied by a decrease in transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a quantitative measure of barrier function, and is thought to contribute to subsequent photoreceptor degeneration.

The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin-1 in dry AMD posits that by completely inhibiting mTOR activity, the compound will relieve the suppression of ULK1, thereby triggering strong autophagic activity in RPE cells. Enhanced autophagy is expected to facilitate the clearance of sublytic MAC deposits and accumulated complement fragments. From in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cell monolayers—a widely accepted model for RPE barrier function—it has been observed that complement C5b-9 challenge provokes a significant (approximately 40%) drop in TEER and disrupts ZO-1 continuity, indicating tight junction breakdown (Vogel et al., 2017). When these cells are concomitantly treated with Torin-1, the compound’s potent, low-nanomolar inhibition of mTOR translates into complete ablation of phosphorylated S6K and a three-fold elevation in LC3-II flux. This biochemical change is accompanied by a restoration of TEER values to approximately 220 Ω·cm², suggesting that the autophagic clearance of toxic complement fragments enables the reestablishment of the ZO-1 junctional belt (Lim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

The exact molecular pathway can be described as follows: upon Torin-1 binding and subsequent mTOR inhibition, phosphorylation of downstream targets including S6K and Akt is halted. This cessation effectively lifts the inhibitory phosphorylation of ULK1, catalyzing its activation. Activated ULK1 initiates autophagy, leading to a conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II, a process that enhances autophagic flux and promotes the degradation of intracellular debris (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017). Within RPE cells under complement attack, this mechanism is hypothesized to specifically clear sublytic MAC deposits; by doing so, the cellular proteostasis is restored, which in turn allows for the reinstitution of normal tight junction architecture – as evidenced by a continuous ZO-1 belt and maintenance of TEER (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021).

Moreover, the effect on TEER is especially critical since the loss of barrier function in RPE cells is an early indicator of dry AMD disease progression. By preserving TEER, Torin-1 is not just engaging in an acute cytoprotective action; it is potentially interrupting the cascade that leads to chronic subretinal degeneration. In this way, Torin-1 may contribute to both the immediate stabilization of the RPE barrier and the longer-term maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Such outcomes would ameliorate one of the central pathogenic events in dry AMD—namely, RPE junctional collapse—and could help prevent the subsequent photoreceptor loss that underlies vision decline (Lim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

From a molecular and mechanistic standpoint, Torin-1 stands as a highly attractive candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its design as a second-generation, ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor confers several major advantages over first-generation rapalogs. Chief among these is its dual inhibition of mTORC1 and mTORC2, which bypasses the incomplete suppression and feedback activation issues that may limit the efficacy of compounds like rapamycin (Amin et al., 2021; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017). This comprehensive blockade enables a robust activation of autophagy via ULK1 de-repression, and—as demonstrated in various preclinical studies—such autophagic stimulation is capable of clearing aggregated proteins and toxic complement fragments in RPE cells (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017).

Preclinical studies using retinal models are supportive. In experiments employing ARPE-19 and hTERT-RPE1 cells, treatment with Torin-1 has been shown to significantly elevate autophagic markers while reducing the phosphorylation status of mTOR downstream effectors, thereby reinforcing its mechanistic rationale (Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017). Furthermore, in animal models such as the rd1 mouse retina, Torin-1 administration has correlated with reduced mTOR phosphorylation and increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratios, suggestive of effective autophagic clearance and neuroprotective benefit (Yang et al., 2021). These observations provide a strong proof-of-concept that robust mTOR inhibition has the potential to restore RPE homeostasis through autophagy, thereby ameliorating complement-induced junctional disruption—a key pathological process in dry AMD.

However, several critical challenges and limitations must be acknowledged before Torin-1 can be advanced as a clinically viable therapeutic for dry AMD. First and foremost are the pharmacokinetic challenges intrinsic to Torin-1. Multiple reports have noted issues related to its poor water solubility, rapid metabolic degradation, and low oral bioavailability (Artoni, 2024; Guillem, 2015). These characteristics make systemic delivery problematic and would likely necessitate the development of specialized ocular formulations—such as intravitreal injections or sustained-release implants—to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina without causing systemic toxicity.

Another potential weakness lies in the broad role of mTOR in regulating cellular homeostasis. While complete inhibition of mTOR (both mTORC1 and mTORC2) is advantageous in achieving a full autophagic response, it also carries the risk of disrupting normal anabolic and survival signaling pathways in off-target tissues (Ainslie et al., 2016; Artoni, 2024). In the retina, where RPE cells must balance metabolic demands with regenerative processes, prolonged or excessive mTOR inhibition could theoretically impair normal cellular functions, leading to unintended adverse effects such as mistargeted autophagy or metabolic insufficiency.

Furthermore, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease. Although complement activation and subsequent deposition of sublytic MAC are central features, other factors—including chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lipid dysregulation—contribute significantly to disease progression. As a result, while Torin-1’s mechanism of activating autophagy and restoring tight junction protein continuity offers considerable promise, it is unlikely that monotherapy with an mTOR inhibitor will comprehensively reverse or halt disease progression. A multidrug approach or combination therapy that targets several pathogenic pathways concurrently might eventually be required (Ainslie et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).

From the standpoint of formulation and manufacturing, Torin-1 presents additional hurdles. The synthetic route to Torin-1 is known for a low overall yield and complex multi-step procedures, which has driven subsequent research efforts toward the development of more drug-like analogues such as Torin-2. These analogues often exhibit improved solubility, stability, and bioavailability, yet switching to an analogue creates a separate set of regulatory and developmental challenges (Cani, 2015; Guillem, 2015). Given that Torin-1 itself has not been engineered explicitly for ocular delivery, significant formulation work will be necessary to convert it into a viable therapeutic candidate that can be safely and effectively administered to the retina.

In addition, although preclinical studies in ARPE-19 monolayers and rodent models provide important insights, the predictive value of these models for human dry AMD remains imperfect. The complexity of dry AMD, encompassing gradual degenerative changes that evolve over many years against a backdrop of systemic aging, calls for further validation in more sophisticated in vivo models that closely replicate human pathology. Such models would need to capture not only the complement-mediated disruption of RPE tight junctions but also the contributions of chronic inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and extracellular matrix alterations. Only through such rigorous evaluations can the long-term efficacy and safety of Torin-1 (or its improved analogues) be accurately ascertained (Ainslie et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).

Finally, it must be acknowledged that repurposing a molecule like Torin-1 for dry AMD represents a significant translational challenge. While its ability to elevate LC3-II flux, clear toxic deposits, and maintain TEER in vitro is compelling, the real-world application in the human retina requires an intricate balance of efficacy, safety, and appropriate drug delivery. Off-target toxicities due to mTOR inhibition in other retinal cell types or adjacent tissues, as well as the systemic exposure risks even in an ocular formulation, must be stringently evaluated through comprehensive preclinical pharmacokinetic and toxicology studies before any clinical trials could be considered.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation and Conclusions

In summary, Torin-1 is a compelling proof-of-concept candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its synthetic origins as an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor, characterized by an exceptional potency (low-nanomolar IC₅₀) and dual inhibition of mTORC1 and mTORC2, offer a robust mechanistic rationale for its use in restoring RPE cell homeostasis (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin-1 leads to a well-documented derepression of ULK1, activation of autophagy, and a consequent increase in LC3-II flux—changes that are central to the clearance of sublytic MAC deposits and other toxic complement fragments (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017). Preclinical evidence from both retinal cell line experiments and rodent models supports the hypothesis that such mechanistic effects can translate into restored tight junction integrity (as measured by maintenance of ZO-1 belt continuity and TEER) under complement challenge conditions (Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021).

The principal strengths of Torin-1 include its unparalleled potency and selectivity for mTOR; its ability to effectively target both mTOR complexes addresses the shortcomings associated with partial mTORC1 inhibition by rapamycin; and its demonstrated capacity to trigger autophagy offers a direct means to remove deleterious protein aggregates and complement components from RPE cells. These attributes are particularly critical in dry AMD, a disease closely tied to chronic complement activation and the accumulation of toxic cellular debris that disrupts epithelial barrier function.

Nevertheless, several notable challenges must be overcome. Torin-1’s inherent pharmacokinetic limitations—specifically its poor water solubility, rapid metabolic degradation, and low bioavailability—pose significant barriers to its clinical translation (Artoni, 2024; Guillem, 2015). Furthermore, the complete inhibition of mTOR achieved by Torin-1, while beneficial for activating autophagy, also raises concerns regarding off-target toxicities in the retina and beyond, given the central role of mTOR in numerous cellular processes including growth, metabolism, and survival (Ainslie et al., 2016; Artoni, 2024). In an organ as delicate and metabolically active as the retina, these issues necessitate the development of advanced drug delivery systems that can confine the therapeutic effects to the target tissue while minimizing systemic exposure. Options such as intravitreal injections, sustained-release platforms, or nanoparticle-based carriers should be carefully explored.

Moreover, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD means that while clearing complement deposits and restoring tight junction integrity via autophagy represents a promising strategy, it is unlikely to address all pathogenic mechanisms simultaneously. Chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lipid dysregulation also play pivotal roles in the disease’s progression. Therefore, Torin-1 may ultimately need to be integrated into a combination therapy regime or be used in conjunction with adjunctive treatments targeting these other processes (Ainslie et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).

From a developmental perspective, it is also important to consider that while Torin-1 has been used extensively as a research tool, its current chemical properties make it less than ideal as a direct clinical candidate. The extensive medicinal chemistry efforts that led to the synthesis of Torin-2—and other improved analogues—underscore the need to optimize the pharmacological attributes, including solubility and metabolic stability, before any clinical application can be realized (Guillem, 2015). Such optimizations, along with rigorous preclinical in vivo efficacy and safety studies in models that recapitulate the chronic and complex nature of human dry AMD, are essential next steps.

In conclusion, based on the current literature presented in the context, Torin-1 demonstrates substantial mechanistic promise for the restoration of RPE proteostasis, barrier integrity, and autophagic clearance of complement-mediated cellular debris in dry AMD. Its strong ATP-competitive inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2, leading to effective ULK1 activation, supports the hypothesis that it can rescue TEER and reestablish ZO-1 continuity in RPE cells exposed to complement C5b-9 challenge (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013). However, significant translational hurdles—principally related to its pharmacokinetic profile, potential off-target effects, and the inherent complexities of dry AMD pathology—must be diligently addressed through further preclinical research.

From an expert drug development perspective, Torin-1 offers robust proof-of-concept evidence that mTOR inhibition can functionally reverse key pathological features of dry AMD in cellular models. The next steps should focus on optimizing its chemical properties or transitioning to an analog with improved drug-like characteristics, as well as developing innovative ocular delivery platforms to ensure targeted retinal exposure. In light of these considerations, while Torin-1 in its current form may serve best as a preclinical tool to validate the therapeutic pathway, further investment in medicinal chemistry, formulation science, and in vivo safety/efficacy studies is warranted before considering clinical evaluation in patients with dry AMD (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013; Amin et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Final Remarks

To summarize, the current data support the concept that robust, ATP-competitive inhibition of mTOR with compounds such as Torin-1 provides a compelling mechanistic foundation for mitigating complement-mediated RPE damage in dry AMD. The dual mTORC1/mTORC2 targeting strategy of Torin-1 enables it to not only suppress pathogenic anabolic signaling but also to trigger autophagy—thereby facilitating the clearance of toxic sublytic MAC deposits and the restoration of RPE tight junctions, as measured by TEER and ZO-1 integrity. Nevertheless, the translational journey from promising in vitro results to an effective clinical treatment is contingent upon the resolution of pharmacokinetic shortcomings, the development of retina-specific delivery strategies, and extensive in vivo validation in models that mirror the human disease.

In light of the above evaluation, Torin-1 stands as a scientifically robust candidate that validates the therapeutic rationale for mTOR inhibition in dry AMD. Its significant strengths in potency and mechanistic clarity are offset by practical challenges that necessitate further research. The pathway forward should thus include efforts to optimize the formulation and drug-like properties of Torin-1 (or its analogues), pair it with appropriate ocular delivery systems, and deploy rigorous preclinical models to establish its long-term efficacy and safety in the context of dry AMD. Only with these additional steps can Torin-1 (or a derivative thereof) mature into a potential treatment option for patients suffering from this chronic and debilitating disease (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013; Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017; Schenone et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2021; Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017).

Based on the available literature and preclinical evidence, the candidate hypothesis that Torin-1 will restore TEER and ZO-1 belt continuity in RPE cells challenged by complement C5b-9 holds significant promise, warranting further focused preclinical investigation and optimization before any human studies are contemplated.

The hypothesis under evaluation is that inhibition of LOXL2 by PXS-5153A will prevent pathogenic collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in Bruch’s membrane (BM), reduce matrix stiffness, and by indirectly alleviating abnormal mechanical tension on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell receptors, stabilize RPE tight junction anchors (ZO-1/occludin). The following sections provide a detailed analysis of the candidate’s origins, therapeutic history, mechanism of action, expected effects in relevant assays, and a balanced overall evaluation based on the current literature.

I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PXS-5153A is a synthetically derived molecule that belongs to the class of selective lysyl oxidase inhibitors. In its design, medicinal chemistry efforts focused on optimizing potency and selectivity for LOXL2, along with activity against LOXL3, two members of the lysyl oxidase family that catalyze the oxidative deamination of lysine residues in collagens and elastin to promote covalent crosslink formation. These crosslinks confer the mechanical strength and stiffness of extracellular matrices (ECMs) such as Bruch’s membrane. Synthetic routes to compounds like PXS-5153A typically rely on structure-based design and iterative optimization to achieve potent enzyme inhibition with favorable pharmacokinetic properties (Lin et al., 2020). The compound, commercially available under MedChemExpress HY-111217, is representative of a new therapeutic class that has been primarily explored in the context of fibrosis and tumor microenvironment modulation. Given that ECM stiffening is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, targeting LOXL2 represents a novel approach compared to conventional anti-inflammatory or anti-angiogenic strategies.

II. Therapeutic History  
The LOXL2 inhibitor class, including molecules such as PXS-5153A, has been extensively tested in preclinical models of fibrosis and cancer. For example, within non-ocular systems, LOXL2 activity has been linked to increased tissue stiffness that fosters metastatic progression and desmoplastic reactions in tumors, and selective inhibition of LOXL2 has been shown to reduce crosslink density, attenuating fibrotic remodeling (Lin et al., 2020). Experimental inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity using non-selective agents like β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) has also been applied to in vitro and in vivo models to modulate ECM assembly, with effects on barrier function observed in RPE cultures co-treated with endothelial cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). Although LOXL2 inhibitors have not traditionally been used to treat dry AMD, evidence underscores the centrality of aberrant ECM crosslinking in BM thickening observed during aging and AMD progression (Wang et al., 2025). In particular, the endothelial cell–RPE crosstalk studies demonstrate a critical role for lysyl oxidase activity in regulating collagen bundle formation and in establishing RPE barrier properties (Benedicto et al., 2017). Accordingly, while there is no direct clinical or preclinical record of PXS-5153A in AMD, the antifibrotic profile of the compound and its impact on extracellular matrix mechanics in other disease contexts serve as a compelling rationale to explore its application in dry AMD.

III. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, LOXL2 catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of lysine or hydroxylysine residues present in collagens and elastin. This reaction is critical for the formation of covalent crosslinks that stabilize the ECM. Overexpression or hyperactivity of LOXL2 results in an excessively crosslinked and stiff matrix. In the eye, particularly within Bruch’s membrane—which is a complex, stratified ECM structure located between the RPE and the choroid—aberrant collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking are known to increase mechanical tension. Such mechanical changes are thought to adversely affect RPE cell function by interfering with integrin-mediated cell–matrix interactions and perturbing the proper localization of tight junction proteins, including ZO-1 and occludin (Benedicto et al., 2017).

PXS-5153A functions by binding to the catalytic pocket of LOXL2, thereby preventing its enzymatic activity. By blocking the oxidative deamination step, PXS-5153A reduces the formation of both immature and mature crosslinks in ECM proteins. The anticipated outcome is a lower crosslink density in Bruch’s membrane, resulting in a softer, more compliant matrix environment. This reduction in mechanical stiffness is expected to diminish abnormal mechanosignaling through β1 integrins, which are integral to the assembly and maintenance of tight junctions on RPE cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). The downstream consequences of reduced integrin activation include dampening of Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways, which in turn facilitate the stabilization and proper localization of tight junction proteins at the RPE cell membranes (Benedicto et al., 2017). Restoration of these junctional complexes correlates with improved barrier function, typically measured as an increased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in cell culture models. This mechanism is supported by studies in which inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity—by pharmacological agents such as BAPN—led to alterations in RPE barrier properties and tight junction morphology (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by directly targeting LOXL2, PXS-5153A is proposed to correct the pathological ECM remodeling that underlies BM stiffening in dry AMD while re-establishing proper RPE barrier integrity.

IV. Expected Effect  
The expected therapeutic effect of PXS-5153A in dry AMD centers on normalization of the BM ECM and concomitant restoration of RPE barrier function. In the proposed experimental model—an in vitro co-culture system where human fetal RPE (hfRPE) cells are grown on a substrate mimicking BM with defined stiffness—the application of PXS-5153A at concentrations around 5 µM is anticipated to yield a number of favorable outcomes.

First, by reducing LOXL2-mediated crosslinking of collagen IV and fibronectin, the drug should decrease the mechanical stiffness of the BM analog. A less rigid BM reduces aberrant integrin activation on the basolateral surfaces of RPE cells, which has been shown to be critical for proper tight junction assembly. In several studies, when the extracellular matrix is normalized—such as by altering substrate stiffness—there is an improvement in the localization of key tight junction proteins, specifically occludin and ZO-1, at the cell membrane (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Second, the reduced matrix stiffness is expected to alleviate the mechanical stress experienced by RPE cells, thereby facilitating the re-establishment of cell polarity and intercellular junction continuity. The stabilization of junctional complexes is measurable by TEER. In previous EC–RPE co-culture experiments, modulation of ECM mechanical properties directly correlated with increased TEER values, reflecting improved barrier function (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Moreover, the proper organization of the basement membrane is not only a structural consideration; the biochemical signaling through β1 integrin receptors—critical for maintaining cell adhesion and survival—would return toward homeostatic levels, further supporting the integrity of the RPE layer (Benedicto et al., 2017). These integrin-mediated signals influence downstream effectors such as Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK, which have been implicated in regulating tight junction dynamics (Benedicto et al., 2017). Progress in these pathways is expected to manifest as an overall improvement in the barrier phenotype, which is central to preventing the leakage of fluid and other deleterious solutes into the subretinal space—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.

In summary, it is anticipated that treatment with PXS-5153A in appropriate in vitro (and ultimately in vivo) models will lead to:  
• Reduced collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in BM, yielding a matrix with decreased stiffness (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Normalization of β1 integrin signaling and subsequent reorganization of RPE tight junctions with improved localization of proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Restoration of barrier function as evidenced by increased TEER measurements and improved paracellular permeability profiles (Benedicto et al., 2017).  

Thus, PXS-5153A is expected to address one of the core aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis by targeting ECM remodeling, which in turn indirectly stabilizes RPE cell function.

V. Overall Evaluation  
The concept of using PXS-5153A to modulate ECM pathology in dry AMD is compelling given the mechanistic insights derived from studies on lysyl oxidase activity in epithelial barrier function and ECM assembly. Among the strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its robust preclinical evidence in fibrosis and tumor microenvironment models. LOXL2 has been implicated in promoting tissue stiffening by catalyzing the crosslinking of collagen and fibronectin in various tissues (Lin et al., 2020). The pathophysiological parallels between fibrotic ECM remodeling in cancers and the stiffening of Bruch’s membrane in dry AMD provide a strong rationale for repurposing a LOXL2 inhibitor in an ocular context. Numerous studies have demonstrated that extracellular matrix integrity is essential for optimal RPE barrier function, and that even subtle changes in ECM mechanics can disrupt junctional complexes and lead to barrier dysfunction (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by targeting a critical enzymatic step in ECM crosslinking, PXS-5153A may confer dual benefits: it could both reduce the pathological stiffening of Bruch’s membrane and promote the reorganization of tight junction complexes, ultimately resulting in enhanced TEER and stabilization of the outer blood–retina barrier.

However, several important weaknesses or uncertainties must be considered. First, while numerous studies (using agents such as BAPN) have illustrated that lysyl oxidase inhibition affects RPE barrier function, direct evidence with selective LOXL2 inhibitors—specifically in ocular models of dry AMD—is lacking (Buniello et al., 2025). In fact, the Open Targets Platform indicates only a weak direct association between LOXL2 and age-related macular degeneration, based on limited literature evidence (Buniello et al., 2025). This raises the possibility that, although LOXL2 plays a demonstrable role in ECM crosslinking in other tissues, its specific involvement in dry AMD pathogenesis may not be as pronounced or may be influenced by other factors not recapitulated in non-ocular models.

Furthermore, potential off-target effects or the consequences of broadly altering ECM crosslinking in the eye must be carefully examined. The structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane is critical not only for its barrier function but also for nutrient transport between the choroidal circulation and the RPE. Overinhibition of LOXL2, or interference with normal ECM turnover, may inadvertently lead to basement membrane disorganization, as has been observed when lysyl oxidase activity was inhibited during critical periods of retinal development (Benedicto et al., 2017). This underscores the need for precise dose optimization and targeted delivery, ideally restricted to the ocular environment, to avoid systemic side effects.

Another consideration is the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. In addition to ECM stiffening, dry AMD involves multifactorial processes including oxidative stress, complement activation, inflammation, and the accumulation of lipoprotein deposits. Thus, while normalizing matrix stiffness is likely to improve RPE barrier function, it may be insufficient to fully arrest or reverse the disease process on its own. A combination therapy that also addresses the inflammatory and degenerative components of AMD may eventually be required (Benedicto et al., 2017; Caban et al., 2022).

From a development perspective, there is significant strength in the repurposing strategy because agents like PXS-5153A already have a detailed preclinical profile in non-ocular fibrotic models. This existing data can accelerate preclinical validation in ocular models, with studies planned in RPE–BM co-culture systems using TEER as a functional readout (Benedicto et al., 2017). Furthermore, leveraging well-characterized in vitro assays (such as those involving decellularized ECM and substrate stiffness modulation as described in the context) offers a clear experimental framework to evaluate whether the normalization of BM stiffness by PXS-5153A is sufficient to restore RPE tight junction integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017).

Nonetheless, one notable weakness is the limited direct evidence linking LOXL2 specifically to dry AMD. Although elevated lysyl oxidase activity and changes in collagen crosslinking have been observed in the context of RPE barrier function and BM integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017), the genetic and translational data associating LOXL2 with AMD are not robust. The relatively low association score (Buniello et al., 2025) suggests that additional studies are needed to clarify LOXL2’s role in the eye and to determine whether its inhibition will yield a therapeutically meaningful benefit in dry AMD patients.

In conclusion, repurposing PXS-5153A for dry AMD represents an innovative strategy that leverages the known antifibrotic effects of LOXL2 inhibition to address the deleterious ECM remodeling observed in aged Bruch’s membrane. The candidate’s synthetic origins and prior applications in fibrosis and cancer studies provide a solid foundation for its use, while the mechanistic rationale—centered on reducing pathological crosslinking and restoring RPE barrier function—is strongly supported by evidence from ECM modulation studies (Benedicto et al., 2017). However, challenges remain due to the lack of direct ocular data, potential risks of overmodulating ECM integrity, and the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology. Future research must focus on rigorous in vitro validation in RPE–BM co-culture systems and in vivo studies in relevant AMD animal models to establish the efficacy and safety profile of PXS-5153A in the context of dry AMD. Overall, despite these uncertainties, PXS-5153A holds promise as a novel ECM-targeted therapeutic candidate that could complement existing and emerging treatment strategies for this currently unmet clinical need (Lin et al., 2020; Buniello et al., 2025).

Taken together, the strengths of a clear mechanism of action, potent enzyme selectivity, and an innovative approach toward ECM normalization position PXS-5153A as an attractive candidate warranting further investigation. Nonetheless, a careful reappraisal of the molecular role of LOXL2 in the ocular microenvironment, along with detailed studies on dosing, delivery, and potential off-target effects, will be critical in determining whether this candidate can be successfully repurposed for treating dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Arimoclomol (also known as BRX-345) is a synthetic hydroxylamine/hydroxamic-acid–derived small molecule developed as a heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducer that amplifies stress-inducible transcription of heat shock genes under conditions of proteotoxic stress, principally through prolongation and potentiation of heat shock factor-1 (HSF1) activation on heat shock elements (HSEs) in target promoters (Penke et al., 2018; Parfitt et al., 2014; O’Leary, 2019). In the hydroximic-acid derivative family (bimoclomol, arimoclomol, NG-094, BGP-15), several members synergistically enhance heat-induced Hsp expression; arimoclomol and bimoclomol have been shown to increase HSF1 activity via hyperphosphorylation and to amplify heat-shock gene expression in eukaryotic cells while sparing basal Hsp expression in unstressed cells, thereby acting as bona fide co-inducers rather than primary HSF1 agonists (Penke et al., 2018). The compound was originally advanced from the bimoclomol chemotype as a more drug-like analogue with similar HSR-potentiating properties and improved pharmacology, and it falls within a broader class of pharmacologic HSP70/HSF1 modulators investigated for neurodegenerative protein-misfolding diseases (e.g., ALS, NPC, tauopathies), as well as select retinal degeneration models (rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa) (Parfitt et al., 2014; Venediktov et al., 2023; Penke et al., 2018). At the biophysical level, hydroximic-acid derivatives can intercalate into cellular membranes, a property hypothesized to contribute to regulation of HSF1 activation/attenuation kinetics and restoration of a protective Hsp profile under stress (Penke et al., 2018). In neuronal cell systems, arimoclomol has also been used in combination with primary HSF1 activators (e.g., celastrol) to achieve robust induction of inducible Hsp70s (HSPA1A, HSPA6) and other stress response proteins at lower inducer doses, consistent with its role as a co-inducer that amplifies pre-existing HSF1 activation (Deane, 2019).

Within the retina, arimoclomol has been evaluated in rod photoreceptor models of misfolded rhodopsin (P23H transgenic rats), where it enhanced Hsp70/Hsp90 expression and improved proteostasis, photoreceptor structure, and visual function; however, there is no published evidence in dry AMD models or direct demonstrations of RPE barrier rescue by arimoclomol, and at least one PRPF31-mutant RPE (RP11) cell system screening showed no aggregate-reducing effect of arimoclomol while an mTOR inhibitor (rapamycin) reduced aggregate burden via autophagy induction (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021). The broader Hsp70/Hsc70 system, chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), and macroautophagy are mechanistically central to RPE proteostasis and AMD pathobiology, establishing a strong rationale for HSF1–HSP70–targeted therapy, but translation from photoreceptor models and exogenous Hsp70 delivery to endogenous induction in RPE remains to be validated for this agent (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Subrizi et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History  
Arimoclomol’s development history is anchored in neurodegeneration and protein-misfolding indications. In SOD1-mutant ALS mice, arimoclomol increased Hsp70 expression and improved motor neuron survival and function, extending lifespan; it progressed to human ALS trials (including a phase 3 program), with mixed outcomes across adult and pediatric indications (O’Leary, 2019; Venediktov et al., 2023). Mechanistically consistent with HSF1 co-induction, arimoclomol is positioned to upregulate a suite of inducible chaperones and components of the proteostasis network rather than single chaperone overexpression, a strategy considered preferable for matching the endogenous disaggregation/refolding machinery and preserving feedback attenuation (O’Leary, 2019).

In the retina, arimoclomol has been tested extensively in rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa (RP) models driven by the P23H misfolding mutation. In P23H-GFP cell models, arimoclomol reduced inclusion incidence and insoluble rod opsin, decreased higher-molecular-weight rhodopsin species, and improved viability, with contemporaneous increases in Hsp70/Hsp90 implying potentiation of the HSR in stressed photoreceptors (Parfitt et al., 2014). In P23H transgenic rats, daily intraperitoneal dosing (10 mg/kg) improved scotopic ERG a- and b-waves, preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness, increased outer segment (OS) length, and improved ultrastructure, consistent with disease modification through HSR and unfolded protein response (UPR) potentiation; Hsp70, Hsp90, and HSF1 were assayed directly in these studies (Parfitt et al., 2014). The authors further observed increased eIF2α phosphorylation and discussed enhanced IRE1/XBP1 activity, indicating crosstalk with ER stress responses (Parfitt et al., 2014). Of note, arimoclomol’s activity appeared contingent on the presence of misfolded-protein stress (i.e., stress-selective action), potentially limiting off-target effects in healthy tissue (Parfitt et al., 2014).

Beyond photoreceptors, the Hsp co-inducer class has retinal neuroprotective precedents: bimoclomol improved early electrophysiologic signs in diabetic rat retina, and the Hsp inducer geranylgeranylacetone protected retinal ganglion cells in a rat glaucoma model, underscoring that Hsp70 induction can be protective across retinal cell types and diseases of proteostasis and stress, although these are class exemplars rather than arimoclomol-specific RPE data (Hesselink, 2016). Separately, exogenous Hsp70 protein delivery to RPE has shown diffusion to the retina and RPE after intravitreal administration, intracellular uptake, lysosomal localization, and protection from oxidative stress and inflammation in ARPE-19 cells, supporting the concept that increasing Hsp70 activity in RPE can be beneficial, albeit via protein pharmacology rather than endogenous induction (Subrizi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Crucially for dry AMD translation, the current literature set provides no in vivo animal or clinical study of arimoclomol in AMD/dry AMD, and no direct measurements of RPE barrier integrity (tight-junction protein preservation or transepithelial electrical resistance [TEER]) following arimoclomol in RPE or AMD models; an RPE disease model of PRPF31 mutation with progressive aggregate accumulation reported that arimoclomol failed to reduce aggregates, whereas rapamycin decreased aggregate load and induced LC3 processing consistent with autophagy activation (LAMP1 and p62 remained unchanged), highlighting context-dependent efficacy and suggesting autophagy induction may be more decisive than Hsp co-induction in some RPE aggregate pathologies (Georgiou, 2021). Thus, while arimoclomol has a positive retinal track record in photoreceptor proteotoxicity and a robust extraocular development history, there is no direct evidence yet of arimoclomol ameliorating dry AMD phenotypes or preserving RPE barrier function in disease-relevant systems (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Arimoclomol is an HSR co-inducer that amplifies HSF1-driven transcription of inducible heat shock proteins under pre-existing cellular stress. Mechanistically, arimoclomol prolongs HSF1 binding to HSEs, increases HSF1 activity (e.g., hyperphosphorylation), and thereby increases transcription of Hsp70/Hsp90 and related chaperones, with limited impact in unstressed cells (i.e., stressor-dependent co-induction) (Penke et al., 2018; O’Leary, 2019; Parfitt et al., 2014). In neuronal cells, arimoclomol enhanced celastrol-induced HSF1 activation to elevate HSPA6, HSPA1A, HSPB1, DNAJB1, and HO-1 at doses that preserved viability and differentiated morphology, supporting efficient co-induction when paired with a primary HSF1 activator (Deane, 2019). In P23H photoreceptor models, arimoclomol reduced insoluble rhodopsin and inclusion incidence, decreased high-molecular-weight species, increased retinal Hsp70/Hsp90, and improved ERG/ONL/OS outcomes; the study observed increased eIF2α phosphorylation and discussed potentiation of the UPR (BiP/IRE1/XBP1), consistent with arimoclomol acting at the intersection of cytosolic HSR and ER homeostasis (Parfitt et al., 2014).

Hsp70 Biology in RPE and AMD. Inducible Hsp70 (HSPA1A/Hsp70-1) is a central, evolutionarily conserved ATPase chaperone that assists folding of nascent chains, refolds damaged/misfolded proteins, buffers aggregation, facilitates “protein triage” toward degradation pathways, and protects cells from apoptosis and inflammatory signaling (e.g., NF-κB pathway), with expression controlled by HSF1 (Ryhänen, 2011; Kivinen, 2018). In the RPE, Hsp70/Hsc70 function intersects both the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) and lysosome-dependent proteolysis. Hsp70 can present misfolded proteins to the UPS via CHIP E3 ligase, regulate disaggregation with co-chaperones HSP40/HSP90/HIP/HOP, and is required for aggregate handling; in proteasome failure, protein aggregates in ARPE-19 cells co-localize with Hsp70 and p62, with p62 undergoing autophagic clearance while Hsp70 binds reversibly and evades autophagic degradation (Kumar et al., 2020; Kivinen et al., 2014; Ryhänen, 2011). Hsp70 is also integral to chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA): cytosolic Hsc70/Hsp70 recognizes KFERQ-containing substrates, delivers them to LAMP-2A at the lysosomal membrane, and ATPase-driven “entropic pulling” and luminal chaperones enable translocation and degradation; oxidative stress reduces HSP70 expression in RPE, impairs CMA, and can dysregulate macroautophagy cross-talk, contributing to RPE death (Chang et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020). Extracellular Hsp70 roles in RPE are complex: exogenous rhHsp70 injections protected against subretinal fibrosis via TLR2/TLR4 and IL-10 induction, while oxidized-lipid stress (4-HNE) can increase extracellular Hsp70 efflux and pro-inflammatory cytokines, indicating that compartmental localization of Hsp70 critically determines immunomodulatory outcomes (Kumar et al., 2020).

Evidence for arimoclomol in RPE cells. Direct mechanistic evidence for arimoclomol action in RPE is limited. A cell-culture report in ARPE-19 asserts that Hsp70 overexpression “with the help of a co-inducer like arimoclomol” suppressed IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α and increased IL-10 and TGF-β1, consistent with Hsp70-mediated IκK/NF-κB inhibition; however, the study details are summarized in low-quality review literature, and direct demonstration of arimoclomol-driven HSF1 activation in RPE is not provided (Kumar et al., 2020). Another ARPE-19-focused review excerpt states that arimoclomol acts on HSF1 to increase cytosolic Hsp70 without increasing extracellular Hsp70 and improved resistance to 4-HNE–induced oxidative stress (relative to paeoniflorin); again, the primary data are not provided here and the review is of limited quality, so these findings should be treated as provisional until replicated (Kumar et al., 2020). Importantly, in an isogenic patient-derived PRPF31-mutant RPE (RP11) model with progressive cytoplasmic aggregate accumulation, a 7-day treatment screen across HSR/UPR/autophagy modulators showed that rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibitor) reduced aggregate load and shifted LC3-I to LC3-II, whereas arimoclomol did not reduce aggregates under the conditions tested, arguing that in this RPE disease context autophagy activation via mTOR inhibition outperformed Hsp co-induction (Georgiou, 2021).

Non-pharmacological Hsp70 induction and autophagy in RPE inform plausibility. Subthreshold retinal thermal stimulation in pig and mouse RPE in vivo induced HSF1 and Hsp70, increased LC3B-II and decreased p62 (consistent with autophagy activation), and increased LAMP2, suggesting potential CMA upregulation, without apoptosis at ~44 °C, confirming that RPE supports coordinated HSR–autophagy programs with an exploitable therapeutic window (but autophagic flux was not directly quantified in vivo) (Amirkavei et al., 2022; Amirkavei et al., 2020). These data reinforce the therapeutic logic for HSF1–Hsp70 upregulation in RPE to restore proteostasis but do not directly validate arimoclomol’s efficacy in RPE (Amirkavei et al., 2022; Amirkavei et al., 2020). Exogenous rhHsp70 trafficking to lysosomes and protection against oxidative stress in ARPE-19 further supports the notion that increasing Hsp70 activity, whether by protein delivery or endogenous induction, can be beneficial to RPE survival under AMD-relevant stressors (Subrizi et al., 2015).

Autophagy and barrier integrity under AMD-relevant stressors. AMD-relevant toxicities (Aβ, lipofuscin/A2E, oxidants) perturb autophagy/lysosomes in RPE, with Aβ decreasing occludin and ZO-1 in ARPE-19 and activating autophagy markers in vitro and in vivo, and A2E promoting lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cell death; impaired UPS and autophagy with aging lead to aggregate accumulation (including p62-positive aggregates) in RPE and drusen, highlighting the importance of restoring both proteasomal and autophagic clearance to protect RPE function and barrier integrity (Wang et al., 2023; Viiri, 2019; Ryhänen, 2011). Hsp70/p62 roles in this axis are mechanistically established: Hsp70 prevents aggregation and participates in aggregate handling, while p62 is an autophagic receptor degraded by autophagy and accumulates when autophagy is impaired; pharmacologic AMPK activation can accelerate p62 clearance during proteasome inhibition and improve RPE survival (Viiri, 2019). To date, arimoclomol has not been shown to modulate CMA or macroautophagy in RPE, nor to preserve tight junctions or TEER in AMD-relevant models (Georgiou, 2021; Kumar et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay hypothesis and rationale. The working hypothesis is that arimoclomol will potentiate stress-triggered HSF1 activity in RPE, elevating inducible Hsp70 and coordinated chaperone networks to stabilize junctional proteostasis, reduce misfolded protein burden, and normalize autophagy (including potentially CMA), thereby preventing degradation of occludin/claudin and restoring TEER under oxidative or drusen-like stress (e.g., H2O2/4-HNE, A2E/lipofuscin, Aβ) (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). This mechanism is biologically plausible: Hsp70 is abundantly expressed in RPE under stress and supports folding and refolding, substrate triage to proteasome via CHIP, and delivery of specific substrates to CMA via Hsc70/LAMP-2A; its induction suppresses NF-κB–driven pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and can raise IL-10/TGF-β1, which together could indirectly protect junctional complexes from cytokine- and stress-mediated degradation (Kumar et al., 2020). Reducing intracellular aggregate load and restoring proteostasis would be expected to mitigate the downstream cascade of mTORC1 activation, p62/LC3-I accumulation, and tight-junction disruption observed in stressed RPE models (e.g., PRPF31-RPE), although in that system arimoclomol was ineffective while rapamycin reduced aggregates, underscoring that Hsp co-induction alone may be insufficient when autophagy is the principal bottleneck (Georgiou, 2021).

Evidence supporting expected effects in RPE assays:  
- Hsp70 induction in retinal tissues has been achieved via HSF1 activation by heat or pharmacologic inducers; in photoreceptor P23H models, arimoclomol increased Hsp70/Hsp90 and reduced aggregation/toxicity, consistent with the proximal arm of the proposed mechanism (HSF1→Hsp70→improved proteostasis) (Parfitt et al., 2014; Amirkavei et al., 2020).  
- In ARPE-19 summaries, arimoclomol increased intracellular (not extracellular) Hsp70 and improved resistance to 4-HNE oxidative stress, and Hsp70 overexpression with help of a co-inducer like arimoclomol suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines, supporting cell-autonomous proteostasis and anti-inflammatory contributions that would be favorable for junctional stability (Kumar et al., 2020).  
- Exogenous rhHsp70 delivery to RPE localizes to lysosomes and reduces oxidative toxicity and inflammation, demonstrating that raising functional Hsp70 in RPE is sufficient to afford cytoprotection, a downstream functional goal of HSF1 co-induction (Subrizi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Evidence arguing for tempered expectations and the need for combination strategies:  
- In PRPF31-mutant RPE, arimoclomol did not reduce aggregates in a 7-day screen, whereas rapamycin shifted LC3 processing and reduced aggregate markers, suggesting that when autophagy is the limiting axis, direct autophagy activation (e.g., mTORC1 inhibition) is required; Hsp co-induction alone may not clear established aggregates or repair autophagic flux (Georgiou, 2021).  
- In primary neuronal ALS models, arimoclomol often failed to induce measurable HSPA1A/HSPA8 and its protective actions occurred without detectable Hsp70 upregulation; HDAC inhibition enhanced Hsp induction by other inducers, arguing that Hsp co-induction efficacy is cell-type and chromatin-context dependent and may require combination therapy to overcome induction thresholds in some cells (potentially relevant to differentiated RPE) (Comaduran et al., 2024).  
- AMD-relevant stressors directly disrupt tight junctions (Aβ reduces occludin and ZO-1 in ARPE-19) and invoke autophagy/lysosomal dysfunction; because arimoclomol’s effects on CMA/macroautophagy in RPE are unproven, barrier rescue may not occur unless autophagic flux is also corrected (Wang et al., 2023).

Assay implementation guidance for decision-making:  
- In vitro human RPE models (primary/donor iPSC-RPE monolayers with high TEER) should be stressed with 4-HNE, H2O2, A2E, or Aβ to recapitulate AMD-relevant proteotoxic and inflammatory conditions, and arimoclomol tested across concentrations paralleling prior cell work (e.g., 10–100 µM) with and without a priming HSF1 activator (celastrol ≤0.3 µM) to evaluate requirement for co-induction, keeping in mind the neuronal data identifying 50 µM arimoclomol + 0.3 µM celastrol as an optimized low-toxicity combination (Deane, 2019).  
- Primary readouts: HSF1 activation (nuclear translocation, Ser phosphorylation), Hsp70/Hsp90 induction (immunoblot, qPCR), autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover with/without bafilomycin, p62 dynamics), CMA markers (LAMP-2A levels, lysosomal Hsc70/Hsp70 substrate colocalization), proteasome activity, aggregate load (FK1, ubiquitin, p62 bodies), and barrier integrity (TEER, ZO-1/occludin/claudin-19 immunostaining continuity) (Kivinen et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2015; Viiri, 2019; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Cytokine profiling (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10, TGF-β1) to detect Hsp70-linked NF-κB effects reported in ARPE-19 (Kumar et al., 2020).  
- Positive comparators: rapamycin for autophagy induction; exogenous rhHsp70 as a proteostasis rescue control; heat-based Hsp70 induction within non-damaging windows to confirm pathway responsiveness (Georgiou, 2021; Subrizi et al., 2015; Amirkavei et al., 2020).

Given the aggregate of evidence, the most realistic expectation is that arimoclomol will increase inducible Hsp70 in stressed RPE if HSF1 can be productively co-induced, reduce misfolded protein accumulation and inflammatory signaling, and potentially improve barrier metrics indirectly by attenuating stressors that degrade junctional complexes; however, without concurrent normalization of autophagic flux and CMA, tight-junction rescue and TEER restoration are uncertain, particularly in models where autophagy is the primary deficit (Georgiou, 2021; Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths supporting arimoclomol for dry AMD RPE barrier rescue:  
- Mechanistic fit: Hsp70/Hsc70 are central “gatekeepers” of RPE proteostasis across the UPS and lysosomal systems, including CMA; restoring inducible Hsp70 via HSF1 co-induction directly targets key failure nodes in RPE aging and AMD pathogenesis (aggregation, impaired clearance, inflammation), aligning with known disease biology (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Kivinen, 2018).  
- Demonstrated retinal efficacy in proteostasis-driven degeneration: arimoclomol increased Hsp70/Hsp90, reduced mutant rhodopsin aggregation, and preserved photoreceptor structure/function in P23H rats, with evidence of concurrent UPR potentiation; this validates the platform concept that HSF1 co-induction plus ER stress modulation can modify retinal degeneration, albeit in photoreceptors rather than RPE (Parfitt et al., 2014).  
- RPE permissiveness to Hsp70-based cytoprotection: exogenous rhHsp70 diffuses to RPE, is internalized, localizes to endolysosomal compartments, reduces IL-6 and cytolysis, and improves viability in oxidative stress paradigms; thus, augmenting Hsp70 in RPE is sufficient to produce protective effects, supporting the feasibility of endogenous induction with a co-inducer if pharmacology is adequate (Subrizi et al., 2015).  
- Stress-selective amplification: arimoclomol preferentially acts in stressed cells, limiting risks of unwanted Hsp70 induction in healthy tissue; this attribute is advantageous for chronic ocular therapy where avoiding constitutive pathway activation is desirable (Parfitt et al., 2014).  
- Clinical development and safety experience: extensive non-ocular development in ALS/NPC provides informative safety and pharmacology context; while ocular distribution is not established in these sources, the systemic safety window is a favorable starting point for repurposing (Venediktov et al., 2023; O’Leary, 2019).

Key weaknesses and uncertainties:  
- Lack of direct evidence in dry AMD/RPE barrier endpoints: no published data demonstrate arimoclomol preserves RPE tight junctions (ZO-1/occludin/claudin), restores TEER, or improves drusen-like pathology in vivo; ARPE-19 reports of arimoclomol-induced Hsp70 and anti-inflammatory effects are secondary summaries in low-quality reviews without primary detail (Kumar et al., 2020). In contrast, direct AMD-relevant in vitro data show that Aβ disrupts tight junction proteins, and autophagy failure correlates with p62 accumulation and aggregate burden, but the ability of arimoclomol to reverse these specific defects in RPE is untested (Wang et al., 2023; Viiri, 2019).  
- Negative/neutral result in PRPF31-RPE aggregation screen: arimoclomol did not reduce cytoplasmic aggregates in a rigorous 7-day screen in RP11-RPE; rapamycin reduced aggregates and shifted LC3 processing, suggesting that in certain RPE aggregate pathologies, autophagy activators outperform Hsp co-induction; whether arimoclomol could complement autophagy induction to achieve barrier rescue remains to be determined (Georgiou, 2021).  
- Uncertain induction competence in differentiated RPE: Primary neurons display high thresholds for inducible Hsp70 (HSPA1A) induction, with arimoclomol often failing to raise Hsp70; Hsp induction can be enhanced by HDAC inhibition, implying that chromatin accessibility and cell state are important variables; differentiated RPE monolayers may similarly require co-induction strategies (e.g., low-dose celastrol or epigenetic modulators) to achieve robust Hsp70 upregulation (Comaduran et al., 2024; Deane, 2019). If arimoclomol cannot reliably induce Hsp70 in mature RPE under clinically relevant stress, the strategy will falter.  
- CMA/macroautophagy modulation by arimoclomol in RPE not established: despite Hsp70’s mechanistic role in CMA, no data show arimoclomol improves CMA or autophagic flux in RPE, which are crucial to clearing damaged proteins/lipids under AMD stress; relying on Hsp70 alone without restoring autophagic flux may be insufficient to protect tight junctions (Chang et al., 2015; Georgiou, 2021).  
- Translational pharmacology: Retinal/RPE exposure of arimoclomol following systemic dosing is not presented in this corpus; ocular delivery strategies and RPE pharmacokinetics for arimoclomol are undefined here, in contrast to exogenous Hsp70 delivery where diffusion and tissue uptake were measured (Subrizi et al., 2015). Without ocular PK/PD and RPE Hsp70 induction data, dosing strategies for barrier rescue remain speculative.

Recommendation and development path:  
- Proceed to targeted preclinical validation in human iPSC-RPE monolayers and AMD-relevant stress paradigms, with rigorous endpoint panels including HSF1–Hsp70 induction, autophagic flux/CMA markers, aggregate clearance, cytokine modulation, and barrier integrity (TEER, ZO-1/occludin continuity), using rapamycin and rhHsp70 as comparators and benchmarking against known disruptions by Aβ and A2E (Georgiou, 2021; Subrizi et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Explore co-induction strategies: combine arimoclomol with low-dose celastrol to lower the induction threshold, and/or with autophagy activators (rapalogs/AMPK agonists) to correct flux while elevating chaperone capacity; justify combinations by neuronal data demonstrating enhanced Hsp induction and by RPE data showing autophagy dependence of aggregate clearance (Deane, 2019; Viiri, 2019; Georgiou, 2021).  
- If cell data are positive (robust Hsp70 induction, reduced aggregate burden, TEER protection), advance to ex vivo retina or small-animal models of RPE oxidative/drusen-like stress, with ocular pharmacokinetic measurements to confirm RPE exposure and on-target Hsp70 induction; consider local ocular delivery if systemic exposure is inadequate (Subrizi et al., 2015).  
- Maintain a realistic risk view: if arimoclomol fails to induce Hsp70 adequately in differentiated RPE or fails to impact autophagic flux, pivot to alternative HSF1 activators or to exogenous Hsp70 delivery or autophagy-centric therapies, where evidence in RPE is stronger (Subrizi et al., 2015; Georgiou, 2021).

In sum, arimoclomol is a mechanistically coherent candidate for restoring RPE proteostasis via HSF1–Hsp70 co-induction, supported by strong photoreceptor data and broad neurodegeneration experience, but it lacks direct evidence in dry AMD models and has an RPE aggregation screen result that favors autophagy induction over Hsp co-induction; rigorous, well-controlled RPE studies with barrier readouts are required before committing to translational development for dry AMD (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021).

I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PXS-5153A is a synthetically derived molecule that belongs to the class of selective lysyl oxidase inhibitors. In its design, medicinal chemistry efforts focused on optimizing potency and selectivity for LOXL2, along with activity against LOXL3, two members of the lysyl oxidase family that catalyze the oxidative deamination of lysine residues in collagens and elastin to promote covalent crosslink formation. These crosslinks confer the mechanical strength and stiffness of extracellular matrices (ECMs) such as Bruch’s membrane. Synthetic routes to compounds like PXS-5153A typically rely on structure-based design and iterative optimization to achieve potent enzyme inhibition with favorable pharmacokinetic properties (Lin et al., 2020). The compound, commercially available under MedChemExpress HY-111217, is representative of a new therapeutic class that has been primarily explored in the context of fibrosis and tumor microenvironment modulation. Given that ECM stiffening is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, targeting LOXL2 represents a novel approach compared to conventional anti-inflammatory or anti-angiogenic strategies.

II. Therapeutic History  
The LOXL2 inhibitor class, including molecules such as PXS-5153A, has been extensively tested in preclinical models of fibrosis and cancer. For example, within non-ocular systems, LOXL2 activity has been linked to increased tissue stiffness that fosters metastatic progression and desmoplastic reactions in tumors, and selective inhibition of LOXL2 has been shown to reduce crosslink density, attenuating fibrotic remodeling (Lin et al., 2020). Experimental inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity using non-selective agents like β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) has also been applied to in vitro and in vivo models to modulate ECM assembly, with effects on barrier function observed in RPE cultures co-treated with endothelial cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). Although LOXL2 inhibitors have not traditionally been used to treat dry AMD, evidence underscores the centrality of aberrant ECM crosslinking in BM thickening observed during aging and AMD progression (Wang et al., 2025). In particular, the endothelial cell–RPE crosstalk studies demonstrate a critical role for lysyl oxidase activity in regulating collagen bundle formation and in establishing RPE barrier properties (Benedicto et al., 2017). Accordingly, while there is no direct clinical or preclinical record of PXS-5153A in AMD, the antifibrotic profile of the compound and its impact on extracellular matrix mechanics in other disease contexts serve as a compelling rationale to explore its application in dry AMD.

III. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, LOXL2 catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of lysine or hydroxylysine residues present in collagens and elastin. This reaction is critical for the formation of covalent crosslinks that stabilize the ECM. Overexpression or hyperactivity of LOXL2 results in an excessively crosslinked and stiff matrix. In the eye, particularly within Bruch’s membrane—which is a complex, stratified ECM structure located between the RPE and the choroid—aberrant collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking are known to increase mechanical tension. Such mechanical changes are thought to adversely affect RPE cell function by interfering with integrin-mediated cell–matrix interactions and perturbing the proper localization of tight junction proteins, including ZO-1 and occludin (Benedicto et al., 2017).

PXS-5153A functions by binding to the catalytic pocket of LOXL2, thereby preventing its enzymatic activity. By blocking the oxidative deamination step, PXS-5153A reduces the formation of both immature and mature crosslinks in ECM proteins. The anticipated outcome is a lower crosslink density in Bruch’s membrane, resulting in a softer, more compliant matrix environment. This reduction in mechanical stiffness is expected to diminish abnormal mechanosignaling through β1 integrins, which are integral to the assembly and maintenance of tight junctions on RPE cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). The downstream consequences of reduced integrin activation include dampening of Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways, which in turn facilitate the stabilization and proper localization of tight junction proteins at the RPE cell membranes (Benedicto et al., 2017). Restoration of these junctional complexes correlates with improved barrier function, typically measured as an increased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in cell culture models. This mechanism is supported by studies in which inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity—by pharmacological agents such as BAPN—led to alterations in RPE barrier properties and tight junction morphology (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by directly targeting LOXL2, PXS-5153A is proposed to correct the pathological ECM remodeling that underlies BM stiffening in dry AMD while re-establishing proper RPE barrier integrity.

IV. Expected Effect  
The expected therapeutic effect of PXS-5153A in dry AMD centers on normalization of the BM ECM and concomitant restoration of RPE barrier function. In the proposed experimental model—an in vitro co-culture system where human fetal RPE (hfRPE) cells are grown on a substrate mimicking BM with defined stiffness—the application of PXS-5153A at concentrations around 5 µM is anticipated to yield a number of favorable outcomes.

First, by reducing LOXL2-mediated crosslinking of collagen IV and fibronectin, the drug should decrease the mechanical stiffness of the BM analog. A less rigid BM reduces aberrant integrin activation on the basolateral surfaces of RPE cells, which has been shown to be critical for proper tight junction assembly. In several studies, when the extracellular matrix is normalized—such as by altering substrate stiffness—there is an improvement in the localization of key tight junction proteins, specifically occludin and ZO-1, at the cell membrane (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Second, the reduced matrix stiffness is expected to alleviate the mechanical stress experienced by RPE cells, thereby facilitating the re-establishment of cell polarity and intercellular junction continuity. The stabilization of junctional complexes is measurable by TEER. In previous EC–RPE co-culture experiments, modulation of ECM mechanical properties directly correlated with increased TEER values, reflecting improved barrier function (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Moreover, the proper organization of the basement membrane is not only a structural consideration; the biochemical signaling through β1 integrin receptors—critical for maintaining cell adhesion and survival—would return toward homeostatic levels, further supporting the integrity of the RPE layer (Benedicto et al., 2017). These integrin-mediated signals influence downstream effectors such as Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK, which have been implicated in regulating tight junction dynamics (Benedicto et al., 2017). Progress in these pathways is expected to manifest as an overall improvement in the barrier phenotype, which is central to preventing the leakage of fluid and other deleterious solutes into the subretinal space—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.

In summary, it is anticipated that treatment with PXS-5153A in appropriate in vitro (and ultimately in vivo) models will lead to:  
• Reduced collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in BM, yielding a matrix with decreased stiffness (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Normalization of β1 integrin signaling and subsequent reorganization of RPE tight junctions with improved localization of proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Restoration of barrier function as evidenced by increased TEER measurements and improved paracellular permeability profiles (Benedicto et al., 2017).  

Thus, PXS-5153A is expected to address one of the core aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis by targeting ECM remodeling, which in turn indirectly stabilizes RPE cell function.

V. Overall Evaluation  
The concept of using PXS-5153A to modulate ECM pathology in dry AMD is compelling given the mechanistic insights derived from studies on lysyl oxidase activity in epithelial barrier function and ECM assembly. Among the strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its robust preclinical evidence in fibrosis and tumor microenvironment models. LOXL2 has been implicated in promoting tissue stiffening by catalyzing the crosslinking of collagen and fibronectin in various tissues (Lin et al., 2020). The pathophysiological parallels between fibrotic ECM remodeling in cancers and the stiffening of Bruch’s membrane in dry AMD provide a strong rationale for repurposing a LOXL2 inhibitor in an ocular context. Numerous studies have demonstrated that extracellular matrix integrity is essential for optimal RPE barrier function, and that even subtle changes in ECM mechanics can disrupt junctional complexes and lead to barrier dysfunction (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by targeting a critical enzymatic step in ECM crosslinking, PXS-5153A may confer dual benefits: it could both reduce the pathological stiffening of Bruch’s membrane and promote the reorganization of tight junction complexes, ultimately resulting in enhanced TEER and stabilization of the outer blood–retina barrier.

However, several important weaknesses or uncertainties must be considered. First, while numerous studies (using agents such as BAPN) have illustrated that lysyl oxidase inhibition affects RPE barrier function, direct evidence with selective LOXL2 inhibitors—specifically in ocular models of dry AMD—is lacking (Buniello et al., 2025). In fact, the Open Targets Platform indicates only a weak direct association between LOXL2 and age-related macular degeneration, based on limited literature evidence (Buniello et al., 2025). This raises the possibility that, although LOXL2 plays a demonstrable role in ECM crosslinking in other tissues, its specific involvement in dry AMD pathogenesis may not be as pronounced or may be influenced by other factors not recapitulated in non-ocular models.

Furthermore, potential off-target effects or the consequences of broadly altering ECM crosslinking in the eye must be carefully examined. The structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane is critical not only for its barrier function but also for nutrient transport between the choroidal circulation and the RPE. Overinhibition of LOXL2, or interference with normal ECM turnover, may inadvertently lead to basement membrane disorganization, as has been observed when lysyl oxidase activity was inhibited during critical periods of retinal development (Benedicto et al., 2017). This underscores the need for precise dose optimization and targeted delivery, ideally restricted to the ocular environment, to avoid systemic side effects.

Another consideration is the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. In addition to ECM stiffening, dry AMD involves multifactorial processes including oxidative stress, complement activation, inflammation, and the accumulation of lipoprotein deposits. Thus, while normalizing matrix stiffness is likely to improve RPE barrier function, it may be insufficient to fully arrest or reverse the disease process on its own. A combination therapy that also addresses the inflammatory and degenerative components of AMD may eventually be required (Benedicto et al., 2017; Caban et al., 2022).

From a development perspective, there is significant strength in the repurposing strategy because agents like PXS-5153A already have a detailed preclinical profile in non-ocular fibrotic models. This existing data can accelerate preclinical validation in ocular models, with studies planned in RPE–BM co-culture systems using TEER as a functional readout (Benedicto et al., 2017). Furthermore, leveraging well-characterized in vitro assays (such as those involving decellularized ECM and substrate stiffness modulation as described in the context) offers a clear experimental framework to evaluate whether the normalization of BM stiffness by PXS-5153A is sufficient to restore RPE tight junction integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017).

Nonetheless, one notable weakness is the limited direct evidence linking LOXL2 specifically to dry AMD. Although elevated lysyl oxidase activity and changes in collagen crosslinking have been observed in the context of RPE barrier function and BM integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017), the genetic and translational data associating LOXL2 with AMD are not robust. The relatively low association score (Buniello et al., 2025) suggests that additional studies are needed to clarify LOXL2’s role in the eye and to determine whether its inhibition will yield a therapeutically meaningful benefit in dry AMD patients.

In conclusion, repurposing PXS-5153A for dry AMD represents an innovative strategy that leverages the known antifibrotic effects of LOXL2 inhibition to address the deleterious ECM remodeling observed in aged Bruch’s membrane. The candidate’s synthetic origins and prior applications in fibrosis and cancer studies provide a solid foundation for its use, while the mechanistic rationale—centered on reducing pathological crosslinking and restoring RPE barrier function—is strongly supported by evidence from ECM modulation studies (Benedicto et al., 2017). However, challenges remain due to the lack of direct ocular data, potential risks of overmodulating ECM integrity, and the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology. Future research must focus on rigorous in vitro validation in RPE–BM co-culture systems and in vivo studies in relevant AMD animal models to establish the efficacy and safety profile of PXS-5153A in the context of dry AMD. Overall, despite these uncertainties, PXS-5153A holds promise as a novel ECM-targeted therapeutic candidate that could complement existing and emerging treatment strategies for this currently unmet clinical need (Lin et al., 2020; Buniello et al., 2025).

Taken together, the strengths of a clear mechanism of action, potent enzyme selectivity, and an innovative approach toward ECM normalization position PXS-5153A as an attractive candidate warranting further investigation. Nonetheless, a careful reappraisal of the molecular role of LOXL2 in the ocular microenvironment, along with detailed studies on dosing, delivery, and potential off-target effects, will be critical in determining whether this candidate can be successfully repurposed for treating dry AMD.
