Go/no-go assessment and recommendations  
- Go decision for mechanism-driven validation in dry AMD-relevant preclinical systems, but with a revised primary hypothesis and fit-for-purpose endpoints. The most compelling AMD-relevant mechanism for JQ1 is epigenetic suppression of cGAS–STING and NF-κB inflammatory programs in RPE and resident microglia, plus autophagy-mediated clearance of cytosolic DNA, not direct activation of tight-junction gene enhancers (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017).  
- Replace the current primary mechanistic claim (increased H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19) with a testable, literature-anchored hypothesis: JQ1 prevents inflammation- and oxidative-stress–induced RPE barrier breakdown by (i) repressing STING transcription and dampening cGAS–STING signaling; (ii) promoting autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA; and (iii) suppressing NF-κB–driven cytokines in RPE and microglia that secondarily disturb junctional integrity. TEER and junctional continuity should be primary outcomes, but mechanistic attribution should center on cGAS–STING/NF-κB and autophagy rather than TJ enhancer activation (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Shahid et al., 2022).  
- Rapid experimental plan:  
  • ARPE-19 and/or primary human RPE on transwells: TEER, paracellular flux, ZO-1/CLDN19 localization under IL-1β or TNF-α ± JQ1 (0.1–1 µM), with NF-κB activity, cytokine ELISAs, STING expression, LC3 flux, and dsDNA imaging to anchor mechanism (Hytti et al., 2016; Shahid et al., 2022; Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Oxidative stress model (H2O2 or SI-conditioned medium) ± JQ1: replicate cGAS–STING repression and autophagy findings in RPE; use autophagy inhibitors to confirm flux-dependence (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • ChIP-qPCR/ATAC at STING and at TJP1/CLDN19 enhancers/promoters to directly test the tight-junction enhancer hypothesis; set expectation that STING chromatin accessibility/acetylation will decline with JQ1, while TJ loci changes are unknown and likely neutral or reduced (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Microglia–RPE co-culture: test whether microglial cytokine suppression by JQ1 protects RPE TEER/barrier vs IL-1β, isolating paracrine contributions (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • In vivo oxidative-injury model (SI) with intraocular slow-release JQ1 (eNano-JQ1) to assess RPE barrier integrity (flat-mount ZO-1 continuity), microglial recruitment (IBA1), and function, leveraging prior safety/feasibility data (Liao et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2022).  
- Modality strategy: Given compensatory BRD4 upregulation with JQ1 and BD2 dominance in microglial activation, parallel exploration of BD2-selective ligands (e.g., apabetalone analogs) or BET degraders (dBET6-like) for retina-directed delivery is warranted to optimize therapeutic index while maintaining target engagement (Zhu et al., 2023; Shahid et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2017).

Conclusion  
JQ1 is a mechanistically well-grounded epigenetic modulator that suppresses inflammatory transcriptional programs and innate immune activation in retina/RPE and microglia, protects photoreceptors and RPE from oxidative and inflammatory injury in vivo, and has feasible ocular delivery paths with encouraging preclinical safety signals (Zou et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2017; Liao et al., 2024). These features position BET inhibition as a credible therapeutic strategy for dry AMD, targeting core disease drivers (oxidative stress, cytosolic DNA sensing via cGAS–STING, chronic NF-κB activation, microglial recruitment) rather than exclusively downstream consequences (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). However, the specific hypothesis that JQ1 restores RPE barrier function by increasing H3K27ac at tight-junction loci (TJP1/CLDN19) is not supported by available evidence; on the contrary, BET inhibition generally reduces histone acetylation/accessibility at target loci like STING, and RPE barrier metrics after JQ1 remain unreported (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016). We therefore recommend proceeding with JQ1 (or improved BET-modality variants) in dry AMD-relevant models with primary endpoints focused on cGAS–STING/NF-κB suppression, autophagy-dependent cytosolic DNA clearance, microglial modulation, and functional RPE barrier preservation (TEER, ZO-1/CLDN19 continuity), while explicitly testing and likely revising the proposed tight-junction enhancer mechanism based on direct chromatin measurements (Zou et al., 2022; Shahid et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative that belongs to the fibrate class of hypolipidemic agents. Originally developed to address dyslipidemia, fenofibrate was synthesized via chemical modifications of the fibric acid scaffold to yield an amphipathic carboxylic acid derivative, designed specifically to modulate lipid metabolism. As a member of the fibrate drug class, fenofibrate exerts its primary effects through activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα), a nuclear receptor that regulates the transcription of a variety of genes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, lipid transport, and overall metabolic homeostasis (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2). Over the past several decades, fibrates have been widely used in clinical practice to lower triglycerides, reduce low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, and elevate high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, significantly contributing to cardiovascular risk management. In addition, the repurposing efforts for fenofibrate in ocular conditions have generated interest based on its ability to modulate inflammatory and metabolic pathways in retinal tissues (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11).

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate’s therapeutic history is well established in the management of dyslipidemia and in reducing cardiovascular risk. Its clinical use dates back several decades, during which it has demonstrated efficacy in lowering plasma triglyceride levels, reducing total cholesterol, and favorably shifting the LDL particle size toward a less atherogenic profile (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9). Beyond its lipid-lowering effects, fenofibrate has been extensively evaluated in the context of diabetic retinopathy. Large-scale clinical trials such as the FIELD (Fenofibrate Intervention and Event Lowering in Diabetes) study and the ACCORD (Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes) Eye study have provided robust evidence that fenofibrate can slow the progression of diabetic retinopathy, reduce the severity of retinal microvascular abnormalities, and decrease the need for laser photocoagulation (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12). Although these studies primarily targeted diabetic retinal changes, the underlying pathophysiology – which includes oxidative stress, inflammation, and lipid accumulation in retinal tissues – overlaps with that observed in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11). Preclinical studies using in vitro models of RPE cells, where saturated fatty acids like palmitate are used to mimic lipotoxic stress, have demonstrated that fenofibrate can reduce lipid droplet accumulation and improve barrier function as measured by trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 8–11). In addition, in vivo studies in high-fat diet–fed mice have shown that fenofibrate treatment partially restores the function of the RPE, as evidenced by improved electroretinography (ERG) parameters and reduced markers of oxidative damage and inflammation (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8, 8–11). While there is no large-scale clinical trial data directly targeting dry AMD with fenofibrate, its documented benefits in diabetic retinopathy and its mechanistic overlap with dry AMD pathology make it an intriguing candidate for repurposing in this disease setting (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action is multifaceted and is primarily mediated by its role as a PPARα agonist. Binding of fenofibrate (or its active metabolite, fenofibric acid) to PPARα leads to the formation of a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor (RXR), which then binds to peroxisome proliferator responsive elements (PPREs) in the promoters of target genes. This transcriptional activation upregulates a suite of enzymes involved in fatty acid uptake and mitochondrial β-oxidation, such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) (Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12; Zhao et al., 2015, pp. 5–7). Increased expression of these catabolic enzymes enhances the degradation of fatty acids, thereby reducing intracellular lipid accumulation. In the context of lipid-loaded RPE cells – a condition that contributes to the disruption of tight junctions and subsequent barrier dysfunction – fenofibrate’s enhancement of fatty acid β-oxidation is hypothesized to lower intracellular lipid levels and consequently mitigate the lipotoxic stress imposed on junctional complexes (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11).  

Beyond its metabolic effects, fenofibrate has been reported to exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions. It downregulates markers of oxidative stress such as NOX4 and 3-nitrotyrosine and attenuates the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNFα, ICAM1, and VEGF in retinal tissues (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 8–11). Importantly, fenofibrate appears to modulate the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway in RPE cells. Under conditions of lipotoxicity induced by saturated fatty acids (e.g., palmitate), the PI3K/AKT pathway is downregulated, leading to increased oxidative stress and inflammation. Fenofibrate treatment has been shown to restore the p-AKT/AKT ratio, suggesting its ability to activate survival and anti-apoptotic pathways that are vital for maintaining RPE integrity (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8). Also, some evidence points to additional PPARα-independent mechanisms that may contribute to fenofibrate’s protective effects, such as modulation of AMPK signaling, which further reinforces mitochondrial function and promotes cell survival (Fu et al., 2020, pp. 6–8; Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15). Overall, fenofibrate’s molecular actions converge on enhancing fatty acid catabolism, reducing oxidative stress, suppressing inflammation, and supporting the survival of RPE cells – all of which are key factors in maintaining the structure and function of the outer blood–retina barrier, a critical component affected in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Zhao et al., 2015, pp. 5–7).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis under investigation posits that fenofibrate-mediated PPARα activation will drive a metabolic shift in lipid-loaded RPE cells by increasing fatty acid β-oxidation and thereby reducing the intracellular accumulation of lipid droplets. In an in vitro model using ARPE-19 cells, treatment with palmitate induces lipotoxic stress that disrupts tight junction complexes, leading to decreased TEER and mislocalization of occludin – an essential tight junction protein. The expected effect of fenofibrate in this assay is twofold. First, by upregulating CPT1A and other enzymes involved in fatty acid metabolism, fenofibrate should reduce the intracellular lipid burden. Such a reduction is anticipated to alleviate the lipotoxic stress that compromises the junctional integrity of RPE cells (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12). Second, through its activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway and potential AMPK signaling modulation, fenofibrate is expected to restore the proper localization of occludin and improve TEER by approximately 30%, as observed in preliminary studies using a 50 µM concentration of the drug (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). These effects are bolstered by previous evidence showing that fenofibrate can reduce oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators that are known to further damage tight junctions in the RPE (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8; Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15). Since PPARα is expressed in retinal cells, including the RPE, and is essential for lipid oxidation and energy metabolism, its activation by fenofibrate in the assay is well supported by the underlying biochemistry (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12). The ultimate expectation is that the improved barrier function in vitro will translate into a therapeutic benefit for dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction and compromised barrier integrity are central to disease progression (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11).

Overall Evaluation:  
Fenofibrate presents several compelling strengths as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. One of its primary advantages is its long-established safety and efficacy profile in clinical use for dyslipidemia. Decades of systemic administration in patients have provided robust safety data and have demonstrated that fenofibrate is well tolerated in the majority of cases (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9). Moreover, the substantial clinical data from the FIELD and ACCORD Eye studies establish its beneficial effects on retinal microvascular complications in diabetic patients, indicating a therapeutic potential that may extend to other retinal diseases with overlapping pathophysiological features, such as dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12).

Mechanistically, fenofibrate’s ability to activate PPARα and enhance fatty acid β-oxidation addresses a critical aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis: the accumulation of lipids within RPE cells that contributes to oxidative stress and impairs junctional integrity. The reduction in lipid accumulation not only decreases lipotoxic stress but also supports cellular energy production, thereby enabling the restoration of tight junction proteins such as occludin (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 6–8). The concomitant activation of survival pathways, notably the PI3K/AKT cascade, further reinforces the protective milieu in RPE cells. These multifactorial actions of fenofibrate – targeting lipid metabolism, oxidative damage, inflammation, and cellular survival – collectively provide a strong mechanistic rationale for its use in preserving RPE barrier function in the context of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–12).

Another strength lies in the potential to repurpose an already approved drug. This approach can significantly shorten the development timeline and reduce costs, as fenofibrate’s pharmacokinetics, dosing ranges, and safety profile are well documented. Additionally, innovative ocular delivery methods, such as nano-emulsion eye drops or localized intraocular administration, have been explored to overcome the limitations of systemic drug delivery in targeting the retina (Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). These novel delivery approaches could maximize retinal drug exposure while minimizing systemic side effects, ensuring that effective concentrations of fenofibrate reach the RPE.

Despite these promising attributes, several challenges must be acknowledged. One primary concern is that the majority of clinical evidence for fenofibrate’s efficacy in retinal conditions comes from diabetic retinopathy studies rather than direct investigations in dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 12–13). Although there is significant overlap in the pathological processes underlying both conditions—such as oxidative stress, inflammation, and RPE dysfunction—the direct translation of benefits from diabetic retinopathy to dry AMD is not yet fully established. Preclinical studies in dry AMD models are therefore essential to validate whether the observed improvements in in vitro RPE barrier function (e.g., increased TEER and proper occludin localization) will translate into clinically meaningful outcomes for patients (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–12).

Another limitation is the duality of fenofibrate’s mechanism of action. While PPARα activation is a well-characterized pathway, available evidence indicates that fenofibrate may also act through PPARα-independent mechanisms, including AMPK activation and inhibition of cytochrome P450 epoxygenase activities (Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11; Qiu et al., 2019, p. 12). This multiplicity of actions, while potentially beneficial, also raises questions about off-target effects that could complicate the therapeutic profile when applied to a sensitive tissue such as the retina. Moreover, fenofibrate’s poor aqueous solubility poses challenges for direct ocular delivery, although recent advances in formulation science (such as nano-emulsion systems) are promising solutions to this problem (Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

A further challenge is that the ideal dosing for maximal retinal efficacy without systemic toxicity remains to be determined. The preliminary in vitro data indicating a 30% improvement in TEER at 50 µM fenofibrate is encouraging; however, scaling these concentrations appropriately for in vivo use in the retina will require careful pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies. In addition, the variability in RPE cell responses due to differences in cellular metabolism, donor characteristics, or disease stage could impact the consistency of the therapeutic response in a clinical setting (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8, 8–11).

In summary, fenofibrate exhibits significant promise as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its strengths include an extensive track record in managing dyslipidemia, well-documented retinal benefits in diabetic retinopathy, and a robust mechanistic rationale grounded in PPARα activation and enhanced fatty acid oxidation. These effects are supported by preclinical data demonstrating improvements in RPE barrier function under lipotoxic conditions, aligning with the pathogenic processes observed in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11). However, to fully establish fenofibrate’s potential in dry AMD, further targeted research is required. This should include advanced in vitro and in vivo models that specifically recapitulate the dry AMD phenotype, detailed investigations into ocular pharmacokinetics and optimal delivery methods, and ultimately, clinical trials that evaluate efficacy and safety in patients with dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 6–8).

Overall, fenofibrate’s ability to reduce intracellular lipid accumulation, diminish oxidative and inflammatory stress, and restore junctional integrity in RPE cells makes it a promising therapeutic candidate. While there are challenges to be addressed—notably, the translation of findings from diabetic retinopathy to dry AMD and the need for precise ocular delivery formulations—the established clinical profile of fenofibrate coupled with its multifaceted mechanisms of action provide a compelling scientific rationale for further exploration in dry AMD. The convergence of metabolic modulation, anti-inflammatory action, and barrier restoration positions fenofibrate as a novel metabolic intervention that could fill an unmet need in a patient population with limited treatment options (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Zhao et al., 2015, pp. 5–7; Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15).

In conclusion, from a drug development perspective, fenofibrate is an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its synthetic derivation and established use as a lipid-lowering agent, combined with revealed preclinical efficacy in preserving RPE function under lipotoxic conditions, align well with the hypothesized benefit of enhancing fatty acid β-oxidation to alleviate junctional stress. The promising in vitro improvements in TEER and occludin localization provide a solid foundation for further research, while the favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profile support its viability for ocular applications. Critical next steps include refining ocular delivery strategies, conducting detailed mechanistic studies in dry AMD-relevant models, and initiating early-phase clinical trials to assess both efficacy and safety in the target population. If these studies confirm the preclinical promise of fenofibrate, this candidate could ultimately be integrated into combination therapeutic strategies—possibly alongside anti-VEGF therapies—to comprehensively address the multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8, 8–11, 11–12).

I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SMER28 is a small‐molecule enhancer of autophagy originally identified through high‐throughput chemical screens designed to activate intracellular clearance pathways. It is chemically characterized as a bromo‐substituted quinazoline and belongs to a series of “SMER” compounds initially disclosed by leading research institutions to augment autophagy independently of mTOR signaling (Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013; Sarkar & Rubinsztein, 2008). The synthesis of SMER28 has been streamlined into a three‐step process using accessible reagents such as 2-amino-5-bromobenzoic acid and 1,1′-carbonyldiimidazole (CDI), facilitating its large-scale preparation without requiring extensive purification of intermediates (Koukourakis et al., 2018). Originally, SMER28 was discovered during efforts to identify compounds that could promote autophagy and protein clearance, a focus that later expanded its potential use to diseases characterized by proteostatic stress. Its structure–activity relationships and ease of synthesis render SMER28 an attractive candidate for drug repurposing strategies beyond its initial applications, particularly in diseases where defective autophagy contributes to pathogenesis. This candidate’s established role in enhancing cellular clearance mechanisms positions it well for evaluation in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a condition marked by impaired removal of misfolded proteins and lipids in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Doulatov et al., 2017; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013).

II. Therapeutic History  
SMER28 has an extensive preclinical history that underscores its potential for broad therapeutic applications. In initial studies focused on Diamond-Blackfan Anemia (DBA), SMER28 was shown to promote erythropoiesis and enhance hemoglobin expression in both in vitro systems and zebrafish models of DBA, where ribosomal protein mutations lead to anemia-like phenotypes (Doulatov et al., 2017). These findings indicated that SMER28 could effectively modulate cellular differentiation and survival pathways in stressed cell populations. Subsequent investigations expanded its evaluation to radioprotection, where SMER28 demonstrated protective effects in mouse bone marrow and liver tissues subjected to irradiation. These studies revealed that SMER28’s activation of autophagy could preserve normal tissue architecture and improve recovery after cellular injury (Koukourakis et al., 2018). Furthermore, in models of neurodegenerative diseases, SMER28 has been implicated in enhancing both autophagic and proteasomal clearance mechanisms to reduce the burden of misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins such as mutant huntingtin and polyQ-expanded proteins (Wrobel, Hill, & Rubinsztein, 2023). Although none of these prior studies were conducted directly in ocular tissues, their outcomes suggest that the underlying mechanism of SMER28—enhancement of the intracellular degradation machinery—is broadly applicable. Given that the RPE in dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and lipid deposits due to defective autophagy (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021), repurposing SMER28 for dry AMD addresses a significant disease mechanism while potentially leveraging its established safety and efficacy in other systems.

III. Mechanism of Action  
SMER28’s mechanism of action is defined by its ability to induce autophagy in an mTOR-independent manner—a key advantage over conventional autophagy modulators that act via mTOR inhibition. At the molecular level, SMER28 binds directly to the Valosin Containing Protein (VCP/p97), an essential chaperone involved in protein quality control and degradation pathways (Wrobel et al., 2022). This binding stabilizes VCP and stimulates its D1 ATPase activity, thereby enhancing both the formation and maturation of autophagosomes. An increase in VCP activity is known to promote the formation of phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI(3)P), a lipid mediator critical for the nucleation of autophagic vesicles (Wrobel et al., 2022). Downstream of PI(3)P production, the assembly of the lipidation machinery—including LC3, a ubiquitin-like protein requisite for autophagosome elongation—is enhanced, as indicated by increased LC3-II formation in cells treated with SMER28 (Wrobel et al., 2022).

Simultaneously, SMER28’s action is dependent on Beclin 1, whose involvement in autophagy initiation further supports the autophagic flux observed upon treatment (Wrobel et al., 2022). Importantly, these effects are achieved without a detectable alteration in the downstream effectors of mTOR signaling; measurements of AKT activation and other mTOR-related pathways remain unaffected, affirming the compound’s mTOR-independent operation (Wrobel et al., 2022; Koukourakis et al., 2018). In parallel, the compound also appears to enhance the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), an additional degradation pathway, in a manner that is similarly VCP-dependent (Wrobel, Hill, & Rubinsztein, 2023). The convergence of autophagy and UPS pathways is particularly relevant in cellular systems where proteostasis is compromised.

While there is robust evidence supporting the activation of autophagic flux via VCP and Beclin 1, the specific hypothesis for dry AMD posits that SMER28 may also engage ULK1-dependent autophagy mechanisms. ULK1 (UNC-51-like kinase 1) is a serine/threonine kinase upstream in the autophagy cascade that integrates stress signals to initiate autophagy, and genetic ablation of ULK1 or ATG5 has been shown to replicate RPE barrier defects (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015). However, the current literature does not provide direct evidence linking SMER28 with ULK1 activation; rather, the bulk of mechanistic data implicates the compound in VCP-mediated processes (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013). Despite this gap, the overall mode of action—enhancing autophagic and proteasomal clearance pathways while bypassing mTOR—remains firmly established. Thus, SMER28 targets a network of molecular interactions, pivoting on the modulation of VCP’s activity, increased PI(3)P production, and subsequent LC3 lipidation, all of which consolidate its role as an effective autophagy inducer (Wrobel et al., 2022).

IV. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of SMER28 in dry AMD is that its administration will lead to activation of autophagy in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, thereby promoting the clearance of accumulated lipids and misfolded proteins at cell–cell contacts. In dry AMD, the RPE exhibits dysfunctional autophagy, which contributes to the accumulation of toxic compounds such as A2E—a lipofuscin precursor known to induce oxidative stress and compromise cellular architecture (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014). By facilitating the removal of these deleterious aggregates, SMER28 is expected to alleviate proteostatic and lipotoxic stress within the RPE.

Although most studies elucidating SMER28’s effects have been performed in non-ocular systems, the mechanistic insights gained can be extrapolated to the RPE environment. Specifically, SMER28’s ability to increase LC3 lipidation and enhance autophagic flux—as evidenced by changes in LC3-II levels and Beclin 1 dependency—offers a promising strategy for reducing intracellular lipid droplets and misfolded protein aggregates (Wrobel et al., 2022). This improved clearance should, in turn, restore proper intracellular communication and protein homeostasis near cell–cell junctions.

A critical consequence of this process is the anticipated reassembly of tight junction proteins, particularly ZO-1 and occludin. These proteins are essential for maintaining barrier integrity in the RPE, and their disassembly under stress conditions leads to a decrease in trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a surrogate marker for barrier function (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015). By reducing the cellular burden of lipid and protein aggregates, SMER28 may enable the reformation of ZO-1 and occludin belts at cell–cell contacts, thereby improving TEER. Although direct measurements of ZO-1 and occludin reassembly following SMER28 treatment have not been detailed in the existing literature, analogous improvements in tight junction morphology have been observed in other proteostatic and neurodegenerative models where SMER28 enhanced cellular protein clearance (Wrobel, Hill, & Rubinsztein, 2023).

Furthermore, SMER28’s mTOR-independent nature is expected to confer a selective therapeutic advantage. Unlike mTOR inhibitors, which often exert widespread metabolic effects that could be harmful in chronic conditions, SMER28’s mechanism minimizes the risk of systemic side effects while still promoting the clearance of pathogenic intracellular substrates (Wrobel et al., 2022). In the proposed assay, RPE cells challenged with A2E or other proteostatic stressors would ideally show increased markers of autophagy (e.g., LC3-II accumulation, reduced p62 levels) alongside functional restoration of barrier properties as measured by TEER assays. The improvement in barrier integrity is expected to reflect not only the biochemical clearance of toxic aggregates but also structural reorganization at intercellular junctions—a dual benefit that addresses key pathogenic features of dry AMD (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021).

Additionally, the genetic correlations drawn from studies where knockdown of crucial autophagy regulators such as ULK1 or ATG5 leads to RPE barrier defects further support the notion that pharmacological enhancement of autophagy may reverse such phenotypes. Although direct evidence linking SMER28 with ULK1 activation in RPE cells is sparse, the overall strategy of boosting autophagic flux to restore cellular homeostasis remains compelling (Davis, 2015; Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021). In summary, SMER28 is expected to work by reducing intracellular accumulations of harmful proteins and lipids, promoting the reassembly of ZO-1 and occludin at cell–cell contacts, and improving TEER under conditions that mimic the stress found in dry AMD.

V. Overall Evaluation  
SMER28 presents several compelling strengths as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, yet it also faces challenges that must be addressed through further targeted research.

Strengths:  
One of the foremost strengths of SMER28 is its robust ability to induce autophagy through mechanisms independent of mTOR inhibition. This property is vital because mTOR inhibitors, while effective at promoting autophagic activity, can induce broad, deleterious metabolic effects not well tolerated in chronic conditions such as AMD (Wrobel et al., 2022). By bypassing mTOR, SMER28 offers a more selective approach that focuses on enhancing intracellular clearance pathways while maintaining the overall metabolic balance. The molecular interactions it engages—predominantly through binding and activating VCP/p97, stimulating the production of PI(3)P, and driving LC3 lipidation—are well documented in several studies (Wrobel et al., 2022). This dual modulation of both autophagic and proteasomal pathways not only promotes protein aggregate clearance but also potentially addresses the accumulation of toxic lipids, which is central to AMD pathogenesis.

The extensive preclinical data supporting SMER28’s efficacy in models of Diamond-Blackfan Anemia, radioprotection, and neurodegenerative diseases offers reassurance regarding its safety profile and mechanism of action (Doulatov et al., 2017; Koukourakis et al., 2018; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013; Sarkar & Rubinsztein, 2008). The compound’s success in these diverse models underscores its versatility and hints at its capacity to produce similar benefits in the RPE, a tissue highly sensitive to proteostatic imbalances. Furthermore, its inclusion in the SMER series—where analogous molecules have been effective in clearing aggregation-prone proteins in neurodegeneration—adds credence to the hypothesis that SMER28 could alleviate the intracellular debris that contributes to dry AMD (Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013; Sarkar & Rubinsztein, 2008).

Weaknesses:  
Despite the promising attributes outlined above, significant gaps in the current literature present challenges for the immediate repurposing of SMER28 for dry AMD. The most notable gap lies in the lack of direct evidence concerning its effects on RPE cells, specifically regarding the reassembly of tight junction proteins like ZO-1 and occludin. The hypothesis that SMER28 will restore TEER by promoting the reformation of these junctional complexes is logically sound given the role of autophagy in RPE homeostasis (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014), yet direct mechanistic and functional data in ocular models remain sparse.

Moreover, while the literature robustly supports a mechanism involving VCP/p97 and subsequent autophagic flux, there is currently no conclusive evidence establishing that SMER28 activates ULK1-dependent autophagy within RPE cells. Studies have indicated that SMER28 predominantly functions via VCP-mediated pathways and enhances LC3 lipidation without evidence of direct ULK1 or ATG5 activation (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013). Given that genetic knockdown of ULK1 and ATG5 replicates detrimental RPE barrier defects, the absence of clear data on SMER28’s influence on these upstream regulators introduces uncertainty regarding the full scope of its autophagic modulation in the context of dry AMD.

Another potential weakness is the translatability of findings from non-ocular systems to the RPE environment. The RPE is a highly specialized cell type with unique metabolic requirements and structural features. Its reliance on constant autophagic turnover to manage oxidative stress and lipid accumulation means that interventions must be finely tuned. Although SMER28’s impact on proteostasis in other tissues is well established, its precise effects on RPE cell physiology—especially under circumstances of A2E-induced stress—must be rigorously validated through dedicated in vitro and in vivo studies.

In addition, most of the supportive studies for SMER28 have been conducted in contexts of systemic or neurodegenerative challenges rather than in ocular models. This necessitates caution when extrapolating positive outcomes from models of Diamond-Blackfan Anemia or radioprotection to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Doulatov et al., 2017; Koukourakis et al., 2018). The hypothesis that SMER28 will facilitate the reassembly of ZO-1/occludin belts and restore TEER, while promising, remains speculative until confirmed by functional assays in RPE cell cultures and suitable animal models of AMD.

Overall, SMER28 combines a favorable mechanism of action with a promising preclinical safety and efficacy record that renders it an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its selective activation of autophagic clearance pathways without engaging mTOR minimizes potential off-target effects, making it particularly suitable for chronic administration in age-related diseases. However, critical unanswered questions regarding its direct impact on RPE barrier function, particularly the reassembly of tight junction proteins and TEER restoration, must be addressed in future studies (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014; Davis, 2015). Moreover, the putative involvement of ULK1-dependent autophagy in SMER28’s mechanism remains to be definitively characterized in ocular models (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019).

In conclusion, while SMER28 has yet to be directly evaluated in ocular systems, its strong mechanistic foundation—as evidenced by its ability to enhance autophagy and proteasomal clearance via VCP stimulation, LC3 lipidation, and Beclin 1 dependency—supports its potential utility in mitigating the autophagic deficits observed in dry AMD (Wrobel et al., 2022). The anticipated clearance of lipid droplets and misfolded proteins, combined with the potential for facilitating the reassembly of ZO-1 and occludin at cell–cell junctions, collectively addresses two critical aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis. Consequently, SMER28 emerges as a promising candidate with significant potential to restore RPE function and barrier integrity, provided that future empirical studies confirm these effects in the appropriate ocular models (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015; Koukourakis et al., 2018).

As an expert drug development team leader evaluating novel therapeutic candidates, I recommend progressing SMER28 to the next stage of rigorous, mechanism-focused preclinical studies using RPE cell cultures and relevant animal models of dry AMD. Emphasis should be placed on detailed analyses of autophagic flux, ULK1 activation status, and the integrity of tight junction reassembly under conditions of A2E-induced or proteostatic stress. This targeted approach will help clarify SMER28’s full mechanistic profile in RPE cells and validate its potential to restore TEER and overall barrier function, thereby establishing its viability as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD (Wrobel et al., 2022; Davis, 2015).

Overall, SMER28 stands out due to its mTOR-independent autophagy induction, dual engagement of autophagic and proteasomal pathways, and a well-established preclinical background in diverse stress models, all of which offer promising avenues for counteracting the cellular dysfunctions underlying dry AMD. Nonetheless, further studies are essential to bridge the current knowledge gap regarding its specific effects on ULK1-dependent autophagy and tight junction reassembly in RPE cells, which are fundamental for achieving the desired therapeutic outcomes in dry AMD (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019; Davis, 2015).

While the theoretical framework suggests that SMER28 may ameliorate the proteostatic and lipotoxic stress impairing RPE function—thereby restoring the reassembly of ZO-1/occludin belts and improving TEER—the success of this therapeutic strategy will ultimately depend on empirical validation in ocular-specific studies. Given the convergence of mechanistic insights, preclinical efficacy in multiple models, and the compelling need for improved therapeutic strategies in dry AMD, SMER28 merits prioritization for further research. Its progression into RPE-based studies could potentially pave the way for a new class of autophagy-modulating, mTOR-independent therapeutics aimed at restoring RPE function and halting the progression of dry AMD, thereby offering hope for improved outcomes in this prevalent cause of vision loss (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015; Koukourakis et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Pioglitazone is a synthetic thiazolidinedione (TZD) that was initially discovered and developed as an antidiabetic agent for type 2 diabetes mellitus. As a member of the glitazone family, its structure is centered on a thiazolidinedione ring that is critical for binding to the nuclear receptor peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). Its discovery by medicinal chemists led to its widespread clinical use as an insulin sensitizer, with the molecule synthesized through conventional organic synthesis methods that allow for high purity and reproducibility. The compound is commercially available from research suppliers, such as Sigma (PHR 1043), and has been extensively studied not only in metabolic disorders but also for its vascular protective and anti‐inflammatory properties. Within its drug class, thiazolidinediones have been used successfully in managing hyperglycemia in diabetic patients and have also been investigated in various preclinical models for their potential in modulating inflammatory responses and oxidative stress, capabilities that are hypothesized to be beneficial in chronic degenerative conditions like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, pioglitazone is approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, where its activation of PPARγ leads to enhanced insulin sensitivity, alterations in adipocyte differentiation, and modulation of lipid metabolism. Over the years, its favorable safety profile in diabetic populations has been well documented. Outside of metabolic disease, growing interest in its pleiotropic effects has led to investigations of its potential for vascular protection and anti‐inflammatory actions in ocular tissues. Some studies have proposed that PPARγ agonists may have a role in retinal diseases due to the expression of this nuclear receptor in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Simpson-Haidaris et al., 2010, pp. 18–19). However, when specifically tested in dry AMD models, such as oxLDL-induced RPE cell death assays, pioglitazone—as well as other PPARγ agonists like ciglitazone and rosiglitazone—did not afford significant protection, whereas troglitazone was the only compound to show marked cytoprotective effects (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). In the clinical arena, a study conducted in diabetic patients with neovascular AMD receiving anti-VEGF therapy showed that thiazolidinedione use was associated with some beneficial anatomical changes in subretinal fluid and tissue complex thickness (Core et al., 2023, pp. 2–4). Nonetheless, these clinical investigations have been primarily confined to the context of neovascular AMD rather than dry AMD, and there is limited direct clinical evidence for pioglitazone being repurposed for dry AMD. Thus, while the drug’s history in diabetes and its secondary vascular effects offer a rationale for repurposing, its track record specifically in dry AMD remains inconclusive.

Mechanism of Action:  
Pioglitazone exerts its primary pharmacological activity through binding to and activating PPARγ, a ligand-dependent transcription factor that modulates the expression of genes involved in glucose metabolism, lipid handling, and inflammatory responses (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). Activation of PPARγ typically leads to downstream transcriptional events that include the upregulation of antioxidant enzymes such as Cu/Zn-superoxide dismutase (SOD) and suppression of NADPH oxidase expression, thereby reducing oxidative stress (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). In theory, within RPE cells, PPARγ activation could also promote the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. PGC-1α is known to drive mitochondrial replication, increase the expression of genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation, and upregulate a suite of antioxidant defenses; these effects have been associated with enhanced cell survival under oxidative stress conditions in RPE models (Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 12–13). Moreover, because RPE cells are characterized by high metabolic demand and are particularly susceptible to ROS-induced damage, induction of mitochondrial biogenesis could mitigate oxidative stress and preserve intracellular energy metabolism. 

The central hypothesis for the repurposing of pioglitazone in dry AMD is that PPARγ activation by this agonist will induce a PGC-1α–driven mitochondrial biogenesis pathway in RPE cells under oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂ stress). This induction is expected to lead to enhanced mitochondrial function, lower mitochondrial ROS (mito-ROS) production, and an overall reduction in oxidative damage. By decreasing ROS levels, the cascade that normally leads to the degradation of key junctional proteins—specifically claudin-19 and ZO-1, which are critical for maintaining the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier—could be interrupted. Thus, preservation or restoration of these junctional complexes could recover the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity of the RPE (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). However, existing in vitro studies in RPE models have shown that among several tested PPARγ agonists, pioglitazone did not replicate the cytoprotective effects seen with troglitazone, and the beneficial effects in these studies were found to be independent of PPARγ activation (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). This discrepancy raises questions about whether pioglitazone can induce the PGC-1α pathway effectively in this context. Nonetheless, the mechanistic rationale remains centered on the possibility that reducing oxidative stress through enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis might preserve cell junction integrity in the RPE, an approach that is biologically plausible based on the roles of both PPARγ and PGC-1α in other tissues and in some retinal models.

Expected Effect:  
According to the proposed hypothesis, when ARPE-19 cells are challenged with H₂O₂ to simulate oxidative stress, treatment with 1 µM pioglitazone is expected to initiate a cascade of molecular events: First, pioglitazone should activate PPARγ, which in turn would upregulate PGC-1α expression. This upregulation is anticipated to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and function, resulting in a measurable decrease in mitochondrial ROS production as detected by MitoSOX fluorescence assays. In addition, by lowering ROS levels, the compound is expected to protect against the degradation of cell junction proteins such as claudin-19 and ZO-1. These proteins are essential for the formation and maintenance of the tight junction belts in RPE cells, contributing to the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier. The experimental readouts proposed include a 45% recovery in TEER, a surrogate marker for barrier integrity, suggesting that pioglitazone would restore functional barrier properties that are compromised under oxidative stress conditions (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). It is important to note, however, that while these effects have been observed in some isolated experiments, the majority of the literature on PPARγ agonists in RPE models has primarily highlighted that only troglitazone, rather than pioglitazone, yielded significant cytoprotection against oxidative insults (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). Thus, while the expected effect is biologically coherent with the ideal model of reducing ROS-mediated junction protein degradation and restoring TEER, the existing experimental evidence raises concerns regarding whether pioglitazone is capable of achieving these outcomes under the conditions outlined.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the repurposing strategy of using pioglitazone for the treatment of dry AMD is based on a sound mechanistic rationale that integrates several interrelated pathways: the PPARγ-mediated modulation of inflammatory and oxidative stress responses, the PGC-1α–driven enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis, and the consequent protection of RPE junctional integrity. The well-established clinical safety profile of pioglitazone in diabetic populations is an important strength, as it facilitates potential rapid translation to clinical trials for new indications. Additionally, the notion that mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS overproduction play central roles in RPE degeneration and barrier disruption in dry AMD provides a compelling target for therapeutic intervention (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).

However, there are several weaknesses and limitations to consider. First, while pioglitazone has demonstrated vascular protective and anti-inflammatory properties in other contexts, the literature on its direct effects in RPE cells under oxidative stress is mixed. Notably, in multiple in vitro studies investigating PPARγ agonists in models of oxidative stress-induced RPE cell death, pioglitazone—as well as other compounds such as ciglitazone and rosiglitazone—failed to confer significant cytoprotection, with only troglitazone showing robust protective effects (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 31–37, 37–42). This discrepancy suggests that either pioglitazone does not effectively induce the mitochondrial biogenesis pathway via PGC-1α in RPE cells or that its mechanism of action may not directly translate into the preservation of tight junction proteins like claudin-19 and ZO-1 under oxidative stress. Given these considerations, the overall evaluation of pioglitazone as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is mixed. Its strengths lie in its well-characterized safety profile, established use as a PPARγ agonist, and the plausible mechanistic link between reduced ROS production and preservation of barrier integrity in RPE cells. However, the weaknesses are notable—most prominently, the inconsistent preclinical efficacy observed in RPE models of oxidative stress and the lack of robust evidence demonstrating that pioglitazone can drive PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial biogenesis in this context. The literature does not strongly support the hypothesis that pioglitazone will prevent ROS-mediated degradation of junction proteins or restore TEER in RPE cells, as only alternative compounds (e.g., troglitazone) have shown such effects in some studies (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42).

In conclusion, while the molecular rationale for targeting mitochondrial dysfunction and junctional breakdown in dry AMD is compelling, and the repurposing of a clinically validated drug like pioglitazone is attractive from a safety and translational standpoint, the current experimental evidence raises significant doubts about its efficacy in this specific application. Further comprehensive studies are needed to resolve these discrepancies—ideally through optimized in vitro models that replicate the oxidative and metabolic challenges of dry AMD, and through detailed mechanistic studies that can confirm or refute the induction of PGC-1α and subsequent mitochondrial biogenesis by pioglitazone in RPE cells. Moreover, alternative PPARγ agonists or combination strategies that pair pioglitazone with agents known to specifically enhance mitochondrial function might offer a more viable therapeutic strategy. Until such additional data become available, the repurposing of pioglitazone for dry AMD should be considered with caution, and resources may better be allocated towards candidates with more consistent preclinical efficacy in relevant RPE models (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Vatiquinone (EPI-743) is a synthetic, tocopherol-derived quinone originally developed as a vitamin E analogue to counteract inherited mitochondrial diseases. It was synthesized through modifications of the natural vitamin E structure, where oxidation of the tocopherol leads to the formation of a quinone moiety. This design enhances its electron transfer capabilities and confers improved bioavailability and tissue penetration, including the ability to cross the blood–brain barrier. As a member of the quinone class of antioxidants, vatiquinone belongs to a group of compounds that have historically been leveraged to modulate redox homeostasis in tissues under oxidative stress. This class of compounds has been applied in diverse therapeutic areas ranging from neurodegenerative disorders to mitochondrial dysfunction, and its mechanism is chiefly considered beneficial in circumstances where oxidative stress and compromised mitochondrial integrity are primary pathological drivers (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

In addition to its synthetic origins, the pharmacological profile of vatiquinone is characterized by its potent antioxidant activity that exceeds that of traditional compounds like Coenzyme Q10 or idebenone. Its chemical structure allows it to interface efficiently with cellular redox enzymes such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1). The high-affinity interaction between vatiquinone and NQO1 is central to its function, as it is hypothesized to regenerate reduced forms of coenzyme Q and thus support the recycling of critical cellular antioxidants such as glutathione. The ability to catalyze these reactions positions vatiquinone as a compelling agent for therapeutic interventions in conditions marked by chronic oxidative stress, an attribute that underpins the rationale for its proposed use in dry age‐related macular degeneration (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Vatiquinone’s therapeutic history is strongly associated with its development for inherited mitochondrial disorders, most notably Friedreich’s ataxia (FRDA) and Leigh syndrome. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated that vatiquinone modulates oxidative stress response pathways and protects mitochondrial function. In clinical trials conducted in patients with FRDA, vatiquinone was shown to regulate key antioxidant defenses by enhancing the expression of genes such as NQO1 and those involved in glutathione synthesis via activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. This led to improvements in neurological function and confirmed its favorable safety profile, thereby validating its use in outpatient settings for mitochondrial disorders (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Beyond its application in mitochondrial disorders, vatiquinone has been explored in the context of various neurodegenerative diseases, reflecting its capacity to preserve mitochondrial health and ameliorate oxidative injury in neural tissues. Its potent neuroprotective properties, which include mitigating oxidative insults and modulating redox-sensitive signaling pathways, have led to its FDA orphan drug designation for Friedrich’s ataxia. Although the primary focus of vatiquinone research has been in neurodegeneration and mitochondrial impairments, the underlying mechanisms that confer mitochondrial protection and support antioxidant defenses have raised interest in its potential application in ocular diseases such as dry age‐related macular degeneration. Notably, preclinical and anecdotal data have suggested that similar redox imbalances found in inherited mitochondrial diseases are also present in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of patients with dry AMD. However, while the compound’s efficacy and safety have been established in the neurological context, no formal clinical investigations have directly addressed its potential in treating dry AMD or in modulating RPE function (Cores et al., 2023; Chang & Chen, 2024).

The translation of vatiquinone’s antioxidant properties to dry AMD is based on the shared underlying pathology of chronic oxidative stress. Pilot data even indicate viability improvements in ARPE-19, a widely used RPE cell model, under stress conditions. Although these data are preliminary and unpublished, they offer a promising foundation for further research into whether the molecule can enhance RPE barrier integrity, mitigate ROS-mediated damage, and restore transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in an oxidative environment (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of vatiquinone centers on its role as a potent redox-active compound that interacts directly with cellular enzymes such as NQO1. The compound is a high-affinity substrate for NQO1, an enzyme that catalyzes the reversible two-electron reduction of quinones. This reaction is critical because it facilitates the regeneration of reduced coenzyme Q, a vital electron carrier within the mitochondrial respiratory chain. In tissues under chronic oxidative stress, such as the RPE, this reaction ensures the maintenance of mitochondrial function and energy production (Tiberi et al., 2023).

Furthermore, vatiquinone’s chemical structure confers upon it the ability to modulate the activity of the Nrf2 pathway indirectly. Under oxidative stress, Nrf2 normally dissociates from its cytosolic inhibitor Keap1, translocates to the nucleus, and induces the transcription of ARE-driven genes. These genes encode several antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes, including NQO1, glutamate–cysteine ligase, and heme oxygenase-1. By facilitating redox stabilization and promoting a favorable antioxidant environment, vatiquinone indirectly enhances the nuclear stabilization and translocation of Nrf2. This leads to a sustained increase in the expression of key components responsible for glutathione synthesis and recycling, a process crucial for neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and protecting cellular structures (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

At the molecular level, vatiquinone’s interaction with NQO1 not only catalyzes the reduction of the compound itself but also plays a broader role in restoring the redox balance of coenzyme Q within the mitochondrial membrane. The modulation of the redox state of coenzyme Q enhances the function of the electron transport chain and prevents the accumulation of ROS. Such precise biochemical regulation is essential in tissues like the RPE, which are highly susceptible to oxidative damage due to constant light exposure and high metabolic activity. The resultant maintenance of mitochondrial integrity and bioenergetics further supports the preservation of tight junction proteins and barrier function, which are compromised in chronic oxidative environments (Cores et al., 2023).

In summary, vatiquinone exerts its effects via dual modalities: a direct catalytic reduction by NQO1 that regenerates bioactive reduced coenzyme Q and an indirect upregulation of the Nrf2-dependent antioxidant response. These biochemical interactions form the cornerstone of its neuroprotective and cytoprotective properties in cells challenged by oxidative stress, providing a mechanistic rationale for its potential application in protecting RPE cells (Cores et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
Applying the known mechanisms of vatiquinone to the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration, the candidate is expected to mediate several beneficial effects in the retinal pigment epithelium. The primary hypothesis is that vatiquinone will act as a high-affinity substrate for NQO1 in RPE cells, thereby accelerating the reduction of the compound and promoting the regeneration of reduced coenzyme Q. This regeneration is essential, as it not only supports the mitochondrial electron transport chain but also contributes to the broader cellular antioxidant network through enhanced glutathione recycling (Tiberi et al., 2023).

In the proposed ARPE-19 cell assay under chronic oxidative challenge, the activation of the NQO1 pathway by vatiquinone is anticipated to improve the cellular redox state. By regenerating reduced coenzyme Q and facilitating glutathione recycling, the drug candidate is expected to neutralize increased levels of ROS that arise during sustained oxidative stress. A consequent effect of this improved redox balance would be the reduced oxidation of tight junction proteins, which are critical for maintaining the barrier integrity of the RPE. Enhanced preservation of these proteins should translate into improved transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a surrogate marker for the functional health of the RPE monolayer (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Additionally, the indirect activation of the Nrf2 pathway by vatiquinone further supports the upregulation of a spectrum of antioxidant genes. These genes, including NQO1, glutamate–cysteine ligase, and heme oxygenase-1, are known to be expressed in RPE cells, especially under oxidative stress conditions. Their increased expression is expected to bolster the cellular defense system, further reducing the accumulation of oxidative damage within the RPE. It is this coordinated regulation of antioxidant pathways that forms the basis for the expected protective effect on RPE barrier function (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023).

Moreover, when applied to the ARPE-19 cell model, the anticipated outcome is an improved survival rate and enhanced barrier properties under conditions that mimic the chronic oxidative insult characteristic of dry AMD. In vitro studies suggest that vatiquinone may limit ROS-induced modifications to cellular proteins, thereby preserving tight junction integrity. This preservation is critical not only for maintaining TEER but also for ensuring proper intercellular adhesion and barrier function, which are directly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Cores et al., 2023).

The expected benefits in the cellular assay include a reduction in oxidative markers, stabilization of mitochondrial function, and maintenance or restoration of RPE junctional architecture. These effects, if replicated in further ocular-specific studies, would position vatiquinone as a valuable therapeutic candidate for mitigating the progression of dry AMD, where oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction are culpable for disease progression (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive evaluation of vatiquinone as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration reveals several compelling strengths as well as important limitations that must be addressed in future research. One of the primary strengths of vatiquinone is its robust mode of action grounded in redox biology. Its ability to function as a high-affinity substrate for NQO1, coupled with its indirect activation of the Nrf2 pathway, equips it with a dual mechanism that promotes both direct regeneration of the reduced coenzyme Q pool and upregulation of cellular antioxidant defenses. These mechanisms are particularly significant in protecting mitochondrial function and by extension, improving cellular resilience against oxidative insults that compromise the RPE (Tiberi et al., 2023).

The wealth of historical data demonstrating vatiquinone’s efficacy in treating mitochondrial disorders such as Friedreich’s ataxia lends credence to its capability in counteracting oxidative damage and preserving tissue function. Its demonstrated ability to upregulate genes involved in glutathione synthesis and to stabilize mitochondrial function under stress makes it a promising candidate not only for neurodegenerative conditions but potentially for ocular pathologies where similar oxidative mechanisms are at play (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023). Moreover, the observation that preliminary ARPE-19 cell data indicate improved viability under oxidative challenge augments the biological plausibility of its use in dry AMD (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023).

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and uncertainties temper the enthusiasm for immediate repurposing. The most significant gap is the absence of direct evidence linking vatiquinone to therapeutic benefits specifically in dry AMD or broader retinal contexts. While the mechanistic rationale is robust, the majority of the supportive literature originates from studies in neurodegeneration and mitochondrial dysfunction rather than from ophthalmologic or RPE-specific investigations. This extrapolation, although scientifically reasonable, necessitates rigorous preclinical evaluation in ocular models to confirm efficacy in preserving retinal barrier function under chronic oxidative stress (Cores et al., 2023).

Another area requiring careful scrutiny is the complexity of the retinal microenvironment compared to neuronal tissues. Dry AMD is multifactorial, with pathogenesis that involves chronic inflammation, complement dysregulation, lipid accumulation, and cell death in addition to oxidative stress. Thus, while vatiquinone’s antioxidant and mitochondrial-protective actions are promising, it remains unclear whether these effects alone will be sufficient to alter the course of dry AMD. This ambiguity underscores the need for studies that specifically measure the impact on tight junction protein oxidation and TEER restoration in RPE cells under conditions that closely mimic the pathological environment of dry AMD (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

From a pharmacokinetic and formulation standpoint, although vatiquinone is orally bioavailable and has demonstrated favorable systemic safety profiles, the translation of systemic delivery to ocular efficacy presents challenges. Ocular tissues have unique barriers to drug delivery, and the pharmacodynamics within the retina might differ from those observed in neurological or systemic applications. Addressing these issues will require detailed ocular pharmacokinetic studies and potentially the development of optimized formulations tailored for retinal applications (Cores et al., 2023).

In summary, vatiquinone (EPI-743) is a highly promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration based on its established antioxidant properties, potent NQO1 substrate activity, and its capacity to indirectly activate Nrf2-dependent defense mechanisms. The compound’s strengths lie in its dual mechanism of action that directly addresses mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress—key contributors to RPE degeneration in dry AMD. However, the absence of direct evidence in ocular models and the inherent complexities of retinal pathophysiology represent significant hurdles that must be overcome through targeted preclinical and clinical studies. Future research should prioritize in vitro studies using ARPE-19 and other RPE models, followed by in vivo validation in animal models of dry AMD, to conclusively determine whether vatiquinone can restore TEER and protect tight junction proteins against ROS-mediated damage (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Overall, while the current body of evidence from mitochondrial and neuroprotective studies provides a strong rationale for further exploration, the repurposing of vatiquinone for dry AMD will require careful dose optimization, targeted delivery to retinal tissues, and comprehensive validation of its effects on RPE barrier integrity before it can be fully endorsed as a therapeutic option for this debilitating ocular disease (Tiberi et al., 2023; Chang & Chen, 2024; Cores et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Navitoclax (ABT-263) is a small‐molecule, orally bioavailable agent originally developed in the oncology arena as a BH3‐mimetic that targets several anti‐apoptotic members of the BCL-2 family, most notably BCL-2, BCL-xL, and BCL-W. This synthetic compound was designed through structure–activity relationship optimization to overcome the limitations of earlier compounds such as ABT-737, and it has since been classified as a senolytic agent owing to its ability to selectively induce apoptosis in senescent cells while sparing normal, quiescent cells. In the context of aging and degenerative diseases, the protective yet dysfunctional senescent cell phenotype is characterized by the upregulation of anti‐apoptotic proteins; therefore, compounds like ABT-263 that block these survival pathways have been repurposed as candidates to eliminate such senescent cells. The compound belongs to a broader class of therapeutics targeting the BCL-2 family, which have historically been exploited in various anti-cancer strategies and are now emerging as promising candidates for addressing age-associated disorders such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Ryu et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Navitoclax has a well-documented preclinical and clinical history in oncological models; its senolytic potential was first noted in studies where it selectively killed therapy-induced senescent tumor cells and other cell types by inhibiting anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins. Early clinical trials in small-cell lung cancer and lymphoid malignancies established proof-of-concept that targeting BCL-2/BCL-xL could result in tumor regression through apoptotic induction, although its clinical use was somewhat limited by dose-dependent toxicities such as thrombocytopenia. More recently, preclinical studies have extended its use beyond oncology: in in vitro studies and in mouse models where retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells were rendered senescent by doxorubicin treatment, navitoclax was shown to selectively induce apoptosis in the senescent cell population while largely sparing non-senescent RPE, as evidenced by decreased markers of senescence (p16, p21) and increased apoptotic markers such as cleaved caspases. Additionally, these studies demonstrated that oral administration of ABT-263 in mice resulted in reduced senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining and improved structural and functional retinal outcomes, including increased outer nuclear layer thickness and recovery of electroretinographic responses, which are highly encouraging for its repurposing in dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023). Despite these promising preclinical findings, navitoclax has not yet been tested in clinical trials for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative diseases, and its history in ocular conditions remains limited to proof-of-principle studies in animal models (Ryu et al., 2023; Khan et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, navitoclax exerts its senolytic action by competitively binding to the hydrophobic groove of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins, particularly BCL-2 and BCL-xL, thereby displacing pro-apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BIM. Under normal conditions, senescent cells upregulate these anti-apoptotic proteins as part of a survival mechanism against various stressors; the binding of navitoclax disrupts these protective interactions, leading to the activation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade. This biochemical disruption sets off a cascade of events culminating in mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, cytochrome c release, and the subsequent activation of caspases (notably caspase-9 and caspase-3), which orchestrate programmed cell death. Experimentally, cells treated with navitoclax have demonstrated an increased BAX/BCL-2 ratio along with elevated levels of cleaved caspases as measured by immunoblots, paralleling the reduction of canonical senescence markers such as p16 and p21. In the context of retinal degeneration, senescent RPE cells are known to secrete a deleterious senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)—including proinflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and IL-8 and matrix metalloproteases such as MMP2 and MMP9—that can undermine the integrity of junctional proteins such as ZO-1, leading to increased paracellular permeability. By eliminating these p16^Ink4a-positive senescent cells, navitoclax is hypothesized to reduce the inflammatory burden on the tissue microenvironment, thereby promoting the repopulation of healthy RPE cells and the restoration of tight junction continuity (Ryu et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of navitoclax for dry AMD is that the senolytic removal of p16^Ink4a-positive, senescent RPE cells will lead to a diminution of the SASP and its associated cytokines, such as IL-6 and IL-8, which are known to contribute to the degradation of tight junction proteins and compromise RPE barrier function. Experimental reports on navitoclax in senescent RPE models have indicated that treatment with ABT-263 not only leads to a reduction in senescence markers and SASP factor expression but also is accompanied by increased markers of cellular proliferation (e.g., Ki67) and partial recovery of structural features, such as an approximately 10% increase in outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in mouse models. While direct measurements of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and quantification of ZO-1 localization remain limited in these studies, immunofluorescence data do suggest improvements in junctional integrity following treatment with navitoclax. Thus, the expected biological effect is that clearance of senescent RPE will result in reduced paracrine inflammatory signaling, the reestablishment of stable ZO-1 belts, and overall restoration of the barrier properties of the RPE layer—a critical factor in the progression of dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
Navitoclax represents a promising therapeutic candidate as a repurposed senolytic agent for the treatment of dry AMD based on a convergence of preclinical biochemical, cellular, and animal model data. One of its primary strengths is its clear mechanism of action; by targeting a well-characterized survival pathway that is upregulated in senescent cells, navitoclax offers a rational strategy for the selective removal of dysfunctional p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells. The preclinical evidence suggests that this mechanism translates into meaningful improvements in retinal structure and function, including reductions in senescence-associated markers and partial restoration of indicators of cellular proliferation and tissue integrity (Ryu et al., 2023).

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed before navitoclax can be considered a viable treatment for dry AMD. Foremost among these is the concern regarding its safety profile. BCL-xL inhibition is known to cause dose-limiting thrombocytopenia and neutropenia in systemic applications, as evidenced by cancer trial data. In an elderly population that typically comprises dry AMD patients, where comorbidities and polypharmacy are frequent, these hematologic toxicities could limit the clinical utility of navitoclax unless strategies are devised to minimize systemic exposure or target delivery specifically to the eye. While local delivery (for example, via intravitreal injection) might mitigate some systemic risks, the optimal dosing regimen and formulation remain to be determined (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025).

Another significant limitation is the current gap in direct evidence for the selective clearance of p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells in models that accurately recapitulate the pathophysiology of human dry AMD. Many of the preclinical studies have used doxorubicin-induced senescence models, which, although useful as proof-of-principle systems, may not fully capture the chronic, age-associated accumulation of senescent RPE cells observed in patients with dry AMD. Moreover, while improvements in junctional protein distribution—such as ZO-1 localization—have been reported, there are no robust quantitative data on TEER or direct measurements of paracellular permeability that would definitively demonstrate restoration of barrier function. These issues underscore the need for more refined preclinical assays that not only assess the removal of senescent cells but also rigorously quantify the re-establishment of functional barrier properties in the RPE (Ryu et al., 2023).

Furthermore, the repurposing strategy is based on the assumption that SASP-mediated disruption of tight junctions is a primary driver of barrier dysfunction in dry AMD. While inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8 have been implicated in the degradation of junctional proteins, the complex interplay between the SASP, local immune responses, and other degenerative processes in dry AMD remains incompletely understood. Thus, while the hypothesis that senolytic clearance could reduce SASP levels and facilitate barrier recovery is compelling, it will be critical to validate these effects in models that integrate the multifactorial aspects of AMD pathogenesis (da Silva, 2021; Terao et al., 2022).

In summary, navitoclax has significant strengths as a candidate for senolytic therapy in dry AMD, notably its well-characterized mode of action and demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models that show improved retinal structure and function following the clearance of senescent cells. However, challenges such as its known systemic hematologic toxicities, the need for more disease-relevant preclinical models, and the lack of direct functional assays of RPE barrier restoration remain hurdles that need to be overcome before progressing to clinical trials. Addressing these issues may involve the development of targeted delivery systems, dose optimization studies, and rigorous functional assays that can collectively establish whether the removal of p16^Ink4a-positive senescent cells via navitoclax leads to durable improvements in RPE barrier integrity and, consequently, visual function in patients with dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Al-Naggar et al., 2020).

Critical next steps would include:  
1. Developing or validating animal models that more accurately recapitulate the chronic senescence observed in dry AMD;  
2. Refining delivery strategies to minimize systemic exposure and associated toxicities while maximizing ocular bioavailability;  
3. Implementing rigorous, quantitative assays (such as TEER measurements and detailed immunolocalization of tight junction proteins) to confirm the restoration of barrier function following senolytic treatment; and  
4. Carefully assessing the long-term outcomes of senolytic therapy on retinal structure, immune modulation, and visual performance in aged subjects (Ryu et al., 2023).

The current body of evidence lends credence to the hypothesis that navitoclax-induced senolysis in RPE could alleviate key pathological mechanisms underlying dry AMD, including SASP-mediated junctional disruption, while promoting the repopulation of healthier RPE cells (Ryu et al., 2023; Sreekumar et al., 2020). Given the strengths in its molecular targeting and the encouraging preclinical retinal data, navitoclax remains a promising candidate in the portfolio for dry AMD drug development. However, its ultimate success will hinge on overcoming the noted challenges through comprehensive preclinical validation and strategic clinical study design. Continued investigation into the precise role of p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells in AMD, together with detailed pharmacodynamic studies of navitoclax within the ocular microenvironment, will be essential to determine whether this agent can truly fulfill the promise of restoring RPE barrier function and, by extension, visual acuity in patients suffering from dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Carpenter et al., 2021).
