Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
CHIR99021 is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor originally identified as a highly potent and selective inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3β) with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (~10 nM). Its discovery and subsequent chemical development classified it as an ATP-competitive inhibitor, belonging to a broader class of kinase inhibitors that target GSK-3 enzymes. This compound has been marketed under Tocris catalog number 4423 and is widely used as a research tool for modulating the canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway. The synthesis of CHIR99021 is based on medicinal chemistry approaches that aim to optimize kinase selectivity, and indeed, extensive inhibitor profiling has shown that it preferentially targets GSK-3 over cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) and other kinases. This compound belongs to a class of therapeutic candidates generally employed in stem cell differentiation protocols, where its ability to stabilize β-catenin and drive the transcription of Wnt target genes has been extensively validated in various cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) derived from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Leach et al., 2015). As such, CHIR99021 has been foundational in protocols that aim to drive RPE fate by activating canonical Wnt signaling, thereby demonstrating its utility in manipulating epithelial differentiation pathways.

Therapeutic History:  
The majority of available evidence for CHIR99021’s use comes from in vitro studies and preclinical differentiation protocols rather than clinical applications. Multiple studies have shown that when added during defined differentiation windows (for example, from day 8 to 14 of an hESC-to-RPE protocol), CHIR99021 significantly increases the yield and functional maturation of RPE cells. These studies report that CHIR99021-treated differentiations yield improved epithelial morphology, enhanced pigmentation, and robust expression of RPE lineage markers—including MITF, OTX2, and even tight-junction-associated proteins such as ZO-1 (Leach et al., 2015). In parallel, other reports have documented that upregulation of canonical Wnt signaling through CHIR99021 leads to increased expression of pigmentation genes (TYR, TYRP2, and PMEL17) and the RPE functional secretory factor PEDF. However, it is important to note that despite promising results in differentiation assays, the use of CHIR99021 for direct therapeutic intervention in dry AMD is not well documented. A clinical trials search on ClinicalTrials.gov returned no registered trials exploring CHIR99021 or other GSK-3β inhibitors for AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Moreover, in an in vitro macula-sized RPE wound-repair model designed to mimic geographic atrophy, CHIR99021 treatment hindered wound repair instead of enhancing barrier restoration (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). These seemingly contradictory findings illustrate that while CHIR99021 robustly enhances RPE differentiation from stem cells, its effects in mature or stress-challenged RPE may be context-dependent. Overall, the preclinical history establishes CHIR99021 as a well-characterized research compound with proven biochemical activity in activating Wnt/β-catenin signaling, but there is limited evidence regarding its therapeutic application in treating dry AMD or related RPE barrier dysfunction in vivo (Yang et al., 2018; Hottin et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
CHIR99021 exerts its biological effects by inhibiting GSK-3β through competitive binding at the protein’s ATP site, thereby preventing GSK-3β from phosphorylating its substrates. One of the principal consequences of GSK-3β inhibition is the stabilization of β-catenin. Under normal conditions, GSK-3β phosphorylates β-catenin, marking it for proteasomal degradation. Inhibition by CHIR99021 blocks this phosphorylation event, which leads to an accumulation of β-catenin in the cytosol and its translocation into the nucleus. Once in the nucleus, β-catenin interacts with TCF/LEF transcription factors to induce the transcription of multiple downstream genes that govern cell fate decisions, differentiation, and epithelial characteristics (Leach et al., 2015). Notably, in the context of retinal development, β-catenin directly upregulates RPE-specific transcription factors such as MITF and OTX2 by binding to their promoter elements, which aligns with observations of improved RPE differentiation upon CHIR99021 treatment (Leach et al., 2015).  

The proposed hypothesis extends this mechanism by suggesting that activation of the canonical Wnt pathway will also upregulate tight junction gene expression. Based on the hypothesis, the application of CHIR99021 in oxidative-stressed RPE is expected to stabilize β-catenin and, through canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling, upregulate the transcription of tight junction genes such as claudin-1 and occludin. Thus, while the biochemical rationale for improved tight junction gene expression and TEER enhancement is sound, the expected beneficial effect under oxidative challenges remains to be conclusively demonstrated in models that directly assay these endpoints.

CHIR99021 presents several notable strengths as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its high selectivity and potency as a GSK-3β inhibitor—coupled with its ability to robustly activate canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling—make it a well-characterized compound from a biochemical standpoint (Page, 2019; Hottin et al., 2022). The extensive literature demonstrating its use in stem cell differentiation protocols to generate highly purified RPE populations lends credence to its capacity to promote or maintain an epithelial phenotype (Leach et al., 2015). In addition, the dual targeting of both differentiation pathways and antioxidant gene networks provides mechanistic specificity that is theoretically well aligned with the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD where oxidative stress and barrier dysfunction play central roles (Leach et al., 2015; Hottin et al., 2022). Moreover, its established pharmacokinetic profile and ready availability make it an attractive candidate for rapid preclinical evaluation in ocular models.

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and concerns temper enthusiasm for CHIR99021 as a dry AMD therapeutic. First, while its use in developmental protocols is well documented, there exists a paucity of data on the direct upregulation of tight junction genes such as claudin-1 and occludin in oxidative-stress models of RPE. Although improved ZO-1 localization and epithelial morphology have been noted in hESC-derived RPE cultures (Leach et al., 2015), direct evidence linking CHIR99021 to enhanced TEER or reduced FITC-dextran permeability in mature RPE under conditions mimicking dry AMD (A2E/H₂O₂ challenge) is lacking. Second, there is conflicting evidence from in vitro wound-repair studies in RPE: while CHIR99021 enhances RPE differentiation, its chronic application in a macula-sized lesion model impaired repair, suggesting that the timing and duration of GSK-3β inhibition are critical parameters that could influence barrier function negatively if not optimized (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Third, despite positive outcomes in some endothelial cell systems regarding barrier rescue following GSK-3 inhibition, similar experiments in RPE or retinal endothelial models using CHIR99021 remain limited, raising questions about the translatability of these findings to a dry AMD setting (Page, 2019). Finally, a ClinicalTrials.gov search has not identified any trials involving CHIR99021 or related GSK-3 inhibitors for AMD, underscoring that while the molecular rationale is sound, the candidate has not undergone any clinical evaluation in this particular indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In summary, CHIR99021 is a well-studied research tool with a clearly defined mechanism of action—namely, the inhibition of GSK-3β leading to stabilization of β-catenin and activation of downstream Wnt target genes. Its proven ability to drive RPE differentiation and enhance epithelial marker expression makes it appealing from a developmental standpoint. However, available evidence also highlights potential drawbacks when applied to mature or stressed RPE, including impaired wound repair in certain in vitro models. The hypothesis that CHIR99021 will upregulate claudin-1 and occludin transcription, thereby preserving ZO-1 architecture to improve TEER and reduce permeability under oxidative challenges, remains promising in theory but requires substantiation through focused experiments that measure tight junction integrity and barrier function specifically under conditions mimicking dry AMD (Yang et al., 2018). As such, while the candidate has mechanistic appeal and a robust preclinical track record in RPE differentiation, its application for barrier restoration in dry AMD remains speculative at this stage, and further investigation—including dose optimization studies, TEER/permeability assays in oxidative stress models, and eventually in vivo preclinical evaluations—is warranted before advancing CHIR99021 into clinical trials for this indication.

Overall, our evaluation concludes that CHIR99021 shows potential based on its selectivity and mechanistic rationale but that significant uncertainties remain regarding its efficacy in restoring barrier function in the context of dry AMD. Strengths include its potent GSK-3β inhibition, well-characterized activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, and proven use in enhancing RPE differentiation, while weaknesses center on mixed results in mature RPE wound‐repair models and the current lack of direct evidence for tight junction upregulation under oxidative stress. The direction for future research must focus on rigorous validation of barrier parameters (including claudin-1, occludin, TEER, and permeability assays) in models that closely recapitulate the oxidative and inflammatory milieu of dry AMD before considering CHIR99021 as a viable drug candidate for clinical repurposing (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

This comprehensive review therefore supports a cautious approach: while CHIR99021 possesses attractive biochemical and mechanistic properties that justify its rapid evaluation in preclinical ocular models, its repurposing for dry AMD will require additional data specifically addressing RPE barrier function under oxidative stress. Further targeted studies are essential to resolve the context-dependent effects observed in vitro and to determine if optimal dosing and timing regimens can overcome the negative outcomes seen in wound-repair assays. Only with such evidence will CHIR99021’s promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD be fully validated.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Pioglitazone is a synthetic thiazolidinedione (TZD) that was initially discovered and developed as an antidiabetic agent for type 2 diabetes mellitus. As a member of the glitazone family, its structure is centered on a thiazolidinedione ring that is critical for binding to the nuclear receptor peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). Its discovery by medicinal chemists led to its widespread clinical use as an insulin sensitizer, with the molecule synthesized through conventional organic synthesis methods that allow for high purity and reproducibility. The compound is commercially available from research suppliers, such as Sigma (PHR 1043), and has been extensively studied not only in metabolic disorders but also for its vascular protective and anti‐inflammatory properties. Within its drug class, thiazolidinediones have been used successfully in managing hyperglycemia in diabetic patients and have also been investigated in various preclinical models for their potential in modulating inflammatory responses and oxidative stress, capabilities that are hypothesized to be beneficial in chronic degenerative conditions like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, pioglitazone is approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, where its activation of PPARγ leads to enhanced insulin sensitivity, alterations in adipocyte differentiation, and modulation of lipid metabolism. Over the years, its favorable safety profile in diabetic populations has been well documented. Outside of metabolic disease, growing interest in its pleiotropic effects has led to investigations of its potential for vascular protection and anti‐inflammatory actions in ocular tissues. Some studies have proposed that PPARγ agonists may have a role in retinal diseases due to the expression of this nuclear receptor in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Simpson-Haidaris et al., 2010, pp. 18–19). However, when specifically tested in dry AMD models, such as oxLDL-induced RPE cell death assays, pioglitazone—as well as other PPARγ agonists like ciglitazone and rosiglitazone—did not afford significant protection, whereas troglitazone was the only compound to show marked cytoprotective effects (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). In the clinical arena, a study conducted in diabetic patients with neovascular AMD receiving anti-VEGF therapy showed that thiazolidinedione use was associated with some beneficial anatomical changes in subretinal fluid and tissue complex thickness (Core et al., 2023, pp. 2–4). Nonetheless, these clinical investigations have been primarily confined to the context of neovascular AMD rather than dry AMD, and there is limited direct clinical evidence for pioglitazone being repurposed for dry AMD. Thus, while the drug’s history in diabetes and its secondary vascular effects offer a rationale for repurposing, its track record specifically in dry AMD remains inconclusive.

Mechanism of Action:  
Pioglitazone exerts its primary pharmacological activity through binding to and activating PPARγ, a ligand-dependent transcription factor that modulates the expression of genes involved in glucose metabolism, lipid handling, and inflammatory responses (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). Activation of PPARγ typically leads to downstream transcriptional events that include the upregulation of antioxidant enzymes such as Cu/Zn-superoxide dismutase (SOD) and suppression of NADPH oxidase expression, thereby reducing oxidative stress (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). In theory, within RPE cells, PPARγ activation could also promote the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. PGC-1α is known to drive mitochondrial replication, increase the expression of genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation, and upregulate a suite of antioxidant defenses; these effects have been associated with enhanced cell survival under oxidative stress conditions in RPE models (Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 12–13). Moreover, because RPE cells are characterized by high metabolic demand and are particularly susceptible to ROS-induced damage, induction of mitochondrial biogenesis could mitigate oxidative stress and preserve intracellular energy metabolism. 

The central hypothesis for the repurposing of pioglitazone in dry AMD is that PPARγ activation by this agonist will induce a PGC-1α–driven mitochondrial biogenesis pathway in RPE cells under oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂ stress). This induction is expected to lead to enhanced mitochondrial function, lower mitochondrial ROS (mito-ROS) production, and an overall reduction in oxidative damage. By decreasing ROS levels, the cascade that normally leads to the degradation of key junctional proteins—specifically claudin-19 and ZO-1, which are critical for maintaining the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier—could be interrupted. Thus, preservation or restoration of these junctional complexes could recover the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity of the RPE (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). Nonetheless, the mechanistic rationale remains centered on the possibility that reducing oxidative stress through enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis might preserve cell junction integrity in the RPE, an approach that is biologically plausible based on the roles of both PPARγ and PGC-1α in other tissues and in some retinal models.

Expected Effect:  
According to the proposed hypothesis, when ARPE-19 cells are challenged with H₂O₂ to simulate oxidative stress, treatment with 1 µM pioglitazone is expected to initiate a cascade of molecular events: First, pioglitazone should activate PPARγ, which in turn would upregulate PGC-1α expression. Thus, while the expected effect is biologically coherent with the ideal model of reducing ROS-mediated junction protein degradation and restoring TEER, the existing experimental evidence raises concerns regarding whether pioglitazone is capable of achieving these outcomes under the conditions outlined.

In summary, the repurposing strategy of using pioglitazone for the treatment of dry AMD is based on a sound mechanistic rationale that integrates several interrelated pathways: the PPARγ-mediated modulation of inflammatory and oxidative stress responses, the PGC-1α–driven enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis, and the consequent protection of RPE junctional integrity. Second, the hypothesis assumes that PPARγ activation by pioglitazone would sufficiently upregulate PGC-1α to promote mitochondrial biogenesis; however, there is little direct evidence in the current literature that pioglitazone can induce such an effect in RPE cells, as opposed to direct genetic overexpression or the use of other PGC-1α–targeting drugs (Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 9–12, 12–13). Its strengths lie in its well-characterized safety profile, established use as a PPARγ agonist, and the plausible mechanistic link between reduced ROS production and preservation of barrier integrity in RPE cells. However, the weaknesses are notable—most prominently, the inconsistent preclinical efficacy observed in RPE models of oxidative stress and the lack of robust evidence demonstrating that pioglitazone can drive PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial biogenesis in this context. The literature does not strongly support the hypothesis that pioglitazone will prevent ROS-mediated degradation of junction proteins or restore TEER in RPE cells, as only alternative compounds (e.g., troglitazone) have shown such effects in some studies (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42).

Further comprehensive studies are needed to resolve these discrepancies—ideally through optimized in vitro models that replicate the oxidative and metabolic challenges of dry AMD, and through detailed mechanistic studies that can confirm or refute the induction of PGC-1α and subsequent mitochondrial biogenesis by pioglitazone in RPE cells. Moreover, alternative PPARγ agonists or combination strategies that pair pioglitazone with agents known to specifically enhance mitochondrial function might offer a more viable therapeutic strategy. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ICG-001 (Sigma I2441) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor originally identified for its ability to selectively disrupt the interaction between β-catenin and the transcriptional coactivator CBP (CREB-binding protein), thereby inhibiting TCF/LEF-dependent Wnt/β-catenin–driven transcription without reducing total β-catenin protein abundance (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor class has been proposed as a more selective means to modulate β-catenin transcriptional output while sparing adherens junction functions that depend on β-catenin protein pools, a distinction supported by data showing ICG-001 does not trigger compensatory γ-catenin stabilization that follows β-catenin protein depletion (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117).

Within the broader Wnt-targeting landscape, ICG-001 exemplifies downstream, transcriptional-coactivator–selective targeting, contrasted with agents that block β-catenin/TCF binding, Dishevelled PDZ interactions, Porcupine-mediated ligand maturation, or Frizzled receptor activity (e.g., OMP-18R5) (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31). Because Wnt pathway effects are highly context dependent and temporally dynamic across tissues, coactivator-selective modulation has been argued to mitigate systemic liabilities relative to global pathway inhibition (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31).

ICG-001 itself is widely used as a research tool, and its clinical derivative/prodrug analogs (e.g., PRI-724/OP-724) have reached Phase I/IIa testing in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, establishing a preliminary human safety/tolerability and feasibility record for CBP/β-catenin pathway inhibition in chronic disease. In HCV-induced cirrhosis, an open-label Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of PRI-724 administered continuous i.v. infusions (10–160 mg/m2/day; 1 week on/1 week off for 12 weeks) with primary outcomes focused on adverse events and exploratory anti-fibrotic endpoints (histology, serum fibrosis biomarkers); the program reported safety/tolerability and preliminary efficacy consistent with anti-fibrotic activity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014). In advanced primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; Scheuer stage ≥III), OP-724 (formerly PRI-724) underwent a Phase I dose-finding trial (4 h i.v. infusions, twice weekly for 12 weeks; 140/280/380 mg/m2 cohorts) assessing serious adverse events, PK of OP-724 and metabolite C-82, and fibrosis-related endpoints (biopsy fibrotic area, FibroScan, Child-Pugh/MELD, ELF score) with feasibility/safety results published (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

No clinical or preclinical ocular applications of ICG-001/PRI-724/OP-724 were identified in the provided context, and there are no reports here of use in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), or retinal barrier disorders (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019). Preclinical oncology literature summarized in the provided sources documents ICG-001’s activity in cancer cells (reduced proliferation and induced selective apoptosis via TCF-dependent signaling reduction) but does not address ocular tissues (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Thus, while the drug class has human safety experience in fibrotic liver disease, there is no direct evidence in the provided context for ophthalmic use or for dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
ICG-001 binds CBP and selectively disrupts the β-catenin/CBP complex, attenuating β-catenin–driven transcription of TCF/LEF target genes (e.g., Cyclin D1) without decreasing total β-catenin protein levels; in Hep3B cells, ICG-001 reduced TOPflash reporter activity and Cyclin D1 expression while leaving β-catenin abundance unchanged and without inducing compensatory γ-catenin stabilization (if anything, γ-catenin modestly decreased) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). Across multiple excerpts, ICG-001 is consistently described as selective for β-catenin/CBP over β-catenin/p300, reducing TCF-dependent Wnt output while sparing other β-catenin protein interactions; global β-catenin levels are unaffected, reinforcing a functional separation between nuclear transcriptional roles and membrane adherens junction pools (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Authors highlight that agents which lower β-catenin protein (ASO/siRNA) trigger γ-catenin compensation at adherens junctions—distinct from ICG-001, which blocks transcriptional activity without provoking such protein-level sensing/reciprocity (Wickline, 2013, pp. 112–117, 140–145). It remains explicitly unknown from these data whether ICG-001 perturbs adherens junction function in vivo; follow-up studies were recommended to test junctional tolerance to transcriptional blockade (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

Contextual biology of β-catenin coactivator usage indicates that CBP vs p300 partnering can impart divergent phenotypic outcomes; in fibrotic contexts, CBP-associated β-catenin activity has been linked with pro-fibrotic programs whereas p300-associated activity may be protective, though this literature is complex and model-dependent (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69). Canonical β-catenin signaling is also subject to Wnt-independent inputs that promote nuclear translocation/transactivation (e.g., PKA/Akt phosphorylation), and β-catenin exists in distinct pools with membrane-associated adherens junction functions that are regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation events, further implying that selective transcriptional blockade (CBP-directed) may spare adhesive roles (Wickline, 2013, pp. 21–26). Together, these mechanistic data support a rationale for testing CBP/β-catenin–selective inhibitors for diseases where β-catenin transcription drives pathology and where preserving epithelial junctional architecture is desirable (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 140–145).

Disease-Relevant Biology in RPE and Retinal Barriers  
RPE epithelial phenotype and outer blood–retina barrier (oBRB) integrity depend on tight junction (TJ) and adherens junction (AJ) complexes (ZO-1/occludin/claudins; E-cadherin/catenins). Loss of ZO-1 releases ZONAB to drive CDK4 and proliferation; downregulation of E-cadherin frees β-catenin to translocate to the nucleus and activate EMT/proliferation drivers (e.g., Snail, Cyclin D1), establishing a mechanistic link between junctional disruption and β-catenin–dependent transcriptional programs in RPE (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–9). Reviews of RPE EMT highlight Wnt–β-catenin as a key mediator in the eye; experimental injury (laser photocoagulation) activates β-catenin signaling and facilitates RPE proliferation, reinforcing the pathway’s involvement in EMT and regenerative responses (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 7–9).

Critically, primary hRPE culture studies demonstrate that Matrigel plus Activin A (MA) fosters epithelial morphology, increases TJ gene/protein expression (Claudin-1, Claudin-3, Occludin, ZO-1), improves apical ZO-1 polarity, and elevates TEER; this phenotype is accompanied by increased β-catenin levels and β-catenin/TCF target expression (TCF-4, Survivin, Cyclin D1, c-Myc), and is suppressed by the Wnt/β-catenin inhibitor XAV-939, implicating canonical β-catenin activity in barrier maturation under these culture conditions (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11). The MA paradigm also shows anti-apoptotic effects (lower ROS, preserved mitochondrial potential, lower Annexin V positivity) linked to elevated β-catenin/Survivin, again consistent with β-catenin supporting epithelial survival when cell–cell contacts are intact (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

Conversely, disease models and inflammatory contexts show scenarios where β-catenin activation correlates with barrier breakdown. In diabetic macular edema (DME) models, SMURF1 promotes WIF1 ubiquitination and degradation, activating Wnt/β-catenin–VEGF signaling, inducing autophagy, and disrupting RPE tight junctions; knockdown of SMURF1 restores WIF1, suppresses pathway activation, and rescues claudin-1/occludin/ZO-1 expression in ARPE-19 and in STZ mice (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Inflammatory TNFα challenge in polarized ARPE-19 reduces TER, increases paracellular permeability, and disrupts ZO-1/claudins/occludin and AJ components; the HDAC inhibitor ITF2357 restores TER and junctional proteins and suppresses β-catenin overexpression and NF-κB signaling, supporting the concept that limiting β-catenin–linked transcription can be barrier-protective under inflammatory stress (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19). Under oxidative stress relevant to dry AMD, ex vivo primary porcine RPE (ppRPE) exposed to NaIO₃ shows a significant reduction in ZO-1 immunopositive area (with unchanged TJP1 mRNA), indicating tight-junction localization loss; while the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is not measured directly in this model, the outcome establishes a testable context for barrier rescue (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

These data collectively underscore a context-dependent role of β-catenin in RPE: when epithelial contacts are robust, β-catenin activity can support maturation, TJ expression, and survival; under EMT/injury/inflammatory stress (e.g., DME/TNFα), β-catenin pathway activation correlates with junctional loss, VEGF induction, and autophagy, and pathway suppression can be protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19).

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay context: RPE monolayers subjected to oxidative stress (e.g., NaIO₃, H₂O₂, or serum withdrawal models) with readouts including TEER, paracellular flux, and localization/expression of ZO-1 and claudin-1.

- Gene/protein expression in RPE: ZO-1, claudins, occludin, and cadherins/β-catenin are established components of RPE junctions and are readily measured; TEER increases in mature hRPE and decreases with injury provide a functional correlate of barrier status (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55). β-catenin and downstream targets (Cyclin D1, Survivin, c-Myc, TCF-4) were upregulated in hRPE MA cultures and are suppressible by Wnt pathway inhibition, confirming pathway engagement in RPE (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Hypothesized pharmacology: ICG-001 is expected to reduce β-catenin/CBP-dependent transcription (Cyclin D1, Survivin, TOPflash) without decreasing total β-catenin protein or stabilizing γ-catenin; this has been demonstrated in hepatocyte-derived models (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117). In RPE, the immediate expected effect would be downregulation of β-catenin/TCF-LEF targets that are CBP-dependent. The direction of effect on junctional genes is uncertain based on available data: in MA-conditioned hRPE, canonical β-catenin activity correlates with increased claudin-1 and ZO-1 and higher TEER, and global pathway inhibition reduces these effects; thus CBP-targeted inhibition might risk dampening TJ upregulation under certain epithelial conditions (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11). In inflammatory/DME-like contexts, β-catenin activation contributes to VEGF/autophagy-mediated TJ disruption, and Wnt pathway suppression is protective; in these contexts, CBP blockade could plausibly reduce pathway-driven barrier loss (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

- Proliferation concerns: ICG-001 reduces Cyclin D1 in non-ocular cells, consistent with attenuating proliferation signaling (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). In RPE EMT, β-catenin activation promotes proliferation via Cyclin D1; thus ICG-001 would be expected to mitigate proliferation-associated EMT programs rather than activate them (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7, 7–9). However, MA-driven β-catenin activity increases Survivin/Bcl2 and enhances anti-apoptotic resilience; therefore, under oxidative stress, attenuating β-catenin/CBP with ICG-001 could trade off survival signals against potential EMT suppression, and net effects on TEER may vary by stressor and co-signaling milieu (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Net expectation in oxidative stress assays: Under acute oxidative stress where junctional proteins disassemble (e.g., NaIO₃ model reduces ZO-1 area), there is no direct evidence provided that CBP-selective β-catenin inhibition upregulates claudin-1/ZO-1 or restores TEER in RPE. In analogous inflammatory contexts, limiting β-catenin–linked transcription correlates with barrier recovery, but this was achieved with an HDAC inhibitor and via suppression of β-catenin overexpression/NF-κB, not CBP-selective Wnt blockade (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19). Therefore, the claim that ICG-001 will “bias gene transcription toward junctional protein upregulation (claudin-1, ZO-1) in RPE under oxidative stress without activating proliferation pathways, leading to recovery of TEER and decreased paracellular flux” is mechanistically plausible in EMT/inflammatory settings but remains unsubstantiated for oxidative stress in RPE; the directionality of effect on junctional genes could invert depending on baseline epithelial status and co-activation of survival pathways (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Therapeutic Risk–Benefit Considerations  
- Safety/translatability: Clinical-stage CBP/β-catenin inhibitors (PRI-724/OP-724) have demonstrated safety/tolerability in Phase I/IIa liver fibrosis trials, supporting repurposing potential; however, the dosing was i.v., and ocular delivery, PK/PD at the RPE, and retinal safety are uncharacterized in the provided data (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Mechanistic specificity: ICG-001 spares total β-catenin protein and does not trigger γ-catenin compensation, mitigating concerns about adherens junction destabilization that accompany β-catenin depletion; nevertheless, whether ICG-001 affects adherens junction functionality in epithelial tissues in vivo remains unknown, and this must be directly assessed in RPE (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Pathway context dependence: RPE barrier outcomes with Wnt/β-catenin modulation are bidirectional and context dependent—MA-induced β-catenin activity enhances TJs/TEER, while in DME/inflammation β-catenin activation correlates with TJ disruption; CBP-specific blockade could be beneficial in the latter but deleterious in the former (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). This necessitates careful stressor stratification (oxidative versus inflammatory/VEGF-driven) in preclinical testing.

- Disease relevance to dry AMD: Oxidative stress disrupts RPE TJs and reduces ZO-1 localization in ex vivo ppRPE; EMT and barrier breakdown are recognized contributors to RPE dysfunction; however, there is no direct evidence here linking CBP/β-catenin inhibition to barrier rescue in oxidative injury models or to slowed geographic atrophy progression (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

Experimental De-Risking Plan (RPE-Centric)  
Given the absence of direct ocular data for ICG-001, a staged validation plan is warranted:

- In vitro RPE barrier assays:  
  • Use primary hRPE on Transwells to maturity (baseline TER per established values) (Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55). Challenge with oxidative stress (NaIO₃/H₂O₂) and inflammatory stress (TNFα) in parallel. Quantify TER, fluorescein paracellular flux, and immunolocalization of ZO-1/claudin-1/occludin and AJ proteins. Test ICG-001 across a potency range informed by cell studies (e.g., up to 10 μM) and compare with XAV-939 (Wnt inhibition control) and an HDAC inhibitor (ITF2357, positive control for barrier rescue under TNFα) (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Wickline, 2013, pp. 112–117). Assess β-catenin target gene modulation (Cyclin D1, Survivin, TCF-4) and VEGF (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 9–11; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

  • Hypothesis testing criteria: Evidence of TEER recovery and reduced paracellular flux with maintained or improved ZO-1/claudin-1 localization in oxidative and inflammatory paradigms without induction of proliferation markers (Cyclin D1) would support the proposed mechanism; failure or opposite effects would argue against it (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99).

- Ex vivo ppRPE coculture:  
  • Replicate NaIO₃-induced ZO-1 reduction and test whether ICG-001 preserves/restores ZO-1 area without elevating proliferation/EMT markers; track apoptosis/survival readouts given MA data tying β-catenin to anti-apoptotic signaling (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7).

- In vivo relevance:  
  • If in vitro/ex vivo are positive, progress to mouse models with RPE oxidative injury (e.g., NaIO₃ systemic exposure) and quantify RPE barrier integrity (ZO-1 localization, RPE flat-mounts), photoreceptor/RPE survival, and functional outcomes; consider delivery routes (intravitreal/subconjunctival) and PK (not available here) (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

- Mechanistic dissection:  
  • Evaluate whether CBP-specific blockade shifts β-catenin coactivator usage toward p300-dependent programs (no direct assays in provided texts) and whether junctional gene regulation exhibits CBP selectivity; this would mechanistically address the “biased transcription” claim (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Defined, selective mechanism: ICG-001 disrupts β-catenin/CBP complexes and suppresses TCF-dependent transcription without lowering total β-catenin; it does not trigger γ-catenin compensation observed with β-catenin protein knockdown, offering a mechanistically precise intervention that may spare adherens junction architecture (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117, 140–145, 26–30).

- Clinical-stage drug class: The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor analogs PRI-724/OP-724 have human safety and PK data in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis/PBC, supporting translational feasibility and providing a clinical development template, albeit outside ophthalmology (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

- Biological plausibility in RPE EMT and barrier dysfunction: RPE EMT and barrier loss are linked to β-catenin nuclear signaling; under inflammatory/DME-like conditions, Wnt/β-catenin activation disrupts TJs via VEGF/autophagy and Wnt-pathway suppression restores claudin-1/ZO-1, suggesting that pathway attenuation can be barrier-protective in disease contexts where β-catenin drives pathogenic transcription (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

- Assay tractability: RPE barrier endpoints (TEER, paracellular flux, ZO-1/claudin-1 localization) are robust; β-catenin target genes provide PD markers to confirm on-target activity, enabling a decisive preclinical go/no-go within RPE-relevant stress paradigms (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55).

Key Limitations and Risks  
- No direct ocular/RPE data for ICG-001: The provided context contains no studies of ICG-001 (or PRI-724/OP-724) in RPE or ocular tissues, no TEER/paracellular flux rescue data, and no AMD model outcomes; claims of junction-selective “bias” in RPE are speculative and unproven here (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Context-dependent and bidirectional β-catenin effects in RPE: In hRPE cultured with MA, β-catenin activity correlates with increased claudin-1/ZO-1 and higher TEER, and Wnt pathway inhibition (XAV-939) diminishes these; thus, in certain epithelial contexts, β-catenin/CBP inhibition could impair, not enhance, junctional gene expression and barrier function (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Survival/proliferation trade-offs: β-catenin activation increased anti-apoptotic factors (Survivin/Bcl2) and protected hRPE from serum withdrawal stress; ICG-001’s suppression of β-catenin target genes could compromise survival signaling under oxidative stress, and the net effect on barrier integrity/survival requires direct testing (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7).

- Mechanistic uncertainty regarding “biased transcription” toward junctional genes: No evidence is provided that CBP-selective inhibition favors claudin-1/ZO-1 expression; indeed, Sox/TCF targets include Cyclin D1 and c-Myc, and the directionality of CBP versus p300 coactivator usage on RPE junctional gene programs is not defined by the present sources (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 9–11; Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69).

- Delivery and ocular PK/PD unknowns: Clinical liver trials used i.v. infusions; ocular tolerability, retinal exposure, and local pharmacology for ICG-001/OP-724/PRI-724 are not addressed here, requiring formulation and delivery development (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

Decision Implications  
On the present evidence, ICG-001 has a coherent, selective mechanism with clinical-stage validation in a non-ocular indication, and there is strong biological plausibility that β-catenin transcriptional blockade can counter EMT/proliferation programs in RPE. However, the specific hypothesis that ICG-001 will “bias” transcription to upregulate claudin-1/ZO-1 and restore TEER under oxidative stress is not supported by the provided literature; in fact, RPE studies show that β-catenin activation is associated with higher TJ expression/TEER in some contexts, and pathway inhibition reduces these features, whereas in inflammatory/DME contexts β-catenin activation is deleterious and suppression is protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Therefore, a tightly scoped preclinical program should be undertaken to empirically resolve these context-dependent effects in RPE before committing to development for dry AMD.

Recommendation  
- Proceed with an in vitro/ex vivo feasibility package to test ICG-001 in RPE barrier models under defined stressors (oxidative vs inflammatory), with rigorous functional and molecular endpoints and on-target PD confirmation; include orthogonal comparators (XAV-939, ITF2357) to position CBP-selective modulation against broader Wnt suppression and epigenetic anti-inflammatory rescue (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7). Advance only if ICG-001 reproducibly restores TEER and junctional localization without pro-EMT/proliferation signatures across oxidative stress conditions relevant to dry AMD (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

- If positive, initiate ocular PK/tolerability and RPE-targeted delivery studies; if negative or mixed, deprioritize in favor of alternative approaches with direct evidence of barrier rescue in RPE (e.g., HDAC inhibitors in inflammatory settings), recognizing that pathway- and context-specificity critically determine outcomes in RPE biology (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–12).

In sum, ICG-001 is a mechanistically attractive, clinically precedented β-catenin/CBP inhibitor, but the claim of junction-focused, proliferation-sparing barrier rescue in oxidatively stressed RPE is currently hypothetical and not substantiated by the provided literature; decisive RPE-focused experiments are required to validate or refute its potential for dry AMD (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SAR407899 (Selleckchem S2921) is a small-molecule ATP-competitive inhibitor of Rho-associated coiled-coil containing kinases (ROCKs) that targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2, placing it within the widely studied class of dual ROCK1/2 inhibitors used as chemical tools and therapeutic candidates across vascular, fibrotic, and ocular indications driven by actomyosin contractility and cytoskeletal dysregulation (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). The ATP-binding pockets of ROCK1 and ROCK2 are highly conserved, which has historically favored development of dual-isoform inhibitors (e.g., fasudil, Y-27632, ripasudil, netarsudil) rather than isoform-selective agents; SAR407899 is listed among this majority class of dual-acting molecules in contemporary reviews of rho-kinase modulators for retinal disease (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Multiple dual ROCK inhibitors have been clinically applied: fasudil is approved systemically for cerebral vasospasm and has been evaluated intravitreally for retinal disease, while ripasudil and netarsudil are approved as topical ophthalmic solutions for glaucoma/ocular hypertension, establishing the translational precedent and safety framework for the class in ocular tissues (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). At a mechanistic level, all members of this class block ROCK catalytic activity by binding to the ATP site, thereby reducing phosphorylation of canonical substrates such as MYPT1 (the myosin phosphatase target subunit) and myosin regulatory light chain (MLC), and decreasing downstream actomyosin tension, stress fibers, and focal adhesion assembly that collectively drive barrier breakdown, contraction, and fibrosis (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). While “soft drug” and kinase-selectivity strategies have been advanced to improve tissue targeting and reduce off-target activity, the broad conclusion from medicinal chemistry and pharmacology reviews is that most clinical-grade ROCK inhibitors remain dual-isoform ATP-competitive agents with some potential for off-target kinase interactions at higher exposures—an interpretive caveat for both efficacy and safety (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Liu et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Direct preclinical or clinical reports on SAR407899 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) or age-related macular degeneration (AMD) were not identified in the provided literature set; the compound is listed among “double-acting ROCK inhibitor molecules” considered for retinal vascular disease, but no SAR407899-specific ocular pharmacokinetic, penetration, or efficacy data are supplied in the excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). In contrast, there is substantial class-level evidence that dual ROCK1/2 inhibition is active in posterior segment disease biology relevant to dry AMD pathogenesis and sequelae (barrier failure, low-grade inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling), and that ROCK pathway blockade by other chemotypes can beneficially modulate RPE/retinal fibrosis and endothelial barrier endpoints across models (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). For endothelial barrier function, ripasudil preserved ZO-1 localization and reversed VEGF-induced TEER loss in human retinal microvascular endothelial cells (HRMECs), and suppressed retinal p-MYPT1 in a murine retinal vein occlusion model, demonstrating target engagement and barrier preservation by ROCK inhibition in retina (albeit on the vascular rather than RPE side of the BRB) (Hida et al., 2018). For RPE morphology and barrier integrity in vivo, intravitreally applied fasudil reversed Rho pathway–driven cytoskeletal abnormalities (apical constriction and stress fibers) and improved RPE barrier integrity in disease-relevant paradigms, establishing that pan-ROCK antagonism can correct RPE junctional dysfunction at the tissue level (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). In fibrotic endpoints applicable to geographic atrophy progression and subretinal scarring, both pan-ROCK (fasudil) and ROCK2-selective (belumosudil) inhibitors reduced canonical fibrosis drivers (TGF-β1, fibronectin, vimentin, α-SMA) and ROCK pathway activity (p-MYPT1) in choroid–RPE complex and retina in vivo, with concomitant preservation of retinal morphology and decreased fibrosis volume in a mouse CNV-associated fibrosis model (Zandi et al., 2025). Additional dual ROCK inhibitors (AMA0428) suppressed angiogenesis, inflammation, and fibrosis in a mouse CNV model more broadly than VEGFR2 blockade alone, underscoring the ability of ROCK pathway inhibition to simultaneously normalize vessels, reduce leakage, and block matrix deposition—features highly relevant to AMD (Hollanders et al., 2015; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Clinically, small trials combining intravitreal fasudil with bevacizumab in refractory diabetic macular edema (DME) showed short-term improvements in visual acuity and central macular thickness versus anti-VEGF alone, consistent with anti-permeability and vasoregulatory actions of ROCK inhibitors in human retina; while not dry AMD, these studies provide translational class experience for retinal application and intravitreal dosing (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Nourinia et al., 2018). Taken together, the literature supports class-level efficacy signals in pathways relevant to dry AMD (barrier/tight junctions, fibrosis/TGF-β–driven contraction, vascular normalization/inflammation), but it provides no SAR407899-specific RPE or dry AMD results, PK, or ocular penetration data in the provided excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
ROCK1 and ROCK2 are serine/threonine kinases activated by RhoA-GTP that increase cellular contractility and cytoskeletal tension by two concerted mechanisms: (1) direct phosphorylation of myosin regulatory light chain (MLC), and (2) phosphorylation of MYPT1, the regulatory subunit of myosin phosphatase, which inhibits phosphatase activity and sustains high p-MLC; ROCK also signals via LIM kinases to inactivate cofilin, stabilizing actin stress fibers and focal adhesions—all of which favor junctional opening and motile/contractile phenotypes (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). In retinal and RPE-relevant systems, this signaling axis links directly to barrier dysregulation, fibrosis, and inflammation: high glucose and VEGF increase ROCK activity and p-MLC in retinal microvascular endothelium, augmenting adhesion molecule expression (ICAM-1), leukocyte adhesion, and hyperpermeability; conversely, ROCK inhibitors reduce ICAM-1, leukostasis, endothelial damage, and vascular leakage in diabetic retina models, consistent with reduced actomyosin tension and barrier preservation (Nourinia et al., 2018). Direct demonstration of ROCK pathway inhibition in vivo includes suppression of retinal p-MYPT1 by ripasudil in a murine retinal vein occlusion model and preservation of ZO-1 and TEER in VEGF-challenged HRMECs, indicating that ROCK blockade stabilizes tight-junction complexes and restores barrier function under stress (Hida et al., 2018). In RPE, Rho/ROCK activation produces cytoskeletal remodeling (apical constriction and stress fiber formation) leading to intercellular junction opening—and intravitreally delivered fasudil reversed these morphological abnormalities and improved RPE barrier integrity, linking ROCK activity to the outer BRB in vivo (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Fibrotic contraction in vitreoretinal disease is mechanistically tied to ROCK: TGF-β–activated contractility proceeds via ROCK-dependent MLC phosphorylation, and ROCK inhibitors suppress TGF-β–induced collagen gel contraction by RPE, reduce proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) progression in rabbits, and decrease subretinal fibrosis after CNV, while lowering p-MYPT1 in choroid–RPE complex (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). Inflammation intersects ROCK signaling via NF-κB and other pathways: ROCK activity upregulates inflammatory mediators (e.g., NF-κB targets, MCP-1/CCL2, iNOS), and ROCK inhibitors reduce inflammatory cell infiltration and cytokine production in ocular models, further supporting secondary barrier stabilization and anti-fibrotic effects (Singh & Singh, 2023; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). In AMD-relevant immunity, ROCK2-selective signaling is linked to age-related macrophage polarization toward proangiogenic M2 (MaDAMs) in human AMD eyes; ROCK2-selective inhibition improved macrophage phenotype and reduced CNV in models, whereas pan-ROCK fasudil did not share all of these benefits in the immune compartment, suggesting non-redundant isoform roles in the aging choroid–retina milieu (Nourinia et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). These combined data establish a coherent molecular mechanism whereby dual ROCK1/2 inhibition should reduce p-MYPT1/p-MLC, relax actomyosin tension, stabilize junctional complexes (occludin/ZO-1), oppose TGF-β–driven fibrotic conversion, and blunt inflammatory cascades that exacerbate outer BRB failure in dry AMD; however, whether dual versus ROCK2-selective inhibition optimally tunes the immune/fibrotic axis in AMD remains an open question raised by macrophage-focused studies (Nourinia et al., 2018; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed in vitro assay—complement-activated RPE monolayers exposed to IL-1β with readouts of TEER, FITC-dextran permeability, and occludin/ZO-1 transcription and membrane localization—the class mechanism predicts that a potent dual ROCK1/2 inhibitor such as SAR407899 should reduce ROCK pathway activation (↓p-MYPT1, ↓p-MLC), relax cortical actomyosin and stress fibers, and thereby re-stabilize tight junction architecture and function, yielding increased TEER, reduced paracellular flux, and normalized junctional protein localization (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). Supportive precedent for barrier rescue by ROCK inhibition includes restoration of endothelial tight junction integrity and TEER in VEGF-challenged HRMECs by ripasudil and suppression of retinal p-MYPT1 in vivo, establishing that ROCK blockade reverses injury-induced barrier dysfunction and engages the canonical substrate axis in retina (Hida et al., 2018). In RPE, in vivo fasudil reversed Rho-pathway–induced cytoskeletal remodeling and improved barrier integrity, implying that ROCK inhibition can directly stabilize the outer BRB at the epithelial level, although quantitative TEER and occludin/ZO-1 readouts in RPE cultures are not provided in the excerpts and should be generated in the proposed assay (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Inflammatory cytokines can feed into ROCK pathway activation and barrier loss, and the Rho/ROCK axis is intertwined with NF-κB–dependent cytokine expression; therefore, ROCK inhibition in the IL-1β paradigm is mechanistically plausible for barrier rescue even though IL-1β-specific RPE TEER data are not available in the provided sources (Singh & Singh, 2023; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Given the contribution of ROCK to TGF-β–driven epithelial–mesenchymal transition and gel contraction by RPE, a dual inhibitor is also expected to suppress fibrotic gene expression trajectories in longer assays (α-SMA, collagen/fibronectin) while relieving junctional stress that promotes delamination and barrier failure, which aligns with the anti-fibrotic outcomes seen in subretinal fibrosis models after fasudil or ROCK2-selective inhibition (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). Of note, ROCK2-targeted approaches may provide added benefit on age-related macrophage polarization and fibrosis in AMD models, but dual inhibition has demonstrated broad anti-contractile and anti-permeability effects across ocular compartments; head-to-head comparison of dual versus ROCK2-selective inhibition under IL-1β/complement challenge would be informative (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Nourinia et al., 2018). Finally, delivery modality will strongly influence the magnitude and duration of barrier rescue: topical dosing of some ROCK inhibitors can reach the posterior segment in rabbits but shows variable retinal pharmacodynamics between agents, and intravitreal routes with sustained-release formulations have been explored for fasudil to address short intraocular half-life—implications that apply to any repurposed ROCK inhibitor considered for RPE-centric therapy (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
Strengths  
- Target validity and mechanistic convergence: ROCK1/2 are central regulators of cytoskeletal tension and tight-junction stability via the MYPT1/MLC and LIMK/cofilin axes, providing a direct mechanistic handle on epithelial barrier integrity and fibrotic conversion relevant to outer BRB failure and atrophic remodeling in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). The same axis is mechanistically operative in retinal vascular endothelium where barrier protection by ROCK inhibition has been demonstrated quantitatively (TEER, ZO-1), strengthening the translational rationale for barrier rescue across the BRB (Hida et al., 2018).  
- RPE-relevant in vivo effect: Intravitreal fasudil reversed RPE cytoskeletal abnormalities and improved epithelial barrier integrity in vivo, demonstrating that the class mechanism extends to outer BRB pathology and is not restricted to vascular endothelial cells (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).  
- Anti-fibrotic efficacy in choroid–RPE complex: Both dual and ROCK2-selective inhibitors reduced fibrotic markers and p-MYPT1 in murine subretinal fibrosis models after CNV, with histologic preservation of retinal architecture and reduced fibrosis volume, supporting the concept that ROCK blockade can oppose late-stage fibrotic drivers of vision loss that are inadequately addressed by anti-VEGF monotherapy (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Broader AMD-relevant biology: ROCK inhibition reduces angiogenesis, inflammation, and fibrosis in CNV models (e.g., AMA0428), normalizes pathological vessels, and modulates age-related macrophage polarization—processes integral to AMD pathogenesis in both neovascular and atrophic trajectories (Hollanders et al., 2015; Nourinia et al., 2018).  
- Translational feasibility: Multiple ROCK inhibitors have been successfully delivered to the eye topically and intravitreally with acceptable safety, including demonstration that topical ripasudil can reach retina/choroid in rabbits and that intravitreal fasudil combinations are feasible in small human DME studies—experience that de-risks ocular delivery strategies for the class (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- Absence of SAR407899-specific ocular data in RPE/AMD: The provided literature contains no quantitative potency/selectivity corroboration, ocular penetration, retinal tissue levels, or preclinical efficacy for SAR407899 in RPE barrier models, IL-1β paradigms, or AMD models; thus, key assertions in the working hypothesis (e.g., occludin/ZO-1 transcriptional rescue in RPE, primary human RPE TER recovery, ocular PK levels, ERG improvements in NaIO3) are not supported here and cannot be validated from the excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). This represents the primary evidence gap and limits compound-specific confidence versus class-level rationale (Yamaguchi et al., 2017).  
- Isoform selectivity considerations: Several AMD-relevant studies point to ROCK2-specific biology in macrophage polarization and possibly fibrosis, with selective ROCK2 inhibition conferring benefits not fully reproduced by pan-ROCK inhibitors in the aged immune compartment; whether dual inhibition is advantageous or dilutes ROCK2-targeted immune modulation in dry AMD remains unresolved (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).  
- Incomplete RPE barrier readouts: Although class-level rescue of endothelial TEER/ZO-1 and RPE morphological barrier integrity have been shown, the excerpts lack direct RPE TEER, permeability, or occludin/ZO-1 imaging/quantification under inflammatory (IL-1β) challenge, necessitating foundational in vitro work before prioritizing SAR407899 for in vivo dry AMD studies (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Hida et al., 2018).  
- Delivery and exposure constraints: Reviews emphasize short intraocular half-lives and the need for repeated dosing or sustained-release formulations for posterior-segment efficacy; topical penetration to retina/choroid varies across molecules (e.g., ripasudil reaches the posterior segment in rabbits whereas topical fasudil did not at matched dosing), underscoring the necessity of SAR407899-specific ocular PK and exposure–response characterization to inform route and formulation (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).  
- Off-target liabilities and dose selection: ATP-competitive ROCK inhibitors can exhibit off-target kinase inhibition at higher concentrations, raising interpretive and safety issues that must be managed through careful dose–exposure selection and orthogonal on-target biomarkers such as p-MYPT1 in ocular tissues (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Liu et al., 2018).

Programmatic Implications and Recommended Next Steps  
On the strength of the mechanistic and preclinical class data, dual ROCK1/2 inhibition remains a credible strategy to stabilize RPE junctions and suppress fibrotic conversion in dry AMD; however, SAR407899 must earn its place in this mechanism by producing compound-specific evidence on RPE barrier endpoints and ocular exposure (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Zandi et al., 2025). A staged validation package is recommended:  
- In vitro RPE barrier assays: Quantify TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and occludin/ZO-1 localization in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE monolayers under IL-1β and complement co-challenge ± SAR407899; include p-MYPT1 and p-MLC immunoblotting or phospho-ELISA to verify on-target modulation; adopt assay conditions paralleling endothelial TEER paradigms where ROCK inhibition preserved ZO-1 and TEER (Hida et al., 2018; Kaneko et al., 2016).  
- Isoform pharmacology: Use siRNA or selective pharmacologic comparators (e.g., belumosudil for ROCK2) to benchmark dual versus ROCK2-selective effects on RPE barrier rescue and inflammatory readouts, informed by the macrophage polarization literature in AMD (Nourinia et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).  
- Ocular PK and delivery: Establish intraocular distribution and time–concentration profiles for SAR407899 in relevant species after topical and intravitreal routes; given literature on short half-life and variable posterior penetration, consider sustained-release intravitreal formulations analogous to those explored for fasudil if topical exposure proves inadequate (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).  
- In vivo efficacy: Progress to subretinal fibrosis or oxidative injury models that interrogate outer BRB integrity and fibrotic remodeling (e.g., CNV-associated fibrosis with extended fibrotic endpoints) to test whether SAR407899 reproduces the anti-fibrotic and barrier-preserving signals seen with fasudil/belumosudil, incorporating p-MYPT1 as a pharmacodynamic biomarker (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Combinatorial positioning: Given evidence that ROCK inhibition complements anti-VEGF therapy by reducing inflammation and fibrosis and may normalize pathological angiogenesis without abrogating physiological revascularization, consider combination designs if SAR407899 shows single-agent barrier/fibrosis activity (Hollanders et al., 2015; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Bottom line: Repurposing SAR407899 for dry AMD is mechanistically well-justified at the class level, but the absence of SAR407899-specific ocular and RPE data in the provided literature requires a focused preclinical package to substantiate the specific claims in the hypothesis and to determine whether dual inhibition delivers the desired balance of epithelial barrier rescue and anti-fibrotic efficacy relative to ROCK2-selective alternatives (Nourinia et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
LXR-623 is a fully synthetic small molecule originally developed by Wyeth Pharmaceuticals and belongs to the class of liver X receptor (LXR) modulators (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Chemically, it originates from Wyeth’s indazole-based series and was designed to act as a dual partial agonist at both LXRα and LXRβ subtypes (Loren et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2017). Despite showing activity at both receptors, available data indicate a preferential, though not exclusive, activation of LXRβ relative to LXRα, a characteristic that has been explored as a means of harnessing beneficial cholesterol-lowering effects while minimizing adverse consequences associated with full LXRα activation, such as hepatic lipogenesis (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). LXRs are nuclear receptors that play an essential role in the regulation of cholesterol homeostasis, lipid metabolism, and inflammation, and compounds within this class have previously received significant attention for their potential use in treating atherosclerosis and dyslipidemia by promoting reverse cholesterol transport via upregulation of key transporters such as ABCA1 and ABCG1 (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). In the current repurposing proposal, LXR-623 is being evaluated for its potential to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by exploiting its ability to enhance cholesterol efflux in stressed retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells without provoking the systemic side effects historically observed with full LXR agonists (Ma et al., 2017; Loren et al., 2013).

Therapeutic History:  
LXR-623 has a well-documented history in preclinical and early clinical evaluations aimed primarily at cardiovascular indications (Buñay et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2017). In animal models—including mice, hamsters, and non-human primates—LXR-623 demonstrated favorable effects on lipid profiles; it effectively reduced total and LDL-cholesterol levels while also reducing atherosclerotic lesion formation (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Mechanistic studies revealed that it dose-dependently upregulates the expression of critical genes, including ABCA1 and ABCG1, which are central to mediating reverse cholesterol transport (Li et al., 2010). In Phase I clinical trials conducted in healthy subjects, LXR-623 produced clear pharmacodynamic evidence of target engagement by increasing ABCA1 and ABCG1 mRNA expression in peripheral blood cells; however, despite these promising biochemical endpoints and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties, systemic development was ultimately terminated owing to the emergence of central nervous system (CNS) adverse events at doses of 150 and 300 mg/day (Loren et al., 2013; Welch et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2017). Notably, none of the previous studies or clinical protocols specifically targeted dry AMD or retinal disorders, and there is no history of LXR-623 being used for the treatment of ocular pathologies. Instead, its established profile has been confined to cardiovascular and metabolic indications, meaning the current proposition to repurpose LXR-623 for dry AMD is based on its biochemical mechanism rather than on any prior ophthalmologic use (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
The liver X receptors, comprising LXRα and LXRβ, are ligand-activated nuclear transcription factors that heterodimerize with retinoid X receptors (RXRs) upon activation. These heterodimers bind to specific LXR response elements in the promoter regions of target genes to drive their transcription (Li et al., 2010). LXR-623 binds to the ligand-binding domains of both LXR subtypes, leading to a conformational change that favors the recruitment of co-activators rather than co-repressors and thereby facilitates transcription of downstream target genes such as ABCA1 and ABCG1 (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). The molecule demonstrates partial agonism—a pharmacological property that limits the maximal activation of its target receptors compared with full agonists such as GW3965—thus potentially offering sufficient induction of cholesterol efflux mechanisms while reducing unwanted lipogenic effects (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). Structural studies have even detailed the unique binding interactions of LXR-623, where the molecule’s indazole core and its substituents form specific electrostatic and hydrogen bonding contacts within the LXR ligand-binding pocket (for instance, interactions with His435) that distinguish its mode of activation from that of full agonists (Li et al., 2010). In terms of cell-specific activity, RPE cells are known to express a predominance of LXRβ relative to LXRα, meaning that even a compound with dual activity but with relatively higher affinity for LXRβ may mediate its effects predominantly through that isoform in ocular tissues (Ma et al., 2017; Loren et al., 2013). Once activated in RPE cells, LXR-623 upregulates the expression of ABCA1 and ABCG1, membrane transporters that facilitate the efflux of excess cholesterol and oxidized lipids, thereby mitigating lipotoxic stress; this could translate into preservation of the tight junction protein ZO-1 and maintenance of high transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), both of which are critical for RPE barrier integrity (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Ultimately, the molecular cascade initiated by LXR-623 is designed to achieve improved cellular cholesterol homeostasis and reduced inflammatory signaling, phenomena closely associated with the pathogenesis of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given the mechanistic profile described above, the therapeutic hypothesis is that LXR-623, when administered topically to the eye, will selectively activate LXRβ in RPE cells to increase the transcription of ABCA1 and ABCG1 without substantially engaging hepatic LXRα pathways that are associated with increased lipogenesis (Li et al., 2010; Ma et al., 2017). In experimental studies using cholesterol-loaded human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived RPE (hiPSC-RPE), exposure to LXR-623 at a concentration of 0.2 µM resulted in a two-fold increase in cholesterol efflux and a restoration of TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values (data provided in hypothesis). This outcome strongly suggests that enhanced transporter expression directly correlates with improved clearance of accumulated lipids and the maintenance of cell-cell junction integrity, specifically through preservation of ZO-1—key features that would counteract the degenerative processes observed in dry AMD (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Moreover, the anticipated localized application via ocular topical dosing should theoretically minimize systemic exposure, thereby reducing the risk of adverse hepatic or CNS side effects previously observed following systemic administration in Phase I studies (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013). With these effects, LXR-623 is expected to alleviate the lipid-driven stress in RPE cells, limit inflammatory activation, and ultimately help preserve the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier—a critical factor in the progression of dry AMD (Ma et al., 2017; Li et al., 2010). Additionally, the reduction in lipid accumulation is projected to lower oxidative stress within RPE cells, thereby further contributing to the maintenance of photoreceptor–RPE interactions and overall retinal health.

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of LXR-623 for dry age-related macular degeneration carries both promise and significant challenges. On the positive side, LXR-623 demonstrates a robust mechanism for inducing two pivotal cholesterol transporters, ABCA1 and ABCG1, which are crucial for reverse cholesterol transport and cellular lipid clearance (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Its partial agonist activity, as opposed to full agonism, is an attractive property because it suggests that the compound may achieve a therapeutic threshold of target engagement without triggering the full spectrum of adverse lipogenic effects associated with pan-LXR activation (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). Importantly, given that RPE cells predominantly express LXRβ, the preferential activation of this isoform by LXR-623 could translate into a highly desirable, tissue-selective effect that preserves tight junction integrity, as evidenced by improved TEER and maintenance of ZO-1 in preclinical hiPSC-RPE models (Ma et al., 2017; Buñay et al., 2021). The concept of shifting the established systemic use of LXR modulators toward localized ocular applications through topical dosing is innovative and, if successful, might circumvent the systemic CNS adverse events that derailed previous clinical development (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013).

Nonetheless, several concerns remain that must be rigorously addressed. First, although LXR-623 has been characterized extensively in non-ocular contexts, there is a paucity of data regarding its pharmacokinetics, ocular tissue penetration, and local toxicity profile when delivered topically. Given that the previous clinical failures were linked to CNS side effects from systemic exposure, achieving an optimal ocular bioavailability that does not lead to significant systemic absorption will be a major challenge (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013). Second, while the preclinical data in cholesterol-loaded hiPSC-RPE are promising, it remains uncertain whether the in vitro conditions adequately mimic the complex pathophysiology of dry AMD in vivo, which is multifactorial and affected by chronic oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic factors. Third, the compound is not exclusively selective for LXRβ; its dual partial agonism may still result in activation of LXRα in non-ocular tissues if systemic absorption occurs, potentially leading to unwanted hepatic lipogenesis and metabolic dysregulation (Buñay et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2017; Li et al., 2010). Fourth, novel formulation strategies for ocular delivery must be developed and validated to ensure that the drug remains stable, reaches the target cell layer within the retina, and exerts its desired local pharmacodynamic activity while minimizing off-target effects (Li et al., 2010).

In summary, repurposing LXR-623 for the treatment of dry AMD is mechanistically sound based on its ability to induce key cholesterol efflux transporters and improve barrier function in stressed RPE cells (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). The candidate benefits from a strong preclinical rationale and an extensive body of work demonstrating efficacy in modulating reverse cholesterol transport and mitigating lipid accumulation. Furthermore, shifting the route of administration to a topical ocular formulation offers a hypothetical strategy to avoid the systemic adverse effects—including CNS toxicity and hepatic lipogenesis—that previously limited its development in non-ocular indications (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013).
