Below is a comprehensive evaluation of SB‐431542 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). The report is organized into five sections: an overview of the therapeutic candidate, a review of its therapeutic history, a detailed discussion of its molecular mechanism of action, an explanation of the expected effects in the proposed assay and ocular environment, and an overall evaluation of its potential strengths and weaknesses for treating dry AMD.

    1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB‐431542 is a fully synthetic small molecule that was discovered through high‐throughput screening efforts at GlaxoSmithKline and further optimized via systematic structure–activity relationship studies. Its chemical identity is defined by the IUPAC name 4-[4-(3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl)-5-(2-pyridyl)-1H-imidazol-2-yl]-benzamide, and it belongs to the triarylimidazole/benzamide structural class (Markell, 2010; Fuchs, 2011). During its development, medicinal chemists employed target-hopping strategies that involved modifying substituents – for example, replacing a 4-pyridyl group with a 2-pyridyl moiety and adding a 3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl ring – to retain TGF-β type I receptor (ALK5) inhibitory potency while minimizing unwanted inhibition of other kinases such as p38 MAPK (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This precise engineering ensures that SB-431542 acts as a competitive inhibitor at the ATP‐binding site of ALK5, thereby conferring selectivity relative to other kinases (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). As a member of a well‐defined class of small molecule kinase inhibitors, SB-431542 has been used extensively as a research tool in studies of TGF-β signaling and fibrosis, and its chemical properties suggest that it belongs to a broader family of agents that modulate receptor kinases via competitive binding (Laping et al., 2002).

    2. Therapeutic History  
SB-431542 has been at the forefront of preclinical research into TGF-β signaling because of its capacity to selectively block ALK5 and, to a lesser extent, related receptors such as ALK4 and ALK7 (Laping et al., 2002; Ge et al., 2004). Its primary use has been as a chemical probe to elucidate the role of TGF-β in diverse fibrotic and oncologic settings. In multiple in vitro and in vivo studies, SB-431542 has been shown to effectively inhibit TGF-β1-induced upregulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components including collagen Iα1, fibronectin, and plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI-1) in renal epithelial cells and fibroblast cultures (Laping et al., 2002). Its potent antifibrotic activity has also been demonstrated in ocular applications; for example, it has been utilized in experimental models of glaucoma filtration surgery to reduce subconjunctival scarring by curtailing fibroblast proliferation, myofibroblast transdifferentiation, and ECM deposition (Wang et al., 2017). Although SB-431542 has not yet been approved for clinical use in AMD or other retinal disorders, its well‐documented ability to inhibit TGF-β–mediated fibrosis in ocular tissues suggests that it holds promise for these indications (Teplitsky et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2009). In addition, the compound’s extensive deployment in cancer studies – where it is used to block the epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and invasion – further verifies its capacity to modulate key pathological processes that also underlie fibrotic changes observed in retinal degeneration (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010).

    3. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, SB-431542 functions as a competitive inhibitor of the TGF-β type I receptor (ALK5) by binding to its ATP binding site. Upon the engagement of TGF-β ligands with cell surface receptors, the type II receptor phosphorylates and activates ALK5. Activated ALK5 then phosphorylates receptor-regulated Smad proteins (Smad2 and Smad3), which subsequently form complexes with Smad4 and translocate into the nucleus to drive the transcription of genes encoding ECM proteins and other pro-fibrotic factors (Laping et al., 2002). SB-431542 directly inhibits this kinase activity by occupying the ATP pocket, thereby blocking the phosphorylation of Smad2/3 and preventing their nuclear accumulation (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This interruption of TGF-β signaling ultimately suppresses the induction of pro-fibrotic genes such as those for collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002).

Importantly, SB-431542 is characterized by its selectivity. Despite the structural similarities among kinases in the TGF-β receptor superfamily, the unique conformational features of ALK5 permit SB-431542 to inhibit it to a significantly greater extent than BMP receptors (ALK2, ALK3, and ALK6) or other non-Smad pathways such as those mediated by ERK, JNK, and p38 MAPK (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This selectivity minimizes off-target effects and allows the compound to function as a precise modulator of TGF-β–dependent fibrotic signaling (Laping et al., 2002; Ling & Lee, 2011). Moreover, by inhibiting ALK5 activity, SB-431542 not only downregulates ECM protein production but also interferes with EMT processes, which are implicated in the phenotypic conversion of epithelial cells to a more mesenchymal and migratory state – a conversion that has been observed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells under stress conditions (Radeke et al., 2015; Yoon et al., 2018). In this regard, SB-431542’s molecular interactions encompass hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic contacts within the ALK5 catalytic pocket, ensuring that its inhibitory activity is both potent (with reported IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range) and selective for the intended target (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002).

    4. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis for repurposing SB-431542 in dry AMD is that inhibiting TGF-β receptor activity in RPE cells and choroidal fibroblasts will reduce pathological ECM overproduction. In dry AMD, elevated levels of TGF-β1 have been implicated in promoting the deposition of fibrotic ECM components in Bruch’s membrane, leading to increased stiffness and altered mechanical forces on the RPE monolayer (Laping et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2009). The resulting stiffening of the extracellular matrix is believed to disrupt the normal anchorage of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity and transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) of the RPE barrier (Xiao et al., 2009; Teplitsky et al., 2023).

By blocking ALK5 and thereby attenuating Smad2/3 activation, SB-431542 is expected to suppress the transcription of genes encoding collagen Iα1, fibronectin, and PAI-1. A reduction in the synthesis and deposition of these ECM components should translate into a decrease in Bruch’s membrane stiffness and the mechanical tension imposed on the RPE (Laping et al., 2002). This, in turn, is anticipated to allow the re-establishment of a continuous network of tight junctions between RPE cells as ZO-1 and occludin are able to reassemble without the interference of a pathological ECM environment (Radeke et al., 2015; Higashijima et al., 2023). When tested in ECM-coated Transwell assays, the expectation is that treatment with SB-431542 will result in improved TEER readings and a restoration of barrier function indicative of normalized RPE physiology (Xiao et al., 2009; Yoon et al., 2018).

Furthermore, TGF-β signaling in RPE cells has been associated with epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a process that not only promotes fibrosis but also deteriorates the well-ordered epithelial phenotype critical for retinal homeostasis (Radeke et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2009). Inhibition of ALK5 is predicted to counteract EMT, thereby preserving the native epithelial characteristics of RPE cells. In this context, the reduction of fibrotic ECM production and the prevention of EMT would act in synergy to reduce the abnormal mechanical stresses on RPE, enhance the continuity of tight junction proteins, and ultimately help restore retinal barrier function (Laping et al., 2002).

Given that both RPE cells and choroidal fibroblasts express TGF-β receptors and respond to TGF-β stimulation, the application of SB-431542 in co-culture models or animal studies is expected to normalize the extracellular microenvironment. This normalization could rescue the mechanical integrity of Bruch’s membrane and improve nutrient/waste exchange across the RPE monolayer—factors that are crucial in slowing or reversing the degenerative progression in dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2009).

    5. Overall Evaluation  
An overall review of SB-431542 indicates that it is a scientifically compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its proven ability to modulate TGF-β signaling and its well-documented anti-fibrotic effects. One major strength of SB-431542 is its high degree of selectivity for ALK5; by competitively inhibiting the ATP binding site on this receptor, the compound effectively blocks the Smad2/3 phosphorylation cascade that ultimately leads to ECM overproduction (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This mechanism has been validated in multiple preclinical models of fibrosis and ocular scarring, indicating that a similar strategy may be effective in the context of dry AMD where excessive ECM deposition in Bruch’s membrane is a central pathogenic feature (Xiao et al., 2009; Teplitsky et al., 2023).

Another point in favor of SB-431542 is its extensive use as a research tool in the investigation of TGF-β–dependent processes in both fibrosis and cancer. Its ability to reduce collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 levels in diverse cellular models underscores its therapeutic potential for attenuating pathological ECM production—a direct mechanism that could alleviate mechanical stress on RPE tight junctions and help restore barrier function, as measured by increased TEER and continuity of ZO-1/occludin (Laping et al., 2002).

From a mechanistic perspective, the detailed molecular interactions of SB-431542 have been characterized to a high degree, with studies demonstrating that its binding to the ALK5 catalytic pocket results in a clear inhibition of the profibrotic gene expression program (Laping et al., 2002; Ling & Lee, 2011). This precision in targeting is particularly important when considering ocular applications, as the retina is highly sensitive to off-target effects. By sparing other signaling pathways—such as those mediated by BMP receptors or Smad-independent cascades—the compound minimizes potential systemic or retinal toxicity (Laping et al., 2002).

Despite these strengths, there are also several challenges that must be addressed for SB-431542 to be successfully repurposed for dry AMD. One of the primary concerns is its pharmacokinetic profile. Preclinical studies in animal models have indicated that SB-431542 may have a relatively short half-life and rapid clearance, which raises questions about achieving sustained intraocular concentrations necessary for chronic conditions such as dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). To address this, development of a controlled-release ocular formulation—such as an intravitreal implant, microsphere-based delivery, or other sustained-release vehicle—will be essential for maintaining therapeutic levels over extended periods without systemic exposure.

Another significant challenge is the duality inherent in TGF-β signaling. While excessive TGF-β activity is responsible for the fibrotic changes observed in AMD, TGF-β also plays an important role in immune regulation, tissue repair, and maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Long-term blockade of TGF-β signaling may therefore carry inherent risks, including potential adverse effects on normal repair mechanisms or the promotion of unanticipated cellular changes such as malignant transformation (Markell, 2010; Schindeler et al., 2010). Careful dose-response studies and localized delivery strategies will be imperative to ensure that therapeutic benefits are achieved without tipping the balance toward deleterious side effects.

Moreover, although the preclinical data in ocular fibrosis models—such as those involving subconjunctival scarring after glaucoma filtration surgery—provide a promising rationale for the use of TGF-β inhibitors, direct evidence in models that recapitulate the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains limited (Xiao et al., 2009). Dry AMD is a complex disease involving not only fibrotic ECM accumulation but also oxidative stress, chronic low-grade inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation. Therefore, while the mechanistic rationale for using SB-431542 to reduce ECM production and restore RPE integrity is sound, it will likely need to be integrated into a broader therapeutic strategy that addresses these additional pathological drivers (Schindeler et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2017).

On the formulation front, the small molecule nature of SB-431542 offers both advantages and challenges. Its chemical tractability allows for modifications that could improve its ocular stability and bioavailability; however, achieving homogeneous distribution within the eye, ensuring drug stability in the vitreous environment, and avoiding direct retinal toxicity remain non-trivial challenges (Fuchs, 2011; Markell, 2010). Additionally, by virtue of its design as a competitive inhibitor, careful titration of dose will be required to ensure that effective ALK5 inhibition is sustained while minimizing interference with other cellular kinases that are essential for retinal cell survival.

In summary, SB-431542 shows significant promise as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to selectively inhibit ALK5 and thereby block the central pro-fibrotic Smad2/3 signaling axis aligns well with the mechanistic hypothesis that targeting TGF-β–mediated ECM overproduction can restore the biomechanical homeostasis of Bruch’s membrane and improve RPE barrier function (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). Furthermore, preliminary ocular studies using SB-431542 in models of surgical scarring provide an encouraging precedent for its application in the retina (Wang et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2009).

However, the pathway to clinical translation is not without hurdles. The pharmacokinetics of SB-431542, characterized by a relatively short half-life, necessitate the development of innovative drug delivery systems to sustain intraocular levels over the chronic course of AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). Additionally, the multifaceted role of TGF-β in ocular physiology requires that any therapeutic intervention be carefully calibrated to avoid impairing normal tissue repair or immunologic function (Markell, 2010; Schindeler et al., 2010). Finally, given that dry AMD is a multifactorial disease rather than being driven solely by fibrosis, further preclinical studies employing comprehensive AMD models that encompass oxidative stress and inflammation will be crucial to validate the therapeutic potential of SB-431542 in this context (Teplitsky et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025).

Overall, SB-431542 represents a scientifically robust and mechanistically well-justified candidate for repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD. Its targeted inhibition of ALK5 offers a strategic means to reduce pathological ECM deposition and thereby alleviate the mechanical stress that undermines RPE tight junction integrity—a key factor implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). The strengths of SB-431542 include its potency, selectivity, and extensive preclinical validation in fibrotic and ocular injury models. In contrast, its weaknesses center on pharmacokinetic limitations, the challenges of ocular delivery, and the complexity of broadly inhibiting a cytokine pathway that also serves beneficial roles.  

In conclusion, while additional formulation work and targeted preclinical studies remain essential, the accumulated evidence from biochemical, cellular, and ocular studies strongly supports the further evaluation of SB-431542 as part of a mechanobiology‐based therapeutic strategy for dry AMD. Given that dry AMD currently lacks effective treatments and that pathological ECM accumulation in Bruch’s membrane is a critical driver of disease progression, the repurposing of SB-431542 could provide a novel means to restore RPE barrier function by reducing ECM stiffness and re-establishing tight junction continuity (Xiao et al., 2009). Future research should focus on optimizing local delivery—potentially via sustained-release intravitreal formulations—and integrating SB-431542 within a combination therapy framework that additionally targets oxidative stress and inflammation. With these measures in place, SB-431542 holds significant promise as an innovative candidate in the quest for effective treatments for dry AMD (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002).

Thus, based on its synthetic origin, proven preclinical anti-fibrotic and anti-EMT effects, and detailed mechanistic rationale, SB-431542 merits further development for dry AMD. A rigorous, methodologically robust preclinical program – including pharmacokinetic optimization, ocular toxicity studies, and validation in relevant AMD models – will be crucial to determine whether the benefits observed in laboratory assays can be translated into meaningful clinical improvements in retinal structure and function.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SS-31, also known as Elamipretide, is a synthetic, cell‐permeable tetrapeptide that was originally discovered serendipitously during efforts to optimize opioid receptor peptide analogs and has since been rationally designed to target mitochondria by binding the lipid cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3). Its chemical structure, typically denoted as D-Arg-Dmt-Lys-Phe-NH₂—with “Dmt” representing 2,6-dimethyltyrosine—confers a unique alternating pattern of cationic and aromatic residues that endows the compound with high membrane permeability and preferential accumulation in the mitochondrial inner membrane (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 2–5). The molecular weight of SS-31 is approximately 639.8 g/mol, and its synthesis is generally performed via solid-phase peptide synthesis, which allows for efficient production and structural modification; this synthetic origin situates SS-31 within the class of mitochondria-targeting peptides or “stealth peptides” that have been extensively studied for their bioenergetic and cytoprotective properties (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In addition to its capacity to target cardiolipin, the compound’s design leverages both electrostatic attraction—owing to its positively charged arginine and lysine residues—and hydrophobic interactions from its aromatic side chains to facilitate a stable binding to the anionic membranes of mitochondria (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). As a member of a broader therapeutic class initially developed to improve mitochondrial function, SS-31 has been applied across various models of mitochondrial dysfunction, making it a promising repurposed candidate for diseases where mitochondrial impairment is a key pathological driver, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SS-31 is extensive and spans several preclinical and early-phase clinical investigations across a range of indications characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction. Preclinical studies across more than 150 peer-reviewed publications have demonstrated that SS-31 exerts robust mitochondrial protection in models of cardiac and skeletal muscle myopathies, where it improves mitochondrial structure, enhances ATP production, reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and ultimately ameliorates organ dysfunction (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3, 10–11). In the cardiovascular arena, animal models of heart failure and ischemia-reperfusion injury have documented that SS-31 treatment leads to improved left ventricular function and reduced tissue biomarkers of injury, effects that are attributed to its ability to stabilize cardiolipin and maintain the integrity of the electron transport system (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 10–12). Further, in neuromuscular and metabolic disease models, the compound has been shown to enhance mitochondrial ATP production and reduce oxidative stress, with early clinical studies in rare mitochondrial disorders such as Barth syndrome (a condition involving cardiolipin abnormalities) and primary mitochondrial myopathy providing supportive translational evidence (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 10–11, 16–22). More recently, SS-31 has been explored in the context of ocular diseases, including nonneovascular age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) and diabetic macular edema, where preclinical studies in murine models report that subcutaneous administration of SS-31 can reverse electroretinographic deficits, facilitate the clearance of sub-retinal pigment epithelium (sub‐RPE) deposits, and ultimately reverse vision loss (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Clinical trials—such as the Phase I ReCLAIM study in intermediate AMD and the ongoing Phase II ReCLAIM-2 trial—have begun to assess SS-31’s safety profile, pharmacokinetics, and preliminary efficacy in preserving visual function, thereby positioning it as a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Although its use in dry AMD is relatively novel compared to its established preclinical record in other mitochondrial disorders, the existing scientific and regulatory trajectory supports its potential repurposing for diseases in which mitochondrial dysfunction is a central pathogenic mechanism (Nashine, 2021, pp. 9–11, 16).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism by which SS-31 exerts its cytoprotective effects is centered on its highly specific interaction with cardiolipin, an anionic phospholipid unique to the mitochondrial inner membrane that plays a pivotal role in maintaining the structural integrity of cristae and the proper assembly and function of electron transport chain complexes (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). Detailed biophysical studies, including nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations, have demonstrated that SS-31 binds to cardiolipin via both electrostatic interactions (through its basic residues) and hydrophobic interactions (via its aromatic side chains), resulting in the “neutralization” of the negative surface charge on mitochondrial membranes and a favorable modulation of membrane fluidity and curvature (Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4; Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 16–22). This binding not only stabilizes cardiolipin against oxidative peroxidation but also promotes the optimal assembly of electron transport chain complexes into respiratory supercomplexes, thereby enhancing electron flow, reducing electron leakage, and ultimately decreasing the generation of ROS (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 4–6, 15–16). In addition, SS-31 has been shown to mitigate proton leakage and restore pH stress resistance in aged mitochondria by enhancing the function of critical proteins such as the adenine nucleotide translocator (ANT), which is central to ADP/ATP exchange and overall mitochondrial bioenergetics (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 10–12). Although SS-31 was initially characterized as an antioxidant, its primary mode of action is now understood to be the preservation of mitochondrial structure and function through cardiolipin stabilization rather than direct radical scavenging alone (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4). In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress—a key pathological hallmark of dry AMD—the hypothesis posits that by stabilizing mitochondria via cardiolipin binding, SS-31 will maintain normal electron transport chain efficiency, preserve ATP production, and limit ROS production, thereby protecting the integrity of RPE cells (Tong et al., 2022, pp. 14–16). Although direct experimental evidence linking SS-31 to the preservation of tight junction proteins such as ZO-1/occludin or to the restoration of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE cells is limited in the current literature, the well-documented mitochondrial protection afforded by SS-31 in other cellular models suggests that secondary benefits on cellular barrier function are plausible given the tight coupling between mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and loss of epithelial integrity (Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). In an experimental setting where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative stress—for example, through hydrogen peroxide treatment—the administration of SS-31 is anticipated to result in the selective binding to cardiolipin within RPE mitochondria; this interaction should stabilize inner mitochondrial membrane architecture, preserve cristae morphology, and enhance the efficiency of electron transport, leading to robust ATP production and reduced ROS levels (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). Overall, SS-31 (Elamipretide) presents as a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, with several key strengths that support its potential utility and a few noteworthy challenges that will need to be addressed in further research. One of the primary strengths of SS-31 is its well-characterized mechanism of action; its ability to bind cardiolipin and thereby stabilize mitochondrial inner membrane structure, enhance electron transport chain efficiency, and reduce ROS generation is supported by robust preclinical data across multiple models of mitochondrial dysfunction, including cardiac, skeletal muscle, and retinal systems (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4). Furthermore, early-phase clinical studies in ocular disease have demonstrated that SS-31 is safe and well tolerated and have hinted at functional improvements in visual acuity and reduced progression of retinal degeneration, which supports its translational viability (Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5). The repurposing of SS-31 from conditions such as heart failure and primary mitochondrial myopathy to an ocular application leverages its established bioenergetic benefits and broad mitochondrial stabilization properties, thereby enhancing its appeal as a novel intervention for dry AMD (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 10–11, 16–22).

Third, while the pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of SS-31 appear favorable for reaching mitochondrial targets, ensuring sufficient ocular penetration and accumulation in the RPE—whether via systemic subcutaneous administration or topical formulations—remains a logistical and pharmacological challenge that must be addressed in future clinical development (Tong et al., 2022, pp. 14–16; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Pioglitazone is a synthetic thiazolidinedione (TZD) that was initially discovered and developed as an antidiabetic agent for type 2 diabetes mellitus. As a member of the glitazone family, its structure is centered on a thiazolidinedione ring that is critical for binding to the nuclear receptor peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). Its discovery by medicinal chemists led to its widespread clinical use as an insulin sensitizer, with the molecule synthesized through conventional organic synthesis methods that allow for high purity and reproducibility. The compound is commercially available from research suppliers, such as Sigma (PHR 1043), and has been extensively studied not only in metabolic disorders but also for its vascular protective and anti‐inflammatory properties. Within its drug class, thiazolidinediones have been used successfully in managing hyperglycemia in diabetic patients and have also been investigated in various preclinical models for their potential in modulating inflammatory responses and oxidative stress, capabilities that are hypothesized to be beneficial in chronic degenerative conditions like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, pioglitazone is approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, where its activation of PPARγ leads to enhanced insulin sensitivity, alterations in adipocyte differentiation, and modulation of lipid metabolism. Over the years, its favorable safety profile in diabetic populations has been well documented. Outside of metabolic disease, growing interest in its pleiotropic effects has led to investigations of its potential for vascular protection and anti‐inflammatory actions in ocular tissues. Some studies have proposed that PPARγ agonists may have a role in retinal diseases due to the expression of this nuclear receptor in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Simpson-Haidaris et al., 2010, pp. 18–19). However, when specifically tested in dry AMD models, such as oxLDL-induced RPE cell death assays, pioglitazone—as well as other PPARγ agonists like ciglitazone and rosiglitazone—did not afford significant protection, whereas troglitazone was the only compound to show marked cytoprotective effects (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). In the clinical arena, a study conducted in diabetic patients with neovascular AMD receiving anti-VEGF therapy showed that thiazolidinedione use was associated with some beneficial anatomical changes in subretinal fluid and tissue complex thickness (Core et al., 2023, pp. 2–4). Nonetheless, these clinical investigations have been primarily confined to the context of neovascular AMD rather than dry AMD, and there is limited direct clinical evidence for pioglitazone being repurposed for dry AMD. Thus, while the drug’s history in diabetes and its secondary vascular effects offer a rationale for repurposing, its track record specifically in dry AMD remains inconclusive.

Mechanism of Action:  
Pioglitazone exerts its primary pharmacological activity through binding to and activating PPARγ, a ligand-dependent transcription factor that modulates the expression of genes involved in glucose metabolism, lipid handling, and inflammatory responses (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). Activation of PPARγ typically leads to downstream transcriptional events that include the upregulation of antioxidant enzymes such as Cu/Zn-superoxide dismutase (SOD) and suppression of NADPH oxidase expression, thereby reducing oxidative stress (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). In theory, within RPE cells, PPARγ activation could also promote the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. PGC-1α is known to drive mitochondrial replication, increase the expression of genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation, and upregulate a suite of antioxidant defenses; these effects have been associated with enhanced cell survival under oxidative stress conditions in RPE models (Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 12–13). Moreover, because RPE cells are characterized by high metabolic demand and are particularly susceptible to ROS-induced damage, induction of mitochondrial biogenesis could mitigate oxidative stress and preserve intracellular energy metabolism. 

The central hypothesis for the repurposing of pioglitazone in dry AMD is that PPARγ activation by this agonist will induce a PGC-1α–driven mitochondrial biogenesis pathway in RPE cells under oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂ stress). This induction is expected to lead to enhanced mitochondrial function, lower mitochondrial ROS (mito-ROS) production, and an overall reduction in oxidative damage. By decreasing ROS levels, the cascade that normally leads to the degradation of key junctional proteins—specifically claudin-19 and ZO-1, which are critical for maintaining the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier—could be interrupted. Thus, preservation or restoration of these junctional complexes could recover the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity of the RPE (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). However, existing in vitro studies in RPE models have shown that among several tested PPARγ agonists, pioglitazone did not replicate the cytoprotective effects seen with troglitazone, and the beneficial effects in these studies were found to be independent of PPARγ activation (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). This discrepancy raises questions about whether pioglitazone can induce the PGC-1α pathway effectively in this context. Nonetheless, the mechanistic rationale remains centered on the possibility that reducing oxidative stress through enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis might preserve cell junction integrity in the RPE, an approach that is biologically plausible based on the roles of both PPARγ and PGC-1α in other tissues and in some retinal models.

Expected Effect:  
According to the proposed hypothesis, when ARPE-19 cells are challenged with H₂O₂ to simulate oxidative stress, treatment with 1 µM pioglitazone is expected to initiate a cascade of molecular events: First, pioglitazone should activate PPARγ, which in turn would upregulate PGC-1α expression. This upregulation is anticipated to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and function, resulting in a measurable decrease in mitochondrial ROS production as detected by MitoSOX fluorescence assays. In addition, by lowering ROS levels, the compound is expected to protect against the degradation of cell junction proteins such as claudin-19 and ZO-1. These proteins are essential for the formation and maintenance of the tight junction belts in RPE cells, contributing to the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier. The experimental readouts proposed include a 45% recovery in TEER, a surrogate marker for barrier integrity, suggesting that pioglitazone would restore functional barrier properties that are compromised under oxidative stress conditions (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). It is important to note, however, that while these effects have been observed in some isolated experiments, the majority of the literature on PPARγ agonists in RPE models has primarily highlighted that only troglitazone, rather than pioglitazone, yielded significant cytoprotection against oxidative insults (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). Thus, while the expected effect is biologically coherent with the ideal model of reducing ROS-mediated junction protein degradation and restoring TEER, the existing experimental evidence raises concerns regarding whether pioglitazone is capable of achieving these outcomes under the conditions outlined.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the repurposing strategy of using pioglitazone for the treatment of dry AMD is based on a sound mechanistic rationale that integrates several interrelated pathways: the PPARγ-mediated modulation of inflammatory and oxidative stress responses, the PGC-1α–driven enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis, and the consequent protection of RPE junctional integrity. The well-established clinical safety profile of pioglitazone in diabetic populations is an important strength, as it facilitates potential rapid translation to clinical trials for new indications. Additionally, the notion that mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS overproduction play central roles in RPE degeneration and barrier disruption in dry AMD provides a compelling target for therapeutic intervention (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).

However, there are several weaknesses and limitations to consider. First, while pioglitazone has demonstrated vascular protective and anti-inflammatory properties in other contexts, the literature on its direct effects in RPE cells under oxidative stress is mixed. Notably, in multiple in vitro studies investigating PPARγ agonists in models of oxidative stress-induced RPE cell death, pioglitazone—as well as other compounds such as ciglitazone and rosiglitazone—failed to confer significant cytoprotection, with only troglitazone showing robust protective effects (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 31–37, 37–42). This discrepancy suggests that either pioglitazone does not effectively induce the mitochondrial biogenesis pathway via PGC-1α in RPE cells or that its mechanism of action may not directly translate into the preservation of tight junction proteins like claudin-19 and ZO-1 under oxidative stress. Second, the hypothesis assumes that PPARγ activation by pioglitazone would sufficiently upregulate PGC-1α to promote mitochondrial biogenesis; however, there is little direct evidence in the current literature that pioglitazone can induce such an effect in RPE cells, as opposed to direct genetic overexpression or the use of other PGC-1α–targeting drugs (Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 9–12, 12–13). Third, while a reported experimental observation of a 45% recovery in TEER in H₂O₂-challenged ARPE-19 cells treated with 1 µM pioglitazone is promising, it is in marked contrast to the majority of findings in similar oxidative stress assays, calling for cautious interpretation and independent validation (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Given these considerations, the overall evaluation of pioglitazone as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is mixed. Its strengths lie in its well-characterized safety profile, established use as a PPARγ agonist, and the plausible mechanistic link between reduced ROS production and preservation of barrier integrity in RPE cells. However, the weaknesses are notable—most prominently, the inconsistent preclinical efficacy observed in RPE models of oxidative stress and the lack of robust evidence demonstrating that pioglitazone can drive PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial biogenesis in this context. The literature does not strongly support the hypothesis that pioglitazone will prevent ROS-mediated degradation of junction proteins or restore TEER in RPE cells, as only alternative compounds (e.g., troglitazone) have shown such effects in some studies (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42).

In conclusion, while the molecular rationale for targeting mitochondrial dysfunction and junctional breakdown in dry AMD is compelling, and the repurposing of a clinically validated drug like pioglitazone is attractive from a safety and translational standpoint, the current experimental evidence raises significant doubts about its efficacy in this specific application. Further comprehensive studies are needed to resolve these discrepancies—ideally through optimized in vitro models that replicate the oxidative and metabolic challenges of dry AMD, and through detailed mechanistic studies that can confirm or refute the induction of PGC-1α and subsequent mitochondrial biogenesis by pioglitazone in RPE cells. Moreover, alternative PPARγ agonists or combination strategies that pair pioglitazone with agents known to specifically enhance mitochondrial function might offer a more viable therapeutic strategy. Until such additional data become available, the repurposing of pioglitazone for dry AMD should be considered with caution, and resources may better be allocated towards candidates with more consistent preclinical efficacy in relevant RPE models (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ripasudil, also known by its research designation Y-39983 and commercially available as Selleckchem S8443, is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor developed originally as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil containing protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. It belongs to a class of therapeutics that act in an ATP‐competitive manner to inhibit the activity of ROCK isoforms, enzymes that are critical regulators of actomyosin contractility and cell adhesion. Ripasudil was synthesized following the structural optimization of earlier compounds such as fasudil and Y-27632, with the aim of increasing both potency and ocular tolerability. Its chemical origins are linked to the rational design strategies that sought to improve enzyme inhibitory selectivity and to enhance the pharmacokinetic profile for local ocular application. Members of the ROCK inhibitor class have seen prior use in settings that require modulation of actin cytoskeleton dynamics, such as the treatment of glaucoma via enhanced aqueous humor outflow, and have also been explored in contexts involving wound healing and anti-fibrotic effects in various ocular tissues (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, ripasudil has been approved in Japan for the treatment of glaucoma and ocular hypertension, where it is delivered topically in the form of eye drops, demonstrating a well-established safety profile and a low incidence of systemic adverse effects. In preclinical models, it has demonstrated efficacy by increasing ocular blood flow, modifying trabecular meshwork cell contractility, and reducing intraocular pressure, thereby serving as a stepping stone and proof-of-concept for the utility of ROCK inhibitors in ocular disorders. Beyond its approved use in glaucoma, investigations of ROCK inhibitors—including ripasudil—have extended into experimental applications in corneal endothelial regeneration and have been evaluated in combination with anti-VEGF therapies for diabetic macular edema. Although direct clinical evidence specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is not available, multiple lines of preclinical research have shown that the ROCK inhibitor class modulates pathways which are believed to underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Notably, the mechanistic studies have identified the role of ROCK signaling in cytoskeletal reorganization, matrix contractility, and fibrosis, all of which are processes particularly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier dysfunction seen in dry AMD (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Moreover, the ocular pharmacokinetic profile of ripasudil—demonstrated by rabbit intravitreal studies showing a half-life of approximately 14 hours and negligible systemic exposure—is supportive of repurposing this candidate for posterior segment indications, including dry AMD (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ripasudil exerts its therapeutic activity by competitively inhibiting the ATP-binding site of ROCK isoforms, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of downstream effectors such as myosin light-chain (MLC), myosin-binding subunit of MLC phosphatase (MYPT1), and LIM kinase. These phosphorylation events normally lead to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, focal adhesion assembly, and ultimately contribute to a contractile, stiffened cell phenotype. In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, this contractility is thought to be exacerbated under conditions of oxidative stress, contributing to disassembly or mislocalization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity. By inhibiting ROCK, ripasudil reduces actomyosin-driven contraction and stress-fiber formation, thereby promoting cortical F-actin remodeling and facilitating the proper membrane relocalization of tight-junction proteins. The specificity of ripasudil has been demonstrated by its greater than 100-fold selectivity against other kinases such as protein kinase C (PKC) and myotonic dystrophy kinase-related Cdc42-binding kinase (MRCK), highlighting the mechanistic precision by which it modulates ROCK-dependent signaling cascades (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Additionally, while several studies indicate that the ROCK inhibitor class generally targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2 isoforms, quantitative biochemical data have shown that ripasudil exhibits potent enzyme inhibitory activity with IC₅₀s in the low nanomolar range (with values reported around 51 nM for ROCK1 and 19 nM for ROCK2 in some studies, though the candidate hypothesis posits values of approximately 29 nM for ROCK1 and 68 nM for ROCK2). This inhibitory profile is particularly relevant because emerging research indicates that ROCK2, in particular, is upregulated in the pathological conditions of dry AMD and plays a key role in mediating cytoskeletal changes that disrupt RPE tight junction integrity (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). The inhibition of ROCK thereby is expected to have a dual benefit of cytoprotection and restoration of cell junction architecture, ultimately leading to improved barrier function (Ghenciu et al., 2025; Singh & Singh, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing ripasudil for dry AMD is that by blocking ROCK activity in oxidatively stressed retinal pigment epithelium cells, the compound will lead to a reduction in actomyosin contractility, thereby alleviating the formation of pathological stress fibers that otherwise disrupt the organization of tight junction complexes. Under normal physiological conditions, tight junction proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin are localized at the plasma membrane in a continuous, belt-like manner that is essential to maintain TEER and restrict paracellular permeability. However, in dry AMD, oxidative damage, inflammation, and mechanical stress lead to cytoskeletal reorganization and a discontinuous distribution of these critical proteins, resulting in impaired barrier function and contributing to the pathogenesis of the disease. Preclinical studies, particularly those employing ARPE-19 cell models subjected to toxic insults such as paraquat or sodium iodate (NaIO₃), have demonstrated that ROCK inhibitors can dose-dependently restore TEER (with reported improvements up to 70%) and re-establish the membrane continuity of ZO-1, suggesting that these agents can “rescue” the RPE barrier phenotype under injurious conditions (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). It is expected that ripasudil, with its potent ROCK-inhibitory activity and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics (including intravitreal retention times supportive of sustained action), will similarly promote the cortical redistribution of F-actin, leading to the re-localization of junctional molecules back to the cell membrane. This mechanistic restoration should result in improved transepithelial electrical resistance and a concomitant reduction in paracellular permeability, effectively reinforcing the RPE barrier—a central therapeutic target in dry AMD. Moreover, the activation of protective cellular pathways through ROCK inhibition may also confer additional anti-apoptotic and anti-inflammatory effects, further contributing to the survival and functional integrity of the RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating ripasudil as a candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths become apparent. First, its established clinical use for glaucoma means that its safety, tolerability, and ocular pharmacokinetic properties are well characterized—attributes that significantly lower the translational barrier for its application in other ocular diseases. The intravitreal pharmacokinetic data, with a half-life of approximately 14 hours in rabbit models and negligible systemic exposure, suggest that therapeutic concentrations capable of modulating ROCK activity in the retina can be achieved with acceptable dosing regimens (Yamaguchi et al., 2016). Second, the mechanistic rationale is compelling: ROCK signaling is intimately involved in mediating actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, and subsequent disruption of tight junction architecture in epithelial cells. Given that ROCK2 in particular is implicated in the pathological processes observed in the RPE in dry AMD, the ability of ripasudil to inhibit this pathway could translate into measurable improvements in barrier function, as indicated by preclinical assays demonstrating TEER restoration and the re-localization of ZO-1 in ARPE-19 cells (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Third, the compound exhibits a favorable selectivity profile, with negligible off-target activity against other kinases such as PKC and MRCK, which minimizes the risk of unintended effects in non-target tissues. This specificity is critical when repurposing drugs for chronic conditions such as dry AMD, where long-term ocular safety is paramount (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Despite these strengths, there are notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before ripasudil can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. A primary limitation is the paucity of direct experimental evidence in RPE models of dry AMD. While the hypothesis is supported by data from related in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative stress), robust in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of dry AMD pathophysiology are still needed. In particular, data demonstrating that ripasudil can restore tight junction integrity and improve TEER in the context of chronic, progressive RPE dysfunction remain limited (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Furthermore, although the compound’s ROCK inhibitory activity is well documented, the available literature does not consistently detail the isoform-specific effects in RPE cells; given that ROCK1 and ROCK2 may play distinct roles in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, clarifying the relative contributions of each isoform is essential. The candidate hypothesis posits specific IC₅₀ values for ROCK1 and ROCK2, yet discrepancies exist across reported studies regarding the precise inhibitory concentrations, which indicates that further biochemical characterization is warranted (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). Another consideration is the potential for adverse effects when repurposing a drug originally optimized for anterior-segment diseases for posterior-segment applications. Although the ocular safety profile of ripasudil in glaucoma is well established, the long-term impact of ROCK inhibition on RPE cell biology in an aged population—especially in the context of dry AMD—remains uncertain. Off-target cytoskeletal effects in other retinal cell types, possible modulation of inflammatory responses, and the risk of inadvertently triggering compensatory signaling pathways are all factors that must be carefully evaluated in preclinical studies (Iancu et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2025). Lastly, while the pharmacokinetic data support retinal exposure after intravitreal or possibly topical administration, optimizing the delivery method to ensure sustained and localized drug levels in the RPE without causing ocular surface toxicity (such as conjunctival hyperemia or corneal epithelial disturbances) will be critical. Innovative delivery systems, such as sustained-release intravitreal implants or depot formulations, may offer solutions but require further development (Yamaguchi et al., 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023).

In conclusion, the repurposing of ripasudil for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and a favorable safety profile derived from its established use in glaucoma. The compound’s capacity to inhibit ROCK-mediated actomyosin contraction and promote cortical F-actin remodeling positions it as a promising agent for restoring RPE barrier function—one of the key pathological features of dry AMD. However, the current literature reveals significant gaps in direct evidence regarding its effects on RPE tight junction proteins, TEER restoration, and the isoform-specific roles of ROCK in the RPE under oxidative stress. To advance ripasudil as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, additional preclinical investigations—ideally incorporating robust animal models of dry AMD and detailed biochemical analyses of ROCK isoform activity in RPE cells—are required. Additionally, optimizations in drug delivery methodology to achieve sustained posterior-segment exposure while minimizing adverse ocular events will be imperative. Overall, ripasudil presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, with its strengths in mechanistic specificity, favorable ocular pharmacokinetics, and established clinical safety underscoring its potential. Nonetheless, the outlined weaknesses and knowledge gaps necessitate a rigorous program of targeted research to validate its efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity and to ensure its long-term safety in the intended patient population (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023; Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Adams & Papillon, 2020; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Pioglitazone is a synthetic thiazolidinedione (TZD) that was initially discovered and developed as an antidiabetic agent for type 2 diabetes mellitus. As a member of the glitazone family, its structure is centered on a thiazolidinedione ring that is critical for binding to the nuclear receptor peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). Its discovery by medicinal chemists led to its widespread clinical use as an insulin sensitizer, with the molecule synthesized through conventional organic synthesis methods that allow for high purity and reproducibility. The compound is commercially available from research suppliers, such as Sigma (PHR 1043), and has been extensively studied not only in metabolic disorders but also for its vascular protective and anti‐inflammatory properties. Within its drug class, thiazolidinediones have been used successfully in managing hyperglycemia in diabetic patients and have also been investigated in various preclinical models for their potential in modulating inflammatory responses and oxidative stress, capabilities that are hypothesized to be beneficial in chronic degenerative conditions like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, pioglitazone is approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, where its activation of PPARγ leads to enhanced insulin sensitivity, alterations in adipocyte differentiation, and modulation of lipid metabolism. Over the years, its favorable safety profile in diabetic populations has been well documented. Outside of metabolic disease, growing interest in its pleiotropic effects has led to investigations of its potential for vascular protection and anti‐inflammatory actions in ocular tissues. Some studies have proposed that PPARγ agonists may have a role in retinal diseases due to the expression of this nuclear receptor in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Simpson-Haidaris et al., 2010, pp. 18–19). However, when specifically tested in dry AMD models, such as oxLDL-induced RPE cell death assays, pioglitazone—as well as other PPARγ agonists like ciglitazone and rosiglitazone—did not afford significant protection, whereas troglitazone was the only compound to show marked cytoprotective effects (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). In the clinical arena, a study conducted in diabetic patients with neovascular AMD receiving anti-VEGF therapy showed that thiazolidinedione use was associated with some beneficial anatomical changes in subretinal fluid and tissue complex thickness (Core et al., 2023, pp. 2–4). Nonetheless, these clinical investigations have been primarily confined to the context of neovascular AMD rather than dry AMD, and there is limited direct clinical evidence for pioglitazone being repurposed for dry AMD. Thus, while the drug’s history in diabetes and its secondary vascular effects offer a rationale for repurposing, its track record specifically in dry AMD remains inconclusive.

Mechanism of Action:  
Pioglitazone exerts its primary pharmacological activity through binding to and activating PPARγ, a ligand-dependent transcription factor that modulates the expression of genes involved in glucose metabolism, lipid handling, and inflammatory responses (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). Activation of PPARγ typically leads to downstream transcriptional events that include the upregulation of antioxidant enzymes such as Cu/Zn-superoxide dismutase (SOD) and suppression of NADPH oxidase expression, thereby reducing oxidative stress (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). In theory, within RPE cells, PPARγ activation could also promote the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. PGC-1α is known to drive mitochondrial replication, increase the expression of genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation, and upregulate a suite of antioxidant defenses; these effects have been associated with enhanced cell survival under oxidative stress conditions in RPE models (Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 12–13). Moreover, because RPE cells are characterized by high metabolic demand and are particularly susceptible to ROS-induced damage, induction of mitochondrial biogenesis could mitigate oxidative stress and preserve intracellular energy metabolism. 

The central hypothesis for the repurposing of pioglitazone in dry AMD is that PPARγ activation by this agonist will induce a PGC-1α–driven mitochondrial biogenesis pathway in RPE cells under oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂ stress). This induction is expected to lead to enhanced mitochondrial function, lower mitochondrial ROS (mito-ROS) production, and an overall reduction in oxidative damage. By decreasing ROS levels, the cascade that normally leads to the degradation of key junctional proteins—specifically claudin-19 and ZO-1, which are critical for maintaining the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier—could be interrupted. Thus, preservation or restoration of these junctional complexes could recover the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity of the RPE (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). However, existing in vitro studies in RPE models have shown that among several tested PPARγ agonists, pioglitazone did not replicate the cytoprotective effects seen with troglitazone, and the beneficial effects in these studies were found to be independent of PPARγ activation (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). This discrepancy raises questions about whether pioglitazone can induce the PGC-1α pathway effectively in this context. Nonetheless, the mechanistic rationale remains centered on the possibility that reducing oxidative stress through enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis might preserve cell junction integrity in the RPE, an approach that is biologically plausible based on the roles of both PPARγ and PGC-1α in other tissues and in some retinal models.

Expected Effect:  
According to the proposed hypothesis, when ARPE-19 cells are challenged with H₂O₂ to simulate oxidative stress, treatment with 1 µM pioglitazone is expected to initiate a cascade of molecular events: First, pioglitazone should activate PPARγ, which in turn would upregulate PGC-1α expression. This upregulation is anticipated to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and function, resulting in a measurable decrease in mitochondrial ROS production as detected by MitoSOX fluorescence assays. In addition, by lowering ROS levels, the compound is expected to protect against the degradation of cell junction proteins such as claudin-19 and ZO-1. These proteins are essential for the formation and maintenance of the tight junction belts in RPE cells, contributing to the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier. The experimental readouts proposed include a 45% recovery in TEER, a surrogate marker for barrier integrity, suggesting that pioglitazone would restore functional barrier properties that are compromised under oxidative stress conditions (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). It is important to note, however, that while these effects have been observed in some isolated experiments, the majority of the literature on PPARγ agonists in RPE models has primarily highlighted that only troglitazone, rather than pioglitazone, yielded significant cytoprotection against oxidative insults (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). Thus, while the expected effect is biologically coherent with the ideal model of reducing ROS-mediated junction protein degradation and restoring TEER, the existing experimental evidence raises concerns regarding whether pioglitazone is capable of achieving these outcomes under the conditions outlined.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the repurposing strategy of using pioglitazone for the treatment of dry AMD is based on a sound mechanistic rationale that integrates several interrelated pathways: the PPARγ-mediated modulation of inflammatory and oxidative stress responses, the PGC-1α–driven enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis, and the consequent protection of RPE junctional integrity. The well-established clinical safety profile of pioglitazone in diabetic populations is an important strength, as it facilitates potential rapid translation to clinical trials for new indications. Additionally, the notion that mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS overproduction play central roles in RPE degeneration and barrier disruption in dry AMD provides a compelling target for therapeutic intervention (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).

However, there are several weaknesses and limitations to consider. First, while pioglitazone has demonstrated vascular protective and anti-inflammatory properties in other contexts, the literature on its direct effects in RPE cells under oxidative stress is mixed. Notably, in multiple in vitro studies investigating PPARγ agonists in models of oxidative stress-induced RPE cell death, pioglitazone—as well as other compounds such as ciglitazone and rosiglitazone—failed to confer significant cytoprotection, with only troglitazone showing robust protective effects (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 31–37, 37–42). This discrepancy suggests that either pioglitazone does not effectively induce the mitochondrial biogenesis pathway via PGC-1α in RPE cells or that its mechanism of action may not directly translate into the preservation of tight junction proteins like claudin-19 and ZO-1 under oxidative stress. Second, the hypothesis assumes that PPARγ activation by pioglitazone would sufficiently upregulate PGC-1α to promote mitochondrial biogenesis; however, there is little direct evidence in the current literature that pioglitazone can induce such an effect in RPE cells, as opposed to direct genetic overexpression or the use of other PGC-1α–targeting drugs (Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 9–12, 12–13). Third, while a reported experimental observation of a 45% recovery in TEER in H₂O₂-challenged ARPE-19 cells treated with 1 µM pioglitazone is promising, it is in marked contrast to the majority of findings in similar oxidative stress assays, calling for cautious interpretation and independent validation (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Given these considerations, the overall evaluation of pioglitazone as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is mixed. Its strengths lie in its well-characterized safety profile, established use as a PPARγ agonist, and the plausible mechanistic link between reduced ROS production and preservation of barrier integrity in RPE cells. However, the weaknesses are notable—most prominently, the inconsistent preclinical efficacy observed in RPE models of oxidative stress and the lack of robust evidence demonstrating that pioglitazone can drive PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial biogenesis in this context. The literature does not strongly support the hypothesis that pioglitazone will prevent ROS-mediated degradation of junction proteins or restore TEER in RPE cells, as only alternative compounds (e.g., troglitazone) have shown such effects in some studies (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42).

In conclusion, while the molecular rationale for targeting mitochondrial dysfunction and junctional breakdown in dry AMD is compelling, and the repurposing of a clinically validated drug like pioglitazone is attractive from a safety and translational standpoint, the current experimental evidence raises significant doubts about its efficacy in this specific application. Further comprehensive studies are needed to resolve these discrepancies—ideally through optimized in vitro models that replicate the oxidative and metabolic challenges of dry AMD, and through detailed mechanistic studies that can confirm or refute the induction of PGC-1α and subsequent mitochondrial biogenesis by pioglitazone in RPE cells. Moreover, alternative PPARγ agonists or combination strategies that pair pioglitazone with agents known to specifically enhance mitochondrial function might offer a more viable therapeutic strategy. Until such additional data become available, the repurposing of pioglitazone for dry AMD should be considered with caution, and resources may better be allocated towards candidates with more consistent preclinical efficacy in relevant RPE models (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Navitoclax (ABT-263) is a small‐molecule, orally bioavailable agent originally developed in the oncology arena as a BH3‐mimetic that targets several anti‐apoptotic members of the BCL-2 family, most notably BCL-2, BCL-xL, and BCL-W. This synthetic compound was designed through structure–activity relationship optimization to overcome the limitations of earlier compounds such as ABT-737, and it has since been classified as a senolytic agent owing to its ability to selectively induce apoptosis in senescent cells while sparing normal, quiescent cells. In the context of aging and degenerative diseases, the protective yet dysfunctional senescent cell phenotype is characterized by the upregulation of anti‐apoptotic proteins; therefore, compounds like ABT-263 that block these survival pathways have been repurposed as candidates to eliminate such senescent cells. The compound belongs to a broader class of therapeutics targeting the BCL-2 family, which have historically been exploited in various anti-cancer strategies and are now emerging as promising candidates for addressing age-associated disorders such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Ryu et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Navitoclax has a well-documented preclinical and clinical history in oncological models; its senolytic potential was first noted in studies where it selectively killed therapy-induced senescent tumor cells and other cell types by inhibiting anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins. Early clinical trials in small-cell lung cancer and lymphoid malignancies established proof-of-concept that targeting BCL-2/BCL-xL could result in tumor regression through apoptotic induction, although its clinical use was somewhat limited by dose-dependent toxicities such as thrombocytopenia. More recently, preclinical studies have extended its use beyond oncology: in in vitro studies and in mouse models where retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells were rendered senescent by doxorubicin treatment, navitoclax was shown to selectively induce apoptosis in the senescent cell population while largely sparing non-senescent RPE, as evidenced by decreased markers of senescence (p16, p21) and increased apoptotic markers such as cleaved caspases. Additionally, these studies demonstrated that oral administration of ABT-263 in mice resulted in reduced senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining and improved structural and functional retinal outcomes, including increased outer nuclear layer thickness and recovery of electroretinographic responses, which are highly encouraging for its repurposing in dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023). Despite these promising preclinical findings, navitoclax has not yet been tested in clinical trials for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative diseases, and its history in ocular conditions remains limited to proof-of-principle studies in animal models (Ryu et al., 2023; Khan et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, navitoclax exerts its senolytic action by competitively binding to the hydrophobic groove of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins, particularly BCL-2 and BCL-xL, thereby displacing pro-apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BIM. Under normal conditions, senescent cells upregulate these anti-apoptotic proteins as part of a survival mechanism against various stressors; the binding of navitoclax disrupts these protective interactions, leading to the activation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade. This biochemical disruption sets off a cascade of events culminating in mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, cytochrome c release, and the subsequent activation of caspases (notably caspase-9 and caspase-3), which orchestrate programmed cell death. Experimentally, cells treated with navitoclax have demonstrated an increased BAX/BCL-2 ratio along with elevated levels of cleaved caspases as measured by immunoblots, paralleling the reduction of canonical senescence markers such as p16 and p21. In the context of retinal degeneration, senescent RPE cells are known to secrete a deleterious senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)—including proinflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and IL-8 and matrix metalloproteases such as MMP2 and MMP9—that can undermine the integrity of junctional proteins such as ZO-1, leading to increased paracellular permeability. By eliminating these p16^Ink4a-positive senescent cells, navitoclax is hypothesized to reduce the inflammatory burden on the tissue microenvironment, thereby promoting the repopulation of healthy RPE cells and the restoration of tight junction continuity (Ryu et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of navitoclax for dry AMD is that the senolytic removal of p16^Ink4a-positive, senescent RPE cells will lead to a diminution of the SASP and its associated cytokines, such as IL-6 and IL-8, which are known to contribute to the degradation of tight junction proteins and compromise RPE barrier function. Experimental reports on navitoclax in senescent RPE models have indicated that treatment with ABT-263 not only leads to a reduction in senescence markers and SASP factor expression but also is accompanied by increased markers of cellular proliferation (e.g., Ki67) and partial recovery of structural features, such as an approximately 10% increase in outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in mouse models. While direct measurements of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and quantification of ZO-1 localization remain limited in these studies, immunofluorescence data do suggest improvements in junctional integrity following treatment with navitoclax. Thus, the expected biological effect is that clearance of senescent RPE will result in reduced paracrine inflammatory signaling, the reestablishment of stable ZO-1 belts, and overall restoration of the barrier properties of the RPE layer—a critical factor in the progression of dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
Navitoclax represents a promising therapeutic candidate as a repurposed senolytic agent for the treatment of dry AMD based on a convergence of preclinical biochemical, cellular, and animal model data. One of its primary strengths is its clear mechanism of action; by targeting a well-characterized survival pathway that is upregulated in senescent cells, navitoclax offers a rational strategy for the selective removal of dysfunctional p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells. The preclinical evidence suggests that this mechanism translates into meaningful improvements in retinal structure and function, including reductions in senescence-associated markers and partial restoration of indicators of cellular proliferation and tissue integrity (Ryu et al., 2023).

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed before navitoclax can be considered a viable treatment for dry AMD. Foremost among these is the concern regarding its safety profile. BCL-xL inhibition is known to cause dose-limiting thrombocytopenia and neutropenia in systemic applications, as evidenced by cancer trial data. In an elderly population that typically comprises dry AMD patients, where comorbidities and polypharmacy are frequent, these hematologic toxicities could limit the clinical utility of navitoclax unless strategies are devised to minimize systemic exposure or target delivery specifically to the eye. While local delivery (for example, via intravitreal injection) might mitigate some systemic risks, the optimal dosing regimen and formulation remain to be determined (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025).

Another significant limitation is the current gap in direct evidence for the selective clearance of p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells in models that accurately recapitulate the pathophysiology of human dry AMD. Many of the preclinical studies have used doxorubicin-induced senescence models, which, although useful as proof-of-principle systems, may not fully capture the chronic, age-associated accumulation of senescent RPE cells observed in patients with dry AMD. Moreover, while improvements in junctional protein distribution—such as ZO-1 localization—have been reported, there are no robust quantitative data on TEER or direct measurements of paracellular permeability that would definitively demonstrate restoration of barrier function. These issues underscore the need for more refined preclinical assays that not only assess the removal of senescent cells but also rigorously quantify the re-establishment of functional barrier properties in the RPE (Ryu et al., 2023).

Furthermore, the repurposing strategy is based on the assumption that SASP-mediated disruption of tight junctions is a primary driver of barrier dysfunction in dry AMD. While inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8 have been implicated in the degradation of junctional proteins, the complex interplay between the SASP, local immune responses, and other degenerative processes in dry AMD remains incompletely understood. Thus, while the hypothesis that senolytic clearance could reduce SASP levels and facilitate barrier recovery is compelling, it will be critical to validate these effects in models that integrate the multifactorial aspects of AMD pathogenesis (da Silva, 2021; Terao et al., 2022).

In summary, navitoclax has significant strengths as a candidate for senolytic therapy in dry AMD, notably its well-characterized mode of action and demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models that show improved retinal structure and function following the clearance of senescent cells. However, challenges such as its known systemic hematologic toxicities, the need for more disease-relevant preclinical models, and the lack of direct functional assays of RPE barrier restoration remain hurdles that need to be overcome before progressing to clinical trials. Addressing these issues may involve the development of targeted delivery systems, dose optimization studies, and rigorous functional assays that can collectively establish whether the removal of p16^Ink4a-positive senescent cells via navitoclax leads to durable improvements in RPE barrier integrity and, consequently, visual function in patients with dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Al-Naggar et al., 2020).

Critical next steps would include:  
1. Developing or validating animal models that more accurately recapitulate the chronic senescence observed in dry AMD;  
2. Refining delivery strategies to minimize systemic exposure and associated toxicities while maximizing ocular bioavailability;  
3. Implementing rigorous, quantitative assays (such as TEER measurements and detailed immunolocalization of tight junction proteins) to confirm the restoration of barrier function following senolytic treatment; and  
4. Carefully assessing the long-term outcomes of senolytic therapy on retinal structure, immune modulation, and visual performance in aged subjects (Ryu et al., 2023).

The current body of evidence lends credence to the hypothesis that navitoclax-induced senolysis in RPE could alleviate key pathological mechanisms underlying dry AMD, including SASP-mediated junctional disruption, while promoting the repopulation of healthier RPE cells (Ryu et al., 2023; Sreekumar et al., 2020). Given the strengths in its molecular targeting and the encouraging preclinical retinal data, navitoclax remains a promising candidate in the portfolio for dry AMD drug development. However, its ultimate success will hinge on overcoming the noted challenges through comprehensive preclinical validation and strategic clinical study design. Continued investigation into the precise role of p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells in AMD, together with detailed pharmacodynamic studies of navitoclax within the ocular microenvironment, will be essential to determine whether this agent can truly fulfill the promise of restoring RPE barrier function and, by extension, visual acuity in patients suffering from dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Carpenter et al., 2021).
