Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose (α,α-trehalose) is a naturally occurring, nonreducing disaccharide composed of two d-glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond; it is broadly found in bacteria, fungi, insects, invertebrates, and plants but is not synthesized by vertebrates, including humans (trehalase in the small intestine hydrolyzes ingested trehalose to glucose) (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). Trehalose’s physicochemical properties include high aqueous solubility, chemical stability, and resistance to glucosidases; it has been mass-produced since the 1990s via enzymatic methods and has been approved for food use by EU regulators and the US FDA, with human exposure generally safe apart from low incidences of malabsorption (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). In drug-development parlance, trehalose is a small-molecule, carbohydrate autophagy modulator and proteostasis regulator; it exhibits both biophysical “chemical chaperone” activity that stabilizes macromolecules and biologic activity that induces the autophagy–lysosome program via TFEB/TFE3 activation and related nutrient-sensing pathways (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Jeong et al., 2021, pp. 1–3, 12–13; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). As a class, autophagy-enhancing small molecules (including trehalose) have been utilized across neurodegeneration and metabolic disease models to promote clearance of toxic protein aggregates or dysfunctional organelles and to restore lysosomal function, with trehalose showing efficacy signals in preclinical Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, Huntington’s disease, and lysosomal storage–related models (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Lotfi et al., 2018, pp. 12–15). Within ophthalmology, trehalose has established use as a topical osmoprotectant/bioprotective excipient in eye-drop formulations for dry-eye disease (commonly 3% w/v), and it is under active investigation for posterior-segment neuroprotection, including age-related retinal degeneration models relevant to AMD (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 18–20; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 10–13).

Therapeutic History  
Clinical/translational use: Trehalose is approved as a safe food ingredient and has been widely used in humans, including topical ophthalmic preparations for dry eye disease and post-LASIK care, with multiple clinical trials and a marketed formulation (e.g., Thealoz Duo, 3% trehalose plus hyaluronic acid) supporting ocular-surface safety and symptomatic benefit; the patented formulation increased tear film thickness after a single drop in clinical testing (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 18–20). Safety data support tolerability of topical trehalose in humans and of high-concentration in vitro exposure across multiple cell types; ocular-surface animal models show safety and barrier-protective effects, and in vitro human RPE studies report no loss of viability up to 200 mM for 24 h, though dosing windows matter for efficacy (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 5–7). Oral trehalose is hydrolyzed by intestinal trehalase and exhibits poor systemic bioavailability, limiting efficacy for some systemic indications; parenteral trehalose achieves low-millimolar plasma levels transiently, which can activate TFEB/TFE3 in macrophages in vivo, but oral exposure is generally insufficient to reach such systemic concentrations in mice in atherosclerosis models (Evans et al., 2018, pp. 2–3). Nonetheless, oral trehalose has shown retinal effects in mice, improving autophagy pathways and preserving cone ERG responses during aging, suggesting either BRB permeability or indirect choroidal effects; the authors noted that establishing BRB permeability is important for translation (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 181–188).

Ocular/retinal preclinical evidence: Multiple independent groups demonstrate mechanistic and functional efficacy of trehalose in RPE/retinal models relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology. In human RPE cell systems (ARPE-19, haRPE, and iPSC-RPE), trehalose increases autophagic flux (LC3-II accumulation with CQ, free GFP readouts), upregulates lysosomal biogenesis markers (LAMP-1/2, cathepsin D), elevates TFEB transcripts and protein, expands the lysosomal compartment (Lysotracker), engages both macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy, and confers autophagy-dependent protection against oxidative stressors such as hydroquinone (HQ), a cigarette smoke–derived oxidant implicated in AMD (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 151–160; Fisher et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). In primary murine RPE, trehalose restored autophagic flux under oxidative stress and improved mitochondrial respiratory function in vitro (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In vivo, topical trehalose eye drops increase autophagy–lysosome activity in mouse RPE (LC3B turnover, p62 degradation, LC3B–LAMP1 colocalization) and protect against light-induced outer retinal degeneration (preserving ONL thickness, RPE morphology, and junctional F-actin) without overt changes in unchallenged retina (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 10–13). Oral trehalose increased retinal autophagy and improved cone photopic ERG with age, and in a lysosomal enzyme-deficiency model (MPS IIIB) trehalose reduced retinal degeneration, restored retinal structure/function, and extended lifespan, with effects dependent on canonical autophagy and TFEB activation; trehalose increased TFEB nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene expression in brain and rescued retinal phenotypes (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 181–188; Lotfi et al., 2018, pp. 12–15).

AMD-model efficacy: In an APOE knockout model that recapitulates early AMD features (decreased retinal function, Bruch’s membrane thickening), chronic trehalose treatment ameliorated functional loss and reduced Bruch’s membrane thickening while normalizing autophagy markers (restoring LC3-II:LC3-I to WT, increasing LC3/LAMP1 labeling and autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE), with pathway analyses pointing to ATM–AMPK activation and, for trehalose, increased p38/MAPK14 signaling (Vessey et al., 2022, pp. 1–2, 11–13). Clinical status for AMD: A ClinicalTrials.gov query indicates at least two registered trials for “Trehalose AND macular degeneration,” but the excerpt provides no identifiers or results, so clinical evidence in AMD is presently insufficient for efficacy conclusions (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Collectively, these histories support trehalose as an autophagy/lysosome-modulating candidate with direct RPE/retina efficacy signals in AMD-relevant models, established human ocular-surface safety, and translational rationale for non-neovascular AMD (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Vessey et al., 2022, p. 1).

Both candidates target key pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD, but their supporting evidence and translational readiness differ markedly. Candidate 1, LXR-623, is a partial LXRα/β agonist with in vitro data in cholesterol-loaded hiPSC-RPE showing upregulation of ABCA1/ABCG1, restored TEER, and preservation of ZO-1. Candidate 2, JQ1, is a pan-BET bromodomain inhibitor with deep mechanistic validation of cGAS–STING repression, NF-κB suppression, and autophagy enhancement in RPE and retinal microglia. Multiple in vivo ophthalmic models (rd10 photoreceptor degeneration, sodium iodate RPE injury, light damage, PVR) demonstrate robust neuroprotection, barrier preservation, reduced microglial infiltration, and favorable ocular safety after intravitreal or sustained intraocular delivery. Ocular PK challenges (short half-life) are addressed by nanoparticle and PROTAC strategies, and local delivery minimizes systemic liabilities. While direct RPE TEER data for JQ1 are lacking, endothelial and microglial barrier precedents and in vivo functional endpoints strongly support its efficacy. The target biology (innate immunity, inflammation, microglia) aligns closely with dry AMD pathogenesis and has been validated in AMD-relevant injury models.
Overall, JQ1 offers a more mature preclinical data package with in vivo ocular efficacy, clear translational delivery strategies, and a safety profile in ocular contexts, whereas LXR-623 remains at early in vitro proof-of-concept without ocular data or confirmed delivery and safety in the eye.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
LXR-623 is a fully synthetic small molecule originally developed by Wyeth Pharmaceuticals and belongs to the class of liver X receptor (LXR) modulators (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Chemically, it originates from Wyeth’s indazole-based series and was designed to act as a dual partial agonist at both LXRα and LXRβ subtypes (Loren et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2017). Despite showing activity at both receptors, available data indicate a preferential, though not exclusive, activation of LXRβ relative to LXRα, a characteristic that has been explored as a means of harnessing beneficial cholesterol-lowering effects while minimizing adverse consequences associated with full LXRα activation, such as hepatic lipogenesis (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). LXRs are nuclear receptors that play an essential role in the regulation of cholesterol homeostasis, lipid metabolism, and inflammation, and compounds within this class have previously received significant attention for their potential use in treating atherosclerosis and dyslipidemia by promoting reverse cholesterol transport via upregulation of key transporters such as ABCA1 and ABCG1 (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). In the current repurposing proposal, LXR-623 is being evaluated for its potential to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by exploiting its ability to enhance cholesterol efflux in stressed retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells without provoking the systemic side effects historically observed with full LXR agonists (Ma et al., 2017; Loren et al., 2013).

Therapeutic History:  
LXR-623 has a well-documented history in preclinical and early clinical evaluations aimed primarily at cardiovascular indications (Buñay et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2017). In animal models—including mice, hamsters, and non-human primates—LXR-623 demonstrated favorable effects on lipid profiles; it effectively reduced total and LDL-cholesterol levels while also reducing atherosclerotic lesion formation (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Mechanistic studies revealed that it dose-dependently upregulates the expression of critical genes, including ABCA1 and ABCG1, which are central to mediating reverse cholesterol transport (Li et al., 2010). In Phase I clinical trials conducted in healthy subjects, LXR-623 produced clear pharmacodynamic evidence of target engagement by increasing ABCA1 and ABCG1 mRNA expression in peripheral blood cells; however, despite these promising biochemical endpoints and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties, systemic development was ultimately terminated owing to the emergence of central nervous system (CNS) adverse events at doses of 150 and 300 mg/day (Loren et al., 2013; Welch et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2017). Notably, none of the previous studies or clinical protocols specifically targeted dry AMD or retinal disorders, and there is no history of LXR-623 being used for the treatment of ocular pathologies. Instead, its established profile has been confined to cardiovascular and metabolic indications, meaning the current proposition to repurpose LXR-623 for dry AMD is based on its biochemical mechanism rather than on any prior ophthalmologic use (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
The liver X receptors, comprising LXRα and LXRβ, are ligand-activated nuclear transcription factors that heterodimerize with retinoid X receptors (RXRs) upon activation. These heterodimers bind to specific LXR response elements in the promoter regions of target genes to drive their transcription (Li et al., 2010). LXR-623 binds to the ligand-binding domains of both LXR subtypes, leading to a conformational change that favors the recruitment of co-activators rather than co-repressors and thereby facilitates transcription of downstream target genes such as ABCA1 and ABCG1 (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). The molecule demonstrates partial agonism—a pharmacological property that limits the maximal activation of its target receptors compared with full agonists such as GW3965—thus potentially offering sufficient induction of cholesterol efflux mechanisms while reducing unwanted lipogenic effects (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). Structural studies have even detailed the unique binding interactions of LXR-623, where the molecule’s indazole core and its substituents form specific electrostatic and hydrogen bonding contacts within the LXR ligand-binding pocket (for instance, interactions with His435) that distinguish its mode of activation from that of full agonists (Li et al., 2010). In terms of cell-specific activity, RPE cells are known to express a predominance of LXRβ relative to LXRα, meaning that even a compound with dual activity but with relatively higher affinity for LXRβ may mediate its effects predominantly through that isoform in ocular tissues (Ma et al., 2017; Loren et al., 2013). Once activated in RPE cells, LXR-623 upregulates the expression of ABCA1 and ABCG1, membrane transporters that facilitate the efflux of excess cholesterol and oxidized lipids, thereby mitigating lipotoxic stress; this could translate into preservation of the tight junction protein ZO-1 and maintenance of high transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), both of which are critical for RPE barrier integrity (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Ultimately, the molecular cascade initiated by LXR-623 is designed to achieve improved cellular cholesterol homeostasis and reduced inflammatory signaling, phenomena closely associated with the pathogenesis of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given the mechanistic profile described above, the therapeutic hypothesis is that LXR-623, when administered topically to the eye, will selectively activate LXRβ in RPE cells to increase the transcription of ABCA1 and ABCG1 without substantially engaging hepatic LXRα pathways that are associated with increased lipogenesis (Li et al., 2010; Ma et al., 2017). In experimental studies using cholesterol-loaded human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived RPE (hiPSC-RPE), exposure to LXR-623 at a concentration of 0.2 µM resulted in a two-fold increase in cholesterol efflux and a restoration of TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values (data provided in hypothesis). This outcome strongly suggests that enhanced transporter expression directly correlates with improved clearance of accumulated lipids and the maintenance of cell-cell junction integrity, specifically through preservation of ZO-1—key features that would counteract the degenerative processes observed in dry AMD (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Moreover, the anticipated localized application via ocular topical dosing should theoretically minimize systemic exposure, thereby reducing the risk of adverse hepatic or CNS side effects previously observed following systemic administration in Phase I studies (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013). With these effects, LXR-623 is expected to alleviate the lipid-driven stress in RPE cells, limit inflammatory activation, and ultimately help preserve the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier—a critical factor in the progression of dry AMD (Ma et al., 2017; Li et al., 2010). Additionally, the reduction in lipid accumulation is projected to lower oxidative stress within RPE cells, thereby further contributing to the maintenance of photoreceptor–RPE interactions and overall retinal health.

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of LXR-623 for dry age-related macular degeneration carries both promise and significant challenges. On the positive side, LXR-623 demonstrates a robust mechanism for inducing two pivotal cholesterol transporters, ABCA1 and ABCG1, which are crucial for reverse cholesterol transport and cellular lipid clearance (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Its partial agonist activity, as opposed to full agonism, is an attractive property because it suggests that the compound may achieve a therapeutic threshold of target engagement without triggering the full spectrum of adverse lipogenic effects associated with pan-LXR activation (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). Importantly, given that RPE cells predominantly express LXRβ, the preferential activation of this isoform by LXR-623 could translate into a highly desirable, tissue-selective effect that preserves tight junction integrity, as evidenced by improved TEER and maintenance of ZO-1 in preclinical hiPSC-RPE models (Ma et al., 2017; Buñay et al., 2021). The concept of shifting the established systemic use of LXR modulators toward localized ocular applications through topical dosing is innovative and, if successful, might circumvent the systemic CNS adverse events that derailed previous clinical development (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013).

Nonetheless, several concerns remain that must be rigorously addressed. First, although LXR-623 has been characterized extensively in non-ocular contexts, there is a paucity of data regarding its pharmacokinetics, ocular tissue penetration, and local toxicity profile when delivered topically. Given that the previous clinical failures were linked to CNS side effects from systemic exposure, achieving an optimal ocular bioavailability that does not lead to significant systemic absorption will be a major challenge (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013). Second, while the preclinical data in cholesterol-loaded hiPSC-RPE are promising, it remains uncertain whether the in vitro conditions adequately mimic the complex pathophysiology of dry AMD in vivo, which is multifactorial and affected by chronic oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic factors. Third, the compound is not exclusively selective for LXRβ; its dual partial agonism may still result in activation of LXRα in non-ocular tissues if systemic absorption occurs, potentially leading to unwanted hepatic lipogenesis and metabolic dysregulation (Buñay et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2017; Li et al., 2010). Fourth, novel formulation strategies for ocular delivery must be developed and validated to ensure that the drug remains stable, reaches the target cell layer within the retina, and exerts its desired local pharmacodynamic activity while minimizing off-target effects (Li et al., 2010).

In summary, repurposing LXR-623 for the treatment of dry AMD is mechanistically sound based on its ability to induce key cholesterol efflux transporters and improve barrier function in stressed RPE cells (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). The candidate benefits from a strong preclinical rationale and an extensive body of work demonstrating efficacy in modulating reverse cholesterol transport and mitigating lipid accumulation. Furthermore, shifting the route of administration to a topical ocular formulation offers a hypothetical strategy to avoid the systemic adverse effects—including CNS toxicity and hepatic lipogenesis—that previously limited its development in non-ocular indications (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
JQ1 (Selleck S7110) is a synthetic small-molecule thienotriazolodiazepine developed as a first-in-class, highly selective competitive inhibitor of the bromodomain and extra-terminal (BET) acetyl-lysine reader family (BRD2/3/4, BRDT) that binds the acetyl-lysine pocket of BET bromodomains (BD1 and BD2) to displace BET proteins from chromatin and suppress transcription at dependent enhancers and promoters (pan-BET, BD1/BD2 non-selective) (Zhao et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2023). BET bromodomains recognize acetylated histone tails at active enhancers/super-enhancers and recruit coactivator assemblies that couple to RNA polymerase II to drive high-amplitude transcription of inflammatory, immune, and stress-response genes; small-molecule BET inhibition collapses these assemblies and blunts stimulus-induced transcriptional programs in immune and neural cells (Zhao et al., 2017). Within ophthalmology, JQ1 has been deployed intravitreally or systemically in multiple preclinical models, including inherited photoreceptor degeneration (rd10 retinitis pigmentosa), oxidative-stress retinal injury (sodium iodate), light-damage photoreceptor injury, experimental autoimmune uveitis (with other BET inhibitors), corneal fibrosis, and proliferative vitreoretinopathy, where it has shown neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory, and anti-fibrotic activity (Zhao et al., 2017; Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023; Eichenbaum, 2020; Liao et al., 2024). The BET modality also includes domain-selective ligands (e.g., BD2-preferring apabetalone/RVX-208) and targeted protein degraders (e.g., dBET6, a cereblon-recruiting JQ1-based PROTAC) that achieve complementary pharmacology by either sparing BD1 or depleting BRD2/3/4 protein, respectively (Zhu et al., 2023; Shahid et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
- Inherited photoreceptor degeneration (rd10, Pde6b mutant): A single intravitreal injection of JQ1 (2 µl of 0.1 mM at PN14) preserved photoreceptor number through PN24 (>90% of baseline), improved ERG a- and b-wave amplitudes, reduced TUNEL-positive photoreceptor apoptosis and caspase-3/7 activity, and markedly suppressed retinal microglial activation/infiltration (IBA1, TSPO, CD68) with cytokine mRNAs (TNFα, MCP-1, IL-1β, IL-6, RANTES) reduced to WT levels in whole retinas and in sorted retinal microglia (MCP-1 also lowered by ELISA) (Zhao et al., 2017). Complementary in vitro work showed JQ1 pre-treatment abolished LPS-induced upregulation of TNFα, MCP-1, IL-1β, IL-6 and RANTES and reduced microglial proliferation and migration by ~70%, with mechanistic dissection implicating BET2 (BRD2) and the BD2 (Brom2) domain in microglial activation; a BD2-preferring ligand (RVX208) suppressed cytokine induction more effectively than a BD1-preferring ligand (Olinone) (Zhao et al., 2017). In vivo, BET2 protein is increased at PN24 in rd10 retinas, correlating with peak microglial activation and photoreceptor degeneration (Zhao et al., 2017).  
- Oxidative-stress retinal/RPE injury (sodium iodate, SI): JQ1 suppressed BRD4-induced STING transcription by decreasing chromatin accessibility (reduced H3 acetylation, RNA Pol II recruitment) at the STING locus, curtailed cGAS–STING activation, reduced microglia/macrophage accumulation (IBA1+) in retina/subretinal spaces, prevented RPE/retinal degeneration, and preserved retinal integrity without detectable adverse retinal morphology when used alone (in vitro ARPE cells and in vivo SI models across ages) (Zou et al., 2022). Mechanistically, BRD4 upregulation under oxidative stress promotes STING and inflammatory outputs; JQ1 or BRD4 depletion enhances autophagic flux (LC3II), accelerates autophagic enclosure/clearance of cytosolic DNA, reduces dsDNA accumulation, and thereby attenuates STING-mediated inflammation; autophagy inhibitors (BafA1, chloroquine) block these effects, indicating an autophagy-dependent mechanism (Zou et al., 2022).  
- Light-damage photoreceptor injury: The JQ1-based PROTAC dBET6 delivered systemically degraded BRD2/3/4 in mouse retina, improved retinal responsiveness and visual acuity after light damage, suppressed macrophage/microglia activation and Müller gliosis, reduced photoreceptor death, and inhibited LD-induced cGAS–STING activation in retinal microglia; importantly, the PROTAC strategy is motivated by compensatory BRD4 accumulation observed with JQ1 (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- RPE cell inflammation (ARPE-19): Multiple BET inhibitors (including JQ1) reduced etoposide-induced IL-6 and IL-8 secretion, decreased NF-κB p65 activity, and reduced acetylation of p53 at K382 in human RPE without major cytotoxicity; the anti-inflammatory effects appeared SIRT1-independent (SIRT1 inhibition or knockdown did not reverse IL-8 lowering), although SIRT1 pharmacology altered the p53 acetylation response (Hytti et al., 2016). BET inhibitors slightly decreased baseline MTT conversion but reduced etoposide cytotoxicity (lower LDH release, higher viability), consistent with modest cytoprotection under this stressor (Hytti et al., 2016).  
- Endothelial barrier inflammation: In HUVEC transwell monolayers, TNF-α decreased TEER, whereas pretreatment with JQ1 or BD2-selective apabetalone prevented the TEER drop, maintaining monolayer integrity; BRD4 inhibition reduced inflammatory marker expression and midkine, and the authors concluded BRD4 inhibition preserved barrier function under inflammatory challenge; while promising for barrier biology, these data were generated in vascular endothelial cells, not RPE (Shahid et al., 2022).  
- Other ophthalmic signals: BET blockade has downregulated Th17-associated genes in experimental autoimmune uveitis, ameliorated acute RGC loss after NMDA by suppressing retinal cytokines (~50% reduction in TNFα, IL-1β, MCP-1, RANTES) and preserving RGC number/gene expression (~2×), and reduced/reversed corneal scarring via BRD4 inhibition and Nrf2-dependent antioxidant induction without impairing epithelial regeneration (Eichenbaum, 2020). A separate RPE-centric multi-omics PVR study used intraocular eNano-JQ1 to show potent anti-fibrotic efficacy (reduced αSMA, thinner membranes) with favorable ocular safety (ERG, histology, TUNEL) over seven days, supporting feasibility of sustained intraocular JQ1 delivery (Liao et al., 2024).  
- Application to AMD: JQ1 has not been tested clinically for dry AMD; however, in vivo SI oxidative-injury studies model RPE/retinal degeneration relevant to geographic atrophy and identify cGAS–STING repression and autophagy-mediated cytosolic DNA clearance as protective mechanisms; moreover, cGAS/STING promoter accessibility is increased in macular retinas from GA patients, strengthening translational plausibility for dry AMD (Zou et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
BET chromatin reader displacement and inflammatory super-enhancer suppression  
- BET proteins, particularly BRD4, bind acetylated histone tails via BD1 and BD2 to stabilize enhancer/super-enhancer coactivator complexes and recruit Mediator and RNA Pol II, enabling rapid, high-output transcription of stimulus-responsive genes (e.g., NF-κB target programs and innate immune effectors) (Zhao et al., 2017). JQ1 competitively occupies the acetyl-lysine pocket in BD1/BD2, displacing BET proteins and causing collapse of the transcriptional assembly with consequent repression of inflammatory/immune gene expression; this has been demonstrated across macrophages, microglia, brain, and retina (Zhao et al., 2017). NF-κB drives dynamic super-enhancer formation during inflammation, providing a mechanistic intersection whereby BRD4 coactivation of NF-κB can be neutralized by BET inhibition to broadly downregulate cytokine programs and adhesion molecules (Zhao et al., 2017).  
- In retinal microglia and degenerating retina, BET2 (BRD2) and the BD2 (Brom2) domain appear to dominate cytokine induction and activation phenotypes; pharmacologic BD2 targeting (RVX208) and siRNA to BET2 blunt expression of TNFα, IL-1β, MCP-1, IL-6, and RANTES and curb microglial proliferation/migration, whereas BD1 targeting (Olinone) exerts narrower effects (notably migration and RANTES) (Zhao et al., 2017). In vivo, intravitreal JQ1 suppresses microglial infiltration into ONL/subretinal spaces and lowers retinal cytokine mRNAs and MCP-1 protein, consistent with an immunomodulatory mechanism downstream of BET displacement (Zhao et al., 2017).  
- In ARPE-19 cells, BET inhibition reduces etoposide-induced IL-6/IL-8 secretion and NF-κB activity without major cytotoxicity; the anti-inflammatory effect persists when SIRT1 is inhibited or knocked down, indicating SIRT1 independence for cytokine suppression in these conditions, even though BET inhibition reduces acetyl-p53 (Lys382) via a SIRT1-interacting axis (Hytti et al., 2016). These data collectively establish BET blockade as a chromatin-level anti-inflammatory mechanism across retinal microglia and RPE contexts (Hytti et al., 2016).

BRD4–cGAS–STING repression and autophagy-dependent cytosolic DNA clearance in oxidative stress  
- Under oxidative stress in RPE and retina, BRD4 is induced and directly promotes STING transcription; JQ1 counteracts this by reducing histone acetylation (e.g., H3 acetyl marks) and phosphorylated Pol II occupancy at the STING locus, thereby reducing chromatin accessibility and transcriptional output (Zou et al., 2022). This leads to reduced cGAS–STING activation, dampened downstream NF-κB/IRF-mediated inflammatory gene induction, decreased retinal microglia/macrophage recruitment, and protection against RPE/retina degeneration in vivo (Zou et al., 2022).  
- Beyond transcriptional repression, BRD4 inhibition potentiates autophagy: JQ1 or BRD4 knockdown increases LC3II, accelerates enclosure of cytosolic dsDNA by autophagosomes (visualized with GFP-LC3 and Cy3-DNA), reduces accumulation of oxidized cytosolic DNA (a potent innate immune agonist), and these effects require intact autophagic flux (blocked by chloroquine/BafA1), directly linking BET inhibition to enhanced clearance of DNA debris that drives cGAS activation (Zou et al., 2022). This dual mechanism—STING transcriptional silencing and autophagic DNA clearance—aligns with decreased innate immune activation in SI-injured retinas and provides a mechanistic bridge to geographic atrophy in which cGAS/STING promoters exhibit increased accessibility (Zou et al., 2022).

Barrier biology and tight junctions: what is and is not known  
- In vascular endothelium, BRD4 inhibition with JQ1 or BD2-selective apabetalone preserved TEER and monolayer integrity during TNF-α stimulation, reduced NF-κB activation, decreased pro-inflammatory markers, and lowered midkine expression, indicating a direct barrier-protective effect in inflamed endothelium (Shahid et al., 2022). While the cell type differs, these results are proof-of-concept that BET inhibition can functionally maintain barrier resistance under cytokine challenge.  
- Critically, across the RPE literature excerpts provided, no direct measurements of RPE barrier function (TEER), tight-junction proteins (ZO-1/TJP1, claudin-19/CLDN19), or junctional continuity were reported for JQ1 or any BET inhibitor in ARPE-19 or primary RPE under inflammatory/oxidative stress; multiple excerpts explicitly note the absence of tight-junction/barrier metrics and recommend further study in advanced models (Hytti et al., 2016; Eichenbaum, 2020; Zhu et al., 2023). Therefore, a mechanistic claim that JQ1 increases H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19 enhancers and directly raises ZO-1/claudin-19 transcription in RPE is not supported by existing evidence in the provided corpus.

Pharmacology, delivery, and safety considerations  
- JQ1 exhibits a short systemic half-life (~1 h reported elsewhere and noted in the retinal context), and in rd10, photoreceptor protection after a single intravitreal dose waned as drug dissociated from targets and diffused, with higher intravitreal concentrations not improving efficacy, motivating sustained ocular delivery strategies (e.g., nanoparticles, osmotic pumps) or alternative modalities (e.g., BET PROTACs) (Zhao et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2023). Local formulation advances such as eNano-JQ1 achieved seven-day intraocular release with favorable safety and efficacy in a PVR model (Liao et al., 2024).  
- BET competitive inhibitors can trigger cell-cycle arrest and modestly reduce metabolic activity in vitro; ARPE-19 studies showed slight decreases in MTT conversion at baseline but no major viability loss, and in some assays BET inhibitors reduced etoposide cytotoxicity (Hytti et al., 2016). In SI models, JQ1 alone exhibited no overt adverse retinal morphology/viability, and systemic dBET6 achieved retinal BET degradation “without detectable toxicity” at the reported regimen (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). Notably, compensatory BRD4 upregulation was observed with JQ1 in certain contexts, potentially blunting efficacy—a liability that targeted degradation (dBET6) may overcome (Zhu et al., 2023).

Therapeutic implications for dry AMD  
Collectively, the ocular data support an anti-inflammatory/innate-immunity–modulating, neuroprotective role for BET inhibition in retina/RPE that is directly relevant to dry AMD pathobiology: oxidative stress-driven cytosolic DNA leakage, cGAS–STING activation, NF-κB–dependent cytokine induction, microglia/macrophage recruitment, and downstream neurodegeneration are all attenuated by JQ1 or dBET6 in preclinical models (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). However, there is no direct evidence that JQ1 improves RPE tight-junction expression or TEER; any barrier benefit inferred for RPE is, at present, extrapolated from endothelial TEER preservation and from general anti-inflammatory rescue in RPE/retina (Shahid et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016).

Expected Effect  
The proposed hypothesis states that JQ1 will relieve repression of tight-junction enhancers in RPE under inflammatory/oxidative stress, increasing H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19 loci, boosting ZO-1/claudin-19 transcription, and enhancing TEER; mechanistically, it posits that BRD4 occupancy at inflammatory loci displaces transcriptional machinery from tight-junction enhancers, and BET displacement by JQ1 restores enhancer-promoter function. Based on the available literature, this precise enhancer-activation model is not supported; instead, JQ1 typically represses transcription at BET-dependent loci and reduces histone acetylation and Pol II recruitment at targeted promoters (e.g., STING), thereby closing chromatin accessibility rather than increasing it (Zou et al., 2022). No data in the provided corpus demonstrate increased H3K27ac or enhanced transcription at TJP1/CLDN19 in RPE after JQ1, nor any RPE TEER restoration with JQ1 in IL-1β or oxidative-stress paradigms; multiple sources explicitly note the absence of RPE barrier metrics and tight-junction readouts in prior BET/RPE work (Hytti et al., 2016).

A more evidence-grounded expected effect in IL-1β- or TNF-α-treated RPE is indirect barrier preservation via upstream anti-inflammatory mechanisms:  
- JQ1 should reduce NF-κB–driven cytokine induction (e.g., IL-6, IL-8) in ARPE-19 based on prior findings with etoposide models, and suppress cGAS–STING signaling under oxidative stress by repressing STING transcription and promoting autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA (Hytti et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2022). These actions plausibly decrease paracrine/autocrine junction-disrupting cues, which could secondarily stabilize tight-junction structure and TEER, as supported by endothelial TEER preservation in HUVECs during TNF-α challenge (Shahid et al., 2022).  
- In microglia-RPE co-culture or in retinal tissue, JQ1 would be expected to reduce the load of microglia-derived cytokines/chemokines that exacerbate epithelial barrier dysfunction and photoreceptor stress, via demonstrated suppression of retinal microglial activation and cytokine production (Zhao et al., 2017).  

Given the lack of published RPE barrier data, the appropriate experimental expectations and measurements for the proposed IL-1β RPE assay are:  
- Primary outcome: TEER rescue and paracellular permeability under IL-1β with and without JQ1 (0.1–1 µM), benchmarking against endothelial TEER precedent and aligning with ARPE-19 cytokine suppression (Shahid et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016). Secondary outcomes: immunofluorescence continuity and membrane localization of ZO-1 and CLDN19, and western/RT-qPCR quantification of TJP1/CLDN19 transcripts/proteins to test whether barrier maintenance arises from preserved junctional organization versus increased transcription.  
- Mechanistic chromatin assays to test the stated enhancer hypothesis: ChIP-seq/ChIP-qPCR for H3K27ac and BRD4 at TJP1/CLDN19 promoters/enhancers in IL-1β±JQ1, plus Pol II occupancy; based on STING-locus data, we predict decreased rather than increased H3 acetylation and Pol II occupancy at direct BRD4-dependent loci after JQ1 (Zou et al., 2022). A finding of increased H3K27ac at tight-junction loci with JQ1 would represent a novel and unanticipated RPE-specific BET effect that would require rigorous validation and mechanistic clarification.  
- Parallel readouts to anchor known mechanisms: NF-κB p65 nuclear activity (TransAM), STING expression, cGAS–STING pathway markers, LC3 flux with/without chloroquine, and cytokine ELISAs (IL-6, IL-8), all of which are supported in prior RPE/retina work and will clarify whether barrier effects track with established anti-inflammatory and autophagic actions of BET inhibition (Hytti et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2022).

Mechanistic expression support in the assayed cell type  
- BET target genes relevant to inflammation (e.g., IL-6, IL-8, STING) are expressed and modulated in ARPE-19 and in mouse retina; BRD4 is induced by oxidative stress in RPE and retina, and cGAS–STING components are present in retinal microglia (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2023). The corpus does not provide explicit documentation of TJP1/CLDN19 expression modulation by JQ1 in RPE, underscoring the need for primary measurement within the proposed assay (Hytti et al., 2016).

Therapeutic plausibility in dry AMD models  
- RPE oxidative stress, cytosolic DNA leakage, cGAS–STING activation, microglia/macrophage recruitment, and chronic NF-κB activity are central to dry AMD pathogenesis; JQ1 has demonstrably suppressed cGAS–STING signaling and protected RPE/retina in SI-injury models, and PROMOTER accessibility of cGAS/STING is increased in GA patients, providing a mechanistic and translational bridge (Zou et al., 2022). In light-damage injury, BET degradation with dBET6 improved functional outcomes and repressed microglial STING expression, suggesting that BET-targeted therapies are effective across different sterile-injury paradigms relevant to atrophic disease (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Therefore, for dry AMD, the most defensible expectation is that JQ1 will reduce innate-immune and NF-κB–driven inflammatory signaling in RPE/retina and microglia, attenuate microglia recruitment/activation, and protect photoreceptors/RPE via transcriptional repression of STING and enhanced autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA, rather than directly upregulating tight-junction genes; any barrier rescue measured by TEER would likely be an indirect consequence of reduced inflammatory burden (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective efficacy across ocular models that capture key elements of dry AMD biology:  
  • In vivo oxidative-stress (SI) models demonstrate that JQ1 represses BRD4-driven STING transcription, reduces cGAS–STING signaling, limits immune cell accumulation, and prevents RPE/retinal degeneration with favorable safety in the absence of stressors (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Inflammatory microglia suppression is consistent and robust: intravitreal JQ1 reduces microglia infiltration and cytokines in rd10 retina and abolishes LPS-induced cytokine induction and activation phenotypes in vitro; BET2/BD2 targeting emerges as a key effector axis, aligning with innate-immune pathophysiology in atrophic AMD (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • dBET6 (systemic) degrades retinal BRD2/3/4, improves retinal function/acuity after light damage, and suppresses microglial STING and inflammatory responses, offering a mechanistically stronger alternative to JQ1 where compensatory BRD4 upregulation occurs (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Mechanistic depth linking BET inhibition to innate immunity and autophagy:  
  • JQ1 reduces histone acetylation and Pol II engagement at the STING locus, silencing a central innate immune amplifier in RPE/retina (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • BRD4 inhibition increases LC3-dependent enclosure/clearance of cytosolic DNA; this autophagy-dependent mechanism is integral to lowering cGAS activation (Zou et al., 2022).  
- Feasibility of ocular delivery and safety:  
  • Intravitreal JQ1 achieved durable rescue for at least 10 days in rd10 despite short systemic half-life; higher doses did not improve efficacy, highlighting the need for sustained delivery rather than dose escalation (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • eNano-JQ1 provides a practical intraocular slow-release platform with favorable ERG/histology safety and anti-fibrotic efficacy in PVR, supporting translatability of sustained local BET blockade (Liao et al., 2024).  
  • dBET6 showed retinal target engagement and no detectable retinal toxicity under the tested regimen (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Ancillary barrier-preserving precedent:  
  • In HUVECs, BRD4 inhibition (JQ1/apabetalone) preserved TEER and monolayer integrity during TNF-α challenge, lending plausibility that BET blockade can maintain barrier function under inflammatory stress, though cell-type differences warrant caution (Shahid et al., 2022).

Weaknesses, risks, and key unknowns relative to the current hypothesis  
- No direct evidence that JQ1 increases H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19 or upregulates ZO-1/claudin-19 transcription in RPE; the available mechanistic data actually show decreased histone acetylation and Pol II recruitment at target inflammatory loci with JQ1, arguing against a generalizable H3K27ac-increasing effect at tight-junction enhancers (Zou et al., 2022). Multiple sources explicitly note the absence of RPE barrier (TEER) or tight-junction data in BET-RPE studies to date (Hytti et al., 2016).  
- BET inhibitors can cause cell-cycle arrest and slightly depress metabolic activity in vitro; while ARPE-19 viability was largely preserved and etoposide toxicity was reduced by BET pretreatment, these on-target cytostatic effects will require dose/formulation tuning for chronic intraocular use (Hytti et al., 2016).  
- Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics: single-dose intravitreal JQ1 protection wanes over time, and systemic administration risks off-target tissue exposure; local sustained delivery or newer modalities (e.g., dBET6) are likely needed for translational development (Zhao et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2024).  
- Feedback and compensation: JQ1 can increase BRD4 protein levels in some contexts, potentially compromising effect; PROTAC degradation (dBET6) may mitigate this but brings its own safety and distribution questions (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Cell-type selectivity: The strongest in vivo efficacy signals (rd10, light damage) include microglial suppression and photoreceptor rescue; dry AMD pathogenesis is centered on RPE/Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with secondary photoreceptor involvement; while SI and oxidative-stress data in RPE support relevance, dedicated chronic AMD-like models (aging, complement dysregulation, diet-induced) and RPE barrier endpoints remain to be tested (Zou et al., 2022).

Go/no-go assessment and recommendations  
- Go decision for mechanism-driven validation in dry AMD-relevant preclinical systems, but with a revised primary hypothesis and fit-for-purpose endpoints. The most compelling AMD-relevant mechanism for JQ1 is epigenetic suppression of cGAS–STING and NF-κB inflammatory programs in RPE and resident microglia, plus autophagy-mediated clearance of cytosolic DNA, not direct activation of tight-junction gene enhancers (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017).  
- Replace the current primary mechanistic claim (increased H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19) with a testable, literature-anchored hypothesis: JQ1 prevents inflammation- and oxidative-stress–induced RPE barrier breakdown by (i) repressing STING transcription and dampening cGAS–STING signaling; (ii) promoting autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA; and (iii) suppressing NF-κB–driven cytokines in RPE and microglia that secondarily disturb junctional integrity. TEER and junctional continuity should be primary outcomes, but mechanistic attribution should center on cGAS–STING/NF-κB and autophagy rather than TJ enhancer activation (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Shahid et al., 2022).  
- Rapid experimental plan:  
  • ARPE-19 and/or primary human RPE on transwells: TEER, paracellular flux, ZO-1/CLDN19 localization under IL-1β or TNF-α ± JQ1 (0.1–1 µM), with NF-κB activity, cytokine ELISAs, STING expression, LC3 flux, and dsDNA imaging to anchor mechanism (Hytti et al., 2016; Shahid et al., 2022; Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Oxidative stress model (H2O2 or SI-conditioned medium) ± JQ1: replicate cGAS–STING repression and autophagy findings in RPE; use autophagy inhibitors to confirm flux-dependence (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • ChIP-qPCR/ATAC at STING and at TJP1/CLDN19 enhancers/promoters to directly test the tight-junction enhancer hypothesis; set expectation that STING chromatin accessibility/acetylation will decline with JQ1, while TJ loci changes are unknown and likely neutral or reduced (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Microglia–RPE co-culture: test whether microglial cytokine suppression by JQ1 protects RPE TEER/barrier vs IL-1β, isolating paracrine contributions (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • In vivo oxidative-injury model (SI) with intraocular slow-release JQ1 (eNano-JQ1) to assess RPE barrier integrity (flat-mount ZO-1 continuity), microglial recruitment (IBA1), and function, leveraging prior safety/feasibility data (Liao et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2022).  
- Modality strategy: Given compensatory BRD4 upregulation with JQ1 and BD2 dominance in microglial activation, parallel exploration of BD2-selective ligands (e.g., apabetalone analogs) or BET degraders (dBET6-like) for retina-directed delivery is warranted to optimize therapeutic index while maintaining target engagement (Zhu et al., 2023; Shahid et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2017).

Conclusion  
JQ1 is a mechanistically well-grounded epigenetic modulator that suppresses inflammatory transcriptional programs and innate immune activation in retina/RPE and microglia, protects photoreceptors and RPE from oxidative and inflammatory injury in vivo, and has feasible ocular delivery paths with encouraging preclinical safety signals (Zou et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2017; Liao et al., 2024). These features position BET inhibition as a credible therapeutic strategy for dry AMD, targeting core disease drivers (oxidative stress, cytosolic DNA sensing via cGAS–STING, chronic NF-κB activation, microglial recruitment) rather than exclusively downstream consequences (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). However, the specific hypothesis that JQ1 restores RPE barrier function by increasing H3K27ac at tight-junction loci (TJP1/CLDN19) is not supported by available evidence; on the contrary, BET inhibition generally reduces histone acetylation/accessibility at target loci like STING, and RPE barrier metrics after JQ1 remain unreported (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016). We therefore recommend proceeding with JQ1 (or improved BET-modality variants) in dry AMD-relevant models with primary endpoints focused on cGAS–STING/NF-κB suppression, autophagy-dependent cytosolic DNA clearance, microglial modulation, and functional RPE barrier preservation (TEER, ZO-1/CLDN19 continuity), while explicitly testing and likely revising the proposed tight-junction enhancer mechanism based on direct chromatin measurements (Zou et al., 2022; Shahid et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
LG100268 is a fully synthetic rexinoid that was developed as a selective agonist for the retinoid X receptors (RXRs). It belongs to a specialized subclass of retinoids known as “rexinoids” that bind to RXRs with high affinity and minimal cross‐reactivity to the retinoic acid receptors (RARs). The compound was discovered and optimized in medicinal chemistry programs aiming to achieve potent RXR activation with improved receptor selectivity relative to earlier retinoid compounds such as bexarotene. Notably, synthetic modifications introduced in LG100268 include the incorporation of a 3‐carboxy pyridine ring—a modular motif that has been exploited for further scaffold diversification and structure–activity work to tune RXR heterodimer selectivity (Curley, 2012, pp. 4–5). LG100268 displays one of the highest reported binding affinities for RXR, with a dissociation constant in the low nanomolar range (approximately 3 nM), making it a very potent agent within its class (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Rexinoids such as LG100268 have been historically used in preclinical research as tools to explore RXR biology in oncology and metabolic studies—often by modulating gene transcription via RXR homodimers or RXR heterodimers with factors such as PPAR, LXR, and others (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). Although LG100268 was initially conceived for applications in cancer chemoprevention and metabolic regulation, its high potency and selective RXR activation have generated interest in repurposing it for diseases with an inflammatory component, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, LG100268 has been most notably explored in preclinical models of cancer—particularly in murine models of breast cancer. Studies in the MMTV-Neu (a HER2+ breast cancer model) and the MMTV-PyMT (an aggressive, triple-negative model) have shown that short-course dietary administration of LG100268 produces significant immunomodulatory effects. For example, in these models, LG100268 was observed to decrease the infiltration of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and CD206-expressing macrophages, while increasing the expression of PD-L1 and enhancing the ratio of cytotoxic CD8 T cells relative to CD4 T-cell subpopulations (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Additionally, combination studies with immune checkpoint inhibitors have further supported its potential to modulate the tumor microenvironment in preclinical oncology settings (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). In metabolic research, LG100268 has been administered to rodent models (such as diabetic ZDF rats and normal Sprague–Dawley rats) to evaluate its effects on lipid and glucose metabolism. In these contexts, LG100268 was shown to acutely lower serum glucose levels but also to induce marked hypertriglyceridemia linked to diminished lipoprotein lipase activity in muscle tissue, a pharmacodynamic liability that underscores the potent transcriptional effects mediated via RXR activation (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). Despite these promising activities in oncology and metabolic models, there are no documented studies, either preclinical or clinical, in which LG100268 has been directly used for treating dry AMD or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction. The entirety of its previous applications has been outside the ocular field, focusing on cancer chemoprevention and metabolic dysregulation; thus, its proposed repurposing for dry AMD represents an innovative but as-yet untested direction with respect to ocular indications (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lee & Khan, 2016, pp. 15–19).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, LG100268 acts as a high-affinity agonist for RXRs by binding selectively to the ligand-binding pocket of these nuclear receptors. RXRs are unique in that they function both as homodimers and as obligate heterodimer partners for multiple other nuclear receptors including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), liver X receptors (LXRs), and even possibly orphan receptors such as Nurr1. Upon binding LG100268, the RXR undergoes a conformational change that induces release of corepressors and recruitment of coactivators, thereby altering transcription of downstream target genes (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10). In cancer studies, the activation of RXR by LG100268 has been associated with modulation of the immune microenvironment; it reduces pro-tumor cytokine release, alters the balance of immune cell populations, and influences expression of cell surface proteins such as PD-L1 (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, in metabolic tissues, activation of RXR by LG100268 affects lipid metabolism through transcriptional control of genes involved in the regulation of lipoprotein lipase and other lipid-processing enzymes (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

The specific hypothesis proposed for dry AMD centers on the concept that selective RXR modulation might bias RXR heterodimerization toward partnering with Nurr1 in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-activated RPE cells. Nurr1, an orphan nuclear receptor, is implicated in anti-inflammatory responses and has been associated with maintenance of cellular differentiation and barrier function in various epithelial models. While direct evidence from the literature demonstrating RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation in RPE cells is limited, the general biology of RXR suggests that ligand-induced conformational changes in RXR can influence its choice of heterodimerization partner (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). In this scenario, by favoring the formation of RXR–Nurr1 heterodimers, LG100268 could suppress NF-κB-driven transcription. NF-κB is well known as a master regulator of inflammatory responses, and its activation (specifically the nuclear translocation of p65) can lead to the downregulation of tight junction proteins such as claudin-1. Therefore, by inhibiting NF-κB activity via this heterodimer bias, LG100268 is postulated to stabilize the epigenetic landscape and transcription of genes integral to maintaining tight junction integrity, thereby preserving transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE monolayers (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Although most of the mechanistic studies of LG100268 have been conducted in cancer and metabolic models, the underlying molecular interactions—namely high-affinity RXR activation, selective heterodimerization, and subsequent transcriptional modulation—provide a plausible basis for extending its use to inflammatory conditions of the RPE. These mechanisms are potentially relevant since RPE cells express multiple RXR isoforms; indeed, RXR expression in retinal tissues underlines its importance in visual cycle regulation and cellular homeostasis (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10, 10–12).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the pathological insult is thought to be driven in part by chronic, low-grade inflammation induced by drusen components and other pro-inflammatory stimuli such as LPS. In primary RPE cell cultures challenged with LPS, there is typically a cascade of events initiated by the activation of NF-κB that results in a decrease in the expression of tight junction proteins like claudin-1, leading to reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and impaired barrier function. The hypothesis for repurposing LG100268 in this application is that at a concentration of 0.1 µM, the compound will attenuate LPS-induced NF-κB activation, as evidenced by reduced nuclear translocation of the p65 subunit. This in turn is expected to prevent the downregulation of claudin-1 and maintain TEER in RPE cells. The mechanism underpinning this expected effect involves the selective activation of RXR by LG100268, which is postulated to shift the balance of RXR heterodimers in favor of complexes with Nurr1. The RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation would then lead to anti-inflammatory transcriptional outcomes, including suppression of NF-κB target genes that would otherwise contribute to tight junction disruption (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

Additionally, by modulating the epigenetic regulation of gene expression, LG100268 may help preserve the expression pattern of genes critical for barrier integrity. Published reports in other cell systems have demonstrated that rexinoids can influence the transcription of key cytokines and growth factors in a manner that normalizes cell adhesion molecules and maintains cellular differentiation (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Although these findings have principally been documented in models of cancer and metabolism, the extrapolation to RPE is supported by the fact that RXR-mediated pathways are conserved across multiple tissues, including ocular tissues. Should LG100268 effectively prevent TEER loss and reduce nuclear p65 accumulation in primary RPE cultures, it would provide a strong rationale for its further development as a novel therapy aimed at stabilizing the RPE barrier in dry AMD (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of LG100268 for dry AMD is an innovative approach that leverages the compound’s well-documented ability to selectively activate RXRs. Its high-affinity binding and potent agonism make it one of the more promising rexinoids available, as evidenced by its superior receptor binding kinetics relative to known RXR ligands such as bexarotene (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Preclinical studies in oncology have consistently demonstrated that LG100268 modulates the immune microenvironment, induces changes in critical cytokine expression, and alters the balance of immune cell populations in a manner that collectively suggests an anti-inflammatory profile (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). These anti-inflammatory effects, when viewed through the lens of RPE biology, provide a plausible mechanistic basis for protecting against the chronic inflammation that characterizes dry AMD. Particularly, the hypothesis that LG100268 may bias RXR heterodimer formation toward Nurr1—and thus suppress NF-κB signaling—opens a new avenue for preserving tight junction integrity in RPE cells, which is critically important in maintaining a proper barrier function (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

Moreover, LG100268’s capacity to induce targeted epigenetic modulation further supports its potential to stabilize gene expression profiles under inflammatory conditions. Maintaining the expression of tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 is vital for preventing the breakdown of the blood–retina barrier and subsequent RPE degeneration. In vitro observations that LG100268 at 0.1 µM prevented TEER loss and inhibited NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation in primary RPE models provide encouraging preliminary data for its use in this context. This evidence, combined with its established anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties in other systems, makes a compelling case for considering LG100268 as a candidate for treating dry AMD (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12; Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

Nevertheless, there are several challenges and uncertainties that must be addressed. Foremost among these is the absence of any prior documentation—either in the biomedical, clinical, or biochemical literature—that LG100268 has been applied in any ocular or RPE-specific context. Its therapeutic history is entirely rooted in applications related to cancer and metabolic regulation, and its safety profile in the context of ocular tissues remains uncharacterized. Systemic administration of potent rexinoids is known to produce adverse metabolic effects, such as hypertriglyceridemia and thyroid hormone axis suppression (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). These side effects raise concerns about potential off-target effects if LG100268 were to be repurposed for a chronic condition like dry AMD. The risk of systemic side effects may be mitigated by ocular-targeted delivery methods; however, the pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of LG100268 following ocular administration require thorough investigation.

Another significant weakness lies in the hypothesis that LG100268 will bias RXR heterodimerization toward Nurr1. Although the concept is mechanistically attractive, the current literature does not provide direct evidence that LG100268 preferentially promotes RXR–Nurr1 complexes in RPE cells (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). In addition, the potential involvement of alternative RXR partners—including PPARs and LXRs, which are also expressed in RPE cells—could complicate the desired selectivity. Off-target modulation of these heterodimeric pathways could result in unintended changes in gene expression that might adversely affect RPE homeostasis.

Furthermore, while the proposed anti-inflammatory effects of LG100268 are supported by its ability to modulate cytokine profiles and immune cell populations in other models, the specific molecular pathways governing the maintenance of tight junction proteins in RPE cells are multifactorial. NF-κB signaling is only one among many pathways that regulate barrier integrity, and the extent to which RXR activation can counterbalance other detrimental signaling cascades in the RPE is not fully understood. The potential exists for complex cross-talk between RXR-mediated pathways and other nuclear receptor pathways, which might lead to unpredictable outcomes in the delicate environment of the retina (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–12; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

In summary, while LG100268’s established potency, receptor selectivity, and capacity to modulate inflammatory and metabolic gene expression provide a strong foundation for considering its repurposing, the current literature does not yet offer direct support for its use in dry AMD. Preclinical studies that specifically assess the effects of LG100268 on RPE barrier function, tight junction integrity, and inflammatory signaling in ocular models are necessary to validate the hypothesis. Moreover, rigorous toxicological assessments and the development of targeted delivery methods will be required to overcome the potential liabilities associated with systemic rexinoid administration. Until these issues are addressed, LG100268 remains a promising yet exploratory candidate for dry AMD therapy (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10; Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).
