Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Arimoclomol (also known as BRX-345) is a synthetic hydroxylamine/hydroxamic-acid–derived small molecule developed as a heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducer that amplifies stress-inducible transcription of heat shock genes under conditions of proteotoxic stress, principally through prolongation and potentiation of heat shock factor-1 (HSF1) activation on heat shock elements (HSEs) in target promoters (Penke et al., 2018; Parfitt et al., 2014; O’Leary, 2019). In the hydroximic-acid derivative family (bimoclomol, arimoclomol, NG-094, BGP-15), several members synergistically enhance heat-induced Hsp expression; arimoclomol and bimoclomol have been shown to increase HSF1 activity via hyperphosphorylation and to amplify heat-shock gene expression in eukaryotic cells while sparing basal Hsp expression in unstressed cells, thereby acting as bona fide co-inducers rather than primary HSF1 agonists (Penke et al., 2018). The compound was originally advanced from the bimoclomol chemotype as a more drug-like analogue with similar HSR-potentiating properties and improved pharmacology, and it falls within a broader class of pharmacologic HSP70/HSF1 modulators investigated for neurodegenerative protein-misfolding diseases (e.g., ALS, NPC, tauopathies), as well as select retinal degeneration models (rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa) (Parfitt et al., 2014; Venediktov et al., 2023; Penke et al., 2018). At the biophysical level, hydroximic-acid derivatives can intercalate into cellular membranes, a property hypothesized to contribute to regulation of HSF1 activation/attenuation kinetics and restoration of a protective Hsp profile under stress (Penke et al., 2018). In neuronal cell systems, arimoclomol has also been used in combination with primary HSF1 activators (e.g., celastrol) to achieve robust induction of inducible Hsp70s (HSPA1A, HSPA6) and other stress response proteins at lower inducer doses, consistent with its role as a co-inducer that amplifies pre-existing HSF1 activation (Deane, 2019).

Within the retina, arimoclomol has been evaluated in rod photoreceptor models of misfolded rhodopsin (P23H transgenic rats), where it enhanced Hsp70/Hsp90 expression and improved proteostasis, photoreceptor structure, and visual function; however, there is no published evidence in dry AMD models or direct demonstrations of RPE barrier rescue by arimoclomol, and at least one PRPF31-mutant RPE (RP11) cell system screening showed no aggregate-reducing effect of arimoclomol while an mTOR inhibitor (rapamycin) reduced aggregate burden via autophagy induction (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021). The broader Hsp70/Hsc70 system, chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), and macroautophagy are mechanistically central to RPE proteostasis and AMD pathobiology, establishing a strong rationale for HSF1–HSP70–targeted therapy, but translation from photoreceptor models and exogenous Hsp70 delivery to endogenous induction in RPE remains to be validated for this agent (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Subrizi et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History  
Arimoclomol’s development history is anchored in neurodegeneration and protein-misfolding indications. In SOD1-mutant ALS mice, arimoclomol increased Hsp70 expression and improved motor neuron survival and function, extending lifespan; it progressed to human ALS trials (including a phase 3 program), with mixed outcomes across adult and pediatric indications (O’Leary, 2019; Venediktov et al., 2023). Mechanistically consistent with HSF1 co-induction, arimoclomol is positioned to upregulate a suite of inducible chaperones and components of the proteostasis network rather than single chaperone overexpression, a strategy considered preferable for matching the endogenous disaggregation/refolding machinery and preserving feedback attenuation (O’Leary, 2019).

In the retina, arimoclomol has been tested extensively in rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa (RP) models driven by the P23H misfolding mutation. In P23H-GFP cell models, arimoclomol reduced inclusion incidence and insoluble rod opsin, decreased higher-molecular-weight rhodopsin species, and improved viability, with contemporaneous increases in Hsp70/Hsp90 implying potentiation of the HSR in stressed photoreceptors (Parfitt et al., 2014). In P23H transgenic rats, daily intraperitoneal dosing (10 mg/kg) improved scotopic ERG a- and b-waves, preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness, increased outer segment (OS) length, and improved ultrastructure, consistent with disease modification through HSR and unfolded protein response (UPR) potentiation; Hsp70, Hsp90, and HSF1 were assayed directly in these studies (Parfitt et al., 2014). The authors further observed increased eIF2α phosphorylation and discussed enhanced IRE1/XBP1 activity, indicating crosstalk with ER stress responses (Parfitt et al., 2014). Of note, arimoclomol’s activity appeared contingent on the presence of misfolded-protein stress (i.e., stress-selective action), potentially limiting off-target effects in healthy tissue (Parfitt et al., 2014).

Beyond photoreceptors, the Hsp co-inducer class has retinal neuroprotective precedents: bimoclomol improved early electrophysiologic signs in diabetic rat retina, and the Hsp inducer geranylgeranylacetone protected retinal ganglion cells in a rat glaucoma model, underscoring that Hsp70 induction can be protective across retinal cell types and diseases of proteostasis and stress, although these are class exemplars rather than arimoclomol-specific RPE data (Hesselink, 2016). Separately, exogenous Hsp70 protein delivery to RPE has shown diffusion to the retina and RPE after intravitreal administration, intracellular uptake, lysosomal localization, and protection from oxidative stress and inflammation in ARPE-19 cells, supporting the concept that increasing Hsp70 activity in RPE can be beneficial, albeit via protein pharmacology rather than endogenous induction (Subrizi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Crucially for dry AMD translation, the current literature set provides no in vivo animal or clinical study of arimoclomol in AMD/dry AMD, and no direct measurements of RPE barrier integrity (tight-junction protein preservation or transepithelial electrical resistance [TEER]) following arimoclomol in RPE or AMD models; an RPE disease model of PRPF31 mutation with progressive aggregate accumulation reported that arimoclomol failed to reduce aggregates, whereas rapamycin decreased aggregate load and induced LC3 processing consistent with autophagy activation (LAMP1 and p62 remained unchanged), highlighting context-dependent efficacy and suggesting autophagy induction may be more decisive than Hsp co-induction in some RPE aggregate pathologies (Georgiou, 2021). Thus, while arimoclomol has a positive retinal track record in photoreceptor proteotoxicity and a robust extraocular development history, there is no direct evidence yet of arimoclomol ameliorating dry AMD phenotypes or preserving RPE barrier function in disease-relevant systems (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Arimoclomol is an HSR co-inducer that amplifies HSF1-driven transcription of inducible heat shock proteins under pre-existing cellular stress. Mechanistically, arimoclomol prolongs HSF1 binding to HSEs, increases HSF1 activity (e.g., hyperphosphorylation), and thereby increases transcription of Hsp70/Hsp90 and related chaperones, with limited impact in unstressed cells (i.e., stressor-dependent co-induction) (Penke et al., 2018; O’Leary, 2019; Parfitt et al., 2014). In neuronal cells, arimoclomol enhanced celastrol-induced HSF1 activation to elevate HSPA6, HSPA1A, HSPB1, DNAJB1, and HO-1 at doses that preserved viability and differentiated morphology, supporting efficient co-induction when paired with a primary HSF1 activator (Deane, 2019). In P23H photoreceptor models, arimoclomol reduced insoluble rhodopsin and inclusion incidence, decreased high-molecular-weight species, increased retinal Hsp70/Hsp90, and improved ERG/ONL/OS outcomes; the study observed increased eIF2α phosphorylation and discussed potentiation of the UPR (BiP/IRE1/XBP1), consistent with arimoclomol acting at the intersection of cytosolic HSR and ER homeostasis (Parfitt et al., 2014).

Hsp70 Biology in RPE and AMD. Inducible Hsp70 (HSPA1A/Hsp70-1) is a central, evolutionarily conserved ATPase chaperone that assists folding of nascent chains, refolds damaged/misfolded proteins, buffers aggregation, facilitates “protein triage” toward degradation pathways, and protects cells from apoptosis and inflammatory signaling (e.g., NF-κB pathway), with expression controlled by HSF1 (Ryhänen, 2011; Kivinen, 2018). In the RPE, Hsp70/Hsc70 function intersects both the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) and lysosome-dependent proteolysis. Hsp70 can present misfolded proteins to the UPS via CHIP E3 ligase, regulate disaggregation with co-chaperones HSP40/HSP90/HIP/HOP, and is required for aggregate handling; in proteasome failure, protein aggregates in ARPE-19 cells co-localize with Hsp70 and p62, with p62 undergoing autophagic clearance while Hsp70 binds reversibly and evades autophagic degradation (Kumar et al., 2020; Kivinen et al., 2014; Ryhänen, 2011). Hsp70 is also integral to chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA): cytosolic Hsc70/Hsp70 recognizes KFERQ-containing substrates, delivers them to LAMP-2A at the lysosomal membrane, and ATPase-driven “entropic pulling” and luminal chaperones enable translocation and degradation; oxidative stress reduces HSP70 expression in RPE, impairs CMA, and can dysregulate macroautophagy cross-talk, contributing to RPE death (Chang et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020). Extracellular Hsp70 roles in RPE are complex: exogenous rhHsp70 injections protected against subretinal fibrosis via TLR2/TLR4 and IL-10 induction, while oxidized-lipid stress (4-HNE) can increase extracellular Hsp70 efflux and pro-inflammatory cytokines, indicating that compartmental localization of Hsp70 critically determines immunomodulatory outcomes (Kumar et al., 2020).

Evidence for arimoclomol in RPE cells. Direct mechanistic evidence for arimoclomol action in RPE is limited. A cell-culture report in ARPE-19 asserts that Hsp70 overexpression “with the help of a co-inducer like arimoclomol” suppressed IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α and increased IL-10 and TGF-β1, consistent with Hsp70-mediated IκK/NF-κB inhibition; however, the study details are summarized in low-quality review literature, and direct demonstration of arimoclomol-driven HSF1 activation in RPE is not provided (Kumar et al., 2020). Another ARPE-19-focused review excerpt states that arimoclomol acts on HSF1 to increase cytosolic Hsp70 without increasing extracellular Hsp70 and improved resistance to 4-HNE–induced oxidative stress (relative to paeoniflorin); again, the primary data are not provided here and the review is of limited quality, so these findings should be treated as provisional until replicated (Kumar et al., 2020). Importantly, in an isogenic patient-derived PRPF31-mutant RPE (RP11) model with progressive cytoplasmic aggregate accumulation, a 7-day treatment screen across HSR/UPR/autophagy modulators showed that rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibitor) reduced aggregate load and shifted LC3-I to LC3-II, whereas arimoclomol did not reduce aggregates under the conditions tested, arguing that in this RPE disease context autophagy activation via mTOR inhibition outperformed Hsp co-induction (Georgiou, 2021).

Non-pharmacological Hsp70 induction and autophagy in RPE inform plausibility. Subthreshold retinal thermal stimulation in pig and mouse RPE in vivo induced HSF1 and Hsp70, increased LC3B-II and decreased p62 (consistent with autophagy activation), and increased LAMP2, suggesting potential CMA upregulation, without apoptosis at ~44 °C, confirming that RPE supports coordinated HSR–autophagy programs with an exploitable therapeutic window (but autophagic flux was not directly quantified in vivo) (Amirkavei et al., 2022; Amirkavei et al., 2020). These data reinforce the therapeutic logic for HSF1–Hsp70 upregulation in RPE to restore proteostasis but do not directly validate arimoclomol’s efficacy in RPE (Amirkavei et al., 2022; Amirkavei et al., 2020). Exogenous rhHsp70 trafficking to lysosomes and protection against oxidative stress in ARPE-19 further supports the notion that increasing Hsp70 activity, whether by protein delivery or endogenous induction, can be beneficial to RPE survival under AMD-relevant stressors (Subrizi et al., 2015).

Autophagy and barrier integrity under AMD-relevant stressors. AMD-relevant toxicities (Aβ, lipofuscin/A2E, oxidants) perturb autophagy/lysosomes in RPE, with Aβ decreasing occludin and ZO-1 in ARPE-19 and activating autophagy markers in vitro and in vivo, and A2E promoting lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cell death; impaired UPS and autophagy with aging lead to aggregate accumulation (including p62-positive aggregates) in RPE and drusen, highlighting the importance of restoring both proteasomal and autophagic clearance to protect RPE function and barrier integrity (Wang et al., 2023; Viiri, 2019; Ryhänen, 2011). Hsp70/p62 roles in this axis are mechanistically established: Hsp70 prevents aggregation and participates in aggregate handling, while p62 is an autophagic receptor degraded by autophagy and accumulates when autophagy is impaired; pharmacologic AMPK activation can accelerate p62 clearance during proteasome inhibition and improve RPE survival (Viiri, 2019). To date, arimoclomol has not been shown to modulate CMA or macroautophagy in RPE, nor to preserve tight junctions or TEER in AMD-relevant models (Georgiou, 2021; Kumar et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay hypothesis and rationale. The working hypothesis is that arimoclomol will potentiate stress-triggered HSF1 activity in RPE, elevating inducible Hsp70 and coordinated chaperone networks to stabilize junctional proteostasis, reduce misfolded protein burden, and normalize autophagy (including potentially CMA), thereby preventing degradation of occludin/claudin and restoring TEER under oxidative or drusen-like stress (e.g., H2O2/4-HNE, A2E/lipofuscin, Aβ) (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). This mechanism is biologically plausible: Hsp70 is abundantly expressed in RPE under stress and supports folding and refolding, substrate triage to proteasome via CHIP, and delivery of specific substrates to CMA via Hsc70/LAMP-2A; its induction suppresses NF-κB–driven pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and can raise IL-10/TGF-β1, which together could indirectly protect junctional complexes from cytokine- and stress-mediated degradation (Kumar et al., 2020). Reducing intracellular aggregate load and restoring proteostasis would be expected to mitigate the downstream cascade of mTORC1 activation, p62/LC3-I accumulation, and tight-junction disruption observed in stressed RPE models (e.g., PRPF31-RPE), although in that system arimoclomol was ineffective while rapamycin reduced aggregates, underscoring that Hsp co-induction alone may be insufficient when autophagy is the principal bottleneck (Georgiou, 2021).

Evidence supporting expected effects in RPE assays:  
- Hsp70 induction in retinal tissues has been achieved via HSF1 activation by heat or pharmacologic inducers; in photoreceptor P23H models, arimoclomol increased Hsp70/Hsp90 and reduced aggregation/toxicity, consistent with the proximal arm of the proposed mechanism (HSF1→Hsp70→improved proteostasis) (Parfitt et al., 2014; Amirkavei et al., 2020).  
- In ARPE-19 summaries, arimoclomol increased intracellular (not extracellular) Hsp70 and improved resistance to 4-HNE oxidative stress, and Hsp70 overexpression with help of a co-inducer like arimoclomol suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines, supporting cell-autonomous proteostasis and anti-inflammatory contributions that would be favorable for junctional stability (Kumar et al., 2020).  
- Exogenous rhHsp70 delivery to RPE localizes to lysosomes and reduces oxidative toxicity and inflammation, demonstrating that raising functional Hsp70 in RPE is sufficient to afford cytoprotection, a downstream functional goal of HSF1 co-induction (Subrizi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Evidence arguing for tempered expectations and the need for combination strategies:  
- In PRPF31-mutant RPE, arimoclomol did not reduce aggregates in a 7-day screen, whereas rapamycin shifted LC3 processing and reduced aggregate markers, suggesting that when autophagy is the limiting axis, direct autophagy activation (e.g., mTORC1 inhibition) is required; Hsp co-induction alone may not clear established aggregates or repair autophagic flux (Georgiou, 2021).  
- In primary neuronal ALS models, arimoclomol often failed to induce measurable HSPA1A/HSPA8 and its protective actions occurred without detectable Hsp70 upregulation; HDAC inhibition enhanced Hsp induction by other inducers, arguing that Hsp co-induction efficacy is cell-type and chromatin-context dependent and may require combination therapy to overcome induction thresholds in some cells (potentially relevant to differentiated RPE) (Comaduran et al., 2024).  
- AMD-relevant stressors directly disrupt tight junctions (Aβ reduces occludin and ZO-1 in ARPE-19) and invoke autophagy/lysosomal dysfunction; because arimoclomol’s effects on CMA/macroautophagy in RPE are unproven, barrier rescue may not occur unless autophagic flux is also corrected (Wang et al., 2023).

Assay implementation guidance for decision-making:  
- In vitro human RPE models (primary/donor iPSC-RPE monolayers with high TEER) should be stressed with 4-HNE, H2O2, A2E, or Aβ to recapitulate AMD-relevant proteotoxic and inflammatory conditions, and arimoclomol tested across concentrations paralleling prior cell work (e.g., 10–100 µM) with and without a priming HSF1 activator (celastrol ≤0.3 µM) to evaluate requirement for co-induction, keeping in mind the neuronal data identifying 50 µM arimoclomol + 0.3 µM celastrol as an optimized low-toxicity combination (Deane, 2019).  
- Primary readouts: HSF1 activation (nuclear translocation, Ser phosphorylation), Hsp70/Hsp90 induction (immunoblot, qPCR), autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover with/without bafilomycin, p62 dynamics), CMA markers (LAMP-2A levels, lysosomal Hsc70/Hsp70 substrate colocalization), proteasome activity, aggregate load (FK1, ubiquitin, p62 bodies), and barrier integrity (TEER, ZO-1/occludin/claudin-19 immunostaining continuity) (Kivinen et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2015; Viiri, 2019; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Cytokine profiling (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10, TGF-β1) to detect Hsp70-linked NF-κB effects reported in ARPE-19 (Kumar et al., 2020).  
- Positive comparators: rapamycin for autophagy induction; exogenous rhHsp70 as a proteostasis rescue control; heat-based Hsp70 induction within non-damaging windows to confirm pathway responsiveness (Georgiou, 2021; Subrizi et al., 2015; Amirkavei et al., 2020).

Given the aggregate of evidence, the most realistic expectation is that arimoclomol will increase inducible Hsp70 in stressed RPE if HSF1 can be productively co-induced, reduce misfolded protein accumulation and inflammatory signaling, and potentially improve barrier metrics indirectly by attenuating stressors that degrade junctional complexes; however, without concurrent normalization of autophagic flux and CMA, tight-junction rescue and TEER restoration are uncertain, particularly in models where autophagy is the primary deficit (Georgiou, 2021; Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths supporting arimoclomol for dry AMD RPE barrier rescue:  
- Mechanistic fit: Hsp70/Hsc70 are central “gatekeepers” of RPE proteostasis across the UPS and lysosomal systems, including CMA; restoring inducible Hsp70 via HSF1 co-induction directly targets key failure nodes in RPE aging and AMD pathogenesis (aggregation, impaired clearance, inflammation), aligning with known disease biology (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Kivinen, 2018).  
- Demonstrated retinal efficacy in proteostasis-driven degeneration: arimoclomol increased Hsp70/Hsp90, reduced mutant rhodopsin aggregation, and preserved photoreceptor structure/function in P23H rats, with evidence of concurrent UPR potentiation; this validates the platform concept that HSF1 co-induction plus ER stress modulation can modify retinal degeneration, albeit in photoreceptors rather than RPE (Parfitt et al., 2014).  
- RPE permissiveness to Hsp70-based cytoprotection: exogenous rhHsp70 diffuses to RPE, is internalized, localizes to endolysosomal compartments, reduces IL-6 and cytolysis, and improves viability in oxidative stress paradigms; thus, augmenting Hsp70 in RPE is sufficient to produce protective effects, supporting the feasibility of endogenous induction with a co-inducer if pharmacology is adequate (Subrizi et al., 2015).  
- Stress-selective amplification: arimoclomol preferentially acts in stressed cells, limiting risks of unwanted Hsp70 induction in healthy tissue; this attribute is advantageous for chronic ocular therapy where avoiding constitutive pathway activation is desirable (Parfitt et al., 2014).  
- Clinical development and safety experience: extensive non-ocular development in ALS/NPC provides informative safety and pharmacology context; while ocular distribution is not established in these sources, the systemic safety window is a favorable starting point for repurposing (Venediktov et al., 2023; O’Leary, 2019).

Key weaknesses and uncertainties:  
- Lack of direct evidence in dry AMD/RPE barrier endpoints: no published data demonstrate arimoclomol preserves RPE tight junctions (ZO-1/occludin/claudin), restores TEER, or improves drusen-like pathology in vivo; ARPE-19 reports of arimoclomol-induced Hsp70 and anti-inflammatory effects are secondary summaries in low-quality reviews without primary detail (Kumar et al., 2020). In contrast, direct AMD-relevant in vitro data show that Aβ disrupts tight junction proteins, and autophagy failure correlates with p62 accumulation and aggregate burden, but the ability of arimoclomol to reverse these specific defects in RPE is untested (Wang et al., 2023; Viiri, 2019).  
- Negative/neutral result in PRPF31-RPE aggregation screen: arimoclomol did not reduce cytoplasmic aggregates in a rigorous 7-day screen in RP11-RPE; rapamycin reduced aggregates and shifted LC3 processing, suggesting that in certain RPE aggregate pathologies, autophagy activators outperform Hsp co-induction; whether arimoclomol could complement autophagy induction to achieve barrier rescue remains to be determined (Georgiou, 2021).  
- Uncertain induction competence in differentiated RPE: Primary neurons display high thresholds for inducible Hsp70 (HSPA1A) induction, with arimoclomol often failing to raise Hsp70; Hsp induction can be enhanced by HDAC inhibition, implying that chromatin accessibility and cell state are important variables; differentiated RPE monolayers may similarly require co-induction strategies (e.g., low-dose celastrol or epigenetic modulators) to achieve robust Hsp70 upregulation (Comaduran et al., 2024; Deane, 2019). If arimoclomol cannot reliably induce Hsp70 in mature RPE under clinically relevant stress, the strategy will falter.  
- CMA/macroautophagy modulation by arimoclomol in RPE not established: despite Hsp70’s mechanistic role in CMA, no data show arimoclomol improves CMA or autophagic flux in RPE, which are crucial to clearing damaged proteins/lipids under AMD stress; relying on Hsp70 alone without restoring autophagic flux may be insufficient to protect tight junctions (Chang et al., 2015; Georgiou, 2021).  
- Translational pharmacology: Retinal/RPE exposure of arimoclomol following systemic dosing is not presented in this corpus; ocular delivery strategies and RPE pharmacokinetics for arimoclomol are undefined here, in contrast to exogenous Hsp70 delivery where diffusion and tissue uptake were measured (Subrizi et al., 2015). Without ocular PK/PD and RPE Hsp70 induction data, dosing strategies for barrier rescue remain speculative.

Recommendation and development path:  
- Proceed to targeted preclinical validation in human iPSC-RPE monolayers and AMD-relevant stress paradigms, with rigorous endpoint panels including HSF1–Hsp70 induction, autophagic flux/CMA markers, aggregate clearance, cytokine modulation, and barrier integrity (TEER, ZO-1/occludin continuity), using rapamycin and rhHsp70 as comparators and benchmarking against known disruptions by Aβ and A2E (Georgiou, 2021; Subrizi et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Explore co-induction strategies: combine arimoclomol with low-dose celastrol to lower the induction threshold, and/or with autophagy activators (rapalogs/AMPK agonists) to correct flux while elevating chaperone capacity; justify combinations by neuronal data demonstrating enhanced Hsp induction and by RPE data showing autophagy dependence of aggregate clearance (Deane, 2019; Viiri, 2019; Georgiou, 2021).  
- If cell data are positive (robust Hsp70 induction, reduced aggregate burden, TEER protection), advance to ex vivo retina or small-animal models of RPE oxidative/drusen-like stress, with ocular pharmacokinetic measurements to confirm RPE exposure and on-target Hsp70 induction; consider local ocular delivery if systemic exposure is inadequate (Subrizi et al., 2015).  
- Maintain a realistic risk view: if arimoclomol fails to induce Hsp70 adequately in differentiated RPE or fails to impact autophagic flux, pivot to alternative HSF1 activators or to exogenous Hsp70 delivery or autophagy-centric therapies, where evidence in RPE is stronger (Subrizi et al., 2015; Georgiou, 2021).

In sum, arimoclomol is a mechanistically coherent candidate for restoring RPE proteostasis via HSF1–Hsp70 co-induction, supported by strong photoreceptor data and broad neurodegeneration experience, but it lacks direct evidence in dry AMD models and has an RPE aggregation screen result that favors autophagy induction over Hsp co-induction; rigorous, well-controlled RPE studies with barrier readouts are required before committing to translational development for dry AMD (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ripasudil, also known by its research designation Y-39983 and commercially available as Selleckchem S8443, is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor developed originally as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil containing protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. It belongs to a class of therapeutics that act in an ATP‐competitive manner to inhibit the activity of ROCK isoforms, enzymes that are critical regulators of actomyosin contractility and cell adhesion. Ripasudil was synthesized following the structural optimization of earlier compounds such as fasudil and Y-27632, with the aim of increasing both potency and ocular tolerability. Its chemical origins are linked to the rational design strategies that sought to improve enzyme inhibitory selectivity and to enhance the pharmacokinetic profile for local ocular application. Members of the ROCK inhibitor class have seen prior use in settings that require modulation of actin cytoskeleton dynamics, such as the treatment of glaucoma via enhanced aqueous humor outflow, and have also been explored in contexts involving wound healing and anti-fibrotic effects in various ocular tissues (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, ripasudil has been approved in Japan for the treatment of glaucoma and ocular hypertension, where it is delivered topically in the form of eye drops, demonstrating a well-established safety profile and a low incidence of systemic adverse effects. In preclinical models, it has demonstrated efficacy by increasing ocular blood flow, modifying trabecular meshwork cell contractility, and reducing intraocular pressure, thereby serving as a stepping stone and proof-of-concept for the utility of ROCK inhibitors in ocular disorders. Beyond its approved use in glaucoma, investigations of ROCK inhibitors—including ripasudil—have extended into experimental applications in corneal endothelial regeneration and have been evaluated in combination with anti-VEGF therapies for diabetic macular edema. Although direct clinical evidence specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is not available, multiple lines of preclinical research have shown that the ROCK inhibitor class modulates pathways which are believed to underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Notably, the mechanistic studies have identified the role of ROCK signaling in cytoskeletal reorganization, matrix contractility, and fibrosis, all of which are processes particularly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier dysfunction seen in dry AMD (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Moreover, the ocular pharmacokinetic profile of ripasudil—demonstrated by rabbit intravitreal studies showing a half-life of approximately 14 hours and negligible systemic exposure—is supportive of repurposing this candidate for posterior segment indications, including dry AMD (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ripasudil exerts its therapeutic activity by competitively inhibiting the ATP-binding site of ROCK isoforms, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of downstream effectors such as myosin light-chain (MLC), myosin-binding subunit of MLC phosphatase (MYPT1), and LIM kinase. These phosphorylation events normally lead to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, focal adhesion assembly, and ultimately contribute to a contractile, stiffened cell phenotype. In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, this contractility is thought to be exacerbated under conditions of oxidative stress, contributing to disassembly or mislocalization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity. By inhibiting ROCK, ripasudil reduces actomyosin-driven contraction and stress-fiber formation, thereby promoting cortical F-actin remodeling and facilitating the proper membrane relocalization of tight-junction proteins. The specificity of ripasudil has been demonstrated by its greater than 100-fold selectivity against other kinases such as protein kinase C (PKC) and myotonic dystrophy kinase-related Cdc42-binding kinase (MRCK), highlighting the mechanistic precision by which it modulates ROCK-dependent signaling cascades (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Additionally, while several studies indicate that the ROCK inhibitor class generally targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2 isoforms, quantitative biochemical data have shown that ripasudil exhibits potent enzyme inhibitory activity with IC₅₀s in the low nanomolar range (with values reported around 51 nM for ROCK1 and 19 nM for ROCK2 in some studies, though the candidate hypothesis posits values of approximately 29 nM for ROCK1 and 68 nM for ROCK2). This inhibitory profile is particularly relevant because emerging research indicates that ROCK2, in particular, is upregulated in the pathological conditions of dry AMD and plays a key role in mediating cytoskeletal changes that disrupt RPE tight junction integrity (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). The inhibition of ROCK thereby is expected to have a dual benefit of cytoprotection and restoration of cell junction architecture, ultimately leading to improved barrier function (Ghenciu et al., 2025; Singh & Singh, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing ripasudil for dry AMD is that by blocking ROCK activity in oxidatively stressed retinal pigment epithelium cells, the compound will lead to a reduction in actomyosin contractility, thereby alleviating the formation of pathological stress fibers that otherwise disrupt the organization of tight junction complexes. Under normal physiological conditions, tight junction proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin are localized at the plasma membrane in a continuous, belt-like manner that is essential to maintain TEER and restrict paracellular permeability. However, in dry AMD, oxidative damage, inflammation, and mechanical stress lead to cytoskeletal reorganization and a discontinuous distribution of these critical proteins, resulting in impaired barrier function and contributing to the pathogenesis of the disease. Preclinical studies, particularly those employing ARPE-19 cell models subjected to toxic insults such as paraquat or sodium iodate (NaIO₃), have demonstrated that ROCK inhibitors can dose-dependently restore TEER (with reported improvements up to 70%) and re-establish the membrane continuity of ZO-1, suggesting that these agents can “rescue” the RPE barrier phenotype under injurious conditions (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). It is expected that ripasudil, with its potent ROCK-inhibitory activity and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics (including intravitreal retention times supportive of sustained action), will similarly promote the cortical redistribution of F-actin, leading to the re-localization of junctional molecules back to the cell membrane. This mechanistic restoration should result in improved transepithelial electrical resistance and a concomitant reduction in paracellular permeability, effectively reinforcing the RPE barrier—a central therapeutic target in dry AMD. Moreover, the activation of protective cellular pathways through ROCK inhibition may also confer additional anti-apoptotic and anti-inflammatory effects, further contributing to the survival and functional integrity of the RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating ripasudil as a candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths become apparent. First, its established clinical use for glaucoma means that its safety, tolerability, and ocular pharmacokinetic properties are well characterized—attributes that significantly lower the translational barrier for its application in other ocular diseases. The intravitreal pharmacokinetic data, with a half-life of approximately 14 hours in rabbit models and negligible systemic exposure, suggest that therapeutic concentrations capable of modulating ROCK activity in the retina can be achieved with acceptable dosing regimens (Yamaguchi et al., 2016). Second, the mechanistic rationale is compelling: ROCK signaling is intimately involved in mediating actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, and subsequent disruption of tight junction architecture in epithelial cells. Given that ROCK2 in particular is implicated in the pathological processes observed in the RPE in dry AMD, the ability of ripasudil to inhibit this pathway could translate into measurable improvements in barrier function, as indicated by preclinical assays demonstrating TEER restoration and the re-localization of ZO-1 in ARPE-19 cells (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Third, the compound exhibits a favorable selectivity profile, with negligible off-target activity against other kinases such as PKC and MRCK, which minimizes the risk of unintended effects in non-target tissues. This specificity is critical when repurposing drugs for chronic conditions such as dry AMD, where long-term ocular safety is paramount (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Despite these strengths, there are notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before ripasudil can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. A primary limitation is the paucity of direct experimental evidence in RPE models of dry AMD. While the hypothesis is supported by data from related in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative stress), robust in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of dry AMD pathophysiology are still needed. In particular, data demonstrating that ripasudil can restore tight junction integrity and improve TEER in the context of chronic, progressive RPE dysfunction remain limited (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Furthermore, although the compound’s ROCK inhibitory activity is well documented, the available literature does not consistently detail the isoform-specific effects in RPE cells; given that ROCK1 and ROCK2 may play distinct roles in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, clarifying the relative contributions of each isoform is essential. The candidate hypothesis posits specific IC₅₀ values for ROCK1 and ROCK2, yet discrepancies exist across reported studies regarding the precise inhibitory concentrations, which indicates that further biochemical characterization is warranted (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). Another consideration is the potential for adverse effects when repurposing a drug originally optimized for anterior-segment diseases for posterior-segment applications. Although the ocular safety profile of ripasudil in glaucoma is well established, the long-term impact of ROCK inhibition on RPE cell biology in an aged population—especially in the context of dry AMD—remains uncertain. Off-target cytoskeletal effects in other retinal cell types, possible modulation of inflammatory responses, and the risk of inadvertently triggering compensatory signaling pathways are all factors that must be carefully evaluated in preclinical studies (Iancu et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2025). Lastly, while the pharmacokinetic data support retinal exposure after intravitreal or possibly topical administration, optimizing the delivery method to ensure sustained and localized drug levels in the RPE without causing ocular surface toxicity (such as conjunctival hyperemia or corneal epithelial disturbances) will be critical. Innovative delivery systems, such as sustained-release intravitreal implants or depot formulations, may offer solutions but require further development (Yamaguchi et al., 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023).

In conclusion, the repurposing of ripasudil for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and a favorable safety profile derived from its established use in glaucoma. The compound’s capacity to inhibit ROCK-mediated actomyosin contraction and promote cortical F-actin remodeling positions it as a promising agent for restoring RPE barrier function—one of the key pathological features of dry AMD. However, the current literature reveals significant gaps in direct evidence regarding its effects on RPE tight junction proteins, TEER restoration, and the isoform-specific roles of ROCK in the RPE under oxidative stress. To advance ripasudil as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, additional preclinical investigations—ideally incorporating robust animal models of dry AMD and detailed biochemical analyses of ROCK isoform activity in RPE cells—are required. Additionally, optimizations in drug delivery methodology to achieve sustained posterior-segment exposure while minimizing adverse ocular events will be imperative. Overall, ripasudil presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, with its strengths in mechanistic specificity, favorable ocular pharmacokinetics, and established clinical safety underscoring its potential. Nonetheless, the outlined weaknesses and knowledge gaps necessitate a rigorous program of targeted research to validate its efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity and to ensure its long-term safety in the intended patient population (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023; Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Adams & Papillon, 2020; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR, chemically known as 5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide, is an endogenous purine biosynthetic intermediate that has been harnessed as a synthetic, cell‐permeable AMP analog to activate AMP‐activated protein kinase (AMPK) pharmacologically (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Originally identified as a naturally occurring metabolic intermediate, AICAR gained prominence when researchers recognized that its structural similarity to AMP enables it to mimic cellular energetic stress conditions, thereby initiating AMPK‐mediated cellular responses (Green, 2013). In its synthetic format, AICAR is produced and purified to high standards by vendors such as Selleckchem and Sigma (S1802; A9978), and belongs to the broader class of nucleoside analogs used as metabolic regulators. Compounds belonging to this class have historically been employed to interrogate and modulate energy sensing and substrate utilization in diverse cell types, ranging from skeletal muscle to vascular smooth muscle (Pokrywka et al., 2014). This same class of metabolic modulators has demonstrated efficacy in experimental models of mitochondrial disease and muscle wasting by stimulating AMPK‐dependent pathways that augment mitochondrial biogenesis and restore energy balance (Green, 2013). Owing to its capacity to influence the phosphorylation of key enzymes and transcription factors, AICAR has found applications not only in elucidating fundamental bioenergetic pathways but also as a candidate to ameliorate conditions where energy homeostasis is disrupted. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, where the maintenance of tight junction integrity is crucial for barrier function and homeostasis, AICAR’s mechanism of action offers a rationale for its repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Historically, metabolic modulation via AMPK activators has been extensively investigated in various systems, and AICAR has been a workhorse agent in these studies owing to its reliable pharmacological profile (Pokrywka et al., 2014). Biochemically, AICAR has been widely used to stimulate AMPK in cell culture and animal models, resulting in a host of downstream effects that include enhanced fatty acid oxidation, increased glucose uptake, and modulated lipid synthesis (Green, 2013). In addition, AICAR’s ability to promote autophagy through the inhibition of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) cascade has been observed across various cell types, including those derived from retinal tissues (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Clinical investigations have predominantly focused on its metabolic effects in conditions such as diabetes and ischemia, although its application in ocular diseases has been comparatively less explored (Pokrywka et al., 2014). In the field of ophthalmology, research into the role of AMPK in retinal health has uncovered that AMPK activation influences key RPE functions including autophagy, inflammatory cytokine production, and tight junction integrity (Qin, 2012). Notably, investigations in RPE-related models have demonstrated that pharmacologic modulation of AMPK can either protect or impair barrier function, depending on the context and isoform engaged (Qin & De Vries, 2008). While AICAR itself has not been approved explicitly for the treatment of dry AMD, its well–established use in preclinical studies, combined with its demonstrated ability to rescue barrier integrity in RPE under oxidative stress conditions, supports its potential repurposing for this indication (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011). Thus, the accumulated literature demonstrates that AMPK activators, and AICAR in particular, offer promising mechanistic pathways to address cellular energy deficits and junctional disintegration, both critical features of dry AMD pathology (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which AICAR exerts its therapeutic effects begins with its cellular uptake through nucleoside transporters such as ENT1 and ENT2, a process that ensures its intracellular availability (Dolinar et al., 2018). Once internalized, AICAR is rapidly phosphorylated by adenosine kinase, converting it into 5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate (ZMP) (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). ZMP, as an AMP analog, binds to the γ subunit of AMPK, eliciting conformational changes that not only enhance its allosteric activation but also protect it from dephosphorylation (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). Concurrently, the binding of ZMP to AMPK facilitates the phosphorylation of the catalytic α‐subunit at Thr172, thereby augmenting the kinase’s catalytic activity to phosphorylate downstream targets such as acetyl‐CoA carboxylase (ACC) (Qin & De Vries, 2008). The phosphorylation and inactivation of ACC lead to decreased fatty acid synthesis and enhanced fatty acid oxidation, contributing significantly to improved energy homeostasis (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Green, 2013). Notably, in the retinal pigment epithelium, robust AMPK activation is implicated in the stabilization of tight junction proteins and in the promotion of autophagy, a process that is essential for removal of damaged organelles and protein aggregates under oxidative stress conditions (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Furthermore, the role of AICAR in modulating tight junction dynamics is complex and intersects with its influence on autophagic flux; AMPK activation can downregulate mTOR signaling, which not only contributes to increased autophagic clearance but also appears to correlate with improved organization of junctional proteins, ultimately enhancing transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). In experimental settings using RPE cells, the administration of AICAR under oxidative or high‐glucose stress conditions leads to a cascade of phosphorylation events that foster an environment conducive to tight junction assembly while simultaneously stabilizing cellular energy stores (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This biochemical cascade is further verified by the reversal of the observed effects upon the use of compound C, an AMPK inhibitor, which underscores the specificity of AICAR’s action being mediated through AMPK activation (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Villarroel et al., 2011).

It is also critical to note that the effects of AICAR on AMPK activity are influenced not only by its rapid intracellular conversion but also by the intrinsic cellular context—including the balance of energy substrates, the presence of other nucleosides, and the isoform‐specific roles of AMPK (Qin & De Vries, 2008). The resultant activation of AMPK leads to multifaceted downstream responses, such as cellular adaptation to metabolic stress, regulation of inflammatory mediators, and modulation of cytoskeletal elements that cooperate in the maintenance of cell–cell adhesion within the RPE monolayer (Villarroel et al., 2011). This detailed mechanistic insight provides the foundation for hypothesizing that AICAR may effectively drive energy homeostasis and promote tight junction assembly in RPE cells, addressing one of the core pathological features of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
In the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration, the primary pathological hallmark is the degeneration of the RPE accompanied by impaired tight junction integrity and compromised barrier function, resulting in increased paracellular permeability and accumulation of metabolic waste. Based on the observed effects of AICAR in in vitro RPE models, it is expected that AICAR will allosterically activate AMPK within RPE cells, leading to enhanced energy homeostasis and improved assembly of tight junctions (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Experimental data have demonstrated that when induced with oxidative stress, as is common in AMD, treatment with 500 µM AICAR increased TEER from 90 to 135 Ω·cm²—a clear indicator of enhanced barrier integrity (Miyagishima et al., 2021). This increase in TEER is paralleled by a 2.8‐fold elevation in phosphorylated AMPK levels, which confirms that AICAR is effectively engaging its intended target in these cells (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011).

The underlying mechanism for this improved barrier function is thought to be twofold. First, through ACC inhibition—mediated by AMPK activation—there is a shift in the cellular lipid economy, reducing the deleterious lipid accumulation that can disrupt tight junction architecture (Qin & De Vries, 2008). Second, the activation of autophagic pathways facilitates the clearance of oxidatively damaged proteins and organelles, thereby enhancing the overall health of the RPE and reinforcing its capacity to maintain tight junction complexes (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). This dual action not only addresses the immediate energetic deficit induced by oxidative stress but also contributes to the structural resilience of the RPE monolayer.

Moreover, the observed reversal of AICAR’s protective effects by compound C serves as strong evidence that the benefit is specifically mediated through the AMPK pathway rather than off‐target effects (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014). This mechanistic specificity is critical when evaluating a compound for clinical translation, as it suggests that downstream effects such as TEER enhancement, tight junction stabilization, and modulation of paracellular flux are directly attributable to AMPK activation. Additionally, AICAR‐mediated autophagy has been implicated in maintaining cellular integrity under chronic oxidative stress—a condition that is intrinsically linked to the progression of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Given the central role of AMPK in RPE physiology, particularly in the regulation of junction protein stability and energy metabolism, the expected therapeutic effect of AICAR in dry AMD is to restore and preserve RPE barrier function. This restoration is anticipated to limit paracellular fluid leakage, reduce the deposition of extracellular debris, and ultimately slow the degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011). The projected outcome is an improvement in cellular homeostasis and reduced progression of retinal degeneration, which translates into a potential clinical benefit for patients with dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History and Prior Applications:  
AICAR’s journey from a metabolic intermediate to a pharmacologically active compound has been well documented across a range of biomedical research areas. In preclinical studies, AICAR has been extensively utilized to activate AMPK in various cellular models, thereby providing critical insights into the regulation of energy balance, mitochondrial biogenesis, and lipid metabolism (Green, 2013; Pokrywka et al., 2014). Its early applications in skeletal muscle and cancer cells underscored its ability to stimulate glucose uptake and shift cellular energy dynamics in favor of catabolic pathways (Dolinar et al., 2018; Longnus et al., 2003).

In cardiovascular research, AICAR was instrumental in elucidating the mechanisms underlying glycogenolysis and vasorelaxation, where its conversion to ZMP led to the activation of AMPK in vascular smooth muscle cells, resulting in beneficial metabolic adaptations (Pyla et al., 2022). Although these studies did not directly target ocular tissues, they established a robust framework for understanding how AMPK activation can mediate protective responses under conditions of metabolic stress.

The transition of AICAR into the realm of ophthalmological research was driven by the observation that AMPK is a pivotal regulator of RPE function and tight junction assembly. Publications have demonstrated that oxidative stress—a significant contributor to AMD pathology—can impair RPE barrier integrity by disrupting the organization of tight junction proteins, while AMPK activation appears to counteract these deleterious changes (Qin, 2012; Villarroel et al., 2011). Furthermore, the dual role of AMPK in regulating autophagy and lipid metabolism has been a focal point in dry AMD research, as dysfunctional autophagy and lipid accumulation are hallmarks of RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011). The protective effects of AMPK activators in other models of cellular stress, such as in cardiomyocytes and hepatocarcinoma cells, lend additional support to the hypothesis that similar mechanisms may be beneficial in preserving RPE function (Kawashima et al., 2020; Sid et al., 2014).

Despite these promising findings, it is important to note that the therapeutic history of AICAR in the context of ocular diseases remains in the preclinical phase, with limited direct clinical evaluation for dry AMD. Some studies have even suggested that AMPK activation in the RPE could have dual outcomes, potentially inhibiting phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments under oxidative conditions (Qin & De Vries, 2008). This observation highlights the intricacies of AMPK signaling in retinal cells and underscores the need for rigorous dose–response and context–specific studies. Nonetheless, the accumulated preclinical data from both ocular and non‐ocular systems provide a strong rationale for further exploring AICAR as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Expected Impact on RPE Function and Dry AMD Pathology:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of AICAR in dry AMD is that its ability to activate AMPK will lead to a concerted improvement in RPE barrier function and energy homeostasis—two crucial aspects compromised in AMD. In vitro models of RPE, particularly those derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC‐RPE), have shown that exposure to oxidative stress causes significant deterioration in tight junction assembly and barrier integrity, as measured by transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Miyagishima et al., 2021).

When these stressed RPE cells are treated with AICAR, a rapid increase in TEER from approximately 90 Ω·cm² to 135 Ω·cm² has been observed, indicating a substantial enhancement in tight junction integrity (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). At the molecular level, this improvement correlates with a 2.8‐fold rise in phosphorylated AMPK, which is directly associated with the activation of energy restoration pathways and the stabilization of tight junction proteins (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011).

The benefits conferred by AMPK activation are expected to be multifaceted. On one hand, the inhibition of ACC through phosphorylation is anticipated to reduce aberrant lipid synthesis and promote fatty acid oxidation, thereby alleviating metabolic stress within RPE cells (Qin & De Vries, 2008). On the other hand, enhanced autophagic flux driven by AMPK is likely to facilitate the removal of oxidatively damaged proteins and organelles, contributing to cellular repair processes that are pivotal in slowing the progression of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

These laboratory observations have practical implications. In a dysregulated retinal environment—characterized by oxidative damage, inflammatory cytokine presence, and disrupted tight junctions—the activation of AMPK by AICAR could serve as a countermeasure to re‐establish and maintain the critical barrier functions of the RPE (Villarroel et al., 2011). Moreover, by diminishing paracellular leak and preserving the integrity of junctional complexes, AICAR may reduce the accumulation of metabolic waste products and drusen, which are pathological hallmarks of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

It is also noteworthy that the experimental reversal of AICAR’s protective effects by compound C—a well‐known AMPK inhibitor—provides definitive evidence that the beneficial outcomes observed in RPE cells are mediated specifically through AMPK signaling (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014). This on‐target specificity increases the confidence that the observed improvements in TEER are attributable to the intended mechanism rather than off‐target pharmacological actions. Consequently, the expected therapeutic effect in dry AMD would involve enhanced RPE cell viability, reduced cellular stress, and a restored barrier function that together could slow or even halt the progressive degeneration observed in patients (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Overall Evaluation:  
When evaluating AICAR as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, several strengths are immediately apparent, along with a number of challenges that must be carefully addressed during further development. One of the foremost strengths of AICAR is its well–characterized mechanism of action. By serving as an AMP analog that is intracellularly converted to ZMP, AICAR robustly activates AMPK—a key cellular energy sensor that orchestrates a wide range of metabolic responses (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). This activation is tightly coupled to downstream effects such as ACC inhibition, enhanced fatty acid oxidation, and the promotion of autophagy, which are all beneficial in counteracting the metabolic and oxidative stresses inherent in dry AMD (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012).

Furthermore, the experimental data indicating a significant increase in TEER and a concomitant rise in phosphorylated AMPK levels in oxidatively stressed iPSC‐RPE cells provide compelling evidence that AICAR can restore RPE barrier function (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This is particularly important because tight junction integrity and paracellular barrier properties are central to the maintenance of retinal homeostasis and are critically impaired in dry AMD (Villarroel et al., 2011). The demonstration that the beneficial effects of AICAR are reversible by an AMPK inhibitor further reinforces the concept that the drug’s actions are on–target and biologically relevant (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014).

Nevertheless, several potential weaknesses require cautious evaluation. First, while AMPK activation is generally associated with enhanced cellular resilience, some studies have reported that excessive or isoform‐specific activation of AMPK in RPE cells may lead to unintended consequences, such as the inhibition of photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis—a process vital for retinal renewal (Qin & De Vries, 2008). Such a dualistic role of AMPK creates a delicate balance whereby the same pathway that is intended to improve barrier function might also impede essential RPE functions if not precisely modulated.

Additionally, the data in the literature suggest that under certain circumstances, AMPK activation might even contribute to increased epithelial permeability rather than a strengthening of tight junctions (Villarroel et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This paradoxical effect raises concerns about potential context–dependent outcomes of AICAR treatment. For example, while low‐to‐moderate activation of AMPK might support tight junction assembly and autophagy, hyperactivation under severe metabolic or oxidative stress could exacerbate junctional disorganization, thereby counteracting any beneficial effects (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Another challenge is the potential for systemic side effects arising from AICAR’s widespread actions in other tissues. Given that AICAR has been employed in models of diabetes, cardiac metabolism, and even cancer, its pleiotropic effects could impose additional safety considerations when repurposed for ocular use (Pokrywka et al., 2014; Viglino et al., 2019). There is also the issue of dosage; concentrations of 500 µM are effective in vitro, but translating such dosages to in vivo ocular applications requires careful pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies to ensure that therapeutic levels are achieved locally without eliciting undesirable systemic responses (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Asby et al., 2015).

Moreover, given the complex interplay between AMPK signaling, autophagy, and cellular differentiation processes, it is essential to thoroughly understand the long‐term implications of chronic AMPK activation in the RPE. While short‐term activation may be protective, persistent stimulation could lead to energy depletion or maladaptive remodeling of the RPE cytoskeleton, which in turn could affect visual function (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). This underscores the need for extensive preclinical studies that evaluate both the efficacy and the safety profile of AICAR over prolonged periods.

Finally, the inherent variability in patient responses due to genetic, metabolic, and environmental factors presents an additional hurdle. The RPE’s response to oxidative stress, and hence its sensitivity to AMPK modulation, may vary widely among individuals with dry AMD. It will be crucial to identify biomarkers that predict response to AICAR treatment and to tailor dosing regimens accordingly (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

In summary, while AICAR shows considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD by virtue of its well‐established mechanism of AMPK activation, experimental data demonstrating tight junction rescue in RPE cells, and its ability to promote autophagic processes that counteract oxidative stress, its repurposing is tempered by concerns regarding the dualistic effects of AMPK signaling in the RPE, potential systemic side effects, and the challenges associated with dosage translation from in vitro to in vivo applications (Villarroel et al., 2011). The overall evaluation is that AICAR exhibits several compelling advantages—including mechanistic clarity, on‐target efficacy, and a robust preclinical rationale—that substantiate further investigation through rigorous preclinical and, eventually, clinical studies. With a careful approach that addresses the aforementioned weaknesses, AICAR may ultimately emerge as a valuable addition to the therapeutic arsenal against dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

To fully validate AICAR’s potential for treating dry AMD, a series of detailed investigations is warranted. In parallel, investigating the interplay between AICAR‐induced AMPK activation and autophagic pathways in the RPE will shed light on how tightly coupled these processes are in the context of dry AMD. Since autophagy is vital for clearing oxidatively damaged cellular components and supporting cell survival, it will be important to determine whether prolonged AMPK activation fosters a beneficial autophagic flux or rather leads to autophagy dysregulation over time (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). Strategies that involve monitoring autophagic markers along with TEER measurements and junction protein expression could provide a comprehensive picture of cellular health in AICAR‐treated RPE cells.

Given the concerns regarding potential systemic effects, advanced drug delivery systems such as localized intraocular injections or biodegradable implants could be considered for delivering AICAR directly to the retina, thereby limiting systemic exposure and enhancing local efficacy (Viglino et al., 2019; Sid et al., 2014). Preclinical animal models that mimic the pathological features of dry AMD will be indispensable in evaluating the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and therapeutic windows of AICAR in an in vivo setting. Such studies would also be instrumental in identifying potential adverse effects and assessing the long‐term safety profile of AICAR when administered via ocular routes.

Another key consideration is the potential for combination therapy. Since some reports indicate that AMPK activation by AICAR might impair certain RPE functions such as phagocytosis if excessively activated, combining AICAR with other agents that either modulate AMPK isoform activity or protect against excessive autophagic stimulation may provide a synergistic benefit (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Villarroel et al., 2011). Genetic or epigenetic factors that predispose individuals to variations in RPE responsiveness may also be identified, thereby enabling personalized medicine approaches for patients with dry AMD.

In conclusion, while there remain numerous challenges and uncertainties, AICAR represents a highly promising candidate for repurposing as a barrier‐protective agent in dry AMD. Its capacity to robustly activate AMPK, improve cellular energy homeostasis, promote autophagy, and restore tight junction integrity in RPE cells offers a multifaceted mode of action that addresses several key pathological features of dry AMD. With targeted preclinical studies that unpack the complexity of AMPK signaling in retinal tissues and strategic clinical trial designs that mitigate potential adverse effects, AICAR could conceivably fill a significant therapeutic gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012; Villarroel et al., 2011).

AICAR’s well‐documented ability to mimic AMP—thereby inducing AMPK activation—and its established role in regulating cellular energy balance and autophagy place it squarely in the category of compounds with high therapeutic potential for metabolic disorders. Emerging evidence in retinal models, particularly those simulating the oxidative stress and barrier dysfunction typical of dry AMD, further reinforces the rationale behind its repurposing. Despite these challenges, the convergence of multiple lines of evidence—from improved TEER measurements and specific molecular activation to supportive mechanistic studies—strongly advocates for further research into AICAR as a viable therapeutic strategy for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Future studies that focus on fine‐tuning its dosage, delivery, and integrated combination therapies hold the key to unlocking its full therapeutic potential and advancing it from the bench to the clinic (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012).

Taking into account the strengths of its well‐defined mechanism, the reproducible experimental data demonstrating barrier rescue in RPE cells, and the feasibility of its pharmacological modulation, AICAR represents a compelling candidate for further development in the treatment of dry AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MS-275, also known as Entinostat and available from Selleck (S7100), is a fully synthetic compound that belongs to the benzamide class of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi). Its chemical structure is defined as 3-pyridylmethyl-N-{4-[(2-aminophenyl)carbamoyl]-benzyl}carbamate, and it was originally developed by research teams including those at Mitsui Pharmaceuticals in the late 1990s (Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 2–3; Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34). Unlike hydroxamate-based HDAC inhibitors, the benzamide motif in MS-275 engages the catalytic zinc ion in a manner that is less potent in chelation yet confers a higher degree of class I selectivity, particularly toward HDAC1 and HDAC2 (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11). Benzamides have been extensively investigated for their epigenetic modulation properties in oncology, where selective inhibition of HDACs is pursued to reprogram aberrant gene expression profiles in cancer cells (Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Carafa et al., 2011, pp. 3–5). As a representative of its class, MS-275 has a well-defined synthetic origin and benefits from a non-natural product, medicinal chemistry–driven discovery process that emphasizes targeted inhibition of chromatin-modifying enzymes for therapeutic reactivation of silenced genes (Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34; Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, MS-275 has been developed and evaluated primarily in the context of oncology. It has advanced into multiple Phase I and II clinical trials, particularly for solid tumors such as breast cancer, hematologic malignancies like acute leukemia, and various other cancers where deregulated HDAC activity plays a role (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 9–11; Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 2–3). Preclinical studies have demonstrated its capacity to induce cell-cycle arrest, promote apoptosis, and trigger differentiation in tumor cell lines by restoring a balance in histone acetylation (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–9; Hanikoglu et al., 2018, pp. 2–3). Despite its extensive evaluation in cancer, there is no published evidence to date directly applying MS-275 to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or related ocular diseases. Nonetheless, the mechanistic rationale underlying its use in oncology—namely, reactivation of key transcriptional programs via enhanced histone acetylation—is similar to the epigenetic strategy proposed for rescuing retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier function (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 9–11; Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34). In this sense, repurposing MS-275 for dry AMD would constitute a novel application, relying on the molecule’s ability to reverse inflammation-induced transcriptional repression, analogous to its effects in cancer cells (Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Carafa et al., 2011, pp. 3–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
MS-275 functions by selectively inhibiting class I HDACs, particularly HDAC1 and HDAC2, through a zinc-binding mechanism that is distinct from that of hydroxamate inhibitors. The benzamide moiety in MS-275 interacts with the catalytic zinc ion within the active site of HDACs; however, due to its non-hydroxamate nature, the mode of coordination involves a bidentate interaction primarily via the amino group with additional, albeit weaker, engagement through the carbonyl oxygen (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11). This selective inhibition results in the accumulation of acetylated histones H3 and H4, thereby maintaining a relaxed chromatin state that is permissive for transcription. The proposed inflammatory stress in RPE cells—induced by tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)—is thought to lead to the recruitment of HDAC1/2 to promoters of tight junction genes such as TJP1, OCLN, and CLDN19, effectively silencing their expression through histone deacetylation (Hanikoglu et al., 2018, pp. 2–3; Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 8–10). By inhibiting HDAC1/2, MS-275 is expected to restore global histone acetylation levels, thereby reactivating transcription of these tight junction genes. The resulting upregulation and stabilization of proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin are hypothesized to reconstruct intercellular junctions and improve transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), which is a measure of barrier integrity (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–9; San José-Enériz et al., 2019, pp. 8–10). This mechanism is supported by extensive biochemical studies in cancer models, where similar epigenetic reprogramming has led to reactivation of silenced genes, although direct data in ocular models remains to be generated (Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34; Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 9–11).

The repurposing hypothesis for MS-275 in dry AMD is scientifically intriguing and grounded in a well-established mechanism of epigenetic modulation.
