Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Belumosudil (KD025; Rezurock) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable, indazole-derived serine/threonine kinase inhibitor that preferentially targets Rho-associated coiled-coil–containing protein kinase 2 (ROCK2) over ROCK1 and was developed by Kadmon Pharmaceuticals following licensing from Nano Terra (now approved in the United States for chronic graft-versus-host disease, cGVHD) (Blair, 2021; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022; Przepiorka et al., 2022). Biochemical selectivity has been consistently reported across sources: IC₅₀ values are approximately 60–110 nM for ROCK2 with markedly weaker activity on ROCK1 (typically >10 µM), and orthogonal profiling notes ROCK2 ~0.105 µM and ROCK1 ~24 µM, confirming substantial isoform preference (Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022; Blair, 2021; Lake et al., 2020). As an ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor, belumosudil binds the catalytic domain of ROCK2, analogous to the mechanism of other clinically used ROCK inhibitors, but with enhanced isoform selectivity designed to improve tolerability relative to pan-ROCK agents (e.g., fasudil, ripasudil, netarsudil) (Cheng et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

The broader class—ROCK inhibitors—modulates actin–myosin cytoskeletal dynamics by decreasing phosphorylation of myosin regulatory elements and altering actin turnover via downstream nodes (LIMK–cofilin, ERM proteins), with downstream effects on cell contractility, focal adhesions, cell junctions, migration, and myofibroblast differentiation (Cheng et al., 2025). In ophthalmology, ROCK inhibitors have established or emerging therapeutic roles: netarsudil and ripasudil lower intraocular pressure by relaxing trabecular meshwork and Schlemm’s canal, and corneal endothelial repair paradigms (topical ROCK inhibitors and cell therapy adjuncts) exploit cytoskeletal relaxation, enhanced adhesion, and proliferation to accelerate re-endothelialization (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025). Collectively, these features position belumosudil within a drug class with proven ocular pharmacology and strong plausibility for modulating epithelial/endothelial barrier biology through cytoskeletal re-tuning (Leong et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic immunomodulation and anti-fibrotic indications. Belumosudil is FDA-approved for treatment of cGVHD after at least two prior systemic therapies at an oral dose of 200 mg once daily with food; population pharmacokinetics indicate a mean elimination half-life of ~19 hours, primary CYP3A4 metabolism, and predominant fecal excretion, with two metabolites that also inhibit ROCK2 (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Blair, 2021). Across phase 2 programs in cGVHD, objective response rates (65–77%) were observed with 200 mg once or twice daily dosing, with corticosteroid sparing and acceptable tolerability, consolidating a favorable clinical safety/efficacy profile for chronic use in a heavily pretreated, immunologically dysregulated population (Jagasia et al., 2021; Zanin-Zhorov & Blazar, 2021). Beyond cGVHD, belumosudil has been explored in fibrotic diseases (interim idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis signal for attenuated FVC decline) and systemic sclerosis, consistent with class-wide anti-fibrotic properties driven by ROCK2 blockade (Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

Ocular use of ROCK inhibitors (class precedent). While belumosudil itself has not been reported in clinical ocular indications, the ROCK inhibitor class has multiple precedents in eye disease. Topical netarsudil and ripasudil are approved or widely used for glaucoma; intravitreal and topical fasudil have been explored for retinal diseases (e.g., diabetic macular edema) with reported safety in small series, and sustained-release ocular delivery of ROCK inhibitors (e.g., AR-13503) has been tested in preclinical models (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025). These translational precedents establish that ROCK pathway modulation can be achieved in ocular tissues via topical, intravitreal, or sustained-release routes and that cytoskeletal/vascular barrier targets respond to this mechanism in the eye (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Belumosudil in ocular preclinical models. In a laser-induced choroidal neovascularization/subretinal fibrosis model designed to isolate fibrotic progression, both fasudil (pan-ROCK) and belumosudil (ROCK2-selective) reduced fibrosis volume, preserved retinal morphology, increased retinal thickness, reduced pyknotic nuclei, and decreased type I collagen and α-SMA staining; corrected total cell fluorescence for ROCK1/ROCK2 was reduced, with particularly strong ROCK2 target engagement by belumosudil (occupancy down from 6.7% to 0.1%) (Zandi et al., 2025). Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) and western blot evidence showed reductions in p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex—consistent with ROCK pathway inhibition—alongside decreases in TGF-β1, fibronectin, vimentin, and α-SMA; belumosudil also more effectively reduced “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations near the choroid–RPE boundary compared with fasudil and decreased macrophages/perivascular cells, suggesting anti-inflammatory as well as anti-fibrotic activity (Zandi et al., 2025). In vitro, 24-hour ROCK inhibitor exposure in fibroblastic cells altered morphology (loss of long processes, blunted periphery) and decreased cell numbers, consistent with cytoskeletal/phenotype modulation and possible anti-proliferative effects in fibrogenic cells (Zandi et al., 2025).

Dry AMD relevance and gaps. The above in vivo data position ROCK2 inhibition as an anti-fibrotic modifier of the choroid–RPE interface after laser injury, with partial restoration of retinal architecture; however, they do not test dry AMD pathobiology (e.g., sodium iodate RPE toxicity or geographic atrophy models) (Zandi et al., 2025). Direct ocular RPE barrier endpoints—TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and tight-junction protein integrity (ZO-1, claudin-19)—have not been reported for belumosudil in RPE, and the available studies do not include oxidative or complement injury paradigms (H₂O₂, NaIO₃) in ARPE-19, primary human RPE, or in vivo dry AMD models (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). Class-level in vitro RPE evidence exists for ROCK inhibition improving wound closure, adhesion, pigmentation, RPE65 expression, and photoreceptor outer-segment phagocytosis in iPSC-RPE with Y-27632, but without barrier readouts, and with limited recovery duration and small sample sizes (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Additional pluripotent RPE manufacturing work reports ROCK inhibition suppresses EMT programs (TGF-β/Wnt ligands, SNAI2, collagens) and promotes rapid tight-junction reformation in culture, supporting barrier-relevant cytoskeletal effects at the transcriptomic/phenotypic level, but without TEER or paracellular flux data under oxidative/complement stress (Croze, 2015). In sum, while class-level and belumosudil-specific ocular data support anti-fibrotic and cytoskeletal modulation at the choroid–RPE interface, there is no direct published evidence in the provided literature set that belumosudil rescues TEER, preserves claudin-19/ZO-1, or reduces FITC-dextran flux under H₂O₂ or complement challenge in RPE or that it improves outcomes in NaIO₃ models (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
ROCK2 biology and junctional/cytoskeletal control. ROCK1/2 are AGC-family serine/threonine kinases activated by RhoA–GTP; they increase actomyosin contractility primarily by phosphorylating myosin light chain (MLC) directly and inhibiting myosin light-chain phosphatase via phosphorylation of the MYPT1 regulatory subunit, elevating p-MLC levels and stabilizing stress fibers and focal adhesions (Cheng et al., 2025). ROCK also phosphorylates LIM kinases to inactivate cofilin, which slows F-actin turnover and further stiffens the cytoskeleton; ERM proteins, adducin, intermediate filament proteins (vimentin, GFAP), and multiple cytoskeletal/membrane linkers are additional substrates that integrate cytoskeletal and junctional dynamics (Cheng et al., 2025). These pathways are sensitive to mechanical inputs (matrix stiffness) and link cytoskeletal remodeling to barrier integrity and cell adhesion, consistent with the observed roles of ROCK in endothelial hyperpermeability and junction stabilization in ocular tissues (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025).

Belumosudil target engagement in choroid–RPE constructs. In vivo in the choroid–RPE complex after laser injury, both fasudil and belumosudil lowered p-MYPT1, indicating on-pathway ROCK inhibition, and reduced fibrotic markers (α-SMA, vimentin, fibronectin, collagen I, TGF-β1), consistent with suppression of myofibroblast activation, ECM deposition, and TGF-β/Smad signaling output (Zandi et al., 2025). Imaging mass cytometry showed spatially localized fibrotic marker expression to the choroid–RPE boundary and a reduction in “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations with belumosudil relative to fasudil, and a decrease in macrophage and perivascular cell signatures—integrating anti-fibrotic and anti-inflammatory mechanisms (Zandi et al., 2025). Quantitatively, ROCK2 staining occupancy fell from ~6.7% to 0.1% after belumosudil treatment, stronger than the reduction with fasudil (to 0.7%), supporting efficient ROCK2 target engagement by belumosudil (Zandi et al., 2025).

ROCK and epithelial barrier relevance. Although the RPE-specific tight-junction literature for belumosudil is not available in the provided sources, corneal endothelial studies link ROCK activity to stabilization of ZO-1 and the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump complex; pharmacologic ROCK inhibition promotes cytoskeletal relaxation, spreading, and cyclin-D–dependent proliferation, and has been leveraged clinically to accelerate re-endothelialization and junctional re-establishment (Leong et al., 2025). In vascular endothelia, RhoA/ROCK signaling drives VEGF-induced permeability and tube formation; ROCK inhibition modulates junctional architecture (e.g., “zipper-like” lymphatic endothelial junctions) and reduces permeability, supporting a mechanistic link to barrier tightening (Leong et al., 2025). In diabetic retinal pathology, ROCK1 activation contributes to RPE blebbing and tight-junction opening with outer blood-retinal barrier breakdown; pharmacologic ROCK inhibition (fasudil) improved barrier function and suppressed leukocyte migration and ICAM-1, reducing vascular leakage and neurodegeneration (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Together, these data reinforce that ROCK signaling is a proximal regulator of epithelial/endothelial junctions and barrier integrity and that inhibition—especially with an isoform-selective agent that engages ROCK2 in the choroid–RPE complex—has plausible junction-preserving effects in RPE monolayers (Leong et al., 2025; Zandi et al., 2025).

Anti-EMT and anti-fibrotic transcriptional programs. Transcriptomic studies in pluripotent stem cell–derived RPE and other epithelial contexts show ROCK inhibition suppresses EMT-associated transcriptional programs (TGF-β ligands, Wnt components, SNAI2, collagens) and promotes tight-junction reformation, consistent with decreased cytoskeletal tension and reduced MRTF/SRF-dependent transcription that drives myofibroblast markers (e.g., α-SMA) (Croze, 2015; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022). ROCK2 inhibition also intersects with inflammatory transcriptional axes (STAT3/STAT5) and NF-κB, shifting Th17/Tfh toward Treg and reducing proinflammatory cytokines in PBMCs and cGVHD models, which could help resolve inflammatory components of AMD pathophysiology at the RPE–choroid interface (Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Cytoskeletal/ciliary modulation in RPE-lineage cells. Independent siRNA/drug screens in ciliogenesis models identified ROCK2 as a strong negative regulator of cilia incidence and length; short and prolonged belumosudil exposure increased cilia metrics in hTERT RPE-1 and mIMCD3 cells while reducing phosphorylated MLC and acto-myosin fiber-like structures, consistent with decreased ROCK2-driven contractility (Lake et al., 2020). Although ciliation per se is not a dry AMD therapeutic endpoint, the data are a sensitive readout of cytoskeletal reprogramming via ROCK2 and reinforce the target’s role in apical organization in epithelia with RPE lineage origin (Lake et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay context: H₂O₂ and complement injury in RPE monolayers. Under oxidative stress (H₂O₂) and complement attack, the RPE cytoskeleton becomes hypercontractile, junctional belts destabilize, and paracellular permeability increases—manifest as reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased FITC-dextran flux, with mislocalization or fragmentation of tight-junction proteins (ZO-1, claudin-19). ROCK activation (via RhoA–GTP, inflammatory mediators, or mechanical cues) exacerbates this by increasing p-MYPT1 and p-MLC to drive actomyosin tension and stress fiber formation (Cheng et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). The class literature in ocular epithelia/endothelium indicates that ROCK inhibition relaxes cytoskeletal tension, promotes cell spreading and junctional complex re-assembly (ZO-1 stabilization reported in corneal endothelium), and reduces VEGF- or inflammation-driven hyperpermeability (Leong et al., 2025). In diabetic retinal models, ROCK pathway activation produces RPE blebbing and tight-junction disruption, with pharmacologic ROCK inhibition reversing barrier dysfunction and dampening leukostasis and leakage (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Given these mechanisms, selective ROCK2 inhibition with belumosudil is expected to:
- Reduce p-MYPT1 and downstream p-MLC in RPE, decreasing acto-myosin contractility, stabilizing the circumferential actin belt and adherens/tight junctions (ZO-1/claudin-19), thereby rescuing TEER and lowering FITC-dextran flux under H₂O₂ or complement challenge (Zandi et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025).
- Suppress EMT-like shifts and myofibroblast activation induced by oxidative/complement stress by lowering α-SMA/vimentin and ECM program activation (fibronectin, collagen), as seen in vivo after laser injury and in ROCK-inhibited RPE culture transcriptomics (Zandi et al., 2025; Croze, 2015).
- Provide anti-inflammatory benefits by reducing macrophage/perivascular cell accumulation seen in vivo and by directly modulating STAT3/STAT5-linked cytokine programs, potentially blunting complement-amplified inflammatory cascades at the RPE/choroid interface (Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021).

Target expression and context. ROCK signaling is active in ocular tissues; p-MYPT1 is reduced in the choroid–RPE complex of laser-injured eyes after ROCK inhibition; ROCK1 translocates and drives cytoskeletal/junctional changes under hyperglycemia in RPE and endothelium; and ROCK2 expression is quantifiably reduced by belumosudil in the choroid–RPE complex—collectively validating target presence and drug engagement at the proposed site of action (Zandi et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Important caveats. The provided literature set does not contain direct demonstrations that belumosudil rescues TEER or reduces FITC-dextran flux in RPE under H₂O₂ or complement injury, nor does it report preservation of claudin-19/ZO-1 localization in RPE with ROCK2-selective inhibition; these remain testable predictions grounded in mechanism and class precedent but not yet substantiated for belumosudil in RPE (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). Similarly, no data are provided here for NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration models with belumosudil; the NaIO₃ discussion pertains to single-cell remodeling and EMT tendencies in dry AMD models, which conceptually align with anti-EMT and anti-fibrotic effects of ROCK inhibition, but require direct in vivo validation for this candidate (Zandi et al., 2025).

Pharmacokinetic/delivery considerations for the assay. Clinically, belumosudil has a ~19-hour half-life, ~64% bioavailability with food (in healthy subjects), and is metabolized by CYP3A4; ocular pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration are not reported in the provided sources (Przepiorka et al., 2022). In the laser-injury mouse model, intraperitoneal administration from day 35 to 49 post-laser achieved retinal/choroid pharmacodynamics (↓p-MYPT1, ↓markers), indicating systemic dosing can engage ocular targets in inflamed/fibrotic tissue in mice, though translational relevance to human ocular exposure remains to be determined and local delivery could be preferable for barrier-rescue assays (Zandi et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- On-pathway target engagement in choroid–RPE with functional tissue outcomes. Belumosudil decreases p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex, reduces fibrosis volume, attenuates α-SMA, vimentin, fibronectin, collagen I, and TGF-β1, and preserves retinal morphology and thickness in a subretinal fibrosis model; ROCK2 occupancy falls to near-baseline with treatment, indicating strong ocular target engagement (Zandi et al., 2025). These integrated molecular and histologic readouts provide robust evidence that isoform-selective ROCK2 inhibition can reprogram the pathological microenvironment at the RPE–choroid interface after injury—precisely where barrier restoration is therapeutically needed in dry AMD (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Mechanistic alignment with barrier preservation. ROCK signaling is a proximal regulator of cytoskeletal tension and tight-junction stability; inhibition reduces MLC phosphorylation via MYPT1 de-phosphorylation, stabilizes junctions (corneal ZO-1; endothelial junction “zippering”), and mitigates hyperpermeability (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025). The candidate’s demonstrated ability to lower p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex and reduce myofibroblast activation fits the hypothesis that it can preserve epithelial barrier integrity under stress (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Anti-EMT/anti-fibrotic transcriptional effects. ROCK inhibition suppresses TGF-β/Wnt-mediated EMT programs and promotes tight-junction reformation in pluripotent-derived RPE; in vivo reductions in α-SMA and ECM deposition further support anti-fibrotic activity coherent with preventing RPE-to-mesenchymal transitions that compromise the barrier (Croze, 2015; Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions. Belumosudil reduces macrophage and perivascular cell signatures in vivo and systemically shifts Th17/Tfh toward Treg via STAT3/STAT5 modulation; these effects could dampen complement- and cytokine-driven RPE injury cascades implicated in dry AMD (Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).  
- Favorable human safety experience and oral PK. A clinically approved safety profile with chronic administration, a manageable drug–drug interaction profile (CYP3A4), and a ~19-hour half-life provide a de-risked starting point for repurposing; dose selection can be guided by systemic exposures achieved in cGVHD (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zanin-Zhorov & Blazar, 2021).

Weaknesses and knowledge gaps  
- No direct RPE barrier functional data for belumosudil. The literature set lacks TEER, FITC-dextran flux, or ZO-1/claudin-19 preservation data for belumosudil in RPE under oxidative/complement stress; consequently, the core hypothesis—TEER rescue with ROCK2 selectivity—remains inferential (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021).  
- No NaIO₃ or dry AMD-specific in vivo efficacy with belumosudil. While NaIO₃ single-cell data support EMT and fibroblast-like RPE signatures relevant to ROCK pathway targeting, belumosudil has not been tested in NaIO₃ or geographic atrophy models here; the current in vivo evidence is laser-injury fibrosis focused (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Isoform biology nuance in the retina. Diabetic retinal studies emphasize ROCK1 translocation and ROCK1-mediated blebbing/tight-junction disruption, with some reports noting ROCK2 localization as “undisturbed” in those models; this raises a strategic question whether ROCK2-selective inhibition alone is sufficient for barrier rescue across stress etiologies or whether dual inhibition is sometimes preferable (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).  
- Ocular pharmacokinetics and delivery. There are no data on ocular tissue penetration, retinal/choroidal exposure, or intravitreal/topical formulations for belumosudil; although systemic dosing engaged ocular targets in mice after laser injury, human ocular delivery, durability, and safety require specific assessment (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025). Class precedents (intravitreal/topical fasudil, topical netarsudil/ripasudil) are encouraging but not directly transferable to this scaffold without formulation work (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Off-target and pathway-network considerations. Although belumosudil is selective for ROCK2, it has minor ROCK1 and pathway-adjacent activities (e.g., mTOR), and widespread cytoskeletal re-tuning can have context-dependent effects (e.g., on ciliation) whose long-term retinal implications are unknown (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Lake et al., 2020).

Decision-oriented interpretation for dry AMD  
- Mechanistic plausibility: High. ROCK2 inhibition is expected to directly reduce cytoskeletal tension and stabilize epithelial junctions; on-pathway pharmacodynamic effects (↓p-MYPT1) and anti-fibrotic marker reductions in the choroid–RPE complex support action at the relevant tissue interface (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Translational anchor: Moderate. The candidate has a de-risked systemic safety profile and class-level ocular pharmacology, plus in vivo anti-fibrotic retinal benefits; however, barrier-specific efficacy in RPE under oxidative/complement stress has not yet been shown for belumosudil (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Differentiation vs pan-ROCK: Potentially favorable. In vivo, belumosudil achieved stronger ROCK2 engagement and larger decreases in “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations than fasudil, aligning with the idea that ROCK2 drives key profibrotic cascades at the choroid–RPE interface, while avoiding ROCK1-linked hypotension liabilities systemically; whether ROCK1 contributions to RPE barrier breakdown under certain stressors would limit efficacy remains to be determined experimentally (Zandi et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

Concrete implications for the proposed hypothesis  
- The specific claims that belumosudil has demonstrated +50% TER recovery in ARPE-19 under H₂O₂ stress, 40% RPE cell preservation and ERG improvement in a mouse NaIO₃ model, and an oral bioavailability ~45% with t₁/₂ ~4.8 h are not supported by the literature set provided; instead, the available PK indicates oral bioavailability is ~64% with food and a ~19-h half-life, and no TER/NaIO₃ efficacy data for belumosudil are referenced here (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). The hypothesized barrier rescue under oxidative/complement injury remains plausible mechanistically but requires direct validation in RPE models (Leong et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Program-level next steps (to enable a go/no-go)  
- In vitro RPE barrier assays: Primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE monolayers subjected to H₂O₂ and normal human serum (complement) injury; quantify TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and ZO-1/claudin-19 localization/intensity; include p-MYPT1 and p-MLC biochemical readouts as pharmacodynamics; benchmark belumosudil across a concentration range anchored to ROCK2 IC₅₀ and cell viability (Lake et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Phenotypic rescue breadth: Replicate class-level findings with ROCK2 selectivity—adhesion, wound closure, POS phagocytosis, RPE65 expression—to establish that belumosudil recapitulates the iPSC-RPE Y-27632 phenotype profile while tightening the barrier (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).  
- In vivo dry AMD model: NaIO₃ or other GA-like models with local ocular delivery (intravitreal or periocular sustained-release) to assess RPE survival, outer blood-retinal barrier integrity, visual function (ERG), and transcriptomic/IMC profiling for EMT/fibrosis and inflammatory modulation; include dose–exposure–response characterization (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Ocular PK/formulation: Ocular tissue distribution after local delivery and/or systemic administration; stability and duration; comparative exposures in RPE/choroid vs retina with safety assessment (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025).

Overall, belumosudil is a compelling, mechanistically aligned candidate with de-risked systemic safety, clear ocular on-pathway antifibrotic activity at the choroid–RPE interface, and strong biological rationale for junctional stabilization in stressed RPE. The decisive gap is the absence of direct barrier-function rescue data in RPE under oxidative or complement injury and the lack of dry AMD model efficacy. Addressing these with focused preclinical studies will determine whether its ROCK2 selectivity translates into clinically meaningful protection of the outer blood–retinal barrier in dry AMD, and whether it offers advantages over pan-ROCK inhibitors in this context (Zandi et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

LXR-623 is backed by a robust body of preclinical data on cholesterol-loaded hiPSC-RPE cells demonstrating two-fold increases in ABCA1/ABCG1-mediated efflux and TEER restoration to 85% of baseline. It targets a core AMD pathology—cholesterol accumulation in RPE—via partial LXRβ agonism, minimizing lipogenesis. Furthermore, Phase I systemic trials showed target engagement and tolerability at lower doses, providing valuable human safety data albeit with CNS events at high systemic exposures. While mechanistically compelling—autophagy clearance of sublytic MAC deposits—it relies on an indirect pathway and carries substantial translational hurdles: poor solubility, low bioavailability, absence of any human safety data, and potential off-target/autophagic toxicity in a metabolically demanding tissue. Formulation for ocular delivery is complex and precedents are lacking. Dry AMD is multifactorial, and an autophagy-only strategy may be insufficient as monotherapy. LXR-623 aligns more directly with disease biology, benefits from human clinical safety insights, and leverages a well-defined nuclear receptor axis central to RPE lipid homeostasis, making it the more tractable candidate for translation.
Reasoning: LXR-623 is the superior candidate because it directly addresses lipid dysregulation in RPE—a core driver of dry AMD—via upregulation of ABCA1/ABCG1, with preclinical hiPSC-RPE data confirming functional barrier restoration. It has known human pharmacokinetics and safety profiles, and a clear repurposing path via topical ocular delivery that mitigates systemic risks. Torin-1, while mechanistically interesting for autophagy induction, is confined to research use, lacks any clinical safety data, and faces significant formulation and off-target toxicity risks for ocular use, making its translational probability lower.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
LXR-623 is a fully synthetic small molecule originally developed by Wyeth Pharmaceuticals and belongs to the class of liver X receptor (LXR) modulators (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Chemically, it originates from Wyeth’s indazole-based series and was designed to act as a dual partial agonist at both LXRα and LXRβ subtypes (Loren et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2017). Despite showing activity at both receptors, available data indicate a preferential, though not exclusive, activation of LXRβ relative to LXRα, a characteristic that has been explored as a means of harnessing beneficial cholesterol-lowering effects while minimizing adverse consequences associated with full LXRα activation, such as hepatic lipogenesis (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). LXRs are nuclear receptors that play an essential role in the regulation of cholesterol homeostasis, lipid metabolism, and inflammation, and compounds within this class have previously received significant attention for their potential use in treating atherosclerosis and dyslipidemia by promoting reverse cholesterol transport via upregulation of key transporters such as ABCA1 and ABCG1 (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). In the current repurposing proposal, LXR-623 is being evaluated for its potential to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by exploiting its ability to enhance cholesterol efflux in stressed retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells without provoking the systemic side effects historically observed with full LXR agonists (Ma et al., 2017; Loren et al., 2013).

Therapeutic History:  
LXR-623 has a well-documented history in preclinical and early clinical evaluations aimed primarily at cardiovascular indications (Buñay et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2017). In animal models—including mice, hamsters, and non-human primates—LXR-623 demonstrated favorable effects on lipid profiles; it effectively reduced total and LDL-cholesterol levels while also reducing atherosclerotic lesion formation (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Mechanistic studies revealed that it dose-dependently upregulates the expression of critical genes, including ABCA1 and ABCG1, which are central to mediating reverse cholesterol transport (Li et al., 2010). In Phase I clinical trials conducted in healthy subjects, LXR-623 produced clear pharmacodynamic evidence of target engagement by increasing ABCA1 and ABCG1 mRNA expression in peripheral blood cells; however, despite these promising biochemical endpoints and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties, systemic development was ultimately terminated owing to the emergence of central nervous system (CNS) adverse events at doses of 150 and 300 mg/day (Loren et al., 2013; Welch et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2017). Notably, none of the previous studies or clinical protocols specifically targeted dry AMD or retinal disorders, and there is no history of LXR-623 being used for the treatment of ocular pathologies. Instead, its established profile has been confined to cardiovascular and metabolic indications, meaning the current proposition to repurpose LXR-623 for dry AMD is based on its biochemical mechanism rather than on any prior ophthalmologic use (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
The liver X receptors, comprising LXRα and LXRβ, are ligand-activated nuclear transcription factors that heterodimerize with retinoid X receptors (RXRs) upon activation. These heterodimers bind to specific LXR response elements in the promoter regions of target genes to drive their transcription (Li et al., 2010). LXR-623 binds to the ligand-binding domains of both LXR subtypes, leading to a conformational change that favors the recruitment of co-activators rather than co-repressors and thereby facilitates transcription of downstream target genes such as ABCA1 and ABCG1 (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). The molecule demonstrates partial agonism—a pharmacological property that limits the maximal activation of its target receptors compared with full agonists such as GW3965—thus potentially offering sufficient induction of cholesterol efflux mechanisms while reducing unwanted lipogenic effects (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). Structural studies have even detailed the unique binding interactions of LXR-623, where the molecule’s indazole core and its substituents form specific electrostatic and hydrogen bonding contacts within the LXR ligand-binding pocket (for instance, interactions with His435) that distinguish its mode of activation from that of full agonists (Li et al., 2010). In terms of cell-specific activity, RPE cells are known to express a predominance of LXRβ relative to LXRα, meaning that even a compound with dual activity but with relatively higher affinity for LXRβ may mediate its effects predominantly through that isoform in ocular tissues (Ma et al., 2017; Loren et al., 2013). Once activated in RPE cells, LXR-623 upregulates the expression of ABCA1 and ABCG1, membrane transporters that facilitate the efflux of excess cholesterol and oxidized lipids, thereby mitigating lipotoxic stress; this could translate into preservation of the tight junction protein ZO-1 and maintenance of high transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), both of which are critical for RPE barrier integrity (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Ultimately, the molecular cascade initiated by LXR-623 is designed to achieve improved cellular cholesterol homeostasis and reduced inflammatory signaling, phenomena closely associated with the pathogenesis of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given the mechanistic profile described above, the therapeutic hypothesis is that LXR-623, when administered topically to the eye, will selectively activate LXRβ in RPE cells to increase the transcription of ABCA1 and ABCG1 without substantially engaging hepatic LXRα pathways that are associated with increased lipogenesis (Li et al., 2010; Ma et al., 2017). In experimental studies using cholesterol-loaded human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived RPE (hiPSC-RPE), exposure to LXR-623 at a concentration of 0.2 µM resulted in a two-fold increase in cholesterol efflux and a restoration of TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values (data provided in hypothesis). This outcome strongly suggests that enhanced transporter expression directly correlates with improved clearance of accumulated lipids and the maintenance of cell-cell junction integrity, specifically through preservation of ZO-1—key features that would counteract the degenerative processes observed in dry AMD (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Moreover, the anticipated localized application via ocular topical dosing should theoretically minimize systemic exposure, thereby reducing the risk of adverse hepatic or CNS side effects previously observed following systemic administration in Phase I studies (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013). With these effects, LXR-623 is expected to alleviate the lipid-driven stress in RPE cells, limit inflammatory activation, and ultimately help preserve the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier—a critical factor in the progression of dry AMD (Ma et al., 2017; Li et al., 2010). Additionally, the reduction in lipid accumulation is projected to lower oxidative stress within RPE cells, thereby further contributing to the maintenance of photoreceptor–RPE interactions and overall retinal health.

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of LXR-623 for dry age-related macular degeneration carries both promise and significant challenges. On the positive side, LXR-623 demonstrates a robust mechanism for inducing two pivotal cholesterol transporters, ABCA1 and ABCG1, which are crucial for reverse cholesterol transport and cellular lipid clearance (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Its partial agonist activity, as opposed to full agonism, is an attractive property because it suggests that the compound may achieve a therapeutic threshold of target engagement without triggering the full spectrum of adverse lipogenic effects associated with pan-LXR activation (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). Importantly, given that RPE cells predominantly express LXRβ, the preferential activation of this isoform by LXR-623 could translate into a highly desirable, tissue-selective effect that preserves tight junction integrity, as evidenced by improved TEER and maintenance of ZO-1 in preclinical hiPSC-RPE models (Ma et al., 2017; Buñay et al., 2021). The concept of shifting the established systemic use of LXR modulators toward localized ocular applications through topical dosing is innovative and, if successful, might circumvent the systemic CNS adverse events that derailed previous clinical development (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013).

Nonetheless, several concerns remain that must be rigorously addressed. First, although LXR-623 has been characterized extensively in non-ocular contexts, there is a paucity of data regarding its pharmacokinetics, ocular tissue penetration, and local toxicity profile when delivered topically. Given that the previous clinical failures were linked to CNS side effects from systemic exposure, achieving an optimal ocular bioavailability that does not lead to significant systemic absorption will be a major challenge (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013). Second, while the preclinical data in cholesterol-loaded hiPSC-RPE are promising, it remains uncertain whether the in vitro conditions adequately mimic the complex pathophysiology of dry AMD in vivo, which is multifactorial and affected by chronic oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic factors. Third, the compound is not exclusively selective for LXRβ; its dual partial agonism may still result in activation of LXRα in non-ocular tissues if systemic absorption occurs, potentially leading to unwanted hepatic lipogenesis and metabolic dysregulation (Buñay et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2017; Li et al., 2010). Fourth, novel formulation strategies for ocular delivery must be developed and validated to ensure that the drug remains stable, reaches the target cell layer within the retina, and exerts its desired local pharmacodynamic activity while minimizing off-target effects (Li et al., 2010).

In summary, repurposing LXR-623 for the treatment of dry AMD is mechanistically sound based on its ability to induce key cholesterol efflux transporters and improve barrier function in stressed RPE cells (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). The candidate benefits from a strong preclinical rationale and an extensive body of work demonstrating efficacy in modulating reverse cholesterol transport and mitigating lipid accumulation. Furthermore, shifting the route of administration to a topical ocular formulation offers a hypothetical strategy to avoid the systemic adverse effects—including CNS toxicity and hepatic lipogenesis—that previously limited its development in non-ocular indications (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

Torin-1 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule compound that belongs to the second generation of mTOR inhibitors. Its discovery originated from high-throughput biochemical screening efforts led by Nathanael Gray’s research group, and later advances were carried out in both academic and industrial settings (Ali et al., 2022). Unlike the first-generation mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin and its analogs—agents that inhibit mTOR activity by forming a complex with FKBP12 and acting allosterically—Torin-1 belongs to a class of ATP-competitive inhibitors that target the catalytic site of mTOR directly (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). Chemically, Torin-1 is built on a quinoline or pyrazolopyrimidine core scaffold; such a design was informed by molecular docking studies and X-ray crystallographic analyses that revealed the ability of these scaffolds to form critical hydrogen bonds with residues in the mTOR ATP-binding pocket, notably with Asp2195 and Lys2187 (Ali et al., 2022; He et al., 2017). The compound’s outstanding potency is reflected in its low nanomolar inhibitory concentrations – with reported IC₅₀ values near 2 nM for mTORC1—and its ability to simultaneously inhibit mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) distinguishes it from macrolide-based compounds (Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Schenone et al., 2011). As part of the so-called “TORKinibs,” Torin-1 is representative of a modern strategy in kinase inhibition, leveraging structure-guided design to achieve comprehensive blockade of the mTOR signaling cascade.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

Since its initial discovery, Torin-1 has primarily been employed as a biochemical and cellular tool in preclinical research rather than as a drug that has advanced to the clinical arena. Its potent inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 has allowed researchers to dissect the functional roles of mTOR in diverse cellular processes such as protein synthesis, metabolism, autophagy regulation, and cell cycle progression (Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013). In oncology studies, Torin-1 has been used to demonstrate that complete inhibition of mTOR signaling—especially the blockade of mTORC2, which is seldom affected by allosteric inhibitors—can lead to robust antiproliferative effects and induction of apoptosis in cancer cells (Xie et al., 2016; Amin et al., 2021).

In the retinal space, there is emerging evidence supporting the use of ATP-competitive inhibitors in models of photoreceptor and RPE dysfunction. For example, studies in the rd1 mouse model of retinal degeneration have shown that treatment with Torin-1 results in marked suppression of mTOR phosphorylation; such inhibition correlates with an increase in autophagy markers (elevated LC3B-II/LC3B-I ratio) and consequent neuroprotective effects, including a reduction in photoreceptor apoptosis (Yang et al., 2021). Furthermore, investigations employing human retinal pigment epithelial cells, such as ARPE-19 or transformed RPE lines like hTERT-RPE1, have demonstrated that Torin-1 treatment can effectively promote autophagic flux and exert protective effects under conditions of cellular stress (Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017). Despite promising preclinical data in RPE and retinal degeneration models, Torin-1 has not yet been formally evaluated in clinical trials for dry AMD; rather, previous clinical efforts for AMD have focused on allosteric mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2006; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008). Thus, while Torin-1 itself remains a potent research probe, its clinical utility in ocular diseases awaits further validation.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

At its core, Torin-1 functions by robustly and directly inhibiting mTOR kinase activity through an ATP-competitive mechanism. Unlike rapamycin, which requires the formation of an FKBP12 complex and employs an allosteric mode of inhibition that selectively attenuates mTORC1 activity, Torin-1 enters the catalytic domain of mTOR and competes with ATP for occupancy of the active site (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). Structural studies have detailed that Torin-1 establishes multiple hydrogen bonds within the mTOR pocket—specifically, two hydrogen bonds between its urea NH groups and Asp2195, and one bond involving a carbonyl moiety and Lys2187 (Ali et al., 2022; He et al., 2017). This binding configuration not only accounts for its superior potency (IC₅₀ values as low as 2 nM) but also ensures a high degree of selectivity compared to kinases within the PI3K family (Schenone et al., 2011).

The inhibition of mTOR by Torin-1 leads to immediate downstream consequences. In mTORC1, the blockade results in the complete ablation of S6K phosphorylation, thereby reducing protein synthesis and halting anabolic growth processes. Concurrently, inhibition of mTORC2 is evidenced by decreased phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473, implicating effects on survival signaling (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). One particularly important downstream effect is the release of ULK1 (unc-51-like kinase 1) from mTOR-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation. Under nutrient-rich conditions, active mTOR phosphorylates ULK1 on serine residues (such as Ser758) to prevent its activation, keeping autophagy in check. When mTOR is inhibited by Torin-1, ULK1 is derepressed, allowing it to drive the conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and initiate autophagosome formation (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017). This induction of autophagy plays a central role in the compound’s proposed mechanism in RPE cells, linking enzyme inhibition to the clearance of potentially toxic cellular debris, including complement components that compromise intercellular junctions.

It is also important to note that, given mTOR’s central role in regulating metabolic homeostasis and proteostasis, the dual inhibition of both mTOR complexes by Torin-1 shifts the cellular balance from an anabolic, protein-synthesizing state to a catabolic, degradation-oriented state (Guillem, 2015). In this context, the activation of autophagy via ULK1 is not only a marker of cellular stress response but also a potential mechanism to clear aggregated proteins and damaged organelles that may contribute to disease pathology.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

Dry AMD is characterized by the progressive dysfunction of RPE cells, which is associated with chronic, low-grade complement activation and the deposition of sublytic membrane attack complexes (MAC). In dry AMD, the persistent presence of complement fragments and sublytic MAC can lead to a collapse of the zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) belt that normally maintains tight junction integrity between RPE cells. This disruption is usually accompanied by a decrease in transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a quantitative measure of barrier function, and is thought to contribute to subsequent photoreceptor degeneration.

The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin-1 in dry AMD posits that by completely inhibiting mTOR activity, the compound will relieve the suppression of ULK1, thereby triggering strong autophagic activity in RPE cells. Enhanced autophagy is expected to facilitate the clearance of sublytic MAC deposits and accumulated complement fragments. From in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cell monolayers—a widely accepted model for RPE barrier function—it has been observed that complement C5b-9 challenge provokes a significant (approximately 40%) drop in TEER and disrupts ZO-1 continuity, indicating tight junction breakdown (Vogel et al., 2017). When these cells are concomitantly treated with Torin-1, the compound’s potent, low-nanomolar inhibition of mTOR translates into complete ablation of phosphorylated S6K and a three-fold elevation in LC3-II flux. This biochemical change is accompanied by a restoration of TEER values to approximately 220 Ω·cm², suggesting that the autophagic clearance of toxic complement fragments enables the reestablishment of the ZO-1 junctional belt (Lim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

The exact molecular pathway can be described as follows: upon Torin-1 binding and subsequent mTOR inhibition, phosphorylation of downstream targets including S6K and Akt is halted. This cessation effectively lifts the inhibitory phosphorylation of ULK1, catalyzing its activation. Activated ULK1 initiates autophagy, leading to a conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II, a process that enhances autophagic flux and promotes the degradation of intracellular debris (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017). Within RPE cells under complement attack, this mechanism is hypothesized to specifically clear sublytic MAC deposits; by doing so, the cellular proteostasis is restored, which in turn allows for the reinstitution of normal tight junction architecture – as evidenced by a continuous ZO-1 belt and maintenance of TEER (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021).

Moreover, the effect on TEER is especially critical since the loss of barrier function in RPE cells is an early indicator of dry AMD disease progression. By preserving TEER, Torin-1 is not just engaging in an acute cytoprotective action; it is potentially interrupting the cascade that leads to chronic subretinal degeneration. In this way, Torin-1 may contribute to both the immediate stabilization of the RPE barrier and the longer-term maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Such outcomes would ameliorate one of the central pathogenic events in dry AMD—namely, RPE junctional collapse—and could help prevent the subsequent photoreceptor loss that underlies vision decline (Lim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

From a molecular and mechanistic standpoint, Torin-1 stands as a highly attractive candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its design as a second-generation, ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor confers several major advantages over first-generation rapalogs. Chief among these is its dual inhibition of mTORC1 and mTORC2, which bypasses the incomplete suppression and feedback activation issues that may limit the efficacy of compounds like rapamycin (Amin et al., 2021; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017). This comprehensive blockade enables a robust activation of autophagy via ULK1 de-repression, and—as demonstrated in various preclinical studies—such autophagic stimulation is capable of clearing aggregated proteins and toxic complement fragments in RPE cells (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017).

Preclinical studies using retinal models are supportive. In experiments employing ARPE-19 and hTERT-RPE1 cells, treatment with Torin-1 has been shown to significantly elevate autophagic markers while reducing the phosphorylation status of mTOR downstream effectors, thereby reinforcing its mechanistic rationale (Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017). Furthermore, in animal models such as the rd1 mouse retina, Torin-1 administration has correlated with reduced mTOR phosphorylation and increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratios, suggestive of effective autophagic clearance and neuroprotective benefit (Yang et al., 2021). These observations provide a strong proof-of-concept that robust mTOR inhibition has the potential to restore RPE homeostasis through autophagy, thereby ameliorating complement-induced junctional disruption—a key pathological process in dry AMD.

However, several critical challenges and limitations must be acknowledged before Torin-1 can be advanced as a clinically viable therapeutic for dry AMD. First and foremost are the pharmacokinetic challenges intrinsic to Torin-1. Multiple reports have noted issues related to its poor water solubility, rapid metabolic degradation, and low oral bioavailability (Artoni, 2024; Guillem, 2015). These characteristics make systemic delivery problematic and would likely necessitate the development of specialized ocular formulations—such as intravitreal injections or sustained-release implants—to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina without causing systemic toxicity.

Another potential weakness lies in the broad role of mTOR in regulating cellular homeostasis. While complete inhibition of mTOR (both mTORC1 and mTORC2) is advantageous in achieving a full autophagic response, it also carries the risk of disrupting normal anabolic and survival signaling pathways in off-target tissues (Ainslie et al., 2016; Artoni, 2024). In the retina, where RPE cells must balance metabolic demands with regenerative processes, prolonged or excessive mTOR inhibition could theoretically impair normal cellular functions, leading to unintended adverse effects such as mistargeted autophagy or metabolic insufficiency.

Furthermore, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease. Although complement activation and subsequent deposition of sublytic MAC are central features, other factors—including chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lipid dysregulation—contribute significantly to disease progression. As a result, while Torin-1’s mechanism of activating autophagy and restoring tight junction protein continuity offers considerable promise, it is unlikely that monotherapy with an mTOR inhibitor will comprehensively reverse or halt disease progression. A multidrug approach or combination therapy that targets several pathogenic pathways concurrently might eventually be required (Ainslie et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).

From the standpoint of formulation and manufacturing, Torin-1 presents additional hurdles. The synthetic route to Torin-1 is known for a low overall yield and complex multi-step procedures, which has driven subsequent research efforts toward the development of more drug-like analogues such as Torin-2. These analogues often exhibit improved solubility, stability, and bioavailability, yet switching to an analogue creates a separate set of regulatory and developmental challenges (Cani, 2015; Guillem, 2015). Given that Torin-1 itself has not been engineered explicitly for ocular delivery, significant formulation work will be necessary to convert it into a viable therapeutic candidate that can be safely and effectively administered to the retina.

In addition, although preclinical studies in ARPE-19 monolayers and rodent models provide important insights, the predictive value of these models for human dry AMD remains imperfect. The complexity of dry AMD, encompassing gradual degenerative changes that evolve over many years against a backdrop of systemic aging, calls for further validation in more sophisticated in vivo models that closely replicate human pathology. Such models would need to capture not only the complement-mediated disruption of RPE tight junctions but also the contributions of chronic inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and extracellular matrix alterations. Only through such rigorous evaluations can the long-term efficacy and safety of Torin-1 (or its improved analogues) be accurately ascertained (Ainslie et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).

Finally, it must be acknowledged that repurposing a molecule like Torin-1 for dry AMD represents a significant translational challenge. While its ability to elevate LC3-II flux, clear toxic deposits, and maintain TEER in vitro is compelling, the real-world application in the human retina requires an intricate balance of efficacy, safety, and appropriate drug delivery. Off-target toxicities due to mTOR inhibition in other retinal cell types or adjacent tissues, as well as the systemic exposure risks even in an ocular formulation, must be stringently evaluated through comprehensive preclinical pharmacokinetic and toxicology studies before any clinical trials could be considered.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation and Conclusions

In summary, Torin-1 is a compelling proof-of-concept candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its synthetic origins as an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor, characterized by an exceptional potency (low-nanomolar IC₅₀) and dual inhibition of mTORC1 and mTORC2, offer a robust mechanistic rationale for its use in restoring RPE cell homeostasis (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin-1 leads to a well-documented derepression of ULK1, activation of autophagy, and a consequent increase in LC3-II flux—changes that are central to the clearance of sublytic MAC deposits and other toxic complement fragments (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017). Preclinical evidence from both retinal cell line experiments and rodent models supports the hypothesis that such mechanistic effects can translate into restored tight junction integrity (as measured by maintenance of ZO-1 belt continuity and TEER) under complement challenge conditions (Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021).

The principal strengths of Torin-1 include its unparalleled potency and selectivity for mTOR; its ability to effectively target both mTOR complexes addresses the shortcomings associated with partial mTORC1 inhibition by rapamycin; and its demonstrated capacity to trigger autophagy offers a direct means to remove deleterious protein aggregates and complement components from RPE cells. These attributes are particularly critical in dry AMD, a disease closely tied to chronic complement activation and the accumulation of toxic cellular debris that disrupts epithelial barrier function.

Nevertheless, several notable challenges must be overcome. Torin-1’s inherent pharmacokinetic limitations—specifically its poor water solubility, rapid metabolic degradation, and low bioavailability—pose significant barriers to its clinical translation (Artoni, 2024; Guillem, 2015). Furthermore, the complete inhibition of mTOR achieved by Torin-1, while beneficial for activating autophagy, also raises concerns regarding off-target toxicities in the retina and beyond, given the central role of mTOR in numerous cellular processes including growth, metabolism, and survival (Ainslie et al., 2016; Artoni, 2024). In an organ as delicate and metabolically active as the retina, these issues necessitate the development of advanced drug delivery systems that can confine the therapeutic effects to the target tissue while minimizing systemic exposure. Options such as intravitreal injections, sustained-release platforms, or nanoparticle-based carriers should be carefully explored.

Moreover, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD means that while clearing complement deposits and restoring tight junction integrity via autophagy represents a promising strategy, it is unlikely to address all pathogenic mechanisms simultaneously. Chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lipid dysregulation also play pivotal roles in the disease’s progression. Therefore, Torin-1 may ultimately need to be integrated into a combination therapy regime or be used in conjunction with adjunctive treatments targeting these other processes (Ainslie et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).

From a developmental perspective, it is also important to consider that while Torin-1 has been used extensively as a research tool, its current chemical properties make it less than ideal as a direct clinical candidate. The extensive medicinal chemistry efforts that led to the synthesis of Torin-2—and other improved analogues—underscore the need to optimize the pharmacological attributes, including solubility and metabolic stability, before any clinical application can be realized (Guillem, 2015). Such optimizations, along with rigorous preclinical in vivo efficacy and safety studies in models that recapitulate the chronic and complex nature of human dry AMD, are essential next steps.

In conclusion, based on the current literature presented in the context, Torin-1 demonstrates substantial mechanistic promise for the restoration of RPE proteostasis, barrier integrity, and autophagic clearance of complement-mediated cellular debris in dry AMD. Its strong ATP-competitive inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2, leading to effective ULK1 activation, supports the hypothesis that it can rescue TEER and reestablish ZO-1 continuity in RPE cells exposed to complement C5b-9 challenge (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013). However, significant translational hurdles—principally related to its pharmacokinetic profile, potential off-target effects, and the inherent complexities of dry AMD pathology—must be diligently addressed through further preclinical research.

From an expert drug development perspective, Torin-1 offers robust proof-of-concept evidence that mTOR inhibition can functionally reverse key pathological features of dry AMD in cellular models. The next steps should focus on optimizing its chemical properties or transitioning to an analog with improved drug-like characteristics, as well as developing innovative ocular delivery platforms to ensure targeted retinal exposure. In light of these considerations, while Torin-1 in its current form may serve best as a preclinical tool to validate the therapeutic pathway, further investment in medicinal chemistry, formulation science, and in vivo safety/efficacy studies is warranted before considering clinical evaluation in patients with dry AMD (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013; Amin et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Final Remarks

To summarize, the current data support the concept that robust, ATP-competitive inhibition of mTOR with compounds such as Torin-1 provides a compelling mechanistic foundation for mitigating complement-mediated RPE damage in dry AMD. The dual mTORC1/mTORC2 targeting strategy of Torin-1 enables it to not only suppress pathogenic anabolic signaling but also to trigger autophagy—thereby facilitating the clearance of toxic sublytic MAC deposits and the restoration of RPE tight junctions, as measured by TEER and ZO-1 integrity. Nevertheless, the translational journey from promising in vitro results to an effective clinical treatment is contingent upon the resolution of pharmacokinetic shortcomings, the development of retina-specific delivery strategies, and extensive in vivo validation in models that mirror the human disease.

In light of the above evaluation, Torin-1 stands as a scientifically robust candidate that validates the therapeutic rationale for mTOR inhibition in dry AMD. Its significant strengths in potency and mechanistic clarity are offset by practical challenges that necessitate further research. The pathway forward should thus include efforts to optimize the formulation and drug-like properties of Torin-1 (or its analogues), pair it with appropriate ocular delivery systems, and deploy rigorous preclinical models to establish its long-term efficacy and safety in the context of dry AMD. Only with these additional steps can Torin-1 (or a derivative thereof) mature into a potential treatment option for patients suffering from this chronic and debilitating disease (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013; Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017; Schenone et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2021; Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017).

Based on the available literature and preclinical evidence, the candidate hypothesis that Torin-1 will restore TEER and ZO-1 belt continuity in RPE cells challenged by complement C5b-9 holds significant promise, warranting further focused preclinical investigation and optimization before any human studies are contemplated.

The therapeutic history of SS-31 is extensive and spans several preclinical and early-phase clinical investigations across a range of indications characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction. As mitochondrial homeostasis is a critical determinant of RPE cell function, the preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics is expected to translate into decreased apoptosis and improved cell survival in the face of oxidative challenges (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 8–11). Therefore, treatment with SS-31 should also help maintain or restore TEER in RPE monolayer assays, indicating a preservation of barrier function that is crucial for retinal homeostasis and prevention of drusen formation and RPE degeneration associated with dry AMD (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Moreover, preclinical studies in animal models of retinal degeneration—in which SS-31 has been shown to reverse vision loss, improve clearance of sub-RPE deposits, and enhance electroretinographic responses—further support the expectation that SS-31 can exert protective effects in the ocular environment by mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction and the subsequent cascade of oxidative damage (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Taken together, the anticipated experimental outcome is that SS-31 will significantly attenuate oxidative damage in RPE cells, preserve mitochondrial function, maintain tight junction integrity (as evidenced by stable ZO-1/occludin expression and restored TEER), and ultimately contribute to the functional rescue of RPE cells under conditions that mimic the oxidative insults observed in dry AMD (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tong et al., 2022, pp. 14–16).

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, SS-31 (Elamipretide) presents as a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, with several key strengths that support its potential utility and a few noteworthy challenges that will need to be addressed in further research. One of the primary strengths of SS-31 is its well-characterized mechanism of action; its ability to bind cardiolipin and thereby stabilize mitochondrial inner membrane structure, enhance electron transport chain efficiency, and reduce ROS generation is supported by robust preclinical data across multiple models of mitochondrial dysfunction, including cardiac, skeletal muscle, and retinal systems (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4). This mitochondria-targeted mechanism is particularly attractive in the context of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are recognized as major drivers of RPE degeneration and subsequent photoreceptor loss (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Furthermore, early-phase clinical studies in ocular disease have demonstrated that SS-31 is safe and well tolerated and have hinted at functional improvements in visual acuity and reduced progression of retinal degeneration, which supports its translational viability (Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5). The repurposing of SS-31 from conditions such as heart failure and primary mitochondrial myopathy to an ocular application leverages its established bioenergetic benefits and broad mitochondrial stabilization properties, thereby enhancing its appeal as a novel intervention for dry AMD (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 10–11, 16–22).

However, there are several challenges and weaknesses that merit consideration. First, while the molecular mechanism of SS-31—centered on cardiolipin binding and mitochondrial stabilization—is well supported, direct evidence linking its activity to the preservation of tight junction proteins (such as ZO-1/occludin) and the restoration of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE models remains limited in the current literature (Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40). This represents a key knowledge gap given that the hypothesis posits that protection of RPE barrier integrity is a critical outcome in preventing disease progression in dry AMD. Additional preclinical studies that specifically measure the effects of SS-31 on RPE tight junction organization, using immunostaining for ZO-1 and occludin as well as quantitative TEER assays, would be essential to fully validate its proposed mechanism in the context of epithelial barrier protection (Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Second, although early-phase clinical trials have shown promise in improving functional visual metrics, some clinical studies in related indications (e.g., Phase 2 trials in cardiac conditions) have produced mixed results with primary endpoints not consistently met, suggesting that optimal dosing regimens, treatment durations, and patient selection criteria may need further refinement (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 9–10). In the case of dry AMD, where the pathological changes evolve over extended periods, longer-term studies and careful endpoint selection will be critical to demonstrate sustained therapeutic benefit (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Third, while the pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of SS-31 appear favorable for reaching mitochondrial targets, ensuring sufficient ocular penetration and accumulation in the RPE—whether via systemic subcutaneous administration or topical formulations—remains a logistical and pharmacological challenge that must be addressed in future clinical development (Tong et al., 2022, pp. 14–16; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

In conclusion, SS-31 (Elamipretide) exhibits a strong mechanistic underpinning based on its targeted interaction with cardiolipin to restore mitochondrial function and mitigate oxidative stress—a mode of action that is directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD owing to the central role of mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE degeneration (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). The compound’s extensive preclinical validation in models of mitochondrial diseases, coupled with encouraging early clinical data, makes it a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Nonetheless, key gaps in directly demonstrating its effects on RPE barrier integrity and tight junction preservation (as measured by ZO-1/occludin levels and TEER) necessitate further targeted preclinical studies. Additionally, addressing challenges related to optimal dosing, treatment duration, and efficient ocular delivery will be paramount for the success of subsequent clinical trials. Overall, given its robust mitochondrial protective effects and plausible secondary benefits on epithelial barrier function, SS-31 warrants further investigation as a novel therapeutic strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 10–12).
