Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ripasudil, also known by its research designation Y-39983 and commercially available as Selleckchem S8443, is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor developed originally as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil containing protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. It belongs to a class of therapeutics that act in an ATP‐competitive manner to inhibit the activity of ROCK isoforms, enzymes that are critical regulators of actomyosin contractility and cell adhesion. Ripasudil was synthesized following the structural optimization of earlier compounds such as fasudil and Y-27632, with the aim of increasing both potency and ocular tolerability. Its chemical origins are linked to the rational design strategies that sought to improve enzyme inhibitory selectivity and to enhance the pharmacokinetic profile for local ocular application. Members of the ROCK inhibitor class have seen prior use in settings that require modulation of actin cytoskeleton dynamics, such as the treatment of glaucoma via enhanced aqueous humor outflow, and have also been explored in contexts involving wound healing and anti-fibrotic effects in various ocular tissues (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, ripasudil has been approved in Japan for the treatment of glaucoma and ocular hypertension, where it is delivered topically in the form of eye drops, demonstrating a well-established safety profile and a low incidence of systemic adverse effects. In preclinical models, it has demonstrated efficacy by increasing ocular blood flow, modifying trabecular meshwork cell contractility, and reducing intraocular pressure, thereby serving as a stepping stone and proof-of-concept for the utility of ROCK inhibitors in ocular disorders. Beyond its approved use in glaucoma, investigations of ROCK inhibitors—including ripasudil—have extended into experimental applications in corneal endothelial regeneration and have been evaluated in combination with anti-VEGF therapies for diabetic macular edema. Although direct clinical evidence specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is not available, multiple lines of preclinical research have shown that the ROCK inhibitor class modulates pathways which are believed to underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Notably, the mechanistic studies have identified the role of ROCK signaling in cytoskeletal reorganization, matrix contractility, and fibrosis, all of which are processes particularly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier dysfunction seen in dry AMD (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Moreover, the ocular pharmacokinetic profile of ripasudil—demonstrated by rabbit intravitreal studies showing a half-life of approximately 14 hours and negligible systemic exposure—is supportive of repurposing this candidate for posterior segment indications, including dry AMD (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ripasudil exerts its therapeutic activity by competitively inhibiting the ATP-binding site of ROCK isoforms, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of downstream effectors such as myosin light-chain (MLC), myosin-binding subunit of MLC phosphatase (MYPT1), and LIM kinase. These phosphorylation events normally lead to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, focal adhesion assembly, and ultimately contribute to a contractile, stiffened cell phenotype. In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, this contractility is thought to be exacerbated under conditions of oxidative stress, contributing to disassembly or mislocalization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity. By inhibiting ROCK, ripasudil reduces actomyosin-driven contraction and stress-fiber formation, thereby promoting cortical F-actin remodeling and facilitating the proper membrane relocalization of tight-junction proteins. The specificity of ripasudil has been demonstrated by its greater than 100-fold selectivity against other kinases such as protein kinase C (PKC) and myotonic dystrophy kinase-related Cdc42-binding kinase (MRCK), highlighting the mechanistic precision by which it modulates ROCK-dependent signaling cascades (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Additionally, while several studies indicate that the ROCK inhibitor class generally targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2 isoforms, quantitative biochemical data have shown that ripasudil exhibits potent enzyme inhibitory activity with IC₅₀s in the low nanomolar range (with values reported around 51 nM for ROCK1 and 19 nM for ROCK2 in some studies, though the candidate hypothesis posits values of approximately 29 nM for ROCK1 and 68 nM for ROCK2). This inhibitory profile is particularly relevant because emerging research indicates that ROCK2, in particular, is upregulated in the pathological conditions of dry AMD and plays a key role in mediating cytoskeletal changes that disrupt RPE tight junction integrity (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). The inhibition of ROCK thereby is expected to have a dual benefit of cytoprotection and restoration of cell junction architecture, ultimately leading to improved barrier function (Ghenciu et al., 2025; Singh & Singh, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing ripasudil for dry AMD is that by blocking ROCK activity in oxidatively stressed retinal pigment epithelium cells, the compound will lead to a reduction in actomyosin contractility, thereby alleviating the formation of pathological stress fibers that otherwise disrupt the organization of tight junction complexes. Under normal physiological conditions, tight junction proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin are localized at the plasma membrane in a continuous, belt-like manner that is essential to maintain TEER and restrict paracellular permeability. However, in dry AMD, oxidative damage, inflammation, and mechanical stress lead to cytoskeletal reorganization and a discontinuous distribution of these critical proteins, resulting in impaired barrier function and contributing to the pathogenesis of the disease. Preclinical studies, particularly those employing ARPE-19 cell models subjected to toxic insults such as paraquat or sodium iodate (NaIO₃), have demonstrated that ROCK inhibitors can dose-dependently restore TEER (with reported improvements up to 70%) and re-establish the membrane continuity of ZO-1, suggesting that these agents can “rescue” the RPE barrier phenotype under injurious conditions (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). It is expected that ripasudil, with its potent ROCK-inhibitory activity and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics (including intravitreal retention times supportive of sustained action), will similarly promote the cortical redistribution of F-actin, leading to the re-localization of junctional molecules back to the cell membrane. This mechanistic restoration should result in improved transepithelial electrical resistance and a concomitant reduction in paracellular permeability, effectively reinforcing the RPE barrier—a central therapeutic target in dry AMD. Moreover, the activation of protective cellular pathways through ROCK inhibition may also confer additional anti-apoptotic and anti-inflammatory effects, further contributing to the survival and functional integrity of the RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating ripasudil as a candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths become apparent. First, its established clinical use for glaucoma means that its safety, tolerability, and ocular pharmacokinetic properties are well characterized—attributes that significantly lower the translational barrier for its application in other ocular diseases. The intravitreal pharmacokinetic data, with a half-life of approximately 14 hours in rabbit models and negligible systemic exposure, suggest that therapeutic concentrations capable of modulating ROCK activity in the retina can be achieved with acceptable dosing regimens (Yamaguchi et al., 2016). Second, the mechanistic rationale is compelling: ROCK signaling is intimately involved in mediating actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, and subsequent disruption of tight junction architecture in epithelial cells. Given that ROCK2 in particular is implicated in the pathological processes observed in the RPE in dry AMD, the ability of ripasudil to inhibit this pathway could translate into measurable improvements in barrier function, as indicated by preclinical assays demonstrating TEER restoration and the re-localization of ZO-1 in ARPE-19 cells (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Third, the compound exhibits a favorable selectivity profile, with negligible off-target activity against other kinases such as PKC and MRCK, which minimizes the risk of unintended effects in non-target tissues. This specificity is critical when repurposing drugs for chronic conditions such as dry AMD, where long-term ocular safety is paramount (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Despite these strengths, there are notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before ripasudil can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. A primary limitation is the paucity of direct experimental evidence in RPE models of dry AMD. While the hypothesis is supported by data from related in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative stress), robust in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of dry AMD pathophysiology are still needed. In particular, data demonstrating that ripasudil can restore tight junction integrity and improve TEER in the context of chronic, progressive RPE dysfunction remain limited (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Furthermore, although the compound’s ROCK inhibitory activity is well documented, the available literature does not consistently detail the isoform-specific effects in RPE cells; given that ROCK1 and ROCK2 may play distinct roles in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, clarifying the relative contributions of each isoform is essential. The candidate hypothesis posits specific IC₅₀ values for ROCK1 and ROCK2, yet discrepancies exist across reported studies regarding the precise inhibitory concentrations, which indicates that further biochemical characterization is warranted (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). Another consideration is the potential for adverse effects when repurposing a drug originally optimized for anterior-segment diseases for posterior-segment applications. Although the ocular safety profile of ripasudil in glaucoma is well established, the long-term impact of ROCK inhibition on RPE cell biology in an aged population—especially in the context of dry AMD—remains uncertain. Off-target cytoskeletal effects in other retinal cell types, possible modulation of inflammatory responses, and the risk of inadvertently triggering compensatory signaling pathways are all factors that must be carefully evaluated in preclinical studies (Iancu et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2025). Lastly, while the pharmacokinetic data support retinal exposure after intravitreal or possibly topical administration, optimizing the delivery method to ensure sustained and localized drug levels in the RPE without causing ocular surface toxicity (such as conjunctival hyperemia or corneal epithelial disturbances) will be critical. Innovative delivery systems, such as sustained-release intravitreal implants or depot formulations, may offer solutions but require further development (Yamaguchi et al., 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023).

In conclusion, the repurposing of ripasudil for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and a favorable safety profile derived from its established use in glaucoma. The compound’s capacity to inhibit ROCK-mediated actomyosin contraction and promote cortical F-actin remodeling positions it as a promising agent for restoring RPE barrier function—one of the key pathological features of dry AMD. However, the current literature reveals significant gaps in direct evidence regarding its effects on RPE tight junction proteins, TEER restoration, and the isoform-specific roles of ROCK in the RPE under oxidative stress. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative that belongs to the fibrate class of hypolipidemic agents. Originally developed to address dyslipidemia, fenofibrate was synthesized via chemical modifications of the fibric acid scaffold to yield an amphipathic carboxylic acid derivative, designed specifically to modulate lipid metabolism. As a member of the fibrate drug class, fenofibrate exerts its primary effects through activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα), a nuclear receptor that regulates the transcription of a variety of genes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, lipid transport, and overall metabolic homeostasis (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2). Over the past several decades, fibrates have been widely used in clinical practice to lower triglycerides, reduce low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, and elevate high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, significantly contributing to cardiovascular risk management. In addition, the repurposing efforts for fenofibrate in ocular conditions have generated interest based on its ability to modulate inflammatory and metabolic pathways in retinal tissues (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11).

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate’s therapeutic history is well established in the management of dyslipidemia and in reducing cardiovascular risk. Its clinical use dates back several decades, during which it has demonstrated efficacy in lowering plasma triglyceride levels, reducing total cholesterol, and favorably shifting the LDL particle size toward a less atherogenic profile (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9). Beyond its lipid-lowering effects, fenofibrate has been extensively evaluated in the context of diabetic retinopathy. Large-scale clinical trials such as the FIELD (Fenofibrate Intervention and Event Lowering in Diabetes) study and the ACCORD (Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes) Eye study have provided robust evidence that fenofibrate can slow the progression of diabetic retinopathy, reduce the severity of retinal microvascular abnormalities, and decrease the need for laser photocoagulation (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12). Although these studies primarily targeted diabetic retinal changes, the underlying pathophysiology – which includes oxidative stress, inflammation, and lipid accumulation in retinal tissues – overlaps with that observed in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11). Preclinical studies using in vitro models of RPE cells, where saturated fatty acids like palmitate are used to mimic lipotoxic stress, have demonstrated that fenofibrate can reduce lipid droplet accumulation and improve barrier function as measured by trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 8–11). In addition, in vivo studies in high-fat diet–fed mice have shown that fenofibrate treatment partially restores the function of the RPE, as evidenced by improved electroretinography (ERG) parameters and reduced markers of oxidative damage and inflammation (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8, 8–11). While there is no large-scale clinical trial data directly targeting dry AMD with fenofibrate, its documented benefits in diabetic retinopathy and its mechanistic overlap with dry AMD pathology make it an intriguing candidate for repurposing in this disease setting (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action is multifaceted and is primarily mediated by its role as a PPARα agonist. Binding of fenofibrate (or its active metabolite, fenofibric acid) to PPARα leads to the formation of a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor (RXR), which then binds to peroxisome proliferator responsive elements (PPREs) in the promoters of target genes. This transcriptional activation upregulates a suite of enzymes involved in fatty acid uptake and mitochondrial β-oxidation, such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) (Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12; Zhao et al., 2015, pp. 5–7). Increased expression of these catabolic enzymes enhances the degradation of fatty acids, thereby reducing intracellular lipid accumulation. In the context of lipid-loaded RPE cells – a condition that contributes to the disruption of tight junctions and subsequent barrier dysfunction – fenofibrate’s enhancement of fatty acid β-oxidation is hypothesized to lower intracellular lipid levels and consequently mitigate the lipotoxic stress imposed on junctional complexes (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11).  

Beyond its metabolic effects, fenofibrate has been reported to exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions. It downregulates markers of oxidative stress such as NOX4 and 3-nitrotyrosine and attenuates the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNFα, ICAM1, and VEGF in retinal tissues (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 8–11). Importantly, fenofibrate appears to modulate the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway in RPE cells. Under conditions of lipotoxicity induced by saturated fatty acids (e.g., palmitate), the PI3K/AKT pathway is downregulated, leading to increased oxidative stress and inflammation. Fenofibrate treatment has been shown to restore the p-AKT/AKT ratio, suggesting its ability to activate survival and anti-apoptotic pathways that are vital for maintaining RPE integrity (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8). Also, some evidence points to additional PPARα-independent mechanisms that may contribute to fenofibrate’s protective effects, such as modulation of AMPK signaling, which further reinforces mitochondrial function and promotes cell survival (Fu et al., 2020, pp. 6–8; Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15). Overall, fenofibrate’s molecular actions converge on enhancing fatty acid catabolism, reducing oxidative stress, suppressing inflammation, and supporting the survival of RPE cells – all of which are key factors in maintaining the structure and function of the outer blood–retina barrier, a critical component affected in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Zhao et al., 2015, pp. 5–7).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis under investigation posits that fenofibrate-mediated PPARα activation will drive a metabolic shift in lipid-loaded RPE cells by increasing fatty acid β-oxidation and thereby reducing the intracellular accumulation of lipid droplets. In an in vitro model using ARPE-19 cells, treatment with palmitate induces lipotoxic stress that disrupts tight junction complexes, leading to decreased TEER and mislocalization of occludin – an essential tight junction protein. The expected effect of fenofibrate in this assay is twofold. First, by upregulating CPT1A and other enzymes involved in fatty acid metabolism, fenofibrate should reduce the intracellular lipid burden. Such a reduction is anticipated to alleviate the lipotoxic stress that compromises the junctional integrity of RPE cells (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12). Second, through its activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway and potential AMPK signaling modulation, fenofibrate is expected to restore the proper localization of occludin and improve TEER by approximately 30%, as observed in preliminary studies using a 50 µM concentration of the drug (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). These effects are bolstered by previous evidence showing that fenofibrate can reduce oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators that are known to further damage tight junctions in the RPE (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8; Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15). Since PPARα is expressed in retinal cells, including the RPE, and is essential for lipid oxidation and energy metabolism, its activation by fenofibrate in the assay is well supported by the underlying biochemistry (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12). The ultimate expectation is that the improved barrier function in vitro will translate into a therapeutic benefit for dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction and compromised barrier integrity are central to disease progression (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11).

Overall Evaluation:  
Fenofibrate presents several compelling strengths as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. One of its primary advantages is its long-established safety and efficacy profile in clinical use for dyslipidemia. Decades of systemic administration in patients have provided robust safety data and have demonstrated that fenofibrate is well tolerated in the majority of cases (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9). Moreover, the substantial clinical data from the FIELD and ACCORD Eye studies establish its beneficial effects on retinal microvascular complications in diabetic patients, indicating a therapeutic potential that may extend to other retinal diseases with overlapping pathophysiological features, such as dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12).

Mechanistically, fenofibrate’s ability to activate PPARα and enhance fatty acid β-oxidation addresses a critical aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis: the accumulation of lipids within RPE cells that contributes to oxidative stress and impairs junctional integrity. The reduction in lipid accumulation not only decreases lipotoxic stress but also supports cellular energy production, thereby enabling the restoration of tight junction proteins such as occludin (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 6–8). The concomitant activation of survival pathways, notably the PI3K/AKT cascade, further reinforces the protective milieu in RPE cells. These multifactorial actions of fenofibrate – targeting lipid metabolism, oxidative damage, inflammation, and cellular survival – collectively provide a strong mechanistic rationale for its use in preserving RPE barrier function in the context of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–12).

Another strength lies in the potential to repurpose an already approved drug. This approach can significantly shorten the development timeline and reduce costs, as fenofibrate’s pharmacokinetics, dosing ranges, and safety profile are well documented. Additionally, innovative ocular delivery methods, such as nano-emulsion eye drops or localized intraocular administration, have been explored to overcome the limitations of systemic drug delivery in targeting the retina (Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). These novel delivery approaches could maximize retinal drug exposure while minimizing systemic side effects, ensuring that effective concentrations of fenofibrate reach the RPE.

Despite these promising attributes, several challenges must be acknowledged. One primary concern is that the majority of clinical evidence for fenofibrate’s efficacy in retinal conditions comes from diabetic retinopathy studies rather than direct investigations in dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 12–13). Although there is significant overlap in the pathological processes underlying both conditions—such as oxidative stress, inflammation, and RPE dysfunction—the direct translation of benefits from diabetic retinopathy to dry AMD is not yet fully established. Preclinical studies in dry AMD models are therefore essential to validate whether the observed improvements in in vitro RPE barrier function (e.g., increased TEER and proper occludin localization) will translate into clinically meaningful outcomes for patients (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–12).

Another limitation is the duality of fenofibrate’s mechanism of action. While PPARα activation is a well-characterized pathway, available evidence indicates that fenofibrate may also act through PPARα-independent mechanisms, including AMPK activation and inhibition of cytochrome P450 epoxygenase activities (Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11; Qiu et al., 2019, p. 12). This multiplicity of actions, while potentially beneficial, also raises questions about off-target effects that could complicate the therapeutic profile when applied to a sensitive tissue such as the retina. Moreover, fenofibrate’s poor aqueous solubility poses challenges for direct ocular delivery, although recent advances in formulation science (such as nano-emulsion systems) are promising solutions to this problem (Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

A further challenge is that the ideal dosing for maximal retinal efficacy without systemic toxicity remains to be determined. The preliminary in vitro data indicating a 30% improvement in TEER at 50 µM fenofibrate is encouraging; however, scaling these concentrations appropriately for in vivo use in the retina will require careful pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies. In addition, the variability in RPE cell responses due to differences in cellular metabolism, donor characteristics, or disease stage could impact the consistency of the therapeutic response in a clinical setting (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8, 8–11).

In summary, fenofibrate exhibits significant promise as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its strengths include an extensive track record in managing dyslipidemia, well-documented retinal benefits in diabetic retinopathy, and a robust mechanistic rationale grounded in PPARα activation and enhanced fatty acid oxidation. These effects are supported by preclinical data demonstrating improvements in RPE barrier function under lipotoxic conditions, aligning with the pathogenic processes observed in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11). However, to fully establish fenofibrate’s potential in dry AMD, further targeted research is required. This should include advanced in vitro and in vivo models that specifically recapitulate the dry AMD phenotype, detailed investigations into ocular pharmacokinetics and optimal delivery methods, and ultimately, clinical trials that evaluate efficacy and safety in patients with dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 6–8).

Overall, fenofibrate’s ability to reduce intracellular lipid accumulation, diminish oxidative and inflammatory stress, and restore junctional integrity in RPE cells makes it a promising therapeutic candidate. While there are challenges to be addressed—notably, the translation of findings from diabetic retinopathy to dry AMD and the need for precise ocular delivery formulations—the established clinical profile of fenofibrate coupled with its multifaceted mechanisms of action provide a compelling scientific rationale for further exploration in dry AMD. The convergence of metabolic modulation, anti-inflammatory action, and barrier restoration positions fenofibrate as a novel metabolic intervention that could fill an unmet need in a patient population with limited treatment options (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Zhao et al., 2015, pp. 5–7; Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15).

In conclusion, from a drug development perspective, fenofibrate is an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its synthetic derivation and established use as a lipid-lowering agent, combined with revealed preclinical efficacy in preserving RPE function under lipotoxic conditions, align well with the hypothesized benefit of enhancing fatty acid β-oxidation to alleviate junctional stress. The promising in vitro improvements in TEER and occludin localization provide a solid foundation for further research, while the favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profile support its viability for ocular applications. Critical next steps include refining ocular delivery strategies, conducting detailed mechanistic studies in dry AMD-relevant models, and initiating early-phase clinical trials to assess both efficacy and safety in the target population. If these studies confirm the preclinical promise of fenofibrate, this candidate could ultimately be integrated into combination therapeutic strategies—possibly alongside anti-VEGF therapies—to comprehensively address the multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8, 8–11, 11–12).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BCX9930 is a novel, orally bioavailable, low-molecular-weight small molecule that functions as a selective inhibitor of complement factor D (FD). It was originally discovered through a rigorous drug discovery program that combined high-throughput screening with structure‐based rational design strategies to identify potent, non-covalent inhibitors of the serine protease FD, an essential enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. This candidate belongs to the class of factor D inhibitors, compounds that have previously been developed for complement-mediated diseases including complement 3 glomerulopathy (Chen et al., 2022). The synthesis and discovery process for BCX9930 involved chemical scaffold optimization to enhance both potency and selectivity; for instance, by specifically non-covalently occupying the S1 pocket of FD, BCX9930 is able to achieve an IC₅₀ value as low as 4 nM, a potency level that places it among the most active agents in its category. Its chemical attributes also include more than a 500-fold selectivity over related serine proteases, thereby reducing the potential for off-target effects—a critical factor for chronic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where long-term safety is paramount (Schubart et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
The development of BCX9930 is emblematic of the broader evolution in complement therapeutics. Historically, the complement system has been successfully targeted in several diseases where dysregulated complement activity plays a pathogenic role. Prior studies have established the role of FD in both the amplification loop of the alternative pathway and its subsequent effects on complement-mediated damage. BCX9930 and similar agents emerged from early research efforts that investigated FD inhibition as a means to alter pathologic complement activation. In clinical studies, similar agents targeting factor D (for example, danicopan) have demonstrated significant suppression of alternative pathway activity in conditions such as PNH, with reports noting reductions in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels and improvements in hemoglobin that facilitated transfusion independence (Schubart et al., 2023; Risitano et al., 2020). Although the majority of these pilots have been focused on hematological disorders and C3G, the mechanistic rationale for FD inhibition directly applies to dry AMD as well. Preclinical models have documented that, when the alternative pathway is excessively activated—as is theorized in dry AMD—even minute amounts of FD can trigger a cascade of destructive complement activity (Schubart et al., 2023; Gavriilaki et al., 2022). In animal models, FD inhibitors have demonstrated promising outcomes including the reduction of complement deposition and preservation of retinal architecture (Ong et al., 2024). Despite the encouraging therapeutic history of FD inhibitors in other indications, it is important to note that clinical trials evaluating FD inhibitors specifically for dry AMD or geographic atrophy have produced mixed results; one high-profile example is the failure of Lampalizumab (an FD inhibitor) to meet meaningful endpoints in pivotal phase 3 trials (Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019). Nonetheless, BCX9930 has distinct chemical and pharmacological properties that differentiate it from earlier candidates, including its strong potency, favorable oral bioavailability, and robust preclinical barrier rescue effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, making it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
The pathologic basis for many complement-mediated diseases, including dry AMD, lies in the dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, in which factor D plays a pivotal role. Normally, FD is the rate-limiting enzyme required to generate the AP C3 convertase by cleaving factor B complexed with C3b, which fuels an amplification loop and leads to the generation of downstream proinflammatory mediators such as C3a and C5a as well as opsonins that promote inflammation and tissue damage (Gavriilaki et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024). BCX9930 exerts its therapeutic effect by binding non-covalently in the S1 pocket of FD. This binding is characterized by exceptionally high affinity, with an IC₅₀ value of 4 nM, and by stringent selectivity that minimizes interference with other serine proteases. By occupying this key binding site, BCX9930 effectively prevents FD from interacting with its natural substrate, thereby arresting the production of the AP C3 convertase. This inhibition leads to a subsequent decrease in C3 cleavage and a reduction in the generation of complement split products, which are known to instigate an inflammatory response (Chen et al., 2022).  
Molecularly, the non-covalent nature of BCX9930’s interaction with factor D confers several advantages. First, such interactions allow reversible inhibition, providing the potential for controlled dosing and the fine-tuning of complement activity. Second, the selectivity profile of BCX9930 results from structural modifications aimed at optimizing the fit within the S1 pocket, ensuring that the inhibitor does not inadvertently affect enzymes with similar active site geometries. This precision is crucial, as systemic blockade of the complement system can result in significant immunosuppression. Thus, the protection of the retinal environment—by specifically inhibiting the amplification loop of the alternative pathway—offers a mechanistic rationale for the use of BCX9930 in diseases where complement overactivation is implicated, notably in the disruption of RPE tight junction integrity (Gavriilaki et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024). Additionally, the compound’s design ensures that while it attenuates pathogenic complement activity, it spares the classical and lectin pathways, reducing the risk of systemic immunocompromise.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for BCX9930 in the treatment of dry AMD is based on its ability to mitigate complement-mediated damage to the retinal pigment epithelium. In vitro studies in primary human RPE cells have shown that under conditions of serum-mediated complement activation, there is a decline in trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and disruption of critical tight junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and claudin-19. These proteins are essential for maintaining the barrier integrity of the RPE, and their dysregulation is a hallmark of retinal degeneration in AMD (Gavriilaki et al., 2022).  
The working hypothesis posits that by non-covalently occupying the S1 pocket of factor D, BCX9930 can inhibit the formation of the alternative pathway C3 convertase, thereby reducing the production of the inflammatory complement split products. This reduction is expected to lead to a decrease in complement-driven RPE tight junction disruption. Experimental data indicate that the addition of 500 nM BCX9930 to primary human RPE cultures challenged with serum results in a recovery of TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values. This recovery is associated with the restoration of tight junction integrity, as evidenced by the maintenance of ZO-1 and claudin-19 continuity, both of which are critical determinants of the barrier function (Chen et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024).  
In parallel, in vivo studies using Factor H-knockout animal models have provided supportive data for BCX9930’s therapeutic effect. In these animal models, which exhibit heightened complement activation and subsequent retinal damage similar to that seen in dry AMD, BCX9930 administered at 5 mg/kg twice daily resulted in a 70% reduction in complement C3 deposition on Bruch’s membrane and preservation of the outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness. These endpoints serve as surrogate indicators for photoreceptor protection and overall retinal health. Taken together, these findings underscore the capacity of BCX9930 not only to neutralize the biochemical drivers of complement activation but also to translate this inhibition into meaningful structural and functional preservation within the retina (Ong et al., 2024).  
Mechanistically, the expected effect hinges on the sustained and robust suppression of the alternative complement pathway, which under normal pathological conditions contributes significantly to the inflammatory milieu and structural degeneration characteristic of dry AMD. The reduction in complement activation is anticipated to curtail downstream inflammatory cascades that can disrupt RPE tight junctions, thereby stabilizing TEER and maintaining the integrity of the retinal barrier. Given that chronic complement activation has been implicated in accelerating the progression of dry AMD, the capacity of BCX9930 to restore and maintain RPE function could slow or even arrest disease progression, offering a novel therapeutic avenue for a condition currently lacking effective interventions (Chen et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating BCX9930 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key strengths and potential limitations must be considered. On the strength side, BCX9930 exhibits an exceptionally high potency (IC₅₀ = 4 nM) and selectivity profile that is well aligned with the intended mechanism of action. Its ability to non-covalently target the S1 pocket of factor D ensures that the inhibition of the alternative pathway is both potent and reversible, thereby allowing for controlled pharmacodynamic effects. The high degree of selectivity—exceeding 500-fold over related serine proteases—not only reduces the likelihood of off-target toxicity but also supports the feasibility of long-term administration required for chronic diseases such as dry AMD (Schubart et al., 2023).  
Preclinical studies provide compelling support for the candidate’s mechanism. The demonstration that 500 nM BCX9930 can recover TEER to 85% of baseline in human RPE cultures suggests that the compound effectively counteracts the complement-mediated disruption of intercellular tight junctions. Furthermore, animal data showing that a dosing regimen of 5 mg/kg BID can reduce Bruch’s membrane C3 deposition by 70% and preserve ONL thickness indicates that BCX9930 not only exerts biochemical effects but also translates these into anatomical preservation within the retina (Ong et al., 2024). Such findings are particularly relevant given the importance of maintaining RPE barrier function and photoreceptor viability in halting the progression of dry AMD.  
Another strong point in favor of BCX9930 is its oral bioavailability, which is a significant advantage over therapies that require invasive delivery methods (for example, intravitreal injections). An oral agent would potentially improve patient compliance and reduce the risks associated with repeated intraocular procedures. This is particularly critical in a disease like dry AMD, where the patient population is predominantly elderly, and minimizing treatment burden is essential (Chen et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).

One major concern pertains to the historical track record of complement inhibitors in the treatment of dry AMD. Previous clinical trials with other agents targeting the alternative pathway—such as Lampalizumab—have ultimately failed to demonstrate robust clinical efficacy in phase 3 trials despite encouraging preclinical data (Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019). Such outcomes underscore the difficulty of translating complement inhibition into meaningful clinical benefits in retinal degenerative diseases. The complexity of AMD pathophysiology, which involves not only complement dysregulation but also oxidative stress, genetic predispositions, and environmental factors, means that addressing a single pathway may not be sufficient to fully arrest disease progression.  
Additionally, while the preclinical data for BCX9930 are encouraging, there is still a gap in clinical evidence demonstrating its efficacy specifically in dry AMD. Most of the clinical data currently available for BCX9930 have been derived from studies in conditions like C3G and PNH, where the pathobiology is somewhat different from that of retinal degenerative diseases. It is essential that further clinical studies with BCX9930 incorporate rigorous monitoring of potential systemic toxicities and immune-related adverse effects, especially given the chronic nature of dry AMD therapy. Long-term data will be critical in confirming that the inhibition of the alternative pathway does not compromise overall host defense mechanisms or lead to other unexpected off-target consequences.  
Finally, the complexity of dry AMD as a clinical entity must guide any decision regarding the advancement of BCX9930. Complement-driven RPE disruption is only one facet of AMD pathogenesis; a multifactorial disease mechanism implies that combination therapies or multimodal approaches may eventually be needed to achieve optimal clinical outcomes. In this context, BCX9930 might best be positioned as part of a combination regimen, potentially alongside agents that address oxidative damage or other pathogenic mechanisms in AMD. Alternatively, biomarkers may need to be better defined so that patients most likely to benefit from complement inhibition can be identified and targeted in clinical trials (Kassa et al., 2019; Ong et al., 2024).  

In summary, BCX9930 represents a highly promising therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its potent and selective inhibition of factor D, a critical enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. The underlying rationale is strongly supported by both molecular and preclinical evidence: by binding non-covalently to the S1 pocket of factor D, BCX9930 effectively blocks the formation of the C3 convertase, thereby mitigating complement activation that is postulated to drive RPE tight junction disruption. In vitro studies have already demonstrated that BCX9930 can restore trans-epithelial electrical resistance and preserve the continuity of crucial tight junction proteins in human RPE cells under complement challenge. Additionally, animal models have provided evidence for significant reductions in complement deposition and the preservation of retinal architecture. These findings collectively indicate that BCX9930 has the potential to protect retinal tissue from complement-mediated injury, a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024).  

However, the transition from preclinical promise to clinical success remains a challenge, as highlighted by the mixed outcomes seen with previous factor D inhibitors in the AMD space. The failure of some earlier agents, despite robust biochemical data, emphasizes that the path from molecular inhibition to effective disease modification is complex and fraught with challenges. Critical areas of future research include the establishment of clear biomarkers that correlate with clinical outcomes in dry AMD, careful delineation of the safety profile specific to the elderly patient population, and the exploration of appropriate combination strategies that might enhance therapeutic efficacy.  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and encouraging preclinical data, BCX9930 stands out as a compelling candidate for further evaluation in clinical trials targeting dry AMD. Its precise mechanism of action and the potential for oral administration offer distinct advantages and may help overcome some of the limitations encountered with earlier complement inhibitors. Ultimately, while caution is warranted due to the historical challenges in this therapeutic area, the overall evaluation supports the advancement of BCX9930 for further development and rigorous clinical testing in dry AMD patients (Schubart et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ripasudil, also known by its research designation Y-39983 and commercially available as Selleckchem S8443, is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor developed originally as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil containing protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. It belongs to a class of therapeutics that act in an ATP‐competitive manner to inhibit the activity of ROCK isoforms, enzymes that are critical regulators of actomyosin contractility and cell adhesion. Ripasudil was synthesized following the structural optimization of earlier compounds such as fasudil and Y-27632, with the aim of increasing both potency and ocular tolerability. Its chemical origins are linked to the rational design strategies that sought to improve enzyme inhibitory selectivity and to enhance the pharmacokinetic profile for local ocular application. Members of the ROCK inhibitor class have seen prior use in settings that require modulation of actin cytoskeleton dynamics, such as the treatment of glaucoma via enhanced aqueous humor outflow, and have also been explored in contexts involving wound healing and anti-fibrotic effects in various ocular tissues (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, ripasudil has been approved in Japan for the treatment of glaucoma and ocular hypertension, where it is delivered topically in the form of eye drops, demonstrating a well-established safety profile and a low incidence of systemic adverse effects. In preclinical models, it has demonstrated efficacy by increasing ocular blood flow, modifying trabecular meshwork cell contractility, and reducing intraocular pressure, thereby serving as a stepping stone and proof-of-concept for the utility of ROCK inhibitors in ocular disorders. Beyond its approved use in glaucoma, investigations of ROCK inhibitors—including ripasudil—have extended into experimental applications in corneal endothelial regeneration and have been evaluated in combination with anti-VEGF therapies for diabetic macular edema. Although direct clinical evidence specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is not available, multiple lines of preclinical research have shown that the ROCK inhibitor class modulates pathways which are believed to underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Notably, the mechanistic studies have identified the role of ROCK signaling in cytoskeletal reorganization, matrix contractility, and fibrosis, all of which are processes particularly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier dysfunction seen in dry AMD (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Moreover, the ocular pharmacokinetic profile of ripasudil—demonstrated by rabbit intravitreal studies showing a half-life of approximately 14 hours and negligible systemic exposure—is supportive of repurposing this candidate for posterior segment indications, including dry AMD (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ripasudil exerts its therapeutic activity by competitively inhibiting the ATP-binding site of ROCK isoforms, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of downstream effectors such as myosin light-chain (MLC), myosin-binding subunit of MLC phosphatase (MYPT1), and LIM kinase. These phosphorylation events normally lead to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, focal adhesion assembly, and ultimately contribute to a contractile, stiffened cell phenotype. In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, this contractility is thought to be exacerbated under conditions of oxidative stress, contributing to disassembly or mislocalization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity. By inhibiting ROCK, ripasudil reduces actomyosin-driven contraction and stress-fiber formation, thereby promoting cortical F-actin remodeling and facilitating the proper membrane relocalization of tight-junction proteins. The specificity of ripasudil has been demonstrated by its greater than 100-fold selectivity against other kinases such as protein kinase C (PKC) and myotonic dystrophy kinase-related Cdc42-binding kinase (MRCK), highlighting the mechanistic precision by which it modulates ROCK-dependent signaling cascades (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Additionally, while several studies indicate that the ROCK inhibitor class generally targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2 isoforms, quantitative biochemical data have shown that ripasudil exhibits potent enzyme inhibitory activity with IC₅₀s in the low nanomolar range (with values reported around 51 nM for ROCK1 and 19 nM for ROCK2 in some studies, though the candidate hypothesis posits values of approximately 29 nM for ROCK1 and 68 nM for ROCK2). This inhibitory profile is particularly relevant because emerging research indicates that ROCK2, in particular, is upregulated in the pathological conditions of dry AMD and plays a key role in mediating cytoskeletal changes that disrupt RPE tight junction integrity (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). The inhibition of ROCK thereby is expected to have a dual benefit of cytoprotection and restoration of cell junction architecture, ultimately leading to improved barrier function (Ghenciu et al., 2025; Singh & Singh, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing ripasudil for dry AMD is that by blocking ROCK activity in oxidatively stressed retinal pigment epithelium cells, the compound will lead to a reduction in actomyosin contractility, thereby alleviating the formation of pathological stress fibers that otherwise disrupt the organization of tight junction complexes. Under normal physiological conditions, tight junction proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin are localized at the plasma membrane in a continuous, belt-like manner that is essential to maintain TEER and restrict paracellular permeability. However, in dry AMD, oxidative damage, inflammation, and mechanical stress lead to cytoskeletal reorganization and a discontinuous distribution of these critical proteins, resulting in impaired barrier function and contributing to the pathogenesis of the disease. Preclinical studies, particularly those employing ARPE-19 cell models subjected to toxic insults such as paraquat or sodium iodate (NaIO₃), have demonstrated that ROCK inhibitors can dose-dependently restore TEER (with reported improvements up to 70%) and re-establish the membrane continuity of ZO-1, suggesting that these agents can “rescue” the RPE barrier phenotype under injurious conditions (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). It is expected that ripasudil, with its potent ROCK-inhibitory activity and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics (including intravitreal retention times supportive of sustained action), will similarly promote the cortical redistribution of F-actin, leading to the re-localization of junctional molecules back to the cell membrane. This mechanistic restoration should result in improved transepithelial electrical resistance and a concomitant reduction in paracellular permeability, effectively reinforcing the RPE barrier—a central therapeutic target in dry AMD. Moreover, the activation of protective cellular pathways through ROCK inhibition may also confer additional anti-apoptotic and anti-inflammatory effects, further contributing to the survival and functional integrity of the RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating ripasudil as a candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths become apparent. First, its established clinical use for glaucoma means that its safety, tolerability, and ocular pharmacokinetic properties are well characterized—attributes that significantly lower the translational barrier for its application in other ocular diseases. The intravitreal pharmacokinetic data, with a half-life of approximately 14 hours in rabbit models and negligible systemic exposure, suggest that therapeutic concentrations capable of modulating ROCK activity in the retina can be achieved with acceptable dosing regimens (Yamaguchi et al., 2016). Second, the mechanistic rationale is compelling: ROCK signaling is intimately involved in mediating actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, and subsequent disruption of tight junction architecture in epithelial cells. Given that ROCK2 in particular is implicated in the pathological processes observed in the RPE in dry AMD, the ability of ripasudil to inhibit this pathway could translate into measurable improvements in barrier function, as indicated by preclinical assays demonstrating TEER restoration and the re-localization of ZO-1 in ARPE-19 cells (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Third, the compound exhibits a favorable selectivity profile, with negligible off-target activity against other kinases such as PKC and MRCK, which minimizes the risk of unintended effects in non-target tissues. This specificity is critical when repurposing drugs for chronic conditions such as dry AMD, where long-term ocular safety is paramount (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Despite these strengths, there are notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before ripasudil can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. A primary limitation is the paucity of direct experimental evidence in RPE models of dry AMD. While the hypothesis is supported by data from related in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative stress), robust in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of dry AMD pathophysiology are still needed. In particular, data demonstrating that ripasudil can restore tight junction integrity and improve TEER in the context of chronic, progressive RPE dysfunction remain limited (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Furthermore, although the compound’s ROCK inhibitory activity is well documented, the available literature does not consistently detail the isoform-specific effects in RPE cells; given that ROCK1 and ROCK2 may play distinct roles in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, clarifying the relative contributions of each isoform is essential. The candidate hypothesis posits specific IC₅₀ values for ROCK1 and ROCK2, yet discrepancies exist across reported studies regarding the precise inhibitory concentrations, which indicates that further biochemical characterization is warranted (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). Another consideration is the potential for adverse effects when repurposing a drug originally optimized for anterior-segment diseases for posterior-segment applications. Although the ocular safety profile of ripasudil in glaucoma is well established, the long-term impact of ROCK inhibition on RPE cell biology in an aged population—especially in the context of dry AMD—remains uncertain. Off-target cytoskeletal effects in other retinal cell types, possible modulation of inflammatory responses, and the risk of inadvertently triggering compensatory signaling pathways are all factors that must be carefully evaluated in preclinical studies (Iancu et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2025). Lastly, while the pharmacokinetic data support retinal exposure after intravitreal or possibly topical administration, optimizing the delivery method to ensure sustained and localized drug levels in the RPE without causing ocular surface toxicity (such as conjunctival hyperemia or corneal epithelial disturbances) will be critical. Innovative delivery systems, such as sustained-release intravitreal implants or depot formulations, may offer solutions but require further development (Yamaguchi et al., 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023).

In conclusion, the repurposing of ripasudil for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and a favorable safety profile derived from its established use in glaucoma. The compound’s capacity to inhibit ROCK-mediated actomyosin contraction and promote cortical F-actin remodeling positions it as a promising agent for restoring RPE barrier function—one of the key pathological features of dry AMD. However, the current literature reveals significant gaps in direct evidence regarding its effects on RPE tight junction proteins, TEER restoration, and the isoform-specific roles of ROCK in the RPE under oxidative stress. To advance ripasudil as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, additional preclinical investigations—ideally incorporating robust animal models of dry AMD and detailed biochemical analyses of ROCK isoform activity in RPE cells—are required. Additionally, optimizations in drug delivery methodology to achieve sustained posterior-segment exposure while minimizing adverse ocular events will be imperative. Overall, ripasudil presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, with its strengths in mechanistic specificity, favorable ocular pharmacokinetics, and established clinical safety underscoring its potential. Nonetheless, the outlined weaknesses and knowledge gaps necessitate a rigorous program of targeted research to validate its efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity and to ensure its long-term safety in the intended patient population (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023; Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Adams & Papillon, 2020; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of TTA‐P2 as a repurposed candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD):

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
TTA‐P2 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed to target T‐type voltage‐gated calcium channels (VGCCs), which belong to the CaV3 family (CaV3.1, CaV3.2, CaV3.3). Its chemical structure, described as 3,5‐dichloro-N-[1-(2,2-dimethyl-tetrahydro-pyran-4-ylmethyl)-4-fluoro-piperidin-4-ylmethyl]-benzamide, was established via medicinal chemistry optimization strategies aimed at increasing potency and selectivity for the T‐type channels relative to high-voltage-activated channels (Choe et al., 2011). Originally discovered and characterized in the context of neuronal excitability studies, TTA‐P2 has been shown to block T‐type calcium currents in rat sensory neurons with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range; this high potency is matched by an excellent selectivity profile given that its inhibitory concentration for high-voltage-activated channels is orders of magnitude higher (Choe et al., 2011). As a member of the T‐type calcium channel blocker class, TTA‐P2 is representative of compounds that modulate low-voltage-activated channels involved in a variety of cell functions, ranging from neuronal burst firing to hormone release. In the context of drug development, this compound is categorized as a channel-modulating agent, and its synthetic origins as a small molecule rendered it amenable to structural modification for improved pharmacokinetics in various tissue systems (Choe et al., 2011). Although historically used primarily in neuronal studies, its inherent properties have prompted consideration of its repurposing for non-neuronal tissues, such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where T‐type channels have been shown to contribute to key physiological processes (Jazouli, 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TTA‐P2 has been investigated in the context of neuropathic pain and epilepsy, where T‐type calcium channels are integral to the regulation of neuronal excitability. In experimental models involving rat sensory neurons, TTA‐P2 demonstrated marked antinociceptive properties and produced significant reductions in neuronal burst firing by selectively blocking T‐type calcium currents (Choe et al., 2011). This evidence underlines the compound’s effectiveness in modulating calcium influx in hyperexcitable systems. Beyond its neurological applications, there have been several studies in which compounds targeting T‐type CaV channels were applied to non-neuronal cells. For instance, work in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) demonstrated that T‐type calcium channels are expressed and functionally important in these cells, although in those studies a different inhibitor—TTA‐A2—was used to evaluate effects on phagocytosis and VEGF secretion (Jazouli, 2022). Moreover, complementary work in RPE models has noted that T‐type channels appear to localize specifically to the apical membrane, with subtypes such as CaV3.1 and CaV3.3 being especially prominent (Jazouli, 2022). Despite extensive preclinical work in neuronal systems, there is no published record, to our knowledge, that TTA‐P2 has been tested directly in AMD or other ocular disease models. However, evidence gleaned from cerebral endothelia studies—where inhibition of CaV3.1/CaV3.2 ameliorates inflammatory barrier disruption—suggests that a similar strategy may be beneficial in preserving the function of the RPE barrier (Unknown Reference). Thus, while TTA‐P2 has a well-established history in neurological studies, its repurposing for dry AMD is based on the emerging understanding that T‐type channels contribute to RPE function and that their inhibition may counter inflammatory and degenerative signals (Jazouli, 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism by which TTA‐P2 exerts its effects is through selective inhibition of T‐type calcium channels. Detailed electrophysiological studies in rat sensory neurons have shown that TTA‐P2 binds preferentially to the inactivated state of these channels, thereby stabilizing them in a non-conducting conformation. This binding results in a significant hyperpolarizing shift (approximately 20 mV) in the steady-state inactivation curves and an incomplete recovery from inactivation, meaning that the channels remain non-functional for a longer period after brief depolarizations (Choe et al., 2011). Such effects effectively reduce the calcium influx that would normally occur during depolarization-driven events. In RPE cells, there is a body of evidence indicating that T‐type calcium channels (particularly CaV3.1 and CaV3.3) contribute to the formation of localized Ca²⁺ microdomains that play a role in regulating tight junction dynamics (Jazouli, 2022). Under inflammatory conditions—such as those induced by TNF-α or complement activation—excessive Ca²⁺ influx via these channels may trigger signaling cascades that lead to the disassembly of adherens junctions and tight junctions, ultimately compromising the integrity of the epithelial barrier. TTA‐P2’s ability to suppress the T‐type currents would, therefore, limit the depolarization-driven Ca²⁺ microdomain formation in RPE cells (Choe et al., 2011). In addition, the selective binding to the inactivated state minimizes off-target effects on channels that have higher activation thresholds, such as L-type channels, thereby preserving other essential calcium-dependent processes. The blockade of T‐type channels is particularly relevant because these channels typically open at more negative membrane potentials, a regime that is critical for maintaining the delicate Ca²⁺ balance in nonexcitable cells such as the RPE (Choe et al., 2011; Jazouli, 2022). Consequently, by dampening the Ca²⁺ entry through these channels, TTA‐P2 could play a protective role against inflammation-induced barrier disruption.

Expected Effect:  
According to the proposal, the central hypothesis is that a pan–T‐type CaV blockade by TTA‐P2 (with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, here cited as approximately 20 nM) will suppress the formation of harmful Ca²⁺ microdomains in RPE cells, thereby preventing the downstream signaling events that lead to the disassembly of tight junctions. The integrity of RPE monolayers is often assessed by measurements such as transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and permeability assays (e.g., FITC-dextran flux). In the presence of inflammatory insults like TNF-α or complement factors—both of which can mimic some of the pathophysiological aspects of dry AMD—the excessive calcium influx through T‐type channels may cause rearrangement or breakdown of tight junction proteins (such as occludin and claudins), leading to compromised barrier function and increased paracellular permeability (Jazouli, 2022).  
By inhibiting these channels, TTA‐P2 is expected to reduce intracellular Ca²⁺ accumulation that drives disassembly of junctional complexes, thereby restoring normal TEER values and reducing the passage of molecules like FITC-dextran across the RPE monolayer. Patch-clamp studies would further validate that TTA‐P2 effectively suppresses the T‐type Ca²⁺ currents in these cells, reinforcing the direct link between calcium channel inhibition and improved barrier integrity (Choe et al., 2011). Moreover, considering that similar principles have been applied in cerebral endothelial models—where T‐type channel inhibition reduced inflammatory barrier disruption—it is plausible that the RPE, which shares some functional similarities as a barrier tissue, may respond in a comparable manner (Korkka, n.d.). It is also important to note that the expression of CaV3.1 and CaV3.3 in RPE cells has been confirmed by immunolabeling and electrophysiological studies, thereby providing a direct anatomical and functional basis for this therapeutic approach (Jazouli, 2022). This expected effect of preserving tight junction integrity makes TTA‐P2 an attractive candidate for therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction and barrier breakdown contribute to disease progression.

Overall Evaluation:  
TTA‐P2 offers several compelling strengths as a potential repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, its high potency and selectivity for T‐type calcium channels have been robustly demonstrated in neuronal systems, and these properties bode well for achieving effective inhibition in RPE cells, where even relatively minor shifts in calcium homeostasis may have significant pathophysiological implications (Choe et al., 2011). Second, the strategy of targeting T‐type channels in the RPE is grounded in evidence that these channels are involved in channel-mediated inflammatory responses and barrier disruption, processes known to play a key role in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Jazouli, 2022). Third, TTA‐P2 works through a mechanism that is distinct from conventional anti-inflammatory agents or anti-VEGF therapies; instead, it modulates a very early step in the cascade—namely, the depolarization-driven Ca²⁺ entry that acts as a trigger for tight junction disassembly. This novel mechanism, if validated, could complement existing therapies or offer a new avenue for intervention in cases where traditional therapeutics have limited efficacy.  

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be acknowledged. Foremost among these is the fact that, to date, no direct studies have been published demonstrating the efficacy of TTA‐P2 in RPE cells or in animal models of dry AMD. The majority of the literature supporting its use comes from neurological applications, and although there are analogous studies in RPE using other T‐type channel blockers (e.g., TTA‐A2), the extrapolation of neuronal pharmacodynamics to ocular tissues is not guaranteed (Jazouli, 2022). Furthermore, it is well recognized that T‐type channels in the RPE also play roles in physiological processes such as phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and the regulation of growth factor secretion (Jazouli, 2022). Thus, chronic inhibition of these channels could potentially disrupt normal RPE function if not properly dosed or targeted, leading to adverse effects that may offset the benefits of barrier preservation. Additionally, the therapeutic index of TTA‐P2 in the ocular milieu remains unknown. While its selectivity in neuronal tissues suggests that off-target effects might be limited, the unique environment of the retina—characterized by tightly regulated ionic gradients and specialized cell–cell interactions—could render RPE cells more sensitive to perturbations in calcium signaling (Jazouli, 2022).  

Another issue that warrants consideration is the delivery of TTA‐P2 to the RPE. The retina poses several pharmacokinetic challenges due to its blood-retina barrier; hence, any candidate must be capable of penetrating ocular tissues effectively, achieving therapeutic concentrations in the RPE while minimizing systemic exposure. While there are established methods for ocular drug delivery, such as intravitreal injections or topical formulations, the physicochemical properties of TTA‐P2 will need careful evaluation in this context. Additionally, given that the proposed mechanism involves modulating rapid Ca²⁺ microdomains, the temporal dynamics of channel blockade versus normal calcium signaling must be precisely controlled. If TTA‐P2 alters RPE calcium homeostasis too profoundly or indiscriminately, it might interfere with essential cellular processes, including phagocytosis, which is critical for retinal maintenance and health (Jazouli, 2022).  

Safety considerations are also paramount. T‐type calcium channels are expressed in multiple tissues, and systemic administration of a potent blocker like TTA‐P2 could lead to unintended side effects in other organ systems, particularly in the cardiovascular and central nervous systems. Although the ocular route of administration could mitigate these systemic effects, the risk of local toxicity and potential interference with normal retinal signaling remains. In summary, while the mechanistic rationale for using TTA‐P2 as a barrier-preserving agent in dry AMD is scientifically sound and innovative, considerable preclinical work is required. This would ideally include comprehensive studies in RPE monolayer models under inflammatory conditions to quantitatively assess TEER restoration and junctional protein preservation, as well as in vivo models of dry AMD to evaluate functional and structural outcomes following TTA‐P2 treatment.

In conclusion, TTA‐P2 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its high potency and selectivity for T‐type calcium channels, coupled with its novel mechanism—stabilizing the inactivated state of these channels and thereby reducing deleterious Ca²⁺ microdomain formation—provide a strong rationale for further investigation (Choe et al., 2011). The hypothesis that such blockade can prevent inflammatory insult-induced tight junction disassembly in RPE cells is supported by observations in both neuronal systems and studies of RPE channel expression (Jazouli, 2022). Nevertheless, gaps remain in our direct understanding of how TTA‐P2 behaves in ocular tissues, and careful evaluation of its impact on essential RPE functions—such as phagocytosis and growth factor secretion—is crucial. Safety, ocular bioavailability, and potential off-target effects are also significant areas for investigation. Overall, while TTA‐P2’s repurposing for dry AMD is still in the exploratory phase, its unique targeting of Ca²⁺ entry and potential to restore barrier integrity make it a compelling candidate that merits further preclinical validation.

Given these considerations, the next steps should include:  
1. In vitro studies using hiPSC-derived RPE cultures subjected to TNF-α or complement challenge, with detailed monitoring of TEER, FITC-dextran permeability, and tight junction protein localization following TTA‐P2 treatment.  
2. Electrophysiological recordings (patch clamp) to verify effective suppression of T‐type channel currents in RPE under both basal and inflammatory conditions, comparing TTA‐P2 with other established blockers (e.g., TTA‐A2) as controls.  
3. In vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD to assess not only RPE barrier function and retinal morphology but also functional visual outcomes after local (intravitreal) administration of TTA‐P2.  
4. Pharmacokinetic and safety evaluations specifically tailored for ocular delivery, to ascertain the optimal dosing regimen that maximizes local efficacy without compromising systemic or retinal cell functions.

Strengths of TTA‐P2 include its well-documented biophysical potency and specificity (Choe et al., 2011); its proposed mechanism, which innovatively focuses on modulating an early, calcium-dependent step in the cascade leading to barrier breakdown; and its potential to synergize with or complement existing therapies for AMD that have primarily targeted angiogenesis or inflammation by offering a strategy focused on preserving RPE junctional integrity (Jazouli, 2022). Weaknesses include the current lack of direct data in RPE or AMD models, potential adverse effects on other RPE functions (such as phagocytosis and growth factor secretion), challenges in ocular drug delivery, and the possibility of off-target effects given the ubiquitous expression of T‐type channels in various tissues (Jazouli, 2022).

Overall, while there is promising scientific rationale behind the use of TTA‐P2 for protecting RPE barrier function under inflammatory conditions reminiscent of dry AMD, the candidate remains at an early repurposing stage. The transition from successful neuronal applications to effective retinal therapies requires extensive adaptation and validation. However, if its efficacy and safety can be confirmed in detailed RPE and in vivo AMD models, TTA‐P2 could emerge as a novel therapeutic tool addressing an unmet clinical need in dry AMD. In summary, TTA‐P2’s mechanism of action—based on precise, state-dependent inhibition of T-type Ca²⁺ channels—coupled with its potential to stabilize RPE tight junctions under pathogenic stress, positions it as an exciting candidate for further investigation in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (Choe et al., 2011; Jazouli, 2022).

This evaluation suggests that while the candidate has substantial merit and promise, the lack of direct preclinical evidence in RPE models means that a dedicated series of studies (both in vitro and in vivo) will be essential before moving toward clinical trials. The potential for TTA‐P2 to fill a therapeutic gap by directly targeting Ca²⁺ entry and preserving RPE barrier function provides a unique and fresh mechanism compared with existing treatments, but its ultimate success will depend on how well these preclinical models predict efficacy and safety in patients with dry AMD.
