Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
5‐Azacytidine is a synthetically produced nucleoside analogue of cytidine originally derived by chemical modification of the natural ribonucleoside. In 5‐azacytidine the normal carbon atom at the 5‐position of the pyrimidine ring is replaced with a nitrogen atom, a modification that critically alters its biochemical properties. This compound is classified as an azanucleoside and has been widely studied as a DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) inhibitor. Its discovery and subsequent synthesis have enabled researchers to interrogate the role of DNA methylation in gene regulation. In its typical biological usage, after cellular uptake mediated by nucleoside transporters, 5‐azacytidine is phosphorylated by cellular kinases into its active triphosphate form (5‐aza‐CTP) and can become incorporated into RNA as well as into DNA, although only around 10–20% is converted to the deoxyribonucleotide form prior to DNA incorporation. This unique feature is a double‐edged sword: on one hand, it allows modulation of cytosine methylation patterns within genomic DNA by trapping DNMTs; on the other, its incorporation into RNA can perturb protein synthesis and contributes to its cytotoxic profile. Chemically, its structure and mode of synthesis place it within a well‐characterized class of antimetabolite agents whose utility extends beyond oncology into other fields where epigenetic modifications are implicated (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, 5‐azacytidine and its deoxy analogue 5‐aza‐2′‐deoxycytidine (decitabine) were first developed as antimetabolite chemotherapy agents for hematologic malignancies. Their clinical utility in treating conditions such as myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) is well established, with DNA demethylation and tumor suppressor gene reactivation being central to their antineoplastic efficacy. Over the years, the successful repurposing of these nucleoside analogues has led to extensive studies investigating their potential effects beyond oncology. In cancer cells, the irreversible binding of DNMT enzymes to DNA following incorporation of 5‐azacytidine has been shown to produce passive demethylation during cell division and consequent gene reactivation (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). In more recent years, researchers have begun to consider the roles of aberrant DNA methylation in non‐cancer diseases, including ocular pathologies like age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). Reviews in ocular epigenetics have noted that epigenetic dysregulation, including hypermethylation of promoters for antioxidant enzymes and other protective genes, may contribute to RPE dysfunction in AMD (Li et al., 2020). For instance, studies in cultured RPE cells and AMD cybrid models have observed tolerability of DNMT inhibitors, as exemplified by experiments where polarized RPE monolayers treated with 5‐aza‐2′‐deoxycytidine showed no significant disruption in barrier markers such as ZO‐1 or cytokeratin, and even demonstrated gene reactivation effects such as upregulation of clusterin (Li et al., 2020). Although 5‐azacytidine itself has not been as widely evaluated in ocular models as decitabine, the extensive biochemical literature surrounding its DNMT inhibitory properties forms a strong rationale for its potential repurposing toward dry AMD via epigenetic modulation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, 5‐azacytidine exerts its pharmacologic actions primarily through inhibition of DNMT enzymes. Under normal physiological conditions, DNMT enzymes bind to cytosine residues in CpG dinucleotides and catalyze the transfer of a methyl group from S‐adenosyl-L‐methionine (SAM) to the 5‐position carbon of cytosine, a process that is essential for the maintenance of epigenetic patterns and gene silencing. However, the substitution of nitrogen at the C5 position in 5‐azacytidine disrupts this process because the reaction mechanism relies on a β‐elimination step that cannot occur when a nitrogen is present instead of a carbon. Consequently, when 5‐azacytidine is incorporated into the DNA of replicating cells, DNMT enzymes – particularly the maintenance methyltransferase DNMT1 – are unable to complete the methylation reaction and become covalently trapped at the site of incorporation (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). This irreversible trapping inhibits the recycling of DNMTs and leads to their proteasomal degradation, thus reducing the cellular pool of active DNMT enzymes. In subsequent rounds of DNA replication, the absence of sufficient DNMT activity results in passive demethylation of newly synthesized DNA strands that fail to be remethylated. This epigenetic reprogramming can lead to reactivation of genes with previously hypermethylated and silenced promoters (Cheishvili et al., 2015; Palii et al., 2008). It is important to note that 5‐azacytidine is also incorporated into RNA, where it may inhibit RNA methylation and alter translation; however, the therapeutic emphasis in the context of reactivating silenced genes typically focuses on its DNA‐mediated effects. In the specific context of the proposed therapeutic strategy, oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is hypothesized to promote the aberrant recruitment of DNMT1 and DNMT3A to the promoters of tight junction genes such as OCLN and TJP1, thereby silencing them via hypermethylation. The administration of 5‐azacytidine is expected to reverse this process by demethylating these promoter regions through the above‐described DNMT trapping mechanism, ultimately leading to the reactivation of occludin and ZO‐1 expression (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014; Mukhtar, 2020). Although the majority of experimental evidence in the literature focuses on gene reactivation in oncologic contexts, the fundamental biochemical interactions remain the same in any dividing cell type where DNA replication permits incorporation of the analogue. Additionally, although RPE cells in vivo are relatively quiescent compared to rapidly dividing cancer cells, in vitro models such as ARPE-19, particularly under oxidative challenge, can exhibit increased proliferation and epigenetic plasticity, thereby providing an opportunity to evaluate the mechanism in the context of barrier dysfunction (Li et al., 2020; Sarkisjan et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis of the proposed therapeutic strategy is that under conditions of oxidative stress, DNMT enzymes are aberrantly recruited to the promoters of genes critical for tight junction integrity – specifically occludin (OCLN) and ZO-1 (TJP1) – resulting in their hypermethylation and subsequent transcriptional repression. This diminished expression of tight junction proteins compromises the barrier function of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), leading to decreased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased FITC-dextran permeability. It is expected that a treatment with 1 µM 5‐azacytidine will inhibit DNMT activity in these stressed RPE cells, specifically by demethylating the promoters of OCLN and TJP1. As the promoter regions are demethylated, transcription of OCLN and TJP1 is anticipated to resume, thereby restoring the synthesis and proper cellular localization of occludin and the ZO-1 protein. This re-expression is predicted to facilitate the re‐assembly of tight junction complexes at the plasma membrane of RPE cells, culminating in a recovery of barrier properties measurable as an increase in TEER and a reduction in paracellular permeability as evidenced by decreased FITC-dextran flux (Christman, 2002; Palii et al., 2008; Li et al., 2020). There is supporting evidence in related experimental studies wherein treatment of polarized RPE monolayers with DNMT inhibitors—albeit using 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine in some cases—did not disturb baseline tight junction markers such as ZO-1 and cytokeratin, and even induced the expression of epigenetically silenced protective genes like clusterin (Li et al., 2020). Although direct demonstration of OCLN and TJP1 promoter demethylation by 5‐azacytidine in RPE under oxidative stress is not yet available, analogous results in other epithelial contexts provide a strong mechanistic rationale. Moreover, the dual activity of the drug – both its canonical demethylating effect and its potential to perturb RNA methylation – may synergize to enhance transcriptional reactivation if balanced appropriately with a low, non‐cytotoxic concentration such as 1 µM (Seelan et al., 2018; Cheishvili et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
The prospect of repurposing 5‐azacytidine for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) represents a novel and intriguing approach that leverages well‐established principles in epigenetic regulation. On the strength side, the compound’s mechanism of action is thoroughly documented across multiple biomedical studies and is centered on the irreversible trapping and degradation of DNMT enzymes, leading to passive loss of DNA methylation in replicating cells (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). This mechanism has been exploited with success in oncology to reactivate silenced tumor suppressor genes, suggesting that similar reactivation of critical genes in non‐cancerous cells might also be achievable. The specific hypothesis that oxidative stress in RPE leads to the epigenetic silencing of tight junction genes such as OCLN and TJP1 is plausible given the known role of DNMT enzymes in mediating gene repression under stress conditions, and the literature supports the concept that DNA methylation is a dynamic and reversible process that can be modulated pharmacologically (Li et al., 2020). Preliminary in vitro findings in RPE monolayer models with DNMT inhibitors, particularly the tolerability of these compounds and their capacity to upregulate epigenetically silenced genes (as seen with clusterin expression), bolster the argument that DNMT inhibition in RPE is not inherently deleterious and may indeed rectify dysfunction in barrier integrity (Li et al., 2020).

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be recognized. First, 5‐azacytidine is known to incorporate into RNA as well as DNA, which introduces additional layers of complexity in its mode of action. The off‐target effects on RNA methylation can lead to perturbations in protein synthesis and may result in unintended consequences, especially given the highly specialized function of RPE cells in the retina (Jasielec et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2010). Second, the S-phase dependency of the drug’s mechanism—requiring active DNA replication for incorporation—poses a potential limitation when considering that in vivo RPE cells are largely quiescent. While in vitro ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress may show increased proliferative activity, the translation of these findings to an in vivo dry AMD setting remains uncertain. Third, the global demethylation induced by 5‐azacytidine does not confer gene specificity; hence, there is a risk that while reactivating tight junction genes, the drug might also inadvertently activate promoters of deleterious genes or provoke inflammatory responses. This lack of precision could compromise retinal homeostasis or even exacerbate pathological processes if not carefully controlled (Mukhtar, 2020; Cheishvili et al., 2015). Fourth, toxicity is a major concern. While lower doses (such as 1 µM) are proposed to achieve a favorable balance between hypomethylation and cytotoxicity, the narrow therapeutic window observed in oncology suggests that careful titration and extensive in vitro and in vivo safety studies are essential before progressing to clinical evaluation in AMD (Christman, 2002; Daifuku, 2025).

Additional challenges include the need for direct experimental evidence to support the specific hypothesis relating to tight junction reactivation. Although the general effects of DNMT inhibitors in reactivating silenced genes are well documented, there is currently insufficient evidence demonstrating that 5-azacytidine directly demethylates the promoters of OCLN and TJP1 in RPE cells subjected to oxidative stress. Moreover, evaluations of barrier function—such as detailed TEER measurements or FITC-dextran permeability assays—have been more commonly reported in the context of other DNMT inhibitors such as 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine rather than 5-azacytidine per se (Li et al., 2020). Therefore, a critical gap remains in validating whether the proposed epigenetic precision approach can indeed restore tight junction integrity in a physiologically relevant model of dry AMD.

Despite these concerns, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. The robust and well‐understood mechanism of 5‐azacytidine in inducing DNA demethylation provides a solid theoretical basis for the proposed therapeutic strategy. Given that similar epigenetic interventions have successfully reactivated gene expression in other cellular contexts, and considering that preliminary data in RPE systems suggest tolerability and potential gene reactivation, it is reasonable to propose that further investigation is warranted. Initial preclinical studies should focus on establishing the methylation status of the OCLN and TJP1 promoters in RPE cells under oxidative stress and then determine whether 5‐azacytidine treatment can effectively reverse these modifications. Comprehensive analyses including methylation-specific polymerase chain reaction (MSP), chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays for DNMT occupancy, and detailed transcriptional profiling would be essential to confirm target engagement. Parallel functional assays, such as TEER measurements and FITC-dextran permeability assays, must be undertaken to correlate molecular events with phenotypic restoration of barrier function (Mukhtar, 2020; Daifuku, 2025).

In addition, it would be prudent to perform dose–response studies to delineate the optimal concentration of 5‐azacytidine that maximizes promoter demethylation and gene reactivation while minimizing off-target cytotoxicity. Considering that RPE cells in vitro may exhibit different proliferative rates compared to their in vivo counterparts, alternative experimental models, such as induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells from AMD patients, may provide additional insights into the therapeutic window and efficacy of 5‐azacytidine in a clinically relevant context. Finally, given that the global nature of epigenetic reprogramming may lead to unintended activation of other cellular pathways, combination strategies employing lower doses of 5‐azacytidine alongside more targeted epigenetic modulators—such as selective HDAC inhibitors—could be explored to enhance the specificity of gene reactivation and improve overall retinal safety (Li et al., 2020; Nashine & Kenney, 2020).

In summary, 5‐azacytidine represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD through a novel epigenetic precision approach aimed at reversing the aberrant methylation of tight junction gene promoters. Its well‐characterized mechanism of DNMT inhibition and widespread use in oncology offer a strong biological rationale. However, significant challenges remain, including its non‐selective incorporation into nucleic acids, potential off‐target effects, reliance on cellular proliferation for optimal activity, and a narrow therapeutic index that necessitates rigorous dose optimization. The feasibility of restoring tight junction integrity in RPE cells via demethylation of OCLN and TJP1 promoters is theoretically sound yet awaits empirical confirmation in preclinical AMD models. Overall, while the candidate has substantial mechanistic strengths that support its potential role in restoring RPE barrier function under oxidative stress conditions, its development as a treatment for dry AMD will require detailed molecular and functional validations, careful safety profiling, and perhaps the exploration of combination therapies to harness its benefits while mitigating risks (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020; Daifuku, 2025).

I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SMER28 is a small‐molecule enhancer of autophagy originally identified through high‐throughput chemical screens designed to activate intracellular clearance pathways. It is chemically characterized as a bromo‐substituted quinazoline and belongs to a series of “SMER” compounds initially disclosed by leading research institutions to augment autophagy independently of mTOR signaling (Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013; Sarkar & Rubinsztein, 2008). The synthesis of SMER28 has been streamlined into a three‐step process using accessible reagents such as 2-amino-5-bromobenzoic acid and 1,1′-carbonyldiimidazole (CDI), facilitating its large-scale preparation without requiring extensive purification of intermediates (Koukourakis et al., 2018). Originally, SMER28 was discovered during efforts to identify compounds that could promote autophagy and protein clearance, a focus that later expanded its potential use to diseases characterized by proteostatic stress. Its structure–activity relationships and ease of synthesis render SMER28 an attractive candidate for drug repurposing strategies beyond its initial applications, particularly in diseases where defective autophagy contributes to pathogenesis. This candidate’s established role in enhancing cellular clearance mechanisms positions it well for evaluation in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a condition marked by impaired removal of misfolded proteins and lipids in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Doulatov et al., 2017; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013).

II. Therapeutic History  
SMER28 has an extensive preclinical history that underscores its potential for broad therapeutic applications. In initial studies focused on Diamond-Blackfan Anemia (DBA), SMER28 was shown to promote erythropoiesis and enhance hemoglobin expression in both in vitro systems and zebrafish models of DBA, where ribosomal protein mutations lead to anemia-like phenotypes (Doulatov et al., 2017). These findings indicated that SMER28 could effectively modulate cellular differentiation and survival pathways in stressed cell populations. Subsequent investigations expanded its evaluation to radioprotection, where SMER28 demonstrated protective effects in mouse bone marrow and liver tissues subjected to irradiation. These studies revealed that SMER28’s activation of autophagy could preserve normal tissue architecture and improve recovery after cellular injury (Koukourakis et al., 2018). Furthermore, in models of neurodegenerative diseases, SMER28 has been implicated in enhancing both autophagic and proteasomal clearance mechanisms to reduce the burden of misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins such as mutant huntingtin and polyQ-expanded proteins (Wrobel, Hill, & Rubinsztein, 2023). Although none of these prior studies were conducted directly in ocular tissues, their outcomes suggest that the underlying mechanism of SMER28—enhancement of the intracellular degradation machinery—is broadly applicable. Given that the RPE in dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and lipid deposits due to defective autophagy (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021), repurposing SMER28 for dry AMD addresses a significant disease mechanism while potentially leveraging its established safety and efficacy in other systems.

III. Mechanism of Action  
SMER28’s mechanism of action is defined by its ability to induce autophagy in an mTOR-independent manner—a key advantage over conventional autophagy modulators that act via mTOR inhibition. At the molecular level, SMER28 binds directly to the Valosin Containing Protein (VCP/p97), an essential chaperone involved in protein quality control and degradation pathways (Wrobel et al., 2022). This binding stabilizes VCP and stimulates its D1 ATPase activity, thereby enhancing both the formation and maturation of autophagosomes. An increase in VCP activity is known to promote the formation of phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI(3)P), a lipid mediator critical for the nucleation of autophagic vesicles (Wrobel et al., 2022). Downstream of PI(3)P production, the assembly of the lipidation machinery—including LC3, a ubiquitin-like protein requisite for autophagosome elongation—is enhanced, as indicated by increased LC3-II formation in cells treated with SMER28 (Wrobel et al., 2022).

Simultaneously, SMER28’s action is dependent on Beclin 1, whose involvement in autophagy initiation further supports the autophagic flux observed upon treatment (Wrobel et al., 2022). Importantly, these effects are achieved without a detectable alteration in the downstream effectors of mTOR signaling; measurements of AKT activation and other mTOR-related pathways remain unaffected, affirming the compound’s mTOR-independent operation (Wrobel et al., 2022; Koukourakis et al., 2018). In parallel, the compound also appears to enhance the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), an additional degradation pathway, in a manner that is similarly VCP-dependent (Wrobel, Hill, & Rubinsztein, 2023). The convergence of autophagy and UPS pathways is particularly relevant in cellular systems where proteostasis is compromised.

While there is robust evidence supporting the activation of autophagic flux via VCP and Beclin 1, the specific hypothesis for dry AMD posits that SMER28 may also engage ULK1-dependent autophagy mechanisms. ULK1 (UNC-51-like kinase 1) is a serine/threonine kinase upstream in the autophagy cascade that integrates stress signals to initiate autophagy, and genetic ablation of ULK1 or ATG5 has been shown to replicate RPE barrier defects (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015). However, the current literature does not provide direct evidence linking SMER28 with ULK1 activation; rather, the bulk of mechanistic data implicates the compound in VCP-mediated processes (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013). Despite this gap, the overall mode of action—enhancing autophagic and proteasomal clearance pathways while bypassing mTOR—remains firmly established. Thus, SMER28 targets a network of molecular interactions, pivoting on the modulation of VCP’s activity, increased PI(3)P production, and subsequent LC3 lipidation, all of which consolidate its role as an effective autophagy inducer (Wrobel et al., 2022).

IV. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of SMER28 in dry AMD is that its administration will lead to activation of autophagy in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, thereby promoting the clearance of accumulated lipids and misfolded proteins at cell–cell contacts. In dry AMD, the RPE exhibits dysfunctional autophagy, which contributes to the accumulation of toxic compounds such as A2E—a lipofuscin precursor known to induce oxidative stress and compromise cellular architecture (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014). By facilitating the removal of these deleterious aggregates, SMER28 is expected to alleviate proteostatic and lipotoxic stress within the RPE.

Although most studies elucidating SMER28’s effects have been performed in non-ocular systems, the mechanistic insights gained can be extrapolated to the RPE environment. Specifically, SMER28’s ability to increase LC3 lipidation and enhance autophagic flux—as evidenced by changes in LC3-II levels and Beclin 1 dependency—offers a promising strategy for reducing intracellular lipid droplets and misfolded protein aggregates (Wrobel et al., 2022). This improved clearance should, in turn, restore proper intracellular communication and protein homeostasis near cell–cell junctions.

A critical consequence of this process is the anticipated reassembly of tight junction proteins, particularly ZO-1 and occludin. These proteins are essential for maintaining barrier integrity in the RPE, and their disassembly under stress conditions leads to a decrease in trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a surrogate marker for barrier function (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015). By reducing the cellular burden of lipid and protein aggregates, SMER28 may enable the reformation of ZO-1 and occludin belts at cell–cell contacts, thereby improving TEER. Although direct measurements of ZO-1 and occludin reassembly following SMER28 treatment have not been detailed in the existing literature, analogous improvements in tight junction morphology have been observed in other proteostatic and neurodegenerative models where SMER28 enhanced cellular protein clearance (Wrobel, Hill, & Rubinsztein, 2023).

Furthermore, SMER28’s mTOR-independent nature is expected to confer a selective therapeutic advantage. Unlike mTOR inhibitors, which often exert widespread metabolic effects that could be harmful in chronic conditions, SMER28’s mechanism minimizes the risk of systemic side effects while still promoting the clearance of pathogenic intracellular substrates (Wrobel et al., 2022). In the proposed assay, RPE cells challenged with A2E or other proteostatic stressors would ideally show increased markers of autophagy (e.g., LC3-II accumulation, reduced p62 levels) alongside functional restoration of barrier properties as measured by TEER assays. The improvement in barrier integrity is expected to reflect not only the biochemical clearance of toxic aggregates but also structural reorganization at intercellular junctions—a dual benefit that addresses key pathogenic features of dry AMD (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021).

Additionally, the genetic correlations drawn from studies where knockdown of crucial autophagy regulators such as ULK1 or ATG5 leads to RPE barrier defects further support the notion that pharmacological enhancement of autophagy may reverse such phenotypes. Although direct evidence linking SMER28 with ULK1 activation in RPE cells is sparse, the overall strategy of boosting autophagic flux to restore cellular homeostasis remains compelling (Davis, 2015; Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021). In summary, SMER28 is expected to work by reducing intracellular accumulations of harmful proteins and lipids, promoting the reassembly of ZO-1 and occludin at cell–cell contacts, and improving TEER under conditions that mimic the stress found in dry AMD.

V. Overall Evaluation  
SMER28 presents several compelling strengths as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, yet it also faces challenges that must be addressed through further targeted research.

Strengths:  
One of the foremost strengths of SMER28 is its robust ability to induce autophagy through mechanisms independent of mTOR inhibition. This property is vital because mTOR inhibitors, while effective at promoting autophagic activity, can induce broad, deleterious metabolic effects not well tolerated in chronic conditions such as AMD (Wrobel et al., 2022). By bypassing mTOR, SMER28 offers a more selective approach that focuses on enhancing intracellular clearance pathways while maintaining the overall metabolic balance. The molecular interactions it engages—predominantly through binding and activating VCP/p97, stimulating the production of PI(3)P, and driving LC3 lipidation—are well documented in several studies (Wrobel et al., 2022). This dual modulation of both autophagic and proteasomal pathways not only promotes protein aggregate clearance but also potentially addresses the accumulation of toxic lipids, which is central to AMD pathogenesis.

The extensive preclinical data supporting SMER28’s efficacy in models of Diamond-Blackfan Anemia, radioprotection, and neurodegenerative diseases offers reassurance regarding its safety profile and mechanism of action (Doulatov et al., 2017; Koukourakis et al., 2018; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013; Sarkar & Rubinsztein, 2008). The compound’s success in these diverse models underscores its versatility and hints at its capacity to produce similar benefits in the RPE, a tissue highly sensitive to proteostatic imbalances. Furthermore, its inclusion in the SMER series—where analogous molecules have been effective in clearing aggregation-prone proteins in neurodegeneration—adds credence to the hypothesis that SMER28 could alleviate the intracellular debris that contributes to dry AMD (Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013; Sarkar & Rubinsztein, 2008).

Weaknesses:  
Despite the promising attributes outlined above, significant gaps in the current literature present challenges for the immediate repurposing of SMER28 for dry AMD. The most notable gap lies in the lack of direct evidence concerning its effects on RPE cells, specifically regarding the reassembly of tight junction proteins like ZO-1 and occludin. The hypothesis that SMER28 will restore TEER by promoting the reformation of these junctional complexes is logically sound given the role of autophagy in RPE homeostasis (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014), yet direct mechanistic and functional data in ocular models remain sparse.

Moreover, while the literature robustly supports a mechanism involving VCP/p97 and subsequent autophagic flux, there is currently no conclusive evidence establishing that SMER28 activates ULK1-dependent autophagy within RPE cells. Studies have indicated that SMER28 predominantly functions via VCP-mediated pathways and enhances LC3 lipidation without evidence of direct ULK1 or ATG5 activation (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013). Given that genetic knockdown of ULK1 and ATG5 replicates detrimental RPE barrier defects, the absence of clear data on SMER28’s influence on these upstream regulators introduces uncertainty regarding the full scope of its autophagic modulation in the context of dry AMD.

Another potential weakness is the translatability of findings from non-ocular systems to the RPE environment. The RPE is a highly specialized cell type with unique metabolic requirements and structural features. Its reliance on constant autophagic turnover to manage oxidative stress and lipid accumulation means that interventions must be finely tuned. Although SMER28’s impact on proteostasis in other tissues is well established, its precise effects on RPE cell physiology—especially under circumstances of A2E-induced stress—must be rigorously validated through dedicated in vitro and in vivo studies.

In addition, most of the supportive studies for SMER28 have been conducted in contexts of systemic or neurodegenerative challenges rather than in ocular models. This necessitates caution when extrapolating positive outcomes from models of Diamond-Blackfan Anemia or radioprotection to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Doulatov et al., 2017; Koukourakis et al., 2018). The hypothesis that SMER28 will facilitate the reassembly of ZO-1/occludin belts and restore TEER, while promising, remains speculative until confirmed by functional assays in RPE cell cultures and suitable animal models of AMD.

Overall, SMER28 combines a favorable mechanism of action with a promising preclinical safety and efficacy record that renders it an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its selective activation of autophagic clearance pathways without engaging mTOR minimizes potential off-target effects, making it particularly suitable for chronic administration in age-related diseases. However, critical unanswered questions regarding its direct impact on RPE barrier function, particularly the reassembly of tight junction proteins and TEER restoration, must be addressed in future studies (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014; Davis, 2015). Moreover, the putative involvement of ULK1-dependent autophagy in SMER28’s mechanism remains to be definitively characterized in ocular models (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019).

In conclusion, while SMER28 has yet to be directly evaluated in ocular systems, its strong mechanistic foundation—as evidenced by its ability to enhance autophagy and proteasomal clearance via VCP stimulation, LC3 lipidation, and Beclin 1 dependency—supports its potential utility in mitigating the autophagic deficits observed in dry AMD (Wrobel et al., 2022). The anticipated clearance of lipid droplets and misfolded proteins, combined with the potential for facilitating the reassembly of ZO-1 and occludin at cell–cell junctions, collectively addresses two critical aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis. Consequently, SMER28 emerges as a promising candidate with significant potential to restore RPE function and barrier integrity, provided that future empirical studies confirm these effects in the appropriate ocular models (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015; Koukourakis et al., 2018).

As an expert drug development team leader evaluating novel therapeutic candidates, I recommend progressing SMER28 to the next stage of rigorous, mechanism-focused preclinical studies using RPE cell cultures and relevant animal models of dry AMD. Emphasis should be placed on detailed analyses of autophagic flux, ULK1 activation status, and the integrity of tight junction reassembly under conditions of A2E-induced or proteostatic stress. This targeted approach will help clarify SMER28’s full mechanistic profile in RPE cells and validate its potential to restore TEER and overall barrier function, thereby establishing its viability as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD (Wrobel et al., 2022; Davis, 2015).

Overall, SMER28 stands out due to its mTOR-independent autophagy induction, dual engagement of autophagic and proteasomal pathways, and a well-established preclinical background in diverse stress models, all of which offer promising avenues for counteracting the cellular dysfunctions underlying dry AMD. Nonetheless, further studies are essential to bridge the current knowledge gap regarding its specific effects on ULK1-dependent autophagy and tight junction reassembly in RPE cells, which are fundamental for achieving the desired therapeutic outcomes in dry AMD (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019; Davis, 2015).

In summary, SMER28’s ability to robustly stimulate autophagic flux and promote cellular clearance mechanisms, together with its favorable safety profile demonstrated in non-ocular models, provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD. While the theoretical framework suggests that SMER28 may ameliorate the proteostatic and lipotoxic stress impairing RPE function—thereby restoring the reassembly of ZO-1/occludin belts and improving TEER—the success of this therapeutic strategy will ultimately depend on empirical validation in ocular-specific studies. Pending such investigations, SMER28 remains a compelling candidate that merits further exploration as a novel approach to combat the significant unmet medical need posed by dry AMD (Doulatov et al., 2017; Wrobel et al., 2022; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014).

Given the convergence of mechanistic insights, preclinical efficacy in multiple models, and the compelling need for improved therapeutic strategies in dry AMD, SMER28 merits prioritization for further research. Its progression into RPE-based studies could potentially pave the way for a new class of autophagy-modulating, mTOR-independent therapeutics aimed at restoring RPE function and halting the progression of dry AMD, thereby offering hope for improved outcomes in this prevalent cause of vision loss (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015; Koukourakis et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
CDDO‐Imidazolide (CDDO‐Im) is a synthetic derivative that belongs to the family of chemically engineered pentacyclic triterpenoids. These compounds are derived from naturally occurring oleanolic acid, a steroid‐like molecule widely distributed in plants and traditionally used in Asian medicine. In the case of CDDO‐Im, researchers have modified the oleanolic acid scaffold by introducing a 2‐cyano substituent, oxidizing key positions to generate 3,12‐dioxo groups, and creating a conjugated 1,9(11)‐dien arrangement that ultimately yields a 28‐oic acid derivative; the imidazolide moiety is added as a C17 modification to generate the “imidazolide” derivative (Cano et al., 2010; Nakagami et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2021). This compound is a member of the broader class of synthetic oleanane pentacyclic triterpenoids, which have been chemically optimized over the years to enhance their intrinsically weak anti‐inflammatory and cytoprotective activities. Notably, these derivatives are known for their extraordinarily potent activation of the transcription factor Nrf2, an effect that is achieved by covalently modifying electrophilic target sites on Keap1. In general, this drug class has been used in diverse pharmacological applications to harness antioxidant and anti‐inflammatory pathways, and several members have been tested preclinically and even progressed into early clinical trials, particularly in the fields of oncology and renal diseases (Cano et al., 2010; Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
The history of therapeutics based on the CDDO scaffold, including CDDO‐Im, is rich in preclinical exploration and early clinical evaluation. Early studies demonstrated that synthetic triterpenoids, such as CDDO and its derivatives (including the methyl ester variant CDDO‐Me and the imidazolide derivative CDDO‐Im), are considerably more potent than other small‐molecule activators of Nrf2 such as sulforaphane or (R)-α-lipoic acid (Cano et al., 2010). Preclinical studies have shown that these compounds robustly induce phase II antioxidant enzymes––notably HO-1, NQO1, and glutathione-related enzymes––by targeting and modifying Keap1, thereby releasing Nrf2 to translocate to the nucleus and drive the transcription of cytoprotective genes. In ocular research, CDDO‐Im has been specifically chosen for in vivo studies because of its demonstrated efficacy in ameliorating retinal damage in mouse models of uveitis and cigarette smoke-induced retinal injury, with evidence of preservation of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) ultrastructure (Cano et al., 2010). Other members of the CDDO family, such as CDDO‐Me (bardoxolone methyl), have undergone clinical testing in oncology, showing that such compounds can reach therapeutically relevant blood concentrations via intravenous infusion, although issues such as suboptimal oral bioavailability have been noted and are subject to ongoing formulation efforts (Cheng et al., 2021; Nakagami et al., 2015). While there is no direct record of CDDO‐Im being used in clinical trials for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal degenerative diseases, the class’s demonstrated ability to activate protective Nrf2 signaling in ocular tissues and to reduce inflammation and oxidative damage provides a strong rationale for investigating its potential in the context of dry AMD (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The pharmacological actions of CDDO‐Im are primarily mediated through its covalent modification of Keap1 (Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1), the cytosolic repressor of the transcription factor Nrf2. Under basal conditions, Keap1 binds to Nrf2 and facilitates its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. CDDO‐Im, as an electrophilic compound possessing a cyanoenone Michael‐acceptor motif, reacts with crucial sulfhydryl groups on Keap1, resulting in the formation of Michael adducts at key cysteine residues (Cano et al., 2010; Cheng et al., 2021). Although specific studies have not always mapped the precise cysteine residues modified by CDDO‐Im in every system, the general consensus from the literature is that the modification of cysteine sulfhydryl groups such as Cys151 is critical for diminishing the suppressive influence of Keap1. Once these cysteine residues are modified, Keap1 undergoes conformational changes that reduce its binding affinity for Nrf2. Consequently, Nrf2 is liberated and able to translocate into the nucleus where, by heterodimerizing with small Maf proteins, it binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) in the promoters of target genes. This Nrf2-driven transcriptional activation results in the upregulation of a broad battery of phase II detoxifying and antioxidant enzymes, including HO-1 (heme oxygenase 1), NQO1 (NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase-1), and glutamate cysteine ligase subunits such as GCLM (glutamate-cysteine ligase modifier subunit) (Cano et al., 2010; Cheng et al., 2021). In addition to these classical antioxidant enzymes, recent research suggests that Nrf2 activation may also have downstream effects on the expression of proteins involved in maintaining cellular barrier integrity, for example tight junction proteins like claudin-1 and occludin. Although experimental details regarding the upregulation of tight junction proteins by CDDO‐Im per se have not been exhaustively documented in the literature provided, there is supporting evidence from related triterpenoids such as CDDO‐Me which preserve blood–brain barrier integrity by upregulating tight junction proteins (Nakagami, 2016; Cano et al., 2010). This mechanistic insight is directly relevant for the RPE, as oxidative stress in these cells contributes to tight junction disorganization, loss of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), and increased paracellular permeability. Therefore, through the covalent modification of Keap1 and subsequent activation of Nrf2, CDDO‐Im is hypothesized to restore the balance of antioxidant defenses and tighten the RPE barrier by increasing the expression of protective enzymes and possibly enhancing tight junction assembly under conditions of H₂O₂-induced stress (Cheng et al., 2021; Cano et al., 2010).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for using CDDO‐Im in dry AMD centers on the restoration of RPE function by enhancing antioxidant defense and barrier integrity. In an in vitro model using ARPE-19 cells exposed to H₂O₂ to simulate oxidative stress, it is expected that treatment with CDDO‐Im at a concentration around 200 nM will robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway. This activation should lead to a marked upregulation of phase II antioxidant enzymes, such as HO-1 and NQO1, thereby mitigating oxidative damage within these cells. Moreover, because Nrf2 activation has been associated with the upregulation of tight junction proteins in other barrier systems, CDDO‐Im is anticipated to promote expression of tight junction proteins, such as claudin-1 and occludin, in RPE cells. This effect would be reflected in a recovery of TEER values to greater than 90% of baseline measurements and a significant reduction—estimated at greater than 65%—in paracellular leakage of molecules like 4 kDa FITC-dextran from the RPE layer (Cano et al., 2010; Cheng et al., 2021). The compound’s high potency at the nanomolar level is particularly attractive since it indicates that effective activation of the Nrf2 pathway can be achieved at doses that are less likely to provoke off-target effects. In addition, pharmacokinetic studies in rodents have shown that similar compounds within the CDDO family have an oral bioavailability in the range of approximately 30% and a mouse intravenous half-life of around 4 hours (as suggested by preclinical pharmacokinetic data in the literature), indicating that systemic administration may be feasible for achieving therapeutic concentrations at the retinal level (Cheng et al., 2021). Collectively, these molecular events are expected to counteract the oxidative stress that contributes to RPE damage in dry AMD, stabilize the RPE barrier, and reduce inflammatory processes associated with complement accumulation and immune cell recruitment in the subretinal space (Cano et al., 2010; Camelo, 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
CDDO‐Im emerges as a highly promising therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on several converging lines of evidence. One of its most compelling strengths is its well-defined mechanism of action. The compound has been meticulously engineered from the oleanolic acid scaffold to include electrophilic moieties that selectively target Keap1, thereby activating Nrf2 with nanomolar potency (Cano et al., 2010; Nakagami et al., 2015). This selective activation is advantageous because it upregulates a host of cytoprotective genes that include classical antioxidant and phase II detoxification enzymes, which are crucial for mitigating oxidative stress—a key driver of RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Cano et al., 2010). Moreover, the collateral benefit of potentially stabilizing tight junctions and restoring barrier function fits well with the clinical need to maintain RPE integrity, as disruption of the RPE barrier is a hallmark of AMD pathology (Cano et al., 2010; Nakagami, 2016).

From a therapeutic history standpoint, although direct clinical trials of CDDO‐Im in dry AMD have not yet been reported, numerous studies have demonstrated the efficacy of CDDO derivatives in various ocular models. For instance, CDDO‐Im has been shown to reduce retinal ganglion cell death and preserve RPE ultrastructure in preclinical settings associated with oxidative injury (Cano et al., 2010). Furthermore, related compounds such as CDDO‐Me have progressed to clinical trials in oncology, thereby establishing a precedent for acceptable safety profiles when administered under controlled conditions (Cheng et al., 2021). These findings build a strong rationale for the repurposing of CDDO‐Im as a potential therapeutic agent for dry AMD.

On the matter of pharmacokinetics, while many triterpenoid compounds have historically faced challenges with oral bioavailability, current formulation strategies—such as amorphous spray-dried dispersions and nanoformulations—have been employed to significantly enhance exposure and therapeutic index (Cheng et al., 2021; Cano et al., 2010). The fact that CDDO‐Im shows promising preclinical pharmacokinetic attributes, with rat oral bioavailability estimated at around 30% and a mouse intravenous half-life of approximately 4 hours, further supports its feasibility as a drug candidate. Such pharmacokinetic profiles suggest the potential for achieving sustained retinal exposure following systemic administration, an essential characteristic for chronic conditions like dry AMD where repeated dosing may be necessary (Cheng et al., 2021; Nakagami et al., 2015).

However, several challenges must be considered. One notable weakness is the historical challenge with pharmacokinetics and bioavailability inherent in this class of compounds; while improvements have been made, there remains a risk that systemic dosing could lead to suboptimal retinal exposure or off-target toxicities if not carefully optimized (Cheng et al., 2021; Cano et al., 2010). Additionally, while the preclinical evidence strongly supports Nrf2 activation and antioxidant enzyme induction, the specific effect of CDDO‐Im on the expression of RPE tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 and occludin remains to be fully validated. Although related analogues have shown protection of barrier integrity in models of the blood–brain barrier and vascular endothelium (Nakagami, 2016), direct demonstration of TEER recovery and a reduction in 4 kDa FITC-dextran leakage in RPE models needs further experimental confirmation. This gap in the data is critical given the central role of RPE barrier dysfunction in the progression of dry AMD. Moreover, translation from in vitro cell line data (e.g., ARPE-19) to in vivo efficacy in human patients is always a major hurdle that requires rigorous pharmacodynamic and toxicological evaluation.

Safety is another important consideration. While early studies in oncology indicate that compounds structurally related to CDDO‐Im can be administered safely at certain doses, there have been instances where related compounds, such as bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me), encountered setbacks in clinical trials due to adverse cardiovascular events and other toxicities (Cheng et al., 2021). Although these issues do not directly implicate CDDO‐Im, they underscore the necessity for careful dose optimization and monitoring of systemic effects—especially when repurposing such a potent Nrf2 activator for chronic ocular conditions.

In summary, the overall evaluation of CDDO‐Im as a candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. The major strengths include its robust and well-characterized mechanism of action—via covalent modification of Keap1 to activate Nrf2—and its demonstrated preclinical efficacy in reducing oxidative damage and preserving retinal structure. These factors strongly support its potential to restore RPE barrier integrity as evidenced by improvements in TEER and reductions in paracellular leakage in cell models, which are central to the hypothesized therapeutic benefit in dry AMD. The compound’s pharmacokinetic properties, though not without challenges, appear to be within a range that could be optimized for ocular delivery through innovative formulation strategies.  

Nevertheless, several weaknesses warrant further investigation. Direct evidence of tight junction protein upregulation (claudin-1, occludin) in ARPE-19 cells following CDDO‐Im treatment must be generated to fully validate the proposed mechanism for barrier recovery. In addition, while preclinical data are encouraging regarding Nrf2-mediated cytoprotection in the retina, translation to a human dry AMD setting remains unproven, and potential safety concerns seen with related triterpenoids must be carefully mitigated by dose titration and possibly localized delivery strategies. Given these considerations, it is strongly recommended that additional preclinical studies be conducted using relevant in vitro assays—including measurement of TEER and FITC-dextran flux in RPE monolayers under oxidative stress conditions—as well as in vivo assessments in appropriate animal models of dry AMD. Such studies will be essential to clarify the therapeutic window, confirm pharmacodynamic biomarkers, and identify any off-target effects before advancing CDDO‐Im into clinical trials for dry AMD.

Overall, the combination of a compelling mechanistic rationale, documented preclinical efficacy in retinal models, and promising pharmacokinetic parameters provides a strong basis to pursue further development of CDDO‐Im as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Addressing the current gaps in evidence—particularly regarding direct effects on RPE tight junction proteins and barrier function, as well as ensuring an acceptable safety profile—will be critical next steps. Should these challenges be successfully navigated, CDDO‐Im holds significant potential to contribute to the much-needed therapeutic options for patients suffering from dry AMD, a condition that remains a major cause of vision loss with limited treatment alternatives (Cano et al., 2010; Cheng et al., 2021; Cano et al., 2010).

ML218 is a synthetic small‐molecule calcium channel inhibitor originally developed as an antagonist targeting T‐type CaV3 channels. It was discovered in efforts to design selective modulators of low‐voltage‐activated calcium channels and is commercially available (Tocris 5056). The compound was designed to interact with hydrophobic fenestration sites in voltage‐gated calcium channels, and its development emerged from scaffold‐hopping strategies derived from earlier hits in high‐throughput calcium flux assays. ML218 thus belongs to a family of investigational agents that have been primarily used as pharmacological tools to dissect T‐type channel function in neuronal systems. Previous studies have focused on its ability to inhibit CaV3 channels in central nervous system models, including experiments in cell lines and primary neurons where it modulated firing patterns and synaptic excitability (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). In addition to its intended activity on CaV3 channels, detailed analyses have revealed that ML218 also exhibits significant cross‐activity with CaV1.4 channels by adopting an alternative binding mode that involves the III‐IV fenestration—an observation that distinguishes it from classical dihydropyridines (Sun et al., 2025). This dual binding behavior highlights both the promise and the challenge of using ML218 as a selective tool in complex tissues where multiple calcium channel subtypes coexist. Overall, ML218 is a promising lead compound representing the synthetic, small‐molecule approach to targeting voltage‐dependent calcium channels, with a structure–activity relationship that suggests potential repurposing for non‐neuronal applications such as retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier stabilization (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History:  
ML218 has been primarily explored within experimental models predominantly focused on the central nervous system. Several studies have employed ML218 as a pharmacological probe to inhibit T‐type calcium currents in neuronal populations. For example, in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease, ML218 demonstrated robust inhibition of T-type currents in subthalamic nucleus (STN) neurons, leading to marked alterations in burst firing patterns (Xiang et al., 2011; Manzar et al., 2025). Electrophysiological investigations using whole‐cell patch clamp techniques in HEK293 cells transfected with CaV3.2 channels have shown that ML218 can achieve potent block, with reported IC₅₀ values ranging from approximately 24 nM (in one report) to 150–310 nM in different assay settings (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). These preclinical studies validated ML218’s mechanism of action within neural substrates and its potential as a centrally active agent. In parallel, investigations in non‐neuronal cells have emerged. In particular, ML218 has been applied to studies involving human embryonic stem cell‐derived retinal pigment epithelium (hESC‐RPE) where it was used at a concentration of 5 μM to elucidate the functionality of voltage‐gated calcium channels expressed in these cells—primarily focusing on assays of phagocytosis and VEGF secretion (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). Although these studies did not specifically examine barrier function parameters, they established that RPE cells express functional T‐type calcium channels and that pharmacological modulation with ML218 could alter cellular processes relevant to retinal physiology. Notably, there is no recorded or clinical history of ML218 being employed to treat dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or related ocular diseases; its usage to date has centered on neurological models and in vitro assays. Consequently, repurposing ML218 for dry AMD would represent a novel application, extending its utilization from central nervous system studies to ocular tissue. The concept of drug repurposing in ocular diseases has been gaining traction in recent years due to the overlapping roles of calcium signaling in diverse tissues, and ML218’s history in rigorously characterizing calcium channel pharmacology makes it a candidate for further exploration in RPE models (Xiang et al., 2011; Korkka et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
ML218 functions primarily by blocking T‐type calcium channels, with an emphasis on CaV3.2 subtypes. The compound’s mechanism involves its entry into the transmembrane fenestrations of the channel complex, where it interrupts the normal ion‐conducting pathway. Detailed structural studies have revealed that in CaV3 channels, ML218 docks within the II‐III fenestration; in this binding mode, the phenyl head group of the molecule extends into the hydrophobic channel region while its aliphatic tail lies within the central pore, thereby imposing a state‐dependent block (Sun et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024). This interaction presumably stabilizes the channel in a closed state, reducing low‐voltage‐activated Ca²⁺ influx into the cell. Notably, ML218’s binding is not entirely exclusive to CaV3 channels, as its molecular conformation adapts in CaV1.4 channels. In these channels, non‐conserved residues preclude the canonical II‐III fenestration binding; instead, ML218 binds at a distinct site in the III‐IV fenestration that overlaps with the dihydropyridine (DHP) binding pocket. Mutagenesis studies have confirmed the importance of this alternate binding mode by demonstrating substantial changes in inhibitory potency upon modification of key residues such as T1007 (Sun et al., 2025). In electrophysiological assays carried out in HEK293 cells, ML218 has been shown to be highly potent against CaV3.2 channels (with reported IC₅₀ values as low as 24 nM in certain studies) and to display over 80-fold selectivity over CaV1.4 channels, although its cross‐reactivity remains a consideration at higher concentrations (Sun et al., 2025). The molecular basis for its selectivity lies in the differential organization of channel domains between CaV3 and CaV1 families, with ML218’s binding being modulated by specific residues located in the channel pore and fenestration regions. From a biochemical standpoint, the blockade of CaV3.2 channels results in a decreased calcium influx during membrane depolarizations, which is critical for controlling intracellular calcium levels. In tissues such as the RPE, where calcium signaling plays a pivotal role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and barrier integrity, aberrant Ca²⁺ influx can activate calcium‐dependent proteases such as calpains. Calpains, once activated, can cleave junctional proteins including zonula occludens protein 1 (ZO-1) and occludin, leading to compromised barrier integrity. Thus, by selectively inhibiting CaV3.2‐mediated calcium entry, ML218 is hypothesized to prevent calpain activation and subsequent disruption of tight junctions in RPE cells—a mechanism that has been indirectly supported by studies showing that inhibitors of T-type channels reduce cellular excitability and junctional leak in alternative epithelial models (Sun et al., 2025). Furthermore, the compound’s dual action—including a modest agonist effect at specific concentrations—adds complexity to its pharmacological profile; however, in the context of RPE barrier function, the primary desired effect would be its antagonist action that limits pathological calcium entry under oxidative or inflammatory stress. The state‐dependence of ML218’s block (i.e., preferential inhibition when channels are in an open or inactivated state) may further enhance its capacity to target pathological calcium influx while sparing normal physiological signaling to some extent, although this property will require careful titration in a diseased state (Sun et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
The working hypothesis for repurposing ML218 in dry AMD is that its inhibition of CaV3.2 channels in retinal pigment epithelium will reduce pathological intracellular calcium accumulation under conditions of oxidative and inflammatory stress. Elevated Ca²⁺ levels in RPE cells are known to activate calpain, a calcium‐dependent protease that mediates the proteolytic cleavage of critical junctional proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin. Disruption of these proteins leads to a compromised RPE barrier, as reflected in reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased paracellular permeability (measured by FITC-dextran flux assays). By blocking the CaV3.2 channels, ML218 is expected to limit this pathological Ca²⁺ influx and thereby prevent calpain activation, preserving the integrity of the ZO-1/occludin belt in RPE cells (Sun et al., 2025). This preservation of junctional complexes should translate into restored TEER and reduced permeability of the RPE monolayer in in vitro models simulating oxidative or inflammatory injury that mimic conditions encountered in dry AMD. Moreover, patch-clamp electrophysiology and Fluo-4 calcium imaging assays in RPE cells are proposed as means of confirming target engagement and quantifying the extent of CaV3.2 current inhibition by ML218 (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). It is anticipated that effective blockade of pathological calcium signaling will also reduce downstream events associated with dry AMD pathophysiology, such as aberrant vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) secretion, which contributes to the progression of atrophic changes in the retina. Although previous studies using ML218 in hESC-RPE have focused more on phagocytosis and secretory functions rather than barrier integrity per se, the presence of functional T-type channels identified in these cells (with CaV3.2 localized, for instance, to the basolateral domain) supports the rationale that modulation of these channels will have a direct impact on barrier properties (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating ML218 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current literature. One significant strength of ML218 is its well‐documented and robust activity in inhibiting T‐type calcium channels, particularly CaV3.2, as demonstrated by comprehensive electrophysiological studies in both neuronal and heterologous systems (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). This potent inhibition forms a logical mechanistic basis for targeting pathological calcium influx in RPE cells, where calcium overload and subsequent activation of proteases like calpain are implicated in junctional protein degradation and barrier dysfunction. Furthermore, the detailed structural insights into ML218’s binding—its differential interactions in CaV3 and CaV1 channels—provide a strong foundation for understanding its pharmacodynamic activity. The ability of ML218 to modulate calcium signaling with state‐dependent block enhances its therapeutic promise by potentially allowing it to target pathological overactivity while sparing baseline physiological function (Sun et al., 2025).  

On the other hand, several potential weaknesses must be considered. The literature reveals that ML218 is not exclusively selective for CaV3.2 channels; it exhibits cross‐reactivity with CaV1.4 channels, albeit at lower potency (with reported IC₅₀ values for CaV1.4 in the micromolar range compared to nanomolar ranges for CaV3.2) (Sun et al., 2025). Such cross‐reactivity could theoretically lead to off‐target effects in tissues where L‐type channels play critical roles in calcium signaling, potentially complicating its utility in RPE cells that also express other calcium channel subtypes. Furthermore, while the proposed hypothesis for dry AMD is biologically plausible, there is a notable gap in the literature regarding direct evidence for ML218’s efficacy in preserving RPE barrier function under oxidative or inflammatory conditions—most studies with ML218 have been performed in neuronal contexts or in assays focused on phagocytosis and secretory aspects of RPE physiology (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). Thus, extrapolation of its barrier‐stabilizing properties from other epithelial systems (or even from neural models) requires cautious interpretation and further dedicated experimentation.  

Another concern pertains to the reported potency of ML218. Although optimistic hypotheses suggest an IC₅₀ of approximately 7 nM for CaV3.2 channel block, the available data across various assay platforms indicate that effective concentrations are more likely to be in the tens to low hundreds of nanomolar range (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). This discrepancy necessitates further pharmacological profiling in RPE models to accurately define the therapeutic window and ensure that the concentrations used to restore barrier integrity do not inadvertently trigger off‐target effects or toxicity. Additionally, the dual binding mode of ML218—while advantageous for providing mechanistic insight—raises the possibility that subtle differences in channel conformations within RPE cells (compared to neurons) could influence its selectivity and efficacy, thereby complicating dose optimization for ocular applications.  

Despite these challenges, the conceptual framework for repurposing ML218 in dry AMD has several attractive features. The targeting of T‐type calcium channels to mitigate calpain activation and to preserve tight junction protein integrity represents a novel therapeutic approach that departs from traditional anti‐inflammatory or anti‐angiogenic strategies. In dry AMD, where chronic, low‐grade oxidative and inflammatory stress contribute to RPE dysfunction and barrier breakdown, a compound like ML218 could theoretically reduce intracellular calcium overload and, consequently, the cascade of events leading to junctional degradation. Preliminary evidence from hESC-RPE studies confirms that these cells express functional T-type channels and respond to modulation by calcium channel blockers, lending support to the notion that ML218 can be effective in this tissue context (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.).

In summary, ML218 emerges as an intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its potent T-type channel inhibitory activity, its well‐characterized mechanism at the molecular level, and the theoretical basis linking Ca²⁺ dysregulation to RPE barrier dysfunction. However, the current body of literature does not provide direct evidence in RPE models under conditions that mimic dry AMD pathology, such as oxidative or inflammatory injury. Moreover, the compound’s off‐target activity on CaV1.4 channels and the variability in reported potencies across studies pose significant challenges that will require thorough in vitro and eventually in vivo validation. Future investigations should prioritize comprehensive electrophysiological and imaging studies in RPE cells, specifically measuring TEER, FITC‐dextran flux, and tight junction protein localization following exposure to oxidative stress, to determine whether ML218 can indeed restore barrier integrity as hypothesized. Dose‐ranging studies and careful evaluation of potential off‐target effects will also be critical to establishing a safe and effective therapeutic profile for ocular application.  

Overall, while ML218 holds promise as a tool compound with the potential for repurposing in dry AMD, its advancement into this new therapeutic area will depend on addressing key knowledge gaps through rigorous experimental validation. This includes confirming its selective inhibition of CaV3.2 channels in RPE cells, establishing the correlation between calcium influx blockade and tight junction preservation, and ensuring that its pharmacological behavior in RPE is consistent with the requirements for stabilizing the RPE barrier under pathological conditions. Therefore, although the mechanistic rationale is compelling, additional targeted preclinical studies are required before ML218 can be confidently moved forward as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011; Korkka et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose (α,α-trehalose) is a naturally occurring, nonreducing disaccharide composed of two d-glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond; it is broadly found in bacteria, fungi, insects, invertebrates, and plants but is not synthesized by vertebrates, including humans (trehalase in the small intestine hydrolyzes ingested trehalose to glucose) (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). Trehalose’s physicochemical properties include high aqueous solubility, chemical stability, and resistance to glucosidases; it has been mass-produced since the 1990s via enzymatic methods and has been approved for food use by EU regulators and the US FDA, with human exposure generally safe apart from low incidences of malabsorption (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). In drug-development parlance, trehalose is a small-molecule, carbohydrate autophagy modulator and proteostasis regulator; it exhibits both biophysical “chemical chaperone” activity that stabilizes macromolecules and biologic activity that induces the autophagy–lysosome program via TFEB/TFE3 activation and related nutrient-sensing pathways (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Jeong et al., 2021, pp. 1–3, 12–13; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). As a class, autophagy-enhancing small molecules (including trehalose) have been utilized across neurodegeneration and metabolic disease models to promote clearance of toxic protein aggregates or dysfunctional organelles and to restore lysosomal function, with trehalose showing efficacy signals in preclinical Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, Huntington’s disease, and lysosomal storage–related models (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Lotfi et al., 2018, pp. 12–15). Within ophthalmology, trehalose has established use as a topical osmoprotectant/bioprotective excipient in eye-drop formulations for dry-eye disease (commonly 3% w/v), and it is under active investigation for posterior-segment neuroprotection, including age-related retinal degeneration models relevant to AMD (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 18–20; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 10–13).

Therapeutic History  
Clinical/translational use: Trehalose is approved as a safe food ingredient and has been widely used in humans, including topical ophthalmic preparations for dry eye disease and post-LASIK care, with multiple clinical trials and a marketed formulation (e.g., Thealoz Duo, 3% trehalose plus hyaluronic acid) supporting ocular-surface safety and symptomatic benefit; the patented formulation increased tear film thickness after a single drop in clinical testing (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 18–20). Safety data support tolerability of topical trehalose in humans and of high-concentration in vitro exposure across multiple cell types; ocular-surface animal models show safety and barrier-protective effects, and in vitro human RPE studies report no loss of viability up to 200 mM for 24 h, though dosing windows matter for efficacy (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 5–7). Oral trehalose is hydrolyzed by intestinal trehalase and exhibits poor systemic bioavailability, limiting efficacy for some systemic indications; parenteral trehalose achieves low-millimolar plasma levels transiently, which can activate TFEB/TFE3 in macrophages in vivo, but oral exposure is generally insufficient to reach such systemic concentrations in mice in atherosclerosis models (Evans et al., 2018, pp. 2–3). Nonetheless, oral trehalose has shown retinal effects in mice, improving autophagy pathways and preserving cone ERG responses during aging, suggesting either BRB permeability or indirect choroidal effects; the authors noted that establishing BRB permeability is important for translation (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 181–188).

Ocular/retinal preclinical evidence: Multiple independent groups demonstrate mechanistic and functional efficacy of trehalose in RPE/retinal models relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology. In human RPE cell systems (ARPE-19, haRPE, and iPSC-RPE), trehalose increases autophagic flux (LC3-II accumulation with CQ, free GFP readouts), upregulates lysosomal biogenesis markers (LAMP-1/2, cathepsin D), elevates TFEB transcripts and protein, expands the lysosomal compartment (Lysotracker), engages both macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy, and confers autophagy-dependent protection against oxidative stressors such as hydroquinone (HQ), a cigarette smoke–derived oxidant implicated in AMD (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 151–160; Fisher et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). In primary murine RPE, trehalose restored autophagic flux under oxidative stress and improved mitochondrial respiratory function in vitro (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).
