Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ripasudil, also known by its research designation Y-39983 and commercially available as Selleckchem S8443, is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor developed originally as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil containing protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. It belongs to a class of therapeutics that act in an ATP‐competitive manner to inhibit the activity of ROCK isoforms, enzymes that are critical regulators of actomyosin contractility and cell adhesion. Ripasudil was synthesized following the structural optimization of earlier compounds such as fasudil and Y-27632, with the aim of increasing both potency and ocular tolerability. Its chemical origins are linked to the rational design strategies that sought to improve enzyme inhibitory selectivity and to enhance the pharmacokinetic profile for local ocular application. Members of the ROCK inhibitor class have seen prior use in settings that require modulation of actin cytoskeleton dynamics, such as the treatment of glaucoma via enhanced aqueous humor outflow, and have also been explored in contexts involving wound healing and anti-fibrotic effects in various ocular tissues (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, ripasudil has been approved in Japan for the treatment of glaucoma and ocular hypertension, where it is delivered topically in the form of eye drops, demonstrating a well-established safety profile and a low incidence of systemic adverse effects. In preclinical models, it has demonstrated efficacy by increasing ocular blood flow, modifying trabecular meshwork cell contractility, and reducing intraocular pressure, thereby serving as a stepping stone and proof-of-concept for the utility of ROCK inhibitors in ocular disorders. Beyond its approved use in glaucoma, investigations of ROCK inhibitors—including ripasudil—have extended into experimental applications in corneal endothelial regeneration and have been evaluated in combination with anti-VEGF therapies for diabetic macular edema. Although direct clinical evidence specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is not available, multiple lines of preclinical research have shown that the ROCK inhibitor class modulates pathways which are believed to underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Notably, the mechanistic studies have identified the role of ROCK signaling in cytoskeletal reorganization, matrix contractility, and fibrosis, all of which are processes particularly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier dysfunction seen in dry AMD (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Moreover, the ocular pharmacokinetic profile of ripasudil—demonstrated by rabbit intravitreal studies showing a half-life of approximately 14 hours and negligible systemic exposure—is supportive of repurposing this candidate for posterior segment indications, including dry AMD (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ripasudil exerts its therapeutic activity by competitively inhibiting the ATP-binding site of ROCK isoforms, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of downstream effectors such as myosin light-chain (MLC), myosin-binding subunit of MLC phosphatase (MYPT1), and LIM kinase. These phosphorylation events normally lead to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, focal adhesion assembly, and ultimately contribute to a contractile, stiffened cell phenotype. In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, this contractility is thought to be exacerbated under conditions of oxidative stress, contributing to disassembly or mislocalization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity. By inhibiting ROCK, ripasudil reduces actomyosin-driven contraction and stress-fiber formation, thereby promoting cortical F-actin remodeling and facilitating the proper membrane relocalization of tight-junction proteins. The specificity of ripasudil has been demonstrated by its greater than 100-fold selectivity against other kinases such as protein kinase C (PKC) and myotonic dystrophy kinase-related Cdc42-binding kinase (MRCK), highlighting the mechanistic precision by which it modulates ROCK-dependent signaling cascades (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Additionally, while several studies indicate that the ROCK inhibitor class generally targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2 isoforms, quantitative biochemical data have shown that ripasudil exhibits potent enzyme inhibitory activity with IC₅₀s in the low nanomolar range (with values reported around 51 nM for ROCK1 and 19 nM for ROCK2 in some studies, though the candidate hypothesis posits values of approximately 29 nM for ROCK1 and 68 nM for ROCK2). This inhibitory profile is particularly relevant because emerging research indicates that ROCK2, in particular, is upregulated in the pathological conditions of dry AMD and plays a key role in mediating cytoskeletal changes that disrupt RPE tight junction integrity (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). The inhibition of ROCK thereby is expected to have a dual benefit of cytoprotection and restoration of cell junction architecture, ultimately leading to improved barrier function (Ghenciu et al., 2025; Singh & Singh, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing ripasudil for dry AMD is that by blocking ROCK activity in oxidatively stressed retinal pigment epithelium cells, the compound will lead to a reduction in actomyosin contractility, thereby alleviating the formation of pathological stress fibers that otherwise disrupt the organization of tight junction complexes. Under normal physiological conditions, tight junction proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin are localized at the plasma membrane in a continuous, belt-like manner that is essential to maintain TEER and restrict paracellular permeability. However, in dry AMD, oxidative damage, inflammation, and mechanical stress lead to cytoskeletal reorganization and a discontinuous distribution of these critical proteins, resulting in impaired barrier function and contributing to the pathogenesis of the disease. Preclinical studies, particularly those employing ARPE-19 cell models subjected to toxic insults such as paraquat or sodium iodate (NaIO₃), have demonstrated that ROCK inhibitors can dose-dependently restore TEER (with reported improvements up to 70%) and re-establish the membrane continuity of ZO-1, suggesting that these agents can “rescue” the RPE barrier phenotype under injurious conditions (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). It is expected that ripasudil, with its potent ROCK-inhibitory activity and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics (including intravitreal retention times supportive of sustained action), will similarly promote the cortical redistribution of F-actin, leading to the re-localization of junctional molecules back to the cell membrane. This mechanistic restoration should result in improved transepithelial electrical resistance and a concomitant reduction in paracellular permeability, effectively reinforcing the RPE barrier—a central therapeutic target in dry AMD. Moreover, the activation of protective cellular pathways through ROCK inhibition may also confer additional anti-apoptotic and anti-inflammatory effects, further contributing to the survival and functional integrity of the RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating ripasudil as a candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths become apparent. First, its established clinical use for glaucoma means that its safety, tolerability, and ocular pharmacokinetic properties are well characterized—attributes that significantly lower the translational barrier for its application in other ocular diseases. The intravitreal pharmacokinetic data, with a half-life of approximately 14 hours in rabbit models and negligible systemic exposure, suggest that therapeutic concentrations capable of modulating ROCK activity in the retina can be achieved with acceptable dosing regimens (Yamaguchi et al., 2016). Second, the mechanistic rationale is compelling: ROCK signaling is intimately involved in mediating actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, and subsequent disruption of tight junction architecture in epithelial cells. Given that ROCK2 in particular is implicated in the pathological processes observed in the RPE in dry AMD, the ability of ripasudil to inhibit this pathway could translate into measurable improvements in barrier function, as indicated by preclinical assays demonstrating TEER restoration and the re-localization of ZO-1 in ARPE-19 cells (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Third, the compound exhibits a favorable selectivity profile, with negligible off-target activity against other kinases such as PKC and MRCK, which minimizes the risk of unintended effects in non-target tissues. This specificity is critical when repurposing drugs for chronic conditions such as dry AMD, where long-term ocular safety is paramount (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Despite these strengths, there are notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before ripasudil can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. A primary limitation is the paucity of direct experimental evidence in RPE models of dry AMD. While the hypothesis is supported by data from related in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative stress), robust in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of dry AMD pathophysiology are still needed. In particular, data demonstrating that ripasudil can restore tight junction integrity and improve TEER in the context of chronic, progressive RPE dysfunction remain limited (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Furthermore, although the compound’s ROCK inhibitory activity is well documented, the available literature does not consistently detail the isoform-specific effects in RPE cells; given that ROCK1 and ROCK2 may play distinct roles in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, clarifying the relative contributions of each isoform is essential. The candidate hypothesis posits specific IC₅₀ values for ROCK1 and ROCK2, yet discrepancies exist across reported studies regarding the precise inhibitory concentrations, which indicates that further biochemical characterization is warranted (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). Another consideration is the potential for adverse effects when repurposing a drug originally optimized for anterior-segment diseases for posterior-segment applications. Although the ocular safety profile of ripasudil in glaucoma is well established, the long-term impact of ROCK inhibition on RPE cell biology in an aged population—especially in the context of dry AMD—remains uncertain. Off-target cytoskeletal effects in other retinal cell types, possible modulation of inflammatory responses, and the risk of inadvertently triggering compensatory signaling pathways are all factors that must be carefully evaluated in preclinical studies (Iancu et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2025). Lastly, while the pharmacokinetic data support retinal exposure after intravitreal or possibly topical administration, optimizing the delivery method to ensure sustained and localized drug levels in the RPE without causing ocular surface toxicity (such as conjunctival hyperemia or corneal epithelial disturbances) will be critical. Innovative delivery systems, such as sustained-release intravitreal implants or depot formulations, may offer solutions but require further development (Yamaguchi et al., 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023).

In conclusion, the repurposing of ripasudil for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and a favorable safety profile derived from its established use in glaucoma. The compound’s capacity to inhibit ROCK-mediated actomyosin contraction and promote cortical F-actin remodeling positions it as a promising agent for restoring RPE barrier function—one of the key pathological features of dry AMD. However, the current literature reveals significant gaps in direct evidence regarding its effects on RPE tight junction proteins, TEER restoration, and the isoform-specific roles of ROCK in the RPE under oxidative stress. To advance ripasudil as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, additional preclinical investigations—ideally incorporating robust animal models of dry AMD and detailed biochemical analyses of ROCK isoform activity in RPE cells—are required. Additionally, optimizations in drug delivery methodology to achieve sustained posterior-segment exposure while minimizing adverse ocular events will be imperative. Overall, ripasudil presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, with its strengths in mechanistic specificity, favorable ocular pharmacokinetics, and established clinical safety underscoring its potential. Nonetheless, the outlined weaknesses and knowledge gaps necessitate a rigorous program of targeted research to validate its efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity and to ensure its long-term safety in the intended patient population (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023; Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Adams & Papillon, 2020; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AZD8055 is a synthetically derived small‐molecule inhibitor designed to target the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway. It belongs to the second‐generation class of mTOR inhibitors, which are structurally and functionally distinct from the first‐generation rapalogs that were originally isolated from Streptomyces species. In contrast to natural product–derived mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin, AZD8055 was developed through rational drug design to achieve high potency and dual inhibition of both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2. Its ATP-competitive binding to the kinase domain endows it with a very high selectivity profile, exhibiting an IC₅₀ of approximately 0.8 nM against mTOR as originally reported, while also limiting activity against other phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) family members (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10). In the context of drug classes, AZD8055 is categorized alongside other small-molecule kinase inhibitors that have been principally exploited in oncology to curb aberrant cell growth; however, the modality by which it inhibits mTOR via direct competition at the ATP-binding pocket distinguishes it from allosteric inhibitors. The development program underlying AZD8055 focused on enhancing both the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic properties to not only achieve a potent biochemical inhibition but also allow for a cleaner kinase selectivity profile, which is essential for targeted clinical interventions. Although primarily intended for oncology indications, this engineered selectivity coupled with its capacity to modulate autophagy has prompted investigation into its potential repurposing for diseases characterized by autophagic dysregulation, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

Historically, mTOR inhibitors have been extensively studied in the context of cancer, with rapamycin and its analogs (rapalogs) serving as prototype compounds for targeting dysregulated mTOR signaling in malignant cells. AZD8055, a second-generation inhibitor, was developed to overcome limitations associated with rapalogs, including incomplete mTORC1 inhibition and the inadvertent activation of compensatory pro-survival signals mediated through mTORC2 and AKT feedback loops. Preclinical studies and phase I clinical evaluations in oncology have demonstrated that AZD8055 can effectively induce cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis by simultaneously suppressing mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis and mTORC2-mediated survival signals (Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10; Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 4–5). Its clinical development history has largely focused on cancers such as Her2-positive breast cancers and gliomas, where its ability to modulate PI3K/AKT signaling has been of particular advantage in overcoming resistance mechanisms. Although the majority of the therapeutic history of AZD8055 has been in cancer, the underlying molecular rationale for its use has provided impetus for exploring its repurposing in non-oncological diseases. In the realm of ocular diseases, particularly dry AMD, the mTOR pathway has been implicated in the regulation of autophagy and cellular homeostasis within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). While traditional mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin have been tested in ocular settings, their clinical efficacy has been inconsistent, partly due to the inability to inhibit mTORC2-driven feedback loops. AZD8055’s dual inhibition mechanism could potentially address these shortcomings by providing a more balanced modulation of the mTOR pathway, although to date there is limited direct clinical or preclinical evidence of its use specifically in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 9–10, 16–17).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, AZD8055 exerts its pharmacological effects through ATP-competitive inhibition of the catalytic domain of mTOR, thereby targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes. mTORC1 is primarily responsible for regulating protein synthesis through substrates such as 4EBP1 and S6 kinase, while mTORC2 is integral to the phosphorylation and activation of AKT, a key mediator of cell survival and metabolism. The simultaneous inhibition of both complexes by AZD8055 prevents the compensatory activation of AKT that is typically observed with rapalogs, which primarily target mTORC1 and leave mTORC2 functionally active (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Downstream effects of this mechanism include rapid dephosphorylation of 4EBP1, which in turn halts cap-dependent mRNA translation, and the induction of autophagy as a result of relieving the suppression of upstream autophagy initiating factors such as ULK1 and transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10). In ocular applications, particularly within RPE cells, the impairment of autophagy is thought to contribute to the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and damaged cellular components. By enhancing autophagic flux, AZD8055 can facilitate the autophagosome–lysosome fusion critical to the degradation and clearance of damaged junctional proteins. The resultant restoration of the tight junction integrity—measurable via trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—is believed to underlie the therapeutic rationale for its use in dry AMD. As a dual mTOR inhibitor with high potency, AZD8055’s molecular interactions within the mTOR kinase domain contribute not only to the suppression of pathological signaling but also promote cellular recycling processes that maintain RPE function and homeostasis (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 4–6). The proposed study hypothesis posits that 50 nM AZD8055 will effectively restore and enhance barrier function in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells that have been subjected to oxidative stress via H₂O₂ exposure. In evaluating AZD8055 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key strengths and potential challenges must be considered. A notable strength of AZD8055 lies in its dual inhibition profile, which addresses the limitations inherent in rapalog therapy by effectively targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2. Chemically, spermidine is classified as a small aliphatic polyamine with the structure H₂N(CH₂)₃NH(CH₂)₄NH₂, and it is biosynthesized from precursor amino acids such as ornithine and arginine via enzymatic steps involving decarboxylation reactions. Its discovery, dating back to early biochemical studies, has led to its isolation from various natural sources, including soybeans, aged cheese, mushrooms, and citrus fruits, and it is now commercially available as a highly purified compound (Sigma S3266). As a member of the polyamine family, spermidine is well known for its roles in modulating cell growth, autophagy, DNA stability, and the regulation of ion channels. These characteristics have fostered significant interest in its application as a dietary supplement with potential anti-aging properties, and more recently, its use has been explored in the context of ocular diseases due to its ability to induce autophagy and mitigate oxidative stress (Han et al., 2022; Hassani et al., 2022). Spermidine’s therapeutic history spans a broad array of biomedical investigations, including diverse preclinical studies in ocular as well as non‐ocular contexts. Initially, its anti‐aging and autophagy‐inducing properties were recognized through studies that linked its supplementation to longevity and enhanced cellular survival under stress conditions. This foundational work, while largely performed in non‐ocular systems, subsequently prompted researchers to explore its use in neuroprotection and the management of chronic conditions associated with oxidative damage. In ocular models, particularly, spermidine has been examined for its potential to mitigate oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), which are critical cell types for retinal function and vision. For instance, several in vitro and preclinical studies have demonstrated that spermidine can mitigate oxidative stress, suppress apoptotic pathways, and promote survival in retinal cells through the chelation of excess calcium and upregulation of antioxidant enzymes (Han et al., 2022). Preclinical animal models of glaucoma and optic nerve injury have provided evidence that spermidine can facilitate optic nerve regeneration and improve RGC survival, suggesting beneficial neuroprotective effects that may be relevant to retinal degenerative diseases (Han et al., 2022).

More specifically, in the context of retinal degenerative diseases such as age‐related macular degeneration, studies have shown that spermidine supplementation may protect RPE cells from oxidative insults by restoring calcium homeostasis and enhancing the expression of intrinsic antioxidant enzymes, thereby preserving cellular integrity (Han et al., 2022). However, these studies also highlight a critical caveat: the effects of spermidine are dose‐dependent, with excessive concentrations leading to oxidative stress and cytotoxicity that may exacerbate retinal damage (Han et al., 2022). In addition to its direct cellular effects, spermidine has been implicated in modulating immune responses in the ocular environment, including influencing the polarization of retinal microglia and T cell differentiation—a factor that could have implications not only for neurodegenerative processes but also for inflammatory disorders such as dry eye syndrome and autoimmune uveitis (Han et al., 2022). Despite promising preclinical data, direct evidence supporting spermidine’s therapeutic efficacy specifically in dry AMD remains limited, thus necessitating further targeted studies; some reviews have advocated for its potential given the broad spectrum of its bioactivities and safety as a dietary supplement, even as they call for careful dose optimization (Han et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesis central to the current proposal is that spermidine mediates EP300 inhibition, thereby facilitating the deacetylation of autophagy-related proteins in RPE cells. EP300 (also known as p300) is a well-characterized histone acetyltransferase that plays a critical role in mediating acetylation on both histone and non-histone proteins, which in turn influences chromatin remodeling, gene expression, and multiple cellular processes including autophagy. Hyperacetylation of autophagy-related proteins by EP300 is thought to impair autophagic flux—a process essential for the removal of damaged organelles and misfolded proteins in RPE cells. At the molecular level, the inhibition of EP300 by spermidine may restore a balance between acetylation and deacetylation events within the RPE cell cytoplasm. In vitro studies have documented that spermidine acts not only as an inducer of autophagy but also as a modulator of inflammatory and apoptotic pathways, particularly under oxidative challenge. Moreover, previous work has suggested that autophagy induced by spermidine can also lead to improvements in mitochondrial function and energy metabolism, which are crucial for maintaining RPE cell viability during chronic oxidative stress common in dry AMD (Rivera et al., 2024; Han et al., 2022). Thus, the proposed mechanism of action—selective inhibition of EP300 to enhance autophagic clearance and preserve junctional integrity—integrates multiple lines of evidence regarding the protective and rejuvenating effects of spermidine in cellular systems exposed to oxidative and metabolic stress (Luo et al., 2025; Han et al., 2022).

This reactivation should, in turn, lead to the clearance of accumulated A2E and other toxic lipofuscin components, mitigating their deleterious effects on RPE cell function (Han et al., 2022).

The preservation of ZO-1 and occludin belts is critical in maintaining the barrier integrity of the RPE monolayer, which is essential not only for preventing the translocation of toxic substances but also for sustaining proper retinal homeostasis. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
LG100268 is a fully synthetic rexinoid that was developed as a selective agonist for the retinoid X receptors (RXRs). It belongs to a specialized subclass of retinoids known as “rexinoids” that bind to RXRs with high affinity and minimal cross‐reactivity to the retinoic acid receptors (RARs). The compound was discovered and optimized in medicinal chemistry programs aiming to achieve potent RXR activation with improved receptor selectivity relative to earlier retinoid compounds such as bexarotene. Notably, synthetic modifications introduced in LG100268 include the incorporation of a 3‐carboxy pyridine ring—a modular motif that has been exploited for further scaffold diversification and structure–activity work to tune RXR heterodimer selectivity (Curley, 2012, pp. 4–5). LG100268 displays one of the highest reported binding affinities for RXR, with a dissociation constant in the low nanomolar range (approximately 3 nM), making it a very potent agent within its class (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Rexinoids such as LG100268 have been historically used in preclinical research as tools to explore RXR biology in oncology and metabolic studies—often by modulating gene transcription via RXR homodimers or RXR heterodimers with factors such as PPAR, LXR, and others (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). Although LG100268 was initially conceived for applications in cancer chemoprevention and metabolic regulation, its high potency and selective RXR activation have generated interest in repurposing it for diseases with an inflammatory component, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, LG100268 has been most notably explored in preclinical models of cancer—particularly in murine models of breast cancer. Studies in the MMTV-Neu (a HER2+ breast cancer model) and the MMTV-PyMT (an aggressive, triple-negative model) have shown that short-course dietary administration of LG100268 produces significant immunomodulatory effects. For example, in these models, LG100268 was observed to decrease the infiltration of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and CD206-expressing macrophages, while increasing the expression of PD-L1 and enhancing the ratio of cytotoxic CD8 T cells relative to CD4 T-cell subpopulations (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Additionally, combination studies with immune checkpoint inhibitors have further supported its potential to modulate the tumor microenvironment in preclinical oncology settings (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). In metabolic research, LG100268 has been administered to rodent models (such as diabetic ZDF rats and normal Sprague–Dawley rats) to evaluate its effects on lipid and glucose metabolism. In these contexts, LG100268 was shown to acutely lower serum glucose levels but also to induce marked hypertriglyceridemia linked to diminished lipoprotein lipase activity in muscle tissue, a pharmacodynamic liability that underscores the potent transcriptional effects mediated via RXR activation (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). Despite these promising activities in oncology and metabolic models, there are no documented studies, either preclinical or clinical, in which LG100268 has been directly used for treating dry AMD or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction. The entirety of its previous applications has been outside the ocular field, focusing on cancer chemoprevention and metabolic dysregulation; thus, its proposed repurposing for dry AMD represents an innovative but as-yet untested direction with respect to ocular indications (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lee & Khan, 2016, pp. 15–19).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, LG100268 acts as a high-affinity agonist for RXRs by binding selectively to the ligand-binding pocket of these nuclear receptors. RXRs are unique in that they function both as homodimers and as obligate heterodimer partners for multiple other nuclear receptors including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), liver X receptors (LXRs), and even possibly orphan receptors such as Nurr1. Upon binding LG100268, the RXR undergoes a conformational change that induces release of corepressors and recruitment of coactivators, thereby altering transcription of downstream target genes (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10). In cancer studies, the activation of RXR by LG100268 has been associated with modulation of the immune microenvironment; it reduces pro-tumor cytokine release, alters the balance of immune cell populations, and influences expression of cell surface proteins such as PD-L1 (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, in metabolic tissues, activation of RXR by LG100268 affects lipid metabolism through transcriptional control of genes involved in the regulation of lipoprotein lipase and other lipid-processing enzymes (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

The specific hypothesis proposed for dry AMD centers on the concept that selective RXR modulation might bias RXR heterodimerization toward partnering with Nurr1 in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-activated RPE cells. Nurr1, an orphan nuclear receptor, is implicated in anti-inflammatory responses and has been associated with maintenance of cellular differentiation and barrier function in various epithelial models. While direct evidence from the literature demonstrating RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation in RPE cells is limited, the general biology of RXR suggests that ligand-induced conformational changes in RXR can influence its choice of heterodimerization partner (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). In this scenario, by favoring the formation of RXR–Nurr1 heterodimers, LG100268 could suppress NF-κB-driven transcription. NF-κB is well known as a master regulator of inflammatory responses, and its activation (specifically the nuclear translocation of p65) can lead to the downregulation of tight junction proteins such as claudin-1. Therefore, by inhibiting NF-κB activity via this heterodimer bias, LG100268 is postulated to stabilize the epigenetic landscape and transcription of genes integral to maintaining tight junction integrity, thereby preserving transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE monolayers (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Although most of the mechanistic studies of LG100268 have been conducted in cancer and metabolic models, the underlying molecular interactions—namely high-affinity RXR activation, selective heterodimerization, and subsequent transcriptional modulation—provide a plausible basis for extending its use to inflammatory conditions of the RPE. These mechanisms are potentially relevant since RPE cells express multiple RXR isoforms; indeed, RXR expression in retinal tissues underlines its importance in visual cycle regulation and cellular homeostasis (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10, 10–12).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the pathological insult is thought to be driven in part by chronic, low-grade inflammation induced by drusen components and other pro-inflammatory stimuli such as LPS. In primary RPE cell cultures challenged with LPS, there is typically a cascade of events initiated by the activation of NF-κB that results in a decrease in the expression of tight junction proteins like claudin-1, leading to reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and impaired barrier function. The hypothesis for repurposing LG100268 in this application is that at a concentration of 0.1 µM, the compound will attenuate LPS-induced NF-κB activation, as evidenced by reduced nuclear translocation of the p65 subunit. This in turn is expected to prevent the downregulation of claudin-1 and maintain TEER in RPE cells. The mechanism underpinning this expected effect involves the selective activation of RXR by LG100268, which is postulated to shift the balance of RXR heterodimers in favor of complexes with Nurr1. The RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation would then lead to anti-inflammatory transcriptional outcomes, including suppression of NF-κB target genes that would otherwise contribute to tight junction disruption (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

Additionally, by modulating the epigenetic regulation of gene expression, LG100268 may help preserve the expression pattern of genes critical for barrier integrity. Published reports in other cell systems have demonstrated that rexinoids can influence the transcription of key cytokines and growth factors in a manner that normalizes cell adhesion molecules and maintains cellular differentiation (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Should LG100268 effectively prevent TEER loss and reduce nuclear p65 accumulation in primary RPE cultures, it would provide a strong rationale for its further development as a novel therapy aimed at stabilizing the RPE barrier in dry AMD (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

The repurposing of LG100268 for dry AMD is an innovative approach that leverages the compound’s well-documented ability to selectively activate RXRs. Its high-affinity binding and potent agonism make it one of the more promising rexinoids available, as evidenced by its superior receptor binding kinetics relative to known RXR ligands such as bexarotene (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Preclinical studies in oncology have consistently demonstrated that LG100268 modulates the immune microenvironment, induces changes in critical cytokine expression, and alters the balance of immune cell populations in a manner that collectively suggests an anti-inflammatory profile (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). These anti-inflammatory effects, when viewed through the lens of RPE biology, provide a plausible mechanistic basis for protecting against the chronic inflammation that characterizes dry AMD. Particularly, the hypothesis that LG100268 may bias RXR heterodimer formation toward Nurr1—and thus suppress NF-κB signaling—opens a new avenue for preserving tight junction integrity in RPE cells, which is critically important in maintaining a proper barrier function (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

Moreover, LG100268’s capacity to induce targeted epigenetic modulation further supports its potential to stabilize gene expression profiles under inflammatory conditions. Maintaining the expression of tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 is vital for preventing the breakdown of the blood–retina barrier and subsequent RPE degeneration. In vitro observations that LG100268 at 0.1 µM prevented TEER loss and inhibited NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation in primary RPE models provide encouraging preliminary data for its use in this context. This evidence, combined with its established anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties in other systems, makes a compelling case for considering LG100268 as a candidate for treating dry AMD (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12; Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

Nevertheless, there are several challenges and uncertainties that must be addressed. Foremost among these is the absence of any prior documentation—either in the biomedical, clinical, or biochemical literature—that LG100268 has been applied in any ocular or RPE-specific context. Its therapeutic history is entirely rooted in applications related to cancer and metabolic regulation, and its safety profile in the context of ocular tissues remains uncharacterized. Systemic administration of potent rexinoids is known to produce adverse metabolic effects, such as hypertriglyceridemia and thyroid hormone axis suppression (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). The risk of systemic side effects may be mitigated by ocular-targeted delivery methods; however, the pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of LG100268 following ocular administration require thorough investigation.

Another significant weakness lies in the hypothesis that LG100268 will bias RXR heterodimerization toward Nurr1. Although the concept is mechanistically attractive, the current literature does not provide direct evidence that LG100268 preferentially promotes RXR–Nurr1 complexes in RPE cells (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). In addition, the potential involvement of alternative RXR partners—including PPARs and LXRs, which are also expressed in RPE cells—could complicate the desired selectivity. NF-κB signaling is only one among many pathways that regulate barrier integrity, and the extent to which RXR activation can counterbalance other detrimental signaling cascades in the RPE is not fully understood. The potential exists for complex cross-talk between RXR-mediated pathways and other nuclear receptor pathways, which might lead to unpredictable outcomes in the delicate environment of the retina (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–12; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

In summary, while LG100268’s established potency, receptor selectivity, and capacity to modulate inflammatory and metabolic gene expression provide a strong foundation for considering its repurposing, the current literature does not yet offer direct support for its use in dry AMD. Preclinical studies that specifically assess the effects of LG100268 on RPE barrier function, tight junction integrity, and inflammatory signaling in ocular models are necessary to validate the hypothesis. Moreover, rigorous toxicological assessments and the development of targeted delivery methods will be required to overcome the potential liabilities associated with systemic rexinoid administration. Until these issues are addressed, LG100268 remains a promising yet exploratory candidate for dry AMD therapy (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10; Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PF-06409577 [6-chloro-5-(4-(1-hydroxycyclobutyl)phenyl)-1H-indole-3-carboxylic acid] is a synthetic, indole-3-carboxylic acid small molecule discovered in a Pfizer program to generate direct, isoform-selective activators of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) for metabolic and renal indications (notably diabetic nephropathy) (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Webb et al., 2019). Medicinal chemistry and structural biology work established PF-06409577 as a direct allosteric AMPK activator that binds the α1β1γ1 heterotrimer and engages the so-called allosteric drug and metabolite (ADaM) site at the α–β interface, with co-crystallization data reported for the parent and its metabolites bound to α1β1γ1 (Ryder et al., 2018; Steinberg & Carling, 2019). In biochemical assays and surface plasmon resonance (SPR), PF-06409577 and related indole-3-carboxylic acids preferentially activate and bind β1-containing AMPK isoforms, with little-to-no activity against β2-containing human AMPK heterotrimers under the conditions reported; notably, the acyl glucuronide conjugates (M1–M3) retain β1-selective AMPK activation with reduced potency relative to the parent (Ryder et al., 2018). Consistent with β-subunit–driven selectivity of ADaM ligands, prior work with thienopyridone A-769662 and benzimidazole 991 demonstrates β1 > β2 preference and mechanistic dependence on β1-Ser108, a key determinant of ADaM-site responsiveness (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).

PF-06409577 belongs to the class of direct, small-molecule AMPK activators designed to allosterically activate the kinase and protect Thr172 phosphorylation from dephosphorylation, in contrast to indirect mitochondrial poisons (e.g., metformin, phenformin, berberine) that raise cellular AMP/ADP and secondarily activate AMPK (Steinberg & Carling, 2019). Within this class, multiple chemotypes (thienopyridones, benzimidazoles, indole acids, and pan-activators such as MK-8722) have been used to probe metabolism, autophagy/mitophagy, and lipid homeostasis in vivo, with both efficacy signals (e.g., cholesterol lowering, NAFLD correction, organ protection) and safety liabilities (e.g., cardiac hypertrophy with a pan-activator) documented across programs (Behl et al., 2021; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2019).

Beyond primary pharmacology, PF-06409577 and congeners are extensively glucuronidated in animals and humans; unusually, the resulting acyl glucuronides remain pharmacologically active at AMPK, preserving β1-selective activation and direct binding to α1β1γ1 in vitro (albeit with 9–19-fold lower potency than the parent), a property with implications for exposure, distribution, and safety (Ryder et al., 2018). The acyl glucuronides of this series were reported to be relatively stable to hydrolysis and acyl migration at physiological pH (t1/2 > 21 h in buffer), a feature that lowers, but does not eliminate, typical concerns about acyl glucuronide–mediated covalent protein modification and idiosyncratic toxicity in carboxylic acid drugs (Ryder et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History  
PF-06409577 was developed as a β1-selective AMPK activator for diabetic nephropathy; it achieved Phase I clinical testing but was discontinued (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), and there is no report of ophthalmic or AMD use in the available sources (Webb et al., 2019). Preclinically, selective activation of β1-containing AMPK isoforms has been linked to improved kidney function in rat nephropathy models, and liver-targeted activation by PF-06409577 corrected NAFLD and lowered cholesterol in rodent and primate studies, with target engagement tracked via ACC phosphorylation (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019). In contrast to pan-activators such as MK-8722 that improved systemic glucose homeostasis but caused cardiac hypertrophy with glycogen accumulation in rodents and primates, β1-selective strategies are viewed as potentially safer with respect to cardiac glycogen loading and skeletal muscle glucose uptake, although this requires empirical confirmation per compound and tissue (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Behl et al., 2021). Of note, β1-biased activation by PF-06409577 has been reported to increase plasma ketone bodies and reduce hepatic triacylglycerol and cholesterol without lowering blood glucose—an important metabolic profile distinction (Behl et al., 2021).

In ocular biology, PF-06409577 has been directly tested in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells in vitro. Li et al. (2018) reported that PF-06409577 activates AMPK signaling and protects both ARPE-19 and primary murine RPEs from ultraviolet radiation (UVR), reducing ROS, lipid peroxidation, DNA damage, apoptosis, and cell death, with accompanying increases in NADPH activity and Nrf2-dependent antioxidant gene expression (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC, GCLM). The protective effects were strictly AMPKα1-dependent (shRNA, dominant-negative T172A, and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout each abrogated PF-mediated protection and AMPK activation), establishing on-target mechanism in RPE under oxidative stress (Li et al., 2018). The paper presents dose–response and time-course data showing AMPKα Thr172 and ACC Ser79 phosphorylation in ARPE-19 over ~0.1–1.0 μM PF-06409577, with 0.03 μM ineffective; parallel experiments in primary RPE at 0.3 μM showed similar activation (Li et al., 2018). The authors also describe PF-06409577 potency as “nM” in RPE in narrative discussion, consistent with direct engagement yet not fully aligned with the 0.03 μM threshold in their western blot data; together, these findings indicate sub- to low-micromolar cellular potencies in RPE compatible with direct ADaM-site engagement (Li et al., 2018). Importantly, the RPE literature to date contains no reports of PF-06409577 use in AMD patients, no in vivo AMD models with PF-06409577, and no published measurements of RPE tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin) or transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) for this agent (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).

Additional translational history for PF-06409577 includes use as a host-directed antiviral tool; AMPK activation by PF-06409577 inhibited replication of flaviviruses (WNV, ZIKV, DENV-2) by interfering with replication complex development linked to host membrane rearrangements and lipid synthesis, at micromolar EC50s with acceptable in vitro selectivity indices (Jiménez de Oya et al., 2018). This antiviral application further underscores the compound’s capacity to reprogram lipid metabolism in stressed cells, relevant to lipid-rich pathology in AMD.

Within the broader therapeutic class, indirect AMPK activators (notably metformin) have been repeatedly associated with retinal protection: metformin reduces drusen formation via LXR/ABCA1/G1-mediated cholesterol efflux, suppresses inflammation (e.g., NLRP3 inflammasome), protects RPE and photoreceptors via PGC-1α/mitochondrial regulation, induces autophagy via AMPK–mTOR, and dampens VEGF signaling in vascular endothelium (all AMPK-dependent), strengthening the conceptual precedent that AMPK activation is protective in retinal degenerations (Dang et al., 2021). However, these metformin data do not establish PF-06409577-specific safety or efficacy in RPE barrier endpoints such as ZO-1, occludin, or TEER (Dang et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Direct binding and isoform selectivity. PF-06409577 and its acyl glucuronide metabolites bind directly to AMPK α1β1γ1 at the ADaM site at the α–β interface, driving allosteric activation and protection against Thr172 dephosphorylation of the α subunit; β1-selective activation is borne out across biochemical and SPR binding assays, and the acyl glucuronides retain β1 selectivity albeit at lower potency (Ryder et al., 2018). ADaM-site pharmacology is isoform-sensitive: conformational and sequence differences in the αC helix and β-subunit (including the β C-interacting helix) modulate ligand responsiveness, with β1-Ser108 phosphorylation enabling synergism between nucleotide- and ADaM-site activation (e.g., AMP plus A-769662/991), and mutation at α Leu166 selectively reduces activation by certain ligands (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019). These structural determinants rationalize β1 preference for ADaM-site ligands and inform tissue-selectivity hypotheses in β1-rich cells (Steinberg & Carling, 2019).

RPE cell signaling and cytoprotection. In ARPE-19 and primary murine RPEs, PF-06409577 rapidly increases AMPKα1 Thr172 phosphorylation and phosphorylation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) at Ser79, a canonical AMPK substrate, with parallel increases in AMPK activity (Li et al., 2018). Functionally, PF-06409577 pretreatment reduces UVR-induced ROS (DCFH-DA), lipid peroxidation (TBARs), DNA damage (p-γH2AX), apoptosis (ssDNA, cleaved caspase-3, Annexin-V/PI), and cell death (LDH), while improving viability (CCK-8), in both ARPE-19 and primary RPE cultures (Li et al., 2018). The compound enhances cellular NADPH activity and stabilizes Nrf2 protein with induction of classical Nrf2 target genes (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC, GCLM), consistent with increased antioxidant capacity and a transcriptional response favoring cytoprotection (Li et al., 2018). Genetic disruption of AMPKα1 (shRNA, dominant-negative T172A mutant, or CRISPR/Cas9 knockout) abrogates both AMPK signaling and PF-mediated protection, demonstrating that AMPKα1 is necessary for the observed effects (Li et al., 2018). Mechanistically, AMPK can preserve NADPH through ACC inactivation (limiting de novo lipogenesis and malonyl-CoA production) and by promoting fatty acid oxidation, both of which improve redox balance; AMPK also phosphorylates Nrf2 at Ser550 to facilitate nuclear translocation and transactivation, with additional indirect support via inhibition of GSK3β-driven nuclear exclusion and p62/SQSTM1-mediated KEAP1 autophagic degradation, all of which are documented upstream regulatory routes present in RPE cells (Hu et al., 2024).

Metabolic control, autophagy, and lipid handling. AMPK is a master regulator of lipid metabolism and autophagy: it phosphorylates and inhibits ACC1/ACC2 to reduce de novo lipogenesis and lower malonyl-CoA, promoting mitochondrial fatty acid import and β-oxidation; AMPK also phosphorylates ULK1 to initiate autophagy and can activate PGC-1α to drive mitochondrial biogenesis, enhance mitophagy, and improve mitochondrial quality control (Webb et al., 2019). Although the RPE PF-06409577 literature does not yet report autophagy markers (LC3-II, p62) or lipid droplet turnover, studies in ARPE-19 with an independent AMPK-activating intervention (liraglutide) show that AMPK activation in FFA-loaded RPE restores autophagy/lipophagy (↑LC3-II, ↓p62, ↓p-mTOR), reduces ROS and lipid droplet burden, rescues EMT markers, and restores ZO-1 localization at the membrane—effects blocked by pharmacologic AMPK inhibition—thereby validating these AMPK-dependent axes in RPE (Tsou et al., 2025). More generally, AICAR activation of AMPK upregulated ABCA1/ABCG1 in RPE and reduced Bruch’s membrane lipid deposition in ApoE⁻/⁻ mice, connecting AMPK to cholesterol efflux pathways relevant to drusen biogenesis (Hu et al., 2024). Collectively, these mechanisms support the plausibility that a direct AMPK activator such as PF-06409577 can modulate autophagy and lipid metabolism in RPE even though PF-specific autophagy/lipophagy data in RPE have not yet been reported (Li et al., 2018; Tsou et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).

Barrier integrity and tight-junction assembly. AMPK has been mechanistically linked to tight-junction assembly in epithelial systems: it promotes ZO-1 reassembly at paracellular contacts, phosphorylates claudin-1 (preventing degradation) and claudin-4 (promoting occludin binding), and phosphorylates scaffold proteins (e.g., cingulin, afadin) and MLCK to tune actin–junction interactions and permeability (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). In RPE specifically, liraglutide’s AMPK-dependent rescue of ZO-1 distribution under FFA challenge suggests that AMPK activation can re-normalize barrier-associated proteins in RPE cultures, although TEER was not reported in that study and the journal quality warrants cautious interpretation (Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). To date, no published data directly demonstrate effects of PF-06409577 on ZO-1/occludin or TEER in RPE; thus, junctional rescue by PF-06409577 remains a testable hypothesis rather than an established mechanism (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).

Systemic pharmacology and safety context. In liver and kidney settings, PF-06409577 engages AMPK in vivo (e.g., pACC biomarker), lowers hepatic lipogenesis, corrects NAFLD, and confers renal protection in β1-focused pharmacology paradigms, while β1 activation by PF-06409577 has been noted to not lower blood glucose (Behl et al., 2021). Pan-activation by MK-8722 in renal disease improved mitochondrial quality control, reduced lipotoxicity and fibrosis, and improved function but highlighted a class-level safety risk—cardiac hypertrophy with glycogen accumulation under some dosing regimens—underscoring the importance of subunit selectivity and tissue targeting for chronic use (Zhou et al., 2019; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). The acyl glucuronide metabolites of PF-06409577 are pharmacologically active and chemically stable in buffer; however, acyl glucuronides as a class have been implicated in idiosyncratic immune toxicities, and careful metabolite profiling and reactive metabolite risk assessment will be required for ocular delivery strategies (Ryder et al., 2018).

Expected Effect  
Rationale in dry AMD pathobiology. Oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/mitophagy, and dysregulated lipid handling are central to RPE dysfunction and drusen biogenesis in dry AMD, with age-related decline in Nrf2-mediated antioxidant defense and lysosome–phagosome fusion defects compounding vulnerability (Hu et al., 2024). AMPK activation is positioned to counter these processes by: (1) improving NADPH homeostasis and activating Nrf2 target gene programs, (2) initiating autophagy/mitophagy via ULK1 while suppressing mTORC1 signaling, (3) reducing lipogenesis (via ACC) and supporting fatty acid oxidation and cholesterol efflux (via LXR–ABCA1/G1), and (4) stabilizing/assembling tight junctions through claudin/occludin/ZO-1 scaffold and cytoskeletal phosphorylation events (Li et al., 2018; Dang et al., 2021; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).

What PF-06409577 is expected to do in RPE assays. Based on the published RPE data and AMPK biology, the following effects are expected if PF-06409577 is applied to human RPE cultures (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary RPE) under oxidative and lipid-loading stress:
- Oxidative stress resistance: Increased AMPKα Thr172 and ACC Ser79 phosphorylation, elevated NADPH/NADP⁺, stabilization of Nrf2 protein, and induction of antioxidant genes (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC, GCLM), with reduced ROS, lipid peroxidation and DNA damage under UVR or oxidant challenges, as shown directly in ARPE-19 and primary RPE by Li et al. (Li et al., 2018). These endpoints should be AMPKα1-dependent (loss-of-function tamps down PF effects) (Li et al., 2018).
- Lipid handling and autophagy: Although untested for PF-06409577 in RPE, AMPK activation in ARPE-19 (with liraglutide) restored autophagy and lipophagy markers (↑LC3-II, ↓p62, ↓p-mTOR), reduced lipid droplet number/size, and normalized lipophagy/lysosome gene expression (ATG5, LIPA, RAB7A, LAMP2) in an AMPK-dependent manner; PF-06409577 should be evaluated for these endpoints under free fatty acid or oxLDL loading where AMPK effects are mechanistically expected (Tsou et al., 2025). Independent RPE evidence that AMPK activation increases ABCA1/ABCG1 and decreases Bruch’s membrane lipid deposition supports anticipated benefits on cholesterol efflux (Hu et al., 2024).
- Barrier integrity: AMPK’s direct effects on tight-junction components and scaffolds in epithelial systems suggest PF-06409577 could improve ZO-1/occludin organization and paracellular barrier function (TEER), but no PF-06409577 data exist in RPE; therefore, ZO-1/occludin immunolocalization and TEER must be prospectively measured. The liraglutide ARPE-19 study showing AMPK-dependent restoration of ZO-1 under FFA stress provides a relevant positive control framework for assay design, with the caveat of study quality and absence of TEER measurements (Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).
- Dosing/target engagement: In ARPE-19 and primary RPE, AMPK activation by PF-06409577 occurred with sub- to low-micromolar exposure (0.1–1.0 μM active, 0.03 μM inactive in westerns), with 0.3 μM effective in primary RPE; therefore, a concentration range of ~0.03–1 μM should be explored with pACC and pAMPKα as engagement biomarkers and NADPH/Nrf2 targets as pharmacodynamic readouts (Li et al., 2018). Biochemical potency of PF-06409577 can be in the single-digit nanomolar range against recombinant AMPK and cellular potency for pACC has been described as “nM” in RPE contexts; nonetheless, empirical titration in RPE is warranted given observed cell-assay thresholds (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).
- Isoform selectivity in RPE: PF-06409577 is β1-selective, and ADaM-site ligand responsiveness is strongly β-isoform-dependent; however, AMPK β isoform expression distribution in human RPE is not provided in the current sources and should be profiled (mRNA/protein) to confirm the β1 hypothesis before assuming superior tissue selectivity (Ryder et al., 2018; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).
- Network cross-talk and safety in vitro: Co-activation of AMPK and mTORC1 has been associated with cytotoxic outcomes in some cell types; assays should monitor mTORC1 readouts (p-S6K, p-4EBP1) alongside autophagy flux to ensure PF-06409577 produces the expected AMPK→mTORC1 inhibition and does not trigger maladaptive co-activation contexts in RPE (Li et al., 2018).

Collectively, the expected proximal effects of PF-06409577 in RPE are robust AMPK activation with antioxidant and metabolic reprogramming, and the expected distal outcomes include reduced oxidative injury and improved lipid/autophagy balance. Barrier strengthening (ZO-1/occludin, TEER) is mechanistically plausible based on AMPK biology and AMPK-dependent rescue with alternative activators in ARPE-19, but must be experimentally demonstrated for PF-06409577 (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Tsou et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Direct, β1-selective AMPK activation with structural, biophysical, and biochemical support. PF-06409577 directly binds and activates AMPK α1β1γ1 at the ADaM site and shows clear β1 selectivity across parents and acyl glucuronide metabolites; this selectivity is a desirable property for limiting pan-AMPK liabilities observed with compounds like MK-8722 (e.g., cardiac glycogen accumulation) (Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).  
- Demonstrated on-target cytoprotection in RPE. Li et al. (2018) show AMPKα1-dependent protection of ARPE-19 and primary RPE against UVR, with mechanistic readouts aligned to AMD pathogenesis: increased NADPH, Nrf2 target induction, reduced ROS, lipid peroxidation, DNA damage, apoptosis, and cell death—providing a strong cell-biological foundation for further RPE work (Li et al., 2018).  
- Mechanistic fit to AMD drivers. AMPK activation intersects the principal RPE failure modes in AMD—redox imbalance (Nrf2), impaired autophagy/mitophagy (ULK1/mTORC1), and lipid dysregulation (ACC, FAO, LXR/ABCA1/G1)—and AMPK-dependent restoration of autophagy/lipophagy and barrier proteins has been demonstrated in ARPE-19 using a different AMPK-activating intervention (liraglutide), making PF-06409577 a mechanistically well-targeted candidate to modulate those pathways (Dang et al., 2021; Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).  
- Favorable metabolic profile and organ-protection precedent. PF-06409577 corrected NAFLD and lowered cholesterol in rodent/primate models with liver AMPK dependence, improved renal endpoints in β1-focused paradigms, and did not lower blood glucose in reported contexts, all suggesting a differentiated systemic pharmacology relative to pan-activators and indirect mitochondrial inhibitors (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).  
- Metabolite pharmacology understood. Active acyl glucuronides have been characterized structurally and functionally and exhibit β1-selective AMPK activation with notable stability, reducing concern about unstable, highly reactive acyl glucuronide species (while not fully removing risk), and informing PK/distribution planning for ocular routes (Ryder et al., 2018).

Key Gaps and Risks  
- No published junctional/TEER data for PF-06409577 in RPE. The project’s central claim—restoration of RPE junction integrity (ZO-1/occludin localization, TEER elevation, reduced paracellular permeability)—has not been demonstrated for PF-06409577 in any RPE model in the sources provided; this is the most critical data gap for the proposed indication (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).  
- No PF-06409577 autophagy/lipophagy data in RPE. While AMPK activation in ARPE-19 by liraglutide restored autophagy/lipophagy and rescued ZO-1 in an AMPK-dependent manner, PF-06409577-specific data on ULK1 phosphorylation, LC3 flux, p62 turnover, lysosome–autophagosome fusion, and lipid droplet dynamics in RPE are absent and must be generated (Tsou et al., 2025).  
- AMPK β isoform expression in human RPE is not established in the provided literature. Although ADaM ligands are β1-preferring and PF-06409577 is β1-selective, we do not have direct evidence here that β1 predominates in mature human RPE; consequently, isoform profiling is a necessary early-stage risk-reduction step (Steinberg & Carling, 2019; Ryder et al., 2018).  
- Cellular potency window in RPE requires clarification. Li et al. (2018) show a clear activation threshold between 0.03 μM (inactive) and 0.1–1.0 μM (active) for AMPKα phosphorylation in ARPE-19 and efficacy at 0.3 μM in primary RPE, whereas narrative text suggests “nM” activation; this discrepancy underscores the need for rigorous concentration–response across engagement and functional endpoints in relevant human RPE models (Li et al., 2018).  
- Clinical development discontinued; no ocular safety data. PF-06409577’s clinical program was halted at Phase I for non-ocular indications; no ophthalmic tolerability, ocular PK, or on-target/off-target safety in retinal tissues has been reported here. Acyl glucuronides, while stable in vitro for this series, can pose idiosyncratic risk; pan-AMPK activation has known cardiac liabilities; and network cross-talk (e.g., co-activation of AMPK and mTORC1) could be deleterious in some contexts—all argue for early safety de-risking (Webb et al., 2019; Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).

Programmatic Recommendations  
Near-term, decision-making studies should prioritize: (1) RPE isoform mapping (AMPK α/β/γ mRNA and protein), (2) dose–response and time-course profiling of PF-06409577 in human primary RPE or iPSC-RPE (pAMPKα Thr172, pACC Ser79, NADPH/NADP⁺, Nrf2 protein and targets), (3) autophagy/lipophagy flux assays (LC3-II turnover with/without lysosomal blockade, p62 degradation, ULK1 phosphorylation, mTORC1 markers), (4) lipid droplet quantification (number, size distribution) under FFA or oxLDL loading, (5) junctional biology (ZO-1/occludin claudin-1/4 localization and levels, cingulin/afadin phosphorylation status) and barrier function (TEER, FITC-dextran permeability), and (6) safety pharmacology in RPE (viability, apoptosis, senescence markers; exploration of AMPK–mTORC1 co-activation risk) across 0.03–1.0 μM with pACC-guided on-target exposure (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).

If in vitro RPE data are supportive, next steps include: (7) ocular PK after topical/periocular dosing (parent and acyl glucuronides in RPE/choroid), (8) metabolite profiling and covalent adduct risk assessment in ocular tissues, (9) in vivo efficacy in AMD-relevant models (e.g., light damage, Alu RNA–induced RPE degeneration, HFD/oxLDL models) with barrier and lipid endpoints, and (10) safety screens for cardiac glycogen accumulation under systemic exposure (to benchmark β1 selectivity advantages) (Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
PF-06409577 is a well-characterized, β1-selective, direct AMPK activator with on-target, AMPKα1-dependent cytoprotective activity in RPE cells under oxidative stress, and with strong mechanistic alignment to dry AMD pathobiology via NADPH/Nrf2, autophagy/mitophagy, and lipid metabolism pathways (Li et al., 2018). Class knowledge and comparator interventions support the plausibility that AMPK activation can restore RPE lipid homeostasis and barrier protein organization; however, critical indication-specific evidence—PF-06409577’s effects on RPE autophagy/lipophagy and junctional/TEER endpoints—is currently missing and must be generated before advancing (Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). The compound’s β1 selectivity, favorable metabolic efficacy profile (NAFLD/kidney), and lack of glucose-lowering are attractive, but the discontinued clinical status, the pharmacologically active acyl glucuronides, and known liabilities with pan-AMPK activation emphasize the need for deliberate safety de-risking and ocular PK/metabolite work (Behl et al., 2021; Ryder et al., 2018; Webb et al., 2019; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).

On balance, PF-06409577 merits a focused, RPE-centric preclinical validation campaign for dry AMD that directly tests barrier and lipid endpoints while monitoring canonical AMPK engagement and redox rescue. Positive readouts across ZO-1/occludin/TEER, autophagy/lipophagy markers, and lipid droplet turnover—together with preservation of mitochondrial/antioxidant markers—would substantially de-risk the mechanistic hypothesis and justify advancement toward ocular PK/safety studies and in vivo efficacy models (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024). At present, claims of TEER restoration and junctional upregulation by PF-06409577 in RPE cannot be substantiated from the available literature and should be considered unproven working hypotheses pending experimental confirmation (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History (Expanded Summary)  
- Origin/chemotype: Indole-3-carboxylic acid, direct ADaM-site AMPK activator; discovered and preclinically characterized by Pfizer for diabetic nephropathy (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Strang et al., 2025).  
- Selectivity/biophysics: Direct binding to α1β1γ1 with β1 selectivity; acyl glucuronide metabolites retain β1 activity with lower potency; likely mode includes allosteric activation and protection from Thr172 dephosphorylation (Ryder et al., 2018; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).  
- Systemic pharmacology: Liver AMPK activation corrected NAFLD and lowered cholesterol in rodents and primates; β1 activation improved kidney function in rodent models (Behl et al., 2021).  
- Safety-class signals: Pan-activator MK-8722 causes cardiac hypertrophy with glycogen in rodents/primate models; PF-06409577 reported not to lower blood glucose; acyl glucuronides stable but class risk remains (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Behl et al., 2021; Ryder et al., 2018).  
- Ocular biology: Direct RPE cytoprotection against UVR via AMPKα1-dependent signaling; no published PF-06409577 data on RPE junctions/TEER/autophagy endpoints (Li et al., 2018).

Mechanistic Integration in AMD Context  
- AMPK→Nrf2 redox axis: AMPK phosphorylation of Nrf2 (Ser550), indirect relief of KEAP1 repression (via GSK3β inhibition and p62-mediated KEAP1 autophagic degradation), and upregulation of antioxidant enzymes; these are operative in RPE and are enhanced by PF-06409577 in vitro (Hu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2018).  
- AMPK→ULK1/mTOR/autophagy: AMPK initiates autophagy, antagonizes mTORC1, and in RPE models AMPK activation restores autophagy/lipophagy, reduces EMT, and normalizes barrier protein localization under lipid stress—mechanistic endpoints to quantify for PF-06409577 (Dang et al., 2021; Tsou et al., 2025).  
- AMPK→ACC/FAO/lipogenesis: ACC inhibition reduces DNL and malonyl-CoA, permitting FAO flux; in RPE, this is expected to reduce lipid droplet accrual and lipoperoxidation burden central to drusen precursor formation (Webb et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2024).  
- AMPK→junction assembly: Phosphorylation of claudins and scaffold proteins, ZO-1 reassembly, and cytoskeletal remodeling provide a direct mechanistic route for barrier strengthening; this is plausible in RPE but requires PF-06409577-specific testing (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).

Decision Framework for Advancement  
- Go/No-Go criteria: Require demonstration that PF-06409577 increases pAMPKα/pACC and Nrf2 targets; reduces ROS/lipid peroxidation/DNA damage in RPE; increases autophagy flux and reduces lipid droplets under FFA or oxLDL; and improves ZO-1/occludin organization with increased TEER and reduced paracellular permeability, all in an AMPK-dependent manner (Li et al., 2018; Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).  
- Risk mitigation: Profile β isoform expression in human RPE; measure mTORC1 to exclude maladaptive co-activation; characterize ocular PK and acyl glucuronide distribution after topical/periocular delivery; benchmark systemic exposure to avoid cardiac glycogen liabilities (Steinberg & Carling, 2019; Li et al., 2018; Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).  
- Comparative positioning: If PF-06409577 proves effective on junctions and lipid/autophagy endpoints, its β1 selectivity and direct mechanism position it favorably versus indirect activators (metformin) and pan-activators (MK-8722); conversely, lack of junctional efficacy or safety signals would shift focus to alternative AMPK modulators or upstream modulators that converge on AMPK/Nrf2 with better ocular PK (Dang et al., 2021; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).

In summary, PF-06409577 has clear mechanistic and cellular evidence to support further exploration in dry AMD, with the caveat that the most clinically salient endpoints for RPE barrier restoration and lipid clearance remain to be proven for this agent. A disciplined experimental plan targeting these gaps will determine whether PF-06409577 advances as a credible candidate for RPE junction restoration in dry AMD (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024; Behl et al., 2021).

Multiple independent studies in human RPE-derived cell models and in vivo retinal injury models demonstrate that SFN robustly activates Nrf2/ARE-dependent antioxidant enzymes (NQO1, HO-1, GSTs, Trx1), elevates GSH, suppresses proinflammatory mediators (ICAM-1, MCP-1, NF-κB), and preserves retinal and RPE function (ERG rescue, cone function) in oxidative or phototoxic injury. The primary gaps are direct TEER/FITC-dextran barrier assays in RPE and optimized ocular delivery, but these are addressable with focused PK/PD and functional barrier experiments. CHIR99021 (ID: 31), by contrast, is a potent research-tool GSK-3β inhibitor that drives Wnt/β-catenin and RPE differentiation from stem cells, yet lacks in vivo or clinical data for dry AMD. There is no direct evidence that CHIR99021 upregulates tight junction genes or restores barrier function under oxidative stress; in fact, it impaired wound repair in an RPE wound model. Its safety in humans is uncharacterized, and drug delivery to the RPE remains unexplored. While CHIR99021 has mechanistic plausibility for epithelial differentiation, its relevance to mature, stressed RPE barrier rescue is speculative and context-dependent.
Reasoning: Sulforaphane emerges as the superior candidate because it has robust, disease-relevant preclinical efficacy in both cellular and animal models of retinal oxidative injury, a well-validated and multitargeted mechanism directly addressing core AMD pathology, and an established safety and translational profile in humans. CHIR99021, although biochemically specific and powerful for stem cell differentiation, lacks direct evidence of barrier restoration in oxidative stress models, shows contradictory effects in mature RPE, and has no clinical safety data or repurposing history.
