Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate generated from the glucosinolate glucoraphanin by the β-thioglucosidase myrosinase, which is abundant in cruciferous vegetables (notably broccoli sprouts). Its electrophilic –N=C=S moiety underlies covalent reactivity with nucleophilic cysteines on sensor proteins, most prominently Keap1, and thereby triggers a broad antioxidant and cytoprotective transcriptional response controlled by Nrf2 (NFE2L2) via antioxidant response elements (AREs) in gene promoters (phase-2 enzymes, redox systems, and detoxification pathways) (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). In retinal and epithelial contexts, SFN has been repeatedly characterized as an “indirect antioxidant” that elevates glutathione (GSH) and induces ARE-dependent enzymes such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1/HMOX1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and thioredoxin (Trx1), among others (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Tanito et al., 2005; Liu & Yan, 2018). In human RPE-derived cell models, SFN increased GSH and induced NQO1 and GST, consistent with canonical ARE program activation (Zhou et al., 2006). In vivo ocular models show SFN attenuates retinal light damage and improves functional outcomes, further anchoring its relevance to oxidative injury in the outer retina and RPE (Tanito et al., 2005; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Within its class, SFN is a prototypical dietary electrophile that activates Nrf2 signaling; this class has been broadly studied for chemoprevention and cytoprotection across organs. In ocular tissues, SFN has been shown to protect RPE and photoreceptors from diverse oxidative and phototoxic insults, often in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Yang et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025). Beyond Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α cross-talk, PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ stress-response nodes, and autophagy/lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs (TFEB/TFE3), all of which intersect with oxidative, inflammatory, and proteostasis stress pathways in RPE biology (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025).

Practical development considerations include bioavailability and delivery. Human studies and reviews indicate that the bioactive isothiocyanate is formed from glucoraphanin in a process heavily dependent on myrosinase (plant or microbiota), with documented systemic exposure and biomarker modulation in clinical settings; however, SFN’s oral bioavailability is limited by solubility, first-pass metabolism, and short plasma half-life, posing translational challenges for ocular exposure through blood–ocular barriers (Zhang et al., 2024). Preclinical delivery strategies such as nanoparticle and albumin carrier systems have been proposed to overcome ocular delivery constraints (Zhang et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
SFN and related Nrf2 activators have a long history as cytoprotective agents in preclinical models spanning oncology prevention, vascular and metabolic protection, and neuroprotection. In humans, SFN or broccoli sprout preparations have been administered in controlled trials with documented pharmacodynamic biomarker changes and well-characterized disposition and metabolism; crossover and dose-response studies highlight interconversion with related isothiocyanates (erucin) and underscore the importance of active myrosinase for consistent systemic exposure (Zhang et al., 2024; Qin, 2007). A pilot study detected SFN metabolites in human breast tissue after a single oral broccoli sprout dose, demonstrating tissue penetration to an epithelial compartment and supporting oral bioavailability to peripheral tissues (Qin, 2007). Although multiple clinical contexts are covered in these translational reviews and trials, there are no reported clinical trials of SFN specifically targeting dry AMD or RPE degeneration in the provided material (Zhang et al., 2024).

In ocular systems, the compound’s therapeutic history is robust at the preclinical level. In cultured human RPE, SFN protects against photooxidative injury (A2E/blue light) and chemical oxidants, increases GSH, and induces phase-2 enzymes including NQO1 and GST (Zhou et al., 2006). Microarray and validation work in human RPE-19 cells demonstrate SFN-induced nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and upregulation of thioredoxin-1, with enhanced oxidative stress resistance following H₂O₂ (Ye et al., 2013). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage in mice through ARE-mediated upregulation of thioredoxin (Trx1), and recovers cone function in a model of RPE oxidative stress in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025). SFN also protects rodent retinas from ischemia–reperfusion injury by increasing Nrf2 nuclear accumulation and HO-1 expression; pharmacologic inhibition of HO-1 abolishes protection, causally implicating HO-1 (Pan et al., 2014). In inherited retinal degeneration models (rd10 and tubby), systemic SFN improves retinal function and reduces degeneration, with evidence that ERK signaling and the Trx/TrxR/Nrf2 axis mediate effects in some settings (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Comparable ocular benefits have been shown in non-RPE tissues. For example, human corneal endothelial FECD cells exhibit SFN-induced Nrf2 nuclear translocation and upregulation of canonical ARE genes (NQO1, HO-1), with reduced ROS and apoptosis (Ziaei et al., 2013). In corneal surface epithelium, SFN protects against oxidative stress via Nrf2/HO-1 activation, supporting generalizability across ocular epithelial cell types (Liu & Yan, 2018). These data reinforce the core mechanism and pharmacology relevant to RPE while underlining the absence of AMD-specific clinical translation to date (Zhang et al., 2024).

Notably, although there is a recent report in an inflamed ARPE-19 model that vitamin D and SFN (alone and combined) reduced ROS, reduced IL-6/IL-8, lowered VEGF, and restored epithelial integrity markers including ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression, the provided material does not include functional barrier endpoints (TEER or FITC-dextran permeability), and claudin-1 is not shown (Bergandi et al., 2024). Thus, while “marker restoration” has been reported for ZO-1 and claudin-4 under TGF-β stress, quantitative barrier function restoration has not yet been demonstrated within the provided sources (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary mechanism—Keap1 cysteine targeting and Nrf2 activation: SFN’s electrophilic isothiocyanate group reacts with redox-sensitive cysteines on Keap1 (notably Cys151), disrupting the Cul3–Keap1 E3 ligase complex and stabilizing Nrf2, which accumulates and translocates to the nucleus. There, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences to upregulate a broad enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant and detoxification program (e.g., NQO1, HO-1, GSTs, GCLM, Trx1, SRXN1), increasing cellular reductive capacity (GSH pools, thiol buffering) and restoring redox homeostasis under oxidative stress (Chang et al., 2020; Ziaei et al., 2013; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). In RPE models, SFN does not consistently increase Nrf2 transcription but promotes nuclear translocation and DNA-binding activity, consistent with post-translational stabilization and activation; ARE target induction follows (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). In ARPE-19, SFN preconditioning increases NQO1 mRNA/activity, boosts cellular GSH, and increases GST activity; microarray and validation data add induction of SRXN1, GCLM, and Trx1 with concurrent Txnip downregulation, aligning with amplified reductive and detoxification capacity (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Under t-BHP stress, SFN increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, elevates NQO1, GR, and GPx1 transcripts, and drives HO-1, NQO1, and GR protein induction (with partial discordance between GPx1 mRNA and protein), while reducing proinflammatory ICAM-1 and MCP-1 (Chang et al., 2020).

Nrf2-dependent ocular efficacy: In vivo, SFN protection from retinal ischemia–reperfusion requires HO-1, as HO-1 inhibition reverses neuroprotection (Pan et al., 2014). In a model of RPE oxidative stress in middle-aged mice, SFN restores cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, underscoring that Nrf2 is the mechanistic driver in that age-relevant retinal context (Falcão et al., 2025).

Nrf2-independent and auxiliary mechanisms: RPE protection is not exclusively Nrf2-dependent. SFN has been shown to promote mitochondrial fusion and reduce Drp1-mediated fission, conferring anti-apoptotic benefit even in CRISPR/Cas9 Nrf2-depleted RPE cells (RPE-1), indicating a parallel mitochondrial protective program (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). SFN also engages the PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ axis: SFN or its metabolites can blunt damage-induced PARylation via direct PARP1 interactions, alleviating SIRT1 inhibition, promoting autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis, and decreasing inflammation in RPE models (Wang & Tang, 2022). In blue light–exposed RPE, SFN activates the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 axis, upregulates HO-1 and thioredoxin-1, blocks NF-κB nuclear translocation, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, and enhances autophagy, all contributing to cytoprotection; Nrf2 inhibition abrogates SFN’s protective effect in this system (Yang et al., 2021). SFN can also activate lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs that mitigate oxidative stress; KEAP1–NRF2 cross-talk with TFEB/TFE3 and macroautophagy has been documented, offering a mechanistic link between Nrf2 activation and proteostasis/autophagy enhancement relevant to RPE degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025).

Anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic effects: Across RPE models, SFN suppresses proinflammatory mediators and pathways (e.g., reduces ICAM-1 and MCP-1; inhibits NF-κB activation), and in TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19 reduces VEGF secretion, which is relevant to para-inflammatory remodeling in AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024). These effects likely contribute to preservation of junctional homeostasis by dampening cytokine-driven disruption.

Cell-type and context dependence: SFN response varies by cell type, stressor, and age-dependent pathway integrity. In some models, HO-1 mRNA is not induced even when protein rises, and under reduced Nrf2 function (as may occur in aged RPE), SFN efficacy can be limited, indicating a dependence on intact Nrf2 signaling and potential post-transcriptional regulation (Chang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Dosing and context also matter: low micromolar SFN protects RPE under oxidative stress, whereas very high concentrations can be deleterious in vitro (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Evidence for barrier-relevant endpoints: The provided sources do not present RPE TEER or FITC-dextran permeability data for SFN, and do not demonstrate claudin-1 induction in RPE (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024). One in vitro ARPE-19 TGF-β model reports that SFN (alone and with vitamin D) restores expression of ZO-1 and claudin-4 suppressed by TGF-β, reduces ROS and VEGF, and decreases proinflammatory cytokines; however, functional permeability or TEER measures were not included, and claudin-1 was not assessed (Bergandi et al., 2024). Therefore, SFN’s capacity to restore RPE barrier function remains mechanistically plausible—through redox normalization, suppression of inflammatory junctional disruption, and potential transcriptional effects on junctional proteins—but is not directly proven by barrier-function assays in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Assay context and rationale: The proposed assays—RPE monolayers subjected to A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ oxidative injury—interrogate oxidative stress pathways central to dry AMD pathophysiology and RPE barrier integrity. A2E/blue light models replicate lipofuscin-photosensitized oxidative injury; NaIO₃ models RPE oxidative cytotoxicity. In both settings, ROS accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, cytokine induction, and downstream tight-junction disruption degrade barrier integrity. The expectation is that SFN will activate Nrf2, increase reductive and detoxifying capacity (GSH, NQO1, HO-1, Trx1, GST), suppress NF-κB–driven inflammation, stabilize mitochondrial function, and secondarily preserve or restore tight-junction protein expression and continuity, resulting in improved TEER and reduced macromolecular flux (FITC-dextran) across the RPE monolayer.

Support for oxidative injury protection in RPE: In A2E/blue light–injured ARPE-19 monolayers, SFN preconditioning increases cell survival, elevates GSH, and induces NQO1 and GST—outcomes mechanistically consistent with improved tolerance to phototoxic oxidative stress (Zhou et al., 2006). In RPE challenged by chemical oxidants (t-BHP, H₂O₂), SFN reduces ROS, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, and induces NQO1, HO-1 (protein), GR, and GPx1 transcripts while suppressing ICAM-1 and MCP-1, thereby addressing both oxidative and inflammatory drivers of junctional disruption (Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013).

Support for HO-1/Nrf2 and auxiliary pathways: Under blue-light exposure, SFN activates Nrf2 and HO-1 in RPE with evidence of mechanistic necessity (Nrf2 inhibitor blocks protection), promotes autophagy (LC3BII and p62), and suppresses NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation—all changes that favor barrier preservation by limiting stress signaling and enhancing cellular cleanup mechanisms (Yang et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and RPE oxidative-stress mouse models, SFN-mediated rescue of retinal function depends on Nrf2 and HO-1, supporting the expected relevance of these axes in RPE-derived stress contexts (Pan et al., 2014; Falcão et al., 2025).

Evidence for junctional protein rescue: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, a recent report shows SFN (particularly with vitamin D) restores ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression suppressed by TGF-β, reduces IL-6/IL-8, reduces VEGF, and normalizes respiratory gene overexpression; this supports the expectation that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven loss of epithelial integrity markers (Bergandi et al., 2024). However, the provided material does not report TEER or FITC-dextran for SFN in RPE, and no data are provided for claudin-1 induction or ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity in oxidative (A2E/NaIO₃) models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Thus, while SFN is expected to improve TEER and reduce FITC-dextran flux in A2E or NaIO₃ assays through Nrf2-driven antioxidant enhancement and suppression of inflammatory/junctional injury, this is an unproven extrapolation that requires direct measurement in the proposed models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).

Target expression in RPE: All principal molecular targets are expressed in human RPE. Nrf2 activation and nuclear translocation occur in SFN-treated RPE-19/ARPE-19, with demonstrated induction of NQO1, HO-1 (protein in some contexts), thioredoxin-1, GCLM, and GST, and suppression of Txnip, ICAM-1, and MCP-1, anchoring the feasibility of modulating these axes in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2006). HO-1 induction in RPE is clearly shown under blue-light stress; in vivo retinal protection requires HO-1, reinforcing target relevance to oxidative retinal injury (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014).

Assay caveats: The provided literature does not contain RPE TEER or macromolecular flux data for SFN, nor does it document claudin-1 induction in RPE. Therefore, while SFN is expected to preserve barrier function, success criteria must include de novo demonstration of TEER rescue, FITC-dextran flux reduction, and ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity under A2E or NaIO₃ stress; these are critical data gaps to address in the proposed work (Zhang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic foundation in RPE and retina: SFN is a well-validated Nrf2 activator that increases GSH and induces multiple ARE-dependent genes (NQO1, GSTs, Trx1, GCLM; HO-1 in several ocular contexts) in RPE and retinal models, with reproducible protection against oxidative and phototoxic injury (A2E/blue light; H₂O₂/t-BHP) and anti-inflammatory activity (reduced ICAM-1, MCP-1, NF-κB signaling) (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage, improves ERG outcomes, rescues cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, and protects against ischemia–reperfusion via HO-1—clear evidence that the compound engages relevant biology and can deliver functional benefit in the retina (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2014).  
- Multiple converging protective axes: Beyond KEAP1–Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling, suppresses PARP1 overactivation to preserve NAD+/SIRT1, promotes autophagy/lysosome programs (TFEB/TFE3 linkage), and modulates mitochondrial dynamics (promotes fusion; reduces Drp1-mediated fission) even when Nrf2 is compromised. This polymechanistic profile is advantageous in RPE, where oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy, and inflammation co-drive degeneration (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2021; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).  
- Preliminary evidence for epithelial integrity marker restoration: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, SFN (especially with vitamin D) restored ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression and reduced VEGF, providing the first reported signal that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven epithelial marker loss in an RPE model (albeit without functional barrier assays) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Translational plausibility and human experience: SFN is orally administrable, with documented human systemic exposure and biomarker modulation; myrosinase co-administration enhances bioavailability from glucoraphanin. Although not yet tested clinically in dry AMD, SFN has a favorable translational narrative as a nutraceutical-derived Nrf2 activator with a safety and PD data trail in other indications (Zhang et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and gaps  
- No direct RPE barrier-function data: Across the provided literature there are no TEER or FITC-dextran permeability results for SFN in RPE monolayers, and no quantified immunofluorescence continuity data for ZO-1 or claudin-1 under oxidative stress. The sole report of “restored markers” addresses ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression after TGF-β, not barrier function or claudin-1 (Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024). The proposal’s assertion of TEER rescue and FITC-dextran reduction remains speculative pending direct measurement in A2E or NaIO₃ models (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Uncertain regulation of tight junction gene set: The provided RPE datasets document induction of canonical Nrf2 targets (NQO1, HO-1 in some contexts, Trx1, GCLM, GSTs), but do not demonstrate SFN induction of claudin-1 in RPE. Without evidence that SFN directly upregulates claudin-1 or stabilizes its junctional localization in RPE, the hypothesis of “junction-supporting gene induction” should be reframed as “junction-preserving via redox and anti-inflammatory mechanisms” until proven otherwise (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Delivery and exposure to the RPE: SFN’s solubility, short half-life, and first-pass metabolism limit systemic exposure; blood–ocular barriers further constrain retinal delivery. Several in vivo retinal studies used intraperitoneal dosing, and one report found i.p. more effective than oral for light-damage protection, emphasizing the need to optimize delivery for ocular targets. Nanocarriers and formulation strategies are promising but remain preclinical (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Dependence on Nrf2 competence and context: In models with impaired Nrf2 (potentially mirroring aged RPE), SFN efficacy is reduced; mechanisms such as mitochondrial fusion may provide partial rescue, but translational effect sizes could be diminished in elderly patients with Nrf2 decline. Additionally, gene-level responses show discordances (e.g., HO-1 mRNA vs protein), indicating context- and post-transcriptional control that complicate predictable pharmacodynamics (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity: Some cited studies are from lower-quality journals; while the core mechanistic findings are corroborated by higher-quality work (e.g., IOVS, Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology, PLoS ONE), the barrier-marker restoration report requires independent replication with functional readouts and in primary human RPE to solidify translational credibility (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Bergandi et al., 2024).

Decision implications and next steps  
Given the robust Nrf2/ARE activation, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory efficacy in RPE/retina, and the breadth of auxiliary protective mechanisms, SFN remains a mechanistically precise candidate for RPE oxidative injury relevant to dry AMD. However, the core claim of “barrier restoration” is currently supported only by marker-expression rescue (ZO-1 and claudin-4) in an inflamed ARPE-19 model without functional permeability data, and there is no evidence for claudin-1 induction or barrier rescue in A2E or NaIO₃ models in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). To de-risk the program and validate the hypothesis, the following experiments are mandatory:  
- TEER and FITC-dextran assays in differentiated human RPE (primary or iPSC-RPE) under A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ insult, with SFN dose–response and timing; include positive controls for barrier rescue (e.g., dexamethasone) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Quantitative junctional immunofluorescence (ZO-1, claudin-1, claudin-4, occludin) with continuity analysis; test whether SFN normalizes localization and expression under oxidative/cytokine stress (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Nrf2 pathway necessity tests (ML385, Nrf2 siRNA) and HO-1 inhibition (ZnPP) to define mechanism-of-action in barrier rescue; given HO-1’s necessity in vivo, confirm whether HO-1 contributes to barrier endpoints in RPE (Pan et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2021).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics and autophagy readouts (Drp1, Mfn2, LC3BII/p62) to quantify auxiliary pathways that may mediate barrier preservation when Nrf2 is compromised (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021).  
- PK/PD bridging: quantify SFN (and metabolites) in plasma and ocular tissues after oral vs i.p. dosing in rodents; evaluate delivery systems (e.g., albumin nanocarriers) for RPE exposure; incorporate myrosinase co-administration for oral strategies; relate exposures to effective in vitro EC₅₀s for barrier rescue (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Aged and Nrf2-impaired models: evaluate efficacy in aged RPE or Nrf2-hypomorphic contexts to assess translational robustness (Zhang et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

If TEER and permeability rescue are demonstrated with mechanistic attribution to Nrf2/HO-1 and/or auxiliary pathways, and if ocular PK can be solved to achieve efficacious exposures, SFN would merit progression to in vivo dry AMD–relevant models (e.g., subretinal NaIO₃, chronic photo-oxidative stress) with structural (OCT) and functional (ERG) endpoints, plus RPE barrier imaging, before considering a human proof-of-concept study.

In sum, the totality of evidence strongly supports SFN for oxidative and inflammatory protection of RPE and retina with multiple convergent mechanisms and translational plausibility. The critical missing element is direct demonstration that these effects translate into bona fide RPE barrier restoration (TEER/permeability) under AMD-relevant oxidative stress, and a practical path to deliver sufficient drug to the RPE in humans. Addressing these gaps should be the focus of immediate preclinical validation (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024).

Below is our comprehensive evaluation of CHIR99021 as a repurposed candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), with detailed discussion of its origins, history, mechanism, expected effects, and overall strengths and weaknesses. In this report, cited evidence is drawn directly from the provided context.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
CHIR99021 is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor originally identified as a highly potent and selective inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3β) with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (~10 nM). Its discovery and subsequent chemical development classified it as an ATP-competitive inhibitor, belonging to a broader class of kinase inhibitors that target GSK-3 enzymes. This compound has been marketed under Tocris catalog number 4423 and is widely used as a research tool for modulating the canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway. The synthesis of CHIR99021 is based on medicinal chemistry approaches that aim to optimize kinase selectivity, and indeed, extensive inhibitor profiling has shown that it preferentially targets GSK-3 over cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) and other kinases. This compound belongs to a class of therapeutic candidates generally employed in stem cell differentiation protocols, where its ability to stabilize β-catenin and drive the transcription of Wnt target genes has been extensively validated in various cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) derived from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Leach et al., 2015). As such, CHIR99021 has been foundational in protocols that aim to drive RPE fate by activating canonical Wnt signaling, thereby demonstrating its utility in manipulating epithelial differentiation pathways.

Therapeutic History:  
The majority of available evidence for CHIR99021’s use comes from in vitro studies and preclinical differentiation protocols rather than clinical applications. Multiple studies have shown that when added during defined differentiation windows (for example, from day 8 to 14 of an hESC-to-RPE protocol), CHIR99021 significantly increases the yield and functional maturation of RPE cells. These studies report that CHIR99021-treated differentiations yield improved epithelial morphology, enhanced pigmentation, and robust expression of RPE lineage markers—including MITF, OTX2, and even tight-junction-associated proteins such as ZO-1 (Leach et al., 2015). In parallel, other reports have documented that upregulation of canonical Wnt signaling through CHIR99021 leads to increased expression of pigmentation genes (TYR, TYRP2, and PMEL17) and the RPE functional secretory factor PEDF. However, it is important to note that despite promising results in differentiation assays, the use of CHIR99021 for direct therapeutic intervention in dry AMD is not well documented. A clinical trials search on ClinicalTrials.gov returned no registered trials exploring CHIR99021 or other GSK-3β inhibitors for AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Moreover, in an in vitro macula-sized RPE wound-repair model designed to mimic geographic atrophy, CHIR99021 treatment hindered wound repair instead of enhancing barrier restoration (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). These seemingly contradictory findings illustrate that while CHIR99021 robustly enhances RPE differentiation from stem cells, its effects in mature or stress-challenged RPE may be context-dependent. Overall, the preclinical history establishes CHIR99021 as a well-characterized research compound with proven biochemical activity in activating Wnt/β-catenin signaling, but there is limited evidence regarding its therapeutic application in treating dry AMD or related RPE barrier dysfunction in vivo (Yang et al., 2018; Hottin et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
CHIR99021 exerts its biological effects by inhibiting GSK-3β through competitive binding at the protein’s ATP site, thereby preventing GSK-3β from phosphorylating its substrates. One of the principal consequences of GSK-3β inhibition is the stabilization of β-catenin. Under normal conditions, GSK-3β phosphorylates β-catenin, marking it for proteasomal degradation. Inhibition by CHIR99021 blocks this phosphorylation event, which leads to an accumulation of β-catenin in the cytosol and its translocation into the nucleus. Once in the nucleus, β-catenin interacts with TCF/LEF transcription factors to induce the transcription of multiple downstream genes that govern cell fate decisions, differentiation, and epithelial characteristics (Leach et al., 2015). Notably, in the context of retinal development, β-catenin directly upregulates RPE-specific transcription factors such as MITF and OTX2 by binding to their promoter elements, which aligns with observations of improved RPE differentiation upon CHIR99021 treatment (Leach et al., 2015).  

The proposed hypothesis extends this mechanism by suggesting that activation of the canonical Wnt pathway will also upregulate tight junction gene expression. Although specific data on claudin-1 and occludin transcription in response to CHIR99021 in RPE under oxidative stress are not directly provided in the available literature, several studies have shown that Wnt/β-catenin signaling positively correlates with the expression of junctional proteins and may help preserve the architecture of the ZO-1 belt (Leach et al., 2015). In endothelial cell models, GSK-3 inhibition has been associated with favorable modulation of barrier proteins and improved barrier function, suggesting a mechanistic plausibility for a similar effect in RPE cells (Page, 2019; Hottin et al., 2022). Moreover, the dual action of CHIR99021 in modulating both Wnt targets and supporting antioxidant gene networks may provide additional cytoprotective effects under oxidative stress conditions relevant to dry AMD (Leach et al., 2015; Hottin et al., 2022). However, it must be noted that in certain experimental settings, such as in an in vitro RPE wound-repair assay, prolonged exposure to CHIR99021 led to impaired wound healing, indicating that the degree and context of canonical pathway activation are critical determinants of outcome (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis, the application of CHIR99021 in oxidative-stressed RPE is expected to stabilize β-catenin and, through canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling, upregulate the transcription of tight junction genes such as claudin-1 and occludin. This molecular cascade is anticipated to preserve or even restore the ZO-1 belt architecture—the structural hallmark of an intact epithelial barrier—and thereby improve functional barrier properties as measured by an increase in transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and a reduction in FITC-dextran permeability under stress challenges induced by A2E or H₂O₂. In ARPE-19 cell models, limited data suggest that stabilization of β-catenin can counteract H₂O₂-induced loss of cell–cell junctions, with reports of a TEER improvement of approximately 35% (Yang et al., 2018). The expected outcome is therefore two-fold: first, the promotion of a differentiated epithelial phenotype with enhanced expression of RPE-specific markers (MITF, OTX2, PMEL17, and ZO-1); and second, the maintenance or restoration of barrier integrity under conditions that mimic oxidative stress encountered in dry AMD. It is important to consider, however, that while CHIR99021 has been shown to improve differentiation when applied during early stages of RPE development (Leach et al., 2015), its application in mature, stressed RPE may have unintended effects. In one in vitro model simulating GA-like lesions, chronic exposure to CHIR99021 resulted in hindered wound repair, suggesting that the dynamics of Wnt activation—and possibly feedback regulation of junctional pathways—must be finely balanced (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Thus, while the biochemical rationale for improved tight junction gene expression and TEER enhancement is sound, the expected beneficial effect under oxidative challenges remains to be conclusively demonstrated in models that directly assay these endpoints.

Overall Evaluation:  
CHIR99021 presents several notable strengths as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its high selectivity and potency as a GSK-3β inhibitor—coupled with its ability to robustly activate canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling—make it a well-characterized compound from a biochemical standpoint (Page, 2019; Hottin et al., 2022). The extensive literature demonstrating its use in stem cell differentiation protocols to generate highly purified RPE populations lends credence to its capacity to promote or maintain an epithelial phenotype (Leach et al., 2015). In addition, the dual targeting of both differentiation pathways and antioxidant gene networks provides mechanistic specificity that is theoretically well aligned with the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD where oxidative stress and barrier dysfunction play central roles (Leach et al., 2015; Hottin et al., 2022). Moreover, its established pharmacokinetic profile and ready availability make it an attractive candidate for rapid preclinical evaluation in ocular models.

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and concerns temper enthusiasm for CHIR99021 as a dry AMD therapeutic. First, while its use in developmental protocols is well documented, there exists a paucity of data on the direct upregulation of tight junction genes such as claudin-1 and occludin in oxidative-stress models of RPE. Although improved ZO-1 localization and epithelial morphology have been noted in hESC-derived RPE cultures (Leach et al., 2015), direct evidence linking CHIR99021 to enhanced TEER or reduced FITC-dextran permeability in mature RPE under conditions mimicking dry AMD (A2E/H₂O₂ challenge) is lacking. Second, there is conflicting evidence from in vitro wound-repair studies in RPE: while CHIR99021 enhances RPE differentiation, its chronic application in a macula-sized lesion model impaired repair, suggesting that the timing and duration of GSK-3β inhibition are critical parameters that could influence barrier function negatively if not optimized (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Third, despite positive outcomes in some endothelial cell systems regarding barrier rescue following GSK-3 inhibition, similar experiments in RPE or retinal endothelial models using CHIR99021 remain limited, raising questions about the translatability of these findings to a dry AMD setting (Page, 2019). Finally, a ClinicalTrials.gov search has not identified any trials involving CHIR99021 or related GSK-3 inhibitors for AMD, underscoring that while the molecular rationale is sound, the candidate has not undergone any clinical evaluation in this particular indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In summary, CHIR99021 is a well-studied research tool with a clearly defined mechanism of action—namely, the inhibition of GSK-3β leading to stabilization of β-catenin and activation of downstream Wnt target genes. Its proven ability to drive RPE differentiation and enhance epithelial marker expression makes it appealing from a developmental standpoint. However, available evidence also highlights potential drawbacks when applied to mature or stressed RPE, including impaired wound repair in certain in vitro models. The hypothesis that CHIR99021 will upregulate claudin-1 and occludin transcription, thereby preserving ZO-1 architecture to improve TEER and reduce permeability under oxidative challenges, remains promising in theory but requires substantiation through focused experiments that measure tight junction integrity and barrier function specifically under conditions mimicking dry AMD (Yang et al., 2018). As such, while the candidate has mechanistic appeal and a robust preclinical track record in RPE differentiation, its application for barrier restoration in dry AMD remains speculative at this stage, and further investigation—including dose optimization studies, TEER/permeability assays in oxidative stress models, and eventually in vivo preclinical evaluations—is warranted before advancing CHIR99021 into clinical trials for this indication.

Overall, our evaluation concludes that CHIR99021 shows potential based on its selectivity and mechanistic rationale but that significant uncertainties remain regarding its efficacy in restoring barrier function in the context of dry AMD. Strengths include its potent GSK-3β inhibition, well-characterized activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, and proven use in enhancing RPE differentiation, while weaknesses center on mixed results in mature RPE wound‐repair models and the current lack of direct evidence for tight junction upregulation under oxidative stress. The direction for future research must focus on rigorous validation of barrier parameters (including claudin-1, occludin, TEER, and permeability assays) in models that closely recapitulate the oxidative and inflammatory milieu of dry AMD before considering CHIR99021 as a viable drug candidate for clinical repurposing (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

This comprehensive review therefore supports a cautious approach: while CHIR99021 possesses attractive biochemical and mechanistic properties that justify its rapid evaluation in preclinical ocular models, its repurposing for dry AMD will require additional data specifically addressing RPE barrier function under oxidative stress. Further targeted studies are essential to resolve the context-dependent effects observed in vitro and to determine if optimal dosing and timing regimens can overcome the negative outcomes seen in wound-repair assays. Only with such evidence will CHIR99021’s promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD be fully validated.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SAR407899 (Selleckchem S2921) is a small-molecule ATP-competitive inhibitor of Rho-associated coiled-coil containing kinases (ROCKs) that targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2, placing it within the widely studied class of dual ROCK1/2 inhibitors used as chemical tools and therapeutic candidates across vascular, fibrotic, and ocular indications driven by actomyosin contractility and cytoskeletal dysregulation (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). The ATP-binding pockets of ROCK1 and ROCK2 are highly conserved, which has historically favored development of dual-isoform inhibitors (e.g., fasudil, Y-27632, ripasudil, netarsudil) rather than isoform-selective agents; SAR407899 is listed among this majority class of dual-acting molecules in contemporary reviews of rho-kinase modulators for retinal disease (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Multiple dual ROCK inhibitors have been clinically applied: fasudil is approved systemically for cerebral vasospasm and has been evaluated intravitreally for retinal disease, while ripasudil and netarsudil are approved as topical ophthalmic solutions for glaucoma/ocular hypertension, establishing the translational precedent and safety framework for the class in ocular tissues (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). At a mechanistic level, all members of this class block ROCK catalytic activity by binding to the ATP site, thereby reducing phosphorylation of canonical substrates such as MYPT1 (the myosin phosphatase target subunit) and myosin regulatory light chain (MLC), and decreasing downstream actomyosin tension, stress fibers, and focal adhesion assembly that collectively drive barrier breakdown, contraction, and fibrosis (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). While “soft drug” and kinase-selectivity strategies have been advanced to improve tissue targeting and reduce off-target activity, the broad conclusion from medicinal chemistry and pharmacology reviews is that most clinical-grade ROCK inhibitors remain dual-isoform ATP-competitive agents with some potential for off-target kinase interactions at higher exposures—an interpretive caveat for both efficacy and safety (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Liu et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Direct preclinical or clinical reports on SAR407899 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) or age-related macular degeneration (AMD) were not identified in the provided literature set; the compound is listed among “double-acting ROCK inhibitor molecules” considered for retinal vascular disease, but no SAR407899-specific ocular pharmacokinetic, penetration, or efficacy data are supplied in the excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). In contrast, there is substantial class-level evidence that dual ROCK1/2 inhibition is active in posterior segment disease biology relevant to dry AMD pathogenesis and sequelae (barrier failure, low-grade inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling), and that ROCK pathway blockade by other chemotypes can beneficially modulate RPE/retinal fibrosis and endothelial barrier endpoints across models (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). For endothelial barrier function, ripasudil preserved ZO-1 localization and reversed VEGF-induced TEER loss in human retinal microvascular endothelial cells (HRMECs), and suppressed retinal p-MYPT1 in a murine retinal vein occlusion model, demonstrating target engagement and barrier preservation by ROCK inhibition in retina (albeit on the vascular rather than RPE side of the BRB) (Hida et al., 2018). For RPE morphology and barrier integrity in vivo, intravitreally applied fasudil reversed Rho pathway–driven cytoskeletal abnormalities (apical constriction and stress fibers) and improved RPE barrier integrity in disease-relevant paradigms, establishing that pan-ROCK antagonism can correct RPE junctional dysfunction at the tissue level (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). In fibrotic endpoints applicable to geographic atrophy progression and subretinal scarring, both pan-ROCK (fasudil) and ROCK2-selective (belumosudil) inhibitors reduced canonical fibrosis drivers (TGF-β1, fibronectin, vimentin, α-SMA) and ROCK pathway activity (p-MYPT1) in choroid–RPE complex and retina in vivo, with concomitant preservation of retinal morphology and decreased fibrosis volume in a mouse CNV-associated fibrosis model (Zandi et al., 2025). Additional dual ROCK inhibitors (AMA0428) suppressed angiogenesis, inflammation, and fibrosis in a mouse CNV model more broadly than VEGFR2 blockade alone, underscoring the ability of ROCK pathway inhibition to simultaneously normalize vessels, reduce leakage, and block matrix deposition—features highly relevant to AMD (Hollanders et al., 2015; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Clinically, small trials combining intravitreal fasudil with bevacizumab in refractory diabetic macular edema (DME) showed short-term improvements in visual acuity and central macular thickness versus anti-VEGF alone, consistent with anti-permeability and vasoregulatory actions of ROCK inhibitors in human retina; while not dry AMD, these studies provide translational class experience for retinal application and intravitreal dosing (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Nourinia et al., 2018). Taken together, the literature supports class-level efficacy signals in pathways relevant to dry AMD (barrier/tight junctions, fibrosis/TGF-β–driven contraction, vascular normalization/inflammation), but it provides no SAR407899-specific RPE or dry AMD results, PK, or ocular penetration data in the provided excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
ROCK1 and ROCK2 are serine/threonine kinases activated by RhoA-GTP that increase cellular contractility and cytoskeletal tension by two concerted mechanisms: (1) direct phosphorylation of myosin regulatory light chain (MLC), and (2) phosphorylation of MYPT1, the regulatory subunit of myosin phosphatase, which inhibits phosphatase activity and sustains high p-MLC; ROCK also signals via LIM kinases to inactivate cofilin, stabilizing actin stress fibers and focal adhesions—all of which favor junctional opening and motile/contractile phenotypes (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). In retinal and RPE-relevant systems, this signaling axis links directly to barrier dysregulation, fibrosis, and inflammation: high glucose and VEGF increase ROCK activity and p-MLC in retinal microvascular endothelium, augmenting adhesion molecule expression (ICAM-1), leukocyte adhesion, and hyperpermeability; conversely, ROCK inhibitors reduce ICAM-1, leukostasis, endothelial damage, and vascular leakage in diabetic retina models, consistent with reduced actomyosin tension and barrier preservation (Nourinia et al., 2018). Direct demonstration of ROCK pathway inhibition in vivo includes suppression of retinal p-MYPT1 by ripasudil in a murine retinal vein occlusion model and preservation of ZO-1 and TEER in VEGF-challenged HRMECs, indicating that ROCK blockade stabilizes tight-junction complexes and restores barrier function under stress (Hida et al., 2018). In RPE, Rho/ROCK activation produces cytoskeletal remodeling (apical constriction and stress fiber formation) leading to intercellular junction opening—and intravitreally delivered fasudil reversed these morphological abnormalities and improved RPE barrier integrity, linking ROCK activity to the outer BRB in vivo (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Fibrotic contraction in vitreoretinal disease is mechanistically tied to ROCK: TGF-β–activated contractility proceeds via ROCK-dependent MLC phosphorylation, and ROCK inhibitors suppress TGF-β–induced collagen gel contraction by RPE, reduce proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) progression in rabbits, and decrease subretinal fibrosis after CNV, while lowering p-MYPT1 in choroid–RPE complex (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). Inflammation intersects ROCK signaling via NF-κB and other pathways: ROCK activity upregulates inflammatory mediators (e.g., NF-κB targets, MCP-1/CCL2, iNOS), and ROCK inhibitors reduce inflammatory cell infiltration and cytokine production in ocular models, further supporting secondary barrier stabilization and anti-fibrotic effects (Singh & Singh, 2023; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). In AMD-relevant immunity, ROCK2-selective signaling is linked to age-related macrophage polarization toward proangiogenic M2 (MaDAMs) in human AMD eyes; ROCK2-selective inhibition improved macrophage phenotype and reduced CNV in models, whereas pan-ROCK fasudil did not share all of these benefits in the immune compartment, suggesting non-redundant isoform roles in the aging choroid–retina milieu (Nourinia et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). These combined data establish a coherent molecular mechanism whereby dual ROCK1/2 inhibition should reduce p-MYPT1/p-MLC, relax actomyosin tension, stabilize junctional complexes (occludin/ZO-1), oppose TGF-β–driven fibrotic conversion, and blunt inflammatory cascades that exacerbate outer BRB failure in dry AMD; however, whether dual versus ROCK2-selective inhibition optimally tunes the immune/fibrotic axis in AMD remains an open question raised by macrophage-focused studies (Nourinia et al., 2018; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Supportive precedent for barrier rescue by ROCK inhibition includes restoration of endothelial tight junction integrity and TEER in VEGF-challenged HRMECs by ripasudil and suppression of retinal p-MYPT1 in vivo, establishing that ROCK blockade reverses injury-induced barrier dysfunction and engages the canonical substrate axis in retina (Hida et al., 2018). In RPE, in vivo fasudil reversed Rho-pathway–induced cytoskeletal remodeling and improved barrier integrity, implying that ROCK inhibition can directly stabilize the outer BRB at the epithelial level, although quantitative TEER and occludin/ZO-1 readouts in RPE cultures are not provided in the excerpts and should be generated in the proposed assay (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Inflammatory cytokines can feed into ROCK pathway activation and barrier loss, and the Rho/ROCK axis is intertwined with NF-κB–dependent cytokine expression; therefore, ROCK inhibition in the IL-1β paradigm is mechanistically plausible for barrier rescue even though IL-1β-specific RPE TEER data are not available in the provided sources (Singh & Singh, 2023; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Given the contribution of ROCK to TGF-β–driven epithelial–mesenchymal transition and gel contraction by RPE, a dual inhibitor is also expected to suppress fibrotic gene expression trajectories in longer assays (α-SMA, collagen/fibronectin) while relieving junctional stress that promotes delamination and barrier failure, which aligns with the anti-fibrotic outcomes seen in subretinal fibrosis models after fasudil or ROCK2-selective inhibition (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). - Target validity and mechanistic convergence: ROCK1/2 are central regulators of cytoskeletal tension and tight-junction stability via the MYPT1/MLC and LIMK/cofilin axes, providing a direct mechanistic handle on epithelial barrier integrity and fibrotic conversion relevant to outer BRB failure and atrophic remodeling in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). The same axis is mechanistically operative in retinal vascular endothelium where barrier protection by ROCK inhibition has been demonstrated quantitatively (TEER, ZO-1), strengthening the translational rationale for barrier rescue across the BRB (Hida et al., 2018).  
- RPE-relevant in vivo effect: Intravitreal fasudil reversed RPE cytoskeletal abnormalities and improved epithelial barrier integrity in vivo, demonstrating that the class mechanism extends to outer BRB pathology and is not restricted to vascular endothelial cells (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- Absence of SAR407899-specific ocular data in RPE/AMD: The provided literature contains no quantitative potency/selectivity corroboration, ocular penetration, retinal tissue levels, or preclinical efficacy for SAR407899 in RPE barrier models, IL-1β paradigms, or AMD models; thus, key assertions in the working hypothesis (e.g., occludin/ZO-1 transcriptional rescue in RPE, primary human RPE TER recovery, ocular PK levels, ERG improvements in NaIO3) are not supported here and cannot be validated from the excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Programmatic Implications and Recommended Next Steps  
On the strength of the mechanistic and preclinical class data, dual ROCK1/2 inhibition remains a credible strategy to stabilize RPE junctions and suppress fibrotic conversion in dry AMD; however, SAR407899 must earn its place in this mechanism by producing compound-specific evidence on RPE barrier endpoints and ocular exposure (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Zandi et al., 2025). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Arimoclomol (also known as BRX-345) is a synthetic hydroxylamine/hydroxamic-acid–derived small molecule developed as a heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducer that amplifies stress-inducible transcription of heat shock genes under conditions of proteotoxic stress, principally through prolongation and potentiation of heat shock factor-1 (HSF1) activation on heat shock elements (HSEs) in target promoters (Penke et al., 2018; Parfitt et al., 2014; O’Leary, 2019). In the hydroximic-acid derivative family (bimoclomol, arimoclomol, NG-094, BGP-15), several members synergistically enhance heat-induced Hsp expression; arimoclomol and bimoclomol have been shown to increase HSF1 activity via hyperphosphorylation and to amplify heat-shock gene expression in eukaryotic cells while sparing basal Hsp expression in unstressed cells, thereby acting as bona fide co-inducers rather than primary HSF1 agonists (Penke et al., 2018). The compound was originally advanced from the bimoclomol chemotype as a more drug-like analogue with similar HSR-potentiating properties and improved pharmacology, and it falls within a broader class of pharmacologic HSP70/HSF1 modulators investigated for neurodegenerative protein-misfolding diseases (e.g., ALS, NPC, tauopathies), as well as select retinal degeneration models (rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa) (Parfitt et al., 2014; Venediktov et al., 2023; Penke et al., 2018). At the biophysical level, hydroximic-acid derivatives can intercalate into cellular membranes, a property hypothesized to contribute to regulation of HSF1 activation/attenuation kinetics and restoration of a protective Hsp profile under stress (Penke et al., 2018). In neuronal cell systems, arimoclomol has also been used in combination with primary HSF1 activators (e.g., celastrol) to achieve robust induction of inducible Hsp70s (HSPA1A, HSPA6) and other stress response proteins at lower inducer doses, consistent with its role as a co-inducer that amplifies pre-existing HSF1 activation (Deane, 2019).

Within the retina, arimoclomol has been evaluated in rod photoreceptor models of misfolded rhodopsin (P23H transgenic rats), where it enhanced Hsp70/Hsp90 expression and improved proteostasis, photoreceptor structure, and visual function; however, there is no published evidence in dry AMD models or direct demonstrations of RPE barrier rescue by arimoclomol, and at least one PRPF31-mutant RPE (RP11) cell system screening showed no aggregate-reducing effect of arimoclomol while an mTOR inhibitor (rapamycin) reduced aggregate burden via autophagy induction (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021). The broader Hsp70/Hsc70 system, chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), and macroautophagy are mechanistically central to RPE proteostasis and AMD pathobiology, establishing a strong rationale for HSF1–HSP70–targeted therapy, but translation from photoreceptor models and exogenous Hsp70 delivery to endogenous induction in RPE remains to be validated for this agent (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Subrizi et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History  
Arimoclomol’s development history is anchored in neurodegeneration and protein-misfolding indications. In SOD1-mutant ALS mice, arimoclomol increased Hsp70 expression and improved motor neuron survival and function, extending lifespan; it progressed to human ALS trials (including a phase 3 program), with mixed outcomes across adult and pediatric indications (O’Leary, 2019; Venediktov et al., 2023). Mechanistically consistent with HSF1 co-induction, arimoclomol is positioned to upregulate a suite of inducible chaperones and components of the proteostasis network rather than single chaperone overexpression, a strategy considered preferable for matching the endogenous disaggregation/refolding machinery and preserving feedback attenuation (O’Leary, 2019).

In the retina, arimoclomol has been tested extensively in rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa (RP) models driven by the P23H misfolding mutation. In P23H-GFP cell models, arimoclomol reduced inclusion incidence and insoluble rod opsin, decreased higher-molecular-weight rhodopsin species, and improved viability, with contemporaneous increases in Hsp70/Hsp90 implying potentiation of the HSR in stressed photoreceptors (Parfitt et al., 2014). In P23H transgenic rats, daily intraperitoneal dosing (10 mg/kg) improved scotopic ERG a- and b-waves, preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness, increased outer segment (OS) length, and improved ultrastructure, consistent with disease modification through HSR and unfolded protein response (UPR) potentiation; Hsp70, Hsp90, and HSF1 were assayed directly in these studies (Parfitt et al., 2014). The authors further observed increased eIF2α phosphorylation and discussed enhanced IRE1/XBP1 activity, indicating crosstalk with ER stress responses (Parfitt et al., 2014). Of note, arimoclomol’s activity appeared contingent on the presence of misfolded-protein stress (i.e., stress-selective action), potentially limiting off-target effects in healthy tissue (Parfitt et al., 2014).

Beyond photoreceptors, the Hsp co-inducer class has retinal neuroprotective precedents: bimoclomol improved early electrophysiologic signs in diabetic rat retina, and the Hsp inducer geranylgeranylacetone protected retinal ganglion cells in a rat glaucoma model, underscoring that Hsp70 induction can be protective across retinal cell types and diseases of proteostasis and stress, although these are class exemplars rather than arimoclomol-specific RPE data (Hesselink, 2016). Separately, exogenous Hsp70 protein delivery to RPE has shown diffusion to the retina and RPE after intravitreal administration, intracellular uptake, lysosomal localization, and protection from oxidative stress and inflammation in ARPE-19 cells, supporting the concept that increasing Hsp70 activity in RPE can be beneficial, albeit via protein pharmacology rather than endogenous induction (Subrizi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Crucially for dry AMD translation, the current literature set provides no in vivo animal or clinical study of arimoclomol in AMD/dry AMD, and no direct measurements of RPE barrier integrity (tight-junction protein preservation or transepithelial electrical resistance [TEER]) following arimoclomol in RPE or AMD models; an RPE disease model of PRPF31 mutation with progressive aggregate accumulation reported that arimoclomol failed to reduce aggregates, whereas rapamycin decreased aggregate load and induced LC3 processing consistent with autophagy activation (LAMP1 and p62 remained unchanged), highlighting context-dependent efficacy and suggesting autophagy induction may be more decisive than Hsp co-induction in some RPE aggregate pathologies (Georgiou, 2021). Thus, while arimoclomol has a positive retinal track record in photoreceptor proteotoxicity and a robust extraocular development history, there is no direct evidence yet of arimoclomol ameliorating dry AMD phenotypes or preserving RPE barrier function in disease-relevant systems (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Arimoclomol is an HSR co-inducer that amplifies HSF1-driven transcription of inducible heat shock proteins under pre-existing cellular stress. Mechanistically, arimoclomol prolongs HSF1 binding to HSEs, increases HSF1 activity (e.g., hyperphosphorylation), and thereby increases transcription of Hsp70/Hsp90 and related chaperones, with limited impact in unstressed cells (i.e., stressor-dependent co-induction) (Penke et al., 2018; O’Leary, 2019; Parfitt et al., 2014). In neuronal cells, arimoclomol enhanced celastrol-induced HSF1 activation to elevate HSPA6, HSPA1A, HSPB1, DNAJB1, and HO-1 at doses that preserved viability and differentiated morphology, supporting efficient co-induction when paired with a primary HSF1 activator (Deane, 2019). In P23H photoreceptor models, arimoclomol reduced insoluble rhodopsin and inclusion incidence, decreased high-molecular-weight species, increased retinal Hsp70/Hsp90, and improved ERG/ONL/OS outcomes; the study observed increased eIF2α phosphorylation and discussed potentiation of the UPR (BiP/IRE1/XBP1), consistent with arimoclomol acting at the intersection of cytosolic HSR and ER homeostasis (Parfitt et al., 2014).

Hsp70 Biology in RPE and AMD. Inducible Hsp70 (HSPA1A/Hsp70-1) is a central, evolutionarily conserved ATPase chaperone that assists folding of nascent chains, refolds damaged/misfolded proteins, buffers aggregation, facilitates “protein triage” toward degradation pathways, and protects cells from apoptosis and inflammatory signaling (e.g., NF-κB pathway), with expression controlled by HSF1 (Ryhänen, 2011; Kivinen, 2018). In the RPE, Hsp70/Hsc70 function intersects both the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) and lysosome-dependent proteolysis. Hsp70 can present misfolded proteins to the UPS via CHIP E3 ligase, regulate disaggregation with co-chaperones HSP40/HSP90/HIP/HOP, and is required for aggregate handling; in proteasome failure, protein aggregates in ARPE-19 cells co-localize with Hsp70 and p62, with p62 undergoing autophagic clearance while Hsp70 binds reversibly and evades autophagic degradation (Kumar et al., 2020; Kivinen et al., 2014; Ryhänen, 2011). Hsp70 is also integral to chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA): cytosolic Hsc70/Hsp70 recognizes KFERQ-containing substrates, delivers them to LAMP-2A at the lysosomal membrane, and ATPase-driven “entropic pulling” and luminal chaperones enable translocation and degradation; oxidative stress reduces HSP70 expression in RPE, impairs CMA, and can dysregulate macroautophagy cross-talk, contributing to RPE death (Chang et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020). Extracellular Hsp70 roles in RPE are complex: exogenous rhHsp70 injections protected against subretinal fibrosis via TLR2/TLR4 and IL-10 induction, while oxidized-lipid stress (4-HNE) can increase extracellular Hsp70 efflux and pro-inflammatory cytokines, indicating that compartmental localization of Hsp70 critically determines immunomodulatory outcomes (Kumar et al., 2020).

Evidence for arimoclomol in RPE cells. Direct mechanistic evidence for arimoclomol action in RPE is limited. A cell-culture report in ARPE-19 asserts that Hsp70 overexpression “with the help of a co-inducer like arimoclomol” suppressed IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α and increased IL-10 and TGF-β1, consistent with Hsp70-mediated IκK/NF-κB inhibition; however, the study details are summarized in low-quality review literature, and direct demonstration of arimoclomol-driven HSF1 activation in RPE is not provided (Kumar et al., 2020). Another ARPE-19-focused review excerpt states that arimoclomol acts on HSF1 to increase cytosolic Hsp70 without increasing extracellular Hsp70 and improved resistance to 4-HNE–induced oxidative stress (relative to paeoniflorin); again, the primary data are not provided here and the review is of limited quality, so these findings should be treated as provisional until replicated (Kumar et al., 2020). Importantly, in an isogenic patient-derived PRPF31-mutant RPE (RP11) model with progressive cytoplasmic aggregate accumulation, a 7-day treatment screen across HSR/UPR/autophagy modulators showed that rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibitor) reduced aggregate load and shifted LC3-I to LC3-II, whereas arimoclomol did not reduce aggregates under the conditions tested, arguing that in this RPE disease context autophagy activation via mTOR inhibition outperformed Hsp co-induction (Georgiou, 2021).

Non-pharmacological Hsp70 induction and autophagy in RPE inform plausibility. Subthreshold retinal thermal stimulation in pig and mouse RPE in vivo induced HSF1 and Hsp70, increased LC3B-II and decreased p62 (consistent with autophagy activation), and increased LAMP2, suggesting potential CMA upregulation, without apoptosis at ~44 °C, confirming that RPE supports coordinated HSR–autophagy programs with an exploitable therapeutic window (but autophagic flux was not directly quantified in vivo) (Amirkavei et al., 2022; Amirkavei et al., 2020). These data reinforce the therapeutic logic for HSF1–Hsp70 upregulation in RPE to restore proteostasis but do not directly validate arimoclomol’s efficacy in RPE (Amirkavei et al., 2022; Amirkavei et al., 2020). Exogenous rhHsp70 trafficking to lysosomes and protection against oxidative stress in ARPE-19 further supports the notion that increasing Hsp70 activity, whether by protein delivery or endogenous induction, can be beneficial to RPE survival under AMD-relevant stressors (Subrizi et al., 2015).

Autophagy and barrier integrity under AMD-relevant stressors. AMD-relevant toxicities (Aβ, lipofuscin/A2E, oxidants) perturb autophagy/lysosomes in RPE, with Aβ decreasing occludin and ZO-1 in ARPE-19 and activating autophagy markers in vitro and in vivo, and A2E promoting lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cell death; impaired UPS and autophagy with aging lead to aggregate accumulation (including p62-positive aggregates) in RPE and drusen, highlighting the importance of restoring both proteasomal and autophagic clearance to protect RPE function and barrier integrity (Wang et al., 2023; Viiri, 2019; Ryhänen, 2011). Hsp70/p62 roles in this axis are mechanistically established: Hsp70 prevents aggregation and participates in aggregate handling, while p62 is an autophagic receptor degraded by autophagy and accumulates when autophagy is impaired; pharmacologic AMPK activation can accelerate p62 clearance during proteasome inhibition and improve RPE survival (Viiri, 2019). To date, arimoclomol has not been shown to modulate CMA or macroautophagy in RPE, nor to preserve tight junctions or TEER in AMD-relevant models (Georgiou, 2021; Kumar et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay hypothesis and rationale. The working hypothesis is that arimoclomol will potentiate stress-triggered HSF1 activity in RPE, elevating inducible Hsp70 and coordinated chaperone networks to stabilize junctional proteostasis, reduce misfolded protein burden, and normalize autophagy (including potentially CMA), thereby preventing degradation of occludin/claudin and restoring TEER under oxidative or drusen-like stress (e.g., H2O2/4-HNE, A2E/lipofuscin, Aβ) (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). This mechanism is biologically plausible: Hsp70 is abundantly expressed in RPE under stress and supports folding and refolding, substrate triage to proteasome via CHIP, and delivery of specific substrates to CMA via Hsc70/LAMP-2A; its induction suppresses NF-κB–driven pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and can raise IL-10/TGF-β1, which together could indirectly protect junctional complexes from cytokine- and stress-mediated degradation (Kumar et al., 2020). Reducing intracellular aggregate load and restoring proteostasis would be expected to mitigate the downstream cascade of mTORC1 activation, p62/LC3-I accumulation, and tight-junction disruption observed in stressed RPE models (e.g., PRPF31-RPE), although in that system arimoclomol was ineffective while rapamycin reduced aggregates, underscoring that Hsp co-induction alone may be insufficient when autophagy is the principal bottleneck (Georgiou, 2021).

Evidence supporting expected effects in RPE assays:  
- Hsp70 induction in retinal tissues has been achieved via HSF1 activation by heat or pharmacologic inducers; in photoreceptor P23H models, arimoclomol increased Hsp70/Hsp90 and reduced aggregation/toxicity, consistent with the proximal arm of the proposed mechanism (HSF1→Hsp70→improved proteostasis) (Parfitt et al., 2014; Amirkavei et al., 2020).  
- In ARPE-19 summaries, arimoclomol increased intracellular (not extracellular) Hsp70 and improved resistance to 4-HNE oxidative stress, and Hsp70 overexpression with help of a co-inducer like arimoclomol suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines, supporting cell-autonomous proteostasis and anti-inflammatory contributions that would be favorable for junctional stability (Kumar et al., 2020).  
- Exogenous rhHsp70 delivery to RPE localizes to lysosomes and reduces oxidative toxicity and inflammation, demonstrating that raising functional Hsp70 in RPE is sufficient to afford cytoprotection, a downstream functional goal of HSF1 co-induction (Subrizi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Evidence arguing for tempered expectations and the need for combination strategies:  
- In PRPF31-mutant RPE, arimoclomol did not reduce aggregates in a 7-day screen, whereas rapamycin shifted LC3 processing and reduced aggregate markers, suggesting that when autophagy is the limiting axis, direct autophagy activation (e.g., mTORC1 inhibition) is required; Hsp co-induction alone may not clear established aggregates or repair autophagic flux (Georgiou, 2021).  
- In primary neuronal ALS models, arimoclomol often failed to induce measurable HSPA1A/HSPA8 and its protective actions occurred without detectable Hsp70 upregulation; HDAC inhibition enhanced Hsp induction by other inducers, arguing that Hsp co-induction efficacy is cell-type and chromatin-context dependent and may require combination therapy to overcome induction thresholds in some cells (potentially relevant to differentiated RPE) (Comaduran et al., 2024).  
- AMD-relevant stressors directly disrupt tight junctions (Aβ reduces occludin and ZO-1 in ARPE-19) and invoke autophagy/lysosomal dysfunction; because arimoclomol’s effects on CMA/macroautophagy in RPE are unproven, barrier rescue may not occur unless autophagic flux is also corrected (Wang et al., 2023).

Assay implementation guidance for decision-making:  
- In vitro human RPE models (primary/donor iPSC-RPE monolayers with high TEER) should be stressed with 4-HNE, H2O2, A2E, or Aβ to recapitulate AMD-relevant proteotoxic and inflammatory conditions, and arimoclomol tested across concentrations paralleling prior cell work (e.g., 10–100 µM) with and without a priming HSF1 activator (celastrol ≤0.3 µM) to evaluate requirement for co-induction, keeping in mind the neuronal data identifying 50 µM arimoclomol + 0.3 µM celastrol as an optimized low-toxicity combination (Deane, 2019).  
- Primary readouts: HSF1 activation (nuclear translocation, Ser phosphorylation), Hsp70/Hsp90 induction (immunoblot, qPCR), autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover with/without bafilomycin, p62 dynamics), CMA markers (LAMP-2A levels, lysosomal Hsc70/Hsp70 substrate colocalization), proteasome activity, aggregate load (FK1, ubiquitin, p62 bodies), and barrier integrity (TEER, ZO-1/occludin/claudin-19 immunostaining continuity) (Kivinen et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2015; Viiri, 2019; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Cytokine profiling (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10, TGF-β1) to detect Hsp70-linked NF-κB effects reported in ARPE-19 (Kumar et al., 2020).  
- Positive comparators: rapamycin for autophagy induction; exogenous rhHsp70 as a proteostasis rescue control; heat-based Hsp70 induction within non-damaging windows to confirm pathway responsiveness (Georgiou, 2021; Subrizi et al., 2015; Amirkavei et al., 2020).

Given the aggregate of evidence, the most realistic expectation is that arimoclomol will increase inducible Hsp70 in stressed RPE if HSF1 can be productively co-induced, reduce misfolded protein accumulation and inflammatory signaling, and potentially improve barrier metrics indirectly by attenuating stressors that degrade junctional complexes; however, without concurrent normalization of autophagic flux and CMA, tight-junction rescue and TEER restoration are uncertain, particularly in models where autophagy is the primary deficit (Georgiou, 2021; Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths supporting arimoclomol for dry AMD RPE barrier rescue:  
- Mechanistic fit: Hsp70/Hsc70 are central “gatekeepers” of RPE proteostasis across the UPS and lysosomal systems, including CMA; restoring inducible Hsp70 via HSF1 co-induction directly targets key failure nodes in RPE aging and AMD pathogenesis (aggregation, impaired clearance, inflammation), aligning with known disease biology (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Kivinen, 2018).  
- Demonstrated retinal efficacy in proteostasis-driven degeneration: arimoclomol increased Hsp70/Hsp90, reduced mutant rhodopsin aggregation, and preserved photoreceptor structure/function in P23H rats, with evidence of concurrent UPR potentiation; this validates the platform concept that HSF1 co-induction plus ER stress modulation can modify retinal degeneration, albeit in photoreceptors rather than RPE (Parfitt et al., 2014).  
- RPE permissiveness to Hsp70-based cytoprotection: exogenous rhHsp70 diffuses to RPE, is internalized, localizes to endolysosomal compartments, reduces IL-6 and cytolysis, and improves viability in oxidative stress paradigms; thus, augmenting Hsp70 in RPE is sufficient to produce protective effects, supporting the feasibility of endogenous induction with a co-inducer if pharmacology is adequate (Subrizi et al., 2015).  
- Stress-selective amplification: arimoclomol preferentially acts in stressed cells, limiting risks of unwanted Hsp70 induction in healthy tissue; this attribute is advantageous for chronic ocular therapy where avoiding constitutive pathway activation is desirable (Parfitt et al., 2014).  
- Clinical development and safety experience: extensive non-ocular development in ALS/NPC provides informative safety and pharmacology context; while ocular distribution is not established in these sources, the systemic safety window is a favorable starting point for repurposing (Venediktov et al., 2023; O’Leary, 2019).

Key weaknesses and uncertainties:  
- Lack of direct evidence in dry AMD/RPE barrier endpoints: no published data demonstrate arimoclomol preserves RPE tight junctions (ZO-1/occludin/claudin), restores TEER, or improves drusen-like pathology in vivo; ARPE-19 reports of arimoclomol-induced Hsp70 and anti-inflammatory effects are secondary summaries in low-quality reviews without primary detail (Kumar et al., 2020). In contrast, direct AMD-relevant in vitro data show that Aβ disrupts tight junction proteins, and autophagy failure correlates with p62 accumulation and aggregate burden, but the ability of arimoclomol to reverse these specific defects in RPE is untested (Wang et al., 2023; Viiri, 2019).  
- Negative/neutral result in PRPF31-RPE aggregation screen: arimoclomol did not reduce cytoplasmic aggregates in a rigorous 7-day screen in RP11-RPE; rapamycin reduced aggregates and shifted LC3 processing, suggesting that in certain RPE aggregate pathologies, autophagy activators outperform Hsp co-induction; whether arimoclomol could complement autophagy induction to achieve barrier rescue remains to be determined (Georgiou, 2021).  
- Uncertain induction competence in differentiated RPE: Primary neurons display high thresholds for inducible Hsp70 (HSPA1A) induction, with arimoclomol often failing to raise Hsp70; Hsp induction can be enhanced by HDAC inhibition, implying that chromatin accessibility and cell state are important variables; differentiated RPE monolayers may similarly require co-induction strategies (e.g., low-dose celastrol or epigenetic modulators) to achieve robust Hsp70 upregulation (Comaduran et al., 2024; Deane, 2019). If arimoclomol cannot reliably induce Hsp70 in mature RPE under clinically relevant stress, the strategy will falter.  
- CMA/macroautophagy modulation by arimoclomol in RPE not established: despite Hsp70’s mechanistic role in CMA, no data show arimoclomol improves CMA or autophagic flux in RPE, which are crucial to clearing damaged proteins/lipids under AMD stress; relying on Hsp70 alone without restoring autophagic flux may be insufficient to protect tight junctions (Chang et al., 2015; Georgiou, 2021).  
- Translational pharmacology: Retinal/RPE exposure of arimoclomol following systemic dosing is not presented in this corpus; ocular delivery strategies and RPE pharmacokinetics for arimoclomol are undefined here, in contrast to exogenous Hsp70 delivery where diffusion and tissue uptake were measured (Subrizi et al., 2015). Without ocular PK/PD and RPE Hsp70 induction data, dosing strategies for barrier rescue remain speculative.

Recommendation and development path:  
- Proceed to targeted preclinical validation in human iPSC-RPE monolayers and AMD-relevant stress paradigms, with rigorous endpoint panels including HSF1–Hsp70 induction, autophagic flux/CMA markers, aggregate clearance, cytokine modulation, and barrier integrity (TEER, ZO-1/occludin continuity), using rapamycin and rhHsp70 as comparators and benchmarking against known disruptions by Aβ and A2E (Georgiou, 2021; Subrizi et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023).
