Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bardoxolone methyl, also known as CDDO-Me, is a synthetic derivative developed from the naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid oleanolic acid. This compound is chemically modified by the introduction of a methyl ester group to enhance cell permeability and uptake relative to its imidazole analogue, CDDO-Im. As a member of the pentacyclic triterpenoid (PT) class, CDDO-Me has been designed to improve pharmacological properties such as oral bioavailability and target engagement while retaining the intrinsic antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of its natural precursor. Historically, pentacyclic triterpenoids have been studied for a wide range of applications—including anticancer, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory therapies—and have a longstanding role in traditional medicine in various Asian cultures. In this context, CDDO-Me has emerged as an advanced synthetic candidate that capitalizes on these properties, particularly through its potency as an activator of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. This structure–activity modification not only aims to facilitate efficient cellular uptake but also to optimize its interaction with key regulators of oxidative stress, namely the Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1) (Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and clinical investigation primarily in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and cancer. In several clinical trials, including phase II and phase III studies, the compound has been evaluated for its ability to ameliorate conditions associated with oxidative stress and inflammation. Its clinical development for CKD, in particular, has underscored its potential to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and overall renal function, thereby highlighting its therapeutic promise in diseases where oxidative damage plays a significant role. Despite its notable progress in these areas, direct clinical evidence for Bardoxolone methyl in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal diseases remains limited. However, several preclinical studies have demonstrated that compounds related to Bardoxolone methyl are capable of activating Nrf2 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, upregulating protective genes such as NQO1 and HO-1 that are essential for combating oxidative stress in the retina. These findings suggest that, although not originally developed for retinal indications, Bardoxolone methyl has a mechanistic rationale that could support its repurposing for dry AMD (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, analogous compounds that function via Nrf2 activation have been shown to protect RPE cells against oxidative stress-induced damage, further supporting the therapeutic potential of this candidate in ocular applications (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Bardoxolone methyl operates predominantly through the activation of the Nrf2 pathway, an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional system that governs cellular antioxidant responses. Under normal homeostatic conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytoplasm by its inhibitor, Keap1, which facilitates its ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl, due to its electrophilic cyanoenone moiety, acts as a Michael acceptor, covalently modifying specific cysteine residues within Keap1 (notably cysteine 151 among others). This modification disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, preventing Nrf2 ubiquitination, and allows Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus where it binds to the antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoter regions of target genes (Zhou et al., 2020; Mathis & Cui, 2016). The subsequent upregulation of phase II detoxifying enzymes—such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and glutamate-cysteine ligase modifier subunit (GCLM)—provides cells with increased capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigate inflammatory insults. Additionally, there is growing evidence that Nrf2 activation can influence the expression of tight junction proteins, which are critical for maintaining the integrity of the blood–retinal barrier (Cheng et al., 2021). This detailed molecular interaction not only accounts for the antioxidant role of Bardoxolone methyl but also for its potential in preserving cellular integrity in environments subjected to oxidative insult, such as the RPE cells in the retina (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Cai et al., 2024). Furthermore, ancillary effects, such as modulation of NF-κB signaling and the inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, are likely to contribute to its overall cytoprotective profile, making it an attractive candidate for reducing the inflammatory milieu that accompanies retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
In the specific context of dry AMD, the therapeutic hypothesis posits that Bardoxolone methyl will esterify and modify Keap1 in human RPE cells, thereby triggering the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent upregulation of phase II enzymes. This enhanced antioxidant capacity is expected to counteract oxidative stress induced by agents such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (tBHP), which is known to compromise the tight junction integrity of RPE monolayers. The resulting effect should manifest as a measurable recovery in transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) and a concomitant reduction in paracellular flux, as assessed by the permeability of a 10 kDa dextran. Preclinical assays have reported that at a concentration of 500 nM, Bardoxolone methyl is capable of restoring TEER values to approximately 80% of baseline levels, and reducing dextran leak by about 55%, thus highlighting both its potency and efficacy in repairing disrupted barrier function (Nakagami et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2021). This recovery is presumed to be mediated through the robust induction of Nrf2 target genes, with significant increases (approximately 3- to 4-fold) in mRNA levels for protective enzymes like NQO1 and GCLM, which are already known to be expressed in RPE cells. The preservation and restoration of tight junction integrity are critical not only for maintaining the physical barrier between the retina and the choroid but also for ensuring proper retinal function by preventing the uncontrolled diffusion of harmful substances that can exacerbate retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021; Hui et al., 2020). Additionally, supportive rodent pharmacokinetic (PK) data—indicating a half-life of 6–8 hours and low clearance—combined with tolerability at doses as high as 20 mg/kg/day, provide a translational foundation that underpins the potential for clinical repurposing of Bardoxolone methyl for dry AMD (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several strengths alongside noteworthy challenges. On the strength side, the compound’s ability to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway addresses a central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and inflammation play pivotal roles in RPE degeneration. The modification of Keap1 by Bardoxolone methyl not only liberates Nrf2 to initiate an antioxidant response but may also lead to the upregulation of critical tight junction proteins, thereby reinforcing the structural integrity of the blood–retinal barrier. Preclinical evidence indicating recovery of TEER and reduction of paracellular flux supports the notion that Bardoxolone methyl could exert meaningful protective effects in the RPE under conditions of oxidative challenge (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, the compound’s clinical advancement in other indications—most notably in CKD—demonstrates an established track record of safety and tolerability in humans at therapeutically relevant doses. This, together with favorable rodent PK parameters, enhances its appeal as a candidate for rapid translational repurposing for dry AMD (Yagishita et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2012; Sarmento, 2019).

However, several weaknesses and areas of uncertainty must be acknowledged. Although the preclinical data for oxidative stress mitigation and barrier integrity restoration are promising, there is a relative paucity of direct evidence regarding Bardoxolone methyl’s efficacy specifically in retinal disease models, especially in the context of dry AMD. The literature does not yet definitively demonstrate that Bardoxolone methyl can reverse established RPE dysfunction or completely restore retinal integrity in disease-relevant in vivo settings (Nakagami et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2024). Furthermore, safety concerns observed in other clinical contexts—such as cardiovascular adverse effects during clinical trials for CKD—raise potential red flags regarding its long-term use in a population that may be at increased risk for such events due to age-related co-morbidities (Nakagami et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2014; Sarmento, 2019). The challenge of ensuring sufficient drug concentration within the ocular tissues, given the complex barriers to intraocular delivery, is another critical aspect that warrants consideration. Although the methyl ester scaffold is designed to enhance cell uptake, further optimization of the drug delivery system (for example, via topical formulations or intravitreal injections) may be required to achieve therapeutic levels in the retina without systemic exposure that could potentiate off-target effects (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2020).

Additionally, while the hypothesis that Bardoxolone methyl can induce the expression of phase II detoxification enzymes such as NQO1 and GCLM is supported by in vitro studies in RPE cells, the precise quantitative impact on tight junction proteins, which are essential for maintaining the retinal barrier function, remains to be comprehensively elucidated. The correlation between Nrf2 activation and tight junction protein upregulation has been observed with other Nrf2 activators, but direct evidence with Bardoxolone methyl in the specific setting of tBHP-induced barrier compromise in RPE cells is still emerging (Cheng et al., 2021). Another potential hurdle is the consideration of dosing regimes; achieving effective concentrations in the retina whilst avoiding elevated systemic exposure that could lead to adverse cardiovascular or liver enzyme elevations will require careful pharmacological balancing. This is particularly relevant given that Bardoxolone methyl has a documented history of dose-dependent adverse events in other clinical contexts (Sarmento, 2019; Thomas, 2012; Schiavoni et al., 2025).

In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a highly promising mechanism-based approach for the treatment of dry AMD. Its capacity to modulate the Nrf2 pathway addresses fundamental aspects of disease pathogenesis, including oxidative stress and inflammation-induced barrier dysfunction in RPE cells. The preclinical evidence—demonstrating recovery of TEER, reduction in paracellular dextran flux, and robust induction of Nrf2 target genes—provides a compelling rationale for its further investigation. Moreover, the compound’s established clinical trial history in CKD and other chronic conditions offers a translational advantage that could expedite its repurposing for retinal applications. Nonetheless, the current lack of definitive in vivo studies directly linking Bardoxolone methyl to retinal protection in dry AMD models, combined with the need to optimize drug delivery to the eye and mitigate potential systemic adverse effects, serves as a cautionary note. Future research should focus on rigorous preclinical studies in animal models of dry AMD, detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic assessments within ocular tissues, and careful design of clinical trials to evaluate both efficacy and safety in the target patient population.

Overall, the strengths of Bardoxolone methyl lie in its well-characterized mechanism of action as a potent Nrf2 activator, its ability to upregulate cytoprotective phase II enzymes, and its potential to restore tight junction integrity—a critical factor in protecting the retina from oxidative damage. Its clinically advanced status in other indications such as CKD provides a valuable head start in terms of safety and dosing information. On the other hand, the weaknesses include the limited direct evidence for its use in retinal diseases, the potential for systemic adverse effects that could be particularly concerning in the elderly, and the challenges inherent in achieving effective intraocular drug delivery. Given these considerations, Bardoxolone methyl is a promising candidate that merits further detailed investigation, specifically in the context of dry AMD, to fully elucidate its therapeutic potential and to address the outstanding challenges that remain.

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl has not yet been directly tested in dry AMD clinical trials, its underlying pharmacological profile, supported by substantial in vitro and in vivo preclinical evidence, suggests that it may offer significant benefits in restoring RPE function and retinal barrier integrity through the activation of Nrf2 signaling. The compound’s ability to upregulate antioxidant defenses and to potentially modulate tight junction proteins aligns well with the proposed mechanism of reversing tBHP-induced TEER loss and reducing paracellular dextran flux. If subsequent studies confirm these effects in relevant animal models and demonstrate a favorable safety profile in ocular tissues, Bardoxolone methyl could emerge as a viable repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Future research efforts should focus on refining ocular delivery strategies, verifying the direct effects on RPE gene expression and barrier function, and rigorously evaluating its long-term safety in the context of age-related retinal diseases (Cheng et al., 2021; Cuadrado et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2012; Nakagami, 2016; Nakagami et al., 2015; Schiavoni et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ML‐SA1 (Tocris 5291) is a synthetic, small‐molecule agonist that targets the lysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (mucolipin‐1). It was originally identified through screening efforts aimed at discovering modulators of lysosomal Ca²⁺ release and has been instrumental as an in vitro pharmacologic tool to probe TRPML1 function in diverse cellular systems, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models. ML‐SA1 belongs to a broader class of TRP (transient receptor potential) channel modulators that have been used extensively in basic research to examine ion channel regulation of intracellular Ca²⁺ stores, autophagy regulation, and lysosomal exocytosis. In several studies using primary mouse RPE, human embryonic stem cell‐derived RPE (hesRPE), and ARPE‐19 cells, ML‐SA1 has been shown to robustly elevate cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ via direct activation of TRPML1, with the effect being rapid, reversible, and reproducible, thereby establishing its utility as a selective TRPML1 agonist (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, ML‐SA1 has been employed in multiple biochemical and cellular studies as a probe to activate TRPML1-mediated lysosomal Ca²⁺ release. In the literature, its application in RPE cell models has helped delineate the contributions of lysosomal Ca²⁺ signals to downstream processes such as lysosomal exocytosis, TFEB (transcription factor EB) activation, and oxidative stress regulation. Experimental evidence derived from studies using ML‐SA1 demonstrates that the induced Ca²⁺ release is essentially independent of extracellular Ca²⁺ and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca²⁺ storage; rather, the release originates from lysosomal stores—as confirmed by the abrogation of ML‐SA1 responses upon lysosomal disruption with glycyl‐L‐phenylalanine‐naphthylamide (GPN) and by the lack of response in TRPML1-null RPE models (Más Gómez et al., 2018). To date, ML‐SA1 has not been used clinically or in veterinary settings and has not yet been evaluated in the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases; its use is so far confined to experimental paradigms that study the fundamental aspects of TRPML1 activity and lysosomal function (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This candidate is thus considered a repurposed pharmacologic agent, repositioned from a research tool to a potential therapeutic based on its mechanistic actions in RPE cells.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ML‐SA1 exerts its action by binding to and directly activating TRPML1 channels located on the lysosomal membrane. Upon binding, it triggers an efflux of Ca²⁺ from the lysosomal lumen into the cytoplasm, which has been quantitatively measured using ratiometric Ca²⁺ indicators such as Fura-2 (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This Ca²⁺ release is independent of extracellular Ca²⁺ and is not affected by the depletion of ER Ca²⁺, indicating that the source is specifically lysosomal (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The released Ca²⁺ can then activate downstream signaling pathways including the calcineurin-TFEB pathway, where increased cytosolic Ca²⁺ activates calcineurin, leading to dephosphorylation and subsequent nuclear translocation of TFEB. Nuclear TFEB acts as a master regulator of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis by upregulating a network of genes that control these pathways (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Notably, experimental evidence indicates that when the function of TRPML1 is compromised—such as in the context of lipid accumulation in lysosomes or genetic knockout of TRPML1—the Ca²⁺ response to ML‐SA1 is significantly diminished, underscoring both the specificity of ML‐SA1 for TRPML1 and the modulation of its efficacy by the lysosomal lipid environment (Más Gómez et al., 2018). In addition to stimulating Ca²⁺ release, TRPML1 activation by ML‐SA1 has been linked to beneficial downstream effects such as the induction of lysosomal exocytosis and the enhancement of cathepsin activity, which together contribute to the restoration of lysosomal function and cellular homeostasis (Karema-Jokinen et al., 2023; Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the current hypothesis, ML‐SA1 is expected to act on RPE cells by enhancing lysosomal Ca²⁺ release through TRPML1 activation, thereby stimulating the calcineurin-TFEB signaling cascade. This cascade is anticipated to upregulate the transcription of autophagy and lysosome-related genes, leading to improved autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis. In practical assays, such as those employing lipofuscin-loaded RPE monolayers, ML‐SA1 should facilitate the clearance of misfolded or aggregated tight junction proteins—including ZO-1—thereby restoring disrupted tight junction belts and improving transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) measurements. The activation of cathepsins, as part of the enhanced lysosomal function, is also expected to increase the degradation of accumulated cellular debris, further supporting cellular clearance (Falcão et al., 2025; Más Gómez et al., 2018). In experimental models of epithelial barrier restoration, previous data using TRPML1 agonists have shown that such compounds can rescue autophagic flux and reduce lysosomal storage, which is associated with improved barrier integrity; this supports the mechanism by which ML‐SA1 is expected to normalize the function of RPE cells relevant to dry AMD (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The candidate’s reported effective concentration (EC₅₀ around 45 µM for MCOLN1/TRPML1 activation) further underlines its potential to achieve a pharmacologically relevant activation of the TRPML1 channel in RPE cells, thereby triggering the downstream beneficial effects (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
ML‐SA1 represents a mechanistically innovative therapeutic candidate with a well‐defined mode of action that directly targets lysosomal dysfunction—a key pathological feature in dry AMD. One of the major strengths of ML‐SA1 is its ability to rapidly induce lysosomal Ca²⁺ release by specifically activating TRPML1, which has been documented robustly in various RPE cell models (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling is crucial for the activation of the calcineurin-TFEB pathway, which in turn upregulates lysosomal and autophagy gene networks; such activation is essential for clearing cellular debris, misfolded proteins, and aggregated tight junction components that compromise the integrity of the RPE barrier (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The anticipated effect of restoring TEER in lipofuscin-loaded monolayers is particularly important because impaired barrier function is a hallmark of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, the potential to enhance cathepsin activity and thereby boost lysosomal degradation pathways positions ML‐SA1 as a promising candidate to counteract the autophagy deficits that are observed in diseased RPE cells.

However, there are notable limitations and challenges that must be addressed. First, while the mechanistic data are compelling, ML‐SA1’s efficacy appears to be significantly modulated by the lysosomal lipid environment; in conditions where lipofuscin or other lipid accumulations are prominent, the Ca²⁺ response to ML‐SA1 has been shown to be reduced, suggesting that its beneficial effects might be attenuated in advanced dry AMD where lipid accumulation is extensive (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Second, despite its robust in vitro activity in various RPE models, ML‐SA1 has not yet been advanced into clinical or in vivo models of dry AMD, and thus there is a lack of safety, toxicity, and pharmacokinetics data relevant to chronic administration in the context of retinal diseases (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Additionally, although ML‐SA1 is reported to have an EC₅₀ around 45 µM for TRPML1 activation, the dosing window and potential off-target effects remain to be thoroughly characterized, particularly with respect to a multifactorial disease such as dry AMD that involves chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and photoreceptor degeneration (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

From a drug development perspective, ML‐SA1’s novel lysosomal-targeted mechanism offers significant promise by addressing a critical aspect of RPE dysfunction through the restoration of lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling and autophagy. Its ability to potentially clear misfolded tight junction proteins and recover ZO-1 belts, thereby restoring TEER, could translate into improved barrier integrity—a key determinant of RPE health in the context of dry AMD (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

In conclusion, while ML‐SA1 is a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapy for dry AMD, the current state of evidence is largely preclinical and mechanistic. The compound’s ability to activate TRPML1 and thereby enhance lysosomal Ca²⁺ release—coupled with its downstream activation of calcineurin-TFEB signaling and the potential to restore autophagy and barrier function in RPE—positions it as a strong candidate for further investigation. However, significant challenges remain in translating these in vitro findings into effective in vivo therapies. Future studies should focus on addressing the impact of lysosomal lipid accumulation on ML‐SA1 efficacy, determining the long-term safety and pharmacokinetic profiles in animal models of dry AMD, and establishing whether the observed cellular benefits translate into functional improvements in retinal health and vision preservation. Overall, ML‐SA1’s lysosomal-targeted mechanism and its demonstrated capacity to rescue key RPE functions provide a compelling rationale to pursue this candidate further, albeit with the caveat that extensive preclinical validation is required before clinical development can be contemplated (Falcão et al., 2025; Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Belumosudil (KD025; Rezurock) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable, indazole-derived serine/threonine kinase inhibitor that preferentially targets Rho-associated coiled-coil–containing protein kinase 2 (ROCK2) over ROCK1 and was developed by Kadmon Pharmaceuticals following licensing from Nano Terra (now approved in the United States for chronic graft-versus-host disease, cGVHD) (Blair, 2021; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022; Przepiorka et al., 2022). Biochemical selectivity has been consistently reported across sources: IC₅₀ values are approximately 60–110 nM for ROCK2 with markedly weaker activity on ROCK1 (typically >10 µM), and orthogonal profiling notes ROCK2 ~0.105 µM and ROCK1 ~24 µM, confirming substantial isoform preference (Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022; Blair, 2021; Lake et al., 2020). As an ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor, belumosudil binds the catalytic domain of ROCK2, analogous to the mechanism of other clinically used ROCK inhibitors, but with enhanced isoform selectivity designed to improve tolerability relative to pan-ROCK agents (e.g., fasudil, ripasudil, netarsudil) (Cheng et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

The broader class—ROCK inhibitors—modulates actin–myosin cytoskeletal dynamics by decreasing phosphorylation of myosin regulatory elements and altering actin turnover via downstream nodes (LIMK–cofilin, ERM proteins), with downstream effects on cell contractility, focal adhesions, cell junctions, migration, and myofibroblast differentiation (Cheng et al., 2025). In ophthalmology, ROCK inhibitors have established or emerging therapeutic roles: netarsudil and ripasudil lower intraocular pressure by relaxing trabecular meshwork and Schlemm’s canal, and corneal endothelial repair paradigms (topical ROCK inhibitors and cell therapy adjuncts) exploit cytoskeletal relaxation, enhanced adhesion, and proliferation to accelerate re-endothelialization (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025). Collectively, these features position belumosudil within a drug class with proven ocular pharmacology and strong plausibility for modulating epithelial/endothelial barrier biology through cytoskeletal re-tuning (Leong et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic immunomodulation and anti-fibrotic indications. Belumosudil is FDA-approved for treatment of cGVHD after at least two prior systemic therapies at an oral dose of 200 mg once daily with food; population pharmacokinetics indicate a mean elimination half-life of ~19 hours, primary CYP3A4 metabolism, and predominant fecal excretion, with two metabolites that also inhibit ROCK2 (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Blair, 2021). Across phase 2 programs in cGVHD, objective response rates (65–77%) were observed with 200 mg once or twice daily dosing, with corticosteroid sparing and acceptable tolerability, consolidating a favorable clinical safety/efficacy profile for chronic use in a heavily pretreated, immunologically dysregulated population (Jagasia et al., 2021; Zanin-Zhorov & Blazar, 2021). Beyond cGVHD, belumosudil has been explored in fibrotic diseases (interim idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis signal for attenuated FVC decline) and systemic sclerosis, consistent with class-wide anti-fibrotic properties driven by ROCK2 blockade (Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

Ocular use of ROCK inhibitors (class precedent). While belumosudil itself has not been reported in clinical ocular indications, the ROCK inhibitor class has multiple precedents in eye disease. Topical netarsudil and ripasudil are approved or widely used for glaucoma; intravitreal and topical fasudil have been explored for retinal diseases (e.g., diabetic macular edema) with reported safety in small series, and sustained-release ocular delivery of ROCK inhibitors (e.g., AR-13503) has been tested in preclinical models (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025). These translational precedents establish that ROCK pathway modulation can be achieved in ocular tissues via topical, intravitreal, or sustained-release routes and that cytoskeletal/vascular barrier targets respond to this mechanism in the eye (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Belumosudil in ocular preclinical models. In a laser-induced choroidal neovascularization/subretinal fibrosis model designed to isolate fibrotic progression, both fasudil (pan-ROCK) and belumosudil (ROCK2-selective) reduced fibrosis volume, preserved retinal morphology, increased retinal thickness, reduced pyknotic nuclei, and decreased type I collagen and α-SMA staining; corrected total cell fluorescence for ROCK1/ROCK2 was reduced, with particularly strong ROCK2 target engagement by belumosudil (occupancy down from 6.7% to 0.1%) (Zandi et al., 2025). Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) and western blot evidence showed reductions in p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex—consistent with ROCK pathway inhibition—alongside decreases in TGF-β1, fibronectin, vimentin, and α-SMA; belumosudil also more effectively reduced “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations near the choroid–RPE boundary compared with fasudil and decreased macrophages/perivascular cells, suggesting anti-inflammatory as well as anti-fibrotic activity (Zandi et al., 2025). In vitro, 24-hour ROCK inhibitor exposure in fibroblastic cells altered morphology (loss of long processes, blunted periphery) and decreased cell numbers, consistent with cytoskeletal/phenotype modulation and possible anti-proliferative effects in fibrogenic cells (Zandi et al., 2025).

Dry AMD relevance and gaps. The above in vivo data position ROCK2 inhibition as an anti-fibrotic modifier of the choroid–RPE interface after laser injury, with partial restoration of retinal architecture; however, they do not test dry AMD pathobiology (e.g., sodium iodate RPE toxicity or geographic atrophy models) (Zandi et al., 2025). Direct ocular RPE barrier endpoints—TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and tight-junction protein integrity (ZO-1, claudin-19)—have not been reported for belumosudil in RPE, and the available studies do not include oxidative or complement injury paradigms (H₂O₂, NaIO₃) in ARPE-19, primary human RPE, or in vivo dry AMD models (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). Class-level in vitro RPE evidence exists for ROCK inhibition improving wound closure, adhesion, pigmentation, RPE65 expression, and photoreceptor outer-segment phagocytosis in iPSC-RPE with Y-27632, but without barrier readouts, and with limited recovery duration and small sample sizes (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Additional pluripotent RPE manufacturing work reports ROCK inhibition suppresses EMT programs (TGF-β/Wnt ligands, SNAI2, collagens) and promotes rapid tight-junction reformation in culture, supporting barrier-relevant cytoskeletal effects at the transcriptomic/phenotypic level, but without TEER or paracellular flux data under oxidative/complement stress (Croze, 2015). In sum, while class-level and belumosudil-specific ocular data support anti-fibrotic and cytoskeletal modulation at the choroid–RPE interface, there is no direct published evidence in the provided literature set that belumosudil rescues TEER, preserves claudin-19/ZO-1, or reduces FITC-dextran flux under H₂O₂ or complement challenge in RPE or that it improves outcomes in NaIO₃ models (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
ROCK2 biology and junctional/cytoskeletal control. ROCK1/2 are AGC-family serine/threonine kinases activated by RhoA–GTP; they increase actomyosin contractility primarily by phosphorylating myosin light chain (MLC) directly and inhibiting myosin light-chain phosphatase via phosphorylation of the MYPT1 regulatory subunit, elevating p-MLC levels and stabilizing stress fibers and focal adhesions (Cheng et al., 2025). ROCK also phosphorylates LIM kinases to inactivate cofilin, which slows F-actin turnover and further stiffens the cytoskeleton; ERM proteins, adducin, intermediate filament proteins (vimentin, GFAP), and multiple cytoskeletal/membrane linkers are additional substrates that integrate cytoskeletal and junctional dynamics (Cheng et al., 2025). These pathways are sensitive to mechanical inputs (matrix stiffness) and link cytoskeletal remodeling to barrier integrity and cell adhesion, consistent with the observed roles of ROCK in endothelial hyperpermeability and junction stabilization in ocular tissues (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025).

Belumosudil target engagement in choroid–RPE constructs. In vivo in the choroid–RPE complex after laser injury, both fasudil and belumosudil lowered p-MYPT1, indicating on-pathway ROCK inhibition, and reduced fibrotic markers (α-SMA, vimentin, fibronectin, collagen I, TGF-β1), consistent with suppression of myofibroblast activation, ECM deposition, and TGF-β/Smad signaling output (Zandi et al., 2025). Imaging mass cytometry showed spatially localized fibrotic marker expression to the choroid–RPE boundary and a reduction in “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations with belumosudil relative to fasudil, and a decrease in macrophage and perivascular cell signatures—integrating anti-fibrotic and anti-inflammatory mechanisms (Zandi et al., 2025). Quantitatively, ROCK2 staining occupancy fell from ~6.7% to 0.1% after belumosudil treatment, stronger than the reduction with fasudil (to 0.7%), supporting efficient ROCK2 target engagement by belumosudil (Zandi et al., 2025).

ROCK and epithelial barrier relevance. Although the RPE-specific tight-junction literature for belumosudil is not available in the provided sources, corneal endothelial studies link ROCK activity to stabilization of ZO-1 and the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump complex; pharmacologic ROCK inhibition promotes cytoskeletal relaxation, spreading, and cyclin-D–dependent proliferation, and has been leveraged clinically to accelerate re-endothelialization and junctional re-establishment (Leong et al., 2025). In vascular endothelia, RhoA/ROCK signaling drives VEGF-induced permeability and tube formation; ROCK inhibition modulates junctional architecture (e.g., “zipper-like” lymphatic endothelial junctions) and reduces permeability, supporting a mechanistic link to barrier tightening (Leong et al., 2025). In diabetic retinal pathology, ROCK1 activation contributes to RPE blebbing and tight-junction opening with outer blood-retinal barrier breakdown; pharmacologic ROCK inhibition (fasudil) improved barrier function and suppressed leukocyte migration and ICAM-1, reducing vascular leakage and neurodegeneration (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Together, these data reinforce that ROCK signaling is a proximal regulator of epithelial/endothelial junctions and barrier integrity and that inhibition—especially with an isoform-selective agent that engages ROCK2 in the choroid–RPE complex—has plausible junction-preserving effects in RPE monolayers (Leong et al., 2025; Zandi et al., 2025).

Anti-EMT and anti-fibrotic transcriptional programs. Transcriptomic studies in pluripotent stem cell–derived RPE and other epithelial contexts show ROCK inhibition suppresses EMT-associated transcriptional programs (TGF-β ligands, Wnt components, SNAI2, collagens) and promotes tight-junction reformation, consistent with decreased cytoskeletal tension and reduced MRTF/SRF-dependent transcription that drives myofibroblast markers (e.g., α-SMA) (Croze, 2015; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022). ROCK2 inhibition also intersects with inflammatory transcriptional axes (STAT3/STAT5) and NF-κB, shifting Th17/Tfh toward Treg and reducing proinflammatory cytokines in PBMCs and cGVHD models, which could help resolve inflammatory components of AMD pathophysiology at the RPE–choroid interface (Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Cytoskeletal/ciliary modulation in RPE-lineage cells. Independent siRNA/drug screens in ciliogenesis models identified ROCK2 as a strong negative regulator of cilia incidence and length; short and prolonged belumosudil exposure increased cilia metrics in hTERT RPE-1 and mIMCD3 cells while reducing phosphorylated MLC and acto-myosin fiber-like structures, consistent with decreased ROCK2-driven contractility (Lake et al., 2020). Although ciliation per se is not a dry AMD therapeutic endpoint, the data are a sensitive readout of cytoskeletal reprogramming via ROCK2 and reinforce the target’s role in apical organization in epithelia with RPE lineage origin (Lake et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay context: H₂O₂ and complement injury in RPE monolayers. Under oxidative stress (H₂O₂) and complement attack, the RPE cytoskeleton becomes hypercontractile, junctional belts destabilize, and paracellular permeability increases—manifest as reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased FITC-dextran flux, with mislocalization or fragmentation of tight-junction proteins (ZO-1, claudin-19). ROCK activation (via RhoA–GTP, inflammatory mediators, or mechanical cues) exacerbates this by increasing p-MYPT1 and p-MLC to drive actomyosin tension and stress fiber formation (Cheng et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). The class literature in ocular epithelia/endothelium indicates that ROCK inhibition relaxes cytoskeletal tension, promotes cell spreading and junctional complex re-assembly (ZO-1 stabilization reported in corneal endothelium), and reduces VEGF- or inflammation-driven hyperpermeability (Leong et al., 2025). In diabetic retinal models, ROCK pathway activation produces RPE blebbing and tight-junction disruption, with pharmacologic ROCK inhibition reversing barrier dysfunction and dampening leukostasis and leakage (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Given these mechanisms, selective ROCK2 inhibition with belumosudil is expected to:
- Reduce p-MYPT1 and downstream p-MLC in RPE, decreasing acto-myosin contractility, stabilizing the circumferential actin belt and adherens/tight junctions (ZO-1/claudin-19), thereby rescuing TEER and lowering FITC-dextran flux under H₂O₂ or complement challenge (Zandi et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025).
- Suppress EMT-like shifts and myofibroblast activation induced by oxidative/complement stress by lowering α-SMA/vimentin and ECM program activation (fibronectin, collagen), as seen in vivo after laser injury and in ROCK-inhibited RPE culture transcriptomics (Zandi et al., 2025; Croze, 2015).
- Provide anti-inflammatory benefits by reducing macrophage/perivascular cell accumulation seen in vivo and by directly modulating STAT3/STAT5-linked cytokine programs, potentially blunting complement-amplified inflammatory cascades at the RPE/choroid interface (Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021).

Target expression and context. ROCK signaling is active in ocular tissues; p-MYPT1 is reduced in the choroid–RPE complex of laser-injured eyes after ROCK inhibition; ROCK1 translocates and drives cytoskeletal/junctional changes under hyperglycemia in RPE and endothelium; and ROCK2 expression is quantifiably reduced by belumosudil in the choroid–RPE complex—collectively validating target presence and drug engagement at the proposed site of action (Zandi et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Important caveats. The provided literature set does not contain direct demonstrations that belumosudil rescues TEER or reduces FITC-dextran flux in RPE under H₂O₂ or complement injury, nor does it report preservation of claudin-19/ZO-1 localization in RPE with ROCK2-selective inhibition; these remain testable predictions grounded in mechanism and class precedent but not yet substantiated for belumosudil in RPE (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). Similarly, no data are provided here for NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration models with belumosudil; the NaIO₃ discussion pertains to single-cell remodeling and EMT tendencies in dry AMD models, which conceptually align with anti-EMT and anti-fibrotic effects of ROCK inhibition, but require direct in vivo validation for this candidate (Zandi et al., 2025).

Clinically, belumosudil has a ~19-hour half-life, ~64% bioavailability with food (in healthy subjects), and is metabolized by CYP3A4; ocular pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration are not reported in the provided sources (Przepiorka et al., 2022). In the laser-injury mouse model, intraperitoneal administration from day 35 to 49 post-laser achieved retinal/choroid pharmacodynamics (↓p-MYPT1, ↓markers), indicating systemic dosing can engage ocular targets in inflamed/fibrotic tissue in mice, though translational relevance to human ocular exposure remains to be determined and local delivery could be preferable for barrier-rescue assays (Zandi et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- On-pathway target engagement in choroid–RPE with functional tissue outcomes. Belumosudil decreases p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex, reduces fibrosis volume, attenuates α-SMA, vimentin, fibronectin, collagen I, and TGF-β1, and preserves retinal morphology and thickness in a subretinal fibrosis model; ROCK2 occupancy falls to near-baseline with treatment, indicating strong ocular target engagement (Zandi et al., 2025). - Mechanistic alignment with barrier preservation. ROCK signaling is a proximal regulator of cytoskeletal tension and tight-junction stability; inhibition reduces MLC phosphorylation via MYPT1 de-phosphorylation, stabilizes junctions (corneal ZO-1; endothelial junction “zippering”), and mitigates hyperpermeability (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025). The candidate’s demonstrated ability to lower p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex and reduce myofibroblast activation fits the hypothesis that it can preserve epithelial barrier integrity under stress (Zandi et al., 2025).

ROCK inhibition suppresses TGF-β/Wnt-mediated EMT programs and promotes tight-junction reformation in pluripotent-derived RPE; in vivo reductions in α-SMA and ECM deposition further support anti-fibrotic activity coherent with preventing RPE-to-mesenchymal transitions that compromise the barrier (Croze, 2015; Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions. Belumosudil reduces macrophage and perivascular cell signatures in vivo and systemically shifts Th17/Tfh toward Treg via STAT3/STAT5 modulation; these effects could dampen complement- and cytokine-driven RPE injury cascades implicated in dry AMD (Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

A clinically approved safety profile with chronic administration, a manageable drug–drug interaction profile (CYP3A4), and a ~19-hour half-life provide a de-risked starting point for repurposing; dose selection can be guided by systemic exposures achieved in cGVHD (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zanin-Zhorov & Blazar, 2021).

Weaknesses and knowledge gaps  
- No direct RPE barrier functional data for belumosudil. The literature set lacks TEER, FITC-dextran flux, or ZO-1/claudin-19 preservation data for belumosudil in RPE under oxidative/complement stress; consequently, the core hypothesis—TEER rescue with ROCK2 selectivity—remains inferential (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021).  
- No NaIO₃ or dry AMD-specific in vivo efficacy with belumosudil. While NaIO₃ single-cell data support EMT and fibroblast-like RPE signatures relevant to ROCK pathway targeting, belumosudil has not been tested in NaIO₃ or geographic atrophy models here; the current in vivo evidence is laser-injury fibrosis focused (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Isoform biology nuance in the retina. Diabetic retinal studies emphasize ROCK1 translocation and ROCK1-mediated blebbing/tight-junction disruption, with some reports noting ROCK2 localization as “undisturbed” in those models; this raises a strategic question whether ROCK2-selective inhibition alone is sufficient for barrier rescue across stress etiologies or whether dual inhibition is sometimes preferable (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).  
- Ocular pharmacokinetics and delivery. There are no data on ocular tissue penetration, retinal/choroidal exposure, or intravitreal/topical formulations for belumosudil; although systemic dosing engaged ocular targets in mice after laser injury, human ocular delivery, durability, and safety require specific assessment (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025). Class precedents (intravitreal/topical fasudil, topical netarsudil/ripasudil) are encouraging but not directly transferable to this scaffold without formulation work (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Off-target and pathway-network considerations. Although belumosudil is selective for ROCK2, it has minor ROCK1 and pathway-adjacent activities (e.g., mTOR), and widespread cytoskeletal re-tuning can have context-dependent effects (e.g., on ciliation) whose long-term retinal implications are unknown (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Lake et al., 2020).

Decision-oriented interpretation for dry AMD  
- Mechanistic plausibility: High. ROCK2 inhibition is expected to directly reduce cytoskeletal tension and stabilize epithelial junctions; on-pathway pharmacodynamic effects (↓p-MYPT1) and anti-fibrotic marker reductions in the choroid–RPE complex support action at the relevant tissue interface (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025).

The candidate has a de-risked systemic safety profile and class-level ocular pharmacology, plus in vivo anti-fibrotic retinal benefits; however, barrier-specific efficacy in RPE under oxidative/complement stress has not yet been shown for belumosudil (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Differentiation vs pan-ROCK: Potentially favorable. In vivo, belumosudil achieved stronger ROCK2 engagement and larger decreases in “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations than fasudil, aligning with the idea that ROCK2 drives key profibrotic cascades at the choroid–RPE interface, while avoiding ROCK1-linked hypotension liabilities systemically; whether ROCK1 contributions to RPE barrier breakdown under certain stressors would limit efficacy remains to be determined experimentally (Zandi et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

Concrete implications for the proposed hypothesis  
- The specific claims that belumosudil has demonstrated +50% TER recovery in ARPE-19 under H₂O₂ stress, 40% RPE cell preservation and ERG improvement in a mouse NaIO₃ model, and an oral bioavailability ~45% with t₁/₂ ~4.8 h are not supported by the literature set provided; instead, the available PK indicates oral bioavailability is ~64% with food and a ~19-h half-life, and no TER/NaIO₃ efficacy data for belumosudil are referenced here (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). The hypothesized barrier rescue under oxidative/complement injury remains plausible mechanistically but requires direct validation in RPE models (Leong et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Program-level next steps (to enable a go/no-go)  
- In vitro RPE barrier assays: Primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE monolayers subjected to H₂O₂ and normal human serum (complement) injury; quantify TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and ZO-1/claudin-19 localization/intensity; include p-MYPT1 and p-MLC biochemical readouts as pharmacodynamics; benchmark belumosudil across a concentration range anchored to ROCK2 IC₅₀ and cell viability (Lake et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Phenotypic rescue breadth: Replicate class-level findings with ROCK2 selectivity—adhesion, wound closure, POS phagocytosis, RPE65 expression—to establish that belumosudil recapitulates the iPSC-RPE Y-27632 phenotype profile while tightening the barrier (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

- Ocular PK/formulation: Ocular tissue distribution after local delivery and/or systemic administration; stability and duration; comparative exposures in RPE/choroid vs retina with safety assessment (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025).

Overall, belumosudil is a compelling, mechanistically aligned candidate with de-risked systemic safety, clear ocular on-pathway antifibrotic activity at the choroid–RPE interface, and strong biological rationale for junctional stabilization in stressed RPE. The decisive gap is the absence of direct barrier-function rescue data in RPE under oxidative or complement injury and the lack of dry AMD model efficacy. Addressing these with focused preclinical studies will determine whether its ROCK2 selectivity translates into clinically meaningful protection of the outer blood–retinal barrier in dry AMD, and whether it offers advantages over pan-ROCK inhibitors in this context (Zandi et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ICG-001 (Sigma I2441) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor originally identified for its ability to selectively disrupt the interaction between β-catenin and the transcriptional coactivator CBP (CREB-binding protein), thereby inhibiting TCF/LEF-dependent Wnt/β-catenin–driven transcription without reducing total β-catenin protein abundance (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). Mechanistically, ICG-001 is positioned within a class of β-catenin pathway modulators that block nuclear β-catenin activity rather than decreasing β-catenin protein levels; this distinguishes it from antisense/siRNA approaches and from inhibitors that act upstream in Wnt signaling (e.g., tankyrase inhibitors like XAV-939) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor class has been proposed as a more selective means to modulate β-catenin transcriptional output while sparing adherens junction functions that depend on β-catenin protein pools, a distinction supported by data showing ICG-001 does not trigger compensatory γ-catenin stabilization that follows β-catenin protein depletion (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117).

Within the broader Wnt-targeting landscape, ICG-001 exemplifies downstream, transcriptional-coactivator–selective targeting, contrasted with agents that block β-catenin/TCF binding, Dishevelled PDZ interactions, Porcupine-mediated ligand maturation, or Frizzled receptor activity (e.g., OMP-18R5) (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31). Because Wnt pathway effects are highly context dependent and temporally dynamic across tissues, coactivator-selective modulation has been argued to mitigate systemic liabilities relative to global pathway inhibition (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31).

Therapeutic History  
ICG-001 itself is widely used as a research tool, and its clinical derivative/prodrug analogs (e.g., PRI-724/OP-724) have reached Phase I/IIa testing in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, establishing a preliminary human safety/tolerability and feasibility record for CBP/β-catenin pathway inhibition in chronic disease. In HCV-induced cirrhosis, an open-label Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of PRI-724 administered continuous i.v. infusions (10–160 mg/m2/day; 1 week on/1 week off for 12 weeks) with primary outcomes focused on adverse events and exploratory anti-fibrotic endpoints (histology, serum fibrosis biomarkers); the program reported safety/tolerability and preliminary efficacy consistent with anti-fibrotic activity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014). In HBV/HCV-related cirrhosis, a Phase I/IIa open-label study (twice-weekly 4 h infusions; 140, 280, 380 mg/m2 per 4 h) evaluated safety, PK, and change in liver fibrosis area by biopsy at 12 weeks; the registry cites a derived EBioMedicine report on safety, tolerability, and anti-fibrotic effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2018). In advanced primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; Scheuer stage ≥III), OP-724 (formerly PRI-724) underwent a Phase I dose-finding trial (4 h i.v. infusions, twice weekly for 12 weeks; 140/280/380 mg/m2 cohorts) assessing serious adverse events, PK of OP-724 and metabolite C-82, and fibrosis-related endpoints (biopsy fibrotic area, FibroScan, Child-Pugh/MELD, ELF score) with feasibility/safety results published (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

No clinical or preclinical ocular applications of ICG-001/PRI-724/OP-724 were identified in the provided context, and there are no reports here of use in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), or retinal barrier disorders (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019). Preclinical oncology literature summarized in the provided sources documents ICG-001’s activity in cancer cells (reduced proliferation and induced selective apoptosis via TCF-dependent signaling reduction) but does not address ocular tissues (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Thus, while the drug class has human safety experience in fibrotic liver disease, there is no direct evidence in the provided context for ophthalmic use or for dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
ICG-001 binds CBP and selectively disrupts the β-catenin/CBP complex, attenuating β-catenin–driven transcription of TCF/LEF target genes (e.g., Cyclin D1) without decreasing total β-catenin protein levels; in Hep3B cells, ICG-001 reduced TOPflash reporter activity and Cyclin D1 expression while leaving β-catenin abundance unchanged and without inducing compensatory γ-catenin stabilization (if anything, γ-catenin modestly decreased) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). Across multiple excerpts, ICG-001 is consistently described as selective for β-catenin/CBP over β-catenin/p300, reducing TCF-dependent Wnt output while sparing other β-catenin protein interactions; global β-catenin levels are unaffected, reinforcing a functional separation between nuclear transcriptional roles and membrane adherens junction pools (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Authors highlight that agents which lower β-catenin protein (ASO/siRNA) trigger γ-catenin compensation at adherens junctions—distinct from ICG-001, which blocks transcriptional activity without provoking such protein-level sensing/reciprocity (Wickline, 2013, pp. 112–117, 140–145). It remains explicitly unknown from these data whether ICG-001 perturbs adherens junction function in vivo; follow-up studies were recommended to test junctional tolerance to transcriptional blockade (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

Contextual biology of β-catenin coactivator usage indicates that CBP vs p300 partnering can impart divergent phenotypic outcomes; in fibrotic contexts, CBP-associated β-catenin activity has been linked with pro-fibrotic programs whereas p300-associated activity may be protective, though this literature is complex and model-dependent (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69). Canonical β-catenin signaling is also subject to Wnt-independent inputs that promote nuclear translocation/transactivation (e.g., PKA/Akt phosphorylation), and β-catenin exists in distinct pools with membrane-associated adherens junction functions that are regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation events, further implying that selective transcriptional blockade (CBP-directed) may spare adhesive roles (Wickline, 2013, pp. 21–26). Together, these mechanistic data support a rationale for testing CBP/β-catenin–selective inhibitors for diseases where β-catenin transcription drives pathology and where preserving epithelial junctional architecture is desirable (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 140–145).

Disease-Relevant Biology in RPE and Retinal Barriers  
RPE epithelial phenotype and outer blood–retina barrier (oBRB) integrity depend on tight junction (TJ) and adherens junction (AJ) complexes (ZO-1/occludin/claudins; E-cadherin/catenins). Loss of ZO-1 releases ZONAB to drive CDK4 and proliferation; downregulation of E-cadherin frees β-catenin to translocate to the nucleus and activate EMT/proliferation drivers (e.g., Snail, Cyclin D1), establishing a mechanistic link between junctional disruption and β-catenin–dependent transcriptional programs in RPE (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–9). Reviews of RPE EMT highlight Wnt–β-catenin as a key mediator in the eye; experimental injury (laser photocoagulation) activates β-catenin signaling and facilitates RPE proliferation, reinforcing the pathway’s involvement in EMT and regenerative responses (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 7–9).

Critically, primary hRPE culture studies demonstrate that Matrigel plus Activin A (MA) fosters epithelial morphology, increases TJ gene/protein expression (Claudin-1, Claudin-3, Occludin, ZO-1), improves apical ZO-1 polarity, and elevates TEER; this phenotype is accompanied by increased β-catenin levels and β-catenin/TCF target expression (TCF-4, Survivin, Cyclin D1, c-Myc), and is suppressed by the Wnt/β-catenin inhibitor XAV-939, implicating canonical β-catenin activity in barrier maturation under these culture conditions (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11). The MA paradigm also shows anti-apoptotic effects (lower ROS, preserved mitochondrial potential, lower Annexin V positivity) linked to elevated β-catenin/Survivin, again consistent with β-catenin supporting epithelial survival when cell–cell contacts are intact (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

Conversely, disease models and inflammatory contexts show scenarios where β-catenin activation correlates with barrier breakdown. In diabetic macular edema (DME) models, SMURF1 promotes WIF1 ubiquitination and degradation, activating Wnt/β-catenin–VEGF signaling, inducing autophagy, and disrupting RPE tight junctions; knockdown of SMURF1 restores WIF1, suppresses pathway activation, and rescues claudin-1/occludin/ZO-1 expression in ARPE-19 and in STZ mice (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Inflammatory TNFα challenge in polarized ARPE-19 reduces TER, increases paracellular permeability, and disrupts ZO-1/claudins/occludin and AJ components; the HDAC inhibitor ITF2357 restores TER and junctional proteins and suppresses β-catenin overexpression and NF-κB signaling, supporting the concept that limiting β-catenin–linked transcription can be barrier-protective under inflammatory stress (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19). Under oxidative stress relevant to dry AMD, ex vivo primary porcine RPE (ppRPE) exposed to NaIO₃ shows a significant reduction in ZO-1 immunopositive area (with unchanged TJP1 mRNA), indicating tight-junction localization loss; while the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is not measured directly in this model, the outcome establishes a testable context for barrier rescue (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

These data collectively underscore a context-dependent role of β-catenin in RPE: when epithelial contacts are robust, β-catenin activity can support maturation, TJ expression, and survival; under EMT/injury/inflammatory stress (e.g., DME/TNFα), β-catenin pathway activation correlates with junctional loss, VEGF induction, and autophagy, and pathway suppression can be protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19).

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay context: RPE monolayers subjected to oxidative stress (e.g., NaIO₃, H₂O₂, or serum withdrawal models) with readouts including TEER, paracellular flux, and localization/expression of ZO-1 and claudin-1.

- Gene/protein expression in RPE: ZO-1, claudins, occludin, and cadherins/β-catenin are established components of RPE junctions and are readily measured; TEER increases in mature hRPE and decreases with injury provide a functional correlate of barrier status (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55). β-catenin and downstream targets (Cyclin D1, Survivin, c-Myc, TCF-4) were upregulated in hRPE MA cultures and are suppressible by Wnt pathway inhibition, confirming pathway engagement in RPE (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Hypothesized pharmacology: ICG-001 is expected to reduce β-catenin/CBP-dependent transcription (Cyclin D1, Survivin, TOPflash) without decreasing total β-catenin protein or stabilizing γ-catenin; this has been demonstrated in hepatocyte-derived models (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117). In RPE, the immediate expected effect would be downregulation of β-catenin/TCF-LEF targets that are CBP-dependent. The direction of effect on junctional genes is uncertain based on available data: in MA-conditioned hRPE, canonical β-catenin activity correlates with increased claudin-1 and ZO-1 and higher TEER, and global pathway inhibition reduces these effects; thus CBP-targeted inhibition might risk dampening TJ upregulation under certain epithelial conditions (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11). In inflammatory/DME-like contexts, β-catenin activation contributes to VEGF/autophagy-mediated TJ disruption, and Wnt pathway suppression is protective; in these contexts, CBP blockade could plausibly reduce pathway-driven barrier loss (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

- Proliferation concerns: ICG-001 reduces Cyclin D1 in non-ocular cells, consistent with attenuating proliferation signaling (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). In RPE EMT, β-catenin activation promotes proliferation via Cyclin D1; thus ICG-001 would be expected to mitigate proliferation-associated EMT programs rather than activate them (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7, 7–9). However, MA-driven β-catenin activity increases Survivin/Bcl2 and enhances anti-apoptotic resilience; therefore, under oxidative stress, attenuating β-catenin/CBP with ICG-001 could trade off survival signals against potential EMT suppression, and net effects on TEER may vary by stressor and co-signaling milieu (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Net expectation in oxidative stress assays: Under acute oxidative stress where junctional proteins disassemble (e.g., NaIO₃ model reduces ZO-1 area), there is no direct evidence provided that CBP-selective β-catenin inhibition upregulates claudin-1/ZO-1 or restores TEER in RPE. In analogous inflammatory contexts, limiting β-catenin–linked transcription correlates with barrier recovery, but this was achieved with an HDAC inhibitor and via suppression of β-catenin overexpression/NF-κB, not CBP-selective Wnt blockade (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19). Therefore, the claim that ICG-001 will “bias gene transcription toward junctional protein upregulation (claudin-1, ZO-1) in RPE under oxidative stress without activating proliferation pathways, leading to recovery of TEER and decreased paracellular flux” is mechanistically plausible in EMT/inflammatory settings but remains unsubstantiated for oxidative stress in RPE; the directionality of effect on junctional genes could invert depending on baseline epithelial status and co-activation of survival pathways (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Therapeutic Risk–Benefit Considerations  
- Safety/translatability: Clinical-stage CBP/β-catenin inhibitors (PRI-724/OP-724) have demonstrated safety/tolerability in Phase I/IIa liver fibrosis trials, supporting repurposing potential; however, the dosing was i.v., and ocular delivery, PK/PD at the RPE, and retinal safety are uncharacterized in the provided data (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Mechanistic specificity: ICG-001 spares total β-catenin protein and does not trigger γ-catenin compensation, mitigating concerns about adherens junction destabilization that accompany β-catenin depletion; nevertheless, whether ICG-001 affects adherens junction functionality in epithelial tissues in vivo remains unknown, and this must be directly assessed in RPE (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Pathway context dependence: RPE barrier outcomes with Wnt/β-catenin modulation are bidirectional and context dependent—MA-induced β-catenin activity enhances TJs/TEER, while in DME/inflammation β-catenin activation correlates with TJ disruption; CBP-specific blockade could be beneficial in the latter but deleterious in the former (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). This necessitates careful stressor stratification (oxidative versus inflammatory/VEGF-driven) in preclinical testing.

- Disease relevance to dry AMD: Oxidative stress disrupts RPE TJs and reduces ZO-1 localization in ex vivo ppRPE; EMT and barrier breakdown are recognized contributors to RPE dysfunction; however, there is no direct evidence here linking CBP/β-catenin inhibition to barrier rescue in oxidative injury models or to slowed geographic atrophy progression (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

Experimental De-Risking Plan (RPE-Centric)  
Given the absence of direct ocular data for ICG-001, a staged validation plan is warranted:

- In vitro RPE barrier assays:  
  • Use primary hRPE on Transwells to maturity (baseline TER per established values) (Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55). Challenge with oxidative stress (NaIO₃/H₂O₂) and inflammatory stress (TNFα) in parallel. Quantify TER, fluorescein paracellular flux, and immunolocalization of ZO-1/claudin-1/occludin and AJ proteins. Test ICG-001 across a potency range informed by cell studies (e.g., up to 10 μM) and compare with XAV-939 (Wnt inhibition control) and an HDAC inhibitor (ITF2357, positive control for barrier rescue under TNFα) (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Wickline, 2013, pp. 112–117). Assess β-catenin target gene modulation (Cyclin D1, Survivin, TCF-4) and VEGF (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 9–11; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

  • Hypothesis testing criteria: Evidence of TEER recovery and reduced paracellular flux with maintained or improved ZO-1/claudin-1 localization in oxidative and inflammatory paradigms without induction of proliferation markers (Cyclin D1) would support the proposed mechanism; failure or opposite effects would argue against it (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99).

- Ex vivo ppRPE coculture:  
  • Replicate NaIO₃-induced ZO-1 reduction and test whether ICG-001 preserves/restores ZO-1 area without elevating proliferation/EMT markers; track apoptosis/survival readouts given MA data tying β-catenin to anti-apoptotic signaling (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7).

- In vivo relevance:  
  • If in vitro/ex vivo are positive, progress to mouse models with RPE oxidative injury (e.g., NaIO₃ systemic exposure) and quantify RPE barrier integrity (ZO-1 localization, RPE flat-mounts), photoreceptor/RPE survival, and functional outcomes; consider delivery routes (intravitreal/subconjunctival) and PK (not available here) (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

- Mechanistic dissection:  
  • Evaluate whether CBP-specific blockade shifts β-catenin coactivator usage toward p300-dependent programs (no direct assays in provided texts) and whether junctional gene regulation exhibits CBP selectivity; this would mechanistically address the “biased transcription” claim (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Defined, selective mechanism: ICG-001 disrupts β-catenin/CBP complexes and suppresses TCF-dependent transcription without lowering total β-catenin; it does not trigger γ-catenin compensation observed with β-catenin protein knockdown, offering a mechanistically precise intervention that may spare adherens junction architecture (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117, 140–145, 26–30).

- Clinical-stage drug class: The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor analogs PRI-724/OP-724 have human safety and PK data in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis/PBC, supporting translational feasibility and providing a clinical development template, albeit outside ophthalmology (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

- Biological plausibility in RPE EMT and barrier dysfunction: RPE EMT and barrier loss are linked to β-catenin nuclear signaling; under inflammatory/DME-like conditions, Wnt/β-catenin activation disrupts TJs via VEGF/autophagy and Wnt-pathway suppression restores claudin-1/ZO-1, suggesting that pathway attenuation can be barrier-protective in disease contexts where β-catenin drives pathogenic transcription (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

- Assay tractability: RPE barrier endpoints (TEER, paracellular flux, ZO-1/claudin-1 localization) are robust; β-catenin target genes provide PD markers to confirm on-target activity, enabling a decisive preclinical go/no-go within RPE-relevant stress paradigms (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55).

Key Limitations and Risks  
- No direct ocular/RPE data for ICG-001: The provided context contains no studies of ICG-001 (or PRI-724/OP-724) in RPE or ocular tissues, no TEER/paracellular flux rescue data, and no AMD model outcomes; claims of junction-selective “bias” in RPE are speculative and unproven here (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Context-dependent and bidirectional β-catenin effects in RPE: In hRPE cultured with MA, β-catenin activity correlates with increased claudin-1/ZO-1 and higher TEER, and Wnt pathway inhibition (XAV-939) diminishes these; thus, in certain epithelial contexts, β-catenin/CBP inhibition could impair, not enhance, junctional gene expression and barrier function (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Survival/proliferation trade-offs: β-catenin activation increased anti-apoptotic factors (Survivin/Bcl2) and protected hRPE from serum withdrawal stress; ICG-001’s suppression of β-catenin target genes could compromise survival signaling under oxidative stress, and the net effect on barrier integrity/survival requires direct testing (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7).

- Mechanistic uncertainty regarding “biased transcription” toward junctional genes: No evidence is provided that CBP-selective inhibition favors claudin-1/ZO-1 expression; indeed, Sox/TCF targets include Cyclin D1 and c-Myc, and the directionality of CBP versus p300 coactivator usage on RPE junctional gene programs is not defined by the present sources (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 9–11; Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69).

- Delivery and ocular PK/PD unknowns: Clinical liver trials used i.v. infusions; ocular tolerability, retinal exposure, and local pharmacology for ICG-001/OP-724/PRI-724 are not addressed here, requiring formulation and delivery development (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

Decision Implications  
On the present evidence, ICG-001 has a coherent, selective mechanism with clinical-stage validation in a non-ocular indication, and there is strong biological plausibility that β-catenin transcriptional blockade can counter EMT/proliferation programs in RPE. However, the specific hypothesis that ICG-001 will “bias” transcription to upregulate claudin-1/ZO-1 and restore TEER under oxidative stress is not supported by the provided literature; in fact, RPE studies show that β-catenin activation is associated with higher TJ expression/TEER in some contexts, and pathway inhibition reduces these features, whereas in inflammatory/DME contexts β-catenin activation is deleterious and suppression is protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Therefore, a tightly scoped preclinical program should be undertaken to empirically resolve these context-dependent effects in RPE before committing to development for dry AMD.

Recommendation  
- Proceed with an in vitro/ex vivo feasibility package to test ICG-001 in RPE barrier models under defined stressors (oxidative vs inflammatory), with rigorous functional and molecular endpoints and on-target PD confirmation; include orthogonal comparators (XAV-939, ITF2357) to position CBP-selective modulation against broader Wnt suppression and epigenetic anti-inflammatory rescue (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7). Advance only if ICG-001 reproducibly restores TEER and junctional localization without pro-EMT/proliferation signatures across oxidative stress conditions relevant to dry AMD (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

- If positive, initiate ocular PK/tolerability and RPE-targeted delivery studies; if negative or mixed, deprioritize in favor of alternative approaches with direct evidence of barrier rescue in RPE (e.g., HDAC inhibitors in inflammatory settings), recognizing that pathway- and context-specificity critically determine outcomes in RPE biology (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–12).

In sum, ICG-001 is a mechanistically attractive, clinically precedented β-catenin/CBP inhibitor, but the claim of junction-focused, proliferation-sparing barrier rescue in oxidatively stressed RPE is currently hypothetical and not substantiated by the provided literature; decisive RPE-focused experiments are required to validate or refute its potential for dry AMD (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Vatiquinone (EPI-743) is a potent NQO1 substrate that both regenerates reduced coenzyme Q and indirectly upregulates Nrf2-mediated antioxidant defenses, with robust clinical safety in mitochondrial disorders and preliminary ARPE-19 cell data under oxidative challenge. It is this coordinated regulation of antioxidant pathways that forms the basis for the expected protective effect on RPE barrier function (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023).

The expected benefits in the cellular assay include a reduction in oxidative markers, stabilization of mitochondrial function, and maintenance or restoration of RPE junctional architecture. A comprehensive evaluation of vatiquinone as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration reveals several compelling strengths as well as important limitations that must be addressed in future research.
