Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR, chemically known as 5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide, is an endogenous purine biosynthetic intermediate that has been harnessed as a synthetic, cell‐permeable AMP analog to activate AMP‐activated protein kinase (AMPK) pharmacologically (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Originally identified as a naturally occurring metabolic intermediate, AICAR gained prominence when researchers recognized that its structural similarity to AMP enables it to mimic cellular energetic stress conditions, thereby initiating AMPK‐mediated cellular responses (Green, 2013). In its synthetic format, AICAR is produced and purified to high standards by vendors such as Selleckchem and Sigma (S1802; A9978), and belongs to the broader class of nucleoside analogs used as metabolic regulators. Compounds belonging to this class have historically been employed to interrogate and modulate energy sensing and substrate utilization in diverse cell types, ranging from skeletal muscle to vascular smooth muscle (Pokrywka et al., 2014). This same class of metabolic modulators has demonstrated efficacy in experimental models of mitochondrial disease and muscle wasting by stimulating AMPK‐dependent pathways that augment mitochondrial biogenesis and restore energy balance (Green, 2013). Owing to its capacity to influence the phosphorylation of key enzymes and transcription factors, AICAR has found applications not only in elucidating fundamental bioenergetic pathways but also as a candidate to ameliorate conditions where energy homeostasis is disrupted. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, where the maintenance of tight junction integrity is crucial for barrier function and homeostasis, AICAR’s mechanism of action offers a rationale for its repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Historically, metabolic modulation via AMPK activators has been extensively investigated in various systems, and AICAR has been a workhorse agent in these studies owing to its reliable pharmacological profile (Pokrywka et al., 2014). Biochemically, AICAR has been widely used to stimulate AMPK in cell culture and animal models, resulting in a host of downstream effects that include enhanced fatty acid oxidation, increased glucose uptake, and modulated lipid synthesis (Green, 2013). In addition, AICAR’s ability to promote autophagy through the inhibition of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) cascade has been observed across various cell types, including those derived from retinal tissues (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Clinical investigations have predominantly focused on its metabolic effects in conditions such as diabetes and ischemia, although its application in ocular diseases has been comparatively less explored (Pokrywka et al., 2014). In the field of ophthalmology, research into the role of AMPK in retinal health has uncovered that AMPK activation influences key RPE functions including autophagy, inflammatory cytokine production, and tight junction integrity (Qin, 2012). Notably, investigations in RPE-related models have demonstrated that pharmacologic modulation of AMPK can either protect or impair barrier function, depending on the context and isoform engaged (Qin & De Vries, 2008). While AICAR itself has not been approved explicitly for the treatment of dry AMD, its well–established use in preclinical studies, combined with its demonstrated ability to rescue barrier integrity in RPE under oxidative stress conditions, supports its potential repurposing for this indication (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011). Thus, the accumulated literature demonstrates that AMPK activators, and AICAR in particular, offer promising mechanistic pathways to address cellular energy deficits and junctional disintegration, both critical features of dry AMD pathology (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which AICAR exerts its therapeutic effects begins with its cellular uptake through nucleoside transporters such as ENT1 and ENT2, a process that ensures its intracellular availability (Dolinar et al., 2018). Once internalized, AICAR is rapidly phosphorylated by adenosine kinase, converting it into 5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate (ZMP) (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). ZMP, as an AMP analog, binds to the γ subunit of AMPK, eliciting conformational changes that not only enhance its allosteric activation but also protect it from dephosphorylation (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). Concurrently, the binding of ZMP to AMPK facilitates the phosphorylation of the catalytic α‐subunit at Thr172, thereby augmenting the kinase’s catalytic activity to phosphorylate downstream targets such as acetyl‐CoA carboxylase (ACC) (Qin & De Vries, 2008). The phosphorylation and inactivation of ACC lead to decreased fatty acid synthesis and enhanced fatty acid oxidation, contributing significantly to improved energy homeostasis (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Green, 2013). Notably, in the retinal pigment epithelium, robust AMPK activation is implicated in the stabilization of tight junction proteins and in the promotion of autophagy, a process that is essential for removal of damaged organelles and protein aggregates under oxidative stress conditions (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Furthermore, the role of AICAR in modulating tight junction dynamics is complex and intersects with its influence on autophagic flux; AMPK activation can downregulate mTOR signaling, which not only contributes to increased autophagic clearance but also appears to correlate with improved organization of junctional proteins, ultimately enhancing transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). In experimental settings using RPE cells, the administration of AICAR under oxidative or high‐glucose stress conditions leads to a cascade of phosphorylation events that foster an environment conducive to tight junction assembly while simultaneously stabilizing cellular energy stores (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This biochemical cascade is further verified by the reversal of the observed effects upon the use of compound C, an AMPK inhibitor, which underscores the specificity of AICAR’s action being mediated through AMPK activation (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Villarroel et al., 2011).

It is also critical to note that the effects of AICAR on AMPK activity are influenced not only by its rapid intracellular conversion but also by the intrinsic cellular context—including the balance of energy substrates, the presence of other nucleosides, and the isoform‐specific roles of AMPK (Qin & De Vries, 2008). The resultant activation of AMPK leads to multifaceted downstream responses, such as cellular adaptation to metabolic stress, regulation of inflammatory mediators, and modulation of cytoskeletal elements that cooperate in the maintenance of cell–cell adhesion within the RPE monolayer (Villarroel et al., 2011). This detailed mechanistic insight provides the foundation for hypothesizing that AICAR may effectively drive energy homeostasis and promote tight junction assembly in RPE cells, addressing one of the core pathological features of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
In the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration, the primary pathological hallmark is the degeneration of the RPE accompanied by impaired tight junction integrity and compromised barrier function, resulting in increased paracellular permeability and accumulation of metabolic waste. Based on the observed effects of AICAR in in vitro RPE models, it is expected that AICAR will allosterically activate AMPK within RPE cells, leading to enhanced energy homeostasis and improved assembly of tight junctions (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Experimental data have demonstrated that when induced with oxidative stress, as is common in AMD, treatment with 500 µM AICAR increased TEER from 90 to 135 Ω·cm²—a clear indicator of enhanced barrier integrity (Miyagishima et al., 2021). This increase in TEER is paralleled by a 2.8‐fold elevation in phosphorylated AMPK levels, which confirms that AICAR is effectively engaging its intended target in these cells (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011).

The underlying mechanism for this improved barrier function is thought to be twofold. First, through ACC inhibition—mediated by AMPK activation—there is a shift in the cellular lipid economy, reducing the deleterious lipid accumulation that can disrupt tight junction architecture (Qin & De Vries, 2008). Second, the activation of autophagic pathways facilitates the clearance of oxidatively damaged proteins and organelles, thereby enhancing the overall health of the RPE and reinforcing its capacity to maintain tight junction complexes (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). This dual action not only addresses the immediate energetic deficit induced by oxidative stress but also contributes to the structural resilience of the RPE monolayer.

Moreover, the observed reversal of AICAR’s protective effects by compound C serves as strong evidence that the benefit is specifically mediated through the AMPK pathway rather than off‐target effects (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014). This mechanistic specificity is critical when evaluating a compound for clinical translation, as it suggests that downstream effects such as TEER enhancement, tight junction stabilization, and modulation of paracellular flux are directly attributable to AMPK activation. Additionally, AICAR‐mediated autophagy has been implicated in maintaining cellular integrity under chronic oxidative stress—a condition that is intrinsically linked to the progression of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Given the central role of AMPK in RPE physiology, particularly in the regulation of junction protein stability and energy metabolism, the expected therapeutic effect of AICAR in dry AMD is to restore and preserve RPE barrier function. This restoration is anticipated to limit paracellular fluid leakage, reduce the deposition of extracellular debris, and ultimately slow the degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011). The projected outcome is an improvement in cellular homeostasis and reduced progression of retinal degeneration, which translates into a potential clinical benefit for patients with dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History and Prior Applications:  
AICAR’s journey from a metabolic intermediate to a pharmacologically active compound has been well documented across a range of biomedical research areas. In preclinical studies, AICAR has been extensively utilized to activate AMPK in various cellular models, thereby providing critical insights into the regulation of energy balance, mitochondrial biogenesis, and lipid metabolism (Green, 2013; Pokrywka et al., 2014). Its early applications in skeletal muscle and cancer cells underscored its ability to stimulate glucose uptake and shift cellular energy dynamics in favor of catabolic pathways (Dolinar et al., 2018; Longnus et al., 2003).

In cardiovascular research, AICAR was instrumental in elucidating the mechanisms underlying glycogenolysis and vasorelaxation, where its conversion to ZMP led to the activation of AMPK in vascular smooth muscle cells, resulting in beneficial metabolic adaptations (Pyla et al., 2022). Although these studies did not directly target ocular tissues, they established a robust framework for understanding how AMPK activation can mediate protective responses under conditions of metabolic stress.

The transition of AICAR into the realm of ophthalmological research was driven by the observation that AMPK is a pivotal regulator of RPE function and tight junction assembly. Publications have demonstrated that oxidative stress—a significant contributor to AMD pathology—can impair RPE barrier integrity by disrupting the organization of tight junction proteins, while AMPK activation appears to counteract these deleterious changes (Qin, 2012; Villarroel et al., 2011). In one study, treatment with AICAR in RPE cells under H₂O₂‐induced stress not only increased TEER but also elevated levels of phosphorylated AMPK, thereby indicating enhanced barrier stability (Miyagishima et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the dual role of AMPK in regulating autophagy and lipid metabolism has been a focal point in dry AMD research, as dysfunctional autophagy and lipid accumulation are hallmarks of RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011). The protective effects of AMPK activators in other models of cellular stress, such as in cardiomyocytes and hepatocarcinoma cells, lend additional support to the hypothesis that similar mechanisms may be beneficial in preserving RPE function (Kawashima et al., 2020; Sid et al., 2014).

Despite these promising findings, it is important to note that the therapeutic history of AICAR in the context of ocular diseases remains in the preclinical phase, with limited direct clinical evaluation for dry AMD. Some studies have even suggested that AMPK activation in the RPE could have dual outcomes, potentially inhibiting phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments under oxidative conditions (Qin & De Vries, 2008). This observation highlights the intricacies of AMPK signaling in retinal cells and underscores the need for rigorous dose–response and context–specific studies. Nonetheless, the accumulated preclinical data from both ocular and non‐ocular systems provide a strong rationale for further exploring AICAR as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Expected Impact on RPE Function and Dry AMD Pathology:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of AICAR in dry AMD is that its ability to activate AMPK will lead to a concerted improvement in RPE barrier function and energy homeostasis—two crucial aspects compromised in AMD. In vitro models of RPE, particularly those derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC‐RPE), have shown that exposure to oxidative stress causes significant deterioration in tight junction assembly and barrier integrity, as measured by transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Miyagishima et al., 2021).

When these stressed RPE cells are treated with AICAR, a rapid increase in TEER from approximately 90 Ω·cm² to 135 Ω·cm² has been observed, indicating a substantial enhancement in tight junction integrity (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). At the molecular level, this improvement correlates with a 2.8‐fold rise in phosphorylated AMPK, which is directly associated with the activation of energy restoration pathways and the stabilization of tight junction proteins (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011).

The benefits conferred by AMPK activation are expected to be multifaceted. On one hand, the inhibition of ACC through phosphorylation is anticipated to reduce aberrant lipid synthesis and promote fatty acid oxidation, thereby alleviating metabolic stress within RPE cells (Qin & De Vries, 2008). On the other hand, enhanced autophagic flux driven by AMPK is likely to facilitate the removal of oxidatively damaged proteins and organelles, contributing to cellular repair processes that are pivotal in slowing the progression of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

These laboratory observations have practical implications. In a dysregulated retinal environment—characterized by oxidative damage, inflammatory cytokine presence, and disrupted tight junctions—the activation of AMPK by AICAR could serve as a countermeasure to re‐establish and maintain the critical barrier functions of the RPE (Villarroel et al., 2011). Moreover, by diminishing paracellular leak and preserving the integrity of junctional complexes, AICAR may reduce the accumulation of metabolic waste products and drusen, which are pathological hallmarks of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

It is also noteworthy that the experimental reversal of AICAR’s protective effects by compound C—a well‐known AMPK inhibitor—provides definitive evidence that the beneficial outcomes observed in RPE cells are mediated specifically through AMPK signaling (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014). This on‐target specificity increases the confidence that the observed improvements in TEER are attributable to the intended mechanism rather than off‐target pharmacological actions. Consequently, the expected therapeutic effect in dry AMD would involve enhanced RPE cell viability, reduced cellular stress, and a restored barrier function that together could slow or even halt the progressive degeneration observed in patients (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Overall Evaluation:  
When evaluating AICAR as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, several strengths are immediately apparent, along with a number of challenges that must be carefully addressed during further development. One of the foremost strengths of AICAR is its well–characterized mechanism of action. By serving as an AMP analog that is intracellularly converted to ZMP, AICAR robustly activates AMPK—a key cellular energy sensor that orchestrates a wide range of metabolic responses (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). This activation is tightly coupled to downstream effects such as ACC inhibition, enhanced fatty acid oxidation, and the promotion of autophagy, which are all beneficial in counteracting the metabolic and oxidative stresses inherent in dry AMD (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012).

Furthermore, the experimental data indicating a significant increase in TEER and a concomitant rise in phosphorylated AMPK levels in oxidatively stressed iPSC‐RPE cells provide compelling evidence that AICAR can restore RPE barrier function (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This is particularly important because tight junction integrity and paracellular barrier properties are central to the maintenance of retinal homeostasis and are critically impaired in dry AMD (Villarroel et al., 2011). The demonstration that the beneficial effects of AICAR are reversible by an AMPK inhibitor further reinforces the concept that the drug’s actions are on–target and biologically relevant (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014).

Nevertheless, several potential weaknesses require cautious evaluation. First, while AMPK activation is generally associated with enhanced cellular resilience, some studies have reported that excessive or isoform‐specific activation of AMPK in RPE cells may lead to unintended consequences, such as the inhibition of photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis—a process vital for retinal renewal (Qin & De Vries, 2008). Such a dualistic role of AMPK creates a delicate balance whereby the same pathway that is intended to improve barrier function might also impede essential RPE functions if not precisely modulated.

Additionally, the data in the literature suggest that under certain circumstances, AMPK activation might even contribute to increased epithelial permeability rather than a strengthening of tight junctions (Villarroel et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This paradoxical effect raises concerns about potential context–dependent outcomes of AICAR treatment. For example, while low‐to‐moderate activation of AMPK might support tight junction assembly and autophagy, hyperactivation under severe metabolic or oxidative stress could exacerbate junctional disorganization, thereby counteracting any beneficial effects (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Another challenge is the potential for systemic side effects arising from AICAR’s widespread actions in other tissues. Given that AICAR has been employed in models of diabetes, cardiac metabolism, and even cancer, its pleiotropic effects could impose additional safety considerations when repurposed for ocular use (Pokrywka et al., 2014; Viglino et al., 2019). There is also the issue of dosage; concentrations of 500 µM are effective in vitro, but translating such dosages to in vivo ocular applications requires careful pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies to ensure that therapeutic levels are achieved locally without eliciting undesirable systemic responses (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Asby et al., 2015).

Moreover, given the complex interplay between AMPK signaling, autophagy, and cellular differentiation processes, it is essential to thoroughly understand the long‐term implications of chronic AMPK activation in the RPE. While short‐term activation may be protective, persistent stimulation could lead to energy depletion or maladaptive remodeling of the RPE cytoskeleton, which in turn could affect visual function (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). This underscores the need for extensive preclinical studies that evaluate both the efficacy and the safety profile of AICAR over prolonged periods.

Finally, the inherent variability in patient responses due to genetic, metabolic, and environmental factors presents an additional hurdle. The RPE’s response to oxidative stress, and hence its sensitivity to AMPK modulation, may vary widely among individuals with dry AMD. It will be crucial to identify biomarkers that predict response to AICAR treatment and to tailor dosing regimens accordingly (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

In summary, while AICAR shows considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD by virtue of its well‐established mechanism of AMPK activation, experimental data demonstrating tight junction rescue in RPE cells, and its ability to promote autophagic processes that counteract oxidative stress, its repurposing is tempered by concerns regarding the dualistic effects of AMPK signaling in the RPE, potential systemic side effects, and the challenges associated with dosage translation from in vitro to in vivo applications (Villarroel et al., 2011). The overall evaluation is that AICAR exhibits several compelling advantages—including mechanistic clarity, on‐target efficacy, and a robust preclinical rationale—that substantiate further investigation through rigorous preclinical and, eventually, clinical studies. With a careful approach that addresses the aforementioned weaknesses, AICAR may ultimately emerge as a valuable addition to the therapeutic arsenal against dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Comprehensive Future Directions and Considerations:  
To fully validate AICAR’s potential for treating dry AMD, a series of detailed investigations is warranted. First, further elucidation of the dose–response relationship in RPE cell cultures will be critical. This includes not only establishing the optimal concentration of AICAR to achieve maximal TEER improvement and AMPK activation but also determining whether these effects are sustained over time without incurring cellular toxicity (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011). Long‐term studies are needed to assess whether repeated dosing maintains barrier integrity or if adaptive processes eventually diminish the protective effects of AICAR.

Additionally, it will be necessary to delve deeper into the isoform‐specific effects of AMPK in the RPE. Evidence suggests that the α2 isoform in particular plays a critical role in mediating responses to oxidative stress and that its activation may differ qualitatively from that of the α1 subunit (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012). Understanding these nuances will help design therapeutic strategies that maximize the beneficial aspects of AMPK activation while minimizing potential adverse outcomes, such as impaired phagocytosis or unwanted alterations in cellular metabolism (Qin & De Vries, 2008).

In parallel, investigating the interplay between AICAR‐induced AMPK activation and autophagic pathways in the RPE will shed light on how tightly coupled these processes are in the context of dry AMD. Since autophagy is vital for clearing oxidatively damaged cellular components and supporting cell survival, it will be important to determine whether prolonged AMPK activation fosters a beneficial autophagic flux or rather leads to autophagy dysregulation over time (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). Strategies that involve monitoring autophagic markers along with TEER measurements and junction protein expression could provide a comprehensive picture of cellular health in AICAR‐treated RPE cells.

Given the concerns regarding potential systemic effects, advanced drug delivery systems such as localized intraocular injections or biodegradable implants could be considered for delivering AICAR directly to the retina, thereby limiting systemic exposure and enhancing local efficacy (Viglino et al., 2019; Sid et al., 2014). Preclinical animal models that mimic the pathological features of dry AMD will be indispensable in evaluating the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and therapeutic windows of AICAR in an in vivo setting. Such studies would also be instrumental in identifying potential adverse effects and assessing the long‐term safety profile of AICAR when administered via ocular routes.

Another key consideration is the potential for combination therapy. Since some reports indicate that AMPK activation by AICAR might impair certain RPE functions such as phagocytosis if excessively activated, combining AICAR with other agents that either modulate AMPK isoform activity or protect against excessive autophagic stimulation may provide a synergistic benefit (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Villarroel et al., 2011). For instance, the protective effect of fenofibric acid in preventing AICAR‐induced permeability increases has been documented, suggesting that a combination approach may overcome the limitations of monotherapy (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Finally, translational studies will need to integrate biomarker analyses capable of monitoring AMPK activation status, autophagy markers, and tight junction protein localization in the RPE. These biomarkers could guide dose optimization and serve as early indicators of therapeutic response in clinical trials (Villarroel et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008). Genetic or epigenetic factors that predispose individuals to variations in RPE responsiveness may also be identified, thereby enabling personalized medicine approaches for patients with dry AMD.

In conclusion, while there remain numerous challenges and uncertainties, AICAR represents a highly promising candidate for repurposing as a barrier‐protective agent in dry AMD. Its capacity to robustly activate AMPK, improve cellular energy homeostasis, promote autophagy, and restore tight junction integrity in RPE cells offers a multifaceted mode of action that addresses several key pathological features of dry AMD. With targeted preclinical studies that unpack the complexity of AMPK signaling in retinal tissues and strategic clinical trial designs that mitigate potential adverse effects, AICAR could conceivably fill a significant therapeutic gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012; Villarroel et al., 2011).

AICAR’s well‐documented ability to mimic AMP—thereby inducing AMPK activation—and its established role in regulating cellular energy balance and autophagy place it squarely in the category of compounds with high therapeutic potential for metabolic disorders. Emerging evidence in retinal models, particularly those simulating the oxidative stress and barrier dysfunction typical of dry AMD, further reinforces the rationale behind its repurposing. Nonetheless, while preclinical data are encouraging, careful consideration must be given to the dualistic nature of AMPK signaling in the RPE, as well as the potential systemic risks associated with systemic exposure. Despite these challenges, the convergence of multiple lines of evidence—from improved TEER measurements and specific molecular activation to supportive mechanistic studies—strongly advocates for further research into AICAR as a viable therapeutic strategy for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

In summary, the repurposing of AICAR for dry AMD is supported by both its robust mechanistic underpinnings and its promising preclinical efficacy data, placing it among the most attractive candidates for modulating RPE barrier integrity in this debilitating disease. Future studies that focus on fine‐tuning its dosage, delivery, and integrated combination therapies hold the key to unlocking its full therapeutic potential and advancing it from the bench to the clinic (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012).

Taking into account the strengths of its well‐defined mechanism, the reproducible experimental data demonstrating barrier rescue in RPE cells, and the feasibility of its pharmacological modulation, AICAR represents a compelling candidate for further development in the treatment of dry AMD. With continued advances in targeted drug delivery and combination therapeutics, the prospects for leveraging AICAR’s metabolic and protective effects in the retina are promising, warranting its inclusion in the strategic pipeline for combating age‐related macular degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

This comprehensive evaluation underscores that while challenges remain—including potential dose‐dependent effects, off‐target actions, and the need for precise modulation of AMPK isoforms—the overall body of evidence provides a solid rationale for advancing AICAR in preclinical and ultimately clinical studies focused on dry AMD. Its capacity to restore RPE barrier integrity under oxidative stress, coupled with its well‐established pharmacodynamic properties, offers a therapeutic strategy that could mitigate the progression of retinal degeneration and improve visual outcomes for patients suffering from this currently untreatable condition (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
BIRB 796 (doramapimod) is a small-molecule p38 MAP kinase inhibitor discovered at Boehringer Ingelheim as part of a diaryl urea/pyrazolyl-urea medicinal chemistry effort to exploit an inactive, DFG-out conformation of p38 and thereby achieve high potency and kinase-family selectivity via an allosteric binding site adjacent to the ATP pocket (type II binding) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Bagley et al., 2010; Xing, 2016; Coulthard et al., 2009). In contrast to classical ATP-site inhibitors (e.g., pyridinyl-imidazoles such as SB203580) that anchor in the hinge region and remain in the DFG-in active conformation, BIRB 796 engages a selectivity pocket opened by flipping the Asp-Phe-Gly (DFG) motif to a DFG-out state; this binding mode is incompatible with ATP binding and additionally disrupts the interaction between p38α and its upstream activators MKK3/MKK6 (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Bagley et al., 2010). Structural features include deep insertion of a t-butyl group into the hydrophobic “Phe-pocket” created by the DFG-out rearrangement, naphthyl contacts, favorable packing of a tolyl group in a Glu71-containing hydrophobic pocket, a morpholino that H-bonds with Met109, and a diaryl urea NH that forms an H-bond with Glu71 analogous to the adenine N1 interaction in ATP binding (Bagley et al., 2010). Kinetically, BIRB 796 is a prototypical slow-binding, slow-dissociating p38 inhibitor: association is ~500-fold slower and dissociation ~10^6-fold slower than the ATP-site pyridinyl-imidazole SK&F 86002, consistent with a major conformational rearrangement upon binding and prolonged target residence time (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Biophysically, reported potency is sub-nanomolar in binding assays (Kd ~0.1–<0.8 nM) with functional enzymatic or cellular IC50 values on the order of tens of nanomolar (e.g., ~63 nM), and the compound inhibits all p38 isoforms to varying degrees (pan-p38), with context-dependent reports of minimal or dual activity on JNK2 (Xing, 2016; Bagley et al., 2010; Yong et al., 2009; Coulthard et al., 2009). A microwave-assisted route to BIRB 796 was reported (aminopyrazole formation from pivaloylacetonitrile and p-tolylhydrazine; carbamate and aminonaphthol intermediates; DMSO coupling at 100°C), enabling improved yields for preclinical supply and mechanistic studies (Bagley et al., 2010).

As a chemotype, diaryl/urea-type type II kinase inhibitors that exploit DFG-out conformations were developed to expand selectivity beyond hinge-binding ATP mimetics, often achieving slow off-rates and high apparent affinity; within the p38 field, BIRB 796 became the best-characterized example of this allosteric/selectivity-pocket strategy and served as a clinical tool compound for inflammatory indications (Xing, 2016; Coulthard et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History  
BIRB 796 advanced through Phase I and Phase II programs and was reported as having reached Phase II/III development for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases including rheumatoid arthritis (RA), Crohn’s disease (CD), and psoriasis; a human endotoxemia model was used to demonstrate pharmacodynamic target engagement (suppression of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-8, and effects on coagulation/fibrinolysis/endothelial activation) (Yong et al., 2009; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Coulthard et al., 2009; Xing, 2016). Oral dosing regimens included 5–30 mg twice daily (RA) and 10–60 mg twice daily (CD); in endotoxemia, single doses up to 600 mg were tested and showed robust biomarker modulation (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Yong et al., 2009). Despite clear pharmacodynamic effects, randomized trials failed to demonstrate durable clinical efficacy in Crohn’s disease and psoriasis, and RA efficacy was not substantiated; development was discontinued after Phase II, with repeated administration associated with elevated liver transaminases (class-typical hepatotoxicity) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Mechanistic work implicated a reactive naphthalene-epoxide metabolite (glutathione-conjugated) in the ALT elevations observed in CD patients, supporting on-drug hepatotoxicity as a liability for the chemotype (Machado et al., 2021). More broadly, many clinical p38 inhibitor programs (including BIRB 796) showed a stereotyped pattern of early biomarker suppression (e.g., CRP, soluble TNF receptor) that returned to near baseline by week 12, coincident with a lack of sustained clinical benefit, pointing to network compensation under chronic p38 blockade (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Xing, 2016). These outcomes, together with dose-limiting toxicities seen across the class, drove a field-wide shift toward alternative strategies (substrate-selective or docking-site inhibitors) rather than pan-p38 catalytic inhibition (Burton et al., 2021).

In preclinical and translational settings, BIRB 796 has been widely used as a pharmacological probe: it reduces LPS-induced TNF-α and other cytokines in vitro and in vivo; in a human endotoxemia model a 600 mg dose suppressed coagulation/fibrinolysis and endothelial activation; in tumor-associated contexts it inhibited IL-6 secretion and reduced tumor cell proliferation (Yong et al., 2009). In macrophage-centric COPD studies, BIRB-class inhibitors sometimes failed to suppress IL-8, underscoring cell-type-specific differences in p38 control of cytokine outputs; however, at very low concentrations (1 nM) BIRB-0796 exhibited synergistic cytokine suppression when combined with corticosteroids, reflecting complementary mechanisms (steroids do not block p38-HSP27 phosphorylation) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). In epithelial barrier biology, doramapimod protected the Sertoli cell tight-junction barrier against cadmium-induced injury, preserving localization of ZO-1, claudin-11, occludin, and adherens junction components and rescuing transepithelial electrical resistance (TER), while selectively blocking p38 phosphorylation (without suppressing JNK, CREB, or Akt activation) (Wang et al., 2023).

No registered clinical trials of p38 MAPK inhibitors (including doramapimod) for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are listed on ClinicalTrials.gov under the queried terms, indicating no formal AMD program has been conducted in this class to date (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Mechanistically, p38 signaling has been implicated in retinal vascular and AMD-relevant processes (e.g., VEGF induction, matrix remodeling via MMP-2/MMP-14 and basigin, inflammasome activation, endothelial dysfunction and barrier leakage), which supports biological plausibility but not direct clinical translation for AMD (Burton et al., 2021). There is no RPE- or AMD-specific preclinical study of doramapimod in the provided materials, and none of the cited clinical programs tested dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Burton et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
p38 MAPKs (α/β/γ/δ) are stress-activated serine/threonine kinases that integrate inflammatory cues and drive transcriptional and post-transcriptional control of cytokines including TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8; downstream effectors include MK2/MK3 (MAPKAPK2/3), MSK1/2, and HSP27, which regulate mRNA stability, translation, and cytoskeletal dynamics (Machado et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009; Burton et al., 2021). Canonical activation proceeds via MKK3 and MKK6 phosphorylation of the Thr-Gly-Tyr activation loop, but atypical, TAB1-dependent activation on endosomes also occurs in response to GPCR/cytokine stimuli, fueling vascular inflammation and barrier dysfunction; p38 pathway activity is further modulated by MAPK phosphatases (DUSPs) feeding back on p38 dephosphorylation (Burton et al., 2021).

BIRB 796 binds in a selectivity pocket adjacent to the ATP site and induces a DFG-out conformation that is catalytically incompetent, sterically and conformationally precluding ATP binding and preventing interaction with upstream kinases (MKK3/MKK6) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Bagley et al., 2010). Structural contacts include insertion of a tert-butyl group into the DFG-derived Phe-pocket, hydrophobic contacts by a naphthyl group, a tolyl group accommodated in a Glu71-containing hydrophobic cavity, and a morpholino ring that H-bonds to Met109; importantly, a diaryl urea NH forms a hydrogen bond with Glu71 that mimics the adenine N1 interaction in ATP, highlighting how selectivity-pocket binders can spare classical hinge contacts yet achieve high affinity (Bagley et al., 2010). The kinetic signature of BIRB 796—extremely slow dissociation and slow association—reflects the energetic barrier to reorganize the DFG motif and surrounding activation loop, and is thought to confer prolonged target occupancy in cells (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). As a result, BIRB 796 has sub-nanomolar binding affinity to non-activated p38α (Kd ~0.1–<0.8 nM) with functional inhibitory potency in the low- to mid-nanomolar range in biochemical/cellular assays (Xing, 2016; Bagley et al., 2010).

Isoform and pathway coverage is broad: multiple sources report inhibition of all p38 isoforms (α/β/γ/δ), a property linked to the allosteric binding mode, which avoids the Met109-dependent hinge interaction exploited by ATP-site inhibitors that often lack activity on γ/δ (Coulthard et al., 2009; Xing, 2016). Some profiling described BIRB 796 as selective against JNK2, whereas other reports noted dual p38/JNK activity—differences likely arise from assay format, activation state, and concentration ranges, but the possibility of JNK2 inhibition exists and complicates mechanistic attribution in certain systems (Yong et al., 2009; Bagley et al., 2010). Functionally, BIRB 796 suppresses LPS-induced TNF-α and lowers IL-6 and IL-8 in human endotoxemia, reduces p38 readouts such as phosphorylated HSP27 (a sensitive pharmacodynamic biomarker), and decreases phosphorylation of MK2, consistent with dampened pro-inflammatory transcription and mRNA stabilization (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Yong et al., 2009; Burton et al., 2021). In immortalized Werner syndrome fibroblasts, BIRB 796 prevents p38 activation, reduces pp38 and pHSP27, and thereby modifies senescence-associated phenotypes, reinforcing its activity on the p38→MK2/HSP27 axis in stressed/aged cells (Bagley et al., 2010). In primary Sertoli cells exposed to cadmium, doramapimod specifically blocked p38 phosphorylation, preserved junctional protein localization (e.g., ZO-1, occludin, claudin-11, JAM-A), and maintained barrier function (TER), while not suppressing parallel stress signals (pJNK, p-c-Jun, p-CREB, p-Akt), indicating target-pathway selectivity in vitro (Wang et al., 2023).

Clinical pharmacology confirms human anti-inflammatory effects: a 600 mg dose of BIRB-796BS in endotoxemia suppressed LPS-induced coagulation, fibrinolysis, and endothelial activation (Yong et al., 2009). However, in chronic inflammatory diseases, repeated dosing produced only transient biomarker suppression and limited clinical benefits; repeated administration caused liver-enzyme elevations, and mechanistic toxicology implicated a reactive naphthalene-epoxide metabolite (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Machado et al., 2021). These observations align with broader p38 inhibitor experience: pan-p38 blockade can interrupt beneficial anti-inflammatory signaling (e.g., MSK1/2-mediated) and distort feedback circuits, while disinhibiting upstream kinases (e.g., TAK1, MLK2/3) and activating JNK or NF-κB crosstalk, conferring dose-limiting toxicities and short-lived efficacy (Coulthard et al., 2009).

Expected Effect  
Assay hypothesis: In senescent retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), pharmacologic p38α/β inhibition with BIRB 796 will suppress SASP-like cytokines (particularly IL-6 and IL-8), reducing paracrine/autocrine downregulation of junctional proteins and preserving tight junction belts (e.g., ZO-1) and transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER).

Mechanistic rationale: p38 controls transcriptional and post-transcriptional programs that elevate IL-6 and IL-8 across multiple inflamed tissues and cell types; BIRB 796 lowers IL-6/IL-8 in human endotoxemia and tumor-cell paracrine models, and at low nanomolar concentrations can synergize with corticosteroids to suppress cytokines in macrophage systems, consistent with broad suppression of p38-driven inflammatory outputs (Yong et al., 2009; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Downstream, p38→MK2 phosphorylates HSP27 and RNA-binding proteins (e.g., tristetraprolin/TTP), which increases mRNA stability and translation of cytokine transcripts; BIRB 796 reduces pp38 and pHSP27 in senescence models, matching the predicted SASP attenuation mechanism (Burton et al., 2021; Bagley et al., 2010). In epithelial barrier contexts, doramapimod rescued tight-junction integrity and TER in primary Sertoli monolayers under toxic stress while maintaining junctional protein localization, providing a functional precedent that p38 inhibition can preserve epithelial-like barrier structure and function via junctional/cytoskeletal stabilization (Wang et al., 2023).

RPE disease-context rationale: Although no RPE-specific BIRB 796 data are provided here, p38 signaling is implicated in AMD-relevant processes (e.g., VEGF induction and angiogenesis, MMP-driven matrix remodeling, inflammasome activation, vascular endothelial dysfunction and barrier leakage), making p38 a plausible node in retinal inflammation and barrier pathology (Burton et al., 2021). Given that p38 activity drives IL-6/IL-8 production broadly, and that these cytokines can downregulate junctional proteins and disrupt epithelial barriers in many systems, it is reasonable to expect that BIRB 796 will lower MK2/HSP27 pathway activity, reduce IL-6/IL-8 secretion from senescent RPE, and preserve ZO-1 belts and TEER if p38-dependent SASP is operative in this cell type (Coulthard et al., 2009; Xing, 2016; Burton et al., 2021). Atypical (TAB1-mediated) p38 activation has been linked to endothelial barrier disruption; while not demonstrated in RPE here, such noncanonical activation could also contribute to epithelial stress responses and might be sensitive to allosteric type II inhibition (Burton et al., 2021).

Assay execution considerations: To test the hypothesis rigorously in senescent RPE, readouts should include (1) p38 pathway activity markers (pp38, pMK2, pHSP27), (2) secreted SASP cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), and (3) barrier metrics (continuous ZO-1 belts by immunofluorescence; TER dynamics over time), with BIRB 796 concentration–response spanning low nanomolar to low micromolar given reported cellular potencies and the 10 µM concentration that preserved Sertoli barrier function (Wang et al., 2023; Xing, 2016; Bagley et al., 2010). Given steroid independence of p38 signaling (p-HSP27 is not reduced by steroids), testing BIRB 796 alone and in combination with a glucocorticoid could probe pharmacologic additivity and compensatory pathways in RPE SASP (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Because IL-8 may be variably p38-dependent across cell types, the assay should be powered to detect partial suppression and explore time-dependent compensation (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Finally, inclusion of controls that assess atypical activation (e.g., TAB1–p38 engagement) and post-transcriptional endpoints (TTP phosphorylation status) could sharpen mechanistic attribution (Burton et al., 2021).

Translational considerations: Systemic doramapimod exposure is constrained by hepatotoxicity and lack of durable efficacy in chronic inflammation, plausibly due to network adaptation; any clinical path in dry AMD would require local ocular delivery to minimize systemic exposure and to bypass compensatory systemic responses, a principle consistent with proposed niches for p38 inhibitors in localized/short-term settings (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Coulthard et al., 2009). At present, there are no registered AMD trials of p38 inhibitors, so translational validation must proceed from RPE/retinal preclinical models (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit: p38 MAPK is a master regulator of inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 and IL-8, with well-defined downstream effectors (MK2/MK3, HSP27) that also interface with cytoskeletal and junctional integrity; BIRB 796 potently and durably engages this pathway, reduces p38 phosphorylation readouts, and suppresses IL-6/IL-8 in human endotoxemia and other systems (Machado et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Yong et al., 2009). The proposed RPE SASP-barrier mechanism is therefore biochemically coherent (Burton et al., 2021).  
- High potency and residence time: sub-nanomolar affinity, nanomolar functional inhibition, and extremely slow off-rate support strong target engagement at low free concentrations, which may be advantageous for intraocular dosing strategies designed to minimize systemic exposure (Xing, 2016; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012).  
- Allosteric type II mode and pan-p38 coverage: by stabilizing DFG-out, BIRB 796 inhibits α/β/γ/δ isoforms, potentially covering non-α p38 activity that could contribute to epithelial senescence or retinal inflammation; the allosteric site is exploited with favorable structural interactions and a defined pharmacophore (Coulthard et al., 2009; Bagley et al., 2010; Xing, 2016).  
- Barrier-protection precedent in epithelia: doramapimod preserved ZO-1/occludin/claudin-11 localization and TER in primary Sertoli monolayers under toxic injury while selectively blocking p38 phosphorylation, an effect directionally aligned with the goal of preserving RPE tight junctions and barrier function (Wang et al., 2023).  
- PD biomarkers to guide development: pHSP27 and pMK2 provide sensitive pathway engagement readouts, facilitating translational bridging from in vitro RPE to in vivo ocular models and potentially to human aqueous/vitreous sampling (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Burton et al., 2021).  
- Combination potential: BIRB-class inhibitors can synergize with corticosteroids at very low concentrations in cytokine suppression assays, reflecting complementary mechanisms of action and offering a combination path to mitigate compensation (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of RPE-specific data: No direct evidence in the provided materials demonstrates doramapimod effects on senescent RPE SASP, IL-6/IL-8, ZO-1 belts, or TEER; AMD- or RPE-specific proof of concept remains to be generated (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Burton et al., 2021).  
- Clinical class history of transient efficacy: Across chronic inflammatory indications, p38 inhibitors showed early biomarker suppression followed by reversion toward baseline and lack of durable benefit by ~12 weeks, likely reflecting pathway compensation and complex feedback/crosstalk that may also occur in chronic retinal disease (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Xing, 2016).  
- Hepatotoxicity and metabolic liability: Repeated systemic dosing raised liver enzymes, and mechanistic toxicology implicated a reactive naphthalene-epoxide metabolite for BIRB 796 specifically; while intraocular delivery could mitigate systemic exposure, any repurposing must address ocular-specific safety and formulation (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Machado et al., 2021).  
- Potential dual JNK2 activity: Reports vary on BIRB 796 selectivity; dual p38/JNK2 inhibition has been described, complicating mechanistic interpretation and potentially adding pathway liabilities in some cellular contexts (Bagley et al., 2010; Yong et al., 2009).  
- Isoform- and context-specific cytokine control: In alveolar macrophages and COPD models, IL-8 can be relatively resistant to p38 inhibition, cautioning against assuming uniform suppression of IL-8 in senescent RPE; parallel drivers (e.g., NF-κB) may require combination strategies (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012).  
- Strategic alternatives may be preferable: Substrate-selective p38 pathway interventions (e.g., ED-site inhibitor UM101) that spare beneficial MSK1 signaling, or inhibitors that block atypical TAB1-mediated activation, have shown preclinical advantages and may reduce compensation/toxicity risks compared with pan-p38 catalytic inhibition (Burton et al., 2021).

Decision-oriented assessment for dry AMD  
- Biological plausibility: Strong. p38 controls IL-6/IL-8 and MK2/HSP27 signaling that plausibly drive SASP and barrier dysfunction; doramapimod has repeatedly demonstrated suppression of these axes and preserved epithelial-like barrier function in vitro (Machado et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Translational tractability: Conditional. Systemic use is precluded by hepatotoxicity and lack of durable efficacy; however, local ocular delivery could deliver high intraocular drug levels while limiting systemic exposure, and the slow off-rate may support infrequent dosing, pending ocular PK/toxicity profiling (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Coulthard et al., 2009).  
- Evidence gaps: Critical. No RPE-focused or AMD-model data exist here; there are no registered AMD clinical trials for p38 inhibitors; demonstration in senescent RPE models is essential before advancing (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Recommended next steps  
- In vitro RPE senescence studies: Evaluate BIRB 796 concentration–response (1 nM–10 µM) on pp38/pMK2/pHSP27, IL-6/IL-8 secretion, ZO-1/occludin belt continuity, and TEER in primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE rendered senescent (e.g., replicative or stress-induced senescence) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Burton et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Mechanistic dissection: Assess TTP phosphorylation and mRNA decay of IL-6/IL-8; interrogate atypical TAB1-dependent activation signatures; compare to a substrate-selective p38 modulator where possible to benchmark compensation (Burton et al., 2021).  
- Combination testing: Explore additivity with a glucocorticoid and/or NF-κB modulation to overcome potential IL-8 resistance in RPE; measure durability after washout to probe rebound signaling (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012).  
- Ocular safety and delivery: Conduct ex vivo/in vivo ocular tolerability (ERGs, histology) and intraocular PK in relevant species; leverage the slow target off-rate to test low-dose intravitreal delivery designed to minimize systemic exposure (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Coulthard et al., 2009).  
- Prioritize de-risking strategies: If doramapimod exhibits ocular or systemic liabilities, consider pathway-refined alternatives (e.g., MK2 inhibitors; ED-site p38α inhibitors sparing MSK1; TAB1-site blockers) that may retain anti-SASP efficacy with reduced toxicity and compensation (Burton et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009).

Conclusion  
On mechanistic grounds, BIRB 796 is well-suited to test the SASP-barrier hypothesis in senescent RPE: it is a potent, slow-off, allosteric type II inhibitor that suppresses IL-6/IL-8 outputs and p38→MK2/HSP27 signaling, and it preserves epithelial-like junctional integrity and TER in a primary Sertoli barrier model (Xing, 2016; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Yong et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2023). The absence of RPE- or AMD-specific evidence and the class’s clinical history of transient efficacy and hepatotoxicity are significant liabilities that limit immediate translational prospects; nonetheless, a local-delivery, RPE-focused preclinical program is justified to generate the missing data and to determine whether p38 suppression can stabilize RPE barrier function and SASP in dry AMD models (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Coulthard et al., 2009). If positive, doramapimod could serve as a powerful chemical probe for isoform- and pathway-specific dissection in RPE senescence, while parallel exploration of pathway-refined or substrate-selective p38 modulators may offer a more sustainable clinical trajectory for chronic ocular disease (Burton et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Vatiquinone (EPI-743) is a synthetic, tocopherol-derived quinone originally developed as a vitamin E analogue to counteract inherited mitochondrial diseases. It was synthesized through modifications of the natural vitamin E structure, where oxidation of the tocopherol leads to the formation of a quinone moiety. This design enhances its electron transfer capabilities and confers improved bioavailability and tissue penetration, including the ability to cross the blood–brain barrier. As a member of the quinone class of antioxidants, vatiquinone belongs to a group of compounds that have historically been leveraged to modulate redox homeostasis in tissues under oxidative stress. This class of compounds has been applied in diverse therapeutic areas ranging from neurodegenerative disorders to mitochondrial dysfunction, and its mechanism is chiefly considered beneficial in circumstances where oxidative stress and compromised mitochondrial integrity are primary pathological drivers (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

In addition to its synthetic origins, the pharmacological profile of vatiquinone is characterized by its potent antioxidant activity that exceeds that of traditional compounds like Coenzyme Q10 or idebenone. Its chemical structure allows it to interface efficiently with cellular redox enzymes such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1). The high-affinity interaction between vatiquinone and NQO1 is central to its function, as it is hypothesized to regenerate reduced forms of coenzyme Q and thus support the recycling of critical cellular antioxidants such as glutathione. The ability to catalyze these reactions positions vatiquinone as a compelling agent for therapeutic interventions in conditions marked by chronic oxidative stress, an attribute that underpins the rationale for its proposed use in dry age‐related macular degeneration (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Vatiquinone’s therapeutic history is strongly associated with its development for inherited mitochondrial disorders, most notably Friedreich’s ataxia (FRDA) and Leigh syndrome. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated that vatiquinone modulates oxidative stress response pathways and protects mitochondrial function. In clinical trials conducted in patients with FRDA, vatiquinone was shown to regulate key antioxidant defenses by enhancing the expression of genes such as NQO1 and those involved in glutathione synthesis via activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. This led to improvements in neurological function and confirmed its favorable safety profile, thereby validating its use in outpatient settings for mitochondrial disorders (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Beyond its application in mitochondrial disorders, vatiquinone has been explored in the context of various neurodegenerative diseases, reflecting its capacity to preserve mitochondrial health and ameliorate oxidative injury in neural tissues. Its potent neuroprotective properties, which include mitigating oxidative insults and modulating redox-sensitive signaling pathways, have led to its FDA orphan drug designation for Friedrich’s ataxia. Although the primary focus of vatiquinone research has been in neurodegeneration and mitochondrial impairments, the underlying mechanisms that confer mitochondrial protection and support antioxidant defenses have raised interest in its potential application in ocular diseases such as dry age‐related macular degeneration. Notably, preclinical and anecdotal data have suggested that similar redox imbalances found in inherited mitochondrial diseases are also present in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of patients with dry AMD. However, while the compound’s efficacy and safety have been established in the neurological context, no formal clinical investigations have directly addressed its potential in treating dry AMD or in modulating RPE function (Cores et al., 2023; Chang & Chen, 2024).

The translation of vatiquinone’s antioxidant properties to dry AMD is based on the shared underlying pathology of chronic oxidative stress. Pilot data even indicate viability improvements in ARPE-19, a widely used RPE cell model, under stress conditions. Although these data are preliminary and unpublished, they offer a promising foundation for further research into whether the molecule can enhance RPE barrier integrity, mitigate ROS-mediated damage, and restore transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in an oxidative environment (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of vatiquinone centers on its role as a potent redox-active compound that interacts directly with cellular enzymes such as NQO1. The compound is a high-affinity substrate for NQO1, an enzyme that catalyzes the reversible two-electron reduction of quinones. This reaction is critical because it facilitates the regeneration of reduced coenzyme Q, a vital electron carrier within the mitochondrial respiratory chain. In tissues under chronic oxidative stress, such as the RPE, this reaction ensures the maintenance of mitochondrial function and energy production (Tiberi et al., 2023).

Furthermore, vatiquinone’s chemical structure confers upon it the ability to modulate the activity of the Nrf2 pathway indirectly. Under oxidative stress, Nrf2 normally dissociates from its cytosolic inhibitor Keap1, translocates to the nucleus, and induces the transcription of ARE-driven genes. These genes encode several antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes, including NQO1, glutamate–cysteine ligase, and heme oxygenase-1. By facilitating redox stabilization and promoting a favorable antioxidant environment, vatiquinone indirectly enhances the nuclear stabilization and translocation of Nrf2. This leads to a sustained increase in the expression of key components responsible for glutathione synthesis and recycling, a process crucial for neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and protecting cellular structures (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

At the molecular level, vatiquinone’s interaction with NQO1 not only catalyzes the reduction of the compound itself but also plays a broader role in restoring the redox balance of coenzyme Q within the mitochondrial membrane. The modulation of the redox state of coenzyme Q enhances the function of the electron transport chain and prevents the accumulation of ROS. Such precise biochemical regulation is essential in tissues like the RPE, which are highly susceptible to oxidative damage due to constant light exposure and high metabolic activity. The resultant maintenance of mitochondrial integrity and bioenergetics further supports the preservation of tight junction proteins and barrier function, which are compromised in chronic oxidative environments (Cores et al., 2023).

In summary, vatiquinone exerts its effects via dual modalities: a direct catalytic reduction by NQO1 that regenerates bioactive reduced coenzyme Q and an indirect upregulation of the Nrf2-dependent antioxidant response. These biochemical interactions form the cornerstone of its neuroprotective and cytoprotective properties in cells challenged by oxidative stress, providing a mechanistic rationale for its potential application in protecting RPE cells (Cores et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
Applying the known mechanisms of vatiquinone to the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration, the candidate is expected to mediate several beneficial effects in the retinal pigment epithelium. The primary hypothesis is that vatiquinone will act as a high-affinity substrate for NQO1 in RPE cells, thereby accelerating the reduction of the compound and promoting the regeneration of reduced coenzyme Q. This regeneration is essential, as it not only supports the mitochondrial electron transport chain but also contributes to the broader cellular antioxidant network through enhanced glutathione recycling (Tiberi et al., 2023).

In the proposed ARPE-19 cell assay under chronic oxidative challenge, the activation of the NQO1 pathway by vatiquinone is anticipated to improve the cellular redox state. By regenerating reduced coenzyme Q and facilitating glutathione recycling, the drug candidate is expected to neutralize increased levels of ROS that arise during sustained oxidative stress. A consequent effect of this improved redox balance would be the reduced oxidation of tight junction proteins, which are critical for maintaining the barrier integrity of the RPE. Enhanced preservation of these proteins should translate into improved transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a surrogate marker for the functional health of the RPE monolayer (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Additionally, the indirect activation of the Nrf2 pathway by vatiquinone further supports the upregulation of a spectrum of antioxidant genes. These genes, including NQO1, glutamate–cysteine ligase, and heme oxygenase-1, are known to be expressed in RPE cells, especially under oxidative stress conditions. Their increased expression is expected to bolster the cellular defense system, further reducing the accumulation of oxidative damage within the RPE. It is this coordinated regulation of antioxidant pathways that forms the basis for the expected protective effect on RPE barrier function (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023).

Moreover, when applied to the ARPE-19 cell model, the anticipated outcome is an improved survival rate and enhanced barrier properties under conditions that mimic the chronic oxidative insult characteristic of dry AMD. In vitro studies suggest that vatiquinone may limit ROS-induced modifications to cellular proteins, thereby preserving tight junction integrity. This preservation is critical not only for maintaining TEER but also for ensuring proper intercellular adhesion and barrier function, which are directly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Cores et al., 2023).

The expected benefits in the cellular assay include a reduction in oxidative markers, stabilization of mitochondrial function, and maintenance or restoration of RPE junctional architecture. These effects, if replicated in further ocular-specific studies, would position vatiquinone as a valuable therapeutic candidate for mitigating the progression of dry AMD, where oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction are culpable for disease progression (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive evaluation of vatiquinone as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration reveals several compelling strengths as well as important limitations that must be addressed in future research. One of the primary strengths of vatiquinone is its robust mode of action grounded in redox biology. Its ability to function as a high-affinity substrate for NQO1, coupled with its indirect activation of the Nrf2 pathway, equips it with a dual mechanism that promotes both direct regeneration of the reduced coenzyme Q pool and upregulation of cellular antioxidant defenses. These mechanisms are particularly significant in protecting mitochondrial function and by extension, improving cellular resilience against oxidative insults that compromise the RPE (Tiberi et al., 2023).

The wealth of historical data demonstrating vatiquinone’s efficacy in treating mitochondrial disorders such as Friedreich’s ataxia lends credence to its capability in counteracting oxidative damage and preserving tissue function. Its demonstrated ability to upregulate genes involved in glutathione synthesis and to stabilize mitochondrial function under stress makes it a promising candidate not only for neurodegenerative conditions but potentially for ocular pathologies where similar oxidative mechanisms are at play (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023). Moreover, the observation that preliminary ARPE-19 cell data indicate improved viability under oxidative challenge augments the biological plausibility of its use in dry AMD (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023).

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and uncertainties temper the enthusiasm for immediate repurposing. The most significant gap is the absence of direct evidence linking vatiquinone to therapeutic benefits specifically in dry AMD or broader retinal contexts. While the mechanistic rationale is robust, the majority of the supportive literature originates from studies in neurodegeneration and mitochondrial dysfunction rather than from ophthalmologic or RPE-specific investigations. This extrapolation, although scientifically reasonable, necessitates rigorous preclinical evaluation in ocular models to confirm efficacy in preserving retinal barrier function under chronic oxidative stress (Cores et al., 2023).

Another area requiring careful scrutiny is the complexity of the retinal microenvironment compared to neuronal tissues. Dry AMD is multifactorial, with pathogenesis that involves chronic inflammation, complement dysregulation, lipid accumulation, and cell death in addition to oxidative stress. Thus, while vatiquinone’s antioxidant and mitochondrial-protective actions are promising, it remains unclear whether these effects alone will be sufficient to alter the course of dry AMD. This ambiguity underscores the need for studies that specifically measure the impact on tight junction protein oxidation and TEER restoration in RPE cells under conditions that closely mimic the pathological environment of dry AMD (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

From a pharmacokinetic and formulation standpoint, although vatiquinone is orally bioavailable and has demonstrated favorable systemic safety profiles, the translation of systemic delivery to ocular efficacy presents challenges. Addressing these issues will require detailed ocular pharmacokinetic studies and potentially the development of optimized formulations tailored for retinal applications (Cores et al., 2023).

In summary, vatiquinone (EPI-743) is a highly promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration based on its established antioxidant properties, potent NQO1 substrate activity, and its capacity to indirectly activate Nrf2-dependent defense mechanisms. The compound’s strengths lie in its dual mechanism of action that directly addresses mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress—key contributors to RPE degeneration in dry AMD. However, the absence of direct evidence in ocular models and the inherent complexities of retinal pathophysiology represent significant hurdles that must be overcome through targeted preclinical and clinical studies. Future research should prioritize in vitro studies using ARPE-19 and other RPE models, followed by in vivo validation in animal models of dry AMD, to conclusively determine whether vatiquinone can restore TEER and protect tight junction proteins against ROS-mediated damage (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Overall, while the current body of evidence from mitochondrial and neuroprotective studies provides a strong rationale for further exploration, the repurposing of vatiquinone for dry AMD will require careful dose optimization, targeted delivery to retinal tissues, and comprehensive validation of its effects on RPE barrier integrity before it can be fully endorsed as a therapeutic option for this debilitating ocular disease (Tiberi et al., 2023; Chang & Chen, 2024; Cores et al., 2023).
