Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
BIRB 796 (doramapimod) is a small-molecule p38 MAP kinase inhibitor discovered at Boehringer Ingelheim as part of a diaryl urea/pyrazolyl-urea medicinal chemistry effort to exploit an inactive, DFG-out conformation of p38 and thereby achieve high potency and kinase-family selectivity via an allosteric binding site adjacent to the ATP pocket (type II binding) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Bagley et al., 2010; Xing, 2016; Coulthard et al., 2009). In contrast to classical ATP-site inhibitors (e.g., pyridinyl-imidazoles such as SB203580) that anchor in the hinge region and remain in the DFG-in active conformation, BIRB 796 engages a selectivity pocket opened by flipping the Asp-Phe-Gly (DFG) motif to a DFG-out state; this binding mode is incompatible with ATP binding and additionally disrupts the interaction between p38α and its upstream activators MKK3/MKK6 (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Bagley et al., 2010). Structural features include deep insertion of a t-butyl group into the hydrophobic “Phe-pocket” created by the DFG-out rearrangement, naphthyl contacts, favorable packing of a tolyl group in a Glu71-containing hydrophobic pocket, a morpholino that H-bonds with Met109, and a diaryl urea NH that forms an H-bond with Glu71 analogous to the adenine N1 interaction in ATP binding (Bagley et al., 2010). Kinetically, BIRB 796 is a prototypical slow-binding, slow-dissociating p38 inhibitor: association is ~500-fold slower and dissociation ~10^6-fold slower than the ATP-site pyridinyl-imidazole SK&F 86002, consistent with a major conformational rearrangement upon binding and prolonged target residence time (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Biophysically, reported potency is sub-nanomolar in binding assays (Kd ~0.1–<0.8 nM) with functional enzymatic or cellular IC50 values on the order of tens of nanomolar (e.g., ~63 nM), and the compound inhibits all p38 isoforms to varying degrees (pan-p38), with context-dependent reports of minimal or dual activity on JNK2 (Xing, 2016; Bagley et al., 2010; Yong et al., 2009; Coulthard et al., 2009). A microwave-assisted route to BIRB 796 was reported (aminopyrazole formation from pivaloylacetonitrile and p-tolylhydrazine; carbamate and aminonaphthol intermediates; DMSO coupling at 100°C), enabling improved yields for preclinical supply and mechanistic studies (Bagley et al., 2010).

As a chemotype, diaryl/urea-type type II kinase inhibitors that exploit DFG-out conformations were developed to expand selectivity beyond hinge-binding ATP mimetics, often achieving slow off-rates and high apparent affinity; within the p38 field, BIRB 796 became the best-characterized example of this allosteric/selectivity-pocket strategy and served as a clinical tool compound for inflammatory indications (Xing, 2016; Coulthard et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History  
BIRB 796 advanced through Phase I and Phase II programs and was reported as having reached Phase II/III development for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases including rheumatoid arthritis (RA), Crohn’s disease (CD), and psoriasis; a human endotoxemia model was used to demonstrate pharmacodynamic target engagement (suppression of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-8, and effects on coagulation/fibrinolysis/endothelial activation) (Yong et al., 2009; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Coulthard et al., 2009; Xing, 2016). Oral dosing regimens included 5–30 mg twice daily (RA) and 10–60 mg twice daily (CD); in endotoxemia, single doses up to 600 mg were tested and showed robust biomarker modulation (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Yong et al., 2009). Despite clear pharmacodynamic effects, randomized trials failed to demonstrate durable clinical efficacy in Crohn’s disease and psoriasis, and RA efficacy was not substantiated; development was discontinued after Phase II, with repeated administration associated with elevated liver transaminases (class-typical hepatotoxicity) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Mechanistic work implicated a reactive naphthalene-epoxide metabolite (glutathione-conjugated) in the ALT elevations observed in CD patients, supporting on-drug hepatotoxicity as a liability for the chemotype (Machado et al., 2021). More broadly, many clinical p38 inhibitor programs (including BIRB 796) showed a stereotyped pattern of early biomarker suppression (e.g., CRP, soluble TNF receptor) that returned to near baseline by week 12, coincident with a lack of sustained clinical benefit, pointing to network compensation under chronic p38 blockade (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Xing, 2016). These outcomes, together with dose-limiting toxicities seen across the class, drove a field-wide shift toward alternative strategies (substrate-selective or docking-site inhibitors) rather than pan-p38 catalytic inhibition (Burton et al., 2021).

In preclinical and translational settings, BIRB 796 has been widely used as a pharmacological probe: it reduces LPS-induced TNF-α and other cytokines in vitro and in vivo; in a human endotoxemia model a 600 mg dose suppressed coagulation/fibrinolysis and endothelial activation; in tumor-associated contexts it inhibited IL-6 secretion and reduced tumor cell proliferation (Yong et al., 2009). In macrophage-centric COPD studies, BIRB-class inhibitors sometimes failed to suppress IL-8, underscoring cell-type-specific differences in p38 control of cytokine outputs; however, at very low concentrations (1 nM) BIRB-0796 exhibited synergistic cytokine suppression when combined with corticosteroids, reflecting complementary mechanisms (steroids do not block p38-HSP27 phosphorylation) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). In epithelial barrier biology, doramapimod protected the Sertoli cell tight-junction barrier against cadmium-induced injury, preserving localization of ZO-1, claudin-11, occludin, and adherens junction components and rescuing transepithelial electrical resistance (TER), while selectively blocking p38 phosphorylation (without suppressing JNK, CREB, or Akt activation) (Wang et al., 2023).

No registered clinical trials of p38 MAPK inhibitors (including doramapimod) for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are listed on ClinicalTrials.gov under the queried terms, indicating no formal AMD program has been conducted in this class to date (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Mechanistically, p38 signaling has been implicated in retinal vascular and AMD-relevant processes (e.g., VEGF induction, matrix remodeling via MMP-2/MMP-14 and basigin, inflammasome activation, endothelial dysfunction and barrier leakage), which supports biological plausibility but not direct clinical translation for AMD (Burton et al., 2021). There is no RPE- or AMD-specific preclinical study of doramapimod in the provided materials, and none of the cited clinical programs tested dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Burton et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
p38 MAPKs (α/β/γ/δ) are stress-activated serine/threonine kinases that integrate inflammatory cues and drive transcriptional and post-transcriptional control of cytokines including TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8; downstream effectors include MK2/MK3 (MAPKAPK2/3), MSK1/2, and HSP27, which regulate mRNA stability, translation, and cytoskeletal dynamics (Machado et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009; Burton et al., 2021). Canonical activation proceeds via MKK3 and MKK6 phosphorylation of the Thr-Gly-Tyr activation loop, but atypical, TAB1-dependent activation on endosomes also occurs in response to GPCR/cytokine stimuli, fueling vascular inflammation and barrier dysfunction; p38 pathway activity is further modulated by MAPK phosphatases (DUSPs) feeding back on p38 dephosphorylation (Burton et al., 2021).

BIRB 796 binds in a selectivity pocket adjacent to the ATP site and induces a DFG-out conformation that is catalytically incompetent, sterically and conformationally precluding ATP binding and preventing interaction with upstream kinases (MKK3/MKK6) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Bagley et al., 2010). Structural contacts include insertion of a tert-butyl group into the DFG-derived Phe-pocket, hydrophobic contacts by a naphthyl group, a tolyl group accommodated in a Glu71-containing hydrophobic cavity, and a morpholino ring that H-bonds to Met109; importantly, a diaryl urea NH forms a hydrogen bond with Glu71 that mimics the adenine N1 interaction in ATP, highlighting how selectivity-pocket binders can spare classical hinge contacts yet achieve high affinity (Bagley et al., 2010). The kinetic signature of BIRB 796—extremely slow dissociation and slow association—reflects the energetic barrier to reorganize the DFG motif and surrounding activation loop, and is thought to confer prolonged target occupancy in cells (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). As a result, BIRB 796 has sub-nanomolar binding affinity to non-activated p38α (Kd ~0.1–<0.8 nM) with functional inhibitory potency in the low- to mid-nanomolar range in biochemical/cellular assays (Xing, 2016; Bagley et al., 2010).

Isoform and pathway coverage is broad: multiple sources report inhibition of all p38 isoforms (α/β/γ/δ), a property linked to the allosteric binding mode, which avoids the Met109-dependent hinge interaction exploited by ATP-site inhibitors that often lack activity on γ/δ (Coulthard et al., 2009; Xing, 2016). Some profiling described BIRB 796 as selective against JNK2, whereas other reports noted dual p38/JNK activity—differences likely arise from assay format, activation state, and concentration ranges, but the possibility of JNK2 inhibition exists and complicates mechanistic attribution in certain systems (Yong et al., 2009; Bagley et al., 2010). Functionally, BIRB 796 suppresses LPS-induced TNF-α and lowers IL-6 and IL-8 in human endotoxemia, reduces p38 readouts such as phosphorylated HSP27 (a sensitive pharmacodynamic biomarker), and decreases phosphorylation of MK2, consistent with dampened pro-inflammatory transcription and mRNA stabilization (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Yong et al., 2009; Burton et al., 2021). In immortalized Werner syndrome fibroblasts, BIRB 796 prevents p38 activation, reduces pp38 and pHSP27, and thereby modifies senescence-associated phenotypes, reinforcing its activity on the p38→MK2/HSP27 axis in stressed/aged cells (Bagley et al., 2010). In primary Sertoli cells exposed to cadmium, doramapimod specifically blocked p38 phosphorylation, preserved junctional protein localization (e.g., ZO-1, occludin, claudin-11, JAM-A), and maintained barrier function (TER), while not suppressing parallel stress signals (pJNK, p-c-Jun, p-CREB, p-Akt), indicating target-pathway selectivity in vitro (Wang et al., 2023).

Clinical pharmacology confirms human anti-inflammatory effects: a 600 mg dose of BIRB-796BS in endotoxemia suppressed LPS-induced coagulation, fibrinolysis, and endothelial activation (Yong et al., 2009). However, in chronic inflammatory diseases, repeated dosing produced only transient biomarker suppression and limited clinical benefits; repeated administration caused liver-enzyme elevations, and mechanistic toxicology implicated a reactive naphthalene-epoxide metabolite (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Machado et al., 2021). These observations align with broader p38 inhibitor experience: pan-p38 blockade can interrupt beneficial anti-inflammatory signaling (e.g., MSK1/2-mediated) and distort feedback circuits, while disinhibiting upstream kinases (e.g., TAK1, MLK2/3) and activating JNK or NF-κB crosstalk, conferring dose-limiting toxicities and short-lived efficacy (Coulthard et al., 2009).

Expected Effect  
Assay hypothesis: In senescent retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), pharmacologic p38α/β inhibition with BIRB 796 will suppress SASP-like cytokines (particularly IL-6 and IL-8), reducing paracrine/autocrine downregulation of junctional proteins and preserving tight junction belts (e.g., ZO-1) and transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER).

Mechanistic rationale: p38 controls transcriptional and post-transcriptional programs that elevate IL-6 and IL-8 across multiple inflamed tissues and cell types; BIRB 796 lowers IL-6/IL-8 in human endotoxemia and tumor-cell paracrine models, and at low nanomolar concentrations can synergize with corticosteroids to suppress cytokines in macrophage systems, consistent with broad suppression of p38-driven inflammatory outputs (Yong et al., 2009; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Downstream, p38→MK2 phosphorylates HSP27 and RNA-binding proteins (e.g., tristetraprolin/TTP), which increases mRNA stability and translation of cytokine transcripts; BIRB 796 reduces pp38 and pHSP27 in senescence models, matching the predicted SASP attenuation mechanism (Burton et al., 2021; Bagley et al., 2010). In epithelial barrier contexts, doramapimod rescued tight-junction integrity and TER in primary Sertoli monolayers under toxic stress while maintaining junctional protein localization, providing a functional precedent that p38 inhibition can preserve epithelial-like barrier structure and function via junctional/cytoskeletal stabilization (Wang et al., 2023).

RPE disease-context rationale: Although no RPE-specific BIRB 796 data are provided here, p38 signaling is implicated in AMD-relevant processes (e.g., VEGF induction and angiogenesis, MMP-driven matrix remodeling, inflammasome activation, vascular endothelial dysfunction and barrier leakage), making p38 a plausible node in retinal inflammation and barrier pathology (Burton et al., 2021). Given that p38 activity drives IL-6/IL-8 production broadly, and that these cytokines can downregulate junctional proteins and disrupt epithelial barriers in many systems, it is reasonable to expect that BIRB 796 will lower MK2/HSP27 pathway activity, reduce IL-6/IL-8 secretion from senescent RPE, and preserve ZO-1 belts and TEER if p38-dependent SASP is operative in this cell type (Coulthard et al., 2009; Xing, 2016; Burton et al., 2021). Atypical (TAB1-mediated) p38 activation has been linked to endothelial barrier disruption; while not demonstrated in RPE here, such noncanonical activation could also contribute to epithelial stress responses and might be sensitive to allosteric type II inhibition (Burton et al., 2021).

Assay execution considerations: To test the hypothesis rigorously in senescent RPE, readouts should include (1) p38 pathway activity markers (pp38, pMK2, pHSP27), (2) secreted SASP cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), and (3) barrier metrics (continuous ZO-1 belts by immunofluorescence; TER dynamics over time), with BIRB 796 concentration–response spanning low nanomolar to low micromolar given reported cellular potencies and the 10 µM concentration that preserved Sertoli barrier function (Wang et al., 2023; Xing, 2016; Bagley et al., 2010). Given steroid independence of p38 signaling (p-HSP27 is not reduced by steroids), testing BIRB 796 alone and in combination with a glucocorticoid could probe pharmacologic additivity and compensatory pathways in RPE SASP (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Because IL-8 may be variably p38-dependent across cell types, the assay should be powered to detect partial suppression and explore time-dependent compensation (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Finally, inclusion of controls that assess atypical activation (e.g., TAB1–p38 engagement) and post-transcriptional endpoints (TTP phosphorylation status) could sharpen mechanistic attribution (Burton et al., 2021).

Translational considerations: Systemic doramapimod exposure is constrained by hepatotoxicity and lack of durable efficacy in chronic inflammation, plausibly due to network adaptation; any clinical path in dry AMD would require local ocular delivery to minimize systemic exposure and to bypass compensatory systemic responses, a principle consistent with proposed niches for p38 inhibitors in localized/short-term settings (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Coulthard et al., 2009). At present, there are no registered AMD trials of p38 inhibitors, so translational validation must proceed from RPE/retinal preclinical models (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit: p38 MAPK is a master regulator of inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 and IL-8, with well-defined downstream effectors (MK2/MK3, HSP27) that also interface with cytoskeletal and junctional integrity; BIRB 796 potently and durably engages this pathway, reduces p38 phosphorylation readouts, and suppresses IL-6/IL-8 in human endotoxemia and other systems (Machado et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Yong et al., 2009). The proposed RPE SASP-barrier mechanism is therefore biochemically coherent (Burton et al., 2021).  
- High potency and residence time: sub-nanomolar affinity, nanomolar functional inhibition, and extremely slow off-rate support strong target engagement at low free concentrations, which may be advantageous for intraocular dosing strategies designed to minimize systemic exposure (Xing, 2016; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012).  
- Allosteric type II mode and pan-p38 coverage: by stabilizing DFG-out, BIRB 796 inhibits α/β/γ/δ isoforms, potentially covering non-α p38 activity that could contribute to epithelial senescence or retinal inflammation; the allosteric site is exploited with favorable structural interactions and a defined pharmacophore (Coulthard et al., 2009; Bagley et al., 2010; Xing, 2016).  
- Barrier-protection precedent in epithelia: doramapimod preserved ZO-1/occludin/claudin-11 localization and TER in primary Sertoli monolayers under toxic injury while selectively blocking p38 phosphorylation, an effect directionally aligned with the goal of preserving RPE tight junctions and barrier function (Wang et al., 2023).  
- PD biomarkers to guide development: pHSP27 and pMK2 provide sensitive pathway engagement readouts, facilitating translational bridging from in vitro RPE to in vivo ocular models and potentially to human aqueous/vitreous sampling (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Burton et al., 2021).  
- Combination potential: BIRB-class inhibitors can synergize with corticosteroids at very low concentrations in cytokine suppression assays, reflecting complementary mechanisms of action and offering a combination path to mitigate compensation (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of RPE-specific data: No direct evidence in the provided materials demonstrates doramapimod effects on senescent RPE SASP, IL-6/IL-8, ZO-1 belts, or TEER; AMD- or RPE-specific proof of concept remains to be generated (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Burton et al., 2021).  
- Clinical class history of transient efficacy: Across chronic inflammatory indications, p38 inhibitors showed early biomarker suppression followed by reversion toward baseline and lack of durable benefit by ~12 weeks, likely reflecting pathway compensation and complex feedback/crosstalk that may also occur in chronic retinal disease (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Xing, 2016).  
- Hepatotoxicity and metabolic liability: Repeated systemic dosing raised liver enzymes, and mechanistic toxicology implicated a reactive naphthalene-epoxide metabolite for BIRB 796 specifically; while intraocular delivery could mitigate systemic exposure, any repurposing must address ocular-specific safety and formulation (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Machado et al., 2021).  
- Potential dual JNK2 activity: Reports vary on BIRB 796 selectivity; dual p38/JNK2 inhibition has been described, complicating mechanistic interpretation and potentially adding pathway liabilities in some cellular contexts (Bagley et al., 2010; Yong et al., 2009).  
- Isoform- and context-specific cytokine control: In alveolar macrophages and COPD models, IL-8 can be relatively resistant to p38 inhibition, cautioning against assuming uniform suppression of IL-8 in senescent RPE; parallel drivers (e.g., NF-κB) may require combination strategies (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012).  
- Strategic alternatives may be preferable: Substrate-selective p38 pathway interventions (e.g., ED-site inhibitor UM101) that spare beneficial MSK1 signaling, or inhibitors that block atypical TAB1-mediated activation, have shown preclinical advantages and may reduce compensation/toxicity risks compared with pan-p38 catalytic inhibition (Burton et al., 2021).

Decision-oriented assessment for dry AMD  
- Biological plausibility: Strong. p38 controls IL-6/IL-8 and MK2/HSP27 signaling that plausibly drive SASP and barrier dysfunction; doramapimod has repeatedly demonstrated suppression of these axes and preserved epithelial-like barrier function in vitro (Machado et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Translational tractability: Conditional. Systemic use is precluded by hepatotoxicity and lack of durable efficacy; however, local ocular delivery could deliver high intraocular drug levels while limiting systemic exposure, and the slow off-rate may support infrequent dosing, pending ocular PK/toxicity profiling (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Coulthard et al., 2009).  
- Evidence gaps: Critical. No RPE-focused or AMD-model data exist here; there are no registered AMD clinical trials for p38 inhibitors; demonstration in senescent RPE models is essential before advancing (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Recommended next steps  
- In vitro RPE senescence studies: Evaluate BIRB 796 concentration–response (1 nM–10 µM) on pp38/pMK2/pHSP27, IL-6/IL-8 secretion, ZO-1/occludin belt continuity, and TEER in primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE rendered senescent (e.g., replicative or stress-induced senescence) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Burton et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Mechanistic dissection: Assess TTP phosphorylation and mRNA decay of IL-6/IL-8; interrogate atypical TAB1-dependent activation signatures; compare to a substrate-selective p38 modulator where possible to benchmark compensation (Burton et al., 2021).  
- Combination testing: Explore additivity with a glucocorticoid and/or NF-κB modulation to overcome potential IL-8 resistance in RPE; measure durability after washout to probe rebound signaling (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012).  
- Ocular safety and delivery: Conduct ex vivo/in vivo ocular tolerability (ERGs, histology) and intraocular PK in relevant species; leverage the slow target off-rate to test low-dose intravitreal delivery designed to minimize systemic exposure (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Coulthard et al., 2009).  
- Prioritize de-risking strategies: If doramapimod exhibits ocular or systemic liabilities, consider pathway-refined alternatives (e.g., MK2 inhibitors; ED-site p38α inhibitors sparing MSK1; TAB1-site blockers) that may retain anti-SASP efficacy with reduced toxicity and compensation (Burton et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009).

Conclusion  
On mechanistic grounds, BIRB 796 is well-suited to test the SASP-barrier hypothesis in senescent RPE: it is a potent, slow-off, allosteric type II inhibitor that suppresses IL-6/IL-8 outputs and p38→MK2/HSP27 signaling, and it preserves epithelial-like junctional integrity and TER in a primary Sertoli barrier model (Xing, 2016; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Yong et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2023). The absence of RPE- or AMD-specific evidence and the class’s clinical history of transient efficacy and hepatotoxicity are significant liabilities that limit immediate translational prospects; nonetheless, a local-delivery, RPE-focused preclinical program is justified to generate the missing data and to determine whether p38 suppression can stabilize RPE barrier function and SASP in dry AMD models (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Coulthard et al., 2009). If positive, doramapimod could serve as a powerful chemical probe for isoform- and pathway-specific dissection in RPE senescence, while parallel exploration of pathway-refined or substrate-selective p38 modulators may offer a more sustainable clinical trajectory for chronic ocular disease (Burton et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
H-151 is a small-molecule antagonist of the innate immune adaptor STING (TMEM173) that was developed as part of a chemical class designed to prevent the palmitoylation-dependent activation of STING at the Golgi following cyclic dinucleotide binding and ER-to-Golgi trafficking (i.e., cGAMP-bound STING oligomerization and signalosome assembly) (Decout et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). In its mechanistic class, H-151 is grouped with covalent STING inhibitors that target Cys91 within the transmembrane region–proximal cytosolic interface, thereby preventing activation-induced palmitoylation at Cys88/Cys91 and downstream signaling; nitrofuran analogs such as C-176 and C-178 are the canonical examples where Cys91-directed covalent modification has been mapped by probe chemistry and mass spectrometry (with consequent suppression of type I interferon and IL-6 in vivo) (Decout et al., 2021). STING activation is known to require ligand-induced conformational change, ER exit, and palmitoylation on Cys88/Cys91 to drive oligomerization/polymerization and recruitment of TBK1 and other signal transducers; antagonists that block this palmitoylation step are therefore positioned to broadly prevent both IRF3-dependent type I interferon and NF-κB–dependent inflammatory outputs (Li et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2021).

H-151 has been characterized in inflammatory disease models as a low molecular weight, irreversible inhibitor of human and mouse STING that blocks activation-induced palmitoylation and attenuates downstream signaling (with primary mechanistic references tracing to the discovery work summarized by Pan et al. and by Decout et al.) (Pan et al., 2021; Decout et al., 2021). In keratinocyte and immune-cell systems relevant to psoriatic inflammation, H-151 has reproducibly suppressed STING-dependent NF-κB and IRF3 phosphorylation, inhibited proinflammatory cytokine mRNA induction (e.g., IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α), and reduced STING protein levels, consistent with an antagonist mechanism upstream of canonical downstream effectors (Pan et al., 2021). Conceptually, H-151 belongs to the broader class of cGAS–STING pathway modulators that have been deployed to suppress sterile inflammation across multiple tissues; for the eye and retina, related pathway inhibitors (e.g., C-176, SN-011, cryptotanshinone) have shown efficacy in ischemic and neovascular models via suppression of microglial STING signaling and cytokine/chemokine/protease outputs, supporting the translatability of STING antagonism to ocular tissues (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
There is no reported clinical use of H-151 in humans, and no published veterinary or clinical trials in ophthalmology were identified in the provided literature set; H-151 has been used as a research tool compound in preclinical inflammatory models, most prominently in psoriasis, where it decreased lesion severity and cutaneous inflammatory readouts in the imiquimod model (Pan et al., 2021). In psoriasis-relevant cell systems, H-151 suppressed cGAMP-induced IRF3 and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and reduced IFN-β, IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α expression, consistent with on-pathway inhibition of STING and its downstream transcriptional programs (Pan et al., 2021). In vivo, topical H-151 improved psoriasis-like dermatitis and decreased markers linked to STING/NF-κB signaling, again without human clinical translation to date (Pan et al., 2021).

Ocular/retinal precedent for the STING target is strong even if H-151–specific data are sparse. In multiple retinal contexts, activation of cGAS–STING has been implicated in pathogenesis through DNA-damage and mitochondrial DNA leakage, leading to IRF3/NF-κB activation, SASP-like cytokine induction, angiogenesis, and barrier dysfunction (Hu et al., 2023). Genetic and pharmacologic pathway perturbations show benefit: genetic loss of STING limits endothelial senescence and vascular degeneration in diabetic models (Liu et al., 2023), genetic deletion along the cGAS–STING axis rescues Alu DNA–driven RPE toxicity (implicated in geographic atrophy) (Hu et al., 2023), and pharmacologic STING inhibitors (C-176, SN-011) suppress neovascularization in laser CNV and OIR models (Ni et al., 2024). Importantly for RPE biology, senescent ARPE-19 cells were reported to overproduce VEGF and this overproduction was prevented by H-151, providing a direct albeit single-study line of evidence that H-151 can modulate pathogenic angiogenic/SASP output in an RPE-derived cell line (Hu et al., 2023). Beyond H-151, epigenetic suppression of STING (JQ1), PPARα activation, and visual cycle modulation (reducing toxic retinoid stress) each attenuate cGAS–STING activation and downstream inflammation or degeneration, underscoring the therapeutic appeal of targeting this axis in retinal disease (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
STING biology and the palmitoylation node. STING is a homodimeric ER-resident adaptor with an N-terminal multi-pass transmembrane domain and a cytosolic C-terminal ligand-binding domain; binding of 2’3’-cGAMP (produced by cGAS upon sensing cytosolic dsDNA) induces conformational rearrangements that enable ER exit and trafficking to the Golgi, where palmitoylation of Cys88 and Cys91 is critical for higher-order assembly and recruitment of TBK1 and other signaling proteins (Li et al., 2021). Palmitoylation-driven tetramerization/higher-order oligomerization is a central activation step for STING, and mutational or pharmacologic interference with Cys88/Cys91 palmitoylation abrogates downstream signal propagation (Pan et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). Activated STING scaffolds TBK1 to phosphorylate IRF3 (e.g., at Ser366), triggering type I interferon gene expression, and engages NF-κB to induce a broad proinflammatory transcriptional program, including SASP components (Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2021). In retinal disease contexts, cGAS–STING activation (driven by nuclear/mtDNA release or Alu-derived nucleic acids) is linked to up-regulation of VEGF via NF-κB/HIF-1α in oxidative-stress–induced RPE senescence, endothelial and microglial inflammatory activation, and barrier compromise (Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025).

H-151 and palmitoylation blockade. H-151 is positioned mechanistically among irreversible covalent inhibitors of STING that target Cys91 to prevent activation-associated palmitoylation and signalosome formation (Decout et al., 2021). While detailed covalent adduct chemistry for H-151 itself is not contained in the supplied excerpts, authoritative mechanistic reviews depict H-151 in the “Targeting Cys91” class, alongside nitrofuran inhibitors (C-176, C-178) that have been shown to bind Cys91 selectively and irreversibly (but not Cys88) and that suppress in vivo IFN and IL-6 responses to STING agonism (Decout et al., 2021). Primary disease-model data support a functional blockade of STING signal transmission by H-151: it reduced STING protein abundance in keratinocytes and THP-1 monocytes, inhibited cGAMP-driven IRF3 and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation, and suppressed downstream cytokine expression (IFN-β, IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α) (Pan et al., 2021). In the psoriasis model, H-151 strongly downregulated NF-κB activity and IL-6 and reduced p-p65 and total p65, with a more variable impact on IRF3 phosphorylation depending on system and readout, suggesting it can dominantly blunt the NF-κB arm of STING signaling while at least partially reducing IRF3 activation (Pan et al., 2021). The lack of additivity with an NF-κB inhibitor (BAY 11-7082) on IL-6 suppression implies pathway overlap and supports that H-151’s anti-inflammatory effects in that model are mediated primarily by interference with STING → NF-κB–driven cytokine production (Pan et al., 2021).

Rationale in retinal cells and tissue. cGAS and STING are expressed across retinal cell types (RPE, microglia, endothelial cells, Müller glia, photoreceptors) and are upregulated in disease states (AMD/DR), with promoter accessibility and mRNA levels increased in diseased tissue, positioning the pathway as targetable across multiple ocular compartments (Hu et al., 2023). Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction cause cytosolic mtDNA accumulation that activates cGAS–STING; Alu-derived nucleic acids similarly drive cytosolic DNA sensing and RPE cytotoxicity in GA, with multiple studies showing that genetic deletion along the cGAS–STING axis rescues Alu DNA toxicity (Hu et al., 2023). In RPE biology specifically, STING is implicated in senescence-associated VEGF upregulation, and H-151 prevented VEGF overproduction in senescent ARPE-19 cells, indicating that palmitoylation-targeted STING antagonism can suppress a central angiogenic/SASP mediator in stressed RPE-like cells (Hu et al., 2023). In retinal vascular and microglial compartments, pathway inhibition reduces inflammatory and proteolytic mediators (e.g., lowering Il6 and Mmp9) and blunts vascular leakage and neovascular pathology, as shown with cryptotanshinone, C-176, and SN-011 (Qiu et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024). Collectively, these data situate H-151’s palmitoylation blockade at a nodal point capable of broadly dampening IRF3 and NF-κB outputs in ocular cells that contribute to SASP, MMP expression, VEGF induction, and barrier compromise relevant to dry AMD (Hu et al., 2023).

Important mechanistic caveats. RPE models are heterogeneous in cGAS expression and DNA-sensor usage; some RPE cell lines lack cGAS and instead rely on other nucleic acid sensors (e.g., RIG-I, ZBP1), and the relative contribution of cGAS–STING versus alternative pathways varies by context (Hu et al., 2023). Moreover, the balance of STING outputs (IRF3/type I IFN versus NF-κB) can be cell/state dependent, as reflected by psoriasis-model findings where systemic IFN-β was unchanged despite local suppression of p-IRF3 and p65 in skin (Pan et al., 2021). These observations underscore that while H-151 inhibits upstream STING activation, the phenotype in any given ocular assay will reflect cell-type–specific wiring, stimulus context (Alu vs mtDNA vs oxidant stress), and cross-talk with other innate immune axes (Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023).

Expected Effect  
Assay context and target presence. The proposed assays—senescence models in RPE with readouts including TEER, ZO-1 continuity, SASP cytokines (IL-6/IL-8), and MMPs—interrogate processes (barrier integrity, SASP-driven inflammation, matrix remodeling) that are mechanistically tied to cGAS–STING–NF-κB signaling and are central to dry AMD progression (Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025; Terao et al., 2022). RPE expresses STING and engages cGAS–STING signaling under oxidative and senescent stress; senescent ARPE-19 cells overproduce VEGF via a STING/NF-κB/HIF-1α pathway, and H-151 prevented this VEGF overproduction, providing direct cell-type–relevant evidence of efficacy on a SASP/angiogenic factor in RPE (Hu et al., 2023). In addition, cGAS inhibition alleviates Alu RNA–induced immune responses and cytotoxicity in RPE, consistent with the pathway’s role in dsDNA/dsRNA-triggered sterile inflammation and suggesting that upstream DNA-sensor blockade mitigates RPE injury (Li et al., 2022).

Expected pharmacodynamic effects. Based on H-151’s mechanism at the palmitoylation node and its demonstrated suppression of STING-dependent IRF3 and NF-κB activation in immune and epithelial cells, we expect the following in RPE senescence assays:

- Proximal signaling: reductions in STING abundance (as seen in keratinocytes/THP-1), p-TBK1, p-IRF3, and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation following H-151 treatment under stimuli that engage cGAS–STING (e.g., H₂O₂-induced senescence, Alu cDNA transfection, mtDNA transfection) (Pan et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022).

- Cytokines/SASP: decreased secretion and/or expression of IL-6 and potentially IL-8 and other SASP components; in non-ocular systems H-151 lowered IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, IFN-β, and IFN-stimulated gene signatures, and in ARPE-19 senescence models H-151 prevented VEGF overproduction (Pan et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2023). Because NF-κB is a principal SASP driver in oxidant-stressed RPE, H-151’s suppression of NF-κB should proportionally lower SASP cytokines, including IL-6/IL-8, which are repeatedly implicated in AMD pathobiology (Terao et al., 2022; Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025).

- MMPs and matrix remodeling: in retinal microglia, pharmacologic STING inhibition reduced Mmp9 expression alongside Il6 and diminished vascular leakage in OIR, suggesting that blocking STING can lower proteases that degrade extracellular matrix and compromise barriers (Qiu et al., 2025; Terao et al., 2022). While H-151-specific MMP data in RPE have not been reported here, we would predict a reduction in MMP-9 in senescent RPE given the NF-κB dependence of SASP proteases and the precedent in ocular STING inhibition (Qiu et al., 2025; Terao et al., 2022).

- Barrier integrity (TEER and ZO-1): direct H-151 data on RPE TEER/ZO-1 are unavailable in the provided literature. However, STING activity has been linked to barrier dysfunction in retinal endothelium (inner barrier), with evidence that STING activation through TBK1/IRF3/IFN-β axes amplifies senescence and compromises barrier integrity; genetic STING deficiency mitigates such changes (Wu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). In the outer retina, RPE degeneration driven by inflammatory stimuli is attenuated in STING knockout mice, supporting that STING inhibition can preserve epithelial integrity under inflammatory stress (Hu et al., 2023). Thus, we expect H-151 to preserve TEER and maintain ZO-1 continuity in RPE senescence models where cGAS–STING–NF-κB contributes to junctional remodeling and MMP-driven degradation, but this prediction requires experimental confirmation given the absence of direct H-151 barrier data (Hu et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025).

- Anti-senescence signatures: in non-ocular systems, H-151 treatment decreased cGAS–STING pathway activation, reduced ISGs, lowered P16/P21, and decreased SA-β-gal activity, indicating that STING antagonism can blunt senescence programs and SASP (Ye et al., 2024). Given the overlap between senescence and innate immune signaling in RPE and AMD, we expect H-151 to reduce senescence markers in RPE senescence assays, again pending direct validation in ocular cells (Blasiak, 2020; Terao et al., 2022).

Expression in the assayed RPE lineage is supported by disease-relevant data showing STING expression and activation in retinal tissues and RPE under stress, including oxidative stress and Alu/mtDNA triggers; cGAS–STING pathway genes are broadly expressed in the retina and upregulated in disease, and RPE senescence engages STING-dependent NF-κB/HIF-1α signaling to drive VEGF (Hu et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease-mechanism fit. Dry AMD pathogenesis features chronic oxidative stress, DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and senescence in RPE, with resultant SASP cytokines, VEGF, and MMPs that degrade extracellular matrix and compromise barriers; cGAS–STING is positioned as a key sensor/effector linking cytosolic DNA to NF-κB/IRF3 activation and SASP output in RPE and retinal cell types (Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2023). Genetic and pharmacologic evidence across models (DR endothelium, Alu-driven RPE toxicity, ischemic/neovascular retinopathy) show that suppressing STING signaling reduces inflammation, senescence markers, angiogenic/proteolytic factors, leakage, and degeneration, indicating pathway validity and translational plausibility in the eye (Liu et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

- Direct RPE cell evidence for H-151. H-151 prevented VEGF overproduction in senescent ARPE-19 cells, directly supporting the candidate’s ability to suppress a central SASP/angiogenic mediator in an RPE-derived cell model (Hu et al., 2023). This aligns with the broader observation that STING upregulates VEGF in oxidative stress–induced RPE senescence via NF-κB/HIF-1α (Hu et al., 2023).

- Potent inhibition of NF-κB and cytokine outputs. In preclinical psoriasis systems, H-151 suppressed cGAMP-induced IRF3/NF-κB phosphorylation and reduced IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IFN-β readouts, consistent with broad blockade of the principal proinflammatory axes downstream of STING (Pan et al., 2021). Given that NF-κB is a dominant inducer of SASP components in oxidant-stressed RPE, and IL-6/IL-8 and MMPs are canonical RPE SASP factors in AMD, H-151’s activity is well matched to reduce these pathological outputs (Terao et al., 2022; Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025).

- Target validation in retinal models via related inhibitors/genetics. STING inhibition by C-176/SN-011 reduces neovascularization in CNV/OIR; cryptotanshinone reduces Il6 and Mmp9 and vascular leakage through STING suppression in microglia; STING knockout provides protection against inflammatory retinal degeneration and endothelial senescence and barrier compromise, together providing multi-compartment evidence that STING blockade can ameliorate retinal inflammatory pathology (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023).

- Modality fit for intracellular target. Because cGAS and STING are intracellular, small molecules are preferred for retinal applications; the literature anticipates that blood–retina–penetrant small-molecule cGAS–STING inhibitors will be needed to translate this strategy to the clinic, supporting H-151’s modality selection (Hu et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- Sparse ocular data for H-151. Beyond the ARPE-19 VEGF observation, there are no H-151 data for TEER, ZO-1 continuity, MMP modulation, or in vivo ocular efficacy in dry AMD models in the provided literature, so the central claims around barrier preservation remain predictions that require direct testing (Hu et al., 2023). By contrast, barrier-relevant evidence is stronger for alternative STING inhibitors (cryptotanshinone effects on Mmp9/leakage; C-176/SN-011 in angiogenesis models), indicating pathway relevance but not yet validating H-151 itself in retina (Qiu et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2024).

- Cell-type heterogeneity in DNA sensing. Some RPE models lack cGAS and may rely on other sensors (RIG-I, ZBP1), and the cGAS–STING axis can be variably engaged depending on the nature of the stressor (Alu vs mtDNA vs photo-oxidized A2E), potentially limiting the breadth of H-151’s efficacy across RPE senescence paradigms (Hu et al., 2023). Thorough profiling in human primary RPE and AMD-relevant triggers will be required.

- Pathway-output variability. H-151’s strongest effects in psoriasis were on NF-κB/IL-6, with partial or context-dependent impact on IRF3/IFN-β; while NF-κB is the prime SASP driver in RPE, specific disease contexts (e.g., dsDNA-driven type I IFN) may require robust IRF3 suppression to fully ameliorate pathology (Pan et al., 2021). The differential balance of NF-κB versus IRF3 outputs in RPE under various triggers should be experimentally mapped.

- Covalent inhibitor liabilities. Cysteine-targeting covalent inhibitors can carry risks of off-target reactivity and species-specific metabolic liabilities; development of covalent agents demands careful derisking of reactivity and ocular PK/PD, as underscored in general discussions of covalent inhibitor strategies and metabolism in drug discovery (Wang et al., 2022). Although H-151’s covalent target is genetically unique (Cys91 on STING), comprehensive safety and selectivity profiling—especially for intraocular delivery—is not available here.

- Immunological trade-offs. STING deficiency can increase susceptibility to tumorigenesis and reduce vaccine responses, and human STING haplotypes (e.g., HAQ) show variable responsiveness to cyclic dinucleotides, implying potential population variability in pathway dependence and therapeutic response (Hu et al., 2023). For ocular delivery, local exposure may mitigate systemic risks, but intraocular immunosuppression could theoretically predispose to infections; risk–benefit will need empirical assessment.

Evidence-based development plan (prioritized)  
- In vitro RPE assays. Use human primary RPE and ARPE-19 under AMD-relevant triggers (H₂O₂, Alu cDNA, mtDNA transfection) to quantify: STING pathway activation (p-TBK1, p-IRF3, p65), SASP cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), MMPs (MMP-9), and angiogenic factors (VEGF); barrier metrics by TEER and ZO-1 continuity; and senescence markers (P16, P21, SA-β-gal). Include STING agonist/antagonist controls (e.g., diABZI, C-176), and cGAS/STING knockdown to confirm on-target effects; the goal is to reproduce the VEGF suppression result and extend to barrier preservation and MMP control with H-151 (Hu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022; Terao et al., 2022).

- Retinal explant and in vivo models. Move to sodium iodate or oxidant-driven RPE injury models and to Alu DNA–induced RPE degeneration to test whether H-151 reduces cGAS–STING activation, NF-κB signaling, cytokines/MMPs, and preserves RPE morphology; positive controls include JQ1 and C-176, which have shown efficacy in related contexts (Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024). The LIRD model shows cGAS–STING activation can be modulated upstream by visual-cycle inhibitors; testing H-151 in LIRD would further link pathway suppression to photoreceptor/RPE protection (Wang et al., 2022).

- Delivery and PK/PD. Evaluate intravitreal versus periocular dosing for ocular exposure, using formulation strategies with precedent (e.g., nanoparticle-loaded C-176) to optimize intraocular retention and cell uptake; measure intraocular H-151 levels and target engagement markers (p-STING, p-TBK1, p-IRF3) (Shao et al., 2024).

- Safety and immunology. Profile local tolerability and infection risk in the eye while monitoring systemic spillover; genotype stratification for STING haplotypes can be deferred to later phases but should be considered due to pathway variability (Hu et al., 2023).

Decision context  
On balance, H-151 is a mechanistically compelling, tractable small-molecule inhibitor that targets a validated inflammatory/senescence axis in retinal disease, with one direct RPE line of evidence (suppression of VEGF in senescent ARPE-19) and robust non-ocular and ocular-pathway support via related tools and genetic models (Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). The absence of H-151–specific data on RPE barrier metrics (TEER/ZO-1) and MMP modulation is the principal evidence gap relative to the stated hypothesis; however, the consistent linkage of cGAS–STING to IL-6/VEGF/MMP outputs and barrier failure across retinal compartments supports the plausibility that a palmitoylation-targeted STING antagonist like H-151 will deliver the predicted phenotype in senescent RPE (Hu et al., 2023; Terao et al., 2022; Qiu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025).

Recommendation  
Advance H-151 into AMD-relevant in vitro RPE barrier and senescence assays with rigorous on-target controls and head-to-head comparison against alternative STING inhibitors (C-176/SN-011, cryptotanshinone) to establish class translatability and select the best ocular candidate by efficacy and safety; proceed to in vivo validation contingent on clear demonstration of TEER/ZO-1 preservation, SASP/MMP suppression, and favorable ocular PK/PD (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

Strengths summary: strong mechanistic rationale in AMD, direct RPE evidence for VEGF suppression by H-151, broad anti–NF-κB/SASP activity of H-151 in inflammatory models, and multiple retinal models validating STING inhibition (Hu et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2021; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025). Weaknesses summary: no H-151 data yet on RPE barrier readouts or in vivo retinal protection; covalent-inhibitor liabilities and immunologic trade-offs require careful derisking; cell-type heterogeneity in DNA sensing mandates model selection rigor (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Taken together, H-151 is a high-priority mechanistic probe and a plausible therapeutic lead for dry AMD that merits focused preclinical validation in RPE barrier/senescence systems and in Alu/oxidative injury models of outer retinal degeneration, with parallel medicinal-chemistry and formulation work to address ocular delivery and covalent-inhibitor safety considerations (Hu et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MS-275, also known as Entinostat and available from Selleck (S7100), is a fully synthetic compound that belongs to the benzamide class of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi). Its chemical structure is defined as 3-pyridylmethyl-N-{4-[(2-aminophenyl)carbamoyl]-benzyl}carbamate, and it was originally developed by research teams including those at Mitsui Pharmaceuticals in the late 1990s (Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 2–3; Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34). Unlike hydroxamate-based HDAC inhibitors, the benzamide motif in MS-275 engages the catalytic zinc ion in a manner that is less potent in chelation yet confers a higher degree of class I selectivity, particularly toward HDAC1 and HDAC2 (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11). Benzamides have been extensively investigated for their epigenetic modulation properties in oncology, where selective inhibition of HDACs is pursued to reprogram aberrant gene expression profiles in cancer cells (Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Carafa et al., 2011, pp. 3–5). As a representative of its class, MS-275 has a well-defined synthetic origin and benefits from a non-natural product, medicinal chemistry–driven discovery process that emphasizes targeted inhibition of chromatin-modifying enzymes for therapeutic reactivation of silenced genes (Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34; Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, MS-275 has been developed and evaluated primarily in the context of oncology. It has advanced into multiple Phase I and II clinical trials, particularly for solid tumors such as breast cancer, hematologic malignancies like acute leukemia, and various other cancers where deregulated HDAC activity plays a role (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 9–11; Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 2–3). Preclinical studies have demonstrated its capacity to induce cell-cycle arrest, promote apoptosis, and trigger differentiation in tumor cell lines by restoring a balance in histone acetylation (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–9; Hanikoglu et al., 2018, pp. 2–3). Despite its extensive evaluation in cancer, there is no published evidence to date directly applying MS-275 to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or related ocular diseases. Nonetheless, the mechanistic rationale underlying its use in oncology—namely, reactivation of key transcriptional programs via enhanced histone acetylation—is similar to the epigenetic strategy proposed for rescuing retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier function (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 9–11; Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34). In this sense, repurposing MS-275 for dry AMD would constitute a novel application, relying on the molecule’s ability to reverse inflammation-induced transcriptional repression, analogous to its effects in cancer cells (Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Carafa et al., 2011, pp. 3–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
MS-275 functions by selectively inhibiting class I HDACs, particularly HDAC1 and HDAC2, through a zinc-binding mechanism that is distinct from that of hydroxamate inhibitors. The benzamide moiety in MS-275 interacts with the catalytic zinc ion within the active site of HDACs; however, due to its non-hydroxamate nature, the mode of coordination involves a bidentate interaction primarily via the amino group with additional, albeit weaker, engagement through the carbonyl oxygen (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11). This selective inhibition results in the accumulation of acetylated histones H3 and H4, thereby maintaining a relaxed chromatin state that is permissive for transcription. The proposed inflammatory stress in RPE cells—induced by tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)—is thought to lead to the recruitment of HDAC1/2 to promoters of tight junction genes such as TJP1, OCLN, and CLDN19, effectively silencing their expression through histone deacetylation (Hanikoglu et al., 2018, pp. 2–3; Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 8–10). By inhibiting HDAC1/2, MS-275 is expected to restore global histone acetylation levels, thereby reactivating transcription of these tight junction genes. The resulting upregulation and stabilization of proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin are hypothesized to reconstruct intercellular junctions and improve transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), which is a measure of barrier integrity (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–9; San José-Enériz et al., 2019, pp. 8–10). This mechanism is supported by extensive biochemical studies in cancer models, where similar epigenetic reprogramming has led to reactivation of silenced genes, although direct data in ocular models remains to be generated (Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34; Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 9–11).

Expected Effect in the Proposed Assay:  
In the experimental model using ARPE-19 cells subjected to TNF-α stress, the central hypothesis is that treatment with 0.5 µM MS-275 will be sufficient to inhibit HDAC1/2 activity and restore histone acetylation at tight junction gene promoters. This, in turn, should lead to a reactivation of transcription for TJP1 (encoding ZO-1), OCLN (encoding occludin), and CLDN19 (encoding claudin-19), resulting in an increased synthesis of these key proteins. As tight junction proteins come back online, the structural integrity of the RPE monolayer is expected to improve, which will be reflected by a significant increase in TEER measurements—quantitatively, it is predicted that junction protein levels might be restored by at least twofold, corresponding to a recovery of barrier function (Zhang et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Ruiz et al., 2015, pp. 2–3). ARPE-19 cells are an established model for studying RPE barrier function and are known to express these tight junction components; thus, the assay is well poised to test whether the epigenetic modulation by MS-275 can counteract the deleterious effects of TNF-α (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 17–18; San José-Enériz et al., 2019, pp. 8–10). Moreover, the selective profile of MS-275 against HDAC1/2 is critical because these isoforms have been directly implicated in the repression of gene transcription in inflammatory contexts (Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–9). Consequently, a restored acetylation pattern is expected to facilitate the re-expression of the tight junction gene set and consequently normalize TEER, which is a proxy for the functional integrity of the RPE barrier (Hanikoglu et al., 2018, pp. 2–3; Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 8–10).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing hypothesis for MS-275 in dry AMD is scientifically intriguing and grounded in a well-established mechanism of epigenetic modulation. One of the principal strengths of MS-275 is its robust clinical characterization in oncology, which provides a wealth of safety and pharmacokinetic information, albeit in cancer patients rather than in an ocular context (Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 2–3; Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Its selective inhibition of HDAC1 and HDAC2 is particularly attractive because these isoforms are known to be involved in the aberrant epigenetic silencing observed under conditions of inflammatory stress, and their inhibition has been shown to restore transcriptionally active chromatin states (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11). Additionally, the reversible nature of epigenetic modifications mediated by HDACs means that therapeutic intervention can potentially restore normal gene expression patterns without permanently altering the genomic landscape, an advantage that is particularly relevant in chronic diseases such as dry AMD (Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34; Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 1–2).

However, there are notable challenges as well. Although MS-275 has a well-defined mechanism in cancer, there is a lack of direct preclinical data supporting its use in ocular diseases, and specifically in models of RPE tight junction disruption. This represents a significant gap in the literature that would need to be addressed through targeted studies in ocular cell lines and animal models. Furthermore, MS-275’s pharmacokinetic profile, which has been characterized in the context of systemic cancer therapy, may not directly translate to effective drug delivery or retention in ocular tissues. For instance, issues such as blood–retina barrier penetration, potential ocular toxicity, and the need for specialized formulation strategies (e.g., local delivery through intravitreal injection or topical administration) are important considerations that have not yet been systematically evaluated for this compound (Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 2–3; Ruiz et al., 2015, pp. 1–2). In addition, the broad spectrum of gene reactivation induced by HDAC inhibition may carry the risk of off-target effects, and while the selective inhibition of HDAC1/2 is a strength in terms of targeted epigenetic modulation, chronic inhibition of these enzymes could potentially disrupt normal cellular functions in the retina if not carefully controlled (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11).

Another weakness is the variability inherent in the clinical data for MS-275 observed in oncology, where interpatient differences and dose-dependent toxicities (such as gastrointestinal, hematologic, and metabolic abnormalities) have been reported (Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34; Weber, 2015, pp. 33–34). Although these adverse effects were generally considered manageable in the cancer setting, the risk–benefit balance for treatment of a chronic, non-lethal condition like dry AMD would have to be carefully re-evaluated. It is also worth noting that while MS-275’s epigenetic mechanism is promising for restoring tight junction gene expression, the complex interplay of inflammatory cytokines and multiple HDAC isoforms in the RPE may require combinatorial approaches or more selective targeting strategies than those currently afforded by MS-275 (McCabe, 2019, pp. 23–27; Hanikoglu et al., 2018, pp. 2–3).

In conclusion, MS-275 (Entinostat) presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its established epigenetic mechanism, clinical profile in oncology, and the plausible hypothesis that HDAC1/2 inhibition in RPE cells under inflammatory stress can restore tight junction integrity. Its strengths lie in its synthetic origin, clear mechanism of increasing histone acetylation, and potential to reactivate genes suppressed by pro-inflammatory signaling. However, significant preclinical research is needed to validate its efficacy and safety in ocular models, to optimize its delivery to retinal tissues, and to ensure that its broad effects on gene expression do not result in adverse outcomes when used chronically in a non-oncologic context (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11; Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34; Zhang et al., 2015, pp. 2–3). Overall, while the candidate is promising, a cautious, step-wise approach involving detailed in vitro and in vivo studies in ocular systems is warranted before advancing to clinical trials for dry AMD (Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; San José-Enériz et al., 2019, pp. 8–10; Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 9–11).

I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SMER28 is a small‐molecule enhancer of autophagy originally identified through high‐throughput chemical screens designed to activate intracellular clearance pathways. It is chemically characterized as a bromo‐substituted quinazoline and belongs to a series of “SMER” compounds initially disclosed by leading research institutions to augment autophagy independently of mTOR signaling (Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013; Sarkar & Rubinsztein, 2008). The synthesis of SMER28 has been streamlined into a three‐step process using accessible reagents such as 2-amino-5-bromobenzoic acid and 1,1′-carbonyldiimidazole (CDI), facilitating its large-scale preparation without requiring extensive purification of intermediates (Koukourakis et al., 2018). Originally, SMER28 was discovered during efforts to identify compounds that could promote autophagy and protein clearance, a focus that later expanded its potential use to diseases characterized by proteostatic stress. Its structure–activity relationships and ease of synthesis render SMER28 an attractive candidate for drug repurposing strategies beyond its initial applications, particularly in diseases where defective autophagy contributes to pathogenesis. This candidate’s established role in enhancing cellular clearance mechanisms positions it well for evaluation in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a condition marked by impaired removal of misfolded proteins and lipids in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Doulatov et al., 2017; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013).

II. Therapeutic History  
SMER28 has an extensive preclinical history that underscores its potential for broad therapeutic applications. In initial studies focused on Diamond-Blackfan Anemia (DBA), SMER28 was shown to promote erythropoiesis and enhance hemoglobin expression in both in vitro systems and zebrafish models of DBA, where ribosomal protein mutations lead to anemia-like phenotypes (Doulatov et al., 2017). These findings indicated that SMER28 could effectively modulate cellular differentiation and survival pathways in stressed cell populations. Subsequent investigations expanded its evaluation to radioprotection, where SMER28 demonstrated protective effects in mouse bone marrow and liver tissues subjected to irradiation. These studies revealed that SMER28’s activation of autophagy could preserve normal tissue architecture and improve recovery after cellular injury (Koukourakis et al., 2018). Furthermore, in models of neurodegenerative diseases, SMER28 has been implicated in enhancing both autophagic and proteasomal clearance mechanisms to reduce the burden of misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins such as mutant huntingtin and polyQ-expanded proteins (Wrobel, Hill, & Rubinsztein, 2023). Although none of these prior studies were conducted directly in ocular tissues, their outcomes suggest that the underlying mechanism of SMER28—enhancement of the intracellular degradation machinery—is broadly applicable. Given that the RPE in dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and lipid deposits due to defective autophagy (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021), repurposing SMER28 for dry AMD addresses a significant disease mechanism while potentially leveraging its established safety and efficacy in other systems.

III. Mechanism of Action  
SMER28’s mechanism of action is defined by its ability to induce autophagy in an mTOR-independent manner—a key advantage over conventional autophagy modulators that act via mTOR inhibition. At the molecular level, SMER28 binds directly to the Valosin Containing Protein (VCP/p97), an essential chaperone involved in protein quality control and degradation pathways (Wrobel et al., 2022). This binding stabilizes VCP and stimulates its D1 ATPase activity, thereby enhancing both the formation and maturation of autophagosomes. An increase in VCP activity is known to promote the formation of phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI(3)P), a lipid mediator critical for the nucleation of autophagic vesicles (Wrobel et al., 2022). Downstream of PI(3)P production, the assembly of the lipidation machinery—including LC3, a ubiquitin-like protein requisite for autophagosome elongation—is enhanced, as indicated by increased LC3-II formation in cells treated with SMER28 (Wrobel et al., 2022).

Simultaneously, SMER28’s action is dependent on Beclin 1, whose involvement in autophagy initiation further supports the autophagic flux observed upon treatment (Wrobel et al., 2022). Importantly, these effects are achieved without a detectable alteration in the downstream effectors of mTOR signaling; measurements of AKT activation and other mTOR-related pathways remain unaffected, affirming the compound’s mTOR-independent operation (Wrobel et al., 2022; Koukourakis et al., 2018). In parallel, the compound also appears to enhance the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), an additional degradation pathway, in a manner that is similarly VCP-dependent (Wrobel, Hill, & Rubinsztein, 2023). The convergence of autophagy and UPS pathways is particularly relevant in cellular systems where proteostasis is compromised.

While there is robust evidence supporting the activation of autophagic flux via VCP and Beclin 1, the specific hypothesis for dry AMD posits that SMER28 may also engage ULK1-dependent autophagy mechanisms. ULK1 (UNC-51-like kinase 1) is a serine/threonine kinase upstream in the autophagy cascade that integrates stress signals to initiate autophagy, and genetic ablation of ULK1 or ATG5 has been shown to replicate RPE barrier defects (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015). However, the current literature does not provide direct evidence linking SMER28 with ULK1 activation; rather, the bulk of mechanistic data implicates the compound in VCP-mediated processes (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013). Despite this gap, the overall mode of action—enhancing autophagic and proteasomal clearance pathways while bypassing mTOR—remains firmly established. Thus, SMER28 targets a network of molecular interactions, pivoting on the modulation of VCP’s activity, increased PI(3)P production, and subsequent LC3 lipidation, all of which consolidate its role as an effective autophagy inducer (Wrobel et al., 2022).

IV. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of SMER28 in dry AMD is that its administration will lead to activation of autophagy in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, thereby promoting the clearance of accumulated lipids and misfolded proteins at cell–cell contacts. In dry AMD, the RPE exhibits dysfunctional autophagy, which contributes to the accumulation of toxic compounds such as A2E—a lipofuscin precursor known to induce oxidative stress and compromise cellular architecture (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014). By facilitating the removal of these deleterious aggregates, SMER28 is expected to alleviate proteostatic and lipotoxic stress within the RPE.

Although most studies elucidating SMER28’s effects have been performed in non-ocular systems, the mechanistic insights gained can be extrapolated to the RPE environment. Specifically, SMER28’s ability to increase LC3 lipidation and enhance autophagic flux—as evidenced by changes in LC3-II levels and Beclin 1 dependency—offers a promising strategy for reducing intracellular lipid droplets and misfolded protein aggregates (Wrobel et al., 2022). This improved clearance should, in turn, restore proper intracellular communication and protein homeostasis near cell–cell junctions.

A critical consequence of this process is the anticipated reassembly of tight junction proteins, particularly ZO-1 and occludin. These proteins are essential for maintaining barrier integrity in the RPE, and their disassembly under stress conditions leads to a decrease in trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a surrogate marker for barrier function (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015). By reducing the cellular burden of lipid and protein aggregates, SMER28 may enable the reformation of ZO-1 and occludin belts at cell–cell contacts, thereby improving TEER. Although direct measurements of ZO-1 and occludin reassembly following SMER28 treatment have not been detailed in the existing literature, analogous improvements in tight junction morphology have been observed in other proteostatic and neurodegenerative models where SMER28 enhanced cellular protein clearance (Wrobel, Hill, & Rubinsztein, 2023).

Furthermore, SMER28’s mTOR-independent nature is expected to confer a selective therapeutic advantage. Unlike mTOR inhibitors, which often exert widespread metabolic effects that could be harmful in chronic conditions, SMER28’s mechanism minimizes the risk of systemic side effects while still promoting the clearance of pathogenic intracellular substrates (Wrobel et al., 2022). In the proposed assay, RPE cells challenged with A2E or other proteostatic stressors would ideally show increased markers of autophagy (e.g., LC3-II accumulation, reduced p62 levels) alongside functional restoration of barrier properties as measured by TEER assays. The improvement in barrier integrity is expected to reflect not only the biochemical clearance of toxic aggregates but also structural reorganization at intercellular junctions—a dual benefit that addresses key pathogenic features of dry AMD (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021).

Additionally, the genetic correlations drawn from studies where knockdown of crucial autophagy regulators such as ULK1 or ATG5 leads to RPE barrier defects further support the notion that pharmacological enhancement of autophagy may reverse such phenotypes. Although direct evidence linking SMER28 with ULK1 activation in RPE cells is sparse, the overall strategy of boosting autophagic flux to restore cellular homeostasis remains compelling (Davis, 2015; Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021). In summary, SMER28 is expected to work by reducing intracellular accumulations of harmful proteins and lipids, promoting the reassembly of ZO-1 and occludin at cell–cell contacts, and improving TEER under conditions that mimic the stress found in dry AMD.

V. Overall Evaluation  
SMER28 presents several compelling strengths as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, yet it also faces challenges that must be addressed through further targeted research.

Strengths:  
One of the foremost strengths of SMER28 is its robust ability to induce autophagy through mechanisms independent of mTOR inhibition. This property is vital because mTOR inhibitors, while effective at promoting autophagic activity, can induce broad, deleterious metabolic effects not well tolerated in chronic conditions such as AMD (Wrobel et al., 2022). By bypassing mTOR, SMER28 offers a more selective approach that focuses on enhancing intracellular clearance pathways while maintaining the overall metabolic balance. The molecular interactions it engages—predominantly through binding and activating VCP/p97, stimulating the production of PI(3)P, and driving LC3 lipidation—are well documented in several studies (Wrobel et al., 2022). This dual modulation of both autophagic and proteasomal pathways not only promotes protein aggregate clearance but also potentially addresses the accumulation of toxic lipids, which is central to AMD pathogenesis.

The extensive preclinical data supporting SMER28’s efficacy in models of Diamond-Blackfan Anemia, radioprotection, and neurodegenerative diseases offers reassurance regarding its safety profile and mechanism of action (Doulatov et al., 2017; Koukourakis et al., 2018; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013; Sarkar & Rubinsztein, 2008). The compound’s success in these diverse models underscores its versatility and hints at its capacity to produce similar benefits in the RPE, a tissue highly sensitive to proteostatic imbalances. Furthermore, its inclusion in the SMER series—where analogous molecules have been effective in clearing aggregation-prone proteins in neurodegeneration—adds credence to the hypothesis that SMER28 could alleviate the intracellular debris that contributes to dry AMD (Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013; Sarkar & Rubinsztein, 2008).

Weaknesses:  
Despite the promising attributes outlined above, significant gaps in the current literature present challenges for the immediate repurposing of SMER28 for dry AMD. The most notable gap lies in the lack of direct evidence concerning its effects on RPE cells, specifically regarding the reassembly of tight junction proteins like ZO-1 and occludin. The hypothesis that SMER28 will restore TEER by promoting the reformation of these junctional complexes is logically sound given the role of autophagy in RPE homeostasis (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014), yet direct mechanistic and functional data in ocular models remain sparse.

Moreover, while the literature robustly supports a mechanism involving VCP/p97 and subsequent autophagic flux, there is currently no conclusive evidence establishing that SMER28 activates ULK1-dependent autophagy within RPE cells. Studies have indicated that SMER28 predominantly functions via VCP-mediated pathways and enhances LC3 lipidation without evidence of direct ULK1 or ATG5 activation (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013). Given that genetic knockdown of ULK1 and ATG5 replicates detrimental RPE barrier defects, the absence of clear data on SMER28’s influence on these upstream regulators introduces uncertainty regarding the full scope of its autophagic modulation in the context of dry AMD.

Another potential weakness is the translatability of findings from non-ocular systems to the RPE environment. The RPE is a highly specialized cell type with unique metabolic requirements and structural features. Its reliance on constant autophagic turnover to manage oxidative stress and lipid accumulation means that interventions must be finely tuned. Although SMER28’s impact on proteostasis in other tissues is well established, its precise effects on RPE cell physiology—especially under circumstances of A2E-induced stress—must be rigorously validated through dedicated in vitro and in vivo studies.

In addition, most of the supportive studies for SMER28 have been conducted in contexts of systemic or neurodegenerative challenges rather than in ocular models. This necessitates caution when extrapolating positive outcomes from models of Diamond-Blackfan Anemia or radioprotection to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Doulatov et al., 2017; Koukourakis et al., 2018). The hypothesis that SMER28 will facilitate the reassembly of ZO-1/occludin belts and restore TEER, while promising, remains speculative until confirmed by functional assays in RPE cell cultures and suitable animal models of AMD.

Overall, SMER28 combines a favorable mechanism of action with a promising preclinical safety and efficacy record that renders it an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its selective activation of autophagic clearance pathways without engaging mTOR minimizes potential off-target effects, making it particularly suitable for chronic administration in age-related diseases. However, critical unanswered questions regarding its direct impact on RPE barrier function, particularly the reassembly of tight junction proteins and TEER restoration, must be addressed in future studies (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014; Davis, 2015). Moreover, the putative involvement of ULK1-dependent autophagy in SMER28’s mechanism remains to be definitively characterized in ocular models (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019).

In conclusion, while SMER28 has yet to be directly evaluated in ocular systems, its strong mechanistic foundation—as evidenced by its ability to enhance autophagy and proteasomal clearance via VCP stimulation, LC3 lipidation, and Beclin 1 dependency—supports its potential utility in mitigating the autophagic deficits observed in dry AMD (Wrobel et al., 2022). The anticipated clearance of lipid droplets and misfolded proteins, combined with the potential for facilitating the reassembly of ZO-1 and occludin at cell–cell junctions, collectively addresses two critical aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis. Consequently, SMER28 emerges as a promising candidate with significant potential to restore RPE function and barrier integrity, provided that future empirical studies confirm these effects in the appropriate ocular models (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015; Koukourakis et al., 2018).

As an expert drug development team leader evaluating novel therapeutic candidates, I recommend progressing SMER28 to the next stage of rigorous, mechanism-focused preclinical studies using RPE cell cultures and relevant animal models of dry AMD. Emphasis should be placed on detailed analyses of autophagic flux, ULK1 activation status, and the integrity of tight junction reassembly under conditions of A2E-induced or proteostatic stress. This targeted approach will help clarify SMER28’s full mechanistic profile in RPE cells and validate its potential to restore TEER and overall barrier function, thereby establishing its viability as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD (Wrobel et al., 2022; Davis, 2015).

Overall, SMER28 stands out due to its mTOR-independent autophagy induction, dual engagement of autophagic and proteasomal pathways, and a well-established preclinical background in diverse stress models, all of which offer promising avenues for counteracting the cellular dysfunctions underlying dry AMD. Nonetheless, further studies are essential to bridge the current knowledge gap regarding its specific effects on ULK1-dependent autophagy and tight junction reassembly in RPE cells, which are fundamental for achieving the desired therapeutic outcomes in dry AMD (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019; Davis, 2015).

While the theoretical framework suggests that SMER28 may ameliorate the proteostatic and lipotoxic stress impairing RPE function—thereby restoring the reassembly of ZO-1/occludin belts and improving TEER—the success of this therapeutic strategy will ultimately depend on empirical validation in ocular-specific studies. Given the convergence of mechanistic insights, preclinical efficacy in multiple models, and the compelling need for improved therapeutic strategies in dry AMD, SMER28 merits prioritization for further research. Its progression into RPE-based studies could potentially pave the way for a new class of autophagy-modulating, mTOR-independent therapeutics aimed at restoring RPE function and halting the progression of dry AMD, thereby offering hope for improved outcomes in this prevalent cause of vision loss (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015; Koukourakis et al., 2018).
