Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
5‐Azacytidine is a synthetically produced nucleoside analogue of cytidine originally derived by chemical modification of the natural ribonucleoside. In 5‐azacytidine the normal carbon atom at the 5‐position of the pyrimidine ring is replaced with a nitrogen atom, a modification that critically alters its biochemical properties. This compound is classified as an azanucleoside and has been widely studied as a DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) inhibitor. Its discovery and subsequent synthesis have enabled researchers to interrogate the role of DNA methylation in gene regulation. In its typical biological usage, after cellular uptake mediated by nucleoside transporters, 5‐azacytidine is phosphorylated by cellular kinases into its active triphosphate form (5‐aza‐CTP) and can become incorporated into RNA as well as into DNA, although only around 10–20% is converted to the deoxyribonucleotide form prior to DNA incorporation. This unique feature is a double‐edged sword: on one hand, it allows modulation of cytosine methylation patterns within genomic DNA by trapping DNMTs; on the other, its incorporation into RNA can perturb protein synthesis and contributes to its cytotoxic profile. Chemically, its structure and mode of synthesis place it within a well‐characterized class of antimetabolite agents whose utility extends beyond oncology into other fields where epigenetic modifications are implicated (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, 5‐azacytidine and its deoxy analogue 5‐aza‐2′‐deoxycytidine (decitabine) were first developed as antimetabolite chemotherapy agents for hematologic malignancies. Their clinical utility in treating conditions such as myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) is well established, with DNA demethylation and tumor suppressor gene reactivation being central to their antineoplastic efficacy. Over the years, the successful repurposing of these nucleoside analogues has led to extensive studies investigating their potential effects beyond oncology. In cancer cells, the irreversible binding of DNMT enzymes to DNA following incorporation of 5‐azacytidine has been shown to produce passive demethylation during cell division and consequent gene reactivation (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). In more recent years, researchers have begun to consider the roles of aberrant DNA methylation in non‐cancer diseases, including ocular pathologies like age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). Reviews in ocular epigenetics have noted that epigenetic dysregulation, including hypermethylation of promoters for antioxidant enzymes and other protective genes, may contribute to RPE dysfunction in AMD (Li et al., 2020). For instance, studies in cultured RPE cells and AMD cybrid models have observed tolerability of DNMT inhibitors, as exemplified by experiments where polarized RPE monolayers treated with 5‐aza‐2′‐deoxycytidine showed no significant disruption in barrier markers such as ZO‐1 or cytokeratin, and even demonstrated gene reactivation effects such as upregulation of clusterin (Li et al., 2020). At the molecular level, 5‐azacytidine exerts its pharmacologic actions primarily through inhibition of DNMT enzymes. Under normal physiological conditions, DNMT enzymes bind to cytosine residues in CpG dinucleotides and catalyze the transfer of a methyl group from S‐adenosyl-L‐methionine (SAM) to the 5‐position carbon of cytosine, a process that is essential for the maintenance of epigenetic patterns and gene silencing. Consequently, when 5‐azacytidine is incorporated into the DNA of replicating cells, DNMT enzymes – particularly the maintenance methyltransferase DNMT1 – are unable to complete the methylation reaction and become covalently trapped at the site of incorporation (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). This irreversible trapping inhibits the recycling of DNMTs and leads to their proteasomal degradation, thus reducing the cellular pool of active DNMT enzymes. In subsequent rounds of DNA replication, the absence of sufficient DNMT activity results in passive demethylation of newly synthesized DNA strands that fail to be remethylated. This epigenetic reprogramming can lead to reactivation of genes with previously hypermethylated and silenced promoters (Cheishvili et al., 2015; Palii et al., 2008). It is important to note that 5‐azacytidine is also incorporated into RNA, where it may inhibit RNA methylation and alter translation; however, the therapeutic emphasis in the context of reactivating silenced genes typically focuses on its DNA‐mediated effects. Parallel functional assays, such as TEER measurements and FITC-dextran permeability assays, must be undertaken to correlate molecular events with phenotypic restoration of barrier function (Mukhtar, 2020; Daifuku, 2025).

In addition, it would be prudent to perform dose–response studies to delineate the optimal concentration of 5‐azacytidine that maximizes promoter demethylation and gene reactivation while minimizing off-target cytotoxicity. Considering that RPE cells in vitro may exhibit different proliferative rates compared to their in vivo counterparts, alternative experimental models, such as induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells from AMD patients, may provide additional insights into the therapeutic window and efficacy of 5‐azacytidine in a clinically relevant context. Finally, given that the global nature of epigenetic reprogramming may lead to unintended activation of other cellular pathways, combination strategies employing lower doses of 5‐azacytidine alongside more targeted epigenetic modulators—such as selective HDAC inhibitors—could be explored to enhance the specificity of gene reactivation and improve overall retinal safety (Li et al., 2020; Nashine & Kenney, 2020).

In summary, 5‐azacytidine represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD through a novel epigenetic precision approach aimed at reversing the aberrant methylation of tight junction gene promoters. Its well‐characterized mechanism of DNMT inhibition and widespread use in oncology offer a strong biological rationale. However, significant challenges remain, including its non‐selective incorporation into nucleic acids, potential off‐target effects, reliance on cellular proliferation for optimal activity, and a narrow therapeutic index that necessitates rigorous dose optimization. The feasibility of restoring tight junction integrity in RPE cells via demethylation of OCLN and TJP1 promoters is theoretically sound yet awaits empirical confirmation in preclinical AMD models. Overall, while the candidate has substantial mechanistic strengths that support its potential role in restoring RPE barrier function under oxidative stress conditions, its development as a treatment for dry AMD will require detailed molecular and functional validations, careful safety profiling, and perhaps the exploration of combination therapies to harness its benefits while mitigating risks (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020; Daifuku, 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate generated from the glucosinolate glucoraphanin by the β-thioglucosidase myrosinase, which is abundant in cruciferous vegetables (notably broccoli sprouts). Its electrophilic –N=C=S moiety underlies covalent reactivity with nucleophilic cysteines on sensor proteins, most prominently Keap1, and thereby triggers a broad antioxidant and cytoprotective transcriptional response controlled by Nrf2 (NFE2L2) via antioxidant response elements (AREs) in gene promoters (phase-2 enzymes, redox systems, and detoxification pathways) (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). In retinal and epithelial contexts, SFN has been repeatedly characterized as an “indirect antioxidant” that elevates glutathione (GSH) and induces ARE-dependent enzymes such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1/HMOX1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and thioredoxin (Trx1), among others (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Tanito et al., 2005; Liu & Yan, 2018). In human RPE-derived cell models, SFN increased GSH and induced NQO1 and GST, consistent with canonical ARE program activation (Zhou et al., 2006). In vivo ocular models show SFN attenuates retinal light damage and improves functional outcomes, further anchoring its relevance to oxidative injury in the outer retina and RPE (Tanito et al., 2005; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Within its class, SFN is a prototypical dietary electrophile that activates Nrf2 signaling; this class has been broadly studied for chemoprevention and cytoprotection across organs. In ocular tissues, SFN has been shown to protect RPE and photoreceptors from diverse oxidative and phototoxic insults, often in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Yang et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025). Beyond Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α cross-talk, PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ stress-response nodes, and autophagy/lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs (TFEB/TFE3), all of which intersect with oxidative, inflammatory, and proteostasis stress pathways in RPE biology (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025).

Practical development considerations include bioavailability and delivery. Human studies and reviews indicate that the bioactive isothiocyanate is formed from glucoraphanin in a process heavily dependent on myrosinase (plant or microbiota), with documented systemic exposure and biomarker modulation in clinical settings; however, SFN’s oral bioavailability is limited by solubility, first-pass metabolism, and short plasma half-life, posing translational challenges for ocular exposure through blood–ocular barriers (Zhang et al., 2024). Preclinical delivery strategies such as nanoparticle and albumin carrier systems have been proposed to overcome ocular delivery constraints (Zhang et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
SFN and related Nrf2 activators have a long history as cytoprotective agents in preclinical models spanning oncology prevention, vascular and metabolic protection, and neuroprotection. In humans, SFN or broccoli sprout preparations have been administered in controlled trials with documented pharmacodynamic biomarker changes and well-characterized disposition and metabolism; crossover and dose-response studies highlight interconversion with related isothiocyanates (erucin) and underscore the importance of active myrosinase for consistent systemic exposure (Zhang et al., 2024; Qin, 2007). A pilot study detected SFN metabolites in human breast tissue after a single oral broccoli sprout dose, demonstrating tissue penetration to an epithelial compartment and supporting oral bioavailability to peripheral tissues (Qin, 2007). Although multiple clinical contexts are covered in these translational reviews and trials, there are no reported clinical trials of SFN specifically targeting dry AMD or RPE degeneration in the provided material (Zhang et al., 2024).

In ocular systems, the compound’s therapeutic history is robust at the preclinical level. In cultured human RPE, SFN protects against photooxidative injury (A2E/blue light) and chemical oxidants, increases GSH, and induces phase-2 enzymes including NQO1 and GST (Zhou et al., 2006). Microarray and validation work in human RPE-19 cells demonstrate SFN-induced nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and upregulation of thioredoxin-1, with enhanced oxidative stress resistance following H₂O₂ (Ye et al., 2013). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage in mice through ARE-mediated upregulation of thioredoxin (Trx1), and recovers cone function in a model of RPE oxidative stress in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025). SFN also protects rodent retinas from ischemia–reperfusion injury by increasing Nrf2 nuclear accumulation and HO-1 expression; pharmacologic inhibition of HO-1 abolishes protection, causally implicating HO-1 (Pan et al., 2014). In inherited retinal degeneration models (rd10 and tubby), systemic SFN improves retinal function and reduces degeneration, with evidence that ERK signaling and the Trx/TrxR/Nrf2 axis mediate effects in some settings (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Comparable ocular benefits have been shown in non-RPE tissues. For example, human corneal endothelial FECD cells exhibit SFN-induced Nrf2 nuclear translocation and upregulation of canonical ARE genes (NQO1, HO-1), with reduced ROS and apoptosis (Ziaei et al., 2013). In corneal surface epithelium, SFN protects against oxidative stress via Nrf2/HO-1 activation, supporting generalizability across ocular epithelial cell types (Liu & Yan, 2018). These data reinforce the core mechanism and pharmacology relevant to RPE while underlining the absence of AMD-specific clinical translation to date (Zhang et al., 2024).

Notably, although there is a recent report in an inflamed ARPE-19 model that vitamin D and SFN (alone and combined) reduced ROS, reduced IL-6/IL-8, lowered VEGF, and restored epithelial integrity markers including ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression, the provided material does not include functional barrier endpoints (TEER or FITC-dextran permeability), and claudin-1 is not shown (Bergandi et al., 2024). Thus, while “marker restoration” has been reported for ZO-1 and claudin-4 under TGF-β stress, quantitative barrier function restoration has not yet been demonstrated within the provided sources (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary mechanism—Keap1 cysteine targeting and Nrf2 activation: SFN’s electrophilic isothiocyanate group reacts with redox-sensitive cysteines on Keap1 (notably Cys151), disrupting the Cul3–Keap1 E3 ligase complex and stabilizing Nrf2, which accumulates and translocates to the nucleus. There, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences to upregulate a broad enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant and detoxification program (e.g., NQO1, HO-1, GSTs, GCLM, Trx1, SRXN1), increasing cellular reductive capacity (GSH pools, thiol buffering) and restoring redox homeostasis under oxidative stress (Chang et al., 2020; Ziaei et al., 2013; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). In RPE models, SFN does not consistently increase Nrf2 transcription but promotes nuclear translocation and DNA-binding activity, consistent with post-translational stabilization and activation; ARE target induction follows (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). In ARPE-19, SFN preconditioning increases NQO1 mRNA/activity, boosts cellular GSH, and increases GST activity; microarray and validation data add induction of SRXN1, GCLM, and Trx1 with concurrent Txnip downregulation, aligning with amplified reductive and detoxification capacity (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Under t-BHP stress, SFN increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, elevates NQO1, GR, and GPx1 transcripts, and drives HO-1, NQO1, and GR protein induction (with partial discordance between GPx1 mRNA and protein), while reducing proinflammatory ICAM-1 and MCP-1 (Chang et al., 2020).

Nrf2-dependent ocular efficacy: In vivo, SFN protection from retinal ischemia–reperfusion requires HO-1, as HO-1 inhibition reverses neuroprotection (Pan et al., 2014). In a model of RPE oxidative stress in middle-aged mice, SFN restores cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, underscoring that Nrf2 is the mechanistic driver in that age-relevant retinal context (Falcão et al., 2025).

Nrf2-independent and auxiliary mechanisms: RPE protection is not exclusively Nrf2-dependent. SFN has been shown to promote mitochondrial fusion and reduce Drp1-mediated fission, conferring anti-apoptotic benefit even in CRISPR/Cas9 Nrf2-depleted RPE cells (RPE-1), indicating a parallel mitochondrial protective program (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). SFN also engages the PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ axis: SFN or its metabolites can blunt damage-induced PARylation via direct PARP1 interactions, alleviating SIRT1 inhibition, promoting autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis, and decreasing inflammation in RPE models (Wang & Tang, 2022). In blue light–exposed RPE, SFN activates the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 axis, upregulates HO-1 and thioredoxin-1, blocks NF-κB nuclear translocation, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, and enhances autophagy, all contributing to cytoprotection; Nrf2 inhibition abrogates SFN’s protective effect in this system (Yang et al., 2021). SFN can also activate lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs that mitigate oxidative stress; KEAP1–NRF2 cross-talk with TFEB/TFE3 and macroautophagy has been documented, offering a mechanistic link between Nrf2 activation and proteostasis/autophagy enhancement relevant to RPE degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025).

Anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic effects: Across RPE models, SFN suppresses proinflammatory mediators and pathways (e.g., reduces ICAM-1 and MCP-1; inhibits NF-κB activation), and in TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19 reduces VEGF secretion, which is relevant to para-inflammatory remodeling in AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024). These effects likely contribute to preservation of junctional homeostasis by dampening cytokine-driven disruption.

Cell-type and context dependence: SFN response varies by cell type, stressor, and age-dependent pathway integrity. In some models, HO-1 mRNA is not induced even when protein rises, and under reduced Nrf2 function (as may occur in aged RPE), SFN efficacy can be limited, indicating a dependence on intact Nrf2 signaling and potential post-transcriptional regulation (Chang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Dosing and context also matter: low micromolar SFN protects RPE under oxidative stress, whereas very high concentrations can be deleterious in vitro (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Evidence for barrier-relevant endpoints: The provided sources do not present RPE TEER or FITC-dextran permeability data for SFN, and do not demonstrate claudin-1 induction in RPE (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024). One in vitro ARPE-19 TGF-β model reports that SFN (alone and with vitamin D) restores expression of ZO-1 and claudin-4 suppressed by TGF-β, reduces ROS and VEGF, and decreases proinflammatory cytokines; however, functional permeability or TEER measures were not included, and claudin-1 was not assessed (Bergandi et al., 2024). Therefore, SFN’s capacity to restore RPE barrier function remains mechanistically plausible—through redox normalization, suppression of inflammatory junctional disruption, and potential transcriptional effects on junctional proteins—but is not directly proven by barrier-function assays in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Assay context and rationale: The proposed assays—RPE monolayers subjected to A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ oxidative injury—interrogate oxidative stress pathways central to dry AMD pathophysiology and RPE barrier integrity. A2E/blue light models replicate lipofuscin-photosensitized oxidative injury; NaIO₃ models RPE oxidative cytotoxicity. In both settings, ROS accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, cytokine induction, and downstream tight-junction disruption degrade barrier integrity. The expectation is that SFN will activate Nrf2, increase reductive and detoxifying capacity (GSH, NQO1, HO-1, Trx1, GST), suppress NF-κB–driven inflammation, stabilize mitochondrial function, and secondarily preserve or restore tight-junction protein expression and continuity, resulting in improved TEER and reduced macromolecular flux (FITC-dextran) across the RPE monolayer.

Support for oxidative injury protection in RPE: In A2E/blue light–injured ARPE-19 monolayers, SFN preconditioning increases cell survival, elevates GSH, and induces NQO1 and GST—outcomes mechanistically consistent with improved tolerance to phototoxic oxidative stress (Zhou et al., 2006). In RPE challenged by chemical oxidants (t-BHP, H₂O₂), SFN reduces ROS, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, and induces NQO1, HO-1 (protein), GR, and GPx1 transcripts while suppressing ICAM-1 and MCP-1, thereby addressing both oxidative and inflammatory drivers of junctional disruption (Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013).

Support for HO-1/Nrf2 and auxiliary pathways: Under blue-light exposure, SFN activates Nrf2 and HO-1 in RPE with evidence of mechanistic necessity (Nrf2 inhibitor blocks protection), promotes autophagy (LC3BII and p62), and suppresses NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation—all changes that favor barrier preservation by limiting stress signaling and enhancing cellular cleanup mechanisms (Yang et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and RPE oxidative-stress mouse models, SFN-mediated rescue of retinal function depends on Nrf2 and HO-1, supporting the expected relevance of these axes in RPE-derived stress contexts (Pan et al., 2014; Falcão et al., 2025).

Evidence for junctional protein rescue: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, a recent report shows SFN (particularly with vitamin D) restores ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression suppressed by TGF-β, reduces IL-6/IL-8, reduces VEGF, and normalizes respiratory gene overexpression; this supports the expectation that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven loss of epithelial integrity markers (Bergandi et al., 2024). However, the provided material does not report TEER or FITC-dextran for SFN in RPE, and no data are provided for claudin-1 induction or ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity in oxidative (A2E/NaIO₃) models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Thus, while SFN is expected to improve TEER and reduce FITC-dextran flux in A2E or NaIO₃ assays through Nrf2-driven antioxidant enhancement and suppression of inflammatory/junctional injury, this is an unproven extrapolation that requires direct measurement in the proposed models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).

Target expression in RPE: All principal molecular targets are expressed in human RPE. Nrf2 activation and nuclear translocation occur in SFN-treated RPE-19/ARPE-19, with demonstrated induction of NQO1, HO-1 (protein in some contexts), thioredoxin-1, GCLM, and GST, and suppression of Txnip, ICAM-1, and MCP-1, anchoring the feasibility of modulating these axes in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2006). HO-1 induction in RPE is clearly shown under blue-light stress; in vivo retinal protection requires HO-1, reinforcing target relevance to oxidative retinal injury (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014).

Assay caveats: The provided literature does not contain RPE TEER or macromolecular flux data for SFN, nor does it document claudin-1 induction in RPE. Therefore, while SFN is expected to preserve barrier function, success criteria must include de novo demonstration of TEER rescue, FITC-dextran flux reduction, and ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity under A2E or NaIO₃ stress; these are critical data gaps to address in the proposed work (Zhang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic foundation in RPE and retina: SFN is a well-validated Nrf2 activator that increases GSH and induces multiple ARE-dependent genes (NQO1, GSTs, Trx1, GCLM; HO-1 in several ocular contexts) in RPE and retinal models, with reproducible protection against oxidative and phototoxic injury (A2E/blue light; H₂O₂/t-BHP) and anti-inflammatory activity (reduced ICAM-1, MCP-1, NF-κB signaling) (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage, improves ERG outcomes, rescues cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, and protects against ischemia–reperfusion via HO-1—clear evidence that the compound engages relevant biology and can deliver functional benefit in the retina (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2014).  
- Multiple converging protective axes: Beyond KEAP1–Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling, suppresses PARP1 overactivation to preserve NAD+/SIRT1, promotes autophagy/lysosome programs (TFEB/TFE3 linkage), and modulates mitochondrial dynamics (promotes fusion; reduces Drp1-mediated fission) even when Nrf2 is compromised. This polymechanistic profile is advantageous in RPE, where oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy, and inflammation co-drive degeneration (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2021; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).  
- Preliminary evidence for epithelial integrity marker restoration: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, SFN (especially with vitamin D) restored ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression and reduced VEGF, providing the first reported signal that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven epithelial marker loss in an RPE model (albeit without functional barrier assays) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Translational plausibility and human experience: SFN is orally administrable, with documented human systemic exposure and biomarker modulation; myrosinase co-administration enhances bioavailability from glucoraphanin. Although not yet tested clinically in dry AMD, SFN has a favorable translational narrative as a nutraceutical-derived Nrf2 activator with a safety and PD data trail in other indications (Zhang et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and gaps  
- No direct RPE barrier-function data: Across the provided literature there are no TEER or FITC-dextran permeability results for SFN in RPE monolayers, and no quantified immunofluorescence continuity data for ZO-1 or claudin-1 under oxidative stress. The sole report of “restored markers” addresses ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression after TGF-β, not barrier function or claudin-1 (Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024). The proposal’s assertion of TEER rescue and FITC-dextran reduction remains speculative pending direct measurement in A2E or NaIO₃ models (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Uncertain regulation of tight junction gene set: The provided RPE datasets document induction of canonical Nrf2 targets (NQO1, HO-1 in some contexts, Trx1, GCLM, GSTs), but do not demonstrate SFN induction of claudin-1 in RPE. Without evidence that SFN directly upregulates claudin-1 or stabilizes its junctional localization in RPE, the hypothesis of “junction-supporting gene induction” should be reframed as “junction-preserving via redox and anti-inflammatory mechanisms” until proven otherwise (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Delivery and exposure to the RPE: SFN’s solubility, short half-life, and first-pass metabolism limit systemic exposure; blood–ocular barriers further constrain retinal delivery. Several in vivo retinal studies used intraperitoneal dosing, and one report found i.p. more effective than oral for light-damage protection, emphasizing the need to optimize delivery for ocular targets. Nanocarriers and formulation strategies are promising but remain preclinical (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Dependence on Nrf2 competence and context: In models with impaired Nrf2 (potentially mirroring aged RPE), SFN efficacy is reduced; mechanisms such as mitochondrial fusion may provide partial rescue, but translational effect sizes could be diminished in elderly patients with Nrf2 decline. Additionally, gene-level responses show discordances (e.g., HO-1 mRNA vs protein), indicating context- and post-transcriptional control that complicate predictable pharmacodynamics (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity: Some cited studies are from lower-quality journals; while the core mechanistic findings are corroborated by higher-quality work (e.g., IOVS, Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology, PLoS ONE), the barrier-marker restoration report requires independent replication with functional readouts and in primary human RPE to solidify translational credibility (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Bergandi et al., 2024).

Decision implications and next steps  
Given the robust Nrf2/ARE activation, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory efficacy in RPE/retina, and the breadth of auxiliary protective mechanisms, SFN remains a mechanistically precise candidate for RPE oxidative injury relevant to dry AMD. However, the core claim of “barrier restoration” is currently supported only by marker-expression rescue (ZO-1 and claudin-4) in an inflamed ARPE-19 model without functional permeability data, and there is no evidence for claudin-1 induction or barrier rescue in A2E or NaIO₃ models in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). To de-risk the program and validate the hypothesis, the following experiments are mandatory:  
- TEER and FITC-dextran assays in differentiated human RPE (primary or iPSC-RPE) under A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ insult, with SFN dose–response and timing; include positive controls for barrier rescue (e.g., dexamethasone) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Quantitative junctional immunofluorescence (ZO-1, claudin-1, claudin-4, occludin) with continuity analysis; test whether SFN normalizes localization and expression under oxidative/cytokine stress (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Nrf2 pathway necessity tests (ML385, Nrf2 siRNA) and HO-1 inhibition (ZnPP) to define mechanism-of-action in barrier rescue; given HO-1’s necessity in vivo, confirm whether HO-1 contributes to barrier endpoints in RPE (Pan et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2021).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics and autophagy readouts (Drp1, Mfn2, LC3BII/p62) to quantify auxiliary pathways that may mediate barrier preservation when Nrf2 is compromised (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021).  
- PK/PD bridging: quantify SFN (and metabolites) in plasma and ocular tissues after oral vs i.p. dosing in rodents; evaluate delivery systems (e.g., albumin nanocarriers) for RPE exposure; incorporate myrosinase co-administration for oral strategies; relate exposures to effective in vitro EC₅₀s for barrier rescue (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Aged and Nrf2-impaired models: evaluate efficacy in aged RPE or Nrf2-hypomorphic contexts to assess translational robustness (Zhang et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

If TEER and permeability rescue are demonstrated with mechanistic attribution to Nrf2/HO-1 and/or auxiliary pathways, and if ocular PK can be solved to achieve efficacious exposures, SFN would merit progression to in vivo dry AMD–relevant models (e.g., subretinal NaIO₃, chronic photo-oxidative stress) with structural (OCT) and functional (ERG) endpoints, plus RPE barrier imaging, before considering a human proof-of-concept study.

In sum, the totality of evidence strongly supports SFN for oxidative and inflammatory protection of RPE and retina with multiple convergent mechanisms and translational plausibility. The critical missing element is direct demonstration that these effects translate into bona fide RPE barrier restoration (TEER/permeability) under AMD-relevant oxidative stress, and a practical path to deliver sufficient drug to the RPE in humans. Addressing these gaps should be the focus of immediate preclinical validation (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024).

────────────────────────────────────────────', 'answer': 'Proposal for Torin-1 (Tocris 4247; Cayman 11767)

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of Torin-1 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), structured to address its origin, historical use, molecular mechanism, expected therapeutic effects in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, and an overall assessment of its strengths and limitations based solely on the available context.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

Torin-1 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule compound that belongs to the second generation of mTOR inhibitors. Its discovery originated from high-throughput biochemical screening efforts led by Nathanael Gray’s research group, and later advances were carried out in both academic and industrial settings (Ali et al., 2022). Unlike the first-generation mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin and its analogs—agents that inhibit mTOR activity by forming a complex with FKBP12 and acting allosterically—Torin-1 belongs to a class of ATP-competitive inhibitors that target the catalytic site of mTOR directly (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). Chemically, Torin-1 is built on a quinoline or pyrazolopyrimidine core scaffold; such a design was informed by molecular docking studies and X-ray crystallographic analyses that revealed the ability of these scaffolds to form critical hydrogen bonds with residues in the mTOR ATP-binding pocket, notably with Asp2195 and Lys2187 (Ali et al., 2022; He et al., 2017). The compound’s outstanding potency is reflected in its low nanomolar inhibitory concentrations – with reported IC₅₀ values near 2 nM for mTORC1—and its ability to simultaneously inhibit mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) distinguishes it from macrolide-based compounds (Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Schenone et al., 2011). As part of the so-called “TORKinibs,” Torin-1 is representative of a modern strategy in kinase inhibition, leveraging structure-guided design to achieve comprehensive blockade of the mTOR signaling cascade.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

Since its initial discovery, Torin-1 has primarily been employed as a biochemical and cellular tool in preclinical research rather than as a drug that has advanced to the clinical arena. Its potent inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 has allowed researchers to dissect the functional roles of mTOR in diverse cellular processes such as protein synthesis, metabolism, autophagy regulation, and cell cycle progression (Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013). In oncology studies, Torin-1 has been used to demonstrate that complete inhibition of mTOR signaling—especially the blockade of mTORC2, which is seldom affected by allosteric inhibitors—can lead to robust antiproliferative effects and induction of apoptosis in cancer cells (Xie et al., 2016; Amin et al., 2021).

In the retinal space, there is emerging evidence supporting the use of ATP-competitive inhibitors in models of photoreceptor and RPE dysfunction. For example, studies in the rd1 mouse model of retinal degeneration have shown that treatment with Torin-1 results in marked suppression of mTOR phosphorylation; such inhibition correlates with an increase in autophagy markers (elevated LC3B-II/LC3B-I ratio) and consequent neuroprotective effects, including a reduction in photoreceptor apoptosis (Yang et al., 2021). Furthermore, investigations employing human retinal pigment epithelial cells, such as ARPE-19 or transformed RPE lines like hTERT-RPE1, have demonstrated that Torin-1 treatment can effectively promote autophagic flux and exert protective effects under conditions of cellular stress (Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017). Despite promising preclinical data in RPE and retinal degeneration models, Torin-1 has not yet been formally evaluated in clinical trials for dry AMD; rather, previous clinical efforts for AMD have focused on allosteric mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2006; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008). Thus, while Torin-1 itself remains a potent research probe, its clinical utility in ocular diseases awaits further validation.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

At its core, Torin-1 functions by robustly and directly inhibiting mTOR kinase activity through an ATP-competitive mechanism. Unlike rapamycin, which requires the formation of an FKBP12 complex and employs an allosteric mode of inhibition that selectively attenuates mTORC1 activity, Torin-1 enters the catalytic domain of mTOR and competes with ATP for occupancy of the active site (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). Structural studies have detailed that Torin-1 establishes multiple hydrogen bonds within the mTOR pocket—specifically, two hydrogen bonds between its urea NH groups and Asp2195, and one bond involving a carbonyl moiety and Lys2187 (Ali et al., 2022; He et al., 2017). This binding configuration not only accounts for its superior potency (IC₅₀ values as low as 2 nM) but also ensures a high degree of selectivity compared to kinases within the PI3K family (Schenone et al., 2011).

The inhibition of mTOR by Torin-1 leads to immediate downstream consequences. In mTORC1, the blockade results in the complete ablation of S6K phosphorylation, thereby reducing protein synthesis and halting anabolic growth processes. Concurrently, inhibition of mTORC2 is evidenced by decreased phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473, implicating effects on survival signaling (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). One particularly important downstream effect is the release of ULK1 (unc-51-like kinase 1) from mTOR-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation. Under nutrient-rich conditions, active mTOR phosphorylates ULK1 on serine residues (such as Ser758) to prevent its activation, keeping autophagy in check. When mTOR is inhibited by Torin-1, ULK1 is derepressed, allowing it to drive the conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and initiate autophagosome formation (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017). This induction of autophagy plays a central role in the compound’s proposed mechanism in RPE cells, linking enzyme inhibition to the clearance of potentially toxic cellular debris, including complement components that compromise intercellular junctions.

It is also important to note that, given mTOR’s central role in regulating metabolic homeostasis and proteostasis, the dual inhibition of both mTOR complexes by Torin-1 shifts the cellular balance from an anabolic, protein-synthesizing state to a catabolic, degradation-oriented state (Guillem, 2015). In this context, the activation of autophagy via ULK1 is not only a marker of cellular stress response but also a potential mechanism to clear aggregated proteins and damaged organelles that may contribute to disease pathology.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

Dry AMD is characterized by the progressive dysfunction of RPE cells, which is associated with chronic, low-grade complement activation and the deposition of sublytic membrane attack complexes (MAC). In dry AMD, the persistent presence of complement fragments and sublytic MAC can lead to a collapse of the zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) belt that normally maintains tight junction integrity between RPE cells. This disruption is usually accompanied by a decrease in transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a quantitative measure of barrier function, and is thought to contribute to subsequent photoreceptor degeneration.

The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin-1 in dry AMD posits that by completely inhibiting mTOR activity, the compound will relieve the suppression of ULK1, thereby triggering strong autophagic activity in RPE cells. Enhanced autophagy is expected to facilitate the clearance of sublytic MAC deposits and accumulated complement fragments. From in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cell monolayers—a widely accepted model for RPE barrier function—it has been observed that complement C5b-9 challenge provokes a significant (approximately 40%) drop in TEER and disrupts ZO-1 continuity, indicating tight junction breakdown (Vogel et al., 2017). When these cells are concomitantly treated with Torin-1, the compound’s potent, low-nanomolar inhibition of mTOR translates into complete ablation of phosphorylated S6K and a three-fold elevation in LC3-II flux. This biochemical change is accompanied by a restoration of TEER values to approximately 220 Ω·cm², suggesting that the autophagic clearance of toxic complement fragments enables the reestablishment of the ZO-1 junctional belt (Lim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

The exact molecular pathway can be described as follows: upon Torin-1 binding and subsequent mTOR inhibition, phosphorylation of downstream targets including S6K and Akt is halted. This cessation effectively lifts the inhibitory phosphorylation of ULK1, catalyzing its activation. Activated ULK1 initiates autophagy, leading to a conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II, a process that enhances autophagic flux and promotes the degradation of intracellular debris (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017). Within RPE cells under complement attack, this mechanism is hypothesized to specifically clear sublytic MAC deposits; by doing so, the cellular proteostasis is restored, which in turn allows for the reinstitution of normal tight junction architecture – as evidenced by a continuous ZO-1 belt and maintenance of TEER (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021).

Moreover, the effect on TEER is especially critical since the loss of barrier function in RPE cells is an early indicator of dry AMD disease progression. By preserving TEER, Torin-1 is not just engaging in an acute cytoprotective action; it is potentially interrupting the cascade that leads to chronic subretinal degeneration. In this way, Torin-1 may contribute to both the immediate stabilization of the RPE barrier and the longer-term maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Such outcomes would ameliorate one of the central pathogenic events in dry AMD—namely, RPE junctional collapse—and could help prevent the subsequent photoreceptor loss that underlies vision decline (Lim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

From a molecular and mechanistic standpoint, Torin-1 stands as a highly attractive candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its design as a second-generation, ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor confers several major advantages over first-generation rapalogs. Chief among these is its dual inhibition of mTORC1 and mTORC2, which bypasses the incomplete suppression and feedback activation issues that may limit the efficacy of compounds like rapamycin (Amin et al., 2021; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017). This comprehensive blockade enables a robust activation of autophagy via ULK1 de-repression, and—as demonstrated in various preclinical studies—such autophagic stimulation is capable of clearing aggregated proteins and toxic complement fragments in RPE cells (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017).

Preclinical studies using retinal models are supportive. In experiments employing ARPE-19 and hTERT-RPE1 cells, treatment with Torin-1 has been shown to significantly elevate autophagic markers while reducing the phosphorylation status of mTOR downstream effectors, thereby reinforcing its mechanistic rationale (Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017). Furthermore, in animal models such as the rd1 mouse retina, Torin-1 administration has correlated with reduced mTOR phosphorylation and increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratios, suggestive of effective autophagic clearance and neuroprotective benefit (Yang et al., 2021). These observations provide a strong proof-of-concept that robust mTOR inhibition has the potential to restore RPE homeostasis through autophagy, thereby ameliorating complement-induced junctional disruption—a key pathological process in dry AMD.

However, several critical challenges and limitations must be acknowledged before Torin-1 can be advanced as a clinically viable therapeutic for dry AMD. First and foremost are the pharmacokinetic challenges intrinsic to Torin-1. Multiple reports have noted issues related to its poor water solubility, rapid metabolic degradation, and low oral bioavailability (Artoni, 2024; Guillem, 2015). These characteristics make systemic delivery problematic and would likely necessitate the development of specialized ocular formulations—such as intravitreal injections or sustained-release implants—to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina without causing systemic toxicity.

Another potential weakness lies in the broad role of mTOR in regulating cellular homeostasis. While complete inhibition of mTOR (both mTORC1 and mTORC2) is advantageous in achieving a full autophagic response, it also carries the risk of disrupting normal anabolic and survival signaling pathways in off-target tissues (Ainslie et al., 2016; Artoni, 2024). In the retina, where RPE cells must balance metabolic demands with regenerative processes, prolonged or excessive mTOR inhibition could theoretically impair normal cellular functions, leading to unintended adverse effects such as mistargeted autophagy or metabolic insufficiency.

Furthermore, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease. Although complement activation and subsequent deposition of sublytic MAC are central features, other factors—including chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lipid dysregulation—contribute significantly to disease progression. As a result, while Torin-1’s mechanism of activating autophagy and restoring tight junction protein continuity offers considerable promise, it is unlikely that monotherapy with an mTOR inhibitor will comprehensively reverse or halt disease progression. A multidrug approach or combination therapy that targets several pathogenic pathways concurrently might eventually be required (Ainslie et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).

From the standpoint of formulation and manufacturing, Torin-1 presents additional hurdles. The synthetic route to Torin-1 is known for a low overall yield and complex multi-step procedures, which has driven subsequent research efforts toward the development of more drug-like analogues such as Torin-2. These analogues often exhibit improved solubility, stability, and bioavailability, yet switching to an analogue creates a separate set of regulatory and developmental challenges (Cani, 2015; Guillem, 2015). Given that Torin-1 itself has not been engineered explicitly for ocular delivery, significant formulation work will be necessary to convert it into a viable therapeutic candidate that can be safely and effectively administered to the retina.

In addition, although preclinical studies in ARPE-19 monolayers and rodent models provide important insights, the predictive value of these models for human dry AMD remains imperfect. The complexity of dry AMD, encompassing gradual degenerative changes that evolve over many years against a backdrop of systemic aging, calls for further validation in more sophisticated in vivo models that closely replicate human pathology. Such models would need to capture not only the complement-mediated disruption of RPE tight junctions but also the contributions of chronic inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and extracellular matrix alterations. Only through such rigorous evaluations can the long-term efficacy and safety of Torin-1 (or its improved analogues) be accurately ascertained (Ainslie et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).

Finally, it must be acknowledged that repurposing a molecule like Torin-1 for dry AMD represents a significant translational challenge. While its ability to elevate LC3-II flux, clear toxic deposits, and maintain TEER in vitro is compelling, the real-world application in the human retina requires an intricate balance of efficacy, safety, and appropriate drug delivery. Off-target toxicities due to mTOR inhibition in other retinal cell types or adjacent tissues, as well as the systemic exposure risks even in an ocular formulation, must be stringently evaluated through comprehensive preclinical pharmacokinetic and toxicology studies before any clinical trials could be considered.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation and Conclusions

In summary, Torin-1 is a compelling proof-of-concept candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its synthetic origins as an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor, characterized by an exceptional potency (low-nanomolar IC₅₀) and dual inhibition of mTORC1 and mTORC2, offer a robust mechanistic rationale for its use in restoring RPE cell homeostasis (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin-1 leads to a well-documented derepression of ULK1, activation of autophagy, and a consequent increase in LC3-II flux—changes that are central to the clearance of sublytic MAC deposits and other toxic complement fragments (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017). Preclinical evidence from both retinal cell line experiments and rodent models supports the hypothesis that such mechanistic effects can translate into restored tight junction integrity (as measured by maintenance of ZO-1 belt continuity and TEER) under complement challenge conditions (Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021).

The principal strengths of Torin-1 include its unparalleled potency and selectivity for mTOR; its ability to effectively target both mTOR complexes addresses the shortcomings associated with partial mTORC1 inhibition by rapamycin; and its demonstrated capacity to trigger autophagy offers a direct means to remove deleterious protein aggregates and complement components from RPE cells. These attributes are particularly critical in dry AMD, a disease closely tied to chronic complement activation and the accumulation of toxic cellular debris that disrupts epithelial barrier function.

Nevertheless, several notable challenges must be overcome. Torin-1’s inherent pharmacokinetic limitations—specifically its poor water solubility, rapid metabolic degradation, and low bioavailability—pose significant barriers to its clinical translation (Artoni, 2024; Guillem, 2015). Furthermore, the complete inhibition of mTOR achieved by Torin-1, while beneficial for activating autophagy, also raises concerns regarding off-target toxicities in the retina and beyond, given the central role of mTOR in numerous cellular processes including growth, metabolism, and survival (Ainslie et al., 2016; Artoni, 2024). In an organ as delicate and metabolically active as the retina, these issues necessitate the development of advanced drug delivery systems that can confine the therapeutic effects to the target tissue while minimizing systemic exposure. Options such as intravitreal injections, sustained-release platforms, or nanoparticle-based carriers should be carefully explored.

Moreover, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD means that while clearing complement deposits and restoring tight junction integrity via autophagy represents a promising strategy, it is unlikely to address all pathogenic mechanisms simultaneously. Chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lipid dysregulation also play pivotal roles in the disease’s progression. Therefore, Torin-1 may ultimately need to be integrated into a combination therapy regime or be used in conjunction with adjunctive treatments targeting these other processes (Ainslie et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).

From a developmental perspective, it is also important to consider that while Torin-1 has been used extensively as a research tool, its current chemical properties make it less than ideal as a direct clinical candidate. The extensive medicinal chemistry efforts that led to the synthesis of Torin-2—and other improved analogues—underscore the need to optimize the pharmacological attributes, including solubility and metabolic stability, before any clinical application can be realized (Guillem, 2015). Such optimizations, along with rigorous preclinical in vivo efficacy and safety studies in models that recapitulate the chronic and complex nature of human dry AMD, are essential next steps.

In conclusion, based on the current literature presented in the context, Torin-1 demonstrates substantial mechanistic promise for the restoration of RPE proteostasis, barrier integrity, and autophagic clearance of complement-mediated cellular debris in dry AMD. Its strong ATP-competitive inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2, leading to effective ULK1 activation, supports the hypothesis that it can rescue TEER and reestablish ZO-1 continuity in RPE cells exposed to complement C5b-9 challenge (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013). However, significant translational hurdles—principally related to its pharmacokinetic profile, potential off-target effects, and the inherent complexities of dry AMD pathology—must be diligently addressed through further preclinical research.

From an expert drug development perspective, Torin-1 offers robust proof-of-concept evidence that mTOR inhibition can functionally reverse key pathological features of dry AMD in cellular models. The next steps should focus on optimizing its chemical properties or transitioning to an analog with improved drug-like characteristics, as well as developing innovative ocular delivery platforms to ensure targeted retinal exposure. In light of these considerations, while Torin-1 in its current form may serve best as a preclinical tool to validate the therapeutic pathway, further investment in medicinal chemistry, formulation science, and in vivo safety/efficacy studies is warranted before considering clinical evaluation in patients with dry AMD (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013; Amin et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Final Remarks

To summarize, the current data support the concept that robust, ATP-competitive inhibition of mTOR with compounds such as Torin-1 provides a compelling mechanistic foundation for mitigating complement-mediated RPE damage in dry AMD. The dual mTORC1/mTORC2 targeting strategy of Torin-1 enables it to not only suppress pathogenic anabolic signaling but also to trigger autophagy—thereby facilitating the clearance of toxic sublytic MAC deposits and the restoration of RPE tight junctions, as measured by TEER and ZO-1 integrity. Nevertheless, the translational journey from promising in vitro results to an effective clinical treatment is contingent upon the resolution of pharmacokinetic shortcomings, the development of retina-specific delivery strategies, and extensive in vivo validation in models that mirror the human disease.

In light of the above evaluation, Torin-1 stands as a scientifically robust candidate that validates the therapeutic rationale for mTOR inhibition in dry AMD. Its significant strengths in potency and mechanistic clarity are offset by practical challenges that necessitate further research. The pathway forward should thus include efforts to optimize the formulation and drug-like properties of Torin-1 (or its analogues), pair it with appropriate ocular delivery systems, and deploy rigorous preclinical models to establish its long-term efficacy and safety in the context of dry AMD. Only with these additional steps can Torin-1 (or a derivative thereof) mature into a potential treatment option for patients suffering from this chronic and debilitating disease (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013; Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017; Schenone et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2021; Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017).

The ATP-binding pockets of ROCK1 and ROCK2 are highly conserved, which has historically favored development of dual-isoform inhibitors (e.g., fasudil, Y-27632, ripasudil, netarsudil) rather than isoform-selective agents; SAR407899 is listed among this majority class of dual-acting molecules in contemporary reviews of rho-kinase modulators for retinal disease (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Multiple dual ROCK inhibitors have been clinically applied: fasudil is approved systemically for cerebral vasospasm and has been evaluated intravitreally for retinal disease, while ripasudil and netarsudil are approved as topical ophthalmic solutions for glaucoma/ocular hypertension, establishing the translational precedent and safety framework for the class in ocular tissues (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). At a mechanistic level, all members of this class block ROCK catalytic activity by binding to the ATP site, thereby reducing phosphorylation of canonical substrates such as MYPT1 (the myosin phosphatase target subunit) and myosin regulatory light chain (MLC), and decreasing downstream actomyosin tension, stress fibers, and focal adhesion assembly that collectively drive barrier breakdown, contraction, and fibrosis (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). While “soft drug” and kinase-selectivity strategies have been advanced to improve tissue targeting and reduce off-target activity, the broad conclusion from medicinal chemistry and pharmacology reviews is that most clinical-grade ROCK inhibitors remain dual-isoform ATP-competitive agents with some potential for off-target kinase interactions at higher exposures—an interpretive caveat for both efficacy and safety (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Liu et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Direct preclinical or clinical reports on SAR407899 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) or age-related macular degeneration (AMD) were not identified in the provided literature set; the compound is listed among “double-acting ROCK inhibitor molecules” considered for retinal vascular disease, but no SAR407899-specific ocular pharmacokinetic, penetration, or efficacy data are supplied in the excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). In contrast, there is substantial class-level evidence that dual ROCK1/2 inhibition is active in posterior segment disease biology relevant to dry AMD pathogenesis and sequelae (barrier failure, low-grade inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling), and that ROCK pathway blockade by other chemotypes can beneficially modulate RPE/retinal fibrosis and endothelial barrier endpoints across models (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). For endothelial barrier function, ripasudil preserved ZO-1 localization and reversed VEGF-induced TEER loss in human retinal microvascular endothelial cells (HRMECs), and suppressed retinal p-MYPT1 in a murine retinal vein occlusion model, demonstrating target engagement and barrier preservation by ROCK inhibition in retina (albeit on the vascular rather than RPE side of the BRB) (Hida et al., 2018). For RPE morphology and barrier integrity in vivo, intravitreally applied fasudil reversed Rho pathway–driven cytoskeletal abnormalities (apical constriction and stress fibers) and improved RPE barrier integrity in disease-relevant paradigms, establishing that pan-ROCK antagonism can correct RPE junctional dysfunction at the tissue level (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). In fibrotic endpoints applicable to geographic atrophy progression and subretinal scarring, both pan-ROCK (fasudil) and ROCK2-selective (belumosudil) inhibitors reduced canonical fibrosis drivers (TGF-β1, fibronectin, vimentin, α-SMA) and ROCK pathway activity (p-MYPT1) in choroid–RPE complex and retina in vivo, with concomitant preservation of retinal morphology and decreased fibrosis volume in a mouse CNV-associated fibrosis model (Zandi et al., 2025). Additional dual ROCK inhibitors (AMA0428) suppressed angiogenesis, inflammation, and fibrosis in a mouse CNV model more broadly than VEGFR2 blockade alone, underscoring the ability of ROCK pathway inhibition to simultaneously normalize vessels, reduce leakage, and block matrix deposition—features highly relevant to AMD (Hollanders et al., 2015; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Mechanism of Action:  
ROCK1 and ROCK2 are serine/threonine kinases activated by RhoA-GTP that increase cellular contractility and cytoskeletal tension by two concerted mechanisms: (1) direct phosphorylation of myosin regulatory light chain (MLC), and (2) phosphorylation of MYPT1, the regulatory subunit of myosin phosphatase, which inhibits phosphatase activity and sustains high p-MLC; ROCK also signals via LIM kinases to inactivate cofilin, stabilizing actin stress fibers and focal adhesions—all of which favor junctional opening and motile/contractile phenotypes (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). Inflammation intersects ROCK signaling via NF-κB and other pathways: ROCK activity upregulates inflammatory mediators (e.g., NF-κB targets, MCP-1/CCL2, iNOS), and ROCK inhibitors reduce inflammatory cell infiltration and cytokine production in ocular models, further supporting secondary barrier stabilization and anti-fibrotic effects (Singh & Singh, 2023; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). In AMD-relevant immunity, ROCK2-selective signaling is linked to age-related macrophage polarization toward proangiogenic M2 (MaDAMs) in human AMD eyes; ROCK2-selective inhibition improved macrophage phenotype and reduced CNV in models, whereas pan-ROCK fasudil did not share all of these benefits in the immune compartment, suggesting non-redundant isoform roles in the aging choroid–retina milieu (Nourinia et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). These combined data establish a coherent molecular mechanism whereby dual ROCK1/2 inhibition should reduce p-MYPT1/p-MLC, relax actomyosin tension, stabilize junctional complexes (occludin/ZO-1), oppose TGF-β–driven fibrotic conversion, and blunt inflammatory cascades that exacerbate outer BRB failure in dry AMD; however, whether dual versus ROCK2-selective inhibition optimally tunes the immune/fibrotic axis in AMD remains an open question raised by macrophage-focused studies (Nourinia et al., 2018; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Strengths  
- Target validity and mechanistic convergence: ROCK1/2 are central regulators of cytoskeletal tension and tight-junction stability via the MYPT1/MLC and LIMK/cofilin axes, providing a direct mechanistic handle on epithelial barrier integrity and fibrotic conversion relevant to outer BRB failure and atrophic remodeling in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). - RPE-relevant in vivo effect: Intravitreal fasudil reversed RPE cytoskeletal abnormalities and improved epithelial barrier integrity in vivo, demonstrating that the class mechanism extends to outer BRB pathology and is not restricted to vascular endothelial cells (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

- Absence of SAR407899-specific ocular data in RPE/AMD: The provided literature contains no quantitative potency/selectivity corroboration, ocular penetration, retinal tissue levels, or preclinical efficacy for SAR407899 in RPE barrier models, IL-1β paradigms, or AMD models; thus, key assertions in the working hypothesis (e.g., occludin/ZO-1 transcriptional rescue in RPE, primary human RPE TER recovery, ocular PK levels, ERG improvements in NaIO3) are not supported here and cannot be validated from the excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). On the strength of the mechanistic and preclinical class data, dual ROCK1/2 inhibition remains a credible strategy to stabilize RPE junctions and suppress fibrotic conversion in dry AMD; however, SAR407899 must earn its place in this mechanism by producing compound-specific evidence on RPE barrier endpoints and ocular exposure (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Zandi et al., 2025). - In vitro RPE barrier assays: Quantify TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and occludin/ZO-1 localization in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE monolayers under IL-1β and complement co-challenge ± SAR407899; include p-MYPT1 and p-MLC immunoblotting or phospho-ELISA to verify on-target modulation; adopt assay conditions paralleling endothelial TEER paradigms where ROCK inhibition preserved ZO-1 and TEER (Hida et al., 2018; Kaneko et al., 2016).  
- Isoform pharmacology: Use siRNA or selective pharmacologic comparators (e.g., belumosudil for ROCK2) to benchmark dual versus ROCK2-selective effects on RPE barrier rescue and inflammatory readouts, informed by the macrophage polarization literature in AMD (Nourinia et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

- In vivo efficacy: Progress to subretinal fibrosis or oxidative injury models that interrogate outer BRB integrity and fibrotic remodeling (e.g., CNV-associated fibrosis with extended fibrotic endpoints) to test whether SAR407899 reproduces the anti-fibrotic and barrier-preserving signals seen with fasudil/belumosudil, incorporating p-MYPT1 as a pharmacodynamic biomarker (Zandi et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Alagebrium chloride (ALT-711) is a synthetic small molecule designed as an advanced glycation end product (AGE) crosslink breaker. Chemically identified as 3‐phenacyl‐4,5‐dimethylthiazolium chloride, it belongs to the thiazolium salt family—a class noted for its reactivity toward α-dicarbonyl substrates found in AGE crosslinks. Originally developed as an analog of N-phenacylthiazolium bromide (PTB), ALT-711 was synthesized specifically to overcome the instability and in vivo degradation that hampered PTB’s clinical potential, and thus represented a more stable, easily synthesized candidate with retained crosslink-cleaving activity (Alam, Ahsan, & Alam, 2013; Borg & Forbes, 2016). The design rationale capitalized on the unique nucleophilic properties of the thiazolium core—similar in some respects to the vitamin thiamine structure, though it lacks the pyrimidine moiety—to facilitate cleavage of carbon–carbon bonds between protein-bound glycation products, notably interfering with the formation of deleterious cross-links such as those involving pentosidine (Furber, 2010; Coughlan et al., 2007). Over the past two decades, this class of AGE breakers, including ALT-711, has been primarily explored for applications in cardiovascular and diabetic complications, with the underlying therapeutic hypothesis being that reversal of AGE-mediated crosslinking could restore tissue compliance and function (Kim & Spiegel, 2013; Toprak & Yigitaslan, 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
The historical development of alagebrium is rooted in efforts to counteract the progressive accumulation of AGEs—a hallmark of chronic hyperglycemia and aging—that contribute to decreased protein turnover, tissue stiffening, and dysfunction. ALT-711 was developed and advanced by pharmaceutical entities like Alteon Pharmaceuticals (later Synvista Therapeutics) for its ability to reverse AGE-mediated crosslinking in the extracellular matrix, particularly in collagen and elastin-rich tissues (Alam, Ahsan, & Alam, 2013; Velichkova, 2020). Preclinical studies in diabetic rat models demonstrated that ALT-711 not only increased cardiac output and improved left ventricular diastolic function but also reduced arterial stiffening by breaking protein crosslinks, an effect that was correlated with improved vascular compliance (Coughlan et al., 2007; Kim & Spiegel, 2013). In clinical development, ALT-711 progressed through human trials—being evaluated for conditions such as heart failure, systolic hypertension, and vascular stiffening—although its program ultimately faced setbacks due to financial constraints and discontinuation of further clinical studies (Toprak & Yigitaslan, 2019; Vasan et al., 2003). Despite robust preclinical evidence in cardiovascular models, there is no established record of alagebrium being previously used to treat ocular diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); however, the underlying mechanism of AGE crosslink reversal suggests potential utility in tissues that undergo similar AGE-mediated structural changes, like the Bruch’s membrane (BM) of the eye (Krautwald et al., 2011; Nagai et al., 2012).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of action of ALT-711 centers on its ability to cleave AGE-derived protein crosslinks via a nucleophilic reaction targeting α-dicarbonyl moieties within these adducts. In biochemical models, the thiazolium ring of ALT-711 acts by facilitating the hydrolytic cleavage of carbon–carbon bonds that form between juxtaposed carbonyl groups in AGE crosslinks. This cleavage is thought to reduce the irreversible linkages that normally render long-lived extracellular matrix proteins (such as collagen and elastin) resistant to proteolytic degradation, thereby restoring their turnover and normal biomechanical properties (Borg & Forbes, 2016; Coughlan et al., 2007). Additionally, several studies have indicated that ALT-711 may exert secondary effects such as chelation of transition metals, thereby mitigating metal-catalyzed oxidative modifications that fuel further AGE formation (Kim & Spiegel, 2013; Velichkova, 2020). While there remains some controversy regarding the specificity and efficiency of its crosslink-breaking capacity in complex tissue environments, experimental evidence from enzymatic and cellular assays supports its role in reducing crosslink density in collagen matrices (Velichkova, 2020; Yamagishi, 2013). Molecular modeling studies have further delineated that the compound retains structural homologies with thiamine derivatives, and its phenacyl substituent is critical for reactivity, promoting interactions with dicarbonyl groups and facilitating reversible bond cleavage without extensive disruption of peptide backbones (Krautwald et al., 2011; Chen & Tang, 2007). These combined actions—disruption of AGE crosslinks and antioxidant/chelation activity—constitute the basis for its therapeutic potential in tissues rendered pathologically stiff by AGE accumulation.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration, the central hypothesis posits that ALT-711 can act on the collagen/elastin-rich Bruch’s membrane (BM), a structure whose biomechanical integrity is compromised by AGE accumulation. In dry AMD, AGE crosslinks are believed to induce stiffening of BM and disrupt the tight junctions of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), leading to impaired transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased paracellular permeability. From an overall standpoint, ALT-711 presents a multifaceted candidate with intriguing properties that render it potentially suitable for repurposing in dry AMD. Nevertheless, the extrapolation from cardiovascular tissues to the BM requires careful consideration; ocular-specific delivery methods and dose optimization studies will be critical to determine whether the compound can achieve sufficient local concentration and activity without inducing off-target toxicity.  

Overall, ALT-711 stands as a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its established role as an AGE crosslink breaker and its demonstrated efficacy in softening stiffened extracellular matrices in other disease models. The strength of its scientific rationale is enhanced by its dual mode of action—both direct cleavage of AGE-induced crosslinks and ancillary metal-chelating and antioxidant effects—which may synergize to reduce pathological ECM rigidity. However, its previous clinical setbacks in other indications and the absence of direct ocular data represent significant challenges. A rigorous set of preclinical studies using ocular models of AMD, including drusen-mimic co-culture systems and animal models that recapitulate BM stiffening, will be crucial to validate its efficacy and determine appropriate dosing regimens (Krautwald et al., 2011; Nagai et al., 2012; Velichkova, 2020). Additionally, further molecular characterization of its crosslink-cleaving activity under conditions that mimic the BM environment will be essential to resolve controversies regarding its mechanism and ensure that its benefits outweigh any potential risks in the sensitive ocular setting (Chen & Tang, 2007; Kim & Spiegel, 2013).  

In conclusion, while there is compelling mechanistic rationale and supportive preclinical evidence from non-ocular studies for the repurposing of ALT-711, additional research specific to the ocular milieu is needed to confirm that the therapeutic benefits observed in cardiovascular contexts can be translated effectively to dry AMD. The hypothesis that AGE crosslink cleavage will soften Bruch’s membrane, thereby restoring RPE tight junction integrity and improving barrier function, is scientifically sound but remains to be validated through targeted ocular studies. Given the innovative nature of this extracellular matrix–centric therapeutic approach in a disease with few effective treatments, ALT-711 merits further investigation as a drug candidate for dry AMD, with the caveat that its previous clinical development challenges and current controversies regarding its mechanism necessitate cautious and thorough preclinical validation before any clinical translation can be contemplated (Alam, Ahsan, & Alam, 2013; Velichkova, 2020; Cooper, 2004; Toprak et al., 2017).
