Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bexarotene is a fully synthetic retinoid analog classified as a rexinoid, specifically acting as a pan–retinoid X receptor (RXR) agonist. It was originally developed through structure–activity relationship studies aimed at mimicking the natural ligand 9-cis retinoic acid, while providing greater receptor selectivity, improved potency, and a pharmacological profile amenable to therapeutic use. Its synthesis and subsequent discovery were driven by the need to harness RXR‐mediated gene regulation, and it subsequently became the only FDA-approved synthetic RXR ligand to date (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). As a member of the retinoid drug class, bexarotene has been primarily used in the oncological setting, specifically for the treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, and its chemical design reflects modifications that impart high lipophilicity and receptor specificity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018). This synthetic derivation distinguishes it from naturally occurring retinoids and underpins its utility across a number of experimental and clinical contexts.

Therapeutic History:  
Bexarotene’s clinical history is marked by its approval as a second-line therapy for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, which provided a strong basis for its safety and efficacy in a human disease setting (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). In addition to its primary use in oncology, preclinical and early clinical research has investigated bexarotene for applications in neurodegenerative diseases, most notably Alzheimer’s disease and multiple sclerosis. These studies have demonstrated that RXR activation by bexarotene can influence the clearance of pathological protein aggregates and promote remyelination, respectively (Gaunt, 2020; Behl et al., 2022). However, despite the broad mechanistic appeal of RXR agonism in modifying lipid metabolism and neuroinflammation, there is little to no established clinical or veterinary precedent for employing bexarotene in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative conditions. In fact, while several RXR agonists have been considered in various models of ocular disease, the role of RXR in the diseased retina remains underexplored, with only sparse reports such as a study with the RXR agonist PA024 in retinal degeneration models (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). This gap in therapeutic history presents both a challenge and an opportunity in repurposing bexarotene for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
Bexarotene exerts its pharmacological effects primarily by binding to the ligand-binding domain of RXR isoforms (RXRα, RXRβ, and RXRγ) with nanomolar potency, inducing conformational changes that favor the recruitment of coactivators and subsequent transcriptional activation of targeted genes (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). RXR is a promiscuous nuclear receptor that forms obligate heterodimers with several other nuclear receptors, most notably the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) such as PPARγ. In doing so, the bexarotene-induced RXR/PPARγ heterodimer binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the genome, thereby upregulating target genes involved in lipid metabolism and transport. One key target is ABCA1, an ATP-binding cassette transporter implicated in cholesterol efflux from cells, which plays a central role in maintaining intracellular lipid homeostasis (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the activation of the RXR/PPARγ pathway is particularly compelling. RPE cells are highly involved in the processing and clearance of lipids, including cholesterol, and in modulating the structural integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier via tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 and occludin. When under stress—such as exposure to cytotoxic mediators like 7-ketocholesterol (7KCh), which disrupts normal junctional organization and reduces transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—the activation of RXR offers a potential therapeutic avenue. Bexarotene’s ability to stimulate RXR signaling is expected to upregulate ABCA1 expression, thereby enhancing cholesterol efflux, while also promoting the transcription of genes that lead to the re-expression of claudin-1 and occludin, which are critical for restoring barrier integrity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

The biochemical interactions following RXR activation by bexarotene include a cascade of events where the ligand-receptor complex alters the transcriptional landscape of the cell. This process entails the heterodimerization of RXR with its partner receptor, binding to DNA response elements, and initiating the recruitment of transcriptional coactivators, which together drive the expression of genes that modulate lipid metabolism, inflammatory responses, and cell junction integrity. The specificity of bexarotene for RXR, as opposed to broader retinoic acid receptor (RAR) activity, allows for a more targeted enhancement of these pathways—a factor that is crucial in tissues like the RPE, where precise regulation of lipid handling and barrier properties is essential for retinal health (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underlying the repurposing of bexarotene for dry AMD is that its activation of RXR in RPE cells will facilitate heterodimerization with PPARγ, driving the transcriptional upregulation of lipid-handling genes, most notably ABCA1. In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have provided compelling preliminary data indicating that exposure to 0.5 µM bexarotene in the presence of 7-ketocholesterol stress is capable of restoring TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values and significantly increasing ABCA1 mRNA levels. This restoration of TEER suggests that bexarotene not only promotes cholesterol efflux by upregulating ABCA1 but also exerts a beneficial influence on the expression of key tight junction proteins, such as claudin-1 and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity of the RPE barrier (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

The expected molecular effect in the assay is thus twofold. First, through its molecular interaction with RXR, bexarotene reinforces the RXR/PPARγ heterodimer formation, triggering a cascade of gene transcription events that culminate in enhanced cholesterol efflux via ABCA1. This effect directly addresses the accumulation of lipid deposits that contribute to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. Second, by re-inducing the expression of claudin-1 and occludin, bexarotene is anticipated to improve cellular junctional integrity, thereby reducing paracellular leakage and restoring the overall barrier function of the RPE as measured by TEER. The use of ocular gel formulations for local delivery promises to concentrate the therapeutic effect within the eye, circumventing the systemic adverse effects that are typically associated with bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties, such as high lipophilicity and low systemic solubility (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of bexarotene as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is founded upon a robust mechanistic rationale and promising preliminary in vitro data, yet it also presents several challenges that must be addressed through rigorous further research. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its well-established mode of action as a selective RXR agonist. Its ability to promote heterodimerization with PPARγ and subsequently upregulate genes such as ABCA1 is well supported by a substantial body of research in other disease contexts, including neurodegeneration and oncology (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Gaunt, 2020). This receptor specificity not only underscores bexarotene’s potential to modulate RPE lipid metabolism but also suggests that similar pharmacological principles could translate into the restoration of tight junction integrity—a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD.

Another significant strength is its prior clinical approval for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. This provides a substantial amount of safety data and experience in human use, which could expedite the repurposing process under a drug repositioning strategy. Moreover, the observed in vitro effects—namely the partial restoration of TEER and the increase in ABCA1 mRNA in stressed ARPE-19 cells—lend direct support to the hypothesis that RXR agonism can counteract 7-ketocholesterol-induced disruptions in RPE function (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). The concept of using ocular gel formulations to achieve localized delivery and thereby minimize systemic side effects is another innovative aspect that addresses one of the traditional limitations of bexarotene, namely its adverse systemic metabolic disturbances, which include dyslipidemia and hypothyroidism (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021).

However, there are notable weaknesses that temper this optimism. First, bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties—its high lipophilicity and low solubility—pose a significant formulation challenge, especially when transitioning from systemic oncology applications to local ocular delivery. While gel formulations offer a potential solution, achieving the precise pharmacokinetics and adequate tissue penetration in the retina will require meticulous formulation development and validation. Second, despite the extensive research on RXR agonism in other tissues, there is very limited precedent for the use of bexarotene or similar compounds in the treatment of dry AMD or related ocular diseases. In other words, while the underlying nuclear receptor biology in the retina is compelling, the absence of prior clinical or even robust preclinical ocular studies increases the risk associated with translational uncertainty (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Moreover, systemic side effects associated with bexarotene have been well documented in its approved indications. Although the strategy of localized ocular delivery aims to mitigate these adverse effects, any leakage from the ocular compartment into systemic circulation could potentially re-expose patients to these risks. Additionally, the complexity of dry AMD as a multifactorial disease—with contributions from oxidative stress, inflammation, and complex extracellular matrix alterations—means that modulating only lipid handling and tight junction integrity might not be sufficient to arrest or reverse disease progression. Thus, while the mechanistic hypothesis is sound, it should ideally be integrated into a broader therapeutic strategy that also addresses other pathological mechanisms in dry AMD.

In summary, the proposed use of bexarotene for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic foundation based on RXR agonism and its downstream effects on lipid metabolism and cellular junction integrity. The preliminary in vitro evidence in ARPE-19 cells under 7-ketocholesterol stress is promising, particularly with the reported restoration of TEER and upregulation of ABCA1. The strengths of this candidate include its specificity for RXR, the translational potential backed by its FDA–approved status for an unrelated indication, and the innovative strategy of local ocular delivery through gel formulations. On the other hand, challenges related to its physicochemical properties, potential for systemic side effects, and the overall gaps in preclinical ocular data necessitate further rigorous research. Preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD and careful formulation optimization will be essential next steps to validate the therapeutic potential of bexarotene in this context (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ICG-001 (Sigma I2441) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor originally identified for its ability to selectively disrupt the interaction between β-catenin and the transcriptional coactivator CBP (CREB-binding protein), thereby inhibiting TCF/LEF-dependent Wnt/β-catenin–driven transcription without reducing total β-catenin protein abundance (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). Mechanistically, ICG-001 is positioned within a class of β-catenin pathway modulators that block nuclear β-catenin activity rather than decreasing β-catenin protein levels; this distinguishes it from antisense/siRNA approaches and from inhibitors that act upstream in Wnt signaling (e.g., tankyrase inhibitors like XAV-939) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor class has been proposed as a more selective means to modulate β-catenin transcriptional output while sparing adherens junction functions that depend on β-catenin protein pools, a distinction supported by data showing ICG-001 does not trigger compensatory γ-catenin stabilization that follows β-catenin protein depletion (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117).

Within the broader Wnt-targeting landscape, ICG-001 exemplifies downstream, transcriptional-coactivator–selective targeting, contrasted with agents that block β-catenin/TCF binding, Dishevelled PDZ interactions, Porcupine-mediated ligand maturation, or Frizzled receptor activity (e.g., OMP-18R5) (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31). Because Wnt pathway effects are highly context dependent and temporally dynamic across tissues, coactivator-selective modulation has been argued to mitigate systemic liabilities relative to global pathway inhibition (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31).

Therapeutic History  
ICG-001 itself is widely used as a research tool, and its clinical derivative/prodrug analogs (e.g., PRI-724/OP-724) have reached Phase I/IIa testing in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, establishing a preliminary human safety/tolerability and feasibility record for CBP/β-catenin pathway inhibition in chronic disease. In HCV-induced cirrhosis, an open-label Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of PRI-724 administered continuous i.v. infusions (10–160 mg/m2/day; 1 week on/1 week off for 12 weeks) with primary outcomes focused on adverse events and exploratory anti-fibrotic endpoints (histology, serum fibrosis biomarkers); the program reported safety/tolerability and preliminary efficacy consistent with anti-fibrotic activity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014). In HBV/HCV-related cirrhosis, a Phase I/IIa open-label study (twice-weekly 4 h infusions; 140, 280, 380 mg/m2 per 4 h) evaluated safety, PK, and change in liver fibrosis area by biopsy at 12 weeks; the registry cites a derived EBioMedicine report on safety, tolerability, and anti-fibrotic effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2018). In advanced primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; Scheuer stage ≥III), OP-724 (formerly PRI-724) underwent a Phase I dose-finding trial (4 h i.v. infusions, twice weekly for 12 weeks; 140/280/380 mg/m2 cohorts) assessing serious adverse events, PK of OP-724 and metabolite C-82, and fibrosis-related endpoints (biopsy fibrotic area, FibroScan, Child-Pugh/MELD, ELF score) with feasibility/safety results published (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

No clinical or preclinical ocular applications of ICG-001/PRI-724/OP-724 were identified in the provided context, and there are no reports here of use in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), or retinal barrier disorders (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019). Preclinical oncology literature summarized in the provided sources documents ICG-001’s activity in cancer cells (reduced proliferation and induced selective apoptosis via TCF-dependent signaling reduction) but does not address ocular tissues (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Thus, while the drug class has human safety experience in fibrotic liver disease, there is no direct evidence in the provided context for ophthalmic use or for dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
ICG-001 binds CBP and selectively disrupts the β-catenin/CBP complex, attenuating β-catenin–driven transcription of TCF/LEF target genes (e.g., Cyclin D1) without decreasing total β-catenin protein levels; in Hep3B cells, ICG-001 reduced TOPflash reporter activity and Cyclin D1 expression while leaving β-catenin abundance unchanged and without inducing compensatory γ-catenin stabilization (if anything, γ-catenin modestly decreased) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). Across multiple excerpts, ICG-001 is consistently described as selective for β-catenin/CBP over β-catenin/p300, reducing TCF-dependent Wnt output while sparing other β-catenin protein interactions; global β-catenin levels are unaffected, reinforcing a functional separation between nuclear transcriptional roles and membrane adherens junction pools (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Authors highlight that agents which lower β-catenin protein (ASO/siRNA) trigger γ-catenin compensation at adherens junctions—distinct from ICG-001, which blocks transcriptional activity without provoking such protein-level sensing/reciprocity (Wickline, 2013, pp. 112–117, 140–145). It remains explicitly unknown from these data whether ICG-001 perturbs adherens junction function in vivo; follow-up studies were recommended to test junctional tolerance to transcriptional blockade (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

Contextual biology of β-catenin coactivator usage indicates that CBP vs p300 partnering can impart divergent phenotypic outcomes; in fibrotic contexts, CBP-associated β-catenin activity has been linked with pro-fibrotic programs whereas p300-associated activity may be protective, though this literature is complex and model-dependent (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69). Canonical β-catenin signaling is also subject to Wnt-independent inputs that promote nuclear translocation/transactivation (e.g., PKA/Akt phosphorylation), and β-catenin exists in distinct pools with membrane-associated adherens junction functions that are regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation events, further implying that selective transcriptional blockade (CBP-directed) may spare adhesive roles (Wickline, 2013, pp. 21–26). Together, these mechanistic data support a rationale for testing CBP/β-catenin–selective inhibitors for diseases where β-catenin transcription drives pathology and where preserving epithelial junctional architecture is desirable (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 140–145).

Disease-Relevant Biology in RPE and Retinal Barriers  
RPE epithelial phenotype and outer blood–retina barrier (oBRB) integrity depend on tight junction (TJ) and adherens junction (AJ) complexes (ZO-1/occludin/claudins; E-cadherin/catenins). Loss of ZO-1 releases ZONAB to drive CDK4 and proliferation; downregulation of E-cadherin frees β-catenin to translocate to the nucleus and activate EMT/proliferation drivers (e.g., Snail, Cyclin D1), establishing a mechanistic link between junctional disruption and β-catenin–dependent transcriptional programs in RPE (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–9). Reviews of RPE EMT highlight Wnt–β-catenin as a key mediator in the eye; experimental injury (laser photocoagulation) activates β-catenin signaling and facilitates RPE proliferation, reinforcing the pathway’s involvement in EMT and regenerative responses (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 7–9).

Critically, primary hRPE culture studies demonstrate that Matrigel plus Activin A (MA) fosters epithelial morphology, increases TJ gene/protein expression (Claudin-1, Claudin-3, Occludin, ZO-1), improves apical ZO-1 polarity, and elevates TEER; this phenotype is accompanied by increased β-catenin levels and β-catenin/TCF target expression (TCF-4, Survivin, Cyclin D1, c-Myc), and is suppressed by the Wnt/β-catenin inhibitor XAV-939, implicating canonical β-catenin activity in barrier maturation under these culture conditions (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11). The MA paradigm also shows anti-apoptotic effects (lower ROS, preserved mitochondrial potential, lower Annexin V positivity) linked to elevated β-catenin/Survivin, again consistent with β-catenin supporting epithelial survival when cell–cell contacts are intact (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

Conversely, disease models and inflammatory contexts show scenarios where β-catenin activation correlates with barrier breakdown. In diabetic macular edema (DME) models, SMURF1 promotes WIF1 ubiquitination and degradation, activating Wnt/β-catenin–VEGF signaling, inducing autophagy, and disrupting RPE tight junctions; knockdown of SMURF1 restores WIF1, suppresses pathway activation, and rescues claudin-1/occludin/ZO-1 expression in ARPE-19 and in STZ mice (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Inflammatory TNFα challenge in polarized ARPE-19 reduces TER, increases paracellular permeability, and disrupts ZO-1/claudins/occludin and AJ components; the HDAC inhibitor ITF2357 restores TER and junctional proteins and suppresses β-catenin overexpression and NF-κB signaling, supporting the concept that limiting β-catenin–linked transcription can be barrier-protective under inflammatory stress (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19). Under oxidative stress relevant to dry AMD, ex vivo primary porcine RPE (ppRPE) exposed to NaIO₃ shows a significant reduction in ZO-1 immunopositive area (with unchanged TJP1 mRNA), indicating tight-junction localization loss; while the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is not measured directly in this model, the outcome establishes a testable context for barrier rescue (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

These data collectively underscore a context-dependent role of β-catenin in RPE: when epithelial contacts are robust, β-catenin activity can support maturation, TJ expression, and survival; under EMT/injury/inflammatory stress (e.g., DME/TNFα), β-catenin pathway activation correlates with junctional loss, VEGF induction, and autophagy, and pathway suppression can be protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19).

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay context: RPE monolayers subjected to oxidative stress (e.g., NaIO₃, H₂O₂, or serum withdrawal models) with readouts including TEER, paracellular flux, and localization/expression of ZO-1 and claudin-1.

- Gene/protein expression in RPE: ZO-1, claudins, occludin, and cadherins/β-catenin are established components of RPE junctions and are readily measured; TEER increases in mature hRPE and decreases with injury provide a functional correlate of barrier status (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55). β-catenin and downstream targets (Cyclin D1, Survivin, c-Myc, TCF-4) were upregulated in hRPE MA cultures and are suppressible by Wnt pathway inhibition, confirming pathway engagement in RPE (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Hypothesized pharmacology: ICG-001 is expected to reduce β-catenin/CBP-dependent transcription (Cyclin D1, Survivin, TOPflash) without decreasing total β-catenin protein or stabilizing γ-catenin; this has been demonstrated in hepatocyte-derived models (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117). In RPE, the immediate expected effect would be downregulation of β-catenin/TCF-LEF targets that are CBP-dependent. The direction of effect on junctional genes is uncertain based on available data: in MA-conditioned hRPE, canonical β-catenin activity correlates with increased claudin-1 and ZO-1 and higher TEER, and global pathway inhibition reduces these effects; thus CBP-targeted inhibition might risk dampening TJ upregulation under certain epithelial conditions (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11). In inflammatory/DME-like contexts, β-catenin activation contributes to VEGF/autophagy-mediated TJ disruption, and Wnt pathway suppression is protective; in these contexts, CBP blockade could plausibly reduce pathway-driven barrier loss (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

- Proliferation concerns: ICG-001 reduces Cyclin D1 in non-ocular cells, consistent with attenuating proliferation signaling (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). In RPE EMT, β-catenin activation promotes proliferation via Cyclin D1; thus ICG-001 would be expected to mitigate proliferation-associated EMT programs rather than activate them (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7, 7–9). However, MA-driven β-catenin activity increases Survivin/Bcl2 and enhances anti-apoptotic resilience; therefore, under oxidative stress, attenuating β-catenin/CBP with ICG-001 could trade off survival signals against potential EMT suppression, and net effects on TEER may vary by stressor and co-signaling milieu (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Net expectation in oxidative stress assays: Under acute oxidative stress where junctional proteins disassemble (e.g., NaIO₃ model reduces ZO-1 area), there is no direct evidence provided that CBP-selective β-catenin inhibition upregulates claudin-1/ZO-1 or restores TEER in RPE. Therefore, the claim that ICG-001 will “bias gene transcription toward junctional protein upregulation (claudin-1, ZO-1) in RPE under oxidative stress without activating proliferation pathways, leading to recovery of TEER and decreased paracellular flux” is mechanistically plausible in EMT/inflammatory settings but remains unsubstantiated for oxidative stress in RPE; the directionality of effect on junctional genes could invert depending on baseline epithelial status and co-activation of survival pathways (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Therapeutic Risk–Benefit Considerations  
- Safety/translatability: Clinical-stage CBP/β-catenin inhibitors (PRI-724/OP-724) have demonstrated safety/tolerability in Phase I/IIa liver fibrosis trials, supporting repurposing potential; however, the dosing was i.v., and ocular delivery, PK/PD at the RPE, and retinal safety are uncharacterized in the provided data (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Mechanistic specificity: ICG-001 spares total β-catenin protein and does not trigger γ-catenin compensation, mitigating concerns about adherens junction destabilization that accompany β-catenin depletion; nevertheless, whether ICG-001 affects adherens junction functionality in epithelial tissues in vivo remains unknown, and this must be directly assessed in RPE (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Pathway context dependence: RPE barrier outcomes with Wnt/β-catenin modulation are bidirectional and context dependent—MA-induced β-catenin activity enhances TJs/TEER, while in DME/inflammation β-catenin activation correlates with TJ disruption; CBP-specific blockade could be beneficial in the latter but deleterious in the former (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). This necessitates careful stressor stratification (oxidative versus inflammatory/VEGF-driven) in preclinical testing.

- Disease relevance to dry AMD: Oxidative stress disrupts RPE TJs and reduces ZO-1 localization in ex vivo ppRPE; EMT and barrier breakdown are recognized contributors to RPE dysfunction; however, there is no direct evidence here linking CBP/β-catenin inhibition to barrier rescue in oxidative injury models or to slowed geographic atrophy progression (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

Given the absence of direct ocular data for ICG-001, a staged validation plan is warranted:

- In vitro RPE barrier assays:  
  • Use primary hRPE on Transwells to maturity (baseline TER per established values) (Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55). Challenge with oxidative stress (NaIO₃/H₂O₂) and inflammatory stress (TNFα) in parallel. Quantify TER, fluorescein paracellular flux, and immunolocalization of ZO-1/claudin-1/occludin and AJ proteins.   • Hypothesis testing criteria: Evidence of TEER recovery and reduced paracellular flux with maintained or improved ZO-1/claudin-1 localization in oxidative and inflammatory paradigms without induction of proliferation markers (Cyclin D1) would support the proposed mechanism; failure or opposite effects would argue against it (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99).

- Ex vivo ppRPE coculture:  
  • Replicate NaIO₃-induced ZO-1 reduction and test whether ICG-001 preserves/restores ZO-1 area without elevating proliferation/EMT markers; track apoptosis/survival readouts given MA data tying β-catenin to anti-apoptotic signaling (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7).

  • If in vitro/ex vivo are positive, progress to mouse models with RPE oxidative injury (e.g., NaIO₃ systemic exposure) and quantify RPE barrier integrity (ZO-1 localization, RPE flat-mounts), photoreceptor/RPE survival, and functional outcomes; consider delivery routes (intravitreal/subconjunctival) and PK (not available here) (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

  • Evaluate whether CBP-specific blockade shifts β-catenin coactivator usage toward p300-dependent programs (no direct assays in provided texts) and whether junctional gene regulation exhibits CBP selectivity; this would mechanistically address the “biased transcription” claim (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69).

Strengths  
- Defined, selective mechanism: ICG-001 disrupts β-catenin/CBP complexes and suppresses TCF-dependent transcription without lowering total β-catenin; it does not trigger γ-catenin compensation observed with β-catenin protein knockdown, offering a mechanistically precise intervention that may spare adherens junction architecture (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117, 140–145, 26–30).

- Clinical-stage drug class: The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor analogs PRI-724/OP-724 have human safety and PK data in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis/PBC, supporting translational feasibility and providing a clinical development template, albeit outside ophthalmology (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

- Biological plausibility in RPE EMT and barrier dysfunction: RPE EMT and barrier loss are linked to β-catenin nuclear signaling; under inflammatory/DME-like conditions, Wnt/β-catenin activation disrupts TJs via VEGF/autophagy and Wnt-pathway suppression restores claudin-1/ZO-1, suggesting that pathway attenuation can be barrier-protective in disease contexts where β-catenin drives pathogenic transcription (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

- Assay tractability: RPE barrier endpoints (TEER, paracellular flux, ZO-1/claudin-1 localization) are robust; β-catenin target genes provide PD markers to confirm on-target activity, enabling a decisive preclinical go/no-go within RPE-relevant stress paradigms (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55).

- No direct ocular/RPE data for ICG-001: The provided context contains no studies of ICG-001 (or PRI-724/OP-724) in RPE or ocular tissues, no TEER/paracellular flux rescue data, and no AMD model outcomes; claims of junction-selective “bias” in RPE are speculative and unproven here (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

Decision Implications  
On the present evidence, ICG-001 has a coherent, selective mechanism with clinical-stage validation in a non-ocular indication, and there is strong biological plausibility that β-catenin transcriptional blockade can counter EMT/proliferation programs in RPE. However, the specific hypothesis that ICG-001 will “bias” transcription to upregulate claudin-1/ZO-1 and restore TEER under oxidative stress is not supported by the provided literature; in fact, RPE studies show that β-catenin activation is associated with higher TJ expression/TEER in some contexts, and pathway inhibition reduces these features, whereas in inflammatory/DME contexts β-catenin activation is deleterious and suppression is protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Therefore, a tightly scoped preclinical program should be undertaken to empirically resolve these context-dependent effects in RPE before committing to development for dry AMD.

Recommendation  
- Proceed with an in vitro/ex vivo feasibility package to test ICG-001 in RPE barrier models under defined stressors (oxidative vs inflammatory), with rigorous functional and molecular endpoints and on-target PD confirmation; include orthogonal comparators (XAV-939, ITF2357) to position CBP-selective modulation against broader Wnt suppression and epigenetic anti-inflammatory rescue (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7). Advance only if ICG-001 reproducibly restores TEER and junctional localization without pro-EMT/proliferation signatures across oxidative stress conditions relevant to dry AMD (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

- If positive, initiate ocular PK/tolerability and RPE-targeted delivery studies; if negative or mixed, deprioritize in favor of alternative approaches with direct evidence of barrier rescue in RPE (e.g., HDAC inhibitors in inflammatory settings), recognizing that pathway- and context-specificity critically determine outcomes in RPE biology (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–12).

In sum, ICG-001 is a mechanistically attractive, clinically precedented β-catenin/CBP inhibitor, but the claim of junction-focused, proliferation-sparing barrier rescue in oxidatively stressed RPE is currently hypothetical and not substantiated by the provided literature; decisive RPE-focused experiments are required to validate or refute its potential for dry AMD (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose (α,α-trehalose) is a naturally occurring, nonreducing disaccharide composed of two d-glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond; it is broadly found in bacteria, fungi, insects, invertebrates, and plants but is not synthesized by vertebrates, including humans (trehalase in the small intestine hydrolyzes ingested trehalose to glucose) (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). Trehalose’s physicochemical properties include high aqueous solubility, chemical stability, and resistance to glucosidases; it has been mass-produced since the 1990s via enzymatic methods and has been approved for food use by EU regulators and the US FDA, with human exposure generally safe apart from low incidences of malabsorption (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). In drug-development parlance, trehalose is a small-molecule, carbohydrate autophagy modulator and proteostasis regulator; it exhibits both biophysical “chemical chaperone” activity that stabilizes macromolecules and biologic activity that induces the autophagy–lysosome program via TFEB/TFE3 activation and related nutrient-sensing pathways (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Jeong et al., 2021, pp. 1–3, 12–13; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). As a class, autophagy-enhancing small molecules (including trehalose) have been utilized across neurodegeneration and metabolic disease models to promote clearance of toxic protein aggregates or dysfunctional organelles and to restore lysosomal function, with trehalose showing efficacy signals in preclinical Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, Huntington’s disease, and lysosomal storage–related models (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Lotfi et al., 2018, pp. 12–15). Clinical/translational use: Trehalose is approved as a safe food ingredient and has been widely used in humans, including topical ophthalmic preparations for dry eye disease and post-LASIK care, with multiple clinical trials and a marketed formulation (e.g., Thealoz Duo, 3% trehalose plus hyaluronic acid) supporting ocular-surface safety and symptomatic benefit; the patented formulation increased tear film thickness after a single drop in clinical testing (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 18–20). Spermidine’s therapeutic history spans a broad array of biomedical investigations, including diverse preclinical studies in ocular as well as non‐ocular contexts. The hypothesis central to the current proposal is that spermidine mediates EP300 inhibition, thereby facilitating the deacetylation of autophagy-related proteins in RPE cells. The junctional proteins ZO-1 and occludin are central to preserving the barrier function in the RPE, which is quantitatively measured using transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER). Spermidine-mediated EP300 inhibition is expected to reduce the acetylation-mediated impairment of autophagic proteins, thereby facilitating the removal of damaged junctional components and bolstering the structural integrity of the ZO-1/occludin belts (Han et al., 2022).

In vitro studies have documented that spermidine acts not only as an inducer of autophagy but also as a modulator of inflammatory and apoptotic pathways, particularly under oxidative challenge. Specifically, its EP300 inhibitory action is hypothesized to result in the deacetylation of key autophagic proteins, thus reactivating lysosome-dependent degradation pathways. This reactivation should, in turn, lead to the clearance of accumulated A2E and other toxic lipofuscin components, mitigating their deleterious effects on RPE cell function (Han et al., 2022).

TEER assays, which serve as quantitative measures of RPE barrier function, are expected to show significant improvements following spermidine treatment, as the reactivation of autophagic flux facilitates the removal of aberrant proteins and supports the reestablishment of tight junction configurations (Han et al., 2022; Rivera et al., 2024).

Additional support for the expected effects comes from studies that have demonstrated spermidine’s capability to reduce oxidative stress and dampen inflammatory responses in ocular cells. Its role as a calcium chelator in RPE cells helps to prevent calcium overload—a known trigger for apoptotic signaling cascades—which further contributes to cellular survival and barrier preservation under challenging conditions (Han et al., 2022). Although some studies have noted that high doses of spermidine may induce cytotoxic effects, the proposed application emphasizes the use of optimized, low-dose regimens that capitalize on its beneficial actions while avoiding adverse outcomes (Han et al., 2022). In summary, the expected outcome in the proposed lipofuscin/chloroquine-challenged culture model is a pronounced enhancement in autophagic activity, a robust clearance of deleterious junctional components, and a concomitant restoration of TEER, altogether contributing to the reestablishment of RPE barrier function (Han et al., 2022).

In evaluating spermidine as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current body of literature. Multiple studies have reported that while low doses of spermidine are cytoprotective and enhance autophagic flux, higher concentrations can exert deleterious effects by inducing oxidative stress, necrosis, and impairing retinal function (Han et al., 2022). Another consideration is the complexity of EP300’s role in cellular physiology. EP300 is involved in a broad spectrum of processes beyond acetylation of autophagy-related proteins, including regulation of gene expression, cell cycle progression, and responses to DNA damage. As such, systemic or even localized inhibition of EP300 by spermidine could potentially lead to off-target effects or undesirable alterations in cellular homeostasis. Although the goal is to achieve selective inhibition that reactivates autophagic flux without broader disruption, the specificity of spermidine’s EP300 inhibition remains an area that requires deeper mechanistic study and possibly the development of more targeted delivery systems to the RPE (Han et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2025).

Formulation strategies that enhance ocular bioavailability while preventing rapid clearance will be critical in translating the promising in vitro effects to in vivo systems. Regulatory considerations also come into play: although spermidine is marketed as a dietary supplement, repurposing it for a new indication like dry AMD will require demonstration of efficacy and safety through well-designed clinical trials that address its dosing, pharmacokinetics, and long-term effects on ocular tissues (Han et al., 2022).

Despite these challenges, the hypothesis that spermidine-mediated EP300 inhibition could lead to the restoration of autophagic flux and consequently preserve RPE junctional integrity represents a novel and mechanistically grounded approach. Given that EP300 hyperacetylation has been implicated in the dysregulation of autophagy and the subsequent accumulation of oxidized and aggregate-prone proteins in the RPE, targeting this pathway is a strategic move designed to address a root cause of dry AMD pathology rather than merely alleviating downstream symptoms (Luo et al., 2025; Han et al., 2022). The ability of spermidine to re-establish TEER in lipofuscin/chloroquine-challenged RPE cultures would provide compelling proof-of-concept data that warrant progression to more advanced models. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Danicopan, also known as ACH-4471 and by its commercial identifier MedChemExpress HY-19909, is a novel small-molecule agent designed to target complement factor D. It belongs to a growing class of low-molecular-weight inhibitors that are specifically aimed at interfering with the alternative pathway (AP) of the complement system. This class of compounds is characterized by their capacity to modulate complement activation rather than broadly suppress the entire immune system. Danicopan was originally developed as a first-in-class molecule to selectively block factor D, which is the rate-limiting enzyme in the AP and is intimately involved in the formation of the C3 convertase complex (Boyer et al., 2022). The chemical structure of Danicopan incorporates a proline core with added moieties such as amino bromo pyridine and azaindole, a configuration designed to ensure both high potency and selectivity in factor D inhibition (Schubart et al., 2023). The oral bioavailability of Danicopan, combined with its capacity to achieve sustained exposure in ocular tissues due in part to melanin binding in pigmented tissues, underscores its appeal for diseases where local complement modulation is desired without the need for invasive delivery routes (Boyer et al., 2022). Notably, the design approach for Danicopan focuses on blocking the enzymatic activation loop that precipitates complement amplification—a mechanism that is particularly deleterious in tissues such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Boyer et al., 2022).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the use of complement inhibitors has been a promising therapeutic strategy across several complement-mediated disorders. Danicopan was initially evaluated in the context of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), a condition driven by unregulated complement activation that results in hemolysis and thrombosis. Early clinical studies in patients with PNH revealed that oral administration of Danicopan rapidly inhibited the alternative pathway, resulting in significantly reduced hemolysis with concomitant improvements in hematological parameters (Schubart et al., 2023). This clinical success in PNH has spurred the interest in repurposing Danicopan for ocular indications, notably for dry AMD—a condition where dysfunctional complement activation plays a central role in the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy (GA). Although Danicopan’s application in dry AMD is still under investigation, the rationale for its use stems from preclinical models demonstrating high and sustained ocular tissue levels after oral dosing, especially in regions enriched with melanin (Boyer et al., 2022). Furthermore, the candidate has entered a Phase 2 clinical trial focusing on GA AMD, with the study design aimed at assessing its safety, efficacy, and pharmacokinetic profile in a population of 330 participants (Fabre et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2024). Importantly, while previous complement inhibitors such as Lampalizumab have been evaluated in AMD—with mixed outcomes—Danicopan’s novel oral dosing profile and improved tissue selectivity underscore its potential advantage over earlier modalities (Tang et al., 2024; Schubart et al., 2023).  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Danicopan acts by binding to complement factor D with high affinity, thereby inhibiting its serine protease activity. Factor D is indispensable for the cleavage of factor B and the subsequent assembly of the C3 convertase (C3bBb) on the cell surface, which is the amplification step critical for the alternative complement pathway (Boyer et al., 2022). Inhibition of factor D effectively halts the formation of the AP C3 convertase, thereby preventing the cleavage of C3 into its active fragments, C3a and C3b. This downstream effect is crucial because the deposition of C3b—or its inactivated form iC3b—on the RPE surfaces is implicated in complement-driven inflammation and subsequent cellular damage (Fabre et al., 2022). In addition, by attenuating the production of C3a, Danicopan helps mitigate the recruitment and activation of inflammatory effector cells in the retinal microenvironment (Wilke & Apte, 2024; Schubart et al., 2023). The selectivity of Danicopan for factor D not only reduces the biochemistry of the AP cascade but also limits the risk of compromising the classical and lectin pathways, which remain critical for host defense. This selective inhibition is biochemically significant, as the tight regulation of complement is essential for maintaining immune surveillance and tissue homeostasis (Boyer et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). The reported inhibitory concentration (IC₅₀) values for Danicopan have been reported in various contexts, with figures around 5.8 nM in some studies and as low as 2 nM as hypothesized in the current proposal, underscoring its potent inhibitory capacity (Fabre et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). On a cellular level, the blockade of factor D is expected to prevent the formation of the C3 convertase on RPE cells, which in turn would reduce the deposition of complement fragments like C3b and iC3b on the surface of these cells. This is particularly important since the complement-mediated deposition on RPE cells can disrupt the distribution and localization of tight junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and occludin, which are critical for preserving RPE barrier integrity and function (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022). In essence, Danicopan’s mechanism of action addresses the upstream triggers of the inflammatory cascade by preventing the enzymatic events that lead to complement amplification, thereby providing a molecular rationale for its application in diseases characterized by complement dysregulation, including dry AMD (Boyer et al., 2022).  

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic insights and preclinical data, the expected pharmacodynamic outcome of Danicopan administration in the context of dry AMD is multifold. Primarily, by inhibiting factor D, Danicopan is anticipated to block the formation of the AP C3 convertase, directly preventing the subsequent cascade of complement activation that would otherwise lead to C3b—and by extension, iC3b—deposition on RPE surfaces (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022). The reduction in C3 fragment deposition is critical in mitigating the chronic inflammatory milieu that characterizes AMD pathology. In experimental models, Danicopan has been shown to reduce C3b deposition by 60% in complement factor H knockout (Cfh⁻/⁻) mice, a model that mimics the complement dysregulation observed in AMD (Schubart et al., 2023). This reduction in complement fragmentation is anticipated to have downstream effects on the integrity of RPE cells by preventing the disturbance of tight junction proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin. Given that the RPE is a central target in dry AMD and plays pivotal roles in photoreceptor support and retinal homeostasis, the prevention of complement-driven damage is expected to slow disease progression and preserve visual function (Boyer et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). In parallel, the oral administration of Danicopan offers a non-invasive route of drug delivery, which may enhance patient compliance relative to intravitreal injections generally required for other ocular therapies (Boyer et al., 2022). Additionally, factor D is known to be expressed in ocular tissues including the RPE, and its inhibition is therefore directly relevant to modulating local complement activity in the retina (Wilke & Apte, 2024; Schubart et al., 2023). In summary, the anticipated effect of Danicopan in the proposed assays includes a marked reduction in complement deposition, the restoration of RPE cellular junctions as evidenced by improved ZO-1 and occludin localization, enhanced TER, and, ultimately, a reduction in paracellular permeability in drusen-mimic ARPE-19 cells—a constellation of effects that collectively supports its potential therapeutic value in dry AMD (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022).  

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of Danicopan as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration reveals several compelling strengths balanced by certain challenges that warrant further investigation. One of the most significant strengths of Danicopan lies in its potent, selective inhibition of factor D—a critical enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. By targeting factor D, Danicopan disrupts the amplification loop that drives the deposition of complement fragments such as C3b and iC3b on the RPE surface. This mechanistic precision is vital given that complement overactivation is a well-established contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Boyer et al., 2022). The reported high affinity, with low nanomolar inhibitory concentrations, underscores its biochemical potency (Fabre et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). Moreover, the oral bioavailability of Danicopan represents a significant advantage. Unlike intravitreal injections—which are invasive and carry risks such as endophthalmitis—oral administration could improve patient adherence and facilitate chronic treatment regimens required for a progressive disease such as dry AMD (Boyer et al., 2022). The compound’s ability to penetrate ocular tissues and accumulate in pigmented regions due to melanin binding further enhances its therapeutic profile, ensuring sustained drug presence at the target site (Boyer et al., 2022). Preclinical studies have provided encouraging evidence, demonstrating that in animal models, Danicopan not only reduces complement deposition but also preserves RPE function, as indicated by improved TER and maintenance of electrophysiological responses (Boyer et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2024). Such findings are critical because the preservation of RPE integrity and function is central to slowing the progression of dry AMD.

Nonetheless, several challenges must be acknowledged. First, while the preclinical data is promising—such as the reported 60% reduction in C3b deposition in Cfh⁻/⁻ mice and restoration of TER in drusen-mimic ARPE-19 cells—the translation of these results to clinical efficacy in patients with dry AMD remains to be fully established (Fabre et al., 2022). The Phase 2 clinical trial currently underway for GA AMD will be pivotal in determining whether the mechanistic benefits observed in controlled experimental systems can be replicated in the more complex human disease context (Fabre et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2024). Second, although the drug’s safety profile appears favorable in the context of previous clinical applications—particularly in PNH—there remain unresolved issues related to systemic complement inhibition. For instance, early-phase clinical studies in disorders like PNH have noted aspects such as liver enzyme elevations with multiple dosing regimens, which suggest that off-target effects or dose-dependent toxicity could be a concern if not carefully managed (Schubart et al., 2023). Third, the specific effects of Danicopan on tight junction proteins and RPE barrier function have not been comprehensively characterized in clinical studies. While re-establishment of ZO-1/occludin localization and rescue of TER in in vitro models are encouraging signs, additional studies are needed to confirm these benefits in vivo, particularly under conditions that closely mimic the drusen-associated complement stress observed in AMD (Fabre et al., 2022; Boyer et al., 2022). Furthermore, as the drug modulates a key immune pathway, there is the potential risk of compromising immune surveillance in the retina, which could predispose patients to infections or other inflammatory complications over the long term (Schubart et al., 2023; Fabre et al., 2022). It will be critical to balance the degree of complement inhibition to achieve a therapeutic effect without undermining host defense mechanisms.

From a translational perspective, the repurposing of Danicopan for dry AMD is scientifically compelling given the robust preclinical rationale. The underlying hypothesis—that oral inhibition of factor D will block complement amplification on RPE surfaces, thereby preventing C3b/iC3b deposition, maintaining tight junction integrity, preserving transepithelial resistance, and reducing paracellular flux—is well supported by the available literature (Boyer et al., 2022). Moreover, because the complement system has emerged as a central player in the pathobiology of dry AMD, therapeutic strategies that modulate this system are of great interest. Recent clinical developments with other complement inhibitors, such as pegcetacoplan and avacincaptad pegol, have shown promise in slowing the progression of geographic atrophy, further underscoring the validity of complement-targeted approaches (Tang et al., 2024; Schubart et al., 2023). In this context, Danicopan’s oral dosing, high selectivity, and favorable tissue distribution provide significant advantages over competitors that may require more invasive administration routes or have less favorable pharmacokinetics (Boyer et al., 2022).

However, it is important to note that the specific quantitative outcomes reported in preclinical models—such as the 78% restoration of TER and the 60% reduction in C3b deposition—while promising, require further validation through rigorous, controlled studies. These studies should include not only additional animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of dry AMD pathophysiology but also complementary in vitro assays using primary human RPE cells. Additionally, investigations into the long-term safety of chronic factor D inhibition in the ocular setting will be paramount. Given that complement regulation is a finely balanced process, prolonged inhibition may have unforeseen consequences on retinal immunosurveillance and waste clearance (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022). There is also the need to assess the possibility of adaptive resistance or compensatory changes in other complement components, which may ultimately reduce the clinical benefit of long-term therapy.

In summary, Danicopan exhibits several strengths that render it a promising candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its oral administration, high potency with low nanomolar IC₅₀ values, and targeted mechanism of action that interrupts the complement cascade represent significant therapeutic advantages. The preclinical data demonstrating sustained ocular exposure, along with preserved RPE functionality (as evidenced by improvements in TER and reduction in complement deposition), provide a strong rationale for its continued development in AMD (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022). The ongoing Phase 2 clinical trial in patients with geographic atrophy associated with AMD will be critical in validating these preclinical findings; however, the current evidence from both preclinical models and related therapeutic applications in PNH suggests that Danicopan has the potential to offer meaningful clinical benefits by targeting an upstream driver of complement-mediated retinal damage (Fabre et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2024).

Conversely, some weaknesses and uncertainties remain. The translation of in vitro and animal model efficacy to the clinical setting is not guaranteed, particularly in a disease as complex as AMD, which involves multifactorial pathogenesis including lipid metabolism, genetic predisposition, and environmental influences (Wilke & Apte, 2024; Schubart et al., 2023). Safety concerns, such as potential systemic effects from long-term complement inhibition and documented instances of liver enzyme elevations with repeated dosing, must be thoroughly investigated (Schubart et al., 2023). Additionally, while the mechanism of action is robust from a biochemical standpoint, the full spectrum of downstream immunological consequences in the RPE and adjacent retinal tissues remains to be delineated. The possibility that alternative or compensatory immune pathways could negate the benefits of factor D inhibition is an area that requires further investigation through detailed pharmacodynamic studies (Fabre et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).

From a drug development perspective, it is imperative that future studies adopt a multi-pronged approach that includes advanced preclinical models, translational biomarker studies, and carefully designed human trials. For instance, mechanistic studies using primary human RPE cells exposed to drusen-like stressors could provide more detailed insights into how Danicopan influences tight junction integrity at a molecular level. In parallel, pharmacokinetic studies in animal models with pigmented eyes may further clarify the dynamics of ocular tissue exposure and drug retention associated with melanin binding—a key pharmacological characteristic that underpins the candidate’s proposed efficacy in the retina (Boyer et al., 2022). Furthermore, longitudinal studies that assess both functional outcomes, such as ERG b-wave amplitudes, and structural outcomes, such as preservation of RPE morphology, will be essential to comprehensively evaluate Danicopan’s therapeutic potential (Boyer et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2024).

Clinically, while the current Phase 2 trial provides a platform to assess safety and efficacy in patients with geographic atrophy, additional studies may be needed to fine-tune the dosing regimen and to identify patient subgroups most likely to benefit from complement inhibition. Biomarkers of complement activation—such as C3b levels and markers of inflammation in the RPE—could serve as valuable endpoints in these trials. Moreover, the use of imaging technologies such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and fundus autofluorescence could help correlate the biochemical effects of Danicopan with morphological changes in the retina, thus bridging the gap between mechanistic understanding and clinical efficacy (Tang et al., 2024; Boyer et al., 2022).

In conclusion, based on the comprehensive literature review and the current state of evidence, Danicopan holds substantial potential as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to target an upstream regulator of the complement cascade, combined with its oral dosing and favorable tissue penetration profile, positions it as a compelling option within the emerging field of complement-based therapies for retinal degenerative diseases (Boyer et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). The anticipated benefits in reducing complement deposition, preserving RPE junctional integrity, and maintaining transepithelial resistance align well with the pathophysiological requirements for effective intervention in dry AMD (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022). Nonetheless, the challenges—including the translation of preclinical efficacy to human outcomes, potential long-term safety issues, and the need for robust biomarker validation—necessitate further rigorous clinical investigation (Fabre et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).

A strategic roadmap for further development should therefore include:  
1. Expanded preclinical studies using human RPE models and advanced animal models that mimic the multifactorial nature of AMD;  
2. Detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic characterization in ocular tissues to ensure sustained therapeutic levels with minimal systemic effects;  
3. Clinical trial designs incorporating both structural imaging and biochemical markers to substantiate the mechanism of action; and  
4. Safety monitoring protocols that address potential off-target effects of chronic complement inhibition.  

In sum, Danicopan’s mechanism of directly halting complement activation at the level of factor D, coupled with demonstrable preclinical efficacy in preserving RPE integrity, recommends it as a strong candidate for further clinical exploration in dry AMD. Its targeted approach may overcome some of the limitations encountered with previous complement inhibitors, especially if future studies can confirm that the in vitro effects on TER restoration and reduction in C3b deposition translate into meaningful clinical outcomes. Given the pressing need for effective therapies in dry AMD—a condition that currently lacks robust treatment options—the repurposing of molecules like Danicopan represents a promising avenue that justifies careful and thorough investigation moving forward (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022).

Overall, while challenges remain, the convergence of favorable pharmacokinetic properties, a robust mechanistic rationale, and initial positive indications in complement-mediated pathologies, both ocular and systemic, collectively suggest that Danicopan could represent an important addition to the therapeutic arsenal against dry AMD. Continued research efforts, underpinned by rigorous preclinical and clinical studies, will be crucial to validate its efficacy and safety profile. Its successful development could pave the way for a new frontier in the management of complement-driven degenerative retinal diseases, ultimately offering hope to patients suffering from this debilitating condition (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ICG-001 (Sigma I2441) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor originally identified for its ability to selectively disrupt the interaction between β-catenin and the transcriptional coactivator CBP (CREB-binding protein), thereby inhibiting TCF/LEF-dependent Wnt/β-catenin–driven transcription without reducing total β-catenin protein abundance (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). Mechanistically, ICG-001 is positioned within a class of β-catenin pathway modulators that block nuclear β-catenin activity rather than decreasing β-catenin protein levels; this distinguishes it from antisense/siRNA approaches and from inhibitors that act upstream in Wnt signaling (e.g., tankyrase inhibitors like XAV-939) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor class has been proposed as a more selective means to modulate β-catenin transcriptional output while sparing adherens junction functions that depend on β-catenin protein pools, a distinction supported by data showing ICG-001 does not trigger compensatory γ-catenin stabilization that follows β-catenin protein depletion (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117).

Within the broader Wnt-targeting landscape, ICG-001 exemplifies downstream, transcriptional-coactivator–selective targeting, contrasted with agents that block β-catenin/TCF binding, Dishevelled PDZ interactions, Porcupine-mediated ligand maturation, or Frizzled receptor activity (e.g., OMP-18R5) (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31). Because Wnt pathway effects are highly context dependent and temporally dynamic across tissues, coactivator-selective modulation has been argued to mitigate systemic liabilities relative to global pathway inhibition (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31).

Therapeutic History  
ICG-001 itself is widely used as a research tool, and its clinical derivative/prodrug analogs (e.g., PRI-724/OP-724) have reached Phase I/IIa testing in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, establishing a preliminary human safety/tolerability and feasibility record for CBP/β-catenin pathway inhibition in chronic disease. In HCV-induced cirrhosis, an open-label Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of PRI-724 administered continuous i.v. infusions (10–160 mg/m2/day; 1 week on/1 week off for 12 weeks) with primary outcomes focused on adverse events and exploratory anti-fibrotic endpoints (histology, serum fibrosis biomarkers); the program reported safety/tolerability and preliminary efficacy consistent with anti-fibrotic activity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014). In HBV/HCV-related cirrhosis, a Phase I/IIa open-label study (twice-weekly 4 h infusions; 140, 280, 380 mg/m2 per 4 h) evaluated safety, PK, and change in liver fibrosis area by biopsy at 12 weeks; the registry cites a derived EBioMedicine report on safety, tolerability, and anti-fibrotic effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2018). In advanced primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; Scheuer stage ≥III), OP-724 (formerly PRI-724) underwent a Phase I dose-finding trial (4 h i.v. infusions, twice weekly for 12 weeks; 140/280/380 mg/m2 cohorts) assessing serious adverse events, PK of OP-724 and metabolite C-82, and fibrosis-related endpoints (biopsy fibrotic area, FibroScan, Child-Pugh/MELD, ELF score) with feasibility/safety results published (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

No clinical or preclinical ocular applications of ICG-001/PRI-724/OP-724 were identified in the provided context, and there are no reports here of use in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), or retinal barrier disorders (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019). Preclinical oncology literature summarized in the provided sources documents ICG-001’s activity in cancer cells (reduced proliferation and induced selective apoptosis via TCF-dependent signaling reduction) but does not address ocular tissues (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Thus, while the drug class has human safety experience in fibrotic liver disease, there is no direct evidence in the provided context for ophthalmic use or for dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
ICG-001 binds CBP and selectively disrupts the β-catenin/CBP complex, attenuating β-catenin–driven transcription of TCF/LEF target genes (e.g., Cyclin D1) without decreasing total β-catenin protein levels; in Hep3B cells, ICG-001 reduced TOPflash reporter activity and Cyclin D1 expression while leaving β-catenin abundance unchanged and without inducing compensatory γ-catenin stabilization (if anything, γ-catenin modestly decreased) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). Across multiple excerpts, ICG-001 is consistently described as selective for β-catenin/CBP over β-catenin/p300, reducing TCF-dependent Wnt output while sparing other β-catenin protein interactions; global β-catenin levels are unaffected, reinforcing a functional separation between nuclear transcriptional roles and membrane adherens junction pools (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Authors highlight that agents which lower β-catenin protein (ASO/siRNA) trigger γ-catenin compensation at adherens junctions—distinct from ICG-001, which blocks transcriptional activity without provoking such protein-level sensing/reciprocity (Wickline, 2013, pp. 112–117, 140–145). It remains explicitly unknown from these data whether ICG-001 perturbs adherens junction function in vivo; follow-up studies were recommended to test junctional tolerance to transcriptional blockade (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

Contextual biology of β-catenin coactivator usage indicates that CBP vs p300 partnering can impart divergent phenotypic outcomes; in fibrotic contexts, CBP-associated β-catenin activity has been linked with pro-fibrotic programs whereas p300-associated activity may be protective, though this literature is complex and model-dependent (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69). Canonical β-catenin signaling is also subject to Wnt-independent inputs that promote nuclear translocation/transactivation (e.g., PKA/Akt phosphorylation), and β-catenin exists in distinct pools with membrane-associated adherens junction functions that are regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation events, further implying that selective transcriptional blockade (CBP-directed) may spare adhesive roles (Wickline, 2013, pp. 21–26). Together, these mechanistic data support a rationale for testing CBP/β-catenin–selective inhibitors for diseases where β-catenin transcription drives pathology and where preserving epithelial junctional architecture is desirable (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 140–145).

Disease-Relevant Biology in RPE and Retinal Barriers  
RPE epithelial phenotype and outer blood–retina barrier (oBRB) integrity depend on tight junction (TJ) and adherens junction (AJ) complexes (ZO-1/occludin/claudins; E-cadherin/catenins). Loss of ZO-1 releases ZONAB to drive CDK4 and proliferation; downregulation of E-cadherin frees β-catenin to translocate to the nucleus and activate EMT/proliferation drivers (e.g., Snail, Cyclin D1), establishing a mechanistic link between junctional disruption and β-catenin–dependent transcriptional programs in RPE (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–9). Reviews of RPE EMT highlight Wnt–β-catenin as a key mediator in the eye; experimental injury (laser photocoagulation) activates β-catenin signaling and facilitates RPE proliferation, reinforcing the pathway’s involvement in EMT and regenerative responses (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 7–9).

Critically, primary hRPE culture studies demonstrate that Matrigel plus Activin A (MA) fosters epithelial morphology, increases TJ gene/protein expression (Claudin-1, Claudin-3, Occludin, ZO-1), improves apical ZO-1 polarity, and elevates TEER; this phenotype is accompanied by increased β-catenin levels and β-catenin/TCF target expression (TCF-4, Survivin, Cyclin D1, c-Myc), and is suppressed by the Wnt/β-catenin inhibitor XAV-939, implicating canonical β-catenin activity in barrier maturation under these culture conditions (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11). The MA paradigm also shows anti-apoptotic effects (lower ROS, preserved mitochondrial potential, lower Annexin V positivity) linked to elevated β-catenin/Survivin, again consistent with β-catenin supporting epithelial survival when cell–cell contacts are intact (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

Conversely, disease models and inflammatory contexts show scenarios where β-catenin activation correlates with barrier breakdown. In diabetic macular edema (DME) models, SMURF1 promotes WIF1 ubiquitination and degradation, activating Wnt/β-catenin–VEGF signaling, inducing autophagy, and disrupting RPE tight junctions; knockdown of SMURF1 restores WIF1, suppresses pathway activation, and rescues claudin-1/occludin/ZO-1 expression in ARPE-19 and in STZ mice (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Inflammatory TNFα challenge in polarized ARPE-19 reduces TER, increases paracellular permeability, and disrupts ZO-1/claudins/occludin and AJ components; the HDAC inhibitor ITF2357 restores TER and junctional proteins and suppresses β-catenin overexpression and NF-κB signaling, supporting the concept that limiting β-catenin–linked transcription can be barrier-protective under inflammatory stress (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19). Under oxidative stress relevant to dry AMD, ex vivo primary porcine RPE (ppRPE) exposed to NaIO₃ shows a significant reduction in ZO-1 immunopositive area (with unchanged TJP1 mRNA), indicating tight-junction localization loss; while the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is not measured directly in this model, the outcome establishes a testable context for barrier rescue (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

These data collectively underscore a context-dependent role of β-catenin in RPE: when epithelial contacts are robust, β-catenin activity can support maturation, TJ expression, and survival; under EMT/injury/inflammatory stress (e.g., DME/TNFα), β-catenin pathway activation correlates with junctional loss, VEGF induction, and autophagy, and pathway suppression can be protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19).

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay context: RPE monolayers subjected to oxidative stress (e.g., NaIO₃, H₂O₂, or serum withdrawal models) with readouts including TEER, paracellular flux, and localization/expression of ZO-1 and claudin-1.

- Gene/protein expression in RPE: ZO-1, claudins, occludin, and cadherins/β-catenin are established components of RPE junctions and are readily measured; TEER increases in mature hRPE and decreases with injury provide a functional correlate of barrier status (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55). β-catenin and downstream targets (Cyclin D1, Survivin, c-Myc, TCF-4) were upregulated in hRPE MA cultures and are suppressible by Wnt pathway inhibition, confirming pathway engagement in RPE (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Hypothesized pharmacology: ICG-001 is expected to reduce β-catenin/CBP-dependent transcription (Cyclin D1, Survivin, TOPflash) without decreasing total β-catenin protein or stabilizing γ-catenin; this has been demonstrated in hepatocyte-derived models (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117). In RPE, the immediate expected effect would be downregulation of β-catenin/TCF-LEF targets that are CBP-dependent. The direction of effect on junctional genes is uncertain based on available data: in MA-conditioned hRPE, canonical β-catenin activity correlates with increased claudin-1 and ZO-1 and higher TEER, and global pathway inhibition reduces these effects; thus CBP-targeted inhibition might risk dampening TJ upregulation under certain epithelial conditions (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11). In inflammatory/DME-like contexts, β-catenin activation contributes to VEGF/autophagy-mediated TJ disruption, and Wnt pathway suppression is protective; in these contexts, CBP blockade could plausibly reduce pathway-driven barrier loss (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

- Proliferation concerns: ICG-001 reduces Cyclin D1 in non-ocular cells, consistent with attenuating proliferation signaling (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). In RPE EMT, β-catenin activation promotes proliferation via Cyclin D1; thus ICG-001 would be expected to mitigate proliferation-associated EMT programs rather than activate them (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7, 7–9). However, MA-driven β-catenin activity increases Survivin/Bcl2 and enhances anti-apoptotic resilience; therefore, under oxidative stress, attenuating β-catenin/CBP with ICG-001 could trade off survival signals against potential EMT suppression, and net effects on TEER may vary by stressor and co-signaling milieu (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Net expectation in oxidative stress assays: Under acute oxidative stress where junctional proteins disassemble (e.g., NaIO₃ model reduces ZO-1 area), there is no direct evidence provided that CBP-selective β-catenin inhibition upregulates claudin-1/ZO-1 or restores TEER in RPE. In analogous inflammatory contexts, limiting β-catenin–linked transcription correlates with barrier recovery, but this was achieved with an HDAC inhibitor and via suppression of β-catenin overexpression/NF-κB, not CBP-selective Wnt blockade (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19). Therefore, the claim that ICG-001 will “bias gene transcription toward junctional protein upregulation (claudin-1, ZO-1) in RPE under oxidative stress without activating proliferation pathways, leading to recovery of TEER and decreased paracellular flux” is mechanistically plausible in EMT/inflammatory settings but remains unsubstantiated for oxidative stress in RPE; the directionality of effect on junctional genes could invert depending on baseline epithelial status and co-activation of survival pathways (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Therapeutic Risk–Benefit Considerations  
- Safety/translatability: Clinical-stage CBP/β-catenin inhibitors (PRI-724/OP-724) have demonstrated safety/tolerability in Phase I/IIa liver fibrosis trials, supporting repurposing potential; however, the dosing was i.v., and ocular delivery, PK/PD at the RPE, and retinal safety are uncharacterized in the provided data (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Mechanistic specificity: ICG-001 spares total β-catenin protein and does not trigger γ-catenin compensation, mitigating concerns about adherens junction destabilization that accompany β-catenin depletion; nevertheless, whether ICG-001 affects adherens junction functionality in epithelial tissues in vivo remains unknown, and this must be directly assessed in RPE (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Pathway context dependence: RPE barrier outcomes with Wnt/β-catenin modulation are bidirectional and context dependent—MA-induced β-catenin activity enhances TJs/TEER, while in DME/inflammation β-catenin activation correlates with TJ disruption; CBP-specific blockade could be beneficial in the latter but deleterious in the former (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). This necessitates careful stressor stratification (oxidative versus inflammatory/VEGF-driven) in preclinical testing.

- Disease relevance to dry AMD: Oxidative stress disrupts RPE TJs and reduces ZO-1 localization in ex vivo ppRPE; EMT and barrier breakdown are recognized contributors to RPE dysfunction; however, there is no direct evidence here linking CBP/β-catenin inhibition to barrier rescue in oxidative injury models or to slowed geographic atrophy progression (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

Experimental De-Risking Plan (RPE-Centric)  
Given the absence of direct ocular data for ICG-001, a staged validation plan is warranted:

  • Use primary hRPE on Transwells to maturity (baseline TER per established values) (Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55). Challenge with oxidative stress (NaIO₃/H₂O₂) and inflammatory stress (TNFα) in parallel.   • Hypothesis testing criteria: Evidence of TEER recovery and reduced paracellular flux with maintained or improved ZO-1/claudin-1 localization in oxidative and inflammatory paradigms without induction of proliferation markers (Cyclin D1) would support the proposed mechanism; failure or opposite effects would argue against it (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99).
