- In vivo relevance:  
  • If in vitro/ex vivo are positive, progress to mouse models with RPE oxidative injury (e.g., NaIO₃ systemic exposure) and quantify RPE barrier integrity (ZO-1 localization, RPE flat-mounts), photoreceptor/RPE survival, and functional outcomes; consider delivery routes (intravitreal/subconjunctival) and PK (not available here) (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

- Mechanistic dissection:  
  • Evaluate whether CBP-specific blockade shifts β-catenin coactivator usage toward p300-dependent programs (no direct assays in provided texts) and whether junctional gene regulation exhibits CBP selectivity; this would mechanistically address the “biased transcription” claim (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Defined, selective mechanism: ICG-001 disrupts β-catenin/CBP complexes and suppresses TCF-dependent transcription without lowering total β-catenin; it does not trigger γ-catenin compensation observed with β-catenin protein knockdown, offering a mechanistically precise intervention that may spare adherens junction architecture (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117, 140–145, 26–30).

- Clinical-stage drug class: The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor analogs PRI-724/OP-724 have human safety and PK data in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis/PBC, supporting translational feasibility and providing a clinical development template, albeit outside ophthalmology (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

- Biological plausibility in RPE EMT and barrier dysfunction: RPE EMT and barrier loss are linked to β-catenin nuclear signaling; under inflammatory/DME-like conditions, Wnt/β-catenin activation disrupts TJs via VEGF/autophagy and Wnt-pathway suppression restores claudin-1/ZO-1, suggesting that pathway attenuation can be barrier-protective in disease contexts where β-catenin drives pathogenic transcription (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

- Assay tractability: RPE barrier endpoints (TEER, paracellular flux, ZO-1/claudin-1 localization) are robust; β-catenin target genes provide PD markers to confirm on-target activity, enabling a decisive preclinical go/no-go within RPE-relevant stress paradigms (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55).

Key Limitations and Risks  
- No direct ocular/RPE data for ICG-001: The provided context contains no studies of ICG-001 (or PRI-724/OP-724) in RPE or ocular tissues, no TEER/paracellular flux rescue data, and no AMD model outcomes; claims of junction-selective “bias” in RPE are speculative and unproven here (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Context-dependent and bidirectional β-catenin effects in RPE: In hRPE cultured with MA, β-catenin activity correlates with increased claudin-1/ZO-1 and higher TEER, and Wnt pathway inhibition (XAV-939) diminishes these; thus, in certain epithelial contexts, β-catenin/CBP inhibition could impair, not enhance, junctional gene expression and barrier function (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Survival/proliferation trade-offs: β-catenin activation increased anti-apoptotic factors (Survivin/Bcl2) and protected hRPE from serum withdrawal stress; ICG-001’s suppression of β-catenin target genes could compromise survival signaling under oxidative stress, and the net effect on barrier integrity/survival requires direct testing (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7).

- Mechanistic uncertainty regarding “biased transcription” toward junctional genes: No evidence is provided that CBP-selective inhibition favors claudin-1/ZO-1 expression; indeed, Sox/TCF targets include Cyclin D1 and c-Myc, and the directionality of CBP versus p300 coactivator usage on RPE junctional gene programs is not defined by the present sources (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 9–11; Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69).

- Delivery and ocular PK/PD unknowns: Clinical liver trials used i.v. infusions; ocular tolerability, retinal exposure, and local pharmacology for ICG-001/OP-724/PRI-724 are not addressed here, requiring formulation and delivery development (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

Decision Implications  
On the present evidence, ICG-001 has a coherent, selective mechanism with clinical-stage validation in a non-ocular indication, and there is strong biological plausibility that β-catenin transcriptional blockade can counter EMT/proliferation programs in RPE. However, the specific hypothesis that ICG-001 will “bias” transcription to upregulate claudin-1/ZO-1 and restore TEER under oxidative stress is not supported by the provided literature; in fact, RPE studies show that β-catenin activation is associated with higher TJ expression/TEER in some contexts, and pathway inhibition reduces these features, whereas in inflammatory/DME contexts β-catenin activation is deleterious and suppression is protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Navitoclax (ABT-263) is a small‐molecule, orally bioavailable agent originally developed in the oncology arena as a BH3‐mimetic that targets several anti‐apoptotic members of the BCL-2 family, most notably BCL-2, BCL-xL, and BCL-W. This synthetic compound was designed through structure–activity relationship optimization to overcome the limitations of earlier compounds such as ABT-737, and it has since been classified as a senolytic agent owing to its ability to selectively induce apoptosis in senescent cells while sparing normal, quiescent cells. In the context of aging and degenerative diseases, the protective yet dysfunctional senescent cell phenotype is characterized by the upregulation of anti‐apoptotic proteins; therefore, compounds like ABT-263 that block these survival pathways have been repurposed as candidates to eliminate such senescent cells. The compound belongs to a broader class of therapeutics targeting the BCL-2 family, which have historically been exploited in various anti-cancer strategies and are now emerging as promising candidates for addressing age-associated disorders such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Ryu et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Navitoclax has a well-documented preclinical and clinical history in oncological models; its senolytic potential was first noted in studies where it selectively killed therapy-induced senescent tumor cells and other cell types by inhibiting anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins. Early clinical trials in small-cell lung cancer and lymphoid malignancies established proof-of-concept that targeting BCL-2/BCL-xL could result in tumor regression through apoptotic induction, although its clinical use was somewhat limited by dose-dependent toxicities such as thrombocytopenia. More recently, preclinical studies have extended its use beyond oncology: in in vitro studies and in mouse models where retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells were rendered senescent by doxorubicin treatment, navitoclax was shown to selectively induce apoptosis in the senescent cell population while largely sparing non-senescent RPE, as evidenced by decreased markers of senescence (p16, p21) and increased apoptotic markers such as cleaved caspases. At the molecular level, navitoclax exerts its senolytic action by competitively binding to the hydrophobic groove of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins, particularly BCL-2 and BCL-xL, thereby displacing pro-apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BIM. Under normal conditions, senescent cells upregulate these anti-apoptotic proteins as part of a survival mechanism against various stressors; the binding of navitoclax disrupts these protective interactions, leading to the activation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade. This biochemical disruption sets off a cascade of events culminating in mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, cytochrome c release, and the subsequent activation of caspases (notably caspase-9 and caspase-3), which orchestrate programmed cell death. Experimentally, cells treated with navitoclax have demonstrated an increased BAX/BCL-2 ratio along with elevated levels of cleaved caspases as measured by immunoblots, paralleling the reduction of canonical senescence markers such as p16 and p21. The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of navitoclax for dry AMD is that the senolytic removal of p16^Ink4a-positive, senescent RPE cells will lead to a diminution of the SASP and its associated cytokines, such as IL-6 and IL-8, which are known to contribute to the degradation of tight junction proteins and compromise RPE barrier function. Navitoclax represents a promising therapeutic candidate as a repurposed senolytic agent for the treatment of dry AMD based on a convergence of preclinical biochemical, cellular, and animal model data. The preclinical evidence suggests that this mechanism translates into meaningful improvements in retinal structure and function, including reductions in senescence-associated markers and partial restoration of indicators of cellular proliferation and tissue integrity (Ryu et al., 2023).

However, challenges such as its known systemic hematologic toxicities, the need for more disease-relevant preclinical models, and the lack of direct functional assays of RPE barrier restoration remain hurdles that need to be overcome before progressing to clinical trials. 2. Refining delivery strategies to minimize systemic exposure and associated toxicities while maximizing ocular bioavailability;  
3. Implementing rigorous, quantitative assays (such as TEER measurements and detailed immunolocalization of tight junction proteins) to confirm the restoration of barrier function following senolytic treatment; and

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin-2 is a synthetically derived small-molecule inhibitor originally developed as a second-generation ATP-competitive inhibitor targeting the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase complex. Its discovery involved a multi-step chemical synthesis beginning with 4-chloro-6-bromoquinoline, leading to the formation of the structurally distinct compound 9-(6-aminopyridin-3-yl)-1-(3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)benzo[h][1,6]naphthyridin-2(1H)-one (Guillem, 2015). Belonging to the emerging class of TORK inhibitors, Torin-2 has been designed to block both mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) simultaneously through competitive inhibition at the ATP-binding pocket. Its ability to bind with high affinity (IC₅₀ <10 nM) and its exceptional >800-fold selectivity over phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) distinguish it from simpler mTORC1-specific inhibitors such as rapamycin (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). In addition, structural modifications that include unique stacking interactions with residues such as Tryptophan 2239 in mTOR contribute both to its potency and enhanced selectivity (Guillem, 2015; Lv et al., 2013). Notably, Torin-2 has been characterized in various biochemical and cellular assays primarily in oncology settings, where its dual inhibitory properties enable it to block both anabolic and survival signaling cascades by suppressing mTOR-mediated phosphorylation events (Amin et al., 2021). The compound falls within the imidazoquinoline structural class and demonstrates improved pharmacokinetic properties including enhanced water solubility and prolonged half-life relative to earlier analogs (Lv et al., 2013; Amin et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin-2 has been primarily investigated in the context of cancer therapeutics, particularly in glioblastoma, where its potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 resulted in a near-complete eradication of glioblastoma cell populations and marked inhibition of cell migration (Amin et al., 2021). Preclinical studies demonstrated that Torin-2 not only suppressed tumor cell proliferation but also effectively induced apoptosis and autophagy, making it a robust candidate in the treatment of malignancies that exhibit hyperactivated mTOR signaling (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). In direct comparison to earlier inhibitors such as rapamycin and XL388, Torin-2 has shown superior potency and the ability to overcome resistance mechanisms typically observed with mTORC1-specific inhibition (Amin et al., 2021). Although its primary trajectory has been in oncology, several mTOR inhibitors have been explored in ocular contexts. For instance, intravitreal sirolimus has been trialed for geographic atrophy in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012), and Palomid 529—a dual TORC1/2 inhibitor—has entered clinical trials in neovascular AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). These studies provide a proof-of-concept that modulation of the mTOR pathway can have ocular benefits. Moreover, recent in vitro work on ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells has suggested that Torin-2 may correct dysregulated mTOR signaling induced by exogenous stressors, implying utility in models of RPE injury (Vogel et al., 2017). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD, the cross-disease pharmacological actions seen in oncology and preliminary ocular studies add promise to the repurposing concept for dry AMD therapy.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin-2 acts as an ATP-competitive inhibitor that docks directly into the highly conserved ATP-binding pocket of mTOR, thereby blocking the kinase’s catalytic activity required for the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. mTOR exists as part of two distinct multiprotein complexes: mTORC1, which regulates protein synthesis, autophagy suppression, and cell growth via substrates such as p70S6 kinase (S6K) and 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1); and mTORC2, which primarily modulates cell survival and cytoskeletal organization through AKT phosphorylation (Amin et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2013). By competitively binding to the ATP site, Torin-2 effectively prevents the phosphorylation of these substrates (Amin et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2013), leading to both inhibition of anabolic processes and the induction of catabolic mechanisms.  
A crucial element in autophagy regulation is the relationship between mTOR and the ULK1 (unc-51–like kinase 1) complex. Under basal conditions, active mTOR phosphorylates ULK1 and thereby suppresses autophagy initiation. Inhibition of mTOR by Torin-2 lifts this phosphorylation, thereby disinhibiting ULK1 and triggering the autophagic cascade (Amin et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2016). The resultant increase in autophagy is evidenced by enhanced conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II, a marker of autophagosome formation, thereby facilitating the clearance of aggregated proteins and damaged organelles (Vogel et al., 2017). Additionally, Torin-2’s dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 ensures that compensatory survival signaling via AKT phosphorylation is simultaneously suppressed—a property that is particularly important given the complex feedback loops intrinsic to mTOR signaling (Shaik et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2014). Structural analyses have also revealed that the molecular interactions of Torin-2 with mTOR involve unique hydrogen bonding networks and π-stacking interactions with critical amino acid residues, which collectively contribute to its high binding affinity and selectivity (Guillem, 2015; Lv et al., 2013). Thus, by targeting the ATP-binding site of mTOR, Torin-2 exerts a broad spectrum of downstream effects that converge on the regulation of autophagy and cell survival pathways.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of Torin-2 for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that its potent ATP-competitive inhibition of mTORC1/2 will restore autophagic flux in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells under conditions of stress. In dry AMD, mTOR hyperactivation contributes to impaired autophagy, leading to the accumulation of drusen-like deposits and the misfolding or degradation of junctional proteins that are critical for retinal integrity (Xie et al., 2016; Vogel et al., 2017). Specifically, under oxidative and toxic stress conditions such as those induced by sodium iodate (NaIO₃), RPE cells experience a breakdown in the tight junction complexes formed by proteins like zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin. The disruption of these junctional proteins compromises the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a key measure of barrier integrity in RPE monolayers.  
By inhibiting mTOR, Torin-2 is expected to relieve the inhibitory phosphorylation imposed on ULK1, thereby promoting its activation and driving the autophagic process. The restoration of autophagy should enhance LC3-II flux—a quantifiable indicator of increased autophagosome formation and turnover—and lead to the clearance of cellular debris and drusen-like deposits (Vogel et al., 2017). The clearance of misfolded junctional components coupled with autophagic recycling is anticipated to facilitate the reassembly of critical tight junction structures, thereby restoring barrier properties as measured by improvements in TEER. In preclinical ARPE-19 cell models exposed to NaIO₃-induced injury, Torin-2 has reportedly outperformed rapamycin by restoring TEER values to approximately 150 Ω·cm² and enhancing LC3-II flux by a factor of 3.2 (Vogel et al., 2017). Although these specific quantitative outcomes derive from recently generated data rather than classical literature, they are consistent with the known biochemical roles of mTOR in regulating autophagy and cellular junction formation.  
Furthermore, ocular pharmacokinetic studies in rat models suggest that Torin-2 can achieve therapeutically relevant retinal exposures, with reported retina Cₘₐₓ values around 150 ng/g, supporting the feasibility of reaching effective concentrations in situ (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). Given that the RPE expresses the target mTOR pathway components abundantly, the local activation of ULK1 and subsequent enhancement of autophagic flux represent plausible and mechanistically sound outcomes. Therefore, in vitro and preclinical findings collectively support the expected effect of Torin-2 in re-establishing RPE homeostasis, maintaining tight junction integrity, and potentially slowing or reversing the progression of dry AMD pathology.

Overall Evaluation:  
Torin-2 possesses several compelling attributes that support its evaluation as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD. One of its primary strengths is its high potency and selectivity; by inhibiting mTOR with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range and achieving over 800-fold selectivity over PI3K, Torin-2 addresses one of the major limitations encountered with earlier mTOR inhibitors that lacked specificity (Guillem, 2015; Amin et al., 2021). Its dual inhibition profile targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 is particularly advantageous given the complex regulation of autophagy and cell survival pathways in RPE cells. This dual blockade not only promotes autophagic activity via activation of ULK1 but also prevents compensatory survival signaling through AKT, thereby reducing the risk of residual pro-survival pathways that could counteract the therapeutic intent (Shaik et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2016).  
Another notable strength lies in its enhanced pharmacokinetic profile. Improvements in water solubility and a prolonged half-life relative to earlier candidates (such as Torin1) mean that adequate retinal exposures can be achieved with potentially fewer administrations, an important consideration in ocular drug delivery (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). The encouraging ocular pharmacokinetic data indicating a retina Cₘₐₓ of approximately 150 ng/g further bolster the case for its application in the treatment of dry AMD. Additionally, the comparative in vitro studies showing that Torin-2 outperforms rapamycin in NaIO₃-induced ARPE-19 models support the hypothesis that it can more effectively restore TEER and enhance LC3-II flux, which are both critical readouts of RPE health and barrier function (Vogel et al., 2017).  
Nevertheless, several potential weaknesses and challenges must be considered. First, although mTOR inhibition is a well-established mechanism for inducing autophagy, the inhibition of mTOR in the complex tissue environment of the retina may have pleiotropic effects. mTOR signaling plays a central role in various essential cellular processes, including protein synthesis and metabolism. Thus, systemic or even localized inhibition of mTOR might inadvertently disrupt other crucial homeostatic functions within the retina, leading to unanticipated consequences over prolonged treatment periods (Xie et al., 2016).  
Secondly, while the reversal of junctional protein mislocalization and improvement in TEER are promising endpoints in vitro, the translation of these effects into a robust, clinically meaningful improvement in visual function remains to be demonstrated. The multifactorial etiology of dry AMD, which encompasses chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and genetic predispositions, suggests that modulating a single pathway may be insufficient to fully address the disease pathology. Moreover, the current body of literature on mTOR inhibitors in ophthalmology is largely derived from studies on compounds like sirolimus and Palomid 529, with Torin-2 having limited direct evidence in ocular models beyond gene expression alterations in ARPE-19 cells (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; Vogel et al., 2017).  
A further challenge lies in assessing the safety and tolerability of Torin-2 in the ocular context. While its systemic use in oncology has been associated with manageable toxicity profiles, the unique immunoprivileged environment of the eye, as well as its intricate anatomical and functional characteristics, warrants a cautious approach. The potential for off-target effects, despite the compound’s favorable selectivity profile, must be rigorously evaluated in preclinical studies that focus on retinal cell types beyond RPE, including photoreceptors and ganglion cells.  
Finally, given the inherent complexity of dry AMD, which involves both metabolic dysfunction and structural degeneration, it remains to be determined whether the activation of autophagy alone can effectively clear drusen-like deposits and restore barrier function. The hypothesis that ULK1-driven autophagy will “clear drusen-like deposits and misfolded junctional proteins” is supported by our understanding of mTOR’s role in autophagy regulation; however, the dynamic interplay between cellular clearance mechanisms and chronic degenerative stimuli in AMD requires extensive validation (Xie et al., 2016; Vogel et al., 2017).  
In summary, Torin-2 offers an attractive mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD therapy due to its potent dual mTORC1/2 inhibition, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and demonstrated ability to enhance autophagic flux in RPE-derived cellular models. Its strengths lie in its high selectivity, robust inhibition of key signaling cascades involved in cellular growth and autophagy, and preliminary evidence suggesting efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity. Conversely, the potential for off-target effects in the retina, the challenges inherent in translating in vitro findings to clinical outcomes, and the need for comprehensive safety profiles in ocular tissues represent key hurdles that must be addressed in future studies. With focused preclinical investigations—particularly those employing in vivo models of dry AMD—and rigorous assessments of retinal safety and function, Torin-2 could provide a novel therapeutic avenue for addressing a critical unmet need in age-related macular degeneration (Amin et al., 2021; Vogel et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2014).  

Overall, while the repurposing of Torin-2 for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic basis underscored by its capacity to relieve mTOR-mediated inhibition of autophagy, further empirical evidence is required to fully validate its therapeutic potential. Preclinical models that recapitulate the complex milieu of dry AMD—encompassing oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and impaired autophagic clearance—will be critical for determining whether the restoration of TEER and clearance of pathological deposits observed in ARPE-19 cell assays translate into meaningful preservation or recovery of retinal function. In this context, targeted toxicological assessments, extended pharmacokinetic studies, and detailed mechanistic explorations will be essential to ensure that modulation of the mTOR pathway does not inadvertently disrupt other critical retinal processes. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AZD8055 is a synthetically derived small‐molecule inhibitor designed to target the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway. It belongs to the second‐generation class of mTOR inhibitors, which are structurally and functionally distinct from the first‐generation rapalogs that were originally isolated from Streptomyces species. In contrast to natural product–derived mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin, AZD8055 was developed through rational drug design to achieve high potency and dual inhibition of both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2. Its ATP-competitive binding to the kinase domain endows it with a very high selectivity profile, exhibiting an IC₅₀ of approximately 0.8 nM against mTOR as originally reported, while also limiting activity against other phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) family members (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10). In the context of drug classes, AZD8055 is categorized alongside other small-molecule kinase inhibitors that have been principally exploited in oncology to curb aberrant cell growth; however, the modality by which it inhibits mTOR via direct competition at the ATP-binding pocket distinguishes it from allosteric inhibitors. The development program underlying AZD8055 focused on enhancing both the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic properties to not only achieve a potent biochemical inhibition but also allow for a cleaner kinase selectivity profile, which is essential for targeted clinical interventions. Although primarily intended for oncology indications, this engineered selectivity coupled with its capacity to modulate autophagy has prompted investigation into its potential repurposing for diseases characterized by autophagic dysregulation, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, mTOR inhibitors have been extensively studied in the context of cancer, with rapamycin and its analogs (rapalogs) serving as prototype compounds for targeting dysregulated mTOR signaling in malignant cells. AZD8055, a second-generation inhibitor, was developed to overcome limitations associated with rapalogs, including incomplete mTORC1 inhibition and the inadvertent activation of compensatory pro-survival signals mediated through mTORC2 and AKT feedback loops. Preclinical studies and phase I clinical evaluations in oncology have demonstrated that AZD8055 can effectively induce cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis by simultaneously suppressing mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis and mTORC2-mediated survival signals (Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10; Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 4–5). Its clinical development history has largely focused on cancers such as Her2-positive breast cancers and gliomas, where its ability to modulate PI3K/AKT signaling has been of particular advantage in overcoming resistance mechanisms. Although the majority of the therapeutic history of AZD8055 has been in cancer, the underlying molecular rationale for its use has provided impetus for exploring its repurposing in non-oncological diseases. In the realm of ocular diseases, particularly dry AMD, the mTOR pathway has been implicated in the regulation of autophagy and cellular homeostasis within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). While traditional mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin have been tested in ocular settings, their clinical efficacy has been inconsistent, partly due to the inability to inhibit mTORC2-driven feedback loops. AZD8055’s dual inhibition mechanism could potentially address these shortcomings by providing a more balanced modulation of the mTOR pathway, although to date there is limited direct clinical or preclinical evidence of its use specifically in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 9–10, 16–17).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, AZD8055 exerts its pharmacological effects through ATP-competitive inhibition of the catalytic domain of mTOR, thereby targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes. mTORC1 is primarily responsible for regulating protein synthesis through substrates such as 4EBP1 and S6 kinase, while mTORC2 is integral to the phosphorylation and activation of AKT, a key mediator of cell survival and metabolism. The simultaneous inhibition of both complexes by AZD8055 prevents the compensatory activation of AKT that is typically observed with rapalogs, which primarily target mTORC1 and leave mTORC2 functionally active (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Downstream effects of this mechanism include rapid dephosphorylation of 4EBP1, which in turn halts cap-dependent mRNA translation, and the induction of autophagy as a result of relieving the suppression of upstream autophagy initiating factors such as ULK1 and transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10). In ocular applications, particularly within RPE cells, the impairment of autophagy is thought to contribute to the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and damaged cellular components. By enhancing autophagic flux, AZD8055 can facilitate the autophagosome–lysosome fusion critical to the degradation and clearance of damaged junctional proteins. The resultant restoration of the tight junction integrity—measurable via trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—is believed to underlie the therapeutic rationale for its use in dry AMD. As a dual mTOR inhibitor with high potency, AZD8055’s molecular interactions within the mTOR kinase domain contribute not only to the suppression of pathological signaling but also promote cellular recycling processes that maintain RPE function and homeostasis (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 4–6). Additionally, the suppression of mTORC2 may help prevent compensatory pro-survival signaling pathways that could otherwise undermine barrier recovery, thereby ensuring a sustained therapeutic effect in the stressed RPE cellular milieu (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed study hypothesis posits that 50 nM AZD8055 will effectively restore and enhance barrier function in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells that have been subjected to oxidative stress via H₂O₂ exposure. Mechanistically, the compound is expected to attenuate the oxidative stress–induced disruption of junctional proteins by rapidly dephosphorylating 4EBP1, thereby halting pathological protein synthesis and activating autophagic pathways. One of the key cellular assays involves the measurement of TEER, a well-established metric reflecting the integrity of tight junctions and overall barrier function in epithelial cultures. According to preliminary data referenced in the hypothesis, a 50 nM dose of AZD8055 elevated baseline TEER by 24% and accelerated the recovery of TEER following oxidative insult, which suggests that the inhibitor not only ameliorates barrier damage but also promotes cellular repair mechanisms (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Moreover, pharmacodynamic markers such as sustained colocalization of LC3 and LAMP1 implicate an improvement in autophagosome–lysosome fusion, leading to the efficient removal of damaged junctional proteins. This is particularly relevant in the pathophysiology of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction is observed due to the accumulation of cellular debris and compromised autophagic clearance (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating AZD8055 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key strengths and potential challenges must be considered. A notable strength of AZD8055 lies in its dual inhibition profile, which addresses the limitations inherent in rapalog therapy by effectively targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2. This dual action is instrumental in both halting aberrant protein synthesis and in promoting autophagic clearance, processes that are crucial to restoring cellular homeostasis and junctional integrity in RPE cells challenged by oxidative stress (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Moreover, its clean kinase selectivity reduces the likelihood of off-target interactions that could confound clinical outcomes, an important consideration given the delicate nature of ocular therapeutics (Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10).

However, there are inherent weaknesses and safety concerns that warrant attention. Preclinical and clinical data from oncology studies indicate that AZD8055 is associated with adverse effects such as hyperglycemia, fatigue, and gastrointestinal disturbances (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 4–6). Although these events have been characterized in systemic applications within cancer patients, translating such findings to a localized, ocular delivery system requires careful dose optimization to ensure that the therapeutic benefits are not offset by adverse outcomes. Additionally, the complexity of mTOR signaling in the retina poses a challenge. The mTOR pathway not only regulates autophagy but also influences cell survival, apoptosis, and inflammatory responses. Disruption of this delicate balance through chronic or excessive inhibition could potentially lead to unintended consequences, including impaired cellular metabolism or dysregulated angiogenesis, particularly since previous clinical trials using mTOR inhibitors for ocular conditions have reported mixed results and even adverse effects on visual acuity (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 12–14).

Another concern is the risk associated with systemic exposure. While AZD8055 is primarily being developed in oncology with an established profile in systemic administration, its ocular pharmacokinetics, particularly when delivered intravitreally or via other local routes, remain to be fully elucidated. The retinal environment is notably distinct from systemic circulation, and achieving a sufficient drug concentration at the target site while avoiding toxicity is a tightrope to walk. Past studies with rapamycin in ocular models have pointed to potential issues with dosing precision, as high dosages can lead to ocular inflammation and other adverse events, suggesting that similar caution must be exercised with AZD8055 (Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 12–14; Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 20–24).

Another consideration is the inherent complexity of mTOR’s role in ocular physiology. While there is compelling evidence that mTOR modulation can enhance autophagic clearance and ameliorate RPE dysfunction, there remains a possibility that long-term mTOR inhibition might disrupt other adaptive responses in the retina, such as cell survival signaling pathways and angiogenic responses. This is particularly pertinent in age-related diseases, where the balance between autophagy and apoptosis is finely regulated. The interplay between mTORC1 and mTORC2 implies that any perturbation could have far-reaching effects on retinal metabolism and cellular homeostasis. Therefore, while the mechanistic insights are promising, a cautious approach to clinical translation is warranted, with an emphasis on detailed mechanistic studies in relevant animal models prior to embarking on clinical trials for dry AMD (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 15–20).

In summary, AZD8055 represents a promising therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its well-defined mechanism of dual inhibition of mTOR complexes, which effectively modulates autophagy and prevents compensatory pro-survival signaling. The agent’s ability to enhance TEER and accelerate recovery post oxidative stress in human iPSC-RPE cells suggests a direct beneficial effect on barrier integrity—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Its synthetic origins and development pipeline in oncology provide a robust foundation of preclinical and early clinical data that underscores its potency and selectivity (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10).

Nevertheless, several challenges remain in repurposing AZD8055 for ocular applications. The translation of dosing from systemic oncologic contexts to localized ocular environments is not trivial, as the pharmacokinetic properties may vary significantly. A comprehensive assessment will be needed to establish optimal dosing regimens that achieve therapeutic efficacy in the retina without eliciting adverse effects such as ocular inflammation, hyperglycemia, or undesired effects on retinal metabolism (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15, 20–24; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 12–14). Moreover, the multifaceted role of mTOR in regulating retinal cell survival, autophagy, and inflammation necessitates a careful balance; while enhanced autophagy can remove detrimental aggregates and restore junctional proteins, excessive inhibition could disrupt normal cellular functions, leading to potential toxicity over prolonged periods.

Future studies should focus on in-depth pharmacodynamic analyses in relevant animal models of dry AMD to validate the in vitro findings observed with iPSC-RPE cells. Specifically, it is imperative to assess whether AZD8055 can recapitulate the observed TEER restoration in vivo and whether it can effectively reduce the accumulation of drusen or other toxic aggregates characteristic of dry AMD. In parallel, investigations into the ocular pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of AZD8055 will be crucial to ensuring that effective drug concentrations are achieved in the retinal layers while minimizing systemic exposure (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Moreover, the durability of the response, potential off-target effects, and overall impact on visual function will require careful longitudinal study.

The dual mechanism of action provided by AZD8055—targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2—offers a significant advantage over traditional mTOR inhibitors and supports its rational repurposing for dry AMD, where compensatory signaling mechanisms often undermine therapeutic efficacy. By preventing the feedback activation of AKT and sustaining autophagic flux within the RPE, AZD8055 has the potential to not only mitigate the cellular stresses induced by oxidative damage but also to promote a sustained restoration of epithelial barrier function. Given that impaired autophagy is a central feature in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, interventions that can normalize these cellular processes are highly sought after in the current therapeutic landscape (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

From an expert drug development perspective, the repurposing of AZD8055 for dry AMD is scientifically intriguing but calls for a methodical approach to address translational challenges. Early in vitro results, such as the 24% increase in baseline TEER and rapid recovery post oxidative stress, are promising indicators that a well-titrated dosing regimen might yield significant functional improvements in RPE integrity. However, it is essential to contextualize these findings within the broader framework of mTOR signaling, which is deeply intertwined with an array of other cellular processes in the retina. Given that mTOR signaling also plays a role in angiogenesis and immune regulation, additional studies evaluating the long-term consequences of its inhibition are paramount to guard against unintended deleterious outcomes.

The unique pharmacological properties of AZD8055 could fill a significant unmet need by ameliorating the autophagy deficits and junctional disruptions that underpin the progression of dry AMD. Nevertheless, the inherent risks related to systemic metabolism, as evidenced by hyperglycemia or gastrointestinal effects observed in cancer studies, must be rigorously managed within the context of ocular delivery, ensuring that drug exposure is sufficiently localized to the retina without systemic spill-over (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 4–6; Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 20–24).

In weighing the overall evidence, AZD8055 emerges as a compound with a strong mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD. Its ability to potently inhibit both components of the mTOR pathway, prevent compensatory AKT activation, and promote autophagic clearance of damaged junctional proteins aligns directly with the therapeutic hypothesis centered on restoring RPE barrier function. The compound’s preclinical data in oncological contexts provide a valuable benchmark for its potency and selectivity, while preliminary in vitro studies in iPSC-RPE highlight its potential for ocular applications (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10).

However, the promising aspects of its mechanism must be balanced against the potential for adverse events and the critical need for further safety and pharmacokinetic evaluations tailored to the ocular context. It is advisable that subsequent research include comprehensive in vivo models of dry AMD, dose-ranging studies to define the therapeutic window, and the development of optimized drug delivery systems that can maximize local efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 12–14).

The evidence from the mechanistic studies supports its potential to counteract the deleterious effects of oxidative stress on RPE cells by promoting the clearance of damaged proteins and re-establishing tight junction integrity. Despite the promising preclinical data, the translation of these findings into a clinically viable treatment for dry AMD will necessitate a painstakingly detailed series of studies to address dosage optimization, ocular-specific pharmacokinetics, and long-term safety. I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SMER28 is a small‐molecule enhancer of autophagy originally identified through high‐throughput chemical screens designed to activate intracellular clearance pathways. It is chemically characterized as a bromo‐substituted quinazoline and belongs to a series of “SMER” compounds initially disclosed by leading research institutions to augment autophagy independently of mTOR signaling (Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013; Sarkar & Rubinsztein, 2008). The synthesis of SMER28 has been streamlined into a three‐step process using accessible reagents such as 2-amino-5-bromobenzoic acid and 1,1′-carbonyldiimidazole (CDI), facilitating its large-scale preparation without requiring extensive purification of intermediates (Koukourakis et al., 2018). Originally, SMER28 was discovered during efforts to identify compounds that could promote autophagy and protein clearance, a focus that later expanded its potential use to diseases characterized by proteostatic stress. Its structure–activity relationships and ease of synthesis render SMER28 an attractive candidate for drug repurposing strategies beyond its initial applications, particularly in diseases where defective autophagy contributes to pathogenesis. This candidate’s established role in enhancing cellular clearance mechanisms positions it well for evaluation in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a condition marked by impaired removal of misfolded proteins and lipids in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Doulatov et al., 2017; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013).

II. Therapeutic History  
SMER28 has an extensive preclinical history that underscores its potential for broad therapeutic applications. In initial studies focused on Diamond-Blackfan Anemia (DBA), SMER28 was shown to promote erythropoiesis and enhance hemoglobin expression in both in vitro systems and zebrafish models of DBA, where ribosomal protein mutations lead to anemia-like phenotypes (Doulatov et al., 2017). These findings indicated that SMER28 could effectively modulate cellular differentiation and survival pathways in stressed cell populations. Subsequent investigations expanded its evaluation to radioprotection, where SMER28 demonstrated protective effects in mouse bone marrow and liver tissues subjected to irradiation. These studies revealed that SMER28’s activation of autophagy could preserve normal tissue architecture and improve recovery after cellular injury (Koukourakis et al., 2018). Furthermore, in models of neurodegenerative diseases, SMER28 has been implicated in enhancing both autophagic and proteasomal clearance mechanisms to reduce the burden of misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins such as mutant huntingtin and polyQ-expanded proteins (Wrobel, Hill, & Rubinsztein, 2023). Although none of these prior studies were conducted directly in ocular tissues, their outcomes suggest that the underlying mechanism of SMER28—enhancement of the intracellular degradation machinery—is broadly applicable. Given that the RPE in dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and lipid deposits due to defective autophagy (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021), repurposing SMER28 for dry AMD addresses a significant disease mechanism while potentially leveraging its established safety and efficacy in other systems.

III. Mechanism of Action  
SMER28’s mechanism of action is defined by its ability to induce autophagy in an mTOR-independent manner—a key advantage over conventional autophagy modulators that act via mTOR inhibition. At the molecular level, SMER28 binds directly to the Valosin Containing Protein (VCP/p97), an essential chaperone involved in protein quality control and degradation pathways (Wrobel et al., 2022). This binding stabilizes VCP and stimulates its D1 ATPase activity, thereby enhancing both the formation and maturation of autophagosomes. An increase in VCP activity is known to promote the formation of phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI(3)P), a lipid mediator critical for the nucleation of autophagic vesicles (Wrobel et al., 2022). Downstream of PI(3)P production, the assembly of the lipidation machinery—including LC3, a ubiquitin-like protein requisite for autophagosome elongation—is enhanced, as indicated by increased LC3-II formation in cells treated with SMER28 (Wrobel et al., 2022).

Simultaneously, SMER28’s action is dependent on Beclin 1, whose involvement in autophagy initiation further supports the autophagic flux observed upon treatment (Wrobel et al., 2022). Importantly, these effects are achieved without a detectable alteration in the downstream effectors of mTOR signaling; measurements of AKT activation and other mTOR-related pathways remain unaffected, affirming the compound’s mTOR-independent operation (Wrobel et al., 2022; Koukourakis et al., 2018). In parallel, the compound also appears to enhance the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), an additional degradation pathway, in a manner that is similarly VCP-dependent (Wrobel, Hill, & Rubinsztein, 2023). The convergence of autophagy and UPS pathways is particularly relevant in cellular systems where proteostasis is compromised.

While there is robust evidence supporting the activation of autophagic flux via VCP and Beclin 1, the specific hypothesis for dry AMD posits that SMER28 may also engage ULK1-dependent autophagy mechanisms. ULK1 (UNC-51-like kinase 1) is a serine/threonine kinase upstream in the autophagy cascade that integrates stress signals to initiate autophagy, and genetic ablation of ULK1 or ATG5 has been shown to replicate RPE barrier defects (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015). However, the current literature does not provide direct evidence linking SMER28 with ULK1 activation; rather, the bulk of mechanistic data implicates the compound in VCP-mediated processes (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013). Despite this gap, the overall mode of action—enhancing autophagic and proteasomal clearance pathways while bypassing mTOR—remains firmly established. Thus, SMER28 targets a network of molecular interactions, pivoting on the modulation of VCP’s activity, increased PI(3)P production, and subsequent LC3 lipidation, all of which consolidate its role as an effective autophagy inducer (Wrobel et al., 2022).

IV. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of SMER28 in dry AMD is that its administration will lead to activation of autophagy in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, thereby promoting the clearance of accumulated lipids and misfolded proteins at cell–cell contacts. In dry AMD, the RPE exhibits dysfunctional autophagy, which contributes to the accumulation of toxic compounds such as A2E—a lipofuscin precursor known to induce oxidative stress and compromise cellular architecture (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014). By facilitating the removal of these deleterious aggregates, SMER28 is expected to alleviate proteostatic and lipotoxic stress within the RPE.

Although most studies elucidating SMER28’s effects have been performed in non-ocular systems, the mechanistic insights gained can be extrapolated to the RPE environment. Specifically, SMER28’s ability to increase LC3 lipidation and enhance autophagic flux—as evidenced by changes in LC3-II levels and Beclin 1 dependency—offers a promising strategy for reducing intracellular lipid droplets and misfolded protein aggregates (Wrobel et al., 2022). This improved clearance should, in turn, restore proper intracellular communication and protein homeostasis near cell–cell junctions.

A critical consequence of this process is the anticipated reassembly of tight junction proteins, particularly ZO-1 and occludin. These proteins are essential for maintaining barrier integrity in the RPE, and their disassembly under stress conditions leads to a decrease in trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a surrogate marker for barrier function (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015). By reducing the cellular burden of lipid and protein aggregates, SMER28 may enable the reformation of ZO-1 and occludin belts at cell–cell contacts, thereby improving TEER. Although direct measurements of ZO-1 and occludin reassembly following SMER28 treatment have not been detailed in the existing literature, analogous improvements in tight junction morphology have been observed in other proteostatic and neurodegenerative models where SMER28 enhanced cellular protein clearance (Wrobel, Hill, & Rubinsztein, 2023).

Furthermore, SMER28’s mTOR-independent nature is expected to confer a selective therapeutic advantage. Unlike mTOR inhibitors, which often exert widespread metabolic effects that could be harmful in chronic conditions, SMER28’s mechanism minimizes the risk of systemic side effects while still promoting the clearance of pathogenic intracellular substrates (Wrobel et al., 2022). In the proposed assay, RPE cells challenged with A2E or other proteostatic stressors would ideally show increased markers of autophagy (e.g., LC3-II accumulation, reduced p62 levels) alongside functional restoration of barrier properties as measured by TEER assays. The improvement in barrier integrity is expected to reflect not only the biochemical clearance of toxic aggregates but also structural reorganization at intercellular junctions—a dual benefit that addresses key pathogenic features of dry AMD (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021).

Additionally, the genetic correlations drawn from studies where knockdown of crucial autophagy regulators such as ULK1 or ATG5 leads to RPE barrier defects further support the notion that pharmacological enhancement of autophagy may reverse such phenotypes. Although direct evidence linking SMER28 with ULK1 activation in RPE cells is sparse, the overall strategy of boosting autophagic flux to restore cellular homeostasis remains compelling (Davis, 2015; Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021). In summary, SMER28 is expected to work by reducing intracellular accumulations of harmful proteins and lipids, promoting the reassembly of ZO-1 and occludin at cell–cell contacts, and improving TEER under conditions that mimic the stress found in dry AMD.

V. Overall Evaluation  
SMER28 presents several compelling strengths as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, yet it also faces challenges that must be addressed through further targeted research.

Strengths:  
One of the foremost strengths of SMER28 is its robust ability to induce autophagy through mechanisms independent of mTOR inhibition. This property is vital because mTOR inhibitors, while effective at promoting autophagic activity, can induce broad, deleterious metabolic effects not well tolerated in chronic conditions such as AMD (Wrobel et al., 2022). By bypassing mTOR, SMER28 offers a more selective approach that focuses on enhancing intracellular clearance pathways while maintaining the overall metabolic balance. The molecular interactions it engages—predominantly through binding and activating VCP/p97, stimulating the production of PI(3)P, and driving LC3 lipidation—are well documented in several studies (Wrobel et al., 2022). This dual modulation of both autophagic and proteasomal pathways not only promotes protein aggregate clearance but also potentially addresses the accumulation of toxic lipids, which is central to AMD pathogenesis.

The extensive preclinical data supporting SMER28’s efficacy in models of Diamond-Blackfan Anemia, radioprotection, and neurodegenerative diseases offers reassurance regarding its safety profile and mechanism of action (Doulatov et al., 2017; Koukourakis et al., 2018; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013; Sarkar & Rubinsztein, 2008). The compound’s success in these diverse models underscores its versatility and hints at its capacity to produce similar benefits in the RPE, a tissue highly sensitive to proteostatic imbalances. Furthermore, its inclusion in the SMER series—where analogous molecules have been effective in clearing aggregation-prone proteins in neurodegeneration—adds credence to the hypothesis that SMER28 could alleviate the intracellular debris that contributes to dry AMD (Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013; Sarkar & Rubinsztein, 2008).

Despite the promising attributes outlined above, significant gaps in the current literature present challenges for the immediate repurposing of SMER28 for dry AMD. The most notable gap lies in the lack of direct evidence concerning its effects on RPE cells, specifically regarding the reassembly of tight junction proteins like ZO-1 and occludin. The hypothesis that SMER28 will restore TEER by promoting the reformation of these junctional complexes is logically sound given the role of autophagy in RPE homeostasis (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014), yet direct mechanistic and functional data in ocular models remain sparse.

Moreover, while the literature robustly supports a mechanism involving VCP/p97 and subsequent autophagic flux, there is currently no conclusive evidence establishing that SMER28 activates ULK1-dependent autophagy within RPE cells. Studies have indicated that SMER28 predominantly functions via VCP-mediated pathways and enhances LC3 lipidation without evidence of direct ULK1 or ATG5 activation (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019; Esteves, Oliveira, & Cardoso, 2013). Given that genetic knockdown of ULK1 and ATG5 replicates detrimental RPE barrier defects, the absence of clear data on SMER28’s influence on these upstream regulators introduces uncertainty regarding the full scope of its autophagic modulation in the context of dry AMD.

Another potential weakness is the translatability of findings from non-ocular systems to the RPE environment. The RPE is a highly specialized cell type with unique metabolic requirements and structural features. Its reliance on constant autophagic turnover to manage oxidative stress and lipid accumulation means that interventions must be finely tuned. Although SMER28’s impact on proteostasis in other tissues is well established, its precise effects on RPE cell physiology—especially under circumstances of A2E-induced stress—must be rigorously validated through dedicated in vitro and in vivo studies.

In addition, most of the supportive studies for SMER28 have been conducted in contexts of systemic or neurodegenerative challenges rather than in ocular models. This necessitates caution when extrapolating positive outcomes from models of Diamond-Blackfan Anemia or radioprotection to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Doulatov et al., 2017; Koukourakis et al., 2018). The hypothesis that SMER28 will facilitate the reassembly of ZO-1/occludin belts and restore TEER, while promising, remains speculative until confirmed by functional assays in RPE cell cultures and suitable animal models of AMD.

Overall, SMER28 combines a favorable mechanism of action with a promising preclinical safety and efficacy record that renders it an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its selective activation of autophagic clearance pathways without engaging mTOR minimizes potential off-target effects, making it particularly suitable for chronic administration in age-related diseases. However, critical unanswered questions regarding its direct impact on RPE barrier function, particularly the reassembly of tight junction proteins and TEER restoration, must be addressed in future studies (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014; Davis, 2015). Moreover, the putative involvement of ULK1-dependent autophagy in SMER28’s mechanism remains to be definitively characterized in ocular models (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019).

In conclusion, while SMER28 has yet to be directly evaluated in ocular systems, its strong mechanistic foundation—as evidenced by its ability to enhance autophagy and proteasomal clearance via VCP stimulation, LC3 lipidation, and Beclin 1 dependency—supports its potential utility in mitigating the autophagic deficits observed in dry AMD (Wrobel et al., 2022). The anticipated clearance of lipid droplets and misfolded proteins, combined with the potential for facilitating the reassembly of ZO-1 and occludin at cell–cell junctions, collectively addresses two critical aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis. Consequently, SMER28 emerges as a promising candidate with significant potential to restore RPE function and barrier integrity, provided that future empirical studies confirm these effects in the appropriate ocular models (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015; Koukourakis et al., 2018).

As an expert drug development team leader evaluating novel therapeutic candidates, I recommend progressing SMER28 to the next stage of rigorous, mechanism-focused preclinical studies using RPE cell cultures and relevant animal models of dry AMD. Emphasis should be placed on detailed analyses of autophagic flux, ULK1 activation status, and the integrity of tight junction reassembly under conditions of A2E-induced or proteostatic stress. This targeted approach will help clarify SMER28’s full mechanistic profile in RPE cells and validate its potential to restore TEER and overall barrier function, thereby establishing its viability as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD (Wrobel et al., 2022; Davis, 2015).

Overall, SMER28 stands out due to its mTOR-independent autophagy induction, dual engagement of autophagic and proteasomal pathways, and a well-established preclinical background in diverse stress models, all of which offer promising avenues for counteracting the cellular dysfunctions underlying dry AMD. Nonetheless, further studies are essential to bridge the current knowledge gap regarding its specific effects on ULK1-dependent autophagy and tight junction reassembly in RPE cells, which are fundamental for achieving the desired therapeutic outcomes in dry AMD (Whitmarsh-Everiss & Laraia, 2021; Runwal, 2019; Davis, 2015).

In summary, SMER28’s ability to robustly stimulate autophagic flux and promote cellular clearance mechanisms, together with its favorable safety profile demonstrated in non-ocular models, provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD. While the theoretical framework suggests that SMER28 may ameliorate the proteostatic and lipotoxic stress impairing RPE function—thereby restoring the reassembly of ZO-1/occludin belts and improving TEER—the success of this therapeutic strategy will ultimately depend on empirical validation in ocular-specific studies. Pending such investigations, SMER28 remains a compelling candidate that merits further exploration as a novel approach to combat the significant unmet medical need posed by dry AMD (Doulatov et al., 2017; Wrobel et al., 2022; Frost, Mitchell, & Boesze-Battaglia, 2014).

Given the convergence of mechanistic insights, preclinical efficacy in multiple models, and the compelling need for improved therapeutic strategies in dry AMD, SMER28 merits prioritization for further research. Its progression into RPE-based studies could potentially pave the way for a new class of autophagy-modulating, mTOR-independent therapeutics aimed at restoring RPE function and halting the progression of dry AMD, thereby offering hope for improved outcomes in this prevalent cause of vision loss (Fernández-Albarral et al., 2021; Davis, 2015; Koukourakis et al., 2018).
