I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PXS-5153A is a synthetically derived molecule that belongs to the class of selective lysyl oxidase inhibitors. In its design, medicinal chemistry efforts focused on optimizing potency and selectivity for LOXL2, along with activity against LOXL3, two members of the lysyl oxidase family that catalyze the oxidative deamination of lysine residues in collagens and elastin to promote covalent crosslink formation. These crosslinks confer the mechanical strength and stiffness of extracellular matrices (ECMs) such as Bruch’s membrane. Synthetic routes to compounds like PXS-5153A typically rely on structure-based design and iterative optimization to achieve potent enzyme inhibition with favorable pharmacokinetic properties (Lin et al., 2020). The compound, commercially available under MedChemExpress HY-111217, is representative of a new therapeutic class that has been primarily explored in the context of fibrosis and tumor microenvironment modulation. Given that ECM stiffening is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, targeting LOXL2 represents a novel approach compared to conventional anti-inflammatory or anti-angiogenic strategies.

II. Therapeutic History  
The LOXL2 inhibitor class, including molecules such as PXS-5153A, has been extensively tested in preclinical models of fibrosis and cancer. For example, within non-ocular systems, LOXL2 activity has been linked to increased tissue stiffness that fosters metastatic progression and desmoplastic reactions in tumors, and selective inhibition of LOXL2 has been shown to reduce crosslink density, attenuating fibrotic remodeling (Lin et al., 2020). Experimental inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity using non-selective agents like β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) has also been applied to in vitro and in vivo models to modulate ECM assembly, with effects on barrier function observed in RPE cultures co-treated with endothelial cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). Although LOXL2 inhibitors have not traditionally been used to treat dry AMD, evidence underscores the centrality of aberrant ECM crosslinking in BM thickening observed during aging and AMD progression (Wang et al., 2025). In particular, the endothelial cell–RPE crosstalk studies demonstrate a critical role for lysyl oxidase activity in regulating collagen bundle formation and in establishing RPE barrier properties (Benedicto et al., 2017). Accordingly, while there is no direct clinical or preclinical record of PXS-5153A in AMD, the antifibrotic profile of the compound and its impact on extracellular matrix mechanics in other disease contexts serve as a compelling rationale to explore its application in dry AMD.

III. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, LOXL2 catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of lysine or hydroxylysine residues present in collagens and elastin. This reaction is critical for the formation of covalent crosslinks that stabilize the ECM. Overexpression or hyperactivity of LOXL2 results in an excessively crosslinked and stiff matrix. In the eye, particularly within Bruch’s membrane—which is a complex, stratified ECM structure located between the RPE and the choroid—aberrant collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking are known to increase mechanical tension. Such mechanical changes are thought to adversely affect RPE cell function by interfering with integrin-mediated cell–matrix interactions and perturbing the proper localization of tight junction proteins, including ZO-1 and occludin (Benedicto et al., 2017).

PXS-5153A functions by binding to the catalytic pocket of LOXL2, thereby preventing its enzymatic activity. By blocking the oxidative deamination step, PXS-5153A reduces the formation of both immature and mature crosslinks in ECM proteins. The anticipated outcome is a lower crosslink density in Bruch’s membrane, resulting in a softer, more compliant matrix environment. This reduction in mechanical stiffness is expected to diminish abnormal mechanosignaling through β1 integrins, which are integral to the assembly and maintenance of tight junctions on RPE cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). The downstream consequences of reduced integrin activation include dampening of Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways, which in turn facilitate the stabilization and proper localization of tight junction proteins at the RPE cell membranes (Benedicto et al., 2017). Restoration of these junctional complexes correlates with improved barrier function, typically measured as an increased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in cell culture models. This mechanism is supported by studies in which inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity—by pharmacological agents such as BAPN—led to alterations in RPE barrier properties and tight junction morphology (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by directly targeting LOXL2, PXS-5153A is proposed to correct the pathological ECM remodeling that underlies BM stiffening in dry AMD while re-establishing proper RPE barrier integrity.

IV. Expected Effect  
The expected therapeutic effect of PXS-5153A in dry AMD centers on normalization of the BM ECM and concomitant restoration of RPE barrier function. In the proposed experimental model—an in vitro co-culture system where human fetal RPE (hfRPE) cells are grown on a substrate mimicking BM with defined stiffness—the application of PXS-5153A at concentrations around 5 µM is anticipated to yield a number of favorable outcomes.

First, by reducing LOXL2-mediated crosslinking of collagen IV and fibronectin, the drug should decrease the mechanical stiffness of the BM analog. A less rigid BM reduces aberrant integrin activation on the basolateral surfaces of RPE cells, which has been shown to be critical for proper tight junction assembly. In several studies, when the extracellular matrix is normalized—such as by altering substrate stiffness—there is an improvement in the localization of key tight junction proteins, specifically occludin and ZO-1, at the cell membrane (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Second, the reduced matrix stiffness is expected to alleviate the mechanical stress experienced by RPE cells, thereby facilitating the re-establishment of cell polarity and intercellular junction continuity. The stabilization of junctional complexes is measurable by TEER. In previous EC–RPE co-culture experiments, modulation of ECM mechanical properties directly correlated with increased TEER values, reflecting improved barrier function (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Moreover, the proper organization of the basement membrane is not only a structural consideration; the biochemical signaling through β1 integrin receptors—critical for maintaining cell adhesion and survival—would return toward homeostatic levels, further supporting the integrity of the RPE layer (Benedicto et al., 2017). These integrin-mediated signals influence downstream effectors such as Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK, which have been implicated in regulating tight junction dynamics (Benedicto et al., 2017). Progress in these pathways is expected to manifest as an overall improvement in the barrier phenotype, which is central to preventing the leakage of fluid and other deleterious solutes into the subretinal space—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.

In summary, it is anticipated that treatment with PXS-5153A in appropriate in vitro (and ultimately in vivo) models will lead to:  
• Reduced collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in BM, yielding a matrix with decreased stiffness (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Normalization of β1 integrin signaling and subsequent reorganization of RPE tight junctions with improved localization of proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Restoration of barrier function as evidenced by increased TEER measurements and improved paracellular permeability profiles (Benedicto et al., 2017).  

Thus, PXS-5153A is expected to address one of the core aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis by targeting ECM remodeling, which in turn indirectly stabilizes RPE cell function.

V. Overall Evaluation  
The concept of using PXS-5153A to modulate ECM pathology in dry AMD is compelling given the mechanistic insights derived from studies on lysyl oxidase activity in epithelial barrier function and ECM assembly. Among the strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its robust preclinical evidence in fibrosis and tumor microenvironment models. LOXL2 has been implicated in promoting tissue stiffening by catalyzing the crosslinking of collagen and fibronectin in various tissues (Lin et al., 2020). The pathophysiological parallels between fibrotic ECM remodeling in cancers and the stiffening of Bruch’s membrane in dry AMD provide a strong rationale for repurposing a LOXL2 inhibitor in an ocular context. Numerous studies have demonstrated that extracellular matrix integrity is essential for optimal RPE barrier function, and that even subtle changes in ECM mechanics can disrupt junctional complexes and lead to barrier dysfunction (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by targeting a critical enzymatic step in ECM crosslinking, PXS-5153A may confer dual benefits: it could both reduce the pathological stiffening of Bruch’s membrane and promote the reorganization of tight junction complexes, ultimately resulting in enhanced TEER and stabilization of the outer blood–retina barrier.

However, several important weaknesses or uncertainties must be considered. First, while numerous studies (using agents such as BAPN) have illustrated that lysyl oxidase inhibition affects RPE barrier function, direct evidence with selective LOXL2 inhibitors—specifically in ocular models of dry AMD—is lacking (Buniello et al., 2025). In fact, the Open Targets Platform indicates only a weak direct association between LOXL2 and age-related macular degeneration, based on limited literature evidence (Buniello et al., 2025). This raises the possibility that, although LOXL2 plays a demonstrable role in ECM crosslinking in other tissues, its specific involvement in dry AMD pathogenesis may not be as pronounced or may be influenced by other factors not recapitulated in non-ocular models.

Furthermore, potential off-target effects or the consequences of broadly altering ECM crosslinking in the eye must be carefully examined. The structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane is critical not only for its barrier function but also for nutrient transport between the choroidal circulation and the RPE. Overinhibition of LOXL2, or interference with normal ECM turnover, may inadvertently lead to basement membrane disorganization, as has been observed when lysyl oxidase activity was inhibited during critical periods of retinal development (Benedicto et al., 2017). This underscores the need for precise dose optimization and targeted delivery, ideally restricted to the ocular environment, to avoid systemic side effects.

Another consideration is the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. In addition to ECM stiffening, dry AMD involves multifactorial processes including oxidative stress, complement activation, inflammation, and the accumulation of lipoprotein deposits. Thus, while normalizing matrix stiffness is likely to improve RPE barrier function, it may be insufficient to fully arrest or reverse the disease process on its own. A combination therapy that also addresses the inflammatory and degenerative components of AMD may eventually be required (Benedicto et al., 2017; Caban et al., 2022).

From a development perspective, there is significant strength in the repurposing strategy because agents like PXS-5153A already have a detailed preclinical profile in non-ocular fibrotic models. This existing data can accelerate preclinical validation in ocular models, with studies planned in RPE–BM co-culture systems using TEER as a functional readout (Benedicto et al., 2017). Furthermore, leveraging well-characterized in vitro assays (such as those involving decellularized ECM and substrate stiffness modulation as described in the context) offers a clear experimental framework to evaluate whether the normalization of BM stiffness by PXS-5153A is sufficient to restore RPE tight junction integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017).

Nonetheless, one notable weakness is the limited direct evidence linking LOXL2 specifically to dry AMD. Although elevated lysyl oxidase activity and changes in collagen crosslinking have been observed in the context of RPE barrier function and BM integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017), the genetic and translational data associating LOXL2 with AMD are not robust. The relatively low association score (Buniello et al., 2025) suggests that additional studies are needed to clarify LOXL2’s role in the eye and to determine whether its inhibition will yield a therapeutically meaningful benefit in dry AMD patients.

In conclusion, repurposing PXS-5153A for dry AMD represents an innovative strategy that leverages the known antifibrotic effects of LOXL2 inhibition to address the deleterious ECM remodeling observed in aged Bruch’s membrane. The candidate’s synthetic origins and prior applications in fibrosis and cancer studies provide a solid foundation for its use, while the mechanistic rationale—centered on reducing pathological crosslinking and restoring RPE barrier function—is strongly supported by evidence from ECM modulation studies (Benedicto et al., 2017). However, challenges remain due to the lack of direct ocular data, potential risks of overmodulating ECM integrity, and the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology. Future research must focus on rigorous in vitro validation in RPE–BM co-culture systems and in vivo studies in relevant AMD animal models to establish the efficacy and safety profile of PXS-5153A in the context of dry AMD. Overall, despite these uncertainties, PXS-5153A holds promise as a novel ECM-targeted therapeutic candidate that could complement existing and emerging treatment strategies for this currently unmet clinical need (Lin et al., 2020; Buniello et al., 2025).

Taken together, the strengths of a clear mechanism of action, potent enzyme selectivity, and an innovative approach toward ECM normalization position PXS-5153A as an attractive candidate warranting further investigation. Nonetheless, a careful reappraisal of the molecular role of LOXL2 in the ocular microenvironment, along with detailed studies on dosing, delivery, and potential off-target effects, will be critical in determining whether this candidate can be successfully repurposed for treating dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Belumosudil (KD025; Rezurock) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable, indazole-derived serine/threonine kinase inhibitor that preferentially targets Rho-associated coiled-coil–containing protein kinase 2 (ROCK2) over ROCK1 and was developed by Kadmon Pharmaceuticals following licensing from Nano Terra (now approved in the United States for chronic graft-versus-host disease, cGVHD) (Blair, 2021; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022; Przepiorka et al., 2022). Biochemical selectivity has been consistently reported across sources: IC₅₀ values are approximately 60–110 nM for ROCK2 with markedly weaker activity on ROCK1 (typically >10 µM), and orthogonal profiling notes ROCK2 ~0.105 µM and ROCK1 ~24 µM, confirming substantial isoform preference (Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022; Blair, 2021; Lake et al., 2020). As an ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor, belumosudil binds the catalytic domain of ROCK2, analogous to the mechanism of other clinically used ROCK inhibitors, but with enhanced isoform selectivity designed to improve tolerability relative to pan-ROCK agents (e.g., fasudil, ripasudil, netarsudil) (Cheng et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

The broader class—ROCK inhibitors—modulates actin–myosin cytoskeletal dynamics by decreasing phosphorylation of myosin regulatory elements and altering actin turnover via downstream nodes (LIMK–cofilin, ERM proteins), with downstream effects on cell contractility, focal adhesions, cell junctions, migration, and myofibroblast differentiation (Cheng et al., 2025). In ophthalmology, ROCK inhibitors have established or emerging therapeutic roles: netarsudil and ripasudil lower intraocular pressure by relaxing trabecular meshwork and Schlemm’s canal, and corneal endothelial repair paradigms (topical ROCK inhibitors and cell therapy adjuncts) exploit cytoskeletal relaxation, enhanced adhesion, and proliferation to accelerate re-endothelialization (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025). Collectively, these features position belumosudil within a drug class with proven ocular pharmacology and strong plausibility for modulating epithelial/endothelial barrier biology through cytoskeletal re-tuning (Leong et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic immunomodulation and anti-fibrotic indications. Belumosudil is FDA-approved for treatment of cGVHD after at least two prior systemic therapies at an oral dose of 200 mg once daily with food; population pharmacokinetics indicate a mean elimination half-life of ~19 hours, primary CYP3A4 metabolism, and predominant fecal excretion, with two metabolites that also inhibit ROCK2 (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Blair, 2021). Across phase 2 programs in cGVHD, objective response rates (65–77%) were observed with 200 mg once or twice daily dosing, with corticosteroid sparing and acceptable tolerability, consolidating a favorable clinical safety/efficacy profile for chronic use in a heavily pretreated, immunologically dysregulated population (Jagasia et al., 2021; Zanin-Zhorov & Blazar, 2021). Beyond cGVHD, belumosudil has been explored in fibrotic diseases (interim idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis signal for attenuated FVC decline) and systemic sclerosis, consistent with class-wide anti-fibrotic properties driven by ROCK2 blockade (Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

Ocular use of ROCK inhibitors (class precedent). While belumosudil itself has not been reported in clinical ocular indications, the ROCK inhibitor class has multiple precedents in eye disease. Topical netarsudil and ripasudil are approved or widely used for glaucoma; intravitreal and topical fasudil have been explored for retinal diseases (e.g., diabetic macular edema) with reported safety in small series, and sustained-release ocular delivery of ROCK inhibitors (e.g., AR-13503) has been tested in preclinical models (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025). These translational precedents establish that ROCK pathway modulation can be achieved in ocular tissues via topical, intravitreal, or sustained-release routes and that cytoskeletal/vascular barrier targets respond to this mechanism in the eye (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Belumosudil in ocular preclinical models. In a laser-induced choroidal neovascularization/subretinal fibrosis model designed to isolate fibrotic progression, both fasudil (pan-ROCK) and belumosudil (ROCK2-selective) reduced fibrosis volume, preserved retinal morphology, increased retinal thickness, reduced pyknotic nuclei, and decreased type I collagen and α-SMA staining; corrected total cell fluorescence for ROCK1/ROCK2 was reduced, with particularly strong ROCK2 target engagement by belumosudil (occupancy down from 6.7% to 0.1%) (Zandi et al., 2025). Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) and western blot evidence showed reductions in p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex—consistent with ROCK pathway inhibition—alongside decreases in TGF-β1, fibronectin, vimentin, and α-SMA; belumosudil also more effectively reduced “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations near the choroid–RPE boundary compared with fasudil and decreased macrophages/perivascular cells, suggesting anti-inflammatory as well as anti-fibrotic activity (Zandi et al., 2025). In vitro, 24-hour ROCK inhibitor exposure in fibroblastic cells altered morphology (loss of long processes, blunted periphery) and decreased cell numbers, consistent with cytoskeletal/phenotype modulation and possible anti-proliferative effects in fibrogenic cells (Zandi et al., 2025).

Dry AMD relevance and gaps. The above in vivo data position ROCK2 inhibition as an anti-fibrotic modifier of the choroid–RPE interface after laser injury, with partial restoration of retinal architecture; however, they do not test dry AMD pathobiology (e.g., sodium iodate RPE toxicity or geographic atrophy models) (Zandi et al., 2025). Direct ocular RPE barrier endpoints—TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and tight-junction protein integrity (ZO-1, claudin-19)—have not been reported for belumosudil in RPE, and the available studies do not include oxidative or complement injury paradigms (H₂O₂, NaIO₃) in ARPE-19, primary human RPE, or in vivo dry AMD models (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). Class-level in vitro RPE evidence exists for ROCK inhibition improving wound closure, adhesion, pigmentation, RPE65 expression, and photoreceptor outer-segment phagocytosis in iPSC-RPE with Y-27632, but without barrier readouts, and with limited recovery duration and small sample sizes (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Additional pluripotent RPE manufacturing work reports ROCK inhibition suppresses EMT programs (TGF-β/Wnt ligands, SNAI2, collagens) and promotes rapid tight-junction reformation in culture, supporting barrier-relevant cytoskeletal effects at the transcriptomic/phenotypic level, but without TEER or paracellular flux data under oxidative/complement stress (Croze, 2015). In sum, while class-level and belumosudil-specific ocular data support anti-fibrotic and cytoskeletal modulation at the choroid–RPE interface, there is no direct published evidence in the provided literature set that belumosudil rescues TEER, preserves claudin-19/ZO-1, or reduces FITC-dextran flux under H₂O₂ or complement challenge in RPE or that it improves outcomes in NaIO₃ models (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
ROCK2 biology and junctional/cytoskeletal control. ROCK1/2 are AGC-family serine/threonine kinases activated by RhoA–GTP; they increase actomyosin contractility primarily by phosphorylating myosin light chain (MLC) directly and inhibiting myosin light-chain phosphatase via phosphorylation of the MYPT1 regulatory subunit, elevating p-MLC levels and stabilizing stress fibers and focal adhesions (Cheng et al., 2025). ROCK also phosphorylates LIM kinases to inactivate cofilin, which slows F-actin turnover and further stiffens the cytoskeleton; ERM proteins, adducin, intermediate filament proteins (vimentin, GFAP), and multiple cytoskeletal/membrane linkers are additional substrates that integrate cytoskeletal and junctional dynamics (Cheng et al., 2025). These pathways are sensitive to mechanical inputs (matrix stiffness) and link cytoskeletal remodeling to barrier integrity and cell adhesion, consistent with the observed roles of ROCK in endothelial hyperpermeability and junction stabilization in ocular tissues (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025).

Belumosudil target engagement in choroid–RPE constructs. In vivo in the choroid–RPE complex after laser injury, both fasudil and belumosudil lowered p-MYPT1, indicating on-pathway ROCK inhibition, and reduced fibrotic markers (α-SMA, vimentin, fibronectin, collagen I, TGF-β1), consistent with suppression of myofibroblast activation, ECM deposition, and TGF-β/Smad signaling output (Zandi et al., 2025). Imaging mass cytometry showed spatially localized fibrotic marker expression to the choroid–RPE boundary and a reduction in “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations with belumosudil relative to fasudil, and a decrease in macrophage and perivascular cell signatures—integrating anti-fibrotic and anti-inflammatory mechanisms (Zandi et al., 2025). Quantitatively, ROCK2 staining occupancy fell from ~6.7% to 0.1% after belumosudil treatment, stronger than the reduction with fasudil (to 0.7%), supporting efficient ROCK2 target engagement by belumosudil (Zandi et al., 2025).

ROCK and epithelial barrier relevance. Although the RPE-specific tight-junction literature for belumosudil is not available in the provided sources, corneal endothelial studies link ROCK activity to stabilization of ZO-1 and the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump complex; pharmacologic ROCK inhibition promotes cytoskeletal relaxation, spreading, and cyclin-D–dependent proliferation, and has been leveraged clinically to accelerate re-endothelialization and junctional re-establishment (Leong et al., 2025). In vascular endothelia, RhoA/ROCK signaling drives VEGF-induced permeability and tube formation; ROCK inhibition modulates junctional architecture (e.g., “zipper-like” lymphatic endothelial junctions) and reduces permeability, supporting a mechanistic link to barrier tightening (Leong et al., 2025). In diabetic retinal pathology, ROCK1 activation contributes to RPE blebbing and tight-junction opening with outer blood-retinal barrier breakdown; pharmacologic ROCK inhibition (fasudil) improved barrier function and suppressed leukocyte migration and ICAM-1, reducing vascular leakage and neurodegeneration (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Together, these data reinforce that ROCK signaling is a proximal regulator of epithelial/endothelial junctions and barrier integrity and that inhibition—especially with an isoform-selective agent that engages ROCK2 in the choroid–RPE complex—has plausible junction-preserving effects in RPE monolayers (Leong et al., 2025; Zandi et al., 2025).

Anti-EMT and anti-fibrotic transcriptional programs. Transcriptomic studies in pluripotent stem cell–derived RPE and other epithelial contexts show ROCK inhibition suppresses EMT-associated transcriptional programs (TGF-β ligands, Wnt components, SNAI2, collagens) and promotes tight-junction reformation, consistent with decreased cytoskeletal tension and reduced MRTF/SRF-dependent transcription that drives myofibroblast markers (e.g., α-SMA) (Croze, 2015; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022). ROCK2 inhibition also intersects with inflammatory transcriptional axes (STAT3/STAT5) and NF-κB, shifting Th17/Tfh toward Treg and reducing proinflammatory cytokines in PBMCs and cGVHD models, which could help resolve inflammatory components of AMD pathophysiology at the RPE–choroid interface (Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Cytoskeletal/ciliary modulation in RPE-lineage cells. Independent siRNA/drug screens in ciliogenesis models identified ROCK2 as a strong negative regulator of cilia incidence and length; short and prolonged belumosudil exposure increased cilia metrics in hTERT RPE-1 and mIMCD3 cells while reducing phosphorylated MLC and acto-myosin fiber-like structures, consistent with decreased ROCK2-driven contractility (Lake et al., 2020). Although ciliation per se is not a dry AMD therapeutic endpoint, the data are a sensitive readout of cytoskeletal reprogramming via ROCK2 and reinforce the target’s role in apical organization in epithelia with RPE lineage origin (Lake et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay context: H₂O₂ and complement injury in RPE monolayers. Under oxidative stress (H₂O₂) and complement attack, the RPE cytoskeleton becomes hypercontractile, junctional belts destabilize, and paracellular permeability increases—manifest as reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased FITC-dextran flux, with mislocalization or fragmentation of tight-junction proteins (ZO-1, claudin-19). ROCK activation (via RhoA–GTP, inflammatory mediators, or mechanical cues) exacerbates this by increasing p-MYPT1 and p-MLC to drive actomyosin tension and stress fiber formation (Cheng et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). The class literature in ocular epithelia/endothelium indicates that ROCK inhibition relaxes cytoskeletal tension, promotes cell spreading and junctional complex re-assembly (ZO-1 stabilization reported in corneal endothelium), and reduces VEGF- or inflammation-driven hyperpermeability (Leong et al., 2025). In diabetic retinal models, ROCK pathway activation produces RPE blebbing and tight-junction disruption, with pharmacologic ROCK inhibition reversing barrier dysfunction and dampening leukostasis and leakage (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Given these mechanisms, selective ROCK2 inhibition with belumosudil is expected to:
- Reduce p-MYPT1 and downstream p-MLC in RPE, decreasing acto-myosin contractility, stabilizing the circumferential actin belt and adherens/tight junctions (ZO-1/claudin-19), thereby rescuing TEER and lowering FITC-dextran flux under H₂O₂ or complement challenge (Zandi et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025).
- Suppress EMT-like shifts and myofibroblast activation induced by oxidative/complement stress by lowering α-SMA/vimentin and ECM program activation (fibronectin, collagen), as seen in vivo after laser injury and in ROCK-inhibited RPE culture transcriptomics (Zandi et al., 2025; Croze, 2015).
- Provide anti-inflammatory benefits by reducing macrophage/perivascular cell accumulation seen in vivo and by directly modulating STAT3/STAT5-linked cytokine programs, potentially blunting complement-amplified inflammatory cascades at the RPE/choroid interface (Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021).

Target expression and context. ROCK signaling is active in ocular tissues; p-MYPT1 is reduced in the choroid–RPE complex of laser-injured eyes after ROCK inhibition; ROCK1 translocates and drives cytoskeletal/junctional changes under hyperglycemia in RPE and endothelium; and ROCK2 expression is quantifiably reduced by belumosudil in the choroid–RPE complex—collectively validating target presence and drug engagement at the proposed site of action (Zandi et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Important caveats. The provided literature set does not contain direct demonstrations that belumosudil rescues TEER or reduces FITC-dextran flux in RPE under H₂O₂ or complement injury, nor does it report preservation of claudin-19/ZO-1 localization in RPE with ROCK2-selective inhibition; these remain testable predictions grounded in mechanism and class precedent but not yet substantiated for belumosudil in RPE (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). Similarly, no data are provided here for NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration models with belumosudil; the NaIO₃ discussion pertains to single-cell remodeling and EMT tendencies in dry AMD models, which conceptually align with anti-EMT and anti-fibrotic effects of ROCK inhibition, but require direct in vivo validation for this candidate (Zandi et al., 2025).

Pharmacokinetic/delivery considerations for the assay. Clinically, belumosudil has a ~19-hour half-life, ~64% bioavailability with food (in healthy subjects), and is metabolized by CYP3A4; ocular pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration are not reported in the provided sources (Przepiorka et al., 2022). In the laser-injury mouse model, intraperitoneal administration from day 35 to 49 post-laser achieved retinal/choroid pharmacodynamics (↓p-MYPT1, ↓markers), indicating systemic dosing can engage ocular targets in inflamed/fibrotic tissue in mice, though translational relevance to human ocular exposure remains to be determined and local delivery could be preferable for barrier-rescue assays (Zandi et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- On-pathway target engagement in choroid–RPE with functional tissue outcomes. Belumosudil decreases p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex, reduces fibrosis volume, attenuates α-SMA, vimentin, fibronectin, collagen I, and TGF-β1, and preserves retinal morphology and thickness in a subretinal fibrosis model; ROCK2 occupancy falls to near-baseline with treatment, indicating strong ocular target engagement (Zandi et al., 2025). These integrated molecular and histologic readouts provide robust evidence that isoform-selective ROCK2 inhibition can reprogram the pathological microenvironment at the RPE–choroid interface after injury—precisely where barrier restoration is therapeutically needed in dry AMD (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Mechanistic alignment with barrier preservation. ROCK signaling is a proximal regulator of cytoskeletal tension and tight-junction stability; inhibition reduces MLC phosphorylation via MYPT1 de-phosphorylation, stabilizes junctions (corneal ZO-1; endothelial junction “zippering”), and mitigates hyperpermeability (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025). The candidate’s demonstrated ability to lower p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex and reduce myofibroblast activation fits the hypothesis that it can preserve epithelial barrier integrity under stress (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Anti-EMT/anti-fibrotic transcriptional effects. ROCK inhibition suppresses TGF-β/Wnt-mediated EMT programs and promotes tight-junction reformation in pluripotent-derived RPE; in vivo reductions in α-SMA and ECM deposition further support anti-fibrotic activity coherent with preventing RPE-to-mesenchymal transitions that compromise the barrier (Croze, 2015; Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions. Belumosudil reduces macrophage and perivascular cell signatures in vivo and systemically shifts Th17/Tfh toward Treg via STAT3/STAT5 modulation; these effects could dampen complement- and cytokine-driven RPE injury cascades implicated in dry AMD (Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).  
- Favorable human safety experience and oral PK. A clinically approved safety profile with chronic administration, a manageable drug–drug interaction profile (CYP3A4), and a ~19-hour half-life provide a de-risked starting point for repurposing; dose selection can be guided by systemic exposures achieved in cGVHD (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zanin-Zhorov & Blazar, 2021).

Weaknesses and knowledge gaps  
- No direct RPE barrier functional data for belumosudil. The literature set lacks TEER, FITC-dextran flux, or ZO-1/claudin-19 preservation data for belumosudil in RPE under oxidative/complement stress; consequently, the core hypothesis—TEER rescue with ROCK2 selectivity—remains inferential (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021).  
- No NaIO₃ or dry AMD-specific in vivo efficacy with belumosudil. While NaIO₃ single-cell data support EMT and fibroblast-like RPE signatures relevant to ROCK pathway targeting, belumosudil has not been tested in NaIO₃ or geographic atrophy models here; the current in vivo evidence is laser-injury fibrosis focused (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Isoform biology nuance in the retina. Diabetic retinal studies emphasize ROCK1 translocation and ROCK1-mediated blebbing/tight-junction disruption, with some reports noting ROCK2 localization as “undisturbed” in those models; this raises a strategic question whether ROCK2-selective inhibition alone is sufficient for barrier rescue across stress etiologies or whether dual inhibition is sometimes preferable (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).  
- Ocular pharmacokinetics and delivery. There are no data on ocular tissue penetration, retinal/choroidal exposure, or intravitreal/topical formulations for belumosudil; although systemic dosing engaged ocular targets in mice after laser injury, human ocular delivery, durability, and safety require specific assessment (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025). Class precedents (intravitreal/topical fasudil, topical netarsudil/ripasudil) are encouraging but not directly transferable to this scaffold without formulation work (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Off-target and pathway-network considerations. Although belumosudil is selective for ROCK2, it has minor ROCK1 and pathway-adjacent activities (e.g., mTOR), and widespread cytoskeletal re-tuning can have context-dependent effects (e.g., on ciliation) whose long-term retinal implications are unknown (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Lake et al., 2020).

Decision-oriented interpretation for dry AMD  
- Mechanistic plausibility: High. ROCK2 inhibition is expected to directly reduce cytoskeletal tension and stabilize epithelial junctions; on-pathway pharmacodynamic effects (↓p-MYPT1) and anti-fibrotic marker reductions in the choroid–RPE complex support action at the relevant tissue interface (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Translational anchor: Moderate. The candidate has a de-risked systemic safety profile and class-level ocular pharmacology, plus in vivo anti-fibrotic retinal benefits; however, barrier-specific efficacy in RPE under oxidative/complement stress has not yet been shown for belumosudil (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Differentiation vs pan-ROCK: Potentially favorable. In vivo, belumosudil achieved stronger ROCK2 engagement and larger decreases in “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations than fasudil, aligning with the idea that ROCK2 drives key profibrotic cascades at the choroid–RPE interface, while avoiding ROCK1-linked hypotension liabilities systemically; whether ROCK1 contributions to RPE barrier breakdown under certain stressors would limit efficacy remains to be determined experimentally (Zandi et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

Concrete implications for the proposed hypothesis  
- The specific claims that belumosudil has demonstrated +50% TER recovery in ARPE-19 under H₂O₂ stress, 40% RPE cell preservation and ERG improvement in a mouse NaIO₃ model, and an oral bioavailability ~45% with t₁/₂ ~4.8 h are not supported by the literature set provided; instead, the available PK indicates oral bioavailability is ~64% with food and a ~19-h half-life, and no TER/NaIO₃ efficacy data for belumosudil are referenced here (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). The hypothesized barrier rescue under oxidative/complement injury remains plausible mechanistically but requires direct validation in RPE models (Leong et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Program-level next steps (to enable a go/no-go)  
- In vitro RPE barrier assays: Primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE monolayers subjected to H₂O₂ and normal human serum (complement) injury; quantify TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and ZO-1/claudin-19 localization/intensity; include p-MYPT1 and p-MLC biochemical readouts as pharmacodynamics; benchmark belumosudil across a concentration range anchored to ROCK2 IC₅₀ and cell viability (Lake et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Phenotypic rescue breadth: Replicate class-level findings with ROCK2 selectivity—adhesion, wound closure, POS phagocytosis, RPE65 expression—to establish that belumosudil recapitulates the iPSC-RPE Y-27632 phenotype profile while tightening the barrier (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).  
- In vivo dry AMD model: NaIO₃ or other GA-like models with local ocular delivery (intravitreal or periocular sustained-release) to assess RPE survival, outer blood-retinal barrier integrity, visual function (ERG), and transcriptomic/IMC profiling for EMT/fibrosis and inflammatory modulation; include dose–exposure–response characterization (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Ocular PK/formulation: Ocular tissue distribution after local delivery and/or systemic administration; stability and duration; comparative exposures in RPE/choroid vs retina with safety assessment (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025).

Overall, belumosudil is a compelling, mechanistically aligned candidate with de-risked systemic safety, clear ocular on-pathway antifibrotic activity at the choroid–RPE interface, and strong biological rationale for junctional stabilization in stressed RPE. The decisive gap is the absence of direct barrier-function rescue data in RPE under oxidative or complement injury and the lack of dry AMD model efficacy. Addressing these with focused preclinical studies will determine whether its ROCK2 selectivity translates into clinically meaningful protection of the outer blood–retinal barrier in dry AMD, and whether it offers advantages over pan-ROCK inhibitors in this context (Zandi et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of isradipine as a repurposed candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In this report, we review its chemical origins and classification, historical therapeutic uses, detailed molecular mechanism of action, expected biological effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, and a critical overall assessment from the perspective of drug development for dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

Isradipine is a fully synthetic compound that belongs to the 1,4-dihydropyridine (DHP) class of calcium channel blockers, a family of agents that has been extensively optimized over several decades. The parent chemical scaffold was developed to target L-type voltage-gated calcium channels (LTCCs), particularly CaV1.2 and CaV1.3, which are key regulators of calcium entry in many excitable cells. Originally synthesized under the internal code PN 200-110, isradipine was later marketed for cardiovascular applications such as hypertension and angina pectoris due to its potent vasodilatory effects (Hof & Rüegg, 1988; Triggle, 2006). The design of isradipine is based on a thoroughly studied heterocyclic core that has undergone iterative modifications to yield compounds with improved potency, selectivity, and favorable pharmacokinetic properties. Its ability to achieve effective blockade of LTCCs at submicromolar concentrations—with an IC₅₀ around 0.2 µM—is a hallmark of its pharmacologic profile (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

The DHP class, to which isradipine belongs, has been widely used for its arterial vasodilatory actions in cardiovascular medicine, where selective inhibition of LTCCs in vascular smooth muscle produces systemic blood pressure reductions without significantly impairing cardiac contractility (Schachter, 1991; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011). Over the years, the profile of DHP calcium channel blockers has been expanded beyond their classical cardiovascular indications. More recently, several studies have begun to explore the neuroprotective and neuromodulatory properties of DHPs in models of neurodegeneration. Furthermore, emerging data suggest that alterations in LTCC function in non-vascular tissues—such as the retinal pigment epithelium—may contribute to disease mechanisms in dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025). In particular, mislocalization and dysfunction of the CaV1.3 subtype have been implicated in the degeneration of RPE cells, a central component in the pathogenesis of dry AMD.

Given that isradipine is well known for its high potency and state-dependent blockade of LTCCs, its repurposing for dry AMD is based on the hypothesis that pharmacological control of calcium influx can preserve tight junction integrity in RPE cells. With an established history of safe systemic use and an extensively characterized pharmacologic profile, isradipine emerges as an attractive candidate to modulate aberrant Ca²⁺ homeostasis in the retina (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

─────────────────────────────  
2. Therapeutic History

Clinically, isradipine has been deployed primarily in the management of cardiovascular disorders. Its use in treatment regimens for hypertension and angina pectoris is well documented, with decades of clinical experience supporting its efficacy and safety in reducing peripheral vascular resistance and relieving myocardial ischemia (Schachter, 1991). As a member of the DHP family, its predictable absorption, metabolism, and elimination have rendered it a mainstay in cardiovascular pharmacotherapy, with adverse effects generally limited to dose-dependent vasodilation-related symptoms such as headache and peripheral edema (Hof & Rüegg, 1988; Striessnig, 1999).

Beyond its cardiovascular applications, isradipine has recently been evaluated as a neuroprotective agent in several contexts. Preclinical data indicate that isradipine can reduce harmful calcium influx in neuronal populations, particularly in dopaminergic neurons that are at risk in Parkinson’s disease (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Ilijic et al., 2011). In these studies, isradipine’s ability to cross the blood–brain barrier and selectively inhibit LTCCs has been exploited to mitigate mitochondrial oxidative stress and calcium-mediated neurotoxicity. Although outcomes in clinical trials for neurodegenerative diseases have been mixed, the protective mechanisms observed in animal models provide a mechanistic rationale that could be applicable also beyond the central nervous system (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Nimmrich & Eckert, 2013).

Importantly, there is emerging evidence linking altered L-type calcium channel activity, particularly of the CaV1.3 subtype, to ocular pathology relevant to AMD. Data from the Open Targets Platform, for example, indicate a moderate association between CACNA1D (the gene encoding CaV1.3) and macular degeneration, with studies in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells from AMD patients demonstrating both mislocalization of CaV1.3 channels and reduced intracellular Ca²⁺ levels compared to controls (Buniello et al., 2025). Although isradipine has not previously been used in clinical studies for ocular diseases or for dry AMD specifically, its long-established cardiovascular use, combined with its neuroprotective potential in other cell types, offers an attractive opportunity for repurposing. The safety profile and systemic tolerability of isradipine further support its candidacy for new therapeutic indications in an elderly population commonly affected by AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

─────────────────────────────  
3. Mechanism of Action

At its most fundamental level, isradipine acts by inhibiting LTCCs—integral membrane proteins that mediate voltage-dependent calcium influx into cells. The LTCC family includes several subtypes, among which CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 have been most extensively studied. Isradipine is known to preferentially block these channels in a state-dependent manner, binding with higher affinity to channels that are in either an open or inactivated state and thereby sparing those in the resting state (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Filippini et al., 2023).

More specifically, the molecular interaction between isradipine and LTCCs involves defined transmembrane segments located on the pore-forming α1 subunit. Structural studies have identified that regions such as the IS6 and IVS6 helices form part of the binding pocket responsible for dihydropyridine sensitivity. When isradipine binds to this pocket, it not only obstructs the pore physically but also stabilizes the channel in a nonconducting conformation that precludes further Ca²⁺ entry (Filippini et al., 2023; Lacinová, Klugbauer, & Hofmann, 2000). This blockade leads to a rapid and sustained reduction in intracellular calcium levels, which is critical in tissues where tight junction assembly and maintenance are calcium-dependent processes.

In the context of RPE cells, maintaining appropriate basal Ca²⁺ concentrations is crucial for the integrity and anchoring of tight junction proteins such as occludin and zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1). Under physiological conditions, LTCC-mediated calcium entry provides a signal that regulates calcium-sensitive kinase and phosphatase pathways involved in organizing the cytoskeleton and maintaining cell–cell adhesion. However, in disease conditions such as dry AMD, factors such as pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α) or complement activation can disrupt this finely tuned balance. Excessive Ca²⁺ influx can lead to the activation of calcium-dependent proteases (e.g., calpains) and kinases that precipitate cytoskeletal remodeling and disassembly of tight junction complexes, contributing to a collapse in transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and loss of barrier function (Buniello et al., 2025).

By antagonizing LTCCs, isradipine is hypothesized to counteract these deleterious effects. Its state-dependent, high-affinity binding minimizes excessive Ca²⁺ entry during inflammatory challenges while preserving the minimal calcium flux necessary for normal cellular function (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Rotstein et al., 2015). In addition to its acute blocking effect, there is evidence from studies in neuronal models that prolonged exposure to dihydropyridines may down-regulate LTCC expression, leading to longer-term stabilization of calcium homeostasis (Ilijic et al., 2011; Nimmrich & Eckert, 2013). Therefore, in RPE cells, isradipine could theoretically act via a dual mechanism: an immediate reduction in aberrant calcium entry during cytokine-induced stress and a more prolonged normalization of LTCC density and function.

Furthermore, the selective targeting of CaV1.3 is particularly pertinent in the case of dry AMD because studies have revealed a moderate association between CACNA1D expression and macular degeneration, along with observations of mislocalization of CaV1.3 channels in AMD-derived RPE cells (Buniello et al., 2025). Such mislocalization is associated with reduced intracellular calcium levels which, paradoxically, may contribute to the failure of the tight junction apparatus due to a deficiency in the calcium signal necessary for proper junction assembly. In this scenario, isradipine’s ability to fine-tune calcium influx by blocking excessive but inappropriate LTCC activity may help restore normal intracellular Ca²⁺ dynamics, thereby preserving the localization and function of occludin and ZO-1 (Buniello et al., 2025; Filippini et al., 2023).

In summary, at the molecular level, isradipine’s action involves binding to critical transmembrane segments of LTCCs—particularly those associated with CaV1.2 and CaV1.3—thereby stabilizing these channels in a closed or inactivated state, reducing aberrant calcium influx, and indirectly safeguarding the intracellular signaling pathways that maintain tight junction integrity. This mechanism is central to the proposed therapeutic approach for stabilizing the RPE barrier in dry AMD (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Filippini et al., 2023; Buniello et al., 2025).

─────────────────────────────  
4. Expected Effect

Dry AMD is characterized by chronic RPE cell dysfunction and degeneration leading to breakdown of the outer blood–retinal barrier, a process largely fueled by disruptions in intracellular calcium homeostasis. In this context, inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) play a critical role in triggering disassembly of tight junctions and reducing transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER). Moreover, evidence linking the CaV1.3 channel to macular degeneration underscores the importance of calcium regulation in RPE pathology (Buniello et al., 2025).

The central hypothesis guiding the repurposing of isradipine for dry AMD is that by blocking LTCCs—specifically CaV1.2 and CaV1.3—at an IC₅₀ near 0.2 µM, it is possible to stabilize basal calcium levels in RPE cells. Under inflammatory conditions induced by TNF-α or complement activation, uncontrolled calcium influx would normally activate calcium-dependent proteolytic enzymes and kinases that contribute to the disruption of the cytoskeletal framework and the disassembly of cell–cell junctions. With isradipine’s intervention, the unwanted surge in intracellular calcium would be attenuated, thereby preserving the expression, localization, and function of tight junction proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

In practical in vitro assays—using the human RPE cell line ARPE-19 or primary RPE cultures—exposure to TNF-α typically results in marked declines in TEER, reflecting compromised barrier integrity, alongside mislocalization of occludin and ZO-1 within the cell. Treatment with isradipine is expected to counter these effects. Specifically, by reducing the level of calcium influx across the plasma membrane, isradipine should enable the maintenance of the proper cytoskeletal anchoring of tight junction proteins, which in turn is expected to translate into a stabilization or even enhancement of TEER. Preliminary data in complement-challenged ARPE-19 models have shown that treatment with calcium channel blockers can lead to increased TEER, supporting the concept that pharmacological modulation of calcium entry is beneficial for RPE barrier function (Buniello et al., 2025).

Moreover, the anticipated outcomes include not only the acute preservation of junctional architecture during short-term inflammatory challenges but also potentially the modulation of LTCC expression under chronic stress. Over time, reducing the pathological calcium influx may alleviate the cellular stress that leads to LTCC up-regulation, thereby preventing a vicious cycle of calcium overload and junctional disassembly. Thus, even beyond immediate effects on TEER, isradipine may exert disease-modifying properties by normalizing the intracellular signaling milieu in RPE cells (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Ilijic et al., 2011).

Finally, by maintaining appropriate intracellular Ca²⁺ concentrations, isradipine may also prevent the activation of downstream calcium-dependent effectors—such as calpains and other proteases—that can degrade tight junction proteins directly. This dual action of immediate channel blockade and secondary protection against proteolytic degradation underpins the rationale that isradipine can preserve the barrier function of the RPE, thereby preventing the progression of dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

In essence, the expected effect of isradipine in the proposed assay is multifaceted:
• An immediate stabilization of intracellular calcium levels through LTCC blockade.  
• Prevention of TNF-α–induced tight junction disassembly, with sustained localization of occludin and ZO-1.  
• Improvement or stabilization of TEER in RPE cells under inflammatory or complement-challenge conditions.  
• Potential chronic benefits through secondary down-regulation of LTCC expression and the subsequent maintenance of calcium homeostasis.

Such effects would translate into a pharmacological strategy not only to protect the RPE barrier acutely but also to potentially slow the degenerative process of dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Filippini et al., 2023).

─────────────────────────────  
5. Overall Evaluation

Based on the comprehensive review of the available literature across biochemical, clinical, and preclinical domains, isradipine emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its favorable safety profile, robust historical data in cardiovascular applications, and emerging evidence supporting its neuroprotective and calcium-modulating effects form a strong foundation for exploring its role in ocular diseases.

Strengths of isradipine include its extensive clinical record in hypertension and angina, where decades of use have demonstrated predictable pharmacokinetics and a low incidence of severe adverse effects (Schachter, 1991). The compound’s belonging to the dihydropyridine class further supports its suitability, as this class is characterized by potent and state-dependent blockade of LTCCs—properties that are critical for controlling abnormal calcium influx in pathological situations. In addition, preclinical data documenting abnormal localization of CaV1.3 channels in AMD-affected RPE cells (Buniello et al., 2025) provide a direct link between LTCC dysfunction and retinal barrier breakdown, thereby strengthening the mechanistic rationale for isradipine’s use in dry AMD.

Another major strength is isradipine’s dual mechanism of action. Acutely, it can reduce the extracellular calcium influx that triggers deleterious cell-signaling cascades, and with chronic administration, it may also modulate LTCC expression levels. Such a dual mechanism implies that isradipine might not only preserve junctional integrity during inflammatory insults but also slow the overall progression of RPE degeneration. This is particularly important given that dry AMD is a slowly progressive and multifactorial disease where both acute and chronic therapeutic interventions are needed to achieve meaningful clinical outcomes (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Filippini et al., 2023).

Moreover, isradipine’s pharmacodynamic profile—with an IC₅₀ of approximately 0.2 µM—suggests that at appropriate dosing, it can achieve targeted LTCC inhibition in RPE cells without completely abolishing basal calcium signaling, which is essential for normal cellular functions. This fine balance is crucial in tissues such as the retina where calcium plays a key role not only in tight junction regulation but also in phototransduction and cellular homeostasis (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

Nonetheless, several challenges and limitations must be acknowledged. First, there is a relative paucity of direct ocular data on isradipine. Most of the supporting evidence for its mechanism and effects comes from studies in cardiovascular and neuronal cells. While the fundamental principles of calcium-dependent tight junction regulation are conserved, the specific expression profiles and regulatory mechanisms in RPE cells may differ. Consequently, extensive in vitro studies in RPE cell lines (such as ARPE-19) and primary RPE cultures will be imperative before moving into in vivo evaluations (Buniello et al., 2025).

Another significant limitation concerns drug delivery. Isradipine is predominantly administered systemically for its current indications, and achieving therapeutically relevant concentrations in the retina while minimizing systemic hypotension presents an important formulation challenge. Novel ocular delivery approaches—ranging from topical formulations to intravitreal injections or slow-release implants—must be rigorously developed and optimized. This challenge is compounded by the need to ensure that such delivery methods do not disrupt normal retinal physiology or exacerbate inflammatory responses (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Schachter, 1991).

There is also the potential for off-target effects in the retina. Calcium signaling underpins many essential retinal functions, including the regulation of photoreceptor activity, synaptic transmission, and RPE phagocytosis. Over-inhibition of LTCCs, if not carefully titrated, could compromise these processes. Thus, defining a safe therapeutic window in RPE cells is critical to ensure that the benefits of junctional preservation do not come at the cost of impaired retinal function (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

Finally, while the data linking LTCC dysfunction to AMD provide a compelling rationale for repurposing isradipine, the heterogeneity of LTCC expression across different cell types in the retina may influence treatment efficacy. It will be necessary to characterize not only the levels of CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 in RPE cells but also their functional roles in maintaining barrier integrity. Any variability in channel isoform expression or alternative splicing patterns may require adjustments in dosing or even the exploration of more isoform-selective derivatives (Buniello et al., 2025; Filippini et al., 2023).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation is positive: isradipine is a well-characterized, clinically safe calcium channel blocker with a robust mechanistic basis for repurposing in dry AMD. Its combined acute and chronic actions on LTCCs, along with emerging evidence linking CaV1.3 dysfunction to retinal degeneration, provide a strong rationale for further preclinical investigation. In particular, detailed studies focusing on its effects in human RPE cells under inflammatory conditions will be critical to validate the hypothesis that isradipine can preserve occludin and ZO-1 localization and maintain TEER under TNF-α challenge (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

─────────────────────────────  
6. Future Directions and Recommendations

Based on the evaluation above, the following research directions are recommended to advance isradipine as a potential therapeutic agent for dry AMD:

a) Detailed Characterization in RPE Cells  
It is vital to confirm the expression levels and localization of LTCC subtypes, particularly CaV1.3, in human RPE cells. Techniques such as quantitative PCR, Western blotting, immunocytochemistry, and electrophysiological recordings (e.g., patch-clamp) should be used to assess both basal expression and any alterations under inflammatory conditions. This will establish whether the therapeutic window for isradipine’s action in RPE cells is similar to that observed in neuronal or vascular cells (Buniello et al., 2025).

b) In Vitro Barrier Function Studies  
Establish in vitro models using ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures to evaluate the effects of isradipine on TEER and the immunolocalization of tight junction proteins such as occludin and ZO-1. These studies should employ cytokine challenges (e.g., TNF-α) and complement-mediated insults to simulate the pathological environment associated with dry AMD. Dose–response studies centered around the 0.2 µM IC₅₀ value will help define optimal concentrations for barrier preservation (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

c) Mechanistic Pathway Dissection  
Investigate the downstream signaling cascades following LTCC blockade in RPE cells. This includes evaluating changes in the activation state of calcium-dependent proteases, kinases, and the cytoskeletal proteins that govern tight junction formation. In addition, longitudinal studies should assess whether chronic isradipine exposure modifies LTCC expression itself, providing potential long-term benefits beyond immediate calcium modulation (Ilijic et al., 2011).

d) Development of Ocular Delivery Systems  
Given isradipine’s existing use as an orally administered drug for cardiovascular indications, it is essential to develop ocular-specific formulations that enable efficient delivery to the retina. This could involve exploring topical eye drops, intravitreal injections, or sustained-release implants that achieve high retinal bioavailability with minimal systemic absorption. In vivo pharmacokinetic studies in appropriate animal models will be key to optimizing these delivery systems (Schachter, 1991).

e) In Vivo Efficacy Studies  
Animal models that recapitulate key features of dry AMD, including RPE degeneration and barrier dysfunction, should be employed to assess the functional impact of isradipine on retinal preservation. Outcome measures might include in vivo imaging of retinal structure, ex vivo TEER measurements, histological analysis of tight junction integrity, and functional assessments such as electroretinography.

f) Safety and Tolerability in Retinal Tissues  
Since calcium signaling is critical for many retinal cellular functions, it is imperative to assess whether isradipine—at doses sufficient to block pathological calcium influx—might inadvertently impair normal retinal processes such as photoreceptor function, synaptic transmission, or RPE phagocytosis. Defining a precise therapeutic index in the ocular setting will be crucial for further development.

─────────────────────────────  
7. Overall Conclusion

In conclusion, isradipine represents a highly promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its extensive use in cardiovascular medicine, combined with an emerging body of evidence linking LTCC dysfunction to RPE barrier failure and macular degeneration, provides a strong scientific rationale for its investigation in this novel indication. At the molecular level, isradipine’s state-dependent and selective blockade of CaV1.2/CaV1.3 channels offers a targeted approach to stabilizing intracellular calcium levels and preserving the organization of tight junction proteins critical for maintaining the outer blood–retinal barrier (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

While the majority of the supportive literature originates from studies conducted in cardiovascular and neuronal models, the fundamental role of LTCC-mediated calcium signaling in modulating barrier integrity is highly relevant to RPE physiology. The proposed mechanism—preventing TNF-α–induced junctional disassembly and cytokine-driven TEER collapse by preserving occludin and ZO-1 localization—is both plausible and timely given the persistent unmet need in the treatment of dry AMD.

Nonetheless, key challenges remain. Direct experimental evidence in ocular systems is currently limited, and significant work is needed to optimize the drug formulation for targeted retinal delivery while safeguarding against potential off-target effects. The heterogeneity of LTCC expression in ocular tissues may also necessitate further refinement in dosing strategies. Addressing these challenges through targeted in vitro and in vivo studies will be critical for translating the promising mechanistic insights into clinical benefit.

Overall, the convergence of robust clinical safety data, precise molecular pharmacological action, and emerging evidence linking LTCC dysregulation to RPE dysfunction supports the advancement of isradipine into focused preclinical studies for dry AMD. If studies confirm that isradipine can preserve the integrity of RPE tight junctions under inflammatory conditions, it may offer not only symptomatic relief but also a disease-modifying strategy that slows or prevents the progression of dry AMD—a condition currently lacking effective treatment options (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

Given these considerations, the recommendation is to pursue an accelerated preclinical program that encompasses detailed mechanistic assays in RPE cells, the development of suitable ocular delivery systems, and rigorous in vivo testing in relevant animal models. Success in these areas would justify subsequent clinical trials and could ultimately position isradipine as a transformative therapy for preserving retinal structure and function in patients with dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
Final Summary

Isradipine is a synthetically derived 1,4-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker with a proven record in cardiovascular therapy due to its potent, state-dependent inhibition of LTCCs. Its repurposing for dry age-related macular degeneration is scientifically supported by emerging evidence that links dysregulated CaV1.3 function with RPE barrier breakdown in AMD. By stabilizing basal intracellular Ca²⁺ levels under inflammatory stress, isradipine is expected to prevent TNF-α–induced disassembly of tight junction proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 and thereby maintain TEER. Although direct ocular data are currently limited and significant challenges in retinal drug delivery remain to be addressed, the overall safety profile and well-defined molecular mechanism of isradipine provide a compelling rationale for further preclinical investigation in dry AMD. Advancing isradipine into detailed mechanistic studies in RPE models, coupled with the development of targeted ocular formulations, offers the potential to deliver a first-in-class, disease-modifying treatment for dry AMD—a condition with significant unmet medical need (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

Based solely on the data provided in the current context and using the established literature from cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and emerging ocular studies, isradipine holds considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The proposed mechanism of stabilizing basal Ca²⁺ homeostasis to preserve RPE tight junction integrity is strongly supported, and the path forward includes focused preclinical research to address ocular-specific efficacy and delivery issues. This strategy represents a logical and scientifically grounded approach to expand the therapeutic indications of an already widely used drug, thereby potentially transforming care for patients suffering from dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA-408; also known as CDDO-DFPA; N-(2-Cyano-3,12-dioxo-28-noroleana-1,9(11)-dien-17-yl)-2,2-difluoropropanamide) is a semisynthetic oleanane triterpenoid created by lead optimization of the natural product oleanolic acid, a plant-derived pentacyclic triterpene produced via the mevalonate pathway (squalene → 2,3-oxidosqualene → β-amyrin → erythrodiol → oleanolic acid) and abundantly available from Oleaceae (e.g., olive) and other botanical sources (over 1,600 species; Nakagami, 2016; Masullo et al., 2017; Pollier & Goossens, 2012). The oleanane scaffold was iteratively diversified by Sporn, Gribble, Honda and collaborators to introduce enone and cyanoenone Michael acceptors on rings A and C, yielding the CDDO class (2-cyano-3,12-dioxo-oleana-1,9(11)-dien-28-oic acid and derivatives) as extraordinarily potent anti-inflammatory and Nrf2-inducing agents; C-28 esters/amides and further A/C-ring modifications produced multiple clinical candidates including CDDO-Me (bardoxolone methyl, RTA-402) and RTA-408 (omaveloxolone) (Honda et al., 2000; Pollier & Goossens, 2012; Cheng et al., 2021). RTA-408 specifically is a C17-modified difluoro-propanamide on an oleanane core and belongs to the second generation of synthetic triterpenoids designed to preserve high Nrf2 potency while controlling electrophilicity and pharmacokinetics (Nakagami, 2016; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

At the pharmacological class level, synthetic oleanane triterpenoids are electrophilic “antioxidant inflammation modulators” that activate the KEAP1–NRF2–ARE pathway through covalent (but often reversible) Michael addition to redox-sensitive cysteines on KEAP1, particularly Cys151 on the BTB domain, thereby stabilizing Nrf2 and inducing a coordinated cytoprotective gene program; they concurrently suppress inducible pro-inflammatory mediators (e.g., iNOS, COX-2) with dose-dependent bifunctionality (cytoprotection at low concentrations; pro-oxidant/apoptotic signaling at higher exposure) (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Liby et al., 2007). This scaffold has been extensively explored as a drug platform across oncology, nephrology, cardiopulmonary, inflammatory, and neurological indications, with bardoxolone methyl and omaveloxolone translating to clinical studies and, for omaveloxolone, regulatory approval in Friedreich’s ataxia (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Zahir et al., 2025). Within ophthalmology, oleanane triterpenoids and close congeners (dh404, CDDO-TFEA, CDDO-EA, CDDO-Me) have shown robust Nrf2-mediated protection in retinal models, and RTA-408 itself has been advanced into ocular clinical trials evaluating postoperative ocular pain/inflammation and corneal endothelial cell loss after cataract surgery, positioning this mechanism squarely within ocular translational scope (Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
The oleanane triterpenoid class has a two-decade translational history that began with demonstrations that cyano-enone–bearing derivatives are sub-nanomolar inducers of the Nrf2 transcriptome and suppressors of inflammatory enzymes in vitro and in vivo, a property mapped by SAR to the presence/placement of A-ring 1-en-3-one and C-ring 9(11)-en-12-one Michael acceptors (Honda et al., 2000; Nakagami, 2016). Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me) showed pharmacodynamic activity in humans (ARE-gene induction in tumor biopsies; renal function improvements), but its BEACON Phase 3 trial in advanced CKD was halted for cardiovascular adverse events—an outcome that did not negate class activity but highlighted the need for indication-specific risk management and exclusion criteria (e.g., high BNP, poor baseline eGFR) (Masullo et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Subsequent controlled studies in rarer CKD-associated diseases continued under tighter cardiometabolic selection, while medicinal-chemistry efforts generated second-generation analogs including fluorinated scaffolds (e.g., omaveloxolone) to tune reactivity and PK/PD (Sun et al., 2017).

For omaveloxolone specifically, preclinical pharmacology established Nrf2-dependent induction of glutathione homeostasis genes and improvements in mitochondrial respiration; systemic PK in primates/humans showed dose proportionality and measurable tissue distribution (including liver, lung, brain), with PBMC and tissue Nrf2 target-gene induction at clinically achievable exposures (Reisman et al., 2019). In oncology, a first-in-human dose-escalation study in advanced solid tumors reported acceptable tolerability with pharmacodynamic evidence of Nrf2 pathway activation in PBMCs; in dermatology, topical RTA-408 lotion activated Nrf2 in human skin and was well tolerated (Creelan et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). In neurology, omaveloxolone advanced through the MOXIe program for Friedreich’s ataxia with evidence of neurologic benefit at clinical doses ≥80 mg and exposures concordant with preclinical pharmacology (Naidu & Dinkova-Kostova, 2020; Reisman et al., 2019; Zahir et al., 2025).

Ocularly, multiple oleanane triterpenoid derivatives have shown benefit in retinal oxidative-stress models: dh404 induced canonical Nrf2 target genes (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM), reduced inflammatory mediators, and decreased retinal vascular leakage; CDDO-TFEA and CDDO-EA activated NQO1 in photoreceptor-derived 661W cells and CDDO-TFEA reduced light-induced retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021). RS9, an OA-derived analog generated via microbial transformation, showed superior potency versus CDDO-Me in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) protection, increased retinal HO-1/NQO1 at low doses, and suppressed neovascularization and blood-brain barrier hyperpermeability in vivo, supporting the generalizable ocular protective potential of optimized oleanane triterpenoids (Cheng et al., 2021). Critically for translational relevance, omaveloxolone itself has documented protective activity in human fetal RPE at low-nanomolar concentrations (≤100 nM), where it prevents H₂O₂-induced apoptosis/necrosis by shifting the Bcl-2:Bax ratio and reducing protein glutathionylation—biomarkers linked to oxidative damage and barrier compromise in RPE (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, RTA-408 is the only oleanolic acid analogue noted to have entered clinical trials in ocular indications (cataract-surgery–related pain/inflammation and corneal endothelial cell loss), demonstrating sponsor commitment to ophthalmic development and an initial tolerability signal for ocular use (Cheng et al., 2021). No clinical reports were found in the provided context for omaveloxolone in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) specifically, nor in geographic atrophy; thus, this is a repurposing proposal grounded in mechanistic and preclinical ocular convergence rather than direct AMD clinical precedent (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
The KEAP1–NRF2 node is a cysteine-centric electrophile sensor system that orchestrates the phase-2 antioxidant and cytoprotective response. Under basal conditions, KEAP1 recruits NRF2 to the CUL3 E3 ligase complex for ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover. Electrophiles such as cyano-enone triterpenoids react with KEAP1 cysteine sensors—most prominently Cys151 in the BTB domain—to disrupt CUL3 docking and/or alter KEAP1 conformation, thereby stabilizing NRF2, allowing nuclear translocation, heterodimerization with small Maf proteins, and binding to antioxidant response elements (ARE) to induce a transcriptional battery including NQO1, HO-1 (HMOX1), glutathione biosynthesis enzymes (GCLC, GCLM), thioredoxin and thioredoxin reductase (Txn1, Txnrd1), sulfiredoxin (Srxn1), and other detoxifying/antioxidative genes (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). Belumosudil (KD025; Rezurock) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable, indazole-derived serine/threonine kinase inhibitor that preferentially targets Rho-associated coiled-coil–containing protein kinase 2 (ROCK2) over ROCK1 and was developed by Kadmon Pharmaceuticals following licensing from Nano Terra (now approved in the United States for chronic graft-versus-host disease, cGVHD) (Blair, 2021; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022; Przepiorka et al., 2022). The broader class—ROCK inhibitors—modulates actin–myosin cytoskeletal dynamics by decreasing phosphorylation of myosin regulatory elements and altering actin turnover via downstream nodes (LIMK–cofilin, ERM proteins), with downstream effects on cell contractility, focal adhesions, cell junctions, migration, and myofibroblast differentiation (Cheng et al., 2025). In ophthalmology, ROCK inhibitors have established or emerging therapeutic roles: netarsudil and ripasudil lower intraocular pressure by relaxing trabecular meshwork and Schlemm’s canal, and corneal endothelial repair paradigms (topical ROCK inhibitors and cell therapy adjuncts) exploit cytoskeletal relaxation, enhanced adhesion, and proliferation to accelerate re-endothelialization (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025). Collectively, these features position belumosudil within a drug class with proven ocular pharmacology and strong plausibility for modulating epithelial/endothelial barrier biology through cytoskeletal re-tuning (Leong et al., 2025).

Under oxidative stress (H₂O₂) and complement attack, the RPE cytoskeleton becomes hypercontractile, junctional belts destabilize, and paracellular permeability increases—manifest as reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased FITC-dextran flux, with mislocalization or fragmentation of tight-junction proteins (ZO-1, claudin-19). ROCK activation (via RhoA–GTP, inflammatory mediators, or mechanical cues) exacerbates this by increasing p-MYPT1 and p-MLC to drive actomyosin tension and stress fiber formation (Cheng et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). The class literature in ocular epithelia/endothelium indicates that ROCK inhibition relaxes cytoskeletal tension, promotes cell spreading and junctional complex re-assembly (ZO-1 stabilization reported in corneal endothelium), and reduces VEGF- or inflammation-driven hyperpermeability (Leong et al., 2025). In diabetic retinal models, ROCK pathway activation produces RPE blebbing and tight-junction disruption, with pharmacologic ROCK inhibition reversing barrier dysfunction and dampening leukostasis and leakage (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Given these mechanisms, selective ROCK2 inhibition with belumosudil is expected to:
- Reduce p-MYPT1 and downstream p-MLC in RPE, decreasing acto-myosin contractility, stabilizing the circumferential actin belt and adherens/tight junctions (ZO-1/claudin-19), thereby rescuing TEER and lowering FITC-dextran flux under H₂O₂ or complement challenge (Zandi et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025).
