I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PXS-5153A is a synthetically derived molecule that belongs to the class of selective lysyl oxidase inhibitors. In its design, medicinal chemistry efforts focused on optimizing potency and selectivity for LOXL2, along with activity against LOXL3, two members of the lysyl oxidase family that catalyze the oxidative deamination of lysine residues in collagens and elastin to promote covalent crosslink formation. These crosslinks confer the mechanical strength and stiffness of extracellular matrices (ECMs) such as Bruch’s membrane. Synthetic routes to compounds like PXS-5153A typically rely on structure-based design and iterative optimization to achieve potent enzyme inhibition with favorable pharmacokinetic properties (Lin et al., 2020). The compound, commercially available under MedChemExpress HY-111217, is representative of a new therapeutic class that has been primarily explored in the context of fibrosis and tumor microenvironment modulation. Given that ECM stiffening is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, targeting LOXL2 represents a novel approach compared to conventional anti-inflammatory or anti-angiogenic strategies.

II. Therapeutic History  
The LOXL2 inhibitor class, including molecules such as PXS-5153A, has been extensively tested in preclinical models of fibrosis and cancer. For example, within non-ocular systems, LOXL2 activity has been linked to increased tissue stiffness that fosters metastatic progression and desmoplastic reactions in tumors, and selective inhibition of LOXL2 has been shown to reduce crosslink density, attenuating fibrotic remodeling (Lin et al., 2020). Experimental inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity using non-selective agents like β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) has also been applied to in vitro and in vivo models to modulate ECM assembly, with effects on barrier function observed in RPE cultures co-treated with endothelial cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). Although LOXL2 inhibitors have not traditionally been used to treat dry AMD, evidence underscores the centrality of aberrant ECM crosslinking in BM thickening observed during aging and AMD progression (Wang et al., 2025). In particular, the endothelial cell–RPE crosstalk studies demonstrate a critical role for lysyl oxidase activity in regulating collagen bundle formation and in establishing RPE barrier properties (Benedicto et al., 2017). Accordingly, while there is no direct clinical or preclinical record of PXS-5153A in AMD, the antifibrotic profile of the compound and its impact on extracellular matrix mechanics in other disease contexts serve as a compelling rationale to explore its application in dry AMD.

III. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, LOXL2 catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of lysine or hydroxylysine residues present in collagens and elastin. This reaction is critical for the formation of covalent crosslinks that stabilize the ECM. Overexpression or hyperactivity of LOXL2 results in an excessively crosslinked and stiff matrix. In the eye, particularly within Bruch’s membrane—which is a complex, stratified ECM structure located between the RPE and the choroid—aberrant collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking are known to increase mechanical tension. Such mechanical changes are thought to adversely affect RPE cell function by interfering with integrin-mediated cell–matrix interactions and perturbing the proper localization of tight junction proteins, including ZO-1 and occludin (Benedicto et al., 2017).

PXS-5153A functions by binding to the catalytic pocket of LOXL2, thereby preventing its enzymatic activity. By blocking the oxidative deamination step, PXS-5153A reduces the formation of both immature and mature crosslinks in ECM proteins. The anticipated outcome is a lower crosslink density in Bruch’s membrane, resulting in a softer, more compliant matrix environment. This reduction in mechanical stiffness is expected to diminish abnormal mechanosignaling through β1 integrins, which are integral to the assembly and maintenance of tight junctions on RPE cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). The downstream consequences of reduced integrin activation include dampening of Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways, which in turn facilitate the stabilization and proper localization of tight junction proteins at the RPE cell membranes (Benedicto et al., 2017). Restoration of these junctional complexes correlates with improved barrier function, typically measured as an increased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in cell culture models. This mechanism is supported by studies in which inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity—by pharmacological agents such as BAPN—led to alterations in RPE barrier properties and tight junction morphology (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by directly targeting LOXL2, PXS-5153A is proposed to correct the pathological ECM remodeling that underlies BM stiffening in dry AMD while re-establishing proper RPE barrier integrity.

IV. Expected Effect  
The expected therapeutic effect of PXS-5153A in dry AMD centers on normalization of the BM ECM and concomitant restoration of RPE barrier function. In the proposed experimental model—an in vitro co-culture system where human fetal RPE (hfRPE) cells are grown on a substrate mimicking BM with defined stiffness—the application of PXS-5153A at concentrations around 5 µM is anticipated to yield a number of favorable outcomes.

First, by reducing LOXL2-mediated crosslinking of collagen IV and fibronectin, the drug should decrease the mechanical stiffness of the BM analog. A less rigid BM reduces aberrant integrin activation on the basolateral surfaces of RPE cells, which has been shown to be critical for proper tight junction assembly. In several studies, when the extracellular matrix is normalized—such as by altering substrate stiffness—there is an improvement in the localization of key tight junction proteins, specifically occludin and ZO-1, at the cell membrane (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Second, the reduced matrix stiffness is expected to alleviate the mechanical stress experienced by RPE cells, thereby facilitating the re-establishment of cell polarity and intercellular junction continuity. The stabilization of junctional complexes is measurable by TEER. In previous EC–RPE co-culture experiments, modulation of ECM mechanical properties directly correlated with increased TEER values, reflecting improved barrier function (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Moreover, the proper organization of the basement membrane is not only a structural consideration; the biochemical signaling through β1 integrin receptors—critical for maintaining cell adhesion and survival—would return toward homeostatic levels, further supporting the integrity of the RPE layer (Benedicto et al., 2017). These integrin-mediated signals influence downstream effectors such as Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK, which have been implicated in regulating tight junction dynamics (Benedicto et al., 2017). Progress in these pathways is expected to manifest as an overall improvement in the barrier phenotype, which is central to preventing the leakage of fluid and other deleterious solutes into the subretinal space—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.

In summary, it is anticipated that treatment with PXS-5153A in appropriate in vitro (and ultimately in vivo) models will lead to:  
• Reduced collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in BM, yielding a matrix with decreased stiffness (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Normalization of β1 integrin signaling and subsequent reorganization of RPE tight junctions with improved localization of proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Restoration of barrier function as evidenced by increased TEER measurements and improved paracellular permeability profiles (Benedicto et al., 2017).  

Thus, PXS-5153A is expected to address one of the core aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis by targeting ECM remodeling, which in turn indirectly stabilizes RPE cell function.

V. Overall Evaluation  
The concept of using PXS-5153A to modulate ECM pathology in dry AMD is compelling given the mechanistic insights derived from studies on lysyl oxidase activity in epithelial barrier function and ECM assembly. Among the strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its robust preclinical evidence in fibrosis and tumor microenvironment models. LOXL2 has been implicated in promoting tissue stiffening by catalyzing the crosslinking of collagen and fibronectin in various tissues (Lin et al., 2020). The pathophysiological parallels between fibrotic ECM remodeling in cancers and the stiffening of Bruch’s membrane in dry AMD provide a strong rationale for repurposing a LOXL2 inhibitor in an ocular context. Numerous studies have demonstrated that extracellular matrix integrity is essential for optimal RPE barrier function, and that even subtle changes in ECM mechanics can disrupt junctional complexes and lead to barrier dysfunction (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by targeting a critical enzymatic step in ECM crosslinking, PXS-5153A may confer dual benefits: it could both reduce the pathological stiffening of Bruch’s membrane and promote the reorganization of tight junction complexes, ultimately resulting in enhanced TEER and stabilization of the outer blood–retina barrier.

However, several important weaknesses or uncertainties must be considered. First, while numerous studies (using agents such as BAPN) have illustrated that lysyl oxidase inhibition affects RPE barrier function, direct evidence with selective LOXL2 inhibitors—specifically in ocular models of dry AMD—is lacking (Buniello et al., 2025). In fact, the Open Targets Platform indicates only a weak direct association between LOXL2 and age-related macular degeneration, based on limited literature evidence (Buniello et al., 2025). This raises the possibility that, although LOXL2 plays a demonstrable role in ECM crosslinking in other tissues, its specific involvement in dry AMD pathogenesis may not be as pronounced or may be influenced by other factors not recapitulated in non-ocular models.

Furthermore, potential off-target effects or the consequences of broadly altering ECM crosslinking in the eye must be carefully examined. The structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane is critical not only for its barrier function but also for nutrient transport between the choroidal circulation and the RPE. Overinhibition of LOXL2, or interference with normal ECM turnover, may inadvertently lead to basement membrane disorganization, as has been observed when lysyl oxidase activity was inhibited during critical periods of retinal development (Benedicto et al., 2017). This underscores the need for precise dose optimization and targeted delivery, ideally restricted to the ocular environment, to avoid systemic side effects.

Another consideration is the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. In addition to ECM stiffening, dry AMD involves multifactorial processes including oxidative stress, complement activation, inflammation, and the accumulation of lipoprotein deposits. Thus, while normalizing matrix stiffness is likely to improve RPE barrier function, it may be insufficient to fully arrest or reverse the disease process on its own. A combination therapy that also addresses the inflammatory and degenerative components of AMD may eventually be required (Benedicto et al., 2017; Caban et al., 2022).

From a development perspective, there is significant strength in the repurposing strategy because agents like PXS-5153A already have a detailed preclinical profile in non-ocular fibrotic models. This existing data can accelerate preclinical validation in ocular models, with studies planned in RPE–BM co-culture systems using TEER as a functional readout (Benedicto et al., 2017). Furthermore, leveraging well-characterized in vitro assays (such as those involving decellularized ECM and substrate stiffness modulation as described in the context) offers a clear experimental framework to evaluate whether the normalization of BM stiffness by PXS-5153A is sufficient to restore RPE tight junction integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017).

Nonetheless, one notable weakness is the limited direct evidence linking LOXL2 specifically to dry AMD. Although elevated lysyl oxidase activity and changes in collagen crosslinking have been observed in the context of RPE barrier function and BM integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017), the genetic and translational data associating LOXL2 with AMD are not robust. The relatively low association score (Buniello et al., 2025) suggests that additional studies are needed to clarify LOXL2’s role in the eye and to determine whether its inhibition will yield a therapeutically meaningful benefit in dry AMD patients.

In conclusion, repurposing PXS-5153A for dry AMD represents an innovative strategy that leverages the known antifibrotic effects of LOXL2 inhibition to address the deleterious ECM remodeling observed in aged Bruch’s membrane. The candidate’s synthetic origins and prior applications in fibrosis and cancer studies provide a solid foundation for its use, while the mechanistic rationale—centered on reducing pathological crosslinking and restoring RPE barrier function—is strongly supported by evidence from ECM modulation studies (Benedicto et al., 2017). However, challenges remain due to the lack of direct ocular data, potential risks of overmodulating ECM integrity, and the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology. Future research must focus on rigorous in vitro validation in RPE–BM co-culture systems and in vivo studies in relevant AMD animal models to establish the efficacy and safety profile of PXS-5153A in the context of dry AMD. Overall, despite these uncertainties, PXS-5153A holds promise as a novel ECM-targeted therapeutic candidate that could complement existing and emerging treatment strategies for this currently unmet clinical need (Lin et al., 2020; Buniello et al., 2025).

Taken together, the strengths of a clear mechanism of action, potent enzyme selectivity, and an innovative approach toward ECM normalization position PXS-5153A as an attractive candidate warranting further investigation. Nonetheless, a careful reappraisal of the molecular role of LOXL2 in the ocular microenvironment, along with detailed studies on dosing, delivery, and potential off-target effects, will be critical in determining whether this candidate can be successfully repurposed for treating dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ICG-001 (Sigma I2441) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor originally identified for its ability to selectively disrupt the interaction between β-catenin and the transcriptional coactivator CBP (CREB-binding protein), thereby inhibiting TCF/LEF-dependent Wnt/β-catenin–driven transcription without reducing total β-catenin protein abundance (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). Mechanistically, ICG-001 is positioned within a class of β-catenin pathway modulators that block nuclear β-catenin activity rather than decreasing β-catenin protein levels; this distinguishes it from antisense/siRNA approaches and from inhibitors that act upstream in Wnt signaling (e.g., tankyrase inhibitors like XAV-939) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor class has been proposed as a more selective means to modulate β-catenin transcriptional output while sparing adherens junction functions that depend on β-catenin protein pools, a distinction supported by data showing ICG-001 does not trigger compensatory γ-catenin stabilization that follows β-catenin protein depletion (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117).

Within the broader Wnt-targeting landscape, ICG-001 exemplifies downstream, transcriptional-coactivator–selective targeting, contrasted with agents that block β-catenin/TCF binding, Dishevelled PDZ interactions, Porcupine-mediated ligand maturation, or Frizzled receptor activity (e.g., OMP-18R5) (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31). Because Wnt pathway effects are highly context dependent and temporally dynamic across tissues, coactivator-selective modulation has been argued to mitigate systemic liabilities relative to global pathway inhibition (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31).

Therapeutic History  
ICG-001 itself is widely used as a research tool, and its clinical derivative/prodrug analogs (e.g., PRI-724/OP-724) have reached Phase I/IIa testing in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, establishing a preliminary human safety/tolerability and feasibility record for CBP/β-catenin pathway inhibition in chronic disease. In HCV-induced cirrhosis, an open-label Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of PRI-724 administered continuous i.v. infusions (10–160 mg/m2/day; 1 week on/1 week off for 12 weeks) with primary outcomes focused on adverse events and exploratory anti-fibrotic endpoints (histology, serum fibrosis biomarkers); the program reported safety/tolerability and preliminary efficacy consistent with anti-fibrotic activity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014). In HBV/HCV-related cirrhosis, a Phase I/IIa open-label study (twice-weekly 4 h infusions; 140, 280, 380 mg/m2 per 4 h) evaluated safety, PK, and change in liver fibrosis area by biopsy at 12 weeks; the registry cites a derived EBioMedicine report on safety, tolerability, and anti-fibrotic effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2018). In advanced primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; Scheuer stage ≥III), OP-724 (formerly PRI-724) underwent a Phase I dose-finding trial (4 h i.v. infusions, twice weekly for 12 weeks; 140/280/380 mg/m2 cohorts) assessing serious adverse events, PK of OP-724 and metabolite C-82, and fibrosis-related endpoints (biopsy fibrotic area, FibroScan, Child-Pugh/MELD, ELF score) with feasibility/safety results published (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

No clinical or preclinical ocular applications of ICG-001/PRI-724/OP-724 were identified in the provided context, and there are no reports here of use in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), or retinal barrier disorders (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019). Preclinical oncology literature summarized in the provided sources documents ICG-001’s activity in cancer cells (reduced proliferation and induced selective apoptosis via TCF-dependent signaling reduction) but does not address ocular tissues (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Thus, while the drug class has human safety experience in fibrotic liver disease, there is no direct evidence in the provided context for ophthalmic use or for dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
ICG-001 binds CBP and selectively disrupts the β-catenin/CBP complex, attenuating β-catenin–driven transcription of TCF/LEF target genes (e.g., Cyclin D1) without decreasing total β-catenin protein levels; in Hep3B cells, ICG-001 reduced TOPflash reporter activity and Cyclin D1 expression while leaving β-catenin abundance unchanged and without inducing compensatory γ-catenin stabilization (if anything, γ-catenin modestly decreased) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). Across multiple excerpts, ICG-001 is consistently described as selective for β-catenin/CBP over β-catenin/p300, reducing TCF-dependent Wnt output while sparing other β-catenin protein interactions; global β-catenin levels are unaffected, reinforcing a functional separation between nuclear transcriptional roles and membrane adherens junction pools (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Authors highlight that agents which lower β-catenin protein (ASO/siRNA) trigger γ-catenin compensation at adherens junctions—distinct from ICG-001, which blocks transcriptional activity without provoking such protein-level sensing/reciprocity (Wickline, 2013, pp. 112–117, 140–145). It remains explicitly unknown from these data whether ICG-001 perturbs adherens junction function in vivo; follow-up studies were recommended to test junctional tolerance to transcriptional blockade (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

Contextual biology of β-catenin coactivator usage indicates that CBP vs p300 partnering can impart divergent phenotypic outcomes; in fibrotic contexts, CBP-associated β-catenin activity has been linked with pro-fibrotic programs whereas p300-associated activity may be protective, though this literature is complex and model-dependent (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69). Canonical β-catenin signaling is also subject to Wnt-independent inputs that promote nuclear translocation/transactivation (e.g., PKA/Akt phosphorylation), and β-catenin exists in distinct pools with membrane-associated adherens junction functions that are regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation events, further implying that selective transcriptional blockade (CBP-directed) may spare adhesive roles (Wickline, 2013, pp. 21–26). Together, these mechanistic data support a rationale for testing CBP/β-catenin–selective inhibitors for diseases where β-catenin transcription drives pathology and where preserving epithelial junctional architecture is desirable (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 140–145).

Disease-Relevant Biology in RPE and Retinal Barriers  
RPE epithelial phenotype and outer blood–retina barrier (oBRB) integrity depend on tight junction (TJ) and adherens junction (AJ) complexes (ZO-1/occludin/claudins; E-cadherin/catenins). Loss of ZO-1 releases ZONAB to drive CDK4 and proliferation; downregulation of E-cadherin frees β-catenin to translocate to the nucleus and activate EMT/proliferation drivers (e.g., Snail, Cyclin D1), establishing a mechanistic link between junctional disruption and β-catenin–dependent transcriptional programs in RPE (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–9). Reviews of RPE EMT highlight Wnt–β-catenin as a key mediator in the eye; experimental injury (laser photocoagulation) activates β-catenin signaling and facilitates RPE proliferation, reinforcing the pathway’s involvement in EMT and regenerative responses (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 7–9).

Critically, primary hRPE culture studies demonstrate that Matrigel plus Activin A (MA) fosters epithelial morphology, increases TJ gene/protein expression (Claudin-1, Claudin-3, Occludin, ZO-1), improves apical ZO-1 polarity, and elevates TEER; this phenotype is accompanied by increased β-catenin levels and β-catenin/TCF target expression (TCF-4, Survivin, Cyclin D1, c-Myc), and is suppressed by the Wnt/β-catenin inhibitor XAV-939, implicating canonical β-catenin activity in barrier maturation under these culture conditions (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11). The MA paradigm also shows anti-apoptotic effects (lower ROS, preserved mitochondrial potential, lower Annexin V positivity) linked to elevated β-catenin/Survivin, again consistent with β-catenin supporting epithelial survival when cell–cell contacts are intact (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

Conversely, disease models and inflammatory contexts show scenarios where β-catenin activation correlates with barrier breakdown. In diabetic macular edema (DME) models, SMURF1 promotes WIF1 ubiquitination and degradation, activating Wnt/β-catenin–VEGF signaling, inducing autophagy, and disrupting RPE tight junctions; knockdown of SMURF1 restores WIF1, suppresses pathway activation, and rescues claudin-1/occludin/ZO-1 expression in ARPE-19 and in STZ mice (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Inflammatory TNFα challenge in polarized ARPE-19 reduces TER, increases paracellular permeability, and disrupts ZO-1/claudins/occludin and AJ components; the HDAC inhibitor ITF2357 restores TER and junctional proteins and suppresses β-catenin overexpression and NF-κB signaling, supporting the concept that limiting β-catenin–linked transcription can be barrier-protective under inflammatory stress (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19). Under oxidative stress relevant to dry AMD, ex vivo primary porcine RPE (ppRPE) exposed to NaIO₃ shows a significant reduction in ZO-1 immunopositive area (with unchanged TJP1 mRNA), indicating tight-junction localization loss; while the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is not measured directly in this model, the outcome establishes a testable context for barrier rescue (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

These data collectively underscore a context-dependent role of β-catenin in RPE: when epithelial contacts are robust, β-catenin activity can support maturation, TJ expression, and survival; under EMT/injury/inflammatory stress (e.g., DME/TNFα), β-catenin pathway activation correlates with junctional loss, VEGF induction, and autophagy, and pathway suppression can be protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19).

In inflammatory/DME-like contexts, β-catenin activation contributes to VEGF/autophagy-mediated TJ disruption, and Wnt pathway suppression is protective; in these contexts, CBP blockade could plausibly reduce pathway-driven barrier loss (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

- Proliferation concerns: ICG-001 reduces Cyclin D1 in non-ocular cells, consistent with attenuating proliferation signaling (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). In RPE EMT, β-catenin activation promotes proliferation via Cyclin D1; thus ICG-001 would be expected to mitigate proliferation-associated EMT programs rather than activate them (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7, 7–9). However, MA-driven β-catenin activity increases Survivin/Bcl2 and enhances anti-apoptotic resilience; therefore, under oxidative stress, attenuating β-catenin/CBP with ICG-001 could trade off survival signals against potential EMT suppression, and net effects on TEER may vary by stressor and co-signaling milieu (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

In analogous inflammatory contexts, limiting β-catenin–linked transcription correlates with barrier recovery, but this was achieved with an HDAC inhibitor and via suppression of β-catenin overexpression/NF-κB, not CBP-selective Wnt blockade (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19). Therefore, the claim that ICG-001 will “bias gene transcription toward junctional protein upregulation (claudin-1, ZO-1) in RPE under oxidative stress without activating proliferation pathways, leading to recovery of TEER and decreased paracellular flux” is mechanistically plausible in EMT/inflammatory settings but remains unsubstantiated for oxidative stress in RPE; the directionality of effect on junctional genes could invert depending on baseline epithelial status and co-activation of survival pathways (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Therapeutic Risk–Benefit Considerations  
- Safety/translatability: Clinical-stage CBP/β-catenin inhibitors (PRI-724/OP-724) have demonstrated safety/tolerability in Phase I/IIa liver fibrosis trials, supporting repurposing potential; however, the dosing was i.v., and ocular delivery, PK/PD at the RPE, and retinal safety are uncharacterized in the provided data (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Mechanistic specificity: ICG-001 spares total β-catenin protein and does not trigger γ-catenin compensation, mitigating concerns about adherens junction destabilization that accompany β-catenin depletion; nevertheless, whether ICG-001 affects adherens junction functionality in epithelial tissues in vivo remains unknown, and this must be directly assessed in RPE (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Pathway context dependence: RPE barrier outcomes with Wnt/β-catenin modulation are bidirectional and context dependent—MA-induced β-catenin activity enhances TJs/TEER, while in DME/inflammation β-catenin activation correlates with TJ disruption; CBP-specific blockade could be beneficial in the latter but deleterious in the former (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). This necessitates careful stressor stratification (oxidative versus inflammatory/VEGF-driven) in preclinical testing.

- Disease relevance to dry AMD: Oxidative stress disrupts RPE TJs and reduces ZO-1 localization in ex vivo ppRPE; EMT and barrier breakdown are recognized contributors to RPE dysfunction; however, there is no direct evidence here linking CBP/β-catenin inhibition to barrier rescue in oxidative injury models or to slowed geographic atrophy progression (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

  • Replicate NaIO₃-induced ZO-1 reduction and test whether ICG-001 preserves/restores ZO-1 area without elevating proliferation/EMT markers; track apoptosis/survival readouts given MA data tying β-catenin to anti-apoptotic signaling (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7).

  • If in vitro/ex vivo are positive, progress to mouse models with RPE oxidative injury (e.g., NaIO₃ systemic exposure) and quantify RPE barrier integrity (ZO-1 localization, RPE flat-mounts), photoreceptor/RPE survival, and functional outcomes; consider delivery routes (intravitreal/subconjunctival) and PK (not available here) (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

Strengths  
- Defined, selective mechanism: ICG-001 disrupts β-catenin/CBP complexes and suppresses TCF-dependent transcription without lowering total β-catenin; it does not trigger γ-catenin compensation observed with β-catenin protein knockdown, offering a mechanistically precise intervention that may spare adherens junction architecture (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117, 140–145, 26–30).

- Clinical-stage drug class: The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor analogs PRI-724/OP-724 have human safety and PK data in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis/PBC, supporting translational feasibility and providing a clinical development template, albeit outside ophthalmology (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

- Assay tractability: RPE barrier endpoints (TEER, paracellular flux, ZO-1/claudin-1 localization) are robust; β-catenin target genes provide PD markers to confirm on-target activity, enabling a decisive preclinical go/no-go within RPE-relevant stress paradigms (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55).

Key Limitations and Risks  
- No direct ocular/RPE data for ICG-001: The provided context contains no studies of ICG-001 (or PRI-724/OP-724) in RPE or ocular tissues, no TEER/paracellular flux rescue data, and no AMD model outcomes; claims of junction-selective “bias” in RPE are speculative and unproven here (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

On the present evidence, ICG-001 has a coherent, selective mechanism with clinical-stage validation in a non-ocular indication, and there is strong biological plausibility that β-catenin transcriptional blockade can counter EMT/proliferation programs in RPE. However, the specific hypothesis that ICG-001 will “bias” transcription to upregulate claudin-1/ZO-1 and restore TEER under oxidative stress is not supported by the provided literature; in fact, RPE studies show that β-catenin activation is associated with higher TJ expression/TEER in some contexts, and pathway inhibition reduces these features, whereas in inflammatory/DME contexts β-catenin activation is deleterious and suppression is protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Therefore, a tightly scoped preclinical program should be undertaken to empirically resolve these context-dependent effects in RPE before committing to development for dry AMD.

- Proceed with an in vitro/ex vivo feasibility package to test ICG-001 in RPE barrier models under defined stressors (oxidative vs inflammatory), with rigorous functional and molecular endpoints and on-target PD confirmation; include orthogonal comparators (XAV-939, ITF2357) to position CBP-selective modulation against broader Wnt suppression and epigenetic anti-inflammatory rescue (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7). Advance only if ICG-001 reproducibly restores TEER and junctional localization without pro-EMT/proliferation signatures across oxidative stress conditions relevant to dry AMD (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

In sum, ICG-001 is a mechanistically attractive, clinically precedented β-catenin/CBP inhibitor, but the claim of junction-focused, proliferation-sparing barrier rescue in oxidatively stressed RPE is currently hypothetical and not substantiated by the provided literature; decisive RPE-focused experiments are required to validate or refute its potential for dry AMD (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AZD8055 is a synthetically derived small‐molecule inhibitor designed to target the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway. It belongs to the second‐generation class of mTOR inhibitors, which are structurally and functionally distinct from the first‐generation rapalogs that were originally isolated from Streptomyces species. In contrast to natural product–derived mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin, AZD8055 was developed through rational drug design to achieve high potency and dual inhibition of both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2. Its ATP-competitive binding to the kinase domain endows it with a very high selectivity profile, exhibiting an IC₅₀ of approximately 0.8 nM against mTOR as originally reported, while also limiting activity against other phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) family members (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10). In the context of drug classes, AZD8055 is categorized alongside other small-molecule kinase inhibitors that have been principally exploited in oncology to curb aberrant cell growth; however, the modality by which it inhibits mTOR via direct competition at the ATP-binding pocket distinguishes it from allosteric inhibitors. The development program underlying AZD8055 focused on enhancing both the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic properties to not only achieve a potent biochemical inhibition but also allow for a cleaner kinase selectivity profile, which is essential for targeted clinical interventions. Although primarily intended for oncology indications, this engineered selectivity coupled with its capacity to modulate autophagy has prompted investigation into its potential repurposing for diseases characterized by autophagic dysregulation, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, mTOR inhibitors have been extensively studied in the context of cancer, with rapamycin and its analogs (rapalogs) serving as prototype compounds for targeting dysregulated mTOR signaling in malignant cells. AZD8055, a second-generation inhibitor, was developed to overcome limitations associated with rapalogs, including incomplete mTORC1 inhibition and the inadvertent activation of compensatory pro-survival signals mediated through mTORC2 and AKT feedback loops. Preclinical studies and phase I clinical evaluations in oncology have demonstrated that AZD8055 can effectively induce cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis by simultaneously suppressing mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis and mTORC2-mediated survival signals (Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10; Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 4–5). Its clinical development history has largely focused on cancers such as Her2-positive breast cancers and gliomas, where its ability to modulate PI3K/AKT signaling has been of particular advantage in overcoming resistance mechanisms. Although the majority of the therapeutic history of AZD8055 has been in cancer, the underlying molecular rationale for its use has provided impetus for exploring its repurposing in non-oncological diseases. In the realm of ocular diseases, particularly dry AMD, the mTOR pathway has been implicated in the regulation of autophagy and cellular homeostasis within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). While traditional mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin have been tested in ocular settings, their clinical efficacy has been inconsistent, partly due to the inability to inhibit mTORC2-driven feedback loops. AZD8055’s dual inhibition mechanism could potentially address these shortcomings by providing a more balanced modulation of the mTOR pathway, although to date there is limited direct clinical or preclinical evidence of its use specifically in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 9–10, 16–17).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, AZD8055 exerts its pharmacological effects through ATP-competitive inhibition of the catalytic domain of mTOR, thereby targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes. mTORC1 is primarily responsible for regulating protein synthesis through substrates such as 4EBP1 and S6 kinase, while mTORC2 is integral to the phosphorylation and activation of AKT, a key mediator of cell survival and metabolism. The simultaneous inhibition of both complexes by AZD8055 prevents the compensatory activation of AKT that is typically observed with rapalogs, which primarily target mTORC1 and leave mTORC2 functionally active (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Downstream effects of this mechanism include rapid dephosphorylation of 4EBP1, which in turn halts cap-dependent mRNA translation, and the induction of autophagy as a result of relieving the suppression of upstream autophagy initiating factors such as ULK1 and transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10). In ocular applications, particularly within RPE cells, the impairment of autophagy is thought to contribute to the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and damaged cellular components. By enhancing autophagic flux, AZD8055 can facilitate the autophagosome–lysosome fusion critical to the degradation and clearance of damaged junctional proteins. The resultant restoration of the tight junction integrity—measurable via trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—is believed to underlie the therapeutic rationale for its use in dry AMD. As a dual mTOR inhibitor with high potency, AZD8055’s molecular interactions within the mTOR kinase domain contribute not only to the suppression of pathological signaling but also promote cellular recycling processes that maintain RPE function and homeostasis (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 4–6). Additionally, the suppression of mTORC2 may help prevent compensatory pro-survival signaling pathways that could otherwise undermine barrier recovery, thereby ensuring a sustained therapeutic effect in the stressed RPE cellular milieu (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed study hypothesis posits that 50 nM AZD8055 will effectively restore and enhance barrier function in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells that have been subjected to oxidative stress via H₂O₂ exposure. Mechanistically, the compound is expected to attenuate the oxidative stress–induced disruption of junctional proteins by rapidly dephosphorylating 4EBP1, thereby halting pathological protein synthesis and activating autophagic pathways. One of the key cellular assays involves the measurement of TEER, a well-established metric reflecting the integrity of tight junctions and overall barrier function in epithelial cultures. According to preliminary data referenced in the hypothesis, a 50 nM dose of AZD8055 elevated baseline TEER by 24% and accelerated the recovery of TEER following oxidative insult, which suggests that the inhibitor not only ameliorates barrier damage but also promotes cellular repair mechanisms (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Moreover, pharmacodynamic markers such as sustained colocalization of LC3 and LAMP1 implicate an improvement in autophagosome–lysosome fusion, leading to the efficient removal of damaged junctional proteins. This is particularly relevant in the pathophysiology of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction is observed due to the accumulation of cellular debris and compromised autophagic clearance (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating AZD8055 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key strengths and potential challenges must be considered. A notable strength of AZD8055 lies in its dual inhibition profile, which addresses the limitations inherent in rapalog therapy by effectively targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2. This dual action is instrumental in both halting aberrant protein synthesis and in promoting autophagic clearance, processes that are crucial to restoring cellular homeostasis and junctional integrity in RPE cells challenged by oxidative stress (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Moreover, its clean kinase selectivity reduces the likelihood of off-target interactions that could confound clinical outcomes, an important consideration given the delicate nature of ocular therapeutics (Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10).

However, there are inherent weaknesses and safety concerns that warrant attention. Preclinical and clinical data from oncology studies indicate that AZD8055 is associated with adverse effects such as hyperglycemia, fatigue, and gastrointestinal disturbances (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 4–6). Although these events have been characterized in systemic applications within cancer patients, translating such findings to a localized, ocular delivery system requires careful dose optimization to ensure that the therapeutic benefits are not offset by adverse outcomes. Additionally, the complexity of mTOR signaling in the retina poses a challenge. The mTOR pathway not only regulates autophagy but also influences cell survival, apoptosis, and inflammatory responses. Disruption of this delicate balance through chronic or excessive inhibition could potentially lead to unintended consequences, including impaired cellular metabolism or dysregulated angiogenesis, particularly since previous clinical trials using mTOR inhibitors for ocular conditions have reported mixed results and even adverse effects on visual acuity (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 12–14).

Another concern is the risk associated with systemic exposure. While AZD8055 is primarily being developed in oncology with an established profile in systemic administration, its ocular pharmacokinetics, particularly when delivered intravitreally or via other local routes, remain to be fully elucidated. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BCX9930 is a novel, orally bioavailable, low-molecular-weight small molecule that functions as a selective inhibitor of complement factor D (FD). It was originally discovered through a rigorous drug discovery program that combined high-throughput screening with structure‐based rational design strategies to identify potent, non-covalent inhibitors of the serine protease FD, an essential enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. This candidate belongs to the class of factor D inhibitors, compounds that have previously been developed for complement-mediated diseases including complement 3 glomerulopathy (Chen et al., 2022). The synthesis and discovery process for BCX9930 involved chemical scaffold optimization to enhance both potency and selectivity; for instance, by specifically non-covalently occupying the S1 pocket of FD, BCX9930 is able to achieve an IC₅₀ value as low as 4 nM, a potency level that places it among the most active agents in its category. Its chemical attributes also include more than a 500-fold selectivity over related serine proteases, thereby reducing the potential for off-target effects—a critical factor for chronic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where long-term safety is paramount (Schubart et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
The development of BCX9930 is emblematic of the broader evolution in complement therapeutics. Historically, the complement system has been successfully targeted in several diseases where dysregulated complement activity plays a pathogenic role. Prior studies have established the role of FD in both the amplification loop of the alternative pathway and its subsequent effects on complement-mediated damage. BCX9930 and similar agents emerged from early research efforts that investigated FD inhibition as a means to alter pathologic complement activation. In clinical studies, similar agents targeting factor D (for example, danicopan) have demonstrated significant suppression of alternative pathway activity in conditions such as PNH, with reports noting reductions in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels and improvements in hemoglobin that facilitated transfusion independence (Schubart et al., 2023; Risitano et al., 2020). Although the majority of these pilots have been focused on hematological disorders and C3G, the mechanistic rationale for FD inhibition directly applies to dry AMD as well. Preclinical models have documented that, when the alternative pathway is excessively activated—as is theorized in dry AMD—even minute amounts of FD can trigger a cascade of destructive complement activity (Schubart et al., 2023; Gavriilaki et al., 2022). In animal models, FD inhibitors have demonstrated promising outcomes including the reduction of complement deposition and preservation of retinal architecture (Ong et al., 2024). Despite the encouraging therapeutic history of FD inhibitors in other indications, it is important to note that clinical trials evaluating FD inhibitors specifically for dry AMD or geographic atrophy have produced mixed results; one high-profile example is the failure of Lampalizumab (an FD inhibitor) to meet meaningful endpoints in pivotal phase 3 trials (Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019). Nonetheless, BCX9930 has distinct chemical and pharmacological properties that differentiate it from earlier candidates, including its strong potency, favorable oral bioavailability, and robust preclinical barrier rescue effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, making it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
The pathologic basis for many complement-mediated diseases, including dry AMD, lies in the dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, in which factor D plays a pivotal role. Normally, FD is the rate-limiting enzyme required to generate the AP C3 convertase by cleaving factor B complexed with C3b, which fuels an amplification loop and leads to the generation of downstream proinflammatory mediators such as C3a and C5a as well as opsonins that promote inflammation and tissue damage (Gavriilaki et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024). BCX9930 exerts its therapeutic effect by binding non-covalently in the S1 pocket of FD. This binding is characterized by exceptionally high affinity, with an IC₅₀ value of 4 nM, and by stringent selectivity that minimizes interference with other serine proteases. By occupying this key binding site, BCX9930 effectively prevents FD from interacting with its natural substrate, thereby arresting the production of the AP C3 convertase. This inhibition leads to a subsequent decrease in C3 cleavage and a reduction in the generation of complement split products, which are known to instigate an inflammatory response (Chen et al., 2022).  
Molecularly, the non-covalent nature of BCX9930’s interaction with factor D confers several advantages. First, such interactions allow reversible inhibition, providing the potential for controlled dosing and the fine-tuning of complement activity. Second, the selectivity profile of BCX9930 results from structural modifications aimed at optimizing the fit within the S1 pocket, ensuring that the inhibitor does not inadvertently affect enzymes with similar active site geometries. This precision is crucial, as systemic blockade of the complement system can result in significant immunosuppression. Thus, the protection of the retinal environment—by specifically inhibiting the amplification loop of the alternative pathway—offers a mechanistic rationale for the use of BCX9930 in diseases where complement overactivation is implicated, notably in the disruption of RPE tight junction integrity (Gavriilaki et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024). Additionally, the compound’s design ensures that while it attenuates pathogenic complement activity, it spares the classical and lectin pathways, reducing the risk of systemic immunocompromise.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for BCX9930 in the treatment of dry AMD is based on its ability to mitigate complement-mediated damage to the retinal pigment epithelium. In vitro studies in primary human RPE cells have shown that under conditions of serum-mediated complement activation, there is a decline in trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and disruption of critical tight junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and claudin-19. These proteins are essential for maintaining the barrier integrity of the RPE, and their dysregulation is a hallmark of retinal degeneration in AMD (Gavriilaki et al., 2022).  
The working hypothesis posits that by non-covalently occupying the S1 pocket of factor D, BCX9930 can inhibit the formation of the alternative pathway C3 convertase, thereby reducing the production of the inflammatory complement split products. This reduction is expected to lead to a decrease in complement-driven RPE tight junction disruption. Experimental data indicate that the addition of 500 nM BCX9930 to primary human RPE cultures challenged with serum results in a recovery of TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values. This recovery is associated with the restoration of tight junction integrity, as evidenced by the maintenance of ZO-1 and claudin-19 continuity, both of which are critical determinants of the barrier function (Chen et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024).  
In parallel, in vivo studies using Factor H-knockout animal models have provided supportive data for BCX9930’s therapeutic effect. In these animal models, which exhibit heightened complement activation and subsequent retinal damage similar to that seen in dry AMD, BCX9930 administered at 5 mg/kg twice daily resulted in a 70% reduction in complement C3 deposition on Bruch’s membrane and preservation of the outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness. These endpoints serve as surrogate indicators for photoreceptor protection and overall retinal health. Taken together, these findings underscore the capacity of BCX9930 not only to neutralize the biochemical drivers of complement activation but also to translate this inhibition into meaningful structural and functional preservation within the retina (Ong et al., 2024).  
Mechanistically, the expected effect hinges on the sustained and robust suppression of the alternative complement pathway, which under normal pathological conditions contributes significantly to the inflammatory milieu and structural degeneration characteristic of dry AMD. The reduction in complement activation is anticipated to curtail downstream inflammatory cascades that can disrupt RPE tight junctions, thereby stabilizing TEER and maintaining the integrity of the retinal barrier. Given that chronic complement activation has been implicated in accelerating the progression of dry AMD, the capacity of BCX9930 to restore and maintain RPE function could slow or even arrest disease progression, offering a novel therapeutic avenue for a condition currently lacking effective interventions (Chen et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating BCX9930 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key strengths and potential limitations must be considered. On the strength side, BCX9930 exhibits an exceptionally high potency (IC₅₀ = 4 nM) and selectivity profile that is well aligned with the intended mechanism of action. Its ability to non-covalently target the S1 pocket of factor D ensures that the inhibition of the alternative pathway is both potent and reversible, thereby allowing for controlled pharmacodynamic effects. The high degree of selectivity—exceeding 500-fold over related serine proteases—not only reduces the likelihood of off-target toxicity but also supports the feasibility of long-term administration required for chronic diseases such as dry AMD (Schubart et al., 2023).  
Preclinical studies provide compelling support for the candidate’s mechanism. The demonstration that 500 nM BCX9930 can recover TEER to 85% of baseline in human RPE cultures suggests that the compound effectively counteracts the complement-mediated disruption of intercellular tight junctions. Furthermore, animal data showing that a dosing regimen of 5 mg/kg BID can reduce Bruch’s membrane C3 deposition by 70% and preserve ONL thickness indicates that BCX9930 not only exerts biochemical effects but also translates these into anatomical preservation within the retina (Ong et al., 2024). Such findings are particularly relevant given the importance of maintaining RPE barrier function and photoreceptor viability in halting the progression of dry AMD.  
Another strong point in favor of BCX9930 is its oral bioavailability, which is a significant advantage over therapies that require invasive delivery methods (for example, intravitreal injections). An oral agent would potentially improve patient compliance and reduce the risks associated with repeated intraocular procedures. This is particularly critical in a disease like dry AMD, where the patient population is predominantly elderly, and minimizing treatment burden is essential (Chen et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).  
Despite these promising attributes, there are notable challenges and uncertainties that must be acknowledged. One major concern pertains to the historical track record of complement inhibitors in the treatment of dry AMD. Previous clinical trials with other agents targeting the alternative pathway—such as Lampalizumab—have ultimately failed to demonstrate robust clinical efficacy in phase 3 trials despite encouraging preclinical data (Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019). Such outcomes underscore the difficulty of translating complement inhibition into meaningful clinical benefits in retinal degenerative diseases. The complexity of AMD pathophysiology, which involves not only complement dysregulation but also oxidative stress, genetic predispositions, and environmental factors, means that addressing a single pathway may not be sufficient to fully arrest disease progression.  
Additionally, while the preclinical data for BCX9930 are encouraging, there is still a gap in clinical evidence demonstrating its efficacy specifically in dry AMD. Most of the clinical data currently available for BCX9930 have been derived from studies in conditions like C3G and PNH, where the pathobiology is somewhat different from that of retinal degenerative diseases. There is a high degree of uncertainty as to whether the pharmacodynamic markers observed in these other disease models—such as reductions in complement split products and improved hematological indices—will translate into improved retinal structure and function in AMD patients (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Chen et al., 2022).  
Safety is another domain that necessitates cautious exploration. Although the mechanism of action of BCX9930 suggests an improved tolerability profile owing to its selective inhibition of FD, experiences with analogous compounds (e.g., danicopan) have revealed potential issues such as liver enzyme elevations and other adverse events following sustained treatment (Schubart et al., 2023). Long-term data will be critical in confirming that the inhibition of the alternative pathway does not compromise overall host defense mechanisms or lead to other unexpected off-target consequences.

Complement-driven RPE disruption is only one facet of AMD pathogenesis; a multifactorial disease mechanism implies that combination therapies or multimodal approaches may eventually be needed to achieve optimal clinical outcomes. In this context, BCX9930 might best be positioned as part of a combination regimen, potentially alongside agents that address oxidative damage or other pathogenic mechanisms in AMD. Alternatively, biomarkers may need to be better defined so that patients most likely to benefit from complement inhibition can be identified and targeted in clinical trials (Kassa et al., 2019; Ong et al., 2024).  

In summary, BCX9930 represents a highly promising therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its potent and selective inhibition of factor D, a critical enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. The underlying rationale is strongly supported by both molecular and preclinical evidence: by binding non-covalently to the S1 pocket of factor D, BCX9930 effectively blocks the formation of the C3 convertase, thereby mitigating complement activation that is postulated to drive RPE tight junction disruption. In vitro studies have already demonstrated that BCX9930 can restore trans-epithelial electrical resistance and preserve the continuity of crucial tight junction proteins in human RPE cells under complement challenge. Additionally, animal models have provided evidence for significant reductions in complement deposition and the preservation of retinal architecture. These findings collectively indicate that BCX9930 has the potential to protect retinal tissue from complement-mediated injury, a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024).  

However, the transition from preclinical promise to clinical success remains a challenge, as highlighted by the mixed outcomes seen with previous factor D inhibitors in the AMD space. The failure of some earlier agents, despite robust biochemical data, emphasizes that the path from molecular inhibition to effective disease modification is complex and fraught with challenges. Critical areas of future research include the establishment of clear biomarkers that correlate with clinical outcomes in dry AMD, careful delineation of the safety profile specific to the elderly patient population, and the exploration of appropriate combination strategies that might enhance therapeutic efficacy.  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and encouraging preclinical data, BCX9930 stands out as a compelling candidate for further evaluation in clinical trials targeting dry AMD. Its precise mechanism of action and the potential for oral administration offer distinct advantages and may help overcome some of the limitations encountered with earlier complement inhibitors. Ultimately, while caution is warranted due to the historical challenges in this therapeutic area, the overall evaluation supports the advancement of BCX9930 for further development and rigorous clinical testing in dry AMD patients (Schubart et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
LG100268 is a fully synthetic rexinoid that was developed as a selective agonist for the retinoid X receptors (RXRs). It belongs to a specialized subclass of retinoids known as “rexinoids” that bind to RXRs with high affinity and minimal cross‐reactivity to the retinoic acid receptors (RARs). The compound was discovered and optimized in medicinal chemistry programs aiming to achieve potent RXR activation with improved receptor selectivity relative to earlier retinoid compounds such as bexarotene. Notably, synthetic modifications introduced in LG100268 include the incorporation of a 3‐carboxy pyridine ring—a modular motif that has been exploited for further scaffold diversification and structure–activity work to tune RXR heterodimer selectivity (Curley, 2012, pp. 4–5). LG100268 displays one of the highest reported binding affinities for RXR, with a dissociation constant in the low nanomolar range (approximately 3 nM), making it a very potent agent within its class (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Rexinoids such as LG100268 have been historically used in preclinical research as tools to explore RXR biology in oncology and metabolic studies—often by modulating gene transcription via RXR homodimers or RXR heterodimers with factors such as PPAR, LXR, and others (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). Although LG100268 was initially conceived for applications in cancer chemoprevention and metabolic regulation, its high potency and selective RXR activation have generated interest in repurposing it for diseases with an inflammatory component, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, LG100268 has been most notably explored in preclinical models of cancer—particularly in murine models of breast cancer. Studies in the MMTV-Neu (a HER2+ breast cancer model) and the MMTV-PyMT (an aggressive, triple-negative model) have shown that short-course dietary administration of LG100268 produces significant immunomodulatory effects. For example, in these models, LG100268 was observed to decrease the infiltration of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and CD206-expressing macrophages, while increasing the expression of PD-L1 and enhancing the ratio of cytotoxic CD8 T cells relative to CD4 T-cell subpopulations (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Additionally, combination studies with immune checkpoint inhibitors have further supported its potential to modulate the tumor microenvironment in preclinical oncology settings (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). In metabolic research, LG100268 has been administered to rodent models (such as diabetic ZDF rats and normal Sprague–Dawley rats) to evaluate its effects on lipid and glucose metabolism. In these contexts, LG100268 was shown to acutely lower serum glucose levels but also to induce marked hypertriglyceridemia linked to diminished lipoprotein lipase activity in muscle tissue, a pharmacodynamic liability that underscores the potent transcriptional effects mediated via RXR activation (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). Despite these promising activities in oncology and metabolic models, there are no documented studies, either preclinical or clinical, in which LG100268 has been directly used for treating dry AMD or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction. The entirety of its previous applications has been outside the ocular field, focusing on cancer chemoprevention and metabolic dysregulation; thus, its proposed repurposing for dry AMD represents an innovative but as-yet untested direction with respect to ocular indications (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lee & Khan, 2016, pp. 15–19).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, LG100268 acts as a high-affinity agonist for RXRs by binding selectively to the ligand-binding pocket of these nuclear receptors. RXRs are unique in that they function both as homodimers and as obligate heterodimer partners for multiple other nuclear receptors including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), liver X receptors (LXRs), and even possibly orphan receptors such as Nurr1. Upon binding LG100268, the RXR undergoes a conformational change that induces release of corepressors and recruitment of coactivators, thereby altering transcription of downstream target genes (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10). In cancer studies, the activation of RXR by LG100268 has been associated with modulation of the immune microenvironment; it reduces pro-tumor cytokine release, alters the balance of immune cell populations, and influences expression of cell surface proteins such as PD-L1 (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, in metabolic tissues, activation of RXR by LG100268 affects lipid metabolism through transcriptional control of genes involved in the regulation of lipoprotein lipase and other lipid-processing enzymes (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

The specific hypothesis proposed for dry AMD centers on the concept that selective RXR modulation might bias RXR heterodimerization toward partnering with Nurr1 in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-activated RPE cells. Nurr1, an orphan nuclear receptor, is implicated in anti-inflammatory responses and has been associated with maintenance of cellular differentiation and barrier function in various epithelial models. While direct evidence from the literature demonstrating RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation in RPE cells is limited, the general biology of RXR suggests that ligand-induced conformational changes in RXR can influence its choice of heterodimerization partner (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
CHIR99021 is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor originally identified as a highly potent and selective inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3β) with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (~10 nM). Its discovery and subsequent chemical development classified it as an ATP-competitive inhibitor, belonging to a broader class of kinase inhibitors that target GSK-3 enzymes. This compound has been marketed under Tocris catalog number 4423 and is widely used as a research tool for modulating the canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway. The synthesis of CHIR99021 is based on medicinal chemistry approaches that aim to optimize kinase selectivity, and indeed, extensive inhibitor profiling has shown that it preferentially targets GSK-3 over cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) and other kinases. This compound belongs to a class of therapeutic candidates generally employed in stem cell differentiation protocols, where its ability to stabilize β-catenin and drive the transcription of Wnt target genes has been extensively validated in various cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) derived from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Leach et al., 2015). As such, CHIR99021 has been foundational in protocols that aim to drive RPE fate by activating canonical Wnt signaling, thereby demonstrating its utility in manipulating epithelial differentiation pathways.

Therapeutic History:  
The majority of available evidence for CHIR99021’s use comes from in vitro studies and preclinical differentiation protocols rather than clinical applications. Multiple studies have shown that when added during defined differentiation windows (for example, from day 8 to 14 of an hESC-to-RPE protocol), CHIR99021 significantly increases the yield and functional maturation of RPE cells. These studies report that CHIR99021-treated differentiations yield improved epithelial morphology, enhanced pigmentation, and robust expression of RPE lineage markers—including MITF, OTX2, and even tight-junction-associated proteins such as ZO-1 (Leach et al., 2015). In parallel, other reports have documented that upregulation of canonical Wnt signaling through CHIR99021 leads to increased expression of pigmentation genes (TYR, TYRP2, and PMEL17) and the RPE functional secretory factor PEDF. However, it is important to note that despite promising results in differentiation assays, the use of CHIR99021 for direct therapeutic intervention in dry AMD is not well documented. A clinical trials search on ClinicalTrials.gov returned no registered trials exploring CHIR99021 or other GSK-3β inhibitors for AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Moreover, in an in vitro macula-sized RPE wound-repair model designed to mimic geographic atrophy, CHIR99021 treatment hindered wound repair instead of enhancing barrier restoration (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). These seemingly contradictory findings illustrate that while CHIR99021 robustly enhances RPE differentiation from stem cells, its effects in mature or stress-challenged RPE may be context-dependent. Overall, the preclinical history establishes CHIR99021 as a well-characterized research compound with proven biochemical activity in activating Wnt/β-catenin signaling, but there is limited evidence regarding its therapeutic application in treating dry AMD or related RPE barrier dysfunction in vivo (Yang et al., 2018; Hottin et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
CHIR99021 exerts its biological effects by inhibiting GSK-3β through competitive binding at the protein’s ATP site, thereby preventing GSK-3β from phosphorylating its substrates. One of the principal consequences of GSK-3β inhibition is the stabilization of β-catenin. Under normal conditions, GSK-3β phosphorylates β-catenin, marking it for proteasomal degradation. Inhibition by CHIR99021 blocks this phosphorylation event, which leads to an accumulation of β-catenin in the cytosol and its translocation into the nucleus. Once in the nucleus, β-catenin interacts with TCF/LEF transcription factors to induce the transcription of multiple downstream genes that govern cell fate decisions, differentiation, and epithelial characteristics (Leach et al., 2015). Notably, in the context of retinal development, β-catenin directly upregulates RPE-specific transcription factors such as MITF and OTX2 by binding to their promoter elements, which aligns with observations of improved RPE differentiation upon CHIR99021 treatment (Leach et al., 2015).  

The proposed hypothesis extends this mechanism by suggesting that activation of the canonical Wnt pathway will also upregulate tight junction gene expression. CHIR99021 presents several notable strengths as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. In addition, the dual targeting of both differentiation pathways and antioxidant gene networks provides mechanistic specificity that is theoretically well aligned with the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD where oxidative stress and barrier dysfunction play central roles (Leach et al., 2015; Hottin et al., 2022). Moreover, its established pharmacokinetic profile and ready availability make it an attractive candidate for rapid preclinical evaluation in ocular models.

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and concerns temper enthusiasm for CHIR99021 as a dry AMD therapeutic. First, while its use in developmental protocols is well documented, there exists a paucity of data on the direct upregulation of tight junction genes such as claudin-1 and occludin in oxidative-stress models of RPE. Finally, a ClinicalTrials.gov search has not identified any trials involving CHIR99021 or related GSK-3 inhibitors for AMD, underscoring that while the molecular rationale is sound, the candidate has not undergone any clinical evaluation in this particular indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Its proven ability to drive RPE differentiation and enhance epithelial marker expression makes it appealing from a developmental standpoint. However, available evidence also highlights potential drawbacks when applied to mature or stressed RPE, including impaired wound repair in certain in vitro models. The hypothesis that CHIR99021 will upregulate claudin-1 and occludin transcription, thereby preserving ZO-1 architecture to improve TEER and reduce permeability under oxidative challenges, remains promising in theory but requires substantiation through focused experiments that measure tight junction integrity and barrier function specifically under conditions mimicking dry AMD (Yang et al., 2018). As such, while the candidate has mechanistic appeal and a robust preclinical track record in RPE differentiation, its application for barrier restoration in dry AMD remains speculative at this stage, and further investigation—including dose optimization studies, TEER/permeability assays in oxidative stress models, and eventually in vivo preclinical evaluations—is warranted before advancing CHIR99021 into clinical trials for this indication.

Strengths include its potent GSK-3β inhibition, well-characterized activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, and proven use in enhancing RPE differentiation, while weaknesses center on mixed results in mature RPE wound‐repair models and the current lack of direct evidence for tight junction upregulation under oxidative stress. The direction for future research must focus on rigorous validation of barrier parameters (including claudin-1, occludin, TEER, and permeability assays) in models that closely recapitulate the oxidative and inflammatory milieu of dry AMD before considering CHIR99021 as a viable drug candidate for clinical repurposing (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

This comprehensive review therefore supports a cautious approach: while CHIR99021 possesses attractive biochemical and mechanistic properties that justify its rapid evaluation in preclinical ocular models, its repurposing for dry AMD will require additional data specifically addressing RPE barrier function under oxidative stress. Further targeted studies are essential to resolve the context-dependent effects observed in vitro and to determine if optimal dosing and timing regimens can overcome the negative outcomes seen in wound-repair assays. Only with such evidence will CHIR99021’s promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD be fully validated.

The LOXL2 inhibitor class, including molecules such as PXS-5153A, has been extensively tested in preclinical models of fibrosis and cancer. For example, within non-ocular systems, LOXL2 activity has been linked to increased tissue stiffness that fosters metastatic progression and desmoplastic reactions in tumors, and selective inhibition of LOXL2 has been shown to reduce crosslink density, attenuating fibrotic remodeling (Lin et al., 2020). Experimental inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity using non-selective agents like β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) has also been applied to in vitro and in vivo models to modulate ECM assembly, with effects on barrier function observed in RPE cultures co-treated with endothelial cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). In particular, the endothelial cell–RPE crosstalk studies demonstrate a critical role for lysyl oxidase activity in regulating collagen bundle formation and in establishing RPE barrier properties (Benedicto et al., 2017). Accordingly, while there is no direct clinical or preclinical record of PXS-5153A in AMD, the antifibrotic profile of the compound and its impact on extracellular matrix mechanics in other disease contexts serve as a compelling rationale to explore its application in dry AMD.

At the molecular level, LOXL2 catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of lysine or hydroxylysine residues present in collagens and elastin. The anticipated outcome is a lower crosslink density in Bruch’s membrane, resulting in a softer, more compliant matrix environment. The downstream consequences of reduced integrin activation include dampening of Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways, which in turn facilitate the stabilization and proper localization of tight junction proteins at the RPE cell membranes (Benedicto et al., 2017). First, by reducing LOXL2-mediated crosslinking of collagen IV and fibronectin, the drug should decrease the mechanical stiffness of the BM analog.
