In several studies, when the extracellular matrix is normalized—such as by altering substrate stiffness—there is an improvement in the localization of key tight junction proteins, specifically occludin and ZO-1, at the cell membrane (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Second, the reduced matrix stiffness is expected to alleviate the mechanical stress experienced by RPE cells, thereby facilitating the re-establishment of cell polarity and intercellular junction continuity. The stabilization of junctional complexes is measurable by TEER. In previous EC–RPE co-culture experiments, modulation of ECM mechanical properties directly correlated with increased TEER values, reflecting improved barrier function (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Moreover, the proper organization of the basement membrane is not only a structural consideration; the biochemical signaling through β1 integrin receptors—critical for maintaining cell adhesion and survival—would return toward homeostatic levels, further supporting the integrity of the RPE layer (Benedicto et al., 2017). These integrin-mediated signals influence downstream effectors such as Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK, which have been implicated in regulating tight junction dynamics (Benedicto et al., 2017). Progress in these pathways is expected to manifest as an overall improvement in the barrier phenotype, which is central to preventing the leakage of fluid and other deleterious solutes into the subretinal space—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.

In summary, it is anticipated that treatment with PXS-5153A in appropriate in vitro (and ultimately in vivo) models will lead to:  
• Reduced collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in BM, yielding a matrix with decreased stiffness (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Normalization of β1 integrin signaling and subsequent reorganization of RPE tight junctions with improved localization of proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Restoration of barrier function as evidenced by increased TEER measurements and improved paracellular permeability profiles (Benedicto et al., 2017).  

Thus, PXS-5153A is expected to address one of the core aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis by targeting ECM remodeling, which in turn indirectly stabilizes RPE cell function.

V. Overall Evaluation  
The concept of using PXS-5153A to modulate ECM pathology in dry AMD is compelling given the mechanistic insights derived from studies on lysyl oxidase activity in epithelial barrier function and ECM assembly. Among the strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its robust preclinical evidence in fibrosis and tumor microenvironment models. LOXL2 has been implicated in promoting tissue stiffening by catalyzing the crosslinking of collagen and fibronectin in various tissues (Lin et al., 2020). The pathophysiological parallels between fibrotic ECM remodeling in cancers and the stiffening of Bruch’s membrane in dry AMD provide a strong rationale for repurposing a LOXL2 inhibitor in an ocular context. Numerous studies have demonstrated that extracellular matrix integrity is essential for optimal RPE barrier function, and that even subtle changes in ECM mechanics can disrupt junctional complexes and lead to barrier dysfunction (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by targeting a critical enzymatic step in ECM crosslinking, PXS-5153A may confer dual benefits: it could both reduce the pathological stiffening of Bruch’s membrane and promote the reorganization of tight junction complexes, ultimately resulting in enhanced TEER and stabilization of the outer blood–retina barrier.

However, several important weaknesses or uncertainties must be considered. First, while numerous studies (using agents such as BAPN) have illustrated that lysyl oxidase inhibition affects RPE barrier function, direct evidence with selective LOXL2 inhibitors—specifically in ocular models of dry AMD—is lacking (Buniello et al., 2025). In fact, the Open Targets Platform indicates only a weak direct association between LOXL2 and age-related macular degeneration, based on limited literature evidence (Buniello et al., 2025). This raises the possibility that, although LOXL2 plays a demonstrable role in ECM crosslinking in other tissues, its specific involvement in dry AMD pathogenesis may not be as pronounced or may be influenced by other factors not recapitulated in non-ocular models.

Furthermore, potential off-target effects or the consequences of broadly altering ECM crosslinking in the eye must be carefully examined. The structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane is critical not only for its barrier function but also for nutrient transport between the choroidal circulation and the RPE. Overinhibition of LOXL2, or interference with normal ECM turnover, may inadvertently lead to basement membrane disorganization, as has been observed when lysyl oxidase activity was inhibited during critical periods of retinal development (Benedicto et al., 2017). This underscores the need for precise dose optimization and targeted delivery, ideally restricted to the ocular environment, to avoid systemic side effects.

Another consideration is the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. In addition to ECM stiffening, dry AMD involves multifactorial processes including oxidative stress, complement activation, inflammation, and the accumulation of lipoprotein deposits. Thus, while normalizing matrix stiffness is likely to improve RPE barrier function, it may be insufficient to fully arrest or reverse the disease process on its own. A combination therapy that also addresses the inflammatory and degenerative components of AMD may eventually be required (Benedicto et al., 2017; Caban et al., 2022).

From a development perspective, there is significant strength in the repurposing strategy because agents like PXS-5153A already have a detailed preclinical profile in non-ocular fibrotic models. This existing data can accelerate preclinical validation in ocular models, with studies planned in RPE–BM co-culture systems using TEER as a functional readout (Benedicto et al., 2017). Furthermore, leveraging well-characterized in vitro assays (such as those involving decellularized ECM and substrate stiffness modulation as described in the context) offers a clear experimental framework to evaluate whether the normalization of BM stiffness by PXS-5153A is sufficient to restore RPE tight junction integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017).

Nonetheless, one notable weakness is the limited direct evidence linking LOXL2 specifically to dry AMD. Although elevated lysyl oxidase activity and changes in collagen crosslinking have been observed in the context of RPE barrier function and BM integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017), the genetic and translational data associating LOXL2 with AMD are not robust. The relatively low association score (Buniello et al., 2025) suggests that additional studies are needed to clarify LOXL2’s role in the eye and to determine whether its inhibition will yield a therapeutically meaningful benefit in dry AMD patients.

In conclusion, repurposing PXS-5153A for dry AMD represents an innovative strategy that leverages the known antifibrotic effects of LOXL2 inhibition to address the deleterious ECM remodeling observed in aged Bruch’s membrane. The candidate’s synthetic origins and prior applications in fibrosis and cancer studies provide a solid foundation for its use, while the mechanistic rationale—centered on reducing pathological crosslinking and restoring RPE barrier function—is strongly supported by evidence from ECM modulation studies (Benedicto et al., 2017). However, challenges remain due to the lack of direct ocular data, potential risks of overmodulating ECM integrity, and the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology. Future research must focus on rigorous in vitro validation in RPE–BM co-culture systems and in vivo studies in relevant AMD animal models to establish the efficacy and safety profile of PXS-5153A in the context of dry AMD. Overall, despite these uncertainties, PXS-5153A holds promise as a novel ECM-targeted therapeutic candidate that could complement existing and emerging treatment strategies for this currently unmet clinical need (Lin et al., 2020; Buniello et al., 2025).

Taken together, the strengths of a clear mechanism of action, potent enzyme selectivity, and an innovative approach toward ECM normalization position PXS-5153A as an attractive candidate warranting further investigation. Nonetheless, a careful reappraisal of the molecular role of LOXL2 in the ocular microenvironment, along with detailed studies on dosing, delivery, and potential off-target effects, will be critical in determining whether this candidate can be successfully repurposed for treating dry AMD.

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of TTA‐P2 as a repurposed candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD):

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
TTA‐P2 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed to target T‐type voltage‐gated calcium channels (VGCCs), which belong to the CaV3 family (CaV3.1, CaV3.2, CaV3.3). Its chemical structure, described as 3,5‐dichloro-N-[1-(2,2-dimethyl-tetrahydro-pyran-4-ylmethyl)-4-fluoro-piperidin-4-ylmethyl]-benzamide, was established via medicinal chemistry optimization strategies aimed at increasing potency and selectivity for the T‐type channels relative to high-voltage-activated channels (Choe et al., 2011). Originally discovered and characterized in the context of neuronal excitability studies, TTA‐P2 has been shown to block T‐type calcium currents in rat sensory neurons with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range; this high potency is matched by an excellent selectivity profile given that its inhibitory concentration for high-voltage-activated channels is orders of magnitude higher (Choe et al., 2011). As a member of the T‐type calcium channel blocker class, TTA‐P2 is representative of compounds that modulate low-voltage-activated channels involved in a variety of cell functions, ranging from neuronal burst firing to hormone release. In the context of drug development, this compound is categorized as a channel-modulating agent, and its synthetic origins as a small molecule rendered it amenable to structural modification for improved pharmacokinetics in various tissue systems (Choe et al., 2011). Although historically used primarily in neuronal studies, its inherent properties have prompted consideration of its repurposing for non-neuronal tissues, such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where T‐type channels have been shown to contribute to key physiological processes (Jazouli, 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TTA‐P2 has been investigated in the context of neuropathic pain and epilepsy, where T‐type calcium channels are integral to the regulation of neuronal excitability. In experimental models involving rat sensory neurons, TTA‐P2 demonstrated marked antinociceptive properties and produced significant reductions in neuronal burst firing by selectively blocking T‐type calcium currents (Choe et al., 2011). This evidence underlines the compound’s effectiveness in modulating calcium influx in hyperexcitable systems. Beyond its neurological applications, there have been several studies in which compounds targeting T‐type CaV channels were applied to non-neuronal cells. For instance, work in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) demonstrated that T‐type calcium channels are expressed and functionally important in these cells, although in those studies a different inhibitor—TTA‐A2—was used to evaluate effects on phagocytosis and VEGF secretion (Jazouli, 2022). Moreover, complementary work in RPE models has noted that T‐type channels appear to localize specifically to the apical membrane, with subtypes such as CaV3.1 and CaV3.3 being especially prominent (Jazouli, 2022). Despite extensive preclinical work in neuronal systems, there is no published record, to our knowledge, that TTA‐P2 has been tested directly in AMD or other ocular disease models. However, evidence gleaned from cerebral endothelia studies—where inhibition of CaV3.1/CaV3.2 ameliorates inflammatory barrier disruption—suggests that a similar strategy may be beneficial in preserving the function of the RPE barrier (Unknown Reference). Thus, while TTA‐P2 has a well-established history in neurological studies, its repurposing for dry AMD is based on the emerging understanding that T‐type channels contribute to RPE function and that their inhibition may counter inflammatory and degenerative signals (Jazouli, 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism by which TTA‐P2 exerts its effects is through selective inhibition of T‐type calcium channels. Detailed electrophysiological studies in rat sensory neurons have shown that TTA‐P2 binds preferentially to the inactivated state of these channels, thereby stabilizing them in a non-conducting conformation. This binding results in a significant hyperpolarizing shift (approximately 20 mV) in the steady-state inactivation curves and an incomplete recovery from inactivation, meaning that the channels remain non-functional for a longer period after brief depolarizations (Choe et al., 2011). Such effects effectively reduce the calcium influx that would normally occur during depolarization-driven events. In RPE cells, there is a body of evidence indicating that T‐type calcium channels (particularly CaV3.1 and CaV3.3) contribute to the formation of localized Ca²⁺ microdomains that play a role in regulating tight junction dynamics (Jazouli, 2022). Under inflammatory conditions—such as those induced by TNF-α or complement activation—excessive Ca²⁺ influx via these channels may trigger signaling cascades that lead to the disassembly of adherens junctions and tight junctions, ultimately compromising the integrity of the epithelial barrier. TTA‐P2’s ability to suppress the T‐type currents would, therefore, limit the depolarization-driven Ca²⁺ microdomain formation in RPE cells (Choe et al., 2011). In addition, the selective binding to the inactivated state minimizes off-target effects on channels that have higher activation thresholds, such as L-type channels, thereby preserving other essential calcium-dependent processes. The blockade of T‐type channels is particularly relevant because these channels typically open at more negative membrane potentials, a regime that is critical for maintaining the delicate Ca²⁺ balance in nonexcitable cells such as the RPE (Choe et al., 2011; Jazouli, 2022). Consequently, by dampening the Ca²⁺ entry through these channels, TTA‐P2 could play a protective role against inflammation-induced barrier disruption.

Expected Effect:  
According to the proposal, the central hypothesis is that a pan–T‐type CaV blockade by TTA‐P2 (with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, here cited as approximately 20 nM) will suppress the formation of harmful Ca²⁺ microdomains in RPE cells, thereby preventing the downstream signaling events that lead to the disassembly of tight junctions. The integrity of RPE monolayers is often assessed by measurements such as transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and permeability assays (e.g., FITC-dextran flux). In the presence of inflammatory insults like TNF-α or complement factors—both of which can mimic some of the pathophysiological aspects of dry AMD—the excessive calcium influx through T‐type channels may cause rearrangement or breakdown of tight junction proteins (such as occludin and claudins), leading to compromised barrier function and increased paracellular permeability (Jazouli, 2022).  
By inhibiting these channels, TTA‐P2 is expected to reduce intracellular Ca²⁺ accumulation that drives disassembly of junctional complexes, thereby restoring normal TEER values and reducing the passage of molecules like FITC-dextran across the RPE monolayer. Patch-clamp studies would further validate that TTA‐P2 effectively suppresses the T‐type Ca²⁺ currents in these cells, reinforcing the direct link between calcium channel inhibition and improved barrier integrity (Choe et al., 2011). Moreover, considering that similar principles have been applied in cerebral endothelial models—where T‐type channel inhibition reduced inflammatory barrier disruption—it is plausible that the RPE, which shares some functional similarities as a barrier tissue, may respond in a comparable manner (Korkka, n.d.). It is also important to note that the expression of CaV3.1 and CaV3.3 in RPE cells has been confirmed by immunolabeling and electrophysiological studies, thereby providing a direct anatomical and functional basis for this therapeutic approach (Jazouli, 2022). This expected effect of preserving tight junction integrity makes TTA‐P2 an attractive candidate for therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction and barrier breakdown contribute to disease progression.

Overall Evaluation:  
TTA‐P2 offers several compelling strengths as a potential repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, its high potency and selectivity for T‐type calcium channels have been robustly demonstrated in neuronal systems, and these properties bode well for achieving effective inhibition in RPE cells, where even relatively minor shifts in calcium homeostasis may have significant pathophysiological implications (Choe et al., 2011). Second, the strategy of targeting T‐type channels in the RPE is grounded in evidence that these channels are involved in channel-mediated inflammatory responses and barrier disruption, processes known to play a key role in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Jazouli, 2022). Third, TTA‐P2 works through a mechanism that is distinct from conventional anti-inflammatory agents or anti-VEGF therapies; instead, it modulates a very early step in the cascade—namely, the depolarization-driven Ca²⁺ entry that acts as a trigger for tight junction disassembly. This novel mechanism, if validated, could complement existing therapies or offer a new avenue for intervention in cases where traditional therapeutics have limited efficacy.  

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be acknowledged. Foremost among these is the fact that, to date, no direct studies have been published demonstrating the efficacy of TTA‐P2 in RPE cells or in animal models of dry AMD. The majority of the literature supporting its use comes from neurological applications, and although there are analogous studies in RPE using other T‐type channel blockers (e.g., TTA‐A2), the extrapolation of neuronal pharmacodynamics to ocular tissues is not guaranteed (Jazouli, 2022). Furthermore, it is well recognized that T‐type channels in the RPE also play roles in physiological processes such as phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and the regulation of growth factor secretion (Jazouli, 2022). Thus, chronic inhibition of these channels could potentially disrupt normal RPE function if not properly dosed or targeted, leading to adverse effects that may offset the benefits of barrier preservation. Additionally, the therapeutic index of TTA‐P2 in the ocular milieu remains unknown. While its selectivity in neuronal tissues suggests that off-target effects might be limited, the unique environment of the retina—characterized by tightly regulated ionic gradients and specialized cell–cell interactions—could render RPE cells more sensitive to perturbations in calcium signaling (Jazouli, 2022).  

Another issue that warrants consideration is the delivery of TTA‐P2 to the RPE. The retina poses several pharmacokinetic challenges due to its blood-retina barrier; hence, any candidate must be capable of penetrating ocular tissues effectively, achieving therapeutic concentrations in the RPE while minimizing systemic exposure. While there are established methods for ocular drug delivery, such as intravitreal injections or topical formulations, the physicochemical properties of TTA‐P2 will need careful evaluation in this context. Additionally, given that the proposed mechanism involves modulating rapid Ca²⁺ microdomains, the temporal dynamics of channel blockade versus normal calcium signaling must be precisely controlled. If TTA‐P2 alters RPE calcium homeostasis too profoundly or indiscriminately, it might interfere with essential cellular processes, including phagocytosis, which is critical for retinal maintenance and health (Jazouli, 2022).  

Safety considerations are also paramount. T‐type calcium channels are expressed in multiple tissues, and systemic administration of a potent blocker like TTA‐P2 could lead to unintended side effects in other organ systems, particularly in the cardiovascular and central nervous systems. Although the ocular route of administration could mitigate these systemic effects, the risk of local toxicity and potential interference with normal retinal signaling remains. In summary, while the mechanistic rationale for using TTA‐P2 as a barrier-preserving agent in dry AMD is scientifically sound and innovative, considerable preclinical work is required. This would ideally include comprehensive studies in RPE monolayer models under inflammatory conditions to quantitatively assess TEER restoration and junctional protein preservation, as well as in vivo models of dry AMD to evaluate functional and structural outcomes following TTA‐P2 treatment.

In conclusion, TTA‐P2 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its high potency and selectivity for T‐type calcium channels, coupled with its novel mechanism—stabilizing the inactivated state of these channels and thereby reducing deleterious Ca²⁺ microdomain formation—provide a strong rationale for further investigation (Choe et al., 2011). The hypothesis that such blockade can prevent inflammatory insult-induced tight junction disassembly in RPE cells is supported by observations in both neuronal systems and studies of RPE channel expression (Jazouli, 2022). Nevertheless, gaps remain in our direct understanding of how TTA‐P2 behaves in ocular tissues, and careful evaluation of its impact on essential RPE functions—such as phagocytosis and growth factor secretion—is crucial. Safety, ocular bioavailability, and potential off-target effects are also significant areas for investigation. Overall, while TTA‐P2’s repurposing for dry AMD is still in the exploratory phase, its unique targeting of Ca²⁺ entry and potential to restore barrier integrity make it a compelling candidate that merits further preclinical validation.

Given these considerations, the next steps should include:  
1. In vitro studies using hiPSC-derived RPE cultures subjected to TNF-α or complement challenge, with detailed monitoring of TEER, FITC-dextran permeability, and tight junction protein localization following TTA‐P2 treatment.  
2. Electrophysiological recordings (patch clamp) to verify effective suppression of T‐type channel currents in RPE under both basal and inflammatory conditions, comparing TTA‐P2 with other established blockers (e.g., TTA‐A2) as controls.  
3. In vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD to assess not only RPE barrier function and retinal morphology but also functional visual outcomes after local (intravitreal) administration of TTA‐P2.  
4. Pharmacokinetic and safety evaluations specifically tailored for ocular delivery, to ascertain the optimal dosing regimen that maximizes local efficacy without compromising systemic or retinal cell functions.

Strengths of TTA‐P2 include its well-documented biophysical potency and specificity (Choe et al., 2011); its proposed mechanism, which innovatively focuses on modulating an early, calcium-dependent step in the cascade leading to barrier breakdown; and its potential to synergize with or complement existing therapies for AMD that have primarily targeted angiogenesis or inflammation by offering a strategy focused on preserving RPE junctional integrity (Jazouli, 2022). Weaknesses include the current lack of direct data in RPE or AMD models, potential adverse effects on other RPE functions (such as phagocytosis and growth factor secretion), challenges in ocular drug delivery, and the possibility of off-target effects given the ubiquitous expression of T‐type channels in various tissues (Jazouli, 2022).

Overall, while there is promising scientific rationale behind the use of TTA‐P2 for protecting RPE barrier function under inflammatory conditions reminiscent of dry AMD, the candidate remains at an early repurposing stage. The transition from successful neuronal applications to effective retinal therapies requires extensive adaptation and validation. However, if its efficacy and safety can be confirmed in detailed RPE and in vivo AMD models, TTA‐P2 could emerge as a novel therapeutic tool addressing an unmet clinical need in dry AMD. In summary, TTA‐P2’s mechanism of action—based on precise, state-dependent inhibition of T-type Ca²⁺ channels—coupled with its potential to stabilize RPE tight junctions under pathogenic stress, positions it as an exciting candidate for further investigation in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (Choe et al., 2011; Jazouli, 2022).

This evaluation suggests that while the candidate has substantial merit and promise, the lack of direct preclinical evidence in RPE models means that a dedicated series of studies (both in vitro and in vivo) will be essential before moving toward clinical trials. The potential for TTA‐P2 to fill a therapeutic gap by directly targeting Ca²⁺ entry and preserving RPE barrier function provides a unique and fresh mechanism compared with existing treatments, but its ultimate success will depend on how well these preclinical models predict efficacy and safety in patients with dry AMD.

Thus, by selectively inhibiting CaV3.2‐mediated calcium entry, ML218 is hypothesized to prevent calpain activation and subsequent disruption of tight junctions in RPE cells—a mechanism that has been indirectly supported by studies showing that inhibitors of T-type channels reduce cellular excitability and junctional leak in alternative epithelial models (Sun et al., 2025). The state‐dependence of ML218’s block (i.e., preferential inhibition when channels are in an open or inactivated state) may further enhance its capacity to target pathological calcium influx while sparing normal physiological signaling to some extent, although this property will require careful titration in a diseased state (Sun et al., 2025).

The working hypothesis for repurposing ML218 in dry AMD is that its inhibition of CaV3.2 channels in retinal pigment epithelium will reduce pathological intracellular calcium accumulation under conditions of oxidative and inflammatory stress. Elevated Ca²⁺ levels in RPE cells are known to activate calpain, a calcium‐dependent protease that mediates the proteolytic cleavage of critical junctional proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin. In evaluating ML218 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current literature. This potent inhibition forms a logical mechanistic basis for targeting pathological calcium influx in RPE cells, where calcium overload and subsequent activation of proteases like calpain are implicated in junctional protein degradation and barrier dysfunction. Furthermore, the detailed structural insights into ML218’s binding—its differential interactions in CaV3 and CaV1 channels—provide a strong foundation for understanding its pharmacodynamic activity. The ability of ML218 to modulate calcium signaling with state‐dependent block enhances its therapeutic promise by potentially allowing it to target pathological overactivity while sparing baseline physiological function (Sun et al., 2025).  

On the other hand, several potential weaknesses must be considered. The literature reveals that ML218 is not exclusively selective for CaV3.2 channels; it exhibits cross‐reactivity with CaV1.4 channels, albeit at lower potency (with reported IC₅₀ values for CaV1.4 in the micromolar range compared to nanomolar ranges for CaV3.2) (Sun et al., 2025). Such cross‐reactivity could theoretically lead to off‐target effects in tissues where L‐type channels play critical roles in calcium signaling, potentially complicating its utility in RPE cells that also express other calcium channel subtypes. Furthermore, while the proposed hypothesis for dry AMD is biologically plausible, there is a notable gap in the literature regarding direct evidence for ML218’s efficacy in preserving RPE barrier function under oxidative or inflammatory conditions—most studies with ML218 have been performed in neuronal contexts or in assays focused on phagocytosis and secretory aspects of RPE physiology (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). Although optimistic hypotheses suggest an IC₅₀ of approximately 7 nM for CaV3.2 channel block, the available data across various assay platforms indicate that effective concentrations are more likely to be in the tens to low hundreds of nanomolar range (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). Despite these challenges, the conceptual framework for repurposing ML218 in dry AMD has several attractive features. The targeting of T‐type calcium channels to mitigate calpain activation and to preserve tight junction protein integrity represents a novel therapeutic approach that departs from traditional anti‐inflammatory or anti‐angiogenic strategies. In dry AMD, where chronic, low‐grade oxidative and inflammatory stress contribute to RPE dysfunction and barrier breakdown, a compound like ML218 could theoretically reduce intracellular calcium overload and, consequently, the cascade of events leading to junctional degradation. Moreover, the compound’s off‐target activity on CaV1.4 channels and the variability in reported potencies across studies pose significant challenges that will require thorough in vitro and eventually in vivo validation. Future investigations should prioritize comprehensive electrophysiological and imaging studies in RPE cells, specifically measuring TEER, FITC‐dextran flux, and tight junction protein localization following exposure to oxidative stress, to determine whether ML218 can indeed restore barrier integrity as hypothesized. Dose‐ranging studies and careful evaluation of potential off‐target effects will also be critical to establishing a safe and effective therapeutic profile for ocular application.  

Overall, while ML218 holds promise as a tool compound with the potential for repurposing in dry AMD, its advancement into this new therapeutic area will depend on addressing key knowledge gaps through rigorous experimental validation. This includes confirming its selective inhibition of CaV3.2 channels in RPE cells, establishing the correlation between calcium influx blockade and tight junction preservation, and ensuring that its pharmacological behavior in RPE is consistent with the requirements for stabilizing the RPE barrier under pathological conditions. Therefore, although the mechanistic rationale is compelling, additional targeted preclinical studies are required before ML218 can be confidently moved forward as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011; Korkka et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BCX9930 is a novel, orally bioavailable, low-molecular-weight small molecule that functions as a selective inhibitor of complement factor D (FD). It was originally discovered through a rigorous drug discovery program that combined high-throughput screening with structure‐based rational design strategies to identify potent, non-covalent inhibitors of the serine protease FD, an essential enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. This candidate belongs to the class of factor D inhibitors, compounds that have previously been developed for complement-mediated diseases including complement 3 glomerulopathy (Chen et al., 2022). The synthesis and discovery process for BCX9930 involved chemical scaffold optimization to enhance both potency and selectivity; for instance, by specifically non-covalently occupying the S1 pocket of FD, BCX9930 is able to achieve an IC₅₀ value as low as 4 nM, a potency level that places it among the most active agents in its category. Its chemical attributes also include more than a 500-fold selectivity over related serine proteases, thereby reducing the potential for off-target effects—a critical factor for chronic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where long-term safety is paramount (Schubart et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
The development of BCX9930 is emblematic of the broader evolution in complement therapeutics. Historically, the complement system has been successfully targeted in several diseases where dysregulated complement activity plays a pathogenic role. Prior studies have established the role of FD in both the amplification loop of the alternative pathway and its subsequent effects on complement-mediated damage. BCX9930 and similar agents emerged from early research efforts that investigated FD inhibition as a means to alter pathologic complement activation. In clinical studies, similar agents targeting factor D (for example, danicopan) have demonstrated significant suppression of alternative pathway activity in conditions such as PNH, with reports noting reductions in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels and improvements in hemoglobin that facilitated transfusion independence (Schubart et al., 2023; Risitano et al., 2020). Although the majority of these pilots have been focused on hematological disorders and C3G, the mechanistic rationale for FD inhibition directly applies to dry AMD as well. Preclinical models have documented that, when the alternative pathway is excessively activated—as is theorized in dry AMD—even minute amounts of FD can trigger a cascade of destructive complement activity (Schubart et al., 2023; Gavriilaki et al., 2022). In animal models, FD inhibitors have demonstrated promising outcomes including the reduction of complement deposition and preservation of retinal architecture (Ong et al., 2024). Despite the encouraging therapeutic history of FD inhibitors in other indications, it is important to note that clinical trials evaluating FD inhibitors specifically for dry AMD or geographic atrophy have produced mixed results; one high-profile example is the failure of Lampalizumab (an FD inhibitor) to meet meaningful endpoints in pivotal phase 3 trials (Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019). Nonetheless, BCX9930 has distinct chemical and pharmacological properties that differentiate it from earlier candidates, including its strong potency, favorable oral bioavailability, and robust preclinical barrier rescue effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, making it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
The pathologic basis for many complement-mediated diseases, including dry AMD, lies in the dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, in which factor D plays a pivotal role. Normally, FD is the rate-limiting enzyme required to generate the AP C3 convertase by cleaving factor B complexed with C3b, which fuels an amplification loop and leads to the generation of downstream proinflammatory mediators such as C3a and C5a as well as opsonins that promote inflammation and tissue damage (Gavriilaki et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024). BCX9930 exerts its therapeutic effect by binding non-covalently in the S1 pocket of FD. This binding is characterized by exceptionally high affinity, with an IC₅₀ value of 4 nM, and by stringent selectivity that minimizes interference with other serine proteases. By occupying this key binding site, BCX9930 effectively prevents FD from interacting with its natural substrate, thereby arresting the production of the AP C3 convertase. This inhibition leads to a subsequent decrease in C3 cleavage and a reduction in the generation of complement split products, which are known to instigate an inflammatory response (Chen et al., 2022).  
Molecularly, the non-covalent nature of BCX9930’s interaction with factor D confers several advantages. First, such interactions allow reversible inhibition, providing the potential for controlled dosing and the fine-tuning of complement activity. Second, the selectivity profile of BCX9930 results from structural modifications aimed at optimizing the fit within the S1 pocket, ensuring that the inhibitor does not inadvertently affect enzymes with similar active site geometries. This precision is crucial, as systemic blockade of the complement system can result in significant immunosuppression. Thus, the protection of the retinal environment—by specifically inhibiting the amplification loop of the alternative pathway—offers a mechanistic rationale for the use of BCX9930 in diseases where complement overactivation is implicated, notably in the disruption of RPE tight junction integrity (Gavriilaki et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024). Additionally, the compound’s design ensures that while it attenuates pathogenic complement activity, it spares the classical and lectin pathways, reducing the risk of systemic immunocompromise.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for BCX9930 in the treatment of dry AMD is based on its ability to mitigate complement-mediated damage to the retinal pigment epithelium. In vitro studies in primary human RPE cells have shown that under conditions of serum-mediated complement activation, there is a decline in trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and disruption of critical tight junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and claudin-19. The working hypothesis posits that by non-covalently occupying the S1 pocket of factor D, BCX9930 can inhibit the formation of the alternative pathway C3 convertase, thereby reducing the production of the inflammatory complement split products. This reduction is expected to lead to a decrease in complement-driven RPE tight junction disruption. Experimental data indicate that the addition of 500 nM BCX9930 to primary human RPE cultures challenged with serum results in a recovery of TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values. Mechanistically, the expected effect hinges on the sustained and robust suppression of the alternative complement pathway, which under normal pathological conditions contributes significantly to the inflammatory milieu and structural degeneration characteristic of dry AMD. In evaluating BCX9930 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key strengths and potential limitations must be considered. On the strength side, BCX9930 exhibits an exceptionally high potency (IC₅₀ = 4 nM) and selectivity profile that is well aligned with the intended mechanism of action. Its ability to non-covalently target the S1 pocket of factor D ensures that the inhibition of the alternative pathway is both potent and reversible, thereby allowing for controlled pharmacodynamic effects. The high degree of selectivity—exceeding 500-fold over related serine proteases—not only reduces the likelihood of off-target toxicity but also supports the feasibility of long-term administration required for chronic diseases such as dry AMD (Schubart et al., 2023).  
Preclinical studies provide compelling support for the candidate’s mechanism. Another strong point in favor of BCX9930 is its oral bioavailability, which is a significant advantage over therapies that require invasive delivery methods (for example, intravitreal injections). An oral agent would potentially improve patient compliance and reduce the risks associated with repeated intraocular procedures. This is particularly critical in a disease like dry AMD, where the patient population is predominantly elderly, and minimizing treatment burden is essential (Chen et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).

One major concern pertains to the historical track record of complement inhibitors in the treatment of dry AMD. Previous clinical trials with other agents targeting the alternative pathway—such as Lampalizumab—have ultimately failed to demonstrate robust clinical efficacy in phase 3 trials despite encouraging preclinical data (Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019). The complexity of AMD pathophysiology, which involves not only complement dysregulation but also oxidative stress, genetic predispositions, and environmental factors, means that addressing a single pathway may not be sufficient to fully arrest disease progression.  
Additionally, while the preclinical data for BCX9930 are encouraging, there is still a gap in clinical evidence demonstrating its efficacy specifically in dry AMD. Long-term data will be critical in confirming that the inhibition of the alternative pathway does not compromise overall host defense mechanisms or lead to other unexpected off-target consequences.

Complement-driven RPE disruption is only one facet of AMD pathogenesis; a multifactorial disease mechanism implies that combination therapies or multimodal approaches may eventually be needed to achieve optimal clinical outcomes. In this context, BCX9930 might best be positioned as part of a combination regimen, potentially alongside agents that address oxidative damage or other pathogenic mechanisms in AMD. In summary, BCX9930 represents a highly promising therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its potent and selective inhibition of factor D, a critical enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. In vitro studies have already demonstrated that BCX9930 can restore trans-epithelial electrical resistance and preserve the continuity of crucial tight junction proteins in human RPE cells under complement challenge. Additionally, animal models have provided evidence for significant reductions in complement deposition and the preservation of retinal architecture. These findings collectively indicate that BCX9930 has the potential to protect retinal tissue from complement-mediated injury, a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024).  

However, the transition from preclinical promise to clinical success remains a challenge, as highlighted by the mixed outcomes seen with previous factor D inhibitors in the AMD space. The failure of some earlier agents, despite robust biochemical data, emphasizes that the path from molecular inhibition to effective disease modification is complex and fraught with challenges. Critical areas of future research include the establishment of clear biomarkers that correlate with clinical outcomes in dry AMD, careful delineation of the safety profile specific to the elderly patient population, and the exploration of appropriate combination strategies that might enhance therapeutic efficacy.  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and encouraging preclinical data, BCX9930 stands out as a compelling candidate for further evaluation in clinical trials targeting dry AMD. Its precise mechanism of action and the potential for oral administration offer distinct advantages and may help overcome some of the limitations encountered with earlier complement inhibitors.     2. Therapeutic History  
SB-431542 has been at the forefront of preclinical research into TGF-β signaling because of its capacity to selectively block ALK5 and, to a lesser extent, related receptors such as ALK4 and ALK7 (Laping et al., 2002; Ge et al., 2004). Its primary use has been as a chemical probe to elucidate the role of TGF-β in diverse fibrotic and oncologic settings. In multiple in vitro and in vivo studies, SB-431542 has been shown to effectively inhibit TGF-β1-induced upregulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components including collagen Iα1, fibronectin, and plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI-1) in renal epithelial cells and fibroblast cultures (Laping et al., 2002). In addition, the compound’s extensive deployment in cancer studies – where it is used to block the epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and invasion – further verifies its capacity to modulate key pathological processes that also underlie fibrotic changes observed in retinal degeneration (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010).

Upon the engagement of TGF-β ligands with cell surface receptors, the type II receptor phosphorylates and activates ALK5. Activated ALK5 then phosphorylates receptor-regulated Smad proteins (Smad2 and Smad3), which subsequently form complexes with Smad4 and translocate into the nucleus to drive the transcription of genes encoding ECM proteins and other pro-fibrotic factors (Laping et al., 2002). SB-431542 directly inhibits this kinase activity by occupying the ATP pocket, thereby blocking the phosphorylation of Smad2/3 and preventing their nuclear accumulation (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This interruption of TGF-β signaling ultimately suppresses the induction of pro-fibrotic genes such as those for collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002).

Importantly, SB-431542 is characterized by its selectivity. Despite the structural similarities among kinases in the TGF-β receptor superfamily, the unique conformational features of ALK5 permit SB-431542 to inhibit it to a significantly greater extent than BMP receptors (ALK2, ALK3, and ALK6) or other non-Smad pathways such as those mediated by ERK, JNK, and p38 MAPK (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This selectivity minimizes off-target effects and allows the compound to function as a precise modulator of TGF-β–dependent fibrotic signaling (Laping et al., 2002; Ling & Lee, 2011). Moreover, by inhibiting ALK5 activity, SB-431542 not only downregulates ECM protein production but also interferes with EMT processes, which are implicated in the phenotypic conversion of epithelial cells to a more mesenchymal and migratory state – a conversion that has been observed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells under stress conditions (Radeke et al., 2015; Yoon et al., 2018). In this regard, SB-431542’s molecular interactions encompass hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic contacts within the ALK5 catalytic pocket, ensuring that its inhibitory activity is both potent (with reported IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range) and selective for the intended target (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002).

    4. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis for repurposing SB-431542 in dry AMD is that inhibiting TGF-β receptor activity in RPE cells and choroidal fibroblasts will reduce pathological ECM overproduction. In dry AMD, elevated levels of TGF-β1 have been implicated in promoting the deposition of fibrotic ECM components in Bruch’s membrane, leading to increased stiffness and altered mechanical forces on the RPE monolayer (Laping et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2009). The resulting stiffening of the extracellular matrix is believed to disrupt the normal anchorage of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity and transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) of the RPE barrier (Xiao et al., 2009; Teplitsky et al., 2023).

By blocking ALK5 and thereby attenuating Smad2/3 activation, SB-431542 is expected to suppress the transcription of genes encoding collagen Iα1, fibronectin, and PAI-1. A reduction in the synthesis and deposition of these ECM components should translate into a decrease in Bruch’s membrane stiffness and the mechanical tension imposed on the RPE (Laping et al., 2002). This, in turn, is anticipated to allow the re-establishment of a continuous network of tight junctions between RPE cells as ZO-1 and occludin are able to reassemble without the interference of a pathological ECM environment (Radeke et al., 2015; Higashijima et al., 2023). When tested in ECM-coated Transwell assays, the expectation is that treatment with SB-431542 will result in improved TEER readings and a restoration of barrier function indicative of normalized RPE physiology (Xiao et al., 2009; Yoon et al., 2018).

Furthermore, TGF-β signaling in RPE cells has been associated with epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a process that not only promotes fibrosis but also deteriorates the well-ordered epithelial phenotype critical for retinal homeostasis (Radeke et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2009). Inhibition of ALK5 is predicted to counteract EMT, thereby preserving the native epithelial characteristics of RPE cells. In this context, the reduction of fibrotic ECM production and the prevention of EMT would act in synergy to reduce the abnormal mechanical stresses on RPE, enhance the continuity of tight junction proteins, and ultimately help restore retinal barrier function (Laping et al., 2002).

Given that both RPE cells and choroidal fibroblasts express TGF-β receptors and respond to TGF-β stimulation, the application of SB-431542 in co-culture models or animal studies is expected to normalize the extracellular microenvironment. This normalization could rescue the mechanical integrity of Bruch’s membrane and improve nutrient/waste exchange across the RPE monolayer—factors that are crucial in slowing or reversing the degenerative progression in dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2009).

    5. Overall Evaluation  
An overall review of SB-431542 indicates that it is a scientifically compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its proven ability to modulate TGF-β signaling and its well-documented anti-fibrotic effects. One major strength of SB-431542 is its high degree of selectivity for ALK5; by competitively inhibiting the ATP binding site on this receptor, the compound effectively blocks the Smad2/3 phosphorylation cascade that ultimately leads to ECM overproduction (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This mechanism has been validated in multiple preclinical models of fibrosis and ocular scarring, indicating that a similar strategy may be effective in the context of dry AMD where excessive ECM deposition in Bruch’s membrane is a central pathogenic feature (Xiao et al., 2009; Teplitsky et al., 2023).

Another point in favor of SB-431542 is its extensive use as a research tool in the investigation of TGF-β–dependent processes in both fibrosis and cancer. Its ability to reduce collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 levels in diverse cellular models underscores its therapeutic potential for attenuating pathological ECM production—a direct mechanism that could alleviate mechanical stress on RPE tight junctions and help restore barrier function, as measured by increased TEER and continuity of ZO-1/occludin (Laping et al., 2002).

From a mechanistic perspective, the detailed molecular interactions of SB-431542 have been characterized to a high degree, with studies demonstrating that its binding to the ALK5 catalytic pocket results in a clear inhibition of the profibrotic gene expression program (Laping et al., 2002; Ling & Lee, 2011). This precision in targeting is particularly important when considering ocular applications, as the retina is highly sensitive to off-target effects. By sparing other signaling pathways—such as those mediated by BMP receptors or Smad-independent cascades—the compound minimizes potential systemic or retinal toxicity (Laping et al., 2002).

Despite these strengths, there are also several challenges that must be addressed for SB-431542 to be successfully repurposed for dry AMD. One of the primary concerns is its pharmacokinetic profile. Preclinical studies in animal models have indicated that SB-431542 may have a relatively short half-life and rapid clearance, which raises questions about achieving sustained intraocular concentrations necessary for chronic conditions such as dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). To address this, development of a controlled-release ocular formulation—such as an intravitreal implant, microsphere-based delivery, or other sustained-release vehicle—will be essential for maintaining therapeutic levels over extended periods without systemic exposure.

Another significant challenge is the duality inherent in TGF-β signaling. While excessive TGF-β activity is responsible for the fibrotic changes observed in AMD, TGF-β also plays an important role in immune regulation, tissue repair, and maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Long-term blockade of TGF-β signaling may therefore carry inherent risks, including potential adverse effects on normal repair mechanisms or the promotion of unanticipated cellular changes such as malignant transformation (Markell, 2010; Schindeler et al., 2010). Careful dose-response studies and localized delivery strategies will be imperative to ensure that therapeutic benefits are achieved without tipping the balance toward deleterious side effects.

Moreover, although the preclinical data in ocular fibrosis models—such as those involving subconjunctival scarring after glaucoma filtration surgery—provide a promising rationale for the use of TGF-β inhibitors, direct evidence in models that recapitulate the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains limited (Xiao et al., 2009). Dry AMD is a complex disease involving not only fibrotic ECM accumulation but also oxidative stress, chronic low-grade inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation. On the formulation front, the small molecule nature of SB-431542 offers both advantages and challenges. Its chemical tractability allows for modifications that could improve its ocular stability and bioavailability; however, achieving homogeneous distribution within the eye, ensuring drug stability in the vitreous environment, and avoiding direct retinal toxicity remain non-trivial challenges (Fuchs, 2011; Markell, 2010). In summary, SB-431542 shows significant promise as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to selectively inhibit ALK5 and thereby block the central pro-fibrotic Smad2/3 signaling axis aligns well with the mechanistic hypothesis that targeting TGF-β–mediated ECM overproduction can restore the biomechanical homeostasis of Bruch’s membrane and improve RPE barrier function (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). However, the pathway to clinical translation is not without hurdles. The pharmacokinetics of SB-431542, characterized by a relatively short half-life, necessitate the development of innovative drug delivery systems to sustain intraocular levels over the chronic course of AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). Additionally, the multifaceted role of TGF-β in ocular physiology requires that any therapeutic intervention be carefully calibrated to avoid impairing normal tissue repair or immunologic function (Markell, 2010; Schindeler et al., 2010). Finally, given that dry AMD is a multifactorial disease rather than being driven solely by fibrosis, further preclinical studies employing comprehensive AMD models that encompass oxidative stress and inflammation will be crucial to validate the therapeutic potential of SB-431542 in this context (Teplitsky et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025).

Overall, SB-431542 represents a scientifically robust and mechanistically well-justified candidate for repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD. Its targeted inhibition of ALK5 offers a strategic means to reduce pathological ECM deposition and thereby alleviate the mechanical stress that undermines RPE tight junction integrity—a key factor implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). The strengths of SB-431542 include its potency, selectivity, and extensive preclinical validation in fibrotic and ocular injury models. In contrast, its weaknesses center on pharmacokinetic limitations, the challenges of ocular delivery, and the complexity of broadly inhibiting a cytokine pathway that also serves beneficial roles.  

In conclusion, while additional formulation work and targeted preclinical studies remain essential, the accumulated evidence from biochemical, cellular, and ocular studies strongly supports the further evaluation of SB-431542 as part of a mechanobiology‐based therapeutic strategy for dry AMD. Given that dry AMD currently lacks effective treatments and that pathological ECM accumulation in Bruch’s membrane is a critical driver of disease progression, the repurposing of SB-431542 could provide a novel means to restore RPE barrier function by reducing ECM stiffness and re-establishing tight junction continuity (Xiao et al., 2009). Future research should focus on optimizing local delivery—potentially via sustained-release intravitreal formulations—and integrating SB-431542 within a combination therapy framework that additionally targets oxidative stress and inflammation. With these measures in place, SB-431542 holds significant promise as an innovative candidate in the quest for effective treatments for dry AMD (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002).

Thus, based on its synthetic origin, proven preclinical anti-fibrotic and anti-EMT effects, and detailed mechanistic rationale, SB-431542 merits further development for dry AMD. A rigorous, methodologically robust preclinical program – including pharmacokinetic optimization, ocular toxicity studies, and validation in relevant AMD models – will be crucial to determine whether the benefits observed in laboratory assays can be translated into meaningful clinical improvements in retinal structure and function.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
TTA‐P2 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed to target T‐type voltage‐gated calcium channels (VGCCs), which belong to the CaV3 family (CaV3.1, CaV3.2, CaV3.3). As a member of the T‐type calcium channel blocker class, TTA‐P2 is representative of compounds that modulate low-voltage-activated channels involved in a variety of cell functions, ranging from neuronal burst firing to hormone release. In the context of drug development, this compound is categorized as a channel-modulating agent, and its synthetic origins as a small molecule rendered it amenable to structural modification for improved pharmacokinetics in various tissue systems (Choe et al., 2011). Historically, TTA‐P2 has been investigated in the context of neuropathic pain and epilepsy, where T‐type calcium channels are integral to the regulation of neuronal excitability. In experimental models involving rat sensory neurons, TTA‐P2 demonstrated marked antinociceptive properties and produced significant reductions in neuronal burst firing by selectively blocking T‐type calcium currents (Choe et al., 2011). This evidence underlines the compound’s effectiveness in modulating calcium influx in hyperexcitable systems. Beyond its neurological applications, there have been several studies in which compounds targeting T‐type CaV channels were applied to non-neuronal cells. Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism by which TTA‐P2 exerts its effects is through selective inhibition of T‐type calcium channels. Detailed electrophysiological studies in rat sensory neurons have shown that TTA‐P2 binds preferentially to the inactivated state of these channels, thereby stabilizing them in a non-conducting conformation. This binding results in a significant hyperpolarizing shift (approximately 20 mV) in the steady-state inactivation curves and an incomplete recovery from inactivation, meaning that the channels remain non-functional for a longer period after brief depolarizations (Choe et al., 2011). Such effects effectively reduce the calcium influx that would normally occur during depolarization-driven events. In RPE cells, there is a body of evidence indicating that T‐type calcium channels (particularly CaV3.1 and CaV3.3) contribute to the formation of localized Ca²⁺ microdomains that play a role in regulating tight junction dynamics (Jazouli, 2022). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Danicopan, also known as ACH-4471 and by its commercial identifier MedChemExpress HY-19909, is a novel small-molecule agent designed to target complement factor D. This class of compounds is characterized by their capacity to modulate complement activation rather than broadly suppress the entire immune system. Danicopan was originally developed as a first-in-class molecule to selectively block factor D, which is the rate-limiting enzyme in the AP and is intimately involved in the formation of the C3 convertase complex (Boyer et al., 2022). Historically, the use of complement inhibitors has been a promising therapeutic strategy across several complement-mediated disorders. The evaluation of Danicopan as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration reveals several compelling strengths balanced by certain challenges that warrant further investigation. Its targeted approach may overcome some of the limitations encountered with previous complement inhibitors, especially if future studies can confirm that the in vitro effects on TER restoration and reduction in C3b deposition translate into meaningful clinical outcomes. Navitoclax (ABT-263) is a small‐molecule, orally bioavailable agent originally developed in the oncology arena as a BH3‐mimetic that targets several anti‐apoptotic members of the BCL-2 family, most notably BCL-2, BCL-xL, and BCL-W. This synthetic compound was designed through structure–activity relationship optimization to overcome the limitations of earlier compounds such as ABT-737, and it has since been classified as a senolytic agent owing to its ability to selectively induce apoptosis in senescent cells while sparing normal, quiescent cells. In the context of aging and degenerative diseases, the protective yet dysfunctional senescent cell phenotype is characterized by the upregulation of anti‐apoptotic proteins; therefore, compounds like ABT-263 that block these survival pathways have been repurposed as candidates to eliminate such senescent cells. The compound belongs to a broader class of therapeutics targeting the BCL-2 family, which have historically been exploited in various anti-cancer strategies and are now emerging as promising candidates for addressing age-associated disorders such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Ryu et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Navitoclax has a well-documented preclinical and clinical history in oncological models; its senolytic potential was first noted in studies where it selectively killed therapy-induced senescent tumor cells and other cell types by inhibiting anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins. Early clinical trials in small-cell lung cancer and lymphoid malignancies established proof-of-concept that targeting BCL-2/BCL-xL could result in tumor regression through apoptotic induction, although its clinical use was somewhat limited by dose-dependent toxicities such as thrombocytopenia. More recently, preclinical studies have extended its use beyond oncology: in in vitro studies and in mouse models where retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells were rendered senescent by doxorubicin treatment, navitoclax was shown to selectively induce apoptosis in the senescent cell population while largely sparing non-senescent RPE, as evidenced by decreased markers of senescence (p16, p21) and increased apoptotic markers such as cleaved caspases. Additionally, these studies demonstrated that oral administration of ABT-263 in mice resulted in reduced senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining and improved structural and functional retinal outcomes, including increased outer nuclear layer thickness and recovery of electroretinographic responses, which are highly encouraging for its repurposing in dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023). At the molecular level, navitoclax exerts its senolytic action by competitively binding to the hydrophobic groove of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins, particularly BCL-2 and BCL-xL, thereby displacing pro-apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BIM. Under normal conditions, senescent cells upregulate these anti-apoptotic proteins as part of a survival mechanism against various stressors; the binding of navitoclax disrupts these protective interactions, leading to the activation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade. This biochemical disruption sets off a cascade of events culminating in mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, cytochrome c release, and the subsequent activation of caspases (notably caspase-9 and caspase-3), which orchestrate programmed cell death. Navitoclax represents a promising therapeutic candidate as a repurposed senolytic agent for the treatment of dry AMD based on a convergence of preclinical biochemical, cellular, and animal model data. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MS-275, also known as Entinostat and available from Selleck (S7100), is a fully synthetic compound that belongs to the benzamide class of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi). Its chemical structure is defined as 3-pyridylmethyl-N-{4-[(2-aminophenyl)carbamoyl]-benzyl}carbamate, and it was originally developed by research teams including those at Mitsui Pharmaceuticals in the late 1990s (Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 2–3; Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34). Unlike hydroxamate-based HDAC inhibitors, the benzamide motif in MS-275 engages the catalytic zinc ion in a manner that is less potent in chelation yet confers a higher degree of class I selectivity, particularly toward HDAC1 and HDAC2 (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11). Benzamides have been extensively investigated for their epigenetic modulation properties in oncology, where selective inhibition of HDACs is pursued to reprogram aberrant gene expression profiles in cancer cells (Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Carafa et al., 2011, pp. 3–5). As a representative of its class, MS-275 has a well-defined synthetic origin and benefits from a non-natural product, medicinal chemistry–driven discovery process that emphasizes targeted inhibition of chromatin-modifying enzymes for therapeutic reactivation of silenced genes (Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34; Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, MS-275 has been developed and evaluated primarily in the context of oncology. It has advanced into multiple Phase I and II clinical trials, particularly for solid tumors such as breast cancer, hematologic malignancies like acute leukemia, and various other cancers where deregulated HDAC activity plays a role (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 9–11; Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 2–3). Preclinical studies have demonstrated its capacity to induce cell-cycle arrest, promote apoptosis, and trigger differentiation in tumor cell lines by restoring a balance in histone acetylation (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–9; Hanikoglu et al., 2018, pp. 2–3). Mechanism of Action:  
MS-275 functions by selectively inhibiting class I HDACs, particularly HDAC1 and HDAC2, through a zinc-binding mechanism that is distinct from that of hydroxamate inhibitors. The benzamide moiety in MS-275 interacts with the catalytic zinc ion within the active site of HDACs; however, due to its non-hydroxamate nature, the mode of coordination involves a bidentate interaction primarily via the amino group with additional, albeit weaker, engagement through the carbonyl oxygen (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11).
