Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PF-06409577 [6-chloro-5-(4-(1-hydroxycyclobutyl)phenyl)-1H-indole-3-carboxylic acid] is a synthetic, indole-3-carboxylic acid small molecule discovered in a Pfizer program to generate direct, isoform-selective activators of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) for metabolic and renal indications (notably diabetic nephropathy) (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Webb et al., 2019). Medicinal chemistry and structural biology work established PF-06409577 as a direct allosteric AMPK activator that binds the α1β1γ1 heterotrimer and engages the so-called allosteric drug and metabolite (ADaM) site at the α–β interface, with co-crystallization data reported for the parent and its metabolites bound to α1β1γ1 (Ryder et al., 2018; Steinberg & Carling, 2019). In biochemical assays and surface plasmon resonance (SPR), PF-06409577 and related indole-3-carboxylic acids preferentially activate and bind β1-containing AMPK isoforms, with little-to-no activity against β2-containing human AMPK heterotrimers under the conditions reported; notably, the acyl glucuronide conjugates (M1–M3) retain β1-selective AMPK activation with reduced potency relative to the parent (Ryder et al., 2018). Consistent with β-subunit–driven selectivity of ADaM ligands, prior work with thienopyridone A-769662 and benzimidazole 991 demonstrates β1 > β2 preference and mechanistic dependence on β1-Ser108, a key determinant of ADaM-site responsiveness (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).

PF-06409577 belongs to the class of direct, small-molecule AMPK activators designed to allosterically activate the kinase and protect Thr172 phosphorylation from dephosphorylation, in contrast to indirect mitochondrial poisons (e.g., metformin, phenformin, berberine) that raise cellular AMP/ADP and secondarily activate AMPK (Steinberg & Carling, 2019). Within this class, multiple chemotypes (thienopyridones, benzimidazoles, indole acids, and pan-activators such as MK-8722) have been used to probe metabolism, autophagy/mitophagy, and lipid homeostasis in vivo, with both efficacy signals (e.g., cholesterol lowering, NAFLD correction, organ protection) and safety liabilities (e.g., cardiac hypertrophy with a pan-activator) documented across programs (Behl et al., 2021; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2019).

Beyond primary pharmacology, PF-06409577 and congeners are extensively glucuronidated in animals and humans; unusually, the resulting acyl glucuronides remain pharmacologically active at AMPK, preserving β1-selective activation and direct binding to α1β1γ1 in vitro (albeit with 9–19-fold lower potency than the parent), a property with implications for exposure, distribution, and safety (Ryder et al., 2018). The acyl glucuronides of this series were reported to be relatively stable to hydrolysis and acyl migration at physiological pH (t1/2 > 21 h in buffer), a feature that lowers, but does not eliminate, typical concerns about acyl glucuronide–mediated covalent protein modification and idiosyncratic toxicity in carboxylic acid drugs (Ryder et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History  
PF-06409577 was developed as a β1-selective AMPK activator for diabetic nephropathy; it achieved Phase I clinical testing but was discontinued (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), and there is no report of ophthalmic or AMD use in the available sources (Webb et al., 2019). Preclinically, selective activation of β1-containing AMPK isoforms has been linked to improved kidney function in rat nephropathy models, and liver-targeted activation by PF-06409577 corrected NAFLD and lowered cholesterol in rodent and primate studies, with target engagement tracked via ACC phosphorylation (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019). In contrast to pan-activators such as MK-8722 that improved systemic glucose homeostasis but caused cardiac hypertrophy with glycogen accumulation in rodents and primates, β1-selective strategies are viewed as potentially safer with respect to cardiac glycogen loading and skeletal muscle glucose uptake, although this requires empirical confirmation per compound and tissue (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Behl et al., 2021). Of note, β1-biased activation by PF-06409577 has been reported to increase plasma ketone bodies and reduce hepatic triacylglycerol and cholesterol without lowering blood glucose—an important metabolic profile distinction (Behl et al., 2021).

In ocular biology, PF-06409577 has been directly tested in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells in vitro. Li et al. (2018) reported that PF-06409577 activates AMPK signaling and protects both ARPE-19 and primary murine RPEs from ultraviolet radiation (UVR), reducing ROS, lipid peroxidation, DNA damage, apoptosis, and cell death, with accompanying increases in NADPH activity and Nrf2-dependent antioxidant gene expression (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC, GCLM). The protective effects were strictly AMPKα1-dependent (shRNA, dominant-negative T172A, and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout each abrogated PF-mediated protection and AMPK activation), establishing on-target mechanism in RPE under oxidative stress (Li et al., 2018). The paper presents dose–response and time-course data showing AMPKα Thr172 and ACC Ser79 phosphorylation in ARPE-19 over ~0.1–1.0 μM PF-06409577, with 0.03 μM ineffective; parallel experiments in primary RPE at 0.3 μM showed similar activation (Li et al., 2018). The authors also describe PF-06409577 potency as “nM” in RPE in narrative discussion, consistent with direct engagement yet not fully aligned with the 0.03 μM threshold in their western blot data; together, these findings indicate sub- to low-micromolar cellular potencies in RPE compatible with direct ADaM-site engagement (Li et al., 2018). Importantly, the RPE literature to date contains no reports of PF-06409577 use in AMD patients, no in vivo AMD models with PF-06409577, and no published measurements of RPE tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin) or transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) for this agent (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).

Additional translational history for PF-06409577 includes use as a host-directed antiviral tool; AMPK activation by PF-06409577 inhibited replication of flaviviruses (WNV, ZIKV, DENV-2) by interfering with replication complex development linked to host membrane rearrangements and lipid synthesis, at micromolar EC50s with acceptable in vitro selectivity indices (Jiménez de Oya et al., 2018). This antiviral application further underscores the compound’s capacity to reprogram lipid metabolism in stressed cells, relevant to lipid-rich pathology in AMD.

Within the broader therapeutic class, indirect AMPK activators (notably metformin) have been repeatedly associated with retinal protection: metformin reduces drusen formation via LXR/ABCA1/G1-mediated cholesterol efflux, suppresses inflammation (e.g., NLRP3 inflammasome), protects RPE and photoreceptors via PGC-1α/mitochondrial regulation, induces autophagy via AMPK–mTOR, and dampens VEGF signaling in vascular endothelium (all AMPK-dependent), strengthening the conceptual precedent that AMPK activation is protective in retinal degenerations (Dang et al., 2021). However, these metformin data do not establish PF-06409577-specific safety or efficacy in RPE barrier endpoints such as ZO-1, occludin, or TEER (Dang et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Direct binding and isoform selectivity. PF-06409577 and its acyl glucuronide metabolites bind directly to AMPK α1β1γ1 at the ADaM site at the α–β interface, driving allosteric activation and protection against Thr172 dephosphorylation of the α subunit; β1-selective activation is borne out across biochemical and SPR binding assays, and the acyl glucuronides retain β1 selectivity albeit at lower potency (Ryder et al., 2018). ADaM-site pharmacology is isoform-sensitive: conformational and sequence differences in the αC helix and β-subunit (including the β C-interacting helix) modulate ligand responsiveness, with β1-Ser108 phosphorylation enabling synergism between nucleotide- and ADaM-site activation (e.g., AMP plus A-769662/991), and mutation at α Leu166 selectively reduces activation by certain ligands (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019). These structural determinants rationalize β1 preference for ADaM-site ligands and inform tissue-selectivity hypotheses in β1-rich cells (Steinberg & Carling, 2019).

RPE cell signaling and cytoprotection. In ARPE-19 and primary murine RPEs, PF-06409577 rapidly increases AMPKα1 Thr172 phosphorylation and phosphorylation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) at Ser79, a canonical AMPK substrate, with parallel increases in AMPK activity (Li et al., 2018). Functionally, PF-06409577 pretreatment reduces UVR-induced ROS (DCFH-DA), lipid peroxidation (TBARs), DNA damage (p-γH2AX), apoptosis (ssDNA, cleaved caspase-3, Annexin-V/PI), and cell death (LDH), while improving viability (CCK-8), in both ARPE-19 and primary RPE cultures (Li et al., 2018). The compound enhances cellular NADPH activity and stabilizes Nrf2 protein with induction of classical Nrf2 target genes (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC, GCLM), consistent with increased antioxidant capacity and a transcriptional response favoring cytoprotection (Li et al., 2018). Genetic disruption of AMPKα1 (shRNA, dominant-negative T172A mutant, or CRISPR/Cas9 knockout) abrogates both AMPK signaling and PF-mediated protection, demonstrating that AMPKα1 is necessary for the observed effects (Li et al., 2018). Mechanistically, AMPK can preserve NADPH through ACC inactivation (limiting de novo lipogenesis and malonyl-CoA production) and by promoting fatty acid oxidation, both of which improve redox balance; AMPK also phosphorylates Nrf2 at Ser550 to facilitate nuclear translocation and transactivation, with additional indirect support via inhibition of GSK3β-driven nuclear exclusion and p62/SQSTM1-mediated KEAP1 autophagic degradation, all of which are documented upstream regulatory routes present in RPE cells (Hu et al., 2024).

Metabolic control, autophagy, and lipid handling. AMPK is a master regulator of lipid metabolism and autophagy: it phosphorylates and inhibits ACC1/ACC2 to reduce de novo lipogenesis and lower malonyl-CoA, promoting mitochondrial fatty acid import and β-oxidation; AMPK also phosphorylates ULK1 to initiate autophagy and can activate PGC-1α to drive mitochondrial biogenesis, enhance mitophagy, and improve mitochondrial quality control (Webb et al., 2019). Although the RPE PF-06409577 literature does not yet report autophagy markers (LC3-II, p62) or lipid droplet turnover, studies in ARPE-19 with an independent AMPK-activating intervention (liraglutide) show that AMPK activation in FFA-loaded RPE restores autophagy/lipophagy (↑LC3-II, ↓p62, ↓p-mTOR), reduces ROS and lipid droplet burden, rescues EMT markers, and restores ZO-1 localization at the membrane—effects blocked by pharmacologic AMPK inhibition—thereby validating these AMPK-dependent axes in RPE (Tsou et al., 2025). More generally, AICAR activation of AMPK upregulated ABCA1/ABCG1 in RPE and reduced Bruch’s membrane lipid deposition in ApoE⁻/⁻ mice, connecting AMPK to cholesterol efflux pathways relevant to drusen biogenesis (Hu et al., 2024). Collectively, these mechanisms support the plausibility that a direct AMPK activator such as PF-06409577 can modulate autophagy and lipid metabolism in RPE even though PF-specific autophagy/lipophagy data in RPE have not yet been reported (Li et al., 2018; Tsou et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).

Barrier integrity and tight-junction assembly. AMPK has been mechanistically linked to tight-junction assembly in epithelial systems: it promotes ZO-1 reassembly at paracellular contacts, phosphorylates claudin-1 (preventing degradation) and claudin-4 (promoting occludin binding), and phosphorylates scaffold proteins (e.g., cingulin, afadin) and MLCK to tune actin–junction interactions and permeability (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). In RPE specifically, liraglutide’s AMPK-dependent rescue of ZO-1 distribution under FFA challenge suggests that AMPK activation can re-normalize barrier-associated proteins in RPE cultures, although TEER was not reported in that study and the journal quality warrants cautious interpretation (Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). To date, no published data directly demonstrate effects of PF-06409577 on ZO-1/occludin or TEER in RPE; thus, junctional rescue by PF-06409577 remains a testable hypothesis rather than an established mechanism (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).

Systemic pharmacology and safety context. In liver and kidney settings, PF-06409577 engages AMPK in vivo (e.g., pACC biomarker), lowers hepatic lipogenesis, corrects NAFLD, and confers renal protection in β1-focused pharmacology paradigms, while β1 activation by PF-06409577 has been noted to not lower blood glucose (Behl et al., 2021). Pan-activation by MK-8722 in renal disease improved mitochondrial quality control, reduced lipotoxicity and fibrosis, and improved function but highlighted a class-level safety risk—cardiac hypertrophy with glycogen accumulation under some dosing regimens—underscoring the importance of subunit selectivity and tissue targeting for chronic use (Zhou et al., 2019; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). The acyl glucuronide metabolites of PF-06409577 are pharmacologically active and chemically stable in buffer; however, acyl glucuronides as a class have been implicated in idiosyncratic immune toxicities, and careful metabolite profiling and reactive metabolite risk assessment will be required for ocular delivery strategies (Ryder et al., 2018).

Expected Effect  
Rationale in dry AMD pathobiology. Oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/mitophagy, and dysregulated lipid handling are central to RPE dysfunction and drusen biogenesis in dry AMD, with age-related decline in Nrf2-mediated antioxidant defense and lysosome–phagosome fusion defects compounding vulnerability (Hu et al., 2024). AMPK activation is positioned to counter these processes by: (1) improving NADPH homeostasis and activating Nrf2 target gene programs, (2) initiating autophagy/mitophagy via ULK1 while suppressing mTORC1 signaling, (3) reducing lipogenesis (via ACC) and supporting fatty acid oxidation and cholesterol efflux (via LXR–ABCA1/G1), and (4) stabilizing/assembling tight junctions through claudin/occludin/ZO-1 scaffold and cytoskeletal phosphorylation events (Li et al., 2018; Dang et al., 2021; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).

What PF-06409577 is expected to do in RPE assays. Based on the published RPE data and AMPK biology, the following effects are expected if PF-06409577 is applied to human RPE cultures (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary RPE) under oxidative and lipid-loading stress:
- Oxidative stress resistance: Increased AMPKα Thr172 and ACC Ser79 phosphorylation, elevated NADPH/NADP⁺, stabilization of Nrf2 protein, and induction of antioxidant genes (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC, GCLM), with reduced ROS, lipid peroxidation and DNA damage under UVR or oxidant challenges, as shown directly in ARPE-19 and primary RPE by Li et al. (Li et al., 2018). These endpoints should be AMPKα1-dependent (loss-of-function tamps down PF effects) (Li et al., 2018).
- Lipid handling and autophagy: Although untested for PF-06409577 in RPE, AMPK activation in ARPE-19 (with liraglutide) restored autophagy and lipophagy markers (↑LC3-II, ↓p62, ↓p-mTOR), reduced lipid droplet number/size, and normalized lipophagy/lysosome gene expression (ATG5, LIPA, RAB7A, LAMP2) in an AMPK-dependent manner; PF-06409577 should be evaluated for these endpoints under free fatty acid or oxLDL loading where AMPK effects are mechanistically expected (Tsou et al., 2025). Independent RPE evidence that AMPK activation increases ABCA1/ABCG1 and decreases Bruch’s membrane lipid deposition supports anticipated benefits on cholesterol efflux (Hu et al., 2024).
- Barrier integrity: AMPK’s direct effects on tight-junction components and scaffolds in epithelial systems suggest PF-06409577 could improve ZO-1/occludin organization and paracellular barrier function (TEER), but no PF-06409577 data exist in RPE; therefore, ZO-1/occludin immunolocalization and TEER must be prospectively measured. The liraglutide ARPE-19 study showing AMPK-dependent restoration of ZO-1 under FFA stress provides a relevant positive control framework for assay design, with the caveat of study quality and absence of TEER measurements (Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).
- Dosing/target engagement: In ARPE-19 and primary RPE, AMPK activation by PF-06409577 occurred with sub- to low-micromolar exposure (0.1–1.0 μM active, 0.03 μM inactive in westerns), with 0.3 μM effective in primary RPE; therefore, a concentration range of ~0.03–1 μM should be explored with pACC and pAMPKα as engagement biomarkers and NADPH/Nrf2 targets as pharmacodynamic readouts (Li et al., 2018). Biochemical potency of PF-06409577 can be in the single-digit nanomolar range against recombinant AMPK and cellular potency for pACC has been described as “nM” in RPE contexts; nonetheless, empirical titration in RPE is warranted given observed cell-assay thresholds (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).
- Isoform selectivity in RPE: PF-06409577 is β1-selective, and ADaM-site ligand responsiveness is strongly β-isoform-dependent; however, AMPK β isoform expression distribution in human RPE is not provided in the current sources and should be profiled (mRNA/protein) to confirm the β1 hypothesis before assuming superior tissue selectivity (Ryder et al., 2018; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).
- Network cross-talk and safety in vitro: Co-activation of AMPK and mTORC1 has been associated with cytotoxic outcomes in some cell types; assays should monitor mTORC1 readouts (p-S6K, p-4EBP1) alongside autophagy flux to ensure PF-06409577 produces the expected AMPK→mTORC1 inhibition and does not trigger maladaptive co-activation contexts in RPE (Li et al., 2018).

Collectively, the expected proximal effects of PF-06409577 in RPE are robust AMPK activation with antioxidant and metabolic reprogramming, and the expected distal outcomes include reduced oxidative injury and improved lipid/autophagy balance. Barrier strengthening (ZO-1/occludin, TEER) is mechanistically plausible based on AMPK biology and AMPK-dependent rescue with alternative activators in ARPE-19, but must be experimentally demonstrated for PF-06409577 (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Tsou et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Direct, β1-selective AMPK activation with structural, biophysical, and biochemical support. PF-06409577 directly binds and activates AMPK α1β1γ1 at the ADaM site and shows clear β1 selectivity across parents and acyl glucuronide metabolites; this selectivity is a desirable property for limiting pan-AMPK liabilities observed with compounds like MK-8722 (e.g., cardiac glycogen accumulation) (Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).  
- Demonstrated on-target cytoprotection in RPE. Li et al. (2018) show AMPKα1-dependent protection of ARPE-19 and primary RPE against UVR, with mechanistic readouts aligned to AMD pathogenesis: increased NADPH, Nrf2 target induction, reduced ROS, lipid peroxidation, DNA damage, apoptosis, and cell death—providing a strong cell-biological foundation for further RPE work (Li et al., 2018).  
- Mechanistic fit to AMD drivers. AMPK activation intersects the principal RPE failure modes in AMD—redox imbalance (Nrf2), impaired autophagy/mitophagy (ULK1/mTORC1), and lipid dysregulation (ACC, FAO, LXR/ABCA1/G1)—and AMPK-dependent restoration of autophagy/lipophagy and barrier proteins has been demonstrated in ARPE-19 using a different AMPK-activating intervention (liraglutide), making PF-06409577 a mechanistically well-targeted candidate to modulate those pathways (Dang et al., 2021; Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).  
- Favorable metabolic profile and organ-protection precedent. PF-06409577 corrected NAFLD and lowered cholesterol in rodent/primate models with liver AMPK dependence, improved renal endpoints in β1-focused paradigms, and did not lower blood glucose in reported contexts, all suggesting a differentiated systemic pharmacology relative to pan-activators and indirect mitochondrial inhibitors (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).  
- Metabolite pharmacology understood. Active acyl glucuronides have been characterized structurally and functionally and exhibit β1-selective AMPK activation with notable stability, reducing concern about unstable, highly reactive acyl glucuronide species (while not fully removing risk), and informing PK/distribution planning for ocular routes (Ryder et al., 2018).

Key Gaps and Risks  
- No published junctional/TEER data for PF-06409577 in RPE. The project’s central claim—restoration of RPE junction integrity (ZO-1/occludin localization, TEER elevation, reduced paracellular permeability)—has not been demonstrated for PF-06409577 in any RPE model in the sources provided; this is the most critical data gap for the proposed indication (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).  
- No PF-06409577 autophagy/lipophagy data in RPE. While AMPK activation in ARPE-19 by liraglutide restored autophagy/lipophagy and rescued ZO-1 in an AMPK-dependent manner, PF-06409577-specific data on ULK1 phosphorylation, LC3 flux, p62 turnover, lysosome–autophagosome fusion, and lipid droplet dynamics in RPE are absent and must be generated (Tsou et al., 2025).  
- AMPK β isoform expression in human RPE is not established in the provided literature. Although ADaM ligands are β1-preferring and PF-06409577 is β1-selective, we do not have direct evidence here that β1 predominates in mature human RPE; consequently, isoform profiling is a necessary early-stage risk-reduction step (Steinberg & Carling, 2019; Ryder et al., 2018).  
- Cellular potency window in RPE requires clarification. Li et al. (2018) show a clear activation threshold between 0.03 μM (inactive) and 0.1–1.0 μM (active) for AMPKα phosphorylation in ARPE-19 and efficacy at 0.3 μM in primary RPE, whereas narrative text suggests “nM” activation; this discrepancy underscores the need for rigorous concentration–response across engagement and functional endpoints in relevant human RPE models (Li et al., 2018).  
- Clinical development discontinued; no ocular safety data. PF-06409577’s clinical program was halted at Phase I for non-ocular indications; no ophthalmic tolerability, ocular PK, or on-target/off-target safety in retinal tissues has been reported here. Acyl glucuronides, while stable in vitro for this series, can pose idiosyncratic risk; pan-AMPK activation has known cardiac liabilities; and network cross-talk (e.g., co-activation of AMPK and mTORC1) could be deleterious in some contexts—all argue for early safety de-risking (Webb et al., 2019; Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).

Programmatic Recommendations  
Near-term, decision-making studies should prioritize: (1) RPE isoform mapping (AMPK α/β/γ mRNA and protein), (2) dose–response and time-course profiling of PF-06409577 in human primary RPE or iPSC-RPE (pAMPKα Thr172, pACC Ser79, NADPH/NADP⁺, Nrf2 protein and targets), (3) autophagy/lipophagy flux assays (LC3-II turnover with/without lysosomal blockade, p62 degradation, ULK1 phosphorylation, mTORC1 markers), (4) lipid droplet quantification (number, size distribution) under FFA or oxLDL loading, (5) junctional biology (ZO-1/occludin claudin-1/4 localization and levels, cingulin/afadin phosphorylation status) and barrier function (TEER, FITC-dextran permeability), and (6) safety pharmacology in RPE (viability, apoptosis, senescence markers; exploration of AMPK–mTORC1 co-activation risk) across 0.03–1.0 μM with pACC-guided on-target exposure (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).

If in vitro RPE data are supportive, next steps include: (7) ocular PK after topical/periocular dosing (parent and acyl glucuronides in RPE/choroid), (8) metabolite profiling and covalent adduct risk assessment in ocular tissues, (9) in vivo efficacy in AMD-relevant models (e.g., light damage, Alu RNA–induced RPE degeneration, HFD/oxLDL models) with barrier and lipid endpoints, and (10) safety screens for cardiac glycogen accumulation under systemic exposure (to benchmark β1 selectivity advantages) (Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
PF-06409577 is a well-characterized, β1-selective, direct AMPK activator with on-target, AMPKα1-dependent cytoprotective activity in RPE cells under oxidative stress, and with strong mechanistic alignment to dry AMD pathobiology via NADPH/Nrf2, autophagy/mitophagy, and lipid metabolism pathways (Li et al., 2018). Class knowledge and comparator interventions support the plausibility that AMPK activation can restore RPE lipid homeostasis and barrier protein organization; however, critical indication-specific evidence—PF-06409577’s effects on RPE autophagy/lipophagy and junctional/TEER endpoints—is currently missing and must be generated before advancing (Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). The compound’s β1 selectivity, favorable metabolic efficacy profile (NAFLD/kidney), and lack of glucose-lowering are attractive, but the discontinued clinical status, the pharmacologically active acyl glucuronides, and known liabilities with pan-AMPK activation emphasize the need for deliberate safety de-risking and ocular PK/metabolite work (Behl et al., 2021; Ryder et al., 2018; Webb et al., 2019; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).

On balance, PF-06409577 merits a focused, RPE-centric preclinical validation campaign for dry AMD that directly tests barrier and lipid endpoints while monitoring canonical AMPK engagement and redox rescue. Positive readouts across ZO-1/occludin/TEER, autophagy/lipophagy markers, and lipid droplet turnover—together with preservation of mitochondrial/antioxidant markers—would substantially de-risk the mechanistic hypothesis and justify advancement toward ocular PK/safety studies and in vivo efficacy models (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024). At present, claims of TEER restoration and junctional upregulation by PF-06409577 in RPE cannot be substantiated from the available literature and should be considered unproven working hypotheses pending experimental confirmation (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History (Expanded Summary)  
- Origin/chemotype: Indole-3-carboxylic acid, direct ADaM-site AMPK activator; discovered and preclinically characterized by Pfizer for diabetic nephropathy (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Strang et al., 2025).  
- Selectivity/biophysics: Direct binding to α1β1γ1 with β1 selectivity; acyl glucuronide metabolites retain β1 activity with lower potency; likely mode includes allosteric activation and protection from Thr172 dephosphorylation (Ryder et al., 2018; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).  
- Systemic pharmacology: Liver AMPK activation corrected NAFLD and lowered cholesterol in rodents and primates; β1 activation improved kidney function in rodent models (Behl et al., 2021).  
- Safety-class signals: Pan-activator MK-8722 causes cardiac hypertrophy with glycogen in rodents/primate models; PF-06409577 reported not to lower blood glucose; acyl glucuronides stable but class risk remains (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Behl et al., 2021; Ryder et al., 2018).  
- Ocular biology: Direct RPE cytoprotection against UVR via AMPKα1-dependent signaling; no published PF-06409577 data on RPE junctions/TEER/autophagy endpoints (Li et al., 2018).

Mechanistic Integration in AMD Context  
- AMPK→Nrf2 redox axis: AMPK phosphorylation of Nrf2 (Ser550), indirect relief of KEAP1 repression (via GSK3β inhibition and p62-mediated KEAP1 autophagic degradation), and upregulation of antioxidant enzymes; these are operative in RPE and are enhanced by PF-06409577 in vitro (Hu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2018).  
- AMPK→ULK1/mTOR/autophagy: AMPK initiates autophagy, antagonizes mTORC1, and in RPE models AMPK activation restores autophagy/lipophagy, reduces EMT, and normalizes barrier protein localization under lipid stress—mechanistic endpoints to quantify for PF-06409577 (Dang et al., 2021; Tsou et al., 2025).  
- AMPK→ACC/FAO/lipogenesis: ACC inhibition reduces DNL and malonyl-CoA, permitting FAO flux; in RPE, this is expected to reduce lipid droplet accrual and lipoperoxidation burden central to drusen precursor formation (Webb et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2024).  
- AMPK→junction assembly: Phosphorylation of claudins and scaffold proteins, ZO-1 reassembly, and cytoskeletal remodeling provide a direct mechanistic route for barrier strengthening; this is plausible in RPE but requires PF-06409577-specific testing (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).

Decision Framework for Advancement  
- Go/No-Go criteria: Require demonstration that PF-06409577 increases pAMPKα/pACC and Nrf2 targets; reduces ROS/lipid peroxidation/DNA damage in RPE; increases autophagy flux and reduces lipid droplets under FFA or oxLDL; and improves ZO-1/occludin organization with increased TEER and reduced paracellular permeability, all in an AMPK-dependent manner (Li et al., 2018; Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).  
- Risk mitigation: Profile β isoform expression in human RPE; measure mTORC1 to exclude maladaptive co-activation; characterize ocular PK and acyl glucuronide distribution after topical/periocular delivery; benchmark systemic exposure to avoid cardiac glycogen liabilities (Steinberg & Carling, 2019; Li et al., 2018; Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).  
- Comparative positioning: If PF-06409577 proves effective on junctions and lipid/autophagy endpoints, its β1 selectivity and direct mechanism position it favorably versus indirect activators (metformin) and pan-activators (MK-8722); conversely, lack of junctional efficacy or safety signals would shift focus to alternative AMPK modulators or upstream modulators that converge on AMPK/Nrf2 with better ocular PK (Dang et al., 2021; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).

In summary, PF-06409577 has clear mechanistic and cellular evidence to support further exploration in dry AMD, with the caveat that the most clinically salient endpoints for RPE barrier restoration and lipid clearance remain to be proven for this agent. A disciplined experimental plan targeting these gaps will determine whether PF-06409577 advances as a credible candidate for RPE junction restoration in dry AMD (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024; Behl et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR, chemically known as 5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide, is an endogenous purine biosynthetic intermediate that has been harnessed as a synthetic, cell‐permeable AMP analog to activate AMP‐activated protein kinase (AMPK) pharmacologically (Hyttinen et al., 2011). This same class of metabolic modulators has demonstrated efficacy in experimental models of mitochondrial disease and muscle wasting by stimulating AMPK‐dependent pathways that augment mitochondrial biogenesis and restore energy balance (Green, 2013). Owing to its capacity to influence the phosphorylation of key enzymes and transcription factors, AICAR has found applications not only in elucidating fundamental bioenergetic pathways but also as a candidate to ameliorate conditions where energy homeostasis is disrupted. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, where the maintenance of tight junction integrity is crucial for barrier function and homeostasis, AICAR’s mechanism of action offers a rationale for its repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Historically, metabolic modulation via AMPK activators has been extensively investigated in various systems, and AICAR has been a workhorse agent in these studies owing to its reliable pharmacological profile (Pokrywka et al., 2014). Biochemically, AICAR has been widely used to stimulate AMPK in cell culture and animal models, resulting in a host of downstream effects that include enhanced fatty acid oxidation, increased glucose uptake, and modulated lipid synthesis (Green, 2013). In addition, AICAR’s ability to promote autophagy through the inhibition of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) cascade has been observed across various cell types, including those derived from retinal tissues (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Clinical investigations have predominantly focused on its metabolic effects in conditions such as diabetes and ischemia, although its application in ocular diseases has been comparatively less explored (Pokrywka et al., 2014). In the field of ophthalmology, research into the role of AMPK in retinal health has uncovered that AMPK activation influences key RPE functions including autophagy, inflammatory cytokine production, and tight junction integrity (Qin, 2012). Notably, investigations in RPE-related models have demonstrated that pharmacologic modulation of AMPK can either protect or impair barrier function, depending on the context and isoform engaged (Qin & De Vries, 2008). While AICAR itself has not been approved explicitly for the treatment of dry AMD, its well–established use in preclinical studies, combined with its demonstrated ability to rescue barrier integrity in RPE under oxidative stress conditions, supports its potential repurposing for this indication (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011). The molecular mechanism by which AICAR exerts its therapeutic effects begins with its cellular uptake through nucleoside transporters such as ENT1 and ENT2, a process that ensures its intracellular availability (Dolinar et al., 2018). Once internalized, AICAR is rapidly phosphorylated by adenosine kinase, converting it into 5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate (ZMP) (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). ZMP, as an AMP analog, binds to the γ subunit of AMPK, eliciting conformational changes that not only enhance its allosteric activation but also protect it from dephosphorylation (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). Finally, the inherent variability in patient responses due to genetic, metabolic, and environmental factors presents an additional hurdle. The RPE’s response to oxidative stress, and hence its sensitivity to AMPK modulation, may vary widely among individuals with dry AMD. It will be crucial to identify biomarkers that predict response to AICAR treatment and to tailor dosing regimens accordingly (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

In summary, while AICAR shows considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD by virtue of its well‐established mechanism of AMPK activation, experimental data demonstrating tight junction rescue in RPE cells, and its ability to promote autophagic processes that counteract oxidative stress, its repurposing is tempered by concerns regarding the dualistic effects of AMPK signaling in the RPE, potential systemic side effects, and the challenges associated with dosage translation from in vitro to in vivo applications (Villarroel et al., 2011). The overall evaluation is that AICAR exhibits several compelling advantages—including mechanistic clarity, on‐target efficacy, and a robust preclinical rationale—that substantiate further investigation through rigorous preclinical and, eventually, clinical studies. With a careful approach that addresses the aforementioned weaknesses, AICAR may ultimately emerge as a valuable addition to the therapeutic arsenal against dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Comprehensive Future Directions and Considerations:  
To fully validate AICAR’s potential for treating dry AMD, a series of detailed investigations is warranted. First, further elucidation of the dose–response relationship in RPE cell cultures will be critical. This includes not only establishing the optimal concentration of AICAR to achieve maximal TEER improvement and AMPK activation but also determining whether these effects are sustained over time without incurring cellular toxicity (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011). Long‐term studies are needed to assess whether repeated dosing maintains barrier integrity or if adaptive processes eventually diminish the protective effects of AICAR.

Additionally, it will be necessary to delve deeper into the isoform‐specific effects of AMPK in the RPE. Evidence suggests that the α2 isoform in particular plays a critical role in mediating responses to oxidative stress and that its activation may differ qualitatively from that of the α1 subunit (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012). Understanding these nuances will help design therapeutic strategies that maximize the beneficial aspects of AMPK activation while minimizing potential adverse outcomes, such as impaired phagocytosis or unwanted alterations in cellular metabolism (Qin & De Vries, 2008).

In parallel, investigating the interplay between AICAR‐induced AMPK activation and autophagic pathways in the RPE will shed light on how tightly coupled these processes are in the context of dry AMD. Since autophagy is vital for clearing oxidatively damaged cellular components and supporting cell survival, it will be important to determine whether prolonged AMPK activation fosters a beneficial autophagic flux or rather leads to autophagy dysregulation over time (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). Strategies that involve monitoring autophagic markers along with TEER measurements and junction protein expression could provide a comprehensive picture of cellular health in AICAR‐treated RPE cells.

Given the concerns regarding potential systemic effects, advanced drug delivery systems such as localized intraocular injections or biodegradable implants could be considered for delivering AICAR directly to the retina, thereby limiting systemic exposure and enhancing local efficacy (Viglino et al., 2019; Sid et al., 2014). Preclinical animal models that mimic the pathological features of dry AMD will be indispensable in evaluating the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and therapeutic windows of AICAR in an in vivo setting. Such studies would also be instrumental in identifying potential adverse effects and assessing the long‐term safety profile of AICAR when administered via ocular routes.

Another key consideration is the potential for combination therapy. Since some reports indicate that AMPK activation by AICAR might impair certain RPE functions such as phagocytosis if excessively activated, combining AICAR with other agents that either modulate AMPK isoform activity or protect against excessive autophagic stimulation may provide a synergistic benefit (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Villarroel et al., 2011). For instance, the protective effect of fenofibric acid in preventing AICAR‐induced permeability increases has been documented, suggesting that a combination approach may overcome the limitations of monotherapy (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Finally, translational studies will need to integrate biomarker analyses capable of monitoring AMPK activation status, autophagy markers, and tight junction protein localization in the RPE. These biomarkers could guide dose optimization and serve as early indicators of therapeutic response in clinical trials (Villarroel et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008). Genetic or epigenetic factors that predispose individuals to variations in RPE responsiveness may also be identified, thereby enabling personalized medicine approaches for patients with dry AMD.

In conclusion, while there remain numerous challenges and uncertainties, AICAR represents a highly promising candidate for repurposing as a barrier‐protective agent in dry AMD. Its capacity to robustly activate AMPK, improve cellular energy homeostasis, promote autophagy, and restore tight junction integrity in RPE cells offers a multifaceted mode of action that addresses several key pathological features of dry AMD. With targeted preclinical studies that unpack the complexity of AMPK signaling in retinal tissues and strategic clinical trial designs that mitigate potential adverse effects, AICAR could conceivably fill a significant therapeutic gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Overall Conclusions:  
AICAR’s well‐documented ability to mimic AMP—thereby inducing AMPK activation—and its established role in regulating cellular energy balance and autophagy place it squarely in the category of compounds with high therapeutic potential for metabolic disorders. Emerging evidence in retinal models, particularly those simulating the oxidative stress and barrier dysfunction typical of dry AMD, further reinforces the rationale behind its repurposing. Nonetheless, while preclinical data are encouraging, careful consideration must be given to the dualistic nature of AMPK signaling in the RPE, as well as the potential systemic risks associated with systemic exposure. Despite these challenges, the convergence of multiple lines of evidence—from improved TEER measurements and specific molecular activation to supportive mechanistic studies—strongly advocates for further research into AICAR as a viable therapeutic strategy for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

In summary, the repurposing of AICAR for dry AMD is supported by both its robust mechanistic underpinnings and its promising preclinical efficacy data, placing it among the most attractive candidates for modulating RPE barrier integrity in this debilitating disease. Future studies that focus on fine‐tuning its dosage, delivery, and integrated combination therapies hold the key to unlocking its full therapeutic potential and advancing it from the bench to the clinic (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012).

Taking into account the strengths of its well‐defined mechanism, the reproducible experimental data demonstrating barrier rescue in RPE cells, and the feasibility of its pharmacological modulation, AICAR represents a compelling candidate for further development in the treatment of dry AMD. With continued advances in targeted drug delivery and combination therapeutics, the prospects for leveraging AICAR’s metabolic and protective effects in the retina are promising, warranting its inclusion in the strategic pipeline for combating age‐related macular degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

This comprehensive evaluation underscores that while challenges remain—including potential dose‐dependent effects, off‐target actions, and the need for precise modulation of AMPK isoforms—the overall body of evidence provides a solid rationale for advancing AICAR in preclinical and ultimately clinical studies focused on dry AMD. Its capacity to restore RPE barrier integrity under oxidative stress, coupled with its well‐established pharmacodynamic properties, offers a therapeutic strategy that could mitigate the progression of retinal degeneration and improve visual outcomes for patients suffering from this currently untreatable condition (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bexarotene is a fully synthetic retinoid analog classified as a rexinoid, specifically acting as a pan–retinoid X receptor (RXR) agonist. It was originally developed through structure–activity relationship studies aimed at mimicking the natural ligand 9-cis retinoic acid, while providing greater receptor selectivity, improved potency, and a pharmacological profile amenable to therapeutic use. Its synthesis and subsequent discovery were driven by the need to harness RXR‐mediated gene regulation, and it subsequently became the only FDA-approved synthetic RXR ligand to date (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). As a member of the retinoid drug class, bexarotene has been primarily used in the oncological setting, specifically for the treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, and its chemical design reflects modifications that impart high lipophilicity and receptor specificity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018). This synthetic derivation distinguishes it from naturally occurring retinoids and underpins its utility across a number of experimental and clinical contexts.

Therapeutic History:  
Bexarotene’s clinical history is marked by its approval as a second-line therapy for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, which provided a strong basis for its safety and efficacy in a human disease setting (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). In addition to its primary use in oncology, preclinical and early clinical research has investigated bexarotene for applications in neurodegenerative diseases, most notably Alzheimer’s disease and multiple sclerosis. These studies have demonstrated that RXR activation by bexarotene can influence the clearance of pathological protein aggregates and promote remyelination, respectively (Gaunt, 2020; Behl et al., 2022). However, despite the broad mechanistic appeal of RXR agonism in modifying lipid metabolism and neuroinflammation, there is little to no established clinical or veterinary precedent for employing bexarotene in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative conditions. In fact, while several RXR agonists have been considered in various models of ocular disease, the role of RXR in the diseased retina remains underexplored, with only sparse reports such as a study with the RXR agonist PA024 in retinal degeneration models (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). This gap in therapeutic history presents both a challenge and an opportunity in repurposing bexarotene for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
Bexarotene exerts its pharmacological effects primarily by binding to the ligand-binding domain of RXR isoforms (RXRα, RXRβ, and RXRγ) with nanomolar potency, inducing conformational changes that favor the recruitment of coactivators and subsequent transcriptional activation of targeted genes (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). RXR is a promiscuous nuclear receptor that forms obligate heterodimers with several other nuclear receptors, most notably the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) such as PPARγ. In doing so, the bexarotene-induced RXR/PPARγ heterodimer binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the genome, thereby upregulating target genes involved in lipid metabolism and transport. One key target is ABCA1, an ATP-binding cassette transporter implicated in cholesterol efflux from cells, which plays a central role in maintaining intracellular lipid homeostasis (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the activation of the RXR/PPARγ pathway is particularly compelling. RPE cells are highly involved in the processing and clearance of lipids, including cholesterol, and in modulating the structural integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier via tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 and occludin. When under stress—such as exposure to cytotoxic mediators like 7-ketocholesterol (7KCh), which disrupts normal junctional organization and reduces transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—the activation of RXR offers a potential therapeutic avenue. Bexarotene’s ability to stimulate RXR signaling is expected to upregulate ABCA1 expression, thereby enhancing cholesterol efflux, while also promoting the transcription of genes that lead to the re-expression of claudin-1 and occludin, which are critical for restoring barrier integrity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

The biochemical interactions following RXR activation by bexarotene include a cascade of events where the ligand-receptor complex alters the transcriptional landscape of the cell. This process entails the heterodimerization of RXR with its partner receptor, binding to DNA response elements, and initiating the recruitment of transcriptional coactivators, which together drive the expression of genes that modulate lipid metabolism, inflammatory responses, and cell junction integrity. The specificity of bexarotene for RXR, as opposed to broader retinoic acid receptor (RAR) activity, allows for a more targeted enhancement of these pathways—a factor that is crucial in tissues like the RPE, where precise regulation of lipid handling and barrier properties is essential for retinal health (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underlying the repurposing of bexarotene for dry AMD is that its activation of RXR in RPE cells will facilitate heterodimerization with PPARγ, driving the transcriptional upregulation of lipid-handling genes, most notably ABCA1. In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have provided compelling preliminary data indicating that exposure to 0.5 µM bexarotene in the presence of 7-ketocholesterol stress is capable of restoring TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values and significantly increasing ABCA1 mRNA levels. This restoration of TEER suggests that bexarotene not only promotes cholesterol efflux by upregulating ABCA1 but also exerts a beneficial influence on the expression of key tight junction proteins, such as claudin-1 and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity of the RPE barrier (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

The expected molecular effect in the assay is thus twofold. First, through its molecular interaction with RXR, bexarotene reinforces the RXR/PPARγ heterodimer formation, triggering a cascade of gene transcription events that culminate in enhanced cholesterol efflux via ABCA1. This effect directly addresses the accumulation of lipid deposits that contribute to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. Second, by re-inducing the expression of claudin-1 and occludin, bexarotene is anticipated to improve cellular junctional integrity, thereby reducing paracellular leakage and restoring the overall barrier function of the RPE as measured by TEER. The use of ocular gel formulations for local delivery promises to concentrate the therapeutic effect within the eye, circumventing the systemic adverse effects that are typically associated with bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties, such as high lipophilicity and low systemic solubility (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of bexarotene as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is founded upon a robust mechanistic rationale and promising preliminary in vitro data, yet it also presents several challenges that must be addressed through rigorous further research. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its well-established mode of action as a selective RXR agonist. Its ability to promote heterodimerization with PPARγ and subsequently upregulate genes such as ABCA1 is well supported by a substantial body of research in other disease contexts, including neurodegeneration and oncology (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Gaunt, 2020). This receptor specificity not only underscores bexarotene’s potential to modulate RPE lipid metabolism but also suggests that similar pharmacological principles could translate into the restoration of tight junction integrity—a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD.

Another significant strength is its prior clinical approval for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. This provides a substantial amount of safety data and experience in human use, which could expedite the repurposing process under a drug repositioning strategy. Moreover, the observed in vitro effects—namely the partial restoration of TEER and the increase in ABCA1 mRNA in stressed ARPE-19 cells—lend direct support to the hypothesis that RXR agonism can counteract 7-ketocholesterol-induced disruptions in RPE function (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). The concept of using ocular gel formulations to achieve localized delivery and thereby minimize systemic side effects is another innovative aspect that addresses one of the traditional limitations of bexarotene, namely its adverse systemic metabolic disturbances, which include dyslipidemia and hypothyroidism (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021).

However, there are notable weaknesses that temper this optimism. First, bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties—its high lipophilicity and low solubility—pose a significant formulation challenge, especially when transitioning from systemic oncology applications to local ocular delivery. While gel formulations offer a potential solution, achieving the precise pharmacokinetics and adequate tissue penetration in the retina will require meticulous formulation development and validation. Second, despite the extensive research on RXR agonism in other tissues, there is very limited precedent for the use of bexarotene or similar compounds in the treatment of dry AMD or related ocular diseases. In other words, while the underlying nuclear receptor biology in the retina is compelling, the absence of prior clinical or even robust preclinical ocular studies increases the risk associated with translational uncertainty (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Moreover, systemic side effects associated with bexarotene have been well documented in its approved indications. Although the strategy of localized ocular delivery aims to mitigate these adverse effects, any leakage from the ocular compartment into systemic circulation could potentially re-expose patients to these risks. Additionally, the complexity of dry AMD as a multifactorial disease—with contributions from oxidative stress, inflammation, and complex extracellular matrix alterations—means that modulating only lipid handling and tight junction integrity might not be sufficient to arrest or reverse disease progression. Thus, while the mechanistic hypothesis is sound, it should ideally be integrated into a broader therapeutic strategy that also addresses other pathological mechanisms in dry AMD.

In summary, the proposed use of bexarotene for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic foundation based on RXR agonism and its downstream effects on lipid metabolism and cellular junction integrity. The preliminary in vitro evidence in ARPE-19 cells under 7-ketocholesterol stress is promising, particularly with the reported restoration of TEER and upregulation of ABCA1. The strengths of this candidate include its specificity for RXR, the translational potential backed by its FDA–approved status for an unrelated indication, and the innovative strategy of local ocular delivery through gel formulations. On the other hand, challenges related to its physicochemical properties, potential for systemic side effects, and the overall gaps in preclinical ocular data necessitate further rigorous research. Preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD and careful formulation optimization will be essential next steps to validate the therapeutic potential of bexarotene in this context (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Vatiquinone (EPI-743) is a synthetic, tocopherol-derived quinone originally developed as a vitamin E analogue to counteract inherited mitochondrial diseases. It was synthesized through modifications of the natural vitamin E structure, where oxidation of the tocopherol leads to the formation of a quinone moiety. This design enhances its electron transfer capabilities and confers improved bioavailability and tissue penetration, including the ability to cross the blood–brain barrier. As a member of the quinone class of antioxidants, vatiquinone belongs to a group of compounds that have historically been leveraged to modulate redox homeostasis in tissues under oxidative stress. This class of compounds has been applied in diverse therapeutic areas ranging from neurodegenerative disorders to mitochondrial dysfunction, and its mechanism is chiefly considered beneficial in circumstances where oxidative stress and compromised mitochondrial integrity are primary pathological drivers (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

In addition to its synthetic origins, the pharmacological profile of vatiquinone is characterized by its potent antioxidant activity that exceeds that of traditional compounds like Coenzyme Q10 or idebenone. Its chemical structure allows it to interface efficiently with cellular redox enzymes such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1). The high-affinity interaction between vatiquinone and NQO1 is central to its function, as it is hypothesized to regenerate reduced forms of coenzyme Q and thus support the recycling of critical cellular antioxidants such as glutathione. The ability to catalyze these reactions positions vatiquinone as a compelling agent for therapeutic interventions in conditions marked by chronic oxidative stress, an attribute that underpins the rationale for its proposed use in dry age‐related macular degeneration (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Vatiquinone’s therapeutic history is strongly associated with its development for inherited mitochondrial disorders, most notably Friedreich’s ataxia (FRDA) and Leigh syndrome. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated that vatiquinone modulates oxidative stress response pathways and protects mitochondrial function. In clinical trials conducted in patients with FRDA, vatiquinone was shown to regulate key antioxidant defenses by enhancing the expression of genes such as NQO1 and those involved in glutathione synthesis via activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. This led to improvements in neurological function and confirmed its favorable safety profile, thereby validating its use in outpatient settings for mitochondrial disorders (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Beyond its application in mitochondrial disorders, vatiquinone has been explored in the context of various neurodegenerative diseases, reflecting its capacity to preserve mitochondrial health and ameliorate oxidative injury in neural tissues. Its potent neuroprotective properties, which include mitigating oxidative insults and modulating redox-sensitive signaling pathways, have led to its FDA orphan drug designation for Friedrich’s ataxia. Although the primary focus of vatiquinone research has been in neurodegeneration and mitochondrial impairments, the underlying mechanisms that confer mitochondrial protection and support antioxidant defenses have raised interest in its potential application in ocular diseases such as dry age‐related macular degeneration. Notably, preclinical and anecdotal data have suggested that similar redox imbalances found in inherited mitochondrial diseases are also present in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of patients with dry AMD. However, while the compound’s efficacy and safety have been established in the neurological context, no formal clinical investigations have directly addressed its potential in treating dry AMD or in modulating RPE function (Cores et al., 2023; Chang & Chen, 2024).

The translation of vatiquinone’s antioxidant properties to dry AMD is based on the shared underlying pathology of chronic oxidative stress. Pilot data even indicate viability improvements in ARPE-19, a widely used RPE cell model, under stress conditions. Although these data are preliminary and unpublished, they offer a promising foundation for further research into whether the molecule can enhance RPE barrier integrity, mitigate ROS-mediated damage, and restore transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in an oxidative environment (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of vatiquinone centers on its role as a potent redox-active compound that interacts directly with cellular enzymes such as NQO1. The compound is a high-affinity substrate for NQO1, an enzyme that catalyzes the reversible two-electron reduction of quinones. This reaction is critical because it facilitates the regeneration of reduced coenzyme Q, a vital electron carrier within the mitochondrial respiratory chain. In tissues under chronic oxidative stress, such as the RPE, this reaction ensures the maintenance of mitochondrial function and energy production (Tiberi et al., 2023).

Furthermore, vatiquinone’s chemical structure confers upon it the ability to modulate the activity of the Nrf2 pathway indirectly. Under oxidative stress, Nrf2 normally dissociates from its cytosolic inhibitor Keap1, translocates to the nucleus, and induces the transcription of ARE-driven genes. These genes encode several antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes, including NQO1, glutamate–cysteine ligase, and heme oxygenase-1. By facilitating redox stabilization and promoting a favorable antioxidant environment, vatiquinone indirectly enhances the nuclear stabilization and translocation of Nrf2. This leads to a sustained increase in the expression of key components responsible for glutathione synthesis and recycling, a process crucial for neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and protecting cellular structures (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

At the molecular level, vatiquinone’s interaction with NQO1 not only catalyzes the reduction of the compound itself but also plays a broader role in restoring the redox balance of coenzyme Q within the mitochondrial membrane. The modulation of the redox state of coenzyme Q enhances the function of the electron transport chain and prevents the accumulation of ROS. SAR407899 (Selleckchem S2921) is a small-molecule ATP-competitive inhibitor of Rho-associated coiled-coil containing kinases (ROCKs) that targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2, placing it within the widely studied class of dual ROCK1/2 inhibitors used as chemical tools and therapeutic candidates across vascular, fibrotic, and ocular indications driven by actomyosin contractility and cytoskeletal dysregulation (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). The ATP-binding pockets of ROCK1 and ROCK2 are highly conserved, which has historically favored development of dual-isoform inhibitors (e.g., fasudil, Y-27632, ripasudil, netarsudil) rather than isoform-selective agents; SAR407899 is listed among this majority class of dual-acting molecules in contemporary reviews of rho-kinase modulators for retinal disease (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Multiple dual ROCK inhibitors have been clinically applied: fasudil is approved systemically for cerebral vasospasm and has been evaluated intravitreally for retinal disease, while ripasudil and netarsudil are approved as topical ophthalmic solutions for glaucoma/ocular hypertension, establishing the translational precedent and safety framework for the class in ocular tissues (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). At a mechanistic level, all members of this class block ROCK catalytic activity by binding to the ATP site, thereby reducing phosphorylation of canonical substrates such as MYPT1 (the myosin phosphatase target subunit) and myosin regulatory light chain (MLC), and decreasing downstream actomyosin tension, stress fibers, and focal adhesion assembly that collectively drive barrier breakdown, contraction, and fibrosis (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). While “soft drug” and kinase-selectivity strategies have been advanced to improve tissue targeting and reduce off-target activity, the broad conclusion from medicinal chemistry and pharmacology reviews is that most clinical-grade ROCK inhibitors remain dual-isoform ATP-competitive agents with some potential for off-target kinase interactions at higher exposures—an interpretive caveat for both efficacy and safety (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Liu et al., 2018).
