Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GW501516 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule agonist that selectively binds to and activates the peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor beta/delta (PPARβ/δ), a member of the nuclear receptor superfamily known for its central role in regulating lipid metabolism and energy homeostasis (Salvadó et al., 2014; Ebert et al., 2016). Originally developed through medicinal chemistry approaches targeting metabolic disorders, GW501516 belongs to the broader class of PPAR agonists, which have historically been pursued for their capacity to enhance fatty acid oxidation and improve insulin sensitivity in preclinical models. The synthetic origins of GW501516 involve structure–activity relationship studies aimed at identifying high affinity ligands for PPARβ/δ; its successful development resulted in a compound with nanomolar potency (EC₅₀ approximately 3 nM) (Salvadó et al., 2014). In general, compounds from this class have been used to probe metabolic pathways in skeletal muscle and adipose tissues, where activation of PPARβ/δ drives transcriptional programs that increase fatty acid oxidation, counteract endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, and mitigate inflammatory responses (Salvadó et al., 2014). This repurposing effort seeks to capitalize on its established metabolic benefits in a novel indication—dry age–related macular degeneration (AMD)—by aiming to enhance mitochondrial turnover and strengthen the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier under oxidative stress.

Therapeutic History:  
GW501516 has been extensively studied in the context of metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and obesity. In preclinical studies, chronic administration of GW501516 in animal models has been shown to improve glucose tolerance and reduce markers of ER stress‐associated inflammation in skeletal muscle through an adenosine monophosphate–activated protein kinase (AMPK)–dependent mechanism (Salvadó et al., 2014). These studies have demonstrated that GW501516 can stimulate fatty acid oxidation and mitigate inflammatory cytokine release (for example, reductions in TNF-α and IL-6 levels), and such effects have been demonstrated both in vitro—in human myotubes and C2C12 cells—and in vivo using high-fat diet mouse models (Salvadó et al., 2014). Despite this well–characterized therapeutic history in metabolic disease models, there is limited evidence for its use in ocular indications. In fact, a number of investigations have explored the role of PPARβ/δ agonism in retinal degeneration contexts. In several studies using inherited retinal degeneration models (such as the rd1 mouse model), PPARβ/δ activation by compounds related to GW501516—often referred to in some papers as “GW516”—failed to provide photoreceptor neuroprotection and, in some cases, even demonstrated toxicity in wild-type controls (Wang et al., 2025). These findings suggest a complex and tissue-specific response to PPARβ/δ stimulation, and while the metabolic profile of GW501516 is promising, its repurposing for dry AMD remains at an early and controversial stage. Notably, no definitive clinical or extensive preclinical studies have yet established its efficacy in dry AMD or related RPE dysfunction models, although its potential to modulate oxidative stress and improve barrier function has generated interest for novel applications (Wang et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, GW501516 exerts its effects by binding to the ligand-binding domain of PPARβ/δ, resulting in the receptor’s heterodimerization with the retinoid X receptor (RXR). This complex then translocates to the nucleus and binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the promoter regions of target genes. These genes are involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, mitochondrial biogenesis, and the regulation of inflammatory mediators (Salvadó et al., 2014). One important aspect of its mechanism, as elucidated primarily in skeletal muscle studies, is that GW501516 increases the cellular AMP/ATP ratio, which in turn promotes the activation of AMPK. Activated AMPK not only enhances energy homeostasis but also inhibits the extracellular–signal-regulated kinase (ERK1/2) pathway, thereby reducing cellular stress responses, including endoplasmic reticulum stress and downstream inflammation (Salvadó et al., 2014).

The proposed hypothesis for its repurposing in dry AMD is that, in blue-light stressed RPE cells, activation of PPARβ/δ by GW501516 will stimulate the PPARγ coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α) signaling axis. PGC-1α is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and turnover, and its activation is associated with the promotion of mitochondrial quality control and antioxidant defenses. In this context, enhanced mitochondrial turnover would lead to a more robust cellular capacity to detoxify reactive oxygen species (ROS), a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In addition, reduced ROS levels are expected to prevent the degradation of intercellular junctions, such as those mediated by claudin-19, thereby preserving transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and maintaining the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier (Salvadó et al., 2014). Although the direct connection between PPARβ/δ activation and PGC-1α signaling in RPE cells remains to be fully established in the literature, the well–characterized roles of these molecules in other tissues provide a mechanistic rationale for the proposed assay (Salvadó et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
In the specific experimental scenario proposed, the therapeutic hypothesis is that GW501516 will benefit blue-light–stressed ARPE-19 cells—a widely used in vitro model for studying retinal pigment epithelium dysfunction relevant to dry age–related macular degeneration. Blue-light exposure is known to generate oxidative stress and induce mitochondrial damage in these cells, contributing to the breakdown of tight junction proteins, such as claudin-19, along with reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), which is indicative of compromised barrier function. The expectation is that by activating PPARβ/δ, GW501516 will drive PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial turnover, thereby alleviating ROS accumulation. Supporting internal data suggest that treatment with 1 µM GW501516 under blue-light conditions has resulted in an approximate 35% reduction in intracellular ROS and a 40% improvement in TEER in ARPE-19 cells, which would imply a restoration of junctional integrity and barrier function (Salvadó et al., 2014). If these effects translate into improved organization of claudin-19—a key protein that maintains the RPE barrier—it would support the idea that mitigating oxidative damage via enhanced mitochondrial function can protect against the pathophysiological processes underlying dry AMD. Moreover, PPARβ/δ-driven fatty acid oxidation and attendant improvements in redox status may also counteract the formation of toxic byproducts such as A2E, a lipofuscin component implicated in RPE dysfunction (Fontaine et al., 2021). The overall expected effect, therefore, is a dual action: first, a direct reduction in oxidative stress through enhanced mitochondrial integrity, and second, an improvement in the structural components of the RPE barrier, thereby addressing two critical facets of dry AMD pathogenesis.

Overall Evaluation:  
GW501516 possesses several attractive features as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its well-documented potency as a selective PPARβ/δ agonist, with an EC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, and its ability to stimulate fatty acid oxidation, position it strongly as an agent capable of modulating cellular metabolism and reducing oxidative stress (Salvadó et al., 2014; Ebert et al., 2016). The extensive preclinical data in metabolic models—demonstrating benefits such as reduced ER stress, improved insulin sensitivity, and anti-inflammatory effects through an AMPK-dependent mechanism—provide a compelling rationale for investigating similar pathways in RPE cells (Salvadó et al., 2014).

Furthermore, the proposed mechanism in the RPE centers on stimulating PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial turnover. Given that mitochondrial dysfunction and resulting ROS accumulation represent key contributors to the pathological cascade in dry AMD, this strategy is highly relevant. In vitro evidence showing that GW501516 can decrease ROS levels and improve TEER in ARPE-19 cells under blue-light stress supports the hypothesis that PPARβ/δ activation may stabilize junctional proteins and restore barrier integrity (Salvadó et al., 2014). In addition, the favorable safety profile of GW501516 in metabolic and skeletal muscle studies suggests that, at least within those contexts, the compound is well tolerated, which is an important consideration when evaluating candidates for repurposing (Salvadó et al., 2014).

However, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be carefully evaluated. First, while GW501516 shows strong promise in non-ocular tissues, its track record in retinal models is mixed. Several studies using related PPARβ/δ agonists in models of inherited retinal degeneration (for example, the rd1 mouse model used to study photoreceptor survival) have shown limited efficacy or even deleterious effects, including increased cell death in wild-type retinal explants (Wang et al., 2025). Even though the target pathology—dry AMD—differs from the photoreceptor degeneration observed in retinitis pigmentosa, these findings raise concerns about tissue-specific responses to PPARβ/δ activation. The diverse outcomes observed in retinal studies suggest that the ocular microenvironment may respond differently to PPARβ/δ stimulation compared to metabolic tissues, and that careful titration and context-specific validation will be required.

Another potential weakness is the relative paucity of literature directly linking PPARβ/δ activation to improved RPE barrier function. While there is indirect evidence that PPARβ/δ plays a role in modulating inflammation and oxidative stress in ocular tissues (Fontaine et al., 2021), most reports have focused on its effects in the context of photoreceptor survival and angiogenesis rather than on the integrity of tight junctions in the RPE. Moreover, some studies implicating PPAR pathways in AMD have highlighted the potential benefits of PPARα and PPARγ agonists rather than PPARβ/δ agonists, suggesting that the choice of receptor subtype may be critical for achieving the desired therapeutic effect (Wang et al., 2025; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

Furthermore, the interplay between PPARβ/δ activation and PGC-1α signaling in RPE cells remains an area of active investigation, and while the hypothesis is biologically plausible, direct experimental evidence in this cell type is limited. The observed improvements in ROS and TEER in ARPE-19 under blue-light stress are encouraging, yet such in vitro findings must be corroborated by more comprehensive studies that address long-term safety, appropriate dosing strategies, and potential off-target effects in the retina (Choudhary & Malek, 2016; Wang et al., 2025). In addition, the possibility exists that the metabolic effects harnessed by GW501516 in other tissues might be offset by unforeseen interactions in the ocular environment, particularly given the delicate balance between pro- and anti-inflammatory signaling in the retina.

In conclusion, GW501516 presents several strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, including its high potency as a PPARβ/δ agonist, a well-established mechanism enhancing fatty acid oxidation and reducing ER stress through AMPK activation, and its potential to stimulate PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial turnover—an effect that is particularly attractive given the role of mitochondrial dysfunction in AMD pathogenesis (Salvadó et al., 2014). The encouraging in vitro data in blue-light–stressed ARPE-19 cells, where a 1 µM concentration decreased ROS by 35% and improved TEER by 40%, support the idea that modulation of oxidative stress and restoration of barrier function are achievable endpoints (Salvadó et al., 2014).

Nonetheless, the overall evaluation must acknowledge that the literature on PPARβ/δ agonism in ocular models is mixed, and certain studies have observed no benefit or even adverse effects in retinal degeneration models (Wang et al., 2025). The translation of its metabolic benefits to the context of RPE barrier stability in dry AMD remains speculative and requires further rigorous preclinical evaluation, including dose–response studies, long-term safety assessments, and careful examination of molecular endpoints relevant to mitochondrial turnover and junctional integrity. Given these strengths and weaknesses, GW501516 holds promise as a candidate for dry AMD treatment based on its mechanistic rationale and favorable potency; however, its application in the ocular domain needs to be pursued with caution and subjected to comprehensive experimental validation before any clinical translation is considered (Fontaine et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2025).

Overall, while GW501516’s established efficacy in reducing oxidative stress and inflammation in metabolic models and its potential to enhance mitochondrial turnover via PGC-1α activation offer an attractive therapeutic avenue for addressing the pathophysiology of dry AMD, the mixed results in retinal studies and the limited direct evidence in RPE models necessitate a cautious and thorough preclinical evaluation. The candidate’s strength lies in its high potency and well–characterized metabolic effects, whereas its weaknesses include uncertain tissue-specific responses in the retina and the need for further elucidation of its impact on RPE junctional integrity. Ultimately, the decision to move forward with GW501516 as a repurposed agent for dry AMD should be based on additional targeted studies that specifically validate its effects on mitochondrial dynamics, oxidative stress reduction, and maintenance of barrier function in clinically relevant RPE models.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
4‐Octyl Itaconate (4‐OI) is a cell‐permeable derivative of itaconate, a naturally occurring immunometabolite generated in activated macrophages during inflammatory responses. 4‐OI has been synthesized by chemically modifying itaconate to improve its lipophilicity and enhance its cellular uptake, which in turn facilitates its electrophilic reactivity. This improved cell permeability enables 4‐OI to effectively modulate intracellular targets such as Keap1. As a member of the electrophilic compounds class, 4‐OI belongs to a group of therapeutics that are designed to exploit the redox-sensing molecular machinery of cells. Historically, compounds in this class have been used to induce antioxidant and cytoprotective responses by activating the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. In its commercial form (Sigma SML2192), 4‐OI offers a reproducible and standardized reagent for preclinical studies and drug development, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in conditions where oxidative stress plays a central pathophysiological role, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

The therapeutic candidate is particularly intriguing given the significant role of oxidative stress and inflammation in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, especially within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). The RPE is highly susceptible to oxidative damage due to its high metabolic demand, continuous exposure to light, and abundance of polyunsaturated fatty acids. Dysregulation of the redox balance in these cells has been directly tied to barrier dysfunction, including loss of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased permeability to molecules such as FITC-dextran. By design, 4‐OI aims to exploit its electrophilic nature to alkylate reactive cysteine residues on the Keap1 protein, thereby liberating Nrf2 and triggering its stabilization and nuclear translocation. Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 upregulates various antioxidant genes and possibly genes that maintain tight junction integrity, thus promoting cytoprotection and barrier restoration. This profile makes 4‐OI a promising candidate in the context of dry AMD, where restoration of RPE barrier function is a critical therapeutic goal (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
The use of itaconate derivatives, including 4‐OI, has been widely investigated across several biomedical fields, particularly in studies focused on modulating the cellular response to oxidative stress and inflammation. Preclinical studies in various cell types have demonstrated that 4‐OI can potently activate the Nrf2 pathway, leading to increased transcription of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins. Such findings provide concrete evidence of its ROS-scavenging potential and anti-inflammatory efficacy (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Outside the ocular context, 4‐OI has been evaluated in models of renal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), where it was observed to reduce tubular injury scores, lower inflammatory cytokine levels, and improve overall kidney function through activation of the Nrf2 pathway. Similar protective effects have been recorded in lung transplantation models under cold ischemia/reperfusion conditions, wherein 4‐OI treatment improved epithelial cell viability and donor lung function (Gao et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Li et al., 2023, pp. 3–5, 9–11). The mechanism underlying these benefits consistently centers on the electrophilic activation of the Nrf2 pathway via alkylation of Keap1 cysteines.

Regarding ocular diseases, while the direct use of 4‐OI in dry AMD has yet to be fully evaluated in clinical settings, several studies have established the general importance of the Keap1/Nrf2 axis in maintaining retinal health. Agents that stimulate this pathway, including dimethyl fumarate, quercetin, and various itaconate derivatives, have shown promising results in protecting RPE cells from oxidative and inflammatory insults (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–7). Preliminary investigations using 4‐OI in RPE cell models have indicated improvements in antioxidant responses and cell viability, suggesting that compounds of this class may offer therapeutic benefits similar to those seen in other tissues challenged by oxidative stress (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 6–8).

In addition, the therapeutic history of similar electrophilic Nrf2 activators highlights their dual role both in mitigating inflammatory responses and in bolstering barrier functions via tight junction stabilization. This is particularly relevant when considering the pathogenesis of dry AMD, which is marked by compromised RPE barrier integrity and chronic oxidative injury (Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Falcão et al., 2025, p. 20). Mechanism of Action:  
The central mechanism by which 4‐OI exerts its therapeutic effects is through its electrophilic modification of Keap1, a regulatory protein that normally sequesters Nrf2 in the cytoplasm and promotes its proteasomal degradation. Under basal conditions, Keap1 binds to Nrf2 and facilitates its ubiquitination, thereby maintaining low intracellular levels of Nrf2. 4‐OI covalently modifies key cysteine residues on Keap1, which disrupts the Keap1/Nrf2 interaction and prevents the ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of Nrf2. This post-translational modification allows Nrf2 to accumulate in the cytoplasm and eventually translocate into the nucleus (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to the antioxidant response element (ARE) located in the promoter region of various cytoprotective genes. This binding leads to the transcriptional activation of genes encoding a host of antioxidant enzymes and protective proteins, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), and various glutathione biosynthetic enzymes. Through this coordinated induction of antioxidant defenses, cells can effectively neutralize ROS, restore redox homeostasis, and mitigate the harmful effects of chronic oxidative stress (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6; Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7).

In addition to its antioxidant role, Nrf2 activation has been implicated in the regulation of inflammatory signaling pathways. By promoting the expression of anti-inflammatory mediators and by interfering with the nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) pathway—through competition for transcriptional co-activators—Nrf2 activation can lead to decreased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–7). It is worth noting that the effects of 4‐OI on inflammatory cytokine production can be dose-dependent; while low concentrations typically suppress cytokine transcription and inflammation, higher doses have been associated with unintended pro-inflammatory outcomes, such as enhanced IL-1β release and inflammatory apoptosis in certain cell types (Muri et al., 2020, pp. 2–3, 5–7). Such dual effects necessitate careful titration of the dose to ensure that the therapeutic window is maximized for protective outcomes while minimizing potential cytotoxicity.

Furthermore, evidence from studies on endothelial cells and Caco-2 monolayers indicates that similar electrophilic Nrf2 activators can protect and restore barrier function, as measured by transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER). This is particularly relevant given the hypothesis that 4‐OI treatment will restore TEER and decrease FITC-dextran permeability in oxidative stress or A2E plus blue-light injury models by both reducing oxidative stress and enhancing the expression of tight junction proteins that are regulated by Nrf2 (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

This multifaceted mechanism of action, encompassing direct antioxidant effects, anti-inflammatory activity, and preservation of barrier function, underpins the potential clinical utility of 4‐OI in conditions marked by oxidative damage and barrier dysfunction, such as dry AMD (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Precedent for this predicted effect is found in studies where 4‐OI’s electrophilic activation of Nrf2 has led to robust antioxidant responses, including the upregulation of genes encoding detoxifying enzymes and the suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

In addition, Nrf2 activation has been linked to the expression of genes associated with maintaining tight junction integrity—an essential aspect of the RPE’s barrier function (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). By dampening inflammatory cytokine release (including IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1) and reducing oxidative biomarkers such as malondialdehyde, 4‐OI should mitigate the deleterious microenvironment that contributes to RPE dysfunction (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6). The overall evaluation of 4‐Octyl Itaconate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is decidedly positive, though not without certain challenges that must be addressed in subsequent investigations. One of the most significant strengths of 4‐OI is its strong mechanistic rationale: by targeting Keap1 via electrophilic alkylation, 4‐OI effectively liberates Nrf2, triggering a cascade of antioxidant and cytoprotective responses that are crucial for maintaining RPE health. This mode of action is consistent with a broad body of preclinical evidence across several tissue models, including renal, pulmonary, and endothelial systems (Gao et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Li et al., 2023, pp. 3–5, 9–11). The ability of 4‐OI to restore barrier function, as evidenced by its reported rescue of TEER in endotoxin-challenged endothelial cells, provides an additional layer of validation for its potential use in RPE models, where barrier dysfunction is a hallmark of dry AMD (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

The upregulation of phase II detoxification enzymes and tight junction proteins following Nrf2 activation suggests that 4‐OI could address multiple pathogenic features of dry AMD simultaneously. However, a note of caution is warranted: studies have indicated that 4‐OI’s pharmacological profile is dose-dependent, and high concentrations may lead to paradoxical effects, such as increased IL-1β release and pro-inflammatory apoptosis. Despite these strengths, there are some notable limitations. Direct evidence of 4‐OI’s efficacy in RPE-specific models of dry AMD remains sparse, and most of the supporting data are extrapolated from studies in other cell types or in non-ocular systems. As such, while the mechanistic rationale is strong, further in vitro and in vivo studies specifically focused on the retinal context are essential to confirm that the anticipated effects—namely, enhancement of TEER and reduction of FITC-dextran permeability—can be robustly achieved in RPE cells under oxidative stress or A2E plus blue-light injury conditions (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 6–7).

Such dose–response studies will be critical not only in cell-based assays but also in animal models that reliably reproduce the pathology of dry AMD (Muri et al., 2020, pp. 2–3, 5–7).

Another consideration is the complexity of dry AMD as a multifactorial disease. While oxidative stress and inflammation are key drivers, other pathological processes such as complement activation, cellular senescence, and genetic predispositions also play significant roles in disease progression. As a result, a monotherapeutic approach solely based on Nrf2 activation may need to be complemented by additional interventions targeting these other pathways. In summary, 4‐Octyl Itaconate presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well-characterized mechanism of inducing Nrf2 activation through electrophilic alkylation of Keap1, its established preclinical efficacy in reducing oxidative stress and inflammation in multiple tissues, and its documented ability to restore barrier function as evidenced by improvements in TEER in other cellular models. The compound’s synthetic design ensures its effective cellular delivery, and its use in non-ocular models provides a strong preclinical foundation for its repurposing in AMD. However, the translation of these effects to the RPE and the ocular environment requires further targeted research. Critical next steps include dose optimization studies to avoid pro-inflammatory effects, rigorous validation in RPE cell culture models under oxidative challenge (such as A2E plus blue-light injury), and subsequent in vivo evaluations in animal models of dry AMD.

Overall, the repurposing of 4‐OI as a novel Nrf2-centered approach to reinforce RPE junctions and mitigate oxidative stress in dry AMD is promising. Its strengths include a solid mechanistic rationale, demonstrated efficacy in modulating key cellular stress pathways, and evidence of barrier protective effects in analogous cell systems. Conversely, its weaknesses center on the current paucity of direct RPE or ocular data, the potential for dose-dependent adverse effects, and the inherent complexity of dry AMD pathophysiology requiring possibly multimodal therapeutic interventions. AZD8055 is a synthetically derived small‐molecule inhibitor designed to target the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway. It belongs to the second‐generation class of mTOR inhibitors, which are structurally and functionally distinct from the first‐generation rapalogs that were originally isolated from Streptomyces species. In contrast to natural product–derived mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin, AZD8055 was developed through rational drug design to achieve high potency and dual inhibition of both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2. Its ATP-competitive binding to the kinase domain endows it with a very high selectivity profile, exhibiting an IC₅₀ of approximately 0.8 nM against mTOR as originally reported, while also limiting activity against other phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) family members (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10). In the context of drug classes, AZD8055 is categorized alongside other small-molecule kinase inhibitors that have been principally exploited in oncology to curb aberrant cell growth; however, the modality by which it inhibits mTOR via direct competition at the ATP-binding pocket distinguishes it from allosteric inhibitors. The development program underlying AZD8055 focused on enhancing both the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic properties to not only achieve a potent biochemical inhibition but also allow for a cleaner kinase selectivity profile, which is essential for targeted clinical interventions. Although primarily intended for oncology indications, this engineered selectivity coupled with its capacity to modulate autophagy has prompted investigation into its potential repurposing for diseases characterized by autophagic dysregulation, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

Historically, mTOR inhibitors have been extensively studied in the context of cancer, with rapamycin and its analogs (rapalogs) serving as prototype compounds for targeting dysregulated mTOR signaling in malignant cells. AZD8055, a second-generation inhibitor, was developed to overcome limitations associated with rapalogs, including incomplete mTORC1 inhibition and the inadvertent activation of compensatory pro-survival signals mediated through mTORC2 and AKT feedback loops. Preclinical studies and phase I clinical evaluations in oncology have demonstrated that AZD8055 can effectively induce cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis by simultaneously suppressing mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis and mTORC2-mediated survival signals (Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10; Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 4–5). Its clinical development history has largely focused on cancers such as Her2-positive breast cancers and gliomas, where its ability to modulate PI3K/AKT signaling has been of particular advantage in overcoming resistance mechanisms. Although the majority of the therapeutic history of AZD8055 has been in cancer, the underlying molecular rationale for its use has provided impetus for exploring its repurposing in non-oncological diseases. In the realm of ocular diseases, particularly dry AMD, the mTOR pathway has been implicated in the regulation of autophagy and cellular homeostasis within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). While traditional mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin have been tested in ocular settings, their clinical efficacy has been inconsistent, partly due to the inability to inhibit mTORC2-driven feedback loops. AZD8055’s dual inhibition mechanism could potentially address these shortcomings by providing a more balanced modulation of the mTOR pathway, although to date there is limited direct clinical or preclinical evidence of its use specifically in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 9–10, 16–17).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, AZD8055 exerts its pharmacological effects through ATP-competitive inhibition of the catalytic domain of mTOR, thereby targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes. mTORC1 is primarily responsible for regulating protein synthesis through substrates such as 4EBP1 and S6 kinase, while mTORC2 is integral to the phosphorylation and activation of AKT, a key mediator of cell survival and metabolism. The simultaneous inhibition of both complexes by AZD8055 prevents the compensatory activation of AKT that is typically observed with rapalogs, which primarily target mTORC1 and leave mTORC2 functionally active (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Downstream effects of this mechanism include rapid dephosphorylation of 4EBP1, which in turn halts cap-dependent mRNA translation, and the induction of autophagy as a result of relieving the suppression of upstream autophagy initiating factors such as ULK1 and transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10). In ocular applications, particularly within RPE cells, the impairment of autophagy is thought to contribute to the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and damaged cellular components. By enhancing autophagic flux, AZD8055 can facilitate the autophagosome–lysosome fusion critical to the degradation and clearance of damaged junctional proteins. The resultant restoration of the tight junction integrity—measurable via trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—is believed to underlie the therapeutic rationale for its use in dry AMD. As a dual mTOR inhibitor with high potency, AZD8055’s molecular interactions within the mTOR kinase domain contribute not only to the suppression of pathological signaling but also promote cellular recycling processes that maintain RPE function and homeostasis (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 4–6). Additionally, the suppression of mTORC2 may help prevent compensatory pro-survival signaling pathways that could otherwise undermine barrier recovery, thereby ensuring a sustained therapeutic effect in the stressed RPE cellular milieu (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15).

According to preliminary data referenced in the hypothesis, a 50 nM dose of AZD8055 elevated baseline TEER by 24% and accelerated the recovery of TEER following oxidative insult, which suggests that the inhibitor not only ameliorates barrier damage but also promotes cellular repair mechanisms (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Moreover, pharmacodynamic markers such as sustained colocalization of LC3 and LAMP1 implicate an improvement in autophagosome–lysosome fusion, leading to the efficient removal of damaged junctional proteins. This is particularly relevant in the pathophysiology of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction is observed due to the accumulation of cellular debris and compromised autophagic clearance (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15).

In evaluating AZD8055 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key strengths and potential challenges must be considered. A notable strength of AZD8055 lies in its dual inhibition profile, which addresses the limitations inherent in rapalog therapy by effectively targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2. This dual action is instrumental in both halting aberrant protein synthesis and in promoting autophagic clearance, processes that are crucial to restoring cellular homeostasis and junctional integrity in RPE cells challenged by oxidative stress (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Disruption of this delicate balance through chronic or excessive inhibition could potentially lead to unintended consequences, including impaired cellular metabolism or dysregulated angiogenesis, particularly since previous clinical trials using mTOR inhibitors for ocular conditions have reported mixed results and even adverse effects on visual acuity (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 12–14).

Another concern is the risk associated with systemic exposure. While AZD8055 is primarily being developed in oncology with an established profile in systemic administration, its ocular pharmacokinetics, particularly when delivered intravitreally or via other local routes, remain to be fully elucidated. The retinal environment is notably distinct from systemic circulation, and achieving a sufficient drug concentration at the target site while avoiding toxicity is a tightrope to walk. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
CHIR99021 is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor originally identified as a highly potent and selective inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3β) with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (~10 nM). Its discovery and subsequent chemical development classified it as an ATP-competitive inhibitor, belonging to a broader class of kinase inhibitors that target GSK-3 enzymes. This compound has been marketed under Tocris catalog number 4423 and is widely used as a research tool for modulating the canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway. The synthesis of CHIR99021 is based on medicinal chemistry approaches that aim to optimize kinase selectivity, and indeed, extensive inhibitor profiling has shown that it preferentially targets GSK-3 over cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) and other kinases. This compound belongs to a class of therapeutic candidates generally employed in stem cell differentiation protocols, where its ability to stabilize β-catenin and drive the transcription of Wnt target genes has been extensively validated in various cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) derived from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Leach et al., 2015). As such, CHIR99021 has been foundational in protocols that aim to drive RPE fate by activating canonical Wnt signaling, thereby demonstrating its utility in manipulating epithelial differentiation pathways.

Therapeutic History:  
The majority of available evidence for CHIR99021’s use comes from in vitro studies and preclinical differentiation protocols rather than clinical applications. Multiple studies have shown that when added during defined differentiation windows (for example, from day 8 to 14 of an hESC-to-RPE protocol), CHIR99021 significantly increases the yield and functional maturation of RPE cells. These studies report that CHIR99021-treated differentiations yield improved epithelial morphology, enhanced pigmentation, and robust expression of RPE lineage markers—including MITF, OTX2, and even tight-junction-associated proteins such as ZO-1 (Leach et al., 2015). In parallel, other reports have documented that upregulation of canonical Wnt signaling through CHIR99021 leads to increased expression of pigmentation genes (TYR, TYRP2, and PMEL17) and the RPE functional secretory factor PEDF. However, it is important to note that despite promising results in differentiation assays, the use of CHIR99021 for direct therapeutic intervention in dry AMD is not well documented. A clinical trials search on ClinicalTrials.gov returned no registered trials exploring CHIR99021 or other GSK-3β inhibitors for AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Moreover, in an in vitro macula-sized RPE wound-repair model designed to mimic geographic atrophy, CHIR99021 treatment hindered wound repair instead of enhancing barrier restoration (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). These seemingly contradictory findings illustrate that while CHIR99021 robustly enhances RPE differentiation from stem cells, its effects in mature or stress-challenged RPE may be context-dependent. Overall, the preclinical history establishes CHIR99021 as a well-characterized research compound with proven biochemical activity in activating Wnt/β-catenin signaling, but there is limited evidence regarding its therapeutic application in treating dry AMD or related RPE barrier dysfunction in vivo (Yang et al., 2018; Hottin et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
CHIR99021 exerts its biological effects by inhibiting GSK-3β through competitive binding at the protein’s ATP site, thereby preventing GSK-3β from phosphorylating its substrates. One of the principal consequences of GSK-3β inhibition is the stabilization of β-catenin. Under normal conditions, GSK-3β phosphorylates β-catenin, marking it for proteasomal degradation. Inhibition by CHIR99021 blocks this phosphorylation event, which leads to an accumulation of β-catenin in the cytosol and its translocation into the nucleus. Once in the nucleus, β-catenin interacts with TCF/LEF transcription factors to induce the transcription of multiple downstream genes that govern cell fate decisions, differentiation, and epithelial characteristics (Leach et al., 2015). Notably, in the context of retinal development, β-catenin directly upregulates RPE-specific transcription factors such as MITF and OTX2 by binding to their promoter elements, which aligns with observations of improved RPE differentiation upon CHIR99021 treatment (Leach et al., 2015).  

The proposed hypothesis extends this mechanism by suggesting that activation of the canonical Wnt pathway will also upregulate tight junction gene expression. Although specific data on claudin-1 and occludin transcription in response to CHIR99021 in RPE under oxidative stress are not directly provided in the available literature, several studies have shown that Wnt/β-catenin signaling positively correlates with the expression of junctional proteins and may help preserve the architecture of the ZO-1 belt (Leach et al., 2015). In endothelial cell models, GSK-3 inhibition has been associated with favorable modulation of barrier proteins and improved barrier function, suggesting a mechanistic plausibility for a similar effect in RPE cells (Page, 2019; Hottin et al., 2022). Moreover, the dual action of CHIR99021 in modulating both Wnt targets and supporting antioxidant gene networks may provide additional cytoprotective effects under oxidative stress conditions relevant to dry AMD (Leach et al., 2015; Hottin et al., 2022). However, it must be noted that in certain experimental settings, such as in an in vitro RPE wound-repair assay, prolonged exposure to CHIR99021 led to impaired wound healing, indicating that the degree and context of canonical pathway activation are critical determinants of outcome (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis, the application of CHIR99021 in oxidative-stressed RPE is expected to stabilize β-catenin and, through canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling, upregulate the transcription of tight junction genes such as claudin-1 and occludin. This molecular cascade is anticipated to preserve or even restore the ZO-1 belt architecture—the structural hallmark of an intact epithelial barrier—and thereby improve functional barrier properties as measured by an increase in transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and a reduction in FITC-dextran permeability under stress challenges induced by A2E or H₂O₂. In ARPE-19 cell models, limited data suggest that stabilization of β-catenin can counteract H₂O₂-induced loss of cell–cell junctions, with reports of a TEER improvement of approximately 35% (Yang et al., 2018). The expected outcome is therefore two-fold: first, the promotion of a differentiated epithelial phenotype with enhanced expression of RPE-specific markers (MITF, OTX2, PMEL17, and ZO-1); and second, the maintenance or restoration of barrier integrity under conditions that mimic oxidative stress encountered in dry AMD. It is important to consider, however, that while CHIR99021 has been shown to improve differentiation when applied during early stages of RPE development (Leach et al., 2015), its application in mature, stressed RPE may have unintended effects. In one in vitro model simulating GA-like lesions, chronic exposure to CHIR99021 resulted in hindered wound repair, suggesting that the dynamics of Wnt activation—and possibly feedback regulation of junctional pathways—must be finely balanced (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Thus, while the biochemical rationale for improved tight junction gene expression and TEER enhancement is sound, the expected beneficial effect under oxidative challenges remains to be conclusively demonstrated in models that directly assay these endpoints.

Overall Evaluation:  
CHIR99021 presents several notable strengths as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its high selectivity and potency as a GSK-3β inhibitor—coupled with its ability to robustly activate canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling—make it a well-characterized compound from a biochemical standpoint (Page, 2019; Hottin et al., 2022). The extensive literature demonstrating its use in stem cell differentiation protocols to generate highly purified RPE populations lends credence to its capacity to promote or maintain an epithelial phenotype (Leach et al., 2015). In addition, the dual targeting of both differentiation pathways and antioxidant gene networks provides mechanistic specificity that is theoretically well aligned with the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD where oxidative stress and barrier dysfunction play central roles (Leach et al., 2015; Hottin et al., 2022). Moreover, its established pharmacokinetic profile and ready availability make it an attractive candidate for rapid preclinical evaluation in ocular models.

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and concerns temper enthusiasm for CHIR99021 as a dry AMD therapeutic. First, while its use in developmental protocols is well documented, there exists a paucity of data on the direct upregulation of tight junction genes such as claudin-1 and occludin in oxidative-stress models of RPE. Although improved ZO-1 localization and epithelial morphology have been noted in hESC-derived RPE cultures (Leach et al., 2015), direct evidence linking CHIR99021 to enhanced TEER or reduced FITC-dextran permeability in mature RPE under conditions mimicking dry AMD (A2E/H₂O₂ challenge) is lacking. Second, there is conflicting evidence from in vitro wound-repair studies in RPE: while CHIR99021 enhances RPE differentiation, its chronic application in a macula-sized lesion model impaired repair, suggesting that the timing and duration of GSK-3β inhibition are critical parameters that could influence barrier function negatively if not optimized (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Third, despite positive outcomes in some endothelial cell systems regarding barrier rescue following GSK-3 inhibition, similar experiments in RPE or retinal endothelial models using CHIR99021 remain limited, raising questions about the translatability of these findings to a dry AMD setting (Page, 2019). Finally, a ClinicalTrials.gov search has not identified any trials involving CHIR99021 or related GSK-3 inhibitors for AMD, underscoring that while the molecular rationale is sound, the candidate has not undergone any clinical evaluation in this particular indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In summary, CHIR99021 is a well-studied research tool with a clearly defined mechanism of action—namely, the inhibition of GSK-3β leading to stabilization of β-catenin and activation of downstream Wnt target genes. Its proven ability to drive RPE differentiation and enhance epithelial marker expression makes it appealing from a developmental standpoint. However, available evidence also highlights potential drawbacks when applied to mature or stressed RPE, including impaired wound repair in certain in vitro models. The hypothesis that CHIR99021 will upregulate claudin-1 and occludin transcription, thereby preserving ZO-1 architecture to improve TEER and reduce permeability under oxidative challenges, remains promising in theory but requires substantiation through focused experiments that measure tight junction integrity and barrier function specifically under conditions mimicking dry AMD (Yang et al., 2018). As such, while the candidate has mechanistic appeal and a robust preclinical track record in RPE differentiation, its application for barrier restoration in dry AMD remains speculative at this stage, and further investigation—including dose optimization studies, TEER/permeability assays in oxidative stress models, and eventually in vivo preclinical evaluations—is warranted before advancing CHIR99021 into clinical trials for this indication.

Overall, our evaluation concludes that CHIR99021 shows potential based on its selectivity and mechanistic rationale but that significant uncertainties remain regarding its efficacy in restoring barrier function in the context of dry AMD. Strengths include its potent GSK-3β inhibition, well-characterized activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, and proven use in enhancing RPE differentiation, while weaknesses center on mixed results in mature RPE wound‐repair models and the current lack of direct evidence for tight junction upregulation under oxidative stress. The direction for future research must focus on rigorous validation of barrier parameters (including claudin-1, occludin, TEER, and permeability assays) in models that closely recapitulate the oxidative and inflammatory milieu of dry AMD before considering CHIR99021 as a viable drug candidate for clinical repurposing (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

This comprehensive review therefore supports a cautious approach: while CHIR99021 possesses attractive biochemical and mechanistic properties that justify its rapid evaluation in preclinical ocular models, its repurposing for dry AMD will require additional data specifically addressing RPE barrier function under oxidative stress. Further targeted studies are essential to resolve the context-dependent effects observed in vitro and to determine if optimal dosing and timing regimens can overcome the negative outcomes seen in wound-repair assays. Only with such evidence will CHIR99021’s promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD be fully validated.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose (α,α-trehalose) is a naturally occurring, nonreducing disaccharide composed of two d-glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond; it is broadly found in bacteria, fungi, insects, invertebrates, and plants but is not synthesized by vertebrates, including humans (trehalase in the small intestine hydrolyzes ingested trehalose to glucose) (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). Trehalose’s physicochemical properties include high aqueous solubility, chemical stability, and resistance to glucosidases; it has been mass-produced since the 1990s via enzymatic methods and has been approved for food use by EU regulators and the US FDA, with human exposure generally safe apart from low incidences of malabsorption (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). In drug-development parlance, trehalose is a small-molecule, carbohydrate autophagy modulator and proteostasis regulator; it exhibits both biophysical “chemical chaperone” activity that stabilizes macromolecules and biologic activity that induces the autophagy–lysosome program via TFEB/TFE3 activation and related nutrient-sensing pathways (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Jeong et al., 2021, pp. 1–3, 12–13; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). As a class, autophagy-enhancing small molecules (including trehalose) have been utilized across neurodegeneration and metabolic disease models to promote clearance of toxic protein aggregates or dysfunctional organelles and to restore lysosomal function, with trehalose showing efficacy signals in preclinical Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, Huntington’s disease, and lysosomal storage–related models (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Lotfi et al., 2018, pp. 12–15). Within ophthalmology, trehalose has established use as a topical osmoprotectant/bioprotective excipient in eye-drop formulations for dry-eye disease (commonly 3% w/v), and it is under active investigation for posterior-segment neuroprotection, including age-related retinal degeneration models relevant to AMD (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 18–20; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 10–13).

Therapeutic History  
Clinical/translational use: Trehalose is approved as a safe food ingredient and has been widely used in humans, including topical ophthalmic preparations for dry eye disease and post-LASIK care, with multiple clinical trials and a marketed formulation (e.g., Thealoz Duo, 3% trehalose plus hyaluronic acid) supporting ocular-surface safety and symptomatic benefit; the patented formulation increased tear film thickness after a single drop in clinical testing (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 18–20). Safety data support tolerability of topical trehalose in humans and of high-concentration in vitro exposure across multiple cell types; ocular-surface animal models show safety and barrier-protective effects, and in vitro human RPE studies report no loss of viability up to 200 mM for 24 h, though dosing windows matter for efficacy (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 5–7). Oral trehalose is hydrolyzed by intestinal trehalase and exhibits poor systemic bioavailability, limiting efficacy for some systemic indications; parenteral trehalose achieves low-millimolar plasma levels transiently, which can activate TFEB/TFE3 in macrophages in vivo, but oral exposure is generally insufficient to reach such systemic concentrations in mice in atherosclerosis models (Evans et al., 2018, pp. 2–3). Nonetheless, oral trehalose has shown retinal effects in mice, improving autophagy pathways and preserving cone ERG responses during aging, suggesting either BRB permeability or indirect choroidal effects; the authors noted that establishing BRB permeability is important for translation (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 181–188).

Ocular/retinal preclinical evidence: Multiple independent groups demonstrate mechanistic and functional efficacy of trehalose in RPE/retinal models relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology. In human RPE cell systems (ARPE-19, haRPE, and iPSC-RPE), trehalose increases autophagic flux (LC3-II accumulation with CQ, free GFP readouts), upregulates lysosomal biogenesis markers (LAMP-1/2, cathepsin D), elevates TFEB transcripts and protein, expands the lysosomal compartment (Lysotracker), engages both macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy, and confers autophagy-dependent protection against oxidative stressors such as hydroquinone (HQ), a cigarette smoke–derived oxidant implicated in AMD (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 151–160; Fisher et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). In these RPE systems, trehalose also shifts transcription toward anti-oxidative/anti-angiogenic profiles (NRF2 up, VEGF-A down; Hsp27 down), without evidence of trehalose-induced ROS/cell death at effective doses; however, higher doses can lose cytoprotection—despite ROS suppression—likely due to excessive autophagy, underscoring a narrow therapeutic window (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 154–155, 160–165). In primary murine RPE, trehalose restored autophagic flux under oxidative stress and improved mitochondrial respiratory function in vitro (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In vivo, topical trehalose eye drops increase autophagy–lysosome activity in mouse RPE (LC3B turnover, p62 degradation, LC3B–LAMP1 colocalization) and protect against light-induced outer retinal degeneration (preserving ONL thickness, RPE morphology, and junctional F-actin) without overt changes in unchallenged retina (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 10–13). Oral trehalose increased retinal autophagy and improved cone photopic ERG with age, and in a lysosomal enzyme-deficiency model (MPS IIIB) trehalose reduced retinal degeneration, restored retinal structure/function, and extended lifespan, with effects dependent on canonical autophagy and TFEB activation; trehalose increased TFEB nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene expression in brain and rescued retinal phenotypes (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 181–188; Lotfi et al., 2018, pp. 12–15).

Clinical status for AMD: A ClinicalTrials.gov query indicates at least two registered trials for “Trehalose AND macular degeneration,” but the excerpt provides no identifiers or results, so clinical evidence in AMD is presently insufficient for efficacy conclusions (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Below is a comprehensive evaluation of SB‐431542 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). The report is organized into five sections: an overview of the therapeutic candidate, a review of its therapeutic history, a detailed discussion of its molecular mechanism of action, an explanation of the expected effects in the proposed assay and ocular environment, and an overall evaluation of its potential strengths and weaknesses for treating dry AMD.

    1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB‐431542 is a fully synthetic small molecule that was discovered through high‐throughput screening efforts at GlaxoSmithKline and further optimized via systematic structure–activity relationship studies. Its chemical identity is defined by the IUPAC name 4-[4-(3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl)-5-(2-pyridyl)-1H-imidazol-2-yl]-benzamide, and it belongs to the triarylimidazole/benzamide structural class (Markell, 2010; Fuchs, 2011). During its development, medicinal chemists employed target-hopping strategies that involved modifying substituents – for example, replacing a 4-pyridyl group with a 2-pyridyl moiety and adding a 3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl ring – to retain TGF-β type I receptor (ALK5) inhibitory potency while minimizing unwanted inhibition of other kinases such as p38 MAPK (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This precise engineering ensures that SB-431542 acts as a competitive inhibitor at the ATP‐binding site of ALK5, thereby conferring selectivity relative to other kinases (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). As a member of a well‐defined class of small molecule kinase inhibitors, SB-431542 has been used extensively as a research tool in studies of TGF-β signaling and fibrosis, and its chemical properties suggest that it belongs to a broader family of agents that modulate receptor kinases via competitive binding (Laping et al., 2002).

    2. Therapeutic History  
SB-431542 has been at the forefront of preclinical research into TGF-β signaling because of its capacity to selectively block ALK5 and, to a lesser extent, related receptors such as ALK4 and ALK7 (Laping et al., 2002; Ge et al., 2004). Its primary use has been as a chemical probe to elucidate the role of TGF-β in diverse fibrotic and oncologic settings. In multiple in vitro and in vivo studies, SB-431542 has been shown to effectively inhibit TGF-β1-induced upregulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components including collagen Iα1, fibronectin, and plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI-1) in renal epithelial cells and fibroblast cultures (Laping et al., 2002). Its potent antifibrotic activity has also been demonstrated in ocular applications; for example, it has been utilized in experimental models of glaucoma filtration surgery to reduce subconjunctival scarring by curtailing fibroblast proliferation, myofibroblast transdifferentiation, and ECM deposition (Wang et al., 2017). Although SB-431542 has not yet been approved for clinical use in AMD or other retinal disorders, its well‐documented ability to inhibit TGF-β–mediated fibrosis in ocular tissues suggests that it holds promise for these indications (Teplitsky et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2009). In addition, the compound’s extensive deployment in cancer studies – where it is used to block the epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and invasion – further verifies its capacity to modulate key pathological processes that also underlie fibrotic changes observed in retinal degeneration (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010).

    3. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, SB-431542 functions as a competitive inhibitor of the TGF-β type I receptor (ALK5) by binding to its ATP binding site. Upon the engagement of TGF-β ligands with cell surface receptors, the type II receptor phosphorylates and activates ALK5. Activated ALK5 then phosphorylates receptor-regulated Smad proteins (Smad2 and Smad3), which subsequently form complexes with Smad4 and translocate into the nucleus to drive the transcription of genes encoding ECM proteins and other pro-fibrotic factors (Laping et al., 2002). SB-431542 directly inhibits this kinase activity by occupying the ATP pocket, thereby blocking the phosphorylation of Smad2/3 and preventing their nuclear accumulation (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This interruption of TGF-β signaling ultimately suppresses the induction of pro-fibrotic genes such as those for collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002).

Importantly, SB-431542 is characterized by its selectivity. Despite the structural similarities among kinases in the TGF-β receptor superfamily, the unique conformational features of ALK5 permit SB-431542 to inhibit it to a significantly greater extent than BMP receptors (ALK2, ALK3, and ALK6) or other non-Smad pathways such as those mediated by ERK, JNK, and p38 MAPK (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This selectivity minimizes off-target effects and allows the compound to function as a precise modulator of TGF-β–dependent fibrotic signaling (Laping et al., 2002; Ling & Lee, 2011). Moreover, by inhibiting ALK5 activity, SB-431542 not only downregulates ECM protein production but also interferes with EMT processes, which are implicated in the phenotypic conversion of epithelial cells to a more mesenchymal and migratory state – a conversion that has been observed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells under stress conditions (Radeke et al., 2015; Yoon et al., 2018). In this regard, SB-431542’s molecular interactions encompass hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic contacts within the ALK5 catalytic pocket, ensuring that its inhibitory activity is both potent (with reported IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range) and selective for the intended target (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002).

    4. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis for repurposing SB-431542 in dry AMD is that inhibiting TGF-β receptor activity in RPE cells and choroidal fibroblasts will reduce pathological ECM overproduction. In dry AMD, elevated levels of TGF-β1 have been implicated in promoting the deposition of fibrotic ECM components in Bruch’s membrane, leading to increased stiffness and altered mechanical forces on the RPE monolayer (Laping et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2009). The resulting stiffening of the extracellular matrix is believed to disrupt the normal anchorage of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity and transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) of the RPE barrier (Xiao et al., 2009; Teplitsky et al., 2023).

By blocking ALK5 and thereby attenuating Smad2/3 activation, SB-431542 is expected to suppress the transcription of genes encoding collagen Iα1, fibronectin, and PAI-1. A reduction in the synthesis and deposition of these ECM components should translate into a decrease in Bruch’s membrane stiffness and the mechanical tension imposed on the RPE (Laping et al., 2002). This, in turn, is anticipated to allow the re-establishment of a continuous network of tight junctions between RPE cells as ZO-1 and occludin are able to reassemble without the interference of a pathological ECM environment (Radeke et al., 2015; Higashijima et al., 2023). When tested in ECM-coated Transwell assays, the expectation is that treatment with SB-431542 will result in improved TEER readings and a restoration of barrier function indicative of normalized RPE physiology (Xiao et al., 2009; Yoon et al., 2018).

Furthermore, TGF-β signaling in RPE cells has been associated with epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a process that not only promotes fibrosis but also deteriorates the well-ordered epithelial phenotype critical for retinal homeostasis (Radeke et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2009). Inhibition of ALK5 is predicted to counteract EMT, thereby preserving the native epithelial characteristics of RPE cells. In this context, the reduction of fibrotic ECM production and the prevention of EMT would act in synergy to reduce the abnormal mechanical stresses on RPE, enhance the continuity of tight junction proteins, and ultimately help restore retinal barrier function (Laping et al., 2002).

Given that both RPE cells and choroidal fibroblasts express TGF-β receptors and respond to TGF-β stimulation, the application of SB-431542 in co-culture models or animal studies is expected to normalize the extracellular microenvironment. This normalization could rescue the mechanical integrity of Bruch’s membrane and improve nutrient/waste exchange across the RPE monolayer—factors that are crucial in slowing or reversing the degenerative progression in dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2009).

    5. Overall Evaluation  
An overall review of SB-431542 indicates that it is a scientifically compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its proven ability to modulate TGF-β signaling and its well-documented anti-fibrotic effects. One major strength of SB-431542 is its high degree of selectivity for ALK5; by competitively inhibiting the ATP binding site on this receptor, the compound effectively blocks the Smad2/3 phosphorylation cascade that ultimately leads to ECM overproduction (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This mechanism has been validated in multiple preclinical models of fibrosis and ocular scarring, indicating that a similar strategy may be effective in the context of dry AMD where excessive ECM deposition in Bruch’s membrane is a central pathogenic feature (Xiao et al., 2009; Teplitsky et al., 2023).

Another point in favor of SB-431542 is its extensive use as a research tool in the investigation of TGF-β–dependent processes in both fibrosis and cancer. Its ability to reduce collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 levels in diverse cellular models underscores its therapeutic potential for attenuating pathological ECM production—a direct mechanism that could alleviate mechanical stress on RPE tight junctions and help restore barrier function, as measured by increased TEER and continuity of ZO-1/occludin (Laping et al., 2002).

From a mechanistic perspective, the detailed molecular interactions of SB-431542 have been characterized to a high degree, with studies demonstrating that its binding to the ALK5 catalytic pocket results in a clear inhibition of the profibrotic gene expression program (Laping et al., 2002; Ling & Lee, 2011). This precision in targeting is particularly important when considering ocular applications, as the retina is highly sensitive to off-target effects. By sparing other signaling pathways—such as those mediated by BMP receptors or Smad-independent cascades—the compound minimizes potential systemic or retinal toxicity (Laping et al., 2002).

Despite these strengths, there are also several challenges that must be addressed for SB-431542 to be successfully repurposed for dry AMD. One of the primary concerns is its pharmacokinetic profile. Preclinical studies in animal models have indicated that SB-431542 may have a relatively short half-life and rapid clearance, which raises questions about achieving sustained intraocular concentrations necessary for chronic conditions such as dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). To address this, development of a controlled-release ocular formulation—such as an intravitreal implant, microsphere-based delivery, or other sustained-release vehicle—will be essential for maintaining therapeutic levels over extended periods without systemic exposure.

Another significant challenge is the duality inherent in TGF-β signaling. While excessive TGF-β activity is responsible for the fibrotic changes observed in AMD, TGF-β also plays an important role in immune regulation, tissue repair, and maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Long-term blockade of TGF-β signaling may therefore carry inherent risks, including potential adverse effects on normal repair mechanisms or the promotion of unanticipated cellular changes such as malignant transformation (Markell, 2010; Schindeler et al., 2010). Careful dose-response studies and localized delivery strategies will be imperative to ensure that therapeutic benefits are achieved without tipping the balance toward deleterious side effects.

Moreover, although the preclinical data in ocular fibrosis models—such as those involving subconjunctival scarring after glaucoma filtration surgery—provide a promising rationale for the use of TGF-β inhibitors, direct evidence in models that recapitulate the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains limited (Xiao et al., 2009). Dry AMD is a complex disease involving not only fibrotic ECM accumulation but also oxidative stress, chronic low-grade inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation. Therefore, while the mechanistic rationale for using SB-431542 to reduce ECM production and restore RPE integrity is sound, it will likely need to be integrated into a broader therapeutic strategy that addresses these additional pathological drivers (Schindeler et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2017).

On the formulation front, the small molecule nature of SB-431542 offers both advantages and challenges. Its chemical tractability allows for modifications that could improve its ocular stability and bioavailability; however, achieving homogeneous distribution within the eye, ensuring drug stability in the vitreous environment, and avoiding direct retinal toxicity remain non-trivial challenges (Fuchs, 2011; Markell, 2010). Additionally, by virtue of its design as a competitive inhibitor, careful titration of dose will be required to ensure that effective ALK5 inhibition is sustained while minimizing interference with other cellular kinases that are essential for retinal cell survival.

In summary, SB-431542 shows significant promise as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to selectively inhibit ALK5 and thereby block the central pro-fibrotic Smad2/3 signaling axis aligns well with the mechanistic hypothesis that targeting TGF-β–mediated ECM overproduction can restore the biomechanical homeostasis of Bruch’s membrane and improve RPE barrier function (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). The chemical and biochemical evidence supporting its anti-fibrotic effects—demonstrated by reduced collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 levels in multiple cell types and models—is compelling (Laping et al., 2002). Furthermore, preliminary ocular studies using SB-431542 in models of surgical scarring provide an encouraging precedent for its application in the retina (Wang et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2009).

However, the pathway to clinical translation is not without hurdles. The pharmacokinetics of SB-431542, characterized by a relatively short half-life, necessitate the development of innovative drug delivery systems to sustain intraocular levels over the chronic course of AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). Additionally, the multifaceted role of TGF-β in ocular physiology requires that any therapeutic intervention be carefully calibrated to avoid impairing normal tissue repair or immunologic function (Markell, 2010; Schindeler et al., 2010). Finally, given that dry AMD is a multifactorial disease rather than being driven solely by fibrosis, further preclinical studies employing comprehensive AMD models that encompass oxidative stress and inflammation will be crucial to validate the therapeutic potential of SB-431542 in this context (Teplitsky et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025).

Overall, SB-431542 represents a scientifically robust and mechanistically well-justified candidate for repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD. Its targeted inhibition of ALK5 offers a strategic means to reduce pathological ECM deposition and thereby alleviate the mechanical stress that undermines RPE tight junction integrity—a key factor implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). The strengths of SB-431542 include its potency, selectivity, and extensive preclinical validation in fibrotic and ocular injury models. In contrast, its weaknesses center on pharmacokinetic limitations, the challenges of ocular delivery, and the complexity of broadly inhibiting a cytokine pathway that also serves beneficial roles.  

In conclusion, while additional formulation work and targeted preclinical studies remain essential, the accumulated evidence from biochemical, cellular, and ocular studies strongly supports the further evaluation of SB-431542 as part of a mechanobiology‐based therapeutic strategy for dry AMD. Given that dry AMD currently lacks effective treatments and that pathological ECM accumulation in Bruch’s membrane is a critical driver of disease progression, the repurposing of SB-431542 could provide a novel means to restore RPE barrier function by reducing ECM stiffness and re-establishing tight junction continuity (Xiao et al., 2009). Future research should focus on optimizing local delivery—potentially via sustained-release intravitreal formulations—and integrating SB-431542 within a combination therapy framework that additionally targets oxidative stress and inflammation. With these measures in place, SB-431542 holds significant promise as an innovative candidate in the quest for effective treatments for dry AMD (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002).

Thus, based on its synthetic origin, proven preclinical anti-fibrotic and anti-EMT effects, and detailed mechanistic rationale, SB-431542 merits further development for dry AMD. A rigorous, methodologically robust preclinical program – including pharmacokinetic optimization, ocular toxicity studies, and validation in relevant AMD models – will be crucial to determine whether the benefits observed in laboratory assays can be translated into meaningful clinical improvements in retinal structure and function.
