2. Therapeutic History

Clinically, isradipine has been deployed primarily in the management of cardiovascular disorders. Its use in treatment regimens for hypertension and angina pectoris is well documented, with decades of clinical experience supporting its efficacy and safety in reducing peripheral vascular resistance and relieving myocardial ischemia (Schachter, 1991). As a member of the DHP family, its predictable absorption, metabolism, and elimination have rendered it a mainstay in cardiovascular pharmacotherapy, with adverse effects generally limited to dose-dependent vasodilation-related symptoms such as headache and peripheral edema (Hof & Rüegg, 1988; Striessnig, 1999).

Beyond its cardiovascular applications, isradipine has recently been evaluated as a neuroprotective agent in several contexts. Preclinical data indicate that isradipine can reduce harmful calcium influx in neuronal populations, particularly in dopaminergic neurons that are at risk in Parkinson’s disease (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Ilijic et al., 2011). In these studies, isradipine’s ability to cross the blood–brain barrier and selectively inhibit LTCCs has been exploited to mitigate mitochondrial oxidative stress and calcium-mediated neurotoxicity. Although outcomes in clinical trials for neurodegenerative diseases have been mixed, the protective mechanisms observed in animal models provide a mechanistic rationale that could be applicable also beyond the central nervous system (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Nimmrich & Eckert, 2013).

Importantly, there is emerging evidence linking altered L-type calcium channel activity, particularly of the CaV1.3 subtype, to ocular pathology relevant to AMD. Data from the Open Targets Platform, for example, indicate a moderate association between CACNA1D (the gene encoding CaV1.3) and macular degeneration, with studies in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells from AMD patients demonstrating both mislocalization of CaV1.3 channels and reduced intracellular Ca²⁺ levels compared to controls (Buniello et al., 2025). Although isradipine has not previously been used in clinical studies for ocular diseases or for dry AMD specifically, its long-established cardiovascular use, combined with its neuroprotective potential in other cell types, offers an attractive opportunity for repurposing. The safety profile and systemic tolerability of isradipine further support its candidacy for new therapeutic indications in an elderly population commonly affected by AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

─────────────────────────────  
3. Mechanism of Action

At its most fundamental level, isradipine acts by inhibiting LTCCs—integral membrane proteins that mediate voltage-dependent calcium influx into cells. The LTCC family includes several subtypes, among which CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 have been most extensively studied. Isradipine is known to preferentially block these channels in a state-dependent manner, binding with higher affinity to channels that are in either an open or inactivated state and thereby sparing those in the resting state (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Filippini et al., 2023).

More specifically, the molecular interaction between isradipine and LTCCs involves defined transmembrane segments located on the pore-forming α1 subunit. Structural studies have identified that regions such as the IS6 and IVS6 helices form part of the binding pocket responsible for dihydropyridine sensitivity. When isradipine binds to this pocket, it not only obstructs the pore physically but also stabilizes the channel in a nonconducting conformation that precludes further Ca²⁺ entry (Filippini et al., 2023; Lacinová, Klugbauer, & Hofmann, 2000). This blockade leads to a rapid and sustained reduction in intracellular calcium levels, which is critical in tissues where tight junction assembly and maintenance are calcium-dependent processes.

In the context of RPE cells, maintaining appropriate basal Ca²⁺ concentrations is crucial for the integrity and anchoring of tight junction proteins such as occludin and zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1). Under physiological conditions, LTCC-mediated calcium entry provides a signal that regulates calcium-sensitive kinase and phosphatase pathways involved in organizing the cytoskeleton and maintaining cell–cell adhesion. However, in disease conditions such as dry AMD, factors such as pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α) or complement activation can disrupt this finely tuned balance. Excessive Ca²⁺ influx can lead to the activation of calcium-dependent proteases (e.g., calpains) and kinases that precipitate cytoskeletal remodeling and disassembly of tight junction complexes, contributing to a collapse in transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and loss of barrier function (Buniello et al., 2025).

By antagonizing LTCCs, isradipine is hypothesized to counteract these deleterious effects. Its state-dependent, high-affinity binding minimizes excessive Ca²⁺ entry during inflammatory challenges while preserving the minimal calcium flux necessary for normal cellular function (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Rotstein et al., 2015). In addition to its acute blocking effect, there is evidence from studies in neuronal models that prolonged exposure to dihydropyridines may down-regulate LTCC expression, leading to longer-term stabilization of calcium homeostasis (Ilijic et al., 2011; Nimmrich & Eckert, 2013). Therefore, in RPE cells, isradipine could theoretically act via a dual mechanism: an immediate reduction in aberrant calcium entry during cytokine-induced stress and a more prolonged normalization of LTCC density and function.

Furthermore, the selective targeting of CaV1.3 is particularly pertinent in the case of dry AMD because studies have revealed a moderate association between CACNA1D expression and macular degeneration, along with observations of mislocalization of CaV1.3 channels in AMD-derived RPE cells (Buniello et al., 2025). Such mislocalization is associated with reduced intracellular calcium levels which, paradoxically, may contribute to the failure of the tight junction apparatus due to a deficiency in the calcium signal necessary for proper junction assembly. In this scenario, isradipine’s ability to fine-tune calcium influx by blocking excessive but inappropriate LTCC activity may help restore normal intracellular Ca²⁺ dynamics, thereby preserving the localization and function of occludin and ZO-1 (Buniello et al., 2025; Filippini et al., 2023).

In summary, at the molecular level, isradipine’s action involves binding to critical transmembrane segments of LTCCs—particularly those associated with CaV1.2 and CaV1.3—thereby stabilizing these channels in a closed or inactivated state, reducing aberrant calcium influx, and indirectly safeguarding the intracellular signaling pathways that maintain tight junction integrity. This mechanism is central to the proposed therapeutic approach for stabilizing the RPE barrier in dry AMD (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Filippini et al., 2023; Buniello et al., 2025).

─────────────────────────────  
4. Expected Effect

Dry AMD is characterized by chronic RPE cell dysfunction and degeneration leading to breakdown of the outer blood–retinal barrier, a process largely fueled by disruptions in intracellular calcium homeostasis. In this context, inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) play a critical role in triggering disassembly of tight junctions and reducing transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER). Moreover, evidence linking the CaV1.3 channel to macular degeneration underscores the importance of calcium regulation in RPE pathology (Buniello et al., 2025).

The central hypothesis guiding the repurposing of isradipine for dry AMD is that by blocking LTCCs—specifically CaV1.2 and CaV1.3—at an IC₅₀ near 0.2 µM, it is possible to stabilize basal calcium levels in RPE cells. Under inflammatory conditions induced by TNF-α or complement activation, uncontrolled calcium influx would normally activate calcium-dependent proteolytic enzymes and kinases that contribute to the disruption of the cytoskeletal framework and the disassembly of cell–cell junctions. With isradipine’s intervention, the unwanted surge in intracellular calcium would be attenuated, thereby preserving the expression, localization, and function of tight junction proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

In practical in vitro assays—using the human RPE cell line ARPE-19 or primary RPE cultures—exposure to TNF-α typically results in marked declines in TEER, reflecting compromised barrier integrity, alongside mislocalization of occludin and ZO-1 within the cell. Treatment with isradipine is expected to counter these effects. Specifically, by reducing the level of calcium influx across the plasma membrane, isradipine should enable the maintenance of the proper cytoskeletal anchoring of tight junction proteins, which in turn is expected to translate into a stabilization or even enhancement of TEER. Preliminary data in complement-challenged ARPE-19 models have shown that treatment with calcium channel blockers can lead to increased TEER, supporting the concept that pharmacological modulation of calcium entry is beneficial for RPE barrier function (Buniello et al., 2025).

Moreover, the anticipated outcomes include not only the acute preservation of junctional architecture during short-term inflammatory challenges but also potentially the modulation of LTCC expression under chronic stress. Over time, reducing the pathological calcium influx may alleviate the cellular stress that leads to LTCC up-regulation, thereby preventing a vicious cycle of calcium overload and junctional disassembly. Thus, even beyond immediate effects on TEER, isradipine may exert disease-modifying properties by normalizing the intracellular signaling milieu in RPE cells (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Ilijic et al., 2011).

Finally, by maintaining appropriate intracellular Ca²⁺ concentrations, isradipine may also prevent the activation of downstream calcium-dependent effectors—such as calpains and other proteases—that can degrade tight junction proteins directly. This dual action of immediate channel blockade and secondary protection against proteolytic degradation underpins the rationale that isradipine can preserve the barrier function of the RPE, thereby preventing the progression of dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

In essence, the expected effect of isradipine in the proposed assay is multifaceted:
• An immediate stabilization of intracellular calcium levels through LTCC blockade.  
• Prevention of TNF-α–induced tight junction disassembly, with sustained localization of occludin and ZO-1.  
• Improvement or stabilization of TEER in RPE cells under inflammatory or complement-challenge conditions.  
• Potential chronic benefits through secondary down-regulation of LTCC expression and the subsequent maintenance of calcium homeostasis.

Such effects would translate into a pharmacological strategy not only to protect the RPE barrier acutely but also to potentially slow the degenerative process of dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Filippini et al., 2023).

─────────────────────────────  
5. Overall Evaluation

Based on the comprehensive review of the available literature across biochemical, clinical, and preclinical domains, isradipine emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its favorable safety profile, robust historical data in cardiovascular applications, and emerging evidence supporting its neuroprotective and calcium-modulating effects form a strong foundation for exploring its role in ocular diseases.

Strengths of isradipine include its extensive clinical record in hypertension and angina, where decades of use have demonstrated predictable pharmacokinetics and a low incidence of severe adverse effects (Schachter, 1991). The compound’s belonging to the dihydropyridine class further supports its suitability, as this class is characterized by potent and state-dependent blockade of LTCCs—properties that are critical for controlling abnormal calcium influx in pathological situations. In addition, preclinical data documenting abnormal localization of CaV1.3 channels in AMD-affected RPE cells (Buniello et al., 2025) provide a direct link between LTCC dysfunction and retinal barrier breakdown, thereby strengthening the mechanistic rationale for isradipine’s use in dry AMD.

Another major strength is isradipine’s dual mechanism of action. Acutely, it can reduce the extracellular calcium influx that triggers deleterious cell-signaling cascades, and with chronic administration, it may also modulate LTCC expression levels. Such a dual mechanism implies that isradipine might not only preserve junctional integrity during inflammatory insults but also slow the overall progression of RPE degeneration. This is particularly important given that dry AMD is a slowly progressive and multifactorial disease where both acute and chronic therapeutic interventions are needed to achieve meaningful clinical outcomes (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Filippini et al., 2023).

Moreover, isradipine’s pharmacodynamic profile—with an IC₅₀ of approximately 0.2 µM—suggests that at appropriate dosing, it can achieve targeted LTCC inhibition in RPE cells without completely abolishing basal calcium signaling, which is essential for normal cellular functions. This fine balance is crucial in tissues such as the retina where calcium plays a key role not only in tight junction regulation but also in phototransduction and cellular homeostasis (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

Nonetheless, several challenges and limitations must be acknowledged. First, there is a relative paucity of direct ocular data on isradipine. Most of the supporting evidence for its mechanism and effects comes from studies in cardiovascular and neuronal cells. While the fundamental principles of calcium-dependent tight junction regulation are conserved, the specific expression profiles and regulatory mechanisms in RPE cells may differ. Consequently, extensive in vitro studies in RPE cell lines (such as ARPE-19) and primary RPE cultures will be imperative before moving into in vivo evaluations (Buniello et al., 2025).

Another significant limitation concerns drug delivery. Isradipine is predominantly administered systemically for its current indications, and achieving therapeutically relevant concentrations in the retina while minimizing systemic hypotension presents an important formulation challenge. Novel ocular delivery approaches—ranging from topical formulations to intravitreal injections or slow-release implants—must be rigorously developed and optimized. This challenge is compounded by the need to ensure that such delivery methods do not disrupt normal retinal physiology or exacerbate inflammatory responses (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Schachter, 1991).

There is also the potential for off-target effects in the retina. Calcium signaling underpins many essential retinal functions, including the regulation of photoreceptor activity, synaptic transmission, and RPE phagocytosis. Over-inhibition of LTCCs, if not carefully titrated, could compromise these processes. Thus, defining a safe therapeutic window in RPE cells is critical to ensure that the benefits of junctional preservation do not come at the cost of impaired retinal function (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

Finally, while the data linking LTCC dysfunction to AMD provide a compelling rationale for repurposing isradipine, the heterogeneity of LTCC expression across different cell types in the retina may influence treatment efficacy. It will be necessary to characterize not only the levels of CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 in RPE cells but also their functional roles in maintaining barrier integrity. Any variability in channel isoform expression or alternative splicing patterns may require adjustments in dosing or even the exploration of more isoform-selective derivatives (Buniello et al., 2025; Filippini et al., 2023).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation is positive: isradipine is a well-characterized, clinically safe calcium channel blocker with a robust mechanistic basis for repurposing in dry AMD. Its combined acute and chronic actions on LTCCs, along with emerging evidence linking CaV1.3 dysfunction to retinal degeneration, provide a strong rationale for further preclinical investigation. In particular, detailed studies focusing on its effects in human RPE cells under inflammatory conditions will be critical to validate the hypothesis that isradipine can preserve occludin and ZO-1 localization and maintain TEER under TNF-α challenge (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

─────────────────────────────  
6. Future Directions and Recommendations

Based on the evaluation above, the following research directions are recommended to advance isradipine as a potential therapeutic agent for dry AMD:

a) Detailed Characterization in RPE Cells  
It is vital to confirm the expression levels and localization of LTCC subtypes, particularly CaV1.3, in human RPE cells. Techniques such as quantitative PCR, Western blotting, immunocytochemistry, and electrophysiological recordings (e.g., patch-clamp) should be used to assess both basal expression and any alterations under inflammatory conditions. This will establish whether the therapeutic window for isradipine’s action in RPE cells is similar to that observed in neuronal or vascular cells (Buniello et al., 2025).

b) In Vitro Barrier Function Studies  
Establish in vitro models using ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures to evaluate the effects of isradipine on TEER and the immunolocalization of tight junction proteins such as occludin and ZO-1. These studies should employ cytokine challenges (e.g., TNF-α) and complement-mediated insults to simulate the pathological environment associated with dry AMD. Dose–response studies centered around the 0.2 µM IC₅₀ value will help define optimal concentrations for barrier preservation (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

c) Mechanistic Pathway Dissection  
Investigate the downstream signaling cascades following LTCC blockade in RPE cells. This includes evaluating changes in the activation state of calcium-dependent proteases, kinases, and the cytoskeletal proteins that govern tight junction formation. In addition, longitudinal studies should assess whether chronic isradipine exposure modifies LTCC expression itself, providing potential long-term benefits beyond immediate calcium modulation (Ilijic et al., 2011).

d) Development of Ocular Delivery Systems  
Given isradipine’s existing use as an orally administered drug for cardiovascular indications, it is essential to develop ocular-specific formulations that enable efficient delivery to the retina. This could involve exploring topical eye drops, intravitreal injections, or sustained-release implants that achieve high retinal bioavailability with minimal systemic absorption. In vivo pharmacokinetic studies in appropriate animal models will be key to optimizing these delivery systems (Schachter, 1991).

e) In Vivo Efficacy Studies  
Animal models that recapitulate key features of dry AMD, including RPE degeneration and barrier dysfunction, should be employed to assess the functional impact of isradipine on retinal preservation. Outcome measures might include in vivo imaging of retinal structure, ex vivo TEER measurements, histological analysis of tight junction integrity, and functional assessments such as electroretinography.

f) Safety and Tolerability in Retinal Tissues  
Since calcium signaling is critical for many retinal cellular functions, it is imperative to assess whether isradipine—at doses sufficient to block pathological calcium influx—might inadvertently impair normal retinal processes such as photoreceptor function, synaptic transmission, or RPE phagocytosis. Defining a precise therapeutic index in the ocular setting will be crucial for further development.

─────────────────────────────  
7. Overall Conclusion

In conclusion, isradipine represents a highly promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its extensive use in cardiovascular medicine, combined with an emerging body of evidence linking LTCC dysfunction to RPE barrier failure and macular degeneration, provides a strong scientific rationale for its investigation in this novel indication. At the molecular level, isradipine’s state-dependent and selective blockade of CaV1.2/CaV1.3 channels offers a targeted approach to stabilizing intracellular calcium levels and preserving the organization of tight junction proteins critical for maintaining the outer blood–retinal barrier (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

While the majority of the supportive literature originates from studies conducted in cardiovascular and neuronal models, the fundamental role of LTCC-mediated calcium signaling in modulating barrier integrity is highly relevant to RPE physiology. The proposed mechanism—preventing TNF-α–induced junctional disassembly and cytokine-driven TEER collapse by preserving occludin and ZO-1 localization—is both plausible and timely given the persistent unmet need in the treatment of dry AMD.

Nonetheless, key challenges remain. Direct experimental evidence in ocular systems is currently limited, and significant work is needed to optimize the drug formulation for targeted retinal delivery while safeguarding against potential off-target effects. The heterogeneity of LTCC expression in ocular tissues may also necessitate further refinement in dosing strategies. Addressing these challenges through targeted in vitro and in vivo studies will be critical for translating the promising mechanistic insights into clinical benefit.

Overall, the convergence of robust clinical safety data, precise molecular pharmacological action, and emerging evidence linking LTCC dysregulation to RPE dysfunction supports the advancement of isradipine into focused preclinical studies for dry AMD. If studies confirm that isradipine can preserve the integrity of RPE tight junctions under inflammatory conditions, it may offer not only symptomatic relief but also a disease-modifying strategy that slows or prevents the progression of dry AMD—a condition currently lacking effective treatment options (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

Given these considerations, the recommendation is to pursue an accelerated preclinical program that encompasses detailed mechanistic assays in RPE cells, the development of suitable ocular delivery systems, and rigorous in vivo testing in relevant animal models. Success in these areas would justify subsequent clinical trials and could ultimately position isradipine as a transformative therapy for preserving retinal structure and function in patients with dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
Final Summary

Isradipine is a synthetically derived 1,4-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker with a proven record in cardiovascular therapy due to its potent, state-dependent inhibition of LTCCs. Its repurposing for dry age-related macular degeneration is scientifically supported by emerging evidence that links dysregulated CaV1.3 function with RPE barrier breakdown in AMD. By stabilizing basal intracellular Ca²⁺ levels under inflammatory stress, isradipine is expected to prevent TNF-α–induced disassembly of tight junction proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 and thereby maintain TEER. Although direct ocular data are currently limited and significant challenges in retinal drug delivery remain to be addressed, the overall safety profile and well-defined molecular mechanism of isradipine provide a compelling rationale for further preclinical investigation in dry AMD. Advancing isradipine into detailed mechanistic studies in RPE models, coupled with the development of targeted ocular formulations, offers the potential to deliver a first-in-class, disease-modifying treatment for dry AMD—a condition with significant unmet medical need (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

Based solely on the data provided in the current context and using the established literature from cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and emerging ocular studies, isradipine holds considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The proposed mechanism of stabilizing basal Ca²⁺ homeostasis to preserve RPE tight junction integrity is strongly supported, and the path forward includes focused preclinical research to address ocular-specific efficacy and delivery issues. This strategy represents a logical and scientifically grounded approach to expand the therapeutic indications of an already widely used drug, thereby potentially transforming care for patients suffering from dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

ML‐SA1 (Tocris 5291) is a synthetic, small‐molecule agonist that targets the lysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (mucolipin‐1). Therapeutic History:  
Historically, ML‐SA1 has been employed in multiple biochemical and cellular studies as a probe to activate TRPML1-mediated lysosomal Ca²⁺ release. In the literature, its application in RPE cell models has helped delineate the contributions of lysosomal Ca²⁺ signals to downstream processes such as lysosomal exocytosis, TFEB (transcription factor EB) activation, and oxidative stress regulation. Experimental evidence derived from studies using ML‐SA1 demonstrates that the induced Ca²⁺ release is essentially independent of extracellular Ca²⁺ and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca²⁺ storage; rather, the release originates from lysosomal stores—as confirmed by the abrogation of ML‐SA1 responses upon lysosomal disruption with glycyl‐L‐phenylalanine‐naphthylamide (GPN) and by the lack of response in TRPML1-null RPE models (Más Gómez et al., 2018). To date, ML‐SA1 has not been used clinically or in veterinary settings and has not yet been evaluated in the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases; its use is so far confined to experimental paradigms that study the fundamental aspects of TRPML1 activity and lysosomal function (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This candidate is thus considered a repurposed pharmacologic agent, repositioned from a research tool to a potential therapeutic based on its mechanistic actions in RPE cells.

At the molecular level, ML‐SA1 exerts its action by binding to and directly activating TRPML1 channels located on the lysosomal membrane. The released Ca²⁺ can then activate downstream signaling pathways including the calcineurin-TFEB pathway, where increased cytosolic Ca²⁺ activates calcineurin, leading to dephosphorylation and subsequent nuclear translocation of TFEB. In addition to stimulating Ca²⁺ release, TRPML1 activation by ML‐SA1 has been linked to beneficial downstream effects such as the induction of lysosomal exocytosis and the enhancement of cathepsin activity, which together contribute to the restoration of lysosomal function and cellular homeostasis (Karema-Jokinen et al., 2023; Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Based on the current hypothesis, ML‐SA1 is expected to act on RPE cells by enhancing lysosomal Ca²⁺ release through TRPML1 activation, thereby stimulating the calcineurin-TFEB signaling cascade. Historically, LG100268 has been most notably explored in preclinical models of cancer—particularly in murine models of breast cancer. Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, LG100268 acts as a high-affinity agonist for RXRs by binding selectively to the ligand-binding pocket of these nuclear receptors. RXRs are unique in that they function both as homodimers and as obligate heterodimer partners for multiple other nuclear receptors including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), liver X receptors (LXRs), and even possibly orphan receptors such as Nurr1. Upon binding LG100268, the RXR undergoes a conformational change that induces release of corepressors and recruitment of coactivators, thereby altering transcription of downstream target genes (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10). In cancer studies, the activation of RXR by LG100268 has been associated with modulation of the immune microenvironment; it reduces pro-tumor cytokine release, alters the balance of immune cell populations, and influences expression of cell surface proteins such as PD-L1 (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). The repurposing of LG100268 for dry AMD is an innovative approach that leverages the compound’s well-documented ability to selectively activate RXRs. Its high-affinity binding and potent agonism make it one of the more promising rexinoids available, as evidenced by its superior receptor binding kinetics relative to known RXR ligands such as bexarotene (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Preclinical studies in oncology have consistently demonstrated that LG100268 modulates the immune microenvironment, induces changes in critical cytokine expression, and alters the balance of immune cell populations in a manner that collectively suggests an anti-inflammatory profile (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Particularly, the hypothesis that LG100268 may bias RXR heterodimer formation toward Nurr1—and thus suppress NF-κB signaling—opens a new avenue for preserving tight junction integrity in RPE cells, which is critically important in maintaining a proper barrier function (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

In summary, while LG100268’s established potency, receptor selectivity, and capacity to modulate inflammatory and metabolic gene expression provide a strong foundation for considering its repurposing, the current literature does not yet offer direct support for its use in dry AMD. Below is a comprehensive evaluation of SB‐431542 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). The report is organized into five sections: an overview of the therapeutic candidate, a review of its therapeutic history, a detailed discussion of its molecular mechanism of action, an explanation of the expected effects in the proposed assay and ocular environment, and an overall evaluation of its potential strengths and weaknesses for treating dry AMD.

    1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB‐431542 is a fully synthetic small molecule that was discovered through high‐throughput screening efforts at GlaxoSmithKline and further optimized via systematic structure–activity relationship studies. Its chemical identity is defined by the IUPAC name 4-[4-(3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl)-5-(2-pyridyl)-1H-imidazol-2-yl]-benzamide, and it belongs to the triarylimidazole/benzamide structural class (Markell, 2010; Fuchs, 2011). During its development, medicinal chemists employed target-hopping strategies that involved modifying substituents – for example, replacing a 4-pyridyl group with a 2-pyridyl moiety and adding a 3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl ring – to retain TGF-β type I receptor (ALK5) inhibitory potency while minimizing unwanted inhibition of other kinases such as p38 MAPK (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This precise engineering ensures that SB-431542 acts as a competitive inhibitor at the ATP‐binding site of ALK5, thereby conferring selectivity relative to other kinases (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). As a member of a well‐defined class of small molecule kinase inhibitors, SB-431542 has been used extensively as a research tool in studies of TGF-β signaling and fibrosis, and its chemical properties suggest that it belongs to a broader family of agents that modulate receptor kinases via competitive binding (Laping et al., 2002).

    2. Therapeutic History  
SB-431542 has been at the forefront of preclinical research into TGF-β signaling because of its capacity to selectively block ALK5 and, to a lesser extent, related receptors such as ALK4 and ALK7 (Laping et al., 2002; Ge et al., 2004). Its primary use has been as a chemical probe to elucidate the role of TGF-β in diverse fibrotic and oncologic settings. In multiple in vitro and in vivo studies, SB-431542 has been shown to effectively inhibit TGF-β1-induced upregulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components including collagen Iα1, fibronectin, and plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI-1) in renal epithelial cells and fibroblast cultures (Laping et al., 2002). Its potent antifibrotic activity has also been demonstrated in ocular applications; for example, it has been utilized in experimental models of glaucoma filtration surgery to reduce subconjunctival scarring by curtailing fibroblast proliferation, myofibroblast transdifferentiation, and ECM deposition (Wang et al., 2017). Although SB-431542 has not yet been approved for clinical use in AMD or other retinal disorders, its well‐documented ability to inhibit TGF-β–mediated fibrosis in ocular tissues suggests that it holds promise for these indications (Teplitsky et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2009). In addition, the compound’s extensive deployment in cancer studies – where it is used to block the epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and invasion – further verifies its capacity to modulate key pathological processes that also underlie fibrotic changes observed in retinal degeneration (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010).

    3. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, SB-431542 functions as a competitive inhibitor of the TGF-β type I receptor (ALK5) by binding to its ATP binding site. Upon the engagement of TGF-β ligands with cell surface receptors, the type II receptor phosphorylates and activates ALK5. Activated ALK5 then phosphorylates receptor-regulated Smad proteins (Smad2 and Smad3), which subsequently form complexes with Smad4 and translocate into the nucleus to drive the transcription of genes encoding ECM proteins and other pro-fibrotic factors (Laping et al., 2002). SB-431542 directly inhibits this kinase activity by occupying the ATP pocket, thereby blocking the phosphorylation of Smad2/3 and preventing their nuclear accumulation (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This interruption of TGF-β signaling ultimately suppresses the induction of pro-fibrotic genes such as those for collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002).

Importantly, SB-431542 is characterized by its selectivity. Despite the structural similarities among kinases in the TGF-β receptor superfamily, the unique conformational features of ALK5 permit SB-431542 to inhibit it to a significantly greater extent than BMP receptors (ALK2, ALK3, and ALK6) or other non-Smad pathways such as those mediated by ERK, JNK, and p38 MAPK (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This selectivity minimizes off-target effects and allows the compound to function as a precise modulator of TGF-β–dependent fibrotic signaling (Laping et al., 2002; Ling & Lee, 2011). Moreover, by inhibiting ALK5 activity, SB-431542 not only downregulates ECM protein production but also interferes with EMT processes, which are implicated in the phenotypic conversion of epithelial cells to a more mesenchymal and migratory state – a conversion that has been observed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells under stress conditions (Radeke et al., 2015; Yoon et al., 2018). In this regard, SB-431542’s molecular interactions encompass hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic contacts within the ALK5 catalytic pocket, ensuring that its inhibitory activity is both potent (with reported IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range) and selective for the intended target (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002).

    4. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis for repurposing SB-431542 in dry AMD is that inhibiting TGF-β receptor activity in RPE cells and choroidal fibroblasts will reduce pathological ECM overproduction. In dry AMD, elevated levels of TGF-β1 have been implicated in promoting the deposition of fibrotic ECM components in Bruch’s membrane, leading to increased stiffness and altered mechanical forces on the RPE monolayer (Laping et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2009). The resulting stiffening of the extracellular matrix is believed to disrupt the normal anchorage of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity and transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) of the RPE barrier (Xiao et al., 2009; Teplitsky et al., 2023).

By blocking ALK5 and thereby attenuating Smad2/3 activation, SB-431542 is expected to suppress the transcription of genes encoding collagen Iα1, fibronectin, and PAI-1. A reduction in the synthesis and deposition of these ECM components should translate into a decrease in Bruch’s membrane stiffness and the mechanical tension imposed on the RPE (Laping et al., 2002). This, in turn, is anticipated to allow the re-establishment of a continuous network of tight junctions between RPE cells as ZO-1 and occludin are able to reassemble without the interference of a pathological ECM environment (Radeke et al., 2015; Higashijima et al., 2023). When tested in ECM-coated Transwell assays, the expectation is that treatment with SB-431542 will result in improved TEER readings and a restoration of barrier function indicative of normalized RPE physiology (Xiao et al., 2009; Yoon et al., 2018).

Furthermore, TGF-β signaling in RPE cells has been associated with epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a process that not only promotes fibrosis but also deteriorates the well-ordered epithelial phenotype critical for retinal homeostasis (Radeke et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2009). Inhibition of ALK5 is predicted to counteract EMT, thereby preserving the native epithelial characteristics of RPE cells. In this context, the reduction of fibrotic ECM production and the prevention of EMT would act in synergy to reduce the abnormal mechanical stresses on RPE, enhance the continuity of tight junction proteins, and ultimately help restore retinal barrier function (Laping et al., 2002).

Given that both RPE cells and choroidal fibroblasts express TGF-β receptors and respond to TGF-β stimulation, the application of SB-431542 in co-culture models or animal studies is expected to normalize the extracellular microenvironment. This normalization could rescue the mechanical integrity of Bruch’s membrane and improve nutrient/waste exchange across the RPE monolayer—factors that are crucial in slowing or reversing the degenerative progression in dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2009).

    5. Overall Evaluation  
An overall review of SB-431542 indicates that it is a scientifically compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its proven ability to modulate TGF-β signaling and its well-documented anti-fibrotic effects. One major strength of SB-431542 is its high degree of selectivity for ALK5; by competitively inhibiting the ATP binding site on this receptor, the compound effectively blocks the Smad2/3 phosphorylation cascade that ultimately leads to ECM overproduction (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This mechanism has been validated in multiple preclinical models of fibrosis and ocular scarring, indicating that a similar strategy may be effective in the context of dry AMD where excessive ECM deposition in Bruch’s membrane is a central pathogenic feature (Xiao et al., 2009; Teplitsky et al., 2023).

Another point in favor of SB-431542 is its extensive use as a research tool in the investigation of TGF-β–dependent processes in both fibrosis and cancer. Its ability to reduce collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 levels in diverse cellular models underscores its therapeutic potential for attenuating pathological ECM production—a direct mechanism that could alleviate mechanical stress on RPE tight junctions and help restore barrier function, as measured by increased TEER and continuity of ZO-1/occludin (Laping et al., 2002).

From a mechanistic perspective, the detailed molecular interactions of SB-431542 have been characterized to a high degree, with studies demonstrating that its binding to the ALK5 catalytic pocket results in a clear inhibition of the profibrotic gene expression program (Laping et al., 2002; Ling & Lee, 2011). This precision in targeting is particularly important when considering ocular applications, as the retina is highly sensitive to off-target effects. By sparing other signaling pathways—such as those mediated by BMP receptors or Smad-independent cascades—the compound minimizes potential systemic or retinal toxicity (Laping et al., 2002).

Despite these strengths, there are also several challenges that must be addressed for SB-431542 to be successfully repurposed for dry AMD. One of the primary concerns is its pharmacokinetic profile. Preclinical studies in animal models have indicated that SB-431542 may have a relatively short half-life and rapid clearance, which raises questions about achieving sustained intraocular concentrations necessary for chronic conditions such as dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). To address this, development of a controlled-release ocular formulation—such as an intravitreal implant, microsphere-based delivery, or other sustained-release vehicle—will be essential for maintaining therapeutic levels over extended periods without systemic exposure.

Another significant challenge is the duality inherent in TGF-β signaling. While excessive TGF-β activity is responsible for the fibrotic changes observed in AMD, TGF-β also plays an important role in immune regulation, tissue repair, and maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Long-term blockade of TGF-β signaling may therefore carry inherent risks, including potential adverse effects on normal repair mechanisms or the promotion of unanticipated cellular changes such as malignant transformation (Markell, 2010; Schindeler et al., 2010). Careful dose-response studies and localized delivery strategies will be imperative to ensure that therapeutic benefits are achieved without tipping the balance toward deleterious side effects.

Moreover, although the preclinical data in ocular fibrosis models—such as those involving subconjunctival scarring after glaucoma filtration surgery—provide a promising rationale for the use of TGF-β inhibitors, direct evidence in models that recapitulate the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains limited (Xiao et al., 2009). Dry AMD is a complex disease involving not only fibrotic ECM accumulation but also oxidative stress, chronic low-grade inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation. Therefore, while the mechanistic rationale for using SB-431542 to reduce ECM production and restore RPE integrity is sound, it will likely need to be integrated into a broader therapeutic strategy that addresses these additional pathological drivers (Schindeler et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2017).

On the formulation front, the small molecule nature of SB-431542 offers both advantages and challenges. Its chemical tractability allows for modifications that could improve its ocular stability and bioavailability; however, achieving homogeneous distribution within the eye, ensuring drug stability in the vitreous environment, and avoiding direct retinal toxicity remain non-trivial challenges (Fuchs, 2011; Markell, 2010). Additionally, by virtue of its design as a competitive inhibitor, careful titration of dose will be required to ensure that effective ALK5 inhibition is sustained while minimizing interference with other cellular kinases that are essential for retinal cell survival.

In summary, SB-431542 shows significant promise as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to selectively inhibit ALK5 and thereby block the central pro-fibrotic Smad2/3 signaling axis aligns well with the mechanistic hypothesis that targeting TGF-β–mediated ECM overproduction can restore the biomechanical homeostasis of Bruch’s membrane and improve RPE barrier function (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). The chemical and biochemical evidence supporting its anti-fibrotic effects—demonstrated by reduced collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 levels in multiple cell types and models—is compelling (Laping et al., 2002). Furthermore, preliminary ocular studies using SB-431542 in models of surgical scarring provide an encouraging precedent for its application in the retina (Wang et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2009).

However, the pathway to clinical translation is not without hurdles. The pharmacokinetics of SB-431542, characterized by a relatively short half-life, necessitate the development of innovative drug delivery systems to sustain intraocular levels over the chronic course of AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). Additionally, the multifaceted role of TGF-β in ocular physiology requires that any therapeutic intervention be carefully calibrated to avoid impairing normal tissue repair or immunologic function (Markell, 2010; Schindeler et al., 2010). Finally, given that dry AMD is a multifactorial disease rather than being driven solely by fibrosis, further preclinical studies employing comprehensive AMD models that encompass oxidative stress and inflammation will be crucial to validate the therapeutic potential of SB-431542 in this context (Teplitsky et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025).

Overall, SB-431542 represents a scientifically robust and mechanistically well-justified candidate for repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD. Its targeted inhibition of ALK5 offers a strategic means to reduce pathological ECM deposition and thereby alleviate the mechanical stress that undermines RPE tight junction integrity—a key factor implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). The strengths of SB-431542 include its potency, selectivity, and extensive preclinical validation in fibrotic and ocular injury models. In contrast, its weaknesses center on pharmacokinetic limitations, the challenges of ocular delivery, and the complexity of broadly inhibiting a cytokine pathway that also serves beneficial roles.  

In conclusion, while additional formulation work and targeted preclinical studies remain essential, the accumulated evidence from biochemical, cellular, and ocular studies strongly supports the further evaluation of SB-431542 as part of a mechanobiology‐based therapeutic strategy for dry AMD. Given that dry AMD currently lacks effective treatments and that pathological ECM accumulation in Bruch’s membrane is a critical driver of disease progression, the repurposing of SB-431542 could provide a novel means to restore RPE barrier function by reducing ECM stiffness and re-establishing tight junction continuity (Xiao et al., 2009). Future research should focus on optimizing local delivery—potentially via sustained-release intravitreal formulations—and integrating SB-431542 within a combination therapy framework that additionally targets oxidative stress and inflammation. With these measures in place, SB-431542 holds significant promise as an innovative candidate in the quest for effective treatments for dry AMD (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002).

Thus, based on its synthetic origin, proven preclinical anti-fibrotic and anti-EMT effects, and detailed mechanistic rationale, SB-431542 merits further development for dry AMD. A rigorous, methodologically robust preclinical program – including pharmacokinetic optimization, ocular toxicity studies, and validation in relevant AMD models – will be crucial to determine whether the benefits observed in laboratory assays can be translated into meaningful clinical improvements in retinal structure and function.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bardoxolone methyl, also known as CDDO-Me, is a synthetic derivative developed from the naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid oleanolic acid. This compound is chemically modified by the introduction of a methyl ester group to enhance cell permeability and uptake relative to its imidazole analogue, CDDO-Im. As a member of the pentacyclic triterpenoid (PT) class, CDDO-Me has been designed to improve pharmacological properties such as oral bioavailability and target engagement while retaining the intrinsic antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of its natural precursor. Historically, pentacyclic triterpenoids have been studied for a wide range of applications—including anticancer, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory therapies—and have a longstanding role in traditional medicine in various Asian cultures. In this context, CDDO-Me has emerged as an advanced synthetic candidate that capitalizes on these properties, particularly through its potency as an activator of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. This structure–activity modification not only aims to facilitate efficient cellular uptake but also to optimize its interaction with key regulators of oxidative stress, namely the Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1) (Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and clinical investigation primarily in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and cancer. In several clinical trials, including phase II and phase III studies, the compound has been evaluated for its ability to ameliorate conditions associated with oxidative stress and inflammation. Its clinical development for CKD, in particular, has underscored its potential to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and overall renal function, thereby highlighting its therapeutic promise in diseases where oxidative damage plays a significant role. Despite its notable progress in these areas, direct clinical evidence for Bardoxolone methyl in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal diseases remains limited. However, several preclinical studies have demonstrated that compounds related to Bardoxolone methyl are capable of activating Nrf2 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, upregulating protective genes such as NQO1 and HO-1 that are essential for combating oxidative stress in the retina. These findings suggest that, although not originally developed for retinal indications, Bardoxolone methyl has a mechanistic rationale that could support its repurposing for dry AMD (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, analogous compounds that function via Nrf2 activation have been shown to protect RPE cells against oxidative stress-induced damage, further supporting the therapeutic potential of this candidate in ocular applications (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Bardoxolone methyl operates predominantly through the activation of the Nrf2 pathway, an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional system that governs cellular antioxidant responses. Under normal homeostatic conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytoplasm by its inhibitor, Keap1, which facilitates its ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl, due to its electrophilic cyanoenone moiety, acts as a Michael acceptor, covalently modifying specific cysteine residues within Keap1 (notably cysteine 151 among others). This modification disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, preventing Nrf2 ubiquitination, and allows Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus where it binds to the antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoter regions of target genes (Zhou et al., 2020; Mathis & Cui, 2016). The subsequent upregulation of phase II detoxifying enzymes—such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and glutamate-cysteine ligase modifier subunit (GCLM)—provides cells with increased capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigate inflammatory insults. Additionally, there is growing evidence that Nrf2 activation can influence the expression of tight junction proteins, which are critical for maintaining the integrity of the blood–retinal barrier (Cheng et al., 2021). This detailed molecular interaction not only accounts for the antioxidant role of Bardoxolone methyl but also for its potential in preserving cellular integrity in environments subjected to oxidative insult, such as the RPE cells in the retina (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Cai et al., 2024). Furthermore, ancillary effects, such as modulation of NF-κB signaling and the inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, are likely to contribute to its overall cytoprotective profile, making it an attractive candidate for reducing the inflammatory milieu that accompanies retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
In the specific context of dry AMD, the therapeutic hypothesis posits that Bardoxolone methyl will esterify and modify Keap1 in human RPE cells, thereby triggering the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent upregulation of phase II enzymes. This enhanced antioxidant capacity is expected to counteract oxidative stress induced by agents such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (tBHP), which is known to compromise the tight junction integrity of RPE monolayers. The resulting effect should manifest as a measurable recovery in transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) and a concomitant reduction in paracellular flux, as assessed by the permeability of a 10 kDa dextran. Preclinical assays have reported that at a concentration of 500 nM, Bardoxolone methyl is capable of restoring TEER values to approximately 80% of baseline levels, and reducing dextran leak by about 55%, thus highlighting both its potency and efficacy in repairing disrupted barrier function (Nakagami et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2021). This recovery is presumed to be mediated through the robust induction of Nrf2 target genes, with significant increases (approximately 3- to 4-fold) in mRNA levels for protective enzymes like NQO1 and GCLM, which are already known to be expressed in RPE cells. The preservation and restoration of tight junction integrity are critical not only for maintaining the physical barrier between the retina and the choroid but also for ensuring proper retinal function by preventing the uncontrolled diffusion of harmful substances that can exacerbate retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021; Hui et al., 2020). Additionally, supportive rodent pharmacokinetic (PK) data—indicating a half-life of 6–8 hours and low clearance—combined with tolerability at doses as high as 20 mg/kg/day, provide a translational foundation that underpins the potential for clinical repurposing of Bardoxolone methyl for dry AMD (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several strengths alongside noteworthy challenges. On the strength side, the compound’s ability to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway addresses a central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and inflammation play pivotal roles in RPE degeneration. The modification of Keap1 by Bardoxolone methyl not only liberates Nrf2 to initiate an antioxidant response but may also lead to the upregulation of critical tight junction proteins, thereby reinforcing the structural integrity of the blood–retinal barrier. Preclinical evidence indicating recovery of TEER and reduction of paracellular flux supports the notion that Bardoxolone methyl could exert meaningful protective effects in the RPE under conditions of oxidative challenge (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, the compound’s clinical advancement in other indications—most notably in CKD—demonstrates an established track record of safety and tolerability in humans at therapeutically relevant doses. This, together with favorable rodent PK parameters, enhances its appeal as a candidate for rapid translational repurposing for dry AMD (Yagishita et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2012; Sarmento, 2019).

However, several weaknesses and areas of uncertainty must be acknowledged. Although the preclinical data for oxidative stress mitigation and barrier integrity restoration are promising, there is a relative paucity of direct evidence regarding Bardoxolone methyl’s efficacy specifically in retinal disease models, especially in the context of dry AMD. The literature does not yet definitively demonstrate that Bardoxolone methyl can reverse established RPE dysfunction or completely restore retinal integrity in disease-relevant in vivo settings (Nakagami et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2024). Furthermore, safety concerns observed in other clinical contexts—such as cardiovascular adverse effects during clinical trials for CKD—raise potential red flags regarding its long-term use in a population that may be at increased risk for such events due to age-related co-morbidities (Nakagami et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2014; Sarmento, 2019). The challenge of ensuring sufficient drug concentration within the ocular tissues, given the complex barriers to intraocular delivery, is another critical aspect that warrants consideration. Although the methyl ester scaffold is designed to enhance cell uptake, further optimization of the drug delivery system (for example, via topical formulations or intravitreal injections) may be required to achieve therapeutic levels in the retina without systemic exposure that could potentiate off-target effects (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2020).

Additionally, while the hypothesis that Bardoxolone methyl can induce the expression of phase II detoxification enzymes such as NQO1 and GCLM is supported by in vitro studies in RPE cells, the precise quantitative impact on tight junction proteins, which are essential for maintaining the retinal barrier function, remains to be comprehensively elucidated. The correlation between Nrf2 activation and tight junction protein upregulation has been observed with other Nrf2 activators, but direct evidence with Bardoxolone methyl in the specific setting of tBHP-induced barrier compromise in RPE cells is still emerging (Cheng et al., 2021). Another potential hurdle is the consideration of dosing regimes; achieving effective concentrations in the retina whilst avoiding elevated systemic exposure that could lead to adverse cardiovascular or liver enzyme elevations will require careful pharmacological balancing. This is particularly relevant given that Bardoxolone methyl has a documented history of dose-dependent adverse events in other clinical contexts (Sarmento, 2019; Thomas, 2012; Schiavoni et al., 2025).

In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a highly promising mechanism-based approach for the treatment of dry AMD. Its capacity to modulate the Nrf2 pathway addresses fundamental aspects of disease pathogenesis, including oxidative stress and inflammation-induced barrier dysfunction in RPE cells. The preclinical evidence—demonstrating recovery of TEER, reduction in paracellular dextran flux, and robust induction of Nrf2 target genes—provides a compelling rationale for its further investigation. Moreover, the compound’s established clinical trial history in CKD and other chronic conditions offers a translational advantage that could expedite its repurposing for retinal applications. Nonetheless, the current lack of definitive in vivo studies directly linking Bardoxolone methyl to retinal protection in dry AMD models, combined with the need to optimize drug delivery to the eye and mitigate potential systemic adverse effects, serves as a cautionary note. Future research should focus on rigorous preclinical studies in animal models of dry AMD, detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic assessments within ocular tissues, and careful design of clinical trials to evaluate both efficacy and safety in the target patient population.

Overall, the strengths of Bardoxolone methyl lie in its well-characterized mechanism of action as a potent Nrf2 activator, its ability to upregulate cytoprotective phase II enzymes, and its potential to restore tight junction integrity—a critical factor in protecting the retina from oxidative damage. Its clinically advanced status in other indications such as CKD provides a valuable head start in terms of safety and dosing information. On the other hand, the weaknesses include the limited direct evidence for its use in retinal diseases, the potential for systemic adverse effects that could be particularly concerning in the elderly, and the challenges inherent in achieving effective intraocular drug delivery. Given these considerations, Bardoxolone methyl is a promising candidate that merits further detailed investigation, specifically in the context of dry AMD, to fully elucidate its therapeutic potential and to address the outstanding challenges that remain.

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl has not yet been directly tested in dry AMD clinical trials, its underlying pharmacological profile, supported by substantial in vitro and in vivo preclinical evidence, suggests that it may offer significant benefits in restoring RPE function and retinal barrier integrity through the activation of Nrf2 signaling. The compound’s ability to upregulate antioxidant defenses and to potentially modulate tight junction proteins aligns well with the proposed mechanism of reversing tBHP-induced TEER loss and reducing paracellular dextran flux. If subsequent studies confirm these effects in relevant animal models and demonstrate a favorable safety profile in ocular tissues, Bardoxolone methyl could emerge as a viable repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Future research efforts should focus on refining ocular delivery strategies, verifying the direct effects on RPE gene expression and barrier function, and rigorously evaluating its long-term safety in the context of age-related retinal diseases (Cheng et al., 2021; Cuadrado et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2012; Nakagami, 2016; Nakagami et al., 2015; Schiavoni et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA-408; also known as CDDO-DFPA; N-(2-Cyano-3,12-dioxo-28-noroleana-1,9(11)-dien-17-yl)-2,2-difluoropropanamide) is a semisynthetic oleanane triterpenoid created by lead optimization of the natural product oleanolic acid, a plant-derived pentacyclic triterpene produced via the mevalonate pathway (squalene → 2,3-oxidosqualene → β-amyrin → erythrodiol → oleanolic acid) and abundantly available from Oleaceae (e.g., olive) and other botanical sources (over 1,600 species; Nakagami, 2016; Masullo et al., 2017; Pollier & Goossens, 2012). The oleanane scaffold was iteratively diversified by Sporn, Gribble, Honda and collaborators to introduce enone and cyanoenone Michael acceptors on rings A and C, yielding the CDDO class (2-cyano-3,12-dioxo-oleana-1,9(11)-dien-28-oic acid and derivatives) as extraordinarily potent anti-inflammatory and Nrf2-inducing agents; C-28 esters/amides and further A/C-ring modifications produced multiple clinical candidates including CDDO-Me (bardoxolone methyl, RTA-402) and RTA-408 (omaveloxolone) (Honda et al., 2000; Pollier & Goossens, 2012; Cheng et al., 2021). RTA-408 specifically is a C17-modified difluoro-propanamide on an oleanane core and belongs to the second generation of synthetic triterpenoids designed to preserve high Nrf2 potency while controlling electrophilicity and pharmacokinetics (Nakagami, 2016; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

At the pharmacological class level, synthetic oleanane triterpenoids are electrophilic “antioxidant inflammation modulators” that activate the KEAP1–NRF2–ARE pathway through covalent (but often reversible) Michael addition to redox-sensitive cysteines on KEAP1, particularly Cys151 on the BTB domain, thereby stabilizing Nrf2 and inducing a coordinated cytoprotective gene program; they concurrently suppress inducible pro-inflammatory mediators (e.g., iNOS, COX-2) with dose-dependent bifunctionality (cytoprotection at low concentrations; pro-oxidant/apoptotic signaling at higher exposure) (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Liby et al., 2007). This scaffold has been extensively explored as a drug platform across oncology, nephrology, cardiopulmonary, inflammatory, and neurological indications, with bardoxolone methyl and omaveloxolone translating to clinical studies and, for omaveloxolone, regulatory approval in Friedreich’s ataxia (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Zahir et al., 2025). Within ophthalmology, oleanane triterpenoids and close congeners (dh404, CDDO-TFEA, CDDO-EA, CDDO-Me) have shown robust Nrf2-mediated protection in retinal models, and RTA-408 itself has been advanced into ocular clinical trials evaluating postoperative ocular pain/inflammation and corneal endothelial cell loss after cataract surgery, positioning this mechanism squarely within ocular translational scope (Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
The oleanane triterpenoid class has a two-decade translational history that began with demonstrations that cyano-enone–bearing derivatives are sub-nanomolar inducers of the Nrf2 transcriptome and suppressors of inflammatory enzymes in vitro and in vivo, a property mapped by SAR to the presence/placement of A-ring 1-en-3-one and C-ring 9(11)-en-12-one Michael acceptors (Honda et al., 2000; Nakagami, 2016). Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me) showed pharmacodynamic activity in humans (ARE-gene induction in tumor biopsies; renal function improvements), but its BEACON Phase 3 trial in advanced CKD was halted for cardiovascular adverse events—an outcome that did not negate class activity but highlighted the need for indication-specific risk management and exclusion criteria (e.g., high BNP, poor baseline eGFR) (Masullo et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Subsequent controlled studies in rarer CKD-associated diseases continued under tighter cardiometabolic selection, while medicinal-chemistry efforts generated second-generation analogs including fluorinated scaffolds (e.g., omaveloxolone) to tune reactivity and PK/PD (Sun et al., 2017).

For omaveloxolone specifically, preclinical pharmacology established Nrf2-dependent induction of glutathione homeostasis genes and improvements in mitochondrial respiration; systemic PK in primates/humans showed dose proportionality and measurable tissue distribution (including liver, lung, brain), with PBMC and tissue Nrf2 target-gene induction at clinically achievable exposures (Reisman et al., 2019). In oncology, a first-in-human dose-escalation study in advanced solid tumors reported acceptable tolerability with pharmacodynamic evidence of Nrf2 pathway activation in PBMCs; in dermatology, topical RTA-408 lotion activated Nrf2 in human skin and was well tolerated (Creelan et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). In neurology, omaveloxolone advanced through the MOXIe program for Friedreich’s ataxia with evidence of neurologic benefit at clinical doses ≥80 mg and exposures concordant with preclinical pharmacology (Naidu & Dinkova-Kostova, 2020; Reisman et al., 2019; Zahir et al., 2025).

Ocularly, multiple oleanane triterpenoid derivatives have shown benefit in retinal oxidative-stress models: dh404 induced canonical Nrf2 target genes (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM), reduced inflammatory mediators, and decreased retinal vascular leakage; CDDO-TFEA and CDDO-EA activated NQO1 in photoreceptor-derived 661W cells and CDDO-TFEA reduced light-induced retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021). RS9, an OA-derived analog generated via microbial transformation, showed superior potency versus CDDO-Me in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) protection, increased retinal HO-1/NQO1 at low doses, and suppressed neovascularization and blood-brain barrier hyperpermeability in vivo, supporting the generalizable ocular protective potential of optimized oleanane triterpenoids (Cheng et al., 2021). Critically for translational relevance, omaveloxolone itself has documented protective activity in human fetal RPE at low-nanomolar concentrations (≤100 nM), where it prevents H₂O₂-induced apoptosis/necrosis by shifting the Bcl-2:Bax ratio and reducing protein glutathionylation—biomarkers linked to oxidative damage and barrier compromise in RPE (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, RTA-408 is the only oleanolic acid analogue noted to have entered clinical trials in ocular indications (cataract-surgery–related pain/inflammation and corneal endothelial cell loss), demonstrating sponsor commitment to ophthalmic development and an initial tolerability signal for ocular use (Cheng et al., 2021). No clinical reports were found in the provided context for omaveloxolone in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) specifically, nor in geographic atrophy; thus, this is a repurposing proposal grounded in mechanistic and preclinical ocular convergence rather than direct AMD clinical precedent (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
The KEAP1–NRF2 node is a cysteine-centric electrophile sensor system that orchestrates the phase-2 antioxidant and cytoprotective response. Under basal conditions, KEAP1 recruits NRF2 to the CUL3 E3 ligase complex for ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover. Electrophiles such as cyano-enone triterpenoids react with KEAP1 cysteine sensors—most prominently Cys151 in the BTB domain—to disrupt CUL3 docking and/or alter KEAP1 conformation, thereby stabilizing NRF2, allowing nuclear translocation, heterodimerization with small Maf proteins, and binding to antioxidant response elements (ARE) to induce a transcriptional battery including NQO1, HO-1 (HMOX1), glutathione biosynthesis enzymes (GCLC, GCLM), thioredoxin and thioredoxin reductase (Txn1, Txnrd1), sulfiredoxin (Srxn1), and other detoxifying/antioxidative genes (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). Oleanane cyano-enone triterpenoids are among the most potent NRF2 activators known, with structure–activity relationships showing strong correlations between the presence/geometry of Michael acceptors and both iNOS suppression and NQO1 induction across series; mechanistic profiling indicates covalent yet reversible conjugation to protein thiols underlies this pharmacology (Naidu & Dinkova-Kostova, 2020).

Within this class, omaveloxolone is an electrophilic Michael acceptor–bearing, difluoro-propanamide oleanane that activates Nrf2 at nanomolar concentrations in reporter assays and upregulates canonical ARE-target genes (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, TxnR1), consistent with its cyano-enone pharmacophore engaging KEAP1 Cys151 and allied redox sensors (Sun et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019). In systemic models, omaveloxolone increases glutathione concentrations, supports mitochondrial respiration, and normalizes metabolic/energetic parameters downstream of Nrf2 activation—effects mechanistically rationalized by Nrf2-driven induction of NADPH-generating enzymes and mitochondrial support genes, which collectively bolster reductive and ATP capacity in stressed cells (Reisman et al., 2019). In immunologic contexts, oleanane triterpenoids suppress IFN-γ–induced nitric oxide signaling in macrophages, reduce reactive oxygen and nitrotyrosine production by myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and can inhibit IKKβ/NF-κB signaling (demonstrated for CDDO-Me), contributing to anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions that are secondary but complementary to NRF2-mediated cytoprotection (Creelan et al., 2017; Sporn et al., 2007). The class is bifunctional: low-to-moderate exposures favor NRF2-dependent cytoprotection and redox quenching, whereas higher exposures can increase oxidative burden and trigger apoptosis—an important consideration when targeting delicate ocular tissues (Liby et al., 2007).

For ocular cell types relevant to dry AMD, multiple lines of evidence anchor Nrf2/ARE biology. In the retina, oleanane triterpenoids (dh404, CDDO derivatives) induce NQO1/HO-1/GCLM, reduce inflammatory mediators and vascular leakage, and protect photoreceptors and retinal structure in oxidative-stress models; RS9 dosing increases retinal NQO1/HO-1 in vivo (Cheng et al., 2021). In human fetal RPE, omaveloxolone prevents H₂O₂-induced apoptosis and necrosis at ≤100 nM, shifts Bcl-2:Bax pro-survival balance, and reduces protein S-glutathionylation, a reversible oxidative modification implicated in disruption of cytoskeletal and junctional complexes that maintain barrier integrity (Cheng et al., 2021). Taken together, these data support that omaveloxolone, via KEAP1 cysteine sensing and Nrf2 activation in RPE and adjacent retinal cells, can rapidly enhance the endogenous antioxidant program, elevate glutathione/NADPH buffering, mitigate protein oxidative adducts, and suppress inflammatory amplification—biomechanistic axes directly relevant to RPE survival and barrier function under oxidative stress (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021).

Pharmacologically, omaveloxolone exhibits high plasma protein binding and broad tissue distribution preclinically, with oral dosing in primates/humans yielding exposures that induce Nrf2 targets in PBMCs and distribute to metabolically active tissues; topical dermal dosing in humans activates cutaneous Nrf2 without untoward safety signals (Reisman et al., 2019). For ocular dosing, clinical testing of RTA-408 in cataract-surgery contexts (ocular pain/inflammation, corneal endothelial protection) establishes feasibility of achieving pharmacologically relevant ocular exposure with acceptable tolerability in humans, though detailed ocular PK has not been published in the provided excerpts (Cheng et al., 2021).

Assay and hypothesis: In a human RPE monolayer model subjected to H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury, omaveloxolone is expected to covalently and reversibly modify KEAP1 cysteines (notably Cys151), stabilize and activate Nrf2, and robustly induce the ARE-regulated antioxidant gene set (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, TXNRD1, SRXN1), thereby increasing cellular glutathione, NADPH-dependent antioxidant enzyme activity, and mitochondrial resilience; these changes should reduce protein S-glutathionylation, prevent loss of perijunctional actomyosin integrity, and preserve tight-junction belts, culminating in restoration of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and reduction of paracellular flux (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021). Mechanistic support for each step:
