Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
H-1152 Dihydrochloride is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor discovered and developed as part of the class of ATP‐competitive inhibitors targeting Rho‐associated coiled‐coil kinase (ROCK). It is formulated as a dihydrochloride salt (Tocris 2061) and has been characterized for its exceptional potency against ROCK isoforms, with reported IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range (0.003 µM for ROCK1 and 0.014 µM for ROCK2). As an ATP-competitive type I kinase inhibitor, it possesses a chemical structure that enables it to fit into the highly conserved ATP-binding cavity of ROCK and thereby prevents phosphorylation of downstream targets. This class of compounds has historically been used to explore the roles of ROCK in cytoskeletal dynamics, cell contractility, and migration, and has been applied in various preclinical models of ocular disorders such as glaucoma and corneal endothelial injury (Iancu et al., 2021; Meekins et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Although H-1152 itself has not been clinically approved, its pharmacologic profile as a ROCK inhibitor has been extensively studied in preclinical ocular models. Multiple studies have employed H-1152 in experiments that assessed its effects on corneal endothelial cell migration, proliferation, and wound healing. For instance, in in vitro assays using porcine corneal endothelial cells, H-1152 significantly enhanced cell migration and proliferation compared with control treatments and with other inhibitors like Y-27632. In vivo topical application in rabbit corneal surgical wound models demonstrated accelerated wound closure and resolution of corneal edema without significant toxic effects. These findings underscore its potential utility as a topical therapeutic agent in ocular applications. Moreover, the general class of ROCK inhibitors has been clinically exploited—ripasudil, for example, has been approved for the treatment of glaucoma in Japan, and intravitreal fasudil has been explored for refractory diabetic macular oedema—establishing a safe precedent for ocular delivery of ROCK-targeting molecules. However, while ROCK inhibitors have been investigated in retinal and choroidal vascular pathologies and in conditions marked by barrier dysfunction (such as diabetic macular oedema), there is currently no direct record of H-1152 having been used specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or for RPE-specific pathologies in published clinical or preclinical studies (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, H-1152 acts by competitively inhibiting the kinase activity of both ROCK1 and ROCK2. By binding to the ATP-binding site of the kinase domain, H-1152 prevents the phosphorylation of downstream substrates such as myosin light chain (MLC) and LIM kinases, which in turn results in the reduced phosphorylation of cofilin. This cascade of events inhibits actomyosin contractility and results in the disassembly—or at least, a significant reduction—of actin stress fibers. In cellular contexts, this biochemical action translates into the disruption of stress-fiber–driven cellular contraction and a modulation of both cell–matrix and cell–cell adhesion complexes. In ocular applications, particularly within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), such cytoskeletal reorganization is hypothesized to stabilize junctional complexes by normalizing the localization and organization of critical tight-junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and occludin. Studies in related ocular cell types (e.g., corneal endothelial cells) have documented that ROCK inhibitors induce a rapid collapse of actin stress fibers and result in a transient loss but subsequent restoration of tight-junction architecture over time. Furthermore, ROCK signaling is implicated in mediating the cellular responses to oxidative stress and in promoting VEGF-induced permeability. In models of VEGF stimulation, ROCK inhibition has been associated with a reduction in paracellular leak by preserving tight-junction integrity. Therefore, by potently inhibiting ROCK1/2, H-1152 is proposed to prevent the stress-fiber–mediated disruption of cell–cell junctions and to restore transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE cells subjected to chronic oxidative insult – a mechanism particularly relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology (Meekins et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its mechanism of action and experimental precedent in other ocular models, it is expected that H-1152 will exert a protective effect on RPE cells under conditions of chronic oxidative stress as seen in dry AMD. In vitro, in an ARPE-19 or primary RPE cell model, chronic exposure to low levels of H₂O₂ typically results in a decrease in TEER, disorganization of tight junction proteins (including ZO-1 and occludin), and the formation of abnormal F-actin stress fibers. Treatment with H-1152 in the range of 0.1–1 µM is hypothesized to partially or even substantially reverse these deleterious changes. Specifically, by inhibiting ROCK activity, H-1152 is expected to reduce the formation of stress fibers, thereby reversing the disruption of cell junctions and restoring a more normal distribution of ZO-1 and occludin at the plasma membrane. This should in turn lead to an improvement in TEER – with potential recovery to up to 60% of baseline levels in injured cells – as well as diminish the regulation of VEGF-driven paracellular leak. In addition, pharmacokinetic studies in rabbit models have demonstrated that subconjunctival dosing can achieve ocular RPE/choroid concentrations on the order of ~0.2 µM, which falls within the effective in vitro concentration range. Thus, the expected translational effect is that topical or subconjunctival administration of H-1152 will normalize RPE barrier function, mitigating one of the critical pathological hallmarks of dry AMD, which is the breakdown of the outer blood-retinal barrier that underlies RPE dysfunction and subsequent photoreceptor loss (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Meekins et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the therapeutic candidate H-1152 Dihydrochloride exhibits multiple promising attributes as a repurposed drug for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. One of its primary strengths is its exceptional potency and selectivity toward ROCK1 and ROCK2, with IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range, which is critical given that only minimal inhibition may be required to elicit beneficial cellular modifications in the RPE. Its mechanism of action, relying on the inhibition of the ROCK pathway, directly addresses key pathological processes in dry AMD, notably the stress-fiber–mediated disruption of cell–cell junctions and the abnormal VEGF-driven paracellular leak. Furthermore, successful preclinical studies in corneal endothelial models have demonstrated that H-1152 can modulate cytoskeletal organization and promote wound healing, providing a proof-of-concept for its ability to restore barrier function in ocular tissues. The fact that ocular delivery via topical or subconjunctival routes can achieve therapeutic levels in the RPE/choroid is another advantage that underscores its translational potential, especially when compared with other ROCK inhibitors that have advanced into clinical trials for related ocular conditions such as glaucoma and diabetic macular oedema (Iancu et al., 2021; Meekins et al., 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, there are several important weaknesses and uncertainties that must be addressed. First, the bulk of available preclinical evidence for H-1152 is derived from studies involving corneal endothelial cells rather than RPE cells, and therefore it remains uncertain whether the effects observed in these models will fully translate to the RPE context. The RPE possesses unique structural and functional characteristics that distinguish it from corneal endothelium, and additional targeted experiments in ARPE-19 or primary RPE cell models under conditions of chronic oxidative stress are required to confirm the hypothesized restoration of TEER and normalization of tight-junction proteins. Second, while the ROCK inhibitor class has been used in other areas of ophthalmology with an acceptable safety and tolerability profile, there is currently no direct clinical history of H-1152 being used for dry AMD or even in posterior-segment diseases; most clinical data so far pertains to ROCK inhibitors used in glaucoma or diabetic macular oedema. This means that the long-term safety, potential off-target effects, and optimal dosing regimens for H-1152 in the context of dry AMD remain to be established (Iancu et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Furthermore, some studies in retinal angiogenesis models have reported that certain ROCK inhibitors can produce paradoxical effects, such as increased VEGF-induced angiogenesis via alternative signaling pathways including ERK1/2 activation. Although the candidate hypothesis emphasizes barrier restoration and suppression of VEGF-driven leak, it will be critical to delineate the dose–response relationship and evaluate any potential pro-angiogenic or off-target actions of H-1152 in comprehensive preclinical studies. Establishing robust pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles is essential; while rabbit subconjunctival dosing reportedly achieved ocular RPE/choroid levels around 0.2 µM, it needs to be confirmed that such concentrations are both efficacious and safe in the long term, particularly as the dry AMD population may require chronic dosing (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overall, H-1152 Dihydrochloride presents as a promising candidate for repurposing as a dry AMD therapeutic based on its mechanistic rationale, outstanding potency and selectivity for ROCK inhibition, and the supportive data from ocular surface models. The proposed molecular mechanism—restoring tight-junction integrity through suppression of stress fiber formation and subsequent normalization of ZO-1 and occludin localization—aligns well with the underlying pathology of dry AMD, in which the breakdown of RPE barrier function contributes to disease progression. However, definitive preclinical studies employing RPE-specific models and in vivo evaluations in relevant dry AMD animal models are necessary to solidify its translational potential. Additionally, careful attention must be given to its safety profile, especially given the delicate nature of the posterior segment and the potential for off-target effects on retinal vasculature. In conclusion, while H-1152 shows significant promise based on its pharmacological profile and the mechanistic logic underlying RPE barrier restoration, further research is warranted to bridge the gap between ocular surface models and the RPE-specific pathology encountered in dry AMD. Strategic preclinical investigations, including detailed assessments of TEER restoration, tight junction protein localization under oxidative stress, and the modulation of VEGF signaling, are critical next steps in validating H-1152 as a viable therapeutic candidate for this complex and currently underserved retinal disease (Meekins et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Arimoclomol (also known as BRX-345) is a synthetic hydroxylamine/hydroxamic-acid–derived small molecule developed as a heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducer that amplifies stress-inducible transcription of heat shock genes under conditions of proteotoxic stress, principally through prolongation and potentiation of heat shock factor-1 (HSF1) activation on heat shock elements (HSEs) in target promoters (Penke et al., 2018; Parfitt et al., 2014; O’Leary, 2019). In the hydroximic-acid derivative family (bimoclomol, arimoclomol, NG-094, BGP-15), several members synergistically enhance heat-induced Hsp expression; arimoclomol and bimoclomol have been shown to increase HSF1 activity via hyperphosphorylation and to amplify heat-shock gene expression in eukaryotic cells while sparing basal Hsp expression in unstressed cells, thereby acting as bona fide co-inducers rather than primary HSF1 agonists (Penke et al., 2018). The compound was originally advanced from the bimoclomol chemotype as a more drug-like analogue with similar HSR-potentiating properties and improved pharmacology, and it falls within a broader class of pharmacologic HSP70/HSF1 modulators investigated for neurodegenerative protein-misfolding diseases (e.g., ALS, NPC, tauopathies), as well as select retinal degeneration models (rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa) (Parfitt et al., 2014; Venediktov et al., 2023; Penke et al., 2018). At the biophysical level, hydroximic-acid derivatives can intercalate into cellular membranes, a property hypothesized to contribute to regulation of HSF1 activation/attenuation kinetics and restoration of a protective Hsp profile under stress (Penke et al., 2018). In neuronal cell systems, arimoclomol has also been used in combination with primary HSF1 activators (e.g., celastrol) to achieve robust induction of inducible Hsp70s (HSPA1A, HSPA6) and other stress response proteins at lower inducer doses, consistent with its role as a co-inducer that amplifies pre-existing HSF1 activation (Deane, 2019).

Within the retina, arimoclomol has been evaluated in rod photoreceptor models of misfolded rhodopsin (P23H transgenic rats), where it enhanced Hsp70/Hsp90 expression and improved proteostasis, photoreceptor structure, and visual function; however, there is no published evidence in dry AMD models or direct demonstrations of RPE barrier rescue by arimoclomol, and at least one PRPF31-mutant RPE (RP11) cell system screening showed no aggregate-reducing effect of arimoclomol while an mTOR inhibitor (rapamycin) reduced aggregate burden via autophagy induction (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021). The broader Hsp70/Hsc70 system, chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), and macroautophagy are mechanistically central to RPE proteostasis and AMD pathobiology, establishing a strong rationale for HSF1–HSP70–targeted therapy, but translation from photoreceptor models and exogenous Hsp70 delivery to endogenous induction in RPE remains to be validated for this agent (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Subrizi et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History  
Arimoclomol’s development history is anchored in neurodegeneration and protein-misfolding indications. In SOD1-mutant ALS mice, arimoclomol increased Hsp70 expression and improved motor neuron survival and function, extending lifespan; it progressed to human ALS trials (including a phase 3 program), with mixed outcomes across adult and pediatric indications (O’Leary, 2019; Venediktov et al., 2023). Mechanistically consistent with HSF1 co-induction, arimoclomol is positioned to upregulate a suite of inducible chaperones and components of the proteostasis network rather than single chaperone overexpression, a strategy considered preferable for matching the endogenous disaggregation/refolding machinery and preserving feedback attenuation (O’Leary, 2019).

In the retina, arimoclomol has been tested extensively in rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa (RP) models driven by the P23H misfolding mutation. In P23H-GFP cell models, arimoclomol reduced inclusion incidence and insoluble rod opsin, decreased higher-molecular-weight rhodopsin species, and improved viability, with contemporaneous increases in Hsp70/Hsp90 implying potentiation of the HSR in stressed photoreceptors (Parfitt et al., 2014). In P23H transgenic rats, daily intraperitoneal dosing (10 mg/kg) improved scotopic ERG a- and b-waves, preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness, increased outer segment (OS) length, and improved ultrastructure, consistent with disease modification through HSR and unfolded protein response (UPR) potentiation; Hsp70, Hsp90, and HSF1 were assayed directly in these studies (Parfitt et al., 2014). The authors further observed increased eIF2α phosphorylation and discussed enhanced IRE1/XBP1 activity, indicating crosstalk with ER stress responses (Parfitt et al., 2014). Of note, arimoclomol’s activity appeared contingent on the presence of misfolded-protein stress (i.e., stress-selective action), potentially limiting off-target effects in healthy tissue (Parfitt et al., 2014).

Beyond photoreceptors, the Hsp co-inducer class has retinal neuroprotective precedents: bimoclomol improved early electrophysiologic signs in diabetic rat retina, and the Hsp inducer geranylgeranylacetone protected retinal ganglion cells in a rat glaucoma model, underscoring that Hsp70 induction can be protective across retinal cell types and diseases of proteostasis and stress, although these are class exemplars rather than arimoclomol-specific RPE data (Hesselink, 2016). Separately, exogenous Hsp70 protein delivery to RPE has shown diffusion to the retina and RPE after intravitreal administration, intracellular uptake, lysosomal localization, and protection from oxidative stress and inflammation in ARPE-19 cells, supporting the concept that increasing Hsp70 activity in RPE can be beneficial, albeit via protein pharmacology rather than endogenous induction (Subrizi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Crucially for dry AMD translation, the current literature set provides no in vivo animal or clinical study of arimoclomol in AMD/dry AMD, and no direct measurements of RPE barrier integrity (tight-junction protein preservation or transepithelial electrical resistance [TEER]) following arimoclomol in RPE or AMD models; an RPE disease model of PRPF31 mutation with progressive aggregate accumulation reported that arimoclomol failed to reduce aggregates, whereas rapamycin decreased aggregate load and induced LC3 processing consistent with autophagy activation (LAMP1 and p62 remained unchanged), highlighting context-dependent efficacy and suggesting autophagy induction may be more decisive than Hsp co-induction in some RPE aggregate pathologies (Georgiou, 2021). Thus, while arimoclomol has a positive retinal track record in photoreceptor proteotoxicity and a robust extraocular development history, there is no direct evidence yet of arimoclomol ameliorating dry AMD phenotypes or preserving RPE barrier function in disease-relevant systems (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Arimoclomol is an HSR co-inducer that amplifies HSF1-driven transcription of inducible heat shock proteins under pre-existing cellular stress. Mechanistically, arimoclomol prolongs HSF1 binding to HSEs, increases HSF1 activity (e.g., hyperphosphorylation), and thereby increases transcription of Hsp70/Hsp90 and related chaperones, with limited impact in unstressed cells (i.e., stressor-dependent co-induction) (Penke et al., 2018; O’Leary, 2019; Parfitt et al., 2014). In neuronal cells, arimoclomol enhanced celastrol-induced HSF1 activation to elevate HSPA6, HSPA1A, HSPB1, DNAJB1, and HO-1 at doses that preserved viability and differentiated morphology, supporting efficient co-induction when paired with a primary HSF1 activator (Deane, 2019). In P23H photoreceptor models, arimoclomol reduced insoluble rhodopsin and inclusion incidence, decreased high-molecular-weight species, increased retinal Hsp70/Hsp90, and improved ERG/ONL/OS outcomes; the study observed increased eIF2α phosphorylation and discussed potentiation of the UPR (BiP/IRE1/XBP1), consistent with arimoclomol acting at the intersection of cytosolic HSR and ER homeostasis (Parfitt et al., 2014).

Hsp70 Biology in RPE and AMD. Inducible Hsp70 (HSPA1A/Hsp70-1) is a central, evolutionarily conserved ATPase chaperone that assists folding of nascent chains, refolds damaged/misfolded proteins, buffers aggregation, facilitates “protein triage” toward degradation pathways, and protects cells from apoptosis and inflammatory signaling (e.g., NF-κB pathway), with expression controlled by HSF1 (Ryhänen, 2011; Kivinen, 2018). In the RPE, Hsp70/Hsc70 function intersects both the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) and lysosome-dependent proteolysis. Hsp70 can present misfolded proteins to the UPS via CHIP E3 ligase, regulate disaggregation with co-chaperones HSP40/HSP90/HIP/HOP, and is required for aggregate handling; in proteasome failure, protein aggregates in ARPE-19 cells co-localize with Hsp70 and p62, with p62 undergoing autophagic clearance while Hsp70 binds reversibly and evades autophagic degradation (Kumar et al., 2020; Kivinen et al., 2014; Ryhänen, 2011). Hsp70 is also integral to chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA): cytosolic Hsc70/Hsp70 recognizes KFERQ-containing substrates, delivers them to LAMP-2A at the lysosomal membrane, and ATPase-driven “entropic pulling” and luminal chaperones enable translocation and degradation; oxidative stress reduces HSP70 expression in RPE, impairs CMA, and can dysregulate macroautophagy cross-talk, contributing to RPE death (Chang et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020). Extracellular Hsp70 roles in RPE are complex: exogenous rhHsp70 injections protected against subretinal fibrosis via TLR2/TLR4 and IL-10 induction, while oxidized-lipid stress (4-HNE) can increase extracellular Hsp70 efflux and pro-inflammatory cytokines, indicating that compartmental localization of Hsp70 critically determines immunomodulatory outcomes (Kumar et al., 2020).

Evidence for arimoclomol in RPE cells. Direct mechanistic evidence for arimoclomol action in RPE is limited. A cell-culture report in ARPE-19 asserts that Hsp70 overexpression “with the help of a co-inducer like arimoclomol” suppressed IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α and increased IL-10 and TGF-β1, consistent with Hsp70-mediated IκK/NF-κB inhibition; however, the study details are summarized in low-quality review literature, and direct demonstration of arimoclomol-driven HSF1 activation in RPE is not provided (Kumar et al., 2020). Another ARPE-19-focused review excerpt states that arimoclomol acts on HSF1 to increase cytosolic Hsp70 without increasing extracellular Hsp70 and improved resistance to 4-HNE–induced oxidative stress (relative to paeoniflorin); again, the primary data are not provided here and the review is of limited quality, so these findings should be treated as provisional until replicated (Kumar et al., 2020). Importantly, in an isogenic patient-derived PRPF31-mutant RPE (RP11) model with progressive cytoplasmic aggregate accumulation, a 7-day treatment screen across HSR/UPR/autophagy modulators showed that rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibitor) reduced aggregate load and shifted LC3-I to LC3-II, whereas arimoclomol did not reduce aggregates under the conditions tested, arguing that in this RPE disease context autophagy activation via mTOR inhibition outperformed Hsp co-induction (Georgiou, 2021).

Non-pharmacological Hsp70 induction and autophagy in RPE inform plausibility. Subthreshold retinal thermal stimulation in pig and mouse RPE in vivo induced HSF1 and Hsp70, increased LC3B-II and decreased p62 (consistent with autophagy activation), and increased LAMP2, suggesting potential CMA upregulation, without apoptosis at ~44 °C, confirming that RPE supports coordinated HSR–autophagy programs with an exploitable therapeutic window (but autophagic flux was not directly quantified in vivo) (Amirkavei et al., 2022; Amirkavei et al., 2020). These data reinforce the therapeutic logic for HSF1–Hsp70 upregulation in RPE to restore proteostasis but do not directly validate arimoclomol’s efficacy in RPE (Amirkavei et al., 2022; Amirkavei et al., 2020). Exogenous rhHsp70 trafficking to lysosomes and protection against oxidative stress in ARPE-19 further supports the notion that increasing Hsp70 activity, whether by protein delivery or endogenous induction, can be beneficial to RPE survival under AMD-relevant stressors (Subrizi et al., 2015).

Autophagy and barrier integrity under AMD-relevant stressors. AMD-relevant toxicities (Aβ, lipofuscin/A2E, oxidants) perturb autophagy/lysosomes in RPE, with Aβ decreasing occludin and ZO-1 in ARPE-19 and activating autophagy markers in vitro and in vivo, and A2E promoting lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cell death; impaired UPS and autophagy with aging lead to aggregate accumulation (including p62-positive aggregates) in RPE and drusen, highlighting the importance of restoring both proteasomal and autophagic clearance to protect RPE function and barrier integrity (Wang et al., 2023; Viiri, 2019; Ryhänen, 2011). Hsp70/p62 roles in this axis are mechanistically established: Hsp70 prevents aggregation and participates in aggregate handling, while p62 is an autophagic receptor degraded by autophagy and accumulates when autophagy is impaired; pharmacologic AMPK activation can accelerate p62 clearance during proteasome inhibition and improve RPE survival (Viiri, 2019). To date, arimoclomol has not been shown to modulate CMA or macroautophagy in RPE, nor to preserve tight junctions or TEER in AMD-relevant models (Georgiou, 2021; Kumar et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay hypothesis and rationale. The working hypothesis is that arimoclomol will potentiate stress-triggered HSF1 activity in RPE, elevating inducible Hsp70 and coordinated chaperone networks to stabilize junctional proteostasis, reduce misfolded protein burden, and normalize autophagy (including potentially CMA), thereby preventing degradation of occludin/claudin and restoring TEER under oxidative or drusen-like stress (e.g., H2O2/4-HNE, A2E/lipofuscin, Aβ) (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). This mechanism is biologically plausible: Hsp70 is abundantly expressed in RPE under stress and supports folding and refolding, substrate triage to proteasome via CHIP, and delivery of specific substrates to CMA via Hsc70/LAMP-2A; its induction suppresses NF-κB–driven pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and can raise IL-10/TGF-β1, which together could indirectly protect junctional complexes from cytokine- and stress-mediated degradation (Kumar et al., 2020). Reducing intracellular aggregate load and restoring proteostasis would be expected to mitigate the downstream cascade of mTORC1 activation, p62/LC3-I accumulation, and tight-junction disruption observed in stressed RPE models (e.g., PRPF31-RPE), although in that system arimoclomol was ineffective while rapamycin reduced aggregates, underscoring that Hsp co-induction alone may be insufficient when autophagy is the principal bottleneck (Georgiou, 2021).

Evidence supporting expected effects in RPE assays:  
- Hsp70 induction in retinal tissues has been achieved via HSF1 activation by heat or pharmacologic inducers; in photoreceptor P23H models, arimoclomol increased Hsp70/Hsp90 and reduced aggregation/toxicity, consistent with the proximal arm of the proposed mechanism (HSF1→Hsp70→improved proteostasis) (Parfitt et al., 2014; Amirkavei et al., 2020).  
- In ARPE-19 summaries, arimoclomol increased intracellular (not extracellular) Hsp70 and improved resistance to 4-HNE oxidative stress, and Hsp70 overexpression with help of a co-inducer like arimoclomol suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines, supporting cell-autonomous proteostasis and anti-inflammatory contributions that would be favorable for junctional stability (Kumar et al., 2020).  
- Exogenous rhHsp70 delivery to RPE localizes to lysosomes and reduces oxidative toxicity and inflammation, demonstrating that raising functional Hsp70 in RPE is sufficient to afford cytoprotection, a downstream functional goal of HSF1 co-induction (Subrizi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Evidence arguing for tempered expectations and the need for combination strategies:  
- In PRPF31-mutant RPE, arimoclomol did not reduce aggregates in a 7-day screen, whereas rapamycin shifted LC3 processing and reduced aggregate markers, suggesting that when autophagy is the limiting axis, direct autophagy activation (e.g., mTORC1 inhibition) is required; Hsp co-induction alone may not clear established aggregates or repair autophagic flux (Georgiou, 2021).  
- In primary neuronal ALS models, arimoclomol often failed to induce measurable HSPA1A/HSPA8 and its protective actions occurred without detectable Hsp70 upregulation; HDAC inhibition enhanced Hsp induction by other inducers, arguing that Hsp co-induction efficacy is cell-type and chromatin-context dependent and may require combination therapy to overcome induction thresholds in some cells (potentially relevant to differentiated RPE) (Comaduran et al., 2024).  
- AMD-relevant stressors directly disrupt tight junctions (Aβ reduces occludin and ZO-1 in ARPE-19) and invoke autophagy/lysosomal dysfunction; because arimoclomol’s effects on CMA/macroautophagy in RPE are unproven, barrier rescue may not occur unless autophagic flux is also corrected (Wang et al., 2023).

Assay implementation guidance for decision-making:  
- In vitro human RPE models (primary/donor iPSC-RPE monolayers with high TEER) should be stressed with 4-HNE, H2O2, A2E, or Aβ to recapitulate AMD-relevant proteotoxic and inflammatory conditions, and arimoclomol tested across concentrations paralleling prior cell work (e.g., 10–100 µM) with and without a priming HSF1 activator (celastrol ≤0.3 µM) to evaluate requirement for co-induction, keeping in mind the neuronal data identifying 50 µM arimoclomol + 0.3 µM celastrol as an optimized low-toxicity combination (Deane, 2019).  
- Primary readouts: HSF1 activation (nuclear translocation, Ser phosphorylation), Hsp70/Hsp90 induction (immunoblot, qPCR), autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover with/without bafilomycin, p62 dynamics), CMA markers (LAMP-2A levels, lysosomal Hsc70/Hsp70 substrate colocalization), proteasome activity, aggregate load (FK1, ubiquitin, p62 bodies), and barrier integrity (TEER, ZO-1/occludin/claudin-19 immunostaining continuity) (Kivinen et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2015; Viiri, 2019; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Cytokine profiling (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10, TGF-β1) to detect Hsp70-linked NF-κB effects reported in ARPE-19 (Kumar et al., 2020).  
- Positive comparators: rapamycin for autophagy induction; exogenous rhHsp70 as a proteostasis rescue control; heat-based Hsp70 induction within non-damaging windows to confirm pathway responsiveness (Georgiou, 2021; Subrizi et al., 2015; Amirkavei et al., 2020).

Given the aggregate of evidence, the most realistic expectation is that arimoclomol will increase inducible Hsp70 in stressed RPE if HSF1 can be productively co-induced, reduce misfolded protein accumulation and inflammatory signaling, and potentially improve barrier metrics indirectly by attenuating stressors that degrade junctional complexes; however, without concurrent normalization of autophagic flux and CMA, tight-junction rescue and TEER restoration are uncertain, particularly in models where autophagy is the primary deficit (Georgiou, 2021; Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths supporting arimoclomol for dry AMD RPE barrier rescue:  
- Mechanistic fit: Hsp70/Hsc70 are central “gatekeepers” of RPE proteostasis across the UPS and lysosomal systems, including CMA; restoring inducible Hsp70 via HSF1 co-induction directly targets key failure nodes in RPE aging and AMD pathogenesis (aggregation, impaired clearance, inflammation), aligning with known disease biology (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Kivinen, 2018).  
- Demonstrated retinal efficacy in proteostasis-driven degeneration: arimoclomol increased Hsp70/Hsp90, reduced mutant rhodopsin aggregation, and preserved photoreceptor structure/function in P23H rats, with evidence of concurrent UPR potentiation; this validates the platform concept that HSF1 co-induction plus ER stress modulation can modify retinal degeneration, albeit in photoreceptors rather than RPE (Parfitt et al., 2014).  
- RPE permissiveness to Hsp70-based cytoprotection: exogenous rhHsp70 diffuses to RPE, is internalized, localizes to endolysosomal compartments, reduces IL-6 and cytolysis, and improves viability in oxidative stress paradigms; thus, augmenting Hsp70 in RPE is sufficient to produce protective effects, supporting the feasibility of endogenous induction with a co-inducer if pharmacology is adequate (Subrizi et al., 2015).  
- Stress-selective amplification: arimoclomol preferentially acts in stressed cells, limiting risks of unwanted Hsp70 induction in healthy tissue; this attribute is advantageous for chronic ocular therapy where avoiding constitutive pathway activation is desirable (Parfitt et al., 2014).  
- Clinical development and safety experience: extensive non-ocular development in ALS/NPC provides informative safety and pharmacology context; while ocular distribution is not established in these sources, the systemic safety window is a favorable starting point for repurposing (Venediktov et al., 2023; O’Leary, 2019).

Key weaknesses and uncertainties:  
- Lack of direct evidence in dry AMD/RPE barrier endpoints: no published data demonstrate arimoclomol preserves RPE tight junctions (ZO-1/occludin/claudin), restores TEER, or improves drusen-like pathology in vivo; ARPE-19 reports of arimoclomol-induced Hsp70 and anti-inflammatory effects are secondary summaries in low-quality reviews without primary detail (Kumar et al., 2020). In contrast, direct AMD-relevant in vitro data show that Aβ disrupts tight junction proteins, and autophagy failure correlates with p62 accumulation and aggregate burden, but the ability of arimoclomol to reverse these specific defects in RPE is untested (Wang et al., 2023; Viiri, 2019).  
- Negative/neutral result in PRPF31-RPE aggregation screen: arimoclomol did not reduce cytoplasmic aggregates in a rigorous 7-day screen in RP11-RPE; rapamycin reduced aggregates and shifted LC3 processing, suggesting that in certain RPE aggregate pathologies, autophagy activators outperform Hsp co-induction; whether arimoclomol could complement autophagy induction to achieve barrier rescue remains to be determined (Georgiou, 2021).  
- Uncertain induction competence in differentiated RPE: Primary neurons display high thresholds for inducible Hsp70 (HSPA1A) induction, with arimoclomol often failing to raise Hsp70; Hsp induction can be enhanced by HDAC inhibition, implying that chromatin accessibility and cell state are important variables; differentiated RPE monolayers may similarly require co-induction strategies (e.g., low-dose celastrol or epigenetic modulators) to achieve robust Hsp70 upregulation (Comaduran et al., 2024; Deane, 2019). If arimoclomol cannot reliably induce Hsp70 in mature RPE under clinically relevant stress, the strategy will falter.  
- CMA/macroautophagy modulation by arimoclomol in RPE not established: despite Hsp70’s mechanistic role in CMA, no data show arimoclomol improves CMA or autophagic flux in RPE, which are crucial to clearing damaged proteins/lipids under AMD stress; relying on Hsp70 alone without restoring autophagic flux may be insufficient to protect tight junctions (Chang et al., 2015; Georgiou, 2021).  
- Translational pharmacology: Retinal/RPE exposure of arimoclomol following systemic dosing is not presented in this corpus; ocular delivery strategies and RPE pharmacokinetics for arimoclomol are undefined here, in contrast to exogenous Hsp70 delivery where diffusion and tissue uptake were measured (Subrizi et al., 2015). Without ocular PK/PD and RPE Hsp70 induction data, dosing strategies for barrier rescue remain speculative.

Recommendation and development path:  
- Proceed to targeted preclinical validation in human iPSC-RPE monolayers and AMD-relevant stress paradigms, with rigorous endpoint panels including HSF1–Hsp70 induction, autophagic flux/CMA markers, aggregate clearance, cytokine modulation, and barrier integrity (TEER, ZO-1/occludin continuity), using rapamycin and rhHsp70 as comparators and benchmarking against known disruptions by Aβ and A2E (Georgiou, 2021; Subrizi et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Explore co-induction strategies: combine arimoclomol with low-dose celastrol to lower the induction threshold, and/or with autophagy activators (rapalogs/AMPK agonists) to correct flux while elevating chaperone capacity; justify combinations by neuronal data demonstrating enhanced Hsp induction and by RPE data showing autophagy dependence of aggregate clearance (Deane, 2019; Viiri, 2019; Georgiou, 2021).  
- If cell data are positive (robust Hsp70 induction, reduced aggregate burden, TEER protection), advance to ex vivo retina or small-animal models of RPE oxidative/drusen-like stress, with ocular pharmacokinetic measurements to confirm RPE exposure and on-target Hsp70 induction; consider local ocular delivery if systemic exposure is inadequate (Subrizi et al., 2015).  
- Maintain a realistic risk view: if arimoclomol fails to induce Hsp70 adequately in differentiated RPE or fails to impact autophagic flux, pivot to alternative HSF1 activators or to exogenous Hsp70 delivery or autophagy-centric therapies, where evidence in RPE is stronger (Subrizi et al., 2015; Georgiou, 2021).

In sum, arimoclomol is a mechanistically coherent candidate for restoring RPE proteostasis via HSF1–Hsp70 co-induction, supported by strong photoreceptor data and broad neurodegeneration experience, but it lacks direct evidence in dry AMD models and has an RPE aggregation screen result that favors autophagy induction over Hsp co-induction; rigorous, well-controlled RPE studies with barrier readouts are required before committing to translational development for dry AMD (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021).

Analysis: Both candidates target pathobiological processes implicated in dry AMD, but they differ in evidence depth, mechanism, and translational feasibility. SB-431542 is a well-characterized ALK5 inhibitor with robust anti-fibrotic activity in multiple preclinical models, including ocular fibrosis. It directly blocks TGF-β–Smad2/3 signaling to reduce ECM overproduction, addressing Bruch’s membrane stiffening and RPE barrier disruption. However, SB-431542 lacks direct AMD models; its repurposing relies on extrapolation from glaucoma surgery scarring and non-retinal fibrosis. Chronic TGF-β blockade carries risks to immune regulation, tissue repair, and retinal homeostasis. Its short intraocular half-life necessitates complex sustained-release formulations, and long-term safety in the eye is unproven. In contrast, H-151 antagonizes STING, a key sensor linking cytosolic DNA damage to NF-κB/IRF3-driven inflammation, SASP, VEGF induction, and MMP expression—a constellation of processes central to RPE senescence and barrier failure in AMD. STING inhibition has strong genetic and pharmacologic validation in AMD-relevant contexts (Alu RNA toxicity, endothelial senescence, neovascular models). H-151 itself has direct data in senescent ARPE-19 cells showing VEGF suppression, and related STING inhibitors (C-176, SN-011) preserve barrier integrity and reduce inflammation in retinal models. While H-151’s ocular PK/PD, barrier-specific TEER data, and long-term safety are undemonstrated, its mechanism addresses multiple upstream drivers of dry AMD (oxidative stress, inflammation, senescence, proteolysis) rather than only fibrosis. The immunosuppressive and covalent-inhibitor liabilities of H-151 require derisking, but local intraocular delivery may mitigate systemic concerns. Overall, H-151 shows greater relevance to dry AMD pathology, more direct supportive data in RPE systems, and a broader mechanism tackling key disease axes, whereas SB-431542’s narrow anti-fibrotic focus and unknown AMD safety profile reduce its translatability.
Reasoning: H-151 (ID 33) is preferred because its mechanism of STING palmitoylation blockade cuts across inflammation, senescence, VEGF overproduction, and matrix remodeling—key drivers in dry AMD—and is supported by both genetic and pharmacologic validation in retinal contexts. It already shows direct evidence of VEGF suppression in RPE cells and aligns with multiple in vivo ocular models using related STING inhibitors, whereas SB-431542 (ID 29) is limited to anti-fibrotic action with no direct AMD model data, carries greater risk of interfering with beneficial TGF-β functions, and demands complex formulation to sustain intraocular levels. Consequently, H-151 has a higher likelihood of successful experimental outcome and clinical translation in dry AMD.

The report is organized into five sections: an overview of the therapeutic candidate, a review of its therapeutic history, a detailed discussion of its molecular mechanism of action, an explanation of the expected effects in the proposed assay and ocular environment, and an overall evaluation of its potential strengths and weaknesses for treating dry AMD.

    1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB‐431542 is a fully synthetic small molecule that was discovered through high‐throughput screening efforts at GlaxoSmithKline and further optimized via systematic structure–activity relationship studies. Its chemical identity is defined by the IUPAC name 4-[4-(3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl)-5-(2-pyridyl)-1H-imidazol-2-yl]-benzamide, and it belongs to the triarylimidazole/benzamide structural class (Markell, 2010; Fuchs, 2011). During its development, medicinal chemists employed target-hopping strategies that involved modifying substituents – for example, replacing a 4-pyridyl group with a 2-pyridyl moiety and adding a 3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl ring – to retain TGF-β type I receptor (ALK5) inhibitory potency while minimizing unwanted inhibition of other kinases such as p38 MAPK (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This precise engineering ensures that SB-431542 acts as a competitive inhibitor at the ATP‐binding site of ALK5, thereby conferring selectivity relative to other kinases (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). As a member of a well‐defined class of small molecule kinase inhibitors, SB-431542 has been used extensively as a research tool in studies of TGF-β signaling and fibrosis, and its chemical properties suggest that it belongs to a broader family of agents that modulate receptor kinases via competitive binding (Laping et al., 2002).

    2. Therapeutic History  
SB-431542 has been at the forefront of preclinical research into TGF-β signaling because of its capacity to selectively block ALK5 and, to a lesser extent, related receptors such as ALK4 and ALK7 (Laping et al., 2002; Ge et al., 2004). Its primary use has been as a chemical probe to elucidate the role of TGF-β in diverse fibrotic and oncologic settings. In multiple in vitro and in vivo studies, SB-431542 has been shown to effectively inhibit TGF-β1-induced upregulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components including collagen Iα1, fibronectin, and plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI-1) in renal epithelial cells and fibroblast cultures (Laping et al., 2002). Its potent antifibrotic activity has also been demonstrated in ocular applications; for example, it has been utilized in experimental models of glaucoma filtration surgery to reduce subconjunctival scarring by curtailing fibroblast proliferation, myofibroblast transdifferentiation, and ECM deposition (Wang et al., 2017). Although SB-431542 has not yet been approved for clinical use in AMD or other retinal disorders, its well‐documented ability to inhibit TGF-β–mediated fibrosis in ocular tissues suggests that it holds promise for these indications (Teplitsky et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2009). In addition, the compound’s extensive deployment in cancer studies – where it is used to block the epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and invasion – further verifies its capacity to modulate key pathological processes that also underlie fibrotic changes observed in retinal degeneration (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010).

    3. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, SB-431542 functions as a competitive inhibitor of the TGF-β type I receptor (ALK5) by binding to its ATP binding site. Upon the engagement of TGF-β ligands with cell surface receptors, the type II receptor phosphorylates and activates ALK5. Activated ALK5 then phosphorylates receptor-regulated Smad proteins (Smad2 and Smad3), which subsequently form complexes with Smad4 and translocate into the nucleus to drive the transcription of genes encoding ECM proteins and other pro-fibrotic factors (Laping et al., 2002). SB-431542 directly inhibits this kinase activity by occupying the ATP pocket, thereby blocking the phosphorylation of Smad2/3 and preventing their nuclear accumulation (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This interruption of TGF-β signaling ultimately suppresses the induction of pro-fibrotic genes such as those for collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002).

Importantly, SB-431542 is characterized by its selectivity. Despite the structural similarities among kinases in the TGF-β receptor superfamily, the unique conformational features of ALK5 permit SB-431542 to inhibit it to a significantly greater extent than BMP receptors (ALK2, ALK3, and ALK6) or other non-Smad pathways such as those mediated by ERK, JNK, and p38 MAPK (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This selectivity minimizes off-target effects and allows the compound to function as a precise modulator of TGF-β–dependent fibrotic signaling (Laping et al., 2002; Ling & Lee, 2011). Moreover, by inhibiting ALK5 activity, SB-431542 not only downregulates ECM protein production but also interferes with EMT processes, which are implicated in the phenotypic conversion of epithelial cells to a more mesenchymal and migratory state – a conversion that has been observed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells under stress conditions (Radeke et al., 2015; Yoon et al., 2018). In this regard, SB-431542’s molecular interactions encompass hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic contacts within the ALK5 catalytic pocket, ensuring that its inhibitory activity is both potent (with reported IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range) and selective for the intended target (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002).

    4. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis for repurposing SB-431542 in dry AMD is that inhibiting TGF-β receptor activity in RPE cells and choroidal fibroblasts will reduce pathological ECM overproduction. In dry AMD, elevated levels of TGF-β1 have been implicated in promoting the deposition of fibrotic ECM components in Bruch’s membrane, leading to increased stiffness and altered mechanical forces on the RPE monolayer (Laping et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2009). The resulting stiffening of the extracellular matrix is believed to disrupt the normal anchorage of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity and transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) of the RPE barrier (Xiao et al., 2009; Teplitsky et al., 2023).

By blocking ALK5 and thereby attenuating Smad2/3 activation, SB-431542 is expected to suppress the transcription of genes encoding collagen Iα1, fibronectin, and PAI-1. A reduction in the synthesis and deposition of these ECM components should translate into a decrease in Bruch’s membrane stiffness and the mechanical tension imposed on the RPE (Laping et al., 2002). This, in turn, is anticipated to allow the re-establishment of a continuous network of tight junctions between RPE cells as ZO-1 and occludin are able to reassemble without the interference of a pathological ECM environment (Radeke et al., 2015; Higashijima et al., 2023). When tested in ECM-coated Transwell assays, the expectation is that treatment with SB-431542 will result in improved TEER readings and a restoration of barrier function indicative of normalized RPE physiology (Xiao et al., 2009; Yoon et al., 2018).

Furthermore, TGF-β signaling in RPE cells has been associated with epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a process that not only promotes fibrosis but also deteriorates the well-ordered epithelial phenotype critical for retinal homeostasis (Radeke et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2009). Inhibition of ALK5 is predicted to counteract EMT, thereby preserving the native epithelial characteristics of RPE cells. In this context, the reduction of fibrotic ECM production and the prevention of EMT would act in synergy to reduce the abnormal mechanical stresses on RPE, enhance the continuity of tight junction proteins, and ultimately help restore retinal barrier function (Laping et al., 2002).

Given that both RPE cells and choroidal fibroblasts express TGF-β receptors and respond to TGF-β stimulation, the application of SB-431542 in co-culture models or animal studies is expected to normalize the extracellular microenvironment. This normalization could rescue the mechanical integrity of Bruch’s membrane and improve nutrient/waste exchange across the RPE monolayer—factors that are crucial in slowing or reversing the degenerative progression in dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2009).

    5. Overall Evaluation  
An overall review of SB-431542 indicates that it is a scientifically compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its proven ability to modulate TGF-β signaling and its well-documented anti-fibrotic effects. One major strength of SB-431542 is its high degree of selectivity for ALK5; by competitively inhibiting the ATP binding site on this receptor, the compound effectively blocks the Smad2/3 phosphorylation cascade that ultimately leads to ECM overproduction (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This mechanism has been validated in multiple preclinical models of fibrosis and ocular scarring, indicating that a similar strategy may be effective in the context of dry AMD where excessive ECM deposition in Bruch’s membrane is a central pathogenic feature (Xiao et al., 2009; Teplitsky et al., 2023).

Another point in favor of SB-431542 is its extensive use as a research tool in the investigation of TGF-β–dependent processes in both fibrosis and cancer. Its ability to reduce collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 levels in diverse cellular models underscores its therapeutic potential for attenuating pathological ECM production—a direct mechanism that could alleviate mechanical stress on RPE tight junctions and help restore barrier function, as measured by increased TEER and continuity of ZO-1/occludin (Laping et al., 2002).

From a mechanistic perspective, the detailed molecular interactions of SB-431542 have been characterized to a high degree, with studies demonstrating that its binding to the ALK5 catalytic pocket results in a clear inhibition of the profibrotic gene expression program (Laping et al., 2002; Ling & Lee, 2011). This precision in targeting is particularly important when considering ocular applications, as the retina is highly sensitive to off-target effects. By sparing other signaling pathways—such as those mediated by BMP receptors or Smad-independent cascades—the compound minimizes potential systemic or retinal toxicity (Laping et al., 2002).

Despite these strengths, there are also several challenges that must be addressed for SB-431542 to be successfully repurposed for dry AMD. One of the primary concerns is its pharmacokinetic profile. Preclinical studies in animal models have indicated that SB-431542 may have a relatively short half-life and rapid clearance, which raises questions about achieving sustained intraocular concentrations necessary for chronic conditions such as dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). To address this, development of a controlled-release ocular formulation—such as an intravitreal implant, microsphere-based delivery, or other sustained-release vehicle—will be essential for maintaining therapeutic levels over extended periods without systemic exposure.

Another significant challenge is the duality inherent in TGF-β signaling. While excessive TGF-β activity is responsible for the fibrotic changes observed in AMD, TGF-β also plays an important role in immune regulation, tissue repair, and maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Long-term blockade of TGF-β signaling may therefore carry inherent risks, including potential adverse effects on normal repair mechanisms or the promotion of unanticipated cellular changes such as malignant transformation (Markell, 2010; Schindeler et al., 2010). Careful dose-response studies and localized delivery strategies will be imperative to ensure that therapeutic benefits are achieved without tipping the balance toward deleterious side effects.

Moreover, although the preclinical data in ocular fibrosis models—such as those involving subconjunctival scarring after glaucoma filtration surgery—provide a promising rationale for the use of TGF-β inhibitors, direct evidence in models that recapitulate the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains limited (Xiao et al., 2009). Dry AMD is a complex disease involving not only fibrotic ECM accumulation but also oxidative stress, chronic low-grade inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation. Therefore, while the mechanistic rationale for using SB-431542 to reduce ECM production and restore RPE integrity is sound, it will likely need to be integrated into a broader therapeutic strategy that addresses these additional pathological drivers (Schindeler et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2017).

On the formulation front, the small molecule nature of SB-431542 offers both advantages and challenges. Its chemical tractability allows for modifications that could improve its ocular stability and bioavailability; however, achieving homogeneous distribution within the eye, ensuring drug stability in the vitreous environment, and avoiding direct retinal toxicity remain non-trivial challenges (Fuchs, 2011; Markell, 2010). Additionally, by virtue of its design as a competitive inhibitor, careful titration of dose will be required to ensure that effective ALK5 inhibition is sustained while minimizing interference with other cellular kinases that are essential for retinal cell survival.

In summary, SB-431542 shows significant promise as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to selectively inhibit ALK5 and thereby block the central pro-fibrotic Smad2/3 signaling axis aligns well with the mechanistic hypothesis that targeting TGF-β–mediated ECM overproduction can restore the biomechanical homeostasis of Bruch’s membrane and improve RPE barrier function (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). The chemical and biochemical evidence supporting its anti-fibrotic effects—demonstrated by reduced collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 levels in multiple cell types and models—is compelling (Laping et al., 2002). Furthermore, preliminary ocular studies using SB-431542 in models of surgical scarring provide an encouraging precedent for its application in the retina (Wang et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2009).

However, the pathway to clinical translation is not without hurdles. The pharmacokinetics of SB-431542, characterized by a relatively short half-life, necessitate the development of innovative drug delivery systems to sustain intraocular levels over the chronic course of AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). Additionally, the multifaceted role of TGF-β in ocular physiology requires that any therapeutic intervention be carefully calibrated to avoid impairing normal tissue repair or immunologic function (Markell, 2010; Schindeler et al., 2010). Finally, given that dry AMD is a multifactorial disease rather than being driven solely by fibrosis, further preclinical studies employing comprehensive AMD models that encompass oxidative stress and inflammation will be crucial to validate the therapeutic potential of SB-431542 in this context (Teplitsky et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025).

Overall, SB-431542 represents a scientifically robust and mechanistically well-justified candidate for repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD. Its targeted inhibition of ALK5 offers a strategic means to reduce pathological ECM deposition and thereby alleviate the mechanical stress that undermines RPE tight junction integrity—a key factor implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). The strengths of SB-431542 include its potency, selectivity, and extensive preclinical validation in fibrotic and ocular injury models. In contrast, its weaknesses center on pharmacokinetic limitations, the challenges of ocular delivery, and the complexity of broadly inhibiting a cytokine pathway that also serves beneficial roles.  

In conclusion, while additional formulation work and targeted preclinical studies remain essential, the accumulated evidence from biochemical, cellular, and ocular studies strongly supports the further evaluation of SB-431542 as part of a mechanobiology‐based therapeutic strategy for dry AMD. Given that dry AMD currently lacks effective treatments and that pathological ECM accumulation in Bruch’s membrane is a critical driver of disease progression, the repurposing of SB-431542 could provide a novel means to restore RPE barrier function by reducing ECM stiffness and re-establishing tight junction continuity (Xiao et al., 2009). Future research should focus on optimizing local delivery—potentially via sustained-release intravitreal formulations—and integrating SB-431542 within a combination therapy framework that additionally targets oxidative stress and inflammation. With these measures in place, SB-431542 holds significant promise as an innovative candidate in the quest for effective treatments for dry AMD (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002).

Thus, based on its synthetic origin, proven preclinical anti-fibrotic and anti-EMT effects, and detailed mechanistic rationale, SB-431542 merits further development for dry AMD. A rigorous, methodologically robust preclinical program – including pharmacokinetic optimization, ocular toxicity studies, and validation in relevant AMD models – will be crucial to determine whether the benefits observed in laboratory assays can be translated into meaningful clinical improvements in retinal structure and function.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
H-151 is a small-molecule antagonist of the innate immune adaptor STING (TMEM173) that was developed as part of a chemical class designed to prevent the palmitoylation-dependent activation of STING at the Golgi following cyclic dinucleotide binding and ER-to-Golgi trafficking (i.e., cGAMP-bound STING oligomerization and signalosome assembly) (Decout et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). In its mechanistic class, H-151 is grouped with covalent STING inhibitors that target Cys91 within the transmembrane region–proximal cytosolic interface, thereby preventing activation-induced palmitoylation at Cys88/Cys91 and downstream signaling; nitrofuran analogs such as C-176 and C-178 are the canonical examples where Cys91-directed covalent modification has been mapped by probe chemistry and mass spectrometry (with consequent suppression of type I interferon and IL-6 in vivo) (Decout et al., 2021). STING activation is known to require ligand-induced conformational change, ER exit, and palmitoylation on Cys88/Cys91 to drive oligomerization/polymerization and recruitment of TBK1 and other signal transducers; antagonists that block this palmitoylation step are therefore positioned to broadly prevent both IRF3-dependent type I interferon and NF-κB–dependent inflammatory outputs (Li et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2021).

H-151 has been characterized in inflammatory disease models as a low molecular weight, irreversible inhibitor of human and mouse STING that blocks activation-induced palmitoylation and attenuates downstream signaling (with primary mechanistic references tracing to the discovery work summarized by Pan et al. and by Decout et al.) (Pan et al., 2021; Decout et al., 2021). In keratinocyte and immune-cell systems relevant to psoriatic inflammation, H-151 has reproducibly suppressed STING-dependent NF-κB and IRF3 phosphorylation, inhibited proinflammatory cytokine mRNA induction (e.g., IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α), and reduced STING protein levels, consistent with an antagonist mechanism upstream of canonical downstream effectors (Pan et al., 2021). Conceptually, H-151 belongs to the broader class of cGAS–STING pathway modulators that have been deployed to suppress sterile inflammation across multiple tissues; for the eye and retina, related pathway inhibitors (e.g., C-176, SN-011, cryptotanshinone) have shown efficacy in ischemic and neovascular models via suppression of microglial STING signaling and cytokine/chemokine/protease outputs, supporting the translatability of STING antagonism to ocular tissues (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
There is no reported clinical use of H-151 in humans, and no published veterinary or clinical trials in ophthalmology were identified in the provided literature set; H-151 has been used as a research tool compound in preclinical inflammatory models, most prominently in psoriasis, where it decreased lesion severity and cutaneous inflammatory readouts in the imiquimod model (Pan et al., 2021). In psoriasis-relevant cell systems, H-151 suppressed cGAMP-induced IRF3 and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and reduced IFN-β, IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α expression, consistent with on-pathway inhibition of STING and its downstream transcriptional programs (Pan et al., 2021). In vivo, topical H-151 improved psoriasis-like dermatitis and decreased markers linked to STING/NF-κB signaling, again without human clinical translation to date (Pan et al., 2021).

Ocular/retinal precedent for the STING target is strong even if H-151–specific data are sparse. In multiple retinal contexts, activation of cGAS–STING has been implicated in pathogenesis through DNA-damage and mitochondrial DNA leakage, leading to IRF3/NF-κB activation, SASP-like cytokine induction, angiogenesis, and barrier dysfunction (Hu et al., 2023). Genetic and pharmacologic pathway perturbations show benefit: genetic loss of STING limits endothelial senescence and vascular degeneration in diabetic models (Liu et al., 2023), genetic deletion along the cGAS–STING axis rescues Alu DNA–driven RPE toxicity (implicated in geographic atrophy) (Hu et al., 2023), and pharmacologic STING inhibitors (C-176, SN-011) suppress neovascularization in laser CNV and OIR models (Ni et al., 2024). Importantly for RPE biology, senescent ARPE-19 cells were reported to overproduce VEGF and this overproduction was prevented by H-151, providing a direct albeit single-study line of evidence that H-151 can modulate pathogenic angiogenic/SASP output in an RPE-derived cell line (Hu et al., 2023). Beyond H-151, epigenetic suppression of STING (JQ1), PPARα activation, and visual cycle modulation (reducing toxic retinoid stress) each attenuate cGAS–STING activation and downstream inflammation or degeneration, underscoring the therapeutic appeal of targeting this axis in retinal disease (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
STING biology and the palmitoylation node. STING is a homodimeric ER-resident adaptor with an N-terminal multi-pass transmembrane domain and a cytosolic C-terminal ligand-binding domain; binding of 2’3’-cGAMP (produced by cGAS upon sensing cytosolic dsDNA) induces conformational rearrangements that enable ER exit and trafficking to the Golgi, where palmitoylation of Cys88 and Cys91 is critical for higher-order assembly and recruitment of TBK1 and other signaling proteins (Li et al., 2021). Palmitoylation-driven tetramerization/higher-order oligomerization is a central activation step for STING, and mutational or pharmacologic interference with Cys88/Cys91 palmitoylation abrogates downstream signal propagation (Pan et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). Rationale in retinal cells and tissue. cGAS and STING are expressed across retinal cell types (RPE, microglia, endothelial cells, Müller glia, photoreceptors) and are upregulated in disease states (AMD/DR), with promoter accessibility and mRNA levels increased in diseased tissue, positioning the pathway as targetable across multiple ocular compartments (Hu et al., 2023). Expected pharmacodynamic effects. Based on H-151’s mechanism at the palmitoylation node and its demonstrated suppression of STING-dependent IRF3 and NF-κB activation in immune and epithelial cells, we expect the following in RPE senescence assays:

- Proximal signaling: reductions in STING abundance (as seen in keratinocytes/THP-1), p-TBK1, p-IRF3, and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation following H-151 treatment under stimuli that engage cGAS–STING (e.g., H₂O₂-induced senescence, Alu cDNA transfection, mtDNA transfection) (Pan et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022).

- Cytokines/SASP: decreased secretion and/or expression of IL-6 and potentially IL-8 and other SASP components; in non-ocular systems H-151 lowered IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, IFN-β, and IFN-stimulated gene signatures, and in ARPE-19 senescence models H-151 prevented VEGF overproduction (Pan et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2023). Because NF-κB is a principal SASP driver in oxidant-stressed RPE, H-151’s suppression of NF-κB should proportionally lower SASP cytokines, including IL-6/IL-8, which are repeatedly implicated in AMD pathobiology (Terao et al., 2022; Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025).

- MMPs and matrix remodeling: in retinal microglia, pharmacologic STING inhibition reduced Mmp9 expression alongside Il6 and diminished vascular leakage in OIR, suggesting that blocking STING can lower proteases that degrade extracellular matrix and compromise barriers (Qiu et al., 2025; Terao et al., 2022). While H-151-specific MMP data in RPE have not been reported here, we would predict a reduction in MMP-9 in senescent RPE given the NF-κB dependence of SASP proteases and the precedent in ocular STING inhibition (Qiu et al., 2025; Terao et al., 2022).

- Barrier integrity (TEER and ZO-1): direct H-151 data on RPE TEER/ZO-1 are unavailable in the provided literature. However, STING activity has been linked to barrier dysfunction in retinal endothelium (inner barrier), with evidence that STING activation through TBK1/IRF3/IFN-β axes amplifies senescence and compromises barrier integrity; genetic STING deficiency mitigates such changes (Wu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). In the outer retina, RPE degeneration driven by inflammatory stimuli is attenuated in STING knockout mice, supporting that STING inhibition can preserve epithelial integrity under inflammatory stress (Hu et al., 2023). Thus, we expect H-151 to preserve TEER and maintain ZO-1 continuity in RPE senescence models where cGAS–STING–NF-κB contributes to junctional remodeling and MMP-driven degradation, but this prediction requires experimental confirmation given the absence of direct H-151 barrier data (Hu et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025).

- Anti-senescence signatures: in non-ocular systems, H-151 treatment decreased cGAS–STING pathway activation, reduced ISGs, lowered P16/P21, and decreased SA-β-gal activity, indicating that STING antagonism can blunt senescence programs and SASP (Ye et al., 2024). Given the overlap between senescence and innate immune signaling in RPE and AMD, we expect H-151 to reduce senescence markers in RPE senescence assays, again pending direct validation in ocular cells (Blasiak, 2020; Terao et al., 2022).

Expression in the assayed RPE lineage is supported by disease-relevant data showing STING expression and activation in retinal tissues and RPE under stress, including oxidative stress and Alu/mtDNA triggers; cGAS–STING pathway genes are broadly expressed in the retina and upregulated in disease, and RPE senescence engages STING-dependent NF-κB/HIF-1α signaling to drive VEGF (Hu et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease-mechanism fit. Dry AMD pathogenesis features chronic oxidative stress, DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and senescence in RPE, with resultant SASP cytokines, VEGF, and MMPs that degrade extracellular matrix and compromise barriers; cGAS–STING is positioned as a key sensor/effector linking cytosolic DNA to NF-κB/IRF3 activation and SASP output in RPE and retinal cell types (Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2023). Genetic and pharmacologic evidence across models (DR endothelium, Alu-driven RPE toxicity, ischemic/neovascular retinopathy) show that suppressing STING signaling reduces inflammation, senescence markers, angiogenic/proteolytic factors, leakage, and degeneration, indicating pathway validity and translational plausibility in the eye (Liu et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

- Direct RPE cell evidence for H-151. H-151 prevented VEGF overproduction in senescent ARPE-19 cells, directly supporting the candidate’s ability to suppress a central SASP/angiogenic mediator in an RPE-derived cell model (Hu et al., 2023). This aligns with the broader observation that STING upregulates VEGF in oxidative stress–induced RPE senescence via NF-κB/HIF-1α (Hu et al., 2023).

- Potent inhibition of NF-κB and cytokine outputs. In preclinical psoriasis systems, H-151 suppressed cGAMP-induced IRF3/NF-κB phosphorylation and reduced IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IFN-β readouts, consistent with broad blockade of the principal proinflammatory axes downstream of STING (Pan et al., 2021). Given that NF-κB is a dominant inducer of SASP components in oxidant-stressed RPE, and IL-6/IL-8 and MMPs are canonical RPE SASP factors in AMD, H-151’s activity is well matched to reduce these pathological outputs (Terao et al., 2022; Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025).

- Target validation in retinal models via related inhibitors/genetics. STING inhibition by C-176/SN-011 reduces neovascularization in CNV/OIR; cryptotanshinone reduces Il6 and Mmp9 and vascular leakage through STING suppression in microglia; STING knockout provides protection against inflammatory retinal degeneration and endothelial senescence and barrier compromise, together providing multi-compartment evidence that STING blockade can ameliorate retinal inflammatory pathology (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023).

- Modality fit for intracellular target. Because cGAS and STING are intracellular, small molecules are preferred for retinal applications; the literature anticipates that blood–retina–penetrant small-molecule cGAS–STING inhibitors will be needed to translate this strategy to the clinic, supporting H-151’s modality selection (Hu et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- Sparse ocular data for H-151. Beyond the ARPE-19 VEGF observation, there are no H-151 data for TEER, ZO-1 continuity, MMP modulation, or in vivo ocular efficacy in dry AMD models in the provided literature, so the central claims around barrier preservation remain predictions that require direct testing (Hu et al., 2023). By contrast, barrier-relevant evidence is stronger for alternative STING inhibitors (cryptotanshinone effects on Mmp9/leakage; C-176/SN-011 in angiogenesis models), indicating pathway relevance but not yet validating H-151 itself in retina (Qiu et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2024).

- Cell-type heterogeneity in DNA sensing. Some RPE models lack cGAS and may rely on other sensors (RIG-I, ZBP1), and the cGAS–STING axis can be variably engaged depending on the nature of the stressor (Alu vs mtDNA vs photo-oxidized A2E), potentially limiting the breadth of H-151’s efficacy across RPE senescence paradigms (Hu et al., 2023). Thorough profiling in human primary RPE and AMD-relevant triggers will be required.

- Pathway-output variability. H-151’s strongest effects in psoriasis were on NF-κB/IL-6, with partial or context-dependent impact on IRF3/IFN-β; while NF-κB is the prime SASP driver in RPE, specific disease contexts (e.g., dsDNA-driven type I IFN) may require robust IRF3 suppression to fully ameliorate pathology (Pan et al., 2021). The differential balance of NF-κB versus IRF3 outputs in RPE under various triggers should be experimentally mapped.

- Covalent inhibitor liabilities. Cysteine-targeting covalent inhibitors can carry risks of off-target reactivity and species-specific metabolic liabilities; development of covalent agents demands careful derisking of reactivity and ocular PK/PD, as underscored in general discussions of covalent inhibitor strategies and metabolism in drug discovery (Wang et al., 2022). Although H-151’s covalent target is genetically unique (Cys91 on STING), comprehensive safety and selectivity profiling—especially for intraocular delivery—is not available here.

- Immunological trade-offs. STING deficiency can increase susceptibility to tumorigenesis and reduce vaccine responses, and human STING haplotypes (e.g., HAQ) show variable responsiveness to cyclic dinucleotides, implying potential population variability in pathway dependence and therapeutic response (Hu et al., 2023). For ocular delivery, local exposure may mitigate systemic risks, but intraocular immunosuppression could theoretically predispose to infections; risk–benefit will need empirical assessment.

Evidence-based development plan (prioritized)  
- In vitro RPE assays. Use human primary RPE and ARPE-19 under AMD-relevant triggers (H₂O₂, Alu cDNA, mtDNA transfection) to quantify: STING pathway activation (p-TBK1, p-IRF3, p65), SASP cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), MMPs (MMP-9), and angiogenic factors (VEGF); barrier metrics by TEER and ZO-1 continuity; and senescence markers (P16, P21, SA-β-gal). Include STING agonist/antagonist controls (e.g., diABZI, C-176), and cGAS/STING knockdown to confirm on-target effects; the goal is to reproduce the VEGF suppression result and extend to barrier preservation and MMP control with H-151 (Hu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022; Terao et al., 2022).

- Retinal explant and in vivo models. Move to sodium iodate or oxidant-driven RPE injury models and to Alu DNA–induced RPE degeneration to test whether H-151 reduces cGAS–STING activation, NF-κB signaling, cytokines/MMPs, and preserves RPE morphology; positive controls include JQ1 and C-176, which have shown efficacy in related contexts (Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024). The LIRD model shows cGAS–STING activation can be modulated upstream by visual-cycle inhibitors; testing H-151 in LIRD would further link pathway suppression to photoreceptor/RPE protection (Wang et al., 2022).

- Delivery and PK/PD. Evaluate intravitreal versus periocular dosing for ocular exposure, using formulation strategies with precedent (e.g., nanoparticle-loaded C-176) to optimize intraocular retention and cell uptake; measure intraocular H-151 levels and target engagement markers (p-STING, p-TBK1, p-IRF3) (Shao et al., 2024).

- Safety and immunology. Profile local tolerability and infection risk in the eye while monitoring systemic spillover; genotype stratification for STING haplotypes can be deferred to later phases but should be considered due to pathway variability (Hu et al., 2023).

Decision context  
On balance, H-151 is a mechanistically compelling, tractable small-molecule inhibitor that targets a validated inflammatory/senescence axis in retinal disease, with one direct RPE line of evidence (suppression of VEGF in senescent ARPE-19) and robust non-ocular and ocular-pathway support via related tools and genetic models (Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). The absence of H-151–specific data on RPE barrier metrics (TEER/ZO-1) and MMP modulation is the principal evidence gap relative to the stated hypothesis; however, the consistent linkage of cGAS–STING to IL-6/VEGF/MMP outputs and barrier failure across retinal compartments supports the plausibility that a palmitoylation-targeted STING antagonist like H-151 will deliver the predicted phenotype in senescent RPE (Hu et al., 2023; Terao et al., 2022; Qiu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025).

Recommendation  
Advance H-151 into AMD-relevant in vitro RPE barrier and senescence assays with rigorous on-target controls and head-to-head comparison against alternative STING inhibitors (C-176/SN-011, cryptotanshinone) to establish class translatability and select the best ocular candidate by efficacy and safety; proceed to in vivo validation contingent on clear demonstration of TEER/ZO-1 preservation, SASP/MMP suppression, and favorable ocular PK/PD (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

Strengths summary: strong mechanistic rationale in AMD, direct RPE evidence for VEGF suppression by H-151, broad anti–NF-κB/SASP activity of H-151 in inflammatory models, and multiple retinal models validating STING inhibition (Hu et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2021; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025). Weaknesses summary: no H-151 data yet on RPE barrier readouts or in vivo retinal protection; covalent-inhibitor liabilities and immunologic trade-offs require careful derisking; cell-type heterogeneity in DNA sensing mandates model selection rigor (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Taken together, H-151 is a high-priority mechanistic probe and a plausible therapeutic lead for dry AMD that merits focused preclinical validation in RPE barrier/senescence systems and in Alu/oxidative injury models of outer retinal degeneration, with parallel medicinal-chemistry and formulation work to address ocular delivery and covalent-inhibitor safety considerations (Hu et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2024).
