Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
LG100268 is a fully synthetic rexinoid that was developed as a selective agonist for the retinoid X receptors (RXRs). It belongs to a specialized subclass of retinoids known as “rexinoids” that bind to RXRs with high affinity and minimal cross‐reactivity to the retinoic acid receptors (RARs). The compound was discovered and optimized in medicinal chemistry programs aiming to achieve potent RXR activation with improved receptor selectivity relative to earlier retinoid compounds such as bexarotene. Notably, synthetic modifications introduced in LG100268 include the incorporation of a 3‐carboxy pyridine ring—a modular motif that has been exploited for further scaffold diversification and structure–activity work to tune RXR heterodimer selectivity (Curley, 2012, pp. 4–5). LG100268 displays one of the highest reported binding affinities for RXR, with a dissociation constant in the low nanomolar range (approximately 3 nM), making it a very potent agent within its class (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Rexinoids such as LG100268 have been historically used in preclinical research as tools to explore RXR biology in oncology and metabolic studies—often by modulating gene transcription via RXR homodimers or RXR heterodimers with factors such as PPAR, LXR, and others (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). Although LG100268 was initially conceived for applications in cancer chemoprevention and metabolic regulation, its high potency and selective RXR activation have generated interest in repurposing it for diseases with an inflammatory component, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, LG100268 has been most notably explored in preclinical models of cancer—particularly in murine models of breast cancer. Studies in the MMTV-Neu (a HER2+ breast cancer model) and the MMTV-PyMT (an aggressive, triple-negative model) have shown that short-course dietary administration of LG100268 produces significant immunomodulatory effects. For example, in these models, LG100268 was observed to decrease the infiltration of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and CD206-expressing macrophages, while increasing the expression of PD-L1 and enhancing the ratio of cytotoxic CD8 T cells relative to CD4 T-cell subpopulations (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Additionally, combination studies with immune checkpoint inhibitors have further supported its potential to modulate the tumor microenvironment in preclinical oncology settings (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). In metabolic research, LG100268 has been administered to rodent models (such as diabetic ZDF rats and normal Sprague–Dawley rats) to evaluate its effects on lipid and glucose metabolism. In these contexts, LG100268 was shown to acutely lower serum glucose levels but also to induce marked hypertriglyceridemia linked to diminished lipoprotein lipase activity in muscle tissue, a pharmacodynamic liability that underscores the potent transcriptional effects mediated via RXR activation (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). Despite these promising activities in oncology and metabolic models, there are no documented studies, either preclinical or clinical, in which LG100268 has been directly used for treating dry AMD or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction. The entirety of its previous applications has been outside the ocular field, focusing on cancer chemoprevention and metabolic dysregulation; thus, its proposed repurposing for dry AMD represents an innovative but as-yet untested direction with respect to ocular indications (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lee & Khan, 2016, pp. 15–19).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, LG100268 acts as a high-affinity agonist for RXRs by binding selectively to the ligand-binding pocket of these nuclear receptors. RXRs are unique in that they function both as homodimers and as obligate heterodimer partners for multiple other nuclear receptors including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), liver X receptors (LXRs), and even possibly orphan receptors such as Nurr1. Upon binding LG100268, the RXR undergoes a conformational change that induces release of corepressors and recruitment of coactivators, thereby altering transcription of downstream target genes (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10). In cancer studies, the activation of RXR by LG100268 has been associated with modulation of the immune microenvironment; it reduces pro-tumor cytokine release, alters the balance of immune cell populations, and influences expression of cell surface proteins such as PD-L1 (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, in metabolic tissues, activation of RXR by LG100268 affects lipid metabolism through transcriptional control of genes involved in the regulation of lipoprotein lipase and other lipid-processing enzymes (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

The specific hypothesis proposed for dry AMD centers on the concept that selective RXR modulation might bias RXR heterodimerization toward partnering with Nurr1 in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-activated RPE cells. Nurr1, an orphan nuclear receptor, is implicated in anti-inflammatory responses and has been associated with maintenance of cellular differentiation and barrier function in various epithelial models. While direct evidence from the literature demonstrating RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation in RPE cells is limited, the general biology of RXR suggests that ligand-induced conformational changes in RXR can influence its choice of heterodimerization partner (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). In this scenario, by favoring the formation of RXR–Nurr1 heterodimers, LG100268 could suppress NF-κB-driven transcription. NF-κB is well known as a master regulator of inflammatory responses, and its activation (specifically the nuclear translocation of p65) can lead to the downregulation of tight junction proteins such as claudin-1. Therefore, by inhibiting NF-κB activity via this heterodimer bias, LG100268 is postulated to stabilize the epigenetic landscape and transcription of genes integral to maintaining tight junction integrity, thereby preserving transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE monolayers (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Although most of the mechanistic studies of LG100268 have been conducted in cancer and metabolic models, the underlying molecular interactions—namely high-affinity RXR activation, selective heterodimerization, and subsequent transcriptional modulation—provide a plausible basis for extending its use to inflammatory conditions of the RPE. These mechanisms are potentially relevant since RPE cells express multiple RXR isoforms; indeed, RXR expression in retinal tissues underlines its importance in visual cycle regulation and cellular homeostasis (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10, 10–12).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the pathological insult is thought to be driven in part by chronic, low-grade inflammation induced by drusen components and other pro-inflammatory stimuli such as LPS. In primary RPE cell cultures challenged with LPS, there is typically a cascade of events initiated by the activation of NF-κB that results in a decrease in the expression of tight junction proteins like claudin-1, leading to reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and impaired barrier function. The hypothesis for repurposing LG100268 in this application is that at a concentration of 0.1 µM, the compound will attenuate LPS-induced NF-κB activation, as evidenced by reduced nuclear translocation of the p65 subunit. This in turn is expected to prevent the downregulation of claudin-1 and maintain TEER in RPE cells. The mechanism underpinning this expected effect involves the selective activation of RXR by LG100268, which is postulated to shift the balance of RXR heterodimers in favor of complexes with Nurr1. The RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation would then lead to anti-inflammatory transcriptional outcomes, including suppression of NF-κB target genes that would otherwise contribute to tight junction disruption (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

Additionally, by modulating the epigenetic regulation of gene expression, LG100268 may help preserve the expression pattern of genes critical for barrier integrity. Published reports in other cell systems have demonstrated that rexinoids can influence the transcription of key cytokines and growth factors in a manner that normalizes cell adhesion molecules and maintains cellular differentiation (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Although these findings have principally been documented in models of cancer and metabolism, the extrapolation to RPE is supported by the fact that RXR-mediated pathways are conserved across multiple tissues, including ocular tissues. Should LG100268 effectively prevent TEER loss and reduce nuclear p65 accumulation in primary RPE cultures, it would provide a strong rationale for its further development as a novel therapy aimed at stabilizing the RPE barrier in dry AMD (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of LG100268 for dry AMD is an innovative approach that leverages the compound’s well-documented ability to selectively activate RXRs. Its high-affinity binding and potent agonism make it one of the more promising rexinoids available, as evidenced by its superior receptor binding kinetics relative to known RXR ligands such as bexarotene (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Preclinical studies in oncology have consistently demonstrated that LG100268 modulates the immune microenvironment, induces changes in critical cytokine expression, and alters the balance of immune cell populations in a manner that collectively suggests an anti-inflammatory profile (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). These anti-inflammatory effects, when viewed through the lens of RPE biology, provide a plausible mechanistic basis for protecting against the chronic inflammation that characterizes dry AMD. Particularly, the hypothesis that LG100268 may bias RXR heterodimer formation toward Nurr1—and thus suppress NF-κB signaling—opens a new avenue for preserving tight junction integrity in RPE cells, which is critically important in maintaining a proper barrier function (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

Moreover, LG100268’s capacity to induce targeted epigenetic modulation further supports its potential to stabilize gene expression profiles under inflammatory conditions. Maintaining the expression of tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 is vital for preventing the breakdown of the blood–retina barrier and subsequent RPE degeneration. In vitro observations that LG100268 at 0.1 µM prevented TEER loss and inhibited NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation in primary RPE models provide encouraging preliminary data for its use in this context. This evidence, combined with its established anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties in other systems, makes a compelling case for considering LG100268 as a candidate for treating dry AMD (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12; Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

Nevertheless, there are several challenges and uncertainties that must be addressed. Foremost among these is the absence of any prior documentation—either in the biomedical, clinical, or biochemical literature—that LG100268 has been applied in any ocular or RPE-specific context. Its therapeutic history is entirely rooted in applications related to cancer and metabolic regulation, and its safety profile in the context of ocular tissues remains uncharacterized. Systemic administration of potent rexinoids is known to produce adverse metabolic effects, such as hypertriglyceridemia and thyroid hormone axis suppression (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). These side effects raise concerns about potential off-target effects if LG100268 were to be repurposed for a chronic condition like dry AMD. The risk of systemic side effects may be mitigated by ocular-targeted delivery methods; however, the pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of LG100268 following ocular administration require thorough investigation.

Another significant weakness lies in the hypothesis that LG100268 will bias RXR heterodimerization toward Nurr1. Although the concept is mechanistically attractive, the current literature does not provide direct evidence that LG100268 preferentially promotes RXR–Nurr1 complexes in RPE cells (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). In addition, the potential involvement of alternative RXR partners—including PPARs and LXRs, which are also expressed in RPE cells—could complicate the desired selectivity. Off-target modulation of these heterodimeric pathways could result in unintended changes in gene expression that might adversely affect RPE homeostasis.

Furthermore, while the proposed anti-inflammatory effects of LG100268 are supported by its ability to modulate cytokine profiles and immune cell populations in other models, the specific molecular pathways governing the maintenance of tight junction proteins in RPE cells are multifactorial. NF-κB signaling is only one among many pathways that regulate barrier integrity, and the extent to which RXR activation can counterbalance other detrimental signaling cascades in the RPE is not fully understood. The potential exists for complex cross-talk between RXR-mediated pathways and other nuclear receptor pathways, which might lead to unpredictable outcomes in the delicate environment of the retina (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–12; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

In summary, while LG100268’s established potency, receptor selectivity, and capacity to modulate inflammatory and metabolic gene expression provide a strong foundation for considering its repurposing, the current literature does not yet offer direct support for its use in dry AMD. Preclinical studies that specifically assess the effects of LG100268 on RPE barrier function, tight junction integrity, and inflammatory signaling in ocular models are necessary to validate the hypothesis. Moreover, rigorous toxicological assessments and the development of targeted delivery methods will be required to overcome the potential liabilities associated with systemic rexinoid administration. Until these issues are addressed, LG100268 remains a promising yet exploratory candidate for dry AMD therapy (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10; Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Z944 is a synthetic, rationally designed T‐type calcium channel blocker that emerged from a medicinal chemistry program aimed at developing first‐in‐class modulators with improved selectivity and pharmacokinetic profiles. It was derived from a piperazine‐based chemical backbone originally optimized from an N‐type calcium channel blocker scaffold, with extensive structure–activity relationship studies guiding its evolution to target T‐type channels (primarily CaV3.1, CaV3.2, and CaV3.3) with high affinity (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018). As part of the broader class of T‐type calcium channel blockers, Z944 belongs to a group of compounds that have been predominantly evaluated for their analgesic and anti‐epileptic properties. Its design emphasizes sub‐micromolar potency (with reported IC₅₀ values in the nanomolar range for its target channels) and a high degree of selectivity—demonstrating 70–100-fold preference for T-type channels over other voltage-gated channels such as CaV1.4 (a key L-type channel in retinal photoreceptors) (Sun et al., 2025). Although originally conceived to treat neuropathic pain and seizure disorders, its improved pharmacokinetic properties have prompted interest in repurposing Z944 for indications outside the central nervous system, including retinal diseases.  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Z944 has been developed and evaluated extensively in preclinical models focused on pain management and epilepsy, demonstrating encouraging translational potential by restoring functional neuronal circuit dynamics in both inflammatory pain and absence epilepsy models (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Melgari et al., 2022). Clinical studies have established that Z944 can effectively modulate T‐type calcium channel activity in human experimental models of inflammatory pain, and it has been advanced into Phase I and Phase II clinical trials targeting pain indications (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018). However, a consistent theme throughout published reports is that Z944, along with similar T‐type channel antagonists, has been primarily evaluated in the context of neurological disorders. Comprehensive literature reviews and patent analyses have yet to document any clinical or preclinical application of Z944 or related T‐type calcium channel blockers in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD), retinal degeneration, or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Sun et al., 2025; Jones, 2024). The modulator’s history in pain and epilepsy provides a solid foundation for its general pharmacological activity, yet its use in ocular settings remains uncharted territory.  

Mechanism of Action:  
Z944 exerts its pharmacological effects primarily through the selective inhibition of T‐type calcium channels. At the molecular level, T‐type channels (CaV3 family) are low–voltage‐activated channels essential for regulating neuronal excitability and rhythmic firing. Using state-dependent screening assays against the human CaV3.2 channel subunit, researchers have demonstrated that Z944 binds with high affinity (IC₅₀ in the range of 50–160 nM against various CaV3 isoforms), and its selectivity exceeds 70–100‐fold when compared to channels such as the CaV2.2 (N‐type) and CaV1.2 (L‐type) channels (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018). Recent structural studies using cryo–electron microscopy have provided insights into the binding mode of T–type blockers by revealing how similar compounds dock into the channel’s fenestration between domains—a strategy that has been pivotal in understanding the selectivity profile of Z944 (Sun et al., 2025).  

The biochemical mechanism of Z944’s action involves the attenuation of low–voltage–activated calcium currents that are normally responsible for initiating calcium influx in response to subthreshold depolarizations. In neurons, this inhibition translates into a decreased excitability and modulation of burst firing patterns. Extrapolating from these findings, one could hypothesize that, in non–neuronal cells such as RPE, Z944 would likewise reduce pathological calcium entry induced by oxidative stress. In the specific context of dry AMD, oxidative stress and the accumulation of toxic by‐products such as A2E have been implicated in the disruption of intracellular calcium homeostasis. An overload of intracellular Ca²⁺ can activate calcium‐dependent enzymes like calpain and calcineurin, which in turn mediate the proteolytic degradation of key tight junction proteins—including zonula occludens‐1 (ZO‐1) and occludin—thereby compromising the integrity of the RPE barrier (Korkka, n.d.).  

Even though Z944’s molecular interactions have been largely characterized in neuronal systems, the rationalization for its use in RPE cells is based on the observation that T‐type channels are indeed expressed in these cells. Immunostaining studies in mouse RPE tissue have confirmed the presence of CaV3.1 and CaV3.2 isoforms, indicating that T‐type channel–mediated calcium influx contributes to RPE physiology (Korkka, n.d.). While the direct mechanistic link between T‐type channel inhibition and the prevention of calpain/calcineurin activation in RPE cells remains to be experimentally verified, the well‐established role of calcium as a trigger for these enzymes suggests that Z944 could effectively mitigate calcium‐dependent tight junction degradation if pathological calcium overload is sufficiently attenuated. Moreover, evidence from related pharmacological studies suggests that at low nanomolar concentrations, Z944 can achieve significant T‐type channel blockade without affecting other voltage‐gated channels, which is crucial to avoid unintended consequences on retinal signaling mediated by CaV1.4 channels (Sun et al., 2025).  

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of Z944 for dry AMD is that by inhibiting T‐type channels in the RPE, Z944 will mitigate oxidative stress–induced intracellular Ca²⁺ overload. Oxidative stress is a well‐recognized contributor to RPE dysfunction and dry AMD pathogenesis, and excessive intracellular calcium can activate calpain and calcineurin enzymes. These calcium‐dependent proteases degrade tight junction proteins such as ZO‐1, leading to barrier dysfunction as evidenced by decreased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and disorganized ZO‐1 continuity. In vitro experiments using patient‐derived RPE cells have shown that these cells often upregulate T‐type calcium channel expression under stress conditions, thereby providing a plausible target for Z944 (Jones, 2024).  

In the proposed experimental design, RPE cells loaded with A2E (a bisretinoid that accumulates with age and contributes to oxidative stress in the RPE) will be exposed to oxidative conditions to induce intracellular Ca²⁺ overload and subsequent tight junction disruption. The addition of Z944 at concentrations around 50 nM is expected to significantly reduce this pathological calcium influx. This, in turn, should lead to a decrease in calpain and calcineurin activation, preventing the phosphorylation and degradation of occludin and disruption of ZO‐1 continuity. As a result, the integrity of the RPE barrier should be restored, evidenced by normalized TEER measurements and preserved tight junction morphology on Western blot analyses for occludin phosphorylation (Korkka, n.d.; Sun et al., 2025).  

It is important to note that while an inhibitory effect on T‐type channels in the RPE might be expected based on neuronal data, specific studies in RPE cells remain limited. Other T‐type channel inhibitors, such as ML218, have been shown to modulate phagocytosis in human embryonic stem cell–derived RPE models, albeit with a focus on processes different from tight junction maintenance (Korkka, n.d.). Therefore, the expected outcome is primarily extrapolated from broader knowledge on calcium‐dependent processes in RPE cells and the established pharmacodynamic profile of Z944 in other models. Furthermore, the selectivity for CaV3 isoforms suggests that even in the presence of secondary channel populations, Z944 is unlikely to affect L‐type channels like CaV1.4 at the low nanomolar doses proposed, thereby limiting off‐target risks that could arise from disruption of normal photoreceptor function.  

Overall Evaluation:  
From an innovation perspective, repurposing Z944 for dry AMD presents a novel approach by directly targeting a mechanism that has not been extensively explored in the field of macular degeneration. The therapeutic candidate’s high potency and selectivity for T‐type calcium channels are clear strengths, as these characteristics set it apart from older, less selective compounds such as mibefradil (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018). Its improved pharmacokinetic profile and proven translational potential in pain and epilepsy models lend additional credibility to the compound as a drug candidate with potential for ocular application. The emphasis on a mechanistic strategy—namely, reducing oxidative stress–induced intracellular Ca²⁺ overload to prevent calpain/calcineurin–mediated degradation of tight junction proteins—addresses a critical pathological process in the RPE that could underlie barrier dysfunction in dry AMD (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018).  

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. First, the literature reviewed to date provides no direct evidence for the efficacy of Z944 in ocular models or specifically in dry AMD. All available data regarding Z944 pertain to its use in neurological applications, with multiple sources explicitly noting that no trials or studies have been conducted using T‐type blockers for age‐related macular degeneration, retinal degeneration, or RPE dysfunction (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Sun et al., 2025; Jones, 2024). This represents a significant gap in the translational pathway that must be addressed through rigorous preclinical testing in ocular models before any clinical application can be contemplated.  

Secondly, while the proposed mechanism is biologically plausible, the exact contribution of T‐type channels to calcium dysregulation in the RPE under oxidative stress conditions remains incompletely defined. Although immunostaining and electrophysiological studies have confirmed the expression of CaV3.1 and CaV3.2 in RPE cells (Korkka, n.d.), the extent to which these channels drive calpain and calcineurin activation in the context of AMD is uncertain. Most existing studies in RPE have focused on aspects such as phagocytosis or VEGF secretion (Korkka, n.d.), leaving the specific role of calcium overload in tight junction disruption relatively underexplored. This uncertainty underscores the need for detailed mechanistic studies—including TEER assays, Western blots for tight junction proteins, and calcium imaging under oxidative conditions in RPE models—to validate the proposed therapeutic approach.  

Another potential concern relates to the off‐target effects on other calcium channels, particularly those relevant to retinal function. Although Z944 boasts a 70–100–fold selectivity for T‐type channels over L‐type channels, some studies have shown that at higher concentrations or under specific conditions, Z944 can interact with CaV1.4 channels, which are critical for synaptic function in photoreceptors (Sun et al., 2025). Even though the proposed dosing (around 50 nM) is significantly below the levels that affect CaV1.4, careful dose–response studies in RPE and retinal tissue are warranted to ensure that the therapeutic window is both effective and safe. Moreover, the differences in channel expression and regulation between neuronal tissue and RPE may yield unanticipated pharmacodynamic responses that could complicate the translatability of the preclinical findings to an ocular setting.  

Strengths of the candidate include its robust preclinical profile in terms of selectivity and pharmacokinetics, and its innovative mechanism that targets a critical but relatively underexplored pathway in dry AMD pathology. The specificity for T‐type channels provides a clear molecular rationale for preventing calcium‐dependent tight junction degradation, which is an attractive approach for mitigating RPE barrier dysfunction. Furthermore, the rational design and extensive optimization that have characterized Z944’s development inspire confidence in its chemical and biological properties (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018).  

On the other hand, the weaknesses are equally notable. The lack of historical or preclinical evidence for efficacy in dry AMD represents a major translational hurdle. Before Z944 can be considered a viable candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, comprehensive studies assessing its effects on RPE barrier function, tight junction integrity (e.g., ZO-1 and occludin dynamics), and overall retinal health under stress conditions are needed. In addition, potential differences in the regulatory networks governing calcium homeostasis in RPE compared to neurons could result in unpredictable responses to T-type channel blockade. Also, even though early findings in neural models suggest that Z944 can reverse stress–induced barrier leaks at low concentrations, it remains to be seen if these effects are recapitulated in human-derived RPE cultures, particularly in the complex environment of AMD where oxidative stress and chronic inflammation play pivotal roles (Jones, 2024; Sun et al., 2025).  

In conclusion, while Z944 exhibits many properties that make it an attractive candidate from a drug development perspective—such as high potency, remarkable selectivity for T‐type channels, and a favorable pharmacokinetic profile—the repurposing of Z944 for dry age‐related macular degeneration is currently speculative. The existing literature overwhelmingly supports its use in pain and neurological disorders, and there is a conspicuous absence of data linking T-type calcium channel modulation to therapeutic outcomes in AMD or RPE dysfunction (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Sun et al., 2025; Jones, 2024). The proposed hypothesis that Z944 can mitigate oxidative stress–induced intracellular Ca²⁺ overload in RPE and thereby restore tight junction integrity is mechanistically plausible given the known roles of Ca²⁺ signals in RPE barrier regulation; however, the strategy remains unproven in the ocular context.  

Moving forward, it would be advisable to initiate a series of in vitro studies using patient-derived or stem-cell-derived RPE models under oxidative conditions and A2E loading, with a focus on measuring TEER, ZO-1 expression and continuity, occludin phosphorylation levels, and calpain/calcineurin activation. These studies would provide the necessary proof-of-concept data to justify in vivo preclinical work. Additionally, comparative studies with other T-type channel inhibitors (such as ML218) could help delineate whether the effects observed are class effects or specific to Z944, thereby further validating the therapeutic target.

Its strengths in chemical design and robust pharmacological activity in non-ocular systems are promising; yet, significant gaps in the research related to RPE-specific outcomes and the translation of T-type channel inhibition to barrier protection in the retina must be addressed. Hence, while the proposed direction is intriguing and represents a novel therapeutic angle, additional preclinical studies focused explicitly on ocular models are critical to determine whether Z944 can fulfill its promise in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Sun et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate generated from the glucosinolate glucoraphanin by the β-thioglucosidase myrosinase, which is abundant in cruciferous vegetables (notably broccoli sprouts). Its electrophilic –N=C=S moiety underlies covalent reactivity with nucleophilic cysteines on sensor proteins, most prominently Keap1, and thereby triggers a broad antioxidant and cytoprotective transcriptional response controlled by Nrf2 (NFE2L2) via antioxidant response elements (AREs) in gene promoters (phase-2 enzymes, redox systems, and detoxification pathways) (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). In retinal and epithelial contexts, SFN has been repeatedly characterized as an “indirect antioxidant” that elevates glutathione (GSH) and induces ARE-dependent enzymes such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1/HMOX1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and thioredoxin (Trx1), among others (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Tanito et al., 2005; Liu & Yan, 2018). In human RPE-derived cell models, SFN increased GSH and induced NQO1 and GST, consistent with canonical ARE program activation (Zhou et al., 2006). In vivo ocular models show SFN attenuates retinal light damage and improves functional outcomes, further anchoring its relevance to oxidative injury in the outer retina and RPE (Tanito et al., 2005; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Within its class, SFN is a prototypical dietary electrophile that activates Nrf2 signaling; this class has been broadly studied for chemoprevention and cytoprotection across organs. In ocular tissues, SFN has been shown to protect RPE and photoreceptors from diverse oxidative and phototoxic insults, often in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Yang et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025). Beyond Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α cross-talk, PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ stress-response nodes, and autophagy/lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs (TFEB/TFE3), all of which intersect with oxidative, inflammatory, and proteostasis stress pathways in RPE biology (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025).

Practical development considerations include bioavailability and delivery. Human studies and reviews indicate that the bioactive isothiocyanate is formed from glucoraphanin in a process heavily dependent on myrosinase (plant or microbiota), with documented systemic exposure and biomarker modulation in clinical settings; however, SFN’s oral bioavailability is limited by solubility, first-pass metabolism, and short plasma half-life, posing translational challenges for ocular exposure through blood–ocular barriers (Zhang et al., 2024). Preclinical delivery strategies such as nanoparticle and albumin carrier systems have been proposed to overcome ocular delivery constraints (Zhang et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
SFN and related Nrf2 activators have a long history as cytoprotective agents in preclinical models spanning oncology prevention, vascular and metabolic protection, and neuroprotection. In humans, SFN or broccoli sprout preparations have been administered in controlled trials with documented pharmacodynamic biomarker changes and well-characterized disposition and metabolism; crossover and dose-response studies highlight interconversion with related isothiocyanates (erucin) and underscore the importance of active myrosinase for consistent systemic exposure (Zhang et al., 2024; Qin, 2007). A pilot study detected SFN metabolites in human breast tissue after a single oral broccoli sprout dose, demonstrating tissue penetration to an epithelial compartment and supporting oral bioavailability to peripheral tissues (Qin, 2007). Although multiple clinical contexts are covered in these translational reviews and trials, there are no reported clinical trials of SFN specifically targeting dry AMD or RPE degeneration in the provided material (Zhang et al., 2024).

In ocular systems, the compound’s therapeutic history is robust at the preclinical level. In cultured human RPE, SFN protects against photooxidative injury (A2E/blue light) and chemical oxidants, increases GSH, and induces phase-2 enzymes including NQO1 and GST (Zhou et al., 2006). Microarray and validation work in human RPE-19 cells demonstrate SFN-induced nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and upregulation of thioredoxin-1, with enhanced oxidative stress resistance following H₂O₂ (Ye et al., 2013). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage in mice through ARE-mediated upregulation of thioredoxin (Trx1), and recovers cone function in a model of RPE oxidative stress in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025). SFN also protects rodent retinas from ischemia–reperfusion injury by increasing Nrf2 nuclear accumulation and HO-1 expression; pharmacologic inhibition of HO-1 abolishes protection, causally implicating HO-1 (Pan et al., 2014). In inherited retinal degeneration models (rd10 and tubby), systemic SFN improves retinal function and reduces degeneration, with evidence that ERK signaling and the Trx/TrxR/Nrf2 axis mediate effects in some settings (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Comparable ocular benefits have been shown in non-RPE tissues. For example, human corneal endothelial FECD cells exhibit SFN-induced Nrf2 nuclear translocation and upregulation of canonical ARE genes (NQO1, HO-1), with reduced ROS and apoptosis (Ziaei et al., 2013). In corneal surface epithelium, SFN protects against oxidative stress via Nrf2/HO-1 activation, supporting generalizability across ocular epithelial cell types (Liu & Yan, 2018). These data reinforce the core mechanism and pharmacology relevant to RPE while underlining the absence of AMD-specific clinical translation to date (Zhang et al., 2024).

Notably, although there is a recent report in an inflamed ARPE-19 model that vitamin D and SFN (alone and combined) reduced ROS, reduced IL-6/IL-8, lowered VEGF, and restored epithelial integrity markers including ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression, the provided material does not include functional barrier endpoints (TEER or FITC-dextran permeability), and claudin-1 is not shown (Bergandi et al., 2024). Thus, while “marker restoration” has been reported for ZO-1 and claudin-4 under TGF-β stress, quantitative barrier function restoration has not yet been demonstrated within the provided sources (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary mechanism—Keap1 cysteine targeting and Nrf2 activation: SFN’s electrophilic isothiocyanate group reacts with redox-sensitive cysteines on Keap1 (notably Cys151), disrupting the Cul3–Keap1 E3 ligase complex and stabilizing Nrf2, which accumulates and translocates to the nucleus. There, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences to upregulate a broad enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant and detoxification program (e.g., NQO1, HO-1, GSTs, GCLM, Trx1, SRXN1), increasing cellular reductive capacity (GSH pools, thiol buffering) and restoring redox homeostasis under oxidative stress (Chang et al., 2020; Ziaei et al., 2013; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). In RPE models, SFN does not consistently increase Nrf2 transcription but promotes nuclear translocation and DNA-binding activity, consistent with post-translational stabilization and activation; ARE target induction follows (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). In ARPE-19, SFN preconditioning increases NQO1 mRNA/activity, boosts cellular GSH, and increases GST activity; microarray and validation data add induction of SRXN1, GCLM, and Trx1 with concurrent Txnip downregulation, aligning with amplified reductive and detoxification capacity (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Under t-BHP stress, SFN increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, elevates NQO1, GR, and GPx1 transcripts, and drives HO-1, NQO1, and GR protein induction (with partial discordance between GPx1 mRNA and protein), while reducing proinflammatory ICAM-1 and MCP-1 (Chang et al., 2020).

Nrf2-dependent ocular efficacy: In vivo, SFN protection from retinal ischemia–reperfusion requires HO-1, as HO-1 inhibition reverses neuroprotection (Pan et al., 2014). In a model of RPE oxidative stress in middle-aged mice, SFN restores cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, underscoring that Nrf2 is the mechanistic driver in that age-relevant retinal context (Falcão et al., 2025).

Nrf2-independent and auxiliary mechanisms: RPE protection is not exclusively Nrf2-dependent. SFN has been shown to promote mitochondrial fusion and reduce Drp1-mediated fission, conferring anti-apoptotic benefit even in CRISPR/Cas9 Nrf2-depleted RPE cells (RPE-1), indicating a parallel mitochondrial protective program (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). SFN also engages the PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ axis: SFN or its metabolites can blunt damage-induced PARylation via direct PARP1 interactions, alleviating SIRT1 inhibition, promoting autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis, and decreasing inflammation in RPE models (Wang & Tang, 2022). In blue light–exposed RPE, SFN activates the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 axis, upregulates HO-1 and thioredoxin-1, blocks NF-κB nuclear translocation, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, and enhances autophagy, all contributing to cytoprotection; Nrf2 inhibition abrogates SFN’s protective effect in this system (Yang et al., 2021). SFN can also activate lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs that mitigate oxidative stress; KEAP1–NRF2 cross-talk with TFEB/TFE3 and macroautophagy has been documented, offering a mechanistic link between Nrf2 activation and proteostasis/autophagy enhancement relevant to RPE degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025).

Anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic effects: Across RPE models, SFN suppresses proinflammatory mediators and pathways (e.g., reduces ICAM-1 and MCP-1; inhibits NF-κB activation), and in TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19 reduces VEGF secretion, which is relevant to para-inflammatory remodeling in AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024). These effects likely contribute to preservation of junctional homeostasis by dampening cytokine-driven disruption.

Cell-type and context dependence: SFN response varies by cell type, stressor, and age-dependent pathway integrity. In some models, HO-1 mRNA is not induced even when protein rises, and under reduced Nrf2 function (as may occur in aged RPE), SFN efficacy can be limited, indicating a dependence on intact Nrf2 signaling and potential post-transcriptional regulation (Chang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Dosing and context also matter: low micromolar SFN protects RPE under oxidative stress, whereas very high concentrations can be deleterious in vitro (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Evidence for barrier-relevant endpoints: The provided sources do not present RPE TEER or FITC-dextran permeability data for SFN, and do not demonstrate claudin-1 induction in RPE (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024). One in vitro ARPE-19 TGF-β model reports that SFN (alone and with vitamin D) restores expression of ZO-1 and claudin-4 suppressed by TGF-β, reduces ROS and VEGF, and decreases proinflammatory cytokines; however, functional permeability or TEER measures were not included, and claudin-1 was not assessed (Bergandi et al., 2024). Therefore, SFN’s capacity to restore RPE barrier function remains mechanistically plausible—through redox normalization, suppression of inflammatory junctional disruption, and potential transcriptional effects on junctional proteins—but is not directly proven by barrier-function assays in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Assay context and rationale: The proposed assays—RPE monolayers subjected to A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ oxidative injury—interrogate oxidative stress pathways central to dry AMD pathophysiology and RPE barrier integrity. A2E/blue light models replicate lipofuscin-photosensitized oxidative injury; NaIO₃ models RPE oxidative cytotoxicity. In both settings, ROS accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, cytokine induction, and downstream tight-junction disruption degrade barrier integrity. The expectation is that SFN will activate Nrf2, increase reductive and detoxifying capacity (GSH, NQO1, HO-1, Trx1, GST), suppress NF-κB–driven inflammation, stabilize mitochondrial function, and secondarily preserve or restore tight-junction protein expression and continuity, resulting in improved TEER and reduced macromolecular flux (FITC-dextran) across the RPE monolayer.

Support for oxidative injury protection in RPE: In A2E/blue light–injured ARPE-19 monolayers, SFN preconditioning increases cell survival, elevates GSH, and induces NQO1 and GST—outcomes mechanistically consistent with improved tolerance to phototoxic oxidative stress (Zhou et al., 2006). In RPE challenged by chemical oxidants (t-BHP, H₂O₂), SFN reduces ROS, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, and induces NQO1, HO-1 (protein), GR, and GPx1 transcripts while suppressing ICAM-1 and MCP-1, thereby addressing both oxidative and inflammatory drivers of junctional disruption (Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013).

Support for HO-1/Nrf2 and auxiliary pathways: Under blue-light exposure, SFN activates Nrf2 and HO-1 in RPE with evidence of mechanistic necessity (Nrf2 inhibitor blocks protection), promotes autophagy (LC3BII and p62), and suppresses NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation—all changes that favor barrier preservation by limiting stress signaling and enhancing cellular cleanup mechanisms (Yang et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and RPE oxidative-stress mouse models, SFN-mediated rescue of retinal function depends on Nrf2 and HO-1, supporting the expected relevance of these axes in RPE-derived stress contexts (Pan et al., 2014; Falcão et al., 2025).

Evidence for junctional protein rescue: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, a recent report shows SFN (particularly with vitamin D) restores ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression suppressed by TGF-β, reduces IL-6/IL-8, reduces VEGF, and normalizes respiratory gene overexpression; this supports the expectation that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven loss of epithelial integrity markers (Bergandi et al., 2024). However, the provided material does not report TEER or FITC-dextran for SFN in RPE, and no data are provided for claudin-1 induction or ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity in oxidative (A2E/NaIO₃) models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Thus, while SFN is expected to improve TEER and reduce FITC-dextran flux in A2E or NaIO₃ assays through Nrf2-driven antioxidant enhancement and suppression of inflammatory/junctional injury, this is an unproven extrapolation that requires direct measurement in the proposed models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).

Target expression in RPE: All principal molecular targets are expressed in human RPE. Nrf2 activation and nuclear translocation occur in SFN-treated RPE-19/ARPE-19, with demonstrated induction of NQO1, HO-1 (protein in some contexts), thioredoxin-1, GCLM, and GST, and suppression of Txnip, ICAM-1, and MCP-1, anchoring the feasibility of modulating these axes in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2006). HO-1 induction in RPE is clearly shown under blue-light stress; in vivo retinal protection requires HO-1, reinforcing target relevance to oxidative retinal injury (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014).

Assay caveats: The provided literature does not contain RPE TEER or macromolecular flux data for SFN, nor does it document claudin-1 induction in RPE. Therefore, while SFN is expected to preserve barrier function, success criteria must include de novo demonstration of TEER rescue, FITC-dextran flux reduction, and ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity under A2E or NaIO₃ stress; these are critical data gaps to address in the proposed work (Zhang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic foundation in RPE and retina: SFN is a well-validated Nrf2 activator that increases GSH and induces multiple ARE-dependent genes (NQO1, GSTs, Trx1, GCLM; HO-1 in several ocular contexts) in RPE and retinal models, with reproducible protection against oxidative and phototoxic injury (A2E/blue light; H₂O₂/t-BHP) and anti-inflammatory activity (reduced ICAM-1, MCP-1, NF-κB signaling) (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage, improves ERG outcomes, rescues cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, and protects against ischemia–reperfusion via HO-1—clear evidence that the compound engages relevant biology and can deliver functional benefit in the retina (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2014).  
- Multiple converging protective axes: Beyond KEAP1–Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling, suppresses PARP1 overactivation to preserve NAD+/SIRT1, promotes autophagy/lysosome programs (TFEB/TFE3 linkage), and modulates mitochondrial dynamics (promotes fusion; reduces Drp1-mediated fission) even when Nrf2 is compromised. This polymechanistic profile is advantageous in RPE, where oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy, and inflammation co-drive degeneration (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2021; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).  
- Preliminary evidence for epithelial integrity marker restoration: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, SFN (especially with vitamin D) restored ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression and reduced VEGF, providing the first reported signal that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven epithelial marker loss in an RPE model (albeit without functional barrier assays) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Translational plausibility and human experience: SFN is orally administrable, with documented human systemic exposure and biomarker modulation; myrosinase co-administration enhances bioavailability from glucoraphanin. Although not yet tested clinically in dry AMD, SFN has a favorable translational narrative as a nutraceutical-derived Nrf2 activator with a safety and PD data trail in other indications (Zhang et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and gaps  
- No direct RPE barrier-function data: Across the provided literature there are no TEER or FITC-dextran permeability results for SFN in RPE monolayers, and no quantified immunofluorescence continuity data for ZO-1 or claudin-1 under oxidative stress. The sole report of “restored markers” addresses ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression after TGF-β, not barrier function or claudin-1 (Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024). The proposal’s assertion of TEER rescue and FITC-dextran reduction remains speculative pending direct measurement in A2E or NaIO₃ models (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Uncertain regulation of tight junction gene set: The provided RPE datasets document induction of canonical Nrf2 targets (NQO1, HO-1 in some contexts, Trx1, GCLM, GSTs), but do not demonstrate SFN induction of claudin-1 in RPE. Without evidence that SFN directly upregulates claudin-1 or stabilizes its junctional localization in RPE, the hypothesis of “junction-supporting gene induction” should be reframed as “junction-preserving via redox and anti-inflammatory mechanisms” until proven otherwise (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Delivery and exposure to the RPE: SFN’s solubility, short half-life, and first-pass metabolism limit systemic exposure; blood–ocular barriers further constrain retinal delivery. Several in vivo retinal studies used intraperitoneal dosing, and one report found i.p. more effective than oral for light-damage protection, emphasizing the need to optimize delivery for ocular targets. Nanocarriers and formulation strategies are promising but remain preclinical (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Dependence on Nrf2 competence and context: In models with impaired Nrf2 (potentially mirroring aged RPE), SFN efficacy is reduced; mechanisms such as mitochondrial fusion may provide partial rescue, but translational effect sizes could be diminished in elderly patients with Nrf2 decline. Additionally, gene-level responses show discordances (e.g., HO-1 mRNA vs protein), indicating context- and post-transcriptional control that complicate predictable pharmacodynamics (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity: Some cited studies are from lower-quality journals; while the core mechanistic findings are corroborated by higher-quality work (e.g., IOVS, Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology, PLoS ONE), the barrier-marker restoration report requires independent replication with functional readouts and in primary human RPE to solidify translational credibility (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Bergandi et al., 2024).

Decision implications and next steps  
Given the robust Nrf2/ARE activation, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory efficacy in RPE/retina, and the breadth of auxiliary protective mechanisms, SFN remains a mechanistically precise candidate for RPE oxidative injury relevant to dry AMD. However, the core claim of “barrier restoration” is currently supported only by marker-expression rescue (ZO-1 and claudin-4) in an inflamed ARPE-19 model without functional permeability data, and there is no evidence for claudin-1 induction or barrier rescue in A2E or NaIO₃ models in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). To de-risk the program and validate the hypothesis, the following experiments are mandatory:  
- TEER and FITC-dextran assays in differentiated human RPE (primary or iPSC-RPE) under A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ insult, with SFN dose–response and timing; include positive controls for barrier rescue (e.g., dexamethasone) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Quantitative junctional immunofluorescence (ZO-1, claudin-1, claudin-4, occludin) with continuity analysis; test whether SFN normalizes localization and expression under oxidative/cytokine stress (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Nrf2 pathway necessity tests (ML385, Nrf2 siRNA) and HO-1 inhibition (ZnPP) to define mechanism-of-action in barrier rescue; given HO-1’s necessity in vivo, confirm whether HO-1 contributes to barrier endpoints in RPE (Pan et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2021).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics and autophagy readouts (Drp1, Mfn2, LC3BII/p62) to quantify auxiliary pathways that may mediate barrier preservation when Nrf2 is compromised (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021).  
- PK/PD bridging: quantify SFN (and metabolites) in plasma and ocular tissues after oral vs i.p. dosing in rodents; evaluate delivery systems (e.g., albumin nanocarriers) for RPE exposure; incorporate myrosinase co-administration for oral strategies; relate exposures to effective in vitro EC₅₀s for barrier rescue (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Aged and Nrf2-impaired models: evaluate efficacy in aged RPE or Nrf2-hypomorphic contexts to assess translational robustness (Zhang et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

If TEER and permeability rescue are demonstrated with mechanistic attribution to Nrf2/HO-1 and/or auxiliary pathways, and if ocular PK can be solved to achieve efficacious exposures, SFN would merit progression to in vivo dry AMD–relevant models (e.g., subretinal NaIO₃, chronic photo-oxidative stress) with structural (OCT) and functional (ERG) endpoints, plus RPE barrier imaging, before considering a human proof-of-concept study.

In sum, the totality of evidence strongly supports SFN for oxidative and inflammatory protection of RPE and retina with multiple convergent mechanisms and translational plausibility. The critical missing element is direct demonstration that these effects translate into bona fide RPE barrier restoration (TEER/permeability) under AMD-relevant oxidative stress, and a practical path to deliver sufficient drug to the RPE in humans. Addressing these gaps should be the focus of immediate preclinical validation (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024).

Its clinical development history has largely focused on cancers such as Her2-positive breast cancers and gliomas, where its ability to modulate PI3K/AKT signaling has been of particular advantage in overcoming resistance mechanisms. Although the majority of the therapeutic history of AZD8055 has been in cancer, the underlying molecular rationale for its use has provided impetus for exploring its repurposing in non-oncological diseases. In the realm of ocular diseases, particularly dry AMD, the mTOR pathway has been implicated in the regulation of autophagy and cellular homeostasis within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). While traditional mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin have been tested in ocular settings, their clinical efficacy has been inconsistent, partly due to the inability to inhibit mTORC2-driven feedback loops. AZD8055’s dual inhibition mechanism could potentially address these shortcomings by providing a more balanced modulation of the mTOR pathway, although to date there is limited direct clinical or preclinical evidence of its use specifically in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 9–10, 16–17).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, AZD8055 exerts its pharmacological effects through ATP-competitive inhibition of the catalytic domain of mTOR, thereby targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes. mTORC1 is primarily responsible for regulating protein synthesis through substrates such as 4EBP1 and S6 kinase, while mTORC2 is integral to the phosphorylation and activation of AKT, a key mediator of cell survival and metabolism. The simultaneous inhibition of both complexes by AZD8055 prevents the compensatory activation of AKT that is typically observed with rapalogs, which primarily target mTORC1 and leave mTORC2 functionally active (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Downstream effects of this mechanism include rapid dephosphorylation of 4EBP1, which in turn halts cap-dependent mRNA translation, and the induction of autophagy as a result of relieving the suppression of upstream autophagy initiating factors such as ULK1 and transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10). In ocular applications, particularly within RPE cells, the impairment of autophagy is thought to contribute to the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and damaged cellular components. By enhancing autophagic flux, AZD8055 can facilitate the autophagosome–lysosome fusion critical to the degradation and clearance of damaged junctional proteins. The resultant restoration of the tight junction integrity—measurable via trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—is believed to underlie the therapeutic rationale for its use in dry AMD. As a dual mTOR inhibitor with high potency, AZD8055’s molecular interactions within the mTOR kinase domain contribute not only to the suppression of pathological signaling but also promote cellular recycling processes that maintain RPE function and homeostasis (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 4–6). Additionally, the suppression of mTORC2 may help prevent compensatory pro-survival signaling pathways that could otherwise undermine barrier recovery, thereby ensuring a sustained therapeutic effect in the stressed RPE cellular milieu (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed study hypothesis posits that 50 nM AZD8055 will effectively restore and enhance barrier function in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells that have been subjected to oxidative stress via H₂O₂ exposure. Mechanistically, the compound is expected to attenuate the oxidative stress–induced disruption of junctional proteins by rapidly dephosphorylating 4EBP1, thereby halting pathological protein synthesis and activating autophagic pathways. One of the key cellular assays involves the measurement of TEER, a well-established metric reflecting the integrity of tight junctions and overall barrier function in epithelial cultures. According to preliminary data referenced in the hypothesis, a 50 nM dose of AZD8055 elevated baseline TEER by 24% and accelerated the recovery of TEER following oxidative insult, which suggests that the inhibitor not only ameliorates barrier damage but also promotes cellular repair mechanisms (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Moreover, pharmacodynamic markers such as sustained colocalization of LC3 and LAMP1 implicate an improvement in autophagosome–lysosome fusion, leading to the efficient removal of damaged junctional proteins. This is particularly relevant in the pathophysiology of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction is observed due to the accumulation of cellular debris and compromised autophagic clearance (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating AZD8055 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key strengths and potential challenges must be considered. A notable strength of AZD8055 lies in its dual inhibition profile, which addresses the limitations inherent in rapalog therapy by effectively targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2. This dual action is instrumental in both halting aberrant protein synthesis and in promoting autophagic clearance, processes that are crucial to restoring cellular homeostasis and junctional integrity in RPE cells challenged by oxidative stress (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Moreover, its clean kinase selectivity reduces the likelihood of off-target interactions that could confound clinical outcomes, an important consideration given the delicate nature of ocular therapeutics (Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10).

However, there are inherent weaknesses and safety concerns that warrant attention. Preclinical and clinical data from oncology studies indicate that AZD8055 is associated with adverse effects such as hyperglycemia, fatigue, and gastrointestinal disturbances (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 4–6). Although these events have been characterized in systemic applications within cancer patients, translating such findings to a localized, ocular delivery system requires careful dose optimization to ensure that the therapeutic benefits are not offset by adverse outcomes. Additionally, the complexity of mTOR signaling in the retina poses a challenge. The mTOR pathway not only regulates autophagy but also influences cell survival, apoptosis, and inflammatory responses. Disruption of this delicate balance through chronic or excessive inhibition could potentially lead to unintended consequences, including impaired cellular metabolism or dysregulated angiogenesis, particularly since previous clinical trials using mTOR inhibitors for ocular conditions have reported mixed results and even adverse effects on visual acuity (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 12–14).

Another concern is the risk associated with systemic exposure. While AZD8055 is primarily being developed in oncology with an established profile in systemic administration, its ocular pharmacokinetics, particularly when delivered intravitreally or via other local routes, remain to be fully elucidated. The retinal environment is notably distinct from systemic circulation, and achieving a sufficient drug concentration at the target site while avoiding toxicity is a tightrope to walk. Past studies with rapamycin in ocular models have pointed to potential issues with dosing precision, as high dosages can lead to ocular inflammation and other adverse events, suggesting that similar caution must be exercised with AZD8055 (Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 12–14; Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 20–24).

Another consideration is the inherent complexity of mTOR’s role in ocular physiology. While there is compelling evidence that mTOR modulation can enhance autophagic clearance and ameliorate RPE dysfunction, there remains a possibility that long-term mTOR inhibition might disrupt other adaptive responses in the retina, such as cell survival signaling pathways and angiogenic responses. This is particularly pertinent in age-related diseases, where the balance between autophagy and apoptosis is finely regulated. The interplay between mTORC1 and mTORC2 implies that any perturbation could have far-reaching effects on retinal metabolism and cellular homeostasis. Therefore, while the mechanistic insights are promising, a cautious approach to clinical translation is warranted, with an emphasis on detailed mechanistic studies in relevant animal models prior to embarking on clinical trials for dry AMD (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 15–20).

In summary, AZD8055 represents a promising therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its well-defined mechanism of dual inhibition of mTOR complexes, which effectively modulates autophagy and prevents compensatory pro-survival signaling. The agent’s ability to enhance TEER and accelerate recovery post oxidative stress in human iPSC-RPE cells suggests a direct beneficial effect on barrier integrity—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Its synthetic origins and development pipeline in oncology provide a robust foundation of preclinical and early clinical data that underscores its potency and selectivity (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10).

Nevertheless, several challenges remain in repurposing AZD8055 for ocular applications. The translation of dosing from systemic oncologic contexts to localized ocular environments is not trivial, as the pharmacokinetic properties may vary significantly. A comprehensive assessment will be needed to establish optimal dosing regimens that achieve therapeutic efficacy in the retina without eliciting adverse effects such as ocular inflammation, hyperglycemia, or undesired effects on retinal metabolism (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15, 20–24; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 12–14). Moreover, the multifaceted role of mTOR in regulating retinal cell survival, autophagy, and inflammation necessitates a careful balance; while enhanced autophagy can remove detrimental aggregates and restore junctional proteins, excessive inhibition could disrupt normal cellular functions, leading to potential toxicity over prolonged periods.

Future studies should focus on in-depth pharmacodynamic analyses in relevant animal models of dry AMD to validate the in vitro findings observed with iPSC-RPE cells. Specifically, it is imperative to assess whether AZD8055 can recapitulate the observed TEER restoration in vivo and whether it can effectively reduce the accumulation of drusen or other toxic aggregates characteristic of dry AMD. In parallel, investigations into the ocular pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of AZD8055 will be crucial to ensuring that effective drug concentrations are achieved in the retinal layers while minimizing systemic exposure (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). Moreover, the durability of the response, potential off-target effects, and overall impact on visual function will require careful longitudinal study.

The dual mechanism of action provided by AZD8055—targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2—offers a significant advantage over traditional mTOR inhibitors and supports its rational repurposing for dry AMD, where compensatory signaling mechanisms often undermine therapeutic efficacy. By preventing the feedback activation of AKT and sustaining autophagic flux within the RPE, AZD8055 has the potential to not only mitigate the cellular stresses induced by oxidative damage but also to promote a sustained restoration of epithelial barrier function. Given that impaired autophagy is a central feature in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, interventions that can normalize these cellular processes are highly sought after in the current therapeutic landscape (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

From an expert drug development perspective, the repurposing of AZD8055 for dry AMD is scientifically intriguing but calls for a methodical approach to address translational challenges. The unique pharmacological properties of AZD8055 could fill a significant unmet need by ameliorating the autophagy deficits and junctional disruptions that underpin the progression of dry AMD. Nevertheless, the inherent risks related to systemic metabolism, as evidenced by hyperglycemia or gastrointestinal effects observed in cancer studies, must be rigorously managed within the context of ocular delivery, ensuring that drug exposure is sufficiently localized to the retina without systemic spill-over (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 4–6; Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 20–24).

In weighing the overall evidence, AZD8055 emerges as a compound with a strong mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD. The compound’s preclinical data in oncological contexts provide a valuable benchmark for its potency and selectivity, while preliminary in vitro studies in iPSC-RPE highlight its potential for ocular applications (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10).

However, the promising aspects of its mechanism must be balanced against the potential for adverse events and the critical need for further safety and pharmacokinetic evaluations tailored to the ocular context. The risk of ocular inflammation, off-target pharmacological effects, and the challenge of achieving sustained drug levels in the retinal layers are all factors that will require careful investigation in future studies. It is advisable that subsequent research include comprehensive in vivo models of dry AMD, dose-ranging studies to define the therapeutic window, and the development of optimized drug delivery systems that can maximize local efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure (Yao & van Wijngaarden, 2020, pp. 11–15; Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 12–14).

In conclusion, while AZD8055 has predominantly been explored within oncological settings, its dual inhibitory action on mTORC1 and mTORC2, coupled with its demonstrated capacity to enhance autophagic flux and restore cellular barrier function, render it a compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. The evidence from the mechanistic studies supports its potential to counteract the deleterious effects of oxidative stress on RPE cells by promoting the clearance of damaged proteins and re-establishing tight junction integrity. Despite the promising preclinical data, the translation of these findings into a clinically viable treatment for dry AMD will necessitate a painstakingly detailed series of studies to address dosage optimization, ocular-specific pharmacokinetics, and long-term safety. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Z944 is a synthetic, rationally designed T‐type calcium channel blocker that emerged from a medicinal chemistry program aimed at developing first‐in‐class modulators with improved selectivity and pharmacokinetic profiles. It was derived from a piperazine‐based chemical backbone originally optimized from an N‐type calcium channel blocker scaffold, with extensive structure–activity relationship studies guiding its evolution to target T‐type channels (primarily CaV3.1, CaV3.2, and CaV3.3) with high affinity (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018). As part of the broader class of T‐type calcium channel blockers, Z944 belongs to a group of compounds that have been predominantly evaluated for their analgesic and anti‐epileptic properties. Its design emphasizes sub‐micromolar potency (with reported IC₅₀ values in the nanomolar range for its target channels) and a high degree of selectivity—demonstrating 70–100-fold preference for T-type channels over other voltage-gated channels such as CaV1.4 (a key L-type channel in retinal photoreceptors) (Sun et al., 2025). Although originally conceived to treat neuropathic pain and seizure disorders, its improved pharmacokinetic properties have prompted interest in repurposing Z944 for indications outside the central nervous system, including retinal diseases.

Historically, Z944 has been developed and evaluated extensively in preclinical models focused on pain management and epilepsy, demonstrating encouraging translational potential by restoring functional neuronal circuit dynamics in both inflammatory pain and absence epilepsy models (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Melgari et al., 2022). Clinical studies have established that Z944 can effectively modulate T‐type calcium channel activity in human experimental models of inflammatory pain, and it has been advanced into Phase I and Phase II clinical trials targeting pain indications (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018). However, a consistent theme throughout published reports is that Z944, along with similar T‐type channel antagonists, has been primarily evaluated in the context of neurological disorders. Comprehensive literature reviews and patent analyses have yet to document any clinical or preclinical application of Z944 or related T‐type calcium channel blockers in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD), retinal degeneration, or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Sun et al., 2025; Jones, 2024). Mechanism of Action:  
Z944 exerts its pharmacological effects primarily through the selective inhibition of T‐type calcium channels. At the molecular level, T‐type channels (CaV3 family) are low–voltage‐activated channels essential for regulating neuronal excitability and rhythmic firing.
