Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
LG100268 is a fully synthetic rexinoid that was developed as a selective agonist for the retinoid X receptors (RXRs). It belongs to a specialized subclass of retinoids known as “rexinoids” that bind to RXRs with high affinity and minimal cross‐reactivity to the retinoic acid receptors (RARs). The compound was discovered and optimized in medicinal chemistry programs aiming to achieve potent RXR activation with improved receptor selectivity relative to earlier retinoid compounds such as bexarotene. Notably, synthetic modifications introduced in LG100268 include the incorporation of a 3‐carboxy pyridine ring—a modular motif that has been exploited for further scaffold diversification and structure–activity work to tune RXR heterodimer selectivity (Curley, 2012, pp. 4–5). LG100268 displays one of the highest reported binding affinities for RXR, with a dissociation constant in the low nanomolar range (approximately 3 nM), making it a very potent agent within its class (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Rexinoids such as LG100268 have been historically used in preclinical research as tools to explore RXR biology in oncology and metabolic studies—often by modulating gene transcription via RXR homodimers or RXR heterodimers with factors such as PPAR, LXR, and others (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). Although LG100268 was initially conceived for applications in cancer chemoprevention and metabolic regulation, its high potency and selective RXR activation have generated interest in repurposing it for diseases with an inflammatory component, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, LG100268 has been most notably explored in preclinical models of cancer—particularly in murine models of breast cancer. Studies in the MMTV-Neu (a HER2+ breast cancer model) and the MMTV-PyMT (an aggressive, triple-negative model) have shown that short-course dietary administration of LG100268 produces significant immunomodulatory effects. For example, in these models, LG100268 was observed to decrease the infiltration of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and CD206-expressing macrophages, while increasing the expression of PD-L1 and enhancing the ratio of cytotoxic CD8 T cells relative to CD4 T-cell subpopulations (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Additionally, combination studies with immune checkpoint inhibitors have further supported its potential to modulate the tumor microenvironment in preclinical oncology settings (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). In metabolic research, LG100268 has been administered to rodent models (such as diabetic ZDF rats and normal Sprague–Dawley rats) to evaluate its effects on lipid and glucose metabolism. In these contexts, LG100268 was shown to acutely lower serum glucose levels but also to induce marked hypertriglyceridemia linked to diminished lipoprotein lipase activity in muscle tissue, a pharmacodynamic liability that underscores the potent transcriptional effects mediated via RXR activation (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). Despite these promising activities in oncology and metabolic models, there are no documented studies, either preclinical or clinical, in which LG100268 has been directly used for treating dry AMD or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction. The entirety of its previous applications has been outside the ocular field, focusing on cancer chemoprevention and metabolic dysregulation; thus, its proposed repurposing for dry AMD represents an innovative but as-yet untested direction with respect to ocular indications (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lee & Khan, 2016, pp. 15–19).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, LG100268 acts as a high-affinity agonist for RXRs by binding selectively to the ligand-binding pocket of these nuclear receptors. RXRs are unique in that they function both as homodimers and as obligate heterodimer partners for multiple other nuclear receptors including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), liver X receptors (LXRs), and even possibly orphan receptors such as Nurr1. Upon binding LG100268, the RXR undergoes a conformational change that induces release of corepressors and recruitment of coactivators, thereby altering transcription of downstream target genes (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10). In cancer studies, the activation of RXR by LG100268 has been associated with modulation of the immune microenvironment; it reduces pro-tumor cytokine release, alters the balance of immune cell populations, and influences expression of cell surface proteins such as PD-L1 (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, in metabolic tissues, activation of RXR by LG100268 affects lipid metabolism through transcriptional control of genes involved in the regulation of lipoprotein lipase and other lipid-processing enzymes (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

The specific hypothesis proposed for dry AMD centers on the concept that selective RXR modulation might bias RXR heterodimerization toward partnering with Nurr1 in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-activated RPE cells. Nurr1, an orphan nuclear receptor, is implicated in anti-inflammatory responses and has been associated with maintenance of cellular differentiation and barrier function in various epithelial models. While direct evidence from the literature demonstrating RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation in RPE cells is limited, the general biology of RXR suggests that ligand-induced conformational changes in RXR can influence its choice of heterodimerization partner (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). In this scenario, by favoring the formation of RXR–Nurr1 heterodimers, LG100268 could suppress NF-κB-driven transcription. NF-κB is well known as a master regulator of inflammatory responses, and its activation (specifically the nuclear translocation of p65) can lead to the downregulation of tight junction proteins such as claudin-1. Therefore, by inhibiting NF-κB activity via this heterodimer bias, LG100268 is postulated to stabilize the epigenetic landscape and transcription of genes integral to maintaining tight junction integrity, thereby preserving transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE monolayers (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Although most of the mechanistic studies of LG100268 have been conducted in cancer and metabolic models, the underlying molecular interactions—namely high-affinity RXR activation, selective heterodimerization, and subsequent transcriptional modulation—provide a plausible basis for extending its use to inflammatory conditions of the RPE. These mechanisms are potentially relevant since RPE cells express multiple RXR isoforms; indeed, RXR expression in retinal tissues underlines its importance in visual cycle regulation and cellular homeostasis (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10, 10–12).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the pathological insult is thought to be driven in part by chronic, low-grade inflammation induced by drusen components and other pro-inflammatory stimuli such as LPS. In primary RPE cell cultures challenged with LPS, there is typically a cascade of events initiated by the activation of NF-κB that results in a decrease in the expression of tight junction proteins like claudin-1, leading to reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and impaired barrier function. The hypothesis for repurposing LG100268 in this application is that at a concentration of 0.1 µM, the compound will attenuate LPS-induced NF-κB activation, as evidenced by reduced nuclear translocation of the p65 subunit. This in turn is expected to prevent the downregulation of claudin-1 and maintain TEER in RPE cells. The mechanism underpinning this expected effect involves the selective activation of RXR by LG100268, which is postulated to shift the balance of RXR heterodimers in favor of complexes with Nurr1. The RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation would then lead to anti-inflammatory transcriptional outcomes, including suppression of NF-κB target genes that would otherwise contribute to tight junction disruption (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

Additionally, by modulating the epigenetic regulation of gene expression, LG100268 may help preserve the expression pattern of genes critical for barrier integrity. Published reports in other cell systems have demonstrated that rexinoids can influence the transcription of key cytokines and growth factors in a manner that normalizes cell adhesion molecules and maintains cellular differentiation (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Although these findings have principally been documented in models of cancer and metabolism, the extrapolation to RPE is supported by the fact that RXR-mediated pathways are conserved across multiple tissues, including ocular tissues. Should LG100268 effectively prevent TEER loss and reduce nuclear p65 accumulation in primary RPE cultures, it would provide a strong rationale for its further development as a novel therapy aimed at stabilizing the RPE barrier in dry AMD (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of LG100268 for dry AMD is an innovative approach that leverages the compound’s well-documented ability to selectively activate RXRs. Its high-affinity binding and potent agonism make it one of the more promising rexinoids available, as evidenced by its superior receptor binding kinetics relative to known RXR ligands such as bexarotene (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Preclinical studies in oncology have consistently demonstrated that LG100268 modulates the immune microenvironment, induces changes in critical cytokine expression, and alters the balance of immune cell populations in a manner that collectively suggests an anti-inflammatory profile (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). These anti-inflammatory effects, when viewed through the lens of RPE biology, provide a plausible mechanistic basis for protecting against the chronic inflammation that characterizes dry AMD. Particularly, the hypothesis that LG100268 may bias RXR heterodimer formation toward Nurr1—and thus suppress NF-κB signaling—opens a new avenue for preserving tight junction integrity in RPE cells, which is critically important in maintaining a proper barrier function (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

Moreover, LG100268’s capacity to induce targeted epigenetic modulation further supports its potential to stabilize gene expression profiles under inflammatory conditions. Maintaining the expression of tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 is vital for preventing the breakdown of the blood–retina barrier and subsequent RPE degeneration. In vitro observations that LG100268 at 0.1 µM prevented TEER loss and inhibited NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation in primary RPE models provide encouraging preliminary data for its use in this context. This evidence, combined with its established anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties in other systems, makes a compelling case for considering LG100268 as a candidate for treating dry AMD (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12; Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

Nevertheless, there are several challenges and uncertainties that must be addressed. Foremost among these is the absence of any prior documentation—either in the biomedical, clinical, or biochemical literature—that LG100268 has been applied in any ocular or RPE-specific context. Its therapeutic history is entirely rooted in applications related to cancer and metabolic regulation, and its safety profile in the context of ocular tissues remains uncharacterized. Systemic administration of potent rexinoids is known to produce adverse metabolic effects, such as hypertriglyceridemia and thyroid hormone axis suppression (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). These side effects raise concerns about potential off-target effects if LG100268 were to be repurposed for a chronic condition like dry AMD. The risk of systemic side effects may be mitigated by ocular-targeted delivery methods; however, the pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of LG100268 following ocular administration require thorough investigation.

Another significant weakness lies in the hypothesis that LG100268 will bias RXR heterodimerization toward Nurr1. Although the concept is mechanistically attractive, the current literature does not provide direct evidence that LG100268 preferentially promotes RXR–Nurr1 complexes in RPE cells (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). In addition, the potential involvement of alternative RXR partners—including PPARs and LXRs, which are also expressed in RPE cells—could complicate the desired selectivity. Off-target modulation of these heterodimeric pathways could result in unintended changes in gene expression that might adversely affect RPE homeostasis.

Furthermore, while the proposed anti-inflammatory effects of LG100268 are supported by its ability to modulate cytokine profiles and immune cell populations in other models, the specific molecular pathways governing the maintenance of tight junction proteins in RPE cells are multifactorial. NF-κB signaling is only one among many pathways that regulate barrier integrity, and the extent to which RXR activation can counterbalance other detrimental signaling cascades in the RPE is not fully understood. The potential exists for complex cross-talk between RXR-mediated pathways and other nuclear receptor pathways, which might lead to unpredictable outcomes in the delicate environment of the retina (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–12; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

In summary, while LG100268’s established potency, receptor selectivity, and capacity to modulate inflammatory and metabolic gene expression provide a strong foundation for considering its repurposing, the current literature does not yet offer direct support for its use in dry AMD. Preclinical studies that specifically assess the effects of LG100268 on RPE barrier function, tight junction integrity, and inflammatory signaling in ocular models are necessary to validate the hypothesis. Moreover, rigorous toxicological assessments and the development of targeted delivery methods will be required to overcome the potential liabilities associated with systemic rexinoid administration. Until these issues are addressed, LG100268 remains a promising yet exploratory candidate for dry AMD therapy (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10; Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ (mitoquinone) is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant generated by covalently linking a ubiquinone headgroup to a decyl triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation, yielding a delocalized lipophilic cation that partitions across biological membranes and accumulates several-hundredfold inside the mitochondrial matrix driven by the large negative inner mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Chico et al., 2016; Smith & Murphy, 2010; Fields et al., 2023). Within mitochondria, MitoQ adsorbs predominantly to the matrix-facing leaflet of the inner mitochondrial membrane where the ubiquinone moiety is reduced by the respiratory chain to the corresponding hydroquinone (mitoquinol), which then acts as a chain-breaking antioxidant that intercepts lipid peroxyl radicals and limits cardiolipin and phospholipid peroxidation in situ (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Vlachantoni et al., 2011). The TPP⁺-driven mitochondrial targeting strategy (also used by related agents such as SkQ1, decylTPP conjugates, and TPP-Niacin) was devised to overcome the poor organelle-level bioavailability and off-target scavenging that limited earlier, non-targeted antioxidants in clinical translation (Fields et al., 2023).

The compound and its class were developed and extensively characterized by Murphy and colleagues, including in vitro uptake/antioxidant activity, radiolabeled biodistribution, and oral tablet formulations suitable for animal toxicology and human dosing (Smith & Murphy, 2010). After oral dosing, MitoQ exhibits low but measurable bioavailability (~10%), undergoes first-pass metabolism (intestinal wall and liver), and is excreted as unchanged drug and conjugated metabolites of the reduced quinol form (glucuronides/sulfates), with phase I human pharmacokinetics showing a Cmax ≈33 ng/mL at ~1 hour after an 80 mg dose (Zinovkin & Zamyatnin, 2019; Smith & Murphy, 2010). Long-term oral administration in rodents was tolerated at 500 μM in drinking water without overt toxicity; quantitative LC/MS/MS confirms tissue distribution to heart, liver, brain, and other organs over weeks to months (Smith & Murphy, 2010). In a retinal context, oral MitoQ accumulates in mouse retina to steady-state levels on the order of ~1.3 nmol/g wet tissue (with no retinal toxicity in wild-type mice at 500 μM dosing), establishing biological access to ocular tissues via systemic exposure (Vlachantoni et al., 2011).

MitoQ belongs to the broader class of mitochondria-targeted quinones (short-chain quinones conjugated to lipophilic cations), which includes plastoquinone analogs such as SkQ1 that share the same TPP⁺ carrier but differ in the redox headgroup and, potentially, in reactivity and recycling kinetics within mitochondria (Chico et al., 2016; Baksheeva et al., 2018). This class has been deployed across neurological, cardiovascular, inflammatory, and hepatic models, with mixed clinical translation; importantly for ophthalmology, SkQ1 has advanced to ocular topical formulations (Visomitin) with evidence of retinal protection in animal models of light-induced damage and age-related retinopathy, illustrating that TPP⁺-conjugated antioxidants can reach and act within retinal tissues when appropriately delivered (Baksheeva et al., 2018; Grigoryan et al., 2012; Lukashev et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical and clinical experience with MitoQ spans multiple organ systems and disease models. In animal studies, orally administered MitoQ has shown protective effects in models of ischemia-reperfusion, endotoxin/sepsis, and neurodegeneration, consistent with its mitochondrial antioxidant mechanism and tissue distribution profile (Lukashev et al., 2014; Fields et al., 2023). For example, MitoQ decreased inflammatory cytokines and liver enzyme elevations in sepsis models, reduced neurological deficits in an Alzheimer’s transgenic mouse model, and modestly prolonged survival with improved pathology in the SOD1-G93A ALS mouse model when given chronically in drinking water (Lukashev et al., 2014). Additional preclinical reports include beneficial effects in diabetic kidney disease via Nrf2/PINK1-associated mitophagy and in sensorineural hearing loss driven by mitochondrial ROS, supporting broad bioactivity against mitochondrial oxidative injury across tissues (Shyam et al., 2021).

Human experience includes long-term oral dosing in Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients (40–80 mg/day for 12 months) without slowing disease progression but providing important safety data for year-long administration, as well as shorter trials demonstrating improved vascular function and reduced oxidative stress biomarkers or decreased hepatic transaminases in chronic hepatitis C without antiviral benefit (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Zinovkin & Zamyatnin, 2019; Mason et al., 2022). Across randomized studies of mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, MitoQ was generally well tolerated (with occasional non-serious gastrointestinal adverse events), but the evidence base remains short-term and of low-to-very-low certainty for many endpoints (Mason et al., 2022). Crucially for AMD, no registered human clinical trials testing MitoQ in age-related macular degeneration were identified on ClinicalTrials.gov, indicating an absence of clinical translational activity in this indication to date (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Ocular and retinal history is mixed. On the positive side, MitoQ is orally bioavailable to the retina in mice at nanomole-per-gram levels without overt retinal toxicity in wild-type animals (outer nuclear layer thickness unchanged; no TUNEL-positive photoreceptor cells), supporting general ocular tolerability and access (Vlachantoni et al., 2011). In vitro, MitoQ (as a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant) has been reported to protect RPE cells from blue light–induced oxidative stress, providing cell-level plausibility in a phototoxic paradigm relevant to RPE oxidative injury (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012). However, in an independent oxidative RPE insult model (NaIO₃ in hTERT RPE-1), MitoQ failed to rescue cells from mitochondrial depolarization and apoptosis, whereas a CD36 ligand (MPE-001) that enhanced autophagy did prevent cell death, directly documenting a negative result for MitoQ in this RPE oxidative-stress paradigm (Dorion et al., 2021).

In vivo retinal degeneration models have been largely negative for MitoQ efficacy. Multiple inherited photoreceptor degeneration (IPD) mouse models—Pde6brd1/rd1, Pde6batrd1/atrd1, Rho⁻/⁻, and Prph2rds/rds—showed no mitigation of photoreceptor loss or apoptosis with oral MitoQ; outer nuclear layer degeneration progressed on schedule, and TUNEL-positive cell counts were unaffected by treatment (Vlachantoni et al., 2011). Mechanistic biomarker analyses in these models also failed to show improvements in Complex I activity or reduced glutathione (GSH), consistent with a lack of impact on core mitochondrial oxidative endpoints in this setting (Vlachantoni et al., 2011). These negative outcomes likely reflect the mismatch between MitoQ’s primary antioxidant chemistry and the dominant ROS species present in these models (see Mechanism of Action), as well as disease-specific drivers beyond ROS that dominate in fast-progressing genetic photoreceptor loss (Vlachantoni et al., 2011).

By contrast, SkQ1—another TPP⁺-linked mitochondrial antioxidant with a plastoquinone headgroup—has repeatedly shown retinal protection in animal models, including light-induced retinal damage in rabbits (preservation of photoreceptors, suppression of H₂O₂ accumulation, inhibition of arrestin disulfide dimerization, improvement of antioxidant capacity; topical administration achieved nanomolar retinal levels) and prevention of RPE atrophy and retinopathy in senescence-accelerated OXYS rats (systemic dosing) (Baksheeva et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2022). SkQ1 also protected RPE and choroid structure in long-term organotypic rat posterior eyecup cultures at nanomolar concentrations, reducing apoptosis and preventing RPE detachment from Bruch’s membrane (Grigoryan et al., 2012). Beyond preclinical studies, SkQ1 has been formulated as an ophthalmic solution (Visomitin) and advanced into human trials for dry eye and ocular indications, demonstrating the feasibility of TPP⁺-linked antioxidants in topical ocular delivery; although not directly probative for AMD, this trajectory indicates class-level translational potential with appropriate formulation (Lukashev et al., 2014).

This body of work positions MitoQ as mechanistically plausible for mitigating mitochondrial oxidative damage in RPE and retina, with retinal access established in mice, but with mixed-to-negative efficacy in photoreceptor degeneration models and at least one negative RPE oxidative injury study; critically, there is no published evidence of MitoQ improving RPE barrier function endpoints (TEER, ZO-1/occludin) or preventing RPE atrophy in AMD-like models in vivo (Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Dorion et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
MitoQ exploits the Δψm-dependent electrophoretic uptake of the TPP⁺ carrier to concentrate within mitochondria, where the ubiquinone moiety is reduced by the electron transport chain (predominantly at Complex II) to the hydroquinone mitoquinol, which is the active antioxidant species (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Gueven et al., 2017). The quinol intercalates into the inner membrane lipid bilayer, where it donates hydrogen atoms to lipid peroxyl radicals, terminating chain propagation in lipid peroxidation and thereby preserving mitochondrial membrane integrity and function; it also reduces reactive nitrogen species such as peroxynitrite-derived intermediates in membrane environments (Smith & Murphy, 2010). After oxidation back to ubiquinone, MitoQ is recycled by the respiratory chain to maintain antioxidant capacity, making it a “rechargeable” mitochondrial antioxidant under conditions where electron flow remains sufficient (Zinovkin & Zamyatnin, 2019).

Two mechanistic constraints are salient for RPE/retinal applications:

- ROS selectivity: MitoQ shows negligible direct reactivity toward hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) and has limited ability to decrease mitochondrial superoxide generation; its predominant efficacy is in lipid radical interception within membranes, not in neutralizing aqueous ROS such as H₂O₂ (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Vlachantoni et al., 2011). Under some conditions, MitoQ or the TPP⁺ moiety can exhibit pro-oxidant behavior, increasing ROS in endothelial cells and isolated mitochondria, underscoring context-dependent redox outcomes (Gueven et al., 2017).

- Dependence on Δψm and ETC activity: Uptake and recycling of MitoQ rely on sustained mitochondrial membrane potential and electron transport activity; in severely depolarized RPE mitochondria (for example, after NaIO₃ injury or intense oxidant exposure), mitochondrial accumulation and bioactivation to the quinol may be compromised (Gueven et al., 2017).

In retinal phototoxicity and AMD-relevant oxidative stress, mitochondrial ROS from photoreceptors and RPE are central drivers, with H₂O₂ acting as a major mediator of phototoxicity; oxidative protein modifications such as arrestin disulfide dimerization and lipid peroxidation products (e.g., malondialdehyde) are robust biomarkers in illuminated retina (Baksheeva et al., 2018). In rabbit light-induced retinal damage, a mitochondria-targeted TPP⁺ antioxidant (SkQ1) suppressed H₂O₂ accumulation, prevented protein oxidation, reduced lipid peroxidation, and improved antioxidant enzyme dynamics (AOA, GPx), consistent with neutralizing mitochondrial sources of ROS and stabilizing redox homeostasis in retinal cells (Baksheeva et al., 2018). The success of SkQ1 in H₂O₂-centric retinal injury contexts may reflect differences in redox kinetics or membrane interactions of the plastoquinone headgroup compared to ubiquinone in MitoQ, or differences in delivery (topical eye drops achieving local retinal exposure) (Baksheeva et al., 2018).

For RPE barrier integrity specifically, tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin) and TEER are degraded by oxidative stressors including H₂O₂, blue light in A2E-loaded RPE, and NaIO₃; mitochondrial dysfunction (Δψm loss, increased mitochondrial ROS, impaired ATP generation) is causally linked to RPE injury in these paradigms (Tong et al., 2022). Mitochondria-targeted antioxidants can restore mitochondrial membrane potential and limit mitochondrial ROS in RPE cells, as shown with TPP-Niacin in H₂O₂-challenged ARPE-19, which preserved Δψm, reduced ROS, and upregulated antioxidant and mitochondrial biogenesis programs, albeit without reported barrier readouts (Kim et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022). Related TPP-conjugates (e.g., TPP-D-NAC) demonstrated selective quenching of mitochondrial ROS in RPE and established an experimental pipeline for assessing RPE bioenergetics, mitochondrial ROS, and structural endpoints that would be directly applicable to evaluating MitoQ (Datta et al., 2023).

Taken together, MitoQ’s molecular pharmacology—robust lipid peroxidation interception when mitochondria are polarized, limited H₂O₂ reactivity, dependence on ETC for recycling—supports a priori efficacy in oxidative paradigms dominated by lipid radical propagation and intact Δψm, while suggesting reduced performance in H₂O₂-dominant or severely depolarizing insults (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Gueven et al., 2017).

Expected Effect  
The proposed hypothesis is that MitoQ will accumulate in RPE mitochondria to scavenge mitochondrial superoxide–derived lipid peroxyl radicals, preventing oxidative degradation of tight junction proteins (ZO-1/occludin) and restoring TEER in A2E- or H₂O₂-challenged monolayers. Mechanistically, if Δψm is maintained sufficiently to support TPP⁺-driven uptake and ETC recycling, mitoquinol should suppress membrane lipid peroxidation and secondary oxidative cascades, indirectly preserving junctional complexes that are susceptible to ROS-driven damage (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Gueven et al., 2017). This expectation is supported in part by prior in vitro RPE photostress data where MitoQ afforded protection against blue light–induced oxidative stress, a model in which A2E photosensitization generates lipid peroxidation and singlet oxygen that could be intercepted effectively by a membrane-localized quinol antioxidant (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Tong et al., 2022). In such A2E/blue-light paradigms, measuring reductions in lipid peroxidation endpoints (e.g., MDA/4-HNE) and preservation of ZO-1/occludin belts would be consistent with MitoQ’s established lipid radical scavenging capacity (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Tong et al., 2022).

By contrast, in H₂O₂-dominant paradigms (e.g., acute H₂O₂ challenge), the compound’s negligible direct reactivity toward H₂O₂ and reliance on Δψm for accumulation predict weaker effects, especially if H₂O₂ exposure collapses Δψm and impairs recycling of MitoQ to mitoquinol (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Gueven et al., 2017). Indeed, in an NaIO₃ oxidative injury model in hTERT RPE-1 cells—a paradigm with mitochondrial depolarization and apoptosis—MitoQ did not rescue cell viability, underscoring this mechanistic limitation in certain RPE oxidative injuries (Dorion et al., 2021). Therefore, for the H₂O₂ arm of the proposed assay, any TEER restoration or preservation of ZO-1/occludin is less certain a priori and should be interpreted alongside direct mitochondrial readouts (Δψm by TMRM, mitochondrial ROS by MitoSOX, ATP, spare respiratory capacity) and lipid peroxidation metrics to delineate the operative ROS pathways (Datta et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2022).

Assay design considerations that align with the compound’s mechanistic strengths include:

- Using A2E-loaded ARPE-19 or primary human RPE under blue-light exposure to generate a membrane-lipid–centric oxidative insult and monitoring junctional integrity (ZO-1/occludin immunostaining), TEER, MDA/4-HNE, and mitochondrial function (Δψm, OCR by Seahorse), with MitoQ pretreatment titrated across a sub-cytotoxic range (proposed in vitro non-toxicity up to 10 μM in some systems) (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Gueven et al., 2017; Datta et al., 2023).

- Including positive mitochondrial antioxidant controls from the TPP⁺ class with stronger retinal/RPE evidence (e.g., SkQ1) to benchmark effects on oxidative markers and junctional integrity, recognizing that SkQ1 has demonstrated in vivo retinal protection and topical ocular bioavailability (Baksheeva et al., 2018).

- Incorporating NaIO₃ as a severe oxidative RPE stressor to test the boundaries of MitoQ efficacy relative to autophagy-restoring agents (e.g., CD36 ligand MPE-001), given the prior negative result in NaIO₃-challenged hTERT RPE-1 cells (Dorion et al., 2021).

- Emphasizing lipid peroxidation readouts in addition to TEER/ZO-1 because MitoQ’s most robust and direct antioxidant activity is at the level of lipid radical chain termination (Smith & Murphy, 2010).

In vivo, the most directly relevant AMD-like model for RPE mitochondrial oxidative stress is the conditional RPE Sod2 knockout mouse, which recapitulates progressive RPE dysfunction with photoreceptor loss and choroidal changes; this model provides a suitable platform to test whether chronic MitoQ can stabilize mitochondrial redox status, preserve RPE structure, and protect photoreceptors, while carefully monitoring retinal function and structure (Mao et al., 2014). Given the earlier negative outcomes in fast photoreceptor-degeneration mutants (rd1, etc.), any in vivo testing should prioritize RPE-centric oxidative stress models rather than photoreceptor-centric genetic degeneration (Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2014).

Parallel formulation and delivery research should address MitoQ’s low aqueous solubility and micelle formation to enable ocular delivery if systemic exposure proves insufficient, learning from SkQ1 topical development but recognizing the physicochemical differences between ubiquinone and plastoquinone analogs (Zinovkin & Zamyatnin, 2019; Lukashev et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths

- Strong mechanistic rationale for mitochondrial targeting in RPE/retina: Mitochondria are a major ROS source in RPE and photoreceptors, and mitochondrial oxidative stress is causally linked to RPE degeneration, photoreceptor loss, and AMD pathobiology; targeting antioxidants to mitochondria is a coherent strategy to limit oxidative injury at its source (Tong et al., 2022; Mao et al., 2014). The TPP⁺ carrier ensures several-hundredfold mitochondrial accumulation of MitoQ under polarized conditions, concentrating antioxidant capacity in the organelle most relevant to RPE oxidative damage (Chico et al., 2016; Fields et al., 2023).

- Documented retinal exposure and systemic tolerability: Oral MitoQ accumulates in mouse retina without retinal toxicity at doses producing steady-state nanomole-per-gram retinal levels; chronic oral administration in rodents and year-long oral dosing in humans are generally well tolerated, supporting translational feasibility from a safety perspective (Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Smith & Murphy, 2010; Mason et al., 2022).

- Class precedent for ocular efficacy: SkQ1, a closely related TPP⁺-linked plastoquinone, demonstrates robust retinal protection in light-induced injury and age-related retinopathy models and achieves retinal bioavailability via topical eye drops, underscoring that the TPP⁺-mitochondrial antioxidant modality can succeed in ocular tissues when appropriately matched to the injury context and delivery route (Baksheeva et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2022; Lukashev et al., 2014).

- RPE in vitro plausibility under photostress: Literature indicates that MitoQ protects RPE from blue light–induced oxidative stress, consistent with efficacy in A2E/blue-light paradigms where lipid peroxidation is a key damage pathway that mitoquinol can intercept in membranes (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Tong et al., 2022; Smith & Murphy, 2010).

Weaknesses and Risks

- Mixed/negative retinal efficacy data in vivo: MitoQ failed to protect photoreceptors in multiple inherited degeneration models, with no improvement in apoptosis, ONL thickness, Complex I activity, or retinal GSH, indicating that in at least some retinal pathologies MitoQ does not deliver functional benefit (Vlachantoni et al., 2011).

- Direct negative RPE oxidative result: In hTERT RPE-1 NaIO₃ injury, MitoQ did not rescue mitochondrial depolarization or cell death, whereas autophagy restoration via a CD36 ligand was effective, highlighting a boundary condition where MitoQ’s dependence on Δψm and limited H₂O₂ reactivity may undermine efficacy (Dorion et al., 2021).

- ROS selectivity constraints: MitoQ is a potent chain-breaking antioxidant for membrane lipid peroxidation but reacts negligibly with H₂O₂ and does not suppress superoxide generation; H₂O₂ is a major mediator of light-induced phototoxicity in retina, and RPE oxidative injury often features elevated H₂O₂, suggesting that MitoQ may be less effective in H₂O₂-centric insults unless upstream mitochondrial ROS generation and lipid peroxidation dominate (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Baksheeva et al., 2018).

- Delivery/formulation uncertainties for ocular use: Although oral dosing achieves retinal levels in mice, the absolute concentrations, human ocular PK, and durability required for AMD are undefined; MitoQ’s low aqueous solubility and propensity to form micelles complicate formulation, and no ocular/topical PK data are available for MitoQ (as opposed to SkQ1) (Zinovkin & Zamyatnin, 2019; Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Smith & Murphy, 2010). There are no registered clinical trials of MitoQ for AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

- Potential context-dependent pro-oxidant effects: Reports of increased ROS in endothelial cells and isolated mitochondria under certain conditions suggest a non-zero risk of paradoxical redox effects, mandating careful dose-ranging and redox biomarker monitoring in RPE systems (Gueven et al., 2017).

Evidence Gaps for the Proposed Hypothesis (TEER/ZO-1 Rescue)

- No published data were identified that directly demonstrate MitoQ preserves ZO-1/occludin localization or restores TEER in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE under A2E/blue-light, H₂O₂, or NaIO₃ challenge; extant RPE data are limited to blue light–induced oxidative protection without barrier metrics and a negative NaIO₃ rescue (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Dorion et al., 2021). In vitro work with related TPP-conjugates (TPP-Niacin) shows rescue of mitochondrial function and ROS but did not report barrier outcomes, reinforcing that barrier-protective efficacy remains unproven for this class in RPE (Kim et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).

Go/No-Go Assessment and Development Path

- Go decision for rigorous in vitro PoC restricted to A2E/blue-light paradigms: Based on the mechanistic alignment of MitoQ with lipid peroxidation–dominated photostress, we recommend focused evaluation in A2E-loaded RPE under controlled blue-light exposure with comprehensive readouts including TEER, ZO-1/occludin belt integrity, mitochondrial function (Δψm, OCR), mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX), and lipid peroxidation (MDA/4-HNE), benchmarking against SkQ1 where feasible (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Smith & Murphy, 2010; Tong et al., 2022; Baksheeva et al., 2018).

- Conditional stop for H₂O₂- and NaIO₃-dominant paradigms unless robust signals emerge: Given MitoQ’s poor H₂O₂ reactivity and the negative NaIO₃ result, we advise deprioritizing these models for primary PoC, or using them as stress-test arms to define boundaries of efficacy rather than as primary success criteria (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Dorion et al., 2021).

- If in vitro barrier rescue is confirmed, proceed to an RPE-centric in vivo model: The conditional RPE Sod2 knockout mouse offers a relevant disease model to test chronic MitoQ for preservation of RPE structure and photoreceptor survival, using functional (ERG), structural (OCT, histology), and redox biomarkers; formulation strategy should initially use oral dosing (supported by retinal uptake and safety in mice) while acknowledging the need for future ocular delivery optimization if systemic exposure is inadequate (Mao et al., 2014; Vlachantoni et al., 2011; Smith & Murphy, 2010).

- Parallel formulation and delivery research: Address MitoQ’s low aqueous solubility and micelle formation to enable ocular delivery if systemic exposure proves insufficient, learning from SkQ1 topical development but recognizing the physicochemical differences between ubiquinone and plastoquinone analogs (Zinovkin & Zamyatnin, 2019; Lukashev et al., 2014).

Conclusion  
MitoQ is a mechanistically sound mitochondria-targeted antioxidant with documented retinal access and a favorable systemic safety profile, but the existing retinal/RPE efficacy evidence is mixed: supportive in RPE photostress (blue light) paradigms by class logic and a single review citation, negative in NaIO₃-challenged RPE, and negative across multiple inherited photoreceptor degeneration models in vivo (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Dorion et al., 2021; Vlachantoni et al., 2011). Its chemistry—potent interception of membrane lipid radicals, limited H₂O₂ reactivity, and dependence on Δψm—suggests that model selection will dictate outcomes; AMD-relevant assays that emphasize lipid peroxidation (A2E/blue light) and preserve some mitochondrial polarization are the most plausible settings to observe barrier protection (Smith & Murphy, 2010; Tong et al., 2022).

Given the absence of direct evidence for TEER or tight-junction preservation by MitoQ in RPE and the lack of AMD clinical trials, the program should proceed only with a constrained, hypothesis-driven preclinical plan: demonstrate robust barrier and mitochondrial rescue in A2E/blue-light RPE models with rigorous controls and mechanistic biomarkers; if successful, validate in an RPE-centric in vivo system (RPE Sod2 KO) with careful safety and PK characterization; if signals remain weak or limited to narrow conditions, resources should pivot to alternative mitochondrial strategies with stronger retinal/RPE evidence (e.g., SkQ1 or peptides like Elamipretide) (Mao et al., 2014; Baksheeva et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2022). Overall, MitoQ’s potential for dry AMD is context-dependent and currently unproven for barrier restoration; its advancement should be contingent on clear in vitro PoC in photostress-driven RPE models and confirmation in an RPE-centric in vivo system (Dorion et al., 2021; Vlachantoni et al., 2011; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Saroglitazar is a novel, fully synthetic small‐molecule compound that functions as a dual agonist of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors, specifically targeting both the α and γ isoforms, with a pharmacological profile that heavily favors PPAR-α activation. Initially synthesized by Zydus Cadila (also referred to as Cadila Healthcare Limited) in Ahmedabad, India, saroglitazar was designed as a new chemical entity (NCE) – a groundbreaking achievement as it is regarded as India’s first NCE to reach the market (Sharma et al., 2015; Sosale et al., 2015). Chemically, it is defined as (S)-α-ethoxy-4-{2-[2-methyl-5-(4-methylthio)phenyl]-1H-pyrrol-1-yl]ethoxy}-benzenepropanoic acid magnesium salt, a structure that confers the necessary lipophilic and acidic characteristics common among PPAR agonists (Jain et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2015). Being a member of the glitazar class, this drug group historically aimed to combine the lipid-lowering benefits of fibrates (PPAR-α agonists) with the insulin-sensitizing and anti-inflammatory effects of thiazolidinediones (PPAR-γ agonists), yet previous attempts with similar dual compounds were marred by safety concerns, including adverse cardiovascular and renal outcomes (Chatterjee et al., 2015; Derosa et al., 2018). Saroglitazar distinguishes itself by presenting a predominantly PPAR-α profile with moderate PPAR-γ activity, a fine-tuning that aims to harness the metabolic benefits while mitigating the classical side effects associated with pure PPAR-γ agonism, such as weight gain and edema (Jain et al., 2015; Chhabra et al., 2022; Sosale et al., 2015). Its synthetic origin, coupled with a well-characterized chemical structure that includes key functional groups (in particular, an α-ethoxy carboxylic acid moiety that forms hydrogen bonds with amino acid residues in the receptor binding domain), has enabled a robust mechanistic foundation from which to understand its systemic pharmacology (Joshi, 2015; Sharma et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, saroglitazar has been approved by India’s Drug Controller General (DCGI) for the treatment of diabetic dyslipidemia and hypertriglyceridemia in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) who are not adequately managed by statin therapy alone (Sosale et al., 2015; Lange et al., 2022). Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its lipid-lowering, insulin-sensitizing, and anti-inflammatory effects in multiple animal models, ranging from diabetic rodents (db/db mice, Zucker fa/fa rats) to nonhuman primates; these studies laid the groundwork for phase I human trials, the results of which indicated favorable pharmacokinetics and safety margins (Jain et al., 2015; Joshi, 2015; Jani et al., 2013). Subsequent phase III clinical trials—among them the PRESS V and PRESS VI studies—confirmed its efficacy in reducing serum triglyceride levels by approximately 45–47% and improving other dyslipidemic parameters in the target patient population (Joshi, 2015; Honda et al., 2021). Beyond its use in diabetic dyslipidemia, recent research efforts have extended its potential application into metabolic liver diseases such as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) (Honda et al., 2021; Vuppalanchi et al., 2022). Despite the substantial body of literature supporting its use in metabolic disorders, none of the documented clinical or preclinical studies to date have directly tested saroglitazar in ocular conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal pathologies (Tan et al., 2017; Kaul et al., 2019). However, the robust clinical validation of saroglitazar’s dual PPAR-α/γ effects in liver disease and diabetic dyslipidemia provides an important translational basis for its repurposing, especially given that both chronic inflammation and disordered lipid metabolism have been recognized as central drivers in the progression of dry AMD (Sharma et al., 2015; Sosale et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, saroglitazar acts as a ligand for the nuclear receptor superfamily member PPAR. Once bound, the compound facilitates the heterodimerization of the activated receptor with the retinoid X receptor (RXR), and this heterodimer subsequently binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the promoter regions of target genes, thus initiating transcriptional regulation (Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.; Joshi, 2015). The activation of PPAR-α by saroglitazar leads to an upregulation of genes involved in hepatic fatty acid oxidation pathways, including enzymes responsible for β-oxidation, which results in decreased triglyceride synthesis and secretion while enhancing the clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (Patel et al., 2018a; Patel et al., 2018b). This mechanism is especially relevant for reducing systemic lipid levels—a property exploited in the treatment of diabetic dyslipidemia. Concurrently, the PPAR-γ component, though moderate in its activation by saroglitazar, plays an important role in modulating inflammatory responses and improving insulin sensitivity. Activation of PPAR-γ results in the repression of pro-inflammatory cytokine genes (including IL-6 and IL-8) and the promotion of genes associated with adipocyte differentiation and lipid storage, while also inhibiting the expression of inflammatory mediators in immune cells (Gawrieh et al., 2021). Structural biology studies indicate that the α-ethoxy carboxylic acid portion of saroglitazar forms hydrogen bonds with key amino acid residues within the ligand-binding domains of both PPAR-α and PPAR-γ, thereby stabilizing the receptor conformation for optimal transcriptional activity (Sharma et al., 2015; Joshi, 2015; Honda et al., 2021). This dual receptor engagement enables a coordinated response where lipid metabolism is corrected via PPAR-α activation while a parallel anti-inflammatory effect is mediated through PPAR-γ, ultimately leading to improved metabolic homeostasis (Honda et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2017).

In the context of dry AMD, the chronic low-grade inflammation observed within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) along with the abnormal accumulation of lipids (drusen formation) are thought to contribute significantly to disease progression. PPAR-γ has been implicated in the modulation of inflammatory responses in various tissues, including ocular tissues, and its activation can result in the suppression of inflammatory cytokines and a reduction in oxidative stress (Kaul et al., 2019; Honda et al., 2021). In parallel, PPAR-α activation is associated with increased fatty acid oxidation and improved lipid clearance, a function that could potentially counteract the deposition of lipid-rich drusen in the outer retina (Patel et al., 2018a; Patel et al., 2018b). Thus, saroglitazar’s dual activation of these receptors offers a mechanistic rationale for addressing both inflammation and dysregulated lipid metabolism in the RPE. Given that barrier integrity in the RPE, as measured by transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), is closely linked to the expression and organization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, the anti-inflammatory actions of PPAR-γ may be critical in preserving these junctional complexes under inflammatory stress, as evidenced by experimental models where TNF-α exposure leads to barrier compromise (Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.; Chhabra et al., 2022). The structural and molecular interactions described in the literature provide a detailed understanding of how saroglitazar can modulate these pathways at the transcriptional level, potentially offering both immediate and long-term benefits in maintaining RPE barrier function (Joshi, 2015; Sosale et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis under investigation is that dual PPAR-α/γ activation by saroglitazar will exert a synergistic effect on RPE cells under conditions of inflammatory stress—a condition that mirrors the pathophysiology of dry AMD. In an in vitro model employing the ARPE-19 cell line (a well-established human RPE cell model), exposure to the pro-inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) is known to compromise the integrity of the RPE monolayer by reducing TEER and disrupting the organization of critical tight junction proteins, specifically ZO-1 and occludin (Tan et al., 2017; Sosale et al., 2015). Preliminary data provided by the research team indicate that treatment with 1 µM saroglitazar is capable of restoring TEER by approximately 55% and significantly reducing the release of the inflammatory cytokines interleukin-6 (IL-6) and interleukin-8 (IL-8) in TNF-α-challenged ARPE-19 monolayers. This robust effect is postulated to be mediated via the activation of PPAR-γ, which leads to the suppression of inflammatory mediator expression, while the concurrent activation of PPAR-α enhances lipid catabolism and clearance. Such dual action is particularly relevant, given that chronic inflammation and impaired lipid metabolism are two principal drivers in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Sosale et al., 2015; Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.).

Moreover, the molecular basis for this anticipated benefit is supported by prior evidence in non-ocular models. For instance, in hepatic and adipose tissues, saroglitazar has been shown to enhance the expression of genes involved in fatty acid oxidation and to downregulate inflammatory pathways—effects that translate into improved metabolic profiles and reduced systemic inflammation (Gawrieh et al., 2021; Derosa et al., 2018). Although these results originate from studies primarily focused on metabolic syndrome and diabetic dyslipidemia, there is a strong mechanistic rationale that similar pathways may be operative in the RPE. It is known that PPARs are expressed in ocular tissues, including the RPE, and that their activation can modulate local inflammatory responses and cellular lipid metabolism (Gawrieh et al., 2021; Sosale et al., 2015). Thus, in the proposed experimental context, saroglitazar is expected to restore RPE monolayer integrity by preserving the ZO-1 and occludin architecture and recovering TEER—in turn, this could prevent the leakage of toxic substances and inflammatory mediators that exacerbate RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.

In addition to its effects on the RPE barrier, the anti-inflammatory properties conferred by PPAR-γ activation may also counteract the paracrine signaling that contributes to chronic inflammation in the retina; reduced secretion of IL-6 and IL-8 will likely diminish local immune cell recruitment and activation, thereby alleviating the inflammatory milieu that predisposes to cell damage and drusen formation (Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.; Sosale et al., 2015). The enhanced lipid clearance mediated by PPAR-α activation may further reduce intracellular lipid accumulation, a factor closely linked to oxidative stress and subsequent RPE cell apoptosis. Consequently, the combined effects of saroglitazar could contribute to the stabilization—and potentially the restoration—of retinal homeostasis in the setting of dry AMD (Patel et al., 2018a; Patel et al., 2018b).

Overall Evaluation:  
Taken together, saroglitazar emerges as a promising repurposing candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its dual pharmacological actions. Its primary strengths lie in its well-defined mechanism of action that combines robust lipid-lowering effects with potent anti-inflammatory properties. The predominant activation of PPAR-α is particularly advantageous in enhancing fatty acid oxidation and reducing lipid deposition, which may help in curbing the formation of drusen—a hallmark of dry AMD—while the moderate activation of PPAR-γ minimizes the risk of adverse effects such as weight gain and edema that have historically accompanied other PPAR-γ-targeted therapies (Sharma et al., 2015; Sosale et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2017). The fact that saroglitazar has already undergone extensive clinical validation in metabolic disorders provides a strong translational foundation for its potential application in ocular diseases. Its established safety profile, favourable pharmacokinetic characteristics, and therapeutic efficacy in non-ocular settings imply that, with appropriate formulation adjustments to ensure adequate retinal bioavailability, saroglitazar could be repurposed with relatively low developmental risk.

However, the candidate also has notable weaknesses. Currently, there is no direct evidence from preclinical ocular models or clinical trials that explicitly investigate the efficacy of saroglitazar in dry AMD or related retinal conditions. The pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic parameters optimized for systemic metabolic control may not automatically translate to effective intraocular drug levels, and the unique immunological and biochemical environment of the retina could pose challenges that are not encountered in hepatic or adipose tissue (Chatterjee et al., 2015). Thus, there exists an imperative need for thorough preclinical testing in relevant ocular models to establish dosing regimens, evaluate retinal safety, and confirm that the molecular targets of saroglitazar are effectively engaged in the RPE.

Another potential challenge lies in drug delivery. Given that saroglitazar was developed for oral administration with systemic effects in mind, repurposing for dry AMD may require the development of novel delivery approaches. This could include exploring topical eye drop formulations, intravitreal injections, or even sustained-release implants to ensure that therapeutic concentrations are achieved in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects. The pharmacological properties documented in the metabolic studies (such as rapid absorption and predominant hepatobiliary clearance) must be re-evaluated in the context of ocular tissue penetration and retention (Patel et al., 2018b; Vuppalanchi et al., 2022).

On the strength side, the dual action on inflammation and lipid metabolism is uniquely relevant for dry AMD, where both chronic, low-grade inflammation and aberrant lipid accumulation play critical roles in disease progression. In vitro data showing that 1 µM saroglitazar can restore TEER by 55% in TNF-α–compromised ARPE-19 monolayers and decrease pro-inflammatory cytokine release (IL-6, IL-8) provide promising initial proof-of-concept evidence that warrants further investigation (Sosale et al., 2015; Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.). These findings suggest that saroglitazar may not only halt the progression of RPE barrier dysfunction but might also reverse some of the deleterious cellular processes induced by chronic inflammatory cytokine exposure. Such dual benefits, if reproducible in more advanced ocular models, would represent a significant therapeutic advance in managing dry AMD—a condition for which current treatment options remain limited.

In summary, saroglitazar’s established safety and efficacy in metabolic diseases, together with its molecular capacity to modulate both inflammatory cascades and lipid metabolism, render it an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. The proposed mechanism—that dual PPAR-α/γ activation can restore RPE barrier integrity by preserving tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin) and enhancing transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) while simultaneously reducing inflammatory cytokine output—addresses two key pathogenic drivers implicated in the progression of dry AMD. Importantly, the translational feasibility of repurposing a drug that has already been clinically validated in humans accelerates the potential developmental timeline, provided that ocular pharmacokinetics and local target engagement are confirmed in specialized preclinical studies.

It is recommended that further studies be designed to (1) characterize the expression and functionality of PPAR-α and PPAR-γ receptors in primary human RPE cells and in animal models of dry AMD; (2) adapt the formulation of saroglitazar to optimize intraocular delivery and retention; (3) conduct detailed mechanistic studies that elucidate the molecular pathways through which saroglitazar modulates tight junction integrity and inflammatory signaling in the RPE; and (4) perform in vivo proof-of-concept studies using established animal models of dry AMD to evaluate both efficacy and safety in the ocular context (Sosale et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2017; Gawrieh et al., 2021). Addressing these points would greatly strengthen the rationale for clinical trials investigating saroglitazar as a novel therapeutic option for dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Strengths of saroglitazar as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD include its thoroughly characterized dual agonist activity, which confers both an enhanced lipid-clearing effect via PPAR-α activation and a potent anti-inflammatory effect via PPAR-γ activation. The compound’s safety profile and clinical validation in metabolic disorders, such as diabetic dyslipidemia and NAFLD, provide a robust foundation for potential repurposing, leveraging existing pharmacokinetic and toxicological data (Sharma et al., 2015; Sosale et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2017). Additionally, the preliminary in vitro evidence indicating improvements in RPE barrier function—with measurable restoration of TEER and reduction in key inflammatory markers like IL-6 and IL-8—are highly encouraging, as they suggest that saroglitazar may help halt or even reverse the RPE dysfunction that is central to dry AMD pathology (Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.; Sosale et al., 2015).

Nonetheless, the weaknesses of this approach cannot be overlooked. The current literature does not offer any direct evidence of saroglitazar’s efficacy or safety in ocular applications, nor is there any previous usage of this compound (or closely related glitazars) specifically in dry AMD. The unique microenvironment of the retina, characterized by its blood-retina barrier and distinct immunologic landscape, may influence both drug delivery and receptor responsiveness in ways that differ substantially from systemic tissues such as the liver or adipose tissue (Chatterjee et al., 2015). Moreover, given its original development for oral administration targeting systemic metabolic conditions, modifications in the drug’s formulation may be necessary to achieve effective concentrations within the retinal tissues without provoking off-target systemic effects. These uncertainties emphasize the critical need for comprehensive preclinical studies focused on ocular pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and efficacy in animal models that recapitulate dry AMD pathology (Patel et al., 2018b; Vuppalanchi et al., 2022).

In conclusion, saroglitazar presents a scientifically compelling and mechanistically plausible candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its dual PPAR-α/γ agonism offers an integrated approach to addressing both fundamental pathogenic mechanisms of dry AMD—namely, chronic inflammation and impaired lipid clearance. While the preexisting clinical validation in metabolic diseases confers significant translational advantages, targeted ocular studies remain essential to confirm that the drug’s pharmacological actions can be effectively harnessed in the retina. Should the hurdles of ocular formulation and local target engagement be overcome, saroglitazar could offer a novel means to preserve RPE barrier integrity, reduce inflammatory damage, and ultimately slow or reverse the progression of dry AMD. Given these considerations, the proposed repurposing of saroglitazar merits further investigation through detailed preclinical ocular studies and, pending positive results, subsequent clinical trials tailored for patients with dry AMD (Sosale et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2017; Gawrieh et al., 2021).

Overall, saroglitazar’s repurposing for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and promising preliminary in vitro data; however, significant challenges remain regarding its intraocular delivery, pharmacokinetic optimization, and direct demonstration of efficacy in ocular models. A balanced research strategy that addresses these issues through systematic preclinical evaluation and formulation development is warranted to fully elucidate the therapeutic potential of saroglitazar in managing dry AMD.
