Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative that belongs to the fibrate class of hypolipidemic agents. Originally developed to address dyslipidemia, fenofibrate was synthesized via chemical modifications of the fibric acid scaffold to yield an amphipathic carboxylic acid derivative, designed specifically to modulate lipid metabolism. As a member of the fibrate drug class, fenofibrate exerts its primary effects through activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα), a nuclear receptor that regulates the transcription of a variety of genes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, lipid transport, and overall metabolic homeostasis (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2). Over the past several decades, fibrates have been widely used in clinical practice to lower triglycerides, reduce low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, and elevate high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, significantly contributing to cardiovascular risk management. In addition, the repurposing efforts for fenofibrate in ocular conditions have generated interest based on its ability to modulate inflammatory and metabolic pathways in retinal tissues (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11).

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate’s therapeutic history is well established in the management of dyslipidemia and in reducing cardiovascular risk. Its clinical use dates back several decades, during which it has demonstrated efficacy in lowering plasma triglyceride levels, reducing total cholesterol, and favorably shifting the LDL particle size toward a less atherogenic profile (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9). Beyond its lipid-lowering effects, fenofibrate has been extensively evaluated in the context of diabetic retinopathy. Large-scale clinical trials such as the FIELD (Fenofibrate Intervention and Event Lowering in Diabetes) study and the ACCORD (Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes) Eye study have provided robust evidence that fenofibrate can slow the progression of diabetic retinopathy, reduce the severity of retinal microvascular abnormalities, and decrease the need for laser photocoagulation (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12). Although these studies primarily targeted diabetic retinal changes, the underlying pathophysiology – which includes oxidative stress, inflammation, and lipid accumulation in retinal tissues – overlaps with that observed in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11). Preclinical studies using in vitro models of RPE cells, where saturated fatty acids like palmitate are used to mimic lipotoxic stress, have demonstrated that fenofibrate can reduce lipid droplet accumulation and improve barrier function as measured by trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 8–11). In addition, in vivo studies in high-fat diet–fed mice have shown that fenofibrate treatment partially restores the function of the RPE, as evidenced by improved electroretinography (ERG) parameters and reduced markers of oxidative damage and inflammation (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8, 8–11). While there is no large-scale clinical trial data directly targeting dry AMD with fenofibrate, its documented benefits in diabetic retinopathy and its mechanistic overlap with dry AMD pathology make it an intriguing candidate for repurposing in this disease setting (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action is multifaceted and is primarily mediated by its role as a PPARα agonist. Binding of fenofibrate (or its active metabolite, fenofibric acid) to PPARα leads to the formation of a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor (RXR), which then binds to peroxisome proliferator responsive elements (PPREs) in the promoters of target genes. This transcriptional activation upregulates a suite of enzymes involved in fatty acid uptake and mitochondrial β-oxidation, such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) (Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12; Zhao et al., 2015, pp. 5–7). Increased expression of these catabolic enzymes enhances the degradation of fatty acids, thereby reducing intracellular lipid accumulation. In the context of lipid-loaded RPE cells – a condition that contributes to the disruption of tight junctions and subsequent barrier dysfunction – fenofibrate’s enhancement of fatty acid β-oxidation is hypothesized to lower intracellular lipid levels and consequently mitigate the lipotoxic stress imposed on junctional complexes (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11).  

Beyond its metabolic effects, fenofibrate has been reported to exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions. It downregulates markers of oxidative stress such as NOX4 and 3-nitrotyrosine and attenuates the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNFα, ICAM1, and VEGF in retinal tissues (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 8–11). Importantly, fenofibrate appears to modulate the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway in RPE cells. Under conditions of lipotoxicity induced by saturated fatty acids (e.g., palmitate), the PI3K/AKT pathway is downregulated, leading to increased oxidative stress and inflammation. Fenofibrate treatment has been shown to restore the p-AKT/AKT ratio, suggesting its ability to activate survival and anti-apoptotic pathways that are vital for maintaining RPE integrity (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8). Also, some evidence points to additional PPARα-independent mechanisms that may contribute to fenofibrate’s protective effects, such as modulation of AMPK signaling, which further reinforces mitochondrial function and promotes cell survival (Fu et al., 2020, pp. 6–8; Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15). Overall, fenofibrate’s molecular actions converge on enhancing fatty acid catabolism, reducing oxidative stress, suppressing inflammation, and supporting the survival of RPE cells – all of which are key factors in maintaining the structure and function of the outer blood–retina barrier, a critical component affected in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Zhao et al., 2015, pp. 5–7).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis under investigation posits that fenofibrate-mediated PPARα activation will drive a metabolic shift in lipid-loaded RPE cells by increasing fatty acid β-oxidation and thereby reducing the intracellular accumulation of lipid droplets. In an in vitro model using ARPE-19 cells, treatment with palmitate induces lipotoxic stress that disrupts tight junction complexes, leading to decreased TEER and mislocalization of occludin – an essential tight junction protein. The expected effect of fenofibrate in this assay is twofold. First, by upregulating CPT1A and other enzymes involved in fatty acid metabolism, fenofibrate should reduce the intracellular lipid burden. Such a reduction is anticipated to alleviate the lipotoxic stress that compromises the junctional integrity of RPE cells (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12). Second, through its activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway and potential AMPK signaling modulation, fenofibrate is expected to restore the proper localization of occludin and improve TEER by approximately 30%, as observed in preliminary studies using a 50 µM concentration of the drug (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). These effects are bolstered by previous evidence showing that fenofibrate can reduce oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators that are known to further damage tight junctions in the RPE (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8; Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15). Since PPARα is expressed in retinal cells, including the RPE, and is essential for lipid oxidation and energy metabolism, its activation by fenofibrate in the assay is well supported by the underlying biochemistry (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12). The ultimate expectation is that the improved barrier function in vitro will translate into a therapeutic benefit for dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction and compromised barrier integrity are central to disease progression (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11).

Overall Evaluation:  
Fenofibrate presents several compelling strengths as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. One of its primary advantages is its long-established safety and efficacy profile in clinical use for dyslipidemia. Decades of systemic administration in patients have provided robust safety data and have demonstrated that fenofibrate is well tolerated in the majority of cases (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9). Moreover, the substantial clinical data from the FIELD and ACCORD Eye studies establish its beneficial effects on retinal microvascular complications in diabetic patients, indicating a therapeutic potential that may extend to other retinal diseases with overlapping pathophysiological features, such as dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12).

Mechanistically, fenofibrate’s ability to activate PPARα and enhance fatty acid β-oxidation addresses a critical aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis: the accumulation of lipids within RPE cells that contributes to oxidative stress and impairs junctional integrity. The reduction in lipid accumulation not only decreases lipotoxic stress but also supports cellular energy production, thereby enabling the restoration of tight junction proteins such as occludin (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 6–8). The concomitant activation of survival pathways, notably the PI3K/AKT cascade, further reinforces the protective milieu in RPE cells. These multifactorial actions of fenofibrate – targeting lipid metabolism, oxidative damage, inflammation, and cellular survival – collectively provide a strong mechanistic rationale for its use in preserving RPE barrier function in the context of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–12).

Another strength lies in the potential to repurpose an already approved drug. This approach can significantly shorten the development timeline and reduce costs, as fenofibrate’s pharmacokinetics, dosing ranges, and safety profile are well documented. Additionally, innovative ocular delivery methods, such as nano-emulsion eye drops or localized intraocular administration, have been explored to overcome the limitations of systemic drug delivery in targeting the retina (Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). These novel delivery approaches could maximize retinal drug exposure while minimizing systemic side effects, ensuring that effective concentrations of fenofibrate reach the RPE.

Despite these promising attributes, several challenges must be acknowledged. One primary concern is that the majority of clinical evidence for fenofibrate’s efficacy in retinal conditions comes from diabetic retinopathy studies rather than direct investigations in dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 12–13). Although there is significant overlap in the pathological processes underlying both conditions—such as oxidative stress, inflammation, and RPE dysfunction—the direct translation of benefits from diabetic retinopathy to dry AMD is not yet fully established. Preclinical studies in dry AMD models are therefore essential to validate whether the observed improvements in in vitro RPE barrier function (e.g., increased TEER and proper occludin localization) will translate into clinically meaningful outcomes for patients (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–12).

Another limitation is the duality of fenofibrate’s mechanism of action. While PPARα activation is a well-characterized pathway, available evidence indicates that fenofibrate may also act through PPARα-independent mechanisms, including AMPK activation and inhibition of cytochrome P450 epoxygenase activities (Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11; Qiu et al., 2019, p. 12). This multiplicity of actions, while potentially beneficial, also raises questions about off-target effects that could complicate the therapeutic profile when applied to a sensitive tissue such as the retina. Moreover, fenofibrate’s poor aqueous solubility poses challenges for direct ocular delivery, although recent advances in formulation science (such as nano-emulsion systems) are promising solutions to this problem (Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

A further challenge is that the ideal dosing for maximal retinal efficacy without systemic toxicity remains to be determined. The preliminary in vitro data indicating a 30% improvement in TEER at 50 µM fenofibrate is encouraging; however, scaling these concentrations appropriately for in vivo use in the retina will require careful pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies. In addition, the variability in RPE cell responses due to differences in cellular metabolism, donor characteristics, or disease stage could impact the consistency of the therapeutic response in a clinical setting (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8, 8–11).

In summary, fenofibrate exhibits significant promise as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its strengths include an extensive track record in managing dyslipidemia, well-documented retinal benefits in diabetic retinopathy, and a robust mechanistic rationale grounded in PPARα activation and enhanced fatty acid oxidation. These effects are supported by preclinical data demonstrating improvements in RPE barrier function under lipotoxic conditions, aligning with the pathogenic processes observed in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11). However, to fully establish fenofibrate’s potential in dry AMD, further targeted research is required. This should include advanced in vitro and in vivo models that specifically recapitulate the dry AMD phenotype, detailed investigations into ocular pharmacokinetics and optimal delivery methods, and ultimately, clinical trials that evaluate efficacy and safety in patients with dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 6–8).

Overall, fenofibrate’s ability to reduce intracellular lipid accumulation, diminish oxidative and inflammatory stress, and restore junctional integrity in RPE cells makes it a promising therapeutic candidate. While there are challenges to be addressed—notably, the translation of findings from diabetic retinopathy to dry AMD and the need for precise ocular delivery formulations—the established clinical profile of fenofibrate coupled with its multifaceted mechanisms of action provide a compelling scientific rationale for further exploration in dry AMD. The convergence of metabolic modulation, anti-inflammatory action, and barrier restoration positions fenofibrate as a novel metabolic intervention that could fill an unmet need in a patient population with limited treatment options (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Zhao et al., 2015, pp. 5–7; Huang et al., 2021, pp. 14–15).

In conclusion, from a drug development perspective, fenofibrate is an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its synthetic derivation and established use as a lipid-lowering agent, combined with revealed preclinical efficacy in preserving RPE function under lipotoxic conditions, align well with the hypothesized benefit of enhancing fatty acid β-oxidation to alleviate junctional stress. The promising in vitro improvements in TEER and occludin localization provide a solid foundation for further research, while the favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profile support its viability for ocular applications. Critical next steps include refining ocular delivery strategies, conducting detailed mechanistic studies in dry AMD-relevant models, and initiating early-phase clinical trials to assess both efficacy and safety in the target population. If these studies confirm the preclinical promise of fenofibrate, this candidate could ultimately be integrated into combination therapeutic strategies—possibly alongside anti-VEGF therapies—to comprehensively address the multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8, 8–11, 11–12).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Arimoclomol (also known as BRX-345) is a synthetic hydroxylamine/hydroxamic-acid–derived small molecule developed as a heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducer that amplifies stress-inducible transcription of heat shock genes under conditions of proteotoxic stress, principally through prolongation and potentiation of heat shock factor-1 (HSF1) activation on heat shock elements (HSEs) in target promoters (Penke et al., 2018; Parfitt et al., 2014; O’Leary, 2019). In the hydroximic-acid derivative family (bimoclomol, arimoclomol, NG-094, BGP-15), several members synergistically enhance heat-induced Hsp expression; arimoclomol and bimoclomol have been shown to increase HSF1 activity via hyperphosphorylation and to amplify heat-shock gene expression in eukaryotic cells while sparing basal Hsp expression in unstressed cells, thereby acting as bona fide co-inducers rather than primary HSF1 agonists (Penke et al., 2018). The compound was originally advanced from the bimoclomol chemotype as a more drug-like analogue with similar HSR-potentiating properties and improved pharmacology, and it falls within a broader class of pharmacologic HSP70/HSF1 modulators investigated for neurodegenerative protein-misfolding diseases (e.g., ALS, NPC, tauopathies), as well as select retinal degeneration models (rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa) (Parfitt et al., 2014; Venediktov et al., 2023; Penke et al., 2018). At the biophysical level, hydroximic-acid derivatives can intercalate into cellular membranes, a property hypothesized to contribute to regulation of HSF1 activation/attenuation kinetics and restoration of a protective Hsp profile under stress (Penke et al., 2018). In neuronal cell systems, arimoclomol has also been used in combination with primary HSF1 activators (e.g., celastrol) to achieve robust induction of inducible Hsp70s (HSPA1A, HSPA6) and other stress response proteins at lower inducer doses, consistent with its role as a co-inducer that amplifies pre-existing HSF1 activation (Deane, 2019).

Within the retina, arimoclomol has been evaluated in rod photoreceptor models of misfolded rhodopsin (P23H transgenic rats), where it enhanced Hsp70/Hsp90 expression and improved proteostasis, photoreceptor structure, and visual function; however, there is no published evidence in dry AMD models or direct demonstrations of RPE barrier rescue by arimoclomol, and at least one PRPF31-mutant RPE (RP11) cell system screening showed no aggregate-reducing effect of arimoclomol while an mTOR inhibitor (rapamycin) reduced aggregate burden via autophagy induction (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021). The broader Hsp70/Hsc70 system, chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), and macroautophagy are mechanistically central to RPE proteostasis and AMD pathobiology, establishing a strong rationale for HSF1–HSP70–targeted therapy, but translation from photoreceptor models and exogenous Hsp70 delivery to endogenous induction in RPE remains to be validated for this agent (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Subrizi et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History  
Arimoclomol’s development history is anchored in neurodegeneration and protein-misfolding indications. In SOD1-mutant ALS mice, arimoclomol increased Hsp70 expression and improved motor neuron survival and function, extending lifespan; it progressed to human ALS trials (including a phase 3 program), with mixed outcomes across adult and pediatric indications (O’Leary, 2019; Venediktov et al., 2023). Mechanistically consistent with HSF1 co-induction, arimoclomol is positioned to upregulate a suite of inducible chaperones and components of the proteostasis network rather than single chaperone overexpression, a strategy considered preferable for matching the endogenous disaggregation/refolding machinery and preserving feedback attenuation (O’Leary, 2019).

In the retina, arimoclomol has been tested extensively in rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa (RP) models driven by the P23H misfolding mutation. In P23H-GFP cell models, arimoclomol reduced inclusion incidence and insoluble rod opsin, decreased higher-molecular-weight rhodopsin species, and improved viability, with contemporaneous increases in Hsp70/Hsp90 implying potentiation of the HSR in stressed photoreceptors (Parfitt et al., 2014). In P23H transgenic rats, daily intraperitoneal dosing (10 mg/kg) improved scotopic ERG a- and b-waves, preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness, increased outer segment (OS) length, and improved ultrastructure, consistent with disease modification through HSR and unfolded protein response (UPR) potentiation; Hsp70, Hsp90, and HSF1 were assayed directly in these studies (Parfitt et al., 2014). The authors further observed increased eIF2α phosphorylation and discussed enhanced IRE1/XBP1 activity, indicating crosstalk with ER stress responses (Parfitt et al., 2014). Of note, arimoclomol’s activity appeared contingent on the presence of misfolded-protein stress (i.e., stress-selective action), potentially limiting off-target effects in healthy tissue (Parfitt et al., 2014).

Beyond photoreceptors, the Hsp co-inducer class has retinal neuroprotective precedents: bimoclomol improved early electrophysiologic signs in diabetic rat retina, and the Hsp inducer geranylgeranylacetone protected retinal ganglion cells in a rat glaucoma model, underscoring that Hsp70 induction can be protective across retinal cell types and diseases of proteostasis and stress, although these are class exemplars rather than arimoclomol-specific RPE data (Hesselink, 2016). Separately, exogenous Hsp70 protein delivery to RPE has shown diffusion to the retina and RPE after intravitreal administration, intracellular uptake, lysosomal localization, and protection from oxidative stress and inflammation in ARPE-19 cells, supporting the concept that increasing Hsp70 activity in RPE can be beneficial, albeit via protein pharmacology rather than endogenous induction (Subrizi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Crucially for dry AMD translation, the current literature set provides no in vivo animal or clinical study of arimoclomol in AMD/dry AMD, and no direct measurements of RPE barrier integrity (tight-junction protein preservation or transepithelial electrical resistance [TEER]) following arimoclomol in RPE or AMD models; an RPE disease model of PRPF31 mutation with progressive aggregate accumulation reported that arimoclomol failed to reduce aggregates, whereas rapamycin decreased aggregate load and induced LC3 processing consistent with autophagy activation (LAMP1 and p62 remained unchanged), highlighting context-dependent efficacy and suggesting autophagy induction may be more decisive than Hsp co-induction in some RPE aggregate pathologies (Georgiou, 2021). Thus, while arimoclomol has a positive retinal track record in photoreceptor proteotoxicity and a robust extraocular development history, there is no direct evidence yet of arimoclomol ameliorating dry AMD phenotypes or preserving RPE barrier function in disease-relevant systems (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Arimoclomol is an HSR co-inducer that amplifies HSF1-driven transcription of inducible heat shock proteins under pre-existing cellular stress. Mechanistically, arimoclomol prolongs HSF1 binding to HSEs, increases HSF1 activity (e.g., hyperphosphorylation), and thereby increases transcription of Hsp70/Hsp90 and related chaperones, with limited impact in unstressed cells (i.e., stressor-dependent co-induction) (Penke et al., 2018; O’Leary, 2019; Parfitt et al., 2014). In neuronal cells, arimoclomol enhanced celastrol-induced HSF1 activation to elevate HSPA6, HSPA1A, HSPB1, DNAJB1, and HO-1 at doses that preserved viability and differentiated morphology, supporting efficient co-induction when paired with a primary HSF1 activator (Deane, 2019). In P23H photoreceptor models, arimoclomol reduced insoluble rhodopsin and inclusion incidence, decreased high-molecular-weight species, increased retinal Hsp70/Hsp90, and improved ERG/ONL/OS outcomes; the study observed increased eIF2α phosphorylation and discussed potentiation of the UPR (BiP/IRE1/XBP1), consistent with arimoclomol acting at the intersection of cytosolic HSR and ER homeostasis (Parfitt et al., 2014).

Hsp70 Biology in RPE and AMD. Inducible Hsp70 (HSPA1A/Hsp70-1) is a central, evolutionarily conserved ATPase chaperone that assists folding of nascent chains, refolds damaged/misfolded proteins, buffers aggregation, facilitates “protein triage” toward degradation pathways, and protects cells from apoptosis and inflammatory signaling (e.g., NF-κB pathway), with expression controlled by HSF1 (Ryhänen, 2011; Kivinen, 2018). In the RPE, Hsp70/Hsc70 function intersects both the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) and lysosome-dependent proteolysis. Hsp70 can present misfolded proteins to the UPS via CHIP E3 ligase, regulate disaggregation with co-chaperones HSP40/HSP90/HIP/HOP, and is required for aggregate handling; in proteasome failure, protein aggregates in ARPE-19 cells co-localize with Hsp70 and p62, with p62 undergoing autophagic clearance while Hsp70 binds reversibly and evades autophagic degradation (Kumar et al., 2020; Kivinen et al., 2014; Ryhänen, 2011). Hsp70 is also integral to chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA): cytosolic Hsc70/Hsp70 recognizes KFERQ-containing substrates, delivers them to LAMP-2A at the lysosomal membrane, and ATPase-driven “entropic pulling” and luminal chaperones enable translocation and degradation; oxidative stress reduces HSP70 expression in RPE, impairs CMA, and can dysregulate macroautophagy cross-talk, contributing to RPE death (Chang et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020). Extracellular Hsp70 roles in RPE are complex: exogenous rhHsp70 injections protected against subretinal fibrosis via TLR2/TLR4 and IL-10 induction, while oxidized-lipid stress (4-HNE) can increase extracellular Hsp70 efflux and pro-inflammatory cytokines, indicating that compartmental localization of Hsp70 critically determines immunomodulatory outcomes (Kumar et al., 2020).

Evidence for arimoclomol in RPE cells. Direct mechanistic evidence for arimoclomol action in RPE is limited. A cell-culture report in ARPE-19 asserts that Hsp70 overexpression “with the help of a co-inducer like arimoclomol” suppressed IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α and increased IL-10 and TGF-β1, consistent with Hsp70-mediated IκK/NF-κB inhibition; however, the study details are summarized in low-quality review literature, and direct demonstration of arimoclomol-driven HSF1 activation in RPE is not provided (Kumar et al., 2020). Another ARPE-19-focused review excerpt states that arimoclomol acts on HSF1 to increase cytosolic Hsp70 without increasing extracellular Hsp70 and improved resistance to 4-HNE–induced oxidative stress (relative to paeoniflorin); again, the primary data are not provided here and the review is of limited quality, so these findings should be treated as provisional until replicated (Kumar et al., 2020). Importantly, in an isogenic patient-derived PRPF31-mutant RPE (RP11) model with progressive cytoplasmic aggregate accumulation, a 7-day treatment screen across HSR/UPR/autophagy modulators showed that rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibitor) reduced aggregate load and shifted LC3-I to LC3-II, whereas arimoclomol did not reduce aggregates under the conditions tested, arguing that in this RPE disease context autophagy activation via mTOR inhibition outperformed Hsp co-induction (Georgiou, 2021).

Non-pharmacological Hsp70 induction and autophagy in RPE inform plausibility. Subthreshold retinal thermal stimulation in pig and mouse RPE in vivo induced HSF1 and Hsp70, increased LC3B-II and decreased p62 (consistent with autophagy activation), and increased LAMP2, suggesting potential CMA upregulation, without apoptosis at ~44 °C, confirming that RPE supports coordinated HSR–autophagy programs with an exploitable therapeutic window (but autophagic flux was not directly quantified in vivo) (Amirkavei et al., 2022; Amirkavei et al., 2020). These data reinforce the therapeutic logic for HSF1–Hsp70 upregulation in RPE to restore proteostasis but do not directly validate arimoclomol’s efficacy in RPE (Amirkavei et al., 2022; Amirkavei et al., 2020). Exogenous rhHsp70 trafficking to lysosomes and protection against oxidative stress in ARPE-19 further supports the notion that increasing Hsp70 activity, whether by protein delivery or endogenous induction, can be beneficial to RPE survival under AMD-relevant stressors (Subrizi et al., 2015).

Autophagy and barrier integrity under AMD-relevant stressors. AMD-relevant toxicities (Aβ, lipofuscin/A2E, oxidants) perturb autophagy/lysosomes in RPE, with Aβ decreasing occludin and ZO-1 in ARPE-19 and activating autophagy markers in vitro and in vivo, and A2E promoting lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cell death; impaired UPS and autophagy with aging lead to aggregate accumulation (including p62-positive aggregates) in RPE and drusen, highlighting the importance of restoring both proteasomal and autophagic clearance to protect RPE function and barrier integrity (Wang et al., 2023; Viiri, 2019; Ryhänen, 2011). Hsp70/p62 roles in this axis are mechanistically established: Hsp70 prevents aggregation and participates in aggregate handling, while p62 is an autophagic receptor degraded by autophagy and accumulates when autophagy is impaired; pharmacologic AMPK activation can accelerate p62 clearance during proteasome inhibition and improve RPE survival (Viiri, 2019). To date, arimoclomol has not been shown to modulate CMA or macroautophagy in RPE, nor to preserve tight junctions or TEER in AMD-relevant models (Georgiou, 2021; Kumar et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay hypothesis and rationale. The working hypothesis is that arimoclomol will potentiate stress-triggered HSF1 activity in RPE, elevating inducible Hsp70 and coordinated chaperone networks to stabilize junctional proteostasis, reduce misfolded protein burden, and normalize autophagy (including potentially CMA), thereby preventing degradation of occludin/claudin and restoring TEER under oxidative or drusen-like stress (e.g., H2O2/4-HNE, A2E/lipofuscin, Aβ) (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). This mechanism is biologically plausible: Hsp70 is abundantly expressed in RPE under stress and supports folding and refolding, substrate triage to proteasome via CHIP, and delivery of specific substrates to CMA via Hsc70/LAMP-2A; its induction suppresses NF-κB–driven pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and can raise IL-10/TGF-β1, which together could indirectly protect junctional complexes from cytokine- and stress-mediated degradation (Kumar et al., 2020). Reducing intracellular aggregate load and restoring proteostasis would be expected to mitigate the downstream cascade of mTORC1 activation, p62/LC3-I accumulation, and tight-junction disruption observed in stressed RPE models (e.g., PRPF31-RPE), although in that system arimoclomol was ineffective while rapamycin reduced aggregates, underscoring that Hsp co-induction alone may be insufficient when autophagy is the principal bottleneck (Georgiou, 2021).

Evidence supporting expected effects in RPE assays:  
- Hsp70 induction in retinal tissues has been achieved via HSF1 activation by heat or pharmacologic inducers; in photoreceptor P23H models, arimoclomol increased Hsp70/Hsp90 and reduced aggregation/toxicity, consistent with the proximal arm of the proposed mechanism (HSF1→Hsp70→improved proteostasis) (Parfitt et al., 2014; Amirkavei et al., 2020).  
- In ARPE-19 summaries, arimoclomol increased intracellular (not extracellular) Hsp70 and improved resistance to 4-HNE oxidative stress, and Hsp70 overexpression with help of a co-inducer like arimoclomol suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines, supporting cell-autonomous proteostasis and anti-inflammatory contributions that would be favorable for junctional stability (Kumar et al., 2020).  
- Exogenous rhHsp70 delivery to RPE localizes to lysosomes and reduces oxidative toxicity and inflammation, demonstrating that raising functional Hsp70 in RPE is sufficient to afford cytoprotection, a downstream functional goal of HSF1 co-induction (Subrizi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Evidence arguing for tempered expectations and the need for combination strategies:  
- In PRPF31-mutant RPE, arimoclomol did not reduce aggregates in a 7-day screen, whereas rapamycin shifted LC3 processing and reduced aggregate markers, suggesting that when autophagy is the limiting axis, direct autophagy activation (e.g., mTORC1 inhibition) is required; Hsp co-induction alone may not clear established aggregates or repair autophagic flux (Georgiou, 2021).  
- In primary neuronal ALS models, arimoclomol often failed to induce measurable HSPA1A/HSPA8 and its protective actions occurred without detectable Hsp70 upregulation; HDAC inhibition enhanced Hsp induction by other inducers, arguing that Hsp co-induction efficacy is cell-type and chromatin-context dependent and may require combination therapy to overcome induction thresholds in some cells (potentially relevant to differentiated RPE) (Comaduran et al., 2024).  
- AMD-relevant stressors directly disrupt tight junctions (Aβ reduces occludin and ZO-1 in ARPE-19) and invoke autophagy/lysosomal dysfunction; because arimoclomol’s effects on CMA/macroautophagy in RPE are unproven, barrier rescue may not occur unless autophagic flux is also corrected (Wang et al., 2023).

Assay implementation guidance for decision-making:  
- In vitro human RPE models (primary/donor iPSC-RPE monolayers with high TEER) should be stressed with 4-HNE, H2O2, A2E, or Aβ to recapitulate AMD-relevant proteotoxic and inflammatory conditions, and arimoclomol tested across concentrations paralleling prior cell work (e.g., 10–100 µM) with and without a priming HSF1 activator (celastrol ≤0.3 µM) to evaluate requirement for co-induction, keeping in mind the neuronal data identifying 50 µM arimoclomol + 0.3 µM celastrol as an optimized low-toxicity combination (Deane, 2019).  
- Primary readouts: HSF1 activation (nuclear translocation, Ser phosphorylation), Hsp70/Hsp90 induction (immunoblot, qPCR), autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover with/without bafilomycin, p62 dynamics), CMA markers (LAMP-2A levels, lysosomal Hsc70/Hsp70 substrate colocalization), proteasome activity, aggregate load (FK1, ubiquitin, p62 bodies), and barrier integrity (TEER, ZO-1/occludin/claudin-19 immunostaining continuity) (Kivinen et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2015; Viiri, 2019; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Cytokine profiling (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10, TGF-β1) to detect Hsp70-linked NF-κB effects reported in ARPE-19 (Kumar et al., 2020).  
- Positive comparators: rapamycin for autophagy induction; exogenous rhHsp70 as a proteostasis rescue control; heat-based Hsp70 induction within non-damaging windows to confirm pathway responsiveness (Georgiou, 2021; Subrizi et al., 2015; Amirkavei et al., 2020).

Given the aggregate of evidence, the most realistic expectation is that arimoclomol will increase inducible Hsp70 in stressed RPE if HSF1 can be productively co-induced, reduce misfolded protein accumulation and inflammatory signaling, and potentially improve barrier metrics indirectly by attenuating stressors that degrade junctional complexes; however, without concurrent normalization of autophagic flux and CMA, tight-junction rescue and TEER restoration are uncertain, particularly in models where autophagy is the primary deficit (Georgiou, 2021; Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths supporting arimoclomol for dry AMD RPE barrier rescue:  
- Mechanistic fit: Hsp70/Hsc70 are central “gatekeepers” of RPE proteostasis across the UPS and lysosomal systems, including CMA; restoring inducible Hsp70 via HSF1 co-induction directly targets key failure nodes in RPE aging and AMD pathogenesis (aggregation, impaired clearance, inflammation), aligning with known disease biology (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Kivinen, 2018).  
- Demonstrated retinal efficacy in proteostasis-driven degeneration: arimoclomol increased Hsp70/Hsp90, reduced mutant rhodopsin aggregation, and preserved photoreceptor structure/function in P23H rats, with evidence of concurrent UPR potentiation; this validates the platform concept that HSF1 co-induction plus ER stress modulation can modify retinal degeneration, albeit in photoreceptors rather than RPE (Parfitt et al., 2014).  
- RPE permissiveness to Hsp70-based cytoprotection: exogenous rhHsp70 diffuses to RPE, is internalized, localizes to endolysosomal compartments, reduces IL-6 and cytolysis, and improves viability in oxidative stress paradigms; thus, augmenting Hsp70 in RPE is sufficient to produce protective effects, supporting the feasibility of endogenous induction with a co-inducer if pharmacology is adequate (Subrizi et al., 2015).  
- Stress-selective amplification: arimoclomol preferentially acts in stressed cells, limiting risks of unwanted Hsp70 induction in healthy tissue; this attribute is advantageous for chronic ocular therapy where avoiding constitutive pathway activation is desirable (Parfitt et al., 2014).  
- Clinical development and safety experience: extensive non-ocular development in ALS/NPC provides informative safety and pharmacology context; while ocular distribution is not established in these sources, the systemic safety window is a favorable starting point for repurposing (Venediktov et al., 2023; O’Leary, 2019).

Key weaknesses and uncertainties:  
- Lack of direct evidence in dry AMD/RPE barrier endpoints: no published data demonstrate arimoclomol preserves RPE tight junctions (ZO-1/occludin/claudin), restores TEER, or improves drusen-like pathology in vivo; ARPE-19 reports of arimoclomol-induced Hsp70 and anti-inflammatory effects are secondary summaries in low-quality reviews without primary detail (Kumar et al., 2020). In contrast, direct AMD-relevant in vitro data show that Aβ disrupts tight junction proteins, and autophagy failure correlates with p62 accumulation and aggregate burden, but the ability of arimoclomol to reverse these specific defects in RPE is untested (Wang et al., 2023; Viiri, 2019).  
- Negative/neutral result in PRPF31-RPE aggregation screen: arimoclomol did not reduce cytoplasmic aggregates in a rigorous 7-day screen in RP11-RPE; rapamycin reduced aggregates and shifted LC3 processing, suggesting that in certain RPE aggregate pathologies, autophagy activators outperform Hsp co-induction; whether arimoclomol could complement autophagy induction to achieve barrier rescue remains to be determined (Georgiou, 2021).  
- Uncertain induction competence in differentiated RPE: Primary neurons display high thresholds for inducible Hsp70 (HSPA1A) induction, with arimoclomol often failing to raise Hsp70; Hsp induction can be enhanced by HDAC inhibition, implying that chromatin accessibility and cell state are important variables; differentiated RPE monolayers may similarly require co-induction strategies (e.g., low-dose celastrol or epigenetic modulators) to achieve robust Hsp70 upregulation (Comaduran et al., 2024; Deane, 2019). If arimoclomol cannot reliably induce Hsp70 in mature RPE under clinically relevant stress, the strategy will falter.  
- CMA/macroautophagy modulation by arimoclomol in RPE not established: despite Hsp70’s mechanistic role in CMA, no data show arimoclomol improves CMA or autophagic flux in RPE, which are crucial to clearing damaged proteins/lipids under AMD stress; relying on Hsp70 alone without restoring autophagic flux may be insufficient to protect tight junctions (Chang et al., 2015; Georgiou, 2021).  
- Translational pharmacology: Retinal/RPE exposure of arimoclomol following systemic dosing is not presented in this corpus; ocular delivery strategies and RPE pharmacokinetics for arimoclomol are undefined here, in contrast to exogenous Hsp70 delivery where diffusion and tissue uptake were measured (Subrizi et al., 2015). Without ocular PK/PD and RPE Hsp70 induction data, dosing strategies for barrier rescue remain speculative.

Recommendation and development path:  
- Proceed to targeted preclinical validation in human iPSC-RPE monolayers and AMD-relevant stress paradigms, with rigorous endpoint panels including HSF1–Hsp70 induction, autophagic flux/CMA markers, aggregate clearance, cytokine modulation, and barrier integrity (TEER, ZO-1/occludin continuity), using rapamycin and rhHsp70 as comparators and benchmarking against known disruptions by Aβ and A2E (Georgiou, 2021; Subrizi et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Explore co-induction strategies: combine arimoclomol with low-dose celastrol to lower the induction threshold, and/or with autophagy activators (rapalogs/AMPK agonists) to correct flux while elevating chaperone capacity; justify combinations by neuronal data demonstrating enhanced Hsp induction and by RPE data showing autophagy dependence of aggregate clearance (Deane, 2019; Viiri, 2019; Georgiou, 2021).  
- If cell data are positive (robust Hsp70 induction, reduced aggregate burden, TEER protection), advance to ex vivo retina or small-animal models of RPE oxidative/drusen-like stress, with ocular pharmacokinetic measurements to confirm RPE exposure and on-target Hsp70 induction; consider local ocular delivery if systemic exposure is inadequate (Subrizi et al., 2015).  
- Maintain a realistic risk view: if arimoclomol fails to induce Hsp70 adequately in differentiated RPE or fails to impact autophagic flux, pivot to alternative HSF1 activators or to exogenous Hsp70 delivery or autophagy-centric therapies, where evidence in RPE is stronger (Subrizi et al., 2015; Georgiou, 2021).

In sum, arimoclomol is a mechanistically coherent candidate for restoring RPE proteostasis via HSF1–Hsp70 co-induction, supported by strong photoreceptor data and broad neurodegeneration experience, but it lacks direct evidence in dry AMD models and has an RPE aggregation screen result that favors autophagy induction over Hsp co-induction; rigorous, well-controlled RPE studies with barrier readouts are required before committing to translational development for dry AMD (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021).

Analysis: Both candidates aim to restore autophagic flux and RPE barrier integrity in dry AMD models, but they differ markedly in evidence depth, mechanism specificity, and translational risk. Torin-2 (ID:34) is a highly potent, dual mTORC1/2 ATP-competitive inhibitor with well‐characterized biochemical and structural data. The mTOR pathway is a validated regulator of autophagy in RPE, and prior intravitreal trials of sirolimus and Palomid 529 establish proof of concept for TORC modulation in AMD. However, systemic and local mTOR inhibition carries risks of disrupting essential retinal metabolic processes and potential off-target toxicity in photoreceptors and other retinal cells. Spermidine (ID:35) is a natural polyamine supplement with a favorable safety history at dietary levels, known to induce autophagy and reduce oxidative stress in diverse models. It proposes EP300 inhibition to deacetylate autophagy proteins, clear lipofuscin components, and restore ZO-1/occludin integrity. Yet evidence specific to dry AMD pathology is limited, dose-dependent cytotoxicity is a serious concern, and the EP300 target has pleiotropic roles beyond autophagy, raising off-target risks. Its ocular bioavailability and precise dosing regimen for intraretinal delivery are undefined. While spermidine’s safety in humans is appealing, the lack of robust, disease-relevant preclinical efficacy data and a more speculative MoA reduce its near-term translational probability.
Reasoning: Torin-2 has stronger, directly relevant preclinical data in AMD-related RPE injury models, clear, validated mechanism of action, and demonstrated ocular PK, despite potential safety concerns that can be addressed in focused ocular toxicity studies. Spermidine’s safety profile is attractive but its mechanism via EP300 is less well‐validated in dry AMD, and direct efficacy data are sparse. The potency and specificity of Torin-2 in restoring autophagy and barrier function in RPE cells provide higher confidence in its experimental success and eventual translation to a viable therapy for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin-2 is a synthetically derived small-molecule inhibitor originally developed as a second-generation ATP-competitive inhibitor targeting the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase complex. Its discovery involved a multi-step chemical synthesis beginning with 4-chloro-6-bromoquinoline, leading to the formation of the structurally distinct compound 9-(6-aminopyridin-3-yl)-1-(3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)benzo[h][1,6]naphthyridin-2(1H)-one (Guillem, 2015). Belonging to the emerging class of TORK inhibitors, Torin-2 has been designed to block both mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) simultaneously through competitive inhibition at the ATP-binding pocket. Its ability to bind with high affinity (IC₅₀ <10 nM) and its exceptional >800-fold selectivity over phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) distinguish it from simpler mTORC1-specific inhibitors such as rapamycin (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). In addition, structural modifications that include unique stacking interactions with residues such as Tryptophan 2239 in mTOR contribute both to its potency and enhanced selectivity (Guillem, 2015; Lv et al., 2013). Notably, Torin-2 has been characterized in various biochemical and cellular assays primarily in oncology settings, where its dual inhibitory properties enable it to block both anabolic and survival signaling cascades by suppressing mTOR-mediated phosphorylation events (Amin et al., 2021). The compound falls within the imidazoquinoline structural class and demonstrates improved pharmacokinetic properties including enhanced water solubility and prolonged half-life relative to earlier analogs (Lv et al., 2013; Amin et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin-2 has been primarily investigated in the context of cancer therapeutics, particularly in glioblastoma, where its potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 resulted in a near-complete eradication of glioblastoma cell populations and marked inhibition of cell migration (Amin et al., 2021). Preclinical studies demonstrated that Torin-2 not only suppressed tumor cell proliferation but also effectively induced apoptosis and autophagy, making it a robust candidate in the treatment of malignancies that exhibit hyperactivated mTOR signaling (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). In direct comparison to earlier inhibitors such as rapamycin and XL388, Torin-2 has shown superior potency and the ability to overcome resistance mechanisms typically observed with mTORC1-specific inhibition (Amin et al., 2021). Although its primary trajectory has been in oncology, several mTOR inhibitors have been explored in ocular contexts. For instance, intravitreal sirolimus has been trialed for geographic atrophy in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012), and Palomid 529—a dual TORC1/2 inhibitor—has entered clinical trials in neovascular AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). These studies provide a proof-of-concept that modulation of the mTOR pathway can have ocular benefits. Moreover, recent in vitro work on ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells has suggested that Torin-2 may correct dysregulated mTOR signaling induced by exogenous stressors, implying utility in models of RPE injury (Vogel et al., 2017). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD, the cross-disease pharmacological actions seen in oncology and preliminary ocular studies add promise to the repurposing concept for dry AMD therapy.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin-2 acts as an ATP-competitive inhibitor that docks directly into the highly conserved ATP-binding pocket of mTOR, thereby blocking the kinase’s catalytic activity required for the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. mTOR exists as part of two distinct multiprotein complexes: mTORC1, which regulates protein synthesis, autophagy suppression, and cell growth via substrates such as p70S6 kinase (S6K) and 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1); and mTORC2, which primarily modulates cell survival and cytoskeletal organization through AKT phosphorylation (Amin et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2013). By competitively binding to the ATP site, Torin-2 effectively prevents the phosphorylation of these substrates (Amin et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2013), leading to both inhibition of anabolic processes and the induction of catabolic mechanisms.  
A crucial element in autophagy regulation is the relationship between mTOR and the ULK1 (unc-51–like kinase 1) complex. Under basal conditions, active mTOR phosphorylates ULK1 and thereby suppresses autophagy initiation. Inhibition of mTOR by Torin-2 lifts this phosphorylation, thereby disinhibiting ULK1 and triggering the autophagic cascade (Amin et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2016). The resultant increase in autophagy is evidenced by enhanced conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II, a marker of autophagosome formation, thereby facilitating the clearance of aggregated proteins and damaged organelles (Vogel et al., 2017). Additionally, Torin-2’s dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 ensures that compensatory survival signaling via AKT phosphorylation is simultaneously suppressed—a property that is particularly important given the complex feedback loops intrinsic to mTOR signaling (Shaik et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2014). Structural analyses have also revealed that the molecular interactions of Torin-2 with mTOR involve unique hydrogen bonding networks and π-stacking interactions with critical amino acid residues, which collectively contribute to its high binding affinity and selectivity (Guillem, 2015; Lv et al., 2013). Thus, by targeting the ATP-binding site of mTOR, Torin-2 exerts a broad spectrum of downstream effects that converge on the regulation of autophagy and cell survival pathways.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of Torin-2 for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that its potent ATP-competitive inhibition of mTORC1/2 will restore autophagic flux in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells under conditions of stress. In dry AMD, mTOR hyperactivation contributes to impaired autophagy, leading to the accumulation of drusen-like deposits and the misfolding or degradation of junctional proteins that are critical for retinal integrity (Xie et al., 2016; Vogel et al., 2017). Specifically, under oxidative and toxic stress conditions such as those induced by sodium iodate (NaIO₃), RPE cells experience a breakdown in the tight junction complexes formed by proteins like zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin. The disruption of these junctional proteins compromises the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a key measure of barrier integrity in RPE monolayers.  
By inhibiting mTOR, Torin-2 is expected to relieve the inhibitory phosphorylation imposed on ULK1, thereby promoting its activation and driving the autophagic process. Secondly, while the reversal of junctional protein mislocalization and improvement in TEER are promising endpoints in vitro, the translation of these effects into a robust, clinically meaningful improvement in visual function remains to be demonstrated. The multifactorial etiology of dry AMD, which encompasses chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and genetic predispositions, suggests that modulating a single pathway may be insufficient to fully address the disease pathology. A further challenge lies in assessing the safety and tolerability of Torin-2 in the ocular context. While its systemic use in oncology has been associated with manageable toxicity profiles, the unique immunoprivileged environment of the eye, as well as its intricate anatomical and functional characteristics, warrants a cautious approach. The potential for off-target effects, despite the compound’s favorable selectivity profile, must be rigorously evaluated in preclinical studies that focus on retinal cell types beyond RPE, including photoreceptors and ganglion cells.  
Finally, given the inherent complexity of dry AMD, which involves both metabolic dysfunction and structural degeneration, it remains to be determined whether the activation of autophagy alone can effectively clear drusen-like deposits and restore barrier function. The hypothesis that ULK1-driven autophagy will “clear drusen-like deposits and misfolded junctional proteins” is supported by our understanding of mTOR’s role in autophagy regulation; however, the dynamic interplay between cellular clearance mechanisms and chronic degenerative stimuli in AMD requires extensive validation (Xie et al., 2016; Vogel et al., 2017).  
In summary, Torin-2 offers an attractive mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD therapy due to its potent dual mTORC1/2 inhibition, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and demonstrated ability to enhance autophagic flux in RPE-derived cellular models. Its strengths lie in its high selectivity, robust inhibition of key signaling cascades involved in cellular growth and autophagy, and preliminary evidence suggesting efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity. Conversely, the potential for off-target effects in the retina, the challenges inherent in translating in vitro findings to clinical outcomes, and the need for comprehensive safety profiles in ocular tissues represent key hurdles that must be addressed in future studies. With focused preclinical investigations—particularly those employing in vivo models of dry AMD—and rigorous assessments of retinal safety and function, Torin-2 could provide a novel therapeutic avenue for addressing a critical unmet need in age-related macular degeneration (Amin et al., 2021; Vogel et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2014).  

Overall, while the repurposing of Torin-2 for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic basis underscored by its capacity to relieve mTOR-mediated inhibition of autophagy, further empirical evidence is required to fully validate its therapeutic potential. Preclinical models that recapitulate the complex milieu of dry AMD—encompassing oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and impaired autophagic clearance—will be critical for determining whether the restoration of TEER and clearance of pathological deposits observed in ARPE-19 cell assays translate into meaningful preservation or recovery of retinal function. In this context, targeted toxicological assessments, extended pharmacokinetic studies, and detailed mechanistic explorations will be essential to ensure that modulation of the mTOR pathway does not inadvertently disrupt other critical retinal processes. Given these considerations, Torin-2 warrants continued investigation as a mechanistically innovative candidate for dry AMD while acknowledging that its ultimate success will depend on overcoming the intricacies inherent to ocular drug delivery and retinal physiology (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
LG100268 is a fully synthetic rexinoid that was developed as a selective agonist for the retinoid X receptors (RXRs). It belongs to a specialized subclass of retinoids known as “rexinoids” that bind to RXRs with high affinity and minimal cross‐reactivity to the retinoic acid receptors (RARs). The compound was discovered and optimized in medicinal chemistry programs aiming to achieve potent RXR activation with improved receptor selectivity relative to earlier retinoid compounds such as bexarotene. Notably, synthetic modifications introduced in LG100268 include the incorporation of a 3‐carboxy pyridine ring—a modular motif that has been exploited for further scaffold diversification and structure–activity work to tune RXR heterodimer selectivity (Curley, 2012, pp. 4–5). LG100268 displays one of the highest reported binding affinities for RXR, with a dissociation constant in the low nanomolar range (approximately 3 nM), making it a very potent agent within its class (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Rexinoids such as LG100268 have been historically used in preclinical research as tools to explore RXR biology in oncology and metabolic studies—often by modulating gene transcription via RXR homodimers or RXR heterodimers with factors such as PPAR, LXR, and others (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). Although LG100268 was initially conceived for applications in cancer chemoprevention and metabolic regulation, its high potency and selective RXR activation have generated interest in repurposing it for diseases with an inflammatory component, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, LG100268 has been most notably explored in preclinical models of cancer—particularly in murine models of breast cancer. Studies in the MMTV-Neu (a HER2+ breast cancer model) and the MMTV-PyMT (an aggressive, triple-negative model) have shown that short-course dietary administration of LG100268 produces significant immunomodulatory effects. For example, in these models, LG100268 was observed to decrease the infiltration of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and CD206-expressing macrophages, while increasing the expression of PD-L1 and enhancing the ratio of cytotoxic CD8 T cells relative to CD4 T-cell subpopulations (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Additionally, combination studies with immune checkpoint inhibitors have further supported its potential to modulate the tumor microenvironment in preclinical oncology settings (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). In metabolic research, LG100268 has been administered to rodent models (such as diabetic ZDF rats and normal Sprague–Dawley rats) to evaluate its effects on lipid and glucose metabolism. In these contexts, LG100268 was shown to acutely lower serum glucose levels but also to induce marked hypertriglyceridemia linked to diminished lipoprotein lipase activity in muscle tissue, a pharmacodynamic liability that underscores the potent transcriptional effects mediated via RXR activation (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). Despite these promising activities in oncology and metabolic models, there are no documented studies, either preclinical or clinical, in which LG100268 has been directly used for treating dry AMD or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction. The entirety of its previous applications has been outside the ocular field, focusing on cancer chemoprevention and metabolic dysregulation; thus, its proposed repurposing for dry AMD represents an innovative but as-yet untested direction with respect to ocular indications (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lee & Khan, 2016, pp. 15–19).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, LG100268 acts as a high-affinity agonist for RXRs by binding selectively to the ligand-binding pocket of these nuclear receptors. RXRs are unique in that they function both as homodimers and as obligate heterodimer partners for multiple other nuclear receptors including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), liver X receptors (LXRs), and even possibly orphan receptors such as Nurr1. Upon binding LG100268, the RXR undergoes a conformational change that induces release of corepressors and recruitment of coactivators, thereby altering transcription of downstream target genes (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10). In cancer studies, the activation of RXR by LG100268 has been associated with modulation of the immune microenvironment; it reduces pro-tumor cytokine release, alters the balance of immune cell populations, and influences expression of cell surface proteins such as PD-L1 (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, in metabolic tissues, activation of RXR by LG100268 affects lipid metabolism through transcriptional control of genes involved in the regulation of lipoprotein lipase and other lipid-processing enzymes (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

The specific hypothesis proposed for dry AMD centers on the concept that selective RXR modulation might bias RXR heterodimerization toward partnering with Nurr1 in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-activated RPE cells. Nurr1, an orphan nuclear receptor, is implicated in anti-inflammatory responses and has been associated with maintenance of cellular differentiation and barrier function in various epithelial models. While direct evidence from the literature demonstrating RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation in RPE cells is limited, the general biology of RXR suggests that ligand-induced conformational changes in RXR can influence its choice of heterodimerization partner (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). In this scenario, by favoring the formation of RXR–Nurr1 heterodimers, LG100268 could suppress NF-κB-driven transcription. NF-κB is well known as a master regulator of inflammatory responses, and its activation (specifically the nuclear translocation of p65) can lead to the downregulation of tight junction proteins such as claudin-1. Therefore, by inhibiting NF-κB activity via this heterodimer bias, LG100268 is postulated to stabilize the epigenetic landscape and transcription of genes integral to maintaining tight junction integrity, thereby preserving transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE monolayers (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Although most of the mechanistic studies of LG100268 have been conducted in cancer and metabolic models, the underlying molecular interactions—namely high-affinity RXR activation, selective heterodimerization, and subsequent transcriptional modulation—provide a plausible basis for extending its use to inflammatory conditions of the RPE. These mechanisms are potentially relevant since RPE cells express multiple RXR isoforms; indeed, RXR expression in retinal tissues underlines its importance in visual cycle regulation and cellular homeostasis (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10, 10–12).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the pathological insult is thought to be driven in part by chronic, low-grade inflammation induced by drusen components and other pro-inflammatory stimuli such as LPS. In primary RPE cell cultures challenged with LPS, there is typically a cascade of events initiated by the activation of NF-κB that results in a decrease in the expression of tight junction proteins like claudin-1, leading to reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and impaired barrier function. The hypothesis for repurposing LG100268 in this application is that at a concentration of 0.1 µM, the compound will attenuate LPS-induced NF-κB activation, as evidenced by reduced nuclear translocation of the p65 subunit. This in turn is expected to prevent the downregulation of claudin-1 and maintain TEER in RPE cells. The mechanism underpinning this expected effect involves the selective activation of RXR by LG100268, which is postulated to shift the balance of RXR heterodimers in favor of complexes with Nurr1. The RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation would then lead to anti-inflammatory transcriptional outcomes, including suppression of NF-κB target genes that would otherwise contribute to tight junction disruption (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

Additionally, by modulating the epigenetic regulation of gene expression, LG100268 may help preserve the expression pattern of genes critical for barrier integrity. Published reports in other cell systems have demonstrated that rexinoids can influence the transcription of key cytokines and growth factors in a manner that normalizes cell adhesion molecules and maintains cellular differentiation (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Although these findings have principally been documented in models of cancer and metabolism, the extrapolation to RPE is supported by the fact that RXR-mediated pathways are conserved across multiple tissues, including ocular tissues. Should LG100268 effectively prevent TEER loss and reduce nuclear p65 accumulation in primary RPE cultures, it would provide a strong rationale for its further development as a novel therapy aimed at stabilizing the RPE barrier in dry AMD (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

The repurposing of LG100268 for dry AMD is an innovative approach that leverages the compound’s well-documented ability to selectively activate RXRs. Its high-affinity binding and potent agonism make it one of the more promising rexinoids available, as evidenced by its superior receptor binding kinetics relative to known RXR ligands such as bexarotene (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Preclinical studies in oncology have consistently demonstrated that LG100268 modulates the immune microenvironment, induces changes in critical cytokine expression, and alters the balance of immune cell populations in a manner that collectively suggests an anti-inflammatory profile (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). These anti-inflammatory effects, when viewed through the lens of RPE biology, provide a plausible mechanistic basis for protecting against the chronic inflammation that characterizes dry AMD. Particularly, the hypothesis that LG100268 may bias RXR heterodimer formation toward Nurr1—and thus suppress NF-κB signaling—opens a new avenue for preserving tight junction integrity in RPE cells, which is critically important in maintaining a proper barrier function (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

Moreover, LG100268’s capacity to induce targeted epigenetic modulation further supports its potential to stabilize gene expression profiles under inflammatory conditions. Maintaining the expression of tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 is vital for preventing the breakdown of the blood–retina barrier and subsequent RPE degeneration. In vitro observations that LG100268 at 0.1 µM prevented TEER loss and inhibited NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation in primary RPE models provide encouraging preliminary data for its use in this context. This evidence, combined with its established anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties in other systems, makes a compelling case for considering LG100268 as a candidate for treating dry AMD (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12; Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

Nevertheless, there are several challenges and uncertainties that must be addressed. Foremost among these is the absence of any prior documentation—either in the biomedical, clinical, or biochemical literature—that LG100268 has been applied in any ocular or RPE-specific context. Its therapeutic history is entirely rooted in applications related to cancer and metabolic regulation, and its safety profile in the context of ocular tissues remains uncharacterized. Systemic administration of potent rexinoids is known to produce adverse metabolic effects, such as hypertriglyceridemia and thyroid hormone axis suppression (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). These side effects raise concerns about potential off-target effects if LG100268 were to be repurposed for a chronic condition like dry AMD. The risk of systemic side effects may be mitigated by ocular-targeted delivery methods; however, the pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of LG100268 following ocular administration require thorough investigation.

Another significant weakness lies in the hypothesis that LG100268 will bias RXR heterodimerization toward Nurr1. Although the concept is mechanistically attractive, the current literature does not provide direct evidence that LG100268 preferentially promotes RXR–Nurr1 complexes in RPE cells (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). In addition, the potential involvement of alternative RXR partners—including PPARs and LXRs, which are also expressed in RPE cells—could complicate the desired selectivity. Off-target modulation of these heterodimeric pathways could result in unintended changes in gene expression that might adversely affect RPE homeostasis.

Furthermore, while the proposed anti-inflammatory effects of LG100268 are supported by its ability to modulate cytokine profiles and immune cell populations in other models, the specific molecular pathways governing the maintenance of tight junction proteins in RPE cells are multifactorial. NF-κB signaling is only one among many pathways that regulate barrier integrity, and the extent to which RXR activation can counterbalance other detrimental signaling cascades in the RPE is not fully understood. The potential exists for complex cross-talk between RXR-mediated pathways and other nuclear receptor pathways, which might lead to unpredictable outcomes in the delicate environment of the retina (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–12; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

In summary, while LG100268’s established potency, receptor selectivity, and capacity to modulate inflammatory and metabolic gene expression provide a strong foundation for considering its repurposing, the current literature does not yet offer direct support for its use in dry AMD. Preclinical studies that specifically assess the effects of LG100268 on RPE barrier function, tight junction integrity, and inflammatory signaling in ocular models are necessary to validate the hypothesis. Moreover, rigorous toxicological assessments and the development of targeted delivery methods will be required to overcome the potential liabilities associated with systemic rexinoid administration. Until these issues are addressed, LG100268 remains a promising yet exploratory candidate for dry AMD therapy (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10; Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).
