Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate generated from the glucosinolate glucoraphanin by the β-thioglucosidase myrosinase, which is abundant in cruciferous vegetables (notably broccoli sprouts). Its electrophilic –N=C=S moiety underlies covalent reactivity with nucleophilic cysteines on sensor proteins, most prominently Keap1, and thereby triggers a broad antioxidant and cytoprotective transcriptional response controlled by Nrf2 (NFE2L2) via antioxidant response elements (AREs) in gene promoters (phase-2 enzymes, redox systems, and detoxification pathways) (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). In retinal and epithelial contexts, SFN has been repeatedly characterized as an “indirect antioxidant” that elevates glutathione (GSH) and induces ARE-dependent enzymes such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1/HMOX1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and thioredoxin (Trx1), among others (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Tanito et al., 2005; Liu & Yan, 2018). In human RPE-derived cell models, SFN increased GSH and induced NQO1 and GST, consistent with canonical ARE program activation (Zhou et al., 2006). In vivo ocular models show SFN attenuates retinal light damage and improves functional outcomes, further anchoring its relevance to oxidative injury in the outer retina and RPE (Tanito et al., 2005; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Within its class, SFN is a prototypical dietary electrophile that activates Nrf2 signaling; this class has been broadly studied for chemoprevention and cytoprotection across organs. In ocular tissues, SFN has been shown to protect RPE and photoreceptors from diverse oxidative and phototoxic insults, often in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Yang et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025). Beyond Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α cross-talk, PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ stress-response nodes, and autophagy/lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs (TFEB/TFE3), all of which intersect with oxidative, inflammatory, and proteostasis stress pathways in RPE biology (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025).

Practical development considerations include bioavailability and delivery. Human studies and reviews indicate that the bioactive isothiocyanate is formed from glucoraphanin in a process heavily dependent on myrosinase (plant or microbiota), with documented systemic exposure and biomarker modulation in clinical settings; however, SFN’s oral bioavailability is limited by solubility, first-pass metabolism, and short plasma half-life, posing translational challenges for ocular exposure through blood–ocular barriers (Zhang et al., 2024). Preclinical delivery strategies such as nanoparticle and albumin carrier systems have been proposed to overcome ocular delivery constraints (Zhang et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
SFN and related Nrf2 activators have a long history as cytoprotective agents in preclinical models spanning oncology prevention, vascular and metabolic protection, and neuroprotection. In humans, SFN or broccoli sprout preparations have been administered in controlled trials with documented pharmacodynamic biomarker changes and well-characterized disposition and metabolism; crossover and dose-response studies highlight interconversion with related isothiocyanates (erucin) and underscore the importance of active myrosinase for consistent systemic exposure (Zhang et al., 2024; Qin, 2007). A pilot study detected SFN metabolites in human breast tissue after a single oral broccoli sprout dose, demonstrating tissue penetration to an epithelial compartment and supporting oral bioavailability to peripheral tissues (Qin, 2007). Although multiple clinical contexts are covered in these translational reviews and trials, there are no reported clinical trials of SFN specifically targeting dry AMD or RPE degeneration in the provided material (Zhang et al., 2024).

In ocular systems, the compound’s therapeutic history is robust at the preclinical level. In cultured human RPE, SFN protects against photooxidative injury (A2E/blue light) and chemical oxidants, increases GSH, and induces phase-2 enzymes including NQO1 and GST (Zhou et al., 2006). Thus, while “marker restoration” has been reported for ZO-1 and claudin-4 under TGF-β stress, quantitative barrier function restoration has not yet been demonstrated within the provided sources (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary mechanism—Keap1 cysteine targeting and Nrf2 activation: SFN’s electrophilic isothiocyanate group reacts with redox-sensitive cysteines on Keap1 (notably Cys151), disrupting the Cul3–Keap1 E3 ligase complex and stabilizing Nrf2, which accumulates and translocates to the nucleus. There, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences to upregulate a broad enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant and detoxification program (e.g., NQO1, HO-1, GSTs, GCLM, Trx1, SRXN1), increasing cellular reductive capacity (GSH pools, thiol buffering) and restoring redox homeostasis under oxidative stress (Chang et al., 2020; Ziaei et al., 2013; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). In RPE models, SFN does not consistently increase Nrf2 transcription but promotes nuclear translocation and DNA-binding activity, consistent with post-translational stabilization and activation; ARE target induction follows (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). In ARPE-19, SFN preconditioning increases NQO1 mRNA/activity, boosts cellular GSH, and increases GST activity; microarray and validation data add induction of SRXN1, GCLM, and Trx1 with concurrent Txnip downregulation, aligning with amplified reductive and detoxification capacity (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Under t-BHP stress, SFN increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, elevates NQO1, GR, and GPx1 transcripts, and drives HO-1, NQO1, and GR protein induction (with partial discordance between GPx1 mRNA and protein), while reducing proinflammatory ICAM-1 and MCP-1 (Chang et al., 2020).

Nrf2-dependent ocular efficacy: In vivo, SFN protection from retinal ischemia–reperfusion requires HO-1, as HO-1 inhibition reverses neuroprotection (Pan et al., 2014). In a model of RPE oxidative stress in middle-aged mice, SFN restores cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, underscoring that Nrf2 is the mechanistic driver in that age-relevant retinal context (Falcão et al., 2025).

Nrf2-independent and auxiliary mechanisms: RPE protection is not exclusively Nrf2-dependent. SFN has been shown to promote mitochondrial fusion and reduce Drp1-mediated fission, conferring anti-apoptotic benefit even in CRISPR/Cas9 Nrf2-depleted RPE cells (RPE-1), indicating a parallel mitochondrial protective program (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). SFN also engages the PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ axis: SFN or its metabolites can blunt damage-induced PARylation via direct PARP1 interactions, alleviating SIRT1 inhibition, promoting autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis, and decreasing inflammation in RPE models (Wang & Tang, 2022). In blue light–exposed RPE, SFN activates the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 axis, upregulates HO-1 and thioredoxin-1, blocks NF-κB nuclear translocation, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, and enhances autophagy, all contributing to cytoprotection; Nrf2 inhibition abrogates SFN’s protective effect in this system (Yang et al., 2021). SFN can also activate lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs that mitigate oxidative stress; KEAP1–NRF2 cross-talk with TFEB/TFE3 and macroautophagy has been documented, offering a mechanistic link between Nrf2 activation and proteostasis/autophagy enhancement relevant to RPE degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025).

Anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic effects: Across RPE models, SFN suppresses proinflammatory mediators and pathways (e.g., reduces ICAM-1 and MCP-1; inhibits NF-κB activation), and in TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19 reduces VEGF secretion, which is relevant to para-inflammatory remodeling in AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024). These effects likely contribute to preservation of junctional homeostasis by dampening cytokine-driven disruption.

Cell-type and context dependence: SFN response varies by cell type, stressor, and age-dependent pathway integrity. In some models, HO-1 mRNA is not induced even when protein rises, and under reduced Nrf2 function (as may occur in aged RPE), SFN efficacy can be limited, indicating a dependence on intact Nrf2 signaling and potential post-transcriptional regulation (Chang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Dosing and context also matter: low micromolar SFN protects RPE under oxidative stress, whereas very high concentrations can be deleterious in vitro (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Evidence for barrier-relevant endpoints: The provided sources do not present RPE TEER or FITC-dextran permeability data for SFN, and do not demonstrate claudin-1 induction in RPE (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024). One in vitro ARPE-19 TGF-β model reports that SFN (alone and with vitamin D) restores expression of ZO-1 and claudin-4 suppressed by TGF-β, reduces ROS and VEGF, and decreases proinflammatory cytokines; however, functional permeability or TEER measures were not included, and claudin-1 was not assessed (Bergandi et al., 2024). Therefore, SFN’s capacity to restore RPE barrier function remains mechanistically plausible—through redox normalization, suppression of inflammatory junctional disruption, and potential transcriptional effects on junctional proteins—but is not directly proven by barrier-function assays in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Assay context and rationale: The proposed assays—RPE monolayers subjected to A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ oxidative injury—interrogate oxidative stress pathways central to dry AMD pathophysiology and RPE barrier integrity. A2E/blue light models replicate lipofuscin-photosensitized oxidative injury; NaIO₃ models RPE oxidative cytotoxicity. In both settings, ROS accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, cytokine induction, and downstream tight-junction disruption degrade barrier integrity. The expectation is that SFN will activate Nrf2, increase reductive and detoxifying capacity (GSH, NQO1, HO-1, Trx1, GST), suppress NF-κB–driven inflammation, stabilize mitochondrial function, and secondarily preserve or restore tight-junction protein expression and continuity, resulting in improved TEER and reduced macromolecular flux (FITC-dextran) across the RPE monolayer.

Support for oxidative injury protection in RPE: In A2E/blue light–injured ARPE-19 monolayers, SFN preconditioning increases cell survival, elevates GSH, and induces NQO1 and GST—outcomes mechanistically consistent with improved tolerance to phototoxic oxidative stress (Zhou et al., 2006). In RPE challenged by chemical oxidants (t-BHP, H₂O₂), SFN reduces ROS, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, and induces NQO1, HO-1 (protein), GR, and GPx1 transcripts while suppressing ICAM-1 and MCP-1, thereby addressing both oxidative and inflammatory drivers of junctional disruption (Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013).

Support for HO-1/Nrf2 and auxiliary pathways: Under blue-light exposure, SFN activates Nrf2 and HO-1 in RPE with evidence of mechanistic necessity (Nrf2 inhibitor blocks protection), promotes autophagy (LC3BII and p62), and suppresses NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation—all changes that favor barrier preservation by limiting stress signaling and enhancing cellular cleanup mechanisms (Yang et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and RPE oxidative-stress mouse models, SFN-mediated rescue of retinal function depends on Nrf2 and HO-1, supporting the expected relevance of these axes in RPE-derived stress contexts (Pan et al., 2014; Falcão et al., 2025).

Evidence for junctional protein rescue: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, a recent report shows SFN (particularly with vitamin D) restores ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression suppressed by TGF-β, reduces IL-6/IL-8, reduces VEGF, and normalizes respiratory gene overexpression; this supports the expectation that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven loss of epithelial integrity markers (Bergandi et al., 2024). However, the provided material does not report TEER or FITC-dextran for SFN in RPE, and no data are provided for claudin-1 induction or ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity in oxidative (A2E/NaIO₃) models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Thus, while SFN is expected to improve TEER and reduce FITC-dextran flux in A2E or NaIO₃ assays through Nrf2-driven antioxidant enhancement and suppression of inflammatory/junctional injury, this is an unproven extrapolation that requires direct measurement in the proposed models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).

Target expression in RPE: All principal molecular targets are expressed in human RPE. Nrf2 activation and nuclear translocation occur in SFN-treated RPE-19/ARPE-19, with demonstrated induction of NQO1, HO-1 (protein in some contexts), thioredoxin-1, GCLM, and GST, and suppression of Txnip, ICAM-1, and MCP-1, anchoring the feasibility of modulating these axes in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2006). HO-1 induction in RPE is clearly shown under blue-light stress; in vivo retinal protection requires HO-1, reinforcing target relevance to oxidative retinal injury (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014).

Assay caveats: The provided literature does not contain RPE TEER or macromolecular flux data for SFN, nor does it document claudin-1 induction in RPE. Therefore, while SFN is expected to preserve barrier function, success criteria must include de novo demonstration of TEER rescue, FITC-dextran flux reduction, and ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity under A2E or NaIO₃ stress; these are critical data gaps to address in the proposed work (Zhang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic foundation in RPE and retina: SFN is a well-validated Nrf2 activator that increases GSH and induces multiple ARE-dependent genes (NQO1, GSTs, Trx1, GCLM; HO-1 in several ocular contexts) in RPE and retinal models, with reproducible protection against oxidative and phototoxic injury (A2E/blue light; H₂O₂/t-BHP) and anti-inflammatory activity (reduced ICAM-1, MCP-1, NF-κB signaling) (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage, improves ERG outcomes, rescues cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, and protects against ischemia–reperfusion via HO-1—clear evidence that the compound engages relevant biology and can deliver functional benefit in the retina (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2014).  
- Multiple converging protective axes: Beyond KEAP1–Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling, suppresses PARP1 overactivation to preserve NAD+/SIRT1, promotes autophagy/lysosome programs (TFEB/TFE3 linkage), and modulates mitochondrial dynamics (promotes fusion; reduces Drp1-mediated fission) even when Nrf2 is compromised. This polymechanistic profile is advantageous in RPE, where oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy, and inflammation co-drive degeneration (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2021; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).  
- Preliminary evidence for epithelial integrity marker restoration: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, SFN (especially with vitamin D) restored ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression and reduced VEGF, providing the first reported signal that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven epithelial marker loss in an RPE model (albeit without functional barrier assays) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Translational plausibility and human experience: SFN is orally administrable, with documented human systemic exposure and biomarker modulation; myrosinase co-administration enhances bioavailability from glucoraphanin. Although not yet tested clinically in dry AMD, SFN has a favorable translational narrative as a nutraceutical-derived Nrf2 activator with a safety and PD data trail in other indications (Zhang et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and gaps  
- No direct RPE barrier-function data: Across the provided literature there are no TEER or FITC-dextran permeability results for SFN in RPE monolayers, and no quantified immunofluorescence continuity data for ZO-1 or claudin-1 under oxidative stress. The sole report of “restored markers” addresses ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression after TGF-β, not barrier function or claudin-1 (Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024). The proposal’s assertion of TEER rescue and FITC-dextran reduction remains speculative pending direct measurement in A2E or NaIO₃ models (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Uncertain regulation of tight junction gene set: The provided RPE datasets document induction of canonical Nrf2 targets (NQO1, HO-1 in some contexts, Trx1, GCLM, GSTs), but do not demonstrate SFN induction of claudin-1 in RPE. Without evidence that SFN directly upregulates claudin-1 or stabilizes its junctional localization in RPE, the hypothesis of “junction-supporting gene induction” should be reframed as “junction-preserving via redox and anti-inflammatory mechanisms” until proven otherwise (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Delivery and exposure to the RPE: SFN’s solubility, short half-life, and first-pass metabolism limit systemic exposure; blood–ocular barriers further constrain retinal delivery. Several in vivo retinal studies used intraperitoneal dosing, and one report found i.p. more effective than oral for light-damage protection, emphasizing the need to optimize delivery for ocular targets. Nanocarriers and formulation strategies are promising but remain preclinical (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Dependence on Nrf2 competence and context: In models with impaired Nrf2 (potentially mirroring aged RPE), SFN efficacy is reduced; mechanisms such as mitochondrial fusion may provide partial rescue, but translational effect sizes could be diminished in elderly patients with Nrf2 decline. Additionally, gene-level responses show discordances (e.g., HO-1 mRNA vs protein), indicating context- and post-transcriptional control that complicate predictable pharmacodynamics (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity: Some cited studies are from lower-quality journals; while the core mechanistic findings are corroborated by higher-quality work (e.g., IOVS, Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology, PLoS ONE), the barrier-marker restoration report requires independent replication with functional readouts and in primary human RPE to solidify translational credibility (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Bergandi et al., 2024).

Decision implications and next steps  
Given the robust Nrf2/ARE activation, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory efficacy in RPE/retina, and the breadth of auxiliary protective mechanisms, SFN remains a mechanistically precise candidate for RPE oxidative injury relevant to dry AMD. However, the core claim of “barrier restoration” is currently supported only by marker-expression rescue (ZO-1 and claudin-4) in an inflamed ARPE-19 model without functional permeability data, and there is no evidence for claudin-1 induction or barrier rescue in A2E or NaIO₃ models in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). To de-risk the program and validate the hypothesis, the following experiments are mandatory:  
- TEER and FITC-dextran assays in differentiated human RPE (primary or iPSC-RPE) under A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ insult, with SFN dose–response and timing; include positive controls for barrier rescue (e.g., dexamethasone) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Quantitative junctional immunofluorescence (ZO-1, claudin-1, claudin-4, occludin) with continuity analysis; test whether SFN normalizes localization and expression under oxidative/cytokine stress (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Nrf2 pathway necessity tests (ML385, Nrf2 siRNA) and HO-1 inhibition (ZnPP) to define mechanism-of-action in barrier rescue; given HO-1’s necessity in vivo, confirm whether HO-1 contributes to barrier endpoints in RPE (Pan et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2021).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics and autophagy readouts (Drp1, Mfn2, LC3BII/p62) to quantify auxiliary pathways that may mediate barrier preservation when Nrf2 is compromised (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021).  
- PK/PD bridging: quantify SFN (and metabolites) in plasma and ocular tissues after oral vs i.p. dosing in rodents; evaluate delivery systems (e.g., albumin nanocarriers) for RPE exposure; incorporate myrosinase co-administration for oral strategies; relate exposures to effective in vitro EC₅₀s for barrier rescue (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Aged and Nrf2-impaired models: evaluate efficacy in aged RPE or Nrf2-hypomorphic contexts to assess translational robustness (Zhang et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

If TEER and permeability rescue are demonstrated with mechanistic attribution to Nrf2/HO-1 and/or auxiliary pathways, and if ocular PK can be solved to achieve efficacious exposures, SFN would merit progression to in vivo dry AMD–relevant models (e.g., subretinal NaIO₃, chronic photo-oxidative stress) with structural (OCT) and functional (ERG) endpoints, plus RPE barrier imaging, before considering a human proof-of-concept study.

In sum, the totality of evidence strongly supports SFN for oxidative and inflammatory protection of RPE and retina with multiple convergent mechanisms and translational plausibility. The critical missing element is direct demonstration that these effects translate into bona fide RPE barrier restoration (TEER/permeability) under AMD-relevant oxidative stress, and a practical path to deliver sufficient drug to the RPE in humans. Addressing these gaps should be the focus of immediate preclinical validation (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ML218 is a synthetic small‐molecule calcium channel inhibitor originally developed as an antagonist targeting T‐type CaV3 channels. It was discovered in efforts to design selective modulators of low‐voltage‐activated calcium channels and is commercially available (Tocris 5056). Its chemical structure – featuring a 3,5‐dichlorobenzamide moiety attached to an azabicyclic fragment – places it in the class of benzamide-derived T‐type channel blockers. The compound was designed to interact with hydrophobic fenestration sites in voltage‐gated calcium channels, and its development emerged from scaffold‐hopping strategies derived from earlier hits in high‐throughput calcium flux assays. ML218 thus belongs to a family of investigational agents that have been primarily used as pharmacological tools to dissect T‐type channel function in neuronal systems. Previous studies have focused on its ability to inhibit CaV3 channels in central nervous system models, including experiments in cell lines and primary neurons where it modulated firing patterns and synaptic excitability (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). In addition to its intended activity on CaV3 channels, detailed analyses have revealed that ML218 also exhibits significant cross‐activity with CaV1.4 channels by adopting an alternative binding mode that involves the III‐IV fenestration—an observation that distinguishes it from classical dihydropyridines (Sun et al., 2025). This dual binding behavior highlights both the promise and the challenge of using ML218 as a selective tool in complex tissues where multiple calcium channel subtypes coexist. Overall, ML218 is a promising lead compound representing the synthetic, small‐molecule approach to targeting voltage‐dependent calcium channels, with a structure–activity relationship that suggests potential repurposing for non‐neuronal applications such as retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier stabilization (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History:  
ML218 has been primarily explored within experimental models predominantly focused on the central nervous system. Several studies have employed ML218 as a pharmacological probe to inhibit T‐type calcium currents in neuronal populations. For example, in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease, ML218 demonstrated robust inhibition of T-type currents in subthalamic nucleus (STN) neurons, leading to marked alterations in burst firing patterns (Xiang et al., 2011; Manzar et al., 2025). Electrophysiological investigations using whole‐cell patch clamp techniques in HEK293 cells transfected with CaV3.2 channels have shown that ML218 can achieve potent block, with reported IC₅₀ values ranging from approximately 24 nM (in one report) to 150–310 nM in different assay settings (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). These preclinical studies validated ML218’s mechanism of action within neural substrates and its potential as a centrally active agent. In parallel, investigations in non‐neuronal cells have emerged. In particular, ML218 has been applied to studies involving human embryonic stem cell‐derived retinal pigment epithelium (hESC‐RPE) where it was used at a concentration of 5 μM to elucidate the functionality of voltage‐gated calcium channels expressed in these cells—primarily focusing on assays of phagocytosis and VEGF secretion (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). Although these studies did not specifically examine barrier function parameters, they established that RPE cells express functional T‐type calcium channels and that pharmacological modulation with ML218 could alter cellular processes relevant to retinal physiology. Notably, there is no recorded or clinical history of ML218 being employed to treat dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or related ocular diseases; its usage to date has centered on neurological models and in vitro assays. Consequently, repurposing ML218 for dry AMD would represent a novel application, extending its utilization from central nervous system studies to ocular tissue. The concept of drug repurposing in ocular diseases has been gaining traction in recent years due to the overlapping roles of calcium signaling in diverse tissues, and ML218’s history in rigorously characterizing calcium channel pharmacology makes it a candidate for further exploration in RPE models (Xiang et al., 2011; Korkka et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
ML218 functions primarily by blocking T‐type calcium channels, with an emphasis on CaV3.2 subtypes. The compound’s mechanism involves its entry into the transmembrane fenestrations of the channel complex, where it interrupts the normal ion‐conducting pathway. Detailed structural studies have revealed that in CaV3 channels, ML218 docks within the II‐III fenestration; in this binding mode, the phenyl head group of the molecule extends into the hydrophobic channel region while its aliphatic tail lies within the central pore, thereby imposing a state‐dependent block (Sun et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024). This interaction presumably stabilizes the channel in a closed state, reducing low‐voltage‐activated Ca²⁺ influx into the cell. Notably, ML218’s binding is not entirely exclusive to CaV3 channels, as its molecular conformation adapts in CaV1.4 channels. In these channels, non‐conserved residues preclude the canonical II‐III fenestration binding; instead, ML218 binds at a distinct site in the III‐IV fenestration that overlaps with the dihydropyridine (DHP) binding pocket. Mutagenesis studies have confirmed the importance of this alternate binding mode by demonstrating substantial changes in inhibitory potency upon modification of key residues such as T1007 (Sun et al., 2025). In electrophysiological assays carried out in HEK293 cells, ML218 has been shown to be highly potent against CaV3.2 channels (with reported IC₅₀ values as low as 24 nM in certain studies) and to display over 80-fold selectivity over CaV1.4 channels, although its cross‐reactivity remains a consideration at higher concentrations (Sun et al., 2025). The molecular basis for its selectivity lies in the differential organization of channel domains between CaV3 and CaV1 families, with ML218’s binding being modulated by specific residues located in the channel pore and fenestration regions. From a biochemical standpoint, the blockade of CaV3.2 channels results in a decreased calcium influx during membrane depolarizations, which is critical for controlling intracellular calcium levels. In tissues such as the RPE, where calcium signaling plays a pivotal role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and barrier integrity, aberrant Ca²⁺ influx can activate calcium‐dependent proteases such as calpains. Calpains, once activated, can cleave junctional proteins including zonula occludens protein 1 (ZO-1) and occludin, leading to compromised barrier integrity. Thus, by selectively inhibiting CaV3.2‐mediated calcium entry, ML218 is hypothesized to prevent calpain activation and subsequent disruption of tight junctions in RPE cells—a mechanism that has been indirectly supported by studies showing that inhibitors of T-type channels reduce cellular excitability and junctional leak in alternative epithelial models (Sun et al., 2025). Furthermore, the compound’s dual action—including a modest agonist effect at specific concentrations—adds complexity to its pharmacological profile; however, in the context of RPE barrier function, the primary desired effect would be its antagonist action that limits pathological calcium entry under oxidative or inflammatory stress. The state‐dependence of ML218’s block (i.e., preferential inhibition when channels are in an open or inactivated state) may further enhance its capacity to target pathological calcium influx while sparing normal physiological signaling to some extent, although this property will require careful titration in a diseased state (Sun et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
The working hypothesis for repurposing ML218 in dry AMD is that its inhibition of CaV3.2 channels in retinal pigment epithelium will reduce pathological intracellular calcium accumulation under conditions of oxidative and inflammatory stress. Elevated Ca²⁺ levels in RPE cells are known to activate calpain, a calcium‐dependent protease that mediates the proteolytic cleavage of critical junctional proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin. Disruption of these proteins leads to a compromised RPE barrier, as reflected in reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased paracellular permeability (measured by FITC-dextran flux assays). By blocking the CaV3.2 channels, ML218 is expected to limit this pathological Ca²⁺ influx and thereby prevent calpain activation, preserving the integrity of the ZO-1/occludin belt in RPE cells (Sun et al., 2025). This preservation of junctional complexes should translate into restored TEER and reduced permeability of the RPE monolayer in in vitro models simulating oxidative or inflammatory injury that mimic conditions encountered in dry AMD. Moreover, patch-clamp electrophysiology and Fluo-4 calcium imaging assays in RPE cells are proposed as means of confirming target engagement and quantifying the extent of CaV3.2 current inhibition by ML218 (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). It is anticipated that effective blockade of pathological calcium signaling will also reduce downstream events associated with dry AMD pathophysiology, such as aberrant vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) secretion, which contributes to the progression of atrophic changes in the retina. Although previous studies using ML218 in hESC-RPE have focused more on phagocytosis and secretory functions rather than barrier integrity per se, the presence of functional T-type channels identified in these cells (with CaV3.2 localized, for instance, to the basolateral domain) supports the rationale that modulation of these channels will have a direct impact on barrier properties (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating ML218 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current literature. One significant strength of ML218 is its well‐documented and robust activity in inhibiting T‐type calcium channels, particularly CaV3.2, as demonstrated by comprehensive electrophysiological studies in both neuronal and heterologous systems (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). This potent inhibition forms a logical mechanistic basis for targeting pathological calcium influx in RPE cells, where calcium overload and subsequent activation of proteases like calpain are implicated in junctional protein degradation and barrier dysfunction. Furthermore, the detailed structural insights into ML218’s binding—its differential interactions in CaV3 and CaV1 channels—provide a strong foundation for understanding its pharmacodynamic activity. The ability of ML218 to modulate calcium signaling with state‐dependent block enhances its therapeutic promise by potentially allowing it to target pathological overactivity while sparing baseline physiological function (Sun et al., 2025).  

On the other hand, several potential weaknesses must be considered. The literature reveals that ML218 is not exclusively selective for CaV3.2 channels; it exhibits cross‐reactivity with CaV1.4 channels, albeit at lower potency (with reported IC₅₀ values for CaV1.4 in the micromolar range compared to nanomolar ranges for CaV3.2) (Sun et al., 2025). Additionally, the dual binding mode of ML218—while advantageous for providing mechanistic insight—raises the possibility that subtle differences in channel conformations within RPE cells (compared to neurons) could influence its selectivity and efficacy, thereby complicating dose optimization for ocular applications.  

Despite these challenges, the conceptual framework for repurposing ML218 in dry AMD has several attractive features. The targeting of T‐type calcium channels to mitigate calpain activation and to preserve tight junction protein integrity represents a novel therapeutic approach that departs from traditional anti‐inflammatory or anti‐angiogenic strategies. In dry AMD, where chronic, low‐grade oxidative and inflammatory stress contribute to RPE dysfunction and barrier breakdown, a compound like ML218 could theoretically reduce intracellular calcium overload and, consequently, the cascade of events leading to junctional degradation. In summary, ML218 emerges as an intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its potent T-type channel inhibitory activity, its well‐characterized mechanism at the molecular level, and the theoretical basis linking Ca²⁺ dysregulation to RPE barrier dysfunction. However, the current body of literature does not provide direct evidence in RPE models under conditions that mimic dry AMD pathology, such as oxidative or inflammatory injury. Moreover, the compound’s off‐target activity on CaV1.4 channels and the variability in reported potencies across studies pose significant challenges that will require thorough in vitro and eventually in vivo validation. Future investigations should prioritize comprehensive electrophysiological and imaging studies in RPE cells, specifically measuring TEER, FITC‐dextran flux, and tight junction protein localization following exposure to oxidative stress, to determine whether ML218 can indeed restore barrier integrity as hypothesized. Dose‐ranging studies and careful evaluation of potential off‐target effects will also be critical to establishing a safe and effective therapeutic profile for ocular application.  

Overall, while ML218 holds promise as a tool compound with the potential for repurposing in dry AMD, its advancement into this new therapeutic area will depend on addressing key knowledge gaps through rigorous experimental validation. This includes confirming its selective inhibition of CaV3.2 channels in RPE cells, establishing the correlation between calcium influx blockade and tight junction preservation, and ensuring that its pharmacological behavior in RPE is consistent with the requirements for stabilizing the RPE barrier under pathological conditions. Therefore, although the mechanistic rationale is compelling, additional targeted preclinical studies are required before ML218 can be confidently moved forward as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011; Korkka et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
H-1152 Dihydrochloride is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor discovered and developed as part of the class of ATP‐competitive inhibitors targeting Rho‐associated coiled‐coil kinase (ROCK). It is formulated as a dihydrochloride salt (Tocris 2061) and has been characterized for its exceptional potency against ROCK isoforms, with reported IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range (0.003 µM for ROCK1 and 0.014 µM for ROCK2). As an ATP-competitive type I kinase inhibitor, it possesses a chemical structure that enables it to fit into the highly conserved ATP-binding cavity of ROCK and thereby prevents phosphorylation of downstream targets. This class of compounds has historically been used to explore the roles of ROCK in cytoskeletal dynamics, cell contractility, and migration, and has been applied in various preclinical models of ocular disorders such as glaucoma and corneal endothelial injury (Iancu et al., 2021; Meekins et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Although H-1152 itself has not been clinically approved, its pharmacologic profile as a ROCK inhibitor has been extensively studied in preclinical ocular models. Multiple studies have employed H-1152 in experiments that assessed its effects on corneal endothelial cell migration, proliferation, and wound healing. For instance, in in vitro assays using porcine corneal endothelial cells, H-1152 significantly enhanced cell migration and proliferation compared with control treatments and with other inhibitors like Y-27632. In vivo topical application in rabbit corneal surgical wound models demonstrated accelerated wound closure and resolution of corneal edema without significant toxic effects. These findings underscore its potential utility as a topical therapeutic agent in ocular applications. Moreover, the general class of ROCK inhibitors has been clinically exploited—ripasudil, for example, has been approved for the treatment of glaucoma in Japan, and intravitreal fasudil has been explored for refractory diabetic macular oedema—establishing a safe precedent for ocular delivery of ROCK-targeting molecules. However, while ROCK inhibitors have been investigated in retinal and choroidal vascular pathologies and in conditions marked by barrier dysfunction (such as diabetic macular oedema), there is currently no direct record of H-1152 having been used specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or for RPE-specific pathologies in published clinical or preclinical studies (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, H-1152 acts by competitively inhibiting the kinase activity of both ROCK1 and ROCK2. By binding to the ATP-binding site of the kinase domain, H-1152 prevents the phosphorylation of downstream substrates such as myosin light chain (MLC) and LIM kinases, which in turn results in the reduced phosphorylation of cofilin. This cascade of events inhibits actomyosin contractility and results in the disassembly—or at least, a significant reduction—of actin stress fibers. In cellular contexts, this biochemical action translates into the disruption of stress-fiber–driven cellular contraction and a modulation of both cell–matrix and cell–cell adhesion complexes. In ocular applications, particularly within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), such cytoskeletal reorganization is hypothesized to stabilize junctional complexes by normalizing the localization and organization of critical tight-junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and occludin. Studies in related ocular cell types (e.g., corneal endothelial cells) have documented that ROCK inhibitors induce a rapid collapse of actin stress fibers and result in a transient loss but subsequent restoration of tight-junction architecture over time. Furthermore, ROCK signaling is implicated in mediating the cellular responses to oxidative stress and in promoting VEGF-induced permeability. In models of VEGF stimulation, ROCK inhibition has been associated with a reduction in paracellular leak by preserving tight-junction integrity. Therefore, by potently inhibiting ROCK1/2, H-1152 is proposed to prevent the stress-fiber–mediated disruption of cell–cell junctions and to restore transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE cells subjected to chronic oxidative insult – a mechanism particularly relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology (Meekins et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its mechanism of action and experimental precedent in other ocular models, it is expected that H-1152 will exert a protective effect on RPE cells under conditions of chronic oxidative stress as seen in dry AMD. In vitro, in an ARPE-19 or primary RPE cell model, chronic exposure to low levels of H₂O₂ typically results in a decrease in TEER, disorganization of tight junction proteins (including ZO-1 and occludin), and the formation of abnormal F-actin stress fibers. Treatment with H-1152 in the range of 0.1–1 µM is hypothesized to partially or even substantially reverse these deleterious changes. Specifically, by inhibiting ROCK activity, H-1152 is expected to reduce the formation of stress fibers, thereby reversing the disruption of cell junctions and restoring a more normal distribution of ZO-1 and occludin at the plasma membrane. This should in turn lead to an improvement in TEER – with potential recovery to up to 60% of baseline levels in injured cells – as well as diminish the regulation of VEGF-driven paracellular leak. In addition, pharmacokinetic studies in rabbit models have demonstrated that subconjunctival dosing can achieve ocular RPE/choroid concentrations on the order of ~0.2 µM, which falls within the effective in vitro concentration range. Thus, the expected translational effect is that topical or subconjunctival administration of H-1152 will normalize RPE barrier function, mitigating one of the critical pathological hallmarks of dry AMD, which is the breakdown of the outer blood-retinal barrier that underlies RPE dysfunction and subsequent photoreceptor loss (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Meekins et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the therapeutic candidate H-1152 Dihydrochloride exhibits multiple promising attributes as a repurposed drug for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. One of its primary strengths is its exceptional potency and selectivity toward ROCK1 and ROCK2, with IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range, which is critical given that only minimal inhibition may be required to elicit beneficial cellular modifications in the RPE. Its mechanism of action, relying on the inhibition of the ROCK pathway, directly addresses key pathological processes in dry AMD, notably the stress-fiber–mediated disruption of cell–cell junctions and the abnormal VEGF-driven paracellular leak. Furthermore, successful preclinical studies in corneal endothelial models have demonstrated that H-1152 can modulate cytoskeletal organization and promote wound healing, providing a proof-of-concept for its ability to restore barrier function in ocular tissues. The fact that ocular delivery via topical or subconjunctival routes can achieve therapeutic levels in the RPE/choroid is another advantage that underscores its translational potential, especially when compared with other ROCK inhibitors that have advanced into clinical trials for related ocular conditions such as glaucoma and diabetic macular oedema (Iancu et al., 2021; Meekins et al., 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, there are several important weaknesses and uncertainties that must be addressed. First, the bulk of available preclinical evidence for H-1152 is derived from studies involving corneal endothelial cells rather than RPE cells, and therefore it remains uncertain whether the effects observed in these models will fully translate to the RPE context. The RPE possesses unique structural and functional characteristics that distinguish it from corneal endothelium, and additional targeted experiments in ARPE-19 or primary RPE cell models under conditions of chronic oxidative stress are required to confirm the hypothesized restoration of TEER and normalization of tight-junction proteins. Second, while the ROCK inhibitor class has been used in other areas of ophthalmology with an acceptable safety and tolerability profile, there is currently no direct clinical history of H-1152 being used for dry AMD or even in posterior-segment diseases; most clinical data so far pertains to ROCK inhibitors used in glaucoma or diabetic macular oedema. This means that the long-term safety, potential off-target effects, and optimal dosing regimens for H-1152 in the context of dry AMD remain to be established (Iancu et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Furthermore, some studies in retinal angiogenesis models have reported that certain ROCK inhibitors can produce paradoxical effects, such as increased VEGF-induced angiogenesis via alternative signaling pathways including ERK1/2 activation. Although the candidate hypothesis emphasizes barrier restoration and suppression of VEGF-driven leak, it will be critical to delineate the dose–response relationship and evaluate any potential pro-angiogenic or off-target actions of H-1152 in comprehensive preclinical studies. Establishing robust pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles is essential; while rabbit subconjunctival dosing reportedly achieved ocular RPE/choroid levels around 0.2 µM, it needs to be confirmed that such concentrations are both efficacious and safe in the long term, particularly as the dry AMD population may require chronic dosing (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overall, H-1152 Dihydrochloride presents as a promising candidate for repurposing as a dry AMD therapeutic based on its mechanistic rationale, outstanding potency and selectivity for ROCK inhibition, and the supportive data from ocular surface models. The proposed molecular mechanism—restoring tight-junction integrity through suppression of stress fiber formation and subsequent normalization of ZO-1 and occludin localization—aligns well with the underlying pathology of dry AMD, in which the breakdown of RPE barrier function contributes to disease progression. However, definitive preclinical studies employing RPE-specific models and in vivo evaluations in relevant dry AMD animal models are necessary to solidify its translational potential. Additionally, careful attention must be given to its safety profile, especially given the delicate nature of the posterior segment and the potential for off-target effects on retinal vasculature. In conclusion, while H-1152 shows significant promise based on its pharmacological profile and the mechanistic logic underlying RPE barrier restoration, further research is warranted to bridge the gap between ocular surface models and the RPE-specific pathology encountered in dry AMD. Strategic preclinical investigations, including detailed assessments of TEER restoration, tight junction protein localization under oxidative stress, and the modulation of VEGF signaling, are critical next steps in validating H-1152 as a viable therapeutic candidate for this complex and currently underserved retinal disease (Meekins et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ripasudil, also known by its research designation Y-39983 and commercially available as Selleckchem S8443, is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor developed originally as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil containing protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. It belongs to a class of therapeutics that act in an ATP‐competitive manner to inhibit the activity of ROCK isoforms, enzymes that are critical regulators of actomyosin contractility and cell adhesion. Ripasudil was synthesized following the structural optimization of earlier compounds such as fasudil and Y-27632, with the aim of increasing both potency and ocular tolerability. Its chemical origins are linked to the rational design strategies that sought to improve enzyme inhibitory selectivity and to enhance the pharmacokinetic profile for local ocular application. Members of the ROCK inhibitor class have seen prior use in settings that require modulation of actin cytoskeleton dynamics, such as the treatment of glaucoma via enhanced aqueous humor outflow, and have also been explored in contexts involving wound healing and anti-fibrotic effects in various ocular tissues (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, ripasudil has been approved in Japan for the treatment of glaucoma and ocular hypertension, where it is delivered topically in the form of eye drops, demonstrating a well-established safety profile and a low incidence of systemic adverse effects. In preclinical models, it has demonstrated efficacy by increasing ocular blood flow, modifying trabecular meshwork cell contractility, and reducing intraocular pressure, thereby serving as a stepping stone and proof-of-concept for the utility of ROCK inhibitors in ocular disorders. Beyond its approved use in glaucoma, investigations of ROCK inhibitors—including ripasudil—have extended into experimental applications in corneal endothelial regeneration and have been evaluated in combination with anti-VEGF therapies for diabetic macular edema. Although direct clinical evidence specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is not available, multiple lines of preclinical research have shown that the ROCK inhibitor class modulates pathways which are believed to underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Notably, the mechanistic studies have identified the role of ROCK signaling in cytoskeletal reorganization, matrix contractility, and fibrosis, all of which are processes particularly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier dysfunction seen in dry AMD (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Moreover, the ocular pharmacokinetic profile of ripasudil—demonstrated by rabbit intravitreal studies showing a half-life of approximately 14 hours and negligible systemic exposure—is supportive of repurposing this candidate for posterior segment indications, including dry AMD (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ripasudil exerts its therapeutic activity by competitively inhibiting the ATP-binding site of ROCK isoforms, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of downstream effectors such as myosin light-chain (MLC), myosin-binding subunit of MLC phosphatase (MYPT1), and LIM kinase. These phosphorylation events normally lead to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, focal adhesion assembly, and ultimately contribute to a contractile, stiffened cell phenotype. In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, this contractility is thought to be exacerbated under conditions of oxidative stress, contributing to disassembly or mislocalization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity. By inhibiting ROCK, ripasudil reduces actomyosin-driven contraction and stress-fiber formation, thereby promoting cortical F-actin remodeling and facilitating the proper membrane relocalization of tight-junction proteins. The specificity of ripasudil has been demonstrated by its greater than 100-fold selectivity against other kinases such as protein kinase C (PKC) and myotonic dystrophy kinase-related Cdc42-binding kinase (MRCK), highlighting the mechanistic precision by which it modulates ROCK-dependent signaling cascades (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Additionally, while several studies indicate that the ROCK inhibitor class generally targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2 isoforms, quantitative biochemical data have shown that ripasudil exhibits potent enzyme inhibitory activity with IC₅₀s in the low nanomolar range (with values reported around 51 nM for ROCK1 and 19 nM for ROCK2 in some studies, though the candidate hypothesis posits values of approximately 29 nM for ROCK1 and 68 nM for ROCK2). This inhibitory profile is particularly relevant because emerging research indicates that ROCK2, in particular, is upregulated in the pathological conditions of dry AMD and plays a key role in mediating cytoskeletal changes that disrupt RPE tight junction integrity (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). The inhibition of ROCK thereby is expected to have a dual benefit of cytoprotection and restoration of cell junction architecture, ultimately leading to improved barrier function (Ghenciu et al., 2025; Singh & Singh, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing ripasudil for dry AMD is that by blocking ROCK activity in oxidatively stressed retinal pigment epithelium cells, the compound will lead to a reduction in actomyosin contractility, thereby alleviating the formation of pathological stress fibers that otherwise disrupt the organization of tight junction complexes. Under normal physiological conditions, tight junction proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin are localized at the plasma membrane in a continuous, belt-like manner that is essential to maintain TEER and restrict paracellular permeability. However, in dry AMD, oxidative damage, inflammation, and mechanical stress lead to cytoskeletal reorganization and a discontinuous distribution of these critical proteins, resulting in impaired barrier function and contributing to the pathogenesis of the disease. Preclinical studies, particularly those employing ARPE-19 cell models subjected to toxic insults such as paraquat or sodium iodate (NaIO₃), have demonstrated that ROCK inhibitors can dose-dependently restore TEER (with reported improvements up to 70%) and re-establish the membrane continuity of ZO-1, suggesting that these agents can “rescue” the RPE barrier phenotype under injurious conditions (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). It is expected that ripasudil, with its potent ROCK-inhibitory activity and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics (including intravitreal retention times supportive of sustained action), will similarly promote the cortical redistribution of F-actin, leading to the re-localization of junctional molecules back to the cell membrane. This mechanistic restoration should result in improved transepithelial electrical resistance and a concomitant reduction in paracellular permeability, effectively reinforcing the RPE barrier—a central therapeutic target in dry AMD. Moreover, the activation of protective cellular pathways through ROCK inhibition may also confer additional anti-apoptotic and anti-inflammatory effects, further contributing to the survival and functional integrity of the RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating ripasudil as a candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths become apparent. First, its established clinical use for glaucoma means that its safety, tolerability, and ocular pharmacokinetic properties are well characterized—attributes that significantly lower the translational barrier for its application in other ocular diseases. The intravitreal pharmacokinetic data, with a half-life of approximately 14 hours in rabbit models and negligible systemic exposure, suggest that therapeutic concentrations capable of modulating ROCK activity in the retina can be achieved with acceptable dosing regimens (Yamaguchi et al., 2016). Second, the mechanistic rationale is compelling: ROCK signaling is intimately involved in mediating actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, and subsequent disruption of tight junction architecture in epithelial cells. Given that ROCK2 in particular is implicated in the pathological processes observed in the RPE in dry AMD, the ability of ripasudil to inhibit this pathway could translate into measurable improvements in barrier function, as indicated by preclinical assays demonstrating TEER restoration and the re-localization of ZO-1 in ARPE-19 cells (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Third, the compound exhibits a favorable selectivity profile, with negligible off-target activity against other kinases such as PKC and MRCK, which minimizes the risk of unintended effects in non-target tissues. This specificity is critical when repurposing drugs for chronic conditions such as dry AMD, where long-term ocular safety is paramount (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Despite these strengths, there are notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before ripasudil can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. A primary limitation is the paucity of direct experimental evidence in RPE models of dry AMD. While the hypothesis is supported by data from related in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative stress), robust in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of dry AMD pathophysiology are still needed. In particular, data demonstrating that ripasudil can restore tight junction integrity and improve TEER in the context of chronic, progressive RPE dysfunction remain limited (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Furthermore, although the compound’s ROCK inhibitory activity is well documented, the available literature does not consistently detail the isoform-specific effects in RPE cells; given that ROCK1 and ROCK2 may play distinct roles in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, clarifying the relative contributions of each isoform is essential. The candidate hypothesis posits specific IC₅₀ values for ROCK1 and ROCK2, yet discrepancies exist across reported studies regarding the precise inhibitory concentrations, which indicates that further biochemical characterization is warranted (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). Another consideration is the potential for adverse effects when repurposing a drug originally optimized for anterior-segment diseases for posterior-segment applications. Although the ocular safety profile of ripasudil in glaucoma is well established, the long-term impact of ROCK inhibition on RPE cell biology in an aged population—especially in the context of dry AMD—remains uncertain. Off-target cytoskeletal effects in other retinal cell types, possible modulation of inflammatory responses, and the risk of inadvertently triggering compensatory signaling pathways are all factors that must be carefully evaluated in preclinical studies (Iancu et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2025). Lastly, while the pharmacokinetic data support retinal exposure after intravitreal or possibly topical administration, optimizing the delivery method to ensure sustained and localized drug levels in the RPE without causing ocular surface toxicity (such as conjunctival hyperemia or corneal epithelial disturbances) will be critical. Innovative delivery systems, such as sustained-release intravitreal implants or depot formulations, may offer solutions but require further development (Yamaguchi et al., 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023).

In conclusion, the repurposing of ripasudil for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and a favorable safety profile derived from its established use in glaucoma. The compound’s capacity to inhibit ROCK-mediated actomyosin contraction and promote cortical F-actin remodeling positions it as a promising agent for restoring RPE barrier function—one of the key pathological features of dry AMD. However, the current literature reveals significant gaps in direct evidence regarding its effects on RPE tight junction proteins, TEER restoration, and the isoform-specific roles of ROCK in the RPE under oxidative stress. To advance ripasudil as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, additional preclinical investigations—ideally incorporating robust animal models of dry AMD and detailed biochemical analyses of ROCK isoform activity in RPE cells—are required. Additionally, optimizations in drug delivery methodology to achieve sustained posterior-segment exposure while minimizing adverse ocular events will be imperative. Overall, ripasudil presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, with its strengths in mechanistic specificity, favorable ocular pharmacokinetics, and established clinical safety underscoring its potential. Nonetheless, the outlined weaknesses and knowledge gaps necessitate a rigorous program of targeted research to validate its efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity and to ensure its long-term safety in the intended patient population (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023; Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Adams & Papillon, 2020; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SS-31, also known as Elamipretide, is a synthetic, cell‐permeable tetrapeptide that was originally discovered serendipitously during efforts to optimize opioid receptor peptide analogs and has since been rationally designed to target mitochondria by binding the lipid cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3). Its chemical structure, typically denoted as D-Arg-Dmt-Lys-Phe-NH₂—with “Dmt” representing 2,6-dimethyltyrosine—confers a unique alternating pattern of cationic and aromatic residues that endows the compound with high membrane permeability and preferential accumulation in the mitochondrial inner membrane (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 2–5). The molecular weight of SS-31 is approximately 639.8 g/mol, and its synthesis is generally performed via solid-phase peptide synthesis, which allows for efficient production and structural modification; this synthetic origin situates SS-31 within the class of mitochondria-targeting peptides or “stealth peptides” that have been extensively studied for their bioenergetic and cytoprotective properties (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In addition to its capacity to target cardiolipin, the compound’s design leverages both electrostatic attraction—owing to its positively charged arginine and lysine residues—and hydrophobic interactions from its aromatic side chains to facilitate a stable binding to the anionic membranes of mitochondria (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). As a member of a broader therapeutic class initially developed to improve mitochondrial function, SS-31 has been applied across various models of mitochondrial dysfunction, making it a promising repurposed candidate for diseases where mitochondrial impairment is a key pathological driver, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SS-31 is extensive and spans several preclinical and early-phase clinical investigations across a range of indications characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction. Preclinical studies across more than 150 peer-reviewed publications have demonstrated that SS-31 exerts robust mitochondrial protection in models of cardiac and skeletal muscle myopathies, where it improves mitochondrial structure, enhances ATP production, reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and ultimately ameliorates organ dysfunction (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3, 10–11). In the cardiovascular arena, animal models of heart failure and ischemia-reperfusion injury have documented that SS-31 treatment leads to improved left ventricular function and reduced tissue biomarkers of injury, effects that are attributed to its ability to stabilize cardiolipin and maintain the integrity of the electron transport system (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 10–12). Further, in neuromuscular and metabolic disease models, the compound has been shown to enhance mitochondrial ATP production and reduce oxidative stress, with early clinical studies in rare mitochondrial disorders such as Barth syndrome (a condition involving cardiolipin abnormalities) and primary mitochondrial myopathy providing supportive translational evidence (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 10–11, 16–22). More recently, SS-31 has been explored in the context of ocular diseases, including nonneovascular age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) and diabetic macular edema, where preclinical studies in murine models report that subcutaneous administration of SS-31 can reverse electroretinographic deficits, facilitate the clearance of sub-retinal pigment epithelium (sub‐RPE) deposits, and ultimately reverse vision loss (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Clinical trials—such as the Phase I ReCLAIM study in intermediate AMD and the ongoing Phase II ReCLAIM-2 trial—have begun to assess SS-31’s safety profile, pharmacokinetics, and preliminary efficacy in preserving visual function, thereby positioning it as a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Although its use in dry AMD is relatively novel compared to its established preclinical record in other mitochondrial disorders, the existing scientific and regulatory trajectory supports its potential repurposing for diseases in which mitochondrial dysfunction is a central pathogenic mechanism (Nashine, 2021, pp. 9–11, 16).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism by which SS-31 exerts its cytoprotective effects is centered on its highly specific interaction with cardiolipin, an anionic phospholipid unique to the mitochondrial inner membrane that plays a pivotal role in maintaining the structural integrity of cristae and the proper assembly and function of electron transport chain complexes (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). Detailed biophysical studies, including nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations, have demonstrated that SS-31 binds to cardiolipin via both electrostatic interactions (through its basic residues) and hydrophobic interactions (via its aromatic side chains), resulting in the “neutralization” of the negative surface charge on mitochondrial membranes and a favorable modulation of membrane fluidity and curvature (Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4; Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 16–22). This binding not only stabilizes cardiolipin against oxidative peroxidation but also promotes the optimal assembly of electron transport chain complexes into respiratory supercomplexes, thereby enhancing electron flow, reducing electron leakage, and ultimately decreasing the generation of ROS (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 4–6, 15–16). In addition, SS-31 has been shown to mitigate proton leakage and restore pH stress resistance in aged mitochondria by enhancing the function of critical proteins such as the adenine nucleotide translocator (ANT), which is central to ADP/ATP exchange and overall mitochondrial bioenergetics (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 10–12). Although SS-31 was initially characterized as an antioxidant, its primary mode of action is now understood to be the preservation of mitochondrial structure and function through cardiolipin stabilization rather than direct radical scavenging alone (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4). In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress—a key pathological hallmark of dry AMD—the hypothesis posits that by stabilizing mitochondria via cardiolipin binding, SS-31 will maintain normal electron transport chain efficiency, preserve ATP production, and limit ROS production, thereby protecting the integrity of RPE cells (Tong et al., 2022, pp. 14–16). Although direct experimental evidence linking SS-31 to the preservation of tight junction proteins such as ZO-1/occludin or to the restoration of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE cells is limited in the current literature, the well-documented mitochondrial protection afforded by SS-31 in other cellular models suggests that secondary benefits on cellular barrier function are plausible given the tight coupling between mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and loss of epithelial integrity (Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). In sum, the molecular interactions of SS-31 with mitochondrial membranes serve not only to optimize respiratory chain efficiency and restore bioenergetic balance but also to reduce the biochemical milieu of oxidative stress that is known to compromise cell–cell junctions, thereby providing a strong mechanistic rationale for its application in protecting RPE barrier function in dry AMD (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3, 15–22).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its molecular mechanism, the expected effect of SS-31 in an oxidative-challenge assay using RPE cells is multifaceted. In an experimental setting where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative stress—for example, through hydrogen peroxide treatment—the administration of SS-31 is anticipated to result in the selective binding to cardiolipin within RPE mitochondria; this interaction should stabilize inner mitochondrial membrane architecture, preserve cristae morphology, and enhance the efficiency of electron transport, leading to robust ATP production and reduced ROS levels (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). As mitochondrial homeostasis is a critical determinant of RPE cell function, the preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics is expected to translate into decreased apoptosis and improved cell survival in the face of oxidative challenges (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 8–11). Beyond these direct mitochondrial effects, maintenance of intracellular energy status and lower levels of ROS are essential for the proper localization and preservation of tight junction proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin; oxidative stress is known to disrupt these junctions, leading to loss of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and compromised RPE barrier integrity (Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40). Therefore, treatment with SS-31 should also help maintain or restore TEER in RPE monolayer assays, indicating a preservation of barrier function that is crucial for retinal homeostasis and prevention of drusen formation and RPE degeneration associated with dry AMD (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Moreover, preclinical studies in animal models of retinal degeneration—in which SS-31 has been shown to reverse vision loss, improve clearance of sub-RPE deposits, and enhance electroretinographic responses—further support the expectation that SS-31 can exert protective effects in the ocular environment by mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction and the subsequent cascade of oxidative damage (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Taken together, the anticipated experimental outcome is that SS-31 will significantly attenuate oxidative damage in RPE cells, preserve mitochondrial function, maintain tight junction integrity (as evidenced by stable ZO-1/occludin expression and restored TEER), and ultimately contribute to the functional rescue of RPE cells under conditions that mimic the oxidative insults observed in dry AMD (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tong et al., 2022, pp. 14–16).

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, SS-31 (Elamipretide) presents as a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, with several key strengths that support its potential utility and a few noteworthy challenges that will need to be addressed in further research. One of the primary strengths of SS-31 is its well-characterized mechanism of action; its ability to bind cardiolipin and thereby stabilize mitochondrial inner membrane structure, enhance electron transport chain efficiency, and reduce ROS generation is supported by robust preclinical data across multiple models of mitochondrial dysfunction, including cardiac, skeletal muscle, and retinal systems (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4). This mitochondria-targeted mechanism is particularly attractive in the context of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are recognized as major drivers of RPE degeneration and subsequent photoreceptor loss (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Furthermore, early-phase clinical studies in ocular disease have demonstrated that SS-31 is safe and well tolerated and have hinted at functional improvements in visual acuity and reduced progression of retinal degeneration, which supports its translational viability (Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5). The repurposing of SS-31 from conditions such as heart failure and primary mitochondrial myopathy to an ocular application leverages its established bioenergetic benefits and broad mitochondrial stabilization properties, thereby enhancing its appeal as a novel intervention for dry AMD (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 10–11, 16–22).

However, there are several challenges and weaknesses that merit consideration. First, while the molecular mechanism of SS-31—centered on cardiolipin binding and mitochondrial stabilization—is well supported, direct evidence linking its activity to the preservation of tight junction proteins (such as ZO-1/occludin) and the restoration of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE models remains limited in the current literature (Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40). This represents a key knowledge gap given that the hypothesis posits that protection of RPE barrier integrity is a critical outcome in preventing disease progression in dry AMD. Additional preclinical studies that specifically measure the effects of SS-31 on RPE tight junction organization, using immunostaining for ZO-1 and occludin as well as quantitative TEER assays, would be essential to fully validate its proposed mechanism in the context of epithelial barrier protection (Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Second, although early-phase clinical trials have shown promise in improving functional visual metrics, some clinical studies in related indications (e.g., Phase 2 trials in cardiac conditions) have produced mixed results with primary endpoints not consistently met, suggesting that optimal dosing regimens, treatment durations, and patient selection criteria may need further refinement (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 9–10). In the case of dry AMD, where the pathological changes evolve over extended periods, longer-term studies and careful endpoint selection will be critical to demonstrate sustained therapeutic benefit (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Third, while the pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of SS-31 appear favorable for reaching mitochondrial targets, ensuring sufficient ocular penetration and accumulation in the RPE—whether via systemic subcutaneous administration or topical formulations—remains a logistical and pharmacological challenge that must be addressed in future clinical development (Tong et al., 2022, pp. 14–16; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

In conclusion, SS-31 (Elamipretide) exhibits a strong mechanistic underpinning based on its targeted interaction with cardiolipin to restore mitochondrial function and mitigate oxidative stress—a mode of action that is directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD owing to the central role of mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE degeneration (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). The compound’s extensive preclinical validation in models of mitochondrial diseases, coupled with encouraging early clinical data, makes it a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Nonetheless, key gaps in directly demonstrating its effects on RPE barrier integrity and tight junction preservation (as measured by ZO-1/occludin levels and TEER) necessitate further targeted preclinical studies. Additionally, addressing challenges related to optimal dosing, treatment duration, and efficient ocular delivery will be paramount for the success of subsequent clinical trials. Overall, given its robust mitochondrial protective effects and plausible secondary benefits on epithelial barrier function, SS-31 warrants further investigation as a novel therapeutic strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 10–12).
