The following sections provide a detailed analysis of the candidate’s origins, therapeutic history, mechanism of action, expected effects in relevant assays, and a balanced overall evaluation based on the current literature.

I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PXS-5153A is a synthetically derived molecule that belongs to the class of selective lysyl oxidase inhibitors. In its design, medicinal chemistry efforts focused on optimizing potency and selectivity for LOXL2, along with activity against LOXL3, two members of the lysyl oxidase family that catalyze the oxidative deamination of lysine residues in collagens and elastin to promote covalent crosslink formation. These crosslinks confer the mechanical strength and stiffness of extracellular matrices (ECMs) such as Bruch’s membrane. Synthetic routes to compounds like PXS-5153A typically rely on structure-based design and iterative optimization to achieve potent enzyme inhibition with favorable pharmacokinetic properties (Lin et al., 2020). The compound, commercially available under MedChemExpress HY-111217, is representative of a new therapeutic class that has been primarily explored in the context of fibrosis and tumor microenvironment modulation. Given that ECM stiffening is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, targeting LOXL2 represents a novel approach compared to conventional anti-inflammatory or anti-angiogenic strategies.

II. Therapeutic History  
The LOXL2 inhibitor class, including molecules such as PXS-5153A, has been extensively tested in preclinical models of fibrosis and cancer. For example, within non-ocular systems, LOXL2 activity has been linked to increased tissue stiffness that fosters metastatic progression and desmoplastic reactions in tumors, and selective inhibition of LOXL2 has been shown to reduce crosslink density, attenuating fibrotic remodeling (Lin et al., 2020). Experimental inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity using non-selective agents like β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) has also been applied to in vitro and in vivo models to modulate ECM assembly, with effects on barrier function observed in RPE cultures co-treated with endothelial cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). Although LOXL2 inhibitors have not traditionally been used to treat dry AMD, evidence underscores the centrality of aberrant ECM crosslinking in BM thickening observed during aging and AMD progression (Wang et al., 2025). In particular, the endothelial cell–RPE crosstalk studies demonstrate a critical role for lysyl oxidase activity in regulating collagen bundle formation and in establishing RPE barrier properties (Benedicto et al., 2017). Accordingly, while there is no direct clinical or preclinical record of PXS-5153A in AMD, the antifibrotic profile of the compound and its impact on extracellular matrix mechanics in other disease contexts serve as a compelling rationale to explore its application in dry AMD.

III. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, LOXL2 catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of lysine or hydroxylysine residues present in collagens and elastin. This reaction is critical for the formation of covalent crosslinks that stabilize the ECM. Overexpression or hyperactivity of LOXL2 results in an excessively crosslinked and stiff matrix. In the eye, particularly within Bruch’s membrane—which is a complex, stratified ECM structure located between the RPE and the choroid—aberrant collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking are known to increase mechanical tension. Such mechanical changes are thought to adversely affect RPE cell function by interfering with integrin-mediated cell–matrix interactions and perturbing the proper localization of tight junction proteins, including ZO-1 and occludin (Benedicto et al., 2017).

PXS-5153A functions by binding to the catalytic pocket of LOXL2, thereby preventing its enzymatic activity. By blocking the oxidative deamination step, PXS-5153A reduces the formation of both immature and mature crosslinks in ECM proteins. The anticipated outcome is a lower crosslink density in Bruch’s membrane, resulting in a softer, more compliant matrix environment. This reduction in mechanical stiffness is expected to diminish abnormal mechanosignaling through β1 integrins, which are integral to the assembly and maintenance of tight junctions on RPE cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). The downstream consequences of reduced integrin activation include dampening of Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways, which in turn facilitate the stabilization and proper localization of tight junction proteins at the RPE cell membranes (Benedicto et al., 2017). Restoration of these junctional complexes correlates with improved barrier function, typically measured as an increased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in cell culture models. This mechanism is supported by studies in which inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity—by pharmacological agents such as BAPN—led to alterations in RPE barrier properties and tight junction morphology (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by directly targeting LOXL2, PXS-5153A is proposed to correct the pathological ECM remodeling that underlies BM stiffening in dry AMD while re-establishing proper RPE barrier integrity.

IV. Expected Effect  
The expected therapeutic effect of PXS-5153A in dry AMD centers on normalization of the BM ECM and concomitant restoration of RPE barrier function. In the proposed experimental model—an in vitro co-culture system where human fetal RPE (hfRPE) cells are grown on a substrate mimicking BM with defined stiffness—the application of PXS-5153A at concentrations around 5 µM is anticipated to yield a number of favorable outcomes.

First, by reducing LOXL2-mediated crosslinking of collagen IV and fibronectin, the drug should decrease the mechanical stiffness of the BM analog. A less rigid BM reduces aberrant integrin activation on the basolateral surfaces of RPE cells, which has been shown to be critical for proper tight junction assembly. In several studies, when the extracellular matrix is normalized—such as by altering substrate stiffness—there is an improvement in the localization of key tight junction proteins, specifically occludin and ZO-1, at the cell membrane (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Second, the reduced matrix stiffness is expected to alleviate the mechanical stress experienced by RPE cells, thereby facilitating the re-establishment of cell polarity and intercellular junction continuity. The stabilization of junctional complexes is measurable by TEER. In previous EC–RPE co-culture experiments, modulation of ECM mechanical properties directly correlated with increased TEER values, reflecting improved barrier function (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Moreover, the proper organization of the basement membrane is not only a structural consideration; the biochemical signaling through β1 integrin receptors—critical for maintaining cell adhesion and survival—would return toward homeostatic levels, further supporting the integrity of the RPE layer (Benedicto et al., 2017). These integrin-mediated signals influence downstream effectors such as Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK, which have been implicated in regulating tight junction dynamics (Benedicto et al., 2017). Progress in these pathways is expected to manifest as an overall improvement in the barrier phenotype, which is central to preventing the leakage of fluid and other deleterious solutes into the subretinal space—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.

In summary, it is anticipated that treatment with PXS-5153A in appropriate in vitro (and ultimately in vivo) models will lead to:  
• Reduced collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in BM, yielding a matrix with decreased stiffness (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Normalization of β1 integrin signaling and subsequent reorganization of RPE tight junctions with improved localization of proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Restoration of barrier function as evidenced by increased TEER measurements and improved paracellular permeability profiles (Benedicto et al., 2017).  

Thus, PXS-5153A is expected to address one of the core aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis by targeting ECM remodeling, which in turn indirectly stabilizes RPE cell function.

V. Overall Evaluation  
The concept of using PXS-5153A to modulate ECM pathology in dry AMD is compelling given the mechanistic insights derived from studies on lysyl oxidase activity in epithelial barrier function and ECM assembly. Among the strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its robust preclinical evidence in fibrosis and tumor microenvironment models. LOXL2 has been implicated in promoting tissue stiffening by catalyzing the crosslinking of collagen and fibronectin in various tissues (Lin et al., 2020). The pathophysiological parallels between fibrotic ECM remodeling in cancers and the stiffening of Bruch’s membrane in dry AMD provide a strong rationale for repurposing a LOXL2 inhibitor in an ocular context. Numerous studies have demonstrated that extracellular matrix integrity is essential for optimal RPE barrier function, and that even subtle changes in ECM mechanics can disrupt junctional complexes and lead to barrier dysfunction (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by targeting a critical enzymatic step in ECM crosslinking, PXS-5153A may confer dual benefits: it could both reduce the pathological stiffening of Bruch’s membrane and promote the reorganization of tight junction complexes, ultimately resulting in enhanced TEER and stabilization of the outer blood–retina barrier.

However, several important weaknesses or uncertainties must be considered. First, while numerous studies (using agents such as BAPN) have illustrated that lysyl oxidase inhibition affects RPE barrier function, direct evidence with selective LOXL2 inhibitors—specifically in ocular models of dry AMD—is lacking (Buniello et al., 2025). In fact, the Open Targets Platform indicates only a weak direct association between LOXL2 and age-related macular degeneration, based on limited literature evidence (Buniello et al., 2025). This raises the possibility that, although LOXL2 plays a demonstrable role in ECM crosslinking in other tissues, its specific involvement in dry AMD pathogenesis may not be as pronounced or may be influenced by other factors not recapitulated in non-ocular models.

Furthermore, potential off-target effects or the consequences of broadly altering ECM crosslinking in the eye must be carefully examined. The structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane is critical not only for its barrier function but also for nutrient transport between the choroidal circulation and the RPE. Overinhibition of LOXL2, or interference with normal ECM turnover, may inadvertently lead to basement membrane disorganization, as has been observed when lysyl oxidase activity was inhibited during critical periods of retinal development (Benedicto et al., 2017). This underscores the need for precise dose optimization and targeted delivery, ideally restricted to the ocular environment, to avoid systemic side effects.

Another consideration is the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. In addition to ECM stiffening, dry AMD involves multifactorial processes including oxidative stress, complement activation, inflammation, and the accumulation of lipoprotein deposits. Thus, while normalizing matrix stiffness is likely to improve RPE barrier function, it may be insufficient to fully arrest or reverse the disease process on its own. A combination therapy that also addresses the inflammatory and degenerative components of AMD may eventually be required (Benedicto et al., 2017; Caban et al., 2022).

From a development perspective, there is significant strength in the repurposing strategy because agents like PXS-5153A already have a detailed preclinical profile in non-ocular fibrotic models. This existing data can accelerate preclinical validation in ocular models, with studies planned in RPE–BM co-culture systems using TEER as a functional readout (Benedicto et al., 2017). Furthermore, leveraging well-characterized in vitro assays (such as those involving decellularized ECM and substrate stiffness modulation as described in the context) offers a clear experimental framework to evaluate whether the normalization of BM stiffness by PXS-5153A is sufficient to restore RPE tight junction integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017).

Nonetheless, one notable weakness is the limited direct evidence linking LOXL2 specifically to dry AMD. Although elevated lysyl oxidase activity and changes in collagen crosslinking have been observed in the context of RPE barrier function and BM integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017), the genetic and translational data associating LOXL2 with AMD are not robust. The relatively low association score (Buniello et al., 2025) suggests that additional studies are needed to clarify LOXL2’s role in the eye and to determine whether its inhibition will yield a therapeutically meaningful benefit in dry AMD patients.

In conclusion, repurposing PXS-5153A for dry AMD represents an innovative strategy that leverages the known antifibrotic effects of LOXL2 inhibition to address the deleterious ECM remodeling observed in aged Bruch’s membrane. The candidate’s synthetic origins and prior applications in fibrosis and cancer studies provide a solid foundation for its use, while the mechanistic rationale—centered on reducing pathological crosslinking and restoring RPE barrier function—is strongly supported by evidence from ECM modulation studies (Benedicto et al., 2017). However, challenges remain due to the lack of direct ocular data, potential risks of overmodulating ECM integrity, and the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology. Future research must focus on rigorous in vitro validation in RPE–BM co-culture systems and in vivo studies in relevant AMD animal models to establish the efficacy and safety profile of PXS-5153A in the context of dry AMD. Overall, despite these uncertainties, PXS-5153A holds promise as a novel ECM-targeted therapeutic candidate that could complement existing and emerging treatment strategies for this currently unmet clinical need (Lin et al., 2020; Buniello et al., 2025).

Taken together, the strengths of a clear mechanism of action, potent enzyme selectivity, and an innovative approach toward ECM normalization position PXS-5153A as an attractive candidate warranting further investigation. Nonetheless, a careful reappraisal of the molecular role of LOXL2 in the ocular microenvironment, along with detailed studies on dosing, delivery, and potential off-target effects, will be critical in determining whether this candidate can be successfully repurposed for treating dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ML‐SA1 (Tocris 5291) is a synthetic, small‐molecule agonist that targets the lysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (mucolipin‐1). It was originally identified through screening efforts aimed at discovering modulators of lysosomal Ca²⁺ release and has been instrumental as an in vitro pharmacologic tool to probe TRPML1 function in diverse cellular systems, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models. ML‐SA1 belongs to a broader class of TRP (transient receptor potential) channel modulators that have been used extensively in basic research to examine ion channel regulation of intracellular Ca²⁺ stores, autophagy regulation, and lysosomal exocytosis. In several studies using primary mouse RPE, human embryonic stem cell‐derived RPE (hesRPE), and ARPE‐19 cells, ML‐SA1 has been shown to robustly elevate cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ via direct activation of TRPML1, with the effect being rapid, reversible, and reproducible, thereby establishing its utility as a selective TRPML1 agonist (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, ML‐SA1 has been employed in multiple biochemical and cellular studies as a probe to activate TRPML1-mediated lysosomal Ca²⁺ release. In the literature, its application in RPE cell models has helped delineate the contributions of lysosomal Ca²⁺ signals to downstream processes such as lysosomal exocytosis, TFEB (transcription factor EB) activation, and oxidative stress regulation. Experimental evidence derived from studies using ML‐SA1 demonstrates that the induced Ca²⁺ release is essentially independent of extracellular Ca²⁺ and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca²⁺ storage; rather, the release originates from lysosomal stores—as confirmed by the abrogation of ML‐SA1 responses upon lysosomal disruption with glycyl‐L‐phenylalanine‐naphthylamide (GPN) and by the lack of response in TRPML1-null RPE models (Más Gómez et al., 2018). To date, ML‐SA1 has not been used clinically or in veterinary settings and has not yet been evaluated in the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases; its use is so far confined to experimental paradigms that study the fundamental aspects of TRPML1 activity and lysosomal function (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This candidate is thus considered a repurposed pharmacologic agent, repositioned from a research tool to a potential therapeutic based on its mechanistic actions in RPE cells.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ML‐SA1 exerts its action by binding to and directly activating TRPML1 channels located on the lysosomal membrane. Upon binding, it triggers an efflux of Ca²⁺ from the lysosomal lumen into the cytoplasm, which has been quantitatively measured using ratiometric Ca²⁺ indicators such as Fura-2 (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This Ca²⁺ release is independent of extracellular Ca²⁺ and is not affected by the depletion of ER Ca²⁺, indicating that the source is specifically lysosomal (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The released Ca²⁺ can then activate downstream signaling pathways including the calcineurin-TFEB pathway, where increased cytosolic Ca²⁺ activates calcineurin, leading to dephosphorylation and subsequent nuclear translocation of TFEB. Nuclear TFEB acts as a master regulator of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis by upregulating a network of genes that control these pathways (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Notably, experimental evidence indicates that when the function of TRPML1 is compromised—such as in the context of lipid accumulation in lysosomes or genetic knockout of TRPML1—the Ca²⁺ response to ML‐SA1 is significantly diminished, underscoring both the specificity of ML‐SA1 for TRPML1 and the modulation of its efficacy by the lysosomal lipid environment (Más Gómez et al., 2018). In addition to stimulating Ca²⁺ release, TRPML1 activation by ML‐SA1 has been linked to beneficial downstream effects such as the induction of lysosomal exocytosis and the enhancement of cathepsin activity, which together contribute to the restoration of lysosomal function and cellular homeostasis (Karema-Jokinen et al., 2023; Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the current hypothesis, ML‐SA1 is expected to act on RPE cells by enhancing lysosomal Ca²⁺ release through TRPML1 activation, thereby stimulating the calcineurin-TFEB signaling cascade. This cascade is anticipated to upregulate the transcription of autophagy and lysosome-related genes, leading to improved autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis. In practical assays, such as those employing lipofuscin-loaded RPE monolayers, ML‐SA1 should facilitate the clearance of misfolded or aggregated tight junction proteins—including ZO-1—thereby restoring disrupted tight junction belts and improving transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) measurements. The activation of cathepsins, as part of the enhanced lysosomal function, is also expected to increase the degradation of accumulated cellular debris, further supporting cellular clearance (Falcão et al., 2025; Más Gómez et al., 2018). In experimental models of epithelial barrier restoration, previous data using TRPML1 agonists have shown that such compounds can rescue autophagic flux and reduce lysosomal storage, which is associated with improved barrier integrity; this supports the mechanism by which ML‐SA1 is expected to normalize the function of RPE cells relevant to dry AMD (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Trehalose (α,α-trehalose) is a naturally occurring, nonreducing disaccharide composed of two d-glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond; it is broadly found in bacteria, fungi, insects, invertebrates, and plants but is not synthesized by vertebrates, including humans (trehalase in the small intestine hydrolyzes ingested trehalose to glucose) (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). In drug-development parlance, trehalose is a small-molecule, carbohydrate autophagy modulator and proteostasis regulator; it exhibits both biophysical “chemical chaperone” activity that stabilizes macromolecules and biologic activity that induces the autophagy–lysosome program via TFEB/TFE3 activation and related nutrient-sensing pathways (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Jeong et al., 2021, pp. 1–3, 12–13; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). Clinical/translational use: Trehalose is approved as a safe food ingredient and has been widely used in humans, including topical ophthalmic preparations for dry eye disease and post-LASIK care, with multiple clinical trials and a marketed formulation (e.g., Thealoz Duo, 3% trehalose plus hyaluronic acid) supporting ocular-surface safety and symptomatic benefit; the patented formulation increased tear film thickness after a single drop in clinical testing (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 18–20). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ML218 is a synthetic small‐molecule calcium channel inhibitor originally developed as an antagonist targeting T‐type CaV3 channels. It was discovered in efforts to design selective modulators of low‐voltage‐activated calcium channels and is commercially available (Tocris 5056). Its chemical structure – featuring a 3,5‐dichlorobenzamide moiety attached to an azabicyclic fragment – places it in the class of benzamide-derived T‐type channel blockers. The compound was designed to interact with hydrophobic fenestration sites in voltage‐gated calcium channels, and its development emerged from scaffold‐hopping strategies derived from earlier hits in high‐throughput calcium flux assays. ML218 thus belongs to a family of investigational agents that have been primarily used as pharmacological tools to dissect T‐type channel function in neuronal systems. Previous studies have focused on its ability to inhibit CaV3 channels in central nervous system models, including experiments in cell lines and primary neurons where it modulated firing patterns and synaptic excitability (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). In addition to its intended activity on CaV3 channels, detailed analyses have revealed that ML218 also exhibits significant cross‐activity with CaV1.4 channels by adopting an alternative binding mode that involves the III‐IV fenestration—an observation that distinguishes it from classical dihydropyridines (Sun et al., 2025). This dual binding behavior highlights both the promise and the challenge of using ML218 as a selective tool in complex tissues where multiple calcium channel subtypes coexist. Overall, ML218 is a promising lead compound representing the synthetic, small‐molecule approach to targeting voltage‐dependent calcium channels, with a structure–activity relationship that suggests potential repurposing for non‐neuronal applications such as retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier stabilization (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History:  
ML218 has been primarily explored within experimental models predominantly focused on the central nervous system. Several studies have employed ML218 as a pharmacological probe to inhibit T‐type calcium currents in neuronal populations. For example, in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease, ML218 demonstrated robust inhibition of T-type currents in subthalamic nucleus (STN) neurons, leading to marked alterations in burst firing patterns (Xiang et al., 2011; Manzar et al., 2025). Electrophysiological investigations using whole‐cell patch clamp techniques in HEK293 cells transfected with CaV3.2 channels have shown that ML218 can achieve potent block, with reported IC₅₀ values ranging from approximately 24 nM (in one report) to 150–310 nM in different assay settings (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). These preclinical studies validated ML218’s mechanism of action within neural substrates and its potential as a centrally active agent. In parallel, investigations in non‐neuronal cells have emerged. In particular, ML218 has been applied to studies involving human embryonic stem cell‐derived retinal pigment epithelium (hESC‐RPE) where it was used at a concentration of 5 μM to elucidate the functionality of voltage‐gated calcium channels expressed in these cells—primarily focusing on assays of phagocytosis and VEGF secretion (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). Although these studies did not specifically examine barrier function parameters, they established that RPE cells express functional T‐type calcium channels and that pharmacological modulation with ML218 could alter cellular processes relevant to retinal physiology. Notably, there is no recorded or clinical history of ML218 being employed to treat dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or related ocular diseases; its usage to date has centered on neurological models and in vitro assays. Consequently, repurposing ML218 for dry AMD would represent a novel application, extending its utilization from central nervous system studies to ocular tissue. The concept of drug repurposing in ocular diseases has been gaining traction in recent years due to the overlapping roles of calcium signaling in diverse tissues, and ML218’s history in rigorously characterizing calcium channel pharmacology makes it a candidate for further exploration in RPE models (Xiang et al., 2011; Korkka et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
ML218 functions primarily by blocking T‐type calcium channels, with an emphasis on CaV3.2 subtypes. The compound’s mechanism involves its entry into the transmembrane fenestrations of the channel complex, where it interrupts the normal ion‐conducting pathway. Detailed structural studies have revealed that in CaV3 channels, ML218 docks within the II‐III fenestration; in this binding mode, the phenyl head group of the molecule extends into the hydrophobic channel region while its aliphatic tail lies within the central pore, thereby imposing a state‐dependent block (Sun et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024). This interaction presumably stabilizes the channel in a closed state, reducing low‐voltage‐activated Ca²⁺ influx into the cell. Notably, ML218’s binding is not entirely exclusive to CaV3 channels, as its molecular conformation adapts in CaV1.4 channels. In these channels, non‐conserved residues preclude the canonical II‐III fenestration binding; instead, ML218 binds at a distinct site in the III‐IV fenestration that overlaps with the dihydropyridine (DHP) binding pocket. Mutagenesis studies have confirmed the importance of this alternate binding mode by demonstrating substantial changes in inhibitory potency upon modification of key residues such as T1007 (Sun et al., 2025). In electrophysiological assays carried out in HEK293 cells, ML218 has been shown to be highly potent against CaV3.2 channels (with reported IC₅₀ values as low as 24 nM in certain studies) and to display over 80-fold selectivity over CaV1.4 channels, although its cross‐reactivity remains a consideration at higher concentrations (Sun et al., 2025). The molecular basis for its selectivity lies in the differential organization of channel domains between CaV3 and CaV1 families, with ML218’s binding being modulated by specific residues located in the channel pore and fenestration regions. From a biochemical standpoint, the blockade of CaV3.2 channels results in a decreased calcium influx during membrane depolarizations, which is critical for controlling intracellular calcium levels. In tissues such as the RPE, where calcium signaling plays a pivotal role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and barrier integrity, aberrant Ca²⁺ influx can activate calcium‐dependent proteases such as calpains. Calpains, once activated, can cleave junctional proteins including zonula occludens protein 1 (ZO-1) and occludin, leading to compromised barrier integrity. Thus, by selectively inhibiting CaV3.2‐mediated calcium entry, ML218 is hypothesized to prevent calpain activation and subsequent disruption of tight junctions in RPE cells—a mechanism that has been indirectly supported by studies showing that inhibitors of T-type channels reduce cellular excitability and junctional leak in alternative epithelial models (Sun et al., 2025). Furthermore, the compound’s dual action—including a modest agonist effect at specific concentrations—adds complexity to its pharmacological profile; however, in the context of RPE barrier function, the primary desired effect would be its antagonist action that limits pathological calcium entry under oxidative or inflammatory stress. The state‐dependence of ML218’s block (i.e., preferential inhibition when channels are in an open or inactivated state) may further enhance its capacity to target pathological calcium influx while sparing normal physiological signaling to some extent, although this property will require careful titration in a diseased state (Sun et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
The working hypothesis for repurposing ML218 in dry AMD is that its inhibition of CaV3.2 channels in retinal pigment epithelium will reduce pathological intracellular calcium accumulation under conditions of oxidative and inflammatory stress. Elevated Ca²⁺ levels in RPE cells are known to activate calpain, a calcium‐dependent protease that mediates the proteolytic cleavage of critical junctional proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin. Disruption of these proteins leads to a compromised RPE barrier, as reflected in reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased paracellular permeability (measured by FITC-dextran flux assays). By blocking the CaV3.2 channels, ML218 is expected to limit this pathological Ca²⁺ influx and thereby prevent calpain activation, preserving the integrity of the ZO-1/occludin belt in RPE cells (Sun et al., 2025). This preservation of junctional complexes should translate into restored TEER and reduced permeability of the RPE monolayer in in vitro models simulating oxidative or inflammatory injury that mimic conditions encountered in dry AMD. Moreover, patch-clamp electrophysiology and Fluo-4 calcium imaging assays in RPE cells are proposed as means of confirming target engagement and quantifying the extent of CaV3.2 current inhibition by ML218 (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). It is anticipated that effective blockade of pathological calcium signaling will also reduce downstream events associated with dry AMD pathophysiology, such as aberrant vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) secretion, which contributes to the progression of atrophic changes in the retina. Although previous studies using ML218 in hESC-RPE have focused more on phagocytosis and secretory functions rather than barrier integrity per se, the presence of functional T-type channels identified in these cells (with CaV3.2 localized, for instance, to the basolateral domain) supports the rationale that modulation of these channels will have a direct impact on barrier properties (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating ML218 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current literature. One significant strength of ML218 is its well‐documented and robust activity in inhibiting T‐type calcium channels, particularly CaV3.2, as demonstrated by comprehensive electrophysiological studies in both neuronal and heterologous systems (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). This potent inhibition forms a logical mechanistic basis for targeting pathological calcium influx in RPE cells, where calcium overload and subsequent activation of proteases like calpain are implicated in junctional protein degradation and barrier dysfunction. Furthermore, the detailed structural insights into ML218’s binding—its differential interactions in CaV3 and CaV1 channels—provide a strong foundation for understanding its pharmacodynamic activity. The ability of ML218 to modulate calcium signaling with state‐dependent block enhances its therapeutic promise by potentially allowing it to target pathological overactivity while sparing baseline physiological function (Sun et al., 2025).  

On the other hand, several potential weaknesses must be considered. The literature reveals that ML218 is not exclusively selective for CaV3.2 channels; it exhibits cross‐reactivity with CaV1.4 channels, albeit at lower potency (with reported IC₅₀ values for CaV1.4 in the micromolar range compared to nanomolar ranges for CaV3.2) (Sun et al., 2025). Such cross‐reactivity could theoretically lead to off‐target effects in tissues where L‐type channels play critical roles in calcium signaling, potentially complicating its utility in RPE cells that also express other calcium channel subtypes. Furthermore, while the proposed hypothesis for dry AMD is biologically plausible, there is a notable gap in the literature regarding direct evidence for ML218’s efficacy in preserving RPE barrier function under oxidative or inflammatory conditions—most studies with ML218 have been performed in neuronal contexts or in assays focused on phagocytosis and secretory aspects of RPE physiology (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). Thus, extrapolation of its barrier‐stabilizing properties from other epithelial systems (or even from neural models) requires cautious interpretation and further dedicated experimentation.  

Another concern pertains to the reported potency of ML218. Although optimistic hypotheses suggest an IC₅₀ of approximately 7 nM for CaV3.2 channel block, the available data across various assay platforms indicate that effective concentrations are more likely to be in the tens to low hundreds of nanomolar range (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). This discrepancy necessitates further pharmacological profiling in RPE models to accurately define the therapeutic window and ensure that the concentrations used to restore barrier integrity do not inadvertently trigger off‐target effects or toxicity. Additionally, the dual binding mode of ML218—while advantageous for providing mechanistic insight—raises the possibility that subtle differences in channel conformations within RPE cells (compared to neurons) could influence its selectivity and efficacy, thereby complicating dose optimization for ocular applications.  

Despite these challenges, the conceptual framework for repurposing ML218 in dry AMD has several attractive features. The targeting of T‐type calcium channels to mitigate calpain activation and to preserve tight junction protein integrity represents a novel therapeutic approach that departs from traditional anti‐inflammatory or anti‐angiogenic strategies. In dry AMD, where chronic, low‐grade oxidative and inflammatory stress contribute to RPE dysfunction and barrier breakdown, a compound like ML218 could theoretically reduce intracellular calcium overload and, consequently, the cascade of events leading to junctional degradation. Preliminary evidence from hESC-RPE studies confirms that these cells express functional T-type channels and respond to modulation by calcium channel blockers, lending support to the notion that ML218 can be effective in this tissue context (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.).

In summary, ML218 emerges as an intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its potent T-type channel inhibitory activity, its well‐characterized mechanism at the molecular level, and the theoretical basis linking Ca²⁺ dysregulation to RPE barrier dysfunction. However, the current body of literature does not provide direct evidence in RPE models under conditions that mimic dry AMD pathology, such as oxidative or inflammatory injury. Moreover, the compound’s off‐target activity on CaV1.4 channels and the variability in reported potencies across studies pose significant challenges that will require thorough in vitro and eventually in vivo validation. Future investigations should prioritize comprehensive electrophysiological and imaging studies in RPE cells, specifically measuring TEER, FITC‐dextran flux, and tight junction protein localization following exposure to oxidative stress, to determine whether ML218 can indeed restore barrier integrity as hypothesized. Dose‐ranging studies and careful evaluation of potential off‐target effects will also be critical to establishing a safe and effective therapeutic profile for ocular application.  

Overall, while ML218 holds promise as a tool compound with the potential for repurposing in dry AMD, its advancement into this new therapeutic area will depend on addressing key knowledge gaps through rigorous experimental validation. This includes confirming its selective inhibition of CaV3.2 channels in RPE cells, establishing the correlation between calcium influx blockade and tight junction preservation, and ensuring that its pharmacological behavior in RPE is consistent with the requirements for stabilizing the RPE barrier under pathological conditions. Therefore, although the mechanistic rationale is compelling, additional targeted preclinical studies are required before ML218 can be confidently moved forward as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011; Korkka et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
LG100268 is a fully synthetic rexinoid that was developed as a selective agonist for the retinoid X receptors (RXRs). It belongs to a specialized subclass of retinoids known as “rexinoids” that bind to RXRs with high affinity and minimal cross‐reactivity to the retinoic acid receptors (RARs). The compound was discovered and optimized in medicinal chemistry programs aiming to achieve potent RXR activation with improved receptor selectivity relative to earlier retinoid compounds such as bexarotene. Notably, synthetic modifications introduced in LG100268 include the incorporation of a 3‐carboxy pyridine ring—a modular motif that has been exploited for further scaffold diversification and structure–activity work to tune RXR heterodimer selectivity (Curley, 2012, pp. 4–5). LG100268 displays one of the highest reported binding affinities for RXR, with a dissociation constant in the low nanomolar range (approximately 3 nM), making it a very potent agent within its class (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Rexinoids such as LG100268 have been historically used in preclinical research as tools to explore RXR biology in oncology and metabolic studies—often by modulating gene transcription via RXR homodimers or RXR heterodimers with factors such as PPAR, LXR, and others (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). Although LG100268 was initially conceived for applications in cancer chemoprevention and metabolic regulation, its high potency and selective RXR activation have generated interest in repurposing it for diseases with an inflammatory component, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, LG100268 has been most notably explored in preclinical models of cancer—particularly in murine models of breast cancer. Studies in the MMTV-Neu (a HER2+ breast cancer model) and the MMTV-PyMT (an aggressive, triple-negative model) have shown that short-course dietary administration of LG100268 produces significant immunomodulatory effects. For example, in these models, LG100268 was observed to decrease the infiltration of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and CD206-expressing macrophages, while increasing the expression of PD-L1 and enhancing the ratio of cytotoxic CD8 T cells relative to CD4 T-cell subpopulations (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Additionally, combination studies with immune checkpoint inhibitors have further supported its potential to modulate the tumor microenvironment in preclinical oncology settings (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). In metabolic research, LG100268 has been administered to rodent models (such as diabetic ZDF rats and normal Sprague–Dawley rats) to evaluate its effects on lipid and glucose metabolism. In these contexts, LG100268 was shown to acutely lower serum glucose levels but also to induce marked hypertriglyceridemia linked to diminished lipoprotein lipase activity in muscle tissue, a pharmacodynamic liability that underscores the potent transcriptional effects mediated via RXR activation (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). Despite these promising activities in oncology and metabolic models, there are no documented studies, either preclinical or clinical, in which LG100268 has been directly used for treating dry AMD or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction. The entirety of its previous applications has been outside the ocular field, focusing on cancer chemoprevention and metabolic dysregulation; thus, its proposed repurposing for dry AMD represents an innovative but as-yet untested direction with respect to ocular indications (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lee & Khan, 2016, pp. 15–19).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, LG100268 acts as a high-affinity agonist for RXRs by binding selectively to the ligand-binding pocket of these nuclear receptors. RXRs are unique in that they function both as homodimers and as obligate heterodimer partners for multiple other nuclear receptors including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), liver X receptors (LXRs), and even possibly orphan receptors such as Nurr1. Upon binding LG100268, the RXR undergoes a conformational change that induces release of corepressors and recruitment of coactivators, thereby altering transcription of downstream target genes (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10). In cancer studies, the activation of RXR by LG100268 has been associated with modulation of the immune microenvironment; it reduces pro-tumor cytokine release, alters the balance of immune cell populations, and influences expression of cell surface proteins such as PD-L1 (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, in metabolic tissues, activation of RXR by LG100268 affects lipid metabolism through transcriptional control of genes involved in the regulation of lipoprotein lipase and other lipid-processing enzymes (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

The specific hypothesis proposed for dry AMD centers on the concept that selective RXR modulation might bias RXR heterodimerization toward partnering with Nurr1 in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-activated RPE cells. Nurr1, an orphan nuclear receptor, is implicated in anti-inflammatory responses and has been associated with maintenance of cellular differentiation and barrier function in various epithelial models. While direct evidence from the literature demonstrating RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation in RPE cells is limited, the general biology of RXR suggests that ligand-induced conformational changes in RXR can influence its choice of heterodimerization partner (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). In this scenario, by favoring the formation of RXR–Nurr1 heterodimers, LG100268 could suppress NF-κB-driven transcription. NF-κB is well known as a master regulator of inflammatory responses, and its activation (specifically the nuclear translocation of p65) can lead to the downregulation of tight junction proteins such as claudin-1. Therefore, by inhibiting NF-κB activity via this heterodimer bias, LG100268 is postulated to stabilize the epigenetic landscape and transcription of genes integral to maintaining tight junction integrity, thereby preserving transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE monolayers (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). Although most of the mechanistic studies of LG100268 have been conducted in cancer and metabolic models, the underlying molecular interactions—namely high-affinity RXR activation, selective heterodimerization, and subsequent transcriptional modulation—provide a plausible basis for extending its use to inflammatory conditions of the RPE. These mechanisms are potentially relevant since RPE cells express multiple RXR isoforms; indeed, RXR expression in retinal tissues underlines its importance in visual cycle regulation and cellular homeostasis (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10, 10–12).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the pathological insult is thought to be driven in part by chronic, low-grade inflammation induced by drusen components and other pro-inflammatory stimuli such as LPS. In primary RPE cell cultures challenged with LPS, there is typically a cascade of events initiated by the activation of NF-κB that results in a decrease in the expression of tight junction proteins like claudin-1, leading to reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and impaired barrier function. The hypothesis for repurposing LG100268 in this application is that at a concentration of 0.1 µM, the compound will attenuate LPS-induced NF-κB activation, as evidenced by reduced nuclear translocation of the p65 subunit. This in turn is expected to prevent the downregulation of claudin-1 and maintain TEER in RPE cells. The mechanism underpinning this expected effect involves the selective activation of RXR by LG100268, which is postulated to shift the balance of RXR heterodimers in favor of complexes with Nurr1. The RXR–Nurr1 heterodimer formation would then lead to anti-inflammatory transcriptional outcomes, including suppression of NF-κB target genes that would otherwise contribute to tight junction disruption (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

Additionally, by modulating the epigenetic regulation of gene expression, LG100268 may help preserve the expression pattern of genes critical for barrier integrity. Published reports in other cell systems have demonstrated that rexinoids can influence the transcription of key cytokines and growth factors in a manner that normalizes cell adhesion molecules and maintains cellular differentiation (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). Although these findings have principally been documented in models of cancer and metabolism, the extrapolation to RPE is supported by the fact that RXR-mediated pathways are conserved across multiple tissues, including ocular tissues. Should LG100268 effectively prevent TEER loss and reduce nuclear p65 accumulation in primary RPE cultures, it would provide a strong rationale for its further development as a novel therapy aimed at stabilizing the RPE barrier in dry AMD (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of LG100268 for dry AMD is an innovative approach that leverages the compound’s well-documented ability to selectively activate RXRs. Its high-affinity binding and potent agonism make it one of the more promising rexinoids available, as evidenced by its superior receptor binding kinetics relative to known RXR ligands such as bexarotene (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–10). Preclinical studies in oncology have consistently demonstrated that LG100268 modulates the immune microenvironment, induces changes in critical cytokine expression, and alters the balance of immune cell populations in a manner that collectively suggests an anti-inflammatory profile (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12). These anti-inflammatory effects, when viewed through the lens of RPE biology, provide a plausible mechanistic basis for protecting against the chronic inflammation that characterizes dry AMD. Particularly, the hypothesis that LG100268 may bias RXR heterodimer formation toward Nurr1—and thus suppress NF-κB signaling—opens a new avenue for preserving tight junction integrity in RPE cells, which is critically important in maintaining a proper barrier function (Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15; Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2).

Moreover, LG100268’s capacity to induce targeted epigenetic modulation further supports its potential to stabilize gene expression profiles under inflammatory conditions. Maintaining the expression of tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 is vital for preventing the breakdown of the blood–retina barrier and subsequent RPE degeneration. In vitro observations that LG100268 at 0.1 µM prevented TEER loss and inhibited NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation in primary RPE models provide encouraging preliminary data for its use in this context. This evidence, combined with its established anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties in other systems, makes a compelling case for considering LG100268 as a candidate for treating dry AMD (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 10–12; Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3).

Nevertheless, there are several challenges and uncertainties that must be addressed. Foremost among these is the absence of any prior documentation—either in the biomedical, clinical, or biochemical literature—that LG100268 has been applied in any ocular or RPE-specific context. Its therapeutic history is entirely rooted in applications related to cancer and metabolic regulation, and its safety profile in the context of ocular tissues remains uncharacterized. Systemic administration of potent rexinoids is known to produce adverse metabolic effects, such as hypertriglyceridemia and thyroid hormone axis suppression (Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3). These side effects raise concerns about potential off-target effects if LG100268 were to be repurposed for a chronic condition like dry AMD. The risk of systemic side effects may be mitigated by ocular-targeted delivery methods; however, the pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of LG100268 following ocular administration require thorough investigation.

Another significant weakness lies in the hypothesis that LG100268 will bias RXR heterodimerization toward Nurr1. Although the concept is mechanistically attractive, the current literature does not provide direct evidence that LG100268 preferentially promotes RXR–Nurr1 complexes in RPE cells (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Liby et al., 2007, pp. 8–9). In addition, the potential involvement of alternative RXR partners—including PPARs and LXRs, which are also expressed in RPE cells—could complicate the desired selectivity. Off-target modulation of these heterodimeric pathways could result in unintended changes in gene expression that might adversely affect RPE homeostasis.

Furthermore, while the proposed anti-inflammatory effects of LG100268 are supported by its ability to modulate cytokine profiles and immune cell populations in other models, the specific molecular pathways governing the maintenance of tight junction proteins in RPE cells are multifactorial. NF-κB signaling is only one among many pathways that regulate barrier integrity, and the extent to which RXR activation can counterbalance other detrimental signaling cascades in the RPE is not fully understood. The potential exists for complex cross-talk between RXR-mediated pathways and other nuclear receptor pathways, which might lead to unpredictable outcomes in the delicate environment of the retina (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 7–12; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

In summary, while LG100268’s established potency, receptor selectivity, and capacity to modulate inflammatory and metabolic gene expression provide a strong foundation for considering its repurposing, the current literature does not yet offer direct support for its use in dry AMD. Preclinical studies that specifically assess the effects of LG100268 on RPE barrier function, tight junction integrity, and inflammatory signaling in ocular models are necessary to validate the hypothesis. Moreover, rigorous toxicological assessments and the development of targeted delivery methods will be required to overcome the potential liabilities associated with systemic rexinoid administration. Until these issues are addressed, LG100268 remains a promising yet exploratory candidate for dry AMD therapy (Leal et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–10; Davies et al., 2001, pp. 1–3; Altucci et al., 2007, pp. 14–15).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose (α,α-trehalose) is a naturally occurring, nonreducing disaccharide composed of two d-glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond; it is broadly found in bacteria, fungi, insects, invertebrates, and plants but is not synthesized by vertebrates, including humans (trehalase in the small intestine hydrolyzes ingested trehalose to glucose) (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). Trehalose’s physicochemical properties include high aqueous solubility, chemical stability, and resistance to glucosidases; it has been mass-produced since the 1990s via enzymatic methods and has been approved for food use by EU regulators and the US FDA, with human exposure generally safe apart from low incidences of malabsorption (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3). In drug-development parlance, trehalose is a small-molecule, carbohydrate autophagy modulator and proteostasis regulator; it exhibits both biophysical “chemical chaperone” activity that stabilizes macromolecules and biologic activity that induces the autophagy–lysosome program via TFEB/TFE3 activation and related nutrient-sensing pathways (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Jeong et al., 2021, pp. 1–3, 12–13; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). As a class, autophagy-enhancing small molecules (including trehalose) have been utilized across neurodegeneration and metabolic disease models to promote clearance of toxic protein aggregates or dysfunctional organelles and to restore lysosomal function, with trehalose showing efficacy signals in preclinical Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, Huntington’s disease, and lysosomal storage–related models (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 27–32; Khalifeh et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Lotfi et al., 2018, pp. 12–15). Within ophthalmology, trehalose has established use as a topical osmoprotectant/bioprotective excipient in eye-drop formulations for dry-eye disease (commonly 3% w/v), and it is under active investigation for posterior-segment neuroprotection, including age-related retinal degeneration models relevant to AMD (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 18–20; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 10–13).

Therapeutic History  
Clinical/translational use: Trehalose is approved as a safe food ingredient and has been widely used in humans, including topical ophthalmic preparations for dry eye disease and post-LASIK care, with multiple clinical trials and a marketed formulation (e.g., Thealoz Duo, 3% trehalose plus hyaluronic acid) supporting ocular-surface safety and symptomatic benefit; the patented formulation increased tear film thickness after a single drop in clinical testing (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 18–20). Safety data support tolerability of topical trehalose in humans and of high-concentration in vitro exposure across multiple cell types; ocular-surface animal models show safety and barrier-protective effects, and in vitro human RPE studies report no loss of viability up to 200 mM for 24 h, though dosing windows matter for efficacy (Laihia & Kaarniranta, 2020, pp. 1–3, 5–7). Oral trehalose is hydrolyzed by intestinal trehalase and exhibits poor systemic bioavailability, limiting efficacy for some systemic indications; parenteral trehalose achieves low-millimolar plasma levels transiently, which can activate TFEB/TFE3 in macrophages in vivo, but oral exposure is generally insufficient to reach such systemic concentrations in mice in atherosclerosis models (Evans et al., 2018, pp. 2–3). Nonetheless, oral trehalose has shown retinal effects in mice, improving autophagy pathways and preserving cone ERG responses during aging, suggesting either BRB permeability or indirect choroidal effects; the authors noted that establishing BRB permeability is important for translation (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 181–188).

Ocular/retinal preclinical evidence: Multiple independent groups demonstrate mechanistic and functional efficacy of trehalose in RPE/retinal models relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology. In human RPE cell systems (ARPE-19, haRPE, and iPSC-RPE), trehalose increases autophagic flux (LC3-II accumulation with CQ, free GFP readouts), upregulates lysosomal biogenesis markers (LAMP-1/2, cathepsin D), elevates TFEB transcripts and protein, expands the lysosomal compartment (Lysotracker), engages both macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy, and confers autophagy-dependent protection against oxidative stressors such as hydroquinone (HQ), a cigarette smoke–derived oxidant implicated in AMD (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 151–160; Fisher et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). In these RPE systems, trehalose also shifts transcription toward anti-oxidative/anti-angiogenic profiles (NRF2 up, VEGF-A down; Hsp27 down), without evidence of trehalose-induced ROS/cell death at effective doses; however, higher doses can lose cytoprotection—despite ROS suppression—likely due to excessive autophagy, underscoring a narrow therapeutic window (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 154–155, 160–165). In primary murine RPE, trehalose restored autophagic flux under oxidative stress and improved mitochondrial respiratory function in vitro (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In vivo, topical trehalose eye drops increase autophagy–lysosome activity in mouse RPE (LC3B turnover, p62 degradation, LC3B–LAMP1 colocalization) and protect against light-induced outer retinal degeneration (preserving ONL thickness, RPE morphology, and junctional F-actin) without overt changes in unchallenged retina (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 10–13). Oral trehalose increased retinal autophagy and improved cone photopic ERG with age, and in a lysosomal enzyme-deficiency model (MPS IIIB) trehalose reduced retinal degeneration, restored retinal structure/function, and extended lifespan, with effects dependent on canonical autophagy and TFEB activation; trehalose increased TFEB nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene expression in brain and rescued retinal phenotypes (Abokyi, 2021, pp. 181–188; Lotfi et al., 2018, pp. 12–15).

AMD-model efficacy: In an APOE knockout model that recapitulates early AMD features (decreased retinal function, Bruch’s membrane thickening), chronic trehalose treatment ameliorated functional loss and reduced Bruch’s membrane thickening while normalizing autophagy markers (restoring LC3-II:LC3-I to WT, increasing LC3/LAMP1 labeling and autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE), with pathway analyses pointing to ATM–AMPK activation and, for trehalose, increased p38/MAPK14 signaling (Vessey et al., 2022, pp. 1–2, 11–13). In AMD-relevant human risk models, trehalose rescued lysosomal function in CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE—restoring LAMP1 and cathepsin D/L and reducing intracellular lipid accumulation (BODIPY) and APOE trend—consistent with TFEB activation independent of mTOR; in vivo, trehalose rescued CLEAR network expression and prevented basal laminar deposits in Cryba1 cKO retina and improved early RPE changes in Akt2 KI mice, positioning trehalose as an mTOR-independent TFEB activator that counteracts AKT2-driven lysosomal/autophagy defects (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15, 34–40; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Clinical status for AMD: A ClinicalTrials.gov query indicates at least two registered trials for “Trehalose AND macular degeneration,” but the excerpt provides no identifiers or results, so clinical evidence in AMD is presently insufficient for efficacy conclusions (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Collectively, these histories support trehalose as an autophagy/lysosome-modulating candidate with direct RPE/retina efficacy signals in AMD-relevant models, established human ocular-surface safety, and translational rationale for non-neovascular AMD (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Vessey et al., 2022, p. 1).
