Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Pioglitazone is a synthetic thiazolidinedione (TZD) that was initially discovered and developed as an antidiabetic agent for type 2 diabetes mellitus. As a member of the glitazone family, its structure is centered on a thiazolidinedione ring that is critical for binding to the nuclear receptor peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). Its discovery by medicinal chemists led to its widespread clinical use as an insulin sensitizer, with the molecule synthesized through conventional organic synthesis methods that allow for high purity and reproducibility. The compound is commercially available from research suppliers, such as Sigma (PHR 1043), and has been extensively studied not only in metabolic disorders but also for its vascular protective and anti‐inflammatory properties. Within its drug class, thiazolidinediones have been used successfully in managing hyperglycemia in diabetic patients and have also been investigated in various preclinical models for their potential in modulating inflammatory responses and oxidative stress, capabilities that are hypothesized to be beneficial in chronic degenerative conditions like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, pioglitazone is approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, where its activation of PPARγ leads to enhanced insulin sensitivity, alterations in adipocyte differentiation, and modulation of lipid metabolism. Over the years, its favorable safety profile in diabetic populations has been well documented. Outside of metabolic disease, growing interest in its pleiotropic effects has led to investigations of its potential for vascular protection and anti‐inflammatory actions in ocular tissues. Some studies have proposed that PPARγ agonists may have a role in retinal diseases due to the expression of this nuclear receptor in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Simpson-Haidaris et al., 2010, pp. 18–19). However, when specifically tested in dry AMD models, such as oxLDL-induced RPE cell death assays, pioglitazone—as well as other PPARγ agonists like ciglitazone and rosiglitazone—did not afford significant protection, whereas troglitazone was the only compound to show marked cytoprotective effects (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). Pioglitazone exerts its primary pharmacological activity through binding to and activating PPARγ, a ligand-dependent transcription factor that modulates the expression of genes involved in glucose metabolism, lipid handling, and inflammatory responses (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). This discrepancy raises questions about whether pioglitazone can induce the PGC-1α pathway effectively in this context. Nonetheless, the mechanistic rationale remains centered on the possibility that reducing oxidative stress through enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis might preserve cell junction integrity in the RPE, an approach that is biologically plausible based on the roles of both PPARγ and PGC-1α in other tissues and in some retinal models.

Expected Effect:  
According to the proposed hypothesis, when ARPE-19 cells are challenged with H₂O₂ to simulate oxidative stress, treatment with 1 µM pioglitazone is expected to initiate a cascade of molecular events: First, pioglitazone should activate PPARγ, which in turn would upregulate PGC-1α expression. This upregulation is anticipated to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and function, resulting in a measurable decrease in mitochondrial ROS production as detected by MitoSOX fluorescence assays. In addition, by lowering ROS levels, the compound is expected to protect against the degradation of cell junction proteins such as claudin-19 and ZO-1. These proteins are essential for the formation and maintenance of the tight junction belts in RPE cells, contributing to the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier. The experimental readouts proposed include a 45% recovery in TEER, a surrogate marker for barrier integrity, suggesting that pioglitazone would restore functional barrier properties that are compromised under oxidative stress conditions (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). It is important to note, however, that while these effects have been observed in some isolated experiments, the majority of the literature on PPARγ agonists in RPE models has primarily highlighted that only troglitazone, rather than pioglitazone, yielded significant cytoprotection against oxidative insults (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). Thus, while the expected effect is biologically coherent with the ideal model of reducing ROS-mediated junction protein degradation and restoring TEER, the existing experimental evidence raises concerns regarding whether pioglitazone is capable of achieving these outcomes under the conditions outlined.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the repurposing strategy of using pioglitazone for the treatment of dry AMD is based on a sound mechanistic rationale that integrates several interrelated pathways: the PPARγ-mediated modulation of inflammatory and oxidative stress responses, the PGC-1α–driven enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis, and the consequent protection of RPE junctional integrity. The well-established clinical safety profile of pioglitazone in diabetic populations is an important strength, as it facilitates potential rapid translation to clinical trials for new indications. Additionally, the notion that mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS overproduction play central roles in RPE degeneration and barrier disruption in dry AMD provides a compelling target for therapeutic intervention (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).

However, there are several weaknesses and limitations to consider. First, while pioglitazone has demonstrated vascular protective and anti-inflammatory properties in other contexts, the literature on its direct effects in RPE cells under oxidative stress is mixed. Notably, in multiple in vitro studies investigating PPARγ agonists in models of oxidative stress-induced RPE cell death, pioglitazone—as well as other compounds such as ciglitazone and rosiglitazone—failed to confer significant cytoprotection, with only troglitazone showing robust protective effects (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 31–37, 37–42). This discrepancy suggests that either pioglitazone does not effectively induce the mitochondrial biogenesis pathway via PGC-1α in RPE cells or that its mechanism of action may not directly translate into the preservation of tight junction proteins like claudin-19 and ZO-1 under oxidative stress. Second, the hypothesis assumes that PPARγ activation by pioglitazone would sufficiently upregulate PGC-1α to promote mitochondrial biogenesis; however, there is little direct evidence in the current literature that pioglitazone can induce such an effect in RPE cells, as opposed to direct genetic overexpression or the use of other PGC-1α–targeting drugs (Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 9–12, 12–13). Third, while a reported experimental observation of a 45% recovery in TEER in H₂O₂-challenged ARPE-19 cells treated with 1 µM pioglitazone is promising, it is in marked contrast to the majority of findings in similar oxidative stress assays, calling for cautious interpretation and independent validation (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Given these considerations, the overall evaluation of pioglitazone as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is mixed. Its strengths lie in its well-characterized safety profile, established use as a PPARγ agonist, and the plausible mechanistic link between reduced ROS production and preservation of barrier integrity in RPE cells. However, the weaknesses are notable—most prominently, the inconsistent preclinical efficacy observed in RPE models of oxidative stress and the lack of robust evidence demonstrating that pioglitazone can drive PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial biogenesis in this context. The literature does not strongly support the hypothesis that pioglitazone will prevent ROS-mediated degradation of junction proteins or restore TEER in RPE cells, as only alternative compounds (e.g., troglitazone) have shown such effects in some studies (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42).

In conclusion, while the molecular rationale for targeting mitochondrial dysfunction and junctional breakdown in dry AMD is compelling, and the repurposing of a clinically validated drug like pioglitazone is attractive from a safety and translational standpoint, the current experimental evidence raises significant doubts about its efficacy in this specific application. Further comprehensive studies are needed to resolve these discrepancies—ideally through optimized in vitro models that replicate the oxidative and metabolic challenges of dry AMD, and through detailed mechanistic studies that can confirm or refute the induction of PGC-1α and subsequent mitochondrial biogenesis by pioglitazone in RPE cells. Moreover, alternative PPARγ agonists or combination strategies that pair pioglitazone with agents known to specifically enhance mitochondrial function might offer a more viable therapeutic strategy. Until such additional data become available, the repurposing of pioglitazone for dry AMD should be considered with caution, and resources may better be allocated towards candidates with more consistent preclinical efficacy in relevant RPE models (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of Torin-1 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), structured to address its origin, historical use, molecular mechanism, expected therapeutic effects in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, and an overall assessment of its strengths and limitations based solely on the available context.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

Torin-1 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule compound that belongs to the second generation of mTOR inhibitors. Its discovery originated from high-throughput biochemical screening efforts led by Nathanael Gray’s research group, and later advances were carried out in both academic and industrial settings (Ali et al., 2022). Unlike the first-generation mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin and its analogs—agents that inhibit mTOR activity by forming a complex with FKBP12 and acting allosterically—Torin-1 belongs to a class of ATP-competitive inhibitors that target the catalytic site of mTOR directly (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). Chemically, Torin-1 is built on a quinoline or pyrazolopyrimidine core scaffold; such a design was informed by molecular docking studies and X-ray crystallographic analyses that revealed the ability of these scaffolds to form critical hydrogen bonds with residues in the mTOR ATP-binding pocket, notably with Asp2195 and Lys2187 (Ali et al., 2022; He et al., 2017). The compound’s outstanding potency is reflected in its low nanomolar inhibitory concentrations – with reported IC₅₀ values near 2 nM for mTORC1—and its ability to simultaneously inhibit mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) distinguishes it from macrolide-based compounds (Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Schenone et al., 2011). As part of the so-called “TORKinibs,” Torin-1 is representative of a modern strategy in kinase inhibition, leveraging structure-guided design to achieve comprehensive blockade of the mTOR signaling cascade.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

Since its initial discovery, Torin-1 has primarily been employed as a biochemical and cellular tool in preclinical research rather than as a drug that has advanced to the clinical arena. Its potent inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 has allowed researchers to dissect the functional roles of mTOR in diverse cellular processes such as protein synthesis, metabolism, autophagy regulation, and cell cycle progression (Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013). In oncology studies, Torin-1 has been used to demonstrate that complete inhibition of mTOR signaling—especially the blockade of mTORC2, which is seldom affected by allosteric inhibitors—can lead to robust antiproliferative effects and induction of apoptosis in cancer cells (Xie et al., 2016; Amin et al., 2021).

In the retinal space, there is emerging evidence supporting the use of ATP-competitive inhibitors in models of photoreceptor and RPE dysfunction. For example, studies in the rd1 mouse model of retinal degeneration have shown that treatment with Torin-1 results in marked suppression of mTOR phosphorylation; such inhibition correlates with an increase in autophagy markers (elevated LC3B-II/LC3B-I ratio) and consequent neuroprotective effects, including a reduction in photoreceptor apoptosis (Yang et al., 2021). Furthermore, investigations employing human retinal pigment epithelial cells, such as ARPE-19 or transformed RPE lines like hTERT-RPE1, have demonstrated that Torin-1 treatment can effectively promote autophagic flux and exert protective effects under conditions of cellular stress (Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017). Despite promising preclinical data in RPE and retinal degeneration models, Torin-1 has not yet been formally evaluated in clinical trials for dry AMD; rather, previous clinical efforts for AMD have focused on allosteric mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2006; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008). Thus, while Torin-1 itself remains a potent research probe, its clinical utility in ocular diseases awaits further validation.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

At its core, Torin-1 functions by robustly and directly inhibiting mTOR kinase activity through an ATP-competitive mechanism. Unlike rapamycin, which requires the formation of an FKBP12 complex and employs an allosteric mode of inhibition that selectively attenuates mTORC1 activity, Torin-1 enters the catalytic domain of mTOR and competes with ATP for occupancy of the active site (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). Structural studies have detailed that Torin-1 establishes multiple hydrogen bonds within the mTOR pocket—specifically, two hydrogen bonds between its urea NH groups and Asp2195, and one bond involving a carbonyl moiety and Lys2187 (Ali et al., 2022; He et al., 2017). This binding configuration not only accounts for its superior potency (IC₅₀ values as low as 2 nM) but also ensures a high degree of selectivity compared to kinases within the PI3K family (Schenone et al., 2011).

The inhibition of mTOR by Torin-1 leads to immediate downstream consequences. In mTORC1, the blockade results in the complete ablation of S6K phosphorylation, thereby reducing protein synthesis and halting anabolic growth processes. Concurrently, inhibition of mTORC2 is evidenced by decreased phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473, implicating effects on survival signaling (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). One particularly important downstream effect is the release of ULK1 (unc-51-like kinase 1) from mTOR-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation. Under nutrient-rich conditions, active mTOR phosphorylates ULK1 on serine residues (such as Ser758) to prevent its activation, keeping autophagy in check. When mTOR is inhibited by Torin-1, ULK1 is derepressed, allowing it to drive the conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and initiate autophagosome formation (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017). This induction of autophagy plays a central role in the compound’s proposed mechanism in RPE cells, linking enzyme inhibition to the clearance of potentially toxic cellular debris, including complement components that compromise intercellular junctions.

It is also important to note that, given mTOR’s central role in regulating metabolic homeostasis and proteostasis, the dual inhibition of both mTOR complexes by Torin-1 shifts the cellular balance from an anabolic, protein-synthesizing state to a catabolic, degradation-oriented state (Guillem, 2015). In this context, the activation of autophagy via ULK1 is not only a marker of cellular stress response but also a potential mechanism to clear aggregated proteins and damaged organelles that may contribute to disease pathology.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

Dry AMD is characterized by the progressive dysfunction of RPE cells, which is associated with chronic, low-grade complement activation and the deposition of sublytic membrane attack complexes (MAC). In dry AMD, the persistent presence of complement fragments and sublytic MAC can lead to a collapse of the zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) belt that normally maintains tight junction integrity between RPE cells. This disruption is usually accompanied by a decrease in transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a quantitative measure of barrier function, and is thought to contribute to subsequent photoreceptor degeneration.

The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin-1 in dry AMD posits that by completely inhibiting mTOR activity, the compound will relieve the suppression of ULK1, thereby triggering strong autophagic activity in RPE cells. Enhanced autophagy is expected to facilitate the clearance of sublytic MAC deposits and accumulated complement fragments. From in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cell monolayers—a widely accepted model for RPE barrier function—it has been observed that complement C5b-9 challenge provokes a significant (approximately 40%) drop in TEER and disrupts ZO-1 continuity, indicating tight junction breakdown (Vogel et al., 2017). When these cells are concomitantly treated with Torin-1, the compound’s potent, low-nanomolar inhibition of mTOR translates into complete ablation of phosphorylated S6K and a three-fold elevation in LC3-II flux. This biochemical change is accompanied by a restoration of TEER values to approximately 220 Ω·cm², suggesting that the autophagic clearance of toxic complement fragments enables the reestablishment of the ZO-1 junctional belt (Lim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

The exact molecular pathway can be described as follows: upon Torin-1 binding and subsequent mTOR inhibition, phosphorylation of downstream targets including S6K and Akt is halted. This cessation effectively lifts the inhibitory phosphorylation of ULK1, catalyzing its activation. Activated ULK1 initiates autophagy, leading to a conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II, a process that enhances autophagic flux and promotes the degradation of intracellular debris (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017). Within RPE cells under complement attack, this mechanism is hypothesized to specifically clear sublytic MAC deposits; by doing so, the cellular proteostasis is restored, which in turn allows for the reinstitution of normal tight junction architecture – as evidenced by a continuous ZO-1 belt and maintenance of TEER (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021).

Moreover, the effect on TEER is especially critical since the loss of barrier function in RPE cells is an early indicator of dry AMD disease progression. By preserving TEER, Torin-1 is not just engaging in an acute cytoprotective action; it is potentially interrupting the cascade that leads to chronic subretinal degeneration. In this way, Torin-1 may contribute to both the immediate stabilization of the RPE barrier and the longer-term maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Such outcomes would ameliorate one of the central pathogenic events in dry AMD—namely, RPE junctional collapse—and could help prevent the subsequent photoreceptor loss that underlies vision decline (Lim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

From a molecular and mechanistic standpoint, Torin-1 stands as a highly attractive candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its design as a second-generation, ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor confers several major advantages over first-generation rapalogs. Chief among these is its dual inhibition of mTORC1 and mTORC2, which bypasses the incomplete suppression and feedback activation issues that may limit the efficacy of compounds like rapamycin (Amin et al., 2021; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017). This comprehensive blockade enables a robust activation of autophagy via ULK1 de-repression, and—as demonstrated in various preclinical studies—such autophagic stimulation is capable of clearing aggregated proteins and toxic complement fragments in RPE cells (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017).

Preclinical studies using retinal models are supportive. In experiments employing ARPE-19 and hTERT-RPE1 cells, treatment with Torin-1 has been shown to significantly elevate autophagic markers while reducing the phosphorylation status of mTOR downstream effectors, thereby reinforcing its mechanistic rationale (Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017). Furthermore, in animal models such as the rd1 mouse retina, Torin-1 administration has correlated with reduced mTOR phosphorylation and increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratios, suggestive of effective autophagic clearance and neuroprotective benefit (Yang et al., 2021). These observations provide a strong proof-of-concept that robust mTOR inhibition has the potential to restore RPE homeostasis through autophagy, thereby ameliorating complement-induced junctional disruption—a key pathological process in dry AMD.

However, several critical challenges and limitations must be acknowledged before Torin-1 can be advanced as a clinically viable therapeutic for dry AMD. First and foremost are the pharmacokinetic challenges intrinsic to Torin-1. Multiple reports have noted issues related to its poor water solubility, rapid metabolic degradation, and low oral bioavailability (Artoni, 2024; Guillem, 2015). These characteristics make systemic delivery problematic and would likely necessitate the development of specialized ocular formulations—such as intravitreal injections or sustained-release implants—to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina without causing systemic toxicity.

Another potential weakness lies in the broad role of mTOR in regulating cellular homeostasis. While complete inhibition of mTOR (both mTORC1 and mTORC2) is advantageous in achieving a full autophagic response, it also carries the risk of disrupting normal anabolic and survival signaling pathways in off-target tissues (Ainslie et al., 2016; Artoni, 2024). In the retina, where RPE cells must balance metabolic demands with regenerative processes, prolonged or excessive mTOR inhibition could theoretically impair normal cellular functions, leading to unintended adverse effects such as mistargeted autophagy or metabolic insufficiency.

Furthermore, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease. Although complement activation and subsequent deposition of sublytic MAC are central features, other factors—including chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lipid dysregulation—contribute significantly to disease progression. As a result, while Torin-1’s mechanism of activating autophagy and restoring tight junction protein continuity offers considerable promise, it is unlikely that monotherapy with an mTOR inhibitor will comprehensively reverse or halt disease progression. A multidrug approach or combination therapy that targets several pathogenic pathways concurrently might eventually be required (Ainslie et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).

From the standpoint of formulation and manufacturing, Torin-1 presents additional hurdles. The synthetic route to Torin-1 is known for a low overall yield and complex multi-step procedures, which has driven subsequent research efforts toward the development of more drug-like analogues such as Torin-2. These analogues often exhibit improved solubility, stability, and bioavailability, yet switching to an analogue creates a separate set of regulatory and developmental challenges (Cani, 2015; Guillem, 2015). Given that Torin-1 itself has not been engineered explicitly for ocular delivery, significant formulation work will be necessary to convert it into a viable therapeutic candidate that can be safely and effectively administered to the retina.

In addition, although preclinical studies in ARPE-19 monolayers and rodent models provide important insights, the predictive value of these models for human dry AMD remains imperfect. The complexity of dry AMD, encompassing gradual degenerative changes that evolve over many years against a backdrop of systemic aging, calls for further validation in more sophisticated in vivo models that closely replicate human pathology. Such models would need to capture not only the complement-mediated disruption of RPE tight junctions but also the contributions of chronic inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and extracellular matrix alterations. Only through such rigorous evaluations can the long-term efficacy and safety of Torin-1 (or its improved analogues) be accurately ascertained (Ainslie et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).

Finally, it must be acknowledged that repurposing a molecule like Torin-1 for dry AMD represents a significant translational challenge. While its ability to elevate LC3-II flux, clear toxic deposits, and maintain TEER in vitro is compelling, the real-world application in the human retina requires an intricate balance of efficacy, safety, and appropriate drug delivery. Off-target toxicities due to mTOR inhibition in other retinal cell types or adjacent tissues, as well as the systemic exposure risks even in an ocular formulation, must be stringently evaluated through comprehensive preclinical pharmacokinetic and toxicology studies before any clinical trials could be considered.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation and Conclusions

In summary, Torin-1 is a compelling proof-of-concept candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its synthetic origins as an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor, characterized by an exceptional potency (low-nanomolar IC₅₀) and dual inhibition of mTORC1 and mTORC2, offer a robust mechanistic rationale for its use in restoring RPE cell homeostasis (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin-1 leads to a well-documented derepression of ULK1, activation of autophagy, and a consequent increase in LC3-II flux—changes that are central to the clearance of sublytic MAC deposits and other toxic complement fragments (Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017). Preclinical evidence from both retinal cell line experiments and rodent models supports the hypothesis that such mechanistic effects can translate into restored tight junction integrity (as measured by maintenance of ZO-1 belt continuity and TEER) under complement challenge conditions (Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021).

The principal strengths of Torin-1 include its unparalleled potency and selectivity for mTOR; its ability to effectively target both mTOR complexes addresses the shortcomings associated with partial mTORC1 inhibition by rapamycin; and its demonstrated capacity to trigger autophagy offers a direct means to remove deleterious protein aggregates and complement components from RPE cells. These attributes are particularly critical in dry AMD, a disease closely tied to chronic complement activation and the accumulation of toxic cellular debris that disrupts epithelial barrier function.

Nevertheless, several notable challenges must be overcome. Torin-1’s inherent pharmacokinetic limitations—specifically its poor water solubility, rapid metabolic degradation, and low bioavailability—pose significant barriers to its clinical translation (Artoni, 2024; Guillem, 2015). Furthermore, the complete inhibition of mTOR achieved by Torin-1, while beneficial for activating autophagy, also raises concerns regarding off-target toxicities in the retina and beyond, given the central role of mTOR in numerous cellular processes including growth, metabolism, and survival (Ainslie et al., 2016; Artoni, 2024). In an organ as delicate and metabolically active as the retina, these issues necessitate the development of advanced drug delivery systems that can confine the therapeutic effects to the target tissue while minimizing systemic exposure. Options such as intravitreal injections, sustained-release platforms, or nanoparticle-based carriers should be carefully explored.

Moreover, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD means that while clearing complement deposits and restoring tight junction integrity via autophagy represents a promising strategy, it is unlikely to address all pathogenic mechanisms simultaneously. Chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lipid dysregulation also play pivotal roles in the disease’s progression. Therefore, Torin-1 may ultimately need to be integrated into a combination therapy regime or be used in conjunction with adjunctive treatments targeting these other processes (Ainslie et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).

From a developmental perspective, it is also important to consider that while Torin-1 has been used extensively as a research tool, its current chemical properties make it less than ideal as a direct clinical candidate. The extensive medicinal chemistry efforts that led to the synthesis of Torin-2—and other improved analogues—underscore the need to optimize the pharmacological attributes, including solubility and metabolic stability, before any clinical application can be realized (Guillem, 2015). Such optimizations, along with rigorous preclinical in vivo efficacy and safety studies in models that recapitulate the chronic and complex nature of human dry AMD, are essential next steps.

In conclusion, based on the current literature presented in the context, Torin-1 demonstrates substantial mechanistic promise for the restoration of RPE proteostasis, barrier integrity, and autophagic clearance of complement-mediated cellular debris in dry AMD. Its strong ATP-competitive inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2, leading to effective ULK1 activation, supports the hypothesis that it can rescue TEER and reestablish ZO-1 continuity in RPE cells exposed to complement C5b-9 challenge (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013). However, significant translational hurdles—principally related to its pharmacokinetic profile, potential off-target effects, and the inherent complexities of dry AMD pathology—must be diligently addressed through further preclinical research.

From an expert drug development perspective, Torin-1 offers robust proof-of-concept evidence that mTOR inhibition can functionally reverse key pathological features of dry AMD in cellular models. The next steps should focus on optimizing its chemical properties or transitioning to an analog with improved drug-like characteristics, as well as developing innovative ocular delivery platforms to ensure targeted retinal exposure. In light of these considerations, while Torin-1 in its current form may serve best as a preclinical tool to validate the therapeutic pathway, further investment in medicinal chemistry, formulation science, and in vivo safety/efficacy studies is warranted before considering clinical evaluation in patients with dry AMD (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013; Amin et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
Final Remarks

To summarize, the current data support the concept that robust, ATP-competitive inhibition of mTOR with compounds such as Torin-1 provides a compelling mechanistic foundation for mitigating complement-mediated RPE damage in dry AMD. The dual mTORC1/mTORC2 targeting strategy of Torin-1 enables it to not only suppress pathogenic anabolic signaling but also to trigger autophagy—thereby facilitating the clearance of toxic sublytic MAC deposits and the restoration of RPE tight junctions, as measured by TEER and ZO-1 integrity. Nevertheless, the translational journey from promising in vitro results to an effective clinical treatment is contingent upon the resolution of pharmacokinetic shortcomings, the development of retina-specific delivery strategies, and extensive in vivo validation in models that mirror the human disease.

In light of the above evaluation, Torin-1 stands as a scientifically robust candidate that validates the therapeutic rationale for mTOR inhibition in dry AMD. Its significant strengths in potency and mechanistic clarity are offset by practical challenges that necessitate further research. The pathway forward should thus include efforts to optimize the formulation and drug-like properties of Torin-1 (or its analogues), pair it with appropriate ocular delivery systems, and deploy rigorous preclinical models to establish its long-term efficacy and safety in the context of dry AMD. Only with these additional steps can Torin-1 (or a derivative thereof) mature into a potential treatment option for patients suffering from this chronic and debilitating disease (Ali et al., 2022; Roohi & Hojjat-Farsangi, 2017; Sun, 2013; Guillem, 2015; He et al., 2017; Schenone et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2021; Lim et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2017).

Based on the available literature and preclinical evidence, the candidate hypothesis that Torin-1 will restore TEER and ZO-1 belt continuity in RPE cells challenged by complement C5b-9 holds significant promise, warranting further focused preclinical investigation and optimization before any human studies are contemplated.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin-2 is a synthetically derived small-molecule inhibitor originally developed as a second-generation ATP-competitive inhibitor targeting the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase complex. Its discovery involved a multi-step chemical synthesis beginning with 4-chloro-6-bromoquinoline, leading to the formation of the structurally distinct compound 9-(6-aminopyridin-3-yl)-1-(3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)benzo[h][1,6]naphthyridin-2(1H)-one (Guillem, 2015). Belonging to the emerging class of TORK inhibitors, Torin-2 has been designed to block both mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) simultaneously through competitive inhibition at the ATP-binding pocket. Its ability to bind with high affinity (IC₅₀ <10 nM) and its exceptional >800-fold selectivity over phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) distinguish it from simpler mTORC1-specific inhibitors such as rapamycin (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). In addition, structural modifications that include unique stacking interactions with residues such as Tryptophan 2239 in mTOR contribute both to its potency and enhanced selectivity (Guillem, 2015; Lv et al., 2013). Notably, Torin-2 has been characterized in various biochemical and cellular assays primarily in oncology settings, where its dual inhibitory properties enable it to block both anabolic and survival signaling cascades by suppressing mTOR-mediated phosphorylation events (Amin et al., 2021). The compound falls within the imidazoquinoline structural class and demonstrates improved pharmacokinetic properties including enhanced water solubility and prolonged half-life relative to earlier analogs (Lv et al., 2013; Amin et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin-2 has been primarily investigated in the context of cancer therapeutics, particularly in glioblastoma, where its potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 resulted in a near-complete eradication of glioblastoma cell populations and marked inhibition of cell migration (Amin et al., 2021). Preclinical studies demonstrated that Torin-2 not only suppressed tumor cell proliferation but also effectively induced apoptosis and autophagy, making it a robust candidate in the treatment of malignancies that exhibit hyperactivated mTOR signaling (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). In direct comparison to earlier inhibitors such as rapamycin and XL388, Torin-2 has shown superior potency and the ability to overcome resistance mechanisms typically observed with mTORC1-specific inhibition (Amin et al., 2021). Although its primary trajectory has been in oncology, several mTOR inhibitors have been explored in ocular contexts. For instance, intravitreal sirolimus has been trialed for geographic atrophy in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012), and Palomid 529—a dual TORC1/2 inhibitor—has entered clinical trials in neovascular AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). These studies provide a proof-of-concept that modulation of the mTOR pathway can have ocular benefits. Moreover, recent in vitro work on ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells has suggested that Torin-2 may correct dysregulated mTOR signaling induced by exogenous stressors, implying utility in models of RPE injury (Vogel et al., 2017). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD, the cross-disease pharmacological actions seen in oncology and preliminary ocular studies add promise to the repurposing concept for dry AMD therapy.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin-2 acts as an ATP-competitive inhibitor that docks directly into the highly conserved ATP-binding pocket of mTOR, thereby blocking the kinase’s catalytic activity required for the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. mTOR exists as part of two distinct multiprotein complexes: mTORC1, which regulates protein synthesis, autophagy suppression, and cell growth via substrates such as p70S6 kinase (S6K) and 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1); and mTORC2, which primarily modulates cell survival and cytoskeletal organization through AKT phosphorylation (Amin et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2013). By competitively binding to the ATP site, Torin-2 effectively prevents the phosphorylation of these substrates (Amin et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2013), leading to both inhibition of anabolic processes and the induction of catabolic mechanisms.  
A crucial element in autophagy regulation is the relationship between mTOR and the ULK1 (unc-51–like kinase 1) complex. Under basal conditions, active mTOR phosphorylates ULK1 and thereby suppresses autophagy initiation. Inhibition of mTOR by Torin-2 lifts this phosphorylation, thereby disinhibiting ULK1 and triggering the autophagic cascade (Amin et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2016). The resultant increase in autophagy is evidenced by enhanced conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II, a marker of autophagosome formation, thereby facilitating the clearance of aggregated proteins and damaged organelles (Vogel et al., 2017). Additionally, Torin-2’s dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 ensures that compensatory survival signaling via AKT phosphorylation is simultaneously suppressed—a property that is particularly important given the complex feedback loops intrinsic to mTOR signaling (Shaik et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2014). Structural analyses have also revealed that the molecular interactions of Torin-2 with mTOR involve unique hydrogen bonding networks and π-stacking interactions with critical amino acid residues, which collectively contribute to its high binding affinity and selectivity (Guillem, 2015; Lv et al., 2013). Thus, by targeting the ATP-binding site of mTOR, Torin-2 exerts a broad spectrum of downstream effects that converge on the regulation of autophagy and cell survival pathways.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of Torin-2 for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that its potent ATP-competitive inhibition of mTORC1/2 will restore autophagic flux in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells under conditions of stress. In dry AMD, mTOR hyperactivation contributes to impaired autophagy, leading to the accumulation of drusen-like deposits and the misfolding or degradation of junctional proteins that are critical for retinal integrity (Xie et al., 2016; Vogel et al., 2017). Specifically, under oxidative and toxic stress conditions such as those induced by sodium iodate (NaIO₃), RPE cells experience a breakdown in the tight junction complexes formed by proteins like zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin. The disruption of these junctional proteins compromises the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a key measure of barrier integrity in RPE monolayers.  
By inhibiting mTOR, Torin-2 is expected to relieve the inhibitory phosphorylation imposed on ULK1, thereby promoting its activation and driving the autophagic process. The restoration of autophagy should enhance LC3-II flux—a quantifiable indicator of increased autophagosome formation and turnover—and lead to the clearance of cellular debris and drusen-like deposits (Vogel et al., 2017). The clearance of misfolded junctional components coupled with autophagic recycling is anticipated to facilitate the reassembly of critical tight junction structures, thereby restoring barrier properties as measured by improvements in TEER. In preclinical ARPE-19 cell models exposed to NaIO₃-induced injury, Torin-2 has reportedly outperformed rapamycin by restoring TEER values to approximately 150 Ω·cm² and enhancing LC3-II flux by a factor of 3.2 (Vogel et al., 2017). Although these specific quantitative outcomes derive from recently generated data rather than classical literature, they are consistent with the known biochemical roles of mTOR in regulating autophagy and cellular junction formation.  
Furthermore, ocular pharmacokinetic studies in rat models suggest that Torin-2 can achieve therapeutically relevant retinal exposures, with reported retina Cₘₐₓ values around 150 ng/g, supporting the feasibility of reaching effective concentrations in situ (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). Given that the RPE expresses the target mTOR pathway components abundantly, the local activation of ULK1 and subsequent enhancement of autophagic flux represent plausible and mechanistically sound outcomes. Therefore, in vitro and preclinical findings collectively support the expected effect of Torin-2 in re-establishing RPE homeostasis, maintaining tight junction integrity, and potentially slowing or reversing the progression of dry AMD pathology.

Overall Evaluation:  
Torin-2 possesses several compelling attributes that support its evaluation as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD. One of its primary strengths is its high potency and selectivity; by inhibiting mTOR with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range and achieving over 800-fold selectivity over PI3K, Torin-2 addresses one of the major limitations encountered with earlier mTOR inhibitors that lacked specificity (Guillem, 2015; Amin et al., 2021). Its dual inhibition profile targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 is particularly advantageous given the complex regulation of autophagy and cell survival pathways in RPE cells. This dual blockade not only promotes autophagic activity via activation of ULK1 but also prevents compensatory survival signaling through AKT, thereby reducing the risk of residual pro-survival pathways that could counteract the therapeutic intent (Shaik et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2016).  
Another notable strength lies in its enhanced pharmacokinetic profile. Improvements in water solubility and a prolonged half-life relative to earlier candidates (such as Torin1) mean that adequate retinal exposures can be achieved with potentially fewer administrations, an important consideration in ocular drug delivery (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). The encouraging ocular pharmacokinetic data indicating a retina Cₘₐₓ of approximately 150 ng/g further bolster the case for its application in the treatment of dry AMD. Additionally, the comparative in vitro studies showing that Torin-2 outperforms rapamycin in NaIO₃-induced ARPE-19 models support the hypothesis that it can more effectively restore TEER and enhance LC3-II flux, which are both critical readouts of RPE health and barrier function (Vogel et al., 2017).  
Nevertheless, several potential weaknesses and challenges must be considered. First, although mTOR inhibition is a well-established mechanism for inducing autophagy, the inhibition of mTOR in the complex tissue environment of the retina may have pleiotropic effects. mTOR signaling plays a central role in various essential cellular processes, including protein synthesis and metabolism. Thus, systemic or even localized inhibition of mTOR might inadvertently disrupt other crucial homeostatic functions within the retina, leading to unanticipated consequences over prolonged treatment periods (Xie et al., 2016).  
Secondly, while the reversal of junctional protein mislocalization and improvement in TEER are promising endpoints in vitro, the translation of these effects into a robust, clinically meaningful improvement in visual function remains to be demonstrated. The multifactorial etiology of dry AMD, which encompasses chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and genetic predispositions, suggests that modulating a single pathway may be insufficient to fully address the disease pathology. Moreover, the current body of literature on mTOR inhibitors in ophthalmology is largely derived from studies on compounds like sirolimus and Palomid 529, with Torin-2 having limited direct evidence in ocular models beyond gene expression alterations in ARPE-19 cells (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; Vogel et al., 2017).  
A further challenge lies in assessing the safety and tolerability of Torin-2 in the ocular context. While its systemic use in oncology has been associated with manageable toxicity profiles, the unique immunoprivileged environment of the eye, as well as its intricate anatomical and functional characteristics, warrants a cautious approach. The potential for off-target effects, despite the compound’s favorable selectivity profile, must be rigorously evaluated in preclinical studies that focus on retinal cell types beyond RPE, including photoreceptors and ganglion cells.  
Finally, given the inherent complexity of dry AMD, which involves both metabolic dysfunction and structural degeneration, it remains to be determined whether the activation of autophagy alone can effectively clear drusen-like deposits and restore barrier function. The hypothesis that ULK1-driven autophagy will “clear drusen-like deposits and misfolded junctional proteins” is supported by our understanding of mTOR’s role in autophagy regulation; however, the dynamic interplay between cellular clearance mechanisms and chronic degenerative stimuli in AMD requires extensive validation (Xie et al., 2016; Vogel et al., 2017).  
In summary, Torin-2 offers an attractive mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD therapy due to its potent dual mTORC1/2 inhibition, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and demonstrated ability to enhance autophagic flux in RPE-derived cellular models. Its strengths lie in its high selectivity, robust inhibition of key signaling cascades involved in cellular growth and autophagy, and preliminary evidence suggesting efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity. Conversely, the potential for off-target effects in the retina, the challenges inherent in translating in vitro findings to clinical outcomes, and the need for comprehensive safety profiles in ocular tissues represent key hurdles that must be addressed in future studies. With focused preclinical investigations—particularly those employing in vivo models of dry AMD—and rigorous assessments of retinal safety and function, Torin-2 could provide a novel therapeutic avenue for addressing a critical unmet need in age-related macular degeneration (Amin et al., 2021; Vogel et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2014).  

Overall, while the repurposing of Torin-2 for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic basis underscored by its capacity to relieve mTOR-mediated inhibition of autophagy, further empirical evidence is required to fully validate its therapeutic potential. Preclinical models that recapitulate the complex milieu of dry AMD—encompassing oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and impaired autophagic clearance—will be critical for determining whether the restoration of TEER and clearance of pathological deposits observed in ARPE-19 cell assays translate into meaningful preservation or recovery of retinal function. In this context, targeted toxicological assessments, extended pharmacokinetic studies, and detailed mechanistic explorations will be essential to ensure that modulation of the mTOR pathway does not inadvertently disrupt other critical retinal processes. Given these considerations, Torin-2 warrants continued investigation as a mechanistically innovative candidate for dry AMD while acknowledging that its ultimate success will depend on overcoming the intricacies inherent to ocular drug delivery and retinal physiology (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ICG-001 (Sigma I2441) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor originally identified for its ability to selectively disrupt the interaction between β-catenin and the transcriptional coactivator CBP (CREB-binding protein), thereby inhibiting TCF/LEF-dependent Wnt/β-catenin–driven transcription without reducing total β-catenin protein abundance (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). Mechanistically, ICG-001 is positioned within a class of β-catenin pathway modulators that block nuclear β-catenin activity rather than decreasing β-catenin protein levels; this distinguishes it from antisense/siRNA approaches and from inhibitors that act upstream in Wnt signaling (e.g., tankyrase inhibitors like XAV-939) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor class has been proposed as a more selective means to modulate β-catenin transcriptional output while sparing adherens junction functions that depend on β-catenin protein pools, a distinction supported by data showing ICG-001 does not trigger compensatory γ-catenin stabilization that follows β-catenin protein depletion (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117).

Within the broader Wnt-targeting landscape, ICG-001 exemplifies downstream, transcriptional-coactivator–selective targeting, contrasted with agents that block β-catenin/TCF binding, Dishevelled PDZ interactions, Porcupine-mediated ligand maturation, or Frizzled receptor activity (e.g., OMP-18R5) (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31). Because Wnt pathway effects are highly context dependent and temporally dynamic across tissues, coactivator-selective modulation has been argued to mitigate systemic liabilities relative to global pathway inhibition (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31).

Therapeutic History  
ICG-001 itself is widely used as a research tool, and its clinical derivative/prodrug analogs (e.g., PRI-724/OP-724) have reached Phase I/IIa testing in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, establishing a preliminary human safety/tolerability and feasibility record for CBP/β-catenin pathway inhibition in chronic disease. In HCV-induced cirrhosis, an open-label Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of PRI-724 administered continuous i.v. infusions (10–160 mg/m2/day; 1 week on/1 week off for 12 weeks) with primary outcomes focused on adverse events and exploratory anti-fibrotic endpoints (histology, serum fibrosis biomarkers); the program reported safety/tolerability and preliminary efficacy consistent with anti-fibrotic activity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014). In HBV/HCV-related cirrhosis, a Phase I/IIa open-label study (twice-weekly 4 h infusions; 140, 280, 380 mg/m2 per 4 h) evaluated safety, PK, and change in liver fibrosis area by biopsy at 12 weeks; the registry cites a derived EBioMedicine report on safety, tolerability, and anti-fibrotic effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2018). In advanced primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; Scheuer stage ≥III), OP-724 (formerly PRI-724) underwent a Phase I dose-finding trial (4 h i.v. infusions, twice weekly for 12 weeks; 140/280/380 mg/m2 cohorts) assessing serious adverse events, PK of OP-724 and metabolite C-82, and fibrosis-related endpoints (biopsy fibrotic area, FibroScan, Child-Pugh/MELD, ELF score) with feasibility/safety results published (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

No clinical or preclinical ocular applications of ICG-001/PRI-724/OP-724 were identified in the provided context, and there are no reports here of use in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), or retinal barrier disorders (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019). Preclinical oncology literature summarized in the provided sources documents ICG-001’s activity in cancer cells (reduced proliferation and induced selective apoptosis via TCF-dependent signaling reduction) but does not address ocular tissues (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Thus, while the drug class has human safety experience in fibrotic liver disease, there is no direct evidence in the provided context for ophthalmic use or for dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
ICG-001 binds CBP and selectively disrupts the β-catenin/CBP complex, attenuating β-catenin–driven transcription of TCF/LEF target genes (e.g., Cyclin D1) without decreasing total β-catenin protein levels; in Hep3B cells, ICG-001 reduced TOPflash reporter activity and Cyclin D1 expression while leaving β-catenin abundance unchanged and without inducing compensatory γ-catenin stabilization (if anything, γ-catenin modestly decreased) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). Across multiple excerpts, ICG-001 is consistently described as selective for β-catenin/CBP over β-catenin/p300, reducing TCF-dependent Wnt output while sparing other β-catenin protein interactions; global β-catenin levels are unaffected, reinforcing a functional separation between nuclear transcriptional roles and membrane adherens junction pools (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Authors highlight that agents which lower β-catenin protein (ASO/siRNA) trigger γ-catenin compensation at adherens junctions—distinct from ICG-001, which blocks transcriptional activity without provoking such protein-level sensing/reciprocity (Wickline, 2013, pp. 112–117, 140–145). It remains explicitly unknown from these data whether ICG-001 perturbs adherens junction function in vivo; follow-up studies were recommended to test junctional tolerance to transcriptional blockade (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

Contextual biology of β-catenin coactivator usage indicates that CBP vs p300 partnering can impart divergent phenotypic outcomes; in fibrotic contexts, CBP-associated β-catenin activity has been linked with pro-fibrotic programs whereas p300-associated activity may be protective, though this literature is complex and model-dependent (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69). Canonical β-catenin signaling is also subject to Wnt-independent inputs that promote nuclear translocation/transactivation (e.g., PKA/Akt phosphorylation), and β-catenin exists in distinct pools with membrane-associated adherens junction functions that are regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation events, further implying that selective transcriptional blockade (CBP-directed) may spare adhesive roles (Wickline, 2013, pp. 21–26). Together, these mechanistic data support a rationale for testing CBP/β-catenin–selective inhibitors for diseases where β-catenin transcription drives pathology and where preserving epithelial junctional architecture is desirable (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 140–145).

Disease-Relevant Biology in RPE and Retinal Barriers  
RPE epithelial phenotype and outer blood–retina barrier (oBRB) integrity depend on tight junction (TJ) and adherens junction (AJ) complexes (ZO-1/occludin/claudins; E-cadherin/catenins). Loss of ZO-1 releases ZONAB to drive CDK4 and proliferation; downregulation of E-cadherin frees β-catenin to translocate to the nucleus and activate EMT/proliferation drivers (e.g., Snail, Cyclin D1), establishing a mechanistic link between junctional disruption and β-catenin–dependent transcriptional programs in RPE (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–9). Reviews of RPE EMT highlight Wnt–β-catenin as a key mediator in the eye; experimental injury (laser photocoagulation) activates β-catenin signaling and facilitates RPE proliferation, reinforcing the pathway’s involvement in EMT and regenerative responses (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 7–9).

Critically, primary hRPE culture studies demonstrate that Matrigel plus Activin A (MA) fosters epithelial morphology, increases TJ gene/protein expression (Claudin-1, Claudin-3, Occludin, ZO-1), improves apical ZO-1 polarity, and elevates TEER; this phenotype is accompanied by increased β-catenin levels and β-catenin/TCF target expression (TCF-4, Survivin, Cyclin D1, c-Myc), and is suppressed by the Wnt/β-catenin inhibitor XAV-939, implicating canonical β-catenin activity in barrier maturation under these culture conditions (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11). The MA paradigm also shows anti-apoptotic effects (lower ROS, preserved mitochondrial potential, lower Annexin V positivity) linked to elevated β-catenin/Survivin, again consistent with β-catenin supporting epithelial survival when cell–cell contacts are intact (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

Conversely, disease models and inflammatory contexts show scenarios where β-catenin activation correlates with barrier breakdown. In diabetic macular edema (DME) models, SMURF1 promotes WIF1 ubiquitination and degradation, activating Wnt/β-catenin–VEGF signaling, inducing autophagy, and disrupting RPE tight junctions; knockdown of SMURF1 restores WIF1, suppresses pathway activation, and rescues claudin-1/occludin/ZO-1 expression in ARPE-19 and in STZ mice (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Inflammatory TNFα challenge in polarized ARPE-19 reduces TER, increases paracellular permeability, and disrupts ZO-1/claudins/occludin and AJ components; the HDAC inhibitor ITF2357 restores TER and junctional proteins and suppresses β-catenin overexpression and NF-κB signaling, supporting the concept that limiting β-catenin–linked transcription can be barrier-protective under inflammatory stress (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19). Under oxidative stress relevant to dry AMD, ex vivo primary porcine RPE (ppRPE) exposed to NaIO₃ shows a significant reduction in ZO-1 immunopositive area (with unchanged TJP1 mRNA), indicating tight-junction localization loss; while the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is not measured directly in this model, the outcome establishes a testable context for barrier rescue (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

These data collectively underscore a context-dependent role of β-catenin in RPE: when epithelial contacts are robust, β-catenin activity can support maturation, TJ expression, and survival; under EMT/injury/inflammatory stress (e.g., DME/TNFα), β-catenin pathway activation correlates with junctional loss, VEGF induction, and autophagy, and pathway suppression can be protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19).

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay context: RPE monolayers subjected to oxidative stress (e.g., NaIO₃, H₂O₂, or serum withdrawal models) with readouts including TEER, paracellular flux, and localization/expression of ZO-1 and claudin-1.

- Gene/protein expression in RPE: ZO-1, claudins, occludin, and cadherins/β-catenin are established components of RPE junctions and are readily measured; TEER increases in mature hRPE and decreases with injury provide a functional correlate of barrier status (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55). β-catenin and downstream targets (Cyclin D1, Survivin, c-Myc, TCF-4) were upregulated in hRPE MA cultures and are suppressible by Wnt pathway inhibition, confirming pathway engagement in RPE (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Net expectation in oxidative stress assays: Under acute oxidative stress where junctional proteins disassemble (e.g., NaIO₃ model reduces ZO-1 area), there is no direct evidence provided that CBP-selective β-catenin inhibition upregulates claudin-1/ZO-1 or restores TEER in RPE. In analogous inflammatory contexts, limiting β-catenin–linked transcription correlates with barrier recovery, but this was achieved with an HDAC inhibitor and via suppression of β-catenin overexpression/NF-κB, not CBP-selective Wnt blockade (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19). Therefore, the claim that ICG-001 will “bias gene transcription toward junctional protein upregulation (claudin-1, ZO-1) in RPE under oxidative stress without activating proliferation pathways, leading to recovery of TEER and decreased paracellular flux” is mechanistically plausible in EMT/inflammatory settings but remains unsubstantiated for oxidative stress in RPE; the directionality of effect on junctional genes could invert depending on baseline epithelial status and co-activation of survival pathways (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Therapeutic Risk–Benefit Considerations  
- Safety/translatability: Clinical-stage CBP/β-catenin inhibitors (PRI-724/OP-724) have demonstrated safety/tolerability in Phase I/IIa liver fibrosis trials, supporting repurposing potential; however, the dosing was i.v., and ocular delivery, PK/PD at the RPE, and retinal safety are uncharacterized in the provided data (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Mechanistic specificity: ICG-001 spares total β-catenin protein and does not trigger γ-catenin compensation, mitigating concerns about adherens junction destabilization that accompany β-catenin depletion; nevertheless, whether ICG-001 affects adherens junction functionality in epithelial tissues in vivo remains unknown, and this must be directly assessed in RPE (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Pathway context dependence: RPE barrier outcomes with Wnt/β-catenin modulation are bidirectional and context dependent—MA-induced β-catenin activity enhances TJs/TEER, while in DME/inflammation β-catenin activation correlates with TJ disruption; CBP-specific blockade could be beneficial in the latter but deleterious in the former (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). This necessitates careful stressor stratification (oxidative versus inflammatory/VEGF-driven) in preclinical testing.

- Disease relevance to dry AMD: Oxidative stress disrupts RPE TJs and reduces ZO-1 localization in ex vivo ppRPE; EMT and barrier breakdown are recognized contributors to RPE dysfunction; however, there is no direct evidence here linking CBP/β-catenin inhibition to barrier rescue in oxidative injury models or to slowed geographic atrophy progression (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

Given the absence of direct ocular data for ICG-001, a staged validation plan is warranted:

- In vitro RPE barrier assays:  
  • Use primary hRPE on Transwells to maturity (baseline TER per established values) (Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55). Challenge with oxidative stress (NaIO₃/H₂O₂) and inflammatory stress (TNFα) in parallel. Quantify TER, fluorescein paracellular flux, and immunolocalization of ZO-1/claudin-1/occludin and AJ proteins.   • Hypothesis testing criteria: Evidence of TEER recovery and reduced paracellular flux with maintained or improved ZO-1/claudin-1 localization in oxidative and inflammatory paradigms without induction of proliferation markers (Cyclin D1) would support the proposed mechanism; failure or opposite effects would argue against it (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99).

- Ex vivo ppRPE coculture:  
  • Replicate NaIO₃-induced ZO-1 reduction and test whether ICG-001 preserves/restores ZO-1 area without elevating proliferation/EMT markers; track apoptosis/survival readouts given MA data tying β-catenin to anti-apoptotic signaling (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7).

- In vivo relevance:  
  • If in vitro/ex vivo are positive, progress to mouse models with RPE oxidative injury (e.g., NaIO₃ systemic exposure) and quantify RPE barrier integrity (ZO-1 localization, RPE flat-mounts), photoreceptor/RPE survival, and functional outcomes; consider delivery routes (intravitreal/subconjunctival) and PK (not available here) (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

- Mechanistic dissection:  
  • Evaluate whether CBP-specific blockade shifts β-catenin coactivator usage toward p300-dependent programs (no direct assays in provided texts) and whether junctional gene regulation exhibits CBP selectivity; this would mechanistically address the “biased transcription” claim (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69).

Strengths  
- Defined, selective mechanism: ICG-001 disrupts β-catenin/CBP complexes and suppresses TCF-dependent transcription without lowering total β-catenin; it does not trigger γ-catenin compensation observed with β-catenin protein knockdown, offering a mechanistically precise intervention that may spare adherens junction architecture (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117, 140–145, 26–30).

- Clinical-stage drug class: The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor analogs PRI-724/OP-724 have human safety and PK data in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis/PBC, supporting translational feasibility and providing a clinical development template, albeit outside ophthalmology (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

- Biological plausibility in RPE EMT and barrier dysfunction: RPE EMT and barrier loss are linked to β-catenin nuclear signaling; under inflammatory/DME-like conditions, Wnt/β-catenin activation disrupts TJs via VEGF/autophagy and Wnt-pathway suppression restores claudin-1/ZO-1, suggesting that pathway attenuation can be barrier-protective in disease contexts where β-catenin drives pathogenic transcription (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

- Assay tractability: RPE barrier endpoints (TEER, paracellular flux, ZO-1/claudin-1 localization) are robust; β-catenin target genes provide PD markers to confirm on-target activity, enabling a decisive preclinical go/no-go within RPE-relevant stress paradigms (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55).

Key Limitations and Risks  
- No direct ocular/RPE data for ICG-001: The provided context contains no studies of ICG-001 (or PRI-724/OP-724) in RPE or ocular tissues, no TEER/paracellular flux rescue data, and no AMD model outcomes; claims of junction-selective “bias” in RPE are speculative and unproven here (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Context-dependent and bidirectional β-catenin effects in RPE: In hRPE cultured with MA, β-catenin activity correlates with increased claudin-1/ZO-1 and higher TEER, and Wnt pathway inhibition (XAV-939) diminishes these; thus, in certain epithelial contexts, β-catenin/CBP inhibition could impair, not enhance, junctional gene expression and barrier function (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Survival/proliferation trade-offs: β-catenin activation increased anti-apoptotic factors (Survivin/Bcl2) and protected hRPE from serum withdrawal stress; ICG-001’s suppression of β-catenin target genes could compromise survival signaling under oxidative stress, and the net effect on barrier integrity/survival requires direct testing (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7).

- Mechanistic uncertainty regarding “biased transcription” toward junctional genes: No evidence is provided that CBP-selective inhibition favors claudin-1/ZO-1 expression; indeed, Sox/TCF targets include Cyclin D1 and c-Myc, and the directionality of CBP versus p300 coactivator usage on RPE junctional gene programs is not defined by the present sources (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 9–11; Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69).

- Delivery and ocular PK/PD unknowns: Clinical liver trials used i.v. infusions; ocular tolerability, retinal exposure, and local pharmacology for ICG-001/OP-724/PRI-724 are not addressed here, requiring formulation and delivery development (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

Decision Implications  
On the present evidence, ICG-001 has a coherent, selective mechanism with clinical-stage validation in a non-ocular indication, and there is strong biological plausibility that β-catenin transcriptional blockade can counter EMT/proliferation programs in RPE. However, the specific hypothesis that ICG-001 will “bias” transcription to upregulate claudin-1/ZO-1 and restore TEER under oxidative stress is not supported by the provided literature; in fact, RPE studies show that β-catenin activation is associated with higher TJ expression/TEER in some contexts, and pathway inhibition reduces these features, whereas in inflammatory/DME contexts β-catenin activation is deleterious and suppression is protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Therefore, a tightly scoped preclinical program should be undertaken to empirically resolve these context-dependent effects in RPE before committing to development for dry AMD.

Recommendation  
- Proceed with an in vitro/ex vivo feasibility package to test ICG-001 in RPE barrier models under defined stressors (oxidative vs inflammatory), with rigorous functional and molecular endpoints and on-target PD confirmation; include orthogonal comparators (XAV-939, ITF2357) to position CBP-selective modulation against broader Wnt suppression and epigenetic anti-inflammatory rescue (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7). Advance only if ICG-001 reproducibly restores TEER and junctional localization without pro-EMT/proliferation signatures across oxidative stress conditions relevant to dry AMD (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

- If positive, initiate ocular PK/tolerability and RPE-targeted delivery studies; if negative or mixed, deprioritize in favor of alternative approaches with direct evidence of barrier rescue in RPE (e.g., HDAC inhibitors in inflammatory settings), recognizing that pathway- and context-specificity critically determine outcomes in RPE biology (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–12).

In sum, ICG-001 is a mechanistically attractive, clinically precedented β-catenin/CBP inhibitor, but the claim of junction-focused, proliferation-sparing barrier rescue in oxidatively stressed RPE is currently hypothetical and not substantiated by the provided literature; decisive RPE-focused experiments are required to validate or refute its potential for dry AMD (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PXS-5153A is a synthetically derived molecule that belongs to the class of selective lysyl oxidase inhibitors. In its design, medicinal chemistry efforts focused on optimizing potency and selectivity for LOXL2, along with activity against LOXL3, two members of the lysyl oxidase family that catalyze the oxidative deamination of lysine residues in collagens and elastin to promote covalent crosslink formation. These crosslinks confer the mechanical strength and stiffness of extracellular matrices (ECMs) such as Bruch’s membrane. Synthetic routes to compounds like PXS-5153A typically rely on structure-based design and iterative optimization to achieve potent enzyme inhibition with favorable pharmacokinetic properties (Lin et al., 2020). The compound, commercially available under MedChemExpress HY-111217, is representative of a new therapeutic class that has been primarily explored in the context of fibrosis and tumor microenvironment modulation. Given that ECM stiffening is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, targeting LOXL2 represents a novel approach compared to conventional anti-inflammatory or anti-angiogenic strategies.

II. Therapeutic History  
The LOXL2 inhibitor class, including molecules such as PXS-5153A, has been extensively tested in preclinical models of fibrosis and cancer. For example, within non-ocular systems, LOXL2 activity has been linked to increased tissue stiffness that fosters metastatic progression and desmoplastic reactions in tumors, and selective inhibition of LOXL2 has been shown to reduce crosslink density, attenuating fibrotic remodeling (Lin et al., 2020). Experimental inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity using non-selective agents like β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) has also been applied to in vitro and in vivo models to modulate ECM assembly, with effects on barrier function observed in RPE cultures co-treated with endothelial cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). Although LOXL2 inhibitors have not traditionally been used to treat dry AMD, evidence underscores the centrality of aberrant ECM crosslinking in BM thickening observed during aging and AMD progression (Wang et al., 2025). In particular, the endothelial cell–RPE crosstalk studies demonstrate a critical role for lysyl oxidase activity in regulating collagen bundle formation and in establishing RPE barrier properties (Benedicto et al., 2017). Accordingly, while there is no direct clinical or preclinical record of PXS-5153A in AMD, the antifibrotic profile of the compound and its impact on extracellular matrix mechanics in other disease contexts serve as a compelling rationale to explore its application in dry AMD.

III. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, LOXL2 catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of lysine or hydroxylysine residues present in collagens and elastin. This reaction is critical for the formation of covalent crosslinks that stabilize the ECM. Overexpression or hyperactivity of LOXL2 results in an excessively crosslinked and stiff matrix. In the eye, particularly within Bruch’s membrane—which is a complex, stratified ECM structure located between the RPE and the choroid—aberrant collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking are known to increase mechanical tension. Such mechanical changes are thought to adversely affect RPE cell function by interfering with integrin-mediated cell–matrix interactions and perturbing the proper localization of tight junction proteins, including ZO-1 and occludin (Benedicto et al., 2017).

PXS-5153A functions by binding to the catalytic pocket of LOXL2, thereby preventing its enzymatic activity. By blocking the oxidative deamination step, PXS-5153A reduces the formation of both immature and mature crosslinks in ECM proteins. The anticipated outcome is a lower crosslink density in Bruch’s membrane, resulting in a softer, more compliant matrix environment. This reduction in mechanical stiffness is expected to diminish abnormal mechanosignaling through β1 integrins, which are integral to the assembly and maintenance of tight junctions on RPE cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). The downstream consequences of reduced integrin activation include dampening of Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways, which in turn facilitate the stabilization and proper localization of tight junction proteins at the RPE cell membranes (Benedicto et al., 2017). Restoration of these junctional complexes correlates with improved barrier function, typically measured as an increased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in cell culture models. This mechanism is supported by studies in which inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity—by pharmacological agents such as BAPN—led to alterations in RPE barrier properties and tight junction morphology (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by directly targeting LOXL2, PXS-5153A is proposed to correct the pathological ECM remodeling that underlies BM stiffening in dry AMD while re-establishing proper RPE barrier integrity.

The expected therapeutic effect of PXS-5153A in dry AMD centers on normalization of the BM ECM and concomitant restoration of RPE barrier function.
