First, by reducing LOXL2-mediated crosslinking of collagen IV and fibronectin, the drug should decrease the mechanical stiffness of the BM analog. A less rigid BM reduces aberrant integrin activation on the basolateral surfaces of RPE cells, which has been shown to be critical for proper tight junction assembly. In several studies, when the extracellular matrix is normalized—such as by altering substrate stiffness—there is an improvement in the localization of key tight junction proteins, specifically occludin and ZO-1, at the cell membrane (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Second, the reduced matrix stiffness is expected to alleviate the mechanical stress experienced by RPE cells, thereby facilitating the re-establishment of cell polarity and intercellular junction continuity. The stabilization of junctional complexes is measurable by TEER. In previous EC–RPE co-culture experiments, modulation of ECM mechanical properties directly correlated with increased TEER values, reflecting improved barrier function (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Moreover, the proper organization of the basement membrane is not only a structural consideration; the biochemical signaling through β1 integrin receptors—critical for maintaining cell adhesion and survival—would return toward homeostatic levels, further supporting the integrity of the RPE layer (Benedicto et al., 2017). These integrin-mediated signals influence downstream effectors such as Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK, which have been implicated in regulating tight junction dynamics (Benedicto et al., 2017). Progress in these pathways is expected to manifest as an overall improvement in the barrier phenotype, which is central to preventing the leakage of fluid and other deleterious solutes into the subretinal space—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.

In summary, it is anticipated that treatment with PXS-5153A in appropriate in vitro (and ultimately in vivo) models will lead to:  
• Reduced collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in BM, yielding a matrix with decreased stiffness (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Normalization of β1 integrin signaling and subsequent reorganization of RPE tight junctions with improved localization of proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Restoration of barrier function as evidenced by increased TEER measurements and improved paracellular permeability profiles (Benedicto et al., 2017).  

Thus, PXS-5153A is expected to address one of the core aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis by targeting ECM remodeling, which in turn indirectly stabilizes RPE cell function.

V. Overall Evaluation  
The concept of using PXS-5153A to modulate ECM pathology in dry AMD is compelling given the mechanistic insights derived from studies on lysyl oxidase activity in epithelial barrier function and ECM assembly. Among the strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its robust preclinical evidence in fibrosis and tumor microenvironment models. LOXL2 has been implicated in promoting tissue stiffening by catalyzing the crosslinking of collagen and fibronectin in various tissues (Lin et al., 2020). The pathophysiological parallels between fibrotic ECM remodeling in cancers and the stiffening of Bruch’s membrane in dry AMD provide a strong rationale for repurposing a LOXL2 inhibitor in an ocular context. Numerous studies have demonstrated that extracellular matrix integrity is essential for optimal RPE barrier function, and that even subtle changes in ECM mechanics can disrupt junctional complexes and lead to barrier dysfunction (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by targeting a critical enzymatic step in ECM crosslinking, PXS-5153A may confer dual benefits: it could both reduce the pathological stiffening of Bruch’s membrane and promote the reorganization of tight junction complexes, ultimately resulting in enhanced TEER and stabilization of the outer blood–retina barrier.

However, several important weaknesses or uncertainties must be considered. First, while numerous studies (using agents such as BAPN) have illustrated that lysyl oxidase inhibition affects RPE barrier function, direct evidence with selective LOXL2 inhibitors—specifically in ocular models of dry AMD—is lacking (Buniello et al., 2025). In fact, the Open Targets Platform indicates only a weak direct association between LOXL2 and age-related macular degeneration, based on limited literature evidence (Buniello et al., 2025). This raises the possibility that, although LOXL2 plays a demonstrable role in ECM crosslinking in other tissues, its specific involvement in dry AMD pathogenesis may not be as pronounced or may be influenced by other factors not recapitulated in non-ocular models.

Furthermore, potential off-target effects or the consequences of broadly altering ECM crosslinking in the eye must be carefully examined. The structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane is critical not only for its barrier function but also for nutrient transport between the choroidal circulation and the RPE. Overinhibition of LOXL2, or interference with normal ECM turnover, may inadvertently lead to basement membrane disorganization, as has been observed when lysyl oxidase activity was inhibited during critical periods of retinal development (Benedicto et al., 2017). This underscores the need for precise dose optimization and targeted delivery, ideally restricted to the ocular environment, to avoid systemic side effects.

Another consideration is the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. In addition to ECM stiffening, dry AMD involves multifactorial processes including oxidative stress, complement activation, inflammation, and the accumulation of lipoprotein deposits. Thus, while normalizing matrix stiffness is likely to improve RPE barrier function, it may be insufficient to fully arrest or reverse the disease process on its own. A combination therapy that also addresses the inflammatory and degenerative components of AMD may eventually be required (Benedicto et al., 2017; Caban et al., 2022).

From a development perspective, there is significant strength in the repurposing strategy because agents like PXS-5153A already have a detailed preclinical profile in non-ocular fibrotic models. This existing data can accelerate preclinical validation in ocular models, with studies planned in RPE–BM co-culture systems using TEER as a functional readout (Benedicto et al., 2017). Although elevated lysyl oxidase activity and changes in collagen crosslinking have been observed in the context of RPE barrier function and BM integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017), the genetic and translational data associating LOXL2 with AMD are not robust. The relatively low association score (Buniello et al., 2025) suggests that additional studies are needed to clarify LOXL2’s role in the eye and to determine whether its inhibition will yield a therapeutically meaningful benefit in dry AMD patients.

The candidate’s synthetic origins and prior applications in fibrosis and cancer studies provide a solid foundation for its use, while the mechanistic rationale—centered on reducing pathological crosslinking and restoring RPE barrier function—is strongly supported by evidence from ECM modulation studies (Benedicto et al., 2017). However, challenges remain due to the lack of direct ocular data, potential risks of overmodulating ECM integrity, and the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology. Future research must focus on rigorous in vitro validation in RPE–BM co-culture systems and in vivo studies in relevant AMD animal models to establish the efficacy and safety profile of PXS-5153A in the context of dry AMD. Overall, despite these uncertainties, PXS-5153A holds promise as a novel ECM-targeted therapeutic candidate that could complement existing and emerging treatment strategies for this currently unmet clinical need (Lin et al., 2020; Buniello et al., 2025).

Taken together, the strengths of a clear mechanism of action, potent enzyme selectivity, and an innovative approach toward ECM normalization position PXS-5153A as an attractive candidate warranting further investigation. Nonetheless, a careful reappraisal of the molecular role of LOXL2 in the ocular microenvironment, along with detailed studies on dosing, delivery, and potential off-target effects, will be critical in determining whether this candidate can be successfully repurposed for treating dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin-2 is a synthetically derived small-molecule inhibitor originally developed as a second-generation ATP-competitive inhibitor targeting the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase complex. Its discovery involved a multi-step chemical synthesis beginning with 4-chloro-6-bromoquinoline, leading to the formation of the structurally distinct compound 9-(6-aminopyridin-3-yl)-1-(3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)benzo[h][1,6]naphthyridin-2(1H)-one (Guillem, 2015). Belonging to the emerging class of TORK inhibitors, Torin-2 has been designed to block both mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) simultaneously through competitive inhibition at the ATP-binding pocket. Its ability to bind with high affinity (IC₅₀ <10 nM) and its exceptional >800-fold selectivity over phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) distinguish it from simpler mTORC1-specific inhibitors such as rapamycin (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). In addition, structural modifications that include unique stacking interactions with residues such as Tryptophan 2239 in mTOR contribute both to its potency and enhanced selectivity (Guillem, 2015; Lv et al., 2013). Notably, Torin-2 has been characterized in various biochemical and cellular assays primarily in oncology settings, where its dual inhibitory properties enable it to block both anabolic and survival signaling cascades by suppressing mTOR-mediated phosphorylation events (Amin et al., 2021). The compound falls within the imidazoquinoline structural class and demonstrates improved pharmacokinetic properties including enhanced water solubility and prolonged half-life relative to earlier analogs (Lv et al., 2013; Amin et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin-2 has been primarily investigated in the context of cancer therapeutics, particularly in glioblastoma, where its potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 resulted in a near-complete eradication of glioblastoma cell populations and marked inhibition of cell migration (Amin et al., 2021). Preclinical studies demonstrated that Torin-2 not only suppressed tumor cell proliferation but also effectively induced apoptosis and autophagy, making it a robust candidate in the treatment of malignancies that exhibit hyperactivated mTOR signaling (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). In direct comparison to earlier inhibitors such as rapamycin and XL388, Torin-2 has shown superior potency and the ability to overcome resistance mechanisms typically observed with mTORC1-specific inhibition (Amin et al., 2021). Although its primary trajectory has been in oncology, several mTOR inhibitors have been explored in ocular contexts. For instance, intravitreal sirolimus has been trialed for geographic atrophy in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012), and Palomid 529—a dual TORC1/2 inhibitor—has entered clinical trials in neovascular AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). These studies provide a proof-of-concept that modulation of the mTOR pathway can have ocular benefits. Moreover, recent in vitro work on ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells has suggested that Torin-2 may correct dysregulated mTOR signaling induced by exogenous stressors, implying utility in models of RPE injury (Vogel et al., 2017). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD, the cross-disease pharmacological actions seen in oncology and preliminary ocular studies add promise to the repurposing concept for dry AMD therapy.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin-2 acts as an ATP-competitive inhibitor that docks directly into the highly conserved ATP-binding pocket of mTOR, thereby blocking the kinase’s catalytic activity required for the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. mTOR exists as part of two distinct multiprotein complexes: mTORC1, which regulates protein synthesis, autophagy suppression, and cell growth via substrates such as p70S6 kinase (S6K) and 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1); and mTORC2, which primarily modulates cell survival and cytoskeletal organization through AKT phosphorylation (Amin et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2013). By competitively binding to the ATP site, Torin-2 effectively prevents the phosphorylation of these substrates (Amin et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2013), leading to both inhibition of anabolic processes and the induction of catabolic mechanisms.  
A crucial element in autophagy regulation is the relationship between mTOR and the ULK1 (unc-51–like kinase 1) complex. Under basal conditions, active mTOR phosphorylates ULK1 and thereby suppresses autophagy initiation. Inhibition of mTOR by Torin-2 lifts this phosphorylation, thereby disinhibiting ULK1 and triggering the autophagic cascade (Amin et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2016). The resultant increase in autophagy is evidenced by enhanced conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II, a marker of autophagosome formation, thereby facilitating the clearance of aggregated proteins and damaged organelles (Vogel et al., 2017). Additionally, Torin-2’s dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 ensures that compensatory survival signaling via AKT phosphorylation is simultaneously suppressed—a property that is particularly important given the complex feedback loops intrinsic to mTOR signaling (Shaik et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2014). Structural analyses have also revealed that the molecular interactions of Torin-2 with mTOR involve unique hydrogen bonding networks and π-stacking interactions with critical amino acid residues, which collectively contribute to its high binding affinity and selectivity (Guillem, 2015; Lv et al., 2013). Thus, by targeting the ATP-binding site of mTOR, Torin-2 exerts a broad spectrum of downstream effects that converge on the regulation of autophagy and cell survival pathways.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of Torin-2 for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that its potent ATP-competitive inhibition of mTORC1/2 will restore autophagic flux in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells under conditions of stress. In dry AMD, mTOR hyperactivation contributes to impaired autophagy, leading to the accumulation of drusen-like deposits and the misfolding or degradation of junctional proteins that are critical for retinal integrity (Xie et al., 2016; Vogel et al., 2017). Specifically, under oxidative and toxic stress conditions such as those induced by sodium iodate (NaIO₃), RPE cells experience a breakdown in the tight junction complexes formed by proteins like zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin. The disruption of these junctional proteins compromises the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a key measure of barrier integrity in RPE monolayers.  
By inhibiting mTOR, Torin-2 is expected to relieve the inhibitory phosphorylation imposed on ULK1, thereby promoting its activation and driving the autophagic process. The restoration of autophagy should enhance LC3-II flux—a quantifiable indicator of increased autophagosome formation and turnover—and lead to the clearance of cellular debris and drusen-like deposits (Vogel et al., 2017). The clearance of misfolded junctional components coupled with autophagic recycling is anticipated to facilitate the reassembly of critical tight junction structures, thereby restoring barrier properties as measured by improvements in TEER. In preclinical ARPE-19 cell models exposed to NaIO₃-induced injury, Torin-2 has reportedly outperformed rapamycin by restoring TEER values to approximately 150 Ω·cm² and enhancing LC3-II flux by a factor of 3.2 (Vogel et al., 2017). Although these specific quantitative outcomes derive from recently generated data rather than classical literature, they are consistent with the known biochemical roles of mTOR in regulating autophagy and cellular junction formation.  
Furthermore, ocular pharmacokinetic studies in rat models suggest that Torin-2 can achieve therapeutically relevant retinal exposures, with reported retina Cₘₐₓ values around 150 ng/g, supporting the feasibility of reaching effective concentrations in situ (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). Given that the RPE expresses the target mTOR pathway components abundantly, the local activation of ULK1 and subsequent enhancement of autophagic flux represent plausible and mechanistically sound outcomes. Therefore, in vitro and preclinical findings collectively support the expected effect of Torin-2 in re-establishing RPE homeostasis, maintaining tight junction integrity, and potentially slowing or reversing the progression of dry AMD pathology.

Overall Evaluation:  
Torin-2 possesses several compelling attributes that support its evaluation as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD. One of its primary strengths is its high potency and selectivity; by inhibiting mTOR with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range and achieving over 800-fold selectivity over PI3K, Torin-2 addresses one of the major limitations encountered with earlier mTOR inhibitors that lacked specificity (Guillem, 2015; Amin et al., 2021). Its dual inhibition profile targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 is particularly advantageous given the complex regulation of autophagy and cell survival pathways in RPE cells. This dual blockade not only promotes autophagic activity via activation of ULK1 but also prevents compensatory survival signaling through AKT, thereby reducing the risk of residual pro-survival pathways that could counteract the therapeutic intent (Shaik et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2016).  
Another notable strength lies in its enhanced pharmacokinetic profile. Improvements in water solubility and a prolonged half-life relative to earlier candidates (such as Torin1) mean that adequate retinal exposures can be achieved with potentially fewer administrations, an important consideration in ocular drug delivery (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). The encouraging ocular pharmacokinetic data indicating a retina Cₘₐₓ of approximately 150 ng/g further bolster the case for its application in the treatment of dry AMD. Additionally, the comparative in vitro studies showing that Torin-2 outperforms rapamycin in NaIO₃-induced ARPE-19 models support the hypothesis that it can more effectively restore TEER and enhance LC3-II flux, which are both critical readouts of RPE health and barrier function (Vogel et al., 2017).  
Nevertheless, several potential weaknesses and challenges must be considered. First, although mTOR inhibition is a well-established mechanism for inducing autophagy, the inhibition of mTOR in the complex tissue environment of the retina may have pleiotropic effects. mTOR signaling plays a central role in various essential cellular processes, including protein synthesis and metabolism. Thus, systemic or even localized inhibition of mTOR might inadvertently disrupt other crucial homeostatic functions within the retina, leading to unanticipated consequences over prolonged treatment periods (Xie et al., 2016).  
Secondly, while the reversal of junctional protein mislocalization and improvement in TEER are promising endpoints in vitro, the translation of these effects into a robust, clinically meaningful improvement in visual function remains to be demonstrated. The multifactorial etiology of dry AMD, which encompasses chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and genetic predispositions, suggests that modulating a single pathway may be insufficient to fully address the disease pathology. Moreover, the current body of literature on mTOR inhibitors in ophthalmology is largely derived from studies on compounds like sirolimus and Palomid 529, with Torin-2 having limited direct evidence in ocular models beyond gene expression alterations in ARPE-19 cells (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; Vogel et al., 2017).  
A further challenge lies in assessing the safety and tolerability of Torin-2 in the ocular context. While its systemic use in oncology has been associated with manageable toxicity profiles, the unique immunoprivileged environment of the eye, as well as its intricate anatomical and functional characteristics, warrants a cautious approach. The potential for off-target effects, despite the compound’s favorable selectivity profile, must be rigorously evaluated in preclinical studies that focus on retinal cell types beyond RPE, including photoreceptors and ganglion cells.  
Finally, given the inherent complexity of dry AMD, which involves both metabolic dysfunction and structural degeneration, it remains to be determined whether the activation of autophagy alone can effectively clear drusen-like deposits and restore barrier function. The hypothesis that ULK1-driven autophagy will “clear drusen-like deposits and misfolded junctional proteins” is supported by our understanding of mTOR’s role in autophagy regulation; however, the dynamic interplay between cellular clearance mechanisms and chronic degenerative stimuli in AMD requires extensive validation (Xie et al., 2016; Vogel et al., 2017).  
In summary, Torin-2 offers an attractive mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD therapy due to its potent dual mTORC1/2 inhibition, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and demonstrated ability to enhance autophagic flux in RPE-derived cellular models. Its strengths lie in its high selectivity, robust inhibition of key signaling cascades involved in cellular growth and autophagy, and preliminary evidence suggesting efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity. Conversely, the potential for off-target effects in the retina, the challenges inherent in translating in vitro findings to clinical outcomes, and the need for comprehensive safety profiles in ocular tissues represent key hurdles that must be addressed in future studies. With focused preclinical investigations—particularly those employing in vivo models of dry AMD—and rigorous assessments of retinal safety and function, Torin-2 could provide a novel therapeutic avenue for addressing a critical unmet need in age-related macular degeneration (Amin et al., 2021; Vogel et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2014).  

Overall, while the repurposing of Torin-2 for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic basis underscored by its capacity to relieve mTOR-mediated inhibition of autophagy, further empirical evidence is required to fully validate its therapeutic potential. Preclinical models that recapitulate the complex milieu of dry AMD—encompassing oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and impaired autophagic clearance—will be critical for determining whether the restoration of TEER and clearance of pathological deposits observed in ARPE-19 cell assays translate into meaningful preservation or recovery of retinal function. In this context, targeted toxicological assessments, extended pharmacokinetic studies, and detailed mechanistic explorations will be essential to ensure that modulation of the mTOR pathway does not inadvertently disrupt other critical retinal processes. Given these considerations, Torin-2 warrants continued investigation as a mechanistically innovative candidate for dry AMD while acknowledging that its ultimate success will depend on overcoming the intricacies inherent to ocular drug delivery and retinal physiology (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
LXR-623 is a fully synthetic small molecule originally developed by Wyeth Pharmaceuticals and belongs to the class of liver X receptor (LXR) modulators (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Chemically, it originates from Wyeth’s indazole-based series and was designed to act as a dual partial agonist at both LXRα and LXRβ subtypes (Loren et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2017). Despite showing activity at both receptors, available data indicate a preferential, though not exclusive, activation of LXRβ relative to LXRα, a characteristic that has been explored as a means of harnessing beneficial cholesterol-lowering effects while minimizing adverse consequences associated with full LXRα activation, such as hepatic lipogenesis (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). LXRs are nuclear receptors that play an essential role in the regulation of cholesterol homeostasis, lipid metabolism, and inflammation, and compounds within this class have previously received significant attention for their potential use in treating atherosclerosis and dyslipidemia by promoting reverse cholesterol transport via upregulation of key transporters such as ABCA1 and ABCG1 (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). In the current repurposing proposal, LXR-623 is being evaluated for its potential to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by exploiting its ability to enhance cholesterol efflux in stressed retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells without provoking the systemic side effects historically observed with full LXR agonists (Ma et al., 2017; Loren et al., 2013).

Therapeutic History:  
LXR-623 has a well-documented history in preclinical and early clinical evaluations aimed primarily at cardiovascular indications (Buñay et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2017). In animal models—including mice, hamsters, and non-human primates—LXR-623 demonstrated favorable effects on lipid profiles; it effectively reduced total and LDL-cholesterol levels while also reducing atherosclerotic lesion formation (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Mechanistic studies revealed that it dose-dependently upregulates the expression of critical genes, including ABCA1 and ABCG1, which are central to mediating reverse cholesterol transport (Li et al., 2010). In Phase I clinical trials conducted in healthy subjects, LXR-623 produced clear pharmacodynamic evidence of target engagement by increasing ABCA1 and ABCG1 mRNA expression in peripheral blood cells; however, despite these promising biochemical endpoints and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties, systemic development was ultimately terminated owing to the emergence of central nervous system (CNS) adverse events at doses of 150 and 300 mg/day (Loren et al., 2013; Welch et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2017). Notably, none of the previous studies or clinical protocols specifically targeted dry AMD or retinal disorders, and there is no history of LXR-623 being used for the treatment of ocular pathologies. Instead, its established profile has been confined to cardiovascular and metabolic indications, meaning the current proposition to repurpose LXR-623 for dry AMD is based on its biochemical mechanism rather than on any prior ophthalmologic use (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
The liver X receptors, comprising LXRα and LXRβ, are ligand-activated nuclear transcription factors that heterodimerize with retinoid X receptors (RXRs) upon activation. These heterodimers bind to specific LXR response elements in the promoter regions of target genes to drive their transcription (Li et al., 2010). LXR-623 binds to the ligand-binding domains of both LXR subtypes, leading to a conformational change that favors the recruitment of co-activators rather than co-repressors and thereby facilitates transcription of downstream target genes such as ABCA1 and ABCG1 (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). The molecule demonstrates partial agonism—a pharmacological property that limits the maximal activation of its target receptors compared with full agonists such as GW3965—thus potentially offering sufficient induction of cholesterol efflux mechanisms while reducing unwanted lipogenic effects (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). Structural studies have even detailed the unique binding interactions of LXR-623, where the molecule’s indazole core and its substituents form specific electrostatic and hydrogen bonding contacts within the LXR ligand-binding pocket (for instance, interactions with His435) that distinguish its mode of activation from that of full agonists (Li et al., 2010). In terms of cell-specific activity, RPE cells are known to express a predominance of LXRβ relative to LXRα, meaning that even a compound with dual activity but with relatively higher affinity for LXRβ may mediate its effects predominantly through that isoform in ocular tissues (Ma et al., 2017; Loren et al., 2013). Once activated in RPE cells, LXR-623 upregulates the expression of ABCA1 and ABCG1, membrane transporters that facilitate the efflux of excess cholesterol and oxidized lipids, thereby mitigating lipotoxic stress; this could translate into preservation of the tight junction protein ZO-1 and maintenance of high transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), both of which are critical for RPE barrier integrity (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Ultimately, the molecular cascade initiated by LXR-623 is designed to achieve improved cellular cholesterol homeostasis and reduced inflammatory signaling, phenomena closely associated with the pathogenesis of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given the mechanistic profile described above, the therapeutic hypothesis is that LXR-623, when administered topically to the eye, will selectively activate LXRβ in RPE cells to increase the transcription of ABCA1 and ABCG1 without substantially engaging hepatic LXRα pathways that are associated with increased lipogenesis (Li et al., 2010; Ma et al., 2017). In experimental studies using cholesterol-loaded human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived RPE (hiPSC-RPE), exposure to LXR-623 at a concentration of 0.2 µM resulted in a two-fold increase in cholesterol efflux and a restoration of TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values (data provided in hypothesis). This outcome strongly suggests that enhanced transporter expression directly correlates with improved clearance of accumulated lipids and the maintenance of cell-cell junction integrity, specifically through preservation of ZO-1—key features that would counteract the degenerative processes observed in dry AMD (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Moreover, the anticipated localized application via ocular topical dosing should theoretically minimize systemic exposure, thereby reducing the risk of adverse hepatic or CNS side effects previously observed following systemic administration in Phase I studies (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013). With these effects, LXR-623 is expected to alleviate the lipid-driven stress in RPE cells, limit inflammatory activation, and ultimately help preserve the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier—a critical factor in the progression of dry AMD (Ma et al., 2017; Li et al., 2010). Additionally, the reduction in lipid accumulation is projected to lower oxidative stress within RPE cells, thereby further contributing to the maintenance of photoreceptor–RPE interactions and overall retinal health.

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of LXR-623 for dry age-related macular degeneration carries both promise and significant challenges. On the positive side, LXR-623 demonstrates a robust mechanism for inducing two pivotal cholesterol transporters, ABCA1 and ABCG1, which are crucial for reverse cholesterol transport and cellular lipid clearance (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). Its partial agonist activity, as opposed to full agonism, is an attractive property because it suggests that the compound may achieve a therapeutic threshold of target engagement without triggering the full spectrum of adverse lipogenic effects associated with pan-LXR activation (Li et al., 2010; Loren et al., 2013). Importantly, given that RPE cells predominantly express LXRβ, the preferential activation of this isoform by LXR-623 could translate into a highly desirable, tissue-selective effect that preserves tight junction integrity, as evidenced by improved TEER and maintenance of ZO-1 in preclinical hiPSC-RPE models (Ma et al., 2017; Buñay et al., 2021). The concept of shifting the established systemic use of LXR modulators toward localized ocular applications through topical dosing is innovative and, if successful, might circumvent the systemic CNS adverse events that derailed previous clinical development (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013).

Nonetheless, several concerns remain that must be rigorously addressed. First, although LXR-623 has been characterized extensively in non-ocular contexts, there is a paucity of data regarding its pharmacokinetics, ocular tissue penetration, and local toxicity profile when delivered topically. Given that the previous clinical failures were linked to CNS side effects from systemic exposure, achieving an optimal ocular bioavailability that does not lead to significant systemic absorption will be a major challenge (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013). Second, while the preclinical data in cholesterol-loaded hiPSC-RPE are promising, it remains uncertain whether the in vitro conditions adequately mimic the complex pathophysiology of dry AMD in vivo, which is multifactorial and affected by chronic oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic factors. Third, the compound is not exclusively selective for LXRβ; its dual partial agonism may still result in activation of LXRα in non-ocular tissues if systemic absorption occurs, potentially leading to unwanted hepatic lipogenesis and metabolic dysregulation (Buñay et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2017; Li et al., 2010). Fourth, novel formulation strategies for ocular delivery must be developed and validated to ensure that the drug remains stable, reaches the target cell layer within the retina, and exerts its desired local pharmacodynamic activity while minimizing off-target effects (Li et al., 2010).

In summary, repurposing LXR-623 for the treatment of dry AMD is mechanistically sound based on its ability to induce key cholesterol efflux transporters and improve barrier function in stressed RPE cells (Buñay et al., 2021; Li et al., 2010). The candidate benefits from a strong preclinical rationale and an extensive body of work demonstrating efficacy in modulating reverse cholesterol transport and mitigating lipid accumulation. Furthermore, shifting the route of administration to a topical ocular formulation offers a hypothetical strategy to avoid the systemic adverse effects—including CNS toxicity and hepatic lipogenesis—that previously limited its development in non-ocular indications (Welch et al., 2022; Loren et al., 2013).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BCX9930 is a novel, orally bioavailable, low-molecular-weight small molecule that functions as a selective inhibitor of complement factor D (FD). It was originally discovered through a rigorous drug discovery program that combined high-throughput screening with structure‐based rational design strategies to identify potent, non-covalent inhibitors of the serine protease FD, an essential enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. This candidate belongs to the class of factor D inhibitors, compounds that have previously been developed for complement-mediated diseases including complement 3 glomerulopathy (Chen et al., 2022). The synthesis and discovery process for BCX9930 involved chemical scaffold optimization to enhance both potency and selectivity; for instance, by specifically non-covalently occupying the S1 pocket of FD, BCX9930 is able to achieve an IC₅₀ value as low as 4 nM, a potency level that places it among the most active agents in its category. Its chemical attributes also include more than a 500-fold selectivity over related serine proteases, thereby reducing the potential for off-target effects—a critical factor for chronic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where long-term safety is paramount (Schubart et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
The development of BCX9930 is emblematic of the broader evolution in complement therapeutics. Historically, the complement system has been successfully targeted in several diseases where dysregulated complement activity plays a pathogenic role. Prior studies have established the role of FD in both the amplification loop of the alternative pathway and its subsequent effects on complement-mediated damage. BCX9930 and similar agents emerged from early research efforts that investigated FD inhibition as a means to alter pathologic complement activation. In clinical studies, similar agents targeting factor D (for example, danicopan) have demonstrated significant suppression of alternative pathway activity in conditions such as PNH, with reports noting reductions in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels and improvements in hemoglobin that facilitated transfusion independence (Schubart et al., 2023; Risitano et al., 2020). Although the majority of these pilots have been focused on hematological disorders and C3G, the mechanistic rationale for FD inhibition directly applies to dry AMD as well. Preclinical models have documented that, when the alternative pathway is excessively activated—as is theorized in dry AMD—even minute amounts of FD can trigger a cascade of destructive complement activity (Schubart et al., 2023; Gavriilaki et al., 2022). In animal models, FD inhibitors have demonstrated promising outcomes including the reduction of complement deposition and preservation of retinal architecture (Ong et al., 2024). Despite the encouraging therapeutic history of FD inhibitors in other indications, it is important to note that clinical trials evaluating FD inhibitors specifically for dry AMD or geographic atrophy have produced mixed results; one high-profile example is the failure of Lampalizumab (an FD inhibitor) to meet meaningful endpoints in pivotal phase 3 trials (Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019). Nonetheless, BCX9930 has distinct chemical and pharmacological properties that differentiate it from earlier candidates, including its strong potency, favorable oral bioavailability, and robust preclinical barrier rescue effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, making it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
The pathologic basis for many complement-mediated diseases, including dry AMD, lies in the dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, in which factor D plays a pivotal role. Normally, FD is the rate-limiting enzyme required to generate the AP C3 convertase by cleaving factor B complexed with C3b, which fuels an amplification loop and leads to the generation of downstream proinflammatory mediators such as C3a and C5a as well as opsonins that promote inflammation and tissue damage (Gavriilaki et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024). BCX9930 exerts its therapeutic effect by binding non-covalently in the S1 pocket of FD. This binding is characterized by exceptionally high affinity, with an IC₅₀ value of 4 nM, and by stringent selectivity that minimizes interference with other serine proteases. By occupying this key binding site, BCX9930 effectively prevents FD from interacting with its natural substrate, thereby arresting the production of the AP C3 convertase. This inhibition leads to a subsequent decrease in C3 cleavage and a reduction in the generation of complement split products, which are known to instigate an inflammatory response (Chen et al., 2022).  
Molecularly, the non-covalent nature of BCX9930’s interaction with factor D confers several advantages. First, such interactions allow reversible inhibition, providing the potential for controlled dosing and the fine-tuning of complement activity. Second, the selectivity profile of BCX9930 results from structural modifications aimed at optimizing the fit within the S1 pocket, ensuring that the inhibitor does not inadvertently affect enzymes with similar active site geometries. This precision is crucial, as systemic blockade of the complement system can result in significant immunosuppression. Thus, the protection of the retinal environment—by specifically inhibiting the amplification loop of the alternative pathway—offers a mechanistic rationale for the use of BCX9930 in diseases where complement overactivation is implicated, notably in the disruption of RPE tight junction integrity (Gavriilaki et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024). Additionally, the compound’s design ensures that while it attenuates pathogenic complement activity, it spares the classical and lectin pathways, reducing the risk of systemic immunocompromise.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for BCX9930 in the treatment of dry AMD is based on its ability to mitigate complement-mediated damage to the retinal pigment epithelium. In vitro studies in primary human RPE cells have shown that under conditions of serum-mediated complement activation, there is a decline in trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and disruption of critical tight junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and claudin-19. These proteins are essential for maintaining the barrier integrity of the RPE, and their dysregulation is a hallmark of retinal degeneration in AMD (Gavriilaki et al., 2022).  
The working hypothesis posits that by non-covalently occupying the S1 pocket of factor D, BCX9930 can inhibit the formation of the alternative pathway C3 convertase, thereby reducing the production of the inflammatory complement split products. This reduction is expected to lead to a decrease in complement-driven RPE tight junction disruption. Experimental data indicate that the addition of 500 nM BCX9930 to primary human RPE cultures challenged with serum results in a recovery of TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values. This recovery is associated with the restoration of tight junction integrity, as evidenced by the maintenance of ZO-1 and claudin-19 continuity, both of which are critical determinants of the barrier function (Chen et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024).  
In parallel, in vivo studies using Factor H-knockout animal models have provided supportive data for BCX9930’s therapeutic effect. In these animal models, which exhibit heightened complement activation and subsequent retinal damage similar to that seen in dry AMD, BCX9930 administered at 5 mg/kg twice daily resulted in a 70% reduction in complement C3 deposition on Bruch’s membrane and preservation of the outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness. These endpoints serve as surrogate indicators for photoreceptor protection and overall retinal health. Taken together, these findings underscore the capacity of BCX9930 not only to neutralize the biochemical drivers of complement activation but also to translate this inhibition into meaningful structural and functional preservation within the retina (Ong et al., 2024).  
Mechanistically, the expected effect hinges on the sustained and robust suppression of the alternative complement pathway, which under normal pathological conditions contributes significantly to the inflammatory milieu and structural degeneration characteristic of dry AMD. The reduction in complement activation is anticipated to curtail downstream inflammatory cascades that can disrupt RPE tight junctions, thereby stabilizing TEER and maintaining the integrity of the retinal barrier. Given that chronic complement activation has been implicated in accelerating the progression of dry AMD, the capacity of BCX9930 to restore and maintain RPE function could slow or even arrest disease progression, offering a novel therapeutic avenue for a condition currently lacking effective interventions (Chen et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating BCX9930 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key strengths and potential limitations must be considered. On the strength side, BCX9930 exhibits an exceptionally high potency (IC₅₀ = 4 nM) and selectivity profile that is well aligned with the intended mechanism of action. Its ability to non-covalently target the S1 pocket of factor D ensures that the inhibition of the alternative pathway is both potent and reversible, thereby allowing for controlled pharmacodynamic effects. The high degree of selectivity—exceeding 500-fold over related serine proteases—not only reduces the likelihood of off-target toxicity but also supports the feasibility of long-term administration required for chronic diseases such as dry AMD (Schubart et al., 2023).  
Preclinical studies provide compelling support for the candidate’s mechanism. The demonstration that 500 nM BCX9930 can recover TEER to 85% of baseline in human RPE cultures suggests that the compound effectively counteracts the complement-mediated disruption of intercellular tight junctions. Furthermore, animal data showing that a dosing regimen of 5 mg/kg BID can reduce Bruch’s membrane C3 deposition by 70% and preserve ONL thickness indicates that BCX9930 not only exerts biochemical effects but also translates these into anatomical preservation within the retina (Ong et al., 2024). Such findings are particularly relevant given the importance of maintaining RPE barrier function and photoreceptor viability in halting the progression of dry AMD.  
Another strong point in favor of BCX9930 is its oral bioavailability, which is a significant advantage over therapies that require invasive delivery methods (for example, intravitreal injections). An oral agent would potentially improve patient compliance and reduce the risks associated with repeated intraocular procedures. This is particularly critical in a disease like dry AMD, where the patient population is predominantly elderly, and minimizing treatment burden is essential (Chen et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).  
Despite these promising attributes, there are notable challenges and uncertainties that must be acknowledged. One major concern pertains to the historical track record of complement inhibitors in the treatment of dry AMD. Previous clinical trials with other agents targeting the alternative pathway—such as Lampalizumab—have ultimately failed to demonstrate robust clinical efficacy in phase 3 trials despite encouraging preclinical data (Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019). Such outcomes underscore the difficulty of translating complement inhibition into meaningful clinical benefits in retinal degenerative diseases. The complexity of AMD pathophysiology, which involves not only complement dysregulation but also oxidative stress, genetic predispositions, and environmental factors, means that addressing a single pathway may not be sufficient to fully arrest disease progression.  
Additionally, while the preclinical data for BCX9930 are encouraging, there is still a gap in clinical evidence demonstrating its efficacy specifically in dry AMD. Most of the clinical data currently available for BCX9930 have been derived from studies in conditions like C3G and PNH, where the pathobiology is somewhat different from that of retinal degenerative diseases. There is a high degree of uncertainty as to whether the pharmacodynamic markers observed in these other disease models—such as reductions in complement split products and improved hematological indices—will translate into improved retinal structure and function in AMD patients (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Chen et al., 2022).  
Safety is another domain that necessitates cautious exploration. Although the mechanism of action of BCX9930 suggests an improved tolerability profile owing to its selective inhibition of FD, experiences with analogous compounds (e.g., danicopan) have revealed potential issues such as liver enzyme elevations and other adverse events following sustained treatment (Schubart et al., 2023). It is essential that further clinical studies with BCX9930 incorporate rigorous monitoring of potential systemic toxicities and immune-related adverse effects, especially given the chronic nature of dry AMD therapy. Long-term data will be critical in confirming that the inhibition of the alternative pathway does not compromise overall host defense mechanisms or lead to other unexpected off-target consequences.  
Finally, the complexity of dry AMD as a clinical entity must guide any decision regarding the advancement of BCX9930. Complement-driven RPE disruption is only one facet of AMD pathogenesis; a multifactorial disease mechanism implies that combination therapies or multimodal approaches may eventually be needed to achieve optimal clinical outcomes. In this context, BCX9930 might best be positioned as part of a combination regimen, potentially alongside agents that address oxidative damage or other pathogenic mechanisms in AMD. Alternatively, biomarkers may need to be better defined so that patients most likely to benefit from complement inhibition can be identified and targeted in clinical trials (Kassa et al., 2019; Ong et al., 2024).  

In summary, BCX9930 represents a highly promising therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its potent and selective inhibition of factor D, a critical enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. The underlying rationale is strongly supported by both molecular and preclinical evidence: by binding non-covalently to the S1 pocket of factor D, BCX9930 effectively blocks the formation of the C3 convertase, thereby mitigating complement activation that is postulated to drive RPE tight junction disruption. In vitro studies have already demonstrated that BCX9930 can restore trans-epithelial electrical resistance and preserve the continuity of crucial tight junction proteins in human RPE cells under complement challenge. Additionally, animal models have provided evidence for significant reductions in complement deposition and the preservation of retinal architecture. These findings collectively indicate that BCX9930 has the potential to protect retinal tissue from complement-mediated injury, a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024).  

However, the transition from preclinical promise to clinical success remains a challenge, as highlighted by the mixed outcomes seen with previous factor D inhibitors in the AMD space. The failure of some earlier agents, despite robust biochemical data, emphasizes that the path from molecular inhibition to effective disease modification is complex and fraught with challenges. Critical areas of future research include the establishment of clear biomarkers that correlate with clinical outcomes in dry AMD, careful delineation of the safety profile specific to the elderly patient population, and the exploration of appropriate combination strategies that might enhance therapeutic efficacy.  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and encouraging preclinical data, BCX9930 stands out as a compelling candidate for further evaluation in clinical trials targeting dry AMD. Its precise mechanism of action and the potential for oral administration offer distinct advantages and may help overcome some of the limitations encountered with earlier complement inhibitors. Ultimately, while caution is warranted due to the historical challenges in this therapeutic area, the overall evaluation supports the advancement of BCX9930 for further development and rigorous clinical testing in dry AMD patients (Schubart et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019).

The hypothesis under evaluation is that inhibition of LOXL2 by PXS-5153A will prevent pathogenic collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in Bruch’s membrane (BM), reduce matrix stiffness, and by indirectly alleviating abnormal mechanical tension on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell receptors, stabilize RPE tight junction anchors (ZO-1/occludin). I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PXS-5153A is a synthetically derived molecule that belongs to the class of selective lysyl oxidase inhibitors. In its design, medicinal chemistry efforts focused on optimizing potency and selectivity for LOXL2, along with activity against LOXL3, two members of the lysyl oxidase family that catalyze the oxidative deamination of lysine residues in collagens and elastin to promote covalent crosslink formation. These crosslinks confer the mechanical strength and stiffness of extracellular matrices (ECMs) such as Bruch’s membrane. Synthetic routes to compounds like PXS-5153A typically rely on structure-based design and iterative optimization to achieve potent enzyme inhibition with favorable pharmacokinetic properties (Lin et al., 2020). The compound, commercially available under MedChemExpress HY-111217, is representative of a new therapeutic class that has been primarily explored in the context of fibrosis and tumor microenvironment modulation. Given that ECM stiffening is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, targeting LOXL2 represents a novel approach compared to conventional anti-inflammatory or anti-angiogenic strategies.

II. Therapeutic History  
The LOXL2 inhibitor class, including molecules such as PXS-5153A, has been extensively tested in preclinical models of fibrosis and cancer. For example, within non-ocular systems, LOXL2 activity has been linked to increased tissue stiffness that fosters metastatic progression and desmoplastic reactions in tumors, and selective inhibition of LOXL2 has been shown to reduce crosslink density, attenuating fibrotic remodeling (Lin et al., 2020). Experimental inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity using non-selective agents like β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) has also been applied to in vitro and in vivo models to modulate ECM assembly, with effects on barrier function observed in RPE cultures co-treated with endothelial cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). Although LOXL2 inhibitors have not traditionally been used to treat dry AMD, evidence underscores the centrality of aberrant ECM crosslinking in BM thickening observed during aging and AMD progression (Wang et al., 2025). In particular, the endothelial cell–RPE crosstalk studies demonstrate a critical role for lysyl oxidase activity in regulating collagen bundle formation and in establishing RPE barrier properties (Benedicto et al., 2017). Accordingly, while there is no direct clinical or preclinical record of PXS-5153A in AMD, the antifibrotic profile of the compound and its impact on extracellular matrix mechanics in other disease contexts serve as a compelling rationale to explore its application in dry AMD.

III. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, LOXL2 catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of lysine or hydroxylysine residues present in collagens and elastin. This reaction is critical for the formation of covalent crosslinks that stabilize the ECM. Overexpression or hyperactivity of LOXL2 results in an excessively crosslinked and stiff matrix. In the eye, particularly within Bruch’s membrane—which is a complex, stratified ECM structure located between the RPE and the choroid—aberrant collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking are known to increase mechanical tension. Such mechanical changes are thought to adversely affect RPE cell function by interfering with integrin-mediated cell–matrix interactions and perturbing the proper localization of tight junction proteins, including ZO-1 and occludin (Benedicto et al., 2017).

PXS-5153A functions by binding to the catalytic pocket of LOXL2, thereby preventing its enzymatic activity. By blocking the oxidative deamination step, PXS-5153A reduces the formation of both immature and mature crosslinks in ECM proteins. The anticipated outcome is a lower crosslink density in Bruch’s membrane, resulting in a softer, more compliant matrix environment. This reduction in mechanical stiffness is expected to diminish abnormal mechanosignaling through β1 integrins, which are integral to the assembly and maintenance of tight junctions on RPE cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). The downstream consequences of reduced integrin activation include dampening of Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways, which in turn facilitate the stabilization and proper localization of tight junction proteins at the RPE cell membranes (Benedicto et al., 2017). Restoration of these junctional complexes correlates with improved barrier function, typically measured as an increased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in cell culture models. This mechanism is supported by studies in which inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity—by pharmacological agents such as BAPN—led to alterations in RPE barrier properties and tight junction morphology (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by directly targeting LOXL2, PXS-5153A is proposed to correct the pathological ECM remodeling that underlies BM stiffening in dry AMD while re-establishing proper RPE barrier integrity.

IV. Expected Effect  
The expected therapeutic effect of PXS-5153A in dry AMD centers on normalization of the BM ECM and concomitant restoration of RPE barrier function. In the proposed experimental model—an in vitro co-culture system where human fetal RPE (hfRPE) cells are grown on a substrate mimicking BM with defined stiffness—the application of PXS-5153A at concentrations around 5 µM is anticipated to yield a number of favorable outcomes.

First, by reducing LOXL2-mediated crosslinking of collagen IV and fibronectin, the drug should decrease the mechanical stiffness of the BM analog. A less rigid BM reduces aberrant integrin activation on the basolateral surfaces of RPE cells, which has been shown to be critical for proper tight junction assembly. In several studies, when the extracellular matrix is normalized—such as by altering substrate stiffness—there is an improvement in the localization of key tight junction proteins, specifically occludin and ZO-1, at the cell membrane (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Second, the reduced matrix stiffness is expected to alleviate the mechanical stress experienced by RPE cells, thereby facilitating the re-establishment of cell polarity and intercellular junction continuity. The stabilization of junctional complexes is measurable by TEER. In previous EC–RPE co-culture experiments, modulation of ECM mechanical properties directly correlated with increased TEER values, reflecting improved barrier function (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Moreover, the proper organization of the basement membrane is not only a structural consideration; the biochemical signaling through β1 integrin receptors—critical for maintaining cell adhesion and survival—would return toward homeostatic levels, further supporting the integrity of the RPE layer (Benedicto et al., 2017). These integrin-mediated signals influence downstream effectors such as Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK, which have been implicated in regulating tight junction dynamics (Benedicto et al., 2017). Progress in these pathways is expected to manifest as an overall improvement in the barrier phenotype, which is central to preventing the leakage of fluid and other deleterious solutes into the subretinal space—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.

In summary, it is anticipated that treatment with PXS-5153A in appropriate in vitro (and ultimately in vivo) models will lead to:  
• Reduced collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in BM, yielding a matrix with decreased stiffness (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Normalization of β1 integrin signaling and subsequent reorganization of RPE tight junctions with improved localization of proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Restoration of barrier function as evidenced by increased TEER measurements and improved paracellular permeability profiles (Benedicto et al., 2017).  

Thus, PXS-5153A is expected to address one of the core aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis by targeting ECM remodeling, which in turn indirectly stabilizes RPE cell function.

V. Overall Evaluation  
The concept of using PXS-5153A to modulate ECM pathology in dry AMD is compelling given the mechanistic insights derived from studies on lysyl oxidase activity in epithelial barrier function and ECM assembly. Among the strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its robust preclinical evidence in fibrosis and tumor microenvironment models. LOXL2 has been implicated in promoting tissue stiffening by catalyzing the crosslinking of collagen and fibronectin in various tissues (Lin et al., 2020). The pathophysiological parallels between fibrotic ECM remodeling in cancers and the stiffening of Bruch’s membrane in dry AMD provide a strong rationale for repurposing a LOXL2 inhibitor in an ocular context. Numerous studies have demonstrated that extracellular matrix integrity is essential for optimal RPE barrier function, and that even subtle changes in ECM mechanics can disrupt junctional complexes and lead to barrier dysfunction (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by targeting a critical enzymatic step in ECM crosslinking, PXS-5153A may confer dual benefits: it could both reduce the pathological stiffening of Bruch’s membrane and promote the reorganization of tight junction complexes, ultimately resulting in enhanced TEER and stabilization of the outer blood–retina barrier.

However, several important weaknesses or uncertainties must be considered. First, while numerous studies (using agents such as BAPN) have illustrated that lysyl oxidase inhibition affects RPE barrier function, direct evidence with selective LOXL2 inhibitors—specifically in ocular models of dry AMD—is lacking (Buniello et al., 2025). In fact, the Open Targets Platform indicates only a weak direct association between LOXL2 and age-related macular degeneration, based on limited literature evidence (Buniello et al., 2025). This raises the possibility that, although LOXL2 plays a demonstrable role in ECM crosslinking in other tissues, its specific involvement in dry AMD pathogenesis may not be as pronounced or may be influenced by other factors not recapitulated in non-ocular models.

Furthermore, potential off-target effects or the consequences of broadly altering ECM crosslinking in the eye must be carefully examined. The structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane is critical not only for its barrier function but also for nutrient transport between the choroidal circulation and the RPE. Overinhibition of LOXL2, or interference with normal ECM turnover, may inadvertently lead to basement membrane disorganization, as has been observed when lysyl oxidase activity was inhibited during critical periods of retinal development (Benedicto et al., 2017). This underscores the need for precise dose optimization and targeted delivery, ideally restricted to the ocular environment, to avoid systemic side effects.

Another consideration is the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. In addition to ECM stiffening, dry AMD involves multifactorial processes including oxidative stress, complement activation, inflammation, and the accumulation of lipoprotein deposits. Thus, while normalizing matrix stiffness is likely to improve RPE barrier function, it may be insufficient to fully arrest or reverse the disease process on its own. A combination therapy that also addresses the inflammatory and degenerative components of AMD may eventually be required (Benedicto et al., 2017; Caban et al., 2022).

From a development perspective, there is significant strength in the repurposing strategy because agents like PXS-5153A already have a detailed preclinical profile in non-ocular fibrotic models. This existing data can accelerate preclinical validation in ocular models, with studies planned in RPE–BM co-culture systems using TEER as a functional readout (Benedicto et al., 2017). Furthermore, leveraging well-characterized in vitro assays (such as those involving decellularized ECM and substrate stiffness modulation as described in the context) offers a clear experimental framework to evaluate whether the normalization of BM stiffness by PXS-5153A is sufficient to restore RPE tight junction integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017).

Nonetheless, one notable weakness is the limited direct evidence linking LOXL2 specifically to dry AMD. Although elevated lysyl oxidase activity and changes in collagen crosslinking have been observed in the context of RPE barrier function and BM integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017), the genetic and translational data associating LOXL2 with AMD are not robust. The relatively low association score (Buniello et al., 2025) suggests that additional studies are needed to clarify LOXL2’s role in the eye and to determine whether its inhibition will yield a therapeutically meaningful benefit in dry AMD patients.

In conclusion, repurposing PXS-5153A for dry AMD represents an innovative strategy that leverages the known antifibrotic effects of LOXL2 inhibition to address the deleterious ECM remodeling observed in aged Bruch’s membrane. The candidate’s synthetic origins and prior applications in fibrosis and cancer studies provide a solid foundation for its use, while the mechanistic rationale—centered on reducing pathological crosslinking and restoring RPE barrier function—is strongly supported by evidence from ECM modulation studies (Benedicto et al., 2017). However, challenges remain due to the lack of direct ocular data, potential risks of overmodulating ECM integrity, and the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology. Future research must focus on rigorous in vitro validation in RPE–BM co-culture systems and in vivo studies in relevant AMD animal models to establish the efficacy and safety profile of PXS-5153A in the context of dry AMD. Overall, despite these uncertainties, PXS-5153A holds promise as a novel ECM-targeted therapeutic candidate that could complement existing and emerging treatment strategies for this currently unmet clinical need (Lin et al., 2020; Buniello et al., 2025).

Taken together, the strengths of a clear mechanism of action, potent enzyme selectivity, and an innovative approach toward ECM normalization position PXS-5153A as an attractive candidate warranting further investigation. Nonetheless, a careful reappraisal of the molecular role of LOXL2 in the ocular microenvironment, along with detailed studies on dosing, delivery, and potential off-target effects, will be critical in determining whether this candidate can be successfully repurposed for treating dry AMD.

Z944 is a synthetic, rationally designed T‐type calcium channel blocker that emerged from a medicinal chemistry program aimed at developing first‐in‐class modulators with improved selectivity and pharmacokinetic profiles. Historically, Z944 has been developed and evaluated extensively in preclinical models focused on pain management and epilepsy, demonstrating encouraging translational potential by restoring functional neuronal circuit dynamics in both inflammatory pain and absence epilepsy models (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Melgari et al., 2022). Clinical studies have established that Z944 can effectively modulate T‐type calcium channel activity in human experimental models of inflammatory pain, and it has been advanced into Phase I and Phase II clinical trials targeting pain indications (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018). However, a consistent theme throughout published reports is that Z944, along with similar T‐type channel antagonists, has been primarily evaluated in the context of neurological disorders. Comprehensive literature reviews and patent analyses have yet to document any clinical or preclinical application of Z944 or related T‐type calcium channel blockers in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD), retinal degeneration, or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Sun et al., 2025; Jones, 2024). The modulator’s history in pain and epilepsy provides a solid foundation for its general pharmacological activity, yet its use in ocular settings remains uncharted territory.  

Mechanism of Action:  
Z944 exerts its pharmacological effects primarily through the selective inhibition of T‐type calcium channels. At the molecular level, T‐type channels (CaV3 family) are low–voltage‐activated channels essential for regulating neuronal excitability and rhythmic firing. Using state-dependent screening assays against the human CaV3.2 channel subunit, researchers have demonstrated that Z944 binds with high affinity (IC₅₀ in the range of 50–160 nM against various CaV3 isoforms), and its selectivity exceeds 70–100‐fold when compared to channels such as the CaV2.2 (N‐type) and CaV1.2 (L‐type) channels (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018). In neurons, this inhibition translates into a decreased excitability and modulation of burst firing patterns. Extrapolating from these findings, one could hypothesize that, in non–neuronal cells such as RPE, Z944 would likewise reduce pathological calcium entry induced by oxidative stress. In the specific context of dry AMD, oxidative stress and the accumulation of toxic by‐products such as A2E have been implicated in the disruption of intracellular calcium homeostasis. Immunostaining studies in mouse RPE tissue have confirmed the presence of CaV3.1 and CaV3.2 isoforms, indicating that T‐type channel–mediated calcium influx contributes to RPE physiology (Korkka, n.d.). While the direct mechanistic link between T‐type channel inhibition and the prevention of calpain/calcineurin activation in RPE cells remains to be experimentally verified, the well‐established role of calcium as a trigger for these enzymes suggests that Z944 could effectively mitigate calcium‐dependent tight junction degradation if pathological calcium overload is sufficiently attenuated.
