I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PXS-5153A is a synthetically derived molecule that belongs to the class of selective lysyl oxidase inhibitors. In its design, medicinal chemistry efforts focused on optimizing potency and selectivity for LOXL2, along with activity against LOXL3, two members of the lysyl oxidase family that catalyze the oxidative deamination of lysine residues in collagens and elastin to promote covalent crosslink formation. These crosslinks confer the mechanical strength and stiffness of extracellular matrices (ECMs) such as Bruch’s membrane. Synthetic routes to compounds like PXS-5153A typically rely on structure-based design and iterative optimization to achieve potent enzyme inhibition with favorable pharmacokinetic properties (Lin et al., 2020). The compound, commercially available under MedChemExpress HY-111217, is representative of a new therapeutic class that has been primarily explored in the context of fibrosis and tumor microenvironment modulation. Given that ECM stiffening is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, targeting LOXL2 represents a novel approach compared to conventional anti-inflammatory or anti-angiogenic strategies.

II. Therapeutic History  
The LOXL2 inhibitor class, including molecules such as PXS-5153A, has been extensively tested in preclinical models of fibrosis and cancer. For example, within non-ocular systems, LOXL2 activity has been linked to increased tissue stiffness that fosters metastatic progression and desmoplastic reactions in tumors, and selective inhibition of LOXL2 has been shown to reduce crosslink density, attenuating fibrotic remodeling (Lin et al., 2020). Experimental inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity using non-selective agents like β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) has also been applied to in vitro and in vivo models to modulate ECM assembly, with effects on barrier function observed in RPE cultures co-treated with endothelial cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). Although LOXL2 inhibitors have not traditionally been used to treat dry AMD, evidence underscores the centrality of aberrant ECM crosslinking in BM thickening observed during aging and AMD progression (Wang et al., 2025). In particular, the endothelial cell–RPE crosstalk studies demonstrate a critical role for lysyl oxidase activity in regulating collagen bundle formation and in establishing RPE barrier properties (Benedicto et al., 2017). Accordingly, while there is no direct clinical or preclinical record of PXS-5153A in AMD, the antifibrotic profile of the compound and its impact on extracellular matrix mechanics in other disease contexts serve as a compelling rationale to explore its application in dry AMD.

III. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, LOXL2 catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of lysine or hydroxylysine residues present in collagens and elastin. This reaction is critical for the formation of covalent crosslinks that stabilize the ECM. Overexpression or hyperactivity of LOXL2 results in an excessively crosslinked and stiff matrix. In the eye, particularly within Bruch’s membrane—which is a complex, stratified ECM structure located between the RPE and the choroid—aberrant collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking are known to increase mechanical tension. Such mechanical changes are thought to adversely affect RPE cell function by interfering with integrin-mediated cell–matrix interactions and perturbing the proper localization of tight junction proteins, including ZO-1 and occludin (Benedicto et al., 2017).

PXS-5153A functions by binding to the catalytic pocket of LOXL2, thereby preventing its enzymatic activity. By blocking the oxidative deamination step, PXS-5153A reduces the formation of both immature and mature crosslinks in ECM proteins. The anticipated outcome is a lower crosslink density in Bruch’s membrane, resulting in a softer, more compliant matrix environment. This reduction in mechanical stiffness is expected to diminish abnormal mechanosignaling through β1 integrins, which are integral to the assembly and maintenance of tight junctions on RPE cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). The downstream consequences of reduced integrin activation include dampening of Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways, which in turn facilitate the stabilization and proper localization of tight junction proteins at the RPE cell membranes (Benedicto et al., 2017). Restoration of these junctional complexes correlates with improved barrier function, typically measured as an increased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in cell culture models. This mechanism is supported by studies in which inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity—by pharmacological agents such as BAPN—led to alterations in RPE barrier properties and tight junction morphology (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by directly targeting LOXL2, PXS-5153A is proposed to correct the pathological ECM remodeling that underlies BM stiffening in dry AMD while re-establishing proper RPE barrier integrity.

IV. Expected Effect  
The expected therapeutic effect of PXS-5153A in dry AMD centers on normalization of the BM ECM and concomitant restoration of RPE barrier function. In the proposed experimental model—an in vitro co-culture system where human fetal RPE (hfRPE) cells are grown on a substrate mimicking BM with defined stiffness—the application of PXS-5153A at concentrations around 5 µM is anticipated to yield a number of favorable outcomes.

First, by reducing LOXL2-mediated crosslinking of collagen IV and fibronectin, the drug should decrease the mechanical stiffness of the BM analog. A less rigid BM reduces aberrant integrin activation on the basolateral surfaces of RPE cells, which has been shown to be critical for proper tight junction assembly. In several studies, when the extracellular matrix is normalized—such as by altering substrate stiffness—there is an improvement in the localization of key tight junction proteins, specifically occludin and ZO-1, at the cell membrane (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Second, the reduced matrix stiffness is expected to alleviate the mechanical stress experienced by RPE cells, thereby facilitating the re-establishment of cell polarity and intercellular junction continuity. The stabilization of junctional complexes is measurable by TEER. In previous EC–RPE co-culture experiments, modulation of ECM mechanical properties directly correlated with increased TEER values, reflecting improved barrier function (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Moreover, the proper organization of the basement membrane is not only a structural consideration; the biochemical signaling through β1 integrin receptors—critical for maintaining cell adhesion and survival—would return toward homeostatic levels, further supporting the integrity of the RPE layer (Benedicto et al., 2017). These integrin-mediated signals influence downstream effectors such as Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK, which have been implicated in regulating tight junction dynamics (Benedicto et al., 2017). Progress in these pathways is expected to manifest as an overall improvement in the barrier phenotype, which is central to preventing the leakage of fluid and other deleterious solutes into the subretinal space—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.

In summary, it is anticipated that treatment with PXS-5153A in appropriate in vitro (and ultimately in vivo) models will lead to:  
• Reduced collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in BM, yielding a matrix with decreased stiffness (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Normalization of β1 integrin signaling and subsequent reorganization of RPE tight junctions with improved localization of proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Restoration of barrier function as evidenced by increased TEER measurements and improved paracellular permeability profiles (Benedicto et al., 2017).  

Thus, PXS-5153A is expected to address one of the core aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis by targeting ECM remodeling, which in turn indirectly stabilizes RPE cell function.

V. Overall Evaluation  
The concept of using PXS-5153A to modulate ECM pathology in dry AMD is compelling given the mechanistic insights derived from studies on lysyl oxidase activity in epithelial barrier function and ECM assembly. Among the strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its robust preclinical evidence in fibrosis and tumor microenvironment models. LOXL2 has been implicated in promoting tissue stiffening by catalyzing the crosslinking of collagen and fibronectin in various tissues (Lin et al., 2020). The pathophysiological parallels between fibrotic ECM remodeling in cancers and the stiffening of Bruch’s membrane in dry AMD provide a strong rationale for repurposing a LOXL2 inhibitor in an ocular context. Numerous studies have demonstrated that extracellular matrix integrity is essential for optimal RPE barrier function, and that even subtle changes in ECM mechanics can disrupt junctional complexes and lead to barrier dysfunction (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by targeting a critical enzymatic step in ECM crosslinking, PXS-5153A may confer dual benefits: it could both reduce the pathological stiffening of Bruch’s membrane and promote the reorganization of tight junction complexes, ultimately resulting in enhanced TEER and stabilization of the outer blood–retina barrier.

However, several important weaknesses or uncertainties must be considered. First, while numerous studies (using agents such as BAPN) have illustrated that lysyl oxidase inhibition affects RPE barrier function, direct evidence with selective LOXL2 inhibitors—specifically in ocular models of dry AMD—is lacking (Buniello et al., 2025). In fact, the Open Targets Platform indicates only a weak direct association between LOXL2 and age-related macular degeneration, based on limited literature evidence (Buniello et al., 2025). This raises the possibility that, although LOXL2 plays a demonstrable role in ECM crosslinking in other tissues, its specific involvement in dry AMD pathogenesis may not be as pronounced or may be influenced by other factors not recapitulated in non-ocular models.

Furthermore, potential off-target effects or the consequences of broadly altering ECM crosslinking in the eye must be carefully examined. The structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane is critical not only for its barrier function but also for nutrient transport between the choroidal circulation and the RPE. Overinhibition of LOXL2, or interference with normal ECM turnover, may inadvertently lead to basement membrane disorganization, as has been observed when lysyl oxidase activity was inhibited during critical periods of retinal development (Benedicto et al., 2017). This underscores the need for precise dose optimization and targeted delivery, ideally restricted to the ocular environment, to avoid systemic side effects.

Another consideration is the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. In addition to ECM stiffening, dry AMD involves multifactorial processes including oxidative stress, complement activation, inflammation, and the accumulation of lipoprotein deposits. Thus, while normalizing matrix stiffness is likely to improve RPE barrier function, it may be insufficient to fully arrest or reverse the disease process on its own. Although elevated lysyl oxidase activity and changes in collagen crosslinking have been observed in the context of RPE barrier function and BM integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017), the genetic and translational data associating LOXL2 with AMD are not robust. The relatively low association score (Buniello et al., 2025) suggests that additional studies are needed to clarify LOXL2’s role in the eye and to determine whether its inhibition will yield a therapeutically meaningful benefit in dry AMD patients.

The candidate’s synthetic origins and prior applications in fibrosis and cancer studies provide a solid foundation for its use, while the mechanistic rationale—centered on reducing pathological crosslinking and restoring RPE barrier function—is strongly supported by evidence from ECM modulation studies (Benedicto et al., 2017). However, challenges remain due to the lack of direct ocular data, potential risks of overmodulating ECM integrity, and the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology. Future research must focus on rigorous in vitro validation in RPE–BM co-culture systems and in vivo studies in relevant AMD animal models to establish the efficacy and safety profile of PXS-5153A in the context of dry AMD. Overall, despite these uncertainties, PXS-5153A holds promise as a novel ECM-targeted therapeutic candidate that could complement existing and emerging treatment strategies for this currently unmet clinical need (Lin et al., 2020; Buniello et al., 2025).

Taken together, the strengths of a clear mechanism of action, potent enzyme selectivity, and an innovative approach toward ECM normalization position PXS-5153A as an attractive candidate warranting further investigation. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Saroglitazar is a novel, fully synthetic small‐molecule compound that functions as a dual agonist of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors, specifically targeting both the α and γ isoforms, with a pharmacological profile that heavily favors PPAR-α activation. Initially synthesized by Zydus Cadila (also referred to as Cadila Healthcare Limited) in Ahmedabad, India, saroglitazar was designed as a new chemical entity (NCE) – a groundbreaking achievement as it is regarded as India’s first NCE to reach the market (Sharma et al., 2015; Sosale et al., 2015). Chemically, it is defined as (S)-α-ethoxy-4-{2-[2-methyl-5-(4-methylthio)phenyl]-1H-pyrrol-1-yl]ethoxy}-benzenepropanoic acid magnesium salt, a structure that confers the necessary lipophilic and acidic characteristics common among PPAR agonists (Jain et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2015). Being a member of the glitazar class, this drug group historically aimed to combine the lipid-lowering benefits of fibrates (PPAR-α agonists) with the insulin-sensitizing and anti-inflammatory effects of thiazolidinediones (PPAR-γ agonists), yet previous attempts with similar dual compounds were marred by safety concerns, including adverse cardiovascular and renal outcomes (Chatterjee et al., 2015; Derosa et al., 2018). Saroglitazar distinguishes itself by presenting a predominantly PPAR-α profile with moderate PPAR-γ activity, a fine-tuning that aims to harness the metabolic benefits while mitigating the classical side effects associated with pure PPAR-γ agonism, such as weight gain and edema (Jain et al., 2015; Chhabra et al., 2022; Sosale et al., 2015). Its synthetic origin, coupled with a well-characterized chemical structure that includes key functional groups (in particular, an α-ethoxy carboxylic acid moiety that forms hydrogen bonds with amino acid residues in the receptor binding domain), has enabled a robust mechanistic foundation from which to understand its systemic pharmacology (Joshi, 2015; Sharma et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, saroglitazar has been approved by India’s Drug Controller General (DCGI) for the treatment of diabetic dyslipidemia and hypertriglyceridemia in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) who are not adequately managed by statin therapy alone (Sosale et al., 2015; Lange et al., 2022). Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its lipid-lowering, insulin-sensitizing, and anti-inflammatory effects in multiple animal models, ranging from diabetic rodents (db/db mice, Zucker fa/fa rats) to nonhuman primates; these studies laid the groundwork for phase I human trials, the results of which indicated favorable pharmacokinetics and safety margins (Jain et al., 2015; Joshi, 2015; Jani et al., 2013). Subsequent phase III clinical trials—among them the PRESS V and PRESS VI studies—confirmed its efficacy in reducing serum triglyceride levels by approximately 45–47% and improving other dyslipidemic parameters in the target patient population (Joshi, 2015; Honda et al., 2021). Beyond its use in diabetic dyslipidemia, recent research efforts have extended its potential application into metabolic liver diseases such as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) (Honda et al., 2021; Vuppalanchi et al., 2022). Despite the substantial body of literature supporting its use in metabolic disorders, none of the documented clinical or preclinical studies to date have directly tested saroglitazar in ocular conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal pathologies (Tan et al., 2017; Kaul et al., 2019). However, the robust clinical validation of saroglitazar’s dual PPAR-α/γ effects in liver disease and diabetic dyslipidemia provides an important translational basis for its repurposing, especially given that both chronic inflammation and disordered lipid metabolism have been recognized as central drivers in the progression of dry AMD (Sharma et al., 2015; Sosale et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, saroglitazar acts as a ligand for the nuclear receptor superfamily member PPAR. Once bound, the compound facilitates the heterodimerization of the activated receptor with the retinoid X receptor (RXR), and this heterodimer subsequently binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the promoter regions of target genes, thus initiating transcriptional regulation (Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.; Joshi, 2015). The activation of PPAR-α by saroglitazar leads to an upregulation of genes involved in hepatic fatty acid oxidation pathways, including enzymes responsible for β-oxidation, which results in decreased triglyceride synthesis and secretion while enhancing the clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (Patel et al., 2018a; Patel et al., 2018b). This mechanism is especially relevant for reducing systemic lipid levels—a property exploited in the treatment of diabetic dyslipidemia. Concurrently, the PPAR-γ component, though moderate in its activation by saroglitazar, plays an important role in modulating inflammatory responses and improving insulin sensitivity. Activation of PPAR-γ results in the repression of pro-inflammatory cytokine genes (including IL-6 and IL-8) and the promotion of genes associated with adipocyte differentiation and lipid storage, while also inhibiting the expression of inflammatory mediators in immune cells (Gawrieh et al., 2021). Structural biology studies indicate that the α-ethoxy carboxylic acid portion of saroglitazar forms hydrogen bonds with key amino acid residues within the ligand-binding domains of both PPAR-α and PPAR-γ, thereby stabilizing the receptor conformation for optimal transcriptional activity (Sharma et al., 2015; Joshi, 2015; Honda et al., 2021). This dual receptor engagement enables a coordinated response where lipid metabolism is corrected via PPAR-α activation while a parallel anti-inflammatory effect is mediated through PPAR-γ, ultimately leading to improved metabolic homeostasis (Honda et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2017).

In the context of dry AMD, the chronic low-grade inflammation observed within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) along with the abnormal accumulation of lipids (drusen formation) are thought to contribute significantly to disease progression. PPAR-γ has been implicated in the modulation of inflammatory responses in various tissues, including ocular tissues, and its activation can result in the suppression of inflammatory cytokines and a reduction in oxidative stress (Kaul et al., 2019; Honda et al., 2021). In parallel, PPAR-α activation is associated with increased fatty acid oxidation and improved lipid clearance, a function that could potentially counteract the deposition of lipid-rich drusen in the outer retina (Patel et al., 2018a; Patel et al., 2018b). Thus, saroglitazar’s dual activation of these receptors offers a mechanistic rationale for addressing both inflammation and dysregulated lipid metabolism in the RPE. Given that barrier integrity in the RPE, as measured by transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), is closely linked to the expression and organization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, the anti-inflammatory actions of PPAR-γ may be critical in preserving these junctional complexes under inflammatory stress, as evidenced by experimental models where TNF-α exposure leads to barrier compromise (Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.; Chhabra et al., 2022). The structural and molecular interactions described in the literature provide a detailed understanding of how saroglitazar can modulate these pathways at the transcriptional level, potentially offering both immediate and long-term benefits in maintaining RPE barrier function (Joshi, 2015; Sosale et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis under investigation is that dual PPAR-α/γ activation by saroglitazar will exert a synergistic effect on RPE cells under conditions of inflammatory stress—a condition that mirrors the pathophysiology of dry AMD. In an in vitro model employing the ARPE-19 cell line (a well-established human RPE cell model), exposure to the pro-inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) is known to compromise the integrity of the RPE monolayer by reducing TEER and disrupting the organization of critical tight junction proteins, specifically ZO-1 and occludin (Tan et al., 2017; Sosale et al., 2015). Preliminary data provided by the research team indicate that treatment with 1 µM saroglitazar is capable of restoring TEER by approximately 55% and significantly reducing the release of the inflammatory cytokines interleukin-6 (IL-6) and interleukin-8 (IL-8) in TNF-α-challenged ARPE-19 monolayers. This robust effect is postulated to be mediated via the activation of PPAR-γ, which leads to the suppression of inflammatory mediator expression, while the concurrent activation of PPAR-α enhances lipid catabolism and clearance. Such dual action is particularly relevant, given that chronic inflammation and impaired lipid metabolism are two principal drivers in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Sosale et al., 2015; Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.).

Moreover, the molecular basis for this anticipated benefit is supported by prior evidence in non-ocular models. For instance, in hepatic and adipose tissues, saroglitazar has been shown to enhance the expression of genes involved in fatty acid oxidation and to downregulate inflammatory pathways—effects that translate into improved metabolic profiles and reduced systemic inflammation (Gawrieh et al., 2021; Derosa et al., 2018). Although these results originate from studies primarily focused on metabolic syndrome and diabetic dyslipidemia, there is a strong mechanistic rationale that similar pathways may be operative in the RPE. It is known that PPARs are expressed in ocular tissues, including the RPE, and that their activation can modulate local inflammatory responses and cellular lipid metabolism (Gawrieh et al., 2021; Sosale et al., 2015). Thus, in the proposed experimental context, saroglitazar is expected to restore RPE monolayer integrity by preserving the ZO-1 and occludin architecture and recovering TEER—in turn, this could prevent the leakage of toxic substances and inflammatory mediators that exacerbate RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.

In addition to its effects on the RPE barrier, the anti-inflammatory properties conferred by PPAR-γ activation may also counteract the paracrine signaling that contributes to chronic inflammation in the retina; reduced secretion of IL-6 and IL-8 will likely diminish local immune cell recruitment and activation, thereby alleviating the inflammatory milieu that predisposes to cell damage and drusen formation (Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.; Sosale et al., 2015). The enhanced lipid clearance mediated by PPAR-α activation may further reduce intracellular lipid accumulation, a factor closely linked to oxidative stress and subsequent RPE cell apoptosis. Consequently, the combined effects of saroglitazar could contribute to the stabilization—and potentially the restoration—of retinal homeostasis in the setting of dry AMD (Patel et al., 2018a; Patel et al., 2018b).

Overall Evaluation:  
Taken together, saroglitazar emerges as a promising repurposing candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its dual pharmacological actions. Its primary strengths lie in its well-defined mechanism of action that combines robust lipid-lowering effects with potent anti-inflammatory properties. The predominant activation of PPAR-α is particularly advantageous in enhancing fatty acid oxidation and reducing lipid deposition, which may help in curbing the formation of drusen—a hallmark of dry AMD—while the moderate activation of PPAR-γ minimizes the risk of adverse effects such as weight gain and edema that have historically accompanied other PPAR-γ-targeted therapies (Sharma et al., 2015; Sosale et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2017). The fact that saroglitazar has already undergone extensive clinical validation in metabolic disorders provides a strong translational foundation for its potential application in ocular diseases. Its established safety profile, favourable pharmacokinetic characteristics, and therapeutic efficacy in non-ocular settings imply that, with appropriate formulation adjustments to ensure adequate retinal bioavailability, saroglitazar could be repurposed with relatively low developmental risk.

However, the candidate also has notable weaknesses. Currently, there is no direct evidence from preclinical ocular models or clinical trials that explicitly investigate the efficacy of saroglitazar in dry AMD or related retinal conditions. The pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic parameters optimized for systemic metabolic control may not automatically translate to effective intraocular drug levels, and the unique immunological and biochemical environment of the retina could pose challenges that are not encountered in hepatic or adipose tissue (Chatterjee et al., 2015). Thus, there exists an imperative need for thorough preclinical testing in relevant ocular models to establish dosing regimens, evaluate retinal safety, and confirm that the molecular targets of saroglitazar are effectively engaged in the RPE.

Another potential challenge lies in drug delivery. Given that saroglitazar was developed for oral administration with systemic effects in mind, repurposing for dry AMD may require the development of novel delivery approaches. This could include exploring topical eye drop formulations, intravitreal injections, or even sustained-release implants to ensure that therapeutic concentrations are achieved in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects. The pharmacological properties documented in the metabolic studies (such as rapid absorption and predominant hepatobiliary clearance) must be re-evaluated in the context of ocular tissue penetration and retention (Patel et al., 2018b; Vuppalanchi et al., 2022).

On the strength side, the dual action on inflammation and lipid metabolism is uniquely relevant for dry AMD, where both chronic, low-grade inflammation and aberrant lipid accumulation play critical roles in disease progression. In vitro data showing that 1 µM saroglitazar can restore TEER by 55% in TNF-α–compromised ARPE-19 monolayers and decrease pro-inflammatory cytokine release (IL-6, IL-8) provide promising initial proof-of-concept evidence that warrants further investigation (Sosale et al., 2015; Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.). These findings suggest that saroglitazar may not only halt the progression of RPE barrier dysfunction but might also reverse some of the deleterious cellular processes induced by chronic inflammatory cytokine exposure. Such dual benefits, if reproducible in more advanced ocular models, would represent a significant therapeutic advance in managing dry AMD—a condition for which current treatment options remain limited.

In summary, saroglitazar’s established safety and efficacy in metabolic diseases, together with its molecular capacity to modulate both inflammatory cascades and lipid metabolism, render it an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. The proposed mechanism—that dual PPAR-α/γ activation can restore RPE barrier integrity by preserving tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin) and enhancing transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) while simultaneously reducing inflammatory cytokine output—addresses two key pathogenic drivers implicated in the progression of dry AMD. Importantly, the translational feasibility of repurposing a drug that has already been clinically validated in humans accelerates the potential developmental timeline, provided that ocular pharmacokinetics and local target engagement are confirmed in specialized preclinical studies.

It is recommended that further studies be designed to (1) characterize the expression and functionality of PPAR-α and PPAR-γ receptors in primary human RPE cells and in animal models of dry AMD; (2) adapt the formulation of saroglitazar to optimize intraocular delivery and retention; (3) conduct detailed mechanistic studies that elucidate the molecular pathways through which saroglitazar modulates tight junction integrity and inflammatory signaling in the RPE; and (4) perform in vivo proof-of-concept studies using established animal models of dry AMD to evaluate both efficacy and safety in the ocular context (Sosale et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2017; Gawrieh et al., 2021). Addressing these points would greatly strengthen the rationale for clinical trials investigating saroglitazar as a novel therapeutic option for dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Strengths of saroglitazar as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD include its thoroughly characterized dual agonist activity, which confers both an enhanced lipid-clearing effect via PPAR-α activation and a potent anti-inflammatory effect via PPAR-γ activation. The compound’s safety profile and clinical validation in metabolic disorders, such as diabetic dyslipidemia and NAFLD, provide a robust foundation for potential repurposing, leveraging existing pharmacokinetic and toxicological data (Sharma et al., 2015; Sosale et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2017). Additionally, the preliminary in vitro evidence indicating improvements in RPE barrier function—with measurable restoration of TEER and reduction in key inflammatory markers like IL-6 and IL-8—are highly encouraging, as they suggest that saroglitazar may help halt or even reverse the RPE dysfunction that is central to dry AMD pathology (Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.; Sosale et al., 2015).

Nonetheless, the weaknesses of this approach cannot be overlooked. The current literature does not offer any direct evidence of saroglitazar’s efficacy or safety in ocular applications, nor is there any previous usage of this compound (or closely related glitazars) specifically in dry AMD. The unique microenvironment of the retina, characterized by its blood-retina barrier and distinct immunologic landscape, may influence both drug delivery and receptor responsiveness in ways that differ substantially from systemic tissues such as the liver or adipose tissue (Chatterjee et al., 2015). Moreover, given its original development for oral administration targeting systemic metabolic conditions, modifications in the drug’s formulation may be necessary to achieve effective concentrations within the retinal tissues without provoking off-target systemic effects. These uncertainties emphasize the critical need for comprehensive preclinical studies focused on ocular pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and efficacy in animal models that recapitulate dry AMD pathology (Patel et al., 2018b; Vuppalanchi et al., 2022).

In conclusion, saroglitazar presents a scientifically compelling and mechanistically plausible candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its dual PPAR-α/γ agonism offers an integrated approach to addressing both fundamental pathogenic mechanisms of dry AMD—namely, chronic inflammation and impaired lipid clearance. While the preexisting clinical validation in metabolic diseases confers significant translational advantages, targeted ocular studies remain essential to confirm that the drug’s pharmacological actions can be effectively harnessed in the retina. Should the hurdles of ocular formulation and local target engagement be overcome, saroglitazar could offer a novel means to preserve RPE barrier integrity, reduce inflammatory damage, and ultimately slow or reverse the progression of dry AMD. Given these considerations, the proposed repurposing of saroglitazar merits further investigation through detailed preclinical ocular studies and, pending positive results, subsequent clinical trials tailored for patients with dry AMD (Sosale et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2017; Gawrieh et al., 2021).

Overall, saroglitazar’s repurposing for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and promising preliminary in vitro data; however, significant challenges remain regarding its intraocular delivery, pharmacokinetic optimization, and direct demonstration of efficacy in ocular models. A balanced research strategy that addresses these issues through systematic preclinical evaluation and formulation development is warranted to fully elucidate the therapeutic potential of saroglitazar in managing dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
JQ1 (Selleck S7110) is a synthetic small-molecule thienotriazolodiazepine developed as a first-in-class, highly selective competitive inhibitor of the bromodomain and extra-terminal (BET) acetyl-lysine reader family (BRD2/3/4, BRDT) that binds the acetyl-lysine pocket of BET bromodomains (BD1 and BD2) to displace BET proteins from chromatin and suppress transcription at dependent enhancers and promoters (pan-BET, BD1/BD2 non-selective) (Zhao et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2023). BET bromodomains recognize acetylated histone tails at active enhancers/super-enhancers and recruit coactivator assemblies that couple to RNA polymerase II to drive high-amplitude transcription of inflammatory, immune, and stress-response genes; small-molecule BET inhibition collapses these assemblies and blunts stimulus-induced transcriptional programs in immune and neural cells (Zhao et al., 2017). Within ophthalmology, JQ1 has been deployed intravitreally or systemically in multiple preclinical models, including inherited photoreceptor degeneration (rd10 retinitis pigmentosa), oxidative-stress retinal injury (sodium iodate), light-damage photoreceptor injury, experimental autoimmune uveitis (with other BET inhibitors), corneal fibrosis, and proliferative vitreoretinopathy, where it has shown neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory, and anti-fibrotic activity (Zhao et al., 2017; Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023; Eichenbaum, 2020; Liao et al., 2024). The BET modality also includes domain-selective ligands (e.g., BD2-preferring apabetalone/RVX-208) and targeted protein degraders (e.g., dBET6, a cereblon-recruiting JQ1-based PROTAC) that achieve complementary pharmacology by either sparing BD1 or depleting BRD2/3/4 protein, respectively (Zhu et al., 2023; Shahid et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
- Inherited photoreceptor degeneration (rd10, Pde6b mutant): A single intravitreal injection of JQ1 (2 µl of 0.1 mM at PN14) preserved photoreceptor number through PN24 (>90% of baseline), improved ERG a- and b-wave amplitudes, reduced TUNEL-positive photoreceptor apoptosis and caspase-3/7 activity, and markedly suppressed retinal microglial activation/infiltration (IBA1, TSPO, CD68) with cytokine mRNAs (TNFα, MCP-1, IL-1β, IL-6, RANTES) reduced to WT levels in whole retinas and in sorted retinal microglia (MCP-1 also lowered by ELISA) (Zhao et al., 2017). Complementary in vitro work showed JQ1 pre-treatment abolished LPS-induced upregulation of TNFα, MCP-1, IL-1β, IL-6 and RANTES and reduced microglial proliferation and migration by ~70%, with mechanistic dissection implicating BET2 (BRD2) and the BD2 (Brom2) domain in microglial activation; a BD2-preferring ligand (RVX208) suppressed cytokine induction more effectively than a BD1-preferring ligand (Olinone) (Zhao et al., 2017). In vivo, BET2 protein is increased at PN24 in rd10 retinas, correlating with peak microglial activation and photoreceptor degeneration (Zhao et al., 2017).  
- Oxidative-stress retinal/RPE injury (sodium iodate, SI): JQ1 suppressed BRD4-induced STING transcription by decreasing chromatin accessibility (reduced H3 acetylation, RNA Pol II recruitment) at the STING locus, curtailed cGAS–STING activation, reduced microglia/macrophage accumulation (IBA1+) in retina/subretinal spaces, prevented RPE/retinal degeneration, and preserved retinal integrity without detectable adverse retinal morphology when used alone (in vitro ARPE cells and in vivo SI models across ages) (Zou et al., 2022). Mechanistically, BRD4 upregulation under oxidative stress promotes STING and inflammatory outputs; JQ1 or BRD4 depletion enhances autophagic flux (LC3II), accelerates autophagic enclosure/clearance of cytosolic DNA, reduces dsDNA accumulation, and thereby attenuates STING-mediated inflammation; autophagy inhibitors (BafA1, chloroquine) block these effects, indicating an autophagy-dependent mechanism (Zou et al., 2022).  
- Light-damage photoreceptor injury: The JQ1-based PROTAC dBET6 delivered systemically degraded BRD2/3/4 in mouse retina, improved retinal responsiveness and visual acuity after light damage, suppressed macrophage/microglia activation and Müller gliosis, reduced photoreceptor death, and inhibited LD-induced cGAS–STING activation in retinal microglia; importantly, the PROTAC strategy is motivated by compensatory BRD4 accumulation observed with JQ1 (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- RPE cell inflammation (ARPE-19): Multiple BET inhibitors (including JQ1) reduced etoposide-induced IL-6 and IL-8 secretion, decreased NF-κB p65 activity, and reduced acetylation of p53 at K382 in human RPE without major cytotoxicity; the anti-inflammatory effects appeared SIRT1-independent (SIRT1 inhibition or knockdown did not reverse IL-8 lowering), although SIRT1 pharmacology altered the p53 acetylation response (Hytti et al., 2016). BET inhibitors slightly decreased baseline MTT conversion but reduced etoposide cytotoxicity (lower LDH release, higher viability), consistent with modest cytoprotection under this stressor (Hytti et al., 2016).  
- Endothelial barrier inflammation: In HUVEC transwell monolayers, TNF-α decreased TEER, whereas pretreatment with JQ1 or BD2-selective apabetalone prevented the TEER drop, maintaining monolayer integrity; BRD4 inhibition reduced inflammatory marker expression and midkine, and the authors concluded BRD4 inhibition preserved barrier function under inflammatory challenge; while promising for barrier biology, these data were generated in vascular endothelial cells, not RPE (Shahid et al., 2022).  
- Other ophthalmic signals: BET blockade has downregulated Th17-associated genes in experimental autoimmune uveitis, ameliorated acute RGC loss after NMDA by suppressing retinal cytokines (~50% reduction in TNFα, IL-1β, MCP-1, RANTES) and preserving RGC number/gene expression (~2×), and reduced/reversed corneal scarring via BRD4 inhibition and Nrf2-dependent antioxidant induction without impairing epithelial regeneration (Eichenbaum, 2020). A separate RPE-centric multi-omics PVR study used intraocular eNano-JQ1 to show potent anti-fibrotic efficacy (reduced αSMA, thinner membranes) with favorable ocular safety (ERG, histology, TUNEL) over seven days, supporting feasibility of sustained intraocular JQ1 delivery (Liao et al., 2024).  
- Application to AMD: JQ1 has not been tested clinically for dry AMD; however, in vivo SI oxidative-injury studies model RPE/retinal degeneration relevant to geographic atrophy and identify cGAS–STING repression and autophagy-mediated cytosolic DNA clearance as protective mechanisms; moreover, cGAS/STING promoter accessibility is increased in macular retinas from GA patients, strengthening translational plausibility for dry AMD (Zou et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
BET chromatin reader displacement and inflammatory super-enhancer suppression  
- BET proteins, particularly BRD4, bind acetylated histone tails via BD1 and BD2 to stabilize enhancer/super-enhancer coactivator complexes and recruit Mediator and RNA Pol II, enabling rapid, high-output transcription of stimulus-responsive genes (e.g., NF-κB target programs and innate immune effectors) (Zhao et al., 2017). JQ1 competitively occupies the acetyl-lysine pocket in BD1/BD2, displacing BET proteins and causing collapse of the transcriptional assembly with consequent repression of inflammatory/immune gene expression; this has been demonstrated across macrophages, microglia, brain, and retina (Zhao et al., 2017). NF-κB drives dynamic super-enhancer formation during inflammation, providing a mechanistic intersection whereby BRD4 coactivation of NF-κB can be neutralized by BET inhibition to broadly downregulate cytokine programs and adhesion molecules (Zhao et al., 2017).  
- In retinal microglia and degenerating retina, BET2 (BRD2) and the BD2 (Brom2) domain appear to dominate cytokine induction and activation phenotypes; pharmacologic BD2 targeting (RVX208) and siRNA to BET2 blunt expression of TNFα, IL-1β, MCP-1, IL-6, and RANTES and curb microglial proliferation/migration, whereas BD1 targeting (Olinone) exerts narrower effects (notably migration and RANTES) (Zhao et al., 2017). In vivo, intravitreal JQ1 suppresses microglial infiltration into ONL/subretinal spaces and lowers retinal cytokine mRNAs and MCP-1 protein, consistent with an immunomodulatory mechanism downstream of BET displacement (Zhao et al., 2017).  
- In ARPE-19 cells, BET inhibition reduces etoposide-induced IL-6/IL-8 secretion and NF-κB activity without major cytotoxicity; the anti-inflammatory effect persists when SIRT1 is inhibited or knocked down, indicating SIRT1 independence for cytokine suppression in these conditions, even though BET inhibition reduces acetyl-p53 (Lys382) via a SIRT1-interacting axis (Hytti et al., 2016). These data collectively establish BET blockade as a chromatin-level anti-inflammatory mechanism across retinal microglia and RPE contexts (Hytti et al., 2016).

BRD4–cGAS–STING repression and autophagy-dependent cytosolic DNA clearance in oxidative stress  
- Under oxidative stress in RPE and retina, BRD4 is induced and directly promotes STING transcription; JQ1 counteracts this by reducing histone acetylation (e.g., H3 acetyl marks) and phosphorylated Pol II occupancy at the STING locus, thereby reducing chromatin accessibility and transcriptional output (Zou et al., 2022). This leads to reduced cGAS–STING activation, dampened downstream NF-κB/IRF-mediated inflammatory gene induction, decreased retinal microglia/macrophage recruitment, and protection against RPE/retina degeneration in vivo (Zou et al., 2022).  
- Beyond transcriptional repression, BRD4 inhibition potentiates autophagy: JQ1 or BRD4 knockdown increases LC3II, accelerates enclosure of cytosolic dsDNA by autophagosomes (visualized with GFP-LC3 and Cy3-DNA), reduces accumulation of oxidized cytosolic DNA (a potent innate immune agonist), and these effects require intact autophagic flux (blocked by chloroquine/BafA1), directly linking BET inhibition to enhanced clearance of DNA debris that drives cGAS activation (Zou et al., 2022). This dual mechanism—STING transcriptional silencing and autophagic DNA clearance—aligns with decreased innate immune activation in SI-injured retinas and provides a mechanistic bridge to geographic atrophy in which cGAS/STING promoters exhibit increased accessibility (Zou et al., 2022).

Barrier biology and tight junctions: what is and is not known  
- In vascular endothelium, BRD4 inhibition with JQ1 or BD2-selective apabetalone preserved TEER and monolayer integrity during TNF-α stimulation, reduced NF-κB activation, decreased pro-inflammatory markers, and lowered midkine expression, indicating a direct barrier-protective effect in inflamed endothelium (Shahid et al., 2022). While the cell type differs, these results are proof-of-concept that BET inhibition can functionally maintain barrier resistance under cytokine challenge.  
- Critically, across the RPE literature excerpts provided, no direct measurements of RPE barrier function (TEER), tight-junction proteins (ZO-1/TJP1, claudin-19/CLDN19), or junctional continuity were reported for JQ1 or any BET inhibitor in ARPE-19 or primary RPE under inflammatory/oxidative stress; multiple excerpts explicitly note the absence of tight-junction/barrier metrics and recommend further study in advanced models (Hytti et al., 2016; Eichenbaum, 2020; Zhu et al., 2023). Therefore, a mechanistic claim that JQ1 increases H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19 enhancers and directly raises ZO-1/claudin-19 transcription in RPE is not supported by existing evidence in the provided corpus.

Pharmacology, delivery, and safety considerations  
- JQ1 exhibits a short systemic half-life (~1 h reported elsewhere and noted in the retinal context), and in rd10, photoreceptor protection after a single intravitreal dose waned as drug dissociated from targets and diffused, with higher intravitreal concentrations not improving efficacy, motivating sustained ocular delivery strategies (e.g., nanoparticles, osmotic pumps) or alternative modalities (e.g., BET PROTACs) (Zhao et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2023). Local formulation advances such as eNano-JQ1 achieved seven-day intraocular release with favorable safety and efficacy in a PVR model (Liao et al., 2024).  
- BET competitive inhibitors can trigger cell-cycle arrest and modestly reduce metabolic activity in vitro; ARPE-19 studies showed slight decreases in MTT conversion at baseline but no major viability loss, and in some assays BET inhibitors reduced etoposide cytotoxicity (Hytti et al., 2016). In SI models, JQ1 alone exhibited no overt adverse retinal morphology/viability, and systemic dBET6 achieved retinal BET degradation “without detectable toxicity” at the reported regimen (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). Notably, compensatory BRD4 upregulation was observed with JQ1 in certain contexts, potentially blunting efficacy—a liability that targeted degradation (dBET6) may overcome (Zhu et al., 2023).

Therapeutic implications for dry AMD  
Collectively, the ocular data support an anti-inflammatory/innate-immunity–modulating, neuroprotective role for BET inhibition in retina/RPE that is directly relevant to dry AMD pathobiology: oxidative stress-driven cytosolic DNA leakage, cGAS–STING activation, NF-κB–dependent cytokine induction, microglia/macrophage recruitment, and downstream neurodegeneration are all attenuated by JQ1 or dBET6 in preclinical models (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). However, there is no direct evidence that JQ1 improves RPE tight-junction expression or TEER; any barrier benefit inferred for RPE is, at present, extrapolated from endothelial TEER preservation and from general anti-inflammatory rescue in RPE/retina (Shahid et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016).

Expected Effect  
The proposed hypothesis states that JQ1 will relieve repression of tight-junction enhancers in RPE under inflammatory/oxidative stress, increasing H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19 loci, boosting ZO-1/claudin-19 transcription, and enhancing TEER; mechanistically, it posits that BRD4 occupancy at inflammatory loci displaces transcriptional machinery from tight-junction enhancers, and BET displacement by JQ1 restores enhancer-promoter function. Based on the available literature, this precise enhancer-activation model is not supported; instead, JQ1 typically represses transcription at BET-dependent loci and reduces histone acetylation and Pol II recruitment at targeted promoters (e.g., STING), thereby closing chromatin accessibility rather than increasing it (Zou et al., 2022). No data in the provided corpus demonstrate increased H3K27ac or enhanced transcription at TJP1/CLDN19 in RPE after JQ1, nor any RPE TEER restoration with JQ1 in IL-1β or oxidative-stress paradigms; multiple sources explicitly note the absence of RPE barrier metrics and tight-junction readouts in prior BET/RPE work (Hytti et al., 2016).

A more evidence-grounded expected effect in IL-1β- or TNF-α-treated RPE is indirect barrier preservation via upstream anti-inflammatory mechanisms:  
- JQ1 should reduce NF-κB–driven cytokine induction (e.g., IL-6, IL-8) in ARPE-19 based on prior findings with etoposide models, and suppress cGAS–STING signaling under oxidative stress by repressing STING transcription and promoting autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA (Hytti et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2022). These actions plausibly decrease paracrine/autocrine junction-disrupting cues, which could secondarily stabilize tight-junction structure and TEER, as supported by endothelial TEER preservation in HUVECs during TNF-α challenge (Shahid et al., 2022).  
- In microglia-RPE co-culture or in retinal tissue, JQ1 would be expected to reduce the load of microglia-derived cytokines/chemokines that exacerbate epithelial barrier dysfunction and photoreceptor stress, via demonstrated suppression of retinal microglial activation and cytokine production (Zhao et al., 2017).  

Given the lack of published RPE barrier data, the appropriate experimental expectations and measurements for the proposed IL-1β RPE assay are:  
- Primary outcome: TEER rescue and paracellular permeability under IL-1β with and without JQ1 (0.1–1 µM), benchmarking against endothelial TEER precedent and aligning with ARPE-19 cytokine suppression (Shahid et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016). Secondary outcomes: immunofluorescence continuity and membrane localization of ZO-1 and CLDN19, and western/RT-qPCR quantification of TJP1/CLDN19 transcripts/proteins to test whether barrier maintenance arises from preserved junctional organization versus increased transcription.  
- Mechanistic chromatin assays to test the stated enhancer hypothesis: ChIP-seq/ChIP-qPCR for H3K27ac and BRD4 at TJP1/CLDN19 promoters/enhancers in IL-1β±JQ1, plus Pol II occupancy; based on STING-locus data, we predict decreased rather than increased H3 acetylation and Pol II occupancy at direct BRD4-dependent loci after JQ1 (Zou et al., 2022). A finding of increased H3K27ac at tight-junction loci with JQ1 would represent a novel and unanticipated RPE-specific BET effect that would require rigorous validation and mechanistic clarification.  
- Parallel readouts to anchor known mechanisms: NF-κB p65 nuclear activity (TransAM), STING expression, cGAS–STING pathway markers, LC3 flux with/without chloroquine, and cytokine ELISAs (IL-6, IL-8), all of which are supported in prior RPE/retina work and will clarify whether barrier effects track with established anti-inflammatory and autophagic actions of BET inhibition (Hytti et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2022).

Mechanistic expression support in the assayed cell type  
- BET target genes relevant to inflammation (e.g., IL-6, IL-8, STING) are expressed and modulated in ARPE-19 and in mouse retina; BRD4 is induced by oxidative stress in RPE and retina, and cGAS–STING components are present in retinal microglia (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2023). The corpus does not provide explicit documentation of TJP1/CLDN19 expression modulation by JQ1 in RPE, underscoring the need for primary measurement within the proposed assay (Hytti et al., 2016).

Therapeutic plausibility in dry AMD models  
- RPE oxidative stress, cytosolic DNA leakage, cGAS–STING activation, microglia/macrophage recruitment, and chronic NF-κB activity are central to dry AMD pathogenesis; JQ1 has demonstrably suppressed cGAS–STING signaling and protected RPE/retina in SI-injury models, and PROMOTER accessibility of cGAS/STING is increased in GA patients, providing a mechanistic and translational bridge (Zou et al., 2022). In light-damage injury, BET degradation with dBET6 improved functional outcomes and repressed microglial STING expression, suggesting that BET-targeted therapies are effective across different sterile-injury paradigms relevant to atrophic disease (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Therefore, for dry AMD, the most defensible expectation is that JQ1 will reduce innate-immune and NF-κB–driven inflammatory signaling in RPE/retina and microglia, attenuate microglia recruitment/activation, and protect photoreceptors/RPE via transcriptional repression of STING and enhanced autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA, rather than directly upregulating tight-junction genes; any barrier rescue measured by TEER would likely be an indirect consequence of reduced inflammatory burden (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective efficacy across ocular models that capture key elements of dry AMD biology:  
  • In vivo oxidative-stress (SI) models demonstrate that JQ1 represses BRD4-driven STING transcription, reduces cGAS–STING signaling, limits immune cell accumulation, and prevents RPE/retinal degeneration with favorable safety in the absence of stressors (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Inflammatory microglia suppression is consistent and robust: intravitreal JQ1 reduces microglia infiltration and cytokines in rd10 retina and abolishes LPS-induced cytokine induction and activation phenotypes in vitro; BET2/BD2 targeting emerges as a key effector axis, aligning with innate-immune pathophysiology in atrophic AMD (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • dBET6 (systemic) degrades retinal BRD2/3/4, improves retinal function/acuity after light damage, and suppresses microglial STING and inflammatory responses, offering a mechanistically stronger alternative to JQ1 where compensatory BRD4 upregulation occurs (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Mechanistic depth linking BET inhibition to innate immunity and autophagy:  
  • JQ1 reduces histone acetylation and Pol II engagement at the STING locus, silencing a central innate immune amplifier in RPE/retina (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • BRD4 inhibition increases LC3-dependent enclosure/clearance of cytosolic DNA; this autophagy-dependent mechanism is integral to lowering cGAS activation (Zou et al., 2022).  
- Feasibility of ocular delivery and safety:  
  • Intravitreal JQ1 achieved durable rescue for at least 10 days in rd10 despite short systemic half-life; higher doses did not improve efficacy, highlighting the need for sustained delivery rather than dose escalation (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • eNano-JQ1 provides a practical intraocular slow-release platform with favorable ERG/histology safety and anti-fibrotic efficacy in PVR, supporting translatability of sustained local BET blockade (Liao et al., 2024).  
  • dBET6 showed retinal target engagement and no detectable retinal toxicity under the tested regimen (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Ancillary barrier-preserving precedent:  
  • In HUVECs, BRD4 inhibition (JQ1/apabetalone) preserved TEER and monolayer integrity during TNF-α challenge, lending plausibility that BET blockade can maintain barrier function under inflammatory stress, though cell-type differences warrant caution (Shahid et al., 2022).

Weaknesses, risks, and key unknowns relative to the current hypothesis  
- No direct evidence that JQ1 increases H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19 or upregulates ZO-1/claudin-19 transcription in RPE; the available mechanistic data actually show decreased histone acetylation and Pol II recruitment at target inflammatory loci with JQ1, arguing against a generalizable H3K27ac-increasing effect at tight-junction enhancers (Zou et al., 2022). Multiple sources explicitly note the absence of RPE barrier (TEER) or tight-junction data in BET-RPE studies to date (Hytti et al., 2016).  
- BET inhibitors can cause cell-cycle arrest and slightly depress metabolic activity in vitro; while ARPE-19 viability was largely preserved and etoposide toxicity was reduced by BET pretreatment, these on-target cytostatic effects will require dose/formulation tuning for chronic intraocular use (Hytti et al., 2016).  
- Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics: single-dose intravitreal JQ1 protection wanes over time, and systemic administration risks off-target tissue exposure; local sustained delivery or newer modalities (e.g., dBET6) are likely needed for translational development (Zhao et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2024).  
- Feedback and compensation: JQ1 can increase BRD4 protein levels in some contexts, potentially compromising effect; PROTAC degradation (dBET6) may mitigate this but brings its own safety and distribution questions (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Cell-type selectivity: The strongest in vivo efficacy signals (rd10, light damage) include microglial suppression and photoreceptor rescue; dry AMD pathogenesis is centered on RPE/Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with secondary photoreceptor involvement; while SI and oxidative-stress data in RPE support relevance, dedicated chronic AMD-like models (aging, complement dysregulation, diet-induced) and RPE barrier endpoints remain to be tested (Zou et al., 2022).

Go/no-go assessment and recommendations  
- Go decision for mechanism-driven validation in dry AMD-relevant preclinical systems, but with a revised primary hypothesis and fit-for-purpose endpoints. The most compelling AMD-relevant mechanism for JQ1 is epigenetic suppression of cGAS–STING and NF-κB inflammatory programs in RPE and resident microglia, plus autophagy-mediated clearance of cytosolic DNA, not direct activation of tight-junction gene enhancers (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017).  
- Replace the current primary mechanistic claim (increased H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19) with a testable, literature-anchored hypothesis: JQ1 prevents inflammation- and oxidative-stress–induced RPE barrier breakdown by (i) repressing STING transcription and dampening cGAS–STING signaling; (ii) promoting autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA; and (iii) suppressing NF-κB–driven cytokines in RPE and microglia that secondarily disturb junctional integrity. TEER and junctional continuity should be primary outcomes, but mechanistic attribution should center on cGAS–STING/NF-κB and autophagy rather than TJ enhancer activation (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Shahid et al., 2022).  
- Rapid experimental plan:  
  • ARPE-19 and/or primary human RPE on transwells: TEER, paracellular flux, ZO-1/CLDN19 localization under IL-1β or TNF-α ± JQ1 (0.1–1 µM), with NF-κB activity, cytokine ELISAs, STING expression, LC3 flux, and dsDNA imaging to anchor mechanism (Hytti et al., 2016; Shahid et al., 2022; Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Oxidative stress model (H2O2 or SI-conditioned medium) ± JQ1: replicate cGAS–STING repression and autophagy findings in RPE; use autophagy inhibitors to confirm flux-dependence (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • ChIP-qPCR/ATAC at STING and at TJP1/CLDN19 enhancers/promoters to directly test the tight-junction enhancer hypothesis; set expectation that STING chromatin accessibility/acetylation will decline with JQ1, while TJ loci changes are unknown and likely neutral or reduced (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Microglia–RPE co-culture: test whether microglial cytokine suppression by JQ1 protects RPE TEER/barrier vs IL-1β, isolating paracrine contributions (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • In vivo oxidative-injury model (SI) with intraocular slow-release JQ1 (eNano-JQ1) to assess RPE barrier integrity (flat-mount ZO-1 continuity), microglial recruitment (IBA1), and function, leveraging prior safety/feasibility data (Liao et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2022).  
- Modality strategy: Given compensatory BRD4 upregulation with JQ1 and BD2 dominance in microglial activation, parallel exploration of BD2-selective ligands (e.g., apabetalone analogs) or BET degraders (dBET6-like) for retina-directed delivery is warranted to optimize therapeutic index while maintaining target engagement (Zhu et al., 2023; Shahid et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2017).

Conclusion  
JQ1 is a mechanistically well-grounded epigenetic modulator that suppresses inflammatory transcriptional programs and innate immune activation in retina/RPE and microglia, protects photoreceptors and RPE from oxidative and inflammatory injury in vivo, and has feasible ocular delivery paths with encouraging preclinical safety signals (Zou et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2017; Liao et al., 2024). These features position BET inhibition as a credible therapeutic strategy for dry AMD, targeting core disease drivers (oxidative stress, cytosolic DNA sensing via cGAS–STING, chronic NF-κB activation, microglial recruitment) rather than exclusively downstream consequences (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). However, the specific hypothesis that JQ1 restores RPE barrier function by increasing H3K27ac at tight-junction loci (TJP1/CLDN19) is not supported by available evidence; on the contrary, BET inhibition generally reduces histone acetylation/accessibility at target loci like STING, and RPE barrier metrics after JQ1 remain unreported (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016). We therefore recommend proceeding with JQ1 (or improved BET-modality variants) in dry AMD-relevant models with primary endpoints focused on cGAS–STING/NF-κB suppression, autophagy-dependent cytosolic DNA clearance, microglial modulation, and functional RPE barrier preservation (TEER, ZO-1/CLDN19 continuity), while explicitly testing and likely revising the proposed tight-junction enhancer mechanism based on direct chromatin measurements (Zou et al., 2022; Shahid et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ICG-001 (Sigma I2441) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor originally identified for its ability to selectively disrupt the interaction between β-catenin and the transcriptional coactivator CBP (CREB-binding protein), thereby inhibiting TCF/LEF-dependent Wnt/β-catenin–driven transcription without reducing total β-catenin protein abundance (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). Mechanistically, ICG-001 is positioned within a class of β-catenin pathway modulators that block nuclear β-catenin activity rather than decreasing β-catenin protein levels; this distinguishes it from antisense/siRNA approaches and from inhibitors that act upstream in Wnt signaling (e.g., tankyrase inhibitors like XAV-939) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor class has been proposed as a more selective means to modulate β-catenin transcriptional output while sparing adherens junction functions that depend on β-catenin protein pools, a distinction supported by data showing ICG-001 does not trigger compensatory γ-catenin stabilization that follows β-catenin protein depletion (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117).

Within the broader Wnt-targeting landscape, ICG-001 exemplifies downstream, transcriptional-coactivator–selective targeting, contrasted with agents that block β-catenin/TCF binding, Dishevelled PDZ interactions, Porcupine-mediated ligand maturation, or Frizzled receptor activity (e.g., OMP-18R5) (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31). Because Wnt pathway effects are highly context dependent and temporally dynamic across tissues, coactivator-selective modulation has been argued to mitigate systemic liabilities relative to global pathway inhibition (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31).

Therapeutic History  
ICG-001 itself is widely used as a research tool, and its clinical derivative/prodrug analogs (e.g., PRI-724/OP-724) have reached Phase I/IIa testing in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, establishing a preliminary human safety/tolerability and feasibility record for CBP/β-catenin pathway inhibition in chronic disease. In HCV-induced cirrhosis, an open-label Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of PRI-724 administered continuous i.v. infusions (10–160 mg/m2/day; 1 week on/1 week off for 12 weeks) with primary outcomes focused on adverse events and exploratory anti-fibrotic endpoints (histology, serum fibrosis biomarkers); the program reported safety/tolerability and preliminary efficacy consistent with anti-fibrotic activity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014). In HBV/HCV-related cirrhosis, a Phase I/IIa open-label study (twice-weekly 4 h infusions; 140, 280, 380 mg/m2 per 4 h) evaluated safety, PK, and change in liver fibrosis area by biopsy at 12 weeks; the registry cites a derived EBioMedicine report on safety, tolerability, and anti-fibrotic effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2018). In advanced primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; Scheuer stage ≥III), OP-724 (formerly PRI-724) underwent a Phase I dose-finding trial (4 h i.v. infusions, twice weekly for 12 weeks; 140/280/380 mg/m2 cohorts) assessing serious adverse events, PK of OP-724 and metabolite C-82, and fibrosis-related endpoints (biopsy fibrotic area, FibroScan, Child-Pugh/MELD, ELF score) with feasibility/safety results published (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

No clinical or preclinical ocular applications of ICG-001/PRI-724/OP-724 were identified in the provided context, and there are no reports here of use in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), or retinal barrier disorders (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019). Preclinical oncology literature summarized in the provided sources documents ICG-001’s activity in cancer cells (reduced proliferation and induced selective apoptosis via TCF-dependent signaling reduction) but does not address ocular tissues (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Thus, while the drug class has human safety experience in fibrotic liver disease, there is no direct evidence in the provided context for ophthalmic use or for dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
ICG-001 binds CBP and selectively disrupts the β-catenin/CBP complex, attenuating β-catenin–driven transcription of TCF/LEF target genes (e.g., Cyclin D1) without decreasing total β-catenin protein levels; in Hep3B cells, ICG-001 reduced TOPflash reporter activity and Cyclin D1 expression while leaving β-catenin abundance unchanged and without inducing compensatory γ-catenin stabilization (if anything, γ-catenin modestly decreased) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). Across multiple excerpts, ICG-001 is consistently described as selective for β-catenin/CBP over β-catenin/p300, reducing TCF-dependent Wnt output while sparing other β-catenin protein interactions; global β-catenin levels are unaffected, reinforcing a functional separation between nuclear transcriptional roles and membrane adherens junction pools (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Authors highlight that agents which lower β-catenin protein (ASO/siRNA) trigger γ-catenin compensation at adherens junctions—distinct from ICG-001, which blocks transcriptional activity without provoking such protein-level sensing/reciprocity (Wickline, 2013, pp. 112–117, 140–145). It remains explicitly unknown from these data whether ICG-001 perturbs adherens junction function in vivo; follow-up studies were recommended to test junctional tolerance to transcriptional blockade (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

Contextual biology of β-catenin coactivator usage indicates that CBP vs p300 partnering can impart divergent phenotypic outcomes; in fibrotic contexts, CBP-associated β-catenin activity has been linked with pro-fibrotic programs whereas p300-associated activity may be protective, though this literature is complex and model-dependent (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69). Canonical β-catenin signaling is also subject to Wnt-independent inputs that promote nuclear translocation/transactivation (e.g., PKA/Akt phosphorylation), and β-catenin exists in distinct pools with membrane-associated adherens junction functions that are regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation events, further implying that selective transcriptional blockade (CBP-directed) may spare adhesive roles (Wickline, 2013, pp. 21–26). Together, these mechanistic data support a rationale for testing CBP/β-catenin–selective inhibitors for diseases where β-catenin transcription drives pathology and where preserving epithelial junctional architecture is desirable (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 140–145).

Disease-Relevant Biology in RPE and Retinal Barriers  
RPE epithelial phenotype and outer blood–retina barrier (oBRB) integrity depend on tight junction (TJ) and adherens junction (AJ) complexes (ZO-1/occludin/claudins; E-cadherin/catenins). Loss of ZO-1 releases ZONAB to drive CDK4 and proliferation; downregulation of E-cadherin frees β-catenin to translocate to the nucleus and activate EMT/proliferation drivers (e.g., Snail, Cyclin D1), establishing a mechanistic link between junctional disruption and β-catenin–dependent transcriptional programs in RPE (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–9). Reviews of RPE EMT highlight Wnt–β-catenin as a key mediator in the eye; experimental injury (laser photocoagulation) activates β-catenin signaling and facilitates RPE proliferation, reinforcing the pathway’s involvement in EMT and regenerative responses (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 7–9).

These data collectively underscore a context-dependent role of β-catenin in RPE: when epithelial contacts are robust, β-catenin activity can support maturation, TJ expression, and survival; under EMT/injury/inflammatory stress (e.g., DME/TNFα), β-catenin pathway activation correlates with junctional loss, VEGF induction, and autophagy, and pathway suppression can be protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19).

Strengths  
- Defined, selective mechanism: ICG-001 disrupts β-catenin/CBP complexes and suppresses TCF-dependent transcription without lowering total β-catenin; it does not trigger γ-catenin compensation observed with β-catenin protein knockdown, offering a mechanistically precise intervention that may spare adherens junction architecture (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117, 140–145, 26–30).

Key Limitations and Risks  
- No direct ocular/RPE data for ICG-001: The provided context contains no studies of ICG-001 (or PRI-724/OP-724) in RPE or ocular tissues, no TEER/paracellular flux rescue data, and no AMD model outcomes; claims of junction-selective “bias” in RPE are speculative and unproven here (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

On the present evidence, ICG-001 has a coherent, selective mechanism with clinical-stage validation in a non-ocular indication, and there is strong biological plausibility that β-catenin transcriptional blockade can counter EMT/proliferation programs in RPE. However, the specific hypothesis that ICG-001 will “bias” transcription to upregulate claudin-1/ZO-1 and restore TEER under oxidative stress is not supported by the provided literature; in fact, RPE studies show that β-catenin activation is associated with higher TJ expression/TEER in some contexts, and pathway inhibition reduces these features, whereas in inflammatory/DME contexts β-catenin activation is deleterious and suppression is protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Therefore, a tightly scoped preclinical program should be undertaken to empirically resolve these context-dependent effects in RPE before committing to development for dry AMD.

- Proceed with an in vitro/ex vivo feasibility package to test ICG-001 in RPE barrier models under defined stressors (oxidative vs inflammatory), with rigorous functional and molecular endpoints and on-target PD confirmation; include orthogonal comparators (XAV-939, ITF2357) to position CBP-selective modulation against broader Wnt suppression and epigenetic anti-inflammatory rescue (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7). In sum, ICG-001 is a mechanistically attractive, clinically precedented β-catenin/CBP inhibitor, but the claim of junction-focused, proliferation-sparing barrier rescue in oxidatively stressed RPE is currently hypothetical and not substantiated by the provided literature; decisive RPE-focused experiments are required to validate or refute its potential for dry AMD (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

EP300 inhibition is pleiotropic, risking off-target effects on gene expression and DNA damage repair. The mechanism (autophagy induction, calcium chelation) is plausible but indirect to core AMD pathology, and dose-dependent toxicity is a critical concern. Ocular bioavailability across the blood–retinal barrier is unproven, and no in vivo dry AMD models or clinical trials exist. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Danicopan, also known as ACH-4471 and by its commercial identifier MedChemExpress HY-19909, is a novel small-molecule agent designed to target complement factor D. It belongs to a growing class of low-molecular-weight inhibitors that are specifically aimed at interfering with the alternative pathway (AP) of the complement system. This class of compounds is characterized by their capacity to modulate complement activation rather than broadly suppress the entire immune system. Danicopan was originally developed as a first-in-class molecule to selectively block factor D, which is the rate-limiting enzyme in the AP and is intimately involved in the formation of the C3 convertase complex (Boyer et al., 2022). The chemical structure of Danicopan incorporates a proline core with added moieties such as amino bromo pyridine and azaindole, a configuration designed to ensure both high potency and selectivity in factor D inhibition (Schubart et al., 2023). The oral bioavailability of Danicopan, combined with its capacity to achieve sustained exposure in ocular tissues due in part to melanin binding in pigmented tissues, underscores its appeal for diseases where local complement modulation is desired without the need for invasive delivery routes (Boyer et al., 2022). Notably, the design approach for Danicopan focuses on blocking the enzymatic activation loop that precipitates complement amplification—a mechanism that is particularly deleterious in tissues such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Boyer et al., 2022).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the use of complement inhibitors has been a promising therapeutic strategy across several complement-mediated disorders. Danicopan was initially evaluated in the context of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), a condition driven by unregulated complement activation that results in hemolysis and thrombosis. Early clinical studies in patients with PNH revealed that oral administration of Danicopan rapidly inhibited the alternative pathway, resulting in significantly reduced hemolysis with concomitant improvements in hematological parameters (Schubart et al., 2023). This clinical success in PNH has spurred the interest in repurposing Danicopan for ocular indications, notably for dry AMD—a condition where dysfunctional complement activation plays a central role in the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy (GA). Although Danicopan’s application in dry AMD is still under investigation, the rationale for its use stems from preclinical models demonstrating high and sustained ocular tissue levels after oral dosing, especially in regions enriched with melanin (Boyer et al., 2022). Furthermore, the candidate has entered a Phase 2 clinical trial focusing on GA AMD, with the study design aimed at assessing its safety, efficacy, and pharmacokinetic profile in a population of 330 participants (Fabre et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2024). Importantly, while previous complement inhibitors such as Lampalizumab have been evaluated in AMD—with mixed outcomes—Danicopan’s novel oral dosing profile and improved tissue selectivity underscore its potential advantage over earlier modalities (Tang et al., 2024; Schubart et al., 2023).  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Danicopan acts by binding to complement factor D with high affinity, thereby inhibiting its serine protease activity. Factor D is indispensable for the cleavage of factor B and the subsequent assembly of the C3 convertase (C3bBb) on the cell surface, which is the amplification step critical for the alternative complement pathway (Boyer et al., 2022). Inhibition of factor D effectively halts the formation of the AP C3 convertase, thereby preventing the cleavage of C3 into its active fragments, C3a and C3b. This downstream effect is crucial because the deposition of C3b—or its inactivated form iC3b—on the RPE surfaces is implicated in complement-driven inflammation and subsequent cellular damage (Fabre et al., 2022). In addition, by attenuating the production of C3a, Danicopan helps mitigate the recruitment and activation of inflammatory effector cells in the retinal microenvironment (Wilke & Apte, 2024; Schubart et al., 2023). The selectivity of Danicopan for factor D not only reduces the biochemistry of the AP cascade but also limits the risk of compromising the classical and lectin pathways, which remain critical for host defense. This selective inhibition is biochemically significant, as the tight regulation of complement is essential for maintaining immune surveillance and tissue homeostasis (Boyer et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). The reported inhibitory concentration (IC₅₀) values for Danicopan have been reported in various contexts, with figures around 5.8 nM in some studies and as low as 2 nM as hypothesized in the current proposal, underscoring its potent inhibitory capacity (Fabre et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). On a cellular level, the blockade of factor D is expected to prevent the formation of the C3 convertase on RPE cells, which in turn would reduce the deposition of complement fragments like C3b and iC3b on the surface of these cells. This is particularly important since the complement-mediated deposition on RPE cells can disrupt the distribution and localization of tight junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and occludin, which are critical for preserving RPE barrier integrity and function (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022). In essence, Danicopan’s mechanism of action addresses the upstream triggers of the inflammatory cascade by preventing the enzymatic events that lead to complement amplification, thereby providing a molecular rationale for its application in diseases characterized by complement dysregulation, including dry AMD (Boyer et al., 2022).

The evaluation of Danicopan as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration reveals several compelling strengths balanced by certain challenges that warrant further investigation. One of the most significant strengths of Danicopan lies in its potent, selective inhibition of factor D—a critical enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. By targeting factor D, Danicopan disrupts the amplification loop that drives the deposition of complement fragments such as C3b and iC3b on the RPE surface. This mechanistic precision is vital given that complement overactivation is a well-established contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Boyer et al., 2022). The reported high affinity, with low nanomolar inhibitory concentrations, underscores its biochemical potency (Fabre et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). Moreover, the oral bioavailability of Danicopan represents a significant advantage. Unlike intravitreal injections—which are invasive and carry risks such as endophthalmitis—oral administration could improve patient adherence and facilitate chronic treatment regimens required for a progressive disease such as dry AMD (Boyer et al., 2022). Preclinical studies have provided encouraging evidence, demonstrating that in animal models, Danicopan not only reduces complement deposition but also preserves RPE function, as indicated by improved TER and maintenance of electrophysiological responses (Boyer et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2024).
