Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bardoxolone methyl, also known as CDDO-Me, is a synthetic derivative developed from the naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid oleanolic acid. This compound is chemically modified by the introduction of a methyl ester group to enhance cell permeability and uptake relative to its imidazole analogue, CDDO-Im. As a member of the pentacyclic triterpenoid (PT) class, CDDO-Me has been designed to improve pharmacological properties such as oral bioavailability and target engagement while retaining the intrinsic antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of its natural precursor. Historically, pentacyclic triterpenoids have been studied for a wide range of applications—including anticancer, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory therapies—and have a longstanding role in traditional medicine in various Asian cultures. In this context, CDDO-Me has emerged as an advanced synthetic candidate that capitalizes on these properties, particularly through its potency as an activator of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. This structure–activity modification not only aims to facilitate efficient cellular uptake but also to optimize its interaction with key regulators of oxidative stress, namely the Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1) (Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and clinical investigation primarily in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and cancer. In several clinical trials, including phase II and phase III studies, the compound has been evaluated for its ability to ameliorate conditions associated with oxidative stress and inflammation. Its clinical development for CKD, in particular, has underscored its potential to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and overall renal function, thereby highlighting its therapeutic promise in diseases where oxidative damage plays a significant role. Despite its notable progress in these areas, direct clinical evidence for Bardoxolone methyl in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal diseases remains limited. However, several preclinical studies have demonstrated that compounds related to Bardoxolone methyl are capable of activating Nrf2 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, upregulating protective genes such as NQO1 and HO-1 that are essential for combating oxidative stress in the retina. These findings suggest that, although not originally developed for retinal indications, Bardoxolone methyl has a mechanistic rationale that could support its repurposing for dry AMD (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, analogous compounds that function via Nrf2 activation have been shown to protect RPE cells against oxidative stress-induced damage, further supporting the therapeutic potential of this candidate in ocular applications (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Bardoxolone methyl operates predominantly through the activation of the Nrf2 pathway, an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional system that governs cellular antioxidant responses. Under normal homeostatic conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytoplasm by its inhibitor, Keap1, which facilitates its ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl, due to its electrophilic cyanoenone moiety, acts as a Michael acceptor, covalently modifying specific cysteine residues within Keap1 (notably cysteine 151 among others). This modification disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, preventing Nrf2 ubiquitination, and allows Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus where it binds to the antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoter regions of target genes (Zhou et al., 2020; Mathis & Cui, 2016). The subsequent upregulation of phase II detoxifying enzymes—such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and glutamate-cysteine ligase modifier subunit (GCLM)—provides cells with increased capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigate inflammatory insults. Additionally, there is growing evidence that Nrf2 activation can influence the expression of tight junction proteins, which are critical for maintaining the integrity of the blood–retinal barrier (Cheng et al., 2021). This detailed molecular interaction not only accounts for the antioxidant role of Bardoxolone methyl but also for its potential in preserving cellular integrity in environments subjected to oxidative insult, such as the RPE cells in the retina (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Cai et al., 2024). Furthermore, ancillary effects, such as modulation of NF-κB signaling and the inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, are likely to contribute to its overall cytoprotective profile, making it an attractive candidate for reducing the inflammatory milieu that accompanies retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
In the specific context of dry AMD, the therapeutic hypothesis posits that Bardoxolone methyl will esterify and modify Keap1 in human RPE cells, thereby triggering the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent upregulation of phase II enzymes. This enhanced antioxidant capacity is expected to counteract oxidative stress induced by agents such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (tBHP), which is known to compromise the tight junction integrity of RPE monolayers. The resulting effect should manifest as a measurable recovery in transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) and a concomitant reduction in paracellular flux, as assessed by the permeability of a 10 kDa dextran. Preclinical assays have reported that at a concentration of 500 nM, Bardoxolone methyl is capable of restoring TEER values to approximately 80% of baseline levels, and reducing dextran leak by about 55%, thus highlighting both its potency and efficacy in repairing disrupted barrier function (Nakagami et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2021). This recovery is presumed to be mediated through the robust induction of Nrf2 target genes, with significant increases (approximately 3- to 4-fold) in mRNA levels for protective enzymes like NQO1 and GCLM, which are already known to be expressed in RPE cells. The preservation and restoration of tight junction integrity are critical not only for maintaining the physical barrier between the retina and the choroid but also for ensuring proper retinal function by preventing the uncontrolled diffusion of harmful substances that can exacerbate retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021; Hui et al., 2020). Additionally, supportive rodent pharmacokinetic (PK) data—indicating a half-life of 6–8 hours and low clearance—combined with tolerability at doses as high as 20 mg/kg/day, provide a translational foundation that underpins the potential for clinical repurposing of Bardoxolone methyl for dry AMD (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several strengths alongside noteworthy challenges. On the strength side, the compound’s ability to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway addresses a central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and inflammation play pivotal roles in RPE degeneration. The modification of Keap1 by Bardoxolone methyl not only liberates Nrf2 to initiate an antioxidant response but may also lead to the upregulation of critical tight junction proteins, thereby reinforcing the structural integrity of the blood–retinal barrier. Preclinical evidence indicating recovery of TEER and reduction of paracellular flux supports the notion that Bardoxolone methyl could exert meaningful protective effects in the RPE under conditions of oxidative challenge (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, the compound’s clinical advancement in other indications—most notably in CKD—demonstrates an established track record of safety and tolerability in humans at therapeutically relevant doses. This, together with favorable rodent PK parameters, enhances its appeal as a candidate for rapid translational repurposing for dry AMD (Yagishita et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2012; Sarmento, 2019).

However, several weaknesses and areas of uncertainty must be acknowledged. Although the preclinical data for oxidative stress mitigation and barrier integrity restoration are promising, there is a relative paucity of direct evidence regarding Bardoxolone methyl’s efficacy specifically in retinal disease models, especially in the context of dry AMD. The literature does not yet definitively demonstrate that Bardoxolone methyl can reverse established RPE dysfunction or completely restore retinal integrity in disease-relevant in vivo settings (Nakagami et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2024). Furthermore, safety concerns observed in other clinical contexts—such as cardiovascular adverse effects during clinical trials for CKD—raise potential red flags regarding its long-term use in a population that may be at increased risk for such events due to age-related co-morbidities (Nakagami et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2014; Sarmento, 2019). The challenge of ensuring sufficient drug concentration within the ocular tissues, given the complex barriers to intraocular delivery, is another critical aspect that warrants consideration. Although the methyl ester scaffold is designed to enhance cell uptake, further optimization of the drug delivery system (for example, via topical formulations or intravitreal injections) may be required to achieve therapeutic levels in the retina without systemic exposure that could potentiate off-target effects (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2020).

Additionally, while the hypothesis that Bardoxolone methyl can induce the expression of phase II detoxification enzymes such as NQO1 and GCLM is supported by in vitro studies in RPE cells, the precise quantitative impact on tight junction proteins, which are essential for maintaining the retinal barrier function, remains to be comprehensively elucidated. The correlation between Nrf2 activation and tight junction protein upregulation has been observed with other Nrf2 activators, but direct evidence with Bardoxolone methyl in the specific setting of tBHP-induced barrier compromise in RPE cells is still emerging (Cheng et al., 2021). Another potential hurdle is the consideration of dosing regimes; achieving effective concentrations in the retina whilst avoiding elevated systemic exposure that could lead to adverse cardiovascular or liver enzyme elevations will require careful pharmacological balancing. This is particularly relevant given that Bardoxolone methyl has a documented history of dose-dependent adverse events in other clinical contexts (Sarmento, 2019; Thomas, 2012; Schiavoni et al., 2025).

In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a highly promising mechanism-based approach for the treatment of dry AMD. Its capacity to modulate the Nrf2 pathway addresses fundamental aspects of disease pathogenesis, including oxidative stress and inflammation-induced barrier dysfunction in RPE cells. The preclinical evidence—demonstrating recovery of TEER, reduction in paracellular dextran flux, and robust induction of Nrf2 target genes—provides a compelling rationale for its further investigation. Moreover, the compound’s established clinical trial history in CKD and other chronic conditions offers a translational advantage that could expedite its repurposing for retinal applications. Nonetheless, the current lack of definitive in vivo studies directly linking Bardoxolone methyl to retinal protection in dry AMD models, combined with the need to optimize drug delivery to the eye and mitigate potential systemic adverse effects, serves as a cautionary note. Future research should focus on rigorous preclinical studies in animal models of dry AMD, detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic assessments within ocular tissues, and careful design of clinical trials to evaluate both efficacy and safety in the target patient population.

Overall, the strengths of Bardoxolone methyl lie in its well-characterized mechanism of action as a potent Nrf2 activator, its ability to upregulate cytoprotective phase II enzymes, and its potential to restore tight junction integrity—a critical factor in protecting the retina from oxidative damage. Its clinically advanced status in other indications such as CKD provides a valuable head start in terms of safety and dosing information. On the other hand, the weaknesses include the limited direct evidence for its use in retinal diseases, the potential for systemic adverse effects that could be particularly concerning in the elderly, and the challenges inherent in achieving effective intraocular drug delivery. Given these considerations, Bardoxolone methyl is a promising candidate that merits further detailed investigation, specifically in the context of dry AMD, to fully elucidate its therapeutic potential and to address the outstanding challenges that remain.

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl has not yet been directly tested in dry AMD clinical trials, its underlying pharmacological profile, supported by substantial in vitro and in vivo preclinical evidence, suggests that it may offer significant benefits in restoring RPE function and retinal barrier integrity through the activation of Nrf2 signaling. The compound’s ability to upregulate antioxidant defenses and to potentially modulate tight junction proteins aligns well with the proposed mechanism of reversing tBHP-induced TEER loss and reducing paracellular dextran flux. If subsequent studies confirm these effects in relevant animal models and demonstrate a favorable safety profile in ocular tissues, Bardoxolone methyl could emerge as a viable repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Future research efforts should focus on refining ocular delivery strategies, verifying the direct effects on RPE gene expression and barrier function, and rigorously evaluating its long-term safety in the context of age-related retinal diseases (Cheng et al., 2021; Cuadrado et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2012; Nakagami, 2016; Nakagami et al., 2015; Schiavoni et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
TTA‐P2 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed to target T‐type voltage‐gated calcium channels (VGCCs), which belong to the CaV3 family (CaV3.1, CaV3.2, CaV3.3). Its chemical structure, described as 3,5‐dichloro-N-[1-(2,2-dimethyl-tetrahydro-pyran-4-ylmethyl)-4-fluoro-piperidin-4-ylmethyl]-benzamide, was established via medicinal chemistry optimization strategies aimed at increasing potency and selectivity for the T‐type channels relative to high-voltage-activated channels (Choe et al., 2011). Originally discovered and characterized in the context of neuronal excitability studies, TTA‐P2 has been shown to block T‐type calcium currents in rat sensory neurons with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range; this high potency is matched by an excellent selectivity profile given that its inhibitory concentration for high-voltage-activated channels is orders of magnitude higher (Choe et al., 2011). As a member of the T‐type calcium channel blocker class, TTA‐P2 is representative of compounds that modulate low-voltage-activated channels involved in a variety of cell functions, ranging from neuronal burst firing to hormone release. In the context of drug development, this compound is categorized as a channel-modulating agent, and its synthetic origins as a small molecule rendered it amenable to structural modification for improved pharmacokinetics in various tissue systems (Choe et al., 2011). Although historically used primarily in neuronal studies, its inherent properties have prompted consideration of its repurposing for non-neuronal tissues, such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where T‐type channels have been shown to contribute to key physiological processes (Jazouli, 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TTA‐P2 has been investigated in the context of neuropathic pain and epilepsy, where T‐type calcium channels are integral to the regulation of neuronal excitability. In experimental models involving rat sensory neurons, TTA‐P2 demonstrated marked antinociceptive properties and produced significant reductions in neuronal burst firing by selectively blocking T‐type calcium currents (Choe et al., 2011). This evidence underlines the compound’s effectiveness in modulating calcium influx in hyperexcitable systems. Beyond its neurological applications, there have been several studies in which compounds targeting T‐type CaV channels were applied to non-neuronal cells. For instance, work in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) demonstrated that T‐type calcium channels are expressed and functionally important in these cells, although in those studies a different inhibitor—TTA‐A2—was used to evaluate effects on phagocytosis and VEGF secretion (Jazouli, 2022). Moreover, complementary work in RPE models has noted that T‐type channels appear to localize specifically to the apical membrane, with subtypes such as CaV3.1 and CaV3.3 being especially prominent (Jazouli, 2022). Despite extensive preclinical work in neuronal systems, there is no published record, to our knowledge, that TTA‐P2 has been tested directly in AMD or other ocular disease models. However, evidence gleaned from cerebral endothelia studies—where inhibition of CaV3.1/CaV3.2 ameliorates inflammatory barrier disruption—suggests that a similar strategy may be beneficial in preserving the function of the RPE barrier (Unknown Reference). Thus, while TTA‐P2 has a well-established history in neurological studies, its repurposing for dry AMD is based on the emerging understanding that T‐type channels contribute to RPE function and that their inhibition may counter inflammatory and degenerative signals (Jazouli, 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism by which TTA‐P2 exerts its effects is through selective inhibition of T‐type calcium channels. Detailed electrophysiological studies in rat sensory neurons have shown that TTA‐P2 binds preferentially to the inactivated state of these channels, thereby stabilizing them in a non-conducting conformation. This binding results in a significant hyperpolarizing shift (approximately 20 mV) in the steady-state inactivation curves and an incomplete recovery from inactivation, meaning that the channels remain non-functional for a longer period after brief depolarizations (Choe et al., 2011). Such effects effectively reduce the calcium influx that would normally occur during depolarization-driven events. In RPE cells, there is a body of evidence indicating that T‐type calcium channels (particularly CaV3.1 and CaV3.3) contribute to the formation of localized Ca²⁺ microdomains that play a role in regulating tight junction dynamics (Jazouli, 2022). Under inflammatory conditions—such as those induced by TNF-α or complement activation—excessive Ca²⁺ influx via these channels may trigger signaling cascades that lead to the disassembly of adherens junctions and tight junctions, ultimately compromising the integrity of the epithelial barrier. TTA‐P2’s ability to suppress the T‐type currents would, therefore, limit the depolarization-driven Ca²⁺ microdomain formation in RPE cells (Choe et al., 2011). In addition, the selective binding to the inactivated state minimizes off-target effects on channels that have higher activation thresholds, such as L-type channels, thereby preserving other essential calcium-dependent processes. The blockade of T‐type channels is particularly relevant because these channels typically open at more negative membrane potentials, a regime that is critical for maintaining the delicate Ca²⁺ balance in nonexcitable cells such as the RPE (Choe et al., 2011; Jazouli, 2022). Consequently, by dampening the Ca²⁺ entry through these channels, TTA‐P2 could play a protective role against inflammation-induced barrier disruption.

Expected Effect:  
According to the proposal, the central hypothesis is that a pan–T‐type CaV blockade by TTA‐P2 (with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, here cited as approximately 20 nM) will suppress the formation of harmful Ca²⁺ microdomains in RPE cells, thereby preventing the downstream signaling events that lead to the disassembly of tight junctions. The integrity of RPE monolayers is often assessed by measurements such as transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and permeability assays (e.g., FITC-dextran flux). In the presence of inflammatory insults like TNF-α or complement factors—both of which can mimic some of the pathophysiological aspects of dry AMD—the excessive calcium influx through T‐type channels may cause rearrangement or breakdown of tight junction proteins (such as occludin and claudins), leading to compromised barrier function and increased paracellular permeability (Jazouli, 2022).

TTA‐P2 offers several compelling strengths as a potential repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, its high potency and selectivity for T‐type calcium channels have been robustly demonstrated in neuronal systems, and these properties bode well for achieving effective inhibition in RPE cells, where even relatively minor shifts in calcium homeostasis may have significant pathophysiological implications (Choe et al., 2011). Second, the strategy of targeting T‐type channels in the RPE is grounded in evidence that these channels are involved in channel-mediated inflammatory responses and barrier disruption, processes known to play a key role in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Jazouli, 2022). Third, TTA‐P2 works through a mechanism that is distinct from conventional anti-inflammatory agents or anti-VEGF therapies; instead, it modulates a very early step in the cascade—namely, the depolarization-driven Ca²⁺ entry that acts as a trigger for tight junction disassembly. This novel mechanism, if validated, could complement existing therapies or offer a new avenue for intervention in cases where traditional therapeutics have limited efficacy.  

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be acknowledged. Foremost among these is the fact that, to date, no direct studies have been published demonstrating the efficacy of TTA‐P2 in RPE cells or in animal models of dry AMD. The majority of the literature supporting its use comes from neurological applications, and although there are analogous studies in RPE using other T‐type channel blockers (e.g., TTA‐A2), the extrapolation of neuronal pharmacodynamics to ocular tissues is not guaranteed (Jazouli, 2022). Furthermore, it is well recognized that T‐type channels in the RPE also play roles in physiological processes such as phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and the regulation of growth factor secretion (Jazouli, 2022). Thus, chronic inhibition of these channels could potentially disrupt normal RPE function if not properly dosed or targeted, leading to adverse effects that may offset the benefits of barrier preservation. Additionally, the therapeutic index of TTA‐P2 in the ocular milieu remains unknown. While its selectivity in neuronal tissues suggests that off-target effects might be limited, the unique environment of the retina—characterized by tightly regulated ionic gradients and specialized cell–cell interactions—could render RPE cells more sensitive to perturbations in calcium signaling (Jazouli, 2022).  

Another issue that warrants consideration is the delivery of TTA‐P2 to the RPE. The retina poses several pharmacokinetic challenges due to its blood-retina barrier; hence, any candidate must be capable of penetrating ocular tissues effectively, achieving therapeutic concentrations in the RPE while minimizing systemic exposure. While there are established methods for ocular drug delivery, such as intravitreal injections or topical formulations, the physicochemical properties of TTA‐P2 will need careful evaluation in this context. Additionally, given that the proposed mechanism involves modulating rapid Ca²⁺ microdomains, the temporal dynamics of channel blockade versus normal calcium signaling must be precisely controlled. If TTA‐P2 alters RPE calcium homeostasis too profoundly or indiscriminately, it might interfere with essential cellular processes, including phagocytosis, which is critical for retinal maintenance and health (Jazouli, 2022).  

Safety considerations are also paramount. T‐type calcium channels are expressed in multiple tissues, and systemic administration of a potent blocker like TTA‐P2 could lead to unintended side effects in other organ systems, particularly in the cardiovascular and central nervous systems. Although the ocular route of administration could mitigate these systemic effects, the risk of local toxicity and potential interference with normal retinal signaling remains. This would ideally include comprehensive studies in RPE monolayer models under inflammatory conditions to quantitatively assess TEER restoration and junctional protein preservation, as well as in vivo models of dry AMD to evaluate functional and structural outcomes following TTA‐P2 treatment.

In conclusion, TTA‐P2 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its high potency and selectivity for T‐type calcium channels, coupled with its novel mechanism—stabilizing the inactivated state of these channels and thereby reducing deleterious Ca²⁺ microdomain formation—provide a strong rationale for further investigation (Choe et al., 2011). The hypothesis that such blockade can prevent inflammatory insult-induced tight junction disassembly in RPE cells is supported by observations in both neuronal systems and studies of RPE channel expression (Jazouli, 2022). Nevertheless, gaps remain in our direct understanding of how TTA‐P2 behaves in ocular tissues, and careful evaluation of its impact on essential RPE functions—such as phagocytosis and growth factor secretion—is crucial. Safety, ocular bioavailability, and potential off-target effects are also significant areas for investigation. Overall, while TTA‐P2’s repurposing for dry AMD is still in the exploratory phase, its unique targeting of Ca²⁺ entry and potential to restore barrier integrity make it a compelling candidate that merits further preclinical validation.

Given these considerations, the next steps should include:  
1. In vitro studies using hiPSC-derived RPE cultures subjected to TNF-α or complement challenge, with detailed monitoring of TEER, FITC-dextran permeability, and tight junction protein localization following TTA‐P2 treatment.  
2. Electrophysiological recordings (patch clamp) to verify effective suppression of T‐type channel currents in RPE under both basal and inflammatory conditions, comparing TTA‐P2 with other established blockers (e.g., TTA‐A2) as controls.  
3. In vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD to assess not only RPE barrier function and retinal morphology but also functional visual outcomes after local (intravitreal) administration of TTA‐P2.  
4. Pharmacokinetic and safety evaluations specifically tailored for ocular delivery, to ascertain the optimal dosing regimen that maximizes local efficacy without compromising systemic or retinal cell functions.

Strengths of TTA‐P2 include its well-documented biophysical potency and specificity (Choe et al., 2011); its proposed mechanism, which innovatively focuses on modulating an early, calcium-dependent step in the cascade leading to barrier breakdown; and its potential to synergize with or complement existing therapies for AMD that have primarily targeted angiogenesis or inflammation by offering a strategy focused on preserving RPE junctional integrity (Jazouli, 2022). Weaknesses include the current lack of direct data in RPE or AMD models, potential adverse effects on other RPE functions (such as phagocytosis and growth factor secretion), challenges in ocular drug delivery, and the possibility of off-target effects given the ubiquitous expression of T‐type channels in various tissues (Jazouli, 2022).

Overall, while there is promising scientific rationale behind the use of TTA‐P2 for protecting RPE barrier function under inflammatory conditions reminiscent of dry AMD, the candidate remains at an early repurposing stage. The transition from successful neuronal applications to effective retinal therapies requires extensive adaptation and validation. However, if its efficacy and safety can be confirmed in detailed RPE and in vivo AMD models, TTA‐P2 could emerge as a novel therapeutic tool addressing an unmet clinical need in dry AMD. In summary, TTA‐P2’s mechanism of action—based on precise, state-dependent inhibition of T-type Ca²⁺ channels—coupled with its potential to stabilize RPE tight junctions under pathogenic stress, positions it as an exciting candidate for further investigation in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (Choe et al., 2011; Jazouli, 2022).

This evaluation suggests that while the candidate has substantial merit and promise, the lack of direct preclinical evidence in RPE models means that a dedicated series of studies (both in vitro and in vivo) will be essential before moving toward clinical trials. The potential for TTA‐P2 to fill a therapeutic gap by directly targeting Ca²⁺ entry and preserving RPE barrier function provides a unique and fresh mechanism compared with existing treatments, but its ultimate success will depend on how well these preclinical models predict efficacy and safety in patients with dry AMD.

In contrast to natural product–derived mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin, AZD8055 was developed through rational drug design to achieve high potency and dual inhibition of both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2. The development program underlying AZD8055 focused on enhancing both the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic properties to not only achieve a potent biochemical inhibition but also allow for a cleaner kinase selectivity profile, which is essential for targeted clinical interventions. Although primarily intended for oncology indications, this engineered selectivity coupled with its capacity to modulate autophagy has prompted investigation into its potential repurposing for diseases characterized by autophagic dysregulation, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

Historically, mTOR inhibitors have been extensively studied in the context of cancer, with rapamycin and its analogs (rapalogs) serving as prototype compounds for targeting dysregulated mTOR signaling in malignant cells. AZD8055, a second-generation inhibitor, was developed to overcome limitations associated with rapalogs, including incomplete mTORC1 inhibition and the inadvertent activation of compensatory pro-survival signals mediated through mTORC2 and AKT feedback loops. Preclinical studies and phase I clinical evaluations in oncology have demonstrated that AZD8055 can effectively induce cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis by simultaneously suppressing mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis and mTORC2-mediated survival signals (Walters & Cox, 2018, pp. 8–10; Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 4–5). Its clinical development history has largely focused on cancers such as Her2-positive breast cancers and gliomas, where its ability to modulate PI3K/AKT signaling has been of particular advantage in overcoming resistance mechanisms. Although the majority of the therapeutic history of AZD8055 has been in cancer, the underlying molecular rationale for its use has provided impetus for exploring its repurposing in non-oncological diseases. In the realm of ocular diseases, particularly dry AMD, the mTOR pathway has been implicated in the regulation of autophagy and cellular homeostasis within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). While traditional mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin have been tested in ocular settings, their clinical efficacy has been inconsistent, partly due to the inability to inhibit mTORC2-driven feedback loops. AZD8055’s dual inhibition mechanism could potentially address these shortcomings by providing a more balanced modulation of the mTOR pathway, although to date there is limited direct clinical or preclinical evidence of its use specifically in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 9–10, 16–17).

At a molecular level, AZD8055 exerts its pharmacological effects through ATP-competitive inhibition of the catalytic domain of mTOR, thereby targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes. mTORC1 is primarily responsible for regulating protein synthesis through substrates such as 4EBP1 and S6 kinase, while mTORC2 is integral to the phosphorylation and activation of AKT, a key mediator of cell survival and metabolism. As a dual mTOR inhibitor with high potency, AZD8055’s molecular interactions within the mTOR kinase domain contribute not only to the suppression of pathological signaling but also promote cellular recycling processes that maintain RPE function and homeostasis (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 2–3; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 4–6). In evaluating AZD8055 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key strengths and potential challenges must be considered. A notable strength of AZD8055 lies in its dual inhibition profile, which addresses the limitations inherent in rapalog therapy by effectively targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative that belongs to the fibrate class of hypolipidemic agents. Originally developed to address dyslipidemia, fenofibrate was synthesized via chemical modifications of the fibric acid scaffold to yield an amphipathic carboxylic acid derivative, designed specifically to modulate lipid metabolism. As a member of the fibrate drug class, fenofibrate exerts its primary effects through activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα), a nuclear receptor that regulates the transcription of a variety of genes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, lipid transport, and overall metabolic homeostasis (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2). Over the past several decades, fibrates have been widely used in clinical practice to lower triglycerides, reduce low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, and elevate high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, significantly contributing to cardiovascular risk management. In addition, the repurposing efforts for fenofibrate in ocular conditions have generated interest based on its ability to modulate inflammatory and metabolic pathways in retinal tissues (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11).

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate’s therapeutic history is well established in the management of dyslipidemia and in reducing cardiovascular risk. Its clinical use dates back several decades, during which it has demonstrated efficacy in lowering plasma triglyceride levels, reducing total cholesterol, and favorably shifting the LDL particle size toward a less atherogenic profile (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9). Beyond its lipid-lowering effects, fenofibrate has been extensively evaluated in the context of diabetic retinopathy. Large-scale clinical trials such as the FIELD (Fenofibrate Intervention and Event Lowering in Diabetes) study and the ACCORD (Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes) Eye study have provided robust evidence that fenofibrate can slow the progression of diabetic retinopathy, reduce the severity of retinal microvascular abnormalities, and decrease the need for laser photocoagulation (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12). Although these studies primarily targeted diabetic retinal changes, the underlying pathophysiology – which includes oxidative stress, inflammation, and lipid accumulation in retinal tissues – overlaps with that observed in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11). Preclinical studies using in vitro models of RPE cells, where saturated fatty acids like palmitate are used to mimic lipotoxic stress, have demonstrated that fenofibrate can reduce lipid droplet accumulation and improve barrier function as measured by trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 8–11). While there is no large-scale clinical trial data directly targeting dry AMD with fenofibrate, its documented benefits in diabetic retinopathy and its mechanistic overlap with dry AMD pathology make it an intriguing candidate for repurposing in this disease setting (Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 12–13).

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action is multifaceted and is primarily mediated by its role as a PPARα agonist. Binding of fenofibrate (or its active metabolite, fenofibric acid) to PPARα leads to the formation of a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor (RXR), which then binds to peroxisome proliferator responsive elements (PPREs) in the promoters of target genes. This transcriptional activation upregulates a suite of enzymes involved in fatty acid uptake and mitochondrial β-oxidation, such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) (Qiu et al., 2019, pp. 11–12; Zhao et al., 2015, pp. 5–7). Increased expression of these catabolic enzymes enhances the degradation of fatty acids, thereby reducing intracellular lipid accumulation. In the context of lipid-loaded RPE cells – a condition that contributes to the disruption of tight junctions and subsequent barrier dysfunction – fenofibrate’s enhancement of fatty acid β-oxidation is hypothesized to lower intracellular lipid levels and consequently mitigate the lipotoxic stress imposed on junctional complexes (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 8–11; Fu et al., 2020, pp. 10–11).  

Beyond its metabolic effects, fenofibrate has been reported to exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions. It downregulates markers of oxidative stress such as NOX4 and 3-nitrotyrosine and attenuates the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNFα, ICAM1, and VEGF in retinal tissues (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 8–11). Importantly, fenofibrate appears to modulate the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway in RPE cells. Under conditions of lipotoxicity induced by saturated fatty acids (e.g., palmitate), the PI3K/AKT pathway is downregulated, leading to increased oxidative stress and inflammation. Fenofibrate treatment has been shown to restore the p-AKT/AKT ratio, suggesting its ability to activate survival and anti-apoptotic pathways that are vital for maintaining RPE integrity (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 6–8). Fenofibrate presents several compelling strengths as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. One of its primary advantages is its long-established safety and efficacy profile in clinical use for dyslipidemia. Decades of systemic administration in patients have provided robust safety data and have demonstrated that fenofibrate is well tolerated in the majority of cases (del V Cano & Gehlbach, 2008, pp. 1–2; Fu et al., 2019, pp. 8–9). Mechanistically, fenofibrate’s ability to activate PPARα and enhance fatty acid β-oxidation addresses a critical aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis: the accumulation of lipids within RPE cells that contributes to oxidative stress and impairs junctional integrity. The reduction in lipid accumulation not only decreases lipotoxic stress but also supports cellular energy production, thereby enabling the restoration of tight junction proteins such as occludin (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 4–6, 6–8). In summary, fenofibrate exhibits significant promise as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its synthetic derivation and established use as a lipid-lowering agent, combined with revealed preclinical efficacy in preserving RPE function under lipotoxic conditions, align well with the hypothesized benefit of enhancing fatty acid β-oxidation to alleviate junctional stress. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
CDDO‐Imidazolide (CDDO‐Im) is a synthetic derivative that belongs to the family of chemically engineered pentacyclic triterpenoids. These compounds are derived from naturally occurring oleanolic acid, a steroid‐like molecule widely distributed in plants and traditionally used in Asian medicine. In the case of CDDO‐Im, researchers have modified the oleanolic acid scaffold by introducing a 2‐cyano substituent, oxidizing key positions to generate 3,12‐dioxo groups, and creating a conjugated 1,9(11)‐dien arrangement that ultimately yields a 28‐oic acid derivative; the imidazolide moiety is added as a C17 modification to generate the “imidazolide” derivative (Cano et al., 2010; Nakagami et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2021). This compound is a member of the broader class of synthetic oleanane pentacyclic triterpenoids, which have been chemically optimized over the years to enhance their intrinsically weak anti‐inflammatory and cytoprotective activities. Notably, these derivatives are known for their extraordinarily potent activation of the transcription factor Nrf2, an effect that is achieved by covalently modifying electrophilic target sites on Keap1. In general, this drug class has been used in diverse pharmacological applications to harness antioxidant and anti‐inflammatory pathways, and several members have been tested preclinically and even progressed into early clinical trials, particularly in the fields of oncology and renal diseases (Cano et al., 2010; Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
The history of therapeutics based on the CDDO scaffold, including CDDO‐Im, is rich in preclinical exploration and early clinical evaluation. Early studies demonstrated that synthetic triterpenoids, such as CDDO and its derivatives (including the methyl ester variant CDDO‐Me and the imidazolide derivative CDDO‐Im), are considerably more potent than other small‐molecule activators of Nrf2 such as sulforaphane or (R)-α-lipoic acid (Cano et al., 2010). Preclinical studies have shown that these compounds robustly induce phase II antioxidant enzymes––notably HO-1, NQO1, and glutathione-related enzymes––by targeting and modifying Keap1, thereby releasing Nrf2 to translocate to the nucleus and drive the transcription of cytoprotective genes. In ocular research, CDDO‐Im has been specifically chosen for in vivo studies because of its demonstrated efficacy in ameliorating retinal damage in mouse models of uveitis and cigarette smoke-induced retinal injury, with evidence of preservation of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) ultrastructure (Cano et al., 2010). Other members of the CDDO family, such as CDDO‐Me (bardoxolone methyl), have undergone clinical testing in oncology, showing that such compounds can reach therapeutically relevant blood concentrations via intravenous infusion, although issues such as suboptimal oral bioavailability have been noted and are subject to ongoing formulation efforts (Cheng et al., 2021; Nakagami et al., 2015). While there is no direct record of CDDO‐Im being used in clinical trials for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal degenerative diseases, the class’s demonstrated ability to activate protective Nrf2 signaling in ocular tissues and to reduce inflammation and oxidative damage provides a strong rationale for investigating its potential in the context of dry AMD (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The pharmacological actions of CDDO‐Im are primarily mediated through its covalent modification of Keap1 (Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1), the cytosolic repressor of the transcription factor Nrf2. Under basal conditions, Keap1 binds to Nrf2 and facilitates its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. CDDO‐Im, as an electrophilic compound possessing a cyanoenone Michael‐acceptor motif, reacts with crucial sulfhydryl groups on Keap1, resulting in the formation of Michael adducts at key cysteine residues (Cano et al., 2010; Cheng et al., 2021). Although specific studies have not always mapped the precise cysteine residues modified by CDDO‐Im in every system, the general consensus from the literature is that the modification of cysteine sulfhydryl groups such as Cys151 is critical for diminishing the suppressive influence of Keap1. Once these cysteine residues are modified, Keap1 undergoes conformational changes that reduce its binding affinity for Nrf2. Consequently, Nrf2 is liberated and able to translocate into the nucleus where, by heterodimerizing with small Maf proteins, it binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) in the promoters of target genes. This Nrf2-driven transcriptional activation results in the upregulation of a broad battery of phase II detoxifying and antioxidant enzymes, including HO-1 (heme oxygenase 1), NQO1 (NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase-1), and glutamate cysteine ligase subunits such as GCLM (glutamate-cysteine ligase modifier subunit) (Cano et al., 2010; Cheng et al., 2021). In addition to these classical antioxidant enzymes, recent research suggests that Nrf2 activation may also have downstream effects on the expression of proteins involved in maintaining cellular barrier integrity, for example tight junction proteins like claudin-1 and occludin. Although experimental details regarding the upregulation of tight junction proteins by CDDO‐Im per se have not been exhaustively documented in the literature provided, there is supporting evidence from related triterpenoids such as CDDO‐Me which preserve blood–brain barrier integrity by upregulating tight junction proteins (Nakagami, 2016; Cano et al., 2010). This mechanistic insight is directly relevant for the RPE, as oxidative stress in these cells contributes to tight junction disorganization, loss of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), and increased paracellular permeability. Therefore, through the covalent modification of Keap1 and subsequent activation of Nrf2, CDDO‐Im is hypothesized to restore the balance of antioxidant defenses and tighten the RPE barrier by increasing the expression of protective enzymes and possibly enhancing tight junction assembly under conditions of H₂O₂-induced stress (Cheng et al., 2021; Cano et al., 2010).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for using CDDO‐Im in dry AMD centers on the restoration of RPE function by enhancing antioxidant defense and barrier integrity. In an in vitro model using ARPE-19 cells exposed to H₂O₂ to simulate oxidative stress, it is expected that treatment with CDDO‐Im at a concentration around 200 nM will robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway. This activation should lead to a marked upregulation of phase II antioxidant enzymes, such as HO-1 and NQO1, thereby mitigating oxidative damage within these cells. Moreover, because Nrf2 activation has been associated with the upregulation of tight junction proteins in other barrier systems, CDDO‐Im is anticipated to promote expression of tight junction proteins, such as claudin-1 and occludin, in RPE cells. This effect would be reflected in a recovery of TEER values to greater than 90% of baseline measurements and a significant reduction—estimated at greater than 65%—in paracellular leakage of molecules like 4 kDa FITC-dextran from the RPE layer (Cano et al., 2010; Cheng et al., 2021). The compound’s high potency at the nanomolar level is particularly attractive since it indicates that effective activation of the Nrf2 pathway can be achieved at doses that are less likely to provoke off-target effects. In addition, pharmacokinetic studies in rodents have shown that similar compounds within the CDDO family have an oral bioavailability in the range of approximately 30% and a mouse intravenous half-life of around 4 hours (as suggested by preclinical pharmacokinetic data in the literature), indicating that systemic administration may be feasible for achieving therapeutic concentrations at the retinal level (Cheng et al., 2021). Collectively, these molecular events are expected to counteract the oxidative stress that contributes to RPE damage in dry AMD, stabilize the RPE barrier, and reduce inflammatory processes associated with complement accumulation and immune cell recruitment in the subretinal space (Cano et al., 2010; Camelo, 2025).

CDDO‐Im emerges as a highly promising therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on several converging lines of evidence. One of its most compelling strengths is its well-defined mechanism of action. The compound has been meticulously engineered from the oleanolic acid scaffold to include electrophilic moieties that selectively target Keap1, thereby activating Nrf2 with nanomolar potency (Cano et al., 2010; Nakagami et al., 2015). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
H-1152 Dihydrochloride is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor discovered and developed as part of the class of ATP‐competitive inhibitors targeting Rho‐associated coiled‐coil kinase (ROCK). It is formulated as a dihydrochloride salt (Tocris 2061) and has been characterized for its exceptional potency against ROCK isoforms, with reported IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range (0.003 µM for ROCK1 and 0.014 µM for ROCK2). As an ATP-competitive type I kinase inhibitor, it possesses a chemical structure that enables it to fit into the highly conserved ATP-binding cavity of ROCK and thereby prevents phosphorylation of downstream targets. This class of compounds has historically been used to explore the roles of ROCK in cytoskeletal dynamics, cell contractility, and migration, and has been applied in various preclinical models of ocular disorders such as glaucoma and corneal endothelial injury (Iancu et al., 2021; Meekins et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Although H-1152 itself has not been clinically approved, its pharmacologic profile as a ROCK inhibitor has been extensively studied in preclinical ocular models. Multiple studies have employed H-1152 in experiments that assessed its effects on corneal endothelial cell migration, proliferation, and wound healing. For instance, in in vitro assays using porcine corneal endothelial cells, H-1152 significantly enhanced cell migration and proliferation compared with control treatments and with other inhibitors like Y-27632. In vivo topical application in rabbit corneal surgical wound models demonstrated accelerated wound closure and resolution of corneal edema without significant toxic effects. These findings underscore its potential utility as a topical therapeutic agent in ocular applications. Moreover, the general class of ROCK inhibitors has been clinically exploited—ripasudil, for example, has been approved for the treatment of glaucoma in Japan, and intravitreal fasudil has been explored for refractory diabetic macular oedema—establishing a safe precedent for ocular delivery of ROCK-targeting molecules. However, while ROCK inhibitors have been investigated in retinal and choroidal vascular pathologies and in conditions marked by barrier dysfunction (such as diabetic macular oedema), there is currently no direct record of H-1152 having been used specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or for RPE-specific pathologies in published clinical or preclinical studies (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, H-1152 acts by competitively inhibiting the kinase activity of both ROCK1 and ROCK2. By binding to the ATP-binding site of the kinase domain, H-1152 prevents the phosphorylation of downstream substrates such as myosin light chain (MLC) and LIM kinases, which in turn results in the reduced phosphorylation of cofilin. This cascade of events inhibits actomyosin contractility and results in the disassembly—or at least, a significant reduction—of actin stress fibers. In cellular contexts, this biochemical action translates into the disruption of stress-fiber–driven cellular contraction and a modulation of both cell–matrix and cell–cell adhesion complexes. In ocular applications, particularly within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), such cytoskeletal reorganization is hypothesized to stabilize junctional complexes by normalizing the localization and organization of critical tight-junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and occludin. Studies in related ocular cell types (e.g., corneal endothelial cells) have documented that ROCK inhibitors induce a rapid collapse of actin stress fibers and result in a transient loss but subsequent restoration of tight-junction architecture over time. Furthermore, ROCK signaling is implicated in mediating the cellular responses to oxidative stress and in promoting VEGF-induced permeability. In models of VEGF stimulation, ROCK inhibition has been associated with a reduction in paracellular leak by preserving tight-junction integrity. Therefore, by potently inhibiting ROCK1/2, H-1152 is proposed to prevent the stress-fiber–mediated disruption of cell–cell junctions and to restore transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE cells subjected to chronic oxidative insult – a mechanism particularly relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology (Meekins et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Based on its mechanism of action and experimental precedent in other ocular models, it is expected that H-1152 will exert a protective effect on RPE cells under conditions of chronic oxidative stress as seen in dry AMD. In vitro, in an ARPE-19 or primary RPE cell model, chronic exposure to low levels of H₂O₂ typically results in a decrease in TEER, disorganization of tight junction proteins (including ZO-1 and occludin), and the formation of abnormal F-actin stress fibers. Treatment with H-1152 in the range of 0.1–1 µM is hypothesized to partially or even substantially reverse these deleterious changes. Specifically, by inhibiting ROCK activity, H-1152 is expected to reduce the formation of stress fibers, thereby reversing the disruption of cell junctions and restoring a more normal distribution of ZO-1 and occludin at the plasma membrane. This should in turn lead to an improvement in TEER – with potential recovery to up to 60% of baseline levels in injured cells – as well as diminish the regulation of VEGF-driven paracellular leak. In addition, pharmacokinetic studies in rabbit models have demonstrated that subconjunctival dosing can achieve ocular RPE/choroid concentrations on the order of ~0.2 µM, which falls within the effective in vitro concentration range. Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the therapeutic candidate H-1152 Dihydrochloride exhibits multiple promising attributes as a repurposed drug for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. One of its primary strengths is its exceptional potency and selectivity toward ROCK1 and ROCK2, with IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range, which is critical given that only minimal inhibition may be required to elicit beneficial cellular modifications in the RPE. Its mechanism of action, relying on the inhibition of the ROCK pathway, directly addresses key pathological processes in dry AMD, notably the stress-fiber–mediated disruption of cell–cell junctions and the abnormal VEGF-driven paracellular leak. Second, while the ROCK inhibitor class has been used in other areas of ophthalmology with an acceptable safety and tolerability profile, there is currently no direct clinical history of H-1152 being used for dry AMD or even in posterior-segment diseases; most clinical data so far pertains to ROCK inhibitors used in glaucoma or diabetic macular oedema. Overall, H-1152 Dihydrochloride presents as a promising candidate for repurposing as a dry AMD therapeutic based on its mechanistic rationale, outstanding potency and selectivity for ROCK inhibition, and the supportive data from ocular surface models. The proposed molecular mechanism—restoring tight-junction integrity through suppression of stress fiber formation and subsequent normalization of ZO-1 and occludin localization—aligns well with the underlying pathology of dry AMD, in which the breakdown of RPE barrier function contributes to disease progression. However, definitive preclinical studies employing RPE-specific models and in vivo evaluations in relevant dry AMD animal models are necessary to solidify its translational potential. Additionally, careful attention must be given to its safety profile, especially given the delicate nature of the posterior segment and the potential for off-target effects on retinal vasculature. In conclusion, while H-1152 shows significant promise based on its pharmacological profile and the mechanistic logic underlying RPE barrier restoration, further research is warranted to bridge the gap between ocular surface models and the RPE-specific pathology encountered in dry AMD. Strategic preclinical investigations, including detailed assessments of TEER restoration, tight junction protein localization under oxidative stress, and the modulation of VEGF signaling, are critical next steps in validating H-1152 as a viable therapeutic candidate for this complex and currently underserved retinal disease (Meekins et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of TTA‐P2 as a repurposed candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD):

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
TTA‐P2 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed to target T‐type voltage‐gated calcium channels (VGCCs), which belong to the CaV3 family (CaV3.1, CaV3.2, CaV3.3). Its chemical structure, described as 3,5‐dichloro-N-[1-(2,2-dimethyl-tetrahydro-pyran-4-ylmethyl)-4-fluoro-piperidin-4-ylmethyl]-benzamide, was established via medicinal chemistry optimization strategies aimed at increasing potency and selectivity for the T‐type channels relative to high-voltage-activated channels (Choe et al., 2011). Originally discovered and characterized in the context of neuronal excitability studies, TTA‐P2 has been shown to block T‐type calcium currents in rat sensory neurons with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range; this high potency is matched by an excellent selectivity profile given that its inhibitory concentration for high-voltage-activated channels is orders of magnitude higher (Choe et al., 2011). As a member of the T‐type calcium channel blocker class, TTA‐P2 is representative of compounds that modulate low-voltage-activated channels involved in a variety of cell functions, ranging from neuronal burst firing to hormone release. In the context of drug development, this compound is categorized as a channel-modulating agent, and its synthetic origins as a small molecule rendered it amenable to structural modification for improved pharmacokinetics in various tissue systems (Choe et al., 2011). Although historically used primarily in neuronal studies, its inherent properties have prompted consideration of its repurposing for non-neuronal tissues, such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where T‐type channels have been shown to contribute to key physiological processes (Jazouli, 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TTA‐P2 has been investigated in the context of neuropathic pain and epilepsy, where T‐type calcium channels are integral to the regulation of neuronal excitability. In experimental models involving rat sensory neurons, TTA‐P2 demonstrated marked antinociceptive properties and produced significant reductions in neuronal burst firing by selectively blocking T‐type calcium currents (Choe et al., 2011). This evidence underlines the compound’s effectiveness in modulating calcium influx in hyperexcitable systems. Beyond its neurological applications, there have been several studies in which compounds targeting T‐type CaV channels were applied to non-neuronal cells. For instance, work in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) demonstrated that T‐type calcium channels are expressed and functionally important in these cells, although in those studies a different inhibitor—TTA‐A2—was used to evaluate effects on phagocytosis and VEGF secretion (Jazouli, 2022). Moreover, complementary work in RPE models has noted that T‐type channels appear to localize specifically to the apical membrane, with subtypes such as CaV3.1 and CaV3.3 being especially prominent (Jazouli, 2022). Despite extensive preclinical work in neuronal systems, there is no published record, to our knowledge, that TTA‐P2 has been tested directly in AMD or other ocular disease models. However, evidence gleaned from cerebral endothelia studies—where inhibition of CaV3.1/CaV3.2 ameliorates inflammatory barrier disruption—suggests that a similar strategy may be beneficial in preserving the function of the RPE barrier (Unknown Reference). Thus, while TTA‐P2 has a well-established history in neurological studies, its repurposing for dry AMD is based on the emerging understanding that T‐type channels contribute to RPE function and that their inhibition may counter inflammatory and degenerative signals (Jazouli, 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism by which TTA‐P2 exerts its effects is through selective inhibition of T‐type calcium channels. Detailed electrophysiological studies in rat sensory neurons have shown that TTA‐P2 binds preferentially to the inactivated state of these channels, thereby stabilizing them in a non-conducting conformation. This binding results in a significant hyperpolarizing shift (approximately 20 mV) in the steady-state inactivation curves and an incomplete recovery from inactivation, meaning that the channels remain non-functional for a longer period after brief depolarizations (Choe et al., 2011). Such effects effectively reduce the calcium influx that would normally occur during depolarization-driven events. In RPE cells, there is a body of evidence indicating that T‐type calcium channels (particularly CaV3.1 and CaV3.3) contribute to the formation of localized Ca²⁺ microdomains that play a role in regulating tight junction dynamics (Jazouli, 2022). Under inflammatory conditions—such as those induced by TNF-α or complement activation—excessive Ca²⁺ influx via these channels may trigger signaling cascades that lead to the disassembly of adherens junctions and tight junctions, ultimately compromising the integrity of the epithelial barrier. TTA‐P2’s ability to suppress the T‐type currents would, therefore, limit the depolarization-driven Ca²⁺ microdomain formation in RPE cells (Choe et al., 2011). In addition, the selective binding to the inactivated state minimizes off-target effects on channels that have higher activation thresholds, such as L-type channels, thereby preserving other essential calcium-dependent processes. The blockade of T‐type channels is particularly relevant because these channels typically open at more negative membrane potentials, a regime that is critical for maintaining the delicate Ca²⁺ balance in nonexcitable cells such as the RPE (Choe et al., 2011; Jazouli, 2022). Consequently, by dampening the Ca²⁺ entry through these channels, TTA‐P2 could play a protective role against inflammation-induced barrier disruption.

Expected Effect:  
According to the proposal, the central hypothesis is that a pan–T‐type CaV blockade by TTA‐P2 (with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, here cited as approximately 20 nM) will suppress the formation of harmful Ca²⁺ microdomains in RPE cells, thereby preventing the downstream signaling events that lead to the disassembly of tight junctions. The integrity of RPE monolayers is often assessed by measurements such as transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and permeability assays (e.g., FITC-dextran flux). In the presence of inflammatory insults like TNF-α or complement factors—both of which can mimic some of the pathophysiological aspects of dry AMD—the excessive calcium influx through T‐type channels may cause rearrangement or breakdown of tight junction proteins (such as occludin and claudins), leading to compromised barrier function and increased paracellular permeability (Jazouli, 2022).  
By inhibiting these channels, TTA‐P2 is expected to reduce intracellular Ca²⁺ accumulation that drives disassembly of junctional complexes, thereby restoring normal TEER values and reducing the passage of molecules like FITC-dextran across the RPE monolayer. Patch-clamp studies would further validate that TTA‐P2 effectively suppresses the T‐type Ca²⁺ currents in these cells, reinforcing the direct link between calcium channel inhibition and improved barrier integrity (Choe et al., 2011). Moreover, considering that similar principles have been applied in cerebral endothelial models—where T‐type channel inhibition reduced inflammatory barrier disruption—it is plausible that the RPE, which shares some functional similarities as a barrier tissue, may respond in a comparable manner (Korkka, n.d.). It is also important to note that the expression of CaV3.1 and CaV3.3 in RPE cells has been confirmed by immunolabeling and electrophysiological studies, thereby providing a direct anatomical and functional basis for this therapeutic approach (Jazouli, 2022). This expected effect of preserving tight junction integrity makes TTA‐P2 an attractive candidate for therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction and barrier breakdown contribute to disease progression.

Overall Evaluation:  
TTA‐P2 offers several compelling strengths as a potential repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, its high potency and selectivity for T‐type calcium channels have been robustly demonstrated in neuronal systems, and these properties bode well for achieving effective inhibition in RPE cells, where even relatively minor shifts in calcium homeostasis may have significant pathophysiological implications (Choe et al., 2011). Second, the strategy of targeting T‐type channels in the RPE is grounded in evidence that these channels are involved in channel-mediated inflammatory responses and barrier disruption, processes known to play a key role in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Jazouli, 2022). Third, TTA‐P2 works through a mechanism that is distinct from conventional anti-inflammatory agents or anti-VEGF therapies; instead, it modulates a very early step in the cascade—namely, the depolarization-driven Ca²⁺ entry that acts as a trigger for tight junction disassembly. This novel mechanism, if validated, could complement existing therapies or offer a new avenue for intervention in cases where traditional therapeutics have limited efficacy.  

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be acknowledged. Foremost among these is the fact that, to date, no direct studies have been published demonstrating the efficacy of TTA‐P2 in RPE cells or in animal models of dry AMD. The majority of the literature supporting its use comes from neurological applications, and although there are analogous studies in RPE using other T‐type channel blockers (e.g., TTA‐A2), the extrapolation of neuronal pharmacodynamics to ocular tissues is not guaranteed (Jazouli, 2022). Furthermore, it is well recognized that T‐type channels in the RPE also play roles in physiological processes such as phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and the regulation of growth factor secretion (Jazouli, 2022). Thus, chronic inhibition of these channels could potentially disrupt normal RPE function if not properly dosed or targeted, leading to adverse effects that may offset the benefits of barrier preservation. Additionally, the therapeutic index of TTA‐P2 in the ocular milieu remains unknown. While its selectivity in neuronal tissues suggests that off-target effects might be limited, the unique environment of the retina—characterized by tightly regulated ionic gradients and specialized cell–cell interactions—could render RPE cells more sensitive to perturbations in calcium signaling (Jazouli, 2022).  

Another issue that warrants consideration is the delivery of TTA‐P2 to the RPE. The retina poses several pharmacokinetic challenges due to its blood-retina barrier; hence, any candidate must be capable of penetrating ocular tissues effectively, achieving therapeutic concentrations in the RPE while minimizing systemic exposure. While there are established methods for ocular drug delivery, such as intravitreal injections or topical formulations, the physicochemical properties of TTA‐P2 will need careful evaluation in this context. Additionally, given that the proposed mechanism involves modulating rapid Ca²⁺ microdomains, the temporal dynamics of channel blockade versus normal calcium signaling must be precisely controlled. If TTA‐P2 alters RPE calcium homeostasis too profoundly or indiscriminately, it might interfere with essential cellular processes, including phagocytosis, which is critical for retinal maintenance and health (Jazouli, 2022).  

Safety considerations are also paramount. T‐type calcium channels are expressed in multiple tissues, and systemic administration of a potent blocker like TTA‐P2 could lead to unintended side effects in other organ systems, particularly in the cardiovascular and central nervous systems. Although the ocular route of administration could mitigate these systemic effects, the risk of local toxicity and potential interference with normal retinal signaling remains. In summary, while the mechanistic rationale for using TTA‐P2 as a barrier-preserving agent in dry AMD is scientifically sound and innovative, considerable preclinical work is required. This would ideally include comprehensive studies in RPE monolayer models under inflammatory conditions to quantitatively assess TEER restoration and junctional protein preservation, as well as in vivo models of dry AMD to evaluate functional and structural outcomes following TTA‐P2 treatment.

In conclusion, TTA‐P2 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its high potency and selectivity for T‐type calcium channels, coupled with its novel mechanism—stabilizing the inactivated state of these channels and thereby reducing deleterious Ca²⁺ microdomain formation—provide a strong rationale for further investigation (Choe et al., 2011). The hypothesis that such blockade can prevent inflammatory insult-induced tight junction disassembly in RPE cells is supported by observations in both neuronal systems and studies of RPE channel expression (Jazouli, 2022). Nevertheless, gaps remain in our direct understanding of how TTA‐P2 behaves in ocular tissues, and careful evaluation of its impact on essential RPE functions—such as phagocytosis and growth factor secretion—is crucial. Safety, ocular bioavailability, and potential off-target effects are also significant areas for investigation. Overall, while TTA‐P2’s repurposing for dry AMD is still in the exploratory phase, its unique targeting of Ca²⁺ entry and potential to restore barrier integrity make it a compelling candidate that merits further preclinical validation.

Given these considerations, the next steps should include:  
1. In vitro studies using hiPSC-derived RPE cultures subjected to TNF-α or complement challenge, with detailed monitoring of TEER, FITC-dextran permeability, and tight junction protein localization following TTA‐P2 treatment.  
2. Electrophysiological recordings (patch clamp) to verify effective suppression of T‐type channel currents in RPE under both basal and inflammatory conditions, comparing TTA‐P2 with other established blockers (e.g., TTA‐A2) as controls.  
3. In vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD to assess not only RPE barrier function and retinal morphology but also functional visual outcomes after local (intravitreal) administration of TTA‐P2.  
4. Pharmacokinetic and safety evaluations specifically tailored for ocular delivery, to ascertain the optimal dosing regimen that maximizes local efficacy without compromising systemic or retinal cell functions.

Strengths of TTA‐P2 include its well-documented biophysical potency and specificity (Choe et al., 2011); its proposed mechanism, which innovatively focuses on modulating an early, calcium-dependent step in the cascade leading to barrier breakdown; and its potential to synergize with or complement existing therapies for AMD that have primarily targeted angiogenesis or inflammation by offering a strategy focused on preserving RPE junctional integrity (Jazouli, 2022). Weaknesses include the current lack of direct data in RPE or AMD models, potential adverse effects on other RPE functions (such as phagocytosis and growth factor secretion), challenges in ocular drug delivery, and the possibility of off-target effects given the ubiquitous expression of T‐type channels in various tissues (Jazouli, 2022).

Overall, while there is promising scientific rationale behind the use of TTA‐P2 for protecting RPE barrier function under inflammatory conditions reminiscent of dry AMD, the candidate remains at an early repurposing stage. The transition from successful neuronal applications to effective retinal therapies requires extensive adaptation and validation. However, if its efficacy and safety can be confirmed in detailed RPE and in vivo AMD models, TTA‐P2 could emerge as a novel therapeutic tool addressing an unmet clinical need in dry AMD. In summary, TTA‐P2’s mechanism of action—based on precise, state-dependent inhibition of T-type Ca²⁺ channels—coupled with its potential to stabilize RPE tight junctions under pathogenic stress, positions it as an exciting candidate for further investigation in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (Choe et al., 2011; Jazouli, 2022).

This evaluation suggests that while the candidate has substantial merit and promise, the lack of direct preclinical evidence in RPE models means that a dedicated series of studies (both in vitro and in vivo) will be essential before moving toward clinical trials. The potential for TTA‐P2 to fill a therapeutic gap by directly targeting Ca²⁺ entry and preserving RPE barrier function provides a unique and fresh mechanism compared with existing treatments, but its ultimate success will depend on how well these preclinical models predict efficacy and safety in patients with dry AMD.

Conceptually, H-151 belongs to the broader class of cGAS–STING pathway modulators that have been deployed to suppress sterile inflammation across multiple tissues; for the eye and retina, related pathway inhibitors (e.g., C-176, SN-011, cryptotanshinone) have shown efficacy in ischemic and neovascular models via suppression of microglial STING signaling and cytokine/chemokine/protease outputs, supporting the translatability of STING antagonism to ocular tissues (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
There is no reported clinical use of H-151 in humans, and no published veterinary or clinical trials in ophthalmology were identified in the provided literature set; H-151 has been used as a research tool compound in preclinical inflammatory models, most prominently in psoriasis, where it decreased lesion severity and cutaneous inflammatory readouts in the imiquimod model (Pan et al., 2021). In vivo, topical H-151 improved psoriasis-like dermatitis and decreased markers linked to STING/NF-κB signaling, again without human clinical translation to date (Pan et al., 2021).

Ocular/retinal precedent for the STING target is strong even if H-151–specific data are sparse. In multiple retinal contexts, activation of cGAS–STING has been implicated in pathogenesis through DNA-damage and mitochondrial DNA leakage, leading to IRF3/NF-κB activation, SASP-like cytokine induction, angiogenesis, and barrier dysfunction (Hu et al., 2023). Genetic and pharmacologic pathway perturbations show benefit: genetic loss of STING limits endothelial senescence and vascular degeneration in diabetic models (Liu et al., 2023), genetic deletion along the cGAS–STING axis rescues Alu DNA–driven RPE toxicity (implicated in geographic atrophy) (Hu et al., 2023), and pharmacologic STING inhibitors (C-176, SN-011) suppress neovascularization in laser CNV and OIR models (Ni et al., 2024). STING biology and the palmitoylation node. STING is a homodimeric ER-resident adaptor with an N-terminal multi-pass transmembrane domain and a cytosolic C-terminal ligand-binding domain; binding of 2’3’-cGAMP (produced by cGAS upon sensing cytosolic dsDNA) induces conformational rearrangements that enable ER exit and trafficking to the Golgi, where palmitoylation of Cys88 and Cys91 is critical for higher-order assembly and recruitment of TBK1 and other signaling proteins (Li et al., 2021). Activated STING scaffolds TBK1 to phosphorylate IRF3 (e.g., at Ser366), triggering type I interferon gene expression, and engages NF-κB to induce a broad proinflammatory transcriptional program, including SASP components (Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2021). H-151 is positioned mechanistically among irreversible covalent inhibitors of STING that target Cys91 to prevent activation-associated palmitoylation and signalosome formation (Decout et al., 2021). While detailed covalent adduct chemistry for H-151 itself is not contained in the supplied excerpts, authoritative mechanistic reviews depict H-151 in the “Targeting Cys91” class, alongside nitrofuran inhibitors (C-176, C-178) that have been shown to bind Cys91 selectively and irreversibly (but not Cys88) and that suppress in vivo IFN and IL-6 responses to STING agonism (Decout et al., 2021). Rationale in retinal cells and tissue. cGAS and STING are expressed across retinal cell types (RPE, microglia, endothelial cells, Müller glia, photoreceptors) and are upregulated in disease states (AMD/DR), with promoter accessibility and mRNA levels increased in diseased tissue, positioning the pathway as targetable across multiple ocular compartments (Hu et al., 2023). Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction cause cytosolic mtDNA accumulation that activates cGAS–STING; Alu-derived nucleic acids similarly drive cytosolic DNA sensing and RPE cytotoxicity in GA, with multiple studies showing that genetic deletion along the cGAS–STING axis rescues Alu DNA toxicity (Hu et al., 2023). In RPE biology specifically, STING is implicated in senescence-associated VEGF upregulation, and H-151 prevented VEGF overproduction in senescent ARPE-19 cells, indicating that palmitoylation-targeted STING antagonism can suppress a central angiogenic/SASP mediator in stressed RPE-like cells (Hu et al., 2023).
