RPE models are heterogeneous in cGAS expression and DNA-sensor usage; some RPE cell lines lack cGAS and instead rely on other nucleic acid sensors (e.g., RIG-I, ZBP1), and the relative contribution of cGAS–STING versus alternative pathways varies by context (Hu et al., 2023). Moreover, the balance of STING outputs (IRF3/type I IFN versus NF-κB) can be cell/state dependent, as reflected by psoriasis-model findings where systemic IFN-β was unchanged despite local suppression of p-IRF3 and p65 in skin (Pan et al., 2021). These observations underscore that while H-151 inhibits upstream STING activation, the phenotype in any given ocular assay will reflect cell-type–specific wiring, stimulus context (Alu vs mtDNA vs oxidant stress), and cross-talk with other innate immune axes (Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023).

Expected Effect  
Assay context and target presence. The proposed assays—senescence models in RPE with readouts including TEER, ZO-1 continuity, SASP cytokines (IL-6/IL-8), and MMPs—interrogate processes (barrier integrity, SASP-driven inflammation, matrix remodeling) that are mechanistically tied to cGAS–STING–NF-κB signaling and are central to dry AMD progression (Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025; Terao et al., 2022). RPE expresses STING and engages cGAS–STING signaling under oxidative and senescent stress; senescent ARPE-19 cells overproduce VEGF via a STING/NF-κB/HIF-1α pathway, and H-151 prevented this VEGF overproduction, providing direct cell-type–relevant evidence of efficacy on a SASP/angiogenic factor in RPE (Hu et al., 2023). In addition, cGAS inhibition alleviates Alu RNA–induced immune responses and cytotoxicity in RPE, consistent with the pathway’s role in dsDNA/dsRNA-triggered sterile inflammation and suggesting that upstream DNA-sensor blockade mitigates RPE injury (Li et al., 2022).

Expected pharmacodynamic effects. Based on H-151’s mechanism at the palmitoylation node and its demonstrated suppression of STING-dependent IRF3 and NF-κB activation in immune and epithelial cells, we expect the following in RPE senescence assays:

- Proximal signaling: reductions in STING abundance (as seen in keratinocytes/THP-1), p-TBK1, p-IRF3, and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation following H-151 treatment under stimuli that engage cGAS–STING (e.g., H₂O₂-induced senescence, Alu cDNA transfection, mtDNA transfection) (Pan et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022).

- Cytokines/SASP: decreased secretion and/or expression of IL-6 and potentially IL-8 and other SASP components; in non-ocular systems H-151 lowered IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, IFN-β, and IFN-stimulated gene signatures, and in ARPE-19 senescence models H-151 prevented VEGF overproduction (Pan et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2023). Because NF-κB is a principal SASP driver in oxidant-stressed RPE, H-151’s suppression of NF-κB should proportionally lower SASP cytokines, including IL-6/IL-8, which are repeatedly implicated in AMD pathobiology (Terao et al., 2022; Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025).

- MMPs and matrix remodeling: in retinal microglia, pharmacologic STING inhibition reduced Mmp9 expression alongside Il6 and diminished vascular leakage in OIR, suggesting that blocking STING can lower proteases that degrade extracellular matrix and compromise barriers (Qiu et al., 2025; Terao et al., 2022). While H-151-specific MMP data in RPE have not been reported here, we would predict a reduction in MMP-9 in senescent RPE given the NF-κB dependence of SASP proteases and the precedent in ocular STING inhibition (Qiu et al., 2025; Terao et al., 2022).

- Barrier integrity (TEER and ZO-1): direct H-151 data on RPE TEER/ZO-1 are unavailable in the provided literature. However, STING activity has been linked to barrier dysfunction in retinal endothelium (inner barrier), with evidence that STING activation through TBK1/IRF3/IFN-β axes amplifies senescence and compromises barrier integrity; genetic STING deficiency mitigates such changes (Wu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). In the outer retina, RPE degeneration driven by inflammatory stimuli is attenuated in STING knockout mice, supporting that STING inhibition can preserve epithelial integrity under inflammatory stress (Hu et al., 2023). Thus, we expect H-151 to preserve TEER and maintain ZO-1 continuity in RPE senescence models where cGAS–STING–NF-κB contributes to junctional remodeling and MMP-driven degradation, but this prediction requires experimental confirmation given the absence of direct H-151 barrier data (Hu et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025).

- Anti-senescence signatures: in non-ocular systems, H-151 treatment decreased cGAS–STING pathway activation, reduced ISGs, lowered P16/P21, and decreased SA-β-gal activity, indicating that STING antagonism can blunt senescence programs and SASP (Ye et al., 2024). Given the overlap between senescence and innate immune signaling in RPE and AMD, we expect H-151 to reduce senescence markers in RPE senescence assays, again pending direct validation in ocular cells (Blasiak, 2020; Terao et al., 2022).

Expression in the assayed RPE lineage is supported by disease-relevant data showing STING expression and activation in retinal tissues and RPE under stress, including oxidative stress and Alu/mtDNA triggers; cGAS–STING pathway genes are broadly expressed in the retina and upregulated in disease, and RPE senescence engages STING-dependent NF-κB/HIF-1α signaling to drive VEGF (Hu et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease-mechanism fit. Dry AMD pathogenesis features chronic oxidative stress, DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and senescence in RPE, with resultant SASP cytokines, VEGF, and MMPs that degrade extracellular matrix and compromise barriers; cGAS–STING is positioned as a key sensor/effector linking cytosolic DNA to NF-κB/IRF3 activation and SASP output in RPE and retinal cell types (Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2023). Genetic and pharmacologic evidence across models (DR endothelium, Alu-driven RPE toxicity, ischemic/neovascular retinopathy) show that suppressing STING signaling reduces inflammation, senescence markers, angiogenic/proteolytic factors, leakage, and degeneration, indicating pathway validity and translational plausibility in the eye (Liu et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

- Direct RPE cell evidence for H-151. H-151 prevented VEGF overproduction in senescent ARPE-19 cells, directly supporting the candidate’s ability to suppress a central SASP/angiogenic mediator in an RPE-derived cell model (Hu et al., 2023). This aligns with the broader observation that STING upregulates VEGF in oxidative stress–induced RPE senescence via NF-κB/HIF-1α (Hu et al., 2023).

- Potent inhibition of NF-κB and cytokine outputs. In preclinical psoriasis systems, H-151 suppressed cGAMP-induced IRF3/NF-κB phosphorylation and reduced IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IFN-β readouts, consistent with broad blockade of the principal proinflammatory axes downstream of STING (Pan et al., 2021). Given that NF-κB is a dominant inducer of SASP components in oxidant-stressed RPE, and IL-6/IL-8 and MMPs are canonical RPE SASP factors in AMD, H-151’s activity is well matched to reduce these pathological outputs (Terao et al., 2022; Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025).

- Target validation in retinal models via related inhibitors/genetics. STING inhibition by C-176/SN-011 reduces neovascularization in CNV/OIR; cryptotanshinone reduces Il6 and Mmp9 and vascular leakage through STING suppression in microglia; STING knockout provides protection against inflammatory retinal degeneration and endothelial senescence and barrier compromise, together providing multi-compartment evidence that STING blockade can ameliorate retinal inflammatory pathology (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023).

- Modality fit for intracellular target. Because cGAS and STING are intracellular, small molecules are preferred for retinal applications; the literature anticipates that blood–retina–penetrant small-molecule cGAS–STING inhibitors will be needed to translate this strategy to the clinic, supporting H-151’s modality selection (Hu et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- Sparse ocular data for H-151. Beyond the ARPE-19 VEGF observation, there are no H-151 data for TEER, ZO-1 continuity, MMP modulation, or in vivo ocular efficacy in dry AMD models in the provided literature, so the central claims around barrier preservation remain predictions that require direct testing (Hu et al., 2023). By contrast, barrier-relevant evidence is stronger for alternative STING inhibitors (cryptotanshinone effects on Mmp9/leakage; C-176/SN-011 in angiogenesis models), indicating pathway relevance but not yet validating H-151 itself in retina (Qiu et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2024).

- Cell-type heterogeneity in DNA sensing. Some RPE models lack cGAS and may rely on other sensors (RIG-I, ZBP1), and the cGAS–STING axis can be variably engaged depending on the nature of the stressor (Alu vs mtDNA vs photo-oxidized A2E), potentially limiting the breadth of H-151’s efficacy across RPE senescence paradigms (Hu et al., 2023). Thorough profiling in human primary RPE and AMD-relevant triggers will be required.

- Pathway-output variability. H-151’s strongest effects in psoriasis were on NF-κB/IL-6, with partial or context-dependent impact on IRF3/IFN-β; while NF-κB is the prime SASP driver in RPE, specific disease contexts (e.g., dsDNA-driven type I IFN) may require robust IRF3 suppression to fully ameliorate pathology (Pan et al., 2021). The differential balance of NF-κB versus IRF3 outputs in RPE under various triggers should be experimentally mapped.

- Covalent inhibitor liabilities. Cysteine-targeting covalent inhibitors can carry risks of off-target reactivity and species-specific metabolic liabilities; development of covalent agents demands careful derisking of reactivity and ocular PK/PD, as underscored in general discussions of covalent inhibitor strategies and metabolism in drug discovery (Wang et al., 2022). Although H-151’s covalent target is genetically unique (Cys91 on STING), comprehensive safety and selectivity profiling—especially for intraocular delivery—is not available here.

- Immunological trade-offs. STING deficiency can increase susceptibility to tumorigenesis and reduce vaccine responses, and human STING haplotypes (e.g., HAQ) show variable responsiveness to cyclic dinucleotides, implying potential population variability in pathway dependence and therapeutic response (Hu et al., 2023). For ocular delivery, local exposure may mitigate systemic risks, but intraocular immunosuppression could theoretically predispose to infections; risk–benefit will need empirical assessment.

Evidence-based development plan (prioritized)  
- In vitro RPE assays. Use human primary RPE and ARPE-19 under AMD-relevant triggers (H₂O₂, Alu cDNA, mtDNA transfection) to quantify: STING pathway activation (p-TBK1, p-IRF3, p65), SASP cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), MMPs (MMP-9), and angiogenic factors (VEGF); barrier metrics by TEER and ZO-1 continuity; and senescence markers (P16, P21, SA-β-gal). Include STING agonist/antagonist controls (e.g., diABZI, C-176), and cGAS/STING knockdown to confirm on-target effects; the goal is to reproduce the VEGF suppression result and extend to barrier preservation and MMP control with H-151 (Hu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022; Terao et al., 2022).

- Retinal explant and in vivo models. Move to sodium iodate or oxidant-driven RPE injury models and to Alu DNA–induced RPE degeneration to test whether H-151 reduces cGAS–STING activation, NF-κB signaling, cytokines/MMPs, and preserves RPE morphology; positive controls include JQ1 and C-176, which have shown efficacy in related contexts (Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024). The LIRD model shows cGAS–STING activation can be modulated upstream by visual-cycle inhibitors; testing H-151 in LIRD would further link pathway suppression to photoreceptor/RPE protection (Wang et al., 2022).

- Delivery and PK/PD. Evaluate intravitreal versus periocular dosing for ocular exposure, using formulation strategies with precedent (e.g., nanoparticle-loaded C-176) to optimize intraocular retention and cell uptake; measure intraocular H-151 levels and target engagement markers (p-STING, p-TBK1, p-IRF3) (Shao et al., 2024).

- Safety and immunology. Profile local tolerability and infection risk in the eye while monitoring systemic spillover; genotype stratification for STING haplotypes can be deferred to later phases but should be considered due to pathway variability (Hu et al., 2023).

Decision context  
On balance, H-151 is a mechanistically compelling, tractable small-molecule inhibitor that targets a validated inflammatory/senescence axis in retinal disease, with one direct RPE line of evidence (suppression of VEGF in senescent ARPE-19) and robust non-ocular and ocular-pathway support via related tools and genetic models (Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). The absence of H-151–specific data on RPE barrier metrics (TEER/ZO-1) and MMP modulation is the principal evidence gap relative to the stated hypothesis; however, the consistent linkage of cGAS–STING to IL-6/VEGF/MMP outputs and barrier failure across retinal compartments supports the plausibility that a palmitoylation-targeted STING antagonist like H-151 will deliver the predicted phenotype in senescent RPE (Hu et al., 2023; Terao et al., 2022; Qiu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025).

Recommendation  
Advance H-151 into AMD-relevant in vitro RPE barrier and senescence assays with rigorous on-target controls and head-to-head comparison against alternative STING inhibitors (C-176/SN-011, cryptotanshinone) to establish class translatability and select the best ocular candidate by efficacy and safety; proceed to in vivo validation contingent on clear demonstration of TEER/ZO-1 preservation, SASP/MMP suppression, and favorable ocular PK/PD (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

Strengths summary: strong mechanistic rationale in AMD, direct RPE evidence for VEGF suppression by H-151, broad anti–NF-κB/SASP activity of H-151 in inflammatory models, and multiple retinal models validating STING inhibition (Hu et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2021; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025). Weaknesses summary: no H-151 data yet on RPE barrier readouts or in vivo retinal protection; covalent-inhibitor liabilities and immunologic trade-offs require careful derisking; cell-type heterogeneity in DNA sensing mandates model selection rigor (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Taken together, H-151 is a high-priority mechanistic probe and a plausible therapeutic lead for dry AMD that merits focused preclinical validation in RPE barrier/senescence systems and in Alu/oxidative injury models of outer retinal degeneration, with parallel medicinal-chemistry and formulation work to address ocular delivery and covalent-inhibitor safety considerations (Hu et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR, chemically known as 5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide, is an endogenous purine biosynthetic intermediate that has been harnessed as a synthetic, cell‐permeable AMP analog to activate AMP‐activated protein kinase (AMPK) pharmacologically (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Originally identified as a naturally occurring metabolic intermediate, AICAR gained prominence when researchers recognized that its structural similarity to AMP enables it to mimic cellular energetic stress conditions, thereby initiating AMPK‐mediated cellular responses (Green, 2013). In its synthetic format, AICAR is produced and purified to high standards by vendors such as Selleckchem and Sigma (S1802; A9978), and belongs to the broader class of nucleoside analogs used as metabolic regulators. Compounds belonging to this class have historically been employed to interrogate and modulate energy sensing and substrate utilization in diverse cell types, ranging from skeletal muscle to vascular smooth muscle (Pokrywka et al., 2014). This same class of metabolic modulators has demonstrated efficacy in experimental models of mitochondrial disease and muscle wasting by stimulating AMPK‐dependent pathways that augment mitochondrial biogenesis and restore energy balance (Green, 2013). Owing to its capacity to influence the phosphorylation of key enzymes and transcription factors, AICAR has found applications not only in elucidating fundamental bioenergetic pathways but also as a candidate to ameliorate conditions where energy homeostasis is disrupted. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, where the maintenance of tight junction integrity is crucial for barrier function and homeostasis, AICAR’s mechanism of action offers a rationale for its repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Historically, metabolic modulation via AMPK activators has been extensively investigated in various systems, and AICAR has been a workhorse agent in these studies owing to its reliable pharmacological profile (Pokrywka et al., 2014). Biochemically, AICAR has been widely used to stimulate AMPK in cell culture and animal models, resulting in a host of downstream effects that include enhanced fatty acid oxidation, increased glucose uptake, and modulated lipid synthesis (Green, 2013). In addition, AICAR’s ability to promote autophagy through the inhibition of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) cascade has been observed across various cell types, including those derived from retinal tissues (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Clinical investigations have predominantly focused on its metabolic effects in conditions such as diabetes and ischemia, although its application in ocular diseases has been comparatively less explored (Pokrywka et al., 2014). In the field of ophthalmology, research into the role of AMPK in retinal health has uncovered that AMPK activation influences key RPE functions including autophagy, inflammatory cytokine production, and tight junction integrity (Qin, 2012). Notably, investigations in RPE-related models have demonstrated that pharmacologic modulation of AMPK can either protect or impair barrier function, depending on the context and isoform engaged (Qin & De Vries, 2008). While AICAR itself has not been approved explicitly for the treatment of dry AMD, its well–established use in preclinical studies, combined with its demonstrated ability to rescue barrier integrity in RPE under oxidative stress conditions, supports its potential repurposing for this indication (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011). Thus, the accumulated literature demonstrates that AMPK activators, and AICAR in particular, offer promising mechanistic pathways to address cellular energy deficits and junctional disintegration, both critical features of dry AMD pathology (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which AICAR exerts its therapeutic effects begins with its cellular uptake through nucleoside transporters such as ENT1 and ENT2, a process that ensures its intracellular availability (Dolinar et al., 2018). Once internalized, AICAR is rapidly phosphorylated by adenosine kinase, converting it into 5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate (ZMP) (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). ZMP, as an AMP analog, binds to the γ subunit of AMPK, eliciting conformational changes that not only enhance its allosteric activation but also protect it from dephosphorylation (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). Concurrently, the binding of ZMP to AMPK facilitates the phosphorylation of the catalytic α‐subunit at Thr172, thereby augmenting the kinase’s catalytic activity to phosphorylate downstream targets such as acetyl‐CoA carboxylase (ACC) (Qin & De Vries, 2008). The phosphorylation and inactivation of ACC lead to decreased fatty acid synthesis and enhanced fatty acid oxidation, contributing significantly to improved energy homeostasis (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Green, 2013). Notably, in the retinal pigment epithelium, robust AMPK activation is implicated in the stabilization of tight junction proteins and in the promotion of autophagy, a process that is essential for removal of damaged organelles and protein aggregates under oxidative stress conditions (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Furthermore, the role of AICAR in modulating tight junction dynamics is complex and intersects with its influence on autophagic flux; AMPK activation can downregulate mTOR signaling, which not only contributes to increased autophagic clearance but also appears to correlate with improved organization of junctional proteins, ultimately enhancing transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). In experimental settings using RPE cells, the administration of AICAR under oxidative or high‐glucose stress conditions leads to a cascade of phosphorylation events that foster an environment conducive to tight junction assembly while simultaneously stabilizing cellular energy stores (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This biochemical cascade is further verified by the reversal of the observed effects upon the use of compound C, an AMPK inhibitor, which underscores the specificity of AICAR’s action being mediated through AMPK activation (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Villarroel et al., 2011).

It is also critical to note that the effects of AICAR on AMPK activity are influenced not only by its rapid intracellular conversion but also by the intrinsic cellular context—including the balance of energy substrates, the presence of other nucleosides, and the isoform‐specific roles of AMPK (Qin & De Vries, 2008). The resultant activation of AMPK leads to multifaceted downstream responses, such as cellular adaptation to metabolic stress, regulation of inflammatory mediators, and modulation of cytoskeletal elements that cooperate in the maintenance of cell–cell adhesion within the RPE monolayer (Villarroel et al., 2011). This detailed mechanistic insight provides the foundation for hypothesizing that AICAR may effectively drive energy homeostasis and promote tight junction assembly in RPE cells, addressing one of the core pathological features of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
In the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration, the primary pathological hallmark is the degeneration of the RPE accompanied by impaired tight junction integrity and compromised barrier function, resulting in increased paracellular permeability and accumulation of metabolic waste. Based on the observed effects of AICAR in in vitro RPE models, it is expected that AICAR will allosterically activate AMPK within RPE cells, leading to enhanced energy homeostasis and improved assembly of tight junctions (Hyttinen et al., 2011). Experimental data have demonstrated that when induced with oxidative stress, as is common in AMD, treatment with 500 µM AICAR increased TEER from 90 to 135 Ω·cm²—a clear indicator of enhanced barrier integrity (Miyagishima et al., 2021). This increase in TEER is paralleled by a 2.8‐fold elevation in phosphorylated AMPK levels, which confirms that AICAR is effectively engaging its intended target in these cells (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011).

The underlying mechanism for this improved barrier function is thought to be twofold. First, through ACC inhibition—mediated by AMPK activation—there is a shift in the cellular lipid economy, reducing the deleterious lipid accumulation that can disrupt tight junction architecture (Qin & De Vries, 2008). Second, the activation of autophagic pathways facilitates the clearance of oxidatively damaged proteins and organelles, thereby enhancing the overall health of the RPE and reinforcing its capacity to maintain tight junction complexes (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). This dual action not only addresses the immediate energetic deficit induced by oxidative stress but also contributes to the structural resilience of the RPE monolayer.

Moreover, the observed reversal of AICAR’s protective effects by compound C serves as strong evidence that the benefit is specifically mediated through the AMPK pathway rather than off‐target effects (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014). This mechanistic specificity is critical when evaluating a compound for clinical translation, as it suggests that downstream effects such as TEER enhancement, tight junction stabilization, and modulation of paracellular flux are directly attributable to AMPK activation. Additionally, AICAR‐mediated autophagy has been implicated in maintaining cellular integrity under chronic oxidative stress—a condition that is intrinsically linked to the progression of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011).

Given the central role of AMPK in RPE physiology, particularly in the regulation of junction protein stability and energy metabolism, the expected therapeutic effect of AICAR in dry AMD is to restore and preserve RPE barrier function. This restoration is anticipated to limit paracellular fluid leakage, reduce the deposition of extracellular debris, and ultimately slow the degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011). The projected outcome is an improvement in cellular homeostasis and reduced progression of retinal degeneration, which translates into a potential clinical benefit for patients with dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History and Prior Applications:  
AICAR’s journey from a metabolic intermediate to a pharmacologically active compound has been well documented across a range of biomedical research areas. In preclinical studies, AICAR has been extensively utilized to activate AMPK in various cellular models, thereby providing critical insights into the regulation of energy balance, mitochondrial biogenesis, and lipid metabolism (Green, 2013; Pokrywka et al., 2014). Its early applications in skeletal muscle and cancer cells underscored its ability to stimulate glucose uptake and shift cellular energy dynamics in favor of catabolic pathways (Dolinar et al., 2018; Longnus et al., 2003).

In cardiovascular research, AICAR was instrumental in elucidating the mechanisms underlying glycogenolysis and vasorelaxation, where its conversion to ZMP led to the activation of AMPK in vascular smooth muscle cells, resulting in beneficial metabolic adaptations (Pyla et al., 2022). Although these studies did not directly target ocular tissues, they established a robust framework for understanding how AMPK activation can mediate protective responses under conditions of metabolic stress.

The transition of AICAR into the realm of ophthalmological research was driven by the observation that AMPK is a pivotal regulator of RPE function and tight junction assembly. Publications have demonstrated that oxidative stress—a significant contributor to AMD pathology—can impair RPE barrier integrity by disrupting the organization of tight junction proteins, while AMPK activation appears to counteract these deleterious changes (Qin, 2012; Villarroel et al., 2011). In one study, treatment with AICAR in RPE cells under H₂O₂‐induced stress not only increased TEER but also elevated levels of phosphorylated AMPK, thereby indicating enhanced barrier stability (Miyagishima et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the dual role of AMPK in regulating autophagy and lipid metabolism has been a focal point in dry AMD research, as dysfunctional autophagy and lipid accumulation are hallmarks of RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011). The protective effects of AMPK activators in other models of cellular stress, such as in cardiomyocytes and hepatocarcinoma cells, lend additional support to the hypothesis that similar mechanisms may be beneficial in preserving RPE function (Kawashima et al., 2020; Sid et al., 2014).

Despite these promising findings, it is important to note that the therapeutic history of AICAR in the context of ocular diseases remains in the preclinical phase, with limited direct clinical evaluation for dry AMD. Some studies have even suggested that AMPK activation in the RPE could have dual outcomes, potentially inhibiting phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments under oxidative conditions (Qin & De Vries, 2008). This observation highlights the intricacies of AMPK signaling in retinal cells and underscores the need for rigorous dose–response and context–specific studies. Nonetheless, the accumulated preclinical data from both ocular and non‐ocular systems provide a strong rationale for further exploring AICAR as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

Expected Impact on RPE Function and Dry AMD Pathology:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of AICAR in dry AMD is that its ability to activate AMPK will lead to a concerted improvement in RPE barrier function and energy homeostasis—two crucial aspects compromised in AMD. In vitro models of RPE, particularly those derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC‐RPE), have shown that exposure to oxidative stress causes significant deterioration in tight junction assembly and barrier integrity, as measured by transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Miyagishima et al., 2021).

When these stressed RPE cells are treated with AICAR, a rapid increase in TEER from approximately 90 Ω·cm² to 135 Ω·cm² has been observed, indicating a substantial enhancement in tight junction integrity (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). At the molecular level, this improvement correlates with a 2.8‐fold rise in phosphorylated AMPK, which is directly associated with the activation of energy restoration pathways and the stabilization of tight junction proteins (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011).

The benefits conferred by AMPK activation are expected to be multifaceted. On one hand, the inhibition of ACC through phosphorylation is anticipated to reduce aberrant lipid synthesis and promote fatty acid oxidation, thereby alleviating metabolic stress within RPE cells (Qin & De Vries, 2008). On the other hand, enhanced autophagic flux driven by AMPK is likely to facilitate the removal of oxidatively damaged proteins and organelles, contributing to cellular repair processes that are pivotal in slowing the progression of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

These laboratory observations have practical implications. In a dysregulated retinal environment—characterized by oxidative damage, inflammatory cytokine presence, and disrupted tight junctions—the activation of AMPK by AICAR could serve as a countermeasure to re‐establish and maintain the critical barrier functions of the RPE (Villarroel et al., 2011). Moreover, by diminishing paracellular leak and preserving the integrity of junctional complexes, AICAR may reduce the accumulation of metabolic waste products and drusen, which are pathological hallmarks of dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

It is also noteworthy that the experimental reversal of AICAR’s protective effects by compound C—a well‐known AMPK inhibitor—provides definitive evidence that the beneficial outcomes observed in RPE cells are mediated specifically through AMPK signaling (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014). This on‐target specificity increases the confidence that the observed improvements in TEER are attributable to the intended mechanism rather than off‐target pharmacological actions. Consequently, the expected therapeutic effect in dry AMD would involve enhanced RPE cell viability, reduced cellular stress, and a restored barrier function that together could slow or even halt the progressive degeneration observed in patients (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

Overall Evaluation:  
When evaluating AICAR as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, several strengths are immediately apparent, along with a number of challenges that must be carefully addressed during further development. One of the foremost strengths of AICAR is its well–characterized mechanism of action. By serving as an AMP analog that is intracellularly converted to ZMP, AICAR robustly activates AMPK—a key cellular energy sensor that orchestrates a wide range of metabolic responses (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Green, 2013). This activation is tightly coupled to downstream effects such as ACC inhibition, enhanced fatty acid oxidation, and the promotion of autophagy, which are all beneficial in counteracting the metabolic and oxidative stresses inherent in dry AMD (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012).

Furthermore, the experimental data indicating a significant increase in TEER and a concomitant rise in phosphorylated AMPK levels in oxidatively stressed iPSC‐RPE cells provide compelling evidence that AICAR can restore RPE barrier function (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This is particularly important because tight junction integrity and paracellular barrier properties are central to the maintenance of retinal homeostasis and are critically impaired in dry AMD (Villarroel et al., 2011). The demonstration that the beneficial effects of AICAR are reversible by an AMPK inhibitor further reinforces the concept that the drug’s actions are on–target and biologically relevant (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Sid et al., 2014).

Nevertheless, several potential weaknesses require cautious evaluation. First, while AMPK activation is generally associated with enhanced cellular resilience, some studies have reported that excessive or isoform‐specific activation of AMPK in RPE cells may lead to unintended consequences, such as the inhibition of photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis—a process vital for retinal renewal (Qin & De Vries, 2008). Such a dualistic role of AMPK creates a delicate balance whereby the same pathway that is intended to improve barrier function might also impede essential RPE functions if not precisely modulated.

Additionally, the data in the literature suggest that under certain circumstances, AMPK activation might even contribute to increased epithelial permeability rather than a strengthening of tight junctions (Villarroel et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008). This paradoxical effect raises concerns about potential context–dependent outcomes of AICAR treatment. For example, while low‐to‐moderate activation of AMPK might support tight junction assembly and autophagy, hyperactivation under severe metabolic or oxidative stress could exacerbate junctional disorganization, thereby counteracting any beneficial effects (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Another challenge is the potential for systemic side effects arising from AICAR’s widespread actions in other tissues. Given that AICAR has been employed in models of diabetes, cardiac metabolism, and even cancer, its pleiotropic effects could impose additional safety considerations when repurposed for ocular use (Pokrywka et al., 2014; Viglino et al., 2019). There is also the issue of dosage; concentrations of 500 µM are effective in vitro, but translating such dosages to in vivo ocular applications requires careful pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies to ensure that therapeutic levels are achieved locally without eliciting undesirable systemic responses (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Asby et al., 2015).

Moreover, given the complex interplay between AMPK signaling, autophagy, and cellular differentiation processes, it is essential to thoroughly understand the long‐term implications of chronic AMPK activation in the RPE. While short‐term activation may be protective, persistent stimulation could lead to energy depletion or maladaptive remodeling of the RPE cytoskeleton, which in turn could affect visual function (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). This underscores the need for extensive preclinical studies that evaluate both the efficacy and the safety profile of AICAR over prolonged periods.

Finally, the inherent variability in patient responses due to genetic, metabolic, and environmental factors presents an additional hurdle. The RPE’s response to oxidative stress, and hence its sensitivity to AMPK modulation, may vary widely among individuals with dry AMD. It will be crucial to identify biomarkers that predict response to AICAR treatment and to tailor dosing regimens accordingly (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

In summary, while AICAR shows considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD by virtue of its well‐established mechanism of AMPK activation, experimental data demonstrating tight junction rescue in RPE cells, and its ability to promote autophagic processes that counteract oxidative stress, its repurposing is tempered by concerns regarding the dualistic effects of AMPK signaling in the RPE, potential systemic side effects, and the challenges associated with dosage translation from in vitro to in vivo applications (Villarroel et al., 2011). The overall evaluation is that AICAR exhibits several compelling advantages—including mechanistic clarity, on‐target efficacy, and a robust preclinical rationale—that substantiate further investigation through rigorous preclinical and, eventually, clinical studies. With a careful approach that addresses the aforementioned weaknesses, AICAR may ultimately emerge as a valuable addition to the therapeutic arsenal against dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012).

To fully validate AICAR’s potential for treating dry AMD, a series of detailed investigations is warranted. First, further elucidation of the dose–response relationship in RPE cell cultures will be critical. This includes not only establishing the optimal concentration of AICAR to achieve maximal TEER improvement and AMPK activation but also determining whether these effects are sustained over time without incurring cellular toxicity (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Hyttinen et al., 2011). Long‐term studies are needed to assess whether repeated dosing maintains barrier integrity or if adaptive processes eventually diminish the protective effects of AICAR.

Additionally, it will be necessary to delve deeper into the isoform‐specific effects of AMPK in the RPE. Evidence suggests that the α2 isoform in particular plays a critical role in mediating responses to oxidative stress and that its activation may differ qualitatively from that of the α1 subunit (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012). Understanding these nuances will help design therapeutic strategies that maximize the beneficial aspects of AMPK activation while minimizing potential adverse outcomes, such as impaired phagocytosis or unwanted alterations in cellular metabolism (Qin & De Vries, 2008).

In parallel, investigating the interplay between AICAR‐induced AMPK activation and autophagic pathways in the RPE will shed light on how tightly coupled these processes are in the context of dry AMD. Since autophagy is vital for clearing oxidatively damaged cellular components and supporting cell survival, it will be important to determine whether prolonged AMPK activation fosters a beneficial autophagic flux or rather leads to autophagy dysregulation over time (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012). Strategies that involve monitoring autophagic markers along with TEER measurements and junction protein expression could provide a comprehensive picture of cellular health in AICAR‐treated RPE cells.

Given the concerns regarding potential systemic effects, advanced drug delivery systems such as localized intraocular injections or biodegradable implants could be considered for delivering AICAR directly to the retina, thereby limiting systemic exposure and enhancing local efficacy (Viglino et al., 2019; Sid et al., 2014). Preclinical animal models that mimic the pathological features of dry AMD will be indispensable in evaluating the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and therapeutic windows of AICAR in an in vivo setting. Such studies would also be instrumental in identifying potential adverse effects and assessing the long‐term safety profile of AICAR when administered via ocular routes.

Another key consideration is the potential for combination therapy. Since some reports indicate that AMPK activation by AICAR might impair certain RPE functions such as phagocytosis if excessively activated, combining AICAR with other agents that either modulate AMPK isoform activity or protect against excessive autophagic stimulation may provide a synergistic benefit (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Villarroel et al., 2011). For instance, the protective effect of fenofibric acid in preventing AICAR‐induced permeability increases has been documented, suggesting that a combination approach may overcome the limitations of monotherapy (Villarroel et al., 2011).

These biomarkers could guide dose optimization and serve as early indicators of therapeutic response in clinical trials (Villarroel et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008). Genetic or epigenetic factors that predispose individuals to variations in RPE responsiveness may also be identified, thereby enabling personalized medicine approaches for patients with dry AMD.

In conclusion, while there remain numerous challenges and uncertainties, AICAR represents a highly promising candidate for repurposing as a barrier‐protective agent in dry AMD. Its capacity to robustly activate AMPK, improve cellular energy homeostasis, promote autophagy, and restore tight junction integrity in RPE cells offers a multifaceted mode of action that addresses several key pathological features of dry AMD. With targeted preclinical studies that unpack the complexity of AMPK signaling in retinal tissues and strategic clinical trial designs that mitigate potential adverse effects, AICAR could conceivably fill a significant therapeutic gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin, 2012; Villarroel et al., 2011).

AICAR’s well‐documented ability to mimic AMP—thereby inducing AMPK activation—and its established role in regulating cellular energy balance and autophagy place it squarely in the category of compounds with high therapeutic potential for metabolic disorders. Emerging evidence in retinal models, particularly those simulating the oxidative stress and barrier dysfunction typical of dry AMD, further reinforces the rationale behind its repurposing. Nonetheless, while preclinical data are encouraging, careful consideration must be given to the dualistic nature of AMPK signaling in the RPE, as well as the potential systemic risks associated with systemic exposure. Despite these challenges, the convergence of multiple lines of evidence—from improved TEER measurements and specific molecular activation to supportive mechanistic studies—strongly advocates for further research into AICAR as a viable therapeutic strategy for dry AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Villarroel et al., 2011).

In summary, the repurposing of AICAR for dry AMD is supported by both its robust mechanistic underpinnings and its promising preclinical efficacy data, placing it among the most attractive candidates for modulating RPE barrier integrity in this debilitating disease. Future studies that focus on fine‐tuning its dosage, delivery, and integrated combination therapies hold the key to unlocking its full therapeutic potential and advancing it from the bench to the clinic (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008; Qin, 2012).

Taking into account the strengths of its well‐defined mechanism, the reproducible experimental data demonstrating barrier rescue in RPE cells, and the feasibility of its pharmacological modulation, AICAR represents a compelling candidate for further development in the treatment of dry AMD. With continued advances in targeted drug delivery and combination therapeutics, the prospects for leveraging AICAR’s metabolic and protective effects in the retina are promising, warranting its inclusion in the strategic pipeline for combating age‐related macular degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Qin & De Vries, 2008).

Its capacity to restore RPE barrier integrity under oxidative stress, coupled with its well‐established pharmacodynamic properties, offers a therapeutic strategy that could mitigate the progression of retinal degeneration and improve visual outcomes for patients suffering from this currently untreatable condition (Villarroel et al., 2011).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Danicopan, also known as ACH-4471 and by its commercial identifier MedChemExpress HY-19909, is a novel small-molecule agent designed to target complement factor D. It belongs to a growing class of low-molecular-weight inhibitors that are specifically aimed at interfering with the alternative pathway (AP) of the complement system. This class of compounds is characterized by their capacity to modulate complement activation rather than broadly suppress the entire immune system. Danicopan was originally developed as a first-in-class molecule to selectively block factor D, which is the rate-limiting enzyme in the AP and is intimately involved in the formation of the C3 convertase complex (Boyer et al., 2022). The chemical structure of Danicopan incorporates a proline core with added moieties such as amino bromo pyridine and azaindole, a configuration designed to ensure both high potency and selectivity in factor D inhibition (Schubart et al., 2023). The oral bioavailability of Danicopan, combined with its capacity to achieve sustained exposure in ocular tissues due in part to melanin binding in pigmented tissues, underscores its appeal for diseases where local complement modulation is desired without the need for invasive delivery routes (Boyer et al., 2022). Notably, the design approach for Danicopan focuses on blocking the enzymatic activation loop that precipitates complement amplification—a mechanism that is particularly deleterious in tissues such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Boyer et al., 2022).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the use of complement inhibitors has been a promising therapeutic strategy across several complement-mediated disorders. Danicopan was initially evaluated in the context of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), a condition driven by unregulated complement activation that results in hemolysis and thrombosis. Early clinical studies in patients with PNH revealed that oral administration of Danicopan rapidly inhibited the alternative pathway, resulting in significantly reduced hemolysis with concomitant improvements in hematological parameters (Schubart et al., 2023). This clinical success in PNH has spurred the interest in repurposing Danicopan for ocular indications, notably for dry AMD—a condition where dysfunctional complement activation plays a central role in the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy (GA). Although Danicopan’s application in dry AMD is still under investigation, the rationale for its use stems from preclinical models demonstrating high and sustained ocular tissue levels after oral dosing, especially in regions enriched with melanin (Boyer et al., 2022). Furthermore, the candidate has entered a Phase 2 clinical trial focusing on GA AMD, with the study design aimed at assessing its safety, efficacy, and pharmacokinetic profile in a population of 330 participants (Fabre et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2024). Importantly, while previous complement inhibitors such as Lampalizumab have been evaluated in AMD—with mixed outcomes—Danicopan’s novel oral dosing profile and improved tissue selectivity underscore its potential advantage over earlier modalities (Tang et al., 2024; Schubart et al., 2023).  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Danicopan acts by binding to complement factor D with high affinity, thereby inhibiting its serine protease activity. Factor D is indispensable for the cleavage of factor B and the subsequent assembly of the C3 convertase (C3bBb) on the cell surface, which is the amplification step critical for the alternative complement pathway (Boyer et al., 2022). Inhibition of factor D effectively halts the formation of the AP C3 convertase, thereby preventing the cleavage of C3 into its active fragments, C3a and C3b. This downstream effect is crucial because the deposition of C3b—or its inactivated form iC3b—on the RPE surfaces is implicated in complement-driven inflammation and subsequent cellular damage (Fabre et al., 2022). In addition, by attenuating the production of C3a, Danicopan helps mitigate the recruitment and activation of inflammatory effector cells in the retinal microenvironment (Wilke & Apte, 2024; Schubart et al., 2023). The selectivity of Danicopan for factor D not only reduces the biochemistry of the AP cascade but also limits the risk of compromising the classical and lectin pathways, which remain critical for host defense. This selective inhibition is biochemically significant, as the tight regulation of complement is essential for maintaining immune surveillance and tissue homeostasis (Boyer et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). The reported inhibitory concentration (IC₅₀) values for Danicopan have been reported in various contexts, with figures around 5.8 nM in some studies and as low as 2 nM as hypothesized in the current proposal, underscoring its potent inhibitory capacity (Fabre et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). On a cellular level, the blockade of factor D is expected to prevent the formation of the C3 convertase on RPE cells, which in turn would reduce the deposition of complement fragments like C3b and iC3b on the surface of these cells. This is particularly important since the complement-mediated deposition on RPE cells can disrupt the distribution and localization of tight junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and occludin, which are critical for preserving RPE barrier integrity and function (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022). The evaluation of Danicopan as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration reveals several compelling strengths balanced by certain challenges that warrant further investigation. One of the most significant strengths of Danicopan lies in its potent, selective inhibition of factor D—a critical enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. By targeting factor D, Danicopan disrupts the amplification loop that drives the deposition of complement fragments such as C3b and iC3b on the RPE surface. Moreover, the oral bioavailability of Danicopan represents a significant advantage. Unlike intravitreal injections—which are invasive and carry risks such as endophthalmitis—oral administration could improve patient adherence and facilitate chronic treatment regimens required for a progressive disease such as dry AMD (Boyer et al., 2022). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ripasudil, also known by its research designation Y-39983 and commercially available as Selleckchem S8443, is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor developed originally as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil containing protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. It belongs to a class of therapeutics that act in an ATP‐competitive manner to inhibit the activity of ROCK isoforms, enzymes that are critical regulators of actomyosin contractility and cell adhesion. Ripasudil was synthesized following the structural optimization of earlier compounds such as fasudil and Y-27632, with the aim of increasing both potency and ocular tolerability. Its chemical origins are linked to the rational design strategies that sought to improve enzyme inhibitory selectivity and to enhance the pharmacokinetic profile for local ocular application. Members of the ROCK inhibitor class have seen prior use in settings that require modulation of actin cytoskeleton dynamics, such as the treatment of glaucoma via enhanced aqueous humor outflow, and have also been explored in contexts involving wound healing and anti-fibrotic effects in various ocular tissues (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, ripasudil has been approved in Japan for the treatment of glaucoma and ocular hypertension, where it is delivered topically in the form of eye drops, demonstrating a well-established safety profile and a low incidence of systemic adverse effects. In preclinical models, it has demonstrated efficacy by increasing ocular blood flow, modifying trabecular meshwork cell contractility, and reducing intraocular pressure, thereby serving as a stepping stone and proof-of-concept for the utility of ROCK inhibitors in ocular disorders. Beyond its approved use in glaucoma, investigations of ROCK inhibitors—including ripasudil—have extended into experimental applications in corneal endothelial regeneration and have been evaluated in combination with anti-VEGF therapies for diabetic macular edema. Although direct clinical evidence specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is not available, multiple lines of preclinical research have shown that the ROCK inhibitor class modulates pathways which are believed to underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Notably, the mechanistic studies have identified the role of ROCK signaling in cytoskeletal reorganization, matrix contractility, and fibrosis, all of which are processes particularly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier dysfunction seen in dry AMD (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Moreover, the ocular pharmacokinetic profile of ripasudil—demonstrated by rabbit intravitreal studies showing a half-life of approximately 14 hours and negligible systemic exposure—is supportive of repurposing this candidate for posterior segment indications, including dry AMD (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ripasudil exerts its therapeutic activity by competitively inhibiting the ATP-binding site of ROCK isoforms, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of downstream effectors such as myosin light-chain (MLC), myosin-binding subunit of MLC phosphatase (MYPT1), and LIM kinase. These phosphorylation events normally lead to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, focal adhesion assembly, and ultimately contribute to a contractile, stiffened cell phenotype. In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, this contractility is thought to be exacerbated under conditions of oxidative stress, contributing to disassembly or mislocalization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity. By inhibiting ROCK, ripasudil reduces actomyosin-driven contraction and stress-fiber formation, thereby promoting cortical F-actin remodeling and facilitating the proper membrane relocalization of tight-junction proteins. The specificity of ripasudil has been demonstrated by its greater than 100-fold selectivity against other kinases such as protein kinase C (PKC) and myotonic dystrophy kinase-related Cdc42-binding kinase (MRCK), highlighting the mechanistic precision by which it modulates ROCK-dependent signaling cascades (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Additionally, while several studies indicate that the ROCK inhibitor class generally targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2 isoforms, quantitative biochemical data have shown that ripasudil exhibits potent enzyme inhibitory activity with IC₅₀s in the low nanomolar range (with values reported around 51 nM for ROCK1 and 19 nM for ROCK2 in some studies, though the candidate hypothesis posits values of approximately 29 nM for ROCK1 and 68 nM for ROCK2). Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing ripasudil for dry AMD is that by blocking ROCK activity in oxidatively stressed retinal pigment epithelium cells, the compound will lead to a reduction in actomyosin contractility, thereby alleviating the formation of pathological stress fibers that otherwise disrupt the organization of tight junction complexes. A primary limitation is the paucity of direct experimental evidence in RPE models of dry AMD. Furthermore, although the compound’s ROCK inhibitory activity is well documented, the available literature does not consistently detail the isoform-specific effects in RPE cells; given that ROCK1 and ROCK2 may play distinct roles in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, clarifying the relative contributions of each isoform is essential. Innovative delivery systems, such as sustained-release intravitreal implants or depot formulations, may offer solutions but require further development (Yamaguchi et al., 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023).

CHIR99021 is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor originally identified as a highly potent and selective inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3β) with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (~10 nM). This compound belongs to a class of therapeutic candidates generally employed in stem cell differentiation protocols, where its ability to stabilize β-catenin and drive the transcription of Wnt target genes has been extensively validated in various cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) derived from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Leach et al., 2015). As such, CHIR99021 has been foundational in protocols that aim to drive RPE fate by activating canonical Wnt signaling, thereby demonstrating its utility in manipulating epithelial differentiation pathways.

Therapeutic History:  
The majority of available evidence for CHIR99021’s use comes from in vitro studies and preclinical differentiation protocols rather than clinical applications. Multiple studies have shown that when added during defined differentiation windows (for example, from day 8 to 14 of an hESC-to-RPE protocol), CHIR99021 significantly increases the yield and functional maturation of RPE cells. These studies report that CHIR99021-treated differentiations yield improved epithelial morphology, enhanced pigmentation, and robust expression of RPE lineage markers—including MITF, OTX2, and even tight-junction-associated proteins such as ZO-1 (Leach et al., 2015). In parallel, other reports have documented that upregulation of canonical Wnt signaling through CHIR99021 leads to increased expression of pigmentation genes (TYR, TYRP2, and PMEL17) and the RPE functional secretory factor PEDF. However, it is important to note that despite promising results in differentiation assays, the use of CHIR99021 for direct therapeutic intervention in dry AMD is not well documented. Moreover, in an in vitro macula-sized RPE wound-repair model designed to mimic geographic atrophy, CHIR99021 treatment hindered wound repair instead of enhancing barrier restoration (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). These seemingly contradictory findings illustrate that while CHIR99021 robustly enhances RPE differentiation from stem cells, its effects in mature or stress-challenged RPE may be context-dependent. Overall, the preclinical history establishes CHIR99021 as a well-characterized research compound with proven biochemical activity in activating Wnt/β-catenin signaling, but there is limited evidence regarding its therapeutic application in treating dry AMD or related RPE barrier dysfunction in vivo (Yang et al., 2018; Hottin et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
CHIR99021 exerts its biological effects by inhibiting GSK-3β through competitive binding at the protein’s ATP site, thereby preventing GSK-3β from phosphorylating its substrates. One of the principal consequences of GSK-3β inhibition is the stabilization of β-catenin. Under normal conditions, GSK-3β phosphorylates β-catenin, marking it for proteasomal degradation. CHIR99021 presents several notable strengths as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. As such, while the candidate has mechanistic appeal and a robust preclinical track record in RPE differentiation, its application for barrier restoration in dry AMD remains speculative at this stage, and further investigation—including dose optimization studies, TEER/permeability assays in oxidative stress models, and eventually in vivo preclinical evaluations—is warranted before advancing CHIR99021 into clinical trials for this indication.

Overall, our evaluation concludes that CHIR99021 shows potential based on its selectivity and mechanistic rationale but that significant uncertainties remain regarding its efficacy in restoring barrier function in the context of dry AMD. The direction for future research must focus on rigorous validation of barrier parameters (including claudin-1, occludin, TEER, and permeability assays) in models that closely recapitulate the oxidative and inflammatory milieu of dry AMD before considering CHIR99021 as a viable drug candidate for clinical repurposing (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

This comprehensive review therefore supports a cautious approach: while CHIR99021 possesses attractive biochemical and mechanistic properties that justify its rapid evaluation in preclinical ocular models, its repurposing for dry AMD will require additional data specifically addressing RPE barrier function under oxidative stress. Further targeted studies are essential to resolve the context-dependent effects observed in vitro and to determine if optimal dosing and timing regimens can overcome the negative outcomes seen in wound-repair assays. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
H-151 is a small-molecule antagonist of the innate immune adaptor STING (TMEM173) that was developed as part of a chemical class designed to prevent the palmitoylation-dependent activation of STING at the Golgi following cyclic dinucleotide binding and ER-to-Golgi trafficking (i.e., cGAMP-bound STING oligomerization and signalosome assembly) (Decout et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). In its mechanistic class, H-151 is grouped with covalent STING inhibitors that target Cys91 within the transmembrane region–proximal cytosolic interface, thereby preventing activation-induced palmitoylation at Cys88/Cys91 and downstream signaling; nitrofuran analogs such as C-176 and C-178 are the canonical examples where Cys91-directed covalent modification has been mapped by probe chemistry and mass spectrometry (with consequent suppression of type I interferon and IL-6 in vivo) (Decout et al., 2021). STING activation is known to require ligand-induced conformational change, ER exit, and palmitoylation on Cys88/Cys91 to drive oligomerization/polymerization and recruitment of TBK1 and other signal transducers; antagonists that block this palmitoylation step are therefore positioned to broadly prevent both IRF3-dependent type I interferon and NF-κB–dependent inflammatory outputs (Li et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2021).

H-151 has been characterized in inflammatory disease models as a low molecular weight, irreversible inhibitor of human and mouse STING that blocks activation-induced palmitoylation and attenuates downstream signaling (with primary mechanistic references tracing to the discovery work summarized by Pan et al. and by Decout et al.) (Pan et al., 2021; Decout et al., 2021). In keratinocyte and immune-cell systems relevant to psoriatic inflammation, H-151 has reproducibly suppressed STING-dependent NF-κB and IRF3 phosphorylation, inhibited proinflammatory cytokine mRNA induction (e.g., IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α), and reduced STING protein levels, consistent with an antagonist mechanism upstream of canonical downstream effectors (Pan et al., 2021). Conceptually, H-151 belongs to the broader class of cGAS–STING pathway modulators that have been deployed to suppress sterile inflammation across multiple tissues; for the eye and retina, related pathway inhibitors (e.g., C-176, SN-011, cryptotanshinone) have shown efficacy in ischemic and neovascular models via suppression of microglial STING signaling and cytokine/chemokine/protease outputs, supporting the translatability of STING antagonism to ocular tissues (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
There is no reported clinical use of H-151 in humans, and no published veterinary or clinical trials in ophthalmology were identified in the provided literature set; H-151 has been used as a research tool compound in preclinical inflammatory models, most prominently in psoriasis, where it decreased lesion severity and cutaneous inflammatory readouts in the imiquimod model (Pan et al., 2021). In psoriasis-relevant cell systems, H-151 suppressed cGAMP-induced IRF3 and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and reduced IFN-β, IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α expression, consistent with on-pathway inhibition of STING and its downstream transcriptional programs (Pan et al., 2021). In vivo, topical H-151 improved psoriasis-like dermatitis and decreased markers linked to STING/NF-κB signaling, again without human clinical translation to date (Pan et al., 2021).

Ocular/retinal precedent for the STING target is strong even if H-151–specific data are sparse. In multiple retinal contexts, activation of cGAS–STING has been implicated in pathogenesis through DNA-damage and mitochondrial DNA leakage, leading to IRF3/NF-κB activation, SASP-like cytokine induction, angiogenesis, and barrier dysfunction (Hu et al., 2023). Genetic and pharmacologic pathway perturbations show benefit: genetic loss of STING limits endothelial senescence and vascular degeneration in diabetic models (Liu et al., 2023), genetic deletion along the cGAS–STING axis rescues Alu DNA–driven RPE toxicity (implicated in geographic atrophy) (Hu et al., 2023), and pharmacologic STING inhibitors (C-176, SN-011) suppress neovascularization in laser CNV and OIR models (Ni et al., 2024). Importantly for RPE biology, senescent ARPE-19 cells were reported to overproduce VEGF and this overproduction was prevented by H-151, providing a direct albeit single-study line of evidence that H-151 can modulate pathogenic angiogenic/SASP output in an RPE-derived cell line (Hu et al., 2023). Beyond H-151, epigenetic suppression of STING (JQ1), PPARα activation, and visual cycle modulation (reducing toxic retinoid stress) each attenuate cGAS–STING activation and downstream inflammation or degeneration, underscoring the therapeutic appeal of targeting this axis in retinal disease (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
STING biology and the palmitoylation node. STING is a homodimeric ER-resident adaptor with an N-terminal multi-pass transmembrane domain and a cytosolic C-terminal ligand-binding domain; binding of 2’3’-cGAMP (produced by cGAS upon sensing cytosolic dsDNA) induces conformational rearrangements that enable ER exit and trafficking to the Golgi, where palmitoylation of Cys88 and Cys91 is critical for higher-order assembly and recruitment of TBK1 and other signaling proteins (Li et al., 2021). Palmitoylation-driven tetramerization/higher-order oligomerization is a central activation step for STING, and mutational or pharmacologic interference with Cys88/Cys91 palmitoylation abrogates downstream signal propagation (Pan et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). Activated STING scaffolds TBK1 to phosphorylate IRF3 (e.g., at Ser366), triggering type I interferon gene expression, and engages NF-κB to induce a broad proinflammatory transcriptional program, including SASP components (Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2021). In retinal disease contexts, cGAS–STING activation (driven by nuclear/mtDNA release or Alu-derived nucleic acids) is linked to up-regulation of VEGF via NF-κB/HIF-1α in oxidative-stress–induced RPE senescence, endothelial and microglial inflammatory activation, and barrier compromise (Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025).

Rationale in retinal cells and tissue. cGAS and STING are expressed across retinal cell types (RPE, microglia, endothelial cells, Müller glia, photoreceptors) and are upregulated in disease states (AMD/DR), with promoter accessibility and mRNA levels increased in diseased tissue, positioning the pathway as targetable across multiple ocular compartments (Hu et al., 2023). STING deficiency can increase susceptibility to tumorigenesis and reduce vaccine responses, and human STING haplotypes (e.g., HAQ) show variable responsiveness to cyclic dinucleotides, implying potential population variability in pathway dependence and therapeutic response (Hu et al., 2023). - In vitro RPE assays. Move to sodium iodate or oxidant-driven RPE injury models and to Alu DNA–induced RPE degeneration to test whether H-151 reduces cGAS–STING activation, NF-κB signaling, cytokines/MMPs, and preserves RPE morphology; positive controls include JQ1 and C-176, which have shown efficacy in related contexts (Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024). On balance, H-151 is a mechanistically compelling, tractable small-molecule inhibitor that targets a validated inflammatory/senescence axis in retinal disease, with one direct RPE line of evidence (suppression of VEGF in senescent ARPE-19) and robust non-ocular and ocular-pathway support via related tools and genetic models (Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023).
