Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
5‐Azacytidine is a synthetically produced nucleoside analogue of cytidine originally derived by chemical modification of the natural ribonucleoside. In 5‐azacytidine the normal carbon atom at the 5‐position of the pyrimidine ring is replaced with a nitrogen atom, a modification that critically alters its biochemical properties. This compound is classified as an azanucleoside and has been widely studied as a DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) inhibitor. Its discovery and subsequent synthesis have enabled researchers to interrogate the role of DNA methylation in gene regulation. In its typical biological usage, after cellular uptake mediated by nucleoside transporters, 5‐azacytidine is phosphorylated by cellular kinases into its active triphosphate form (5‐aza‐CTP) and can become incorporated into RNA as well as into DNA, although only around 10–20% is converted to the deoxyribonucleotide form prior to DNA incorporation. This unique feature is a double‐edged sword: on one hand, it allows modulation of cytosine methylation patterns within genomic DNA by trapping DNMTs; on the other, its incorporation into RNA can perturb protein synthesis and contributes to its cytotoxic profile. Chemically, its structure and mode of synthesis place it within a well‐characterized class of antimetabolite agents whose utility extends beyond oncology into other fields where epigenetic modifications are implicated (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, 5‐azacytidine and its deoxy analogue 5‐aza‐2′‐deoxycytidine (decitabine) were first developed as antimetabolite chemotherapy agents for hematologic malignancies. Their clinical utility in treating conditions such as myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) is well established, with DNA demethylation and tumor suppressor gene reactivation being central to their antineoplastic efficacy. Over the years, the successful repurposing of these nucleoside analogues has led to extensive studies investigating their potential effects beyond oncology. In cancer cells, the irreversible binding of DNMT enzymes to DNA following incorporation of 5‐azacytidine has been shown to produce passive demethylation during cell division and consequent gene reactivation (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). In more recent years, researchers have begun to consider the roles of aberrant DNA methylation in non‐cancer diseases, including ocular pathologies like age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). Reviews in ocular epigenetics have noted that epigenetic dysregulation, including hypermethylation of promoters for antioxidant enzymes and other protective genes, may contribute to RPE dysfunction in AMD (Li et al., 2020). For instance, studies in cultured RPE cells and AMD cybrid models have observed tolerability of DNMT inhibitors, as exemplified by experiments where polarized RPE monolayers treated with 5‐aza‐2′‐deoxycytidine showed no significant disruption in barrier markers such as ZO‐1 or cytokeratin, and even demonstrated gene reactivation effects such as upregulation of clusterin (Li et al., 2020). Although 5‐azacytidine itself has not been as widely evaluated in ocular models as decitabine, the extensive biochemical literature surrounding its DNMT inhibitory properties forms a strong rationale for its potential repurposing toward dry AMD via epigenetic modulation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, 5‐azacytidine exerts its pharmacologic actions primarily through inhibition of DNMT enzymes. Under normal physiological conditions, DNMT enzymes bind to cytosine residues in CpG dinucleotides and catalyze the transfer of a methyl group from S‐adenosyl-L‐methionine (SAM) to the 5‐position carbon of cytosine, a process that is essential for the maintenance of epigenetic patterns and gene silencing. However, the substitution of nitrogen at the C5 position in 5‐azacytidine disrupts this process because the reaction mechanism relies on a β‐elimination step that cannot occur when a nitrogen is present instead of a carbon. Consequently, when 5‐azacytidine is incorporated into the DNA of replicating cells, DNMT enzymes – particularly the maintenance methyltransferase DNMT1 – are unable to complete the methylation reaction and become covalently trapped at the site of incorporation (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). This irreversible trapping inhibits the recycling of DNMTs and leads to their proteasomal degradation, thus reducing the cellular pool of active DNMT enzymes. In subsequent rounds of DNA replication, the absence of sufficient DNMT activity results in passive demethylation of newly synthesized DNA strands that fail to be remethylated. This epigenetic reprogramming can lead to reactivation of genes with previously hypermethylated and silenced promoters (Cheishvili et al., 2015; Palii et al., 2008). It is important to note that 5‐azacytidine is also incorporated into RNA, where it may inhibit RNA methylation and alter translation; however, the therapeutic emphasis in the context of reactivating silenced genes typically focuses on its DNA‐mediated effects. In the specific context of the proposed therapeutic strategy, oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is hypothesized to promote the aberrant recruitment of DNMT1 and DNMT3A to the promoters of tight junction genes such as OCLN and TJP1, thereby silencing them via hypermethylation. The administration of 5‐azacytidine is expected to reverse this process by demethylating these promoter regions through the above‐described DNMT trapping mechanism, ultimately leading to the reactivation of occludin and ZO‐1 expression (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014; Mukhtar, 2020). Although the majority of experimental evidence in the literature focuses on gene reactivation in oncologic contexts, the fundamental biochemical interactions remain the same in any dividing cell type where DNA replication permits incorporation of the analogue. Additionally, although RPE cells in vivo are relatively quiescent compared to rapidly dividing cancer cells, in vitro models such as ARPE-19, particularly under oxidative challenge, can exhibit increased proliferation and epigenetic plasticity, thereby providing an opportunity to evaluate the mechanism in the context of barrier dysfunction (Li et al., 2020; Sarkisjan et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis of the proposed therapeutic strategy is that under conditions of oxidative stress, DNMT enzymes are aberrantly recruited to the promoters of genes critical for tight junction integrity – specifically occludin (OCLN) and ZO-1 (TJP1) – resulting in their hypermethylation and subsequent transcriptional repression. This diminished expression of tight junction proteins compromises the barrier function of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), leading to decreased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased FITC-dextran permeability. It is expected that a treatment with 1 µM 5‐azacytidine will inhibit DNMT activity in these stressed RPE cells, specifically by demethylating the promoters of OCLN and TJP1. As the promoter regions are demethylated, transcription of OCLN and TJP1 is anticipated to resume, thereby restoring the synthesis and proper cellular localization of occludin and the ZO-1 protein. This re-expression is predicted to facilitate the re‐assembly of tight junction complexes at the plasma membrane of RPE cells, culminating in a recovery of barrier properties measurable as an increase in TEER and a reduction in paracellular permeability as evidenced by decreased FITC-dextran flux (Christman, 2002; Palii et al., 2008; Li et al., 2020). There is supporting evidence in related experimental studies wherein treatment of polarized RPE monolayers with DNMT inhibitors—albeit using 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine in some cases—did not disturb baseline tight junction markers such as ZO-1 and cytokeratin, and even induced the expression of epigenetically silenced protective genes like clusterin (Li et al., 2020). Although direct demonstration of OCLN and TJP1 promoter demethylation by 5‐azacytidine in RPE under oxidative stress is not yet available, analogous results in other epithelial contexts provide a strong mechanistic rationale. Moreover, the dual activity of the drug – both its canonical demethylating effect and its potential to perturb RNA methylation – may synergize to enhance transcriptional reactivation if balanced appropriately with a low, non‐cytotoxic concentration such as 1 µM (Seelan et al., 2018; Cheishvili et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
The prospect of repurposing 5‐azacytidine for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) represents a novel and intriguing approach that leverages well‐established principles in epigenetic regulation. On the strength side, the compound’s mechanism of action is thoroughly documented across multiple biomedical studies and is centered on the irreversible trapping and degradation of DNMT enzymes, leading to passive loss of DNA methylation in replicating cells (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). This mechanism has been exploited with success in oncology to reactivate silenced tumor suppressor genes, suggesting that similar reactivation of critical genes in non‐cancerous cells might also be achievable. The specific hypothesis that oxidative stress in RPE leads to the epigenetic silencing of tight junction genes such as OCLN and TJP1 is plausible given the known role of DNMT enzymes in mediating gene repression under stress conditions, and the literature supports the concept that DNA methylation is a dynamic and reversible process that can be modulated pharmacologically (Li et al., 2020). Preliminary in vitro findings in RPE monolayer models with DNMT inhibitors, particularly the tolerability of these compounds and their capacity to upregulate epigenetically silenced genes (as seen with clusterin expression), bolster the argument that DNMT inhibition in RPE is not inherently deleterious and may indeed rectify dysfunction in barrier integrity (Li et al., 2020).

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be recognized. First, 5‐azacytidine is known to incorporate into RNA as well as DNA, which introduces additional layers of complexity in its mode of action. The off‐target effects on RNA methylation can lead to perturbations in protein synthesis and may result in unintended consequences, especially given the highly specialized function of RPE cells in the retina (Jasielec et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2010). Second, the S-phase dependency of the drug’s mechanism—requiring active DNA replication for incorporation—poses a potential limitation when considering that in vivo RPE cells are largely quiescent. While in vitro ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress may show increased proliferative activity, the translation of these findings to an in vivo dry AMD setting remains uncertain. Third, the global demethylation induced by 5‐azacytidine does not confer gene specificity; hence, there is a risk that while reactivating tight junction genes, the drug might also inadvertently activate promoters of deleterious genes or provoke inflammatory responses. This lack of precision could compromise retinal homeostasis or even exacerbate pathological processes if not carefully controlled (Mukhtar, 2020; Cheishvili et al., 2015). Fourth, toxicity is a major concern. While lower doses (such as 1 µM) are proposed to achieve a favorable balance between hypomethylation and cytotoxicity, the narrow therapeutic window observed in oncology suggests that careful titration and extensive in vitro and in vivo safety studies are essential before progressing to clinical evaluation in AMD (Christman, 2002; Daifuku, 2025).

Additional challenges include the need for direct experimental evidence to support the specific hypothesis relating to tight junction reactivation. Although the general effects of DNMT inhibitors in reactivating silenced genes are well documented, there is currently insufficient evidence demonstrating that 5-azacytidine directly demethylates the promoters of OCLN and TJP1 in RPE cells subjected to oxidative stress. Moreover, evaluations of barrier function—such as detailed TEER measurements or FITC-dextran permeability assays—have been more commonly reported in the context of other DNMT inhibitors such as 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine rather than 5-azacytidine per se (Li et al., 2020). Therefore, a critical gap remains in validating whether the proposed epigenetic precision approach can indeed restore tight junction integrity in a physiologically relevant model of dry AMD.

Despite these concerns, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. The robust and well‐understood mechanism of 5‐azacytidine in inducing DNA demethylation provides a solid theoretical basis for the proposed therapeutic strategy. Given that similar epigenetic interventions have successfully reactivated gene expression in other cellular contexts, and considering that preliminary data in RPE systems suggest tolerability and potential gene reactivation, it is reasonable to propose that further investigation is warranted. Initial preclinical studies should focus on establishing the methylation status of the OCLN and TJP1 promoters in RPE cells under oxidative stress and then determine whether 5‐azacytidine treatment can effectively reverse these modifications. Comprehensive analyses including methylation-specific polymerase chain reaction (MSP), chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays for DNMT occupancy, and detailed transcriptional profiling would be essential to confirm target engagement. Parallel functional assays, such as TEER measurements and FITC-dextran permeability assays, must be undertaken to correlate molecular events with phenotypic restoration of barrier function (Mukhtar, 2020; Daifuku, 2025).

In addition, it would be prudent to perform dose–response studies to delineate the optimal concentration of 5‐azacytidine that maximizes promoter demethylation and gene reactivation while minimizing off-target cytotoxicity. Considering that RPE cells in vitro may exhibit different proliferative rates compared to their in vivo counterparts, alternative experimental models, such as induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells from AMD patients, may provide additional insights into the therapeutic window and efficacy of 5‐azacytidine in a clinically relevant context. Finally, given that the global nature of epigenetic reprogramming may lead to unintended activation of other cellular pathways, combination strategies employing lower doses of 5‐azacytidine alongside more targeted epigenetic modulators—such as selective HDAC inhibitors—could be explored to enhance the specificity of gene reactivation and improve overall retinal safety (Li et al., 2020; Nashine & Kenney, 2020).

In summary, 5‐azacytidine represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD through a novel epigenetic precision approach aimed at reversing the aberrant methylation of tight junction gene promoters. Its well‐characterized mechanism of DNMT inhibition and widespread use in oncology offer a strong biological rationale. However, significant challenges remain, including its non‐selective incorporation into nucleic acids, potential off‐target effects, reliance on cellular proliferation for optimal activity, and a narrow therapeutic index that necessitates rigorous dose optimization. The feasibility of restoring tight junction integrity in RPE cells via demethylation of OCLN and TJP1 promoters is theoretically sound yet awaits empirical confirmation in preclinical AMD models. Overall, while the candidate has substantial mechanistic strengths that support its potential role in restoring RPE barrier function under oxidative stress conditions, its development as a treatment for dry AMD will require detailed molecular and functional validations, careful safety profiling, and perhaps the exploration of combination therapies to harness its benefits while mitigating risks (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020; Daifuku, 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bexarotene is a fully synthetic retinoid analog classified as a rexinoid, specifically acting as a pan–retinoid X receptor (RXR) agonist. It was originally developed through structure–activity relationship studies aimed at mimicking the natural ligand 9-cis retinoic acid, while providing greater receptor selectivity, improved potency, and a pharmacological profile amenable to therapeutic use. Its synthesis and subsequent discovery were driven by the need to harness RXR‐mediated gene regulation, and it subsequently became the only FDA-approved synthetic RXR ligand to date (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). As a member of the retinoid drug class, bexarotene has been primarily used in the oncological setting, specifically for the treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, and its chemical design reflects modifications that impart high lipophilicity and receptor specificity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018). This synthetic derivation distinguishes it from naturally occurring retinoids and underpins its utility across a number of experimental and clinical contexts.

Therapeutic History:  
Bexarotene’s clinical history is marked by its approval as a second-line therapy for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, which provided a strong basis for its safety and efficacy in a human disease setting (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). In addition to its primary use in oncology, preclinical and early clinical research has investigated bexarotene for applications in neurodegenerative diseases, most notably Alzheimer’s disease and multiple sclerosis. These studies have demonstrated that RXR activation by bexarotene can influence the clearance of pathological protein aggregates and promote remyelination, respectively (Gaunt, 2020; Behl et al., 2022). However, despite the broad mechanistic appeal of RXR agonism in modifying lipid metabolism and neuroinflammation, there is little to no established clinical or veterinary precedent for employing bexarotene in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative conditions. In fact, while several RXR agonists have been considered in various models of ocular disease, the role of RXR in the diseased retina remains underexplored, with only sparse reports such as a study with the RXR agonist PA024 in retinal degeneration models (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). This gap in therapeutic history presents both a challenge and an opportunity in repurposing bexarotene for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
Bexarotene exerts its pharmacological effects primarily by binding to the ligand-binding domain of RXR isoforms (RXRα, RXRβ, and RXRγ) with nanomolar potency, inducing conformational changes that favor the recruitment of coactivators and subsequent transcriptional activation of targeted genes (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). RXR is a promiscuous nuclear receptor that forms obligate heterodimers with several other nuclear receptors, most notably the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) such as PPARγ. In doing so, the bexarotene-induced RXR/PPARγ heterodimer binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the genome, thereby upregulating target genes involved in lipid metabolism and transport. One key target is ABCA1, an ATP-binding cassette transporter implicated in cholesterol efflux from cells, which plays a central role in maintaining intracellular lipid homeostasis (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the activation of the RXR/PPARγ pathway is particularly compelling. RPE cells are highly involved in the processing and clearance of lipids, including cholesterol, and in modulating the structural integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier via tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 and occludin. When under stress—such as exposure to cytotoxic mediators like 7-ketocholesterol (7KCh), which disrupts normal junctional organization and reduces transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—the activation of RXR offers a potential therapeutic avenue. Bexarotene’s ability to stimulate RXR signaling is expected to upregulate ABCA1 expression, thereby enhancing cholesterol efflux, while also promoting the transcription of genes that lead to the re-expression of claudin-1 and occludin, which are critical for restoring barrier integrity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

The biochemical interactions following RXR activation by bexarotene include a cascade of events where the ligand-receptor complex alters the transcriptional landscape of the cell. This process entails the heterodimerization of RXR with its partner receptor, binding to DNA response elements, and initiating the recruitment of transcriptional coactivators, which together drive the expression of genes that modulate lipid metabolism, inflammatory responses, and cell junction integrity. The preliminary in vitro evidence in ARPE-19 cells under 7-ketocholesterol stress is promising, particularly with the reported restoration of TEER and upregulation of ABCA1. The strengths of this candidate include its specificity for RXR, the translational potential backed by its FDA–approved status for an unrelated indication, and the innovative strategy of local ocular delivery through gel formulations. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Navitoclax (ABT-263) is a small‐molecule, orally bioavailable agent originally developed in the oncology arena as a BH3‐mimetic that targets several anti‐apoptotic members of the BCL-2 family, most notably BCL-2, BCL-xL, and BCL-W. This synthetic compound was designed through structure–activity relationship optimization to overcome the limitations of earlier compounds such as ABT-737, and it has since been classified as a senolytic agent owing to its ability to selectively induce apoptosis in senescent cells while sparing normal, quiescent cells. In the context of aging and degenerative diseases, the protective yet dysfunctional senescent cell phenotype is characterized by the upregulation of anti‐apoptotic proteins; therefore, compounds like ABT-263 that block these survival pathways have been repurposed as candidates to eliminate such senescent cells. The compound belongs to a broader class of therapeutics targeting the BCL-2 family, which have historically been exploited in various anti-cancer strategies and are now emerging as promising candidates for addressing age-associated disorders such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Ryu et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Navitoclax has a well-documented preclinical and clinical history in oncological models; its senolytic potential was first noted in studies where it selectively killed therapy-induced senescent tumor cells and other cell types by inhibiting anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins. Early clinical trials in small-cell lung cancer and lymphoid malignancies established proof-of-concept that targeting BCL-2/BCL-xL could result in tumor regression through apoptotic induction, although its clinical use was somewhat limited by dose-dependent toxicities such as thrombocytopenia. More recently, preclinical studies have extended its use beyond oncology: in in vitro studies and in mouse models where retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells were rendered senescent by doxorubicin treatment, navitoclax was shown to selectively induce apoptosis in the senescent cell population while largely sparing non-senescent RPE, as evidenced by decreased markers of senescence (p16, p21) and increased apoptotic markers such as cleaved caspases. Additionally, these studies demonstrated that oral administration of ABT-263 in mice resulted in reduced senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining and improved structural and functional retinal outcomes, including increased outer nuclear layer thickness and recovery of electroretinographic responses, which are highly encouraging for its repurposing in dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023). Despite these promising preclinical findings, navitoclax has not yet been tested in clinical trials for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative diseases, and its history in ocular conditions remains limited to proof-of-principle studies in animal models (Ryu et al., 2023; Khan et al., 2023).

At the molecular level, navitoclax exerts its senolytic action by competitively binding to the hydrophobic groove of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins, particularly BCL-2 and BCL-xL, thereby displacing pro-apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BIM. Under normal conditions, senescent cells upregulate these anti-apoptotic proteins as part of a survival mechanism against various stressors; the binding of navitoclax disrupts these protective interactions, leading to the activation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade. This biochemical disruption sets off a cascade of events culminating in mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, cytochrome c release, and the subsequent activation of caspases (notably caspase-9 and caspase-3), which orchestrate programmed cell death. Experimentally, cells treated with navitoclax have demonstrated an increased BAX/BCL-2 ratio along with elevated levels of cleaved caspases as measured by immunoblots, paralleling the reduction of canonical senescence markers such as p16 and p21. In the context of retinal degeneration, senescent RPE cells are known to secrete a deleterious senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)—including proinflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and IL-8 and matrix metalloproteases such as MMP2 and MMP9—that can undermine the integrity of junctional proteins such as ZO-1, leading to increased paracellular permeability. By eliminating these p16^Ink4a-positive senescent cells, navitoclax is hypothesized to reduce the inflammatory burden on the tissue microenvironment, thereby promoting the repopulation of healthy RPE cells and the restoration of tight junction continuity (Ryu et al., 2023).

The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of navitoclax for dry AMD is that the senolytic removal of p16^Ink4a-positive, senescent RPE cells will lead to a diminution of the SASP and its associated cytokines, such as IL-6 and IL-8, which are known to contribute to the degradation of tight junction proteins and compromise RPE barrier function. Navitoclax represents a promising therapeutic candidate as a repurposed senolytic agent for the treatment of dry AMD based on a convergence of preclinical biochemical, cellular, and animal model data. One of its primary strengths is its clear mechanism of action; by targeting a well-characterized survival pathway that is upregulated in senescent cells, navitoclax offers a rational strategy for the selective removal of dysfunctional p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells. The preclinical evidence suggests that this mechanism translates into meaningful improvements in retinal structure and function, including reductions in senescence-associated markers and partial restoration of indicators of cellular proliferation and tissue integrity (Ryu et al., 2023).

Addressing these issues may involve the development of targeted delivery systems, dose optimization studies, and rigorous functional assays that can collectively establish whether the removal of p16^Ink4a-positive senescent cells via navitoclax leads to durable improvements in RPE barrier integrity and, consequently, visual function in patients with dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Al-Naggar et al., 2020).

1. Developing or validating animal models that more accurately recapitulate the chronic senescence observed in dry AMD;  
2. Refining delivery strategies to minimize systemic exposure and associated toxicities while maximizing ocular bioavailability;  
3. Implementing rigorous, quantitative assays (such as TEER measurements and detailed immunolocalization of tight junction proteins) to confirm the restoration of barrier function following senolytic treatment; and  
4. Carefully assessing the long-term outcomes of senolytic therapy on retinal structure, immune modulation, and visual performance in aged subjects (Ryu et al., 2023).

Continued investigation into the precise role of p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells in AMD, together with detailed pharmacodynamic studies of navitoclax within the ocular microenvironment, will be essential to determine whether this agent can truly fulfill the promise of restoring RPE barrier function and, by extension, visual acuity in patients suffering from dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Carpenter et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Vatiquinone (EPI-743) is a synthetic, tocopherol-derived quinone originally developed as a vitamin E analogue to counteract inherited mitochondrial diseases. It was synthesized through modifications of the natural vitamin E structure, where oxidation of the tocopherol leads to the formation of a quinone moiety. This design enhances its electron transfer capabilities and confers improved bioavailability and tissue penetration, including the ability to cross the blood–brain barrier. As a member of the quinone class of antioxidants, vatiquinone belongs to a group of compounds that have historically been leveraged to modulate redox homeostasis in tissues under oxidative stress. This class of compounds has been applied in diverse therapeutic areas ranging from neurodegenerative disorders to mitochondrial dysfunction, and its mechanism is chiefly considered beneficial in circumstances where oxidative stress and compromised mitochondrial integrity are primary pathological drivers (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

In addition to its synthetic origins, the pharmacological profile of vatiquinone is characterized by its potent antioxidant activity that exceeds that of traditional compounds like Coenzyme Q10 or idebenone. Its chemical structure allows it to interface efficiently with cellular redox enzymes such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1). The high-affinity interaction between vatiquinone and NQO1 is central to its function, as it is hypothesized to regenerate reduced forms of coenzyme Q and thus support the recycling of critical cellular antioxidants such as glutathione. The ability to catalyze these reactions positions vatiquinone as a compelling agent for therapeutic interventions in conditions marked by chronic oxidative stress, an attribute that underpins the rationale for its proposed use in dry age‐related macular degeneration (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Vatiquinone’s therapeutic history is strongly associated with its development for inherited mitochondrial disorders, most notably Friedreich’s ataxia (FRDA) and Leigh syndrome. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated that vatiquinone modulates oxidative stress response pathways and protects mitochondrial function. In clinical trials conducted in patients with FRDA, vatiquinone was shown to regulate key antioxidant defenses by enhancing the expression of genes such as NQO1 and those involved in glutathione synthesis via activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. This led to improvements in neurological function and confirmed its favorable safety profile, thereby validating its use in outpatient settings for mitochondrial disorders (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Beyond its application in mitochondrial disorders, vatiquinone has been explored in the context of various neurodegenerative diseases, reflecting its capacity to preserve mitochondrial health and ameliorate oxidative injury in neural tissues. Its potent neuroprotective properties, which include mitigating oxidative insults and modulating redox-sensitive signaling pathways, have led to its FDA orphan drug designation for Friedrich’s ataxia. Although the primary focus of vatiquinone research has been in neurodegeneration and mitochondrial impairments, the underlying mechanisms that confer mitochondrial protection and support antioxidant defenses have raised interest in its potential application in ocular diseases such as dry age‐related macular degeneration. Notably, preclinical and anecdotal data have suggested that similar redox imbalances found in inherited mitochondrial diseases are also present in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of patients with dry AMD. However, while the compound’s efficacy and safety have been established in the neurological context, no formal clinical investigations have directly addressed its potential in treating dry AMD or in modulating RPE function (Cores et al., 2023; Chang & Chen, 2024).

The translation of vatiquinone’s antioxidant properties to dry AMD is based on the shared underlying pathology of chronic oxidative stress. Pilot data even indicate viability improvements in ARPE-19, a widely used RPE cell model, under stress conditions. Although these data are preliminary and unpublished, they offer a promising foundation for further research into whether the molecule can enhance RPE barrier integrity, mitigate ROS-mediated damage, and restore transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in an oxidative environment (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of vatiquinone centers on its role as a potent redox-active compound that interacts directly with cellular enzymes such as NQO1. The compound is a high-affinity substrate for NQO1, an enzyme that catalyzes the reversible two-electron reduction of quinones. This reaction is critical because it facilitates the regeneration of reduced coenzyme Q, a vital electron carrier within the mitochondrial respiratory chain. In tissues under chronic oxidative stress, such as the RPE, this reaction ensures the maintenance of mitochondrial function and energy production (Tiberi et al., 2023).

Furthermore, vatiquinone’s chemical structure confers upon it the ability to modulate the activity of the Nrf2 pathway indirectly. Under oxidative stress, Nrf2 normally dissociates from its cytosolic inhibitor Keap1, translocates to the nucleus, and induces the transcription of ARE-driven genes. These genes encode several antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes, including NQO1, glutamate–cysteine ligase, and heme oxygenase-1. By facilitating redox stabilization and promoting a favorable antioxidant environment, vatiquinone indirectly enhances the nuclear stabilization and translocation of Nrf2. This leads to a sustained increase in the expression of key components responsible for glutathione synthesis and recycling, a process crucial for neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and protecting cellular structures (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

At the molecular level, vatiquinone’s interaction with NQO1 not only catalyzes the reduction of the compound itself but also plays a broader role in restoring the redox balance of coenzyme Q within the mitochondrial membrane. The modulation of the redox state of coenzyme Q enhances the function of the electron transport chain and prevents the accumulation of ROS. Such precise biochemical regulation is essential in tissues like the RPE, which are highly susceptible to oxidative damage due to constant light exposure and high metabolic activity. The resultant maintenance of mitochondrial integrity and bioenergetics further supports the preservation of tight junction proteins and barrier function, which are compromised in chronic oxidative environments (Cores et al., 2023).

In summary, vatiquinone exerts its effects via dual modalities: a direct catalytic reduction by NQO1 that regenerates bioactive reduced coenzyme Q and an indirect upregulation of the Nrf2-dependent antioxidant response. These biochemical interactions form the cornerstone of its neuroprotective and cytoprotective properties in cells challenged by oxidative stress, providing a mechanistic rationale for its potential application in protecting RPE cells (Cores et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
Applying the known mechanisms of vatiquinone to the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration, the candidate is expected to mediate several beneficial effects in the retinal pigment epithelium. The primary hypothesis is that vatiquinone will act as a high-affinity substrate for NQO1 in RPE cells, thereby accelerating the reduction of the compound and promoting the regeneration of reduced coenzyme Q. This regeneration is essential, as it not only supports the mitochondrial electron transport chain but also contributes to the broader cellular antioxidant network through enhanced glutathione recycling (Tiberi et al., 2023).

In the proposed ARPE-19 cell assay under chronic oxidative challenge, the activation of the NQO1 pathway by vatiquinone is anticipated to improve the cellular redox state. By regenerating reduced coenzyme Q and facilitating glutathione recycling, the drug candidate is expected to neutralize increased levels of ROS that arise during sustained oxidative stress. A consequent effect of this improved redox balance would be the reduced oxidation of tight junction proteins, which are critical for maintaining the barrier integrity of the RPE. Enhanced preservation of these proteins should translate into improved transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a surrogate marker for the functional health of the RPE monolayer (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Additionally, the indirect activation of the Nrf2 pathway by vatiquinone further supports the upregulation of a spectrum of antioxidant genes. These genes, including NQO1, glutamate–cysteine ligase, and heme oxygenase-1, are known to be expressed in RPE cells, especially under oxidative stress conditions. Their increased expression is expected to bolster the cellular defense system, further reducing the accumulation of oxidative damage within the RPE. It is this coordinated regulation of antioxidant pathways that forms the basis for the expected protective effect on RPE barrier function (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023).

Moreover, when applied to the ARPE-19 cell model, the anticipated outcome is an improved survival rate and enhanced barrier properties under conditions that mimic the chronic oxidative insult characteristic of dry AMD. In vitro studies suggest that vatiquinone may limit ROS-induced modifications to cellular proteins, thereby preserving tight junction integrity. This preservation is critical not only for maintaining TEER but also for ensuring proper intercellular adhesion and barrier function, which are directly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Cores et al., 2023).

The expected benefits in the cellular assay include a reduction in oxidative markers, stabilization of mitochondrial function, and maintenance or restoration of RPE junctional architecture. These effects, if replicated in further ocular-specific studies, would position vatiquinone as a valuable therapeutic candidate for mitigating the progression of dry AMD, where oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction are culpable for disease progression (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive evaluation of vatiquinone as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration reveals several compelling strengths as well as important limitations that must be addressed in future research. One of the primary strengths of vatiquinone is its robust mode of action grounded in redox biology. Its ability to function as a high-affinity substrate for NQO1, coupled with its indirect activation of the Nrf2 pathway, equips it with a dual mechanism that promotes both direct regeneration of the reduced coenzyme Q pool and upregulation of cellular antioxidant defenses. These mechanisms are particularly significant in protecting mitochondrial function and by extension, improving cellular resilience against oxidative insults that compromise the RPE (Tiberi et al., 2023).

The wealth of historical data demonstrating vatiquinone’s efficacy in treating mitochondrial disorders such as Friedreich’s ataxia lends credence to its capability in counteracting oxidative damage and preserving tissue function. Its demonstrated ability to upregulate genes involved in glutathione synthesis and to stabilize mitochondrial function under stress makes it a promising candidate not only for neurodegenerative conditions but potentially for ocular pathologies where similar oxidative mechanisms are at play (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023). Moreover, the observation that preliminary ARPE-19 cell data indicate improved viability under oxidative challenge augments the biological plausibility of its use in dry AMD (Cores et al., 2023; Tiberi et al., 2023).

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and uncertainties temper the enthusiasm for immediate repurposing. The most significant gap is the absence of direct evidence linking vatiquinone to therapeutic benefits specifically in dry AMD or broader retinal contexts. While the mechanistic rationale is robust, the majority of the supportive literature originates from studies in neurodegeneration and mitochondrial dysfunction rather than from ophthalmologic or RPE-specific investigations. This extrapolation, although scientifically reasonable, necessitates rigorous preclinical evaluation in ocular models to confirm efficacy in preserving retinal barrier function under chronic oxidative stress (Cores et al., 2023).

Another area requiring careful scrutiny is the complexity of the retinal microenvironment compared to neuronal tissues. Dry AMD is multifactorial, with pathogenesis that involves chronic inflammation, complement dysregulation, lipid accumulation, and cell death in addition to oxidative stress. Thus, while vatiquinone’s antioxidant and mitochondrial-protective actions are promising, it remains unclear whether these effects alone will be sufficient to alter the course of dry AMD. This ambiguity underscores the need for studies that specifically measure the impact on tight junction protein oxidation and TEER restoration in RPE cells under conditions that closely mimic the pathological environment of dry AMD (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

From a pharmacokinetic and formulation standpoint, although vatiquinone is orally bioavailable and has demonstrated favorable systemic safety profiles, the translation of systemic delivery to ocular efficacy presents challenges. Ocular tissues have unique barriers to drug delivery, and the pharmacodynamics within the retina might differ from those observed in neurological or systemic applications. Addressing these issues will require detailed ocular pharmacokinetic studies and potentially the development of optimized formulations tailored for retinal applications (Cores et al., 2023).

In summary, vatiquinone (EPI-743) is a highly promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration based on its established antioxidant properties, potent NQO1 substrate activity, and its capacity to indirectly activate Nrf2-dependent defense mechanisms. The compound’s strengths lie in its dual mechanism of action that directly addresses mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress—key contributors to RPE degeneration in dry AMD. However, the absence of direct evidence in ocular models and the inherent complexities of retinal pathophysiology represent significant hurdles that must be overcome through targeted preclinical and clinical studies. Future research should prioritize in vitro studies using ARPE-19 and other RPE models, followed by in vivo validation in animal models of dry AMD, to conclusively determine whether vatiquinone can restore TEER and protect tight junction proteins against ROS-mediated damage (Tiberi et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023).

Overall, while the current body of evidence from mitochondrial and neuroprotective studies provides a strong rationale for further exploration, the repurposing of vatiquinone for dry AMD will require careful dose optimization, targeted delivery to retinal tissues, and comprehensive validation of its effects on RPE barrier integrity before it can be fully endorsed as a therapeutic option for this debilitating ocular disease (Tiberi et al., 2023; Chang & Chen, 2024; Cores et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Danicopan, also known as ACH-4471 and by its commercial identifier MedChemExpress HY-19909, is a novel small-molecule agent designed to target complement factor D. It belongs to a growing class of low-molecular-weight inhibitors that are specifically aimed at interfering with the alternative pathway (AP) of the complement system. This class of compounds is characterized by their capacity to modulate complement activation rather than broadly suppress the entire immune system. Danicopan was originally developed as a first-in-class molecule to selectively block factor D, which is the rate-limiting enzyme in the AP and is intimately involved in the formation of the C3 convertase complex (Boyer et al., 2022). The chemical structure of Danicopan incorporates a proline core with added moieties such as amino bromo pyridine and azaindole, a configuration designed to ensure both high potency and selectivity in factor D inhibition (Schubart et al., 2023). The oral bioavailability of Danicopan, combined with its capacity to achieve sustained exposure in ocular tissues due in part to melanin binding in pigmented tissues, underscores its appeal for diseases where local complement modulation is desired without the need for invasive delivery routes (Boyer et al., 2022). Notably, the design approach for Danicopan focuses on blocking the enzymatic activation loop that precipitates complement amplification—a mechanism that is particularly deleterious in tissues such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Boyer et al., 2022).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the use of complement inhibitors has been a promising therapeutic strategy across several complement-mediated disorders. Danicopan was initially evaluated in the context of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), a condition driven by unregulated complement activation that results in hemolysis and thrombosis. Early clinical studies in patients with PNH revealed that oral administration of Danicopan rapidly inhibited the alternative pathway, resulting in significantly reduced hemolysis with concomitant improvements in hematological parameters (Schubart et al., 2023). This clinical success in PNH has spurred the interest in repurposing Danicopan for ocular indications, notably for dry AMD—a condition where dysfunctional complement activation plays a central role in the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy (GA). Although Danicopan’s application in dry AMD is still under investigation, the rationale for its use stems from preclinical models demonstrating high and sustained ocular tissue levels after oral dosing, especially in regions enriched with melanin (Boyer et al., 2022). Furthermore, the candidate has entered a Phase 2 clinical trial focusing on GA AMD, with the study design aimed at assessing its safety, efficacy, and pharmacokinetic profile in a population of 330 participants (Fabre et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2024). Importantly, while previous complement inhibitors such as Lampalizumab have been evaluated in AMD—with mixed outcomes—Danicopan’s novel oral dosing profile and improved tissue selectivity underscore its potential advantage over earlier modalities (Tang et al., 2024; Schubart et al., 2023).  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Danicopan acts by binding to complement factor D with high affinity, thereby inhibiting its serine protease activity. Factor D is indispensable for the cleavage of factor B and the subsequent assembly of the C3 convertase (C3bBb) on the cell surface, which is the amplification step critical for the alternative complement pathway (Boyer et al., 2022). Inhibition of factor D effectively halts the formation of the AP C3 convertase, thereby preventing the cleavage of C3 into its active fragments, C3a and C3b. This downstream effect is crucial because the deposition of C3b—or its inactivated form iC3b—on the RPE surfaces is implicated in complement-driven inflammation and subsequent cellular damage (Fabre et al., 2022). In addition, by attenuating the production of C3a, Danicopan helps mitigate the recruitment and activation of inflammatory effector cells in the retinal microenvironment (Wilke & Apte, 2024; Schubart et al., 2023). The selectivity of Danicopan for factor D not only reduces the biochemistry of the AP cascade but also limits the risk of compromising the classical and lectin pathways, which remain critical for host defense. This selective inhibition is biochemically significant, as the tight regulation of complement is essential for maintaining immune surveillance and tissue homeostasis (Boyer et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). The reported inhibitory concentration (IC₅₀) values for Danicopan have been reported in various contexts, with figures around 5.8 nM in some studies and as low as 2 nM as hypothesized in the current proposal, underscoring its potent inhibitory capacity (Fabre et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). On a cellular level, the blockade of factor D is expected to prevent the formation of the C3 convertase on RPE cells, which in turn would reduce the deposition of complement fragments like C3b and iC3b on the surface of these cells. This is particularly important since the complement-mediated deposition on RPE cells can disrupt the distribution and localization of tight junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and occludin, which are critical for preserving RPE barrier integrity and function (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022). In essence, Danicopan’s mechanism of action addresses the upstream triggers of the inflammatory cascade by preventing the enzymatic events that lead to complement amplification, thereby providing a molecular rationale for its application in diseases characterized by complement dysregulation, including dry AMD (Boyer et al., 2022).

Based on the mechanistic insights and preclinical data, the expected pharmacodynamic outcome of Danicopan administration in the context of dry AMD is multifold. Primarily, by inhibiting factor D, Danicopan is anticipated to block the formation of the AP C3 convertase, directly preventing the subsequent cascade of complement activation that would otherwise lead to C3b—and by extension, iC3b—deposition on RPE surfaces (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022). In parallel, the oral administration of Danicopan offers a non-invasive route of drug delivery, which may enhance patient compliance relative to intravitreal injections generally required for other ocular therapies (Boyer et al., 2022). The evaluation of Danicopan as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration reveals several compelling strengths balanced by certain challenges that warrant further investigation. One of the most significant strengths of Danicopan lies in its potent, selective inhibition of factor D—a critical enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. By targeting factor D, Danicopan disrupts the amplification loop that drives the deposition of complement fragments such as C3b and iC3b on the RPE surface. This mechanistic precision is vital given that complement overactivation is a well-established contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Boyer et al., 2022). The reported high affinity, with low nanomolar inhibitory concentrations, underscores its biochemical potency (Fabre et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023). Moreover, the oral bioavailability of Danicopan represents a significant advantage. Unlike intravitreal injections—which are invasive and carry risks such as endophthalmitis—oral administration could improve patient adherence and facilitate chronic treatment regimens required for a progressive disease such as dry AMD (Boyer et al., 2022). Preclinical studies have provided encouraging evidence, demonstrating that in animal models, Danicopan not only reduces complement deposition but also preserves RPE function, as indicated by improved TER and maintenance of electrophysiological responses (Boyer et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2024). First, while the preclinical data is promising—such as the reported 60% reduction in C3b deposition in Cfh⁻/⁻ mice and restoration of TER in drusen-mimic ARPE-19 cells—the translation of these results to clinical efficacy in patients with dry AMD remains to be fully established (Fabre et al., 2022). The underlying hypothesis—that oral inhibition of factor D will block complement amplification on RPE surfaces, thereby preventing C3b/iC3b deposition, maintaining tight junction integrity, preserving transepithelial resistance, and reducing paracellular flux—is well supported by the available literature (Boyer et al., 2022). However, it is important to note that the specific quantitative outcomes reported in preclinical models—such as the 78% restoration of TER and the 60% reduction in C3b deposition—while promising, require further validation through rigorous, controlled studies. In summary, Danicopan exhibits several strengths that render it a promising candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. The preclinical data demonstrating sustained ocular exposure, along with preserved RPE functionality (as evidenced by improvements in TER and reduction in complement deposition), provide a strong rationale for its continued development in AMD (Boyer et al., 2022; Fabre et al., 2022). 3. Clinical trial designs incorporating both structural imaging and biochemical markers to substantiate the mechanism of action; and

Its targeted approach may overcome some of the limitations encountered with previous complement inhibitors, especially if future studies can confirm that the in vitro effects on TER restoration and reduction in C3b deposition translate into meaningful clinical outcomes. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Belumosudil (KD025; Rezurock) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable, indazole-derived serine/threonine kinase inhibitor that preferentially targets Rho-associated coiled-coil–containing protein kinase 2 (ROCK2) over ROCK1 and was developed by Kadmon Pharmaceuticals following licensing from Nano Terra (now approved in the United States for chronic graft-versus-host disease, cGVHD) (Blair, 2021; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022; Przepiorka et al., 2022). Biochemical selectivity has been consistently reported across sources: IC₅₀ values are approximately 60–110 nM for ROCK2 with markedly weaker activity on ROCK1 (typically >10 µM), and orthogonal profiling notes ROCK2 ~0.105 µM and ROCK1 ~24 µM, confirming substantial isoform preference (Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022; Blair, 2021; Lake et al., 2020). As an ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor, belumosudil binds the catalytic domain of ROCK2, analogous to the mechanism of other clinically used ROCK inhibitors, but with enhanced isoform selectivity designed to improve tolerability relative to pan-ROCK agents (e.g., fasudil, ripasudil, netarsudil) (Cheng et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

The broader class—ROCK inhibitors—modulates actin–myosin cytoskeletal dynamics by decreasing phosphorylation of myosin regulatory elements and altering actin turnover via downstream nodes (LIMK–cofilin, ERM proteins), with downstream effects on cell contractility, focal adhesions, cell junctions, migration, and myofibroblast differentiation (Cheng et al., 2025). In ophthalmology, ROCK inhibitors have established or emerging therapeutic roles: netarsudil and ripasudil lower intraocular pressure by relaxing trabecular meshwork and Schlemm’s canal, and corneal endothelial repair paradigms (topical ROCK inhibitors and cell therapy adjuncts) exploit cytoskeletal relaxation, enhanced adhesion, and proliferation to accelerate re-endothelialization (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025). Collectively, these features position belumosudil within a drug class with proven ocular pharmacology and strong plausibility for modulating epithelial/endothelial barrier biology through cytoskeletal re-tuning (Leong et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic immunomodulation and anti-fibrotic indications. Belumosudil is FDA-approved for treatment of cGVHD after at least two prior systemic therapies at an oral dose of 200 mg once daily with food; population pharmacokinetics indicate a mean elimination half-life of ~19 hours, primary CYP3A4 metabolism, and predominant fecal excretion, with two metabolites that also inhibit ROCK2 (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Blair, 2021). Across phase 2 programs in cGVHD, objective response rates (65–77%) were observed with 200 mg once or twice daily dosing, with corticosteroid sparing and acceptable tolerability, consolidating a favorable clinical safety/efficacy profile for chronic use in a heavily pretreated, immunologically dysregulated population (Jagasia et al., 2021; Zanin-Zhorov & Blazar, 2021). Beyond cGVHD, belumosudil has been explored in fibrotic diseases (interim idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis signal for attenuated FVC decline) and systemic sclerosis, consistent with class-wide anti-fibrotic properties driven by ROCK2 blockade (Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

Ocular use of ROCK inhibitors (class precedent). While belumosudil itself has not been reported in clinical ocular indications, the ROCK inhibitor class has multiple precedents in eye disease. Topical netarsudil and ripasudil are approved or widely used for glaucoma; intravitreal and topical fasudil have been explored for retinal diseases (e.g., diabetic macular edema) with reported safety in small series, and sustained-release ocular delivery of ROCK inhibitors (e.g., AR-13503) has been tested in preclinical models (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025). These translational precedents establish that ROCK pathway modulation can be achieved in ocular tissues via topical, intravitreal, or sustained-release routes and that cytoskeletal/vascular barrier targets respond to this mechanism in the eye (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Belumosudil in ocular preclinical models. In a laser-induced choroidal neovascularization/subretinal fibrosis model designed to isolate fibrotic progression, both fasudil (pan-ROCK) and belumosudil (ROCK2-selective) reduced fibrosis volume, preserved retinal morphology, increased retinal thickness, reduced pyknotic nuclei, and decreased type I collagen and α-SMA staining; corrected total cell fluorescence for ROCK1/ROCK2 was reduced, with particularly strong ROCK2 target engagement by belumosudil (occupancy down from 6.7% to 0.1%) (Zandi et al., 2025). Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) and western blot evidence showed reductions in p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex—consistent with ROCK pathway inhibition—alongside decreases in TGF-β1, fibronectin, vimentin, and α-SMA; belumosudil also more effectively reduced “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations near the choroid–RPE boundary compared with fasudil and decreased macrophages/perivascular cells, suggesting anti-inflammatory as well as anti-fibrotic activity (Zandi et al., 2025). In vitro, 24-hour ROCK inhibitor exposure in fibroblastic cells altered morphology (loss of long processes, blunted periphery) and decreased cell numbers, consistent with cytoskeletal/phenotype modulation and possible anti-proliferative effects in fibrogenic cells (Zandi et al., 2025).

Dry AMD relevance and gaps. The above in vivo data position ROCK2 inhibition as an anti-fibrotic modifier of the choroid–RPE interface after laser injury, with partial restoration of retinal architecture; however, they do not test dry AMD pathobiology (e.g., sodium iodate RPE toxicity or geographic atrophy models) (Zandi et al., 2025). Direct ocular RPE barrier endpoints—TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and tight-junction protein integrity (ZO-1, claudin-19)—have not been reported for belumosudil in RPE, and the available studies do not include oxidative or complement injury paradigms (H₂O₂, NaIO₃) in ARPE-19, primary human RPE, or in vivo dry AMD models (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). Class-level in vitro RPE evidence exists for ROCK inhibition improving wound closure, adhesion, pigmentation, RPE65 expression, and photoreceptor outer-segment phagocytosis in iPSC-RPE with Y-27632, but without barrier readouts, and with limited recovery duration and small sample sizes (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Additional pluripotent RPE manufacturing work reports ROCK inhibition suppresses EMT programs (TGF-β/Wnt ligands, SNAI2, collagens) and promotes rapid tight-junction reformation in culture, supporting barrier-relevant cytoskeletal effects at the transcriptomic/phenotypic level, but without TEER or paracellular flux data under oxidative/complement stress (Croze, 2015). In sum, while class-level and belumosudil-specific ocular data support anti-fibrotic and cytoskeletal modulation at the choroid–RPE interface, there is no direct published evidence in the provided literature set that belumosudil rescues TEER, preserves claudin-19/ZO-1, or reduces FITC-dextran flux under H₂O₂ or complement challenge in RPE or that it improves outcomes in NaIO₃ models (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
ROCK2 biology and junctional/cytoskeletal control. ROCK1/2 are AGC-family serine/threonine kinases activated by RhoA–GTP; they increase actomyosin contractility primarily by phosphorylating myosin light chain (MLC) directly and inhibiting myosin light-chain phosphatase via phosphorylation of the MYPT1 regulatory subunit, elevating p-MLC levels and stabilizing stress fibers and focal adhesions (Cheng et al., 2025). ROCK also phosphorylates LIM kinases to inactivate cofilin, which slows F-actin turnover and further stiffens the cytoskeleton; ERM proteins, adducin, intermediate filament proteins (vimentin, GFAP), and multiple cytoskeletal/membrane linkers are additional substrates that integrate cytoskeletal and junctional dynamics (Cheng et al., 2025). These pathways are sensitive to mechanical inputs (matrix stiffness) and link cytoskeletal remodeling to barrier integrity and cell adhesion, consistent with the observed roles of ROCK in endothelial hyperpermeability and junction stabilization in ocular tissues (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025).

Belumosudil target engagement in choroid–RPE constructs. In vivo in the choroid–RPE complex after laser injury, both fasudil and belumosudil lowered p-MYPT1, indicating on-pathway ROCK inhibition, and reduced fibrotic markers (α-SMA, vimentin, fibronectin, collagen I, TGF-β1), consistent with suppression of myofibroblast activation, ECM deposition, and TGF-β/Smad signaling output (Zandi et al., 2025). Imaging mass cytometry showed spatially localized fibrotic marker expression to the choroid–RPE boundary and a reduction in “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations with belumosudil relative to fasudil, and a decrease in macrophage and perivascular cell signatures—integrating anti-fibrotic and anti-inflammatory mechanisms (Zandi et al., 2025). Quantitatively, ROCK2 staining occupancy fell from ~6.7% to 0.1% after belumosudil treatment, stronger than the reduction with fasudil (to 0.7%), supporting efficient ROCK2 target engagement by belumosudil (Zandi et al., 2025).

ROCK and epithelial barrier relevance. Although the RPE-specific tight-junction literature for belumosudil is not available in the provided sources, corneal endothelial studies link ROCK activity to stabilization of ZO-1 and the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump complex; pharmacologic ROCK inhibition promotes cytoskeletal relaxation, spreading, and cyclin-D–dependent proliferation, and has been leveraged clinically to accelerate re-endothelialization and junctional re-establishment (Leong et al., 2025). In vascular endothelia, RhoA/ROCK signaling drives VEGF-induced permeability and tube formation; ROCK inhibition modulates junctional architecture (e.g., “zipper-like” lymphatic endothelial junctions) and reduces permeability, supporting a mechanistic link to barrier tightening (Leong et al., 2025). In diabetic retinal pathology, ROCK1 activation contributes to RPE blebbing and tight-junction opening with outer blood-retinal barrier breakdown; pharmacologic ROCK inhibition (fasudil) improved barrier function and suppressed leukocyte migration and ICAM-1, reducing vascular leakage and neurodegeneration (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Together, these data reinforce that ROCK signaling is a proximal regulator of epithelial/endothelial junctions and barrier integrity and that inhibition—especially with an isoform-selective agent that engages ROCK2 in the choroid–RPE complex—has plausible junction-preserving effects in RPE monolayers (Leong et al., 2025; Zandi et al., 2025).

Anti-EMT and anti-fibrotic transcriptional programs. Transcriptomic studies in pluripotent stem cell–derived RPE and other epithelial contexts show ROCK inhibition suppresses EMT-associated transcriptional programs (TGF-β ligands, Wnt components, SNAI2, collagens) and promotes tight-junction reformation, consistent with decreased cytoskeletal tension and reduced MRTF/SRF-dependent transcription that drives myofibroblast markers (e.g., α-SMA) (Croze, 2015; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022). ROCK2 inhibition also intersects with inflammatory transcriptional axes (STAT3/STAT5) and NF-κB, shifting Th17/Tfh toward Treg and reducing proinflammatory cytokines in PBMCs and cGVHD models, which could help resolve inflammatory components of AMD pathophysiology at the RPE–choroid interface (Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Cytoskeletal/ciliary modulation in RPE-lineage cells. Independent siRNA/drug screens in ciliogenesis models identified ROCK2 as a strong negative regulator of cilia incidence and length; short and prolonged belumosudil exposure increased cilia metrics in hTERT RPE-1 and mIMCD3 cells while reducing phosphorylated MLC and acto-myosin fiber-like structures, consistent with decreased ROCK2-driven contractility (Lake et al., 2020). Although ciliation per se is not a dry AMD therapeutic endpoint, the data are a sensitive readout of cytoskeletal reprogramming via ROCK2 and reinforce the target’s role in apical organization in epithelia with RPE lineage origin (Lake et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay context: H₂O₂ and complement injury in RPE monolayers. Under oxidative stress (H₂O₂) and complement attack, the RPE cytoskeleton becomes hypercontractile, junctional belts destabilize, and paracellular permeability increases—manifest as reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased FITC-dextran flux, with mislocalization or fragmentation of tight-junction proteins (ZO-1, claudin-19). ROCK activation (via RhoA–GTP, inflammatory mediators, or mechanical cues) exacerbates this by increasing p-MYPT1 and p-MLC to drive actomyosin tension and stress fiber formation (Cheng et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). The class literature in ocular epithelia/endothelium indicates that ROCK inhibition relaxes cytoskeletal tension, promotes cell spreading and junctional complex re-assembly (ZO-1 stabilization reported in corneal endothelium), and reduces VEGF- or inflammation-driven hyperpermeability (Leong et al., 2025). In diabetic retinal models, ROCK pathway activation produces RPE blebbing and tight-junction disruption, with pharmacologic ROCK inhibition reversing barrier dysfunction and dampening leukostasis and leakage (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Given these mechanisms, selective ROCK2 inhibition with belumosudil is expected to:
- Reduce p-MYPT1 and downstream p-MLC in RPE, decreasing acto-myosin contractility, stabilizing the circumferential actin belt and adherens/tight junctions (ZO-1/claudin-19), thereby rescuing TEER and lowering FITC-dextran flux under H₂O₂ or complement challenge (Zandi et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025).
- Suppress EMT-like shifts and myofibroblast activation induced by oxidative/complement stress by lowering α-SMA/vimentin and ECM program activation (fibronectin, collagen), as seen in vivo after laser injury and in ROCK-inhibited RPE culture transcriptomics (Zandi et al., 2025; Croze, 2015).
- Provide anti-inflammatory benefits by reducing macrophage/perivascular cell accumulation seen in vivo and by directly modulating STAT3/STAT5-linked cytokine programs, potentially blunting complement-amplified inflammatory cascades at the RPE/choroid interface (Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021).

Target expression and context. ROCK signaling is active in ocular tissues; p-MYPT1 is reduced in the choroid–RPE complex of laser-injured eyes after ROCK inhibition; ROCK1 translocates and drives cytoskeletal/junctional changes under hyperglycemia in RPE and endothelium; and ROCK2 expression is quantifiably reduced by belumosudil in the choroid–RPE complex—collectively validating target presence and drug engagement at the proposed site of action (Zandi et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Important caveats. The provided literature set does not contain direct demonstrations that belumosudil rescues TEER or reduces FITC-dextran flux in RPE under H₂O₂ or complement injury, nor does it report preservation of claudin-19/ZO-1 localization in RPE with ROCK2-selective inhibition; these remain testable predictions grounded in mechanism and class precedent but not yet substantiated for belumosudil in RPE (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). Similarly, no data are provided here for NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration models with belumosudil; the NaIO₃ discussion pertains to single-cell remodeling and EMT tendencies in dry AMD models, which conceptually align with anti-EMT and anti-fibrotic effects of ROCK inhibition, but require direct in vivo validation for this candidate (Zandi et al., 2025).

Pharmacokinetic/delivery considerations for the assay. Clinically, belumosudil has a ~19-hour half-life, ~64% bioavailability with food (in healthy subjects), and is metabolized by CYP3A4; ocular pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration are not reported in the provided sources (Przepiorka et al., 2022). In the laser-injury mouse model, intraperitoneal administration from day 35 to 49 post-laser achieved retinal/choroid pharmacodynamics (↓p-MYPT1, ↓markers), indicating systemic dosing can engage ocular targets in inflamed/fibrotic tissue in mice, though translational relevance to human ocular exposure remains to be determined and local delivery could be preferable for barrier-rescue assays (Zandi et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- On-pathway target engagement in choroid–RPE with functional tissue outcomes. Belumosudil decreases p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex, reduces fibrosis volume, attenuates α-SMA, vimentin, fibronectin, collagen I, and TGF-β1, and preserves retinal morphology and thickness in a subretinal fibrosis model; ROCK2 occupancy falls to near-baseline with treatment, indicating strong ocular target engagement (Zandi et al., 2025). These integrated molecular and histologic readouts provide robust evidence that isoform-selective ROCK2 inhibition can reprogram the pathological microenvironment at the RPE–choroid interface after injury—precisely where barrier restoration is therapeutically needed in dry AMD (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Mechanistic alignment with barrier preservation. ROCK signaling is a proximal regulator of cytoskeletal tension and tight-junction stability; inhibition reduces MLC phosphorylation via MYPT1 de-phosphorylation, stabilizes junctions (corneal ZO-1; endothelial junction “zippering”), and mitigates hyperpermeability (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025). The candidate’s demonstrated ability to lower p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex and reduce myofibroblast activation fits the hypothesis that it can preserve epithelial barrier integrity under stress (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Anti-EMT/anti-fibrotic transcriptional effects. ROCK inhibition suppresses TGF-β/Wnt-mediated EMT programs and promotes tight-junction reformation in pluripotent-derived RPE; in vivo reductions in α-SMA and ECM deposition further support anti-fibrotic activity coherent with preventing RPE-to-mesenchymal transitions that compromise the barrier (Croze, 2015; Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions. Belumosudil reduces macrophage and perivascular cell signatures in vivo and systemically shifts Th17/Tfh toward Treg via STAT3/STAT5 modulation; these effects could dampen complement- and cytokine-driven RPE injury cascades implicated in dry AMD (Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).  
- Favorable human safety experience and oral PK. A clinically approved safety profile with chronic administration, a manageable drug–drug interaction profile (CYP3A4), and a ~19-hour half-life provide a de-risked starting point for repurposing; dose selection can be guided by systemic exposures achieved in cGVHD (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zanin-Zhorov & Blazar, 2021).

Weaknesses and knowledge gaps  
- No direct RPE barrier functional data for belumosudil. The literature set lacks TEER, FITC-dextran flux, or ZO-1/claudin-19 preservation data for belumosudil in RPE under oxidative/complement stress; consequently, the core hypothesis—TEER rescue with ROCK2 selectivity—remains inferential (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021).  
- No NaIO₃ or dry AMD-specific in vivo efficacy with belumosudil. While NaIO₃ single-cell data support EMT and fibroblast-like RPE signatures relevant to ROCK pathway targeting, belumosudil has not been tested in NaIO₃ or geographic atrophy models here; the current in vivo evidence is laser-injury fibrosis focused (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Isoform biology nuance in the retina. Diabetic retinal studies emphasize ROCK1 translocation and ROCK1-mediated blebbing/tight-junction disruption, with some reports noting ROCK2 localization as “undisturbed” in those models; this raises a strategic question whether ROCK2-selective inhibition alone is sufficient for barrier rescue across stress etiologies or whether dual inhibition is sometimes preferable (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).  
- Ocular pharmacokinetics and delivery. There are no data on ocular tissue penetration, retinal/choroidal exposure, or intravitreal/topical formulations for belumosudil; although systemic dosing engaged ocular targets in mice after laser injury, human ocular delivery, durability, and safety require specific assessment (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025). Class precedents (intravitreal/topical fasudil, topical netarsudil/ripasudil) are encouraging but not directly transferable to this scaffold without formulation work (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Off-target and pathway-network considerations. Although belumosudil is selective for ROCK2, it has minor ROCK1 and pathway-adjacent activities (e.g., mTOR), and widespread cytoskeletal re-tuning can have context-dependent effects (e.g., on ciliation) whose long-term retinal implications are unknown (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Lake et al., 2020).

Decision-oriented interpretation for dry AMD  
- Mechanistic plausibility: High. ROCK2 inhibition is expected to directly reduce cytoskeletal tension and stabilize epithelial junctions; on-pathway pharmacodynamic effects (↓p-MYPT1) and anti-fibrotic marker reductions in the choroid–RPE complex support action at the relevant tissue interface (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Translational anchor: Moderate. The candidate has a de-risked systemic safety profile and class-level ocular pharmacology, plus in vivo anti-fibrotic retinal benefits; however, barrier-specific efficacy in RPE under oxidative/complement stress has not yet been shown for belumosudil (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Differentiation vs pan-ROCK: Potentially favorable. In vivo, belumosudil achieved stronger ROCK2 engagement and larger decreases in “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations than fasudil, aligning with the idea that ROCK2 drives key profibrotic cascades at the choroid–RPE interface, while avoiding ROCK1-linked hypotension liabilities systemically; whether ROCK1 contributions to RPE barrier breakdown under certain stressors would limit efficacy remains to be determined experimentally (Zandi et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

Concrete implications for the proposed hypothesis  
- The specific claims that belumosudil has demonstrated +50% TER recovery in ARPE-19 under H₂O₂ stress, 40% RPE cell preservation and ERG improvement in a mouse NaIO₃ model, and an oral bioavailability ~45% with t₁/₂ ~4.8 h are not supported by the literature set provided; instead, the available PK indicates oral bioavailability is ~64% with food and a ~19-h half-life, and no TER/NaIO₃ efficacy data for belumosudil are referenced here (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). The hypothesized barrier rescue under oxidative/complement injury remains plausible mechanistically but requires direct validation in RPE models (Leong et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Program-level next steps (to enable a go/no-go)  
- In vitro RPE barrier assays: Primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE monolayers subjected to H₂O₂ and normal human serum (complement) injury; quantify TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and ZO-1/claudin-19 localization/intensity; include p-MYPT1 and p-MLC biochemical readouts as pharmacodynamics; benchmark belumosudil across a concentration range anchored to ROCK2 IC₅₀ and cell viability (Lake et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Phenotypic rescue breadth: Replicate class-level findings with ROCK2 selectivity—adhesion, wound closure, POS phagocytosis, RPE65 expression—to establish that belumosudil recapitulates the iPSC-RPE Y-27632 phenotype profile while tightening the barrier (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).  
- In vivo dry AMD model: NaIO₃ or other GA-like models with local ocular delivery (intravitreal or periocular sustained-release) to assess RPE survival, outer blood-retinal barrier integrity, visual function (ERG), and transcriptomic/IMC profiling for EMT/fibrosis and inflammatory modulation; include dose–exposure–response characterization (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Ocular PK/formulation: Ocular tissue distribution after local delivery and/or systemic administration; stability and duration; comparative exposures in RPE/choroid vs retina with safety assessment (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025).

Overall, belumosudil is a compelling, mechanistically aligned candidate with de-risked systemic safety, clear ocular on-pathway antifibrotic activity at the choroid–RPE interface, and strong biological rationale for junctional stabilization in stressed RPE. The decisive gap is the absence of direct barrier-function rescue data in RPE under oxidative or complement injury and the lack of dry AMD model efficacy. Addressing these with focused preclinical studies will determine whether its ROCK2 selectivity translates into clinically meaningful protection of the outer blood–retinal barrier in dry AMD, and whether it offers advantages over pan-ROCK inhibitors in this context (Zandi et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).
