Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Navitoclax (ABT-263) is a small‐molecule, orally bioavailable agent originally developed in the oncology arena as a BH3‐mimetic that targets several anti‐apoptotic members of the BCL-2 family, most notably BCL-2, BCL-xL, and BCL-W. This synthetic compound was designed through structure–activity relationship optimization to overcome the limitations of earlier compounds such as ABT-737, and it has since been classified as a senolytic agent owing to its ability to selectively induce apoptosis in senescent cells while sparing normal, quiescent cells. In the context of aging and degenerative diseases, the protective yet dysfunctional senescent cell phenotype is characterized by the upregulation of anti‐apoptotic proteins; therefore, compounds like ABT-263 that block these survival pathways have been repurposed as candidates to eliminate such senescent cells. The compound belongs to a broader class of therapeutics targeting the BCL-2 family, which have historically been exploited in various anti-cancer strategies and are now emerging as promising candidates for addressing age-associated disorders such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Ryu et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Navitoclax has a well-documented preclinical and clinical history in oncological models; its senolytic potential was first noted in studies where it selectively killed therapy-induced senescent tumor cells and other cell types by inhibiting anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins. Early clinical trials in small-cell lung cancer and lymphoid malignancies established proof-of-concept that targeting BCL-2/BCL-xL could result in tumor regression through apoptotic induction, although its clinical use was somewhat limited by dose-dependent toxicities such as thrombocytopenia. More recently, preclinical studies have extended its use beyond oncology: in in vitro studies and in mouse models where retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells were rendered senescent by doxorubicin treatment, navitoclax was shown to selectively induce apoptosis in the senescent cell population while largely sparing non-senescent RPE, as evidenced by decreased markers of senescence (p16, p21) and increased apoptotic markers such as cleaved caspases. Additionally, these studies demonstrated that oral administration of ABT-263 in mice resulted in reduced senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining and improved structural and functional retinal outcomes, including increased outer nuclear layer thickness and recovery of electroretinographic responses, which are highly encouraging for its repurposing in dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023). Despite these promising preclinical findings, navitoclax has not yet been tested in clinical trials for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative diseases, and its history in ocular conditions remains limited to proof-of-principle studies in animal models (Ryu et al., 2023; Khan et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, navitoclax exerts its senolytic action by competitively binding to the hydrophobic groove of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins, particularly BCL-2 and BCL-xL, thereby displacing pro-apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BIM. Under normal conditions, senescent cells upregulate these anti-apoptotic proteins as part of a survival mechanism against various stressors; the binding of navitoclax disrupts these protective interactions, leading to the activation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade. This biochemical disruption sets off a cascade of events culminating in mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, cytochrome c release, and the subsequent activation of caspases (notably caspase-9 and caspase-3), which orchestrate programmed cell death. Experimentally, cells treated with navitoclax have demonstrated an increased BAX/BCL-2 ratio along with elevated levels of cleaved caspases as measured by immunoblots, paralleling the reduction of canonical senescence markers such as p16 and p21. In the context of retinal degeneration, senescent RPE cells are known to secrete a deleterious senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)—including proinflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and IL-8 and matrix metalloproteases such as MMP2 and MMP9—that can undermine the integrity of junctional proteins such as ZO-1, leading to increased paracellular permeability. By eliminating these p16^Ink4a-positive senescent cells, navitoclax is hypothesized to reduce the inflammatory burden on the tissue microenvironment, thereby promoting the repopulation of healthy RPE cells and the restoration of tight junction continuity (Ryu et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of navitoclax for dry AMD is that the senolytic removal of p16^Ink4a-positive, senescent RPE cells will lead to a diminution of the SASP and its associated cytokines, such as IL-6 and IL-8, which are known to contribute to the degradation of tight junction proteins and compromise RPE barrier function. Experimental reports on navitoclax in senescent RPE models have indicated that treatment with ABT-263 not only leads to a reduction in senescence markers and SASP factor expression but also is accompanied by increased markers of cellular proliferation (e.g., Ki67) and partial recovery of structural features, such as an approximately 10% increase in outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in mouse models. While direct measurements of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and quantification of ZO-1 localization remain limited in these studies, immunofluorescence data do suggest improvements in junctional integrity following treatment with navitoclax. Thus, the expected biological effect is that clearance of senescent RPE will result in reduced paracrine inflammatory signaling, the reestablishment of stable ZO-1 belts, and overall restoration of the barrier properties of the RPE layer—a critical factor in the progression of dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
Navitoclax represents a promising therapeutic candidate as a repurposed senolytic agent for the treatment of dry AMD based on a convergence of preclinical biochemical, cellular, and animal model data. One of its primary strengths is its clear mechanism of action; by targeting a well-characterized survival pathway that is upregulated in senescent cells, navitoclax offers a rational strategy for the selective removal of dysfunctional p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells. The following sections provide a detailed analysis of the candidate’s origins, therapeutic history, mechanism of action, expected effects in relevant assays, and a balanced overall evaluation based on the current literature.

I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PXS-5153A is a synthetically derived molecule that belongs to the class of selective lysyl oxidase inhibitors. In its design, medicinal chemistry efforts focused on optimizing potency and selectivity for LOXL2, along with activity against LOXL3, two members of the lysyl oxidase family that catalyze the oxidative deamination of lysine residues in collagens and elastin to promote covalent crosslink formation. These crosslinks confer the mechanical strength and stiffness of extracellular matrices (ECMs) such as Bruch’s membrane. Synthetic routes to compounds like PXS-5153A typically rely on structure-based design and iterative optimization to achieve potent enzyme inhibition with favorable pharmacokinetic properties (Lin et al., 2020). The compound, commercially available under MedChemExpress HY-111217, is representative of a new therapeutic class that has been primarily explored in the context of fibrosis and tumor microenvironment modulation. Given that ECM stiffening is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, targeting LOXL2 represents a novel approach compared to conventional anti-inflammatory or anti-angiogenic strategies.

II. Therapeutic History  
The LOXL2 inhibitor class, including molecules such as PXS-5153A, has been extensively tested in preclinical models of fibrosis and cancer. For example, within non-ocular systems, LOXL2 activity has been linked to increased tissue stiffness that fosters metastatic progression and desmoplastic reactions in tumors, and selective inhibition of LOXL2 has been shown to reduce crosslink density, attenuating fibrotic remodeling (Lin et al., 2020). Experimental inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity using non-selective agents like β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) has also been applied to in vitro and in vivo models to modulate ECM assembly, with effects on barrier function observed in RPE cultures co-treated with endothelial cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). Although LOXL2 inhibitors have not traditionally been used to treat dry AMD, evidence underscores the centrality of aberrant ECM crosslinking in BM thickening observed during aging and AMD progression (Wang et al., 2025). In particular, the endothelial cell–RPE crosstalk studies demonstrate a critical role for lysyl oxidase activity in regulating collagen bundle formation and in establishing RPE barrier properties (Benedicto et al., 2017). Accordingly, while there is no direct clinical or preclinical record of PXS-5153A in AMD, the antifibrotic profile of the compound and its impact on extracellular matrix mechanics in other disease contexts serve as a compelling rationale to explore its application in dry AMD.

III. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, LOXL2 catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of lysine or hydroxylysine residues present in collagens and elastin. This reaction is critical for the formation of covalent crosslinks that stabilize the ECM. Overexpression or hyperactivity of LOXL2 results in an excessively crosslinked and stiff matrix. In the eye, particularly within Bruch’s membrane—which is a complex, stratified ECM structure located between the RPE and the choroid—aberrant collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking are known to increase mechanical tension. Such mechanical changes are thought to adversely affect RPE cell function by interfering with integrin-mediated cell–matrix interactions and perturbing the proper localization of tight junction proteins, including ZO-1 and occludin (Benedicto et al., 2017).

PXS-5153A functions by binding to the catalytic pocket of LOXL2, thereby preventing its enzymatic activity. By blocking the oxidative deamination step, PXS-5153A reduces the formation of both immature and mature crosslinks in ECM proteins. The anticipated outcome is a lower crosslink density in Bruch’s membrane, resulting in a softer, more compliant matrix environment. This reduction in mechanical stiffness is expected to diminish abnormal mechanosignaling through β1 integrins, which are integral to the assembly and maintenance of tight junctions on RPE cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). The downstream consequences of reduced integrin activation include dampening of Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways, which in turn facilitate the stabilization and proper localization of tight junction proteins at the RPE cell membranes (Benedicto et al., 2017). Restoration of these junctional complexes correlates with improved barrier function, typically measured as an increased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in cell culture models. This mechanism is supported by studies in which inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity—by pharmacological agents such as BAPN—led to alterations in RPE barrier properties and tight junction morphology (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by directly targeting LOXL2, PXS-5153A is proposed to correct the pathological ECM remodeling that underlies BM stiffening in dry AMD while re-establishing proper RPE barrier integrity.

IV. Expected Effect  
The expected therapeutic effect of PXS-5153A in dry AMD centers on normalization of the BM ECM and concomitant restoration of RPE barrier function. In the proposed experimental model—an in vitro co-culture system where human fetal RPE (hfRPE) cells are grown on a substrate mimicking BM with defined stiffness—the application of PXS-5153A at concentrations around 5 µM is anticipated to yield a number of favorable outcomes.

First, by reducing LOXL2-mediated crosslinking of collagen IV and fibronectin, the drug should decrease the mechanical stiffness of the BM analog. A less rigid BM reduces aberrant integrin activation on the basolateral surfaces of RPE cells, which has been shown to be critical for proper tight junction assembly. In several studies, when the extracellular matrix is normalized—such as by altering substrate stiffness—there is an improvement in the localization of key tight junction proteins, specifically occludin and ZO-1, at the cell membrane (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Second, the reduced matrix stiffness is expected to alleviate the mechanical stress experienced by RPE cells, thereby facilitating the re-establishment of cell polarity and intercellular junction continuity. The stabilization of junctional complexes is measurable by TEER. In previous EC–RPE co-culture experiments, modulation of ECM mechanical properties directly correlated with increased TEER values, reflecting improved barrier function (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Moreover, the proper organization of the basement membrane is not only a structural consideration; the biochemical signaling through β1 integrin receptors—critical for maintaining cell adhesion and survival—would return toward homeostatic levels, further supporting the integrity of the RPE layer (Benedicto et al., 2017). These integrin-mediated signals influence downstream effectors such as Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK, which have been implicated in regulating tight junction dynamics (Benedicto et al., 2017). Progress in these pathways is expected to manifest as an overall improvement in the barrier phenotype, which is central to preventing the leakage of fluid and other deleterious solutes into the subretinal space—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.

In summary, it is anticipated that treatment with PXS-5153A in appropriate in vitro (and ultimately in vivo) models will lead to:  
• Reduced collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in BM, yielding a matrix with decreased stiffness (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Normalization of β1 integrin signaling and subsequent reorganization of RPE tight junctions with improved localization of proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Restoration of barrier function as evidenced by increased TEER measurements and improved paracellular permeability profiles (Benedicto et al., 2017).  

Thus, PXS-5153A is expected to address one of the core aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis by targeting ECM remodeling, which in turn indirectly stabilizes RPE cell function.

V. Overall Evaluation  
The concept of using PXS-5153A to modulate ECM pathology in dry AMD is compelling given the mechanistic insights derived from studies on lysyl oxidase activity in epithelial barrier function and ECM assembly. Among the strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its robust preclinical evidence in fibrosis and tumor microenvironment models. LOXL2 has been implicated in promoting tissue stiffening by catalyzing the crosslinking of collagen and fibronectin in various tissues (Lin et al., 2020). The pathophysiological parallels between fibrotic ECM remodeling in cancers and the stiffening of Bruch’s membrane in dry AMD provide a strong rationale for repurposing a LOXL2 inhibitor in an ocular context. Numerous studies have demonstrated that extracellular matrix integrity is essential for optimal RPE barrier function, and that even subtle changes in ECM mechanics can disrupt junctional complexes and lead to barrier dysfunction (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by targeting a critical enzymatic step in ECM crosslinking, PXS-5153A may confer dual benefits: it could both reduce the pathological stiffening of Bruch’s membrane and promote the reorganization of tight junction complexes, ultimately resulting in enhanced TEER and stabilization of the outer blood–retina barrier.

However, several important weaknesses or uncertainties must be considered. First, while numerous studies (using agents such as BAPN) have illustrated that lysyl oxidase inhibition affects RPE barrier function, direct evidence with selective LOXL2 inhibitors—specifically in ocular models of dry AMD—is lacking (Buniello et al., 2025). In fact, the Open Targets Platform indicates only a weak direct association between LOXL2 and age-related macular degeneration, based on limited literature evidence (Buniello et al., 2025). This raises the possibility that, although LOXL2 plays a demonstrable role in ECM crosslinking in other tissues, its specific involvement in dry AMD pathogenesis may not be as pronounced or may be influenced by other factors not recapitulated in non-ocular models.

Furthermore, potential off-target effects or the consequences of broadly altering ECM crosslinking in the eye must be carefully examined. The structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane is critical not only for its barrier function but also for nutrient transport between the choroidal circulation and the RPE. Overinhibition of LOXL2, or interference with normal ECM turnover, may inadvertently lead to basement membrane disorganization, as has been observed when lysyl oxidase activity was inhibited during critical periods of retinal development (Benedicto et al., 2017). This underscores the need for precise dose optimization and targeted delivery, ideally restricted to the ocular environment, to avoid systemic side effects.

Another consideration is the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. In addition to ECM stiffening, dry AMD involves multifactorial processes including oxidative stress, complement activation, inflammation, and the accumulation of lipoprotein deposits. Thus, while normalizing matrix stiffness is likely to improve RPE barrier function, it may be insufficient to fully arrest or reverse the disease process on its own. A combination therapy that also addresses the inflammatory and degenerative components of AMD may eventually be required (Benedicto et al., 2017; Caban et al., 2022).

From a development perspective, there is significant strength in the repurposing strategy because agents like PXS-5153A already have a detailed preclinical profile in non-ocular fibrotic models. This existing data can accelerate preclinical validation in ocular models, with studies planned in RPE–BM co-culture systems using TEER as a functional readout (Benedicto et al., 2017). Furthermore, leveraging well-characterized in vitro assays (such as those involving decellularized ECM and substrate stiffness modulation as described in the context) offers a clear experimental framework to evaluate whether the normalization of BM stiffness by PXS-5153A is sufficient to restore RPE tight junction integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017).

Nonetheless, one notable weakness is the limited direct evidence linking LOXL2 specifically to dry AMD. Although elevated lysyl oxidase activity and changes in collagen crosslinking have been observed in the context of RPE barrier function and BM integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017), the genetic and translational data associating LOXL2 with AMD are not robust. The relatively low association score (Buniello et al., 2025) suggests that additional studies are needed to clarify LOXL2’s role in the eye and to determine whether its inhibition will yield a therapeutically meaningful benefit in dry AMD patients.

In conclusion, repurposing PXS-5153A for dry AMD represents an innovative strategy that leverages the known antifibrotic effects of LOXL2 inhibition to address the deleterious ECM remodeling observed in aged Bruch’s membrane. The candidate’s synthetic origins and prior applications in fibrosis and cancer studies provide a solid foundation for its use, while the mechanistic rationale—centered on reducing pathological crosslinking and restoring RPE barrier function—is strongly supported by evidence from ECM modulation studies (Benedicto et al., 2017). However, challenges remain due to the lack of direct ocular data, potential risks of overmodulating ECM integrity, and the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology. Future research must focus on rigorous in vitro validation in RPE–BM co-culture systems and in vivo studies in relevant AMD animal models to establish the efficacy and safety profile of PXS-5153A in the context of dry AMD. Overall, despite these uncertainties, PXS-5153A holds promise as a novel ECM-targeted therapeutic candidate that could complement existing and emerging treatment strategies for this currently unmet clinical need (Lin et al., 2020; Buniello et al., 2025).

Taken together, the strengths of a clear mechanism of action, potent enzyme selectivity, and an innovative approach toward ECM normalization position PXS-5153A as an attractive candidate warranting further investigation. Nonetheless, a careful reappraisal of the molecular role of LOXL2 in the ocular microenvironment, along with detailed studies on dosing, delivery, and potential off-target effects, will be critical in determining whether this candidate can be successfully repurposed for treating dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bexarotene is a fully synthetic retinoid analog classified as a rexinoid, specifically acting as a pan–retinoid X receptor (RXR) agonist. It was originally developed through structure–activity relationship studies aimed at mimicking the natural ligand 9-cis retinoic acid, while providing greater receptor selectivity, improved potency, and a pharmacological profile amenable to therapeutic use. Its synthesis and subsequent discovery were driven by the need to harness RXR‐mediated gene regulation, and it subsequently became the only FDA-approved synthetic RXR ligand to date (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). As a member of the retinoid drug class, bexarotene has been primarily used in the oncological setting, specifically for the treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, and its chemical design reflects modifications that impart high lipophilicity and receptor specificity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018). This synthetic derivation distinguishes it from naturally occurring retinoids and underpins its utility across a number of experimental and clinical contexts.

Therapeutic History:  
Bexarotene’s clinical history is marked by its approval as a second-line therapy for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, which provided a strong basis for its safety and efficacy in a human disease setting (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). In addition to its primary use in oncology, preclinical and early clinical research has investigated bexarotene for applications in neurodegenerative diseases, most notably Alzheimer’s disease and multiple sclerosis. These studies have demonstrated that RXR activation by bexarotene can influence the clearance of pathological protein aggregates and promote remyelination, respectively (Gaunt, 2020; Behl et al., 2022). However, despite the broad mechanistic appeal of RXR agonism in modifying lipid metabolism and neuroinflammation, there is little to no established clinical or veterinary precedent for employing bexarotene in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative conditions. In fact, while several RXR agonists have been considered in various models of ocular disease, the role of RXR in the diseased retina remains underexplored, with only sparse reports such as a study with the RXR agonist PA024 in retinal degeneration models (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). This gap in therapeutic history presents both a challenge and an opportunity in repurposing bexarotene for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
Bexarotene exerts its pharmacological effects primarily by binding to the ligand-binding domain of RXR isoforms (RXRα, RXRβ, and RXRγ) with nanomolar potency, inducing conformational changes that favor the recruitment of coactivators and subsequent transcriptional activation of targeted genes (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). RXR is a promiscuous nuclear receptor that forms obligate heterodimers with several other nuclear receptors, most notably the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) such as PPARγ. In doing so, the bexarotene-induced RXR/PPARγ heterodimer binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the genome, thereby upregulating target genes involved in lipid metabolism and transport. One key target is ABCA1, an ATP-binding cassette transporter implicated in cholesterol efflux from cells, which plays a central role in maintaining intracellular lipid homeostasis (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the activation of the RXR/PPARγ pathway is particularly compelling. RPE cells are highly involved in the processing and clearance of lipids, including cholesterol, and in modulating the structural integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier via tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 and occludin. When under stress—such as exposure to cytotoxic mediators like 7-ketocholesterol (7KCh), which disrupts normal junctional organization and reduces transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—the activation of RXR offers a potential therapeutic avenue. Bexarotene’s ability to stimulate RXR signaling is expected to upregulate ABCA1 expression, thereby enhancing cholesterol efflux, while also promoting the transcription of genes that lead to the re-expression of claudin-1 and occludin, which are critical for restoring barrier integrity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

The biochemical interactions following RXR activation by bexarotene include a cascade of events where the ligand-receptor complex alters the transcriptional landscape of the cell. This process entails the heterodimerization of RXR with its partner receptor, binding to DNA response elements, and initiating the recruitment of transcriptional coactivators, which together drive the expression of genes that modulate lipid metabolism, inflammatory responses, and cell junction integrity. The specificity of bexarotene for RXR, as opposed to broader retinoic acid receptor (RAR) activity, allows for a more targeted enhancement of these pathways—a factor that is crucial in tissues like the RPE, where precise regulation of lipid handling and barrier properties is essential for retinal health (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underlying the repurposing of bexarotene for dry AMD is that its activation of RXR in RPE cells will facilitate heterodimerization with PPARγ, driving the transcriptional upregulation of lipid-handling genes, most notably ABCA1. In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have provided compelling preliminary data indicating that exposure to 0.5 µM bexarotene in the presence of 7-ketocholesterol stress is capable of restoring TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values and significantly increasing ABCA1 mRNA levels. This restoration of TEER suggests that bexarotene not only promotes cholesterol efflux by upregulating ABCA1 but also exerts a beneficial influence on the expression of key tight junction proteins, such as claudin-1 and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity of the RPE barrier (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

The expected molecular effect in the assay is thus twofold. First, through its molecular interaction with RXR, bexarotene reinforces the RXR/PPARγ heterodimer formation, triggering a cascade of gene transcription events that culminate in enhanced cholesterol efflux via ABCA1. This effect directly addresses the accumulation of lipid deposits that contribute to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. Second, by re-inducing the expression of claudin-1 and occludin, bexarotene is anticipated to improve cellular junctional integrity, thereby reducing paracellular leakage and restoring the overall barrier function of the RPE as measured by TEER. The use of ocular gel formulations for local delivery promises to concentrate the therapeutic effect within the eye, circumventing the systemic adverse effects that are typically associated with bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties, such as high lipophilicity and low systemic solubility (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of bexarotene as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is founded upon a robust mechanistic rationale and promising preliminary in vitro data, yet it also presents several challenges that must be addressed through rigorous further research. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its well-established mode of action as a selective RXR agonist. Its ability to promote heterodimerization with PPARγ and subsequently upregulate genes such as ABCA1 is well supported by a substantial body of research in other disease contexts, including neurodegeneration and oncology (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Gaunt, 2020). This receptor specificity not only underscores bexarotene’s potential to modulate RPE lipid metabolism but also suggests that similar pharmacological principles could translate into the restoration of tight junction integrity—a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD.

Another significant strength is its prior clinical approval for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. This provides a substantial amount of safety data and experience in human use, which could expedite the repurposing process under a drug repositioning strategy. Moreover, the observed in vitro effects—namely the partial restoration of TEER and the increase in ABCA1 mRNA in stressed ARPE-19 cells—lend direct support to the hypothesis that RXR agonism can counteract 7-ketocholesterol-induced disruptions in RPE function (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). The concept of using ocular gel formulations to achieve localized delivery and thereby minimize systemic side effects is another innovative aspect that addresses one of the traditional limitations of bexarotene, namely its adverse systemic metabolic disturbances, which include dyslipidemia and hypothyroidism (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021).

However, there are notable weaknesses that temper this optimism. First, bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties—its high lipophilicity and low solubility—pose a significant formulation challenge, especially when transitioning from systemic oncology applications to local ocular delivery. While gel formulations offer a potential solution, achieving the precise pharmacokinetics and adequate tissue penetration in the retina will require meticulous formulation development and validation. Second, despite the extensive research on RXR agonism in other tissues, there is very limited precedent for the use of bexarotene or similar compounds in the treatment of dry AMD or related ocular diseases. In other words, while the underlying nuclear receptor biology in the retina is compelling, the absence of prior clinical or even robust preclinical ocular studies increases the risk associated with translational uncertainty (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Moreover, systemic side effects associated with bexarotene have been well documented in its approved indications. Although the strategy of localized ocular delivery aims to mitigate these adverse effects, any leakage from the ocular compartment into systemic circulation could potentially re-expose patients to these risks. Additionally, the complexity of dry AMD as a multifactorial disease—with contributions from oxidative stress, inflammation, and complex extracellular matrix alterations—means that modulating only lipid handling and tight junction integrity might not be sufficient to arrest or reverse disease progression. Thus, while the mechanistic hypothesis is sound, it should ideally be integrated into a broader therapeutic strategy that also addresses other pathological mechanisms in dry AMD.

In summary, the proposed use of bexarotene for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic foundation based on RXR agonism and its downstream effects on lipid metabolism and cellular junction integrity. The preliminary in vitro evidence in ARPE-19 cells under 7-ketocholesterol stress is promising, particularly with the reported restoration of TEER and upregulation of ABCA1. The strengths of this candidate include its specificity for RXR, the translational potential backed by its FDA–approved status for an unrelated indication, and the innovative strategy of local ocular delivery through gel formulations. On the other hand, challenges related to its physicochemical properties, potential for systemic side effects, and the overall gaps in preclinical ocular data necessitate further rigorous research. Preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD and careful formulation optimization will be essential next steps to validate the therapeutic potential of bexarotene in this context (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate generated from the glucosinolate glucoraphanin by the β-thioglucosidase myrosinase, which is abundant in cruciferous vegetables (notably broccoli sprouts). Its electrophilic –N=C=S moiety underlies covalent reactivity with nucleophilic cysteines on sensor proteins, most prominently Keap1, and thereby triggers a broad antioxidant and cytoprotective transcriptional response controlled by Nrf2 (NFE2L2) via antioxidant response elements (AREs) in gene promoters (phase-2 enzymes, redox systems, and detoxification pathways) (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). In retinal and epithelial contexts, SFN has been repeatedly characterized as an “indirect antioxidant” that elevates glutathione (GSH) and induces ARE-dependent enzymes such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1/HMOX1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and thioredoxin (Trx1), among others (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Tanito et al., 2005; Liu & Yan, 2018). In human RPE-derived cell models, SFN increased GSH and induced NQO1 and GST, consistent with canonical ARE program activation (Zhou et al., 2006). In vivo ocular models show SFN attenuates retinal light damage and improves functional outcomes, further anchoring its relevance to oxidative injury in the outer retina and RPE (Tanito et al., 2005; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Within its class, SFN is a prototypical dietary electrophile that activates Nrf2 signaling; this class has been broadly studied for chemoprevention and cytoprotection across organs. In ocular tissues, SFN has been shown to protect RPE and photoreceptors from diverse oxidative and phototoxic insults, often in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Yang et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025). Beyond Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α cross-talk, PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ stress-response nodes, and autophagy/lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs (TFEB/TFE3), all of which intersect with oxidative, inflammatory, and proteostasis stress pathways in RPE biology (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025).

Practical development considerations include bioavailability and delivery. Human studies and reviews indicate that the bioactive isothiocyanate is formed from glucoraphanin in a process heavily dependent on myrosinase (plant or microbiota), with documented systemic exposure and biomarker modulation in clinical settings; however, SFN’s oral bioavailability is limited by solubility, first-pass metabolism, and short plasma half-life, posing translational challenges for ocular exposure through blood–ocular barriers (Zhang et al., 2024). Preclinical delivery strategies such as nanoparticle and albumin carrier systems have been proposed to overcome ocular delivery constraints (Zhang et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
SFN and related Nrf2 activators have a long history as cytoprotective agents in preclinical models spanning oncology prevention, vascular and metabolic protection, and neuroprotection. In humans, SFN or broccoli sprout preparations have been administered in controlled trials with documented pharmacodynamic biomarker changes and well-characterized disposition and metabolism; crossover and dose-response studies highlight interconversion with related isothiocyanates (erucin) and underscore the importance of active myrosinase for consistent systemic exposure (Zhang et al., 2024; Qin, 2007). A pilot study detected SFN metabolites in human breast tissue after a single oral broccoli sprout dose, demonstrating tissue penetration to an epithelial compartment and supporting oral bioavailability to peripheral tissues (Qin, 2007). Although multiple clinical contexts are covered in these translational reviews and trials, there are no reported clinical trials of SFN specifically targeting dry AMD or RPE degeneration in the provided material (Zhang et al., 2024).

In ocular systems, the compound’s therapeutic history is robust at the preclinical level. In cultured human RPE, SFN protects against photooxidative injury (A2E/blue light) and chemical oxidants, increases GSH, and induces phase-2 enzymes including NQO1 and GST (Zhou et al., 2006). Microarray and validation work in human RPE-19 cells demonstrate SFN-induced nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and upregulation of thioredoxin-1, with enhanced oxidative stress resistance following H₂O₂ (Ye et al., 2013). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage in mice through ARE-mediated upregulation of thioredoxin (Trx1), and recovers cone function in a model of RPE oxidative stress in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025). SFN also protects rodent retinas from ischemia–reperfusion injury by increasing Nrf2 nuclear accumulation and HO-1 expression; pharmacologic inhibition of HO-1 abolishes protection, causally implicating HO-1 (Pan et al., 2014). In inherited retinal degeneration models (rd10 and tubby), systemic SFN improves retinal function and reduces degeneration, with evidence that ERK signaling and the Trx/TrxR/Nrf2 axis mediate effects in some settings (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Comparable ocular benefits have been shown in non-RPE tissues. For example, human corneal endothelial FECD cells exhibit SFN-induced Nrf2 nuclear translocation and upregulation of canonical ARE genes (NQO1, HO-1), with reduced ROS and apoptosis (Ziaei et al., 2013). In corneal surface epithelium, SFN protects against oxidative stress via Nrf2/HO-1 activation, supporting generalizability across ocular epithelial cell types (Liu & Yan, 2018). These data reinforce the core mechanism and pharmacology relevant to RPE while underlining the absence of AMD-specific clinical translation to date (Zhang et al., 2024).

Notably, although there is a recent report in an inflamed ARPE-19 model that vitamin D and SFN (alone and combined) reduced ROS, reduced IL-6/IL-8, lowered VEGF, and restored epithelial integrity markers including ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression, the provided material does not include functional barrier endpoints (TEER or FITC-dextran permeability), and claudin-1 is not shown (Bergandi et al., 2024). Thus, while “marker restoration” has been reported for ZO-1 and claudin-4 under TGF-β stress, quantitative barrier function restoration has not yet been demonstrated within the provided sources (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary mechanism—Keap1 cysteine targeting and Nrf2 activation: SFN’s electrophilic isothiocyanate group reacts with redox-sensitive cysteines on Keap1 (notably Cys151), disrupting the Cul3–Keap1 E3 ligase complex and stabilizing Nrf2, which accumulates and translocates to the nucleus. There, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences to upregulate a broad enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant and detoxification program (e.g., NQO1, HO-1, GSTs, GCLM, Trx1, SRXN1), increasing cellular reductive capacity (GSH pools, thiol buffering) and restoring redox homeostasis under oxidative stress (Chang et al., 2020; Ziaei et al., 2013; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). In RPE models, SFN does not consistently increase Nrf2 transcription but promotes nuclear translocation and DNA-binding activity, consistent with post-translational stabilization and activation; ARE target induction follows (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). In ARPE-19, SFN preconditioning increases NQO1 mRNA/activity, boosts cellular GSH, and increases GST activity; microarray and validation data add induction of SRXN1, GCLM, and Trx1 with concurrent Txnip downregulation, aligning with amplified reductive and detoxification capacity (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Under t-BHP stress, SFN increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, elevates NQO1, GR, and GPx1 transcripts, and drives HO-1, NQO1, and GR protein induction (with partial discordance between GPx1 mRNA and protein), while reducing proinflammatory ICAM-1 and MCP-1 (Chang et al., 2020).

Nrf2-dependent ocular efficacy: In vivo, SFN protection from retinal ischemia–reperfusion requires HO-1, as HO-1 inhibition reverses neuroprotection (Pan et al., 2014). In a model of RPE oxidative stress in middle-aged mice, SFN restores cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, underscoring that Nrf2 is the mechanistic driver in that age-relevant retinal context (Falcão et al., 2025).

Nrf2-independent and auxiliary mechanisms: RPE protection is not exclusively Nrf2-dependent. SFN has been shown to promote mitochondrial fusion and reduce Drp1-mediated fission, conferring anti-apoptotic benefit even in CRISPR/Cas9 Nrf2-depleted RPE cells (RPE-1), indicating a parallel mitochondrial protective program (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). SFN also engages the PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ axis: SFN or its metabolites can blunt damage-induced PARylation via direct PARP1 interactions, alleviating SIRT1 inhibition, promoting autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis, and decreasing inflammation in RPE models (Wang & Tang, 2022). In blue light–exposed RPE, SFN activates the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 axis, upregulates HO-1 and thioredoxin-1, blocks NF-κB nuclear translocation, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, and enhances autophagy, all contributing to cytoprotection; Nrf2 inhibition abrogates SFN’s protective effect in this system (Yang et al., 2021). SFN can also activate lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs that mitigate oxidative stress; KEAP1–NRF2 cross-talk with TFEB/TFE3 and macroautophagy has been documented, offering a mechanistic link between Nrf2 activation and proteostasis/autophagy enhancement relevant to RPE degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025).

Anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic effects: Across RPE models, SFN suppresses proinflammatory mediators and pathways (e.g., reduces ICAM-1 and MCP-1; inhibits NF-κB activation), and in TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19 reduces VEGF secretion, which is relevant to para-inflammatory remodeling in AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024). These effects likely contribute to preservation of junctional homeostasis by dampening cytokine-driven disruption.

Cell-type and context dependence: SFN response varies by cell type, stressor, and age-dependent pathway integrity. In some models, HO-1 mRNA is not induced even when protein rises, and under reduced Nrf2 function (as may occur in aged RPE), SFN efficacy can be limited, indicating a dependence on intact Nrf2 signaling and potential post-transcriptional regulation (Chang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Dosing and context also matter: low micromolar SFN protects RPE under oxidative stress, whereas very high concentrations can be deleterious in vitro (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Evidence for barrier-relevant endpoints: The provided sources do not present RPE TEER or FITC-dextran permeability data for SFN, and do not demonstrate claudin-1 induction in RPE (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024). One in vitro ARPE-19 TGF-β model reports that SFN (alone and with vitamin D) restores expression of ZO-1 and claudin-4 suppressed by TGF-β, reduces ROS and VEGF, and decreases proinflammatory cytokines; however, functional permeability or TEER measures were not included, and claudin-1 was not assessed (Bergandi et al., 2024). Therefore, SFN’s capacity to restore RPE barrier function remains mechanistically plausible—through redox normalization, suppression of inflammatory junctional disruption, and potential transcriptional effects on junctional proteins—but is not directly proven by barrier-function assays in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Assay context and rationale: The proposed assays—RPE monolayers subjected to A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ oxidative injury—interrogate oxidative stress pathways central to dry AMD pathophysiology and RPE barrier integrity. A2E/blue light models replicate lipofuscin-photosensitized oxidative injury; NaIO₃ models RPE oxidative cytotoxicity. In both settings, ROS accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, cytokine induction, and downstream tight-junction disruption degrade barrier integrity. The expectation is that SFN will activate Nrf2, increase reductive and detoxifying capacity (GSH, NQO1, HO-1, Trx1, GST), suppress NF-κB–driven inflammation, stabilize mitochondrial function, and secondarily preserve or restore tight-junction protein expression and continuity, resulting in improved TEER and reduced macromolecular flux (FITC-dextran) across the RPE monolayer.

Support for oxidative injury protection in RPE: In A2E/blue light–injured ARPE-19 monolayers, SFN preconditioning increases cell survival, elevates GSH, and induces NQO1 and GST—outcomes mechanistically consistent with improved tolerance to phototoxic oxidative stress (Zhou et al., 2006). In RPE challenged by chemical oxidants (t-BHP, H₂O₂), SFN reduces ROS, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, and induces NQO1, HO-1 (protein), GR, and GPx1 transcripts while suppressing ICAM-1 and MCP-1, thereby addressing both oxidative and inflammatory drivers of junctional disruption (Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013).

Support for HO-1/Nrf2 and auxiliary pathways: Under blue-light exposure, SFN activates Nrf2 and HO-1 in RPE with evidence of mechanistic necessity (Nrf2 inhibitor blocks protection), promotes autophagy (LC3BII and p62), and suppresses NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation—all changes that favor barrier preservation by limiting stress signaling and enhancing cellular cleanup mechanisms (Yang et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and RPE oxidative-stress mouse models, SFN-mediated rescue of retinal function depends on Nrf2 and HO-1, supporting the expected relevance of these axes in RPE-derived stress contexts (Pan et al., 2014; Falcão et al., 2025).

Evidence for junctional protein rescue: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, a recent report shows SFN (particularly with vitamin D) restores ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression suppressed by TGF-β, reduces IL-6/IL-8, reduces VEGF, and normalizes respiratory gene overexpression; this supports the expectation that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven loss of epithelial integrity markers (Bergandi et al., 2024). However, the provided material does not report TEER or FITC-dextran for SFN in RPE, and no data are provided for claudin-1 induction or ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity in oxidative (A2E/NaIO₃) models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Thus, while SFN is expected to improve TEER and reduce FITC-dextran flux in A2E or NaIO₃ assays through Nrf2-driven antioxidant enhancement and suppression of inflammatory/junctional injury, this is an unproven extrapolation that requires direct measurement in the proposed models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).

Target expression in RPE: All principal molecular targets are expressed in human RPE. Nrf2 activation and nuclear translocation occur in SFN-treated RPE-19/ARPE-19, with demonstrated induction of NQO1, HO-1 (protein in some contexts), thioredoxin-1, GCLM, and GST, and suppression of Txnip, ICAM-1, and MCP-1, anchoring the feasibility of modulating these axes in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2006). HO-1 induction in RPE is clearly shown under blue-light stress; in vivo retinal protection requires HO-1, reinforcing target relevance to oxidative retinal injury (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014).

Assay caveats: The provided literature does not contain RPE TEER or macromolecular flux data for SFN, nor does it document claudin-1 induction in RPE. Therefore, while SFN is expected to preserve barrier function, success criteria must include de novo demonstration of TEER rescue, FITC-dextran flux reduction, and ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity under A2E or NaIO₃ stress; these are critical data gaps to address in the proposed work (Zhang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic foundation in RPE and retina: SFN is a well-validated Nrf2 activator that increases GSH and induces multiple ARE-dependent genes (NQO1, GSTs, Trx1, GCLM; HO-1 in several ocular contexts) in RPE and retinal models, with reproducible protection against oxidative and phototoxic injury (A2E/blue light; H₂O₂/t-BHP) and anti-inflammatory activity (reduced ICAM-1, MCP-1, NF-κB signaling) (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage, improves ERG outcomes, rescues cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, and protects against ischemia–reperfusion via HO-1—clear evidence that the compound engages relevant biology and can deliver functional benefit in the retina (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2014).  
- Multiple converging protective axes: Beyond KEAP1–Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling, suppresses PARP1 overactivation to preserve NAD+/SIRT1, promotes autophagy/lysosome programs (TFEB/TFE3 linkage), and modulates mitochondrial dynamics (promotes fusion; reduces Drp1-mediated fission) even when Nrf2 is compromised. This polymechanistic profile is advantageous in RPE, where oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy, and inflammation co-drive degeneration (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2021; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).  
- Preliminary evidence for epithelial integrity marker restoration: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, SFN (especially with vitamin D) restored ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression and reduced VEGF, providing the first reported signal that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven epithelial marker loss in an RPE model (albeit without functional barrier assays) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Translational plausibility and human experience: SFN is orally administrable, with documented human systemic exposure and biomarker modulation; myrosinase co-administration enhances bioavailability from glucoraphanin. Although not yet tested clinically in dry AMD, SFN has a favorable translational narrative as a nutraceutical-derived Nrf2 activator with a safety and PD data trail in other indications (Zhang et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and gaps  
- No direct RPE barrier-function data: Across the provided literature there are no TEER or FITC-dextran permeability results for SFN in RPE monolayers, and no quantified immunofluorescence continuity data for ZO-1 or claudin-1 under oxidative stress. The sole report of “restored markers” addresses ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression after TGF-β, not barrier function or claudin-1 (Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024). The proposal’s assertion of TEER rescue and FITC-dextran reduction remains speculative pending direct measurement in A2E or NaIO₃ models (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Uncertain regulation of tight junction gene set: The provided RPE datasets document induction of canonical Nrf2 targets (NQO1, HO-1 in some contexts, Trx1, GCLM, GSTs), but do not demonstrate SFN induction of claudin-1 in RPE. Without evidence that SFN directly upregulates claudin-1 or stabilizes its junctional localization in RPE, the hypothesis of “junction-supporting gene induction” should be reframed as “junction-preserving via redox and anti-inflammatory mechanisms” until proven otherwise (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Delivery and exposure to the RPE: SFN’s solubility, short half-life, and first-pass metabolism limit systemic exposure; blood–ocular barriers further constrain retinal delivery. Several in vivo retinal studies used intraperitoneal dosing, and one report found i.p. more effective than oral for light-damage protection, emphasizing the need to optimize delivery for ocular targets. Nanocarriers and formulation strategies are promising but remain preclinical (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Dependence on Nrf2 competence and context: In models with impaired Nrf2 (potentially mirroring aged RPE), SFN efficacy is reduced; mechanisms such as mitochondrial fusion may provide partial rescue, but translational effect sizes could be diminished in elderly patients with Nrf2 decline. Additionally, gene-level responses show discordances (e.g., HO-1 mRNA vs protein), indicating context- and post-transcriptional control that complicate predictable pharmacodynamics (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity: Some cited studies are from lower-quality journals; while the core mechanistic findings are corroborated by higher-quality work (e.g., IOVS, Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology, PLoS ONE), the barrier-marker restoration report requires independent replication with functional readouts and in primary human RPE to solidify translational credibility (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Bergandi et al., 2024).

Decision implications and next steps  
Given the robust Nrf2/ARE activation, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory efficacy in RPE/retina, and the breadth of auxiliary protective mechanisms, SFN remains a mechanistically precise candidate for RPE oxidative injury relevant to dry AMD. However, the core claim of “barrier restoration” is currently supported only by marker-expression rescue (ZO-1 and claudin-4) in an inflamed ARPE-19 model without functional permeability data, and there is no evidence for claudin-1 induction or barrier rescue in A2E or NaIO₃ models in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). To de-risk the program and validate the hypothesis, the following experiments are mandatory:  
- TEER and FITC-dextran assays in differentiated human RPE (primary or iPSC-RPE) under A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ insult, with SFN dose–response and timing; include positive controls for barrier rescue (e.g., dexamethasone) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Quantitative junctional immunofluorescence (ZO-1, claudin-1, claudin-4, occludin) with continuity analysis; test whether SFN normalizes localization and expression under oxidative/cytokine stress (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Nrf2 pathway necessity tests (ML385, Nrf2 siRNA) and HO-1 inhibition (ZnPP) to define mechanism-of-action in barrier rescue; given HO-1’s necessity in vivo, confirm whether HO-1 contributes to barrier endpoints in RPE (Pan et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2021).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics and autophagy readouts (Drp1, Mfn2, LC3BII/p62) to quantify auxiliary pathways that may mediate barrier preservation when Nrf2 is compromised (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021).  
- PK/PD bridging: quantify SFN (and metabolites) in plasma and ocular tissues after oral vs i.p. dosing in rodents; evaluate delivery systems (e.g., albumin nanocarriers) for RPE exposure; incorporate myrosinase co-administration for oral strategies; relate exposures to effective in vitro EC₅₀s for barrier rescue (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Aged and Nrf2-impaired models: evaluate efficacy in aged RPE or Nrf2-hypomorphic contexts to assess translational robustness (Zhang et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

If TEER and permeability rescue are demonstrated with mechanistic attribution to Nrf2/HO-1 and/or auxiliary pathways, and if ocular PK can be solved to achieve efficacious exposures, SFN would merit progression to in vivo dry AMD–relevant models (e.g., subretinal NaIO₃, chronic photo-oxidative stress) with structural (OCT) and functional (ERG) endpoints, plus RPE barrier imaging, before considering a human proof-of-concept study.

In sum, the totality of evidence strongly supports SFN for oxidative and inflammatory protection of RPE and retina with multiple convergent mechanisms and translational plausibility. The critical missing element is direct demonstration that these effects translate into bona fide RPE barrier restoration (TEER/permeability) under AMD-relevant oxidative stress, and a practical path to deliver sufficient drug to the RPE in humans. Addressing these gaps should be the focus of immediate preclinical validation (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024).
