Below is a comprehensive evaluation of SB‐431542 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). The report is organized into five sections: an overview of the therapeutic candidate, a review of its therapeutic history, a detailed discussion of its molecular mechanism of action, an explanation of the expected effects in the proposed assay and ocular environment, and an overall evaluation of its potential strengths and weaknesses for treating dry AMD.

    1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB‐431542 is a fully synthetic small molecule that was discovered through high‐throughput screening efforts at GlaxoSmithKline and further optimized via systematic structure–activity relationship studies. Its chemical identity is defined by the IUPAC name 4-[4-(3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl)-5-(2-pyridyl)-1H-imidazol-2-yl]-benzamide, and it belongs to the triarylimidazole/benzamide structural class (Markell, 2010; Fuchs, 2011). During its development, medicinal chemists employed target-hopping strategies that involved modifying substituents – for example, replacing a 4-pyridyl group with a 2-pyridyl moiety and adding a 3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl ring – to retain TGF-β type I receptor (ALK5) inhibitory potency while minimizing unwanted inhibition of other kinases such as p38 MAPK (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This precise engineering ensures that SB-431542 acts as a competitive inhibitor at the ATP‐binding site of ALK5, thereby conferring selectivity relative to other kinases (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). As a member of a well‐defined class of small molecule kinase inhibitors, SB-431542 has been used extensively as a research tool in studies of TGF-β signaling and fibrosis, and its chemical properties suggest that it belongs to a broader family of agents that modulate receptor kinases via competitive binding (Laping et al., 2002).

    2. Therapeutic History  
SB-431542 has been at the forefront of preclinical research into TGF-β signaling because of its capacity to selectively block ALK5 and, to a lesser extent, related receptors such as ALK4 and ALK7 (Laping et al., 2002; Ge et al., 2004). Its primary use has been as a chemical probe to elucidate the role of TGF-β in diverse fibrotic and oncologic settings. In multiple in vitro and in vivo studies, SB-431542 has been shown to effectively inhibit TGF-β1-induced upregulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components including collagen Iα1, fibronectin, and plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI-1) in renal epithelial cells and fibroblast cultures (Laping et al., 2002). Its potent antifibrotic activity has also been demonstrated in ocular applications; for example, it has been utilized in experimental models of glaucoma filtration surgery to reduce subconjunctival scarring by curtailing fibroblast proliferation, myofibroblast transdifferentiation, and ECM deposition (Wang et al., 2017). Although SB-431542 has not yet been approved for clinical use in AMD or other retinal disorders, its well‐documented ability to inhibit TGF-β–mediated fibrosis in ocular tissues suggests that it holds promise for these indications (Teplitsky et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2009). In addition, the compound’s extensive deployment in cancer studies – where it is used to block the epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and invasion – further verifies its capacity to modulate key pathological processes that also underlie fibrotic changes observed in retinal degeneration (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010).

    3. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, SB-431542 functions as a competitive inhibitor of the TGF-β type I receptor (ALK5) by binding to its ATP binding site. Upon the engagement of TGF-β ligands with cell surface receptors, the type II receptor phosphorylates and activates ALK5. Activated ALK5 then phosphorylates receptor-regulated Smad proteins (Smad2 and Smad3), which subsequently form complexes with Smad4 and translocate into the nucleus to drive the transcription of genes encoding ECM proteins and other pro-fibrotic factors (Laping et al., 2002). SB-431542 directly inhibits this kinase activity by occupying the ATP pocket, thereby blocking the phosphorylation of Smad2/3 and preventing their nuclear accumulation (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This interruption of TGF-β signaling ultimately suppresses the induction of pro-fibrotic genes such as those for collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002).

Importantly, SB-431542 is characterized by its selectivity. Despite the structural similarities among kinases in the TGF-β receptor superfamily, the unique conformational features of ALK5 permit SB-431542 to inhibit it to a significantly greater extent than BMP receptors (ALK2, ALK3, and ALK6) or other non-Smad pathways such as those mediated by ERK, JNK, and p38 MAPK (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This selectivity minimizes off-target effects and allows the compound to function as a precise modulator of TGF-β–dependent fibrotic signaling (Laping et al., 2002; Ling & Lee, 2011). Moreover, by inhibiting ALK5 activity, SB-431542 not only downregulates ECM protein production but also interferes with EMT processes, which are implicated in the phenotypic conversion of epithelial cells to a more mesenchymal and migratory state – a conversion that has been observed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells under stress conditions (Radeke et al., 2015; Yoon et al., 2018). In this regard, SB-431542’s molecular interactions encompass hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic contacts within the ALK5 catalytic pocket, ensuring that its inhibitory activity is both potent (with reported IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range) and selective for the intended target (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002).

    4. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis for repurposing SB-431542 in dry AMD is that inhibiting TGF-β receptor activity in RPE cells and choroidal fibroblasts will reduce pathological ECM overproduction. In dry AMD, elevated levels of TGF-β1 have been implicated in promoting the deposition of fibrotic ECM components in Bruch’s membrane, leading to increased stiffness and altered mechanical forces on the RPE monolayer (Laping et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2009). The resulting stiffening of the extracellular matrix is believed to disrupt the normal anchorage of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity and transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) of the RPE barrier (Xiao et al., 2009; Teplitsky et al., 2023).

By blocking ALK5 and thereby attenuating Smad2/3 activation, SB-431542 is expected to suppress the transcription of genes encoding collagen Iα1, fibronectin, and PAI-1. A reduction in the synthesis and deposition of these ECM components should translate into a decrease in Bruch’s membrane stiffness and the mechanical tension imposed on the RPE (Laping et al., 2002). This, in turn, is anticipated to allow the re-establishment of a continuous network of tight junctions between RPE cells as ZO-1 and occludin are able to reassemble without the interference of a pathological ECM environment (Radeke et al., 2015; Higashijima et al., 2023). When tested in ECM-coated Transwell assays, the expectation is that treatment with SB-431542 will result in improved TEER readings and a restoration of barrier function indicative of normalized RPE physiology (Xiao et al., 2009; Yoon et al., 2018).

Furthermore, TGF-β signaling in RPE cells has been associated with epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a process that not only promotes fibrosis but also deteriorates the well-ordered epithelial phenotype critical for retinal homeostasis (Radeke et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2009). Inhibition of ALK5 is predicted to counteract EMT, thereby preserving the native epithelial characteristics of RPE cells. In this context, the reduction of fibrotic ECM production and the prevention of EMT would act in synergy to reduce the abnormal mechanical stresses on RPE, enhance the continuity of tight junction proteins, and ultimately help restore retinal barrier function (Laping et al., 2002).

Given that both RPE cells and choroidal fibroblasts express TGF-β receptors and respond to TGF-β stimulation, the application of SB-431542 in co-culture models or animal studies is expected to normalize the extracellular microenvironment. This normalization could rescue the mechanical integrity of Bruch’s membrane and improve nutrient/waste exchange across the RPE monolayer—factors that are crucial in slowing or reversing the degenerative progression in dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2009).

    5. Overall Evaluation  
An overall review of SB-431542 indicates that it is a scientifically compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its proven ability to modulate TGF-β signaling and its well-documented anti-fibrotic effects. One major strength of SB-431542 is its high degree of selectivity for ALK5; by competitively inhibiting the ATP binding site on this receptor, the compound effectively blocks the Smad2/3 phosphorylation cascade that ultimately leads to ECM overproduction (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). This mechanism has been validated in multiple preclinical models of fibrosis and ocular scarring, indicating that a similar strategy may be effective in the context of dry AMD where excessive ECM deposition in Bruch’s membrane is a central pathogenic feature (Xiao et al., 2009; Teplitsky et al., 2023).

Another point in favor of SB-431542 is its extensive use as a research tool in the investigation of TGF-β–dependent processes in both fibrosis and cancer. Its ability to reduce collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 levels in diverse cellular models underscores its therapeutic potential for attenuating pathological ECM production—a direct mechanism that could alleviate mechanical stress on RPE tight junctions and help restore barrier function, as measured by increased TEER and continuity of ZO-1/occludin (Laping et al., 2002).

From a mechanistic perspective, the detailed molecular interactions of SB-431542 have been characterized to a high degree, with studies demonstrating that its binding to the ALK5 catalytic pocket results in a clear inhibition of the profibrotic gene expression program (Laping et al., 2002; Ling & Lee, 2011). This precision in targeting is particularly important when considering ocular applications, as the retina is highly sensitive to off-target effects. By sparing other signaling pathways—such as those mediated by BMP receptors or Smad-independent cascades—the compound minimizes potential systemic or retinal toxicity (Laping et al., 2002).

Despite these strengths, there are also several challenges that must be addressed for SB-431542 to be successfully repurposed for dry AMD. One of the primary concerns is its pharmacokinetic profile. Preclinical studies in animal models have indicated that SB-431542 may have a relatively short half-life and rapid clearance, which raises questions about achieving sustained intraocular concentrations necessary for chronic conditions such as dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). To address this, development of a controlled-release ocular formulation—such as an intravitreal implant, microsphere-based delivery, or other sustained-release vehicle—will be essential for maintaining therapeutic levels over extended periods without systemic exposure.

Another significant challenge is the duality inherent in TGF-β signaling. While excessive TGF-β activity is responsible for the fibrotic changes observed in AMD, TGF-β also plays an important role in immune regulation, tissue repair, and maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Long-term blockade of TGF-β signaling may therefore carry inherent risks, including potential adverse effects on normal repair mechanisms or the promotion of unanticipated cellular changes such as malignant transformation (Markell, 2010; Schindeler et al., 2010). Careful dose-response studies and localized delivery strategies will be imperative to ensure that therapeutic benefits are achieved without tipping the balance toward deleterious side effects.

Moreover, although the preclinical data in ocular fibrosis models—such as those involving subconjunctival scarring after glaucoma filtration surgery—provide a promising rationale for the use of TGF-β inhibitors, direct evidence in models that recapitulate the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains limited (Xiao et al., 2009). Dry AMD is a complex disease involving not only fibrotic ECM accumulation but also oxidative stress, chronic low-grade inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation. Therefore, while the mechanistic rationale for using SB-431542 to reduce ECM production and restore RPE integrity is sound, it will likely need to be integrated into a broader therapeutic strategy that addresses these additional pathological drivers (Schindeler et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2017).

On the formulation front, the small molecule nature of SB-431542 offers both advantages and challenges. Its chemical tractability allows for modifications that could improve its ocular stability and bioavailability; however, achieving homogeneous distribution within the eye, ensuring drug stability in the vitreous environment, and avoiding direct retinal toxicity remain non-trivial challenges (Fuchs, 2011; Markell, 2010). Additionally, by virtue of its design as a competitive inhibitor, careful titration of dose will be required to ensure that effective ALK5 inhibition is sustained while minimizing interference with other cellular kinases that are essential for retinal cell survival.

In summary, SB-431542 shows significant promise as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to selectively inhibit ALK5 and thereby block the central pro-fibrotic Smad2/3 signaling axis aligns well with the mechanistic hypothesis that targeting TGF-β–mediated ECM overproduction can restore the biomechanical homeostasis of Bruch’s membrane and improve RPE barrier function (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002). The chemical and biochemical evidence supporting its anti-fibrotic effects—demonstrated by reduced collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 levels in multiple cell types and models—is compelling (Laping et al., 2002). Furthermore, preliminary ocular studies using SB-431542 in models of surgical scarring provide an encouraging precedent for its application in the retina (Wang et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2009).

However, the pathway to clinical translation is not without hurdles. The pharmacokinetics of SB-431542, characterized by a relatively short half-life, necessitate the development of innovative drug delivery systems to sustain intraocular levels over the chronic course of AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). Additionally, the multifaceted role of TGF-β in ocular physiology requires that any therapeutic intervention be carefully calibrated to avoid impairing normal tissue repair or immunologic function (Markell, 2010; Schindeler et al., 2010). Finally, given that dry AMD is a multifactorial disease rather than being driven solely by fibrosis, further preclinical studies employing comprehensive AMD models that encompass oxidative stress and inflammation will be crucial to validate the therapeutic potential of SB-431542 in this context (Teplitsky et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025).

Overall, SB-431542 represents a scientifically robust and mechanistically well-justified candidate for repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD. Its targeted inhibition of ALK5 offers a strategic means to reduce pathological ECM deposition and thereby alleviate the mechanical stress that undermines RPE tight junction integrity—a key factor implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Markell, 2010). The strengths of SB-431542 include its potency, selectivity, and extensive preclinical validation in fibrotic and ocular injury models. In contrast, its weaknesses center on pharmacokinetic limitations, the challenges of ocular delivery, and the complexity of broadly inhibiting a cytokine pathway that also serves beneficial roles.  

In conclusion, while additional formulation work and targeted preclinical studies remain essential, the accumulated evidence from biochemical, cellular, and ocular studies strongly supports the further evaluation of SB-431542 as part of a mechanobiology‐based therapeutic strategy for dry AMD. Given that dry AMD currently lacks effective treatments and that pathological ECM accumulation in Bruch’s membrane is a critical driver of disease progression, the repurposing of SB-431542 could provide a novel means to restore RPE barrier function by reducing ECM stiffness and re-establishing tight junction continuity (Xiao et al., 2009). Future research should focus on optimizing local delivery—potentially via sustained-release intravitreal formulations—and integrating SB-431542 within a combination therapy framework that additionally targets oxidative stress and inflammation. With these measures in place, SB-431542 holds significant promise as an innovative candidate in the quest for effective treatments for dry AMD (Markell, 2010; Laping et al., 2002).

Thus, based on its synthetic origin, proven preclinical anti-fibrotic and anti-EMT effects, and detailed mechanistic rationale, SB-431542 merits further development for dry AMD. A rigorous, methodologically robust preclinical program – including pharmacokinetic optimization, ocular toxicity studies, and validation in relevant AMD models – will be crucial to determine whether the benefits observed in laboratory assays can be translated into meaningful clinical improvements in retinal structure and function.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SAR407899 (Selleckchem S2921) is a small-molecule ATP-competitive inhibitor of Rho-associated coiled-coil containing kinases (ROCKs) that targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2, placing it within the widely studied class of dual ROCK1/2 inhibitors used as chemical tools and therapeutic candidates across vascular, fibrotic, and ocular indications driven by actomyosin contractility and cytoskeletal dysregulation (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). The ATP-binding pockets of ROCK1 and ROCK2 are highly conserved, which has historically favored development of dual-isoform inhibitors (e.g., fasudil, Y-27632, ripasudil, netarsudil) rather than isoform-selective agents; SAR407899 is listed among this majority class of dual-acting molecules in contemporary reviews of rho-kinase modulators for retinal disease (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Multiple dual ROCK inhibitors have been clinically applied: fasudil is approved systemically for cerebral vasospasm and has been evaluated intravitreally for retinal disease, while ripasudil and netarsudil are approved as topical ophthalmic solutions for glaucoma/ocular hypertension, establishing the translational precedent and safety framework for the class in ocular tissues (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). At a mechanistic level, all members of this class block ROCK catalytic activity by binding to the ATP site, thereby reducing phosphorylation of canonical substrates such as MYPT1 (the myosin phosphatase target subunit) and myosin regulatory light chain (MLC), and decreasing downstream actomyosin tension, stress fibers, and focal adhesion assembly that collectively drive barrier breakdown, contraction, and fibrosis (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). While “soft drug” and kinase-selectivity strategies have been advanced to improve tissue targeting and reduce off-target activity, the broad conclusion from medicinal chemistry and pharmacology reviews is that most clinical-grade ROCK inhibitors remain dual-isoform ATP-competitive agents with some potential for off-target kinase interactions at higher exposures—an interpretive caveat for both efficacy and safety (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Liu et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Direct preclinical or clinical reports on SAR407899 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) or age-related macular degeneration (AMD) were not identified in the provided literature set; the compound is listed among “double-acting ROCK inhibitor molecules” considered for retinal vascular disease, but no SAR407899-specific ocular pharmacokinetic, penetration, or efficacy data are supplied in the excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). In contrast, there is substantial class-level evidence that dual ROCK1/2 inhibition is active in posterior segment disease biology relevant to dry AMD pathogenesis and sequelae (barrier failure, low-grade inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling), and that ROCK pathway blockade by other chemotypes can beneficially modulate RPE/retinal fibrosis and endothelial barrier endpoints across models (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). For endothelial barrier function, ripasudil preserved ZO-1 localization and reversed VEGF-induced TEER loss in human retinal microvascular endothelial cells (HRMECs), and suppressed retinal p-MYPT1 in a murine retinal vein occlusion model, demonstrating target engagement and barrier preservation by ROCK inhibition in retina (albeit on the vascular rather than RPE side of the BRB) (Hida et al., 2018). For RPE morphology and barrier integrity in vivo, intravitreally applied fasudil reversed Rho pathway–driven cytoskeletal abnormalities (apical constriction and stress fibers) and improved RPE barrier integrity in disease-relevant paradigms, establishing that pan-ROCK antagonism can correct RPE junctional dysfunction at the tissue level (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). In fibrotic endpoints applicable to geographic atrophy progression and subretinal scarring, both pan-ROCK (fasudil) and ROCK2-selective (belumosudil) inhibitors reduced canonical fibrosis drivers (TGF-β1, fibronectin, vimentin, α-SMA) and ROCK pathway activity (p-MYPT1) in choroid–RPE complex and retina in vivo, with concomitant preservation of retinal morphology and decreased fibrosis volume in a mouse CNV-associated fibrosis model (Zandi et al., 2025). Additional dual ROCK inhibitors (AMA0428) suppressed angiogenesis, inflammation, and fibrosis in a mouse CNV model more broadly than VEGFR2 blockade alone, underscoring the ability of ROCK pathway inhibition to simultaneously normalize vessels, reduce leakage, and block matrix deposition—features highly relevant to AMD (Hollanders et al., 2015; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Clinically, small trials combining intravitreal fasudil with bevacizumab in refractory diabetic macular edema (DME) showed short-term improvements in visual acuity and central macular thickness versus anti-VEGF alone, consistent with anti-permeability and vasoregulatory actions of ROCK inhibitors in human retina; while not dry AMD, these studies provide translational class experience for retinal application and intravitreal dosing (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Nourinia et al., 2018). Taken together, the literature supports class-level efficacy signals in pathways relevant to dry AMD (barrier/tight junctions, fibrosis/TGF-β–driven contraction, vascular normalization/inflammation), but it provides no SAR407899-specific RPE or dry AMD results, PK, or ocular penetration data in the provided excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
ROCK1 and ROCK2 are serine/threonine kinases activated by RhoA-GTP that increase cellular contractility and cytoskeletal tension by two concerted mechanisms: (1) direct phosphorylation of myosin regulatory light chain (MLC), and (2) phosphorylation of MYPT1, the regulatory subunit of myosin phosphatase, which inhibits phosphatase activity and sustains high p-MLC; ROCK also signals via LIM kinases to inactivate cofilin, stabilizing actin stress fibers and focal adhesions—all of which favor junctional opening and motile/contractile phenotypes (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). In retinal and RPE-relevant systems, this signaling axis links directly to barrier dysregulation, fibrosis, and inflammation: high glucose and VEGF increase ROCK activity and p-MLC in retinal microvascular endothelium, augmenting adhesion molecule expression (ICAM-1), leukocyte adhesion, and hyperpermeability; conversely, ROCK inhibitors reduce ICAM-1, leukostasis, endothelial damage, and vascular leakage in diabetic retina models, consistent with reduced actomyosin tension and barrier preservation (Nourinia et al., 2018). Direct demonstration of ROCK pathway inhibition in vivo includes suppression of retinal p-MYPT1 by ripasudil in a murine retinal vein occlusion model and preservation of ZO-1 and TEER in VEGF-challenged HRMECs, indicating that ROCK blockade stabilizes tight-junction complexes and restores barrier function under stress (Hida et al., 2018). In RPE, Rho/ROCK activation produces cytoskeletal remodeling (apical constriction and stress fiber formation) leading to intercellular junction opening—and intravitreally delivered fasudil reversed these morphological abnormalities and improved RPE barrier integrity, linking ROCK activity to the outer BRB in vivo (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Fibrotic contraction in vitreoretinal disease is mechanistically tied to ROCK: TGF-β–activated contractility proceeds via ROCK-dependent MLC phosphorylation, and ROCK inhibitors suppress TGF-β–induced collagen gel contraction by RPE, reduce proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) progression in rabbits, and decrease subretinal fibrosis after CNV, while lowering p-MYPT1 in choroid–RPE complex (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). Inflammation intersects ROCK signaling via NF-κB and other pathways: ROCK activity upregulates inflammatory mediators (e.g., NF-κB targets, MCP-1/CCL2, iNOS), and ROCK inhibitors reduce inflammatory cell infiltration and cytokine production in ocular models, further supporting secondary barrier stabilization and anti-fibrotic effects (Singh & Singh, 2023; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). In AMD-relevant immunity, ROCK2-selective signaling is linked to age-related macrophage polarization toward proangiogenic M2 (MaDAMs) in human AMD eyes; ROCK2-selective inhibition improved macrophage phenotype and reduced CNV in models, whereas pan-ROCK fasudil did not share all of these benefits in the immune compartment, suggesting non-redundant isoform roles in the aging choroid–retina milieu (Nourinia et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). These combined data establish a coherent molecular mechanism whereby dual ROCK1/2 inhibition should reduce p-MYPT1/p-MLC, relax actomyosin tension, stabilize junctional complexes (occludin/ZO-1), oppose TGF-β–driven fibrotic conversion, and blunt inflammatory cascades that exacerbate outer BRB failure in dry AMD; however, whether dual versus ROCK2-selective inhibition optimally tunes the immune/fibrotic axis in AMD remains an open question raised by macrophage-focused studies (Nourinia et al., 2018; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed in vitro assay—complement-activated RPE monolayers exposed to IL-1β with readouts of TEER, FITC-dextran permeability, and occludin/ZO-1 transcription and membrane localization—the class mechanism predicts that a potent dual ROCK1/2 inhibitor such as SAR407899 should reduce ROCK pathway activation (↓p-MYPT1, ↓p-MLC), relax cortical actomyosin and stress fibers, and thereby re-stabilize tight junction architecture and function, yielding increased TEER, reduced paracellular flux, and normalized junctional protein localization (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). Supportive precedent for barrier rescue by ROCK inhibition includes restoration of endothelial tight junction integrity and TEER in VEGF-challenged HRMECs by ripasudil and suppression of retinal p-MYPT1 in vivo, establishing that ROCK blockade reverses injury-induced barrier dysfunction and engages the canonical substrate axis in retina (Hida et al., 2018). In RPE, in vivo fasudil reversed Rho-pathway–induced cytoskeletal remodeling and improved barrier integrity, implying that ROCK inhibition can directly stabilize the outer BRB at the epithelial level, although quantitative TEER and occludin/ZO-1 readouts in RPE cultures are not provided in the excerpts and should be generated in the proposed assay (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Inflammatory cytokines can feed into ROCK pathway activation and barrier loss, and the Rho/ROCK axis is intertwined with NF-κB–dependent cytokine expression; therefore, ROCK inhibition in the IL-1β paradigm is mechanistically plausible for barrier rescue even though IL-1β-specific RPE TEER data are not available in the provided sources (Singh & Singh, 2023; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Given the contribution of ROCK to TGF-β–driven epithelial–mesenchymal transition and gel contraction by RPE, a dual inhibitor is also expected to suppress fibrotic gene expression trajectories in longer assays (α-SMA, collagen/fibronectin) while relieving junctional stress that promotes delamination and barrier failure, which aligns with the anti-fibrotic outcomes seen in subretinal fibrosis models after fasudil or ROCK2-selective inhibition (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). Of note, ROCK2-targeted approaches may provide added benefit on age-related macrophage polarization and fibrosis in AMD models, but dual inhibition has demonstrated broad anti-contractile and anti-permeability effects across ocular compartments; head-to-head comparison of dual versus ROCK2-selective inhibition under IL-1β/complement challenge would be informative (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Nourinia et al., 2018). Finally, delivery modality will strongly influence the magnitude and duration of barrier rescue: topical dosing of some ROCK inhibitors can reach the posterior segment in rabbits but shows variable retinal pharmacodynamics between agents, and intravitreal routes with sustained-release formulations have been explored for fasudil to address short intraocular half-life—implications that apply to any repurposed ROCK inhibitor considered for RPE-centric therapy (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
Strengths  
- Target validity and mechanistic convergence: ROCK1/2 are central regulators of cytoskeletal tension and tight-junction stability via the MYPT1/MLC and LIMK/cofilin axes, providing a direct mechanistic handle on epithelial barrier integrity and fibrotic conversion relevant to outer BRB failure and atrophic remodeling in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). The same axis is mechanistically operative in retinal vascular endothelium where barrier protection by ROCK inhibition has been demonstrated quantitatively (TEER, ZO-1), strengthening the translational rationale for barrier rescue across the BRB (Hida et al., 2018).  
- RPE-relevant in vivo effect: Intravitreal fasudil reversed RPE cytoskeletal abnormalities and improved epithelial barrier integrity in vivo, demonstrating that the class mechanism extends to outer BRB pathology and is not restricted to vascular endothelial cells (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).  
- Anti-fibrotic efficacy in choroid–RPE complex: Both dual and ROCK2-selective inhibitors reduced fibrotic markers and p-MYPT1 in murine subretinal fibrosis models after CNV, with histologic preservation of retinal architecture and reduced fibrosis volume, supporting the concept that ROCK blockade can oppose late-stage fibrotic drivers of vision loss that are inadequately addressed by anti-VEGF monotherapy (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Broader AMD-relevant biology: ROCK inhibition reduces angiogenesis, inflammation, and fibrosis in CNV models (e.g., AMA0428), normalizes pathological vessels, and modulates age-related macrophage polarization—processes integral to AMD pathogenesis in both neovascular and atrophic trajectories (Hollanders et al., 2015; Nourinia et al., 2018).  
- Translational feasibility: Multiple ROCK inhibitors have been successfully delivered to the eye topically and intravitreally with acceptable safety, including demonstration that topical ripasudil can reach retina/choroid in rabbits and that intravitreal fasudil combinations are feasible in small human DME studies—experience that de-risks ocular delivery strategies for the class (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- Absence of SAR407899-specific ocular data in RPE/AMD: The provided literature contains no quantitative potency/selectivity corroboration, ocular penetration, retinal tissue levels, or preclinical efficacy for SAR407899 in RPE barrier models, IL-1β paradigms, or AMD models; thus, key assertions in the working hypothesis (e.g., occludin/ZO-1 transcriptional rescue in RPE, primary human RPE TER recovery, ocular PK levels, ERG improvements in NaIO3) are not supported here and cannot be validated from the excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). This represents the primary evidence gap and limits compound-specific confidence versus class-level rationale (Yamaguchi et al., 2017).  
- Isoform selectivity considerations: Several AMD-relevant studies point to ROCK2-specific biology in macrophage polarization and possibly fibrosis, with selective ROCK2 inhibition conferring benefits not fully reproduced by pan-ROCK inhibitors in the aged immune compartment; whether dual inhibition is advantageous or dilutes ROCK2-targeted immune modulation in dry AMD remains unresolved (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).  
- Incomplete RPE barrier readouts: Although class-level rescue of endothelial TEER/ZO-1 and RPE morphological barrier integrity have been shown, the excerpts lack direct RPE TEER, permeability, or occludin/ZO-1 imaging/quantification under inflammatory (IL-1β) challenge, necessitating foundational in vitro work before prioritizing SAR407899 for in vivo dry AMD studies (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Hida et al., 2018).  
- Delivery and exposure constraints: Reviews emphasize short intraocular half-lives and the need for repeated dosing or sustained-release formulations for posterior-segment efficacy; topical penetration to retina/choroid varies across molecules (e.g., ripasudil reaches the posterior segment in rabbits whereas topical fasudil did not at matched dosing), underscoring the necessity of SAR407899-specific ocular PK and exposure–response characterization to inform route and formulation (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).  
- Off-target liabilities and dose selection: ATP-competitive ROCK inhibitors can exhibit off-target kinase inhibition at higher concentrations, raising interpretive and safety issues that must be managed through careful dose–exposure selection and orthogonal on-target biomarkers such as p-MYPT1 in ocular tissues (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Liu et al., 2018).

Programmatic Implications and Recommended Next Steps  
On the strength of the mechanistic and preclinical class data, dual ROCK1/2 inhibition remains a credible strategy to stabilize RPE junctions and suppress fibrotic conversion in dry AMD; however, SAR407899 must earn its place in this mechanism by producing compound-specific evidence on RPE barrier endpoints and ocular exposure (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Zandi et al., 2025). A staged validation package is recommended:  
- In vitro RPE barrier assays: Quantify TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and occludin/ZO-1 localization in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE monolayers under IL-1β and complement co-challenge ± SAR407899; include p-MYPT1 and p-MLC immunoblotting or phospho-ELISA to verify on-target modulation; adopt assay conditions paralleling endothelial TEER paradigms where ROCK inhibition preserved ZO-1 and TEER (Hida et al., 2018; Kaneko et al., 2016).  
- Isoform pharmacology: Use siRNA or selective pharmacologic comparators (e.g., belumosudil for ROCK2) to benchmark dual versus ROCK2-selective effects on RPE barrier rescue and inflammatory readouts, informed by the macrophage polarization literature in AMD (Nourinia et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).  
- Ocular PK and delivery: Establish intraocular distribution and time–concentration profiles for SAR407899 in relevant species after topical and intravitreal routes; given literature on short half-life and variable posterior penetration, consider sustained-release intravitreal formulations analogous to those explored for fasudil if topical exposure proves inadequate (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).  
- In vivo efficacy: Progress to subretinal fibrosis or oxidative injury models that interrogate outer BRB integrity and fibrotic remodeling (e.g., CNV-associated fibrosis with extended fibrotic endpoints) to test whether SAR407899 reproduces the anti-fibrotic and barrier-preserving signals seen with fasudil/belumosudil, incorporating p-MYPT1 as a pharmacodynamic biomarker (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Combinatorial positioning: Given evidence that ROCK inhibition complements anti-VEGF therapy by reducing inflammation and fibrosis and may normalize pathological angiogenesis without abrogating physiological revascularization, consider combination designs if SAR407899 shows single-agent barrier/fibrosis activity (Hollanders et al., 2015; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Bottom line: Repurposing SAR407899 for dry AMD is mechanistically well-justified at the class level, but the absence of SAR407899-specific ocular and RPE data in the provided literature requires a focused preclinical package to substantiate the specific claims in the hypothesis and to determine whether dual inhibition delivers the desired balance of epithelial barrier rescue and anti-fibrotic efficacy relative to ROCK2-selective alternatives (Nourinia et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

I cannot answer specific claims in the hypothesis regarding SAR407899’s kinase selectivity (>200-fold), ocular penetration to retina (~0.3 µM), full TER recovery in primary human RPE, or functional rescue in NaIO3 models (+28% ERG b-wave), because the provided context contains no SAR407899-specific biochemical, PK, or preclinical efficacy data supporting those statements (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ML‐SA1 (Tocris 5291) is a synthetic, small‐molecule agonist that targets the lysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (mucolipin‐1). It was originally identified through screening efforts aimed at discovering modulators of lysosomal Ca²⁺ release and has been instrumental as an in vitro pharmacologic tool to probe TRPML1 function in diverse cellular systems, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models. ML‐SA1 belongs to a broader class of TRP (transient receptor potential) channel modulators that have been used extensively in basic research to examine ion channel regulation of intracellular Ca²⁺ stores, autophagy regulation, and lysosomal exocytosis. In several studies using primary mouse RPE, human embryonic stem cell‐derived RPE (hesRPE), and ARPE‐19 cells, ML‐SA1 has been shown to robustly elevate cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ via direct activation of TRPML1, with the effect being rapid, reversible, and reproducible, thereby establishing its utility as a selective TRPML1 agonist (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, ML‐SA1 has been employed in multiple biochemical and cellular studies as a probe to activate TRPML1-mediated lysosomal Ca²⁺ release. In the literature, its application in RPE cell models has helped delineate the contributions of lysosomal Ca²⁺ signals to downstream processes such as lysosomal exocytosis, TFEB (transcription factor EB) activation, and oxidative stress regulation. Experimental evidence derived from studies using ML‐SA1 demonstrates that the induced Ca²⁺ release is essentially independent of extracellular Ca²⁺ and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca²⁺ storage; rather, the release originates from lysosomal stores—as confirmed by the abrogation of ML‐SA1 responses upon lysosomal disruption with glycyl‐L‐phenylalanine‐naphthylamide (GPN) and by the lack of response in TRPML1-null RPE models (Más Gómez et al., 2018). To date, ML‐SA1 has not been used clinically or in veterinary settings and has not yet been evaluated in the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases; its use is so far confined to experimental paradigms that study the fundamental aspects of TRPML1 activity and lysosomal function (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This candidate is thus considered a repurposed pharmacologic agent, repositioned from a research tool to a potential therapeutic based on its mechanistic actions in RPE cells.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ML‐SA1 exerts its action by binding to and directly activating TRPML1 channels located on the lysosomal membrane. Upon binding, it triggers an efflux of Ca²⁺ from the lysosomal lumen into the cytoplasm, which has been quantitatively measured using ratiometric Ca²⁺ indicators such as Fura-2 (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This Ca²⁺ release is independent of extracellular Ca²⁺ and is not affected by the depletion of ER Ca²⁺, indicating that the source is specifically lysosomal (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The released Ca²⁺ can then activate downstream signaling pathways including the calcineurin-TFEB pathway, where increased cytosolic Ca²⁺ activates calcineurin, leading to dephosphorylation and subsequent nuclear translocation of TFEB. Nuclear TFEB acts as a master regulator of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis by upregulating a network of genes that control these pathways (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Notably, experimental evidence indicates that when the function of TRPML1 is compromised—such as in the context of lipid accumulation in lysosomes or genetic knockout of TRPML1—the Ca²⁺ response to ML‐SA1 is significantly diminished, underscoring both the specificity of ML‐SA1 for TRPML1 and the modulation of its efficacy by the lysosomal lipid environment (Más Gómez et al., 2018). In addition to stimulating Ca²⁺ release, TRPML1 activation by ML‐SA1 has been linked to beneficial downstream effects such as the induction of lysosomal exocytosis and the enhancement of cathepsin activity, which together contribute to the restoration of lysosomal function and cellular homeostasis (Karema-Jokinen et al., 2023; Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the current hypothesis, ML‐SA1 is expected to act on RPE cells by enhancing lysosomal Ca²⁺ release through TRPML1 activation, thereby stimulating the calcineurin-TFEB signaling cascade. This cascade is anticipated to upregulate the transcription of autophagy and lysosome-related genes, leading to improved autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis. In practical assays, such as those employing lipofuscin-loaded RPE monolayers, ML‐SA1 should facilitate the clearance of misfolded or aggregated tight junction proteins—including ZO-1—thereby restoring disrupted tight junction belts and improving transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) measurements. The activation of cathepsins, as part of the enhanced lysosomal function, is also expected to increase the degradation of accumulated cellular debris, further supporting cellular clearance (Falcão et al., 2025; Más Gómez et al., 2018). In experimental models of epithelial barrier restoration, previous data using TRPML1 agonists have shown that such compounds can rescue autophagic flux and reduce lysosomal storage, which is associated with improved barrier integrity; this supports the mechanism by which ML‐SA1 is expected to normalize the function of RPE cells relevant to dry AMD (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The candidate’s reported effective concentration (EC₅₀ around 45 µM for MCOLN1/TRPML1 activation) further underlines its potential to achieve a pharmacologically relevant activation of the TRPML1 channel in RPE cells, thereby triggering the downstream beneficial effects (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
ML‐SA1 represents a mechanistically innovative therapeutic candidate with a well‐defined mode of action that directly targets lysosomal dysfunction—a key pathological feature in dry AMD. One of the major strengths of ML‐SA1 is its ability to rapidly induce lysosomal Ca²⁺ release by specifically activating TRPML1, which has been documented robustly in various RPE cell models (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling is crucial for the activation of the calcineurin-TFEB pathway, which in turn upregulates lysosomal and autophagy gene networks; such activation is essential for clearing cellular debris, misfolded proteins, and aggregated tight junction components that compromise the integrity of the RPE barrier (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The anticipated effect of restoring TEER in lipofuscin-loaded monolayers is particularly important because impaired barrier function is a hallmark of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, the potential to enhance cathepsin activity and thereby boost lysosomal degradation pathways positions ML‐SA1 as a promising candidate to counteract the autophagy deficits that are observed in diseased RPE cells.

However, there are notable limitations and challenges that must be addressed. First, while the mechanistic data are compelling, ML‐SA1’s efficacy appears to be significantly modulated by the lysosomal lipid environment; in conditions where lipofuscin or other lipid accumulations are prominent, the Ca²⁺ response to ML‐SA1 has been shown to be reduced, suggesting that its beneficial effects might be attenuated in advanced dry AMD where lipid accumulation is extensive (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Second, despite its robust in vitro activity in various RPE models, ML‐SA1 has not yet been advanced into clinical or in vivo models of dry AMD, and thus there is a lack of safety, toxicity, and pharmacokinetics data relevant to chronic administration in the context of retinal diseases (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Additionally, although ML‐SA1 is reported to have an EC₅₀ around 45 µM for TRPML1 activation, the dosing window and potential off-target effects remain to be thoroughly characterized, particularly with respect to a multifactorial disease such as dry AMD that involves chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and photoreceptor degeneration (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

From a drug development perspective, ML‐SA1’s novel lysosomal-targeted mechanism offers significant promise by addressing a critical aspect of RPE dysfunction through the restoration of lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling and autophagy. Its ability to potentially clear misfolded tight junction proteins and recover ZO-1 belts, thereby restoring TEER, could translate into improved barrier integrity—a key determinant of RPE health in the context of dry AMD (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

In conclusion, while ML‐SA1 is a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapy for dry AMD, the current state of evidence is largely preclinical and mechanistic. The compound’s ability to activate TRPML1 and thereby enhance lysosomal Ca²⁺ release—coupled with its downstream activation of calcineurin-TFEB signaling and the potential to restore autophagy and barrier function in RPE—positions it as a strong candidate for further investigation. However, significant challenges remain in translating these in vitro findings into effective in vivo therapies. Future studies should focus on addressing the impact of lysosomal lipid accumulation on ML‐SA1 efficacy, determining the long-term safety and pharmacokinetic profiles in animal models of dry AMD, and establishing whether the observed cellular benefits translate into functional improvements in retinal health and vision preservation. Overall, ML‐SA1’s lysosomal-targeted mechanism and its demonstrated capacity to rescue key RPE functions provide a compelling rationale to pursue this candidate further, albeit with the caveat that extensive preclinical validation is required before clinical development can be contemplated (Falcão et al., 2025; Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Belumosudil (KD025; Rezurock) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable, indazole-derived serine/threonine kinase inhibitor that preferentially targets Rho-associated coiled-coil–containing protein kinase 2 (ROCK2) over ROCK1 and was developed by Kadmon Pharmaceuticals following licensing from Nano Terra (now approved in the United States for chronic graft-versus-host disease, cGVHD) (Blair, 2021; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022; Przepiorka et al., 2022). Biochemical selectivity has been consistently reported across sources: IC₅₀ values are approximately 60–110 nM for ROCK2 with markedly weaker activity on ROCK1 (typically >10 µM), and orthogonal profiling notes ROCK2 ~0.105 µM and ROCK1 ~24 µM, confirming substantial isoform preference (Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022; Blair, 2021; Lake et al., 2020). As an ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor, belumosudil binds the catalytic domain of ROCK2, analogous to the mechanism of other clinically used ROCK inhibitors, but with enhanced isoform selectivity designed to improve tolerability relative to pan-ROCK agents (e.g., fasudil, ripasudil, netarsudil) (Cheng et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

The broader class—ROCK inhibitors—modulates actin–myosin cytoskeletal dynamics by decreasing phosphorylation of myosin regulatory elements and altering actin turnover via downstream nodes (LIMK–cofilin, ERM proteins), with downstream effects on cell contractility, focal adhesions, cell junctions, migration, and myofibroblast differentiation (Cheng et al., 2025). In ophthalmology, ROCK inhibitors have established or emerging therapeutic roles: netarsudil and ripasudil lower intraocular pressure by relaxing trabecular meshwork and Schlemm’s canal, and corneal endothelial repair paradigms (topical ROCK inhibitors and cell therapy adjuncts) exploit cytoskeletal relaxation, enhanced adhesion, and proliferation to accelerate re-endothelialization (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025). Collectively, these features position belumosudil within a drug class with proven ocular pharmacology and strong plausibility for modulating epithelial/endothelial barrier biology through cytoskeletal re-tuning (Leong et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic immunomodulation and anti-fibrotic indications. Belumosudil is FDA-approved for treatment of cGVHD after at least two prior systemic therapies at an oral dose of 200 mg once daily with food; population pharmacokinetics indicate a mean elimination half-life of ~19 hours, primary CYP3A4 metabolism, and predominant fecal excretion, with two metabolites that also inhibit ROCK2 (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Blair, 2021). Across phase 2 programs in cGVHD, objective response rates (65–77%) were observed with 200 mg once or twice daily dosing, with corticosteroid sparing and acceptable tolerability, consolidating a favorable clinical safety/efficacy profile for chronic use in a heavily pretreated, immunologically dysregulated population (Jagasia et al., 2021; Zanin-Zhorov & Blazar, 2021). Beyond cGVHD, belumosudil has been explored in fibrotic diseases (interim idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis signal for attenuated FVC decline) and systemic sclerosis, consistent with class-wide anti-fibrotic properties driven by ROCK2 blockade (Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

Ocular use of ROCK inhibitors (class precedent). While belumosudil itself has not been reported in clinical ocular indications, the ROCK inhibitor class has multiple precedents in eye disease. Topical netarsudil and ripasudil are approved or widely used for glaucoma; intravitreal and topical fasudil have been explored for retinal diseases (e.g., diabetic macular edema) with reported safety in small series, and sustained-release ocular delivery of ROCK inhibitors (e.g., AR-13503) has been tested in preclinical models (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025). These translational precedents establish that ROCK pathway modulation can be achieved in ocular tissues via topical, intravitreal, or sustained-release routes and that cytoskeletal/vascular barrier targets respond to this mechanism in the eye (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Belumosudil in ocular preclinical models. In a laser-induced choroidal neovascularization/subretinal fibrosis model designed to isolate fibrotic progression, both fasudil (pan-ROCK) and belumosudil (ROCK2-selective) reduced fibrosis volume, preserved retinal morphology, increased retinal thickness, reduced pyknotic nuclei, and decreased type I collagen and α-SMA staining; corrected total cell fluorescence for ROCK1/ROCK2 was reduced, with particularly strong ROCK2 target engagement by belumosudil (occupancy down from 6.7% to 0.1%) (Zandi et al., 2025). Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) and western blot evidence showed reductions in p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex—consistent with ROCK pathway inhibition—alongside decreases in TGF-β1, fibronectin, vimentin, and α-SMA; belumosudil also more effectively reduced “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations near the choroid–RPE boundary compared with fasudil and decreased macrophages/perivascular cells, suggesting anti-inflammatory as well as anti-fibrotic activity (Zandi et al., 2025). In vitro, 24-hour ROCK inhibitor exposure in fibroblastic cells altered morphology (loss of long processes, blunted periphery) and decreased cell numbers, consistent with cytoskeletal/phenotype modulation and possible anti-proliferative effects in fibrogenic cells (Zandi et al., 2025).

Dry AMD relevance and gaps. The above in vivo data position ROCK2 inhibition as an anti-fibrotic modifier of the choroid–RPE interface after laser injury, with partial restoration of retinal architecture; however, they do not test dry AMD pathobiology (e.g., sodium iodate RPE toxicity or geographic atrophy models) (Zandi et al., 2025). Direct ocular RPE barrier endpoints—TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and tight-junction protein integrity (ZO-1, claudin-19)—have not been reported for belumosudil in RPE, and the available studies do not include oxidative or complement injury paradigms (H₂O₂, NaIO₃) in ARPE-19, primary human RPE, or in vivo dry AMD models (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). Class-level in vitro RPE evidence exists for ROCK inhibition improving wound closure, adhesion, pigmentation, RPE65 expression, and photoreceptor outer-segment phagocytosis in iPSC-RPE with Y-27632, but without barrier readouts, and with limited recovery duration and small sample sizes (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Additional pluripotent RPE manufacturing work reports ROCK inhibition suppresses EMT programs (TGF-β/Wnt ligands, SNAI2, collagens) and promotes rapid tight-junction reformation in culture, supporting barrier-relevant cytoskeletal effects at the transcriptomic/phenotypic level, but without TEER or paracellular flux data under oxidative/complement stress (Croze, 2015). In sum, while class-level and belumosudil-specific ocular data support anti-fibrotic and cytoskeletal modulation at the choroid–RPE interface, there is no direct published evidence in the provided literature set that belumosudil rescues TEER, preserves claudin-19/ZO-1, or reduces FITC-dextran flux under H₂O₂ or complement challenge in RPE or that it improves outcomes in NaIO₃ models (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
ROCK2 biology and junctional/cytoskeletal control. ROCK1/2 are AGC-family serine/threonine kinases activated by RhoA–GTP; they increase actomyosin contractility primarily by phosphorylating myosin light chain (MLC) directly and inhibiting myosin light-chain phosphatase via phosphorylation of the MYPT1 regulatory subunit, elevating p-MLC levels and stabilizing stress fibers and focal adhesions (Cheng et al., 2025). ROCK also phosphorylates LIM kinases to inactivate cofilin, which slows F-actin turnover and further stiffens the cytoskeleton; ERM proteins, adducin, intermediate filament proteins (vimentin, GFAP), and multiple cytoskeletal/membrane linkers are additional substrates that integrate cytoskeletal and junctional dynamics (Cheng et al., 2025). These pathways are sensitive to mechanical inputs (matrix stiffness) and link cytoskeletal remodeling to barrier integrity and cell adhesion, consistent with the observed roles of ROCK in endothelial hyperpermeability and junction stabilization in ocular tissues (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025).

Belumosudil target engagement in choroid–RPE constructs. In vivo in the choroid–RPE complex after laser injury, both fasudil and belumosudil lowered p-MYPT1, indicating on-pathway ROCK inhibition, and reduced fibrotic markers (α-SMA, vimentin, fibronectin, collagen I, TGF-β1), consistent with suppression of myofibroblast activation, ECM deposition, and TGF-β/Smad signaling output (Zandi et al., 2025). Imaging mass cytometry showed spatially localized fibrotic marker expression to the choroid–RPE boundary and a reduction in “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations with belumosudil relative to fasudil, and a decrease in macrophage and perivascular cell signatures—integrating anti-fibrotic and anti-inflammatory mechanisms (Zandi et al., 2025). Quantitatively, ROCK2 staining occupancy fell from ~6.7% to 0.1% after belumosudil treatment, stronger than the reduction with fasudil (to 0.7%), supporting efficient ROCK2 target engagement by belumosudil (Zandi et al., 2025).

ROCK and epithelial barrier relevance. Although the RPE-specific tight-junction literature for belumosudil is not available in the provided sources, corneal endothelial studies link ROCK activity to stabilization of ZO-1 and the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump complex; pharmacologic ROCK inhibition promotes cytoskeletal relaxation, spreading, and cyclin-D–dependent proliferation, and has been leveraged clinically to accelerate re-endothelialization and junctional re-establishment (Leong et al., 2025). In vascular endothelia, RhoA/ROCK signaling drives VEGF-induced permeability and tube formation; ROCK inhibition modulates junctional architecture (e.g., “zipper-like” lymphatic endothelial junctions) and reduces permeability, supporting a mechanistic link to barrier tightening (Leong et al., 2025). In diabetic retinal pathology, ROCK1 activation contributes to RPE blebbing and tight-junction opening with outer blood-retinal barrier breakdown; pharmacologic ROCK inhibition (fasudil) improved barrier function and suppressed leukocyte migration and ICAM-1, reducing vascular leakage and neurodegeneration (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Together, these data reinforce that ROCK signaling is a proximal regulator of epithelial/endothelial junctions and barrier integrity and that inhibition—especially with an isoform-selective agent that engages ROCK2 in the choroid–RPE complex—has plausible junction-preserving effects in RPE monolayers (Leong et al., 2025; Zandi et al., 2025).

Anti-EMT and anti-fibrotic transcriptional programs. Transcriptomic studies in pluripotent stem cell–derived RPE and other epithelial contexts show ROCK inhibition suppresses EMT-associated transcriptional programs (TGF-β ligands, Wnt components, SNAI2, collagens) and promotes tight-junction reformation, consistent with decreased cytoskeletal tension and reduced MRTF/SRF-dependent transcription that drives myofibroblast markers (e.g., α-SMA) (Croze, 2015; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022). ROCK2 inhibition also intersects with inflammatory transcriptional axes (STAT3/STAT5) and NF-κB, shifting Th17/Tfh toward Treg and reducing proinflammatory cytokines in PBMCs and cGVHD models, which could help resolve inflammatory components of AMD pathophysiology at the RPE–choroid interface (Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Cytoskeletal/ciliary modulation in RPE-lineage cells. Independent siRNA/drug screens in ciliogenesis models identified ROCK2 as a strong negative regulator of cilia incidence and length; short and prolonged belumosudil exposure increased cilia metrics in hTERT RPE-1 and mIMCD3 cells while reducing phosphorylated MLC and acto-myosin fiber-like structures, consistent with decreased ROCK2-driven contractility (Lake et al., 2020). Although ciliation per se is not a dry AMD therapeutic endpoint, the data are a sensitive readout of cytoskeletal reprogramming via ROCK2 and reinforce the target’s role in apical organization in epithelia with RPE lineage origin (Lake et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay context: H₂O₂ and complement injury in RPE monolayers. Under oxidative stress (H₂O₂) and complement attack, the RPE cytoskeleton becomes hypercontractile, junctional belts destabilize, and paracellular permeability increases—manifest as reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased FITC-dextran flux, with mislocalization or fragmentation of tight-junction proteins (ZO-1, claudin-19). ROCK activation (via RhoA–GTP, inflammatory mediators, or mechanical cues) exacerbates this by increasing p-MYPT1 and p-MLC to drive actomyosin tension and stress fiber formation (Cheng et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). The class literature in ocular epithelia/endothelium indicates that ROCK inhibition relaxes cytoskeletal tension, promotes cell spreading and junctional complex re-assembly (ZO-1 stabilization reported in corneal endothelium), and reduces VEGF- or inflammation-driven hyperpermeability (Leong et al., 2025). In diabetic retinal models, ROCK pathway activation produces RPE blebbing and tight-junction disruption, with pharmacologic ROCK inhibition reversing barrier dysfunction and dampening leukostasis and leakage (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Given these mechanisms, selective ROCK2 inhibition with belumosudil is expected to:
- Reduce p-MYPT1 and downstream p-MLC in RPE, decreasing acto-myosin contractility, stabilizing the circumferential actin belt and adherens/tight junctions (ZO-1/claudin-19), thereby rescuing TEER and lowering FITC-dextran flux under H₂O₂ or complement challenge (Zandi et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025).
- Suppress EMT-like shifts and myofibroblast activation induced by oxidative/complement stress by lowering α-SMA/vimentin and ECM program activation (fibronectin, collagen), as seen in vivo after laser injury and in ROCK-inhibited RPE culture transcriptomics (Zandi et al., 2025; Croze, 2015).
- Provide anti-inflammatory benefits by reducing macrophage/perivascular cell accumulation seen in vivo and by directly modulating STAT3/STAT5-linked cytokine programs, potentially blunting complement-amplified inflammatory cascades at the RPE/choroid interface (Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021).

Target expression and context. ROCK signaling is active in ocular tissues; p-MYPT1 is reduced in the choroid–RPE complex of laser-injured eyes after ROCK inhibition; ROCK1 translocates and drives cytoskeletal/junctional changes under hyperglycemia in RPE and endothelium; and ROCK2 expression is quantifiably reduced by belumosudil in the choroid–RPE complex—collectively validating target presence and drug engagement at the proposed site of action (Zandi et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Important caveats. The provided literature set does not contain direct demonstrations that belumosudil rescues TEER or reduces FITC-dextran flux in RPE under H₂O₂ or complement injury, nor does it report preservation of claudin-19/ZO-1 localization in RPE with ROCK2-selective inhibition; these remain testable predictions grounded in mechanism and class precedent but not yet substantiated for belumosudil in RPE (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). Similarly, no data are provided here for NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration models with belumosudil; the NaIO₃ discussion pertains to single-cell remodeling and EMT tendencies in dry AMD models, which conceptually align with anti-EMT and anti-fibrotic effects of ROCK inhibition, but require direct in vivo validation for this candidate (Zandi et al., 2025).

Pharmacokinetic/delivery considerations for the assay. Clinically, belumosudil has a ~19-hour half-life, ~64% bioavailability with food (in healthy subjects), and is metabolized by CYP3A4; ocular pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration are not reported in the provided sources (Przepiorka et al., 2022). In the laser-injury mouse model, intraperitoneal administration from day 35 to 49 post-laser achieved retinal/choroid pharmacodynamics (↓p-MYPT1, ↓markers), indicating systemic dosing can engage ocular targets in inflamed/fibrotic tissue in mice, though translational relevance to human ocular exposure remains to be determined and local delivery could be preferable for barrier-rescue assays (Zandi et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- On-pathway target engagement in choroid–RPE with functional tissue outcomes. Belumosudil decreases p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex, reduces fibrosis volume, attenuates α-SMA, vimentin, fibronectin, collagen I, and TGF-β1, and preserves retinal morphology and thickness in a subretinal fibrosis model; ROCK2 occupancy falls to near-baseline with treatment, indicating strong ocular target engagement (Zandi et al., 2025). These integrated molecular and histologic readouts provide robust evidence that isoform-selective ROCK2 inhibition can reprogram the pathological microenvironment at the RPE–choroid interface after injury—precisely where barrier restoration is therapeutically needed in dry AMD (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Mechanistic alignment with barrier preservation. ROCK signaling is a proximal regulator of cytoskeletal tension and tight-junction stability; inhibition reduces MLC phosphorylation via MYPT1 de-phosphorylation, stabilizes junctions (corneal ZO-1; endothelial junction “zippering”), and mitigates hyperpermeability (Cheng et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025). The candidate’s demonstrated ability to lower p-MYPT1 in the choroid–RPE complex and reduce myofibroblast activation fits the hypothesis that it can preserve epithelial barrier integrity under stress (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Anti-EMT/anti-fibrotic transcriptional effects. ROCK inhibition suppresses TGF-β/Wnt-mediated EMT programs and promotes tight-junction reformation in pluripotent-derived RPE; in vivo reductions in α-SMA and ECM deposition further support anti-fibrotic activity coherent with preventing RPE-to-mesenchymal transitions that compromise the barrier (Croze, 2015; Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions. Belumosudil reduces macrophage and perivascular cell signatures in vivo and systemically shifts Th17/Tfh toward Treg via STAT3/STAT5 modulation; these effects could dampen complement- and cytokine-driven RPE injury cascades implicated in dry AMD (Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021; Jagasia et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).  
- Favorable human safety experience and oral PK. A clinically approved safety profile with chronic administration, a manageable drug–drug interaction profile (CYP3A4), and a ~19-hour half-life provide a de-risked starting point for repurposing; dose selection can be guided by systemic exposures achieved in cGVHD (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zanin-Zhorov & Blazar, 2021).

Weaknesses and knowledge gaps  
- No direct RPE barrier functional data for belumosudil. The literature set lacks TEER, FITC-dextran flux, or ZO-1/claudin-19 preservation data for belumosudil in RPE under oxidative/complement stress; consequently, the core hypothesis—TEER rescue with ROCK2 selectivity—remains inferential (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Blair, 2021).  
- No NaIO₃ or dry AMD-specific in vivo efficacy with belumosudil. While NaIO₃ single-cell data support EMT and fibroblast-like RPE signatures relevant to ROCK pathway targeting, belumosudil has not been tested in NaIO₃ or geographic atrophy models here; the current in vivo evidence is laser-injury fibrosis focused (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Isoform biology nuance in the retina. Diabetic retinal studies emphasize ROCK1 translocation and ROCK1-mediated blebbing/tight-junction disruption, with some reports noting ROCK2 localization as “undisturbed” in those models; this raises a strategic question whether ROCK2-selective inhibition alone is sufficient for barrier rescue across stress etiologies or whether dual inhibition is sometimes preferable (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).  
- Ocular pharmacokinetics and delivery. There are no data on ocular tissue penetration, retinal/choroidal exposure, or intravitreal/topical formulations for belumosudil; although systemic dosing engaged ocular targets in mice after laser injury, human ocular delivery, durability, and safety require specific assessment (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025). Class precedents (intravitreal/topical fasudil, topical netarsudil/ripasudil) are encouraging but not directly transferable to this scaffold without formulation work (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Off-target and pathway-network considerations. Although belumosudil is selective for ROCK2, it has minor ROCK1 and pathway-adjacent activities (e.g., mTOR), and widespread cytoskeletal re-tuning can have context-dependent effects (e.g., on ciliation) whose long-term retinal implications are unknown (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Lake et al., 2020).

Decision-oriented interpretation for dry AMD  
- Mechanistic plausibility: High. ROCK2 inhibition is expected to directly reduce cytoskeletal tension and stabilize epithelial junctions; on-pathway pharmacodynamic effects (↓p-MYPT1) and anti-fibrotic marker reductions in the choroid–RPE complex support action at the relevant tissue interface (Zandi et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Translational anchor: Moderate. The candidate has a de-risked systemic safety profile and class-level ocular pharmacology, plus in vivo anti-fibrotic retinal benefits; however, barrier-specific efficacy in RPE under oxidative/complement stress has not yet been shown for belumosudil (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Differentiation vs pan-ROCK: Potentially favorable. In vivo, belumosudil achieved stronger ROCK2 engagement and larger decreases in “unspecific” fibrogenic cell populations than fasudil, aligning with the idea that ROCK2 drives key profibrotic cascades at the choroid–RPE interface, while avoiding ROCK1-linked hypotension liabilities systemically; whether ROCK1 contributions to RPE barrier breakdown under certain stressors would limit efficacy remains to be determined experimentally (Zandi et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).

Concrete implications for the proposed hypothesis  
- The specific claims that belumosudil has demonstrated +50% TER recovery in ARPE-19 under H₂O₂ stress, 40% RPE cell preservation and ERG improvement in a mouse NaIO₃ model, and an oral bioavailability ~45% with t₁/₂ ~4.8 h are not supported by the literature set provided; instead, the available PK indicates oral bioavailability is ~64% with food and a ~19-h half-life, and no TER/NaIO₃ efficacy data for belumosudil are referenced here (Przepiorka et al., 2022; Zandi et al., 2025; Blair, 2021). The hypothesized barrier rescue under oxidative/complement injury remains plausible mechanistically but requires direct validation in RPE models (Leong et al., 2025; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Program-level next steps (to enable a go/no-go)  
- In vitro RPE barrier assays: Primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE monolayers subjected to H₂O₂ and normal human serum (complement) injury; quantify TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and ZO-1/claudin-19 localization/intensity; include p-MYPT1 and p-MLC biochemical readouts as pharmacodynamics; benchmark belumosudil across a concentration range anchored to ROCK2 IC₅₀ and cell viability (Lake et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2025).  
- Phenotypic rescue breadth: Replicate class-level findings with ROCK2 selectivity—adhesion, wound closure, POS phagocytosis, RPE65 expression—to establish that belumosudil recapitulates the iPSC-RPE Y-27632 phenotype profile while tightening the barrier (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).  
- In vivo dry AMD model: NaIO₃ or other GA-like models with local ocular delivery (intravitreal or periocular sustained-release) to assess RPE survival, outer blood-retinal barrier integrity, visual function (ERG), and transcriptomic/IMC profiling for EMT/fibrosis and inflammatory modulation; include dose–exposure–response characterization (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Ocular PK/formulation: Ocular tissue distribution after local delivery and/or systemic administration; stability and duration; comparative exposures in RPE/choroid vs retina with safety assessment (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2025).

Overall, belumosudil is a compelling, mechanistically aligned candidate with de-risked systemic safety, clear ocular on-pathway antifibrotic activity at the choroid–RPE interface, and strong biological rationale for junctional stabilization in stressed RPE. The decisive gap is the absence of direct barrier-function rescue data in RPE under oxidative or complement injury and the lack of dry AMD model efficacy. Addressing these with focused preclinical studies will determine whether its ROCK2 selectivity translates into clinically meaningful protection of the outer blood–retinal barrier in dry AMD, and whether it offers advantages over pan-ROCK inhibitors in this context (Zandi et al., 2025; Leong et al., 2025; Mendoza & Jimenez, 2022).
