Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PF-06409577 [6-chloro-5-(4-(1-hydroxycyclobutyl)phenyl)-1H-indole-3-carboxylic acid] is a synthetic, indole-3-carboxylic acid small molecule discovered in a Pfizer program to generate direct, isoform-selective activators of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) for metabolic and renal indications (notably diabetic nephropathy) (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Webb et al., 2019). Medicinal chemistry and structural biology work established PF-06409577 as a direct allosteric AMPK activator that binds the α1β1γ1 heterotrimer and engages the so-called allosteric drug and metabolite (ADaM) site at the α–β interface, with co-crystallization data reported for the parent and its metabolites bound to α1β1γ1 (Ryder et al., 2018; Steinberg & Carling, 2019). In biochemical assays and surface plasmon resonance (SPR), PF-06409577 and related indole-3-carboxylic acids preferentially activate and bind β1-containing AMPK isoforms, with little-to-no activity against β2-containing human AMPK heterotrimers under the conditions reported; notably, the acyl glucuronide conjugates (M1–M3) retain β1-selective AMPK activation with reduced potency relative to the parent (Ryder et al., 2018). Consistent with β-subunit–driven selectivity of ADaM ligands, prior work with thienopyridone A-769662 and benzimidazole 991 demonstrates β1 > β2 preference and mechanistic dependence on β1-Ser108, a key determinant of ADaM-site responsiveness (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).

PF-06409577 belongs to the class of direct, small-molecule AMPK activators designed to allosterically activate the kinase and protect Thr172 phosphorylation from dephosphorylation, in contrast to indirect mitochondrial poisons (e.g., metformin, phenformin, berberine) that raise cellular AMP/ADP and secondarily activate AMPK (Steinberg & Carling, 2019). Within this class, multiple chemotypes (thienopyridones, benzimidazoles, indole acids, and pan-activators such as MK-8722) have been used to probe metabolism, autophagy/mitophagy, and lipid homeostasis in vivo, with both efficacy signals (e.g., cholesterol lowering, NAFLD correction, organ protection) and safety liabilities (e.g., cardiac hypertrophy with a pan-activator) documented across programs (Behl et al., 2021; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2019).

Beyond primary pharmacology, PF-06409577 and congeners are extensively glucuronidated in animals and humans; unusually, the resulting acyl glucuronides remain pharmacologically active at AMPK, preserving β1-selective activation and direct binding to α1β1γ1 in vitro (albeit with 9–19-fold lower potency than the parent), a property with implications for exposure, distribution, and safety (Ryder et al., 2018). The acyl glucuronides of this series were reported to be relatively stable to hydrolysis and acyl migration at physiological pH (t1/2 > 21 h in buffer), a feature that lowers, but does not eliminate, typical concerns about acyl glucuronide–mediated covalent protein modification and idiosyncratic toxicity in carboxylic acid drugs (Ryder et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History  
PF-06409577 was developed as a β1-selective AMPK activator for diabetic nephropathy; it achieved Phase I clinical testing but was discontinued (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), and there is no report of ophthalmic or AMD use in the available sources (Webb et al., 2019). Preclinically, selective activation of β1-containing AMPK isoforms has been linked to improved kidney function in rat nephropathy models, and liver-targeted activation by PF-06409577 corrected NAFLD and lowered cholesterol in rodent and primate studies, with target engagement tracked via ACC phosphorylation (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019). In contrast to pan-activators such as MK-8722 that improved systemic glucose homeostasis but caused cardiac hypertrophy with glycogen accumulation in rodents and primates, β1-selective strategies are viewed as potentially safer with respect to cardiac glycogen loading and skeletal muscle glucose uptake, although this requires empirical confirmation per compound and tissue (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Behl et al., 2021). Of note, β1-biased activation by PF-06409577 has been reported to increase plasma ketone bodies and reduce hepatic triacylglycerol and cholesterol without lowering blood glucose—an important metabolic profile distinction (Behl et al., 2021).

In ocular biology, PF-06409577 has been directly tested in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells in vitro. Li et al. (2018) reported that PF-06409577 activates AMPK signaling and protects both ARPE-19 and primary murine RPEs from ultraviolet radiation (UVR), reducing ROS, lipid peroxidation, DNA damage, apoptosis, and cell death, with accompanying increases in NADPH activity and Nrf2-dependent antioxidant gene expression (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC, GCLM). The protective effects were strictly AMPKα1-dependent (shRNA, dominant-negative T172A, and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout each abrogated PF-mediated protection and AMPK activation), establishing on-target mechanism in RPE under oxidative stress (Li et al., 2018). The paper presents dose–response and time-course data showing AMPKα Thr172 and ACC Ser79 phosphorylation in ARPE-19 over ~0.1–1.0 μM PF-06409577, with 0.03 μM ineffective; parallel experiments in primary RPE at 0.3 μM showed similar activation (Li et al., 2018). The authors also describe PF-06409577 potency as “nM” in RPE in narrative discussion, consistent with direct engagement yet not fully aligned with the 0.03 μM threshold in their western blot data; together, these findings indicate sub- to low-micromolar cellular potencies in RPE compatible with direct ADaM-site engagement (Li et al., 2018). Importantly, the RPE literature to date contains no reports of PF-06409577 use in AMD patients, no in vivo AMD models with PF-06409577, and no published measurements of RPE tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin) or transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) for this agent (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).

Additional translational history for PF-06409577 includes use as a host-directed antiviral tool; AMPK activation by PF-06409577 inhibited replication of flaviviruses (WNV, ZIKV, DENV-2) by interfering with replication complex development linked to host membrane rearrangements and lipid synthesis, at micromolar EC50s with acceptable in vitro selectivity indices (Jiménez de Oya et al., 2018). This antiviral application further underscores the compound’s capacity to reprogram lipid metabolism in stressed cells, relevant to lipid-rich pathology in AMD.

Within the broader therapeutic class, indirect AMPK activators (notably metformin) have been repeatedly associated with retinal protection: metformin reduces drusen formation via LXR/ABCA1/G1-mediated cholesterol efflux, suppresses inflammation (e.g., NLRP3 inflammasome), protects RPE and photoreceptors via PGC-1α/mitochondrial regulation, induces autophagy via AMPK–mTOR, and dampens VEGF signaling in vascular endothelium (all AMPK-dependent), strengthening the conceptual precedent that AMPK activation is protective in retinal degenerations (Dang et al., 2021). However, these metformin data do not establish PF-06409577-specific safety or efficacy in RPE barrier endpoints such as ZO-1, occludin, or TEER (Dang et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Direct binding and isoform selectivity. PF-06409577 and its acyl glucuronide metabolites bind directly to AMPK α1β1γ1 at the ADaM site at the α–β interface, driving allosteric activation and protection against Thr172 dephosphorylation of the α subunit; β1-selective activation is borne out across biochemical and SPR binding assays, and the acyl glucuronides retain β1 selectivity albeit at lower potency (Ryder et al., 2018). ADaM-site pharmacology is isoform-sensitive: conformational and sequence differences in the αC helix and β-subunit (including the β C-interacting helix) modulate ligand responsiveness, with β1-Ser108 phosphorylation enabling synergism between nucleotide- and ADaM-site activation (e.g., AMP plus A-769662/991), and mutation at α Leu166 selectively reduces activation by certain ligands (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019). These structural determinants rationalize β1 preference for ADaM-site ligands and inform tissue-selectivity hypotheses in β1-rich cells (Steinberg & Carling, 2019).

RPE cell signaling and cytoprotection. In ARPE-19 and primary murine RPEs, PF-06409577 rapidly increases AMPKα1 Thr172 phosphorylation and phosphorylation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) at Ser79, a canonical AMPK substrate, with parallel increases in AMPK activity (Li et al., 2018). Functionally, PF-06409577 pretreatment reduces UVR-induced ROS (DCFH-DA), lipid peroxidation (TBARs), DNA damage (p-γH2AX), apoptosis (ssDNA, cleaved caspase-3, Annexin-V/PI), and cell death (LDH), while improving viability (CCK-8), in both ARPE-19 and primary RPE cultures (Li et al., 2018). The compound enhances cellular NADPH activity and stabilizes Nrf2 protein with induction of classical Nrf2 target genes (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC, GCLM), consistent with increased antioxidant capacity and a transcriptional response favoring cytoprotection (Li et al., 2018). Genetic disruption of AMPKα1 (shRNA, dominant-negative T172A mutant, or CRISPR/Cas9 knockout) abrogates both AMPK signaling and PF-mediated protection, demonstrating that AMPKα1 is necessary for the observed effects (Li et al., 2018). Mechanistically, AMPK can preserve NADPH through ACC inactivation (limiting de novo lipogenesis and malonyl-CoA production) and by promoting fatty acid oxidation, both of which improve redox balance; AMPK also phosphorylates Nrf2 at Ser550 to facilitate nuclear translocation and transactivation, with additional indirect support via inhibition of GSK3β-driven nuclear exclusion and p62/SQSTM1-mediated KEAP1 autophagic degradation, all of which are documented upstream regulatory routes present in RPE cells (Hu et al., 2024).

Metabolic control, autophagy, and lipid handling. AMPK is a master regulator of lipid metabolism and autophagy: it phosphorylates and inhibits ACC1/ACC2 to reduce de novo lipogenesis and lower malonyl-CoA, promoting mitochondrial fatty acid import and β-oxidation; AMPK also phosphorylates ULK1 to initiate autophagy and can activate PGC-1α to drive mitochondrial biogenesis, enhance mitophagy, and improve mitochondrial quality control (Webb et al., 2019). Although the RPE PF-06409577 literature does not yet report autophagy markers (LC3-II, p62) or lipid droplet turnover, studies in ARPE-19 with an independent AMPK-activating intervention (liraglutide) show that AMPK activation in FFA-loaded RPE restores autophagy/lipophagy (↑LC3-II, ↓p62, ↓p-mTOR), reduces ROS and lipid droplet burden, rescues EMT markers, and restores ZO-1 localization at the membrane—effects blocked by pharmacologic AMPK inhibition—thereby validating these AMPK-dependent axes in RPE (Tsou et al., 2025). More generally, AICAR activation of AMPK upregulated ABCA1/ABCG1 in RPE and reduced Bruch’s membrane lipid deposition in ApoE⁻/⁻ mice, connecting AMPK to cholesterol efflux pathways relevant to drusen biogenesis (Hu et al., 2024). Collectively, these mechanisms support the plausibility that a direct AMPK activator such as PF-06409577 can modulate autophagy and lipid metabolism in RPE even though PF-specific autophagy/lipophagy data in RPE have not yet been reported (Li et al., 2018; Tsou et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).

Barrier integrity and tight-junction assembly. AMPK has been mechanistically linked to tight-junction assembly in epithelial systems: it promotes ZO-1 reassembly at paracellular contacts, phosphorylates claudin-1 (preventing degradation) and claudin-4 (promoting occludin binding), and phosphorylates scaffold proteins (e.g., cingulin, afadin) and MLCK to tune actin–junction interactions and permeability (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). In RPE specifically, liraglutide’s AMPK-dependent rescue of ZO-1 distribution under FFA challenge suggests that AMPK activation can re-normalize barrier-associated proteins in RPE cultures, although TEER was not reported in that study and the journal quality warrants cautious interpretation (Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). To date, no published data directly demonstrate effects of PF-06409577 on ZO-1/occludin or TEER in RPE; thus, junctional rescue by PF-06409577 remains a testable hypothesis rather than an established mechanism (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).

Systemic pharmacology and safety context. In liver and kidney settings, PF-06409577 engages AMPK in vivo (e.g., pACC biomarker), lowers hepatic lipogenesis, corrects NAFLD, and confers renal protection in β1-focused pharmacology paradigms, while β1 activation by PF-06409577 has been noted to not lower blood glucose (Behl et al., 2021). Pan-activation by MK-8722 in renal disease improved mitochondrial quality control, reduced lipotoxicity and fibrosis, and improved function but highlighted a class-level safety risk—cardiac hypertrophy with glycogen accumulation under some dosing regimens—underscoring the importance of subunit selectivity and tissue targeting for chronic use (Zhou et al., 2019; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). The acyl glucuronide metabolites of PF-06409577 are pharmacologically active and chemically stable in buffer; however, acyl glucuronides as a class have been implicated in idiosyncratic immune toxicities, and careful metabolite profiling and reactive metabolite risk assessment will be required for ocular delivery strategies (Ryder et al., 2018).

Expected Effect  
Rationale in dry AMD pathobiology. Oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/mitophagy, and dysregulated lipid handling are central to RPE dysfunction and drusen biogenesis in dry AMD, with age-related decline in Nrf2-mediated antioxidant defense and lysosome–phagosome fusion defects compounding vulnerability (Hu et al., 2024). AMPK activation is positioned to counter these processes by: (1) improving NADPH homeostasis and activating Nrf2 target gene programs, (2) initiating autophagy/mitophagy via ULK1 while suppressing mTORC1 signaling, (3) reducing lipogenesis (via ACC) and supporting fatty acid oxidation and cholesterol efflux (via LXR–ABCA1/G1), and (4) stabilizing/assembling tight junctions through claudin/occludin/ZO-1 scaffold and cytoskeletal phosphorylation events (Li et al., 2018; Dang et al., 2021; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).

What PF-06409577 is expected to do in RPE assays. Based on the published RPE data and AMPK biology, the following effects are expected if PF-06409577 is applied to human RPE cultures (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary RPE) under oxidative and lipid-loading stress:
- Oxidative stress resistance: Increased AMPKα Thr172 and ACC Ser79 phosphorylation, elevated NADPH/NADP⁺, stabilization of Nrf2 protein, and induction of antioxidant genes (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC, GCLM), with reduced ROS, lipid peroxidation and DNA damage under UVR or oxidant challenges, as shown directly in ARPE-19 and primary RPE by Li et al. (Li et al., 2018). These endpoints should be AMPKα1-dependent (loss-of-function tamps down PF effects) (Li et al., 2018).
- Lipid handling and autophagy: Although untested for PF-06409577 in RPE, AMPK activation in ARPE-19 (with liraglutide) restored autophagy and lipophagy markers (↑LC3-II, ↓p62, ↓p-mTOR), reduced lipid droplet number/size, and normalized lipophagy/lysosome gene expression (ATG5, LIPA, RAB7A, LAMP2) in an AMPK-dependent manner; PF-06409577 should be evaluated for these endpoints under free fatty acid or oxLDL loading where AMPK effects are mechanistically expected (Tsou et al., 2025). Independent RPE evidence that AMPK activation increases ABCA1/ABCG1 and decreases Bruch’s membrane lipid deposition supports anticipated benefits on cholesterol efflux (Hu et al., 2024).
- Barrier integrity: AMPK’s direct effects on tight-junction components and scaffolds in epithelial systems suggest PF-06409577 could improve ZO-1/occludin organization and paracellular barrier function (TEER), but no PF-06409577 data exist in RPE; therefore, ZO-1/occludin immunolocalization and TEER must be prospectively measured. The liraglutide ARPE-19 study showing AMPK-dependent restoration of ZO-1 under FFA stress provides a relevant positive control framework for assay design, with the caveat of study quality and absence of TEER measurements (Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).
- Dosing/target engagement: In ARPE-19 and primary RPE, AMPK activation by PF-06409577 occurred with sub- to low-micromolar exposure (0.1–1.0 μM active, 0.03 μM inactive in westerns), with 0.3 μM effective in primary RPE; therefore, a concentration range of ~0.03–1 μM should be explored with pACC and pAMPKα as engagement biomarkers and NADPH/Nrf2 targets as pharmacodynamic readouts (Li et al., 2018). Biochemical potency of PF-06409577 can be in the single-digit nanomolar range against recombinant AMPK and cellular potency for pACC has been described as “nM” in RPE contexts; nonetheless, empirical titration in RPE is warranted given observed cell-assay thresholds (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).
- Isoform selectivity in RPE: PF-06409577 is β1-selective, and ADaM-site ligand responsiveness is strongly β-isoform-dependent; however, AMPK β isoform expression distribution in human RPE is not provided in the current sources and should be profiled (mRNA/protein) to confirm the β1 hypothesis before assuming superior tissue selectivity (Ryder et al., 2018; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).
- Network cross-talk and safety in vitro: Co-activation of AMPK and mTORC1 has been associated with cytotoxic outcomes in some cell types; assays should monitor mTORC1 readouts (p-S6K, p-4EBP1) alongside autophagy flux to ensure PF-06409577 produces the expected AMPK→mTORC1 inhibition and does not trigger maladaptive co-activation contexts in RPE (Li et al., 2018).

Collectively, the expected proximal effects of PF-06409577 in RPE are robust AMPK activation with antioxidant and metabolic reprogramming, and the expected distal outcomes include reduced oxidative injury and improved lipid/autophagy balance. Barrier strengthening (ZO-1/occludin, TEER) is mechanistically plausible based on AMPK biology and AMPK-dependent rescue with alternative activators in ARPE-19, but must be experimentally demonstrated for PF-06409577 (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Tsou et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Direct, β1-selective AMPK activation with structural, biophysical, and biochemical support. PF-06409577 directly binds and activates AMPK α1β1γ1 at the ADaM site and shows clear β1 selectivity across parents and acyl glucuronide metabolites; this selectivity is a desirable property for limiting pan-AMPK liabilities observed with compounds like MK-8722 (e.g., cardiac glycogen accumulation) (Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).  
- Demonstrated on-target cytoprotection in RPE. Li et al. (2018) show AMPKα1-dependent protection of ARPE-19 and primary RPE against UVR, with mechanistic readouts aligned to AMD pathogenesis: increased NADPH, Nrf2 target induction, reduced ROS, lipid peroxidation, DNA damage, apoptosis, and cell death—providing a strong cell-biological foundation for further RPE work (Li et al., 2018).  
- Mechanistic fit to AMD drivers. AMPK activation intersects the principal RPE failure modes in AMD—redox imbalance (Nrf2), impaired autophagy/mitophagy (ULK1/mTORC1), and lipid dysregulation (ACC, FAO, LXR/ABCA1/G1)—and AMPK-dependent restoration of autophagy/lipophagy and barrier proteins has been demonstrated in ARPE-19 using a different AMPK-activating intervention (liraglutide), making PF-06409577 a mechanistically well-targeted candidate to modulate those pathways (Dang et al., 2021; Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).  
- Favorable metabolic profile and organ-protection precedent. PF-06409577 corrected NAFLD and lowered cholesterol in rodent/primate models with liver AMPK dependence, improved renal endpoints in β1-focused paradigms, and did not lower blood glucose in reported contexts, all suggesting a differentiated systemic pharmacology relative to pan-activators and indirect mitochondrial inhibitors (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).  
- Metabolite pharmacology understood. Active acyl glucuronides have been characterized structurally and functionally and exhibit β1-selective AMPK activation with notable stability, reducing concern about unstable, highly reactive acyl glucuronide species (while not fully removing risk), and informing PK/distribution planning for ocular routes (Ryder et al., 2018).

Key Gaps and Risks  
- No published junctional/TEER data for PF-06409577 in RPE. The project’s central claim—restoration of RPE junction integrity (ZO-1/occludin localization, TEER elevation, reduced paracellular permeability)—has not been demonstrated for PF-06409577 in any RPE model in the sources provided; this is the most critical data gap for the proposed indication (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).  
- No PF-06409577 autophagy/lipophagy data in RPE. While AMPK activation in ARPE-19 by liraglutide restored autophagy/lipophagy and rescued ZO-1 in an AMPK-dependent manner, PF-06409577-specific data on ULK1 phosphorylation, LC3 flux, p62 turnover, lysosome–autophagosome fusion, and lipid droplet dynamics in RPE are absent and must be generated (Tsou et al., 2025).  
- AMPK β isoform expression in human RPE is not established in the provided literature. Although ADaM ligands are β1-preferring and PF-06409577 is β1-selective, we do not have direct evidence here that β1 predominates in mature human RPE; consequently, isoform profiling is a necessary early-stage risk-reduction step (Steinberg & Carling, 2019; Ryder et al., 2018).  
- Cellular potency window in RPE requires clarification. Li et al. (2018) show a clear activation threshold between 0.03 μM (inactive) and 0.1–1.0 μM (active) for AMPKα phosphorylation in ARPE-19 and efficacy at 0.3 μM in primary RPE, whereas narrative text suggests “nM” activation; this discrepancy underscores the need for rigorous concentration–response across engagement and functional endpoints in relevant human RPE models (Li et al., 2018).  
- Clinical development discontinued; no ocular safety data. PF-06409577’s clinical program was halted at Phase I for non-ocular indications; no ophthalmic tolerability, ocular PK, or on-target/off-target safety in retinal tissues has been reported here. Acyl glucuronides, while stable in vitro for this series, can pose idiosyncratic risk; pan-AMPK activation has known cardiac liabilities; and network cross-talk (e.g., co-activation of AMPK and mTORC1) could be deleterious in some contexts—all argue for early safety de-risking (Webb et al., 2019; Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).

Programmatic Recommendations  
Near-term, decision-making studies should prioritize: (1) RPE isoform mapping (AMPK α/β/γ mRNA and protein), (2) dose–response and time-course profiling of PF-06409577 in human primary RPE or iPSC-RPE (pAMPKα Thr172, pACC Ser79, NADPH/NADP⁺, Nrf2 protein and targets), (3) autophagy/lipophagy flux assays (LC3-II turnover with/without lysosomal blockade, p62 degradation, ULK1 phosphorylation, mTORC1 markers), (4) lipid droplet quantification (number, size distribution) under FFA or oxLDL loading, (5) junctional biology (ZO-1/occludin claudin-1/4 localization and levels, cingulin/afadin phosphorylation status) and barrier function (TEER, FITC-dextran permeability), and (6) safety pharmacology in RPE (viability, apoptosis, senescence markers; exploration of AMPK–mTORC1 co-activation risk) across 0.03–1.0 μM with pACC-guided on-target exposure (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).

If in vitro RPE data are supportive, next steps include: (7) ocular PK after topical/periocular dosing (parent and acyl glucuronides in RPE/choroid), (8) metabolite profiling and covalent adduct risk assessment in ocular tissues, (9) in vivo efficacy in AMD-relevant models (e.g., light damage, Alu RNA–induced RPE degeneration, HFD/oxLDL models) with barrier and lipid endpoints, and (10) safety screens for cardiac glycogen accumulation under systemic exposure (to benchmark β1 selectivity advantages) (Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
PF-06409577 is a well-characterized, β1-selective, direct AMPK activator with on-target, AMPKα1-dependent cytoprotective activity in RPE cells under oxidative stress, and with strong mechanistic alignment to dry AMD pathobiology via NADPH/Nrf2, autophagy/mitophagy, and lipid metabolism pathways (Li et al., 2018). Class knowledge and comparator interventions support the plausibility that AMPK activation can restore RPE lipid homeostasis and barrier protein organization; however, critical indication-specific evidence—PF-06409577’s effects on RPE autophagy/lipophagy and junctional/TEER endpoints—is currently missing and must be generated before advancing (Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). The compound’s β1 selectivity, favorable metabolic efficacy profile (NAFLD/kidney), and lack of glucose-lowering are attractive, but the discontinued clinical status, the pharmacologically active acyl glucuronides, and known liabilities with pan-AMPK activation emphasize the need for deliberate safety de-risking and ocular PK/metabolite work (Behl et al., 2021; Ryder et al., 2018; Webb et al., 2019; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).

On balance, PF-06409577 merits a focused, RPE-centric preclinical validation campaign for dry AMD that directly tests barrier and lipid endpoints while monitoring canonical AMPK engagement and redox rescue. Positive readouts across ZO-1/occludin/TEER, autophagy/lipophagy markers, and lipid droplet turnover—together with preservation of mitochondrial/antioxidant markers—would substantially de-risk the mechanistic hypothesis and justify advancement toward ocular PK/safety studies and in vivo efficacy models (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024). At present, claims of TEER restoration and junctional upregulation by PF-06409577 in RPE cannot be substantiated from the available literature and should be considered unproven working hypotheses pending experimental confirmation (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History (Expanded Summary)  
- Origin/chemotype: Indole-3-carboxylic acid, direct ADaM-site AMPK activator; discovered and preclinically characterized by Pfizer for diabetic nephropathy (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Strang et al., 2025).  
- Selectivity/biophysics: Direct binding to α1β1γ1 with β1 selectivity; acyl glucuronide metabolites retain β1 activity with lower potency; likely mode includes allosteric activation and protection from Thr172 dephosphorylation (Ryder et al., 2018; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).  
- Systemic pharmacology: Liver AMPK activation corrected NAFLD and lowered cholesterol in rodents and primates; β1 activation improved kidney function in rodent models (Behl et al., 2021).  
- Safety-class signals: Pan-activator MK-8722 causes cardiac hypertrophy with glycogen in rodents/primate models; PF-06409577 reported not to lower blood glucose; acyl glucuronides stable but class risk remains (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Behl et al., 2021; Ryder et al., 2018).  
- Ocular biology: Direct RPE cytoprotection against UVR via AMPKα1-dependent signaling; no published PF-06409577 data on RPE junctions/TEER/autophagy endpoints (Li et al., 2018).

Mechanistic Integration in AMD Context  
- AMPK→Nrf2 redox axis: AMPK phosphorylation of Nrf2 (Ser550), indirect relief of KEAP1 repression (via GSK3β inhibition and p62-mediated KEAP1 autophagic degradation), and upregulation of antioxidant enzymes; these are operative in RPE and are enhanced by PF-06409577 in vitro (Hu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2018).  
- AMPK→ULK1/mTOR/autophagy: AMPK initiates autophagy, antagonizes mTORC1, and in RPE models AMPK activation restores autophagy/lipophagy, reduces EMT, and normalizes barrier protein localization under lipid stress—mechanistic endpoints to quantify for PF-06409577 (Dang et al., 2021; Tsou et al., 2025).  
- AMPK→ACC/FAO/lipogenesis: ACC inhibition reduces DNL and malonyl-CoA, permitting FAO flux; in RPE, this is expected to reduce lipid droplet accrual and lipoperoxidation burden central to drusen precursor formation (Webb et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2024).  
- AMPK→junction assembly: Phosphorylation of claudins and scaffold proteins, ZO-1 reassembly, and cytoskeletal remodeling provide a direct mechanistic route for barrier strengthening; this is plausible in RPE but requires PF-06409577-specific testing (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).

Decision Framework for Advancement  
- Go/No-Go criteria: Require demonstration that PF-06409577 increases pAMPKα/pACC and Nrf2 targets; reduces ROS/lipid peroxidation/DNA damage in RPE; increases autophagy flux and reduces lipid droplets under FFA or oxLDL; and improves ZO-1/occludin organization with increased TEER and reduced paracellular permeability, all in an AMPK-dependent manner (Li et al., 2018; Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).  
- Risk mitigation: Profile β isoform expression in human RPE; measure mTORC1 to exclude maladaptive co-activation; characterize ocular PK and acyl glucuronide distribution after topical/periocular delivery; benchmark systemic exposure to avoid cardiac glycogen liabilities (Steinberg & Carling, 2019; Li et al., 2018; Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).  
- Comparative positioning: If PF-06409577 proves effective on junctions and lipid/autophagy endpoints, its β1 selectivity and direct mechanism position it favorably versus indirect activators (metformin) and pan-activators (MK-8722); conversely, lack of junctional efficacy or safety signals would shift focus to alternative AMPK modulators or upstream modulators that converge on AMPK/Nrf2 with better ocular PK (Dang et al., 2021; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).

In summary, PF-06409577 has clear mechanistic and cellular evidence to support further exploration in dry AMD, with the caveat that the most clinically salient endpoints for RPE barrier restoration and lipid clearance remain to be proven for this agent. A disciplined experimental plan targeting these gaps will determine whether PF-06409577 advances as a credible candidate for RPE junction restoration in dry AMD (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024; Behl et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ML218 is a synthetic small‐molecule calcium channel inhibitor originally developed as an antagonist targeting T‐type CaV3 channels. It was discovered in efforts to design selective modulators of low‐voltage‐activated calcium channels and is commercially available (Tocris 5056). Its chemical structure – featuring a 3,5‐dichlorobenzamide moiety attached to an azabicyclic fragment – places it in the class of benzamide-derived T‐type channel blockers. The compound was designed to interact with hydrophobic fenestration sites in voltage‐gated calcium channels, and its development emerged from scaffold‐hopping strategies derived from earlier hits in high‐throughput calcium flux assays. ML218 thus belongs to a family of investigational agents that have been primarily used as pharmacological tools to dissect T‐type channel function in neuronal systems. Previous studies have focused on its ability to inhibit CaV3 channels in central nervous system models, including experiments in cell lines and primary neurons where it modulated firing patterns and synaptic excitability (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). In addition to its intended activity on CaV3 channels, detailed analyses have revealed that ML218 also exhibits significant cross‐activity with CaV1.4 channels by adopting an alternative binding mode that involves the III‐IV fenestration—an observation that distinguishes it from classical dihydropyridines (Sun et al., 2025). This dual binding behavior highlights both the promise and the challenge of using ML218 as a selective tool in complex tissues where multiple calcium channel subtypes coexist. Overall, ML218 is a promising lead compound representing the synthetic, small‐molecule approach to targeting voltage‐dependent calcium channels, with a structure–activity relationship that suggests potential repurposing for non‐neuronal applications such as retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier stabilization (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History:  
ML218 has been primarily explored within experimental models predominantly focused on the central nervous system. Several studies have employed ML218 as a pharmacological probe to inhibit T‐type calcium currents in neuronal populations. For example, in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease, ML218 demonstrated robust inhibition of T-type currents in subthalamic nucleus (STN) neurons, leading to marked alterations in burst firing patterns (Xiang et al., 2011; Manzar et al., 2025). Electrophysiological investigations using whole‐cell patch clamp techniques in HEK293 cells transfected with CaV3.2 channels have shown that ML218 can achieve potent block, with reported IC₅₀ values ranging from approximately 24 nM (in one report) to 150–310 nM in different assay settings (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). These preclinical studies validated ML218’s mechanism of action within neural substrates and its potential as a centrally active agent. In parallel, investigations in non‐neuronal cells have emerged. In particular, ML218 has been applied to studies involving human embryonic stem cell‐derived retinal pigment epithelium (hESC‐RPE) where it was used at a concentration of 5 μM to elucidate the functionality of voltage‐gated calcium channels expressed in these cells—primarily focusing on assays of phagocytosis and VEGF secretion (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). Consequently, repurposing ML218 for dry AMD would represent a novel application, extending its utilization from central nervous system studies to ocular tissue. The concept of drug repurposing in ocular diseases has been gaining traction in recent years due to the overlapping roles of calcium signaling in diverse tissues, and ML218’s history in rigorously characterizing calcium channel pharmacology makes it a candidate for further exploration in RPE models (Xiang et al., 2011; Korkka et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
ML218 functions primarily by blocking T‐type calcium channels, with an emphasis on CaV3.2 subtypes. The compound’s mechanism involves its entry into the transmembrane fenestrations of the channel complex, where it interrupts the normal ion‐conducting pathway. Detailed structural studies have revealed that in CaV3 channels, ML218 docks within the II‐III fenestration; in this binding mode, the phenyl head group of the molecule extends into the hydrophobic channel region while its aliphatic tail lies within the central pore, thereby imposing a state‐dependent block (Sun et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024). Mutagenesis studies have confirmed the importance of this alternate binding mode by demonstrating substantial changes in inhibitory potency upon modification of key residues such as T1007 (Sun et al., 2025). The molecular basis for its selectivity lies in the differential organization of channel domains between CaV3 and CaV1 families, with ML218’s binding being modulated by specific residues located in the channel pore and fenestration regions. In tissues such as the RPE, where calcium signaling plays a pivotal role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and barrier integrity, aberrant Ca²⁺ influx can activate calcium‐dependent proteases such as calpains. Calpains, once activated, can cleave junctional proteins including zonula occludens protein 1 (ZO-1) and occludin, leading to compromised barrier integrity. Thus, by selectively inhibiting CaV3.2‐mediated calcium entry, ML218 is hypothesized to prevent calpain activation and subsequent disruption of tight junctions in RPE cells—a mechanism that has been indirectly supported by studies showing that inhibitors of T-type channels reduce cellular excitability and junctional leak in alternative epithelial models (Sun et al., 2025). Furthermore, the compound’s dual action—including a modest agonist effect at specific concentrations—adds complexity to its pharmacological profile; however, in the context of RPE barrier function, the primary desired effect would be its antagonist action that limits pathological calcium entry under oxidative or inflammatory stress. The state‐dependence of ML218’s block (i.e., preferential inhibition when channels are in an open or inactivated state) may further enhance its capacity to target pathological calcium influx while sparing normal physiological signaling to some extent, although this property will require careful titration in a diseased state (Sun et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
The working hypothesis for repurposing ML218 in dry AMD is that its inhibition of CaV3.2 channels in retinal pigment epithelium will reduce pathological intracellular calcium accumulation under conditions of oxidative and inflammatory stress. Elevated Ca²⁺ levels in RPE cells are known to activate calpain, a calcium‐dependent protease that mediates the proteolytic cleavage of critical junctional proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin. Disruption of these proteins leads to a compromised RPE barrier, as reflected in reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased paracellular permeability (measured by FITC-dextran flux assays). In evaluating ML218 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current literature. This potent inhibition forms a logical mechanistic basis for targeting pathological calcium influx in RPE cells, where calcium overload and subsequent activation of proteases like calpain are implicated in junctional protein degradation and barrier dysfunction. Furthermore, the detailed structural insights into ML218’s binding—its differential interactions in CaV3 and CaV1 channels—provide a strong foundation for understanding its pharmacodynamic activity. The ability of ML218 to modulate calcium signaling with state‐dependent block enhances its therapeutic promise by potentially allowing it to target pathological overactivity while sparing baseline physiological function (Sun et al., 2025).

The literature reveals that ML218 is not exclusively selective for CaV3.2 channels; it exhibits cross‐reactivity with CaV1.4 channels, albeit at lower potency (with reported IC₅₀ values for CaV1.4 in the micromolar range compared to nanomolar ranges for CaV3.2) (Sun et al., 2025). Furthermore, while the proposed hypothesis for dry AMD is biologically plausible, there is a notable gap in the literature regarding direct evidence for ML218’s efficacy in preserving RPE barrier function under oxidative or inflammatory conditions—most studies with ML218 have been performed in neuronal contexts or in assays focused on phagocytosis and secretory aspects of RPE physiology (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). Another concern pertains to the reported potency of ML218. Although optimistic hypotheses suggest an IC₅₀ of approximately 7 nM for CaV3.2 channel block, the available data across various assay platforms indicate that effective concentrations are more likely to be in the tens to low hundreds of nanomolar range (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). Despite these challenges, the conceptual framework for repurposing ML218 in dry AMD has several attractive features. The targeting of T‐type calcium channels to mitigate calpain activation and to preserve tight junction protein integrity represents a novel therapeutic approach that departs from traditional anti‐inflammatory or anti‐angiogenic strategies. In dry AMD, where chronic, low‐grade oxidative and inflammatory stress contribute to RPE dysfunction and barrier breakdown, a compound like ML218 could theoretically reduce intracellular calcium overload and, consequently, the cascade of events leading to junctional degradation. Dose‐ranging studies and careful evaluation of potential off‐target effects will also be critical to establishing a safe and effective therapeutic profile for ocular application.

In the cardiovascular arena, animal models of heart failure and ischemia-reperfusion injury have documented that SS-31 treatment leads to improved left ventricular function and reduced tissue biomarkers of injury, effects that are attributed to its ability to stabilize cardiolipin and maintain the integrity of the electron transport system (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 10–12). Further, in neuromuscular and metabolic disease models, the compound has been shown to enhance mitochondrial ATP production and reduce oxidative stress, with early clinical studies in rare mitochondrial disorders such as Barth syndrome (a condition involving cardiolipin abnormalities) and primary mitochondrial myopathy providing supportive translational evidence (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 10–11, 16–22). More recently, SS-31 has been explored in the context of ocular diseases, including nonneovascular age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) and diabetic macular edema, where preclinical studies in murine models report that subcutaneous administration of SS-31 can reverse electroretinographic deficits, facilitate the clearance of sub-retinal pigment epithelium (sub‐RPE) deposits, and ultimately reverse vision loss (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Clinical trials—such as the Phase I ReCLAIM study in intermediate AMD and the ongoing Phase II ReCLAIM-2 trial—have begun to assess SS-31’s safety profile, pharmacokinetics, and preliminary efficacy in preserving visual function, thereby positioning it as a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Although its use in dry AMD is relatively novel compared to its established preclinical record in other mitochondrial disorders, the existing scientific and regulatory trajectory supports its potential repurposing for diseases in which mitochondrial dysfunction is a central pathogenic mechanism (Nashine, 2021, pp. 9–11, 16).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism by which SS-31 exerts its cytoprotective effects is centered on its highly specific interaction with cardiolipin, an anionic phospholipid unique to the mitochondrial inner membrane that plays a pivotal role in maintaining the structural integrity of cristae and the proper assembly and function of electron transport chain complexes (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). Detailed biophysical studies, including nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations, have demonstrated that SS-31 binds to cardiolipin via both electrostatic interactions (through its basic residues) and hydrophobic interactions (via its aromatic side chains), resulting in the “neutralization” of the negative surface charge on mitochondrial membranes and a favorable modulation of membrane fluidity and curvature (Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4; Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 16–22). This binding not only stabilizes cardiolipin against oxidative peroxidation but also promotes the optimal assembly of electron transport chain complexes into respiratory supercomplexes, thereby enhancing electron flow, reducing electron leakage, and ultimately decreasing the generation of ROS (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 4–6, 15–16). In addition, SS-31 has been shown to mitigate proton leakage and restore pH stress resistance in aged mitochondria by enhancing the function of critical proteins such as the adenine nucleotide translocator (ANT), which is central to ADP/ATP exchange and overall mitochondrial bioenergetics (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 10–12). Although SS-31 was initially characterized as an antioxidant, its primary mode of action is now understood to be the preservation of mitochondrial structure and function through cardiolipin stabilization rather than direct radical scavenging alone (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4). In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress—a key pathological hallmark of dry AMD—the hypothesis posits that by stabilizing mitochondria via cardiolipin binding, SS-31 will maintain normal electron transport chain efficiency, preserve ATP production, and limit ROS production, thereby protecting the integrity of RPE cells (Tong et al., 2022, pp. 14–16). Although direct experimental evidence linking SS-31 to the preservation of tight junction proteins such as ZO-1/occludin or to the restoration of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE cells is limited in the current literature, the well-documented mitochondrial protection afforded by SS-31 in other cellular models suggests that secondary benefits on cellular barrier function are plausible given the tight coupling between mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and loss of epithelial integrity (Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). In sum, the molecular interactions of SS-31 with mitochondrial membranes serve not only to optimize respiratory chain efficiency and restore bioenergetic balance but also to reduce the biochemical milieu of oxidative stress that is known to compromise cell–cell junctions, thereby providing a strong mechanistic rationale for its application in protecting RPE barrier function in dry AMD (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3, 15–22).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its molecular mechanism, the expected effect of SS-31 in an oxidative-challenge assay using RPE cells is multifaceted. In an experimental setting where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative stress—for example, through hydrogen peroxide treatment—the administration of SS-31 is anticipated to result in the selective binding to cardiolipin within RPE mitochondria; this interaction should stabilize inner mitochondrial membrane architecture, preserve cristae morphology, and enhance the efficiency of electron transport, leading to robust ATP production and reduced ROS levels (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). As mitochondrial homeostasis is a critical determinant of RPE cell function, the preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics is expected to translate into decreased apoptosis and improved cell survival in the face of oxidative challenges (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 8–11). Beyond these direct mitochondrial effects, maintenance of intracellular energy status and lower levels of ROS are essential for the proper localization and preservation of tight junction proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin; oxidative stress is known to disrupt these junctions, leading to loss of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and compromised RPE barrier integrity (Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40). Therefore, treatment with SS-31 should also help maintain or restore TEER in RPE monolayer assays, indicating a preservation of barrier function that is crucial for retinal homeostasis and prevention of drusen formation and RPE degeneration associated with dry AMD (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Moreover, preclinical studies in animal models of retinal degeneration—in which SS-31 has been shown to reverse vision loss, improve clearance of sub-RPE deposits, and enhance electroretinographic responses—further support the expectation that SS-31 can exert protective effects in the ocular environment by mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction and the subsequent cascade of oxidative damage (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Taken together, the anticipated experimental outcome is that SS-31 will significantly attenuate oxidative damage in RPE cells, preserve mitochondrial function, maintain tight junction integrity (as evidenced by stable ZO-1/occludin expression and restored TEER), and ultimately contribute to the functional rescue of RPE cells under conditions that mimic the oxidative insults observed in dry AMD (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tong et al., 2022, pp. 14–16).

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, SS-31 (Elamipretide) presents as a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, with several key strengths that support its potential utility and a few noteworthy challenges that will need to be addressed in further research. One of the primary strengths of SS-31 is its well-characterized mechanism of action; its ability to bind cardiolipin and thereby stabilize mitochondrial inner membrane structure, enhance electron transport chain efficiency, and reduce ROS generation is supported by robust preclinical data across multiple models of mitochondrial dysfunction, including cardiac, skeletal muscle, and retinal systems (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Mitchell et al., 2019, pp. 1–4). This mitochondria-targeted mechanism is particularly attractive in the context of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are recognized as major drivers of RPE degeneration and subsequent photoreceptor loss (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Lenin et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Furthermore, early-phase clinical studies in ocular disease have demonstrated that SS-31 is safe and well tolerated and have hinted at functional improvements in visual acuity and reduced progression of retinal degeneration, which supports its translational viability (Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5). The repurposing of SS-31 from conditions such as heart failure and primary mitochondrial myopathy to an ocular application leverages its established bioenergetic benefits and broad mitochondrial stabilization properties, thereby enhancing its appeal as a novel intervention for dry AMD (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 10–11, 16–22).

However, there are several challenges and weaknesses that merit consideration. First, while the molecular mechanism of SS-31—centered on cardiolipin binding and mitochondrial stabilization—is well supported, direct evidence linking its activity to the preservation of tight junction proteins (such as ZO-1/occludin) and the restoration of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE models remains limited in the current literature (Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40). This represents a key knowledge gap given that the hypothesis posits that protection of RPE barrier integrity is a critical outcome in preventing disease progression in dry AMD. Additional preclinical studies that specifically measure the effects of SS-31 on RPE tight junction organization, using immunostaining for ZO-1 and occludin as well as quantitative TEER assays, would be essential to fully validate its proposed mechanism in the context of epithelial barrier protection (Fisher, 2022, pp. 36–40; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Second, although early-phase clinical trials have shown promise in improving functional visual metrics, some clinical studies in related indications (e.g., Phase 2 trials in cardiac conditions) have produced mixed results with primary endpoints not consistently met, suggesting that optimal dosing regimens, treatment durations, and patient selection criteria may need further refinement (Tung et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 9–10). In the case of dry AMD, where the pathological changes evolve over extended periods, longer-term studies and careful endpoint selection will be critical to demonstrate sustained therapeutic benefit (Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Third, while the pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of SS-31 appear favorable for reaching mitochondrial targets, ensuring sufficient ocular penetration and accumulation in the RPE—whether via systemic subcutaneous administration or topical formulations—remains a logistical and pharmacological challenge that must be addressed in future clinical development (Tong et al., 2022, pp. 14–16; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

In conclusion, SS-31 (Elamipretide) exhibits a strong mechanistic underpinning based on its targeted interaction with cardiolipin to restore mitochondrial function and mitigate oxidative stress—a mode of action that is directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD owing to the central role of mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE degeneration (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). The compound’s extensive preclinical validation in models of mitochondrial diseases, coupled with encouraging early clinical data, makes it a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Nonetheless, key gaps in directly demonstrating its effects on RPE barrier integrity and tight junction preservation (as measured by ZO-1/occludin levels and TEER) necessitate further targeted preclinical studies. Additionally, addressing challenges related to optimal dosing, treatment duration, and efficient ocular delivery will be paramount for the success of subsequent clinical trials. Overall, given its robust mitochondrial protective effects and plausible secondary benefits on epithelial barrier function, SS-31 warrants further investigation as a novel therapeutic strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration (Sabbah et al., 2025, pp. 1–3; Ji et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Kim & Lad, 2021, pp. 4–5; Tung et al., 2025, pp. 10–12).

I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PXS-5153A is a synthetically derived molecule that belongs to the class of selective lysyl oxidase inhibitors. In its design, medicinal chemistry efforts focused on optimizing potency and selectivity for LOXL2, along with activity against LOXL3, two members of the lysyl oxidase family that catalyze the oxidative deamination of lysine residues in collagens and elastin to promote covalent crosslink formation. These crosslinks confer the mechanical strength and stiffness of extracellular matrices (ECMs) such as Bruch’s membrane. Synthetic routes to compounds like PXS-5153A typically rely on structure-based design and iterative optimization to achieve potent enzyme inhibition with favorable pharmacokinetic properties (Lin et al., 2020). The compound, commercially available under MedChemExpress HY-111217, is representative of a new therapeutic class that has been primarily explored in the context of fibrosis and tumor microenvironment modulation. Given that ECM stiffening is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, targeting LOXL2 represents a novel approach compared to conventional anti-inflammatory or anti-angiogenic strategies.

II. Therapeutic History  
The LOXL2 inhibitor class, including molecules such as PXS-5153A, has been extensively tested in preclinical models of fibrosis and cancer. For example, within non-ocular systems, LOXL2 activity has been linked to increased tissue stiffness that fosters metastatic progression and desmoplastic reactions in tumors, and selective inhibition of LOXL2 has been shown to reduce crosslink density, attenuating fibrotic remodeling (Lin et al., 2020). Experimental inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity using non-selective agents like β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) has also been applied to in vitro and in vivo models to modulate ECM assembly, with effects on barrier function observed in RPE cultures co-treated with endothelial cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). Although LOXL2 inhibitors have not traditionally been used to treat dry AMD, evidence underscores the centrality of aberrant ECM crosslinking in BM thickening observed during aging and AMD progression (Wang et al., 2025). In particular, the endothelial cell–RPE crosstalk studies demonstrate a critical role for lysyl oxidase activity in regulating collagen bundle formation and in establishing RPE barrier properties (Benedicto et al., 2017). Accordingly, while there is no direct clinical or preclinical record of PXS-5153A in AMD, the antifibrotic profile of the compound and its impact on extracellular matrix mechanics in other disease contexts serve as a compelling rationale to explore its application in dry AMD.

III. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, LOXL2 catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of lysine or hydroxylysine residues present in collagens and elastin. This reaction is critical for the formation of covalent crosslinks that stabilize the ECM. Overexpression or hyperactivity of LOXL2 results in an excessively crosslinked and stiff matrix. In the eye, particularly within Bruch’s membrane—which is a complex, stratified ECM structure located between the RPE and the choroid—aberrant collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking are known to increase mechanical tension. Such mechanical changes are thought to adversely affect RPE cell function by interfering with integrin-mediated cell–matrix interactions and perturbing the proper localization of tight junction proteins, including ZO-1 and occludin (Benedicto et al., 2017).

PXS-5153A functions by binding to the catalytic pocket of LOXL2, thereby preventing its enzymatic activity. By blocking the oxidative deamination step, PXS-5153A reduces the formation of both immature and mature crosslinks in ECM proteins. The anticipated outcome is a lower crosslink density in Bruch’s membrane, resulting in a softer, more compliant matrix environment. This reduction in mechanical stiffness is expected to diminish abnormal mechanosignaling through β1 integrins, which are integral to the assembly and maintenance of tight junctions on RPE cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). The downstream consequences of reduced integrin activation include dampening of Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways, which in turn facilitate the stabilization and proper localization of tight junction proteins at the RPE cell membranes (Benedicto et al., 2017). Restoration of these junctional complexes correlates with improved barrier function, typically measured as an increased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in cell culture models. This mechanism is supported by studies in which inhibition of lysyl oxidase activity—by pharmacological agents such as BAPN—led to alterations in RPE barrier properties and tight junction morphology (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by directly targeting LOXL2, PXS-5153A is proposed to correct the pathological ECM remodeling that underlies BM stiffening in dry AMD while re-establishing proper RPE barrier integrity.

IV. Expected Effect  
The expected therapeutic effect of PXS-5153A in dry AMD centers on normalization of the BM ECM and concomitant restoration of RPE barrier function. In the proposed experimental model—an in vitro co-culture system where human fetal RPE (hfRPE) cells are grown on a substrate mimicking BM with defined stiffness—the application of PXS-5153A at concentrations around 5 µM is anticipated to yield a number of favorable outcomes.

First, by reducing LOXL2-mediated crosslinking of collagen IV and fibronectin, the drug should decrease the mechanical stiffness of the BM analog. A less rigid BM reduces aberrant integrin activation on the basolateral surfaces of RPE cells, which has been shown to be critical for proper tight junction assembly. In several studies, when the extracellular matrix is normalized—such as by altering substrate stiffness—there is an improvement in the localization of key tight junction proteins, specifically occludin and ZO-1, at the cell membrane (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Second, the reduced matrix stiffness is expected to alleviate the mechanical stress experienced by RPE cells, thereby facilitating the re-establishment of cell polarity and intercellular junction continuity. The stabilization of junctional complexes is measurable by TEER. In previous EC–RPE co-culture experiments, modulation of ECM mechanical properties directly correlated with increased TEER values, reflecting improved barrier function (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
Moreover, the proper organization of the basement membrane is not only a structural consideration; the biochemical signaling through β1 integrin receptors—critical for maintaining cell adhesion and survival—would return toward homeostatic levels, further supporting the integrity of the RPE layer (Benedicto et al., 2017). These integrin-mediated signals influence downstream effectors such as Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK, which have been implicated in regulating tight junction dynamics (Benedicto et al., 2017). Progress in these pathways is expected to manifest as an overall improvement in the barrier phenotype, which is central to preventing the leakage of fluid and other deleterious solutes into the subretinal space—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology.

In summary, it is anticipated that treatment with PXS-5153A in appropriate in vitro (and ultimately in vivo) models will lead to:  
• Reduced collagen IV and fibronectin crosslinking in BM, yielding a matrix with decreased stiffness (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Normalization of β1 integrin signaling and subsequent reorganization of RPE tight junctions with improved localization of proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Benedicto et al., 2017).  
• Restoration of barrier function as evidenced by increased TEER measurements and improved paracellular permeability profiles (Benedicto et al., 2017).  

Thus, PXS-5153A is expected to address one of the core aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis by targeting ECM remodeling, which in turn indirectly stabilizes RPE cell function.

V. Overall Evaluation  
The concept of using PXS-5153A to modulate ECM pathology in dry AMD is compelling given the mechanistic insights derived from studies on lysyl oxidase activity in epithelial barrier function and ECM assembly. Among the strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its robust preclinical evidence in fibrosis and tumor microenvironment models. LOXL2 has been implicated in promoting tissue stiffening by catalyzing the crosslinking of collagen and fibronectin in various tissues (Lin et al., 2020). The pathophysiological parallels between fibrotic ECM remodeling in cancers and the stiffening of Bruch’s membrane in dry AMD provide a strong rationale for repurposing a LOXL2 inhibitor in an ocular context. Numerous studies have demonstrated that extracellular matrix integrity is essential for optimal RPE barrier function, and that even subtle changes in ECM mechanics can disrupt junctional complexes and lead to barrier dysfunction (Benedicto et al., 2017). Thus, by targeting a critical enzymatic step in ECM crosslinking, PXS-5153A may confer dual benefits: it could both reduce the pathological stiffening of Bruch’s membrane and promote the reorganization of tight junction complexes, ultimately resulting in enhanced TEER and stabilization of the outer blood–retina barrier.

However, several important weaknesses or uncertainties must be considered. First, while numerous studies (using agents such as BAPN) have illustrated that lysyl oxidase inhibition affects RPE barrier function, direct evidence with selective LOXL2 inhibitors—specifically in ocular models of dry AMD—is lacking (Buniello et al., 2025). In fact, the Open Targets Platform indicates only a weak direct association between LOXL2 and age-related macular degeneration, based on limited literature evidence (Buniello et al., 2025). This raises the possibility that, although LOXL2 plays a demonstrable role in ECM crosslinking in other tissues, its specific involvement in dry AMD pathogenesis may not be as pronounced or may be influenced by other factors not recapitulated in non-ocular models.

The structural integrity of Bruch’s membrane is critical not only for its barrier function but also for nutrient transport between the choroidal circulation and the RPE. Overinhibition of LOXL2, or interference with normal ECM turnover, may inadvertently lead to basement membrane disorganization, as has been observed when lysyl oxidase activity was inhibited during critical periods of retinal development (Benedicto et al., 2017). Another consideration is the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. In addition to ECM stiffening, dry AMD involves multifactorial processes including oxidative stress, complement activation, inflammation, and the accumulation of lipoprotein deposits. Thus, while normalizing matrix stiffness is likely to improve RPE barrier function, it may be insufficient to fully arrest or reverse the disease process on its own. From a development perspective, there is significant strength in the repurposing strategy because agents like PXS-5153A already have a detailed preclinical profile in non-ocular fibrotic models. This existing data can accelerate preclinical validation in ocular models, with studies planned in RPE–BM co-culture systems using TEER as a functional readout (Benedicto et al., 2017). Nonetheless, one notable weakness is the limited direct evidence linking LOXL2 specifically to dry AMD. Although elevated lysyl oxidase activity and changes in collagen crosslinking have been observed in the context of RPE barrier function and BM integrity (Benedicto et al., 2017), the genetic and translational data associating LOXL2 with AMD are not robust. The relatively low association score (Buniello et al., 2025) suggests that additional studies are needed to clarify LOXL2’s role in the eye and to determine whether its inhibition will yield a therapeutically meaningful benefit in dry AMD patients.

In conclusion, repurposing PXS-5153A for dry AMD represents an innovative strategy that leverages the known antifibrotic effects of LOXL2 inhibition to address the deleterious ECM remodeling observed in aged Bruch’s membrane. The candidate’s synthetic origins and prior applications in fibrosis and cancer studies provide a solid foundation for its use, while the mechanistic rationale—centered on reducing pathological crosslinking and restoring RPE barrier function—is strongly supported by evidence from ECM modulation studies (Benedicto et al., 2017). However, challenges remain due to the lack of direct ocular data, potential risks of overmodulating ECM integrity, and the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology. Future research must focus on rigorous in vitro validation in RPE–BM co-culture systems and in vivo studies in relevant AMD animal models to establish the efficacy and safety profile of PXS-5153A in the context of dry AMD. Overall, despite these uncertainties, PXS-5153A holds promise as a novel ECM-targeted therapeutic candidate that could complement existing and emerging treatment strategies for this currently unmet clinical need (Lin et al., 2020; Buniello et al., 2025).

Taken together, the strengths of a clear mechanism of action, potent enzyme selectivity, and an innovative approach toward ECM normalization position PXS-5153A as an attractive candidate warranting further investigation. Nonetheless, a careful reappraisal of the molecular role of LOXL2 in the ocular microenvironment, along with detailed studies on dosing, delivery, and potential off-target effects, will be critical in determining whether this candidate can be successfully repurposed for treating dry AMD.
