Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
JQ1 (Selleck S7110) is a synthetic small-molecule thienotriazolodiazepine developed as a first-in-class, highly selective competitive inhibitor of the bromodomain and extra-terminal (BET) acetyl-lysine reader family (BRD2/3/4, BRDT) that binds the acetyl-lysine pocket of BET bromodomains (BD1 and BD2) to displace BET proteins from chromatin and suppress transcription at dependent enhancers and promoters (pan-BET, BD1/BD2 non-selective) (Zhao et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2023). BET bromodomains recognize acetylated histone tails at active enhancers/super-enhancers and recruit coactivator assemblies that couple to RNA polymerase II to drive high-amplitude transcription of inflammatory, immune, and stress-response genes; small-molecule BET inhibition collapses these assemblies and blunts stimulus-induced transcriptional programs in immune and neural cells (Zhao et al., 2017). Within ophthalmology, JQ1 has been deployed intravitreally or systemically in multiple preclinical models, including inherited photoreceptor degeneration (rd10 retinitis pigmentosa), oxidative-stress retinal injury (sodium iodate), light-damage photoreceptor injury, experimental autoimmune uveitis (with other BET inhibitors), corneal fibrosis, and proliferative vitreoretinopathy, where it has shown neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory, and anti-fibrotic activity (Zhao et al., 2017; Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023; Eichenbaum, 2020; Liao et al., 2024). The BET modality also includes domain-selective ligands (e.g., BD2-preferring apabetalone/RVX-208) and targeted protein degraders (e.g., dBET6, a cereblon-recruiting JQ1-based PROTAC) that achieve complementary pharmacology by either sparing BD1 or depleting BRD2/3/4 protein, respectively (Zhu et al., 2023; Shahid et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
- Inherited photoreceptor degeneration (rd10, Pde6b mutant): A single intravitreal injection of JQ1 (2 µl of 0.1 mM at PN14) preserved photoreceptor number through PN24 (>90% of baseline), improved ERG a- and b-wave amplitudes, reduced TUNEL-positive photoreceptor apoptosis and caspase-3/7 activity, and markedly suppressed retinal microglial activation/infiltration (IBA1, TSPO, CD68) with cytokine mRNAs (TNFα, MCP-1, IL-1β, IL-6, RANTES) reduced to WT levels in whole retinas and in sorted retinal microglia (MCP-1 also lowered by ELISA) (Zhao et al., 2017). Complementary in vitro work showed JQ1 pre-treatment abolished LPS-induced upregulation of TNFα, MCP-1, IL-1β, IL-6 and RANTES and reduced microglial proliferation and migration by ~70%, with mechanistic dissection implicating BET2 (BRD2) and the BD2 (Brom2) domain in microglial activation; a BD2-preferring ligand (RVX208) suppressed cytokine induction more effectively than a BD1-preferring ligand (Olinone) (Zhao et al., 2017). In vivo, BET2 protein is increased at PN24 in rd10 retinas, correlating with peak microglial activation and photoreceptor degeneration (Zhao et al., 2017).  
- Oxidative-stress retinal/RPE injury (sodium iodate, SI): JQ1 suppressed BRD4-induced STING transcription by decreasing chromatin accessibility (reduced H3 acetylation, RNA Pol II recruitment) at the STING locus, curtailed cGAS–STING activation, reduced microglia/macrophage accumulation (IBA1+) in retina/subretinal spaces, prevented RPE/retinal degeneration, and preserved retinal integrity without detectable adverse retinal morphology when used alone (in vitro ARPE cells and in vivo SI models across ages) (Zou et al., 2022). Mechanistically, BRD4 upregulation under oxidative stress promotes STING and inflammatory outputs; JQ1 or BRD4 depletion enhances autophagic flux (LC3II), accelerates autophagic enclosure/clearance of cytosolic DNA, reduces dsDNA accumulation, and thereby attenuates STING-mediated inflammation; autophagy inhibitors (BafA1, chloroquine) block these effects, indicating an autophagy-dependent mechanism (Zou et al., 2022).  
- Light-damage photoreceptor injury: The JQ1-based PROTAC dBET6 delivered systemically degraded BRD2/3/4 in mouse retina, improved retinal responsiveness and visual acuity after light damage, suppressed macrophage/microglia activation and Müller gliosis, reduced photoreceptor death, and inhibited LD-induced cGAS–STING activation in retinal microglia; importantly, the PROTAC strategy is motivated by compensatory BRD4 accumulation observed with JQ1 (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- RPE cell inflammation (ARPE-19): Multiple BET inhibitors (including JQ1) reduced etoposide-induced IL-6 and IL-8 secretion, decreased NF-κB p65 activity, and reduced acetylation of p53 at K382 in human RPE without major cytotoxicity; the anti-inflammatory effects appeared SIRT1-independent (SIRT1 inhibition or knockdown did not reverse IL-8 lowering), although SIRT1 pharmacology altered the p53 acetylation response (Hytti et al., 2016). BET inhibitors slightly decreased baseline MTT conversion but reduced etoposide cytotoxicity (lower LDH release, higher viability), consistent with modest cytoprotection under this stressor (Hytti et al., 2016).  
- Endothelial barrier inflammation: In HUVEC transwell monolayers, TNF-α decreased TEER, whereas pretreatment with JQ1 or BD2-selective apabetalone prevented the TEER drop, maintaining monolayer integrity; BRD4 inhibition reduced inflammatory marker expression and midkine, and the authors concluded BRD4 inhibition preserved barrier function under inflammatory challenge; while promising for barrier biology, these data were generated in vascular endothelial cells, not RPE (Shahid et al., 2022).  
- Other ophthalmic signals: BET blockade has downregulated Th17-associated genes in experimental autoimmune uveitis, ameliorated acute RGC loss after NMDA by suppressing retinal cytokines (~50% reduction in TNFα, IL-1β, MCP-1, RANTES) and preserving RGC number/gene expression (~2×), and reduced/reversed corneal scarring via BRD4 inhibition and Nrf2-dependent antioxidant induction without impairing epithelial regeneration (Eichenbaum, 2020). A separate RPE-centric multi-omics PVR study used intraocular eNano-JQ1 to show potent anti-fibrotic efficacy (reduced αSMA, thinner membranes) with favorable ocular safety (ERG, histology, TUNEL) over seven days, supporting feasibility of sustained intraocular JQ1 delivery (Liao et al., 2024).  
- Application to AMD: JQ1 has not been tested clinically for dry AMD; however, in vivo SI oxidative-injury studies model RPE/retinal degeneration relevant to geographic atrophy and identify cGAS–STING repression and autophagy-mediated cytosolic DNA clearance as protective mechanisms; moreover, cGAS/STING promoter accessibility is increased in macular retinas from GA patients, strengthening translational plausibility for dry AMD (Zou et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
BET chromatin reader displacement and inflammatory super-enhancer suppression  
- BET proteins, particularly BRD4, bind acetylated histone tails via BD1 and BD2 to stabilize enhancer/super-enhancer coactivator complexes and recruit Mediator and RNA Pol II, enabling rapid, high-output transcription of stimulus-responsive genes (e.g., NF-κB target programs and innate immune effectors) (Zhao et al., 2017). JQ1 competitively occupies the acetyl-lysine pocket in BD1/BD2, displacing BET proteins and causing collapse of the transcriptional assembly with consequent repression of inflammatory/immune gene expression; this has been demonstrated across macrophages, microglia, brain, and retina (Zhao et al., 2017). NF-κB drives dynamic super-enhancer formation during inflammation, providing a mechanistic intersection whereby BRD4 coactivation of NF-κB can be neutralized by BET inhibition to broadly downregulate cytokine programs and adhesion molecules (Zhao et al., 2017).  
- In retinal microglia and degenerating retina, BET2 (BRD2) and the BD2 (Brom2) domain appear to dominate cytokine induction and activation phenotypes; pharmacologic BD2 targeting (RVX208) and siRNA to BET2 blunt expression of TNFα, IL-1β, MCP-1, IL-6, and RANTES and curb microglial proliferation/migration, whereas BD1 targeting (Olinone) exerts narrower effects (notably migration and RANTES) (Zhao et al., 2017). In vivo, intravitreal JQ1 suppresses microglial infiltration into ONL/subretinal spaces and lowers retinal cytokine mRNAs and MCP-1 protein, consistent with an immunomodulatory mechanism downstream of BET displacement (Zhao et al., 2017).  
- In ARPE-19 cells, BET inhibition reduces etoposide-induced IL-6/IL-8 secretion and NF-κB activity without major cytotoxicity; the anti-inflammatory effect persists when SIRT1 is inhibited or knocked down, indicating SIRT1 independence for cytokine suppression in these conditions, even though BET inhibition reduces acetyl-p53 (Lys382) via a SIRT1-interacting axis (Hytti et al., 2016). These data collectively establish BET blockade as a chromatin-level anti-inflammatory mechanism across retinal microglia and RPE contexts (Hytti et al., 2016).

BRD4–cGAS–STING repression and autophagy-dependent cytosolic DNA clearance in oxidative stress  
- Under oxidative stress in RPE and retina, BRD4 is induced and directly promotes STING transcription; JQ1 counteracts this by reducing histone acetylation (e.g., H3 acetyl marks) and phosphorylated Pol II occupancy at the STING locus, thereby reducing chromatin accessibility and transcriptional output (Zou et al., 2022). This leads to reduced cGAS–STING activation, dampened downstream NF-κB/IRF-mediated inflammatory gene induction, decreased retinal microglia/macrophage recruitment, and protection against RPE/retina degeneration in vivo (Zou et al., 2022).  
- Beyond transcriptional repression, BRD4 inhibition potentiates autophagy: JQ1 or BRD4 knockdown increases LC3II, accelerates enclosure of cytosolic dsDNA by autophagosomes (visualized with GFP-LC3 and Cy3-DNA), reduces accumulation of oxidized cytosolic DNA (a potent innate immune agonist), and these effects require intact autophagic flux (blocked by chloroquine/BafA1), directly linking BET inhibition to enhanced clearance of DNA debris that drives cGAS activation (Zou et al., 2022). This dual mechanism—STING transcriptional silencing and autophagic DNA clearance—aligns with decreased innate immune activation in SI-injured retinas and provides a mechanistic bridge to geographic atrophy in which cGAS/STING promoters exhibit increased accessibility (Zou et al., 2022).

Barrier biology and tight junctions: what is and is not known  
- In vascular endothelium, BRD4 inhibition with JQ1 or BD2-selective apabetalone preserved TEER and monolayer integrity during TNF-α stimulation, reduced NF-κB activation, decreased pro-inflammatory markers, and lowered midkine expression, indicating a direct barrier-protective effect in inflamed endothelium (Shahid et al., 2022). While the cell type differs, these results are proof-of-concept that BET inhibition can functionally maintain barrier resistance under cytokine challenge.  
- Critically, across the RPE literature excerpts provided, no direct measurements of RPE barrier function (TEER), tight-junction proteins (ZO-1/TJP1, claudin-19/CLDN19), or junctional continuity were reported for JQ1 or any BET inhibitor in ARPE-19 or primary RPE under inflammatory/oxidative stress; multiple excerpts explicitly note the absence of tight-junction/barrier metrics and recommend further study in advanced models (Hytti et al., 2016; Eichenbaum, 2020; Zhu et al., 2023). Therefore, a mechanistic claim that JQ1 increases H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19 enhancers and directly raises ZO-1/claudin-19 transcription in RPE is not supported by existing evidence in the provided corpus.

Pharmacology, delivery, and safety considerations  
- JQ1 exhibits a short systemic half-life (~1 h reported elsewhere and noted in the retinal context), and in rd10, photoreceptor protection after a single intravitreal dose waned as drug dissociated from targets and diffused, with higher intravitreal concentrations not improving efficacy, motivating sustained ocular delivery strategies (e.g., nanoparticles, osmotic pumps) or alternative modalities (e.g., BET PROTACs) (Zhao et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2023). Local formulation advances such as eNano-JQ1 achieved seven-day intraocular release with favorable safety and efficacy in a PVR model (Liao et al., 2024).  
- BET competitive inhibitors can trigger cell-cycle arrest and modestly reduce metabolic activity in vitro; ARPE-19 studies showed slight decreases in MTT conversion at baseline but no major viability loss, and in some assays BET inhibitors reduced etoposide cytotoxicity (Hytti et al., 2016). In SI models, JQ1 alone exhibited no overt adverse retinal morphology/viability, and systemic dBET6 achieved retinal BET degradation “without detectable toxicity” at the reported regimen (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). Notably, compensatory BRD4 upregulation was observed with JQ1 in certain contexts, potentially blunting efficacy—a liability that targeted degradation (dBET6) may overcome (Zhu et al., 2023).

Therapeutic implications for dry AMD  
Collectively, the ocular data support an anti-inflammatory/innate-immunity–modulating, neuroprotective role for BET inhibition in retina/RPE that is directly relevant to dry AMD pathobiology: oxidative stress-driven cytosolic DNA leakage, cGAS–STING activation, NF-κB–dependent cytokine induction, microglia/macrophage recruitment, and downstream neurodegeneration are all attenuated by JQ1 or dBET6 in preclinical models (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). However, there is no direct evidence that JQ1 improves RPE tight-junction expression or TEER; any barrier benefit inferred for RPE is, at present, extrapolated from endothelial TEER preservation and from general anti-inflammatory rescue in RPE/retina (Shahid et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016).

Expected Effect  
The proposed hypothesis states that JQ1 will relieve repression of tight-junction enhancers in RPE under inflammatory/oxidative stress, increasing H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19 loci, boosting ZO-1/claudin-19 transcription, and enhancing TEER; mechanistically, it posits that BRD4 occupancy at inflammatory loci displaces transcriptional machinery from tight-junction enhancers, and BET displacement by JQ1 restores enhancer-promoter function. Based on the available literature, this precise enhancer-activation model is not supported; instead, JQ1 typically represses transcription at BET-dependent loci and reduces histone acetylation and Pol II recruitment at targeted promoters (e.g., STING), thereby closing chromatin accessibility rather than increasing it (Zou et al., 2022). No data in the provided corpus demonstrate increased H3K27ac or enhanced transcription at TJP1/CLDN19 in RPE after JQ1, nor any RPE TEER restoration with JQ1 in IL-1β or oxidative-stress paradigms; multiple sources explicitly note the absence of RPE barrier metrics and tight-junction readouts in prior BET/RPE work (Hytti et al., 2016).

A more evidence-grounded expected effect in IL-1β- or TNF-α-treated RPE is indirect barrier preservation via upstream anti-inflammatory mechanisms:  
- JQ1 should reduce NF-κB–driven cytokine induction (e.g., IL-6, IL-8) in ARPE-19 based on prior findings with etoposide models, and suppress cGAS–STING signaling under oxidative stress by repressing STING transcription and promoting autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA (Hytti et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2022). These actions plausibly decrease paracrine/autocrine junction-disrupting cues, which could secondarily stabilize tight-junction structure and TEER, as supported by endothelial TEER preservation in HUVECs during TNF-α challenge (Shahid et al., 2022).  
- In microglia-RPE co-culture or in retinal tissue, JQ1 would be expected to reduce the load of microglia-derived cytokines/chemokines that exacerbate epithelial barrier dysfunction and photoreceptor stress, via demonstrated suppression of retinal microglial activation and cytokine production (Zhao et al., 2017).  

Given the lack of published RPE barrier data, the appropriate experimental expectations and measurements for the proposed IL-1β RPE assay are:  
- Primary outcome: TEER rescue and paracellular permeability under IL-1β with and without JQ1 (0.1–1 µM), benchmarking against endothelial TEER precedent and aligning with ARPE-19 cytokine suppression (Shahid et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016). Secondary outcomes: immunofluorescence continuity and membrane localization of ZO-1 and CLDN19, and western/RT-qPCR quantification of TJP1/CLDN19 transcripts/proteins to test whether barrier maintenance arises from preserved junctional organization versus increased transcription.  
- Mechanistic chromatin assays to test the stated enhancer hypothesis: ChIP-seq/ChIP-qPCR for H3K27ac and BRD4 at TJP1/CLDN19 promoters/enhancers in IL-1β±JQ1, plus Pol II occupancy; based on STING-locus data, we predict decreased rather than increased H3 acetylation and Pol II occupancy at direct BRD4-dependent loci after JQ1 (Zou et al., 2022). A finding of increased H3K27ac at tight-junction loci with JQ1 would represent a novel and unanticipated RPE-specific BET effect that would require rigorous validation and mechanistic clarification.  
- Parallel readouts to anchor known mechanisms: NF-κB p65 nuclear activity (TransAM), STING expression, cGAS–STING pathway markers, LC3 flux with/without chloroquine, and cytokine ELISAs (IL-6, IL-8), all of which are supported in prior RPE/retina work and will clarify whether barrier effects track with established anti-inflammatory and autophagic actions of BET inhibition (Hytti et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2022).

Mechanistic expression support in the assayed cell type  
- BET target genes relevant to inflammation (e.g., IL-6, IL-8, STING) are expressed and modulated in ARPE-19 and in mouse retina; BRD4 is induced by oxidative stress in RPE and retina, and cGAS–STING components are present in retinal microglia (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2023). The corpus does not provide explicit documentation of TJP1/CLDN19 expression modulation by JQ1 in RPE, underscoring the need for primary measurement within the proposed assay (Hytti et al., 2016).

Therapeutic plausibility in dry AMD models  
- RPE oxidative stress, cytosolic DNA leakage, cGAS–STING activation, microglia/macrophage recruitment, and chronic NF-κB activity are central to dry AMD pathogenesis; JQ1 has demonstrably suppressed cGAS–STING signaling and protected RPE/retina in SI-injury models, and PROMOTER accessibility of cGAS/STING is increased in GA patients, providing a mechanistic and translational bridge (Zou et al., 2022). In light-damage injury, BET degradation with dBET6 improved functional outcomes and repressed microglial STING expression, suggesting that BET-targeted therapies are effective across different sterile-injury paradigms relevant to atrophic disease (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Therefore, for dry AMD, the most defensible expectation is that JQ1 will reduce innate-immune and NF-κB–driven inflammatory signaling in RPE/retina and microglia, attenuate microglia recruitment/activation, and protect photoreceptors/RPE via transcriptional repression of STING and enhanced autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA, rather than directly upregulating tight-junction genes; any barrier rescue measured by TEER would likely be an indirect consequence of reduced inflammatory burden (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective efficacy across ocular models that capture key elements of dry AMD biology:  
  • In vivo oxidative-stress (SI) models demonstrate that JQ1 represses BRD4-driven STING transcription, reduces cGAS–STING signaling, limits immune cell accumulation, and prevents RPE/retinal degeneration with favorable safety in the absence of stressors (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Inflammatory microglia suppression is consistent and robust: intravitreal JQ1 reduces microglia infiltration and cytokines in rd10 retina and abolishes LPS-induced cytokine induction and activation phenotypes in vitro; BET2/BD2 targeting emerges as a key effector axis, aligning with innate-immune pathophysiology in atrophic AMD (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • dBET6 (systemic) degrades retinal BRD2/3/4, improves retinal function/acuity after light damage, and suppresses microglial STING and inflammatory responses, offering a mechanistically stronger alternative to JQ1 where compensatory BRD4 upregulation occurs (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Mechanistic depth linking BET inhibition to innate immunity and autophagy:  
  • JQ1 reduces histone acetylation and Pol II engagement at the STING locus, silencing a central innate immune amplifier in RPE/retina (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • BRD4 inhibition increases LC3-dependent enclosure/clearance of cytosolic DNA; this autophagy-dependent mechanism is integral to lowering cGAS activation (Zou et al., 2022).  
- Feasibility of ocular delivery and safety:  
  • Intravitreal JQ1 achieved durable rescue for at least 10 days in rd10 despite short systemic half-life; higher doses did not improve efficacy, highlighting the need for sustained delivery rather than dose escalation (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • eNano-JQ1 provides a practical intraocular slow-release platform with favorable ERG/histology safety and anti-fibrotic efficacy in PVR, supporting translatability of sustained local BET blockade (Liao et al., 2024).  
  • dBET6 showed retinal target engagement and no detectable retinal toxicity under the tested regimen (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Ancillary barrier-preserving precedent:  
  • In HUVECs, BRD4 inhibition (JQ1/apabetalone) preserved TEER and monolayer integrity during TNF-α challenge, lending plausibility that BET blockade can maintain barrier function under inflammatory stress, though cell-type differences warrant caution (Shahid et al., 2022).

Weaknesses, risks, and key unknowns relative to the current hypothesis  
- No direct evidence that JQ1 increases H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19 or upregulates ZO-1/claudin-19 transcription in RPE; the available mechanistic data actually show decreased histone acetylation and Pol II recruitment at target inflammatory loci with JQ1, arguing against a generalizable H3K27ac-increasing effect at tight-junction enhancers (Zou et al., 2022). Multiple sources explicitly note the absence of RPE barrier (TEER) or tight-junction data in BET-RPE studies to date (Hytti et al., 2016).  
- BET inhibitors can cause cell-cycle arrest and slightly depress metabolic activity in vitro; while ARPE-19 viability was largely preserved and etoposide toxicity was reduced by BET pretreatment, these on-target cytostatic effects will require dose/formulation tuning for chronic intraocular use (Hytti et al., 2016).  
- Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics: single-dose intravitreal JQ1 protection wanes over time, and systemic administration risks off-target tissue exposure; local sustained delivery or newer modalities (e.g., dBET6) are likely needed for translational development (Zhao et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2024).  
- Feedback and compensation: JQ1 can increase BRD4 protein levels in some contexts, potentially compromising effect; PROTAC degradation (dBET6) may mitigate this but brings its own safety and distribution questions (Zhu et al., 2023).  
- Cell-type selectivity: The strongest in vivo efficacy signals (rd10, light damage) include microglial suppression and photoreceptor rescue; dry AMD pathogenesis is centered on RPE/Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with secondary photoreceptor involvement; while SI and oxidative-stress data in RPE support relevance, dedicated chronic AMD-like models (aging, complement dysregulation, diet-induced) and RPE barrier endpoints remain to be tested (Zou et al., 2022).

Go/no-go assessment and recommendations  
- Go decision for mechanism-driven validation in dry AMD-relevant preclinical systems, but with a revised primary hypothesis and fit-for-purpose endpoints. The most compelling AMD-relevant mechanism for JQ1 is epigenetic suppression of cGAS–STING and NF-κB inflammatory programs in RPE and resident microglia, plus autophagy-mediated clearance of cytosolic DNA, not direct activation of tight-junction gene enhancers (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017).  
- Replace the current primary mechanistic claim (increased H3K27ac at TJP1/CLDN19) with a testable, literature-anchored hypothesis: JQ1 prevents inflammation- and oxidative-stress–induced RPE barrier breakdown by (i) repressing STING transcription and dampening cGAS–STING signaling; (ii) promoting autophagic clearance of cytosolic DNA; and (iii) suppressing NF-κB–driven cytokines in RPE and microglia that secondarily disturb junctional integrity. TEER and junctional continuity should be primary outcomes, but mechanistic attribution should center on cGAS–STING/NF-κB and autophagy rather than TJ enhancer activation (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016; Shahid et al., 2022).  
- Rapid experimental plan:  
  • ARPE-19 and/or primary human RPE on transwells: TEER, paracellular flux, ZO-1/CLDN19 localization under IL-1β or TNF-α ± JQ1 (0.1–1 µM), with NF-κB activity, cytokine ELISAs, STING expression, LC3 flux, and dsDNA imaging to anchor mechanism (Hytti et al., 2016; Shahid et al., 2022; Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Oxidative stress model (H2O2 or SI-conditioned medium) ± JQ1: replicate cGAS–STING repression and autophagy findings in RPE; use autophagy inhibitors to confirm flux-dependence (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • ChIP-qPCR/ATAC at STING and at TJP1/CLDN19 enhancers/promoters to directly test the tight-junction enhancer hypothesis; set expectation that STING chromatin accessibility/acetylation will decline with JQ1, while TJ loci changes are unknown and likely neutral or reduced (Zou et al., 2022).  
  • Microglia–RPE co-culture: test whether microglial cytokine suppression by JQ1 protects RPE TEER/barrier vs IL-1β, isolating paracrine contributions (Zhao et al., 2017).  
  • In vivo oxidative-injury model (SI) with intraocular slow-release JQ1 (eNano-JQ1) to assess RPE barrier integrity (flat-mount ZO-1 continuity), microglial recruitment (IBA1), and function, leveraging prior safety/feasibility data (Liao et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2022).  
- Modality strategy: Given compensatory BRD4 upregulation with JQ1 and BD2 dominance in microglial activation, parallel exploration of BD2-selective ligands (e.g., apabetalone analogs) or BET degraders (dBET6-like) for retina-directed delivery is warranted to optimize therapeutic index while maintaining target engagement (Zhu et al., 2023; Shahid et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2017).

Conclusion  
JQ1 is a mechanistically well-grounded epigenetic modulator that suppresses inflammatory transcriptional programs and innate immune activation in retina/RPE and microglia, protects photoreceptors and RPE from oxidative and inflammatory injury in vivo, and has feasible ocular delivery paths with encouraging preclinical safety signals (Zou et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2017; Liao et al., 2024). These features position BET inhibition as a credible therapeutic strategy for dry AMD, targeting core disease drivers (oxidative stress, cytosolic DNA sensing via cGAS–STING, chronic NF-κB activation, microglial recruitment) rather than exclusively downstream consequences (Zou et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023). However, the specific hypothesis that JQ1 restores RPE barrier function by increasing H3K27ac at tight-junction loci (TJP1/CLDN19) is not supported by available evidence; on the contrary, BET inhibition generally reduces histone acetylation/accessibility at target loci like STING, and RPE barrier metrics after JQ1 remain unreported (Zou et al., 2022; Hytti et al., 2016). We therefore recommend proceeding with JQ1 (or improved BET-modality variants) in dry AMD-relevant models with primary endpoints focused on cGAS–STING/NF-κB suppression, autophagy-dependent cytosolic DNA clearance, microglial modulation, and functional RPE barrier preservation (TEER, ZO-1/CLDN19 continuity), while explicitly testing and likely revising the proposed tight-junction enhancer mechanism based on direct chromatin measurements (Zou et al., 2022; Shahid et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
H-151 is a small-molecule antagonist of the innate immune adaptor STING (TMEM173) that was developed as part of a chemical class designed to prevent the palmitoylation-dependent activation of STING at the Golgi following cyclic dinucleotide binding and ER-to-Golgi trafficking (i.e., cGAMP-bound STING oligomerization and signalosome assembly) (Decout et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). In its mechanistic class, H-151 is grouped with covalent STING inhibitors that target Cys91 within the transmembrane region–proximal cytosolic interface, thereby preventing activation-induced palmitoylation at Cys88/Cys91 and downstream signaling; nitrofuran analogs such as C-176 and C-178 are the canonical examples where Cys91-directed covalent modification has been mapped by probe chemistry and mass spectrometry (with consequent suppression of type I interferon and IL-6 in vivo) (Decout et al., 2021). STING activation is known to require ligand-induced conformational change, ER exit, and palmitoylation on Cys88/Cys91 to drive oligomerization/polymerization and recruitment of TBK1 and other signal transducers; antagonists that block this palmitoylation step are therefore positioned to broadly prevent both IRF3-dependent type I interferon and NF-κB–dependent inflammatory outputs (Li et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2021).

H-151 has been characterized in inflammatory disease models as a low molecular weight, irreversible inhibitor of human and mouse STING that blocks activation-induced palmitoylation and attenuates downstream signaling (with primary mechanistic references tracing to the discovery work summarized by Pan et al. and by Decout et al.) (Pan et al., 2021; Decout et al., 2021). In keratinocyte and immune-cell systems relevant to psoriatic inflammation, H-151 has reproducibly suppressed STING-dependent NF-κB and IRF3 phosphorylation, inhibited proinflammatory cytokine mRNA induction (e.g., IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α), and reduced STING protein levels, consistent with an antagonist mechanism upstream of canonical downstream effectors (Pan et al., 2021). Conceptually, H-151 belongs to the broader class of cGAS–STING pathway modulators that have been deployed to suppress sterile inflammation across multiple tissues; for the eye and retina, related pathway inhibitors (e.g., C-176, SN-011, cryptotanshinone) have shown efficacy in ischemic and neovascular models via suppression of microglial STING signaling and cytokine/chemokine/protease outputs, supporting the translatability of STING antagonism to ocular tissues (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
There is no reported clinical use of H-151 in humans, and no published veterinary or clinical trials in ophthalmology were identified in the provided literature set; H-151 has been used as a research tool compound in preclinical inflammatory models, most prominently in psoriasis, where it decreased lesion severity and cutaneous inflammatory readouts in the imiquimod model (Pan et al., 2021). In psoriasis-relevant cell systems, H-151 suppressed cGAMP-induced IRF3 and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and reduced IFN-β, IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α expression, consistent with on-pathway inhibition of STING and its downstream transcriptional programs (Pan et al., 2021). In vivo, topical H-151 improved psoriasis-like dermatitis and decreased markers linked to STING/NF-κB signaling, again without human clinical translation to date (Pan et al., 2021).

Ocular/retinal precedent for the STING target is strong even if H-151–specific data are sparse. In multiple retinal contexts, activation of cGAS–STING has been implicated in pathogenesis through DNA-damage and mitochondrial DNA leakage, leading to IRF3/NF-κB activation, SASP-like cytokine induction, angiogenesis, and barrier dysfunction (Hu et al., 2023). Genetic and pharmacologic pathway perturbations show benefit: genetic loss of STING limits endothelial senescence and vascular degeneration in diabetic models (Liu et al., 2023), genetic deletion along the cGAS–STING axis rescues Alu DNA–driven RPE toxicity (implicated in geographic atrophy) (Hu et al., 2023), and pharmacologic STING inhibitors (C-176, SN-011) suppress neovascularization in laser CNV and OIR models (Ni et al., 2024). Importantly for RPE biology, senescent ARPE-19 cells were reported to overproduce VEGF and this overproduction was prevented by H-151, providing a direct albeit single-study line of evidence that H-151 can modulate pathogenic angiogenic/SASP output in an RPE-derived cell line (Hu et al., 2023). Beyond H-151, epigenetic suppression of STING (JQ1), PPARα activation, and visual cycle modulation (reducing toxic retinoid stress) each attenuate cGAS–STING activation and downstream inflammation or degeneration, underscoring the therapeutic appeal of targeting this axis in retinal disease (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
STING biology and the palmitoylation node. STING is a homodimeric ER-resident adaptor with an N-terminal multi-pass transmembrane domain and a cytosolic C-terminal ligand-binding domain; binding of 2’3’-cGAMP (produced by cGAS upon sensing cytosolic dsDNA) induces conformational rearrangements that enable ER exit and trafficking to the Golgi, where palmitoylation of Cys88 and Cys91 is critical for higher-order assembly and recruitment of TBK1 and other signaling proteins (Li et al., 2021). Palmitoylation-driven tetramerization/higher-order oligomerization is a central activation step for STING, and mutational or pharmacologic interference with Cys88/Cys91 palmitoylation abrogates downstream signal propagation (Pan et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). Activated STING scaffolds TBK1 to phosphorylate IRF3 (e.g., at Ser366), triggering type I interferon gene expression, and engages NF-κB to induce a broad proinflammatory transcriptional program, including SASP components (Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2021). In retinal disease contexts, cGAS–STING activation (driven by nuclear/mtDNA release or Alu-derived nucleic acids) is linked to up-regulation of VEGF via NF-κB/HIF-1α in oxidative-stress–induced RPE senescence, endothelial and microglial inflammatory activation, and barrier compromise (Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025).

H-151 and palmitoylation blockade. H-151 is positioned mechanistically among irreversible covalent inhibitors of STING that target Cys91 to prevent activation-associated palmitoylation and signalosome formation (Decout et al., 2021). While detailed covalent adduct chemistry for H-151 itself is not contained in the supplied excerpts, authoritative mechanistic reviews depict H-151 in the “Targeting Cys91” class, alongside nitrofuran inhibitors (C-176, C-178) that have been shown to bind Cys91 selectively and irreversibly (but not Cys88) and that suppress in vivo IFN and IL-6 responses to STING agonism (Decout et al., 2021). Primary disease-model data support a functional blockade of STING signal transmission by H-151: it reduced STING protein abundance in keratinocytes and THP-1 monocytes, inhibited cGAMP-driven IRF3 and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation, and suppressed downstream cytokine expression (IFN-β, IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α) (Pan et al., 2021). In the psoriasis model, H-151 strongly downregulated NF-κB activity and IL-6 and reduced p-p65 and total p65, with a more variable impact on IRF3 phosphorylation depending on system and readout, suggesting it can dominantly blunt the NF-κB arm of STING signaling while at least partially reducing IRF3 activation (Pan et al., 2021). The lack of additivity with an NF-κB inhibitor (BAY 11-7082) on IL-6 suppression implies pathway overlap and supports that H-151’s anti-inflammatory effects in that model are mediated primarily by interference with STING → NF-κB–driven cytokine production (Pan et al., 2021).

Rationale in retinal cells and tissue. cGAS and STING are expressed across retinal cell types (RPE, microglia, endothelial cells, Müller glia, photoreceptors) and are upregulated in disease states (AMD/DR), with promoter accessibility and mRNA levels increased in diseased tissue, positioning the pathway as targetable across multiple ocular compartments (Hu et al., 2023). Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction cause cytosolic mtDNA accumulation that activates cGAS–STING; Alu-derived nucleic acids similarly drive cytosolic DNA sensing and RPE cytotoxicity in GA, with multiple studies showing that genetic deletion along the cGAS–STING axis rescues Alu DNA toxicity (Hu et al., 2023). In RPE biology specifically, STING is implicated in senescence-associated VEGF upregulation, and H-151 prevented VEGF overproduction in senescent ARPE-19 cells, indicating that palmitoylation-targeted STING antagonism can suppress a central angiogenic/SASP mediator in stressed RPE-like cells (Hu et al., 2023). In retinal vascular and microglial compartments, pathway inhibition reduces inflammatory and proteolytic mediators (e.g., lowering Il6 and Mmp9) and blunts vascular leakage and neovascular pathology, as shown with cryptotanshinone, C-176, and SN-011 (Qiu et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024). Collectively, these data situate H-151’s palmitoylation blockade at a nodal point capable of broadly dampening IRF3 and NF-κB outputs in ocular cells that contribute to SASP, MMP expression, VEGF induction, and barrier compromise relevant to dry AMD (Hu et al., 2023).

Important mechanistic caveats. RPE models are heterogeneous in cGAS expression and DNA-sensor usage; some RPE cell lines lack cGAS and instead rely on other nucleic acid sensors (e.g., RIG-I, ZBP1), and the relative contribution of cGAS–STING versus alternative pathways varies by context (Hu et al., 2023). Moreover, the balance of STING outputs (IRF3/type I IFN versus NF-κB) can be cell/state dependent, as reflected by psoriasis-model findings where systemic IFN-β was unchanged despite local suppression of p-IRF3 and p65 in skin (Pan et al., 2021). These observations underscore that while H-151 inhibits upstream STING activation, the phenotype in any given ocular assay will reflect cell-type–specific wiring, stimulus context (Alu vs mtDNA vs oxidant stress), and cross-talk with other innate immune axes (Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023).

Expected Effect  
Assay context and target presence. The proposed assays—senescence models in RPE with readouts including TEER, ZO-1 continuity, SASP cytokines (IL-6/IL-8), and MMPs—interrogate processes (barrier integrity, SASP-driven inflammation, matrix remodeling) that are mechanistically tied to cGAS–STING–NF-κB signaling and are central to dry AMD progression (Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025; Terao et al., 2022). RPE expresses STING and engages cGAS–STING signaling under oxidative and senescent stress; senescent ARPE-19 cells overproduce VEGF via a STING/NF-κB/HIF-1α pathway, and H-151 prevented this VEGF overproduction, providing direct cell-type–relevant evidence of efficacy on a SASP/angiogenic factor in RPE (Hu et al., 2023). In addition, cGAS inhibition alleviates Alu RNA–induced immune responses and cytotoxicity in RPE, consistent with the pathway’s role in dsDNA/dsRNA-triggered sterile inflammation and suggesting that upstream DNA-sensor blockade mitigates RPE injury (Li et al., 2022).

Expected pharmacodynamic effects. Based on H-151’s mechanism at the palmitoylation node and its demonstrated suppression of STING-dependent IRF3 and NF-κB activation in immune and epithelial cells, we expect the following in RPE senescence assays:

- Proximal signaling: reductions in STING abundance (as seen in keratinocytes/THP-1), p-TBK1, p-IRF3, and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation following H-151 treatment under stimuli that engage cGAS–STING (e.g., H₂O₂-induced senescence, Alu cDNA transfection, mtDNA transfection) (Pan et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022).

- Cytokines/SASP: decreased secretion and/or expression of IL-6 and potentially IL-8 and other SASP components; in non-ocular systems H-151 lowered IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, IFN-β, and IFN-stimulated gene signatures, and in ARPE-19 senescence models H-151 prevented VEGF overproduction (Pan et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2023). Because NF-κB is a principal SASP driver in oxidant-stressed RPE, H-151’s suppression of NF-κB should proportionally lower SASP cytokines, including IL-6/IL-8, which are repeatedly implicated in AMD pathobiology (Terao et al., 2022; Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025).

- MMPs and matrix remodeling: in retinal microglia, pharmacologic STING inhibition reduced Mmp9 expression alongside Il6 and diminished vascular leakage in OIR, suggesting that blocking STING can lower proteases that degrade extracellular matrix and compromise barriers (Qiu et al., 2025; Terao et al., 2022). While H-151-specific MMP data in RPE have not been reported here, we would predict a reduction in MMP-9 in senescent RPE given the NF-κB dependence of SASP proteases and the precedent in ocular STING inhibition (Qiu et al., 2025; Terao et al., 2022).

- Barrier integrity (TEER and ZO-1): direct H-151 data on RPE TEER/ZO-1 are unavailable in the provided literature. However, STING activity has been linked to barrier dysfunction in retinal endothelium (inner barrier), with evidence that STING activation through TBK1/IRF3/IFN-β axes amplifies senescence and compromises barrier integrity; genetic STING deficiency mitigates such changes (Wu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). In the outer retina, RPE degeneration driven by inflammatory stimuli is attenuated in STING knockout mice, supporting that STING inhibition can preserve epithelial integrity under inflammatory stress (Hu et al., 2023). Thus, we expect H-151 to preserve TEER and maintain ZO-1 continuity in RPE senescence models where cGAS–STING–NF-κB contributes to junctional remodeling and MMP-driven degradation, but this prediction requires experimental confirmation given the absence of direct H-151 barrier data (Hu et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025).

- Anti-senescence signatures: in non-ocular systems, H-151 treatment decreased cGAS–STING pathway activation, reduced ISGs, lowered P16/P21, and decreased SA-β-gal activity, indicating that STING antagonism can blunt senescence programs and SASP (Ye et al., 2024). Given the overlap between senescence and innate immune signaling in RPE and AMD, we expect H-151 to reduce senescence markers in RPE senescence assays, again pending direct validation in ocular cells (Blasiak, 2020; Terao et al., 2022).

Expression in the assayed RPE lineage is supported by disease-relevant data showing STING expression and activation in retinal tissues and RPE under stress, including oxidative stress and Alu/mtDNA triggers; cGAS–STING pathway genes are broadly expressed in the retina and upregulated in disease, and RPE senescence engages STING-dependent NF-κB/HIF-1α signaling to drive VEGF (Hu et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease-mechanism fit. Dry AMD pathogenesis features chronic oxidative stress, DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and senescence in RPE, with resultant SASP cytokines, VEGF, and MMPs that degrade extracellular matrix and compromise barriers; cGAS–STING is positioned as a key sensor/effector linking cytosolic DNA to NF-κB/IRF3 activation and SASP output in RPE and retinal cell types (Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2023). Genetic and pharmacologic evidence across models (DR endothelium, Alu-driven RPE toxicity, ischemic/neovascular retinopathy) show that suppressing STING signaling reduces inflammation, senescence markers, angiogenic/proteolytic factors, leakage, and degeneration, indicating pathway validity and translational plausibility in the eye (Liu et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

- Direct RPE cell evidence for H-151. H-151 prevented VEGF overproduction in senescent ARPE-19 cells, directly supporting the candidate’s ability to suppress a central SASP/angiogenic mediator in an RPE-derived cell model (Hu et al., 2023). This aligns with the broader observation that STING upregulates VEGF in oxidative stress–induced RPE senescence via NF-κB/HIF-1α (Hu et al., 2023).

- Potent inhibition of NF-κB and cytokine outputs. In preclinical psoriasis systems, H-151 suppressed cGAMP-induced IRF3/NF-κB phosphorylation and reduced IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IFN-β readouts, consistent with broad blockade of the principal proinflammatory axes downstream of STING (Pan et al., 2021). Given that NF-κB is a dominant inducer of SASP components in oxidant-stressed RPE, and IL-6/IL-8 and MMPs are canonical RPE SASP factors in AMD, H-151’s activity is well matched to reduce these pathological outputs (Terao et al., 2022; Blasiak, 2020; Ochoa Hernández et al., 2025).

- Target validation in retinal models via related inhibitors/genetics. STING inhibition by C-176/SN-011 reduces neovascularization in CNV/OIR; cryptotanshinone reduces Il6 and Mmp9 and vascular leakage through STING suppression in microglia; STING knockout provides protection against inflammatory retinal degeneration and endothelial senescence and barrier compromise, together providing multi-compartment evidence that STING blockade can ameliorate retinal inflammatory pathology (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023).

- Modality fit for intracellular target. Because cGAS and STING are intracellular, small molecules are preferred for retinal applications; the literature anticipates that blood–retina–penetrant small-molecule cGAS–STING inhibitors will be needed to translate this strategy to the clinic, supporting H-151’s modality selection (Hu et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- Sparse ocular data for H-151. Beyond the ARPE-19 VEGF observation, there are no H-151 data for TEER, ZO-1 continuity, MMP modulation, or in vivo ocular efficacy in dry AMD models in the provided literature, so the central claims around barrier preservation remain predictions that require direct testing (Hu et al., 2023). By contrast, barrier-relevant evidence is stronger for alternative STING inhibitors (cryptotanshinone effects on Mmp9/leakage; C-176/SN-011 in angiogenesis models), indicating pathway relevance but not yet validating H-151 itself in retina (Qiu et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2024).

- Cell-type heterogeneity in DNA sensing. Some RPE models lack cGAS and may rely on other sensors (RIG-I, ZBP1), and the cGAS–STING axis can be variably engaged depending on the nature of the stressor (Alu vs mtDNA vs photo-oxidized A2E), potentially limiting the breadth of H-151’s efficacy across RPE senescence paradigms (Hu et al., 2023). Thorough profiling in human primary RPE and AMD-relevant triggers will be required.

- Pathway-output variability. H-151’s strongest effects in psoriasis were on NF-κB/IL-6, with partial or context-dependent impact on IRF3/IFN-β; while NF-κB is the prime SASP driver in RPE, specific disease contexts (e.g., dsDNA-driven type I IFN) may require robust IRF3 suppression to fully ameliorate pathology (Pan et al., 2021). The differential balance of NF-κB versus IRF3 outputs in RPE under various triggers should be experimentally mapped.

- Covalent inhibitor liabilities. Cysteine-targeting covalent inhibitors can carry risks of off-target reactivity and species-specific metabolic liabilities; development of covalent agents demands careful derisking of reactivity and ocular PK/PD, as underscored in general discussions of covalent inhibitor strategies and metabolism in drug discovery (Wang et al., 2022). Although H-151’s covalent target is genetically unique (Cys91 on STING), comprehensive safety and selectivity profiling—especially for intraocular delivery—is not available here.

- Immunological trade-offs. STING deficiency can increase susceptibility to tumorigenesis and reduce vaccine responses, and human STING haplotypes (e.g., HAQ) show variable responsiveness to cyclic dinucleotides, implying potential population variability in pathway dependence and therapeutic response (Hu et al., 2023). For ocular delivery, local exposure may mitigate systemic risks, but intraocular immunosuppression could theoretically predispose to infections; risk–benefit will need empirical assessment.

Evidence-based development plan (prioritized)  
- In vitro RPE assays. Use human primary RPE and ARPE-19 under AMD-relevant triggers (H₂O₂, Alu cDNA, mtDNA transfection) to quantify: STING pathway activation (p-TBK1, p-IRF3, p65), SASP cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), MMPs (MMP-9), and angiogenic factors (VEGF); barrier metrics by TEER and ZO-1 continuity; and senescence markers (P16, P21, SA-β-gal). Include STING agonist/antagonist controls (e.g., diABZI, C-176), and cGAS/STING knockdown to confirm on-target effects; the goal is to reproduce the VEGF suppression result and extend to barrier preservation and MMP control with H-151 (Hu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022; Terao et al., 2022).

- Retinal explant and in vivo models. Move to sodium iodate or oxidant-driven RPE injury models and to Alu DNA–induced RPE degeneration to test whether H-151 reduces cGAS–STING activation, NF-κB signaling, cytokines/MMPs, and preserves RPE morphology; positive controls include JQ1 and C-176, which have shown efficacy in related contexts (Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024). The LIRD model shows cGAS–STING activation can be modulated upstream by visual-cycle inhibitors; testing H-151 in LIRD would further link pathway suppression to photoreceptor/RPE protection (Wang et al., 2022).

- Delivery and PK/PD. Evaluate intravitreal versus periocular dosing for ocular exposure, using formulation strategies with precedent (e.g., nanoparticle-loaded C-176) to optimize intraocular retention and cell uptake; measure intraocular H-151 levels and target engagement markers (p-STING, p-TBK1, p-IRF3) (Shao et al., 2024).

- Safety and immunology. Profile local tolerability and infection risk in the eye while monitoring systemic spillover; genotype stratification for STING haplotypes can be deferred to later phases but should be considered due to pathway variability (Hu et al., 2023).

Decision context  
On balance, H-151 is a mechanistically compelling, tractable small-molecule inhibitor that targets a validated inflammatory/senescence axis in retinal disease, with one direct RPE line of evidence (suppression of VEGF in senescent ARPE-19) and robust non-ocular and ocular-pathway support via related tools and genetic models (Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). The absence of H-151–specific data on RPE barrier metrics (TEER/ZO-1) and MMP modulation is the principal evidence gap relative to the stated hypothesis; however, the consistent linkage of cGAS–STING to IL-6/VEGF/MMP outputs and barrier failure across retinal compartments supports the plausibility that a palmitoylation-targeted STING antagonist like H-151 will deliver the predicted phenotype in senescent RPE (Hu et al., 2023; Terao et al., 2022; Qiu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025).

Recommendation  
Advance H-151 into AMD-relevant in vitro RPE barrier and senescence assays with rigorous on-target controls and head-to-head comparison against alternative STING inhibitors (C-176/SN-011, cryptotanshinone) to establish class translatability and select the best ocular candidate by efficacy and safety; proceed to in vivo validation contingent on clear demonstration of TEER/ZO-1 preservation, SASP/MMP suppression, and favorable ocular PK/PD (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

Strengths summary: strong mechanistic rationale in AMD, direct RPE evidence for VEGF suppression by H-151, broad anti–NF-κB/SASP activity of H-151 in inflammatory models, and multiple retinal models validating STING inhibition (Hu et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2021; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025). Weaknesses summary: no H-151 data yet on RPE barrier readouts or in vivo retinal protection; covalent-inhibitor liabilities and immunologic trade-offs require careful derisking; cell-type heterogeneity in DNA sensing mandates model selection rigor (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Taken together, H-151 is a high-priority mechanistic probe and a plausible therapeutic lead for dry AMD that merits focused preclinical validation in RPE barrier/senescence systems and in Alu/oxidative injury models of outer retinal degeneration, with parallel medicinal-chemistry and formulation work to address ocular delivery and covalent-inhibitor safety considerations (Hu et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GW501516 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule agonist that selectively binds to and activates the peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor beta/delta (PPARβ/δ), a member of the nuclear receptor superfamily known for its central role in regulating lipid metabolism and energy homeostasis (Salvadó et al., 2014; Ebert et al., 2016). Its intrinsic properties—as a natural polyamine with well-documented autophagy-inducing, anti-inflammatory, and anti-oxidative activities—coupled with a plausible mechanism involving EP300 inhibition, support its potential utility in restoring cellular homeostasis in the RPE. While the therapeutic promise is underscored by a breadth of preclinical data from related ocular models, the specific application to dry AMD requires targeted confirmation through robust experimental paradigms. The strengths of spermidine, including its favorable safety profile as a dietary supplement and its multi-target action, must be balanced against the challenges of dose-dependent toxicity and the necessity for precise modulation of EP300 activity. With careful experimental design and comprehensive preclinical validation, spermidine may indeed progress as a viable strategy to slow or halt the progression of dry AMD, ultimately offering a new avenue of treatment for patients burdened by this degenerative disease (Han et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
T0901317 (TO901317; Cayman 10006515) is a synthetic, non-sterol small-molecule agonist of the liver X receptors (LXRs), discovered in early industry efforts (Tularik) to pharmacologically activate LXRα (NR1H3) and LXRβ (NR1H2) to drive reverse cholesterol transport and exert anti-inflammatory effects; it is widely used as a reference pan-LXR ligand in mechanistic and preclinical studies (Michael, Schkeryantz, & Burris, 2005; Bennett, Cooke, Edwards, Moir, & Ray, 2004; Berrodin et al., 2010). Crystallographic and biophysical data show that T0901317 binds within the LXR ligand-binding domain in a pocket of ~830 Å³, making a key hydrogen-bonding interaction with His435 while otherwise engaging primarily hydrophobic residues, and can adopt multiple conformations consistent with ligand- and promoter-selective cofactor recruitment (Bennett et al., 2004; Mukherjee & Mani, 2010; Berrodin et al., 2010). As a class, LXR agonists heterodimerize with RXR and activate DR-4 LXR response elements, upregulating genes that mediate cholesterol efflux and reverse cholesterol transport, notably ABCA1 and ABCG1, as well as APOE and ABCG5/ABCG8; they also induce lipogenic regulators such as SREBP-1c and downstream fatty acid synthesis genes (FASN, ACC), producing a characteristic lipogenic liability on systemic dosing (elevated triglycerides, hepatomegaly, hepatic steatosis) (Michael et al., 2005; Lund, Menke, & Sparrow, 2003; Bennett et al., 2004). Although T0901317 is prototypical for the LXR agonist class, it is pharmacologically promiscuous, with documented activation of FXR and PXR in addition to LXR, an important consideration for safety and on-target/off-target attribution (Choudhary et al., 2020; Velma et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2013). Within ocular and retinal biology, LXRs are expressed in the posterior eye (retina, RPE, choroid), are activated by endogenous oxysterols, and regulate cholesterol transport and inflammatory gene programs relevant to AMD pathogenesis, positioning T0901317 as a tool compound to probe LXR-dependent mechanisms in the RPE and outer retina (Choudhary et al., 2020; Sene & Apte, 2014; Rao & Fliesler, 2021). The LXR class has been explored preclinically in aging eye disease, with alternative ligands such as GW3965 and DMHCA also tested to dissociate beneficial ABCA1/ABCG1 induction from lipogenic effects and to evaluate local ocular delivery to avoid systemic liabilities (Choudhary et al., 2020; Sene & Apte, 2014; Vieira et al., 2020; El-Darzi et al., 2018; Velma et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Outside ophthalmology, T0901317 and other LXR agonists demonstrated robust induction of ABCA1 and ABCG family transporters across cell and tissue systems, increased macrophage cholesterol efflux, raised HDL, and reduced atherosclerotic lesion burden in mouse models; however, they consistently triggered SREBP-1c–driven lipogenesis, hypertriglyceridemia, and hepatic steatosis in rodents, limiting their systemic therapeutic development (Plösch et al., 2002; Bennett et al., 2004; Lund et al., 2003). For example, T0901317 increased hepatic and intestinal Abca1 expression with ~60% HDL elevation, induced Abcg5/Abcg8, and markedly increased biliary and fecal neutral sterol excretion in mice, but also increased plasma triglycerides and VLDL-TG secretion via LXR-mediated SREBP-1c induction (Plösch et al., 2002; Lund et al., 2003). Adverse lipid effects have proven difficult to avoid even with LXRβ-selective scaffolds in humans (BMS-852927 increased plasma/hepatic triglycerides and LDL-C while lowering neutrophils), underscoring translational risk for the class and motivating local delivery strategies and nonlipogenic ABCA1 inducers (NLAIs) to separate efflux from lipogenesis (Kirchgessner et al., 2016; Velma et al., 2024; Lin & Gustafsson, 2015).

In ocular models, LXR biology has strong genetic and pharmacologic support. Both LXR isoforms are expressed in the RPE/choroid; loss of LXRα (Nr1h3−/−) produces AMD-like sub-RPE extracellular lipid deposits, disrupted RPE basal infoldings, and a pro-inflammatory outer-retina microenvironment with ADGRE1+ macrophage accumulation and cytokine upregulation, while LXRβ loss yields intracellular RPE lipid droplets (lipoidal degeneration), highlighting isoform- and process-specific control of lipid handling (Choudhary et al., 2020). Systemic GW3965 treatment in apoB100 transgenic mice reduced outer retinal inflammatory markers and APOE deposition in Bruch’s membrane, reduced ADGRE1+ cells, and improved RPE ultrastructure without overt systemic lipid perturbations in that setting, demonstrating in vivo ocular benefit from LXR activation (Choudhary et al., 2020).

RPE-directed studies of T0901317 provide mechanistic and functional evidence relevant to dry AMD. In primary human RPE and ARPE-19 challenged with oligomeric Aβ₁₋₄₀, T0901317 increased LXRα and ABCA1 expression and prevented induction of IL-6, IL-8, MCP-1 and p16, with suppression of NF-κB signaling (reduced p-IκB-α), consistent with an LXRα–ABCA1-dependent anti-inflammatory and anti-senescence effect in RPE (Dai et al., 2017). In the same disease framework of oxidative stress and mitochondrial vulnerability, TO901317 protected human RPE mitochondrial membrane potential from NaIO₃, H₂O₂, and cigarette smoke extract injury, while a different agonist (GW3965) was more effective against lipid-induced mitochondrial injury and lipid accumulation, indicating ligand-specific pharmacology and suggesting TO901317’s strengths in oxidant/Aβ stress versus lipid overload per se (Choudhary et al., 2020). Additional RPE-relevant evidence links T0901317 to improved lysosomal/autophagic processing under bisretinoid load: transcriptional upregulation of ABCA1 and ABCG1 by T0901317 in RPE increased cholesterol efflux and relieved A2E-induced deficits in phagosome maturation, situating LXR-driven efflux upstream of improved outer-segment processing, an AMD-relevant phenotype (Rao & Fliesler, 2021). In a distinct photoreceptor/RPE stress model (Abca4−/−), promoting cholesterol efflux with TO901316 reduced early endosome enlargement in RPE, a change linked to complement C3 intake/activation; this provides complementary evidence that LXR agonism can normalize cholesterol-dependent endosomal trafficking in diseased RPE (Landowski & Bowes Rickman, 2022).

With respect to ocular delivery and in vivo efficacy, beyond the apoB100 systemic study with GW3965, class evidence shows that local ocular administration of LXR agonists can restore tissue-specific cholesterol efflux and reduce choroidal neovascularization in aged mice, supporting the translational feasibility of local dosing strategies to avoid systemic triglyceride liabilities; note that these data are for the class and not compound-specific to T0901317 (Sene & Apte, 2014). In a CNV-relevant model, intravitreal TO901317 reduced CNV area and lipid accumulation in the lesion region and suppressed NF-κB signaling, with the authors implicating ABCG1-dependent cholesterol handling in RPE as part of the mechanism; these data reside in a wet AMD context but nevertheless demonstrate ocular bioactivity of intravitreally delivered T0901317 (Wu et al., 2023). At the same time, multiple sources stress that T0901317 has been shown to cause severe lipogenesis in diabetic mice and to activate FXR and PXR, raising safety concerns for systemic use and underscoring the need for local administration and/or next-generation LXR modulators to separate ABCA1/ABCG1 induction from lipogenesis (Vieira et al., 2020; Choudhary et al., 2020; Velma et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
LXRs are oxysterol-sensing nuclear receptors that heterodimerize with RXR and bind DR-4 LXR response elements to regulate transcription of genes central to cholesterol efflux and lipid homeostasis (ABCA1, ABCG1, APOE, ABCG5/G8), while also inducing lipogenic programs via SREBP-1c and FASN (Michael et al., 2005; Lund et al., 2003; Bennett et al., 2004). In the LXR ligand-binding domain, T0901317 engages a conserved hydrogen-bond network (His435 and nearby residues) and induces receptor conformations that determine coactivator/corepressor exchange and gene-selective transactivation; such ligand-induced conformational ensembles help explain differences between T0901317 and GW3965 in gene and cell selectivity (Bennett et al., 2004; Mukherjee & Mani, 2010; Berrodin et al., 2010). At the target-gene level, T0901317 robustly upregulates ABCA1 and ABCG1 mRNAs and proteins in multiple cell types, increases cholesterol efflux to ApoA1/HDL, and elevates APOE expression, consistent with its intended enhancement of reverse cholesterol transport; induction of PLTP and LDLR-modulating IDOL has also been observed with LXR agonism (Michael et al., 2005; Bennett et al., 2004; Plösch et al., 2002; Berrodin et al., 2010; Sene & Apte, 2014). In neurons and astrocytes, T0901317 raised ABCA1 and reduced Aβ secretion, supporting a mechanistic link between ABCA1-mediated membrane cholesterol redistribution and protease access, while in macrophages LXR activation repressed multiple NF-κB–target inflammatory genes (iNOS, COX-2, IL-6, MMP-9), indicating classical LXR anti-inflammatory transrepression (Michael et al., 2005; Bennett et al., 2004; Mukherjee & Mani, 2010).

Mechanistically in the outer retina, RPE and neural retina express LXRα/β, ABCA1, ABCG1, apolipoprotein acceptors (ApoA1/E), and sterol transporters (NPC1, TSPO), assembling the machinery for ABCA1/ABCG1-mediated cholesterol efflux; RPE can form lipoprotein-like particles, and polarized ABCA1-dependent sterol transfer to ApoA1 occurs at both apical and basolateral membranes in differentiated RPE (Rao & Fliesler, 2021). In primary human fetal RPE monolayers, ABCA1-mediated efflux is generally weak under low-lipid media but becomes strongly upregulated on the apical side upon OxLDL loading, consistent with stimulus-responsive ABCA1 function in RPE that may be relevant in AMD-like lipid conditions (Lyssenko et al., 2018). Genetic loss-of-function underscores ABCA1/ABCG1 importance: double knockout in RPE yields cholesteryl ester droplet accumulation and retinal degeneration; notably, Abca1 single knockout alone is sufficient to drive early RPE lipid accumulation and morphological changes, whereas Abcg1 loss alone is milder, implicating ABCA1 as the primary driver at early stages (Rao & Fliesler, 2021; Storti et al., 2019). Oxysterols produced in the outer retina (e.g., 27-hydroxycholesterol) activate LXR to stimulate ABCA1-dependent efflux, linking local sterol metabolism to LXR activation (Rao & Fliesler, 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Pioglitazone is a synthetic thiazolidinedione (TZD) that was initially discovered and developed as an antidiabetic agent for type 2 diabetes mellitus. As a member of the glitazone family, its structure is centered on a thiazolidinedione ring that is critical for binding to the nuclear receptor peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). Its discovery by medicinal chemists led to its widespread clinical use as an insulin sensitizer, with the molecule synthesized through conventional organic synthesis methods that allow for high purity and reproducibility. The compound is commercially available from research suppliers, such as Sigma (PHR 1043), and has been extensively studied not only in metabolic disorders but also for its vascular protective and anti‐inflammatory properties. Within its drug class, thiazolidinediones have been used successfully in managing hyperglycemia in diabetic patients and have also been investigated in various preclinical models for their potential in modulating inflammatory responses and oxidative stress, capabilities that are hypothesized to be beneficial in chronic degenerative conditions like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, pioglitazone is approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, where its activation of PPARγ leads to enhanced insulin sensitivity, alterations in adipocyte differentiation, and modulation of lipid metabolism. Over the years, its favorable safety profile in diabetic populations has been well documented. Outside of metabolic disease, growing interest in its pleiotropic effects has led to investigations of its potential for vascular protection and anti‐inflammatory actions in ocular tissues. Some studies have proposed that PPARγ agonists may have a role in retinal diseases due to the expression of this nuclear receptor in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26; Simpson-Haidaris et al., 2010, pp. 18–19). However, when specifically tested in dry AMD models, such as oxLDL-induced RPE cell death assays, pioglitazone—as well as other PPARγ agonists like ciglitazone and rosiglitazone—did not afford significant protection, whereas troglitazone was the only compound to show marked cytoprotective effects (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). In the clinical arena, a study conducted in diabetic patients with neovascular AMD receiving anti-VEGF therapy showed that thiazolidinedione use was associated with some beneficial anatomical changes in subretinal fluid and tissue complex thickness (Core et al., 2023, pp. 2–4). Nonetheless, these clinical investigations have been primarily confined to the context of neovascular AMD rather than dry AMD, and there is limited direct clinical evidence for pioglitazone being repurposed for dry AMD. Thus, while the drug’s history in diabetes and its secondary vascular effects offer a rationale for repurposing, its track record specifically in dry AMD remains inconclusive.

Mechanism of Action:  
Pioglitazone exerts its primary pharmacological activity through binding to and activating PPARγ, a ligand-dependent transcription factor that modulates the expression of genes involved in glucose metabolism, lipid handling, and inflammatory responses (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). Activation of PPARγ typically leads to downstream transcriptional events that include the upregulation of antioxidant enzymes such as Cu/Zn-superoxide dismutase (SOD) and suppression of NADPH oxidase expression, thereby reducing oxidative stress (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). In theory, within RPE cells, PPARγ activation could also promote the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. PGC-1α is known to drive mitochondrial replication, increase the expression of genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation, and upregulate a suite of antioxidant defenses; these effects have been associated with enhanced cell survival under oxidative stress conditions in RPE models (Iacovelli et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 12–13). Moreover, because RPE cells are characterized by high metabolic demand and are particularly susceptible to ROS-induced damage, induction of mitochondrial biogenesis could mitigate oxidative stress and preserve intracellular energy metabolism. 

The central hypothesis for the repurposing of pioglitazone in dry AMD is that PPARγ activation by this agonist will induce a PGC-1α–driven mitochondrial biogenesis pathway in RPE cells under oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂ stress). This induction is expected to lead to enhanced mitochondrial function, lower mitochondrial ROS (mito-ROS) production, and an overall reduction in oxidative damage. By decreasing ROS levels, the cascade that normally leads to the degradation of key junctional proteins—specifically claudin-19 and ZO-1, which are critical for maintaining the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier—could be interrupted. Thus, preservation or restoration of these junctional complexes could recover the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity of the RPE (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). However, existing in vitro studies in RPE models have shown that among several tested PPARγ agonists, pioglitazone did not replicate the cytoprotective effects seen with troglitazone, and the beneficial effects in these studies were found to be independent of PPARγ activation (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). This discrepancy raises questions about whether pioglitazone can induce the PGC-1α pathway effectively in this context. Nonetheless, the mechanistic rationale remains centered on the possibility that reducing oxidative stress through enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis might preserve cell junction integrity in the RPE, an approach that is biologically plausible based on the roles of both PPARγ and PGC-1α in other tissues and in some retinal models.

Expected Effect:  
According to the proposed hypothesis, when ARPE-19 cells are challenged with H₂O₂ to simulate oxidative stress, treatment with 1 µM pioglitazone is expected to initiate a cascade of molecular events: First, pioglitazone should activate PPARγ, which in turn would upregulate PGC-1α expression. This upregulation is anticipated to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and function, resulting in a measurable decrease in mitochondrial ROS production as detected by MitoSOX fluorescence assays. In addition, by lowering ROS levels, the compound is expected to protect against the degradation of cell junction proteins such as claudin-19 and ZO-1. These proteins are essential for the formation and maintenance of the tight junction belts in RPE cells, contributing to the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier. The experimental readouts proposed include a 45% recovery in TEER, a surrogate marker for barrier integrity, suggesting that pioglitazone would restore functional barrier properties that are compromised under oxidative stress conditions (Fischer, 2016, pp. 23–26). It is important to note, however, that while these effects have been observed in some isolated experiments, the majority of the literature on PPARγ agonists in RPE models has primarily highlighted that only troglitazone, rather than pioglitazone, yielded significant cytoprotection against oxidative insults (Choi, 2019, pp. 25–31, 37–42). Thus, while the expected effect is biologically coherent with the ideal model of reducing ROS-mediated junction protein degradation and restoring TEER, the existing experimental evidence raises concerns regarding whether pioglitazone is capable of achieving these outcomes under the conditions outlined.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the repurposing strategy of using pioglitazone for the treatment of dry AMD is based on a sound mechanistic rationale that integrates several interrelated pathways: the PPARγ-mediated modulation of inflammatory and oxidative stress responses, the PGC-1α–driven enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis, and the consequent protection of RPE junctional integrity. The well-established clinical safety profile of pioglitazone in diabetic populations is an important strength, as it facilitates potential rapid translation to clinical trials for new indications. Further comprehensive studies are needed to resolve these discrepancies—ideally through optimized in vitro models that replicate the oxidative and metabolic challenges of dry AMD, and through detailed mechanistic studies that can confirm or refute the induction of PGC-1α and subsequent mitochondrial biogenesis by pioglitazone in RPE cells. 5‐Azacytidine is a synthetically produced nucleoside analogue of cytidine originally derived by chemical modification of the natural ribonucleoside. This compound is classified as an azanucleoside and has been widely studied as a DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) inhibitor. Its discovery and subsequent synthesis have enabled researchers to interrogate the role of DNA methylation in gene regulation. In its typical biological usage, after cellular uptake mediated by nucleoside transporters, 5‐azacytidine is phosphorylated by cellular kinases into its active triphosphate form (5‐aza‐CTP) and can become incorporated into RNA as well as into DNA, although only around 10–20% is converted to the deoxyribonucleotide form prior to DNA incorporation. This unique feature is a double‐edged sword: on one hand, it allows modulation of cytosine methylation patterns within genomic DNA by trapping DNMTs; on the other, its incorporation into RNA can perturb protein synthesis and contributes to its cytotoxic profile. Chemically, its structure and mode of synthesis place it within a well‐characterized class of antimetabolite agents whose utility extends beyond oncology into other fields where epigenetic modifications are implicated (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, 5‐azacytidine and its deoxy analogue 5‐aza‐2′‐deoxycytidine (decitabine) were first developed as antimetabolite chemotherapy agents for hematologic malignancies. Their clinical utility in treating conditions such as myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) is well established, with DNA demethylation and tumor suppressor gene reactivation being central to their antineoplastic efficacy. Over the years, the successful repurposing of these nucleoside analogues has led to extensive studies investigating their potential effects beyond oncology. In cancer cells, the irreversible binding of DNMT enzymes to DNA following incorporation of 5‐azacytidine has been shown to produce passive demethylation during cell division and consequent gene reactivation (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). In more recent years, researchers have begun to consider the roles of aberrant DNA methylation in non‐cancer diseases, including ocular pathologies like age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). Reviews in ocular epigenetics have noted that epigenetic dysregulation, including hypermethylation of promoters for antioxidant enzymes and other protective genes, may contribute to RPE dysfunction in AMD (Li et al., 2020). For instance, studies in cultured RPE cells and AMD cybrid models have observed tolerability of DNMT inhibitors, as exemplified by experiments where polarized RPE monolayers treated with 5‐aza‐2′‐deoxycytidine showed no significant disruption in barrier markers such as ZO‐1 or cytokeratin, and even demonstrated gene reactivation effects such as upregulation of clusterin (Li et al., 2020). Although 5‐azacytidine itself has not been as widely evaluated in ocular models as decitabine, the extensive biochemical literature surrounding its DNMT inhibitory properties forms a strong rationale for its potential repurposing toward dry AMD via epigenetic modulation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, 5‐azacytidine exerts its pharmacologic actions primarily through inhibition of DNMT enzymes. Under normal physiological conditions, DNMT enzymes bind to cytosine residues in CpG dinucleotides and catalyze the transfer of a methyl group from S‐adenosyl-L‐methionine (SAM) to the 5‐position carbon of cytosine, a process that is essential for the maintenance of epigenetic patterns and gene silencing. However, the substitution of nitrogen at the C5 position in 5‐azacytidine disrupts this process because the reaction mechanism relies on a β‐elimination step that cannot occur when a nitrogen is present instead of a carbon. Consequently, when 5‐azacytidine is incorporated into the DNA of replicating cells, DNMT enzymes – particularly the maintenance methyltransferase DNMT1 – are unable to complete the methylation reaction and become covalently trapped at the site of incorporation (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). This irreversible trapping inhibits the recycling of DNMTs and leads to their proteasomal degradation, thus reducing the cellular pool of active DNMT enzymes. In subsequent rounds of DNA replication, the absence of sufficient DNMT activity results in passive demethylation of newly synthesized DNA strands that fail to be remethylated. This epigenetic reprogramming can lead to reactivation of genes with previously hypermethylated and silenced promoters (Cheishvili et al., 2015; Palii et al., 2008). It is important to note that 5‐azacytidine is also incorporated into RNA, where it may inhibit RNA methylation and alter translation; however, the therapeutic emphasis in the context of reactivating silenced genes typically focuses on its DNA‐mediated effects. Alagebrium chloride (ALT-711) is a synthetic small molecule designed as an advanced glycation end product (AGE) crosslink breaker. Over the past two decades, this class of AGE breakers, including ALT-711, has been primarily explored for applications in cardiovascular and diabetic complications, with the underlying therapeutic hypothesis being that reversal of AGE-mediated crosslinking could restore tissue compliance and function (Kim & Spiegel, 2013; Toprak & Yigitaslan, 2019).
