Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
4‐Octyl Itaconate (4‐OI) is a cell‐permeable derivative of itaconate, a naturally occurring immunometabolite generated in activated macrophages during inflammatory responses. 4‐OI has been synthesized by chemically modifying itaconate to improve its lipophilicity and enhance its cellular uptake, which in turn facilitates its electrophilic reactivity. This improved cell permeability enables 4‐OI to effectively modulate intracellular targets such as Keap1. As a member of the electrophilic compounds class, 4‐OI belongs to a group of therapeutics that are designed to exploit the redox-sensing molecular machinery of cells. Historically, compounds in this class have been used to induce antioxidant and cytoprotective responses by activating the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. In its commercial form (Sigma SML2192), 4‐OI offers a reproducible and standardized reagent for preclinical studies and drug development, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in conditions where oxidative stress plays a central pathophysiological role, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

The therapeutic candidate is particularly intriguing given the significant role of oxidative stress and inflammation in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, especially within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). The RPE is highly susceptible to oxidative damage due to its high metabolic demand, continuous exposure to light, and abundance of polyunsaturated fatty acids. Dysregulation of the redox balance in these cells has been directly tied to barrier dysfunction, including loss of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased permeability to molecules such as FITC-dextran. By design, 4‐OI aims to exploit its electrophilic nature to alkylate reactive cysteine residues on the Keap1 protein, thereby liberating Nrf2 and triggering its stabilization and nuclear translocation. Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 upregulates various antioxidant genes and possibly genes that maintain tight junction integrity, thus promoting cytoprotection and barrier restoration. This profile makes 4‐OI a promising candidate in the context of dry AMD, where restoration of RPE barrier function is a critical therapeutic goal (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
The use of itaconate derivatives, including 4‐OI, has been widely investigated across several biomedical fields, particularly in studies focused on modulating the cellular response to oxidative stress and inflammation. Preclinical studies in various cell types have demonstrated that 4‐OI can potently activate the Nrf2 pathway, leading to increased transcription of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins. For instance, in human retinal pigment epithelium cells exposed to angiotensin II (Ang II), 4‐OI was shown to significantly reduce reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels while concomitantly enhancing superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity. Such findings provide concrete evidence of its ROS-scavenging potential and anti-inflammatory efficacy (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Outside the ocular context, 4‐OI has been evaluated in models of renal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), where it was observed to reduce tubular injury scores, lower inflammatory cytokine levels, and improve overall kidney function through activation of the Nrf2 pathway. Similar protective effects have been recorded in lung transplantation models under cold ischemia/reperfusion conditions, wherein 4‐OI treatment improved epithelial cell viability and donor lung function (Gao et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Li et al., 2023, pp. 3–5, 9–11). The mechanism underlying these benefits consistently centers on the electrophilic activation of the Nrf2 pathway via alkylation of Keap1 cysteines.

Regarding ocular diseases, while the direct use of 4‐OI in dry AMD has yet to be fully evaluated in clinical settings, several studies have established the general importance of the Keap1/Nrf2 axis in maintaining retinal health. Agents that stimulate this pathway, including dimethyl fumarate, quercetin, and various itaconate derivatives, have shown promising results in protecting RPE cells from oxidative and inflammatory insults (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–7). Preliminary investigations using 4‐OI in RPE cell models have indicated improvements in antioxidant responses and cell viability, suggesting that compounds of this class may offer therapeutic benefits similar to those seen in other tissues challenged by oxidative stress (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 6–8).

In addition, the therapeutic history of similar electrophilic Nrf2 activators highlights their dual role both in mitigating inflammatory responses and in bolstering barrier functions via tight junction stabilization. This is particularly relevant when considering the pathogenesis of dry AMD, which is marked by compromised RPE barrier integrity and chronic oxidative injury (Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Falcão et al., 2025, p. 20). Thus, although the direct clinical application of 4‐OI in AMD is still in its early stages, the compound has a well-documented history in preclinical models of oxidative injury and barrier dysfunction, which supports its repurposing for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
The central mechanism by which 4‐OI exerts its therapeutic effects is through its electrophilic modification of Keap1, a regulatory protein that normally sequesters Nrf2 in the cytoplasm and promotes its proteasomal degradation. Under basal conditions, Keap1 binds to Nrf2 and facilitates its ubiquitination, thereby maintaining low intracellular levels of Nrf2. 4‐OI covalently modifies key cysteine residues on Keap1, which disrupts the Keap1/Nrf2 interaction and prevents the ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of Nrf2. This post-translational modification allows Nrf2 to accumulate in the cytoplasm and eventually translocate into the nucleus (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to the antioxidant response element (ARE) located in the promoter region of various cytoprotective genes. This binding leads to the transcriptional activation of genes encoding a host of antioxidant enzymes and protective proteins, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), and various glutathione biosynthetic enzymes. Through this coordinated induction of antioxidant defenses, cells can effectively neutralize ROS, restore redox homeostasis, and mitigate the harmful effects of chronic oxidative stress (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6; Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7).

In addition to its antioxidant role, Nrf2 activation has been implicated in the regulation of inflammatory signaling pathways. By promoting the expression of anti-inflammatory mediators and by interfering with the nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) pathway—through competition for transcriptional co-activators—Nrf2 activation can lead to decreased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–7). It is worth noting that the effects of 4‐OI on inflammatory cytokine production can be dose-dependent; while low concentrations typically suppress cytokine transcription and inflammation, higher doses have been associated with unintended pro-inflammatory outcomes, such as enhanced IL-1β release and inflammatory apoptosis in certain cell types (Muri et al., 2020, pp. 2–3, 5–7). Such dual effects necessitate careful titration of the dose to ensure that the therapeutic window is maximized for protective outcomes while minimizing potential cytotoxicity.

Furthermore, evidence from studies on endothelial cells and Caco-2 monolayers indicates that similar electrophilic Nrf2 activators can protect and restore barrier function, as measured by transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER). In these models, activation of Nrf2 has been linked to the upregulation of tight junction proteins and the maintenance of paracellular integrity (Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Gao et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). Although direct studies of TEER in RPE cells treated with 4‐OI are limited, the underlying molecular logic suggests a similar beneficial impact on RPE barrier function. This is particularly relevant given the hypothesis that 4‐OI treatment will restore TEER and decrease FITC-dextran permeability in oxidative stress or A2E plus blue-light injury models by both reducing oxidative stress and enhancing the expression of tight junction proteins that are regulated by Nrf2 (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Additionally, the specificity of 4‐OI for Keap1’s cysteine residues, along with its favorable cell permeability, positions the compound as a modulatory switch that can trigger a host of downstream protective pathways. This multifaceted mechanism of action, encompassing direct antioxidant effects, anti-inflammatory activity, and preservation of barrier function, underpins the potential clinical utility of 4‐OI in conditions marked by oxidative damage and barrier dysfunction, such as dry AMD (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for employing 4‐OI in dry AMD is that by alkylating Keap1 cysteines in RPE, it will stabilize and induce the nuclear accumulation of Nrf2, thereby upregulating antioxidant defenses and tight junction proteins. The expected outcome in an in vitro model is a restoration of TEER and a decrease in FITC-dextran permeability under conditions of oxidative stress or when RPE cells are challenged with A2E and blue-light exposure. Precedent for this predicted effect is found in studies where 4‐OI’s electrophilic activation of Nrf2 has led to robust antioxidant responses, including the upregulation of genes encoding detoxifying enzymes and the suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Specifically, the anticipated activation of Nrf2 in RPE cells is expected to result in increased expression of key cytoprotective genes such as HO-1 and NQO1, which play crucial roles in combating ROS-mediated cellular damage. In addition, Nrf2 activation has been linked to the expression of genes associated with maintaining tight junction integrity—an essential aspect of the RPE’s barrier function (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Given that reduced TEER and increased FITC-dextran permeability are hallmarks of RPE barrier disruption in dry AMD, the modulation of these parameters by 4‐OI is a central goal of the proposed intervention.

Experimental data from studies in other cell types, such as endothelial cells challenged with endotoxin, have shown that electrophilic Nrf2 activators can rescue TEER to levels exceeding 95%, suggesting that similar outcomes may be achievable in RPE cells (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). In parallel, research using 4‐OI in human primary RPE models has demonstrated a reduction in ROS production, decreased inflammation, and improved cellular viability in the context of oxidative stress induced by agents like angiotensin II (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6, 7–8). These findings lend credence to the expectation that 4‐OI will counteract A2E plus blue-light-induced oxidative damage in RPE cells, thereby reestablishing normal barrier properties.

By dampening inflammatory cytokine release (including IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1) and reducing oxidative biomarkers such as malondialdehyde, 4‐OI should mitigate the deleterious microenvironment that contributes to RPE dysfunction (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6). The net result would be a restoration of cellular homeostasis, improved barrier integrity, and a reduction in the secondary effects of chronic oxidative injury, which collectively translate into a potential therapeutic benefit for dry AMD.

Finally, the anticipated outcomes are supported by the observation that Nrf2 is expressed in RPE cells and is critical for their survival under stress conditions (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Activation of Nrf2 by 4‐OI, therefore, is expected to counteract the pathophysiological mechanisms that precipitate RPE degeneration in dry AMD. These effects could be quantified both by measuring restored TEER values as a proxy for tight junction integrity and by assessing decreased FITC-dextran permeability as an indicator of improved barrier function (Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of 4‐Octyl Itaconate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is decidedly positive, though not without certain challenges that must be addressed in subsequent investigations. One of the most significant strengths of 4‐OI is its strong mechanistic rationale: by targeting Keap1 via electrophilic alkylation, 4‐OI effectively liberates Nrf2, triggering a cascade of antioxidant and cytoprotective responses that are crucial for maintaining RPE health. This mode of action is consistent with a broad body of preclinical evidence across several tissue models, including renal, pulmonary, and endothelial systems (Gao et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Li et al., 2023, pp. 3–5, 9–11). The ability of 4‐OI to restore barrier function, as evidenced by its reported rescue of TEER in endotoxin-challenged endothelial cells, provides an additional layer of validation for its potential use in RPE models, where barrier dysfunction is a hallmark of dry AMD (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

From a therapeutic history perspective, the repurposing of 4‐OI is supported by its documented efficacy in reducing oxidative stress and inflammation in multiple preclinical studies. Its effects have been observed in various experimental systems that mimic the cellular and molecular events underpinning dry AMD, including the activation of the Nrf2 pathway, downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, and protection against ROS-induced apoptosis (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6, 7–8). Although direct clinical evidence in dry AMD models is limited, the robust preclinical data from related systems and the well-established role of the Keap1/Nrf2 pathway in retinal health lend substantial support to the hypothesis that 4‐OI could be effective in ameliorating RPE degeneration.

Mechanistically, 4‐OI offers several advantages. Its specificity for modifying Keap1 and thereby stabilizing Nrf2 is well-documented, and its integration into cellular signaling networks that govern both oxidative stress responses and inflammatory processes is compelling. The upregulation of phase II detoxification enzymes and tight junction proteins following Nrf2 activation suggests that 4‐OI could address multiple pathogenic features of dry AMD simultaneously. However, a note of caution is warranted: studies have indicated that 4‐OI’s pharmacological profile is dose-dependent, and high concentrations may lead to paradoxical effects, such as increased IL-1β release and pro-inflammatory apoptosis. These findings underscore the importance of careful dose optimization and thorough toxicological evaluation in further preclinical work (Muri et al., 2020, pp. 2–3, 5–7).

Another strength lies in the compound’s favorable safety profile in murine models. Studies in renal IRI and lung transplantation models have demonstrated that 4‐OI is not only efficacious but also well-tolerated, with no significant adverse effects observed at therapeutic doses (Gao et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Li et al., 2023, pp. 3–5). This bodes well for its potential translation to ocular applications, where safety is a paramount concern given the delicate nature of retinal tissues. Additionally, the capacity of 4‐OI to achieve near-complete restoration of TEER in other epithelial models suggests that similar barrier-protective effects might be replicated in RPE cells, a hypothesis that is reinforced by the known importance of Nrf2 in maintaining tight junction integrity (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

Despite these strengths, there are some notable limitations. Direct evidence of 4‐OI’s efficacy in RPE-specific models of dry AMD remains sparse, and most of the supporting data are extrapolated from studies in other cell types or in non-ocular systems. As such, while the mechanistic rationale is strong, further in vitro and in vivo studies specifically focused on the retinal context are essential to confirm that the anticipated effects—namely, enhancement of TEER and reduction of FITC-dextran permeability—can be robustly achieved in RPE cells under oxidative stress or A2E plus blue-light injury conditions (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 6–7).

Moreover, the dual activity of 4‐OI, wherein low doses are beneficial while high doses might provoke inflammatory responses, presents a potential challenge for clinical translation. This necessitates precise pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies to define the optimal dosing regimen that maximizes therapeutic benefits while circumventing adverse effects. Such dose–response studies will be critical not only in cell-based assays but also in animal models that reliably reproduce the pathology of dry AMD (Muri et al., 2020, pp. 2–3, 5–7).

Another consideration is the complexity of dry AMD as a multifactorial disease. While oxidative stress and inflammation are key drivers, other pathological processes such as complement activation, cellular senescence, and genetic predispositions also play significant roles in disease progression. As a result, a monotherapeutic approach solely based on Nrf2 activation may need to be complemented by additional interventions targeting these other pathways. Nonetheless, the central role of oxidative stress in RPE degeneration makes the Nrf2 pathway a critical node, and therapeutics like 4‐OI that modulate this pathway could form a valuable component of combination therapies for dry AMD (Cai et al., 2021, pp. 2–3; Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6).

In summary, 4‐Octyl Itaconate presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well-characterized mechanism of inducing Nrf2 activation through electrophilic alkylation of Keap1, its established preclinical efficacy in reducing oxidative stress and inflammation in multiple tissues, and its documented ability to restore barrier function as evidenced by improvements in TEER in other cellular models. The compound’s synthetic design ensures its effective cellular delivery, and its use in non-ocular models provides a strong preclinical foundation for its repurposing in AMD. However, the translation of these effects to the RPE and the ocular environment requires further targeted research. Critical next steps include dose optimization studies to avoid pro-inflammatory effects, rigorous validation in RPE cell culture models under oxidative challenge (such as A2E plus blue-light injury), and subsequent in vivo evaluations in animal models of dry AMD.

Overall, the repurposing of 4‐OI as a novel Nrf2-centered approach to reinforce RPE junctions and mitigate oxidative stress in dry AMD is promising. Its strengths include a solid mechanistic rationale, demonstrated efficacy in modulating key cellular stress pathways, and evidence of barrier protective effects in analogous cell systems. Conversely, its weaknesses center on the current paucity of direct RPE or ocular data, the potential for dose-dependent adverse effects, and the inherent complexity of dry AMD pathophysiology requiring possibly multimodal therapeutic interventions. With these considerations in mind, 4‐Octyl Itaconate merits further investigation as part of a comprehensive drug development strategy for dry AMD, with the goal of establishing robust preclinical evidence to support its advancement toward clinical trials (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–7; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA-408; also known as CDDO-DFPA; N-(2-Cyano-3,12-dioxo-28-noroleana-1,9(11)-dien-17-yl)-2,2-difluoropropanamide) is a semisynthetic oleanane triterpenoid created by lead optimization of the natural product oleanolic acid, a plant-derived pentacyclic triterpene produced via the mevalonate pathway (squalene → 2,3-oxidosqualene → β-amyrin → erythrodiol → oleanolic acid) and abundantly available from Oleaceae (e.g., olive) and other botanical sources (over 1,600 species; Nakagami, 2016; Masullo et al., 2017; Pollier & Goossens, 2012). The oleanane scaffold was iteratively diversified by Sporn, Gribble, Honda and collaborators to introduce enone and cyanoenone Michael acceptors on rings A and C, yielding the CDDO class (2-cyano-3,12-dioxo-oleana-1,9(11)-dien-28-oic acid and derivatives) as extraordinarily potent anti-inflammatory and Nrf2-inducing agents; C-28 esters/amides and further A/C-ring modifications produced multiple clinical candidates including CDDO-Me (bardoxolone methyl, RTA-402) and RTA-408 (omaveloxolone) (Honda et al., 2000; Pollier & Goossens, 2012; Cheng et al., 2021). RTA-408 specifically is a C17-modified difluoro-propanamide on an oleanane core and belongs to the second generation of synthetic triterpenoids designed to preserve high Nrf2 potency while controlling electrophilicity and pharmacokinetics (Nakagami, 2016; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

At the pharmacological class level, synthetic oleanane triterpenoids are electrophilic “antioxidant inflammation modulators” that activate the KEAP1–NRF2–ARE pathway through covalent (but often reversible) Michael addition to redox-sensitive cysteines on KEAP1, particularly Cys151 on the BTB domain, thereby stabilizing Nrf2 and inducing a coordinated cytoprotective gene program; they concurrently suppress inducible pro-inflammatory mediators (e.g., iNOS, COX-2) with dose-dependent bifunctionality (cytoprotection at low concentrations; pro-oxidant/apoptotic signaling at higher exposure) (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Liby et al., 2007). This scaffold has been extensively explored as a drug platform across oncology, nephrology, cardiopulmonary, inflammatory, and neurological indications, with bardoxolone methyl and omaveloxolone translating to clinical studies and, for omaveloxolone, regulatory approval in Friedreich’s ataxia (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Zahir et al., 2025). Within ophthalmology, oleanane triterpenoids and close congeners (dh404, CDDO-TFEA, CDDO-EA, CDDO-Me) have shown robust Nrf2-mediated protection in retinal models, and RTA-408 itself has been advanced into ocular clinical trials evaluating postoperative ocular pain/inflammation and corneal endothelial cell loss after cataract surgery, positioning this mechanism squarely within ocular translational scope (Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
The oleanane triterpenoid class has a two-decade translational history that began with demonstrations that cyano-enone–bearing derivatives are sub-nanomolar inducers of the Nrf2 transcriptome and suppressors of inflammatory enzymes in vitro and in vivo, a property mapped by SAR to the presence/placement of A-ring 1-en-3-one and C-ring 9(11)-en-12-one Michael acceptors (Honda et al., 2000; Nakagami, 2016). Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me) showed pharmacodynamic activity in humans (ARE-gene induction in tumor biopsies; renal function improvements), but its BEACON Phase 3 trial in advanced CKD was halted for cardiovascular adverse events—an outcome that did not negate class activity but highlighted the need for indication-specific risk management and exclusion criteria (e.g., high BNP, poor baseline eGFR) (Masullo et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Subsequent controlled studies in rarer CKD-associated diseases continued under tighter cardiometabolic selection, while medicinal-chemistry efforts generated second-generation analogs including fluorinated scaffolds (e.g., omaveloxolone) to tune reactivity and PK/PD (Sun et al., 2017).

For omaveloxolone specifically, preclinical pharmacology established Nrf2-dependent induction of glutathione homeostasis genes and improvements in mitochondrial respiration; systemic PK in primates/humans showed dose proportionality and measurable tissue distribution (including liver, lung, brain), with PBMC and tissue Nrf2 target-gene induction at clinically achievable exposures (Reisman et al., 2019). In neurology, omaveloxolone advanced through the MOXIe program for Friedreich’s ataxia with evidence of neurologic benefit at clinical doses ≥80 mg and exposures concordant with preclinical pharmacology (Naidu & Dinkova-Kostova, 2020; Reisman et al., 2019; Zahir et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action  
The KEAP1–NRF2 node is a cysteine-centric electrophile sensor system that orchestrates the phase-2 antioxidant and cytoprotective response. Under basal conditions, KEAP1 recruits NRF2 to the CUL3 E3 ligase complex for ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover. Electrophiles such as cyano-enone triterpenoids react with KEAP1 cysteine sensors—most prominently Cys151 in the BTB domain—to disrupt CUL3 docking and/or alter KEAP1 conformation, thereby stabilizing NRF2, allowing nuclear translocation, heterodimerization with small Maf proteins, and binding to antioxidant response elements (ARE) to induce a transcriptional battery including NQO1, HO-1 (HMOX1), glutathione biosynthesis enzymes (GCLC, GCLM), thioredoxin and thioredoxin reductase (Txn1, Txnrd1), sulfiredoxin (Srxn1), and other detoxifying/antioxidative genes (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). Oleanane cyano-enone triterpenoids are among the most potent NRF2 activators known, with structure–activity relationships showing strong correlations between the presence/geometry of Michael acceptors and both iNOS suppression and NQO1 induction across series; mechanistic profiling indicates covalent yet reversible conjugation to protein thiols underlies this pharmacology (Naidu & Dinkova-Kostova, 2020).

Within this class, omaveloxolone is an electrophilic Michael acceptor–bearing, difluoro-propanamide oleanane that activates Nrf2 at nanomolar concentrations in reporter assays and upregulates canonical ARE-target genes (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, TxnR1), consistent with its cyano-enone pharmacophore engaging KEAP1 Cys151 and allied redox sensors (Sun et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019). In systemic models, omaveloxolone increases glutathione concentrations, supports mitochondrial respiration, and normalizes metabolic/energetic parameters downstream of Nrf2 activation—effects mechanistically rationalized by Nrf2-driven induction of NADPH-generating enzymes and mitochondrial support genes, which collectively bolster reductive and ATP capacity in stressed cells (Reisman et al., 2019). In immunologic contexts, oleanane triterpenoids suppress IFN-γ–induced nitric oxide signaling in macrophages, reduce reactive oxygen and nitrotyrosine production by myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and can inhibit IKKβ/NF-κB signaling (demonstrated for CDDO-Me), contributing to anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions that are secondary but complementary to NRF2-mediated cytoprotection (Creelan et al., 2017; Sporn et al., 2007). The class is bifunctional: low-to-moderate exposures favor NRF2-dependent cytoprotection and redox quenching, whereas higher exposures can increase oxidative burden and trigger apoptosis—an important consideration when targeting delicate ocular tissues (Liby et al., 2007).

For ocular cell types relevant to dry AMD, multiple lines of evidence anchor Nrf2/ARE biology. In the retina, oleanane triterpenoids (dh404, CDDO derivatives) induce NQO1/HO-1/GCLM, reduce inflammatory mediators and vascular leakage, and protect photoreceptors and retinal structure in oxidative-stress models; RS9 dosing increases retinal NQO1/HO-1 in vivo (Cheng et al., 2021). Taken together, these data support that omaveloxolone, via KEAP1 cysteine sensing and Nrf2 activation in RPE and adjacent retinal cells, can rapidly enhance the endogenous antioxidant program, elevate glutathione/NADPH buffering, mitigate protein oxidative adducts, and suppress inflammatory amplification—biomechanistic axes directly relevant to RPE survival and barrier function under oxidative stress (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021).

Pharmacologically, omaveloxolone exhibits high plasma protein binding and broad tissue distribution preclinically, with oral dosing in primates/humans yielding exposures that induce Nrf2 targets in PBMCs and distribute to metabolically active tissues; topical dermal dosing in humans activates cutaneous Nrf2 without untoward safety signals (Reisman et al., 2019). For ocular dosing, clinical testing of RTA-408 in cataract-surgery contexts (ocular pain/inflammation, corneal endothelial protection) establishes feasibility of achieving pharmacologically relevant ocular exposure with acceptable tolerability in humans, though detailed ocular PK has not been published in the provided excerpts (Cheng et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Assay and hypothesis: In a human RPE monolayer model subjected to H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury, omaveloxolone is expected to covalently and reversibly modify KEAP1 cysteines (notably Cys151), stabilize and activate Nrf2, and robustly induce the ARE-regulated antioxidant gene set (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, TXNRD1, SRXN1), thereby increasing cellular glutathione, NADPH-dependent antioxidant enzyme activity, and mitochondrial resilience; these changes should reduce protein S-glutathionylation, prevent loss of perijunctional actomyosin integrity, and preserve tight-junction belts, culminating in restoration of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and reduction of paracellular flux (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021). Mechanistic support for each step:

- Target engagement and Nrf2 activation in RPE: Cyano-enone triterpenoids are sensed by KEAP1 Cys151, stabilizing Nrf2; omaveloxolone activates Nrf2 at nanomolar concentrations and induces NQO1/HO-1/GCLM/TxnR1 in human cells, and has shown protection in human fetal RPE at ≤100 nM against H₂O₂-induced death with suppression of protein glutathionylation—an oxidative adduct linked to structural protein dysfunction and barrier failure (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021).

- Evidence that ocular cells mount an ARE program: In retinal models, dh404 and CDDO derivatives upregulate NQO1, HO-1, and GCLM; RS9 increases retinal NQO1/HO-1 in vivo, confirming that ARE-responsive gene expression is present and inducible in ocular tissues relevant to barrier function and oxidative injury (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Mitochondrial and redox effects: Omaveloxolone increases glutathione and promotes mitochondrial respiration in preclinical systems, and Nrf2 regulates a broad antioxidative and bioenergetic program that supplies reductive capacity (NADPH) and detoxifying enzymes, supporting RPE energy-demanding barrier maintenance under stress (Reisman et al., 2019).

- Barrier functional correlates in vivo and in vitro: Oleanane triterpenoids reduce retinal vascular leakage in models of inflammation/oxidative stress, and RTA-408 decreases oxidative protein glutathionylation in RPE—a mechanistic event that plausibly preserves junctional complexes and TEER under H₂O₂ stress, even though explicit TEER data for RTA-408 in RPE are not provided here (Cheng et al., 2021).

Operationally, we anticipate a biphasic exposure–response: low nanomolar concentrations should maximize cytoprotective Nrf2 signaling without triggering the pro-oxidant/apoptotic bifurcation observed at higher exposures for this class (Liby et al., 2007). In line with available RPE data, we would start at 1–100 nM omaveloxolone, quantify early ARE-gene induction (1–6 h), glutathione/NADPH pools, protein S-glutathionylation, and image ZO-1/occludin belts, then assess TEER and fluorescein (or 70 kDa dextran) paracellular flux after H₂O₂ challenge; photoreceptor-derived 661W and co-culture systems can be used to evaluate paracrine rescue (Cheng et al., 2021).

As a translational bridge, we would prioritize in vivo models where oleanane triterpenoids have shown benefit (light-induced retinal damage; ischemia–reperfusion; BRB leakage models) to confirm retinal/RPE exposure and barrier readouts, leveraging prior triterpenoid ocular pharmacology experience (Cheng et al., 2021).

Drug delivery considerations: Given lipophilicity and protein binding typical of this class, formulation will influence retinal/RPE exposure. Approaches used for related triterpenoids—e.g., amorphous solid dispersions for oral delivery (CDDO-Me) or nanoparticle carriers for ocular delivery (demonstrated for ursolic acid)—illustrate feasible strategies to reach ocular tissues while minimizing systemic exposure; the fact that RTA-408 has entered ocular clinical trials (post-cataract endpoints) supports translatable tolerability of ophthalmic administration (Cheng et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit to dry AMD biology: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to RPE degeneration in dry AMD; omaveloxolone engages KEAP1 cysteine sensors to activate Nrf2 and induce a comprehensive, rapid-acting ARE program that elevates glutathione/NADPH, upregulates HO-1/NQO1/GCL-enzymes, and improves mitochondrial bioenergetics—changes expected to blunt H₂O₂-triggered barrier loss and death in RPE (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). The oleanane scaffold’s larger, conformationally constrained electrophile is argued to offer improved selectivity and controllable PK/PD versus small electrophiles, potentially reducing off-target liabilities at therapeutic concentrations (Cuadrado et al., 2019).

- Direct RPE evidence and ocular translational precedent: RTA-408 protects human fetal RPE from H₂O₂-induced apoptosis/necrosis at ≤100 nM and reduces protein S-glutathionylation, a lesion consistent with cytoskeletal/junctional dysfunction; related oleanane triterpenoids induce Nrf2 targets in retina, reduce BRB leak, and attenuate oxidative-stress retinal damage in vivo (Cheng et al., 2021). RTA-408 is the only OA analogue documented to have entered ocular clinical trials (post-cataract endpoints), supporting feasibility of ophthalmic development (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Clinical-stage agent with known human PK/PD: Omaveloxolone has extensive preclinical and early clinical characterization, including primate/human PK with tissue distribution and PBMC Nrf2 target induction, topical proof of mechanism in human skin, and multiple oral clinical programs (oncology, FA), reducing translational uncertainty compared to earlier chemical matter (Reisman et al., 2019; Creelan et al., 2017; Zahir et al., 2025).

- Class potency and breadth: Oleanane cyano-enones are among the most potent known Nrf2 activators; RS9’s superior retinal potency and CDDO tethered analogs’ efficacy in retinal models argue that the scaffold class, optimized for ocular delivery, can achieve pharmacodynamic effects in the eye at low doses (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021).

Risks and weaknesses  
- Electrophile-driven bifunctionality and narrow window: The same α,β-unsaturated carbonyls that confer high potency can, at higher exposures, increase oxidative stress and trigger apoptosis; dose selection and exposure control will be critical in the eye (Liby et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2021).

- Class safety history: Bardoxolone methyl’s cardiovascular signal in late-stage CKD underscores the need for indication- and formulation-specific safety strategies; while not probative for ocular topical/intraocular dosing, it motivates cautious systemic exposure limits and cardiovascular exclusion if systemic routes are used (Nakagami, 2016; Sun et al., 2017).

- Incomplete AMD-specific evidence: The provided literature does not report omaveloxolone in dry AMD or geographic atrophy models; most ocular data derive from oxidative-stress/retinal injury and postoperative inflammation paradigms, which are supportive but not definitive for the multifactorial dry AMD pathobiology (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Delivery and exposure uncertainties: Omaveloxolone’s lipophilicity and strong protein binding complicate prediction of ocular distribution; although ocular clinical testing exists for RTA-408, detailed ocular PK/PD are not included in the excerpts, and tailored ophthalmic formulations may be required to achieve RPE/retinal exposure without anterior-segment sequestration (Reisman et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021).

Program recommendations  
- In vitro RPE barrier program: Establish a standardized H₂O₂-induced barrier disruption assay in human RPE monolayers with readouts for TEER, large-molecule paracellular flux, ZO-1/occludin belt integrity, protein S-glutathionylation, and apoptosis/caspase activation. Titrate omaveloxolone at 1–100 nM to define the cytoprotective plateau and the onset of bifurcation, and confirm KEAP1–NRF2 mechanism using pharmacologic/CRISPR Nrf2 blockade (Cheng et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2017; Liby et al., 2007).

- Ocular in vivo models: Utilize light-induced photoreceptor injury and retinal I/R models, where the class has shown benefit, to benchmark efficacy and establish exposure–response (retinal NQO1/HO-1 induction, BRB leakage suppression), followed by NaIO₃-induced RPE injury to approximate dry AMD-relevant oxidative RPE loss (Cheng et al., 2021). Include RS9 and a non-electrophilic control to contextualize class effects (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Delivery strategy: Develop an ophthalmic formulation (e.g., micelles, lipid nanoparticles) guided by prior triterpenoid formulation successes (amorphous dispersion for CDDO-Me; UA nanoparticles) to target posterior-segment delivery via topical, suprachoroidal, or intravitreal routes depending on PK modeling and in vivo biodistribution; minimize systemic absorption to mitigate class-related CV risk (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Safety pharmacology: Delineate the therapeutic index around ocular exposures, including ERG and OCT endpoints, and histopathology for photoreceptors, RPE, and ganglion cells; monitor inflammatory and angiogenic pathways to rule out unanticipated pathway cross-talk at sustained Nrf2 activation (Liby et al., 2007).

Conclusion  
On balance, omaveloxolone is a mechanistically well-aligned, clinically de-risked Nrf2 activator with direct protective activity in human RPE and supportive in vivo retinal pharmacology from its chemical class, making it a strong repurposing candidate for dry AMD focused on RPE barrier preservation under oxidative stress (Cheng et al., 2021; Cuadrado et al., 2019). The primary development challenges are exposure control to avoid electrophile-mediated bifunctionality, demonstration of efficacy in AMD-relevant RPE injury models and barrier assays (including TEER), and optimization of ocular delivery to achieve posterior-segment pharmacodynamics with minimal systemic exposure (Liby et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2021; Reisman et al., 2019). Given the magnitude of unmet need in dry AMD and the centrality of oxidative injury to RPE pathology, a staged program beginning with RPE barrier assays and retinal oxidative stress models, followed by formulation-enabled ocular PK/PD and safety, is justified and has a reasonable probability of technical success based on the assembled evidence (Cheng et al., 2021; Reisman et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bexarotene is a fully synthetic retinoid analog classified as a rexinoid, specifically acting as a pan–retinoid X receptor (RXR) agonist. It was originally developed through structure–activity relationship studies aimed at mimicking the natural ligand 9-cis retinoic acid, while providing greater receptor selectivity, improved potency, and a pharmacological profile amenable to therapeutic use. Its synthesis and subsequent discovery were driven by the need to harness RXR‐mediated gene regulation, and it subsequently became the only FDA-approved synthetic RXR ligand to date (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). As a member of the retinoid drug class, bexarotene has been primarily used in the oncological setting, specifically for the treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, and its chemical design reflects modifications that impart high lipophilicity and receptor specificity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018). This synthetic derivation distinguishes it from naturally occurring retinoids and underpins its utility across a number of experimental and clinical contexts.

Therapeutic History:  
Bexarotene’s clinical history is marked by its approval as a second-line therapy for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, which provided a strong basis for its safety and efficacy in a human disease setting (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). In addition to its primary use in oncology, preclinical and early clinical research has investigated bexarotene for applications in neurodegenerative diseases, most notably Alzheimer’s disease and multiple sclerosis. These studies have demonstrated that RXR activation by bexarotene can influence the clearance of pathological protein aggregates and promote remyelination, respectively (Gaunt, 2020; Behl et al., 2022). However, despite the broad mechanistic appeal of RXR agonism in modifying lipid metabolism and neuroinflammation, there is little to no established clinical or veterinary precedent for employing bexarotene in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative conditions. In fact, while several RXR agonists have been considered in various models of ocular disease, the role of RXR in the diseased retina remains underexplored, with only sparse reports such as a study with the RXR agonist PA024 in retinal degeneration models (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). This gap in therapeutic history presents both a challenge and an opportunity in repurposing bexarotene for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
Bexarotene exerts its pharmacological effects primarily by binding to the ligand-binding domain of RXR isoforms (RXRα, RXRβ, and RXRγ) with nanomolar potency, inducing conformational changes that favor the recruitment of coactivators and subsequent transcriptional activation of targeted genes (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). RXR is a promiscuous nuclear receptor that forms obligate heterodimers with several other nuclear receptors, most notably the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) such as PPARγ. In doing so, the bexarotene-induced RXR/PPARγ heterodimer binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the genome, thereby upregulating target genes involved in lipid metabolism and transport. One key target is ABCA1, an ATP-binding cassette transporter implicated in cholesterol efflux from cells, which plays a central role in maintaining intracellular lipid homeostasis (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the activation of the RXR/PPARγ pathway is particularly compelling. RPE cells are highly involved in the processing and clearance of lipids, including cholesterol, and in modulating the structural integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier via tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 and occludin. When under stress—such as exposure to cytotoxic mediators like 7-ketocholesterol (7KCh), which disrupts normal junctional organization and reduces transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—the activation of RXR offers a potential therapeutic avenue. Bexarotene’s ability to stimulate RXR signaling is expected to upregulate ABCA1 expression, thereby enhancing cholesterol efflux, while also promoting the transcription of genes that lead to the re-expression of claudin-1 and occludin, which are critical for restoring barrier integrity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

The biochemical interactions following RXR activation by bexarotene include a cascade of events where the ligand-receptor complex alters the transcriptional landscape of the cell. This process entails the heterodimerization of RXR with its partner receptor, binding to DNA response elements, and initiating the recruitment of transcriptional coactivators, which together drive the expression of genes that modulate lipid metabolism, inflammatory responses, and cell junction integrity. The specificity of bexarotene for RXR, as opposed to broader retinoic acid receptor (RAR) activity, allows for a more targeted enhancement of these pathways—a factor that is crucial in tissues like the RPE, where precise regulation of lipid handling and barrier properties is essential for retinal health (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underlying the repurposing of bexarotene for dry AMD is that its activation of RXR in RPE cells will facilitate heterodimerization with PPARγ, driving the transcriptional upregulation of lipid-handling genes, most notably ABCA1. In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have provided compelling preliminary data indicating that exposure to 0.5 µM bexarotene in the presence of 7-ketocholesterol stress is capable of restoring TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values and significantly increasing ABCA1 mRNA levels. This restoration of TEER suggests that bexarotene not only promotes cholesterol efflux by upregulating ABCA1 but also exerts a beneficial influence on the expression of key tight junction proteins, such as claudin-1 and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity of the RPE barrier (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

The expected molecular effect in the assay is thus twofold. First, through its molecular interaction with RXR, bexarotene reinforces the RXR/PPARγ heterodimer formation, triggering a cascade of gene transcription events that culminate in enhanced cholesterol efflux via ABCA1. This effect directly addresses the accumulation of lipid deposits that contribute to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. Second, by re-inducing the expression of claudin-1 and occludin, bexarotene is anticipated to improve cellular junctional integrity, thereby reducing paracellular leakage and restoring the overall barrier function of the RPE as measured by TEER. The use of ocular gel formulations for local delivery promises to concentrate the therapeutic effect within the eye, circumventing the systemic adverse effects that are typically associated with bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties, such as high lipophilicity and low systemic solubility (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of bexarotene as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is founded upon a robust mechanistic rationale and promising preliminary in vitro data, yet it also presents several challenges that must be addressed through rigorous further research. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its well-established mode of action as a selective RXR agonist. Its ability to promote heterodimerization with PPARγ and subsequently upregulate genes such as ABCA1 is well supported by a substantial body of research in other disease contexts, including neurodegeneration and oncology (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Gaunt, 2020). This receptor specificity not only underscores bexarotene’s potential to modulate RPE lipid metabolism but also suggests that similar pharmacological principles could translate into the restoration of tight junction integrity—a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD.

Another significant strength is its prior clinical approval for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. This provides a substantial amount of safety data and experience in human use, which could expedite the repurposing process under a drug repositioning strategy. Moreover, the observed in vitro effects—namely the partial restoration of TEER and the increase in ABCA1 mRNA in stressed ARPE-19 cells—lend direct support to the hypothesis that RXR agonism can counteract 7-ketocholesterol-induced disruptions in RPE function (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). The concept of using ocular gel formulations to achieve localized delivery and thereby minimize systemic side effects is another innovative aspect that addresses one of the traditional limitations of bexarotene, namely its adverse systemic metabolic disturbances, which include dyslipidemia and hypothyroidism (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021).

However, there are notable weaknesses that temper this optimism. First, bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties—its high lipophilicity and low solubility—pose a significant formulation challenge, especially when transitioning from systemic oncology applications to local ocular delivery. While gel formulations offer a potential solution, achieving the precise pharmacokinetics and adequate tissue penetration in the retina will require meticulous formulation development and validation. Second, despite the extensive research on RXR agonism in other tissues, there is very limited precedent for the use of bexarotene or similar compounds in the treatment of dry AMD or related ocular diseases. In other words, while the underlying nuclear receptor biology in the retina is compelling, the absence of prior clinical or even robust preclinical ocular studies increases the risk associated with translational uncertainty (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Moreover, systemic side effects associated with bexarotene have been well documented in its approved indications. Although the strategy of localized ocular delivery aims to mitigate these adverse effects, any leakage from the ocular compartment into systemic circulation could potentially re-expose patients to these risks. Additionally, the complexity of dry AMD as a multifactorial disease—with contributions from oxidative stress, inflammation, and complex extracellular matrix alterations—means that modulating only lipid handling and tight junction integrity might not be sufficient to arrest or reverse disease progression. Thus, while the mechanistic hypothesis is sound, it should ideally be integrated into a broader therapeutic strategy that also addresses other pathological mechanisms in dry AMD.

In summary, the proposed use of bexarotene for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic foundation based on RXR agonism and its downstream effects on lipid metabolism and cellular junction integrity. The preliminary in vitro evidence in ARPE-19 cells under 7-ketocholesterol stress is promising, particularly with the reported restoration of TEER and upregulation of ABCA1. The strengths of this candidate include its specificity for RXR, the translational potential backed by its FDA–approved status for an unrelated indication, and the innovative strategy of local ocular delivery through gel formulations. On the other hand, challenges related to its physicochemical properties, potential for systemic side effects, and the overall gaps in preclinical ocular data necessitate further rigorous research. Preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD and careful formulation optimization will be essential next steps to validate the therapeutic potential of bexarotene in this context (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate generated from the glucosinolate glucoraphanin by the β-thioglucosidase myrosinase, which is abundant in cruciferous vegetables (notably broccoli sprouts). Its electrophilic –N=C=S moiety underlies covalent reactivity with nucleophilic cysteines on sensor proteins, most prominently Keap1, and thereby triggers a broad antioxidant and cytoprotective transcriptional response controlled by Nrf2 (NFE2L2) via antioxidant response elements (AREs) in gene promoters (phase-2 enzymes, redox systems, and detoxification pathways) (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020). In retinal and epithelial contexts, SFN has been repeatedly characterized as an “indirect antioxidant” that elevates glutathione (GSH) and induces ARE-dependent enzymes such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1/HMOX1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and thioredoxin (Trx1), among others (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Tanito et al., 2005; Liu & Yan, 2018). In human RPE-derived cell models, SFN increased GSH and induced NQO1 and GST, consistent with canonical ARE program activation (Zhou et al., 2006). In vivo ocular models show SFN attenuates retinal light damage and improves functional outcomes, further anchoring its relevance to oxidative injury in the outer retina and RPE (Tanito et al., 2005; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Within its class, SFN is a prototypical dietary electrophile that activates Nrf2 signaling; this class has been broadly studied for chemoprevention and cytoprotection across organs. In ocular tissues, SFN has been shown to protect RPE and photoreceptors from diverse oxidative and phototoxic insults, often in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Yang et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025). Beyond Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α cross-talk, PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ stress-response nodes, and autophagy/lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs (TFEB/TFE3), all of which intersect with oxidative, inflammatory, and proteostasis stress pathways in RPE biology (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025).

Practical development considerations include bioavailability and delivery. Human studies and reviews indicate that the bioactive isothiocyanate is formed from glucoraphanin in a process heavily dependent on myrosinase (plant or microbiota), with documented systemic exposure and biomarker modulation in clinical settings; however, SFN’s oral bioavailability is limited by solubility, first-pass metabolism, and short plasma half-life, posing translational challenges for ocular exposure through blood–ocular barriers (Zhang et al., 2024). Preclinical delivery strategies such as nanoparticle and albumin carrier systems have been proposed to overcome ocular delivery constraints (Zhang et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
SFN and related Nrf2 activators have a long history as cytoprotective agents in preclinical models spanning oncology prevention, vascular and metabolic protection, and neuroprotection. In humans, SFN or broccoli sprout preparations have been administered in controlled trials with documented pharmacodynamic biomarker changes and well-characterized disposition and metabolism; crossover and dose-response studies highlight interconversion with related isothiocyanates (erucin) and underscore the importance of active myrosinase for consistent systemic exposure (Zhang et al., 2024; Qin, 2007). A pilot study detected SFN metabolites in human breast tissue after a single oral broccoli sprout dose, demonstrating tissue penetration to an epithelial compartment and supporting oral bioavailability to peripheral tissues (Qin, 2007). Although multiple clinical contexts are covered in these translational reviews and trials, there are no reported clinical trials of SFN specifically targeting dry AMD or RPE degeneration in the provided material (Zhang et al., 2024).

In ocular systems, the compound’s therapeutic history is robust at the preclinical level. In cultured human RPE, SFN protects against photooxidative injury (A2E/blue light) and chemical oxidants, increases GSH, and induces phase-2 enzymes including NQO1 and GST (Zhou et al., 2006). Microarray and validation work in human RPE-19 cells demonstrate SFN-induced nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and upregulation of thioredoxin-1, with enhanced oxidative stress resistance following H₂O₂ (Ye et al., 2013). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage in mice through ARE-mediated upregulation of thioredoxin (Trx1), and recovers cone function in a model of RPE oxidative stress in an Nrf2-dependent manner (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025). SFN also protects rodent retinas from ischemia–reperfusion injury by increasing Nrf2 nuclear accumulation and HO-1 expression; pharmacologic inhibition of HO-1 abolishes protection, causally implicating HO-1 (Pan et al., 2014). In inherited retinal degeneration models (rd10 and tubby), systemic SFN improves retinal function and reduces degeneration, with evidence that ERK signaling and the Trx/TrxR/Nrf2 axis mediate effects in some settings (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Comparable ocular benefits have been shown in non-RPE tissues. For example, human corneal endothelial FECD cells exhibit SFN-induced Nrf2 nuclear translocation and upregulation of canonical ARE genes (NQO1, HO-1), with reduced ROS and apoptosis (Ziaei et al., 2013). In corneal surface epithelium, SFN protects against oxidative stress via Nrf2/HO-1 activation, supporting generalizability across ocular epithelial cell types (Liu & Yan, 2018). These data reinforce the core mechanism and pharmacology relevant to RPE while underlining the absence of AMD-specific clinical translation to date (Zhang et al., 2024).

Notably, although there is a recent report in an inflamed ARPE-19 model that vitamin D and SFN (alone and combined) reduced ROS, reduced IL-6/IL-8, lowered VEGF, and restored epithelial integrity markers including ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression, the provided material does not include functional barrier endpoints (TEER or FITC-dextran permeability), and claudin-1 is not shown (Bergandi et al., 2024). Thus, while “marker restoration” has been reported for ZO-1 and claudin-4 under TGF-β stress, quantitative barrier function restoration has not yet been demonstrated within the provided sources (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary mechanism—Keap1 cysteine targeting and Nrf2 activation: SFN’s electrophilic isothiocyanate group reacts with redox-sensitive cysteines on Keap1 (notably Cys151), disrupting the Cul3–Keap1 E3 ligase complex and stabilizing Nrf2, which accumulates and translocates to the nucleus. There, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences to upregulate a broad enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant and detoxification program (e.g., NQO1, HO-1, GSTs, GCLM, Trx1, SRXN1), increasing cellular reductive capacity (GSH pools, thiol buffering) and restoring redox homeostasis under oxidative stress (Chang et al., 2020; Ziaei et al., 2013; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). In RPE models, SFN does not consistently increase Nrf2 transcription but promotes nuclear translocation and DNA-binding activity, consistent with post-translational stabilization and activation; ARE target induction follows (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020). In ARPE-19, SFN preconditioning increases NQO1 mRNA/activity, boosts cellular GSH, and increases GST activity; microarray and validation data add induction of SRXN1, GCLM, and Trx1 with concurrent Txnip downregulation, aligning with amplified reductive and detoxification capacity (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). Under t-BHP stress, SFN increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, elevates NQO1, GR, and GPx1 transcripts, and drives HO-1, NQO1, and GR protein induction (with partial discordance between GPx1 mRNA and protein), while reducing proinflammatory ICAM-1 and MCP-1 (Chang et al., 2020).

Nrf2-dependent ocular efficacy: In vivo, SFN protection from retinal ischemia–reperfusion requires HO-1, as HO-1 inhibition reverses neuroprotection (Pan et al., 2014). In a model of RPE oxidative stress in middle-aged mice, SFN restores cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, underscoring that Nrf2 is the mechanistic driver in that age-relevant retinal context (Falcão et al., 2025).

Nrf2-independent and auxiliary mechanisms: RPE protection is not exclusively Nrf2-dependent. SFN has been shown to promote mitochondrial fusion and reduce Drp1-mediated fission, conferring anti-apoptotic benefit even in CRISPR/Cas9 Nrf2-depleted RPE cells (RPE-1), indicating a parallel mitochondrial protective program (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019). SFN also engages the PARP1/SIRT1/NAD+ axis: SFN or its metabolites can blunt damage-induced PARylation via direct PARP1 interactions, alleviating SIRT1 inhibition, promoting autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis, and decreasing inflammation in RPE models (Wang & Tang, 2022). In blue light–exposed RPE, SFN activates the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 axis, upregulates HO-1 and thioredoxin-1, blocks NF-κB nuclear translocation, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, and enhances autophagy, all contributing to cytoprotection; Nrf2 inhibition abrogates SFN’s protective effect in this system (Yang et al., 2021). SFN can also activate lysosome-dependent transcriptional programs that mitigate oxidative stress; KEAP1–NRF2 cross-talk with TFEB/TFE3 and macroautophagy has been documented, offering a mechanistic link between Nrf2 activation and proteostasis/autophagy enhancement relevant to RPE degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025).

Anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic effects: Across RPE models, SFN suppresses proinflammatory mediators and pathways (e.g., reduces ICAM-1 and MCP-1; inhibits NF-κB activation), and in TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19 reduces VEGF secretion, which is relevant to para-inflammatory remodeling in AMD (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024). These effects likely contribute to preservation of junctional homeostasis by dampening cytokine-driven disruption.

Cell-type and context dependence: SFN response varies by cell type, stressor, and age-dependent pathway integrity. In some models, HO-1 mRNA is not induced even when protein rises, and under reduced Nrf2 function (as may occur in aged RPE), SFN efficacy can be limited, indicating a dependence on intact Nrf2 signaling and potential post-transcriptional regulation (Chang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Dosing and context also matter: low micromolar SFN protects RPE under oxidative stress, whereas very high concentrations can be deleterious in vitro (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Evidence for barrier-relevant endpoints: The provided sources do not present RPE TEER or FITC-dextran permeability data for SFN, and do not demonstrate claudin-1 induction in RPE (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024). One in vitro ARPE-19 TGF-β model reports that SFN (alone and with vitamin D) restores expression of ZO-1 and claudin-4 suppressed by TGF-β, reduces ROS and VEGF, and decreases proinflammatory cytokines; however, functional permeability or TEER measures were not included, and claudin-1 was not assessed (Bergandi et al., 2024). Therefore, SFN’s capacity to restore RPE barrier function remains mechanistically plausible—through redox normalization, suppression of inflammatory junctional disruption, and potential transcriptional effects on junctional proteins—but is not directly proven by barrier-function assays in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Assay context and rationale: The proposed assays—RPE monolayers subjected to A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ oxidative injury—interrogate oxidative stress pathways central to dry AMD pathophysiology and RPE barrier integrity. A2E/blue light models replicate lipofuscin-photosensitized oxidative injury; NaIO₃ models RPE oxidative cytotoxicity. In both settings, ROS accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, cytokine induction, and downstream tight-junction disruption degrade barrier integrity. The expectation is that SFN will activate Nrf2, increase reductive and detoxifying capacity (GSH, NQO1, HO-1, Trx1, GST), suppress NF-κB–driven inflammation, stabilize mitochondrial function, and secondarily preserve or restore tight-junction protein expression and continuity, resulting in improved TEER and reduced macromolecular flux (FITC-dextran) across the RPE monolayer.

Support for oxidative injury protection in RPE: In A2E/blue light–injured ARPE-19 monolayers, SFN preconditioning increases cell survival, elevates GSH, and induces NQO1 and GST—outcomes mechanistically consistent with improved tolerance to phototoxic oxidative stress (Zhou et al., 2006). In RPE challenged by chemical oxidants (t-BHP, H₂O₂), SFN reduces ROS, preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, increases nuclear Nrf2 DNA-binding, and induces NQO1, HO-1 (protein), GR, and GPx1 transcripts while suppressing ICAM-1 and MCP-1, thereby addressing both oxidative and inflammatory drivers of junctional disruption (Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013).

Support for HO-1/Nrf2 and auxiliary pathways: Under blue-light exposure, SFN activates Nrf2 and HO-1 in RPE with evidence of mechanistic necessity (Nrf2 inhibitor blocks protection), promotes autophagy (LC3BII and p62), and suppresses NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation—all changes that favor barrier preservation by limiting stress signaling and enhancing cellular cleanup mechanisms (Yang et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and RPE oxidative-stress mouse models, SFN-mediated rescue of retinal function depends on Nrf2 and HO-1, supporting the expected relevance of these axes in RPE-derived stress contexts (Pan et al., 2014; Falcão et al., 2025).

Evidence for junctional protein rescue: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, a recent report shows SFN (particularly with vitamin D) restores ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression suppressed by TGF-β, reduces IL-6/IL-8, reduces VEGF, and normalizes respiratory gene overexpression; this supports the expectation that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven loss of epithelial integrity markers (Bergandi et al., 2024). However, the provided material does not report TEER or FITC-dextran for SFN in RPE, and no data are provided for claudin-1 induction or ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity in oxidative (A2E/NaIO₃) models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Thus, while SFN is expected to improve TEER and reduce FITC-dextran flux in A2E or NaIO₃ assays through Nrf2-driven antioxidant enhancement and suppression of inflammatory/junctional injury, this is an unproven extrapolation that requires direct measurement in the proposed models (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).

Target expression in RPE: All principal molecular targets are expressed in human RPE. Nrf2 activation and nuclear translocation occur in SFN-treated RPE-19/ARPE-19, with demonstrated induction of NQO1, HO-1 (protein in some contexts), thioredoxin-1, GCLM, and GST, and suppression of Txnip, ICAM-1, and MCP-1, anchoring the feasibility of modulating these axes in RPE cells (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2006). HO-1 induction in RPE is clearly shown under blue-light stress; in vivo retinal protection requires HO-1, reinforcing target relevance to oxidative retinal injury (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014).

Assay caveats: The provided literature does not contain RPE TEER or macromolecular flux data for SFN, nor does it document claudin-1 induction in RPE. Therefore, while SFN is expected to preserve barrier function, success criteria must include de novo demonstration of TEER rescue, FITC-dextran flux reduction, and ZO-1/claudin-1 continuity under A2E or NaIO₃ stress; these are critical data gaps to address in the proposed work (Zhang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic foundation in RPE and retina: SFN is a well-validated Nrf2 activator that increases GSH and induces multiple ARE-dependent genes (NQO1, GSTs, Trx1, GCLM; HO-1 in several ocular contexts) in RPE and retinal models, with reproducible protection against oxidative and phototoxic injury (A2E/blue light; H₂O₂/t-BHP) and anti-inflammatory activity (reduced ICAM-1, MCP-1, NF-κB signaling) (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). In vivo, SFN attenuates retinal light damage, improves ERG outcomes, rescues cone function in an Nrf2-dependent manner, and protects against ischemia–reperfusion via HO-1—clear evidence that the compound engages relevant biology and can deliver functional benefit in the retina (Tanito et al., 2005; Falcão et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2014).  
- Multiple converging protective axes: Beyond KEAP1–Nrf2, SFN engages SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling, suppresses PARP1 overactivation to preserve NAD+/SIRT1, promotes autophagy/lysosome programs (TFEB/TFE3 linkage), and modulates mitochondrial dynamics (promotes fusion; reduces Drp1-mediated fission) even when Nrf2 is compromised. This polymechanistic profile is advantageous in RPE, where oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy, and inflammation co-drive degeneration (Wang & Tang, 2022; Falcão et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2021; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).  
- Preliminary evidence for epithelial integrity marker restoration: In TGF-β–inflamed ARPE-19, SFN (especially with vitamin D) restored ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression and reduced VEGF, providing the first reported signal that SFN can reverse cytokine-driven epithelial marker loss in an RPE model (albeit without functional barrier assays) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Translational plausibility and human experience: SFN is orally administrable, with documented human systemic exposure and biomarker modulation; myrosinase co-administration enhances bioavailability from glucoraphanin. Although not yet tested clinically in dry AMD, SFN has a favorable translational narrative as a nutraceutical-derived Nrf2 activator with a safety and PD data trail in other indications (Zhang et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and gaps  
- No direct RPE barrier-function data: Across the provided literature there are no TEER or FITC-dextran permeability results for SFN in RPE monolayers, and no quantified immunofluorescence continuity data for ZO-1 or claudin-1 under oxidative stress. The sole report of “restored markers” addresses ZO-1 and claudin-4 expression after TGF-β, not barrier function or claudin-1 (Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024). The proposal’s assertion of TEER rescue and FITC-dextran reduction remains speculative pending direct measurement in A2E or NaIO₃ models (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Uncertain regulation of tight junction gene set: The provided RPE datasets document induction of canonical Nrf2 targets (NQO1, HO-1 in some contexts, Trx1, GCLM, GSTs), but do not demonstrate SFN induction of claudin-1 in RPE. Without evidence that SFN directly upregulates claudin-1 or stabilizes its junctional localization in RPE, the hypothesis of “junction-supporting gene induction” should be reframed as “junction-preserving via redox and anti-inflammatory mechanisms” until proven otherwise (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Delivery and exposure to the RPE: SFN’s solubility, short half-life, and first-pass metabolism limit systemic exposure; blood–ocular barriers further constrain retinal delivery. Several in vivo retinal studies used intraperitoneal dosing, and one report found i.p. more effective than oral for light-damage protection, emphasizing the need to optimize delivery for ocular targets. Nanocarriers and formulation strategies are promising but remain preclinical (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Dependence on Nrf2 competence and context: In models with impaired Nrf2 (potentially mirroring aged RPE), SFN efficacy is reduced; mechanisms such as mitochondrial fusion may provide partial rescue, but translational effect sizes could be diminished in elderly patients with Nrf2 decline. Additionally, gene-level responses show discordances (e.g., HO-1 mRNA vs protein), indicating context- and post-transcriptional control that complicate predictable pharmacodynamics (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity: Some cited studies are from lower-quality journals; while the core mechanistic findings are corroborated by higher-quality work (e.g., IOVS, Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology, PLoS ONE), the barrier-marker restoration report requires independent replication with functional readouts and in primary human RPE to solidify translational credibility (Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Bergandi et al., 2024).

Decision implications and next steps  
Given the robust Nrf2/ARE activation, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory efficacy in RPE/retina, and the breadth of auxiliary protective mechanisms, SFN remains a mechanistically precise candidate for RPE oxidative injury relevant to dry AMD. However, the core claim of “barrier restoration” is currently supported only by marker-expression rescue (ZO-1 and claudin-4) in an inflamed ARPE-19 model without functional permeability data, and there is no evidence for claudin-1 induction or barrier rescue in A2E or NaIO₃ models in the provided literature (Bergandi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). To de-risk the program and validate the hypothesis, the following experiments are mandatory:  
- TEER and FITC-dextran assays in differentiated human RPE (primary or iPSC-RPE) under A2E/blue light or NaIO₃ insult, with SFN dose–response and timing; include positive controls for barrier rescue (e.g., dexamethasone) (Bergandi et al., 2024).  
- Quantitative junctional immunofluorescence (ZO-1, claudin-1, claudin-4, occludin) with continuity analysis; test whether SFN normalizes localization and expression under oxidative/cytokine stress (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Nrf2 pathway necessity tests (ML385, Nrf2 siRNA) and HO-1 inhibition (ZnPP) to define mechanism-of-action in barrier rescue; given HO-1’s necessity in vivo, confirm whether HO-1 contributes to barrier endpoints in RPE (Pan et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2021).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics and autophagy readouts (Drp1, Mfn2, LC3BII/p62) to quantify auxiliary pathways that may mediate barrier preservation when Nrf2 is compromised (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021).  
- PK/PD bridging: quantify SFN (and metabolites) in plasma and ocular tissues after oral vs i.p. dosing in rodents; evaluate delivery systems (e.g., albumin nanocarriers) for RPE exposure; incorporate myrosinase co-administration for oral strategies; relate exposures to effective in vitro EC₅₀s for barrier rescue (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Aged and Nrf2-impaired models: evaluate efficacy in aged RPE or Nrf2-hypomorphic contexts to assess translational robustness (Zhang et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

If TEER and permeability rescue are demonstrated with mechanistic attribution to Nrf2/HO-1 and/or auxiliary pathways, and if ocular PK can be solved to achieve efficacious exposures, SFN would merit progression to in vivo dry AMD–relevant models (e.g., subretinal NaIO₃, chronic photo-oxidative stress) with structural (OCT) and functional (ERG) endpoints, plus RPE barrier imaging, before considering a human proof-of-concept study.

In sum, the totality of evidence strongly supports SFN for oxidative and inflammatory protection of RPE and retina with multiple convergent mechanisms and translational plausibility. The critical missing element is direct demonstration that these effects translate into bona fide RPE barrier restoration (TEER/permeability) under AMD-relevant oxidative stress, and a practical path to deliver sufficient drug to the RPE in humans. Addressing these gaps should be the focus of immediate preclinical validation (Zhou et al., 2006; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2024; Bergandi et al., 2024).
