Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
5‐Azacytidine is a synthetically produced nucleoside analogue of cytidine originally derived by chemical modification of the natural ribonucleoside. In 5‐azacytidine the normal carbon atom at the 5‐position of the pyrimidine ring is replaced with a nitrogen atom, a modification that critically alters its biochemical properties. This compound is classified as an azanucleoside and has been widely studied as a DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) inhibitor. Its discovery and subsequent synthesis have enabled researchers to interrogate the role of DNA methylation in gene regulation. In its typical biological usage, after cellular uptake mediated by nucleoside transporters, 5‐azacytidine is phosphorylated by cellular kinases into its active triphosphate form (5‐aza‐CTP) and can become incorporated into RNA as well as into DNA, although only around 10–20% is converted to the deoxyribonucleotide form prior to DNA incorporation. This unique feature is a double‐edged sword: on one hand, it allows modulation of cytosine methylation patterns within genomic DNA by trapping DNMTs; on the other, its incorporation into RNA can perturb protein synthesis and contributes to its cytotoxic profile. Chemically, its structure and mode of synthesis place it within a well‐characterized class of antimetabolite agents whose utility extends beyond oncology into other fields where epigenetic modifications are implicated (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, 5‐azacytidine and its deoxy analogue 5‐aza‐2′‐deoxycytidine (decitabine) were first developed as antimetabolite chemotherapy agents for hematologic malignancies. Their clinical utility in treating conditions such as myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) is well established, with DNA demethylation and tumor suppressor gene reactivation being central to their antineoplastic efficacy. Over the years, the successful repurposing of these nucleoside analogues has led to extensive studies investigating their potential effects beyond oncology. In cancer cells, the irreversible binding of DNMT enzymes to DNA following incorporation of 5‐azacytidine has been shown to produce passive demethylation during cell division and consequent gene reactivation (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). In more recent years, researchers have begun to consider the roles of aberrant DNA methylation in non‐cancer diseases, including ocular pathologies like age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). Reviews in ocular epigenetics have noted that epigenetic dysregulation, including hypermethylation of promoters for antioxidant enzymes and other protective genes, may contribute to RPE dysfunction in AMD (Li et al., 2020). For instance, studies in cultured RPE cells and AMD cybrid models have observed tolerability of DNMT inhibitors, as exemplified by experiments where polarized RPE monolayers treated with 5‐aza‐2′‐deoxycytidine showed no significant disruption in barrier markers such as ZO‐1 or cytokeratin, and even demonstrated gene reactivation effects such as upregulation of clusterin (Li et al., 2020). Although 5‐azacytidine itself has not been as widely evaluated in ocular models as decitabine, the extensive biochemical literature surrounding its DNMT inhibitory properties forms a strong rationale for its potential repurposing toward dry AMD via epigenetic modulation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, 5‐azacytidine exerts its pharmacologic actions primarily through inhibition of DNMT enzymes. Under normal physiological conditions, DNMT enzymes bind to cytosine residues in CpG dinucleotides and catalyze the transfer of a methyl group from S‐adenosyl-L‐methionine (SAM) to the 5‐position carbon of cytosine, a process that is essential for the maintenance of epigenetic patterns and gene silencing. However, the substitution of nitrogen at the C5 position in 5‐azacytidine disrupts this process because the reaction mechanism relies on a β‐elimination step that cannot occur when a nitrogen is present instead of a carbon. Consequently, when 5‐azacytidine is incorporated into the DNA of replicating cells, DNMT enzymes – particularly the maintenance methyltransferase DNMT1 – are unable to complete the methylation reaction and become covalently trapped at the site of incorporation (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). This irreversible trapping inhibits the recycling of DNMTs and leads to their proteasomal degradation, thus reducing the cellular pool of active DNMT enzymes. In subsequent rounds of DNA replication, the absence of sufficient DNMT activity results in passive demethylation of newly synthesized DNA strands that fail to be remethylated. This epigenetic reprogramming can lead to reactivation of genes with previously hypermethylated and silenced promoters (Cheishvili et al., 2015; Palii et al., 2008). It is important to note that 5‐azacytidine is also incorporated into RNA, where it may inhibit RNA methylation and alter translation; however, the therapeutic emphasis in the context of reactivating silenced genes typically focuses on its DNA‐mediated effects. In the specific context of the proposed therapeutic strategy, oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is hypothesized to promote the aberrant recruitment of DNMT1 and DNMT3A to the promoters of tight junction genes such as OCLN and TJP1, thereby silencing them via hypermethylation. The administration of 5‐azacytidine is expected to reverse this process by demethylating these promoter regions through the above‐described DNMT trapping mechanism, ultimately leading to the reactivation of occludin and ZO‐1 expression (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014; Mukhtar, 2020). Although the majority of experimental evidence in the literature focuses on gene reactivation in oncologic contexts, the fundamental biochemical interactions remain the same in any dividing cell type where DNA replication permits incorporation of the analogue. Additionally, although RPE cells in vivo are relatively quiescent compared to rapidly dividing cancer cells, in vitro models such as ARPE-19, particularly under oxidative challenge, can exhibit increased proliferation and epigenetic plasticity, thereby providing an opportunity to evaluate the mechanism in the context of barrier dysfunction (Li et al., 2020; Sarkisjan et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis of the proposed therapeutic strategy is that under conditions of oxidative stress, DNMT enzymes are aberrantly recruited to the promoters of genes critical for tight junction integrity – specifically occludin (OCLN) and ZO-1 (TJP1) – resulting in their hypermethylation and subsequent transcriptional repression. This diminished expression of tight junction proteins compromises the barrier function of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), leading to decreased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased FITC-dextran permeability. It is expected that a treatment with 1 µM 5‐azacytidine will inhibit DNMT activity in these stressed RPE cells, specifically by demethylating the promoters of OCLN and TJP1. As the promoter regions are demethylated, transcription of OCLN and TJP1 is anticipated to resume, thereby restoring the synthesis and proper cellular localization of occludin and the ZO-1 protein. This re-expression is predicted to facilitate the re‐assembly of tight junction complexes at the plasma membrane of RPE cells, culminating in a recovery of barrier properties measurable as an increase in TEER and a reduction in paracellular permeability as evidenced by decreased FITC-dextran flux (Christman, 2002; Palii et al., 2008; Li et al., 2020). There is supporting evidence in related experimental studies wherein treatment of polarized RPE monolayers with DNMT inhibitors—albeit using 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine in some cases—did not disturb baseline tight junction markers such as ZO-1 and cytokeratin, and even induced the expression of epigenetically silenced protective genes like clusterin (Li et al., 2020). Although direct demonstration of OCLN and TJP1 promoter demethylation by 5‐azacytidine in RPE under oxidative stress is not yet available, analogous results in other epithelial contexts provide a strong mechanistic rationale. Moreover, the dual activity of the drug – both its canonical demethylating effect and its potential to perturb RNA methylation – may synergize to enhance transcriptional reactivation if balanced appropriately with a low, non‐cytotoxic concentration such as 1 µM (Seelan et al., 2018; Cheishvili et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
The prospect of repurposing 5‐azacytidine for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) represents a novel and intriguing approach that leverages well‐established principles in epigenetic regulation. On the strength side, the compound’s mechanism of action is thoroughly documented across multiple biomedical studies and is centered on the irreversible trapping and degradation of DNMT enzymes, leading to passive loss of DNA methylation in replicating cells (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). This mechanism has been exploited with success in oncology to reactivate silenced tumor suppressor genes, suggesting that similar reactivation of critical genes in non‐cancerous cells might also be achievable. The specific hypothesis that oxidative stress in RPE leads to the epigenetic silencing of tight junction genes such as OCLN and TJP1 is plausible given the known role of DNMT enzymes in mediating gene repression under stress conditions, and the literature supports the concept that DNA methylation is a dynamic and reversible process that can be modulated pharmacologically (Li et al., 2020). Preliminary in vitro findings in RPE monolayer models with DNMT inhibitors, particularly the tolerability of these compounds and their capacity to upregulate epigenetically silenced genes (as seen with clusterin expression), bolster the argument that DNMT inhibition in RPE is not inherently deleterious and may indeed rectify dysfunction in barrier integrity (Li et al., 2020).

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be recognized. First, 5‐azacytidine is known to incorporate into RNA as well as DNA, which introduces additional layers of complexity in its mode of action. The off‐target effects on RNA methylation can lead to perturbations in protein synthesis and may result in unintended consequences, especially given the highly specialized function of RPE cells in the retina (Jasielec et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2010). Second, the S-phase dependency of the drug’s mechanism—requiring active DNA replication for incorporation—poses a potential limitation when considering that in vivo RPE cells are largely quiescent. While in vitro ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress may show increased proliferative activity, the translation of these findings to an in vivo dry AMD setting remains uncertain. Third, the global demethylation induced by 5‐azacytidine does not confer gene specificity; hence, there is a risk that while reactivating tight junction genes, the drug might also inadvertently activate promoters of deleterious genes or provoke inflammatory responses. This lack of precision could compromise retinal homeostasis or even exacerbate pathological processes if not carefully controlled (Mukhtar, 2020; Cheishvili et al., 2015). Fourth, toxicity is a major concern. While lower doses (such as 1 µM) are proposed to achieve a favorable balance between hypomethylation and cytotoxicity, the narrow therapeutic window observed in oncology suggests that careful titration and extensive in vitro and in vivo safety studies are essential before progressing to clinical evaluation in AMD (Christman, 2002; Daifuku, 2025).

Additional challenges include the need for direct experimental evidence to support the specific hypothesis relating to tight junction reactivation. Although the general effects of DNMT inhibitors in reactivating silenced genes are well documented, there is currently insufficient evidence demonstrating that 5-azacytidine directly demethylates the promoters of OCLN and TJP1 in RPE cells subjected to oxidative stress. Moreover, evaluations of barrier function—such as detailed TEER measurements or FITC-dextran permeability assays—have been more commonly reported in the context of other DNMT inhibitors such as 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine rather than 5-azacytidine per se (Li et al., 2020). Therefore, a critical gap remains in validating whether the proposed epigenetic precision approach can indeed restore tight junction integrity in a physiologically relevant model of dry AMD.

Despite these concerns, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. The robust and well‐understood mechanism of 5‐azacytidine in inducing DNA demethylation provides a solid theoretical basis for the proposed therapeutic strategy. Given that similar epigenetic interventions have successfully reactivated gene expression in other cellular contexts, and considering that preliminary data in RPE systems suggest tolerability and potential gene reactivation, it is reasonable to propose that further investigation is warranted. Initial preclinical studies should focus on establishing the methylation status of the OCLN and TJP1 promoters in RPE cells under oxidative stress and then determine whether 5‐azacytidine treatment can effectively reverse these modifications. Comprehensive analyses including methylation-specific polymerase chain reaction (MSP), chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays for DNMT occupancy, and detailed transcriptional profiling would be essential to confirm target engagement. Parallel functional assays, such as TEER measurements and FITC-dextran permeability assays, must be undertaken to correlate molecular events with phenotypic restoration of barrier function (Mukhtar, 2020; Daifuku, 2025).

In addition, it would be prudent to perform dose–response studies to delineate the optimal concentration of 5‐azacytidine that maximizes promoter demethylation and gene reactivation while minimizing off-target cytotoxicity. Considering that RPE cells in vitro may exhibit different proliferative rates compared to their in vivo counterparts, alternative experimental models, such as induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells from AMD patients, may provide additional insights into the therapeutic window and efficacy of 5‐azacytidine in a clinically relevant context. Finally, given that the global nature of epigenetic reprogramming may lead to unintended activation of other cellular pathways, combination strategies employing lower doses of 5‐azacytidine alongside more targeted epigenetic modulators—such as selective HDAC inhibitors—could be explored to enhance the specificity of gene reactivation and improve overall retinal safety (Li et al., 2020; Nashine & Kenney, 2020).

In summary, 5‐azacytidine represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD through a novel epigenetic precision approach aimed at reversing the aberrant methylation of tight junction gene promoters. Its well‐characterized mechanism of DNMT inhibition and widespread use in oncology offer a strong biological rationale. However, significant challenges remain, including its non‐selective incorporation into nucleic acids, potential off‐target effects, reliance on cellular proliferation for optimal activity, and a narrow therapeutic index that necessitates rigorous dose optimization. The feasibility of restoring tight junction integrity in RPE cells via demethylation of OCLN and TJP1 promoters is theoretically sound yet awaits empirical confirmation in preclinical AMD models. Overall, while the candidate has substantial mechanistic strengths that support its potential role in restoring RPE barrier function under oxidative stress conditions, its development as a treatment for dry AMD will require detailed molecular and functional validations, careful safety profiling, and perhaps the exploration of combination therapies to harness its benefits while mitigating risks (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020; Daifuku, 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA-408; also known as CDDO-DFPA; N-(2-Cyano-3,12-dioxo-28-noroleana-1,9(11)-dien-17-yl)-2,2-difluoropropanamide) is a semisynthetic oleanane triterpenoid created by lead optimization of the natural product oleanolic acid, a plant-derived pentacyclic triterpene produced via the mevalonate pathway (squalene → 2,3-oxidosqualene → β-amyrin → erythrodiol → oleanolic acid) and abundantly available from Oleaceae (e.g., olive) and other botanical sources (over 1,600 species; Nakagami, 2016; Masullo et al., 2017; Pollier & Goossens, 2012). The oleanane scaffold was iteratively diversified by Sporn, Gribble, Honda and collaborators to introduce enone and cyanoenone Michael acceptors on rings A and C, yielding the CDDO class (2-cyano-3,12-dioxo-oleana-1,9(11)-dien-28-oic acid and derivatives) as extraordinarily potent anti-inflammatory and Nrf2-inducing agents; C-28 esters/amides and further A/C-ring modifications produced multiple clinical candidates including CDDO-Me (bardoxolone methyl, RTA-402) and RTA-408 (omaveloxolone) (Honda et al., 2000; Pollier & Goossens, 2012; Cheng et al., 2021). RTA-408 specifically is a C17-modified difluoro-propanamide on an oleanane core and belongs to the second generation of synthetic triterpenoids designed to preserve high Nrf2 potency while controlling electrophilicity and pharmacokinetics (Nakagami, 2016; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

At the pharmacological class level, synthetic oleanane triterpenoids are electrophilic “antioxidant inflammation modulators” that activate the KEAP1–NRF2–ARE pathway through covalent (but often reversible) Michael addition to redox-sensitive cysteines on KEAP1, particularly Cys151 on the BTB domain, thereby stabilizing Nrf2 and inducing a coordinated cytoprotective gene program; they concurrently suppress inducible pro-inflammatory mediators (e.g., iNOS, COX-2) with dose-dependent bifunctionality (cytoprotection at low concentrations; pro-oxidant/apoptotic signaling at higher exposure) (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Liby et al., 2007). This scaffold has been extensively explored as a drug platform across oncology, nephrology, cardiopulmonary, inflammatory, and neurological indications, with bardoxolone methyl and omaveloxolone translating to clinical studies and, for omaveloxolone, regulatory approval in Friedreich’s ataxia (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Zahir et al., 2025). Within ophthalmology, oleanane triterpenoids and close congeners (dh404, CDDO-TFEA, CDDO-EA, CDDO-Me) have shown robust Nrf2-mediated protection in retinal models, and RTA-408 itself has been advanced into ocular clinical trials evaluating postoperative ocular pain/inflammation and corneal endothelial cell loss after cataract surgery, positioning this mechanism squarely within ocular translational scope (Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
The oleanane triterpenoid class has a two-decade translational history that began with demonstrations that cyano-enone–bearing derivatives are sub-nanomolar inducers of the Nrf2 transcriptome and suppressors of inflammatory enzymes in vitro and in vivo, a property mapped by SAR to the presence/placement of A-ring 1-en-3-one and C-ring 9(11)-en-12-one Michael acceptors (Honda et al., 2000; Nakagami, 2016). Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me) showed pharmacodynamic activity in humans (ARE-gene induction in tumor biopsies; renal function improvements), but its BEACON Phase 3 trial in advanced CKD was halted for cardiovascular adverse events—an outcome that did not negate class activity but highlighted the need for indication-specific risk management and exclusion criteria (e.g., high BNP, poor baseline eGFR) (Masullo et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Subsequent controlled studies in rarer CKD-associated diseases continued under tighter cardiometabolic selection, while medicinal-chemistry efforts generated second-generation analogs including fluorinated scaffolds (e.g., omaveloxolone) to tune reactivity and PK/PD (Sun et al., 2017).

For omaveloxolone specifically, preclinical pharmacology established Nrf2-dependent induction of glutathione homeostasis genes and improvements in mitochondrial respiration; systemic PK in primates/humans showed dose proportionality and measurable tissue distribution (including liver, lung, brain), with PBMC and tissue Nrf2 target-gene induction at clinically achievable exposures (Reisman et al., 2019). In oncology, a first-in-human dose-escalation study in advanced solid tumors reported acceptable tolerability with pharmacodynamic evidence of Nrf2 pathway activation in PBMCs; in dermatology, topical RTA-408 lotion activated Nrf2 in human skin and was well tolerated (Creelan et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). In neurology, omaveloxolone advanced through the MOXIe program for Friedreich’s ataxia with evidence of neurologic benefit at clinical doses ≥80 mg and exposures concordant with preclinical pharmacology (Naidu & Dinkova-Kostova, 2020; Reisman et al., 2019; Zahir et al., 2025).

Ocularly, multiple oleanane triterpenoid derivatives have shown benefit in retinal oxidative-stress models: dh404 induced canonical Nrf2 target genes (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM), reduced inflammatory mediators, and decreased retinal vascular leakage; CDDO-TFEA and CDDO-EA activated NQO1 in photoreceptor-derived 661W cells and CDDO-TFEA reduced light-induced retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021). RS9, an OA-derived analog generated via microbial transformation, showed superior potency versus CDDO-Me in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) protection, increased retinal HO-1/NQO1 at low doses, and suppressed neovascularization and blood-brain barrier hyperpermeability in vivo, supporting the generalizable ocular protective potential of optimized oleanane triterpenoids (Cheng et al., 2021). Critically for translational relevance, omaveloxolone itself has documented protective activity in human fetal RPE at low-nanomolar concentrations (≤100 nM), where it prevents H₂O₂-induced apoptosis/necrosis by shifting the Bcl-2:Bax ratio and reducing protein glutathionylation—biomarkers linked to oxidative damage and barrier compromise in RPE (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, RTA-408 is the only oleanolic acid analogue noted to have entered clinical trials in ocular indications (cataract-surgery–related pain/inflammation and corneal endothelial cell loss), demonstrating sponsor commitment to ophthalmic development and an initial tolerability signal for ocular use (Cheng et al., 2021). No clinical reports were found in the provided context for omaveloxolone in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) specifically, nor in geographic atrophy; thus, this is a repurposing proposal grounded in mechanistic and preclinical ocular convergence rather than direct AMD clinical precedent (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
The KEAP1–NRF2 node is a cysteine-centric electrophile sensor system that orchestrates the phase-2 antioxidant and cytoprotective response. Under basal conditions, KEAP1 recruits NRF2 to the CUL3 E3 ligase complex for ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover. Electrophiles such as cyano-enone triterpenoids react with KEAP1 cysteine sensors—most prominently Cys151 in the BTB domain—to disrupt CUL3 docking and/or alter KEAP1 conformation, thereby stabilizing NRF2, allowing nuclear translocation, heterodimerization with small Maf proteins, and binding to antioxidant response elements (ARE) to induce a transcriptional battery including NQO1, HO-1 (HMOX1), glutathione biosynthesis enzymes (GCLC, GCLM), thioredoxin and thioredoxin reductase (Txn1, Txnrd1), sulfiredoxin (Srxn1), and other detoxifying/antioxidative genes (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). Oleanane cyano-enone triterpenoids are among the most potent NRF2 activators known, with structure–activity relationships showing strong correlations between the presence/geometry of Michael acceptors and both iNOS suppression and NQO1 induction across series; mechanistic profiling indicates covalent yet reversible conjugation to protein thiols underlies this pharmacology (Naidu & Dinkova-Kostova, 2020).

Within this class, omaveloxolone is an electrophilic Michael acceptor–bearing, difluoro-propanamide oleanane that activates Nrf2 at nanomolar concentrations in reporter assays and upregulates canonical ARE-target genes (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, TxnR1), consistent with its cyano-enone pharmacophore engaging KEAP1 Cys151 and allied redox sensors (Sun et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019). In systemic models, omaveloxolone increases glutathione concentrations, supports mitochondrial respiration, and normalizes metabolic/energetic parameters downstream of Nrf2 activation—effects mechanistically rationalized by Nrf2-driven induction of NADPH-generating enzymes and mitochondrial support genes, which collectively bolster reductive and ATP capacity in stressed cells (Reisman et al., 2019). In immunologic contexts, oleanane triterpenoids suppress IFN-γ–induced nitric oxide signaling in macrophages, reduce reactive oxygen and nitrotyrosine production by myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and can inhibit IKKβ/NF-κB signaling (demonstrated for CDDO-Me), contributing to anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions that are secondary but complementary to NRF2-mediated cytoprotection (Creelan et al., 2017; Sporn et al., 2007). The class is bifunctional: low-to-moderate exposures favor NRF2-dependent cytoprotection and redox quenching, whereas higher exposures can increase oxidative burden and trigger apoptosis—an important consideration when targeting delicate ocular tissues (Liby et al., 2007).

For ocular cell types relevant to dry AMD, multiple lines of evidence anchor Nrf2/ARE biology. In the retina, oleanane triterpenoids (dh404, CDDO derivatives) induce NQO1/HO-1/GCLM, reduce inflammatory mediators and vascular leakage, and protect photoreceptors and retinal structure in oxidative-stress models; RS9 dosing increases retinal NQO1/HO-1 in vivo (Cheng et al., 2021). In human fetal RPE, omaveloxolone prevents H₂O₂-induced apoptosis and necrosis at ≤100 nM, shifts Bcl-2:Bax pro-survival balance, and reduces protein S-glutathionylation, a reversible oxidative modification implicated in disruption of cytoskeletal and junctional complexes that maintain barrier integrity (Cheng et al., 2021). Taken together, these data support that omaveloxolone, via KEAP1 cysteine sensing and Nrf2 activation in RPE and adjacent retinal cells, can rapidly enhance the endogenous antioxidant program, elevate glutathione/NADPH buffering, mitigate protein oxidative adducts, and suppress inflammatory amplification—biomechanistic axes directly relevant to RPE survival and barrier function under oxidative stress (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021).

Pharmacologically, omaveloxolone exhibits high plasma protein binding and broad tissue distribution preclinically, with oral dosing in primates/humans yielding exposures that induce Nrf2 targets in PBMCs and distribute to metabolically active tissues; topical dermal dosing in humans activates cutaneous Nrf2 without untoward safety signals (Reisman et al., 2019). For ocular dosing, clinical testing of RTA-408 in cataract-surgery contexts (ocular pain/inflammation, corneal endothelial protection) establishes feasibility of achieving pharmacologically relevant ocular exposure with acceptable tolerability in humans, though detailed ocular PK has not been published in the provided excerpts (Cheng et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Assay and hypothesis: In a human RPE monolayer model subjected to H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury, omaveloxolone is expected to covalently and reversibly modify KEAP1 cysteines (notably Cys151), stabilize and activate Nrf2, and robustly induce the ARE-regulated antioxidant gene set (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, TXNRD1, SRXN1), thereby increasing cellular glutathione, NADPH-dependent antioxidant enzyme activity, and mitochondrial resilience; these changes should reduce protein S-glutathionylation, prevent loss of perijunctional actomyosin integrity, and preserve tight-junction belts, culminating in restoration of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and reduction of paracellular flux (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021). Mechanistic support for each step:

- Target engagement and Nrf2 activation in RPE: Cyano-enone triterpenoids are sensed by KEAP1 Cys151, stabilizing Nrf2; omaveloxolone activates Nrf2 at nanomolar concentrations and induces NQO1/HO-1/GCLM/TxnR1 in human cells, and has shown protection in human fetal RPE at ≤100 nM against H₂O₂-induced death with suppression of protein glutathionylation—an oxidative adduct linked to structural protein dysfunction and barrier failure (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021).

- Barrier functional correlates in vivo and in vitro: Oleanane triterpenoids reduce retinal vascular leakage in models of inflammation/oxidative stress, and RTA-408 decreases oxidative protein glutathionylation in RPE—a mechanistic event that plausibly preserves junctional complexes and TEER under H₂O₂ stress, even though explicit TEER data for RTA-408 in RPE are not provided here (Cheng et al., 2021).

Operationally, we anticipate a biphasic exposure–response: low nanomolar concentrations should maximize cytoprotective Nrf2 signaling without triggering the pro-oxidant/apoptotic bifurcation observed at higher exposures for this class (Liby et al., 2007). Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit to dry AMD biology: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to RPE degeneration in dry AMD; omaveloxolone engages KEAP1 cysteine sensors to activate Nrf2 and induce a comprehensive, rapid-acting ARE program that elevates glutathione/NADPH, upregulates HO-1/NQO1/GCL-enzymes, and improves mitochondrial bioenergetics—changes expected to blunt H₂O₂-triggered barrier loss and death in RPE (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). Conclusion  
On balance, omaveloxolone is a mechanistically well-aligned, clinically de-risked Nrf2 activator with direct protective activity in human RPE and supportive in vivo retinal pharmacology from its chemical class, making it a strong repurposing candidate for dry AMD focused on RPE barrier preservation under oxidative stress (Cheng et al., 2021; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ICG-001 (Sigma I2441) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor originally identified for its ability to selectively disrupt the interaction between β-catenin and the transcriptional coactivator CBP (CREB-binding protein), thereby inhibiting TCF/LEF-dependent Wnt/β-catenin–driven transcription without reducing total β-catenin protein abundance (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). Mechanistically, ICG-001 is positioned within a class of β-catenin pathway modulators that block nuclear β-catenin activity rather than decreasing β-catenin protein levels; this distinguishes it from antisense/siRNA approaches and from inhibitors that act upstream in Wnt signaling (e.g., tankyrase inhibitors like XAV-939) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 112–117). The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor class has been proposed as a more selective means to modulate β-catenin transcriptional output while sparing adherens junction functions that depend on β-catenin protein pools, a distinction supported by data showing ICG-001 does not trigger compensatory γ-catenin stabilization that follows β-catenin protein depletion (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117).

Within the broader Wnt-targeting landscape, ICG-001 exemplifies downstream, transcriptional-coactivator–selective targeting, contrasted with agents that block β-catenin/TCF binding, Dishevelled PDZ interactions, Porcupine-mediated ligand maturation, or Frizzled receptor activity (e.g., OMP-18R5) (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31). Because Wnt pathway effects are highly context dependent and temporally dynamic across tissues, coactivator-selective modulation has been argued to mitigate systemic liabilities relative to global pathway inhibition (Assaf, 2018, pp. 28–31).

Therapeutic History  
ICG-001 itself is widely used as a research tool, and its clinical derivative/prodrug analogs (e.g., PRI-724/OP-724) have reached Phase I/IIa testing in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, establishing a preliminary human safety/tolerability and feasibility record for CBP/β-catenin pathway inhibition in chronic disease. In HCV-induced cirrhosis, an open-label Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of PRI-724 administered continuous i.v. infusions (10–160 mg/m2/day; 1 week on/1 week off for 12 weeks) with primary outcomes focused on adverse events and exploratory anti-fibrotic endpoints (histology, serum fibrosis biomarkers); the program reported safety/tolerability and preliminary efficacy consistent with anti-fibrotic activity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014). In HBV/HCV-related cirrhosis, a Phase I/IIa open-label study (twice-weekly 4 h infusions; 140, 280, 380 mg/m2 per 4 h) evaluated safety, PK, and change in liver fibrosis area by biopsy at 12 weeks; the registry cites a derived EBioMedicine report on safety, tolerability, and anti-fibrotic effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2018). In advanced primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; Scheuer stage ≥III), OP-724 (formerly PRI-724) underwent a Phase I dose-finding trial (4 h i.v. infusions, twice weekly for 12 weeks; 140/280/380 mg/m2 cohorts) assessing serious adverse events, PK of OP-724 and metabolite C-82, and fibrosis-related endpoints (biopsy fibrotic area, FibroScan, Child-Pugh/MELD, ELF score) with feasibility/safety results published (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

No clinical or preclinical ocular applications of ICG-001/PRI-724/OP-724 were identified in the provided context, and there are no reports here of use in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), or retinal barrier disorders (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019). Preclinical oncology literature summarized in the provided sources documents ICG-001’s activity in cancer cells (reduced proliferation and induced selective apoptosis via TCF-dependent signaling reduction) but does not address ocular tissues (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Thus, while the drug class has human safety experience in fibrotic liver disease, there is no direct evidence in the provided context for ophthalmic use or for dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
ICG-001 binds CBP and selectively disrupts the β-catenin/CBP complex, attenuating β-catenin–driven transcription of TCF/LEF target genes (e.g., Cyclin D1) without decreasing total β-catenin protein levels; in Hep3B cells, ICG-001 reduced TOPflash reporter activity and Cyclin D1 expression while leaving β-catenin abundance unchanged and without inducing compensatory γ-catenin stabilization (if anything, γ-catenin modestly decreased) (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99). Across multiple excerpts, ICG-001 is consistently described as selective for β-catenin/CBP over β-catenin/p300, reducing TCF-dependent Wnt output while sparing other β-catenin protein interactions; global β-catenin levels are unaffected, reinforcing a functional separation between nuclear transcriptional roles and membrane adherens junction pools (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30). Authors highlight that agents which lower β-catenin protein (ASO/siRNA) trigger γ-catenin compensation at adherens junctions—distinct from ICG-001, which blocks transcriptional activity without provoking such protein-level sensing/reciprocity (Wickline, 2013, pp. 112–117, 140–145). It remains explicitly unknown from these data whether ICG-001 perturbs adherens junction function in vivo; follow-up studies were recommended to test junctional tolerance to transcriptional blockade (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

Contextual biology of β-catenin coactivator usage indicates that CBP vs p300 partnering can impart divergent phenotypic outcomes; in fibrotic contexts, CBP-associated β-catenin activity has been linked with pro-fibrotic programs whereas p300-associated activity may be protective, though this literature is complex and model-dependent (Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69). Canonical β-catenin signaling is also subject to Wnt-independent inputs that promote nuclear translocation/transactivation (e.g., PKA/Akt phosphorylation), and β-catenin exists in distinct pools with membrane-associated adherens junction functions that are regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation events, further implying that selective transcriptional blockade (CBP-directed) may spare adhesive roles (Wickline, 2013, pp. 21–26). Together, these mechanistic data support a rationale for testing CBP/β-catenin–selective inhibitors for diseases where β-catenin transcription drives pathology and where preserving epithelial junctional architecture is desirable (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30, 140–145).

Disease-Relevant Biology in RPE and Retinal Barriers  
RPE epithelial phenotype and outer blood–retina barrier (oBRB) integrity depend on tight junction (TJ) and adherens junction (AJ) complexes (ZO-1/occludin/claudins; E-cadherin/catenins). Loss of ZO-1 releases ZONAB to drive CDK4 and proliferation; downregulation of E-cadherin frees β-catenin to translocate to the nucleus and activate EMT/proliferation drivers (e.g., Snail, Cyclin D1), establishing a mechanistic link between junctional disruption and β-catenin–dependent transcriptional programs in RPE (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–9). Reviews of RPE EMT highlight Wnt–β-catenin as a key mediator in the eye; experimental injury (laser photocoagulation) activates β-catenin signaling and facilitates RPE proliferation, reinforcing the pathway’s involvement in EMT and regenerative responses (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 7–9).

Critically, primary hRPE culture studies demonstrate that Matrigel plus Activin A (MA) fosters epithelial morphology, increases TJ gene/protein expression (Claudin-1, Claudin-3, Occludin, ZO-1), improves apical ZO-1 polarity, and elevates TEER; this phenotype is accompanied by increased β-catenin levels and β-catenin/TCF target expression (TCF-4, Survivin, Cyclin D1, c-Myc), and is suppressed by the Wnt/β-catenin inhibitor XAV-939, implicating canonical β-catenin activity in barrier maturation under these culture conditions (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11). The MA paradigm also shows anti-apoptotic effects (lower ROS, preserved mitochondrial potential, lower Annexin V positivity) linked to elevated β-catenin/Survivin, again consistent with β-catenin supporting epithelial survival when cell–cell contacts are intact (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

Conversely, disease models and inflammatory contexts show scenarios where β-catenin activation correlates with barrier breakdown. In diabetic macular edema (DME) models, SMURF1 promotes WIF1 ubiquitination and degradation, activating Wnt/β-catenin–VEGF signaling, inducing autophagy, and disrupting RPE tight junctions; knockdown of SMURF1 restores WIF1, suppresses pathway activation, and rescues claudin-1/occludin/ZO-1 expression in ARPE-19 and in STZ mice (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Inflammatory TNFα challenge in polarized ARPE-19 reduces TER, increases paracellular permeability, and disrupts ZO-1/claudins/occludin and AJ components; the HDAC inhibitor ITF2357 restores TER and junctional proteins and suppresses β-catenin overexpression and NF-κB signaling, supporting the concept that limiting β-catenin–linked transcription can be barrier-protective under inflammatory stress (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19). Under oxidative stress relevant to dry AMD, ex vivo primary porcine RPE (ppRPE) exposed to NaIO₃ shows a significant reduction in ZO-1 immunopositive area (with unchanged TJP1 mRNA), indicating tight-junction localization loss; while the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is not measured directly in this model, the outcome establishes a testable context for barrier rescue (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15).

These data collectively underscore a context-dependent role of β-catenin in RPE: when epithelial contacts are robust, β-catenin activity can support maturation, TJ expression, and survival; under EMT/injury/inflammatory stress (e.g., DME/TNFα), β-catenin pathway activation correlates with junctional loss, VEGF induction, and autophagy, and pathway suppression can be protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–19).

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay context: RPE monolayers subjected to oxidative stress (e.g., NaIO₃, H₂O₂, or serum withdrawal models) with readouts including TEER, paracellular flux, and localization/expression of ZO-1 and claudin-1.

- Gene/protein expression in RPE: ZO-1, claudins, occludin, and cadherins/β-catenin are established components of RPE junctions and are readily measured; TEER increases in mature hRPE and decreases with injury provide a functional correlate of barrier status (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Zhou, 2022, pp. 51–55). β-catenin and downstream targets (Cyclin D1, Survivin, c-Myc, TCF-4) were upregulated in hRPE MA cultures and are suppressible by Wnt pathway inhibition, confirming pathway engagement in RPE (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

In RPE, the immediate expected effect would be downregulation of β-catenin/TCF-LEF targets that are CBP-dependent. The direction of effect on junctional genes is uncertain based on available data: in MA-conditioned hRPE, canonical β-catenin activity correlates with increased claudin-1 and ZO-1 and higher TEER, and global pathway inhibition reduces these effects; thus CBP-targeted inhibition might risk dampening TJ upregulation under certain epithelial conditions (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11). In inflammatory/DME-like contexts, β-catenin activation contributes to VEGF/autophagy-mediated TJ disruption, and Wnt pathway suppression is protective; in these contexts, CBP blockade could plausibly reduce pathway-driven barrier loss (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

In RPE EMT, β-catenin activation promotes proliferation via Cyclin D1; thus ICG-001 would be expected to mitigate proliferation-associated EMT programs rather than activate them (Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7, 7–9). However, MA-driven β-catenin activity increases Survivin/Bcl2 and enhances anti-apoptotic resilience; therefore, under oxidative stress, attenuating β-catenin/CBP with ICG-001 could trade off survival signals against potential EMT suppression, and net effects on TEER may vary by stressor and co-signaling milieu (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Mechanistic specificity: ICG-001 spares total β-catenin protein and does not trigger γ-catenin compensation, mitigating concerns about adherens junction destabilization that accompany β-catenin depletion; nevertheless, whether ICG-001 affects adherens junction functionality in epithelial tissues in vivo remains unknown, and this must be directly assessed in RPE (Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Defined, selective mechanism: ICG-001 disrupts β-catenin/CBP complexes and suppresses TCF-dependent transcription without lowering total β-catenin; it does not trigger γ-catenin compensation observed with β-catenin protein knockdown, offering a mechanistically precise intervention that may spare adherens junction architecture (Wickline, 2013, pp. 94–99, 112–117, 140–145, 26–30).

- Clinical-stage drug class: The CBP/β-catenin inhibitor analogs PRI-724/OP-724 have human safety and PK data in liver fibrosis/cirrhosis/PBC, supporting translational feasibility and providing a clinical development template, albeit outside ophthalmology (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014, 2018, 2019).

- Biological plausibility in RPE EMT and barrier dysfunction: RPE EMT and barrier loss are linked to β-catenin nuclear signaling; under inflammatory/DME-like conditions, Wnt/β-catenin activation disrupts TJs via VEGF/autophagy and Wnt-pathway suppression restores claudin-1/ZO-1, suggesting that pathway attenuation can be barrier-protective in disease contexts where β-catenin drives pathogenic transcription (Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

- No direct ocular/RPE data for ICG-001: The provided context contains no studies of ICG-001 (or PRI-724/OP-724) in RPE or ocular tissues, no TEER/paracellular flux rescue data, and no AMD model outcomes; claims of junction-selective “bias” in RPE are speculative and unproven here (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019; Wickline, 2013, pp. 140–145).

- Context-dependent and bidirectional β-catenin effects in RPE: In hRPE cultured with MA, β-catenin activity correlates with increased claudin-1/ZO-1 and higher TEER, and Wnt pathway inhibition (XAV-939) diminishes these; thus, in certain epithelial contexts, β-catenin/CBP inhibition could impair, not enhance, junctional gene expression and barrier function (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–11).

- Survival/proliferation trade-offs: β-catenin activation increased anti-apoptotic factors (Survivin/Bcl2) and protected hRPE from serum withdrawal stress; ICG-001’s suppression of β-catenin target genes could compromise survival signaling under oxidative stress, and the net effect on barrier integrity/survival requires direct testing (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7).

- Mechanistic uncertainty regarding “biased transcription” toward junctional genes: No evidence is provided that CBP-selective inhibition favors claudin-1/ZO-1 expression; indeed, Sox/TCF targets include Cyclin D1 and c-Myc, and the directionality of CBP versus p300 coactivator usage on RPE junctional gene programs is not defined by the present sources (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 9–11; Assaf, 2018, pp. 66–69).

- Delivery and ocular PK/PD unknowns: Clinical liver trials used i.v. infusions; ocular tolerability, retinal exposure, and local pharmacology for ICG-001/OP-724/PRI-724 are not addressed here, requiring formulation and delivery development (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2019).

Decision Implications  
On the present evidence, ICG-001 has a coherent, selective mechanism with clinical-stage validation in a non-ocular indication, and there is strong biological plausibility that β-catenin transcriptional blockade can counter EMT/proliferation programs in RPE. However, the specific hypothesis that ICG-001 will “bias” transcription to upregulate claudin-1/ZO-1 and restore TEER under oxidative stress is not supported by the provided literature; in fact, RPE studies show that β-catenin activation is associated with higher TJ expression/TEER in some contexts, and pathway inhibition reduces these features, whereas in inflammatory/DME contexts β-catenin activation is deleterious and suppression is protective (Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Therefore, a tightly scoped preclinical program should be undertaken to empirically resolve these context-dependent effects in RPE before committing to development for dry AMD.

Recommendation  
- Proceed with an in vitro/ex vivo feasibility package to test ICG-001 in RPE barrier models under defined stressors (oxidative vs inflammatory), with rigorous functional and molecular endpoints and on-target PD confirmation; include orthogonal comparators (XAV-939, ITF2357) to position CBP-selective modulation against broader Wnt suppression and epigenetic anti-inflammatory rescue (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7). Advance only if ICG-001 reproducibly restores TEER and junctional localization without pro-EMT/proliferation signatures across oxidative stress conditions relevant to dry AMD (Wagner et al., 2024, pp. 14–15; Zhou et al., 2020, pp. 6–7).

- If positive, initiate ocular PK/tolerability and RPE-targeted delivery studies; if negative or mixed, deprioritize in favor of alternative approaches with direct evidence of barrier rescue in RPE (e.g., HDAC inhibitors in inflammatory settings), recognizing that pathway- and context-specificity critically determine outcomes in RPE biology (Lim et al., 2024, pp. 15–19; Lim et al., 2024, pp. 10–12).

In sum, ICG-001 is a mechanistically attractive, clinically precedented β-catenin/CBP inhibitor, but the claim of junction-focused, proliferation-sparing barrier rescue in oxidatively stressed RPE is currently hypothetical and not substantiated by the provided literature; decisive RPE-focused experiments are required to validate or refute its potential for dry AMD (Wickline, 2013, pp. 26–30; Guo et al., 2016, pp. 5–7; Liang et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MS-275, also known as Entinostat and available from Selleck (S7100), is a fully synthetic compound that belongs to the benzamide class of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi). Its chemical structure is defined as 3-pyridylmethyl-N-{4-[(2-aminophenyl)carbamoyl]-benzyl}carbamate, and it was originally developed by research teams including those at Mitsui Pharmaceuticals in the late 1990s (Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 2–3; Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34). Unlike hydroxamate-based HDAC inhibitors, the benzamide motif in MS-275 engages the catalytic zinc ion in a manner that is less potent in chelation yet confers a higher degree of class I selectivity, particularly toward HDAC1 and HDAC2 (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11). Benzamides have been extensively investigated for their epigenetic modulation properties in oncology, where selective inhibition of HDACs is pursued to reprogram aberrant gene expression profiles in cancer cells (Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Carafa et al., 2011, pp. 3–5). As a representative of its class, MS-275 has a well-defined synthetic origin and benefits from a non-natural product, medicinal chemistry–driven discovery process that emphasizes targeted inhibition of chromatin-modifying enzymes for therapeutic reactivation of silenced genes (Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34; Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, MS-275 has been developed and evaluated primarily in the context of oncology. It has advanced into multiple Phase I and II clinical trials, particularly for solid tumors such as breast cancer, hematologic malignancies like acute leukemia, and various other cancers where deregulated HDAC activity plays a role (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 9–11; Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 2–3). Preclinical studies have demonstrated its capacity to induce cell-cycle arrest, promote apoptosis, and trigger differentiation in tumor cell lines by restoring a balance in histone acetylation (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–9; Hanikoglu et al., 2018, pp. 2–3). Despite its extensive evaluation in cancer, there is no published evidence to date directly applying MS-275 to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or related ocular diseases. Nonetheless, the mechanistic rationale underlying its use in oncology—namely, reactivation of key transcriptional programs via enhanced histone acetylation—is similar to the epigenetic strategy proposed for rescuing retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier function (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 9–11; Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34). In this sense, repurposing MS-275 for dry AMD would constitute a novel application, relying on the molecule’s ability to reverse inflammation-induced transcriptional repression, analogous to its effects in cancer cells (Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Carafa et al., 2011, pp. 3–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
MS-275 functions by selectively inhibiting class I HDACs, particularly HDAC1 and HDAC2, through a zinc-binding mechanism that is distinct from that of hydroxamate inhibitors. The benzamide moiety in MS-275 interacts with the catalytic zinc ion within the active site of HDACs; however, due to its non-hydroxamate nature, the mode of coordination involves a bidentate interaction primarily via the amino group with additional, albeit weaker, engagement through the carbonyl oxygen (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11). This selective inhibition results in the accumulation of acetylated histones H3 and H4, thereby maintaining a relaxed chromatin state that is permissive for transcription. The proposed inflammatory stress in RPE cells—induced by tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)—is thought to lead to the recruitment of HDAC1/2 to promoters of tight junction genes such as TJP1, OCLN, and CLDN19, effectively silencing their expression through histone deacetylation (Hanikoglu et al., 2018, pp. 2–3; Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 8–10). By inhibiting HDAC1/2, MS-275 is expected to restore global histone acetylation levels, thereby reactivating transcription of these tight junction genes. The resulting upregulation and stabilization of proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin are hypothesized to reconstruct intercellular junctions and improve transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), which is a measure of barrier integrity (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–9; San José-Enériz et al., 2019, pp. 8–10). This mechanism is supported by extensive biochemical studies in cancer models, where similar epigenetic reprogramming has led to reactivation of silenced genes, although direct data in ocular models remains to be generated (Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34; Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 9–11).

Expected Effect in the Proposed Assay:  
In the experimental model using ARPE-19 cells subjected to TNF-α stress, the central hypothesis is that treatment with 0.5 µM MS-275 will be sufficient to inhibit HDAC1/2 activity and restore histone acetylation at tight junction gene promoters. This, in turn, should lead to a reactivation of transcription for TJP1 (encoding ZO-1), OCLN (encoding occludin), and CLDN19 (encoding claudin-19), resulting in an increased synthesis of these key proteins. As tight junction proteins come back online, the structural integrity of the RPE monolayer is expected to improve, which will be reflected by a significant increase in TEER measurements—quantitatively, it is predicted that junction protein levels might be restored by at least twofold, corresponding to a recovery of barrier function (Zhang et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Ruiz et al., 2015, pp. 2–3). ARPE-19 cells are an established model for studying RPE barrier function and are known to express these tight junction components; thus, the assay is well poised to test whether the epigenetic modulation by MS-275 can counteract the deleterious effects of TNF-α (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 17–18; San José-Enériz et al., 2019, pp. 8–10). Consequently, a restored acetylation pattern is expected to facilitate the re-expression of the tight junction gene set and consequently normalize TEER, which is a proxy for the functional integrity of the RPE barrier (Hanikoglu et al., 2018, pp. 2–3; Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 8–10).

The repurposing hypothesis for MS-275 in dry AMD is scientifically intriguing and grounded in a well-established mechanism of epigenetic modulation. Its selective inhibition of HDAC1 and HDAC2 is particularly attractive because these isoforms are known to be involved in the aberrant epigenetic silencing observed under conditions of inflammatory stress, and their inhibition has been shown to restore transcriptionally active chromatin states (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11). However, there are notable challenges as well. Although MS-275 has a well-defined mechanism in cancer, there is a lack of direct preclinical data supporting its use in ocular diseases, and specifically in models of RPE tight junction disruption. This represents a significant gap in the literature that would need to be addressed through targeted studies in ocular cell lines and animal models. Furthermore, MS-275’s pharmacokinetic profile, which has been characterized in the context of systemic cancer therapy, may not directly translate to effective drug delivery or retention in ocular tissues. For instance, issues such as blood–retina barrier penetration, potential ocular toxicity, and the need for specialized formulation strategies (e.g., local delivery through intravitreal injection or topical administration) are important considerations that have not yet been systematically evaluated for this compound (Knipstein & Gore, 2011, pp. 2–3; Ruiz et al., 2015, pp. 1–2). In addition, the broad spectrum of gene reactivation induced by HDAC inhibition may carry the risk of off-target effects, and while the selective inhibition of HDAC1/2 is a strength in terms of targeted epigenetic modulation, chronic inhibition of these enzymes could potentially disrupt normal cellular functions in the retina if not carefully controlled (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11).

Another weakness is the variability inherent in the clinical data for MS-275 observed in oncology, where interpatient differences and dose-dependent toxicities (such as gastrointestinal, hematologic, and metabolic abnormalities) have been reported (Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34; Weber, 2015, pp. 33–34). Although these adverse effects were generally considered manageable in the cancer setting, the risk–benefit balance for treatment of a chronic, non-lethal condition like dry AMD would have to be carefully re-evaluated. It is also worth noting that while MS-275’s epigenetic mechanism is promising for restoring tight junction gene expression, the complex interplay of inflammatory cytokines and multiple HDAC isoforms in the RPE may require combinatorial approaches or more selective targeting strategies than those currently afforded by MS-275 (McCabe, 2019, pp. 23–27; Hanikoglu et al., 2018, pp. 2–3).

In conclusion, MS-275 (Entinostat) presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its established epigenetic mechanism, clinical profile in oncology, and the plausible hypothesis that HDAC1/2 inhibition in RPE cells under inflammatory stress can restore tight junction integrity. Its strengths lie in its synthetic origin, clear mechanism of increasing histone acetylation, and potential to reactivate genes suppressed by pro-inflammatory signaling. However, significant preclinical research is needed to validate its efficacy and safety in ocular models, to optimize its delivery to retinal tissues, and to ensure that its broad effects on gene expression do not result in adverse outcomes when used chronically in a non-oncologic context (Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 7–11; Rossetti, 2023, pp. 31–34; Zhang et al., 2015, pp. 2–3). Overall, while the candidate is promising, a cautious, step-wise approach involving detailed in vitro and in vivo studies in ocular systems is warranted before advancing to clinical trials for dry AMD (Connolly et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; San José-Enériz et al., 2019, pp. 8–10; Hofny et al., n.d., pp. 9–11).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Navitoclax (ABT-263) is a small‐molecule, orally bioavailable agent originally developed in the oncology arena as a BH3‐mimetic that targets several anti‐apoptotic members of the BCL-2 family, most notably BCL-2, BCL-xL, and BCL-W. This synthetic compound was designed through structure–activity relationship optimization to overcome the limitations of earlier compounds such as ABT-737, and it has since been classified as a senolytic agent owing to its ability to selectively induce apoptosis in senescent cells while sparing normal, quiescent cells. In the context of aging and degenerative diseases, the protective yet dysfunctional senescent cell phenotype is characterized by the upregulation of anti‐apoptotic proteins; therefore, compounds like ABT-263 that block these survival pathways have been repurposed as candidates to eliminate such senescent cells. The compound belongs to a broader class of therapeutics targeting the BCL-2 family, which have historically been exploited in various anti-cancer strategies and are now emerging as promising candidates for addressing age-associated disorders such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Ryu et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Navitoclax has a well-documented preclinical and clinical history in oncological models; its senolytic potential was first noted in studies where it selectively killed therapy-induced senescent tumor cells and other cell types by inhibiting anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins. Early clinical trials in small-cell lung cancer and lymphoid malignancies established proof-of-concept that targeting BCL-2/BCL-xL could result in tumor regression through apoptotic induction, although its clinical use was somewhat limited by dose-dependent toxicities such as thrombocytopenia. More recently, preclinical studies have extended its use beyond oncology: in in vitro studies and in mouse models where retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells were rendered senescent by doxorubicin treatment, navitoclax was shown to selectively induce apoptosis in the senescent cell population while largely sparing non-senescent RPE, as evidenced by decreased markers of senescence (p16, p21) and increased apoptotic markers such as cleaved caspases. Additionally, these studies demonstrated that oral administration of ABT-263 in mice resulted in reduced senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining and improved structural and functional retinal outcomes, including increased outer nuclear layer thickness and recovery of electroretinographic responses, which are highly encouraging for its repurposing in dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023). Despite these promising preclinical findings, navitoclax has not yet been tested in clinical trials for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative diseases, and its history in ocular conditions remains limited to proof-of-principle studies in animal models (Ryu et al., 2023; Khan et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, navitoclax exerts its senolytic action by competitively binding to the hydrophobic groove of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins, particularly BCL-2 and BCL-xL, thereby displacing pro-apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BIM. Under normal conditions, senescent cells upregulate these anti-apoptotic proteins as part of a survival mechanism against various stressors; the binding of navitoclax disrupts these protective interactions, leading to the activation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade. This biochemical disruption sets off a cascade of events culminating in mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, cytochrome c release, and the subsequent activation of caspases (notably caspase-9 and caspase-3), which orchestrate programmed cell death. Experimentally, cells treated with navitoclax have demonstrated an increased BAX/BCL-2 ratio along with elevated levels of cleaved caspases as measured by immunoblots, paralleling the reduction of canonical senescence markers such as p16 and p21. In the context of retinal degeneration, senescent RPE cells are known to secrete a deleterious senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)—including proinflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and IL-8 and matrix metalloproteases such as MMP2 and MMP9—that can undermine the integrity of junctional proteins such as ZO-1, leading to increased paracellular permeability. By eliminating these p16^Ink4a-positive senescent cells, navitoclax is hypothesized to reduce the inflammatory burden on the tissue microenvironment, thereby promoting the repopulation of healthy RPE cells and the restoration of tight junction continuity (Ryu et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of navitoclax for dry AMD is that the senolytic removal of p16^Ink4a-positive, senescent RPE cells will lead to a diminution of the SASP and its associated cytokines, such as IL-6 and IL-8, which are known to contribute to the degradation of tight junction proteins and compromise RPE barrier function. Experimental reports on navitoclax in senescent RPE models have indicated that treatment with ABT-263 not only leads to a reduction in senescence markers and SASP factor expression but also is accompanied by increased markers of cellular proliferation (e.g., Ki67) and partial recovery of structural features, such as an approximately 10% increase in outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in mouse models. While direct measurements of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and quantification of ZO-1 localization remain limited in these studies, immunofluorescence data do suggest improvements in junctional integrity following treatment with navitoclax. Thus, the expected biological effect is that clearance of senescent RPE will result in reduced paracrine inflammatory signaling, the reestablishment of stable ZO-1 belts, and overall restoration of the barrier properties of the RPE layer—a critical factor in the progression of dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
Navitoclax represents a promising therapeutic candidate as a repurposed senolytic agent for the treatment of dry AMD based on a convergence of preclinical biochemical, cellular, and animal model data. One of its primary strengths is its clear mechanism of action; by targeting a well-characterized survival pathway that is upregulated in senescent cells, navitoclax offers a rational strategy for the selective removal of dysfunctional p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells. The preclinical evidence suggests that this mechanism translates into meaningful improvements in retinal structure and function, including reductions in senescence-associated markers and partial restoration of indicators of cellular proliferation and tissue integrity (Ryu et al., 2023).

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed before navitoclax can be considered a viable treatment for dry AMD. Foremost among these is the concern regarding its safety profile. BCL-xL inhibition is known to cause dose-limiting thrombocytopenia and neutropenia in systemic applications, as evidenced by cancer trial data. In an elderly population that typically comprises dry AMD patients, where comorbidities and polypharmacy are frequent, these hematologic toxicities could limit the clinical utility of navitoclax unless strategies are devised to minimize systemic exposure or target delivery specifically to the eye. While local delivery (for example, via intravitreal injection) might mitigate some systemic risks, the optimal dosing regimen and formulation remain to be determined (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025).

Another significant limitation is the current gap in direct evidence for the selective clearance of p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells in models that accurately recapitulate the pathophysiology of human dry AMD. Many of the preclinical studies have used doxorubicin-induced senescence models, which, although useful as proof-of-principle systems, may not fully capture the chronic, age-associated accumulation of senescent RPE cells observed in patients with dry AMD. Moreover, while improvements in junctional protein distribution—such as ZO-1 localization—have been reported, there are no robust quantitative data on TEER or direct measurements of paracellular permeability that would definitively demonstrate restoration of barrier function. These issues underscore the need for more refined preclinical assays that not only assess the removal of senescent cells but also rigorously quantify the re-establishment of functional barrier properties in the RPE (Ryu et al., 2023).

Furthermore, the repurposing strategy is based on the assumption that SASP-mediated disruption of tight junctions is a primary driver of barrier dysfunction in dry AMD. While inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8 have been implicated in the degradation of junctional proteins, the complex interplay between the SASP, local immune responses, and other degenerative processes in dry AMD remains incompletely understood. Thus, while the hypothesis that senolytic clearance could reduce SASP levels and facilitate barrier recovery is compelling, it will be critical to validate these effects in models that integrate the multifactorial aspects of AMD pathogenesis (da Silva, 2021; Terao et al., 2022).

In summary, navitoclax has significant strengths as a candidate for senolytic therapy in dry AMD, notably its well-characterized mode of action and demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models that show improved retinal structure and function following the clearance of senescent cells. However, challenges such as its known systemic hematologic toxicities, the need for more disease-relevant preclinical models, and the lack of direct functional assays of RPE barrier restoration remain hurdles that need to be overcome before progressing to clinical trials. Addressing these issues may involve the development of targeted delivery systems, dose optimization studies, and rigorous functional assays that can collectively establish whether the removal of p16^Ink4a-positive senescent cells via navitoclax leads to durable improvements in RPE barrier integrity and, consequently, visual function in patients with dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Al-Naggar et al., 2020).

Critical next steps would include:  
1. Developing or validating animal models that more accurately recapitulate the chronic senescence observed in dry AMD;  
2. Refining delivery strategies to minimize systemic exposure and associated toxicities while maximizing ocular bioavailability;  
3. Implementing rigorous, quantitative assays (such as TEER measurements and detailed immunolocalization of tight junction proteins) to confirm the restoration of barrier function following senolytic treatment; and  
4. Carefully assessing the long-term outcomes of senolytic therapy on retinal structure, immune modulation, and visual performance in aged subjects (Ryu et al., 2023).

The current body of evidence lends credence to the hypothesis that navitoclax-induced senolysis in RPE could alleviate key pathological mechanisms underlying dry AMD, including SASP-mediated junctional disruption, while promoting the repopulation of healthier RPE cells (Ryu et al., 2023; Sreekumar et al., 2020). Given the strengths in its molecular targeting and the encouraging preclinical retinal data, navitoclax remains a promising candidate in the portfolio for dry AMD drug development. However, its ultimate success will hinge on overcoming the noted challenges through comprehensive preclinical validation and strategic clinical study design. Continued investigation into the precise role of p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells in AMD, together with detailed pharmacodynamic studies of navitoclax within the ocular microenvironment, will be essential to determine whether this agent can truly fulfill the promise of restoring RPE barrier function and, by extension, visual acuity in patients suffering from dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Carpenter et al., 2021).

The LOXL2 inhibitor class, including molecules such as PXS-5153A, has been extensively tested in preclinical models of fibrosis and cancer. At the molecular level, LOXL2 catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of lysine or hydroxylysine residues present in collagens and elastin. This reaction is critical for the formation of covalent crosslinks that stabilize the ECM. Overexpression or hyperactivity of LOXL2 results in an excessively crosslinked and stiff matrix. The anticipated outcome is a lower crosslink density in Bruch’s membrane, resulting in a softer, more compliant matrix environment. This reduction in mechanical stiffness is expected to diminish abnormal mechanosignaling through β1 integrins, which are integral to the assembly and maintenance of tight junctions on RPE cells (Benedicto et al., 2017). The downstream consequences of reduced integrin activation include dampening of Rac1 and RhoA/ROCK signaling pathways, which in turn facilitate the stabilization and proper localization of tight junction proteins at the RPE cell membranes (Benedicto et al., 2017). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
CHIR99021 is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor originally identified as a highly potent and selective inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3β) with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range (~10 nM). Its discovery and subsequent chemical development classified it as an ATP-competitive inhibitor, belonging to a broader class of kinase inhibitors that target GSK-3 enzymes. This compound has been marketed under Tocris catalog number 4423 and is widely used as a research tool for modulating the canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway. The synthesis of CHIR99021 is based on medicinal chemistry approaches that aim to optimize kinase selectivity, and indeed, extensive inhibitor profiling has shown that it preferentially targets GSK-3 over cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) and other kinases. This compound belongs to a class of therapeutic candidates generally employed in stem cell differentiation protocols, where its ability to stabilize β-catenin and drive the transcription of Wnt target genes has been extensively validated in various cell types, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) derived from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Leach et al., 2015). As such, CHIR99021 has been foundational in protocols that aim to drive RPE fate by activating canonical Wnt signaling, thereby demonstrating its utility in manipulating epithelial differentiation pathways.

Therapeutic History:  
The majority of available evidence for CHIR99021’s use comes from in vitro studies and preclinical differentiation protocols rather than clinical applications. Multiple studies have shown that when added during defined differentiation windows (for example, from day 8 to 14 of an hESC-to-RPE protocol), CHIR99021 significantly increases the yield and functional maturation of RPE cells. These studies report that CHIR99021-treated differentiations yield improved epithelial morphology, enhanced pigmentation, and robust expression of RPE lineage markers—including MITF, OTX2, and even tight-junction-associated proteins such as ZO-1 (Leach et al., 2015). In parallel, other reports have documented that upregulation of canonical Wnt signaling through CHIR99021 leads to increased expression of pigmentation genes (TYR, TYRP2, and PMEL17) and the RPE functional secretory factor PEDF. However, it is important to note that despite promising results in differentiation assays, the use of CHIR99021 for direct therapeutic intervention in dry AMD is not well documented. A clinical trials search on ClinicalTrials.gov returned no registered trials exploring CHIR99021 or other GSK-3β inhibitors for AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Moreover, in an in vitro macula-sized RPE wound-repair model designed to mimic geographic atrophy, CHIR99021 treatment hindered wound repair instead of enhancing barrier restoration (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). These seemingly contradictory findings illustrate that while CHIR99021 robustly enhances RPE differentiation from stem cells, its effects in mature or stress-challenged RPE may be context-dependent. Overall, the preclinical history establishes CHIR99021 as a well-characterized research compound with proven biochemical activity in activating Wnt/β-catenin signaling, but there is limited evidence regarding its therapeutic application in treating dry AMD or related RPE barrier dysfunction in vivo (Yang et al., 2018; Hottin et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
CHIR99021 exerts its biological effects by inhibiting GSK-3β through competitive binding at the protein’s ATP site, thereby preventing GSK-3β from phosphorylating its substrates. One of the principal consequences of GSK-3β inhibition is the stabilization of β-catenin. Under normal conditions, GSK-3β phosphorylates β-catenin, marking it for proteasomal degradation. Inhibition by CHIR99021 blocks this phosphorylation event, which leads to an accumulation of β-catenin in the cytosol and its translocation into the nucleus. Once in the nucleus, β-catenin interacts with TCF/LEF transcription factors to induce the transcription of multiple downstream genes that govern cell fate decisions, differentiation, and epithelial characteristics (Leach et al., 2015). Notably, in the context of retinal development, β-catenin directly upregulates RPE-specific transcription factors such as MITF and OTX2 by binding to their promoter elements, which aligns with observations of improved RPE differentiation upon CHIR99021 treatment (Leach et al., 2015).  

The proposed hypothesis extends this mechanism by suggesting that activation of the canonical Wnt pathway will also upregulate tight junction gene expression. Although specific data on claudin-1 and occludin transcription in response to CHIR99021 in RPE under oxidative stress are not directly provided in the available literature, several studies have shown that Wnt/β-catenin signaling positively correlates with the expression of junctional proteins and may help preserve the architecture of the ZO-1 belt (Leach et al., 2015). In endothelial cell models, GSK-3 inhibition has been associated with favorable modulation of barrier proteins and improved barrier function, suggesting a mechanistic plausibility for a similar effect in RPE cells (Page, 2019; Hottin et al., 2022). Moreover, the dual action of CHIR99021 in modulating both Wnt targets and supporting antioxidant gene networks may provide additional cytoprotective effects under oxidative stress conditions relevant to dry AMD (Leach et al., 2015; Hottin et al., 2022). However, it must be noted that in certain experimental settings, such as in an in vitro RPE wound-repair assay, prolonged exposure to CHIR99021 led to impaired wound healing, indicating that the degree and context of canonical pathway activation are critical determinants of outcome (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Based on the hypothesis, the application of CHIR99021 in oxidative-stressed RPE is expected to stabilize β-catenin and, through canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling, upregulate the transcription of tight junction genes such as claudin-1 and occludin. This molecular cascade is anticipated to preserve or even restore the ZO-1 belt architecture—the structural hallmark of an intact epithelial barrier—and thereby improve functional barrier properties as measured by an increase in transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and a reduction in FITC-dextran permeability under stress challenges induced by A2E or H₂O₂. In ARPE-19 cell models, limited data suggest that stabilization of β-catenin can counteract H₂O₂-induced loss of cell–cell junctions, with reports of a TEER improvement of approximately 35% (Yang et al., 2018). The expected outcome is therefore two-fold: first, the promotion of a differentiated epithelial phenotype with enhanced expression of RPE-specific markers (MITF, OTX2, PMEL17, and ZO-1); and second, the maintenance or restoration of barrier integrity under conditions that mimic oxidative stress encountered in dry AMD. It is important to consider, however, that while CHIR99021 has been shown to improve differentiation when applied during early stages of RPE development (Leach et al., 2015), its application in mature, stressed RPE may have unintended effects. In one in vitro model simulating GA-like lesions, chronic exposure to CHIR99021 resulted in hindered wound repair, suggesting that the dynamics of Wnt activation—and possibly feedback regulation of junctional pathways—must be finely balanced (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Thus, while the biochemical rationale for improved tight junction gene expression and TEER enhancement is sound, the expected beneficial effect under oxidative challenges remains to be conclusively demonstrated in models that directly assay these endpoints.
