Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BCX9930 is a novel, orally bioavailable, low-molecular-weight small molecule that functions as a selective inhibitor of complement factor D (FD). It was originally discovered through a rigorous drug discovery program that combined high-throughput screening with structure‐based rational design strategies to identify potent, non-covalent inhibitors of the serine protease FD, an essential enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. This candidate belongs to the class of factor D inhibitors, compounds that have previously been developed for complement-mediated diseases including complement 3 glomerulopathy (Chen et al., 2022). The synthesis and discovery process for BCX9930 involved chemical scaffold optimization to enhance both potency and selectivity; for instance, by specifically non-covalently occupying the S1 pocket of FD, BCX9930 is able to achieve an IC₅₀ value as low as 4 nM, a potency level that places it among the most active agents in its category. Its chemical attributes also include more than a 500-fold selectivity over related serine proteases, thereby reducing the potential for off-target effects—a critical factor for chronic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where long-term safety is paramount (Schubart et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
The development of BCX9930 is emblematic of the broader evolution in complement therapeutics. Historically, the complement system has been successfully targeted in several diseases where dysregulated complement activity plays a pathogenic role. Prior studies have established the role of FD in both the amplification loop of the alternative pathway and its subsequent effects on complement-mediated damage. BCX9930 and similar agents emerged from early research efforts that investigated FD inhibition as a means to alter pathologic complement activation. In clinical studies, similar agents targeting factor D (for example, danicopan) have demonstrated significant suppression of alternative pathway activity in conditions such as PNH, with reports noting reductions in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels and improvements in hemoglobin that facilitated transfusion independence (Schubart et al., 2023; Risitano et al., 2020). Although the majority of these pilots have been focused on hematological disorders and C3G, the mechanistic rationale for FD inhibition directly applies to dry AMD as well. Preclinical models have documented that, when the alternative pathway is excessively activated—as is theorized in dry AMD—even minute amounts of FD can trigger a cascade of destructive complement activity (Schubart et al., 2023; Gavriilaki et al., 2022). In animal models, FD inhibitors have demonstrated promising outcomes including the reduction of complement deposition and preservation of retinal architecture (Ong et al., 2024). Despite the encouraging therapeutic history of FD inhibitors in other indications, it is important to note that clinical trials evaluating FD inhibitors specifically for dry AMD or geographic atrophy have produced mixed results; one high-profile example is the failure of Lampalizumab (an FD inhibitor) to meet meaningful endpoints in pivotal phase 3 trials (Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019). Nonetheless, BCX9930 has distinct chemical and pharmacological properties that differentiate it from earlier candidates, including its strong potency, favorable oral bioavailability, and robust preclinical barrier rescue effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, making it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
The pathologic basis for many complement-mediated diseases, including dry AMD, lies in the dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, in which factor D plays a pivotal role. Normally, FD is the rate-limiting enzyme required to generate the AP C3 convertase by cleaving factor B complexed with C3b, which fuels an amplification loop and leads to the generation of downstream proinflammatory mediators such as C3a and C5a as well as opsonins that promote inflammation and tissue damage (Gavriilaki et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024). BCX9930 exerts its therapeutic effect by binding non-covalently in the S1 pocket of FD. This binding is characterized by exceptionally high affinity, with an IC₅₀ value of 4 nM, and by stringent selectivity that minimizes interference with other serine proteases. By occupying this key binding site, BCX9930 effectively prevents FD from interacting with its natural substrate, thereby arresting the production of the AP C3 convertase. This inhibition leads to a subsequent decrease in C3 cleavage and a reduction in the generation of complement split products, which are known to instigate an inflammatory response (Chen et al., 2022).  
Molecularly, the non-covalent nature of BCX9930’s interaction with factor D confers several advantages. First, such interactions allow reversible inhibition, providing the potential for controlled dosing and the fine-tuning of complement activity. Second, the selectivity profile of BCX9930 results from structural modifications aimed at optimizing the fit within the S1 pocket, ensuring that the inhibitor does not inadvertently affect enzymes with similar active site geometries. This precision is crucial, as systemic blockade of the complement system can result in significant immunosuppression. Thus, the protection of the retinal environment—by specifically inhibiting the amplification loop of the alternative pathway—offers a mechanistic rationale for the use of BCX9930 in diseases where complement overactivation is implicated, notably in the disruption of RPE tight junction integrity (Gavriilaki et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024). Additionally, the compound’s design ensures that while it attenuates pathogenic complement activity, it spares the classical and lectin pathways, reducing the risk of systemic immunocompromise.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for BCX9930 in the treatment of dry AMD is based on its ability to mitigate complement-mediated damage to the retinal pigment epithelium. In vitro studies in primary human RPE cells have shown that under conditions of serum-mediated complement activation, there is a decline in trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and disruption of critical tight junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and claudin-19. These proteins are essential for maintaining the barrier integrity of the RPE, and their dysregulation is a hallmark of retinal degeneration in AMD (Gavriilaki et al., 2022).  
The working hypothesis posits that by non-covalently occupying the S1 pocket of factor D, BCX9930 can inhibit the formation of the alternative pathway C3 convertase, thereby reducing the production of the inflammatory complement split products. This reduction is expected to lead to a decrease in complement-driven RPE tight junction disruption. Experimental data indicate that the addition of 500 nM BCX9930 to primary human RPE cultures challenged with serum results in a recovery of TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values. This recovery is associated with the restoration of tight junction integrity, as evidenced by the maintenance of ZO-1 and claudin-19 continuity, both of which are critical determinants of the barrier function (Chen et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024).  
In parallel, in vivo studies using Factor H-knockout animal models have provided supportive data for BCX9930’s therapeutic effect. In these animal models, which exhibit heightened complement activation and subsequent retinal damage similar to that seen in dry AMD, BCX9930 administered at 5 mg/kg twice daily resulted in a 70% reduction in complement C3 deposition on Bruch’s membrane and preservation of the outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness. These endpoints serve as surrogate indicators for photoreceptor protection and overall retinal health. Taken together, these findings underscore the capacity of BCX9930 not only to neutralize the biochemical drivers of complement activation but also to translate this inhibition into meaningful structural and functional preservation within the retina (Ong et al., 2024).  
Mechanistically, the expected effect hinges on the sustained and robust suppression of the alternative complement pathway, which under normal pathological conditions contributes significantly to the inflammatory milieu and structural degeneration characteristic of dry AMD. The reduction in complement activation is anticipated to curtail downstream inflammatory cascades that can disrupt RPE tight junctions, thereby stabilizing TEER and maintaining the integrity of the retinal barrier. Given that chronic complement activation has been implicated in accelerating the progression of dry AMD, the capacity of BCX9930 to restore and maintain RPE function could slow or even arrest disease progression, offering a novel therapeutic avenue for a condition currently lacking effective interventions (Chen et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating BCX9930 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key strengths and potential limitations must be considered. On the strength side, BCX9930 exhibits an exceptionally high potency (IC₅₀ = 4 nM) and selectivity profile that is well aligned with the intended mechanism of action. Its ability to non-covalently target the S1 pocket of factor D ensures that the inhibition of the alternative pathway is both potent and reversible, thereby allowing for controlled pharmacodynamic effects. The high degree of selectivity—exceeding 500-fold over related serine proteases—not only reduces the likelihood of off-target toxicity but also supports the feasibility of long-term administration required for chronic diseases such as dry AMD (Schubart et al., 2023).  
Preclinical studies provide compelling support for the candidate’s mechanism. The demonstration that 500 nM BCX9930 can recover TEER to 85% of baseline in human RPE cultures suggests that the compound effectively counteracts the complement-mediated disruption of intercellular tight junctions. Furthermore, animal data showing that a dosing regimen of 5 mg/kg BID can reduce Bruch’s membrane C3 deposition by 70% and preserve ONL thickness indicates that BCX9930 not only exerts biochemical effects but also translates these into anatomical preservation within the retina (Ong et al., 2024). Such findings are particularly relevant given the importance of maintaining RPE barrier function and photoreceptor viability in halting the progression of dry AMD.  
Another strong point in favor of BCX9930 is its oral bioavailability, which is a significant advantage over therapies that require invasive delivery methods (for example, intravitreal injections). An oral agent would potentially improve patient compliance and reduce the risks associated with repeated intraocular procedures. This is particularly critical in a disease like dry AMD, where the patient population is predominantly elderly, and minimizing treatment burden is essential (Chen et al., 2022; Schubart et al., 2023).  
Despite these promising attributes, there are notable challenges and uncertainties that must be acknowledged. One major concern pertains to the historical track record of complement inhibitors in the treatment of dry AMD. Previous clinical trials with other agents targeting the alternative pathway—such as Lampalizumab—have ultimately failed to demonstrate robust clinical efficacy in phase 3 trials despite encouraging preclinical data (Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019). Such outcomes underscore the difficulty of translating complement inhibition into meaningful clinical benefits in retinal degenerative diseases. The complexity of AMD pathophysiology, which involves not only complement dysregulation but also oxidative stress, genetic predispositions, and environmental factors, means that addressing a single pathway may not be sufficient to fully arrest disease progression.  
Additionally, while the preclinical data for BCX9930 are encouraging, there is still a gap in clinical evidence demonstrating its efficacy specifically in dry AMD. Most of the clinical data currently available for BCX9930 have been derived from studies in conditions like C3G and PNH, where the pathobiology is somewhat different from that of retinal degenerative diseases. There is a high degree of uncertainty as to whether the pharmacodynamic markers observed in these other disease models—such as reductions in complement split products and improved hematological indices—will translate into improved retinal structure and function in AMD patients (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Chen et al., 2022).  
Safety is another domain that necessitates cautious exploration. Although the mechanism of action of BCX9930 suggests an improved tolerability profile owing to its selective inhibition of FD, experiences with analogous compounds (e.g., danicopan) have revealed potential issues such as liver enzyme elevations and other adverse events following sustained treatment (Schubart et al., 2023). It is essential that further clinical studies with BCX9930 incorporate rigorous monitoring of potential systemic toxicities and immune-related adverse effects, especially given the chronic nature of dry AMD therapy. Long-term data will be critical in confirming that the inhibition of the alternative pathway does not compromise overall host defense mechanisms or lead to other unexpected off-target consequences.  
Finally, the complexity of dry AMD as a clinical entity must guide any decision regarding the advancement of BCX9930. Complement-driven RPE disruption is only one facet of AMD pathogenesis; a multifactorial disease mechanism implies that combination therapies or multimodal approaches may eventually be needed to achieve optimal clinical outcomes. In this context, BCX9930 might best be positioned as part of a combination regimen, potentially alongside agents that address oxidative damage or other pathogenic mechanisms in AMD. Alternatively, biomarkers may need to be better defined so that patients most likely to benefit from complement inhibition can be identified and targeted in clinical trials (Kassa et al., 2019; Ong et al., 2024).  

In summary, BCX9930 represents a highly promising therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its potent and selective inhibition of factor D, a critical enzyme in the alternative complement pathway. The underlying rationale is strongly supported by both molecular and preclinical evidence: by binding non-covalently to the S1 pocket of factor D, BCX9930 effectively blocks the formation of the C3 convertase, thereby mitigating complement activation that is postulated to drive RPE tight junction disruption. In vitro studies have already demonstrated that BCX9930 can restore trans-epithelial electrical resistance and preserve the continuity of crucial tight junction proteins in human RPE cells under complement challenge. Additionally, animal models have provided evidence for significant reductions in complement deposition and the preservation of retinal architecture. These findings collectively indicate that BCX9930 has the potential to protect retinal tissue from complement-mediated injury, a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2022; Ong et al., 2024).  

However, the transition from preclinical promise to clinical success remains a challenge, as highlighted by the mixed outcomes seen with previous factor D inhibitors in the AMD space. The failure of some earlier agents, despite robust biochemical data, emphasizes that the path from molecular inhibition to effective disease modification is complex and fraught with challenges. Critical areas of future research include the establishment of clear biomarkers that correlate with clinical outcomes in dry AMD, careful delineation of the safety profile specific to the elderly patient population, and the exploration of appropriate combination strategies that might enhance therapeutic efficacy.  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and encouraging preclinical data, BCX9930 stands out as a compelling candidate for further evaluation in clinical trials targeting dry AMD. Its precise mechanism of action and the potential for oral administration offer distinct advantages and may help overcome some of the limitations encountered with earlier complement inhibitors. Ultimately, while caution is warranted due to the historical challenges in this therapeutic area, the overall evaluation supports the advancement of BCX9930 for further development and rigorous clinical testing in dry AMD patients (Schubart et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of isradipine as a repurposed candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In this report, we review its chemical origins and classification, historical therapeutic uses, detailed molecular mechanism of action, expected biological effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, and a critical overall assessment from the perspective of drug development for dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

Isradipine is a fully synthetic compound that belongs to the 1,4-dihydropyridine (DHP) class of calcium channel blockers, a family of agents that has been extensively optimized over several decades. The parent chemical scaffold was developed to target L-type voltage-gated calcium channels (LTCCs), particularly CaV1.2 and CaV1.3, which are key regulators of calcium entry in many excitable cells. Originally synthesized under the internal code PN 200-110, isradipine was later marketed for cardiovascular applications such as hypertension and angina pectoris due to its potent vasodilatory effects (Hof & Rüegg, 1988; Triggle, 2006). The design of isradipine is based on a thoroughly studied heterocyclic core that has undergone iterative modifications to yield compounds with improved potency, selectivity, and favorable pharmacokinetic properties. Its ability to achieve effective blockade of LTCCs at submicromolar concentrations—with an IC₅₀ around 0.2 µM—is a hallmark of its pharmacologic profile (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

The DHP class, to which isradipine belongs, has been widely used for its arterial vasodilatory actions in cardiovascular medicine, where selective inhibition of LTCCs in vascular smooth muscle produces systemic blood pressure reductions without significantly impairing cardiac contractility (Schachter, 1991; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011). Over the years, the profile of DHP calcium channel blockers has been expanded beyond their classical cardiovascular indications. More recently, several studies have begun to explore the neuroprotective and neuromodulatory properties of DHPs in models of neurodegeneration. Furthermore, emerging data suggest that alterations in LTCC function in non-vascular tissues—such as the retinal pigment epithelium—may contribute to disease mechanisms in dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025). In particular, mislocalization and dysfunction of the CaV1.3 subtype have been implicated in the degeneration of RPE cells, a central component in the pathogenesis of dry AMD.

Given that isradipine is well known for its high potency and state-dependent blockade of LTCCs, its repurposing for dry AMD is based on the hypothesis that pharmacological control of calcium influx can preserve tight junction integrity in RPE cells. With an established history of safe systemic use and an extensively characterized pharmacologic profile, isradipine emerges as an attractive candidate to modulate aberrant Ca²⁺ homeostasis in the retina (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

─────────────────────────────  
2. Therapeutic History

Clinically, isradipine has been deployed primarily in the management of cardiovascular disorders. Its use in treatment regimens for hypertension and angina pectoris is well documented, with decades of clinical experience supporting its efficacy and safety in reducing peripheral vascular resistance and relieving myocardial ischemia (Schachter, 1991). As a member of the DHP family, its predictable absorption, metabolism, and elimination have rendered it a mainstay in cardiovascular pharmacotherapy, with adverse effects generally limited to dose-dependent vasodilation-related symptoms such as headache and peripheral edema (Hof & Rüegg, 1988; Striessnig, 1999).

Beyond its cardiovascular applications, isradipine has recently been evaluated as a neuroprotective agent in several contexts. Preclinical data indicate that isradipine can reduce harmful calcium influx in neuronal populations, particularly in dopaminergic neurons that are at risk in Parkinson’s disease (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Ilijic et al., 2011). In these studies, isradipine’s ability to cross the blood–brain barrier and selectively inhibit LTCCs has been exploited to mitigate mitochondrial oxidative stress and calcium-mediated neurotoxicity. Although outcomes in clinical trials for neurodegenerative diseases have been mixed, the protective mechanisms observed in animal models provide a mechanistic rationale that could be applicable also beyond the central nervous system (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Nimmrich & Eckert, 2013).

Importantly, there is emerging evidence linking altered L-type calcium channel activity, particularly of the CaV1.3 subtype, to ocular pathology relevant to AMD. Data from the Open Targets Platform, for example, indicate a moderate association between CACNA1D (the gene encoding CaV1.3) and macular degeneration, with studies in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells from AMD patients demonstrating both mislocalization of CaV1.3 channels and reduced intracellular Ca²⁺ levels compared to controls (Buniello et al., 2025). Although isradipine has not previously been used in clinical studies for ocular diseases or for dry AMD specifically, its long-established cardiovascular use, combined with its neuroprotective potential in other cell types, offers an attractive opportunity for repurposing. The safety profile and systemic tolerability of isradipine further support its candidacy for new therapeutic indications in an elderly population commonly affected by AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

─────────────────────────────  
3. Mechanism of Action

At its most fundamental level, isradipine acts by inhibiting LTCCs—integral membrane proteins that mediate voltage-dependent calcium influx into cells. The LTCC family includes several subtypes, among which CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 have been most extensively studied. Isradipine is known to preferentially block these channels in a state-dependent manner, binding with higher affinity to channels that are in either an open or inactivated state and thereby sparing those in the resting state (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Filippini et al., 2023).

More specifically, the molecular interaction between isradipine and LTCCs involves defined transmembrane segments located on the pore-forming α1 subunit. Structural studies have identified that regions such as the IS6 and IVS6 helices form part of the binding pocket responsible for dihydropyridine sensitivity. When isradipine binds to this pocket, it not only obstructs the pore physically but also stabilizes the channel in a nonconducting conformation that precludes further Ca²⁺ entry (Filippini et al., 2023; Lacinová, Klugbauer, & Hofmann, 2000). This blockade leads to a rapid and sustained reduction in intracellular calcium levels, which is critical in tissues where tight junction assembly and maintenance are calcium-dependent processes.

In the context of RPE cells, maintaining appropriate basal Ca²⁺ concentrations is crucial for the integrity and anchoring of tight junction proteins such as occludin and zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1). Under physiological conditions, LTCC-mediated calcium entry provides a signal that regulates calcium-sensitive kinase and phosphatase pathways involved in organizing the cytoskeleton and maintaining cell–cell adhesion. However, in disease conditions such as dry AMD, factors such as pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α) or complement activation can disrupt this finely tuned balance. Excessive Ca²⁺ influx can lead to the activation of calcium-dependent proteases (e.g., calpains) and kinases that precipitate cytoskeletal remodeling and disassembly of tight junction complexes, contributing to a collapse in transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and loss of barrier function (Buniello et al., 2025).

By antagonizing LTCCs, isradipine is hypothesized to counteract these deleterious effects. Its state-dependent, high-affinity binding minimizes excessive Ca²⁺ entry during inflammatory challenges while preserving the minimal calcium flux necessary for normal cellular function (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Rotstein et al., 2015). In addition to its acute blocking effect, there is evidence from studies in neuronal models that prolonged exposure to dihydropyridines may down-regulate LTCC expression, leading to longer-term stabilization of calcium homeostasis (Ilijic et al., 2011; Nimmrich & Eckert, 2013). Therefore, in RPE cells, isradipine could theoretically act via a dual mechanism: an immediate reduction in aberrant calcium entry during cytokine-induced stress and a more prolonged normalization of LTCC density and function.

Furthermore, the selective targeting of CaV1.3 is particularly pertinent in the case of dry AMD because studies have revealed a moderate association between CACNA1D expression and macular degeneration, along with observations of mislocalization of CaV1.3 channels in AMD-derived RPE cells (Buniello et al., 2025). Such mislocalization is associated with reduced intracellular calcium levels which, paradoxically, may contribute to the failure of the tight junction apparatus due to a deficiency in the calcium signal necessary for proper junction assembly. In this scenario, isradipine’s ability to fine-tune calcium influx by blocking excessive but inappropriate LTCC activity may help restore normal intracellular Ca²⁺ dynamics, thereby preserving the localization and function of occludin and ZO-1 (Buniello et al., 2025; Filippini et al., 2023).

In summary, at the molecular level, isradipine’s action involves binding to critical transmembrane segments of LTCCs—particularly those associated with CaV1.2 and CaV1.3—thereby stabilizing these channels in a closed or inactivated state, reducing aberrant calcium influx, and indirectly safeguarding the intracellular signaling pathways that maintain tight junction integrity. This mechanism is central to the proposed therapeutic approach for stabilizing the RPE barrier in dry AMD (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Filippini et al., 2023; Buniello et al., 2025).

─────────────────────────────  
4. Expected Effect

Dry AMD is characterized by chronic RPE cell dysfunction and degeneration leading to breakdown of the outer blood–retinal barrier, a process largely fueled by disruptions in intracellular calcium homeostasis. In this context, inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) play a critical role in triggering disassembly of tight junctions and reducing transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER). Moreover, evidence linking the CaV1.3 channel to macular degeneration underscores the importance of calcium regulation in RPE pathology (Buniello et al., 2025).

The central hypothesis guiding the repurposing of isradipine for dry AMD is that by blocking LTCCs—specifically CaV1.2 and CaV1.3—at an IC₅₀ near 0.2 µM, it is possible to stabilize basal calcium levels in RPE cells. Under inflammatory conditions induced by TNF-α or complement activation, uncontrolled calcium influx would normally activate calcium-dependent proteolytic enzymes and kinases that contribute to the disruption of the cytoskeletal framework and the disassembly of cell–cell junctions. With isradipine’s intervention, the unwanted surge in intracellular calcium would be attenuated, thereby preserving the expression, localization, and function of tight junction proteins such as occludin and ZO-1 (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

In practical in vitro assays—using the human RPE cell line ARPE-19 or primary RPE cultures—exposure to TNF-α typically results in marked declines in TEER, reflecting compromised barrier integrity, alongside mislocalization of occludin and ZO-1 within the cell. Treatment with isradipine is expected to counter these effects. Specifically, by reducing the level of calcium influx across the plasma membrane, isradipine should enable the maintenance of the proper cytoskeletal anchoring of tight junction proteins, which in turn is expected to translate into a stabilization or even enhancement of TEER. Preliminary data in complement-challenged ARPE-19 models have shown that treatment with calcium channel blockers can lead to increased TEER, supporting the concept that pharmacological modulation of calcium entry is beneficial for RPE barrier function (Buniello et al., 2025).

Moreover, the anticipated outcomes include not only the acute preservation of junctional architecture during short-term inflammatory challenges but also potentially the modulation of LTCC expression under chronic stress. Over time, reducing the pathological calcium influx may alleviate the cellular stress that leads to LTCC up-regulation, thereby preventing a vicious cycle of calcium overload and junctional disassembly. Thus, even beyond immediate effects on TEER, isradipine may exert disease-modifying properties by normalizing the intracellular signaling milieu in RPE cells (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Ilijic et al., 2011).

Finally, by maintaining appropriate intracellular Ca²⁺ concentrations, isradipine may also prevent the activation of downstream calcium-dependent effectors—such as calpains and other proteases—that can degrade tight junction proteins directly. This dual action of immediate channel blockade and secondary protection against proteolytic degradation underpins the rationale that isradipine can preserve the barrier function of the RPE, thereby preventing the progression of dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

In essence, the expected effect of isradipine in the proposed assay is multifaceted:
• An immediate stabilization of intracellular calcium levels through LTCC blockade.  
• Prevention of TNF-α–induced tight junction disassembly, with sustained localization of occludin and ZO-1.  
• Improvement or stabilization of TEER in RPE cells under inflammatory or complement-challenge conditions.  
• Potential chronic benefits through secondary down-regulation of LTCC expression and the subsequent maintenance of calcium homeostasis.

Such effects would translate into a pharmacological strategy not only to protect the RPE barrier acutely but also to potentially slow the degenerative process of dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Filippini et al., 2023).

─────────────────────────────  
5. Overall Evaluation

Based on the comprehensive review of the available literature across biochemical, clinical, and preclinical domains, isradipine emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. Its favorable safety profile, robust historical data in cardiovascular applications, and emerging evidence supporting its neuroprotective and calcium-modulating effects form a strong foundation for exploring its role in ocular diseases.

Strengths of isradipine include its extensive clinical record in hypertension and angina, where decades of use have demonstrated predictable pharmacokinetics and a low incidence of severe adverse effects (Schachter, 1991). The compound’s belonging to the dihydropyridine class further supports its suitability, as this class is characterized by potent and state-dependent blockade of LTCCs—properties that are critical for controlling abnormal calcium influx in pathological situations. In addition, preclinical data documenting abnormal localization of CaV1.3 channels in AMD-affected RPE cells (Buniello et al., 2025) provide a direct link between LTCC dysfunction and retinal barrier breakdown, thereby strengthening the mechanistic rationale for isradipine’s use in dry AMD.

Another major strength is isradipine’s dual mechanism of action. Acutely, it can reduce the extracellular calcium influx that triggers deleterious cell-signaling cascades, and with chronic administration, it may also modulate LTCC expression levels. Such a dual mechanism implies that isradipine might not only preserve junctional integrity during inflammatory insults but also slow the overall progression of RPE degeneration. This is particularly important given that dry AMD is a slowly progressive and multifactorial disease where both acute and chronic therapeutic interventions are needed to achieve meaningful clinical outcomes (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Filippini et al., 2023).

Moreover, isradipine’s pharmacodynamic profile—with an IC₅₀ of approximately 0.2 µM—suggests that at appropriate dosing, it can achieve targeted LTCC inhibition in RPE cells without completely abolishing basal calcium signaling, which is essential for normal cellular functions. This fine balance is crucial in tissues such as the retina where calcium plays a key role not only in tight junction regulation but also in phototransduction and cellular homeostasis (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

Nonetheless, several challenges and limitations must be acknowledged. First, there is a relative paucity of direct ocular data on isradipine. Most of the supporting evidence for its mechanism and effects comes from studies in cardiovascular and neuronal cells. While the fundamental principles of calcium-dependent tight junction regulation are conserved, the specific expression profiles and regulatory mechanisms in RPE cells may differ. Consequently, extensive in vitro studies in RPE cell lines (such as ARPE-19) and primary RPE cultures will be imperative before moving into in vivo evaluations (Buniello et al., 2025).

Another significant limitation concerns drug delivery. Isradipine is predominantly administered systemically for its current indications, and achieving therapeutically relevant concentrations in the retina while minimizing systemic hypotension presents an important formulation challenge. Novel ocular delivery approaches—ranging from topical formulations to intravitreal injections or slow-release implants—must be rigorously developed and optimized. This challenge is compounded by the need to ensure that such delivery methods do not disrupt normal retinal physiology or exacerbate inflammatory responses (Anekonda & Quinn, 2011; Schachter, 1991).

There is also the potential for off-target effects in the retina. Calcium signaling underpins many essential retinal functions, including the regulation of photoreceptor activity, synaptic transmission, and RPE phagocytosis. Over-inhibition of LTCCs, if not carefully titrated, could compromise these processes. Thus, defining a safe therapeutic window in RPE cells is critical to ensure that the benefits of junctional preservation do not come at the cost of impaired retinal function (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

Finally, while the data linking LTCC dysfunction to AMD provide a compelling rationale for repurposing isradipine, the heterogeneity of LTCC expression across different cell types in the retina may influence treatment efficacy. It will be necessary to characterize not only the levels of CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 in RPE cells but also their functional roles in maintaining barrier integrity. Any variability in channel isoform expression or alternative splicing patterns may require adjustments in dosing or even the exploration of more isoform-selective derivatives (Buniello et al., 2025; Filippini et al., 2023).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation is positive: isradipine is a well-characterized, clinically safe calcium channel blocker with a robust mechanistic basis for repurposing in dry AMD. Its combined acute and chronic actions on LTCCs, along with emerging evidence linking CaV1.3 dysfunction to retinal degeneration, provide a strong rationale for further preclinical investigation. In particular, detailed studies focusing on its effects in human RPE cells under inflammatory conditions will be critical to validate the hypothesis that isradipine can preserve occludin and ZO-1 localization and maintain TEER under TNF-α challenge (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

─────────────────────────────  
6. Future Directions and Recommendations

Based on the evaluation above, the following research directions are recommended to advance isradipine as a potential therapeutic agent for dry AMD:

a) Detailed Characterization in RPE Cells  
It is vital to confirm the expression levels and localization of LTCC subtypes, particularly CaV1.3, in human RPE cells. Techniques such as quantitative PCR, Western blotting, immunocytochemistry, and electrophysiological recordings (e.g., patch-clamp) should be used to assess both basal expression and any alterations under inflammatory conditions. Establish in vitro models using ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures to evaluate the effects of isradipine on TEER and the immunolocalization of tight junction proteins such as occludin and ZO-1. Investigate the downstream signaling cascades following LTCC blockade in RPE cells. This includes evaluating changes in the activation state of calcium-dependent proteases, kinases, and the cytoskeletal proteins that govern tight junction formation. Given isradipine’s existing use as an orally administered drug for cardiovascular indications, it is essential to develop ocular-specific formulations that enable efficient delivery to the retina. This could involve exploring topical eye drops, intravitreal injections, or sustained-release implants that achieve high retinal bioavailability with minimal systemic absorption. In vivo pharmacokinetic studies in appropriate animal models will be key to optimizing these delivery systems (Schachter, 1991).

e) In Vivo Efficacy Studies  
Animal models that recapitulate key features of dry AMD, including RPE degeneration and barrier dysfunction, should be employed to assess the functional impact of isradipine on retinal preservation. Outcome measures might include in vivo imaging of retinal structure, ex vivo TEER measurements, histological analysis of tight junction integrity, and functional assessments such as electroretinography.

f) Safety and Tolerability in Retinal Tissues  
Since calcium signaling is critical for many retinal cellular functions, it is imperative to assess whether isradipine—at doses sufficient to block pathological calcium influx—might inadvertently impair normal retinal processes such as photoreceptor function, synaptic transmission, or RPE phagocytosis. Defining a precise therapeutic index in the ocular setting will be crucial for further development.

7. Overall Conclusion

In conclusion, isradipine represents a highly promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its extensive use in cardiovascular medicine, combined with an emerging body of evidence linking LTCC dysfunction to RPE barrier failure and macular degeneration, provides a strong scientific rationale for its investigation in this novel indication. At the molecular level, isradipine’s state-dependent and selective blockade of CaV1.2/CaV1.3 channels offers a targeted approach to stabilizing intracellular calcium levels and preserving the organization of tight junction proteins critical for maintaining the outer blood–retinal barrier (Buniello et al., 2025; Anekonda & Quinn, 2011).

While the majority of the supportive literature originates from studies conducted in cardiovascular and neuronal models, the fundamental role of LTCC-mediated calcium signaling in modulating barrier integrity is highly relevant to RPE physiology. The proposed mechanism—preventing TNF-α–induced junctional disassembly and cytokine-driven TEER collapse by preserving occludin and ZO-1 localization—is both plausible and timely given the persistent unmet need in the treatment of dry AMD.

Nonetheless, key challenges remain. Direct experimental evidence in ocular systems is currently limited, and significant work is needed to optimize the drug formulation for targeted retinal delivery while safeguarding against potential off-target effects. The heterogeneity of LTCC expression in ocular tissues may also necessitate further refinement in dosing strategies. Addressing these challenges through targeted in vitro and in vivo studies will be critical for translating the promising mechanistic insights into clinical benefit.

Overall, the convergence of robust clinical safety data, precise molecular pharmacological action, and emerging evidence linking LTCC dysregulation to RPE dysfunction supports the advancement of isradipine into focused preclinical studies for dry AMD. If studies confirm that isradipine can preserve the integrity of RPE tight junctions under inflammatory conditions, it may offer not only symptomatic relief but also a disease-modifying strategy that slows or prevents the progression of dry AMD—a condition currently lacking effective treatment options (Buniello et al., 2025; Rotstein et al., 2015).

Given these considerations, the recommendation is to pursue an accelerated preclinical program that encompasses detailed mechanistic assays in RPE cells, the development of suitable ocular delivery systems, and rigorous in vivo testing in relevant animal models. Success in these areas would justify subsequent clinical trials and could ultimately position isradipine as a transformative therapy for preserving retinal structure and function in patients with dry AMD.

Isradipine is a synthetically derived 1,4-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker with a proven record in cardiovascular therapy due to its potent, state-dependent inhibition of LTCCs. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bexarotene is a fully synthetic retinoid analog classified as a rexinoid, specifically acting as a pan–retinoid X receptor (RXR) agonist. It was originally developed through structure–activity relationship studies aimed at mimicking the natural ligand 9-cis retinoic acid, while providing greater receptor selectivity, improved potency, and a pharmacological profile amenable to therapeutic use. Its synthesis and subsequent discovery were driven by the need to harness RXR‐mediated gene regulation, and it subsequently became the only FDA-approved synthetic RXR ligand to date (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). As a member of the retinoid drug class, bexarotene has been primarily used in the oncological setting, specifically for the treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, and its chemical design reflects modifications that impart high lipophilicity and receptor specificity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018). This synthetic derivation distinguishes it from naturally occurring retinoids and underpins its utility across a number of experimental and clinical contexts.

Therapeutic History:  
Bexarotene’s clinical history is marked by its approval as a second-line therapy for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, which provided a strong basis for its safety and efficacy in a human disease setting (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). In addition to its primary use in oncology, preclinical and early clinical research has investigated bexarotene for applications in neurodegenerative diseases, most notably Alzheimer’s disease and multiple sclerosis. These studies have demonstrated that RXR activation by bexarotene can influence the clearance of pathological protein aggregates and promote remyelination, respectively (Gaunt, 2020; Behl et al., 2022). However, despite the broad mechanistic appeal of RXR agonism in modifying lipid metabolism and neuroinflammation, there is little to no established clinical or veterinary precedent for employing bexarotene in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative conditions. In fact, while several RXR agonists have been considered in various models of ocular disease, the role of RXR in the diseased retina remains underexplored, with only sparse reports such as a study with the RXR agonist PA024 in retinal degeneration models (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). This gap in therapeutic history presents both a challenge and an opportunity in repurposing bexarotene for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
Bexarotene exerts its pharmacological effects primarily by binding to the ligand-binding domain of RXR isoforms (RXRα, RXRβ, and RXRγ) with nanomolar potency, inducing conformational changes that favor the recruitment of coactivators and subsequent transcriptional activation of targeted genes (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). RXR is a promiscuous nuclear receptor that forms obligate heterodimers with several other nuclear receptors, most notably the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) such as PPARγ. In doing so, the bexarotene-induced RXR/PPARγ heterodimer binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the genome, thereby upregulating target genes involved in lipid metabolism and transport. One key target is ABCA1, an ATP-binding cassette transporter implicated in cholesterol efflux from cells, which plays a central role in maintaining intracellular lipid homeostasis (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the activation of the RXR/PPARγ pathway is particularly compelling. RPE cells are highly involved in the processing and clearance of lipids, including cholesterol, and in modulating the structural integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier via tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 and occludin. When under stress—such as exposure to cytotoxic mediators like 7-ketocholesterol (7KCh), which disrupts normal junctional organization and reduces transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—the activation of RXR offers a potential therapeutic avenue. Bexarotene’s ability to stimulate RXR signaling is expected to upregulate ABCA1 expression, thereby enhancing cholesterol efflux, while also promoting the transcription of genes that lead to the re-expression of claudin-1 and occludin, which are critical for restoring barrier integrity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

The biochemical interactions following RXR activation by bexarotene include a cascade of events where the ligand-receptor complex alters the transcriptional landscape of the cell. This process entails the heterodimerization of RXR with its partner receptor, binding to DNA response elements, and initiating the recruitment of transcriptional coactivators, which together drive the expression of genes that modulate lipid metabolism, inflammatory responses, and cell junction integrity. The specificity of bexarotene for RXR, as opposed to broader retinoic acid receptor (RAR) activity, allows for a more targeted enhancement of these pathways—a factor that is crucial in tissues like the RPE, where precise regulation of lipid handling and barrier properties is essential for retinal health (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underlying the repurposing of bexarotene for dry AMD is that its activation of RXR in RPE cells will facilitate heterodimerization with PPARγ, driving the transcriptional upregulation of lipid-handling genes, most notably ABCA1. In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have provided compelling preliminary data indicating that exposure to 0.5 µM bexarotene in the presence of 7-ketocholesterol stress is capable of restoring TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values and significantly increasing ABCA1 mRNA levels. This restoration of TEER suggests that bexarotene not only promotes cholesterol efflux by upregulating ABCA1 but also exerts a beneficial influence on the expression of key tight junction proteins, such as claudin-1 and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity of the RPE barrier (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

The expected molecular effect in the assay is thus twofold. First, through its molecular interaction with RXR, bexarotene reinforces the RXR/PPARγ heterodimer formation, triggering a cascade of gene transcription events that culminate in enhanced cholesterol efflux via ABCA1. This effect directly addresses the accumulation of lipid deposits that contribute to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. Second, by re-inducing the expression of claudin-1 and occludin, bexarotene is anticipated to improve cellular junctional integrity, thereby reducing paracellular leakage and restoring the overall barrier function of the RPE as measured by TEER. The use of ocular gel formulations for local delivery promises to concentrate the therapeutic effect within the eye, circumventing the systemic adverse effects that are typically associated with bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties, such as high lipophilicity and low systemic solubility (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of bexarotene as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is founded upon a robust mechanistic rationale and promising preliminary in vitro data, yet it also presents several challenges that must be addressed through rigorous further research. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its well-established mode of action as a selective RXR agonist. Its ability to promote heterodimerization with PPARγ and subsequently upregulate genes such as ABCA1 is well supported by a substantial body of research in other disease contexts, including neurodegeneration and oncology (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Gaunt, 2020). This receptor specificity not only underscores bexarotene’s potential to modulate RPE lipid metabolism but also suggests that similar pharmacological principles could translate into the restoration of tight junction integrity—a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD.

Another significant strength is its prior clinical approval for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. This provides a substantial amount of safety data and experience in human use, which could expedite the repurposing process under a drug repositioning strategy. Moreover, the observed in vitro effects—namely the partial restoration of TEER and the increase in ABCA1 mRNA in stressed ARPE-19 cells—lend direct support to the hypothesis that RXR agonism can counteract 7-ketocholesterol-induced disruptions in RPE function (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). The concept of using ocular gel formulations to achieve localized delivery and thereby minimize systemic side effects is another innovative aspect that addresses one of the traditional limitations of bexarotene, namely its adverse systemic metabolic disturbances, which include dyslipidemia and hypothyroidism (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021).

However, there are notable weaknesses that temper this optimism. First, bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties—its high lipophilicity and low solubility—pose a significant formulation challenge, especially when transitioning from systemic oncology applications to local ocular delivery. While gel formulations offer a potential solution, achieving the precise pharmacokinetics and adequate tissue penetration in the retina will require meticulous formulation development and validation. Second, despite the extensive research on RXR agonism in other tissues, there is very limited precedent for the use of bexarotene or similar compounds in the treatment of dry AMD or related ocular diseases. In other words, while the underlying nuclear receptor biology in the retina is compelling, the absence of prior clinical or even robust preclinical ocular studies increases the risk associated with translational uncertainty (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Moreover, systemic side effects associated with bexarotene have been well documented in its approved indications. Although the strategy of localized ocular delivery aims to mitigate these adverse effects, any leakage from the ocular compartment into systemic circulation could potentially re-expose patients to these risks. Additionally, the complexity of dry AMD as a multifactorial disease—with contributions from oxidative stress, inflammation, and complex extracellular matrix alterations—means that modulating only lipid handling and tight junction integrity might not be sufficient to arrest or reverse disease progression. Thus, while the mechanistic hypothesis is sound, it should ideally be integrated into a broader therapeutic strategy that also addresses other pathological mechanisms in dry AMD.

In summary, the proposed use of bexarotene for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic foundation based on RXR agonism and its downstream effects on lipid metabolism and cellular junction integrity. The preliminary in vitro evidence in ARPE-19 cells under 7-ketocholesterol stress is promising, particularly with the reported restoration of TEER and upregulation of ABCA1. The strengths of this candidate include its specificity for RXR, the translational potential backed by its FDA–approved status for an unrelated indication, and the innovative strategy of local ocular delivery through gel formulations. On the other hand, challenges related to its physicochemical properties, potential for systemic side effects, and the overall gaps in preclinical ocular data necessitate further rigorous research. Preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD and careful formulation optimization will be essential next steps to validate the therapeutic potential of bexarotene in this context (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bardoxolone methyl, also known as CDDO-Me, is a synthetic derivative developed from the naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid oleanolic acid. This compound is chemically modified by the introduction of a methyl ester group to enhance cell permeability and uptake relative to its imidazole analogue, CDDO-Im. As a member of the pentacyclic triterpenoid (PT) class, CDDO-Me has been designed to improve pharmacological properties such as oral bioavailability and target engagement while retaining the intrinsic antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of its natural precursor. Historically, pentacyclic triterpenoids have been studied for a wide range of applications—including anticancer, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory therapies—and have a longstanding role in traditional medicine in various Asian cultures. In this context, CDDO-Me has emerged as an advanced synthetic candidate that capitalizes on these properties, particularly through its potency as an activator of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. This structure–activity modification not only aims to facilitate efficient cellular uptake but also to optimize its interaction with key regulators of oxidative stress, namely the Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1) (Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and clinical investigation primarily in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and cancer. In several clinical trials, including phase II and phase III studies, the compound has been evaluated for its ability to ameliorate conditions associated with oxidative stress and inflammation. Its clinical development for CKD, in particular, has underscored its potential to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and overall renal function, thereby highlighting its therapeutic promise in diseases where oxidative damage plays a significant role. Despite its notable progress in these areas, direct clinical evidence for Bardoxolone methyl in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal diseases remains limited. However, several preclinical studies have demonstrated that compounds related to Bardoxolone methyl are capable of activating Nrf2 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, upregulating protective genes such as NQO1 and HO-1 that are essential for combating oxidative stress in the retina. These findings suggest that, although not originally developed for retinal indications, Bardoxolone methyl has a mechanistic rationale that could support its repurposing for dry AMD (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, analogous compounds that function via Nrf2 activation have been shown to protect RPE cells against oxidative stress-induced damage, further supporting the therapeutic potential of this candidate in ocular applications (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Bardoxolone methyl operates predominantly through the activation of the Nrf2 pathway, an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional system that governs cellular antioxidant responses. Under normal homeostatic conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytoplasm by its inhibitor, Keap1, which facilitates its ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl, due to its electrophilic cyanoenone moiety, acts as a Michael acceptor, covalently modifying specific cysteine residues within Keap1 (notably cysteine 151 among others). This modification disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, preventing Nrf2 ubiquitination, and allows Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus where it binds to the antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoter regions of target genes (Zhou et al., 2020; Mathis & Cui, 2016). The subsequent upregulation of phase II detoxifying enzymes—such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and glutamate-cysteine ligase modifier subunit (GCLM)—provides cells with increased capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigate inflammatory insults. Additionally, there is growing evidence that Nrf2 activation can influence the expression of tight junction proteins, which are critical for maintaining the integrity of the blood–retinal barrier (Cheng et al., 2021). This detailed molecular interaction not only accounts for the antioxidant role of Bardoxolone methyl but also for its potential in preserving cellular integrity in environments subjected to oxidative insult, such as the RPE cells in the retina (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Cai et al., 2024). Furthermore, ancillary effects, such as modulation of NF-κB signaling and the inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, are likely to contribute to its overall cytoprotective profile, making it an attractive candidate for reducing the inflammatory milieu that accompanies retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
In the specific context of dry AMD, the therapeutic hypothesis posits that Bardoxolone methyl will esterify and modify Keap1 in human RPE cells, thereby triggering the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent upregulation of phase II enzymes. This enhanced antioxidant capacity is expected to counteract oxidative stress induced by agents such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (tBHP), which is known to compromise the tight junction integrity of RPE monolayers. The resulting effect should manifest as a measurable recovery in transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) and a concomitant reduction in paracellular flux, as assessed by the permeability of a 10 kDa dextran. Preclinical assays have reported that at a concentration of 500 nM, Bardoxolone methyl is capable of restoring TEER values to approximately 80% of baseline levels, and reducing dextran leak by about 55%, thus highlighting both its potency and efficacy in repairing disrupted barrier function (Nakagami et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2021). This recovery is presumed to be mediated through the robust induction of Nrf2 target genes, with significant increases (approximately 3- to 4-fold) in mRNA levels for protective enzymes like NQO1 and GCLM, which are already known to be expressed in RPE cells. The preservation and restoration of tight junction integrity are critical not only for maintaining the physical barrier between the retina and the choroid but also for ensuring proper retinal function by preventing the uncontrolled diffusion of harmful substances that can exacerbate retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021; Hui et al., 2020). Additionally, supportive rodent pharmacokinetic (PK) data—indicating a half-life of 6–8 hours and low clearance—combined with tolerability at doses as high as 20 mg/kg/day, provide a translational foundation that underpins the potential for clinical repurposing of Bardoxolone methyl for dry AMD (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several strengths alongside noteworthy challenges. On the strength side, the compound’s ability to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway addresses a central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and inflammation play pivotal roles in RPE degeneration. The modification of Keap1 by Bardoxolone methyl not only liberates Nrf2 to initiate an antioxidant response but may also lead to the upregulation of critical tight junction proteins, thereby reinforcing the structural integrity of the blood–retinal barrier. Preclinical evidence indicating recovery of TEER and reduction of paracellular flux supports the notion that Bardoxolone methyl could exert meaningful protective effects in the RPE under conditions of oxidative challenge (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, the compound’s clinical advancement in other indications—most notably in CKD—demonstrates an established track record of safety and tolerability in humans at therapeutically relevant doses. This, together with favorable rodent PK parameters, enhances its appeal as a candidate for rapid translational repurposing for dry AMD (Yagishita et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2012; Sarmento, 2019).

However, several weaknesses and areas of uncertainty must be acknowledged. Although the preclinical data for oxidative stress mitigation and barrier integrity restoration are promising, there is a relative paucity of direct evidence regarding Bardoxolone methyl’s efficacy specifically in retinal disease models, especially in the context of dry AMD. The literature does not yet definitively demonstrate that Bardoxolone methyl can reverse established RPE dysfunction or completely restore retinal integrity in disease-relevant in vivo settings (Nakagami et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2024). Furthermore, safety concerns observed in other clinical contexts—such as cardiovascular adverse effects during clinical trials for CKD—raise potential red flags regarding its long-term use in a population that may be at increased risk for such events due to age-related co-morbidities (Nakagami et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2014; Sarmento, 2019). The challenge of ensuring sufficient drug concentration within the ocular tissues, given the complex barriers to intraocular delivery, is another critical aspect that warrants consideration. Although the methyl ester scaffold is designed to enhance cell uptake, further optimization of the drug delivery system (for example, via topical formulations or intravitreal injections) may be required to achieve therapeutic levels in the retina without systemic exposure that could potentiate off-target effects (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2020).

Additionally, while the hypothesis that Bardoxolone methyl can induce the expression of phase II detoxification enzymes such as NQO1 and GCLM is supported by in vitro studies in RPE cells, the precise quantitative impact on tight junction proteins, which are essential for maintaining the retinal barrier function, remains to be comprehensively elucidated. Future research should focus on rigorous preclinical studies in animal models of dry AMD, detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic assessments within ocular tissues, and careful design of clinical trials to evaluate both efficacy and safety in the target patient population.

Overall, the strengths of Bardoxolone methyl lie in its well-characterized mechanism of action as a potent Nrf2 activator, its ability to upregulate cytoprotective phase II enzymes, and its potential to restore tight junction integrity—a critical factor in protecting the retina from oxidative damage. Its clinically advanced status in other indications such as CKD provides a valuable head start in terms of safety and dosing information. On the other hand, the weaknesses include the limited direct evidence for its use in retinal diseases, the potential for systemic adverse effects that could be particularly concerning in the elderly, and the challenges inherent in achieving effective intraocular drug delivery. Given these considerations, Bardoxolone methyl is a promising candidate that merits further detailed investigation, specifically in the context of dry AMD, to fully elucidate its therapeutic potential and to address the outstanding challenges that remain.

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl has not yet been directly tested in dry AMD clinical trials, its underlying pharmacological profile, supported by substantial in vitro and in vivo preclinical evidence, suggests that it may offer significant benefits in restoring RPE function and retinal barrier integrity through the activation of Nrf2 signaling. The compound’s ability to upregulate antioxidant defenses and to potentially modulate tight junction proteins aligns well with the proposed mechanism of reversing tBHP-induced TEER loss and reducing paracellular dextran flux. If subsequent studies confirm these effects in relevant animal models and demonstrate a favorable safety profile in ocular tissues, Bardoxolone methyl could emerge as a viable repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Future research efforts should focus on refining ocular delivery strategies, verifying the direct effects on RPE gene expression and barrier function, and rigorously evaluating its long-term safety in the context of age-related retinal diseases (Cheng et al., 2021; Cuadrado et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2012; Nakagami, 2016; Nakagami et al., 2015; Schiavoni et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
H-151 is a small-molecule antagonist of the innate immune adaptor STING (TMEM173) that was developed as part of a chemical class designed to prevent the palmitoylation-dependent activation of STING at the Golgi following cyclic dinucleotide binding and ER-to-Golgi trafficking (i.e., cGAMP-bound STING oligomerization and signalosome assembly) (Decout et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). In its mechanistic class, H-151 is grouped with covalent STING inhibitors that target Cys91 within the transmembrane region–proximal cytosolic interface, thereby preventing activation-induced palmitoylation at Cys88/Cys91 and downstream signaling; nitrofuran analogs such as C-176 and C-178 are the canonical examples where Cys91-directed covalent modification has been mapped by probe chemistry and mass spectrometry (with consequent suppression of type I interferon and IL-6 in vivo) (Decout et al., 2021). STING activation is known to require ligand-induced conformational change, ER exit, and palmitoylation on Cys88/Cys91 to drive oligomerization/polymerization and recruitment of TBK1 and other signal transducers; antagonists that block this palmitoylation step are therefore positioned to broadly prevent both IRF3-dependent type I interferon and NF-κB–dependent inflammatory outputs (Li et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2021).

H-151 has been characterized in inflammatory disease models as a low molecular weight, irreversible inhibitor of human and mouse STING that blocks activation-induced palmitoylation and attenuates downstream signaling (with primary mechanistic references tracing to the discovery work summarized by Pan et al. and by Decout et al.) (Pan et al., 2021; Decout et al., 2021). In keratinocyte and immune-cell systems relevant to psoriatic inflammation, H-151 has reproducibly suppressed STING-dependent NF-κB and IRF3 phosphorylation, inhibited proinflammatory cytokine mRNA induction (e.g., IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α), and reduced STING protein levels, consistent with an antagonist mechanism upstream of canonical downstream effectors (Pan et al., 2021). Conceptually, H-151 belongs to the broader class of cGAS–STING pathway modulators that have been deployed to suppress sterile inflammation across multiple tissues; for the eye and retina, related pathway inhibitors (e.g., C-176, SN-011, cryptotanshinone) have shown efficacy in ischemic and neovascular models via suppression of microglial STING signaling and cytokine/chemokine/protease outputs, supporting the translatability of STING antagonism to ocular tissues (Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
There is no reported clinical use of H-151 in humans, and no published veterinary or clinical trials in ophthalmology were identified in the provided literature set; H-151 has been used as a research tool compound in preclinical inflammatory models, most prominently in psoriasis, where it decreased lesion severity and cutaneous inflammatory readouts in the imiquimod model (Pan et al., 2021). In psoriasis-relevant cell systems, H-151 suppressed cGAMP-induced IRF3 and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and reduced IFN-β, IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α expression, consistent with on-pathway inhibition of STING and its downstream transcriptional programs (Pan et al., 2021). In vivo, topical H-151 improved psoriasis-like dermatitis and decreased markers linked to STING/NF-κB signaling, again without human clinical translation to date (Pan et al., 2021).

Ocular/retinal precedent for the STING target is strong even if H-151–specific data are sparse. In multiple retinal contexts, activation of cGAS–STING has been implicated in pathogenesis through DNA-damage and mitochondrial DNA leakage, leading to IRF3/NF-κB activation, SASP-like cytokine induction, angiogenesis, and barrier dysfunction (Hu et al., 2023). Genetic and pharmacologic pathway perturbations show benefit: genetic loss of STING limits endothelial senescence and vascular degeneration in diabetic models (Liu et al., 2023), genetic deletion along the cGAS–STING axis rescues Alu DNA–driven RPE toxicity (implicated in geographic atrophy) (Hu et al., 2023), and pharmacologic STING inhibitors (C-176, SN-011) suppress neovascularization in laser CNV and OIR models (Ni et al., 2024). Importantly for RPE biology, senescent ARPE-19 cells were reported to overproduce VEGF and this overproduction was prevented by H-151, providing a direct albeit single-study line of evidence that H-151 can modulate pathogenic angiogenic/SASP output in an RPE-derived cell line (Hu et al., 2023). Beyond H-151, epigenetic suppression of STING (JQ1), PPARα activation, and visual cycle modulation (reducing toxic retinoid stress) each attenuate cGAS–STING activation and downstream inflammation or degeneration, underscoring the therapeutic appeal of targeting this axis in retinal disease (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
STING biology and the palmitoylation node. STING is a homodimeric ER-resident adaptor with an N-terminal multi-pass transmembrane domain and a cytosolic C-terminal ligand-binding domain; binding of 2’3’-cGAMP (produced by cGAS upon sensing cytosolic dsDNA) induces conformational rearrangements that enable ER exit and trafficking to the Golgi, where palmitoylation of Cys88 and Cys91 is critical for higher-order assembly and recruitment of TBK1 and other signaling proteins (Li et al., 2021). Palmitoylation-driven tetramerization/higher-order oligomerization is a central activation step for STING, and mutational or pharmacologic interference with Cys88/Cys91 palmitoylation abrogates downstream signal propagation (Pan et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). Activated STING scaffolds TBK1 to phosphorylate IRF3 (e.g., at Ser366), triggering type I interferon gene expression, and engages NF-κB to induce a broad proinflammatory transcriptional program, including SASP components (Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2021). In retinal disease contexts, cGAS–STING activation (driven by nuclear/mtDNA release or Alu-derived nucleic acids) is linked to up-regulation of VEGF via NF-κB/HIF-1α in oxidative-stress–induced RPE senescence, endothelial and microglial inflammatory activation, and barrier compromise (Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025).

H-151 and palmitoylation blockade. H-151 is positioned mechanistically among irreversible covalent inhibitors of STING that target Cys91 to prevent activation-associated palmitoylation and signalosome formation (Decout et al., 2021). While detailed covalent adduct chemistry for H-151 itself is not contained in the supplied excerpts, authoritative mechanistic reviews depict H-151 in the “Targeting Cys91” class, alongside nitrofuran inhibitors (C-176, C-178) that have been shown to bind Cys91 selectively and irreversibly (but not Cys88) and that suppress in vivo IFN and IL-6 responses to STING agonism (Decout et al., 2021). Primary disease-model data support a functional blockade of STING signal transmission by H-151: it reduced STING protein abundance in keratinocytes and THP-1 monocytes, inhibited cGAMP-driven IRF3 and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation, and suppressed downstream cytokine expression (IFN-β, IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α) (Pan et al., 2021). In the psoriasis model, H-151 strongly downregulated NF-κB activity and IL-6 and reduced p-p65 and total p65, with a more variable impact on IRF3 phosphorylation depending on system and readout, suggesting it can dominantly blunt the NF-κB arm of STING signaling while at least partially reducing IRF3 activation (Pan et al., 2021). The lack of additivity with an NF-κB inhibitor (BAY 11-7082) on IL-6 suppression implies pathway overlap and supports that H-151’s anti-inflammatory effects in that model are mediated primarily by interference with STING → NF-κB–driven cytokine production (Pan et al., 2021).

Rationale in retinal cells and tissue. cGAS and STING are expressed across retinal cell types (RPE, microglia, endothelial cells, Müller glia, photoreceptors) and are upregulated in disease states (AMD/DR), with promoter accessibility and mRNA levels increased in diseased tissue, positioning the pathway as targetable across multiple ocular compartments (Hu et al., 2023). Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction cause cytosolic mtDNA accumulation that activates cGAS–STING; Alu-derived nucleic acids similarly drive cytosolic DNA sensing and RPE cytotoxicity in GA, with multiple studies showing that genetic deletion along the cGAS–STING axis rescues Alu DNA toxicity (Hu et al., 2023). In RPE biology specifically, STING is implicated in senescence-associated VEGF upregulation, and H-151 prevented VEGF overproduction in senescent ARPE-19 cells, indicating that palmitoylation-targeted STING antagonism can suppress a central angiogenic/SASP mediator in stressed RPE-like cells (Hu et al., 2023). In retinal vascular and microglial compartments, pathway inhibition reduces inflammatory and proteolytic mediators (e.g., lowering Il6 and Mmp9) and blunts vascular leakage and neovascular pathology, as shown with cryptotanshinone, C-176, and SN-011 (Qiu et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024). Collectively, these data situate H-151’s palmitoylation blockade at a nodal point capable of broadly dampening IRF3 and NF-κB outputs in ocular cells that contribute to SASP, MMP expression, VEGF induction, and barrier compromise relevant to dry AMD (Hu et al., 2023).

Important mechanistic caveats. RPE models are heterogeneous in cGAS expression and DNA-sensor usage; some RPE cell lines lack cGAS and instead rely on other nucleic acid sensors (e.g., RIG-I, ZBP1), and the relative contribution of cGAS–STING versus alternative pathways varies by context (Hu et al., 2023). Moreover, the balance of STING outputs (IRF3/type I IFN versus NF-κB) can be cell/state dependent, as reflected by psoriasis-model findings where systemic IFN-β was unchanged despite local suppression of p-IRF3 and p65 in skin (Pan et al., 2021). These observations underscore that while H-151 inhibits upstream STING activation, the phenotype in any given ocular assay will reflect cell-type–specific wiring, stimulus context (Alu vs mtDNA vs oxidant stress), and cross-talk with other innate immune axes (Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023).

Strengths

Genetic and pharmacologic evidence across models (DR endothelium, Alu-driven RPE toxicity, ischemic/neovascular retinopathy) show that suppressing STING signaling reduces inflammation, senescence markers, angiogenic/proteolytic factors, leakage, and degeneration, indicating pathway validity and translational plausibility in the eye (Liu et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).
